claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by thalamus, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure 9a-f
claims.quote: photoinhibition of thalamus hyperpolarized excitatory neurons and reduced the amplitudes of their membrane voltage fluctuations (Supplementary Fig. 9a–e). Onset latency of Vm hyperpolarization induced by thalamus inactivation was 4.2 ms. This was longer than the 2.8-ms latency measured with direct cortical GABAergic activation (Supplementary Fig. 9f)
claims.criterion: The 12 whole-cell L4 E neurons with VPM light (Supplementary Fig. 9c) and the 7 with direct cortical light in VGAT-ChR2 mice (Supplementary Fig. 9f). Resting Vm and Vm variance (high-pass 10 Hz) from Vm outside touch, light against control (Supplementary Fig. 9d,e), windows O5. The latency rule for laser onset is not given; the only onset rule the paper gives is the touch-latency rule (Online Methods), so it is applied to the laser-onset-aligned grand average (Supplementary Fig. 9c,f): dVm/dt crossing 3 x the s.d. of dVm/dt 0 to 25 ms before laser onset, with the crossing taken in the negative direction, dVm/dt at the sampling rate (reading O8; the paper's 4.2 and 2.8 ms are not whole milliseconds, so not 1 ms bins; answer of 2026-10-20). That this rule is the one used is an assumption, recorded as a deviation. The paper reports no test for 9d,e. Reproduced when Vm is lower and variance lower with light in most of the 12 neurons and both latencies are within tolerance with the thalamic one longer; partially reproduced when the Vm and variance parts hold and a latency does not.

claims.statement: Photoinhibiting the thalamus reduces the spike rates of L4 FS interneurons during nonwhisking (to 4% of control), whisking (to 13%) and touch (to 32%), so FS interneurons are driven by thalamic input.
claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by thalamus, paragraph 2; Figure 6d,e; Supplementary Figure 9j
claims.quote: Photoinhibition reduced spike rates in FS interneurons during nonwhisking (to 4% of control ... and whisking epochs (to 13% of control ... as well as in response to touch (to 32% of control ... FS interneurons were thus driven by input from the thalamus.
claims.criterion: The L4 FS cells (ChR2-tagged, thin spikes; Fig. 6e legend) recorded with VPM light. Nonwhisking and whisking rates, and spikes per touch (Fig. 6e axis; Fig. 5 definition), in light trials inside the light against control, windows O5, fractions O6 (Fig. 6e plots population means, which favours O6 a), laser powers O7. Tests are Wilcoxon signed-rank (paired; not named in the Results), two-sided: the paper does not state the sides, but its printed P values match exact two-sided tests at the printed n (n = 13, P = 5 x 10^-4 is the two-sided exact P with one cell of smallest change going up; no one-sided exact P at n = 13 rounds to it; n = 14 and 15 give the two-sided minima 1.2 x 10^-4 and 6.1 x 10^-5), and the analyses were run in Matlab, whose signrank is two-sided by default (answer of 2026-10-20). The one-sided P is reported as a variant and does not enter the outcome. Reproduced when all three tests give p < 0.05 with light lower and the fractions are within tolerance under a reading; partially reproduced when the three tests hold and a fraction is not within tolerance; not reproduced when a test fails.

claims.statement: Monosynaptic rabies tracing from L4 PV interneurons labels thalamic neurons mostly in VPM (>90%) and few in POM (<10%).
claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by thalamus, paragraph 3; Supplementary Figure 10
claims.quote: The vast majority of trans-synaptically labeled thalamic neurons were in VPM (>90%), with only a small minority in POM (<10%; Supplementary Fig. 10).
claims.criterion: Counts of GFP-labeled neurons in VPM and POM from the tracing sections (Online Methods, Virus injection). Reproduced when VPM holds more than 90% of the labeled thalamic neurons. The paper's histology is not described as part of the recordings; the author reports whether the dandiset holds it.

claims.statement: After infraorbital nerve transection, L4 excitatory neurons do not depolarize after touch.
claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by sensory input, paragraph 2; Figure 7b
claims.quote: As expected, L4 excitatory neurons did not depolarize after touch (Fig. 7b).
claims.criterion: The L4 E neurons recorded whole-cell in ION-cut mice (8 in Fig. 7b). The paper reports no test; the claim is one of absence. The post-touch Vm of exc-vm-touch-whisking (Vm at the peak of the neuron's average PSP) is not defined without a PSP: the maximum of a flat average is biased upward. The test therefore uses the paper's touch epoch (4 to 50 ms after onset; Online Methods, distance to threshold): per neuron, the mean Vm 4 to 50 ms after touch onset against the mean 0 to 5 ms before (Supplementary Fig. 4 pre-touch window), compared over neurons by the Methods' paired test (Wilcoxon signed-rank) at 0.05; the peak-based amplitude is shown as a variant. Reproduced when the test finds no depolarization; not reproduced when it finds one. Touch counts per neuron and the mean amplitude are reported, with the 15 matched control neurons as comparison.

claims.statement: After ION transection, whisking-evoked depolarization of L4 excitatory neurons is reduced (0.62 +- 0.50 mV, n = 9) relative to control neurons with matched resting potential (1.54 +- 0.79 mV, n = 15).
claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by sensory input, paragraph 2; Figure 7c,d
claims.quote: Depolarizations in response to whisker movement were reduced (ION cut: mean ± s.d., 0.62 ± 0.50 mV, n = 9 neurons versus Control with matched resting potential: mean ± s.d., 1.54 ± 0.79 mV, n = 15 neurons; P = 0.005, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Fig. 7c,d)
claims.criterion: Whisking depolarization as in exc-vm-touch-whisking, both of its readings (Supplementary Fig. 4 windows; whisking-epoch minus nonwhisking mean Vm). The matching rule for the 15 controls is not given; readings (a) the control whole-cell E neurons whose resting Vm (O4) lies within the range of the 9 ION-cut neurons; (b) the 15 control neurons nearest in resting Vm to the ION-cut median. Reproduced when a Wilcoxon rank-sum test gives p < 0.05 with ION-cut lower and both means are within tolerance under a reading; partially reproduced when only the test holds.

claims.statement: After ION transection, phase-locking of L4 excitatory Vm to whisker movement is abolished (coupling 0.12 +- 0.04 mV against 0.38 +- 0.31 mV in controls).
claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by sensory input, paragraph 2; Figure 7e
claims.quote: phase-locking of membrane potential to whisker movement was abolished (ION cut, 0.12 ± 0.04 mV versus Control, 0.38 ± 0.31 mV; P = 0.005; Fig. 7e)
claims.criterion: Vm (spikes removed) in 12 phase bins during whisking epochs, fitted with a sinusoid; coupling strength is half its peak-to-trough (Online Methods), filters O1. Same ION-cut and matched control neurons as ion-cut-exc-whisking, both readings; unpaired, so a Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Online Methods). Reproduced when the test gives p < 0.05 with ION-cut lower and both means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when only the test holds.

claims.statement: After ION transection, touch does not evoke spikes in L4 FS interneurons.
claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by sensory input, paragraph 3; Figure 7g
claims.quote: Touch did not evoke spikes in FS interneurons (Fig. 7g).
claims.criterion: The 10 L4 FS cells (ChR2-tagged, thin spikes) recorded in ION-cut mice. A claim of absence with no test in the paper; judged by the Methods' paired test (Wilcoxon signed-rank) of per-cell spikes 0 to 50 ms after against 2 x spikes 0 to 25 ms before touch (the Fig. 5 spikes-per-touch terms) at 0.05. Reproduced when no increase is found; not reproduced when one is. The mean spikes per touch is reported against the control FS value (1.9).

claims.statement: After ION transection, the whisking-related activation of L4 FS interneurons is absent in most cells (P = 0.80, n = 10), so their movement-related modulation is reafference driven by sensory input.
claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by sensory input, paragraph 3; Figure 7h,i
claims.quote: In addition, whisking-related activation of FS interneurons was also absent in most cells (P = 0.80, n = 10 neurons; Fig. 7h,i). ... These data show that excitation of L4 excitatory neurons and L4 FS neurons is dominated by sensory input. Modulation correlated with whisker movement in L4 FS neurons constitutes reafference.
claims.criterion: The 10 L4 FS cells in ION-cut mice; nonwhisking and whisking rates as in fs-whisking-rate. A claim of absence judged on the paper's test, a paired test (not named; Wilcoxon signed-rank per the Methods) of per-cell nonwhisking against whisking rate at 0.05. Reproduced when it finds no difference; not reproduced when it finds one. The per-cell rank-sum results (how many cells still increase, readings O2) and the size of the change are reported.

claims.statement: After ION transection, phase-locking of L4 FS spikes to whisker movement is reduced but not entirely abolished.
claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by sensory input, paragraph 3; Supplementary Figure 12
claims.quote: Phase-locking of spikes to whisker movement was reduced but not entirely abolished (Supplementary Fig. 12).
claims.criterion: r2 of the phase fit (sinusoid, or sinusoid plus double frequency as in Supplementary Fig. 7g; 12 bins; filters O1) for the 10 ION-cut FS cells and the control FS cells; Supplementary Fig. 12b compares the two distributions by their medians. The paper reports no test. Reproduced when the ION-cut median r2 is below the control median and at least one ION-cut cell has r2 > 0.25 (Supplementary Fig. 12a); not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Yellow light in PV-IRES-Cre mice expressing eNpHR3.0 strongly inhibits most L4 PV interneurons (3 of 4); their rate falls 3 ms after laser onset and L4 excitatory activity rises 2 ms later.
claims.source: Results, Layer 4 FS interneurons suppress reafference in L4, paragraph 7; Supplementary Figure 13a,c
claims.quote: First, the spike rate of L4 PV interneurons decreased 3 ms after laser onset, and activity in L4 neurons increased only 2 ms later (Supplementary Fig. 13c) ... Four L4 PV interneurons recorded. 3 out of 4 are strongly inhibited by eNpHR stimulation.
claims.criterion: The 4 L4 PV cells and the excitatory cells of PV-IRES-Cre mice; rates in nonwhisking and whisking periods with and without light (Supplementary Fig. 13a, 95% intervals). "Strongly inhibited" is not defined; read as the light-trial rate below the lower bound of the control 95% bootstrap interval in both periods. Grand averages aligned to laser onset (Supplementary Fig. 13c); the latency rule for laser onset is not given, so the Methods' spike-latency rule is applied to the laser-onset-aligned PSTH (1 ms bins; dPSTH/dt crossing 3 x its s.d. 0 to 25 ms before laser onset, downward for PV cells and upward for excitatory cells; readings O8 and O9), an assumption recorded as a deviation. Reproduced when 3 of 4 PV cells are inhibited and the latencies are within tolerance (1 ms bins limit them to whole ms); partially reproduced when only the PV count holds.

claims.statement: Partially suppressing PV (FS) interneurons increases the spike rate of L4 excitatory neurons during nonwhisking (0.6 to 1.6 spikes/s) and whisking (0.8 to 2.7 spikes/s).
claims.source: Results, Layer 4 FS interneurons suppress reafference in L4, paragraph 1; Figure 8b-d; Supplementary Figure 13b
claims.quote: Partially suppressing PV (FS) interneurons changed the responses of excitatory neurons (Fig. 8b–e; P = 1 × 10−6, Kruskal-Wallis test). L4 excitatory neurons increased their spike rate during both nonwhisking periods (from 0.6 ± 0.1 spikes per s to 1.6 ± 0.3 spikes per s; mean ± s.e.m., n = 40 neurons, P = 6 × 10−5) and whisking periods(from 0.8 ± 0.2 spikes per s to 2.7 ± 0.5 spikes per s, P = 2 × 10−6
claims.criterion: The putative excitatory L4 neurons of PV-IRES-Cre eNpHR mice with light trials (40 in the paper; the selection beyond the count is not given). Nonwhisking and whisking rates in light trials inside the light against control, windows O5, filters O1. Kruskal-Wallis over the four groups (nonwhisking and whisking, control and light; Fig. 8b-e; the paper does not name the groups, so this test is reported and does not enter the outcome), and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests per period (paired; not named in the Results). Reproduced when both paired tests give p < 0.05 with light higher and the four rates are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and a rate is not within tolerance; not reproduced when a paired test fails.

claims.statement: With PV interneurons suppressed, L4 excitatory neurons become driven by whisker movement (whisking rate above nonwhisking, P = 0.02), while in control trials they are not (P = 0.55); their selectivity for touch is normally maintained in part by FS interneurons.
claims.source: Results, Layer 4 FS interneurons suppress reafference in L4, paragraph 1; Figure 8d
claims.quote: L4 excitatory neurons were instead driven by whisker movements (P = 0.02, Fig. 8d), implying that their selectivity for touch was normally maintained in part by FS interneurons.
claims.criterion: Same neurons, windows and rates as fs-suppress-movement-spiking. Fig. 8d prints P = 0.55 for nonwhisking against whisking in control and P = 0.02 with eNpHR; the paired test is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Online Methods). Readings O5 and O1. Reproduced when the test in light trials gives p < 0.05 with whisking higher and the test in control trials gives p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when the light test holds and the control test also finds a difference; not reproduced when the light test fails.

claims.statement: PV interneuron suppression does not change mean touch-evoked spiking of L4 excitatory neurons significantly (0.27 to 0.32 spikes per touch, P = 0.09); its effect is heterogeneous, with weakly responding neurons responding more and strongly responding neurons unchanged or less.
claims.source: Results, Layer 4 FS interneurons suppress reafference in L4, paragraph 2; Figure 8e; Supplementary Figure 13b
claims.quote: PV interneuron suppression also modulated touch-evoked spiking in L4 excitatory neurons, but they did so in a heterogeneous manner (mean ± s.e.m., from 0.27 ± 0.06 spikes per touch to 0.32 ± 0.06 spikes per touch, n = 40 neurons, P = 0.09, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Fig. 8e and Supplementary Fig. 13). Neurons that responded weakly to touch tended to respond more strongly with PV interneuron suppression.
claims.criterion: Same 40 neurons. Spikes per touch by the Fig. 8e definition (4 to 20 ms after minus 0 to 16 ms before onset; intertouch interval at least 10 ms), light against control trials. The absence of a mean change is judged on the paper's test, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at 0.05. Reproduced when it gives p >= 0.05 and both means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when p >= 0.05 and a mean is not within tolerance; not reproduced when it finds a change. The heterogeneity is described, not tested, in the paper; the change against the control value is shown per neuron (Fig. 8e) and reported.

claims.statement: Suppressing PV interneurons improves touch detection (AUC) for L4 excitatory neurons with weak touch responses and diminishes it for neurons with robust touch responses.
claims.source: Results, Layer 4 FS interneurons suppress reafference in L4, paragraph 3; Figure 8f,g
claims.quote: Consistent with the heterogeneous changes in spikes per touch, suppression of PV interneurons improved AUC for neurons with weak responses to touch and diminished AUC for neurons with robust responses to touch (Fig. 8f,g).
claims.criterion: Same 40 neurons. ROC per neuron and condition (Online Methods): per trial, spike counts in 250 ms before and after the first touch, or in the sample epoch for trials without touch; touch and no-touch periods resampled 5,000 times; AUC from the threshold sweep of the count difference. Which 250 ms windows of the sample epoch serve in no-touch trials is not given; readings (a) two adjacent 250 ms windows at a random time in the sample epoch; (b) the 250 ms before and after the median first-touch time of touch trials. The touch-evoked rate is the mean rate 0 to 250 ms after minus 0 to 250 ms before touch, control trials (Fig. 8g legend). The paper gives no test; it groups neurons by the sign of the AUC change (Fig. 8h, 19 increased, 21 reduced). Reproduced when the neurons whose AUC rises have a lower mean control touch-evoked rate (the Fig. 8g measure, after minus before) than those whose AUC falls, under both readings; not reproduced otherwise. The 3.4 and 7.3 spikes/s of Fig. 8h are rates 0 to 250 ms after touch without the baseline subtracted (auc-groups), a different measure, and are not the comparison here.

claims.statement: Neurons whose AUC rose with PV suppression gained touch-evoked spiking (3.4 to 8.7 spikes/s); neurons whose AUC fell kept their touch-evoked response (7.3 to 7.0 spikes/s) but had higher baseline rates (0.9 to 2.6 spikes/s).
claims.source: Results, Layer 4 FS interneurons suppress reafference in L4, paragraph 4; Figure 8h
claims.quote: L4 excitatory neurons with increased AUCs showed a population increase in touch-evoked responses on average (from 3.4 ± 0.8 spikes per s to 8.7 ± 1.9 spikes per s, P = 0.0001). Neurons with reduced AUC showed unchanged touchevoked responses as a population (from 7.3 ± 1.5 spikes per s to 7.0 ± 1.4 spikes per s, P = 0.98, average 0–250 ms after touch onset) ... but elevated baseline spike rates (from 0.9 ± 0.2 spikes per s to 2.6 ± 0.6 spikes per s, mean ± s.e.m., P = 0.0002; Fig. 8f–h).
claims.criterion: Groups by the sign of the AUC change (auc-weak-strong, both readings). The touch-evoked response is the mean rate 0 to 250 ms after touch onset (as the sentence says); the baseline is the mean rate 0 to 250 ms before onset (Fig. 8g legend). Paired tests are Wilcoxon signed-rank (Online Methods). Reproduced when the increased-AUC group's rise and the reduced-AUC group's baseline rise give p < 0.05, the reduced-AUC group's touch response shows no change at 0.05, and the means and group sizes are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the three tests hold and a mean or a group size is not within tolerance; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: With PV interneurons suppressed, most mice (6 of 8) are more likely to report touch with the pole out of reach (false alarms on no-lick trials).
claims.source: Results, Layer 4 FS interneurons suppress reafference in L4, paragraph 6; Supplementary Figure 14b,c
claims.quote: with PV interneuron suppressed, most mice (6 of 8) were more likely to report touches with the pole out of reach (Supplementary Fig. 14). ... In 8 mice tested, 6 showed a significant decrease of performance during Nolick trials with PV interneuron inactivation
claims.criterion: For each of the 8 PV-IRES-Cre eNpHR mice, correct responses on no-lick (anterior pole) trials with and without light, compared by a chi-squared test at p < 0.05 (Supplementary Fig. 14c). Whether sessions of a mouse are pooled is not stated; readings (a) all of a mouse's trials pooled; (b) per session, a mouse counting when any session is significant. Nor is a continuity correction stated (answer of 2026-10-20); readings, each run with the others: (i) the Pearson chi-squared test without correction (what Matlab's crosstab, the paper's stated software, returns); (ii) with Yates's correction. Reproduced when 6 of 8 mice show a significant decrease under a reading (5 to 7 partially reproduced); not reproduced when fewer than 5 do.

claims.statement: In L4 excitatory neurons held near 0 mV, inhibitory inputs occur spontaneously but are more prevalent at the onset of whisker movement; after whisking onset, excitation and inhibition increase gradually, with indistinguishable time courses, over about 100 ms.
claims.source: Results, Membrane-potential dynamics of L4 excitatory neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 3e-g
claims.quote: In the absence of touch, inhibitory inputs occurred spontaneously but were more prevalent at onset of whisker movement (Fig. 3e,f). ... After the onset of whisker movement, excitation and inhibition increased gradually, with indistinguishable time courses, over approximately 100 ms (Fig. 3g).
claims.criterion: The 6 L4 E neurons of exc-inhibition-timing. Whisking-onset-aligned average Vm at rest (excitation) and with current (inhibition, sign inverted), over the transitions of the Online Methods (Fig. 3e-g legend, "same as b-d" for whisking onset), each normalized to its peak after onset (Fig. 3g). The paper gives no test and no window for "more prevalent at onset"; it is read with the paper's whisking-onset windows (Supplementary Fig. 4 legend): with current, the mean Vm 100 to 300 ms after onset below the mean 0 to 200 ms before, in the grand average (Fig. 3f) and by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the 6 neurons at 0.05 (the Methods' paired test). "Indistinguishable time courses" is a claim of absence with no test in the paper; it is judged by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at 0.05 of the per-neuron times at which the normalized excitation and inhibition averages first reach half their peak. Reproduced when the inhibition increase holds and the half-maximum times do not differ; partially reproduced when only one part holds. The times to half and full peak of the normalized grand averages are reported against the paper's "approximately 100 ms". With 6 neurons the smallest two-sided signed-rank p is 0.03, so the test has little power; this is reported.

claims.statement: After infraorbital nerve transection, mice still search for the pole by whisking but, unable to sense it, perform the task at chance (48% correct).
claims.source: Results, Inhibition is driven by sensory input, paragraph 2
claims.quote: however, as they were unable to sense the object, ... they performed at chance level (48% correct).
claims.criterion: Trial outcomes of the behavioral sessions of the ION-cut mice (9 mice; Online Methods, Infraorbital nerve transection). The paper does not say how the 48% is averaged. Readings, each run: (a) all ION-cut trials pooled; (b) the mean over recorded cells of the proportion correct during each recording, as the Methods average control performance (Online Methods, Behavior). Reproduced when the proportion is within tolerance under a reading; not reproduced otherwise. The whisking part ("similar whisking amplitudes", data not shown) is not tested; whisking amplitudes in ION-cut and control sessions are reported.

claims.statement: In ALM scRNA-seq, glutamatergic neurons form 27 clusters and PT neurons map to three of them (Slco2a1, and the closely related Npsr1 and Hpgd), and with axonal reconstructions this suggests that PT neurons can be divided into two cell types.
claims.source: Results, Two types of PT neuron in layer 5, paragraphs 1 and 5; Fig. 1
claims.quote: ALM PT neurons mapped to three transcriptomic clusters ... Axonal reconstructions and scRNA-seq data suggest that PT neurons can be divided into two distinct cell types.
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset, which holds electrophysiology only. The cluster count is an exact count (tolerance 0). Counting rule (answer of 2026-10-20) - Fig. 1a names 26 glutamatergic clusters and its legend says "The transcriptomic cluster corresponding to Cajal–Retzius cells was excluded here"; the Methods give "27 glutamatergic" ALM types. So the 27 are the clusters of Fig. 1a plus the Cajal-Retzius cluster. The count is of ALM glutamatergic clusters not named for VISp, the Cajal-Retzius cluster included; the other counts are variants.

claims.statement: Of 12 reconstructed PT neurons, 8 innervate the thalamus.
claims.source: Results, Two types of PT neuron in layer 5, paragraph 2; Fig. 2a, b; Extended Data Fig. 2
claims.quote: Patterns of axonal collaterals revealed two neuron types: one group innervated the thalamus (n = 8; Fig. 2a, b; green hues and Extended Data Fig. 2)
claims.criterion: Answer of 2026-10-20. The 12 neurons and their groups are those of Supplementary data table 1 (complete reconstructions; thalamus-projecting AA0011, AA0114, AA0115, AA0122, AA0181, AA0182, AA0245, AA0261; medulla-projecting AA0012, AA0133, AA0179, AA0180), the same as the hand grouping of Axons/AxonReconstructions.m (in.grnum). The paper gives no rule for "innervated the thalamus"; Extended Data Fig. 2a, c plot thalamic lengths and termini for both groups. Readings, (a) any axon terminus in the thalamus, (b) any axon length in the thalamus, (c) more termini in the thalamus than in the medulla. The 8 is a reported count, so it holds if it matches under one reading; the counts under every reading are shown.

claims.statement: The other 4 of 12 reconstructed PT neurons bypass the thalamus and branch in the medulla, including the reticular nuclei with premotor neurons for orofacial movements.
claims.source: Results, Two types of PT neuron in layer 5, paragraph 2; Fig. 2a, b
claims.quote: the other group bypassed the thalamus and branched in the medulla, including the reticular nuclei containing premotor neurons for orofacial movements23 (n = 4; magenta hues)
claims.criterion: Answer of 2026-10-20. Neurons and groups as in pt-upper-thalamus-projection (Supplementary data table 1). The paper gives no rule for "bypassed the thalamus". Readings, (a) no axon terminus in the thalamus, (b) no axon length in the thalamus, (c) more termini in the medulla than in the thalamus. The 4 is a reported count, so it holds if it matches under one reading; the counts under every reading are shown.

claims.statement: Both PT types project to several shared targets; all reconstructed cells innervate the superior colliculus, and both types send collaterals to the subthalamic nucleus, zona incerta and midbrain reticular nucleus.
claims.source: Results, Two types of PT neuron in layer 5, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 2e legend
claims.quote: All cells innervated the superior colliculus and subsets of both groups branched in other areas ... Both cell types extended axon collaterals locally within the same sublamina as their somata, the subthalamic nucleus, zona incerta, and the midbrain reticular nucleus.
claims.criterion: Answer of 2026-10-20. The first part ("All cells innervated the superior colliculus") is stated of the reconstructions (Results, paragraph 2) and is tested on Axons.zip. The second part (collaterals to the subthalamic nucleus, zona incerta and midbrain reticular nucleus) is stated in the Extended Data Fig. 2e legend of the bulk labelling ("Bulk projections of PTupper and PTlower populations"), and the paper reports it from annotated images, with no measure or count. Its intended test is the bulk labelling images; the paper gives no method to analyse them. A test on the reconstructions (both groups reach all three structures) is a variant, reported as such.

claims.statement: Thalamus-projecting PT neurons lie in upper L5b and medulla-projecting PT neurons in lower L5b; few neurons are co-labelled from thalamus and medulla (2.2%, 22 of 984) while many are co-labelled from thalamus and superior colliculus (77.1%, 687 of 890).
claims.source: Results, Two types of PT neuron in layer 5, paragraph 3; Fig. 2c, d; Extended Data Fig. 3
claims.quote: Few neurons were co-labelled by injections into the thalamus and medulla (2.2%; 22 out of 984 cells labelled from either location), whereas many neurons were co-labelled by injections into the thalamus and superior colliculus (77.1%; 687 out of 890 thalamus-labelled cells)
claims.criterion: Answer of 2026-10-20. Neither the paper nor its code says how labelled and co-labelled cells were counted. The Methods (Histology and imaging) describe sectioning, immunolabelling and imaging only, and the Figshare record holds no anatomy code; Anatomy.zip holds image stacks (folders BL648_Thal_Med_H2b_Ch01 and Ch02, BL772_ThalMed_anterograde_Ch01 and Ch02, BL777_Medulla_ChR2-YFP_Ch01, BL780_Thalamus_ChR2-YFP_Ch01) and no counts. The counting method (cell detection, the area and sections counted, what makes a cell co-labelled) is open; the claim stays methods_underspecified unless the counts can be shown not to depend on it. The folder names name no superior colliculus labelling, which the 77.1% needs.

claims.statement: All 62 medulla-projecting PT neurons map to the Slco2a1 cluster, and 91 of 94 thalamus-projecting PT neurons map to the Npsr1 and Hpgd clusters.
claims.source: Results, Two types of PT neuron in layer 5, paragraph 4; Fig. 2e, f
claims.quote: projecting PT neurons mapped to the Slco2a1 taxonomic cluster. ... Similarly, thalamus-projecting PT neurons mapped to the Npsr1 and Hpgd clusters (91 out of 94
claims.criterion: Answer of 2026-10-20. The paper does not say which annotation field defines the injection groups of Fig. 2f. Its code for the same cells (Seq/SC_correlations_across_clusters.ipynb, Extended Data Fig. 4a-c) groups them by inj_roi_label, matching "IRN" for medulla, "VAL" for thalamus, "PG" for pons and "SC|SCm" for superior colliculus. Readings, (a) that grouping of the code, (b) inj_primary_label grouped with the Allen ontology (medulla IRN, GRN, PARN; thalamus VAL, PF, MD; pons PG, PRNc). Both counts are reported numbers, so the claim holds when both match under one reading; the counts, and the group sizes against the Methods' n (62, 94, 100, 97), are shown under each.

claims.statement: All 18 partially and fully reconstructed PT neurons project to the superior colliculus and none lacks projections to both thalamus and medulla, suggesting that most if not all PT neurons belong to the two types.
claims.source: Results, Two types of PT neuron in layer 5, paragraph 5; Supplementary Table 1 (read 2026-10-20 in the Supplementary Information PDF)
claims.quote: All (18 out of 18) partially and fully reconstructed PT neurons projected to the superior colliculus and no (0 out of 18) PT neurons lacked projections to both the thalamus and medulla
claims.criterion: Answer of 2026-10-20. The 18 neurons are those listed in Supplementary data table 1 - the 12 complete reconstructions of pt-upper-thalamus-projection and 6 partial ones, thalamus-projecting AA0132, AA0135, AA0250 and medulla-projecting AA0131, AA0134, AA0169. The other neurons of Axons.zip are not among them. The paper gives no rule for projecting to a structure; readings, (a) any axon terminus there, (b) any axon length there, both shown.

claims.statement: smFISH confirms Slco2a1 as a PTlower marker and Npnt as a PTupper marker (Slco2a1 puncta IQR 1-2.5 in PTupper against 6-22 in PTlower; Npnt IQR 16-40 in PTupper against 1-9 in PTlower).
claims.source: Results, Two types of PT neuron in layer 5, paragraph 6; Fig. 3c legend
claims.quote: Slco2a1, PTupper: interquartile range (IQR) = 1–2.5 puncta, n = 60; Slco2a1, PTlower: IQR = 6–22, n = 95; Npnt, PTupper: IQR = 16–40, n = 145; Npnt, PTlower: IQR = 1–9, n = 69
claims.criterion: Answer of 2026-10-20. data was elsewhere, with Anatomy.zip as the place; that was wrong about the paper. The Data availability statement names archives for the bulk RNA-seq (GEO GSE119182) and the electrophysiology (CRCNS.org and Figshare) only, and Anatomy.zip holds no smFISH images or puncta counts. The smFISH data are the paper's own recording, deposited in no archive it names, so data is dataset; whether any data the attempt can reach hold them is the author's to find.

claims.statement: Fold changes between PTupper and PTlower of the 200 most discriminative genes correlate between scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq (Pearson's r = 0.87).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4i legend
claims.quote: The correlation coefficient (Pearson’s r) in fold change expression was 0.87 for this set of 200 differentially expressed genes.
claims.criterion: Answer of 2026-10-20. From the Extended Data Fig. 4i legend, fold change is the mean log2(CPM + 1) of the Npsr1-Hpgd cells minus that of the Slco2a1 cells, for scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq; the 200 genes and the cell and replicate groups are those of the code (Seq/bulkVsSC.m on Seq.zip - the 100 genes at each end of the binary detection accuracy, bulk replicates 1, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13 against 2, 4, 7, 10, 12, 14). The code applies log2(x + 1) to the bulk values as stored in bulk_data.txt, which are not CPM (columns sum to about 1e7); where legend and code differ the legend is followed, and the code's version is a variant. Reproduced when r is within tolerance.

claims.statement: The recordings yield 61 identified PTupper cells from 8 mice and 69 identified PTlower neurons from 4 mice after exclusions (130 of 143 tagged units kept).
claims.source: Results, Cell-type-specific recordings, paragraph 2; Methods, Electrophysiology data analysis
claims.quote: (61 PTupper cells, 8 mice; 69 PTlower neurons, 4 mice; Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 5)
claims.criterion: The unit selection of the opening comment, under each of its readings (code's per-unit rule; Methods' session rule), applied to the tagged units of the dandiset. Reproduced when one reading gives both unit counts within tolerance and the mouse counts exactly. The counts under every reading are shown, with the 143 tagged units before exclusion. The reading that matches is the selection the other electrophysiology claims use; when both match, both are carried. Answer of 2026-10-20 - when neither matches (the dandiset lacks sessions the paper used), the other claims use the code's per-unit rule. The Methods report the outcome of the selection ("13 units were rejected; 130 were kept"), and the code's rule is the one that, as the attempt reports, gives it, with 61 and 69, on the paper's processed data (loadAndProcessData.m on Ephys.zip); the Methods' session rule is a variant.

claims.statement: Identified PTupper cells are at more superficial recording depths than PTlower neurons.
claims.source: Results, Cell-type-specific recordings, paragraph 2; Fig. 4e
claims.quote: Identified PTupper cells were at more superficial recording depths than PTlower neurons, consistent with retrograde labelling experiments
claims.criterion: Depth is the micromanipulator reading, uncorrected (Fig. 4e legend, Methods). The code (simplePlots.m, plotDepth) plots each unit's own depth field (meta.depth) and also stores the session's manipulator depth (manipulatorDepth). Answer of 2026-10-20 - Fig. 4e is the plot of the unit depth field, and the Methods say "Unit depths (Fig. 4e) were inferred from manipulator readings only", so the claim is judged on the unit depth; the session manipulator depth is a variant, shown where available. The paper reports no test; Fig. 4e shows mean +/- s.d. Reproduced when the mean depth of included PTupper units is smaller than that of PTlower units. Shown both with all units, as the code's error bars, and without the right-hemisphere PTlower recordings (animals 29.5 and 30.5), which the code leaves out of the plotted points (simplePlots.m, plotDepth).

claims.statement: Baseline and trial-averaged peak spike rates do not differ between PTupper (baseline 4.3 +/- 3.5 Hz, peak 17.7 +/- 13.8 Hz, median +/- s.d.) and PTlower cells (5.2 +/- 4.8 Hz, 17.2 +/- 22 Hz).
claims.source: Results, Cell-type-specific recordings, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Baseline and trial-averaged peak spike rates were not significantly different (P > 0.1, two-sided t-test) in PTupper cells (baseline: 4.3 ± 3.5 Hz; peak: 17.7 ± 13.8 Hz; median ± s.d.) compared to PTlower cells (baseline: 5.2 ± 4.8 Hz; peak: 17.2 ± 22 Hz)
claims.criterion: From the code (simplePlots.m, plotFiringRates). Baseline rate is the mean, over lick left and lick right correct trials, of each trial type's mean rate in the baseline epoch (-3.1 to -2.7 s); peak rate is the maximum over time of the smoothed trial-averaged rate of either trial type. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-sided Student's t-test between the two populations, for baseline and for peak. Reproduced when neither test has p < 0.05 and the four medians are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and a median is out of tolerance; not reproduced when either test has p < 0.05. Whether p exceeds the reported bound 0.1 is reported, as are the s.d.

claims.statement: Spike rates are more heterogeneous across the PTlower population than the PTupper population, for baseline (P = 0.02) and peak rates (P = 3 x 10^-4).
claims.source: Results, Cell-type-specific recordings, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Spike rates in PTlower cells were more heterogeneous across the population (baseline: P = 0.02; peak: P = 3 × 10−4; χ2 test)
claims.criterion: Rates as defined in pt-spike-rates-similar (the definitions only, not that claim's outcome; the dependency was moved to pt-tagged-units on 2026-10-20, as this claim uses no result of pt-spike-rates-similar). The Results name a "χ2 test" without saying which; the Methods name no variance test. The code compares variances with MATLAB's vartest2, a two-sided two-sample F test (simplePlots.m, plotFiringRates). Readings, (a) Bartlett's test, the two-sample variance test with a chi-squared statistic, (b) the code's F test; both are run and the outcome is the one they give. Reproduced when, for both baseline and peak, the PTlower variance is larger and the test has p < 0.05; partially reproduced when that holds for one.

claims.statement: A substantial proportion of PTlower neurons fire bursts (18.8%), which are rare among PTupper cells (3.3%).
claims.source: Results, Cell-type-specific recordings, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 5c
claims.quote: A substantial proportion of PTlower neurons displayed spike bursts (18.8%), which were rare among PTupper cells (3.3%; P = 0.006, Fisher’s exact test; Extended Data Fig. 5c).
claims.criterion: A bursting cell has more than 10% of its inter-spike intervals shorter than 5 ms (Extended Data Fig. 5c legend). From the code (simplePlots.m, showISIHists) intervals are taken within trials only, an interval across a trial boundary being dropped from the count of short intervals but kept in the denominator, over all of the unit's spikes. Reproduced when both percentages are within tolerance and the two-sided Fisher exact test on the 2 x 2 counts has p < 0.05; partially reproduced when the test holds and a percentage is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: Most recorded PT neurons (122 of 130, 94%) have significant trial-type selectivity in at least one task epoch.
claims.source: Results, Cell-type-specific recordings, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Most recorded PT neurons had significant selectivity, defined as the difference in spike rate between trial types (‘lick left’ versus ‘lick right’), during at least one task epoch (P < 0.01, two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test; 122 out of 130; 94%).
claims.criterion: Per unit and epoch, the mean rate of each correct trial in the epoch, lick right against lick left, two-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.01. The code (simplePlots.m, sigCellsByType) counts a unit when any of the sample (-2.5 to -2.1 s), delay (-1.3 to 0 s) and response (0 to 0.4 s) epochs is significant. "Task epoch" in the text can also be read as the full sample epoch (-2.5 to -1.5 s) in place of its first 400 ms; both readings are run, and the count holds if it is within tolerance under one.

claims.statement: Trial-averaged activity patterns are nearly as diverse within each PT population as across all neurons recorded in ALM; cell type explains relatively little of the variance.
claims.source: Results, Cell-type-specific recordings, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 6; Discussion, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Trial-averaged activity patterns were nearly as diverse within each PT population as across all neurons recorded within ALM (Extended Data Fig. 6).
claims.criterion: From the Methods (variance explained paragraph) and the code (VarianceExplained.m). Trial-averaged lick right and lick left rates of each neuron, concatenated and z-scored (Methods); PCA per PT population; fraction of variance explained by 1 to 6 components (the code's Ncomp); compared with 1,000 size-matched samples drawn without replacement from the unidentified units of the same cohort (the code's groups 3 and 4). The paper gives no threshold for "nearly as diverse"; Extended Data Fig. 6b, d plot the ratio of PT to unidentified variance explained on an axis from 1 to 1.3 (the code's ylim). Reproduced when, for both populations, the median ratio is at most 1.3 at every number of components. Variants that do not change the outcome are the code's own choices, which differ from the Methods text (a 100 ms smoothing, sm = 39; baseline subtraction and division by s.d. in place of z-scoring; the first 1,000 time bins; per iteration, 50 trials of each type resampled with replacement for every neuron, PT and unidentified alike; the variance explained taken per neuron and averaged). The asterisks of the figure (ratio above 1, z > 1.645 of the bootstrap) are reported.

claims.statement: Along the late delay coding direction (CDlate) selectivity is substantial in both PT types, with 40 of 61 PTupper and 44 of 69 PTlower neurons selective.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 7a, b
claims.quote: along a different direction in activity space, which maximized selectivity at the end of the delay epoch, CDlate, selectivity was substantial in both cell types18 (Extended Data Fig. 7a, b; PTupper: 40 out of 61 neurons selective; PTlower: 44 out of 69)
claims.criterion: Two parts. (a) Counts from the code (simplePlots.m, sigCellsByType) - a unit is selective when the mean rates of its correct trials in the late delay epoch (-0.4 to 0 s) differ between lick right and lick left by a two-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.01; both counts within tolerance. (b) Selectivity along each population's CDlate, with the shared bootstrap, is significant (5th percentile above zero) over the late delay epoch in both populations, read as (i) at every time bin from -0.4 to 0 s, or (ii) for the mean over that window. Reproduced when both parts hold, partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: Along the early coding direction (CDearly, first 400 ms of the sample epoch), selectivity is larger and more consistent across trials in the PTupper population than in the PTlower population.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity, paragraph 2; Fig. 5a, b
claims.quote: In this projection, selectivity was larger and more consistent across trials in the PTupper population compared to the PTlower population (Fig. 5b).
claims.criterion: CDearly and selectivity with the shared bootstrap. The paper reports no test or window for "larger". Readings for the window over which bootstrap selectivity is averaged, (a) -2.5 to -2.1 s, the CDearly window, (b) the sample epoch -2.5 to -1.5 s. The paper gives no rule for "larger"; readings fixed here, (i) the bootstrap median of the PTupper mean exceeds that of PTlower, (ii) in addition the PTupper 5th percentile exceeds the PTlower median. "More consistent across trials" is read as a smaller spread of the bootstrap (which resamples trials) relative to its median, the s.d. over median; the paper names no measure. Reproduced when both hold, partially reproduced when larger holds alone, not reproduced when larger does not hold. Answer of 2026-10-20 - the paper does not say which rule decides. The Results give "larger" with no number or test, Fig. 5b and its legend show only the bootstrap median and 5-95% band, and Projections.m draws the curves with no comparison between populations. Both rules stay; when they give different outcomes the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In the PTupper population, selectivity along CDearly remains constant through the sample and delay epochs until the go cue.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity, paragraph 2; Fig. 5b
claims.quote: Furthermore, selectivity in the PTupper population remained constant throughout the sample and delay epochs until the go cue, implying retention of decision-related information.
claims.criterion: PTupper selectivity along its CDearly, shared bootstrap. Readings of "remained constant" (the paper names no measure), (a) the 5th percentile is above zero at every time bin from -2.1 s to the go cue; (b) the mean over the last 400 ms before the go cue (-0.4 to 0 s) is significant by the bootstrap (fewer than 5% of iterations at or below zero), the window and test the paper uses for PTlower (pt-lower-cdearly-decay). Reproduced when the readings agree that it holds; the ratio of the mean in -0.4 to 0 s to the mean in -2.5 to -2.1 s is reported.

claims.statement: In the PTlower population, selectivity along CDearly decays rapidly, with no significant selectivity in the 400 ms before the go cue (P = 0.34, bootstrap).
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity, paragraph 2; Fig. 5b
claims.quote: By contrast, selectivity in the PTlower population decayed rapidly along CDearly (no significant selectivity in 400 ms preceding go cue; P = 0.34, bootstrap).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. PTlower selectivity along its CDearly with the shared bootstrap; the p-value is the fraction of iterations in which the mean selectivity over -0.4 to 0 s is at or below zero (one-sided, as the paper's bootstrap tests are). Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The p-value is compared with the reported 0.34, and the selectivity in that window is given either way.

claims.statement: The coding direction stays more similar across the sample and delay epochs in the PTupper population than in the PTlower population, whose delay-epoch coding directions are largely orthogonal to those of the sample epoch.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 7c, d
claims.quote: For the PTupper population, the CD remained more similar across the sample and delay epochs compared to the PTlower population (Extended Data Fig. 7c, d).
claims.criterion: The paper reports no number or test. Two measures from the paper. (a) Extended Data Fig. 7d legend and the code (Projections.m, plotEarlyLateCorr) - Pearson's r across the units of a population between the CDearly and CDlate weights. (b) Methods and the code (CDCorrelation.m, compareEpochs) - the inner product of the unit-normalised CDs of the sample (-2.5 to -2.1 s) and late delay (-0.4 to 0 s) windows, mean over the bootstrap (the code uses 100 iterations, all trials per type up to 500). Reproduced when PTupper's value exceeds PTlower's under both measures. The code's interval (mean +/- 1.96 s.e. over iterations), the r p-values, and the PTlower values (for "largely orthogonal", which the paper does not quantify) are reported.

claims.statement: Individual PTupper neurons have higher early selectivity than PTlower neurons (0.41 +/- 0.04 against 0.25 +/- 0.02, mean +/- s.e.m., P < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity, paragraph 2
claims.quote: exhibited higher early selectivity (PTupper: 0.41 ± 0.04; mean ± s.e.m.; PTlower: 0.25 ± 0.02; P < 0.01)
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the reported s.e.m. The paper does not define "early selectivity" or name the test. Readings of the measure, each from the first 400 ms of the sample epoch (-2.5 to -2.1 s), over correct trials, (a) the absolute value of the unit's CD weight before normalisation, the difference of mean rates over the root of the summed variances (Methods, equation 1); (b) the d' at the accuracy-maximising threshold that decodingAccuracy.m computes (acc.dprime, from doROC.m), as an absolute value. Readings of the test, (i) two-sided Student's t-test (Methods - all two-sample t-tests were Student's), (ii) two-sided Mann-Whitney test (used for the same window in Extended Data Fig. 9; decodingAccuracy.m computes both). The measure is a reading of the reported numbers, so a match under either reading counts. Trials are those of the unit's range (opening comment, settled 2026-10-20 from the processed files); all trials is a variant. The test is an open method detail, so both tests are run on that measure and the outcome is the one they give (methods_underspecified when they differ). Reproduced when, under one reading of the measure, both means are within tolerance and PTupper is higher with p < 0.01 under both tests; partially reproduced when PTupper is higher with p < 0.01 under both tests but a mean is out of tolerance under every reading.

claims.statement: Single PTupper neurons decode trial type better than PTlower neurons in the first 400 ms of the sample epoch; 24.6% (15 of 61) of PTupper and 4.4% (3 of 69) of PTlower neurons reach 70% accuracy, mean accuracy is 64.4 +/- 1.0% against 58.9 +/- 0.6%, and the ten most discriminative neurons are all PTupper.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9a, b legend; Results, Preparatory activity, paragraph 2
claims.quote: 24.6% (15 out of 61) of PTupper neurons predicted trial type with at least 70% accuracy, whereas only 4.4% (3 out of 69) of PTlower neurons did so. Mean accuracy was also significantly higher in PTupper neurons (PTupper: 64.4 ± 1.0%; PTlower: 58.9 ± 0.6%, mean ± s.e.m.; P = 1 × 10−4, two-sided Mann–Whitney test). The ten most discriminative neurons all belonged to the PTupper population.
claims.criterion: Methods (single-cell decoding) and the code (decodingAccuracy.m, doROC.m). Per unit, the mean rate of each correct trial in -2.5 to -2.1 s; every observed rate is a threshold, with the polarity set by the side of the ROC area; accuracy is the maximum over thresholds of the fraction of trials classified correctly. "At least 70% accuracy" has two readings, (a) accuracy >= 0.70, (b) the code's cut (decodingAccuracy.m, calcTail), accuracy above the mean + 1 s.d. of the accuracies of all PT units of both types, which the text reports as 70%; the counts hold if they match under one. Mean tolerances are the reported s.e.m. Reproduced when all four numbers are within tolerance, the two-sided Mann-Whitney test has p < 0.05 with PTupper higher, and the ten most accurate units are all PTupper; partially reproduced when the test holds and some of the rest do not.

claims.statement: Decoding from spike rates rectified at baseline, no PTlower neuron reaches 70% accuracy while the same 24.6% of PTupper neurons do, PTupper neurons make up 20 of the 21 most predictive, and mean accuracy is 62.7 +/- 1.1% against 56.7 +/- 0.4%.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9c, d legend
claims.quote: Disregarding spike rate changes below baseline, no PTlower neurons predicted trial type with at least 70% accuracy, whereas the same 24.6% of PTupper neurons continued to do so and accounted for 20 out of 21 of the most predictive neurons (PTupper: 62.7 ± 1.1%; PTlower: 56.7 ± 0.4%, mean ± s.e.m.; P = 9 × 10−7, two-sided Mann–Whitney test).
claims.criterion: As pt-upper-decoding, after subtracting from each trial's rate the unit's baseline (the mean over the two trial types of their mean rate in -3.1 to -2.7 s) and setting negative values to zero (decodingAccuracy.m, signConstraint 1). Under reading (b) of the 70% cut, the code recomputes the mean + 1 s.d. from the rectified accuracies. Reproduced when all numbers are within tolerance and the Mann-Whitney test has p < 0.05 with PTupper higher; partially reproduced when the test holds and a number is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: PTlower neurons carry late preparatory activity (selectivity along CDlate) and a movement command; along the go cue coding direction (CDgo) selectivity is larger, emerges faster and persists longer in PTlower than in PTupper.
claims.source: Results, Movement commands, paragraph 2; Fig. 6b, c; Extended Data Fig. 7b; Discussion, paragraphs 1 and 3
claims.quote: Along CDgo, selectivity was larger, emerged faster, and persisted longer in the PTlower than in the PTupper population (Fig. 6b, c).
claims.criterion: CDgo (0 to 0.4 s, orthogonalised to CDlate) and selectivity with the shared bootstrap, go-cue aligned. Late preparatory activity is part (b) of pt-preparatory-activity for PTlower. For CDgo, the paper gives no measure; readings fixed here from its words. Larger, (a) the bootstrap median of the mean selectivity over 0 to 0.4 s, (b) the peak of the median selectivity after the go cue; PTlower above PTupper. Emerged faster, from pt-cdgo-onset. Persisted longer, the last time after the go cue of the first run of bins with the 5th percentile above zero is later for PTlower. Reproduced when PTlower CDlate selectivity holds and larger, faster and longer all hold; partially reproduced when some do.

claims.statement: Along CDgo, significant selectivity emerges 24 ms after the go cue in PTlower neurons, faster than in PTupper neurons (48 ms), consistent with a role in movement initiation.
claims.source: Results, Movement commands, paragraph 2; Fig. 6c legend
claims.quote: In the PTlower population, significant selectivity emerged 24 ms after the go cue, faster than in the PTupper population (48 ms) (Fig. 6c).
claims.criterion: Onset is the first time after the go cue at which the 5th percentile of the bootstrap selectivity along CDgo is above zero (Fig. 6c legend, significance as in the Methods). The tolerance is one 5 ms bin, the resolution of the rates (10% of the values is below a bin). Open, with readings - the bin time stamp, (a) bin centre, (b) bin end, (c) bin start; whether onset must be sustained, (i) the first significant bin, (ii) the first of three consecutive significant bins. Reproduced when, under one reading, both onsets are within tolerance and PTlower is earlier; partially reproduced when PTlower is earlier but an onset is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: The first detectable movement occurs about 50 ms after the go cue (99% confidence interval 38 to 56 ms).
claims.source: Results, Movement commands, paragraph 2; Fig. 6c legend; Methods, Videography
claims.quote: The onset of the first detectable movement occurred approximately 50 ms after the go cue onset (99% confidence interval: 38–56 ms).
claims.criterion: Methods, Videography - reaction time from the luminance change in a region of interest just below the jaw in 400 Hz side-view video, averaged over all trials of a session; confidence interval by bootstrapping session means across mice (3) and sessions (14). The Methods say 95% and the Results 99%; both are computed. The region is placed by hand and the onset rule for the luminance trace is not given, so the test needs the video. The tolerance is the paper's own uncertainty, the 99% interval of 38 to 56 ms; the expected entry carries its upper side (6 ms), and the claim is judged on the whole interval. Reproduced when the bootstrap mean lies within 38 to 56 ms and the computed interval overlaps it. Not testable if the dandiset holds no video.

claims.statement: The coding direction changes rapidly at the go cue in the PTlower population, and more slowly, over several hundred milliseconds, in the PTupper population.
claims.source: Results, Movement commands, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 7c, e
claims.quote: The coding direction changed rapidly at the go cue in the PTlower population, and more slowly, over several hundred milliseconds, in the PTupper population (Extended Data Fig. 7c, e).
claims.criterion: Extended Data Fig. 7e legend - the correlation (inner product of unit-normalised CDs, Methods) between the CD at each time bin and CDlate, normalised to its mean in the 400 ms before the go cue; 1,000 bootstrap iterations. The code (CDCorrelation.m) averages the inner product over the CDs of every bin of the delay epoch (-1.3 to 0 s) and normalises to the delay epoch mean, with 100 iterations; this is a variant. The paper does not say how the speed of change is measured. The reading fixed here is the time after the go cue at which the bootstrap median of the normalised correlation first falls below a level, with levels (a) 0.5 and (b) 0.75. Reproduced when PTlower's time is shorter than PTupper's and PTupper's is at least 0.2 s ("several hundred milliseconds"); partially reproduced when PTlower's is shorter only. Answer of 2026-10-20 - neither the paper nor the code fixes a level or a measure of speed. The Extended Data Fig. 7c legend says the change is "abrupt" and "immediately after the go cue onset" in PTlower and, in PTupper, "more slowly (over several hundred milliseconds), largely after initiation of movement"; CDCorrelation.m plots the normalised correlation with a dotted line at 0.05 s (movement onset) and computes no crossing time. Both levels stay; when they give different outcomes the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In PTlower neurons, selectivity along both CDlate and CDgo ceases with the offset of movement (the last lick), together with an abrupt change in the coding direction; this transition is not seen in the PTupper population.
claims.source: Results, Movement commands, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 10a-c
claims.quote: Selectivity along both CDlate and CDgo ceased with the offset of movement (Extended Data Fig. 10a, b), simultaneous with an abrupt change in the coding direction (Extended Data Fig. 10c). This transition was not observed in the dynamics of the PTupper population.
claims.criterion: Rates aligned to the last lick-port contact after the go cue (either side) on correct trials, within each unit's trial range (loadAndProcessData.m, getLickInfo and ObjToLickPSTH), projected on the go-cue CDlate and CDgo of the population, without baseline subtraction (Projections.m), with the shared bootstrap. The paper gives no window. Readings fixed here - (a) the 5th percentile is above zero for most bins of the 200 ms before the last lick and for none of the bins from 0.2 to 0.4 s after it; (b) the same with 400 ms windows before and from 0.1 to 0.5 s after. Reproduced when this holds for PTlower along both CDs; partially reproduced for one CD. The PTupper result along both CDs and the CD correlation matrix after the go cue (Extended Data Fig. 10c, from CDCorrelation.m with lick-aligned rates) are reported, as the paper gives no measure for the abrupt change. Answer of 2026-10-20 - the paper gives no windows. The Extended Data Fig. 10a, b legends give only the 5-95% band, and Projections.m (showProjection) plots the lick-aligned selectivity with no window or test; both window readings stay, and when they differ the claim is methods_underspecified. The last lick is defined by the code (loadAndProcessData.m, getLickInfo) as, per trial, the latest left or right lick after the go cue among the trial's licks. The paper says nothing of rebuilding it when licks are not assigned to trials; a rebuilt last lick is a deviation, acceptable when the outcome is the same with the trials whose rebuilt last lick disagrees with the processed data left out, which is shown.

claims.statement: Differences in coding between PTupper and PTlower neurons are not explained by the animal cohorts; unidentified neurons recorded in the two cohorts give similar coding direction projections, nearly indistinguishable once depth-matched.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 8 legend; Methods, Electrophysiology
claims.quote: Differences in coding between PTupper and PTlower neurons could not be explained by variation across animal cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 8).
claims.criterion: Unidentified single units of each cohort, with the inclusion rule of the opening comment (the code applies it to untagged units, groups 3 and 4; whether the reported counts are before or after it is open, and both are given); depth matching by keeping the PTlower cohort's left ALM recordings only (Methods; the Extended Data Fig. 8 legend says the removed units were from the "contralateral hemisphere" and recorded at a lower depth, which fits the Methods' right ALM only if contralateral is taken relative to the PTupper recordings, so the Methods are followed). Selectivity along CDearly and CDgo computed for each unidentified population as for the PT populations. The paper gives no test for "similar". Reproduced when, for the depth-matched populations, the difference that separates the PT types is absent - the PTlower-cohort population's mean CDearly selectivity over -2.5 to -2.1 s lies inside the PTupper-cohort population's 5-95% bootstrap interval, and the two CDgo onsets (pt-cdgo-onset rule) differ by no more than the difference between the PT types; partially reproduced when one holds. The z-scored variant of the legend's bottom row is shown.

claims.statement: The two PT types have different roles in time; PTupper populations carry early preparatory activity that persists until movement, while PTlower populations mainly carry late preparatory activity and movement commands.
claims.source: Abstract; Discussion, paragraphs 1 and 3
claims.quote: Preparatory activity appeared early and remained persistent in PTupper neurons, whereas movement commands were observed in PTlower neurons.
claims.criterion: The summary of the claims it depends on, with no measure of its own. Reproduced when all six are reproduced; partially reproduced when at least one claim on each side (PTupper early and persistent; PTlower late and motor) is reproduced; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: 1,329 cells from 266 mice passed the initial quality control and were sequenced; the paper's recordings come from these cells.
claims.source: Results, Patch-seq of mouse primary motor cortex, paragraph 1; Methods, Animals
claims.quote: In total, we performed whole-cell recordings from more than 2,000 cells, of which 1,329 cells (from 266 mice) passed initial quality control.
claims.criterion: Counts are exact records, so the tolerance is zero. Cells are counted as distinct recorded cells in the dandiset, mice as distinct subjects. The paper allows two readings of the cell count for a dandiset of recordings, (a) all 1,329 cells, or (b) 1,328, leaving out the one neuron whose electrophysiological recording did not pass quality control (Extended Data Fig. 3 legend; the code's feature table has 1,328 cells). Reproduced when the mouse count is 266 and the cell count matches either reading; partially reproduced when one of the two counts matches.

claims.statement: The mice were 35 to 245 days old, with a median of 75 days and an interquartile range of 64 to 100 days.
claims.source: Methods, Animals; Extended Data Figure 2a
claims.quote: Experiments on adult male and female mice ( n = 266; median age 75 days, interquartile range 64–100, full range 35–245 days, Extended Data Fig. 2a )
claims.criterion: Ages are records in days, so the extremes take a tolerance of zero and the median and quartiles one day, for the rounding of quartiles between neighbouring values. The statistics are over the n = 266 mice, one age per mouse (Methods, Animals; the Extended Data Fig. 2a legend also says "Age distribution of the mice"). Reproduced when every value is within tolerance.

claims.statement: The 266 mice were wild-type C57Bl/6 (27), Viaat-Cre/Ai9 (24), Sst-Cre/Ai9 (75), Vip-Cre/Ai9 (46), Pvalb-Cre/Ai9 (76), Npy-Cre/Ai9 (2), Vipr2-Cre/Ai9 (7), Slc17a8-Cre/Ai9 (6), Gnb4-Cre/Ai9 (1) and Slc17a8-iCre/Ai9 (2).
claims.source: Methods, Animals
claims.quote: were performed on wild-type C57Bl/6 ( n = 27), Viaat -Cre/Ai9 (vesicular inhibitory amino acid transporter, encoded by the Slc32a1 gene, n = 24), Sst -Cre/Ai9 (somatostatin, n = 75), Vip -Cre/Ai9 (vasoactive intestinal polypeptide, n = 46), Pvalb -Cre/Ai9 (parvalbumin, n = 76), Npy -Cre/Ai9 (neuropeptide Y, n = 2), Vipr2 -Cre/Ai9 (vasoactive intestinal peptide receptor 2, n = 7), Scl17a8 -Cre/Ai9 (VGLUT3, vesicular glutamate transporter 3, n = 6), Gnb4 -Cre/Ai9 ( n = 1), and Slc17a8 -iCre/Ai9 ( n = 2) mice
claims.criterion: Counts of distinct subjects by genotype, from the subjects' metadata; exact records, so the tolerance is zero. The paper spells the Slc17a8-Cre line "Scl17a8" once; the two spellings are one line. Reproduced when all ten counts match; partially reproduced when the total is 266 and at least eight counts match.

claims.statement: Each neuron was stimulated with 600 ms current pulses from -200 pA upwards in 20 pA steps up to 1,380 pA (sometimes stopped earlier), with 1.3 or 1.4 s between pulses, and for most neurons the series was repeated several times.
claims.source: Methods, Patch-seq recording procedures, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Each neuron was injected with 600-ms-long current pulses starting from −200 pA and up to 1,380 pA with 20-pA increment steps (in some cases stimulation was stopped before reaching 1,380 pA). There were 1.3- or 1.4-s intervals between successive current pulses, depending on the used setup. For most neurons, the stimulation was then repeated multiple times from the beginning.
claims.criterion: For every cell, the stimulus of each sweep is read from the file. A cell conforms when every step lasts 600 ms (to within 1 ms), the first step of each series is -200 pA, consecutive steps differ by 20 pA, and the largest is at most 1,380 pA. The interval between pulses is taken as onset to onset, the reading the code's 0.1 s to 0.7 s stimulus window within each sweep allows, or as offset to onset; both are reported, and an interval conforms when it is 1.3 or 1.4 s (to within 0.05 s) under either. "Most" neurons repeated is read as more than half of cells with a second series starting again at -200 pA. The paper gives no margins; the 1 ms and 0.05 s timing margins and the 95% and 80% shares of cells are standard choices for "each neuron" under recording jitter, not the paper's, and are named as such. Reproduced when at least 95% of cells conform on steps and intervals and more than half have repeats; partially reproduced when at least 80% conform; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Soma depth was measured for 1,284 of the 1,329 neurons; 45 neurons were recorded with too little biocytin, and the depth could be measured for only 2 of them.
claims.source: Methods, Cortical thickness normalization and layer assignment
claims.quote: We obtained soma depth information for 1,284 neurons out of 1,329 (45 neurons were mistakenly recorded using a solution with insufficient biocytin concentration, and we could measure soma depths for only 2 of those; for 2 other neurons the measurements could not be carried out because the slices were lost).
claims.criterion: Count of cells with a soma depth recorded in the dandiset's metadata; an exact record, so the tolerance is zero. The paper's figure counts differ (1,187 of the 1,227 assigned cells in Fig. 1b); only the Methods count is tested. If the dandiset holds 1,328 cells (see cohort-cells-mice), 1,283 is also accepted when the missing cell is one with a depth.

claims.statement: The features of the example cell of Extended Data Fig. 4 are an input resistance of 274.80 MOhm, a membrane time constant of 21.95 ms, ISI adaptation index 1.26, ISI average adaptation index 1.15, AP amplitude adaptation index 0.91 and its average 0.99, AP threshold -40.18 mV, AP amplitude 81.17 mV, AP width 0.80 ms, AHP -12.60 mV, ADP 0 mV, UDR 1.62, latency 69.28 ms, rheobase 20.44 pA, 32 APs in the highest firing trace, ISI CV 0.27, ISI Fano factor 0.0014, AP CV 0.17, AP Fano factor 1.32, sag ratio 1.17, sag time 0.26, sag area 31.16 mV ms and rebound 17.84 mV.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 4a-f legend
claims.quote: Hyperpolarizing currents were used to compute the input resistance (274.80 MOhm) and membrane time constant tau (21.95 ms). ... It was used to compute AP threshold (−40.18 mV), AP amplitude (81.17 mV), AP width (0.80 ms), AHP (−12.60 mV), ADP (0 mV), UDR (1.62) and latency of the first spike (69.28 ms). d , Regression line gives the rheobase estimate (20.44 pA).
claims.criterion: The legend does not name the cell; the code does. It draws Extended Data Fig. 4 from cell 20181112_sample_11 (subject mouse ZWZEZ, file ses-20181112-sample-11, slice 20181112-slice-7; preprocess-ephys-files.ipynb, cell 60). Features are extracted from that file with the paper's code (preprocess-ephys-files.ipynb, its get_cell_features and extract_spike_features with ephys_extractor.py and ephys_features.py; stimulus window 0.1 to 0.7 s, 10 kHz Bessel filter). Default 10% tolerance, zero for ADP. Two values in the legend disagree with the code's own feature table for this cell. The AP threshold is -43.18 mV in the table against -40.18 mV in the legend; both readings are reported, and -43.18 lies inside the tolerance of -40.18. The sag time is printed "0.26 ms" in the legend and is 0.26 s in the table; it is read in seconds. Reproduced when all 23 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at least 20 are; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: All 17 features used for statistics could be computed for 1,320 cells, of which 1,219 had a t-type assignment.
claims.source: Figure 3a legend; Methods, t-SNE visualization of the morpho-electric phenotypes
claims.quote: n = 1,320 cells used to construct the embedding, 1,219 cells with t-type labels shown.
claims.criterion: Features extracted from every cell's file with the paper's code, as in ed4-example-cell; a cell counts when all 17 features are defined (finite after the log transform). The count depends on the extraction, so it takes the default 10%. A cell has a t-type when it has an assigned t-type and is not an excluded cell (code, phenotype-tsne.ipynb). Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Pvalb neurons are characterized by high firing rates, while Sst neurons have high hyperpolarization sag and rebound.
claims.source: Results, Distinct phenotypes of major families, paragraph 2; Figure 2 (right biplots)
claims.quote: These groups had distinct electrophysiological properties: for example, as expected, Pvalb neurons were characterized by high firing rates while Sst neurons had high values of the hyperpolarization sag and rebound
claims.criterion: The paper shows this in a biplot and gives no test, so the comparison is fixed from its wording. Cells are those with all 17 features, a t-type and no exclusion. Firing rate is the maximum number of APs in the 600 ms window (Methods); sag is the sag ratio and rebound the rebound (mV). "High" is compared with the other families, under two readings, (a) the family median is the highest of the seven families of Fig. 3d (Lamp5, Vip, Sst, Pvalb, IT, ET, CT), or (b) the highest of the five groups Fig. 2 separates (Pvalb, Sst, Vip, Lamp5, and the excitatory class pooled; Results, paragraph after the Fig. 2 legend). The paper gives no test; a two-sided Mann-Whitney test of the group against the other cells is reported for information only and does not decide the outcome. Reproduced when, under one reading, Pvalb has the highest median maximum AP count and Sst the highest median sag ratio and rebound; partially reproduced when two of the three hold.

claims.statement: In a k-nearest-neighbour classification of cells into seven transcriptomic families from electrophysiological features, the confusion matrix is mostly diagonal, with only the ET and IT subclasses strongly overlapping.
claims.source: Results, Distinct phenotypes of major families, paragraph 3; Figure 3a, d
claims.quote: We quantified this separation using a confusion matrix for k -nearest neighbours (kNN) classification of cells into families: it was mostly diagonal, with only the ET and IT subclasses strongly overlapping (Fig. 3d ).
claims.criterion: As the Methods (kNN classification) and the code (get_family_confusion in phenotype-tsne.ipynb) do it. The ephys representation (see the opening comment); k = 10 nearest neighbours by Euclidean distance, the cell itself left out; neighbours drawn from all 1,320 cells with features, those with no t-type labelled as no family; each cell's predicted family is the most common label among its neighbours (ties to the label first in numpy's sort order, code-point order with the no-family label "low quality" last, as numpy's unique and argmax do), and a cell whose prediction is not one of the seven families is not counted. Rows are Lamp5, Vip, Sst, Pvalb, IT, ET, CT (Sncg and NP not used). The excluded cells are handled in two ways, both run, (a) the Methods', as if they had no t-type (no family as neighbours, not counted in rows), and (b) the code's, which keeps each excluded cell's RNA family (4 IT, 1 Sst) both as a row and as a neighbour label. The paper's own threshold for "classified into wrong families" is 25% (Fig. 5a legend). Reproduced when the ET row puts at least 25% into IT or the IT row at least 25% into ET, and every other off-diagonal entry is below 25%; partially reproduced when ET and IT overlap so and one or two other off-diagonal entries reach 25%; not reproduced otherwise. The outcome is the one both handlings of the excluded cells give; if they differ, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified. The 34 degree follow-up of the same overlap is in dandiset 000035 and not tested here.

claims.statement: At room temperature, the features that differ most between layer 5 IT and ET neurons by a two-sided Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test, after omitting the upstroke-to-downstroke ratio, sag time and sag area, are the sag ratio, input resistance, AP width and rebound.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 6a-e legend; the code, physiological-temperature.ipynb, cells 22 and 23
claims.quote: The first four panels correspond to features showing the largest IT/ET differences at room temperature, according to the two-sided Wilcoxon-Mann–Whitney test statistic (and omitting several features that are very correlated with the shown ones ... upstroke-to-downstroke ratio, sag time, and sag area).
claims.criterion: The legend names the features only in the figure; the four are those the code plots (featuresToShow, the first four of sag ratio, input resistance, AP width, rebound, AP threshold). As in the code, layer 5 IT against layer 5 ET cells (family from the t-type, layer as in the opening comment, excluded cells left out), a two-sided Mann-Whitney test for each of the 29 features except rebound number of APs, ranked by p. Reproduced when, after leaving out UDR, sag time and sag area, the four smallest p are those four features in any order; partially reproduced when three of them are.

claims.statement: Follow-up experiments at 34 degrees C confirmed the electrophysiological overlap between IT and ET neurons and the continuous variation of rebound across neighbouring layer 5 Sst t-types.
claims.source: Results, Distinct phenotypes of major families, paragraph 3, and Continuous phenotypic variation, paragraph 2; Methods, Experiments at physiological temperature; Extended Data Figure 6
claims.quote: We confirmed the electrophysiological overlap between IT and ET neurons in follow-up experiments at 34 °C (Extended Data Fig. 6 ).
claims.criterion: Recorded for coverage. The 34 degree recordings (185 neurons from 8 mice; Methods) are not in this dandiset, and the paper gives no measure of the IT/ET overlap at 34 degrees (Extended Data Fig. 6f, g show it in two-dimensional plots only). Not tested here.

claims.statement: After quality control 1,227 neurons had a t-type (817 inhibitory, 410 excitatory), covering 77 of the 90 neuronal t-types of the reference taxonomy.
claims.source: Results, Patch-seq of mouse primary motor cortex, paragraph 3; Figure 1a
claims.quote: leaving 1,227 neurons for further analysis (817 inhibitory, 410 excitatory; 369 and 269 with morphological reconstructions, respectively). The resulting data set covered 77 out of the 90 neuronal t-types (Fig. 1a )
claims.criterion: Counts of the paper's t-type labels for the dandiset's cells, excluded cells left out; exact records, so the tolerance is zero. Inhibitory is the Lamp5, Sncg, Vip, Sst and Pvalb families, excitatory IT, ET, NP and CT (code, ttype-assignment.ipynb). Under reading (b) of cohort-cells-mice, one fewer cell in one class is accepted if the dandiset lacks a cell with a t-type. Reproduced when all four counts match.

claims.statement: Within-type distributions of soma depth agree with the layer-specific names of the excitatory t-types.
claims.source: Results, Patch-seq of mouse primary motor cortex, paragraph 3; Figure 1b
claims.quote: Within-type distributions of soma depths (Fig. 1b ) agreed well with previous data 4 and with the layer-specific nomenclature of excitatory t-types, confirming the validity of our t-type assignment.
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure, so it is fixed from Fig. 1b's legend. Normalized soma depth (depth over cortical thickness) of cells with a t-type, excluded cells left out; for each excitatory t-type with at least three cells (the legend's cut for showing medians), the median depth is placed in a layer by the Nissl boundaries (L1 below 0.07, L2/3 to 0.29, L5 to 0.73, L6 beyond). A t-type agrees when that layer is one its name gives (L2/3; L4/5 as L2/3 or L5; L5; L5/6 as L5 or L6; L6 and L6b as L6). Reproduced when all such t-types agree; partially reproduced when at least 80% do.

claims.statement: The L4/5 IT_1 t-type is located on the boundary between L2/3 and L5, and probably corresponds to the quasi-L4 neurons described before in motor cortex.
claims.source: Results, Patch-seq of mouse primary motor cortex, paragraph 4; Figure 1b
claims.quote: We were also able to identify a t-type, L4/5 IT_1, that was located on the boundary between L2/3 and L5 and probably corresponds to the quasi-L4 neurons described previously in motor cortex 31 .
claims.criterion: Normalized soma depths of L4/5 IT_1 cells (excluded cells left out). The paper's L2/3 to L5 boundary is 0.29 (Fig. 1b legend). The paper gives no measure of "on the boundary"; two readings, both run, (a) the t-type's median depth lies closer to 0.29 than to the middle of either neighbouring layer (0.18 for L2/3, 0.51 for L5), that is between 0.235 and 0.40, and (b) the interquartile range of the t-type's depths contains 0.29. Reproduced when both hold, not reproduced when neither does; when they differ, methods_underspecified. The correspondence to quasi-L4 neurons is an interpretation and is not tested.

claims.statement: Across 200 pairs of t-types from the same family (50 t-types with at least 5 cells), the transcriptomic and electrophysiological distances between t-types are correlated with r = 0.60.
claims.source: Results, Continuous phenotypic variation, paragraph 3; Figure 4c and legend
claims.quote: Pooling the pairs across all families, we found that these two distance measures were correlated, with r = 0.60 (Fig. 4c , n = 200 pairs; Extended Data Fig. 7 ).
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Within-family analysis) and the code (families.ipynb, cell for the main figure) do it. Cells with a t-type, not excluded, with all 17 features; the 17 features (four log-transformed) standardized over all cells with all features. T-types with at least 5 such cells; each t-type's mean feature vector; electrophysiological distance the Euclidean distance between means. Transcriptomic distance is the correlation distance (one minus Pearson r) between the t-types' mean log(x + 1) UMI counts in the reference single-cell 10x v2 data (t-types with at least 10 reference cells), over the 1,000 most variable genes across all neural types. Pairs are within-family by the code's family of each t-type name (L6b counted with CT). Pearson r over within-family pairs. The Methods do not mention excluding any t-type for Fig. 4c; the code leaves out Sst Chodl and Pvalb Vipr2_2.
