claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Selective neurons are contra-preferring when their total spike count over the three epochs is larger on lick right trials (Methods). The paper's test is a two-tailed t-test against 0 of the spike count difference (lick right minus lick left, correct trials) across neurons; reproduced when it gives P >= 0.05 and not reproduced when P < 0.05 with a contralateral excess. The population is open; readings (a) all 1,245 putative pyramidal neurons ("the recorded population"), (b) the 912 selective neurons (Fig. 3f, "all task-selective neurons"). The spike count window is open; readings (i) the three epochs together (the "overall spike count" of Results paragraph 2), (ii) and (iii) the test windows of fig3f-pt-contra-selectivity, where the Results report the same P = 0.13 for all task-selective neurons. The paper gives no test for the proportions of Fig. 2e; the Methods' bootstrap for Fig. 3f, j (neurons resampled with replacement, P the fraction of resamples with more ipsi- than contra-preferring neurons, one-tailed) is used, and must not find a contralateral excess at P < 0.05. The 8% modulation is checked with the readings of fig3f-pt-contra-selectivity; it is reported, and its mismatch alone makes the claim partially reproduced.

claims.statement: Fast-spiking neurons have higher baseline firing rates and are less selective than putative pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: Methods, Electrophysiology data analyses, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 1b to e
claims.quote: Fast-spiking neurons had higher baseline firing rates and were less selective than putative pyramidal neurons (Extended Data Fig. 1)
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test and does not define the baseline. Baseline readings are (a) the 0.5 s before pole movement onset, (b) all the recorded time before pole movement onset in each trial; selectivity readings are (i) the fraction significantly selective by the test of fig2-selective-fraction, (ii) the mean absolute spike rate difference between trial types over the three epochs. Reproduced when, under every reading, the fast-spiking median and mean baseline rates exceed those of putative pyramidal neurons and their selectivity is lower; a two-sided Mann-Whitney test is reported as a variant.

claims.statement: Of 73 neurons antidromically activated from pyramidal tract axons, 45 passed the collision test (PT neurons), 22 failed and 6 could not be tested; of 134 activated from IT axons, 27 passed (IT neurons), 106 failed and 1 could not be tested.
claims.source: Methods, Electrophysiology data analyses, paragraph 4; Extended Data Figure 5f
claims.quote: Neurons that passed the collision test were classified as pyramidal tract neurons (45/73) or intratelencephalic neurons (27/134). Neurons that failed the test were classified as pyramidal-tract-activated (22/73) or intratelencephalic-activated (106/134)
claims.criterion: Counts of units by the labels the dataset gives for tagging outcome. The 6 and 1 untested neurons are reported. The counts in the text add up (45 + 22 + 6 = 73 and 27 + 106 + 1 = 134).

claims.statement: PT neurons had shorter antidromic latencies (mean 2.7 ms) than IT neurons (4.6 ms), and both had smaller jitter (0.1 and 0.2 ms) than activated neurons that failed collision (latency 8.3 and 9.8 ms, jitter 2.8 and 2.4 ms).
claims.source: Methods, Electrophysiology data analyses, paragraph 4; Results, A movement command emerges in the pyramidal tract neurons, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 5e
claims.quote: Pyramidal tract neurons and intratelencephalic neurons had shorter mean antidromic spike latencies (pyramidal tract neurons, 2.7ms; intratelencephalic neurons, 4.6 ms) and smaller temporal jitter (mean s.d. of the antidromic spike latency, pyramidal tract neurons, 0.1 ms; intratelencephalic neurons, 0.2 ms) than the pyramidal-tract-activated (mean latency, 8.3ms; jitter, 2.8ms) and intratelencephalic-activated neurons
claims.criterion: Latency is the time from light pulse onset to the antidromic spike; jitter its s.d. over pulses, per neuron, then averaged over neurons (Methods). Tested only if the dataset holds the tagging trials. Reproduced when PT latency is below IT latency and all values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the order holds but a value falls outside. The jitter of 0.1 and 0.2 ms is printed to one significant figure, so its 10% tolerance is read as the printed precision (within 0.05 ms when rounded to 0.1 ms). The paper gives no rule for which spike counts as antidromic. What it says is that pulses came in pairs 10 ms apart every 500 ms (Methods, Electrophysiology), that IT jitter to the second pulse of a pair was smaller "following a conditioning stimulus" (Methods; Extended Data Fig. 5g), which suggests the reported jitter is to the first pulse, and that the evoked spikes had "sub-millisecond temporal jitter (mean, 0.15 ms)" (Results). Readings are (w) the first spike within a window after the first pulse of each pair, with the window open (the activated neurons' mean latencies of 8.3 and 9.8 ms need one of about 10 ms, up to the second pulse); (c) as (w), leaving out pulses preceded shortly by a spontaneous spike (the collision trials); (r) as (w), with only spikes in the evoked peak of each neuron's latency histogram. Jitter is the s.d. over the pulses kept, per neuron, then averaged.

claims.statement: Both PT and IT neurons show preparatory and movement-related activity.
claims.source: Results, A movement command emerges in the pyramidal tract neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 3e, i
claims.quote: Both intratelencephalic and pyramidal tract neurons displayed preparatory and movement-related activity (Fig. 3e, i)
claims.criterion: The 45 PT and 27 IT neurons classified with the epoch rule and readings of fig2d-preparatory-perimovement. Reproduced when, in each cell type, at least one neuron has preparatory selectivity and at least one peri-movement selectivity; the fractions in each class are reported.

claims.statement: Contra-preferring neurons outnumber ipsi-preferring neurons among PT neurons (P < 0.05, bootstrap) but not among IT neurons (P = 0.74).
claims.source: Results, A movement command emerges in the pyramidal tract neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 3f, j insets
claims.quote: Contra-preferring neurons outnumbered ipsi-preferring neurons for the pyramidal tract neurons (Fig. 3f; P , 0.05, bootstrap, Methods), but not the intratelencephalic neurons (Fig. 3j, P 5 0.74)
claims.criterion: Contra- or ipsi-preferring by total spike count over the three epochs, lick right against lick left, correct trials (Methods). Bootstrap as the Methods, neurons resampled with replacement (10^4 resamples, a standard number that the Methods give for the behavioural bootstrap), P the fraction of resamples with more ipsi- than contra-preferring neurons. Open, which neurons are counted; readings (a) all tagged neurons of the type, (b) only those selective by the test of fig2-selective-fraction. Reproduced when PT gives P < 0.05 under one reading and IT gives P >= 0.05 under the same reading (the IT part is a claim of absence on the paper's test). The inset fractions were not read from the figure.

claims.statement: Contralateral population selectivity emerges in PT neurons from 570 ms before the response epoch (34% spike rate modulation, P < 0.05), but not in IT neurons (-19%, P = 0.40).
claims.source: Results, A movement command emerges in the pyramidal tract neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 3f, j
claims.quote: Robust contralateral selectivity (the spike count differenceforlickrighttrials and licklefttrials) emerged in pyramidal tract neuron responses starting 570 ms before the response epoch (Fig. 3f; 34% spike rate modulation; P , 0.05, two-tailed t-test against0inspikecounts),butnotforintratelencephalicneurons(219%
claims.criterion: Contra-selectivity is the firing rate difference, lick right minus lick left trials, per neuron, correct trials, averaged across neurons (Methods), in 200 ms windows (the averaging window of Fig. 2c). The text reads "-19%" as "219%". Open, with readings - the neurons, (a) all tagged neurons of the type (Fig. 3f legend) or (b) the selective ones (Methods); the test window, (i) from 570 ms before the go cue to the go cue or (ii) the whole delay epoch; the modulation, (x) the population difference divided by the mean rate over both trial types in that window or (y) divided by the lick left rate; the onset, the start of the earliest window from which the population contra-selectivity stays significantly above 0 (two-tailed t-test across neurons, P < 0.05) until the go cue, with windows stepped by 10 ms (a standard choice; it moves the onset by at most 10 ms). The paper does not say which time a 200 ms window stands for, which moves the onset by up to 200 ms; readings are the window's (p) start, (q) centre and (r) end. Reproduced when, under one reading, the PT test gives P < 0.05 with positive selectivity, the IT test P >= 0.05, and the three expected values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the two tests come out so but a value falls outside under every reading.

claims.statement: In two-photon imaging of ALM (59 fields of view, 4 mice), 58% of cells (2,740 of 4,706) were task-related and 57% of those (1,575) trial-type selective, with a slight majority of contra-preferring cells (61%, 971 of 1,575).
claims.source: Methods, Calcium imaging data analyses, paragraphs 2 and 4; Results, A movement command emerges in the pyramidal tract neurons, paragraph 3
claims.quote: This criterion identified 58% (2,740/4,706) cells as task related ... 57% (1575/2740) of task related cell are trial-type selective ... Overall, imaging detected a slight majority of contra-preferring neurons (61%, 971/1,575)
claims.criterion: Task-related when a Kruskal-Wallis test across 0.33 s bins (five frames) during the task rejects equal fluorescence at P < 0.01 in contra or in ipsi trials; selective when a Wilcoxon rank sum test of DF/F between contra and ipsi trials gives P < 0.05; preference by the average calcium signal during the trial epochs (Methods). DF/F0 with F0 the mean over 0.5 s before trial start, if the dataset holds raw fluorescence. Open, with readings - the span of the Kruskal-Wallis bins, (a) sample onset to the end of the response epoch, (b) the whole recorded trial; the response compared by the rank sum test, (i) mean DF/F over the three epochs together, (ii) each epoch separately, selective if any is significant; the trials, correct only or all non-early trials. Reproduced when all values are within tolerance under one reading. The paper gives no length for the response epoch, in imaging or in electrophysiology; the go cue "signalled the beginning of the response epoch" (Results) and Fig. 1b marks only the 1.3 s sample and delay epochs. Readings are (r1) 1.3 s after the go cue, like the other epochs, and (r2) the 1.5 s lick window ("did not lick within a 1.5 s window after the go cue", Methods, Behaviour). Both are run.

claims.statement: Contra- and ipsi-preferring neurons are found in all fields of view and are spatially intermingled; nearest-neighbour selectivity and same-type distances do not differ from shuffled data (P = 0.34 and P = 0.61).
claims.source: Results, A movement command emerges in the pyramidal tract neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 4f; Methods, Calcium imaging data analyses, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Contra-preferring and ipsi-preferring neurons were observed in all fields of view (Fig. 4f; Methods). The probability that nearby neurons share the same selectivity was not different from randomized data (P 5 0.34, bootstrap, Methods). The distance between nearest neurons with the same selectivity was also not different from chance (P 5 0.61, bootstrap)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's two tests (Methods). For the selective cells, (1) the probability that each cell's nearest neighbour has the same preference (the neighbour searched among (a) the selective cells or (b) all cells, a non-selective neighbour counting as not the same; the Methods do not say), against the same probability with preference labels shuffled, P the fraction of shuffles with a larger probability; (2) the mean distance from each cell to the nearest cell of the same preference, against shuffles, P the fraction of shuffles with a smaller distance. Distances from ROI centres within each field of view. Whether labels are shuffled within each field of view or across all is not stated; both are run. 10^4 shuffles (a standard number). Reproduced when both tests give P >= 0.05 and both preferences occur in every field of view; not reproduced when either test gives P < 0.05.

claims.statement: Among layer 5 neurons, about a quarter of labelled PT (182 of 534) and IT (174 of 542) neurons were selective; 67% of selective PT neurons were contra-preferring (P < 0.001, binomial test) but only 48% of IT neurons, and PT neurons were more often contra-preferring than IT neurons (P < 0.001, chi-squared test).
claims.source: Results, A movement command emerges in the pyramidal tract neurons, paragraph 4; Figure 4g, h
claims.quote: we observed more contra-preferring than ipsi-preferring neurons in the pyramidal tract neuron population (67%, 122/182, Fig. 4g, h; P , 0.001, binomial test), but not in the intratelencephalic neurons (fraction of contra-preferring neurons:48%,83/174;Fig.4g,h)
claims.criterion: Labelled PT (RetroBeads) and IT (CTB-647) cells imaged 450 to 700 um deep; selectivity and preference as imaging-selectivity-counts, with its readings. Reproduced when, under one reading, the PT binomial test (against 0.5; the sidedness is not stated, two-sided is used and one-sided reported) gives P < 0.001 with a contralateral majority, the IT binomial test gives P > 0.05, the chi-squared test of PT against IT gives P < 0.001, and the expected values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the three tests come out so and a value falls outside. The text's "approximately a quarter" does not match its own counts (182/534 is 34%, 174/542 is 32%); the counts are what is tested. The paper selects layer 5 only by imaging depth (450 to 700 um, Results) and gives no depth per plane or any other mark of layer 5 (Methods, Two-photon calcium imaging). It also says "intratelencephalic neurons were also found in superficial layers" (Results), so labelled IT cells outside layer 5 are expected and are not the paper's population. Without a depth per plane, all labelled cells is a substitute population, not a reading of the paper; results on it are a variant and are recorded as a deviation. The PT side is less affected, since the paper places PT neurons in layer 5B.

claims.statement: The reaction time after the go cue was 61.1 +/- 10.5 ms (mean +/- s.d. across mice).
claims.source: Results, Pyramidal tract neurons drive upcoming movements, paragraph 1
claims.quote: reactiontimepostcueonsetacrossmice:61.1 6 10.5 ms,mean 6 s.d.
claims.criterion: Reaction time is measured from mouth movements by photodiode and infrared laser (Methods, Behaviour). Tolerance is the paper's stated spread across mice. Open, with readings - the mice, (a) the electrophysiology mice of Fig. 3, (b) all mice in the dataset with mouth-movement data; per-mouse value, (i) mean or (ii) median of per-trial reaction times; the trials, correct trials or all non-early trials. If the dataset holds only lick contacts at the lickport and no mouth-movement signal, the first lick is a different measure; it is shown as a variant and does not decide the claim. The paper gives no rule for reading a reaction time from the photodiode signal; the Methods say only that "Mouth movements were monitored using a photodiode and an infrared laser diode to obtain reaction time measurements". Readings are (k) the first time after the go cue the signal crosses a fixed threshold on the raw signal, and (z) the first time it exceeds the mean plus a number of s.d. of a baseline before the go cue (for example the delay epoch or its last 0.5 s); the threshold, the number of s.d. and the baseline window are open.

claims.statement: Subthreshold photostimulation of PT neurons during the delay epoch biases licking contralaterally; in left ALM it lowers performance on lick left trials, and the reverse holds for right ALM.
claims.source: Results, Pyramidal tract neurons drive upcoming movements, paragraph 2; Figure 5b
claims.quote: Subthreshold stimulation of pyramidal tract neurons in the left ALMproducedarightwardbias,resulting ina decreaseinperformance in the lick left trials and vice versa (Fig. 5)
claims.criterion: Delay-epoch photostimulation trials of the PT (Sim1_KJ18-Cre x Ai32) mice against control trials, per hemisphere and trial type, with the hierarchical bootstrap of fig1d-delay-inhibition-ipsi-bias. Which powers are pooled is inconsistent in the paper; readings (a) 0.12 to 0.8 mW (Fig. 5 legend), (b) the subthreshold powers below 0.25 mW (text; 0.06, 0.12 and 0.24 mW), (c) 0.12 and 0.24 mW (both bounds together). Reproduced when, under one reading, ipsilateral-trial performance falls with P < 0.05 for both hemispheres; partially reproduced for one. The lowest star level of the legend is recorded as the statistic; which panels carry which stars was not read. Extended Data Fig. 6a shows a 95% interval of behavioural variability from resampling control trials only, with trial numbers matched; whether the change falls outside it is shown as a variant and does not decide the claim.

claims.statement: Stimulation of PT neurons during the sample epoch also causes a significant contralateral bias.
claims.source: Results, Pyramidal tract neurons drive upcoming movements, paragraph 3; Figure 5b
claims.quote: Notably, stimulation of pyramidal tract neurons during the sample epochalsocausedasignificantcontralateralbias(Fig.5b)
claims.criterion: As fig5b-pt-delay-activation-contra-bias, with sample-epoch photostimulation trials and the same readings.

claims.statement: The effect of PT photostimulation on licking depends monotonically on laser power.
claims.source: Results, Pyramidal tract neurons drive upcoming movements, paragraph 2; Extended Data Figure 6b
claims.quote: The effect size was monotonically dependent on laser power (Extended Data Fig. 6b)
claims.criterion: Delay-epoch photostimulation only (Extended Data Fig. 6b), per power (0.06, 0.12, 0.24, 0.8 mW where present). The effect size is not defined; readings (a) the performance change on ipsilateral trials, (b) the ipsilateral-trial change minus the contralateral-trial change, both signed so that a contralateral bias is positive. Reproduced when, under each reading, the effect pooled over mice increases with each step of power; the per-mouse curves are reported with the number that are monotonic.

claims.statement: Subthreshold photostimulation of IT neurons changes behaviour, but the changes vary across mice and depend non-monotonically on laser intensity.
claims.source: Results, Pyramidal tract neurons drive upcoming movements, paragraph 4; Extended Data Figure 6c, d
claims.quote: Subthresholdphotostimulationoftheintratelencephalicneuronsalso caused behavioural changes, but these varied across mice and depended non-monotonicallyonlaserintensity(ExtendedDataFig.6d)
claims.criterion: Delay-epoch photostimulation of the IT (Tlx_PL56-Cre x Ai32) mice, effect sizes as ed6b-pt-dose-response with its readings. The paper gives no test. Reproduced when, under each reading, at least two mice show biases of opposite sign at the same power and the effect pooled over mice is not monotonic in power; partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: High-power unilateral photostimulation of ALM PT or IT neurons triggers contralateral licking with short latency, also in untrained mice, and in trained mice produces premature licking in the contralateral direction; vibrissal motor cortex stimulation does not cause licking.
claims.source: Results, Pyramidal tract neurons control directional licking, paragraph 2; Extended Data Figure 3e, f
claims.quote: UnilateralphotostimulationofALM intratelencephalic or pyramidal tract neurons ('high' power, 0.8 mW, 2 mspulsesat20Hz,Methods)triggeredcontralaterallickingwithshort latencies (Extended Data Fig. 3e), even in untrained mice (Extended Data Fig. 3f)
claims.criterion: Trained PT and IT mice, sample- and delay-epoch photostimulation combined (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Per power, the fraction of photostimulation trials with an early lick, and the fraction of early licks to the contralateral port. Reproduced when, at 0.8 mW, the early-lick fraction exceeds that of control trials and most early licks are contralateral, in each cell type; partially reproduced for one cell type. Untrained mice (Extended Data Fig. 3f) and vibrissal motor cortex trials are tested in the same way if present. Latency is reported; the paper gives no number for it.

claims.statement: Subthreshold sample-epoch stimulation of PT neurons, with simultaneous recordings (2 mice, 8 sessions, 91 neurons), changes ALM activity and causes a directional bias that persists for seconds after the photostimulus ends.
claims.source: Results, Pyramidal tract neurons drive upcoming movements, paragraph 3; Extended Data Figure 7
claims.quote: Simultaneous recordings and optogenetics revealed that subthreshold stimulation of pyramidal tract neurons caused changes in ALM activity and a directionalbiasthatpersistedforsecondsaftercessationofthephotostimulus
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure or test for the change in activity. In these sessions, (1) behaviour, the performance change on lick left trials with sample-epoch stimulation of left ALM is negative (contralateral bias; Extended Data Fig. 7b); (2) activity, per neuron a two-tailed t-test (the paper's selectivity test) of delay-epoch spike counts between photostimulation and control trials, correct trials; reproduced when more neurons differ at P < 0.05 than the 95th percentile of a binomial count with p = 0.05, and the population selectivity (preferred minus non-preferred, Extended Data Fig. 7d) during the delay epoch differs between photostimulation and control trials. Partially reproduced when one of (1) and (2) holds.

claims.statement: Retrograde tracers in the ipsilateral pontine nucleus and the contralateral ALM label non-overlapping populations of PT and IT neurons (under 4% double-labelled, 2 mice), intermingled in layer 5B; ALM PT neurons project to the contralateral intermediate reticular nucleus, which is presynaptic to the hypoglossal nucleus.
claims.source: Results, Pyramidal tract neurons control directional licking, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 3a to d
claims.quote: Injection of retrograde tracers in the ipsilateral pontine nucleusandthecontralateralALMlabellednon-overlappingpopulations of intratelencephalic neurons and pyramidal tract neurons (Extended Data Fig. 3d) (doubly labelled neurons, ,4%, n 5 2 mice)
claims.criterion: Histology. Reproduced when double-labelled neurons are under 4.4% (4% widened by 10%) of labelled neurons in each of the 2 mice. The projection findings are tested only if the images are available.

claims.statement: 1012 single units were recorded in left ALM during behaviour in 58 sessions (20 unilateral, 38 bilateral experiment sessions); by spike width 72 were fast-spiking, 890 putative pyramidal, and 50 intermediate and excluded.
claims.source: Methods, Electrophysiology data analysis, paragraph 1
claims.quote: 1012 single units were recorded during behavior across 58 recording sessions (20 sessions of unilateral experiments, Fig. 1 ; 38 sessions of bilateral experiments ... Units with spike width < 0.35 ms were defined as fast-spiking (FS) neurons (72/1012) and units with spike widths > 0.45 ms as putative pyramidal neurons (890/1012). Units with intermediate values (0.35 - 0.45 ms, 50/1012) were excluded
claims.criterion: Width is the trough-to-peak interval of the mean waveform (Methods). Units and sessions of the control mice only; the Results give 12 mice for these 1012 units, so callosotomy and photoactivation recordings are counted apart. Reproduced when all values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Most putative pyramidal neurons distinguished trial types (634 of 890); 176 in the sample epoch, 337 in the delay epoch and 493 in the response epoch.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity in ALM, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 1
claims.quote: Most ALM pyramidal neurons distinguished trial types (634/890, p<0.05, t-test; sample epoch, 176/890; delay epoch, 337/890; response epoch, 493/890, Methods)
claims.criterion: Convention S on the putative pyramidal neurons of unit-classification, control trials. Reproduced when all four counts are within tolerance under one combination of readings (R1 or R2, O1 or O2, a or b). Lick early trials, readings K1 and K2 (convention K, answered 2026-10-21); the outcome must hold under both.

claims.statement: Unilateral photoinhibition of ALM (0.5 s) ending at the go cue caused an ipsilateral response bias.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity after unilateral silencing, paragraph 1; Figure 1d
claims.quote: Transient (duration, 0.5 s) unilateral photoinhibition of ALM up to the ‘go’ cue (late delay) caused an ipsilateral response bias (n = 5 mice, p < 0.01, two-tailed t-test; Fig. 1d )
claims.criterion: Behaviour of the unilateral experiment (convention T, the condition ending 0 s before the go cue). An ipsilateral bias lowers performance on trials whose instructed lick is contralateral to the photoinhibited hemisphere (lick right for left ALM). The measure tested is not stated; readings (M1) performance on contralateral trials, (M2) overall performance (Fig. 1d plots "behavioral performance"). Per mouse, photoinhibition against control (convention P, readings P1 and P2), left and right hemisphere pooled per mouse. Reproduced when performance on photoinhibition trials is lower with p < 0.01 under a reading, and contralateral trial performance falls more than ipsilateral trial performance.

claims.statement: Unilateral photoinhibition ending at least 0.3 s before the go cue had minimal behavioural effects.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity after unilateral silencing, paragraph 1; Figure 1d; Extended Data Figure 3b
claims.quote: In contrast, photoinhibition ending at least 0.3 s prior to the ‘go’ cue produced minimal behavioral effects (middle delay, early delay; p > 0.1, two-tailed t-test)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-tailed t-test of performance on photoinhibition against control trials over the 5 mice (convention P, readings P1 and P2), for the conditions ending 0.8 s and 0.3 s before the go cue. Reproduced when p > 0.1 for both; not reproduced when either has p < 0.1. The change in performance is reported either way. The paper's naming of the conditions differs between Results and Methods (convention T); the sample condition (1.6 s) is reported as a variant.

claims.statement: Performance was not significantly affected when photoinhibition (0.5 s or 1.3 s) ended more than 0.3 s before the go cue, and 0.5 s photoinhibition just before the go cue had an effect similar to photoinhibition over the whole delay epoch.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 3b, d, e
claims.quote: Performance was not significantly affected for T recovery > 0.3s
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the two-tailed t-test of Extended Data Fig. 3b, d against control (convention P), over mice (n = 5 for 3b; not given for 3d). Data of Extended Data Fig. 3c, d have a delay of 1.2 to 1.7 s and 1.3 s photoinhibition. Reproduced when no condition with T recovery above 0.3 s has p < 0.05 in either experiment, and at T recovery 0 the performance under 0.5 s and 1.3 s photoinhibition differ by less than the larger of their s.e.m. over mice; not reproduced otherwise. The second half has no test in the paper; it is a reading of "similar", and its numbers are shown.

claims.statement: Neurons whose spike rates decreased during the delay epoch also recovered after unilateral photoinhibition, returning to the time-matched control trajectory and not decaying to the end-point rate.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 4b, c; Results, Preparatory activity after unilateral silencing, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Spike rate difference relative to time-matched control show significantly smaller root-mean-squared error (RMS) than spike rate difference relative to end point (p<0.001, paired t-test)
claims.criterion: Unilateral experiment recordings. Neurons with a significant spike rate decrease at the end against the beginning of the delay epoch (two-tailed t-test, p < 0.05, 400 ms windows, trial types pooled; Extended Data Fig. 4b). Rate normalised to the neuron's mean rate. For each perturbed condition the RMS, between photoinhibition offset and the go cue, of the perturbed minus time-matched control rate, and of the perturbed rate minus the control rate at the end of the delay. Which photoinhibition conditions are pooled and whether trial types are taken apart (the legend plots preferred and non-preferred) are not given; readings (a) one value per neuron averaged over conditions and trial types, (b) one per neuron, condition and trial type. Reproduced when the time-matched RMS is smaller by a paired t-test with p < 0.001 under a reading. Answered 2026-10-21, not given by the paper; whether the selection t-test is paired over trials or unpaired, readings (s1) paired, (s2) unpaired; the bin of the normalised rate time course, readings (t1) 200 ms (the PSTH of Fig. 1e), (t2) 400 ms (the legend's windows). The outcome must hold under all of s1, s2, t1, t2, and K1, K2 (convention K); the count of 27 is reported against each.

claims.statement: Within 400 ms after unilateral photoinhibition, spike rates became indistinguishable from control in 90% of neurons; 10% retained a sustained change.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity after unilateral silencing, paragraph 2; Figure 1f
claims.quote: Within 400 ms after photoinhibition, spike rates became indistinguishable from the unperturbed condition in 90% of the neurons; only 10% of neurons retained a sustained change in spike rate
claims.criterion: Convention R on putative pyramidal neurons of the unilateral experiment, per condition (Fig. 1f gives n = 168, 168, 175 neurons). The fraction of neurons with a significant change in the 400 ms window at 400 ms after photoinhibition offset (convention T). Open which conditions the 10% describes; readings (a) each of the sample, early delay and late delay conditions, (b) the three pooled. Reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance under one combination of readings (a or b, W1 or W2, with or without exclusion), and under both K1 and K2 (convention K, answered 2026-10-21). The tolerance, 10% of the value, is one percentage point; the counts 168, 168 and 175 are reported against the paper.

claims.statement: After unilateral photoinhibition ALM neurons recovered more than 80% of their control selectivity within about 0.5 s; recovery times were 373 ms (sample), 510 ms (early delay) and 327 ms (late delay).
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity after unilateral silencing, paragraph 2; Figure 1g legend
claims.quote: Green lines, recovery to 80% of control (mean ± s.e.m. bootstrap). Sample, 373±260 ms; early delay, 510±218 ms; late delay, 327±112 ms
claims.criterion: Convention D on the unilateral experiment. Tolerances are the paper's bootstrap s.e.m. The Results give 514 ms as the bound, the legend 510 ms for early delay; the legend values are used. Reproduced when all three times are within tolerance under one bin reading (B1, B2); partially reproduced for two of three. Answered 2026-10-21, the preferred-type window (D1 to D3), the bin label (L1, L2), the search range (E1, E2) and lick early trials (K1, K2) are not given by the paper; the outcome is the one all of them give (convention D, K). The count of 55 is read per condition (N1), with N2 as a variant.

claims.statement: After transient photoactivation of layer 5 intratelencephalic neurons, ALM selectivity recovered on a time course similar to recovery after photoinhibition.
claims.source: Results, Preparatory activity after unilateral silencing, paragraph 2; Extended Data Figure 5f
claims.quote: Sample epoch: 249 ± 68 ms to recover to 80 % of control selectivity; early delay: 275 ± 168 ms; middle delay: 250 ± 218 ms
claims.criterion: Convention D on the photoactivation recordings (2 Tlx_PL56-cre x Ai32 mice, 69 neurons; 20 Hz sinusoid, 0.53 mW, 1.3 s delay; Methods; 500 ms photostimulus, Results). When in the trial the three conditions fall is not given in the text (Extended Data Fig. 5a, b); read from the dataset's trial metadata. Reproduced when all three times are within tolerance under one bin reading.

claims.statement: Photoactivation during the sample epoch excited 19% and suppressed 22% of neurons; during the late delay epoch it excited 15% and suppressed 17%.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 5c
claims.quote: Photoactivation during sample epoch: 19% excited, 22% suppressed; late delay epoch: 15% excited, 17% suppressed
claims.criterion: Convention R during photoactivation (the 400 ms window ending at photostimulus offset, or the window covering the photostimulus, as readings), trial types pooled; denominators 43 and 44 neurons (Extended Data Fig. 5e). Excited or suppressed by the sign of the change. Reproduced when all four are within tolerance under a reading; partially when two or three are.

claims.statement: Ipsilateral and bilateral photoinhibition reduced the activity of putative pyramidal neurons by more than 90%, similarly in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP and PV x ReaChR mice; contralateral photoinhibition had little effect on the average rate.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 2b; Methods, Photoinhibition
claims.quote: Ipsilateral and bilateral photoinhibition similarly silenced neuronal activity. Average spike rate across the population was little affected by contralateral photoinhibition
claims.criterion: Per neuron (mean rate at least 1 spike/s), the rate during photoinhibition over the control rate in the same window. The window is not given; readings (a) the whole photostimulus before the ramp, (b) the last 400 ms of photoinhibition (Extended Data Fig. 2e). Reproduced when the mean normalised rate is below 0.1 for ipsilateral photoinhibition in both mouse lines (experiment 2) and for bilateral photoinhibition, and contralateral photoinhibition leaves it above 0.8. The 0.8 is a reading of "little affected"; the value is reported. Neuron counts per experiment and condition (117, 110, 109; 300, 294, 301; 52, 52, 102) are reported against the legend. Lick early trials, readings K1 and K2 (convention K, answered 2026-10-21); the outcome must hold under both.

claims.statement: Photoinhibition with one laser spot silenced activity in a cortical area of 1 mm radius at half-maximum, through all layers.
claims.source: Methods, Photoinhibition; Extended Data Figure 2d
claims.quote: The photoinhibition silenced 90% of spikes ( Extended Data Fig. 2b ) in a cortical area of 1mm radius (at half-max) through all cortical layers

claims.statement: Trajectory separation along cd at the end of the delay was 0.80 in control, 0.64 after ipsilateral and 0.68 after contralateral four-spot photoinhibition, and 0.54 after bilateral one-spot photoinhibition.

claims.statement: The direction of the lick right minus lick left difference vector was stable over the sample and delay epochs (correlation 0.61 between late sample and late delay).

Reproduced when within the paper's s.e.m. Sessions and neurons by convention A's rule (T1; T2 as a variant) and lick early trials K1, K2 (convention K), answered 2026-10-21; the outcome must hold under K1 and K2.

claims.statement: Projection on cd captured 65.6% of population selectivity and 36.4% of task-related activity variance over the sample and delay epochs; modes 1 to 5 together captured 98.5% of variance and 95.8% of selectivity.

claims.criterion: Convention A. Selectivity is the RMS of the trial-averaged lick right minus lick left rate over neurons and time in the sample and delay epochs; variance is the RMS of the baseline-subtracted trial-averaged activity (Methods). Captured fraction is read as the RMS of the projected quantity over the RMS of the full quantity; whether RMS or its square (variance) enters the ratio is not stated, readings (a) RMS ratio, (b) squared ratio. The baseline is not defined; readings (a) the pre-sample period, (b) the mean over the trial. Modes as in fig3d-persistent-mode and fig3e-ramping-mode. Tolerances are the paper's s.e.m. Reproduced when the cd values are within tolerance under a reading; the mode 1-5 values are reported and must hold for a full reproduction, else partial. Answered 2026-10-21, not given by the paper; which trials give the trial-averaged activity whose captured selectivity and variance are reported, readings (v1) the training trials, (v2) all correct control trials; the outcome must hold under both. Sessions and neurons by convention A's rule (T1; T2 as a variant) and lick early trials K1, K2 (convention K), answered 2026-10-21; the outcome must hold under K1 and K2.

claims.statement: Along cd, trajectories recovered after ipsilateral photoinhibition (ROC 0.73 against 0.76 in control) and were little changed by contralateral photoinhibition (0.74), but were permanently altered by bilateral photoinhibition (0.58).

claims.quote: After ipsilateral photoinhibition the cd mode recovered to trajectories similar to the unperturbed trials ( Fig. 3c ; ROC values between trajectories at the end of delay epoch: control, 0.76 ± 0.03; ipsilateral, 0.73 ± 0.02; mean ± s.e.m. across sessions

claims.statement: During photoinhibition trajectory separation along cd fell to 0.54 (ipsilateral), 0.64 (contralateral) and 0.54 (bilateral), against 0.72 in control.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 8 legend

claims.criterion: Convention A, with cd'x in a window during photoinhibition. Which window is not given; readings (a) the last 400 ms before the ramp, (b) the 400 ms window centred on the photostimulus, (c) the mean over the photostimulus. Reproduced when all four are within tolerance under a reading. claims.statement: Activity along cd predicts the upcoming movement trial by trial; deviations toward the lick right trajectory predict more lick right responses, and vice versa.
claims.source: Results, Robustness along the coding direction, paragraph 1; Figure 3c bottom; Extended Data Figures 8b and 9e
claims.quote: Deviations toward the “lick right” trajectory predicted more frequent “lick right” responses and vice versa
claims.criterion: Convention A. For each session the decision boundary on held-out control trials; for each held-out control and perturbation trial, the distance of cd'x from the boundary in the last 400 ms before the go cue; trials pooled over sessions. The paper gives no test. Measure, the fraction of trials whose lick falls on the side of the boundary (Extended Data Fig. 8b), and performance on lick right and lick left trials binned along the distance (bin 4, Extended Data Fig. 9e). Reproduced, for control and ipsilateral trials, when the fraction predicted is above 0.5 by a one-sided binomial test at p < 0.05 (a reading of above chance) and lick right performance rises and lick left performance falls with distance (Spearman correlation over bins of the right sign, a reading). Sessions and neurons by convention A's rule (T1; T2 as a variant) and lick early trials K1, K2 (convention K), answered 2026-10-21; the outcome must hold under K1 and K2.

claims.statement: A persistent mode, built to capture the sustained effect of ipsilateral perturbation, stays altered past movement onset but neither discriminates trial type nor predicts behaviour on control trials.
claims.source: Results, Robustness along the coding direction, paragraph 1; Figure 3d
claims.quote: By construction, the persistent mode was altered by the perturbation, up to and beyond movement onset. However, this projection did not discriminate trial type nor predict behavior on control trials
claims.criterion: Mode 2 (Methods), the difference of mean response vectors, ipsilateral perturbed minus control lick right trials, correct trials, at the go cue (last 400 ms window). ROC between lick right and lick left control trials on the projection, and the fraction of control trials predicted with a decision boundary made as for cd. The paper gives no test for absence; reproduced when the session mean ROC is within 2 bootstrap s.e.m. of 0.5 and the fraction predicted is not above 0.5 by the one-sided binomial test of fig3c-cd-predicts-movement, while the ipsilateral minus control difference at the go cue is outside 2 s.e.m. of zero (2 s.e.m. is a standard choice; values shown). Ipsilateral trials are split like control trials; the Methods compute the modes from "a subset of control trials (correct trials only) and ipsilateral perturbation trials" and project "independent control trials and perturbation trials", so projected ipsilateral trials are ones not used to build the mode (answered 2026-10-21; the split size follows H1 or H2). Sessions and neurons by convention A's rule (T1; T2 as a variant) and lick early trials K1, K2 (convention K), answered 2026-10-21; the outcome must hold under K1 and K2.

claims.statement: A ramping mode capturing most remaining variance shows non-selective ramping in the delay epoch, does not predict behaviour, and is resistant to unilateral and bilateral perturbation.
claims.source: Results, Robustness along the coding direction, paragraph 1; Figure 3e; Extended Data Figure 8c-e
claims.quote: Third, a mode that maximally captured the remaining activity variance, showed non-selective ramping during the delay epoch, did not predict behavior, and was resistant to unilateral and bilateral perturbations
claims.criterion: Mode 4 (Methods), the first SVD eigenvector of the baseline-subtracted PSTH matrix (lick right and lick left concatenated, sample and delay epochs as a reading of the time range) made orthogonal to modes 1 to 3 by Gram-Schmidt; mode 3 from the lick left difference, made orthogonal to mode 2. Reproduced when the control projection rises over the delay (end minus start of delay, positive in the session mean), its ROC between trial types and its fraction predicted fail the tests of fig3d-persistent-mode, and for ipsilateral, contralateral and bilateral trials the perturbed minus control difference at the go cue is within 2 bootstrap s.e.m. of zero (a standard choice). Mode 5 is reported as a variant. Ipsilateral trials are split as in fig3d-persistent-mode. The sign of mode 4 is not given (answered 2026-10-21); the paper gives no rule to orient an SVD eigenvector, so "rises" is judged on either orientation, readings (g1) the mode oriented to a positive weight sum, (g2) the mode oriented so that the control projection at the go cue exceeds that at delay onset, judging ramping by the size of the delay change against its bootstrap s.e.m. (2 s.e.m., a standard choice); the outcome must hold under both, else methods_underspecified. Sessions and neurons by convention A's rule (T1; T2 as a variant) and lick early trials K1, K2 (convention K), answered 2026-10-21; the outcome must hold under K1 and K2.

claims.statement: Even after bilateral photoinhibition destroys average selectivity, single-trial activity along cd predicts the upcoming movement.

Sessions and neurons by convention A's rule (T1; T2 as a variant) and lick early trials K1, K2 (convention K), answered 2026-10-21; the outcome must hold under K1 and K2.

claims.statement: In each session the behavioural bias after bilateral photoinhibition followed the side of the control trajectory that the perturbed cd trajectory ended closer to.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 6b
claims.quote: The biases in movement were predicted based ALM activity trajectories
claims.criterion: Per session with bilateral photoinhibition, the mean cd'x of bilateral trials at the go cue relative to the decision boundary (convention A), and the behavioural bias of ed6a-bilateral-inconsistent-bias. Reproduced when the signs agree in a majority of sessions above chance by a one-sided binomial test at p < 0.05 (a reading; the paper shows five example sessions and gives no test). Sessions and neurons by convention A's rule (T1; T2 as a variant) and lick early trials K1, K2 (convention K), answered 2026-10-21; the outcome must hold under K1 and K2.

claims.statement: Reaction times were faster on trials whose cd trajectory was far from the decision boundary at the go cue.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 9f
claims.quote: Reaction times are faster on trials in which the trajectory is far from the decision boundary at the time of the ‘go’ cue
claims.criterion: Convention A, 16 sessions. Reaction time, the first lick after the go cue, relative to the session mean; distance, the absolute distance of cd'x from the boundary at the go cue; lick right and lick left trials pooled. Which trial conditions enter is not given; readings (a) control trials, (b) all trials. The paper gives no test. Reproduced when the Spearman correlation between absolute distance and reaction time is negative with p < 0.05 (a reading). How the first lick is detected is not given (answered 2026-10-21); the Methods say only that a two-spout lickport "was used to record answer licks". With only an analogue lick trace in the data, any threshold is a choice the paper does not fix; the outcome stands only if it is the same over the thresholds tried (a fixed threshold on the raw signal, and k standard deviations above the pre-go-cue baseline, over a range of values), else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: The recovery along cd after unilateral perturbation does not depend on the window used to compute cd (first or last 400 ms of the delay epoch).

Reproduced when, for both windows, the ipsilateral ROC at the end of the delay is within 0.05 of the control ROC (a reading of recovery, from the 0.73 against 0.76 of the main result) and the bilateral ROC is lower than the ipsilateral. claims.statement: Bisecting the ALM corpus callosum did not affect performance on control trials.

Reproduced when p > 0.05; not reproduced otherwise. The difference is reported. Needs behaviour sessions before the cut, which the author must find.

claims.statement: After callosotomy, performance became highly sensitive to unilateral (one spot) photoinhibition, with a significant interaction between callosotomy and photoinhibition, and dropped to the level of bilateral photoinhibition in control mice.

claims.criterion: Convention T (C1, C2) and P. ANOVA on per mouse performance with factors callosotomy (before, after) and photoinhibition (control, unilateral one spot), both within mouse. claims.criterion: Conventions R and D on the callosotomy recordings (Fig. 5d n = 325, 322, 313). claims.statement: After callosotomy, selectivity along cd was reduced following ipsilateral photoinhibition.

claims.statement: Monolithic network models (integrator, integrator with corrective feedback, trained random recurrent networks) do not recover the unperturbed trajectory after transient silencing of half their neurons.
claims.source: Results, Robust model networks, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 1f-i

claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. Parameters from the Methods and Extended Data Fig. 1 legend (simple integrator N = 100, tau 100 ms, one eigenvalue 0.99; FORCE network N = 400, tau 200 ms, tanh, p = 0.1, gain 1.5, 30 iterations; silencing 0.2 to 1.0 s of 2 s). The integration step, noise and random seeds are not given; standard choices (1 ms step, fixed seeds, at least 10 networks). Reproduced when, at 2 s, the output of each model differs from its unperturbed output by more than 10% of the unperturbed selectivity (a reading of failure to recover), for the simple integrator and the transient-input FORCE network. The corrective feedback and tamed chaos models lack parameters in the text (weights, tuning threshold) and are reported only if they can be built from the cited methods.

claims.statement: Modular networks of two coupled modules (attractor, integrator, trained recurrent network) recover after silencing of one module; the modular attractor drifts to a random fixed point when both modules are silenced.
claims.source: Results, Robust model networks, paragraph 2; Figure 6b-d
claims.quote: Selective commissural connections restored activity on the other side after unilateral transient silencing ( Fig. 6b ). When the two sides are silenced, the network drifts to one of the fixed points randomly
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. Modular attractor with the Methods' weights (self 0.5235, within-module -0.5235, between-module 0.3), tau 100 ms, f(x) = g(x) - g(0) with g(x) = 1.4 / (1 + exp(-(x - 0.5) / 0.3)), input 0.1 from 0.05 to 0.1 s, tonic 0.5, noise variance 0.01; modular integrator with the 8 by 8 matrix printed in the Methods, tau 10 ms, input 0.04, tonic 40. Integration step and noise scaling with step are not given; standard choice 1 ms with Euler-Maruyama. Answered 2026-10-21, not given by the paper; readings (n1) white noise of intensity 0.01, Euler-Maruyama increments of sd sqrt(0.01 dt)/tau, (n2) a Gaussian sample of variance 0.01 drawn every step and integrated as an input; the outcome must hold under both, else methods_underspecified. The integration step is not given either; readings (h1) 1 ms, (h2) 0.1 ms, under both noise readings. Reproduced when, over 100 simulated trials per trial type, the modular attractor ends at the instructed fixed point in more than 90% of trials after unilateral silencing (0.2 to 1.0 s) and in 30% to 70% after bilateral silencing (the 90% and the 30% to 70% are readings of "restored" and "randomly"; the paper gives no numbers), and the modular integrator returns within 10% of its unperturbed trajectory by 2 s after unilateral silencing. The FORCE modular network is not specified enough to rebuild and is reported only.

claims.statement: The 52 recordings come from 21 mice of four lines, 21 neurons from 7 C57BL/6 mice, 6 from 3 VGAT-ChR2(H134R) mice, 17 from 8 PV-ires-cre mice and 8 from 3 PV-ires-cre x Ai32 mice.

claims.statement: Across the 52 sessions the fraction of trials correct was 0.740 +- 0.086 (mean +- s.d.).
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 1; Figure 1, figure supplement 1B
claims.quote: n = 21 mice, 52 sessions; fraction of trials correct, 0.740 ± 0.086; mean ± s.d.
claims.criterion: Per session, correct trials (hits and correct rejections) over trials. The trials can be read as (a) all trials of the session or (b) the performing trials analysed (Figure 1, figure supplement 1A); the paper does not say how performing trials were chosen, so under (b) the dataset's own marking of trials used, if it has one, is taken. Both are shown.

claims.statement: The sample epoch, when the pole is presented, lasted 1.54 to 4.05 s, 2.39 s on average.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 1
claims.quote: during a sample epoch lasting a few seconds (1.54–4.05, mean 2.39 s), a pole appeared in one of two locations on the right side of the head
claims.criterion: The sample epoch is the period the pole is in reach (Figure 1C legend, Figure 6E legend). Open detail, the unit of the range and mean, read as (a) over all trials pooled or (b) over per-session means. Both are shown; reproduced when all three values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Mice whisked in bouts with a mean duration of 261 ms, a peak-to-peak amplitude of 15.7 deg and a frequency of 15.4 Hz, separated by rest.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 1; Figure 1, figure supplement 1E-G
claims.quote: Mice whisked in bouts (mean bout duration, 261 ms; peak-to-peak amplitude, 15.7°; frequency, 15.4 Hz) interspersed with periods of rest
claims.criterion: Whisking epochs as defined in the Methods (6 to 60 Hz band-pass, Hilbert amplitude >2.5 deg); a bout is a contiguous whisking epoch. As in Figure 1, figure supplement 1E-G, the amplitude is the maximum amplitude of each bout, the duration that of each bout, and the frequency 1/cycle length of each whisk cycle, pooled across all sessions. Open details, (1) whether "peak-to-peak" is twice the Hilbert amplitude or the range of band-passed theta within a cycle, and (2) whether touch periods break a bout. All four combinations are shown; reproduced when all three values are within tolerance under one.

claims.statement: Mice touched the pole 2.33 times on average before responding, and the reaction time from first touch to first lick was 367 +- 234 ms (mean +- s.d.).
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 1; Figure 1, figure supplement 1C-D
claims.quote: Mice touched the pole multiple times (mean number of touches, 2.33) before reporting perceived object location with licking (mean reaction time 367 ± 234 ms; mean ± s.d.)
claims.criterion: Reaction time is the time from the first touch onset to the first lick, for every trial with licks (Methods, Whisker analysis), pooled over all sessions (Figure 1, figure supplement 1D). The number of touches is counted before the response time per trial (figure supplement 1C). Open detail, which trials count touches, read as (a) trials with a lick, the count before the first lick, or (b) all trials with at least one touch, counting touches in the sample epoch when there is no lick. Both are shown.

claims.statement: The example L4 C2 neuron of Figure 1 fired at 0.73 spikes/s in the 500 ms before the sample epoch and 1.91 spikes/s during it, a 2.6-fold increase (Wilcoxon rank sum, p = 3.38e-7).
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 3; Figure 1C-D
claims.quote: The neuron had a low baseline firing (0.73 spk/s; 500 ms before start of sample epoch) that increased substantially during the sample epoch (2.6 fold; to 1.91 spk/s; p = 3.38e-7, Wilcoxon rank sum)
claims.criterion: The paper does not identify the example cell. It is one of the 31 L4 C2 cells; the values are computed for every L4 C2 cell, and the claim holds when one cell matches all three within tolerance and its per-trial baseline and sample-epoch rates differ by a Wilcoxon rank sum test at p < 0.05 (the trials of the cell are the samples, as the test is named). The cell so found is the example cell for the claims that depend on this one. If no cell matches, example-cell claims are judged on the cell nearest in these values, and that is said.

claims.statement: The Fano factor of spike counts over the whole sample epoch was large, 7.51, in the paragraph on the example neuron, which does not say whose value it is.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 4
claims.quote: FF computed by counting spikes over the entire sample epoch (stimulus presentation), was huge (FF = 7.51)
claims.criterion: The variance over the mean of the per-trial spike count in the sample epoch (pole in reach), across trials. The paragraph follows the example cell but does not say whose FF this is, and the L4 C2 population mean for the same count is 6.57 (fig6e-sample-epoch-ff). Readings, (a) the cell identified in example-cell-rates; (b) the mean over all 41 L4 cells; (c) the mean over all 52 cells. Reproduced when the value is within tolerance under one reading; the readings that match are said.

claims.statement: For the example neuron, 74.4% of spikes fell in a window 8 to 40 ms after touch onset, which covers 15.3% of exploration time.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 8; Figure 3A-C
claims.quote: For the neuron illustrated in Figure 3A , 74.4% spikes fall into a time window spanning 8 to 40 ms after touch onset, comprising 15.3% of overall exploration time
claims.criterion: As fig3c-touch-spikes-l4c2, for the cell identified in example-cell-rates. Since a window end is a whole number of ms, the tolerance on 8 and 40 ms is read as at least 1 ms.

claims.statement: For the example neuron, the 10 ms sliding-window Fano factor is about 1 before and after touch, where the mean spike count is about 0.03, and falls near the peak of the touch response, where the mean count is about 0.7.
claims.source: Figure 6B legend; Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Since the spike rate is very low outside of the touch window, the mean spike count is also very low (∼0.03), implying FF of ∼1 for both the binomial and Poisson models. In contrast, around the peak of the touch response the mean spike count is high (∼0.7)
claims.criterion: Figure 6A and B call this neuron "an example neuron" and do not say it is the cell of Figures 1, 3 and 5. Readings, (a) the cell identified in example-cell-rates; (b) any L4 C2 cell, the number of cells that match being reported. Spike counts in 10 ms windows slid in 1 ms steps around touch onset (Figure 6B), across touches with inter-contact interval >250 ms (Methods, Analysis of spike count variance). Reproduced when the mean counts match, the FF before touch is within 0.1 of 1, and the FF at the window of peak mean count is below 1. Open detail, the touches used, read as (a) the >250 ms touches pooled or (b) one of the five clustered groups; both are shown. Reproduced under reading (a) of the cell when it matches there; otherwise the cells that match under (b) are reported, and the claim is reproduced only if one does, with the difference from the Figure 1 cell recorded.

claims.statement: Each touch evoked on the order of one spike (1.51 spikes per first touch, 0.31 per later touch) with an onset latency of 8 ms.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 4; Table 1
claims.quote: Each touch evoked on the order of one spike (1.51 spikes/first touch; 0.31/later touches) with short latency (onset, 8 ms)
claims.criterion: The sentence cites Table 1, whose L4 C2 values (mean 1.36 and 0.74, median 0.87 and 0.33, median latency 8 ms) do not match 1.51 and 0.31, and it sits in the paragraph on the example cell. Readings, (a) the example cell identified in example-cell-rates; (b) the L4 C2 population mean; (c) the L4 C2 population median. Spikes per touch is the mean spike count in the cell's touch spike window (Methods, Spike analysis), first touches of trials apart from later ones. Reproduced when all three values are within tolerance under one reading (latency tolerance at least 1 ms).

claims.statement: Spike rates were low in both whisking (0.67 spikes/s) and non-whisking (0.23 spikes/s) periods.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Firing rates were low in both whisking (0.67 spikes/s) and non-whisking (0.23 spikes/s) periods
claims.criterion: Whisking and non-whisking periods as in the Methods (Whisker analysis). The sentence does not say whose rates these are, and Table 1 (L4 C2 means 1.39 and 1.31, medians 0.33 and 0.32) does not give them. Readings, (a) the example cell identified in example-cell-rates; (b) the L4 C2 mean; (c) the L4 C2 median; (d) the rate over all L4 C2 spikes and time pooled. Open detail, whether whisking periods include touch epochs, read both ways. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: During exploration the example neuron's spikes are coupled to whisking phase, with a modulation depth close to 1 and near zero spiking at phase 0.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 5; Figure 1G-H
claims.quote: Yet during active exploration, the timing of spikes was coupled to the phase of rhythmic whisker movement ( Fee et al., 1997 ; Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009 ), with a modulation depth close to 1
claims.criterion: Methods, Spike analysis, and Figure 1G-H legends. For the cell identified in example-cell-rates, spikes in whisking bouts (amplitude >2.5 deg) of exploration periods excluding touch, assigned a phase by linear interpolation, in a 12-bin histogram of rate (Figure 3, figure supplement 1C; Figure 1H uses 30 deg bins, the same); fitted with A[1 + cos(theta - phi_pref)] + B, A, B > 0; depth A / (A + B). The tolerance is the protocol's 10% of the paper's value 1. The rate in the bin at phase 0 is reported. Fitting as table1-l4-c2.

claims.statement: For the 31 L4 C2 cells Table 1 gives, as mean +- s.d. (median), spikes per first touch 1.36 +- 1.32 (0.87), per later touch 0.74 +- 0.87 (0.33), touch-evoked spikes 70.6 +- 20.9% (74.7%), touch and whisking spikes 75.2 +- 19.0% (80.3%), phase modulation depth 0.67 +- 0.32 (0.70), non-whisking rate 1.31 +- 2.88 (0.32) spikes/s, whisking rate 1.39 +- 2.33 (0.33) spikes/s, onset latency 7.8 +- 3.0 (8) ms and minimum ISI 2.9 +- 1.9 (2.3) ms.
claims.source: Table 1, row L4 Inside C2 (n=31)
claims.criterion: Each measure per cell as defined in the Methods (see the opening comment), then the mean, s.d. and median over the 31 cells. Spikes per touch, mean count in the touch spike window, first touches of trials and later touches apart. Spikes evoked, as fig3c-touch-spikes-l4c2 and fig3d-touch-phase-l4c2. Modulation depth from the cosine fit to the 12-bin phase histogram of spike rate (Figure 3, figure supplement 1C), fitted by least squares with A, B > 0 (the fitting method is not given; least squares is the standard choice and is not expected to change the outcome). Rates in whisking and non-whisking periods. The minimum ISI is the shortest interspike interval of the cell (Figure 2, figure supplement 1C). Latency tolerance for the median is 1 ms, the bin size. Reproduced when at least 15 of the 18 values are within tolerance, partially reproduced for 10 to 14, not reproduced below 10; the medians, which carry the tighter tolerances, are reported apart. Open detail for latency, the PCTH used, read as (a) first touches or (b) all touches (Figure 3, figure supplement 1A shows both); both are shown.

claims.statement: For the 10 L4 cells outside C2 Table 1 gives, as mean +- s.d. (median), spikes per first touch 0.08 +- 0.19 (0), per later touch 0.02 +- 0.04 (0), touch-evoked spikes 9.2 +- 13.7% (3.6%), touch and whisking spikes 33.0 +- 30.2% (23.8%), modulation depth 0.58 +- 0.36 (0.61), non-whisking rate 2.20 +- 2.91 (1.10) spikes/s, whisking rate 2.41 +- 3.48 (1.31) spikes/s, onset latency 18.5 +- 6.0 (18) ms and minimum ISI 3.3 +- 1.3 (2.8) ms.
claims.source: Table 1, row L4 Outside C2 (n=10)
claims.criterion: As table1-l4-c2, over the 10 cells. The medians of spikes per touch (0 and 0) are checked as exact. Latency is over the cells for which one can be determined (four, Figure 2, figure supplement 1A). The Results give 8.4 +- 13.3% for touch-evoked spikes of this group where Table 1 gives 9.2 +- 13.7%; both are within each other's tolerance, and the Table 1 value is used here (fig3c-touch-spikes-outside uses the text). Reproduced when at least 13 of the 17 values are within tolerance, partially for 9 to 12, not reproduced below 9.

claims.statement: For the 11 L5 cells near C2 Table 1 gives, as mean +- s.d. (median), spikes per first touch 1.95 +- 2.96 (0.98), per later touch 1.28 +- 1.88 (0.42), touch-evoked spikes 24.0 +- 18.6% (24.4%), touch and whisking spikes 31.5 +- 16.4% (36.0%), modulation depth 0.18 +- 0.12 (0.13), non-whisking rate 12.0 +- 9.87 (12.8) spikes/s, whisking rate 16.2 +- 15.3 (13.5) spikes/s, onset latency 9.7 +- 5.2 (8) ms and minimum ISI 3.7 +- 2.5 (2.7) ms.
claims.source: Table 1, row L5 Near C2 (n=11)
claims.criterion: As table1-l4-c2, over the 11 cells (latency over the cells for which it can be determined, see latency-determinable). Reproduced when at least 15 of the 18 values are within tolerance, partially for 10 to 14, not reproduced below 10.

claims.statement: A touch-response latency could be determined for all 31 L4 C2 cells but for only four of the 10 L4 cells outside C2, for lack of a touch response.
claims.source: Figure 2, figure supplement 1A legend
claims.quote: Latency from touch onset to onset of spiking response for 31 L4 cells in C2 (red), four L4 outside C2 (grey) and eleven L5 near C2 (yellow). Latencies could not be determined for six L4 outside cells and one L5 cell due to lack of touch response
claims.criterion: Latency as in the Methods (Spike analysis), the first 1 ms PCTH bin after touch onset above the pre-touch mean (-50 to 0 ms) plus two standard deviations; a cell has no latency when no bin crosses. The legend contradicts itself for L5 (eleven plotted, one undetermined, of 11 cells), so L5 is read as 10 or 11 and not judged. Open details, (1) the PCTH used (first touches, or all touches), (2) the standard deviation (across the 50 pre-touch bins), (3) the window searched after onset, not given, read as 0 to 50 ms, the post-touch span of the touch-aligned responses in the Methods (Population decoding). The cell's touch response cutoff cannot bound the search, as it is computed from spikes indexed after the latency. Both readings of (1) are shown; the outcome is the one they both give, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: L4 neurons outside C2 respond much more weakly to touch than L4 neurons in C2, for first and for later touches.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 6; Figure 2B
claims.quote: In L4, but outside of C2, touch responses were much weaker (first touch, p = 1.4e-5; later touches, p = 6.32e-6; Wilcoxon rank sum)
claims.criterion: Spikes per touch per cell as in table1-l4-c2. Reproduced when both rank-sum tests give p < 0.05 with the C2 median higher; partially when one does. Open detail, the measure tested, read as (a) spikes per touch (Table 1 columns 1 and 2) or (b) the peak touch rate (Figure 2C); both are shown, the outcome being the one they agree on, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: L5 neurons near C2 have much higher spike rates than L4 neurons, with more diverse touch responses.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 6; Figure 2B-D; Table 1
claims.quote: Layer 5 neurons near C2 had much higher firing rates, with touch responses that were more diverse
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test. From Table 1, the L5 median non-whisking and whisking rates (12.8 and 13.5 spikes/s) are many times those of L4 C2 (0.32 and 0.33) and of L4 outside C2 (1.10 and 1.31). The sentence compares L5 with the L4 neurons of the paragraph, inside and outside C2. Reproduced when the L5 median is above the median of each L4 group for both rates and a Wilcoxon rank sum (the paper's test for group comparisons) gives p < 0.05 for all four comparisons; partially when only those against L4 C2 do. Diversity is not judged; the touch PSTHs are shown.

claims.statement: Modulation by whisking phase does not differ between L4 neurons inside and outside C2.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 6; Figure 2, figure supplement 1B
claims.quote: Modulation by whisking phase was not significantly different between L4 neurons inside and outside the C2 barrel (p = 0.68)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a Wilcoxon rank sum of per-cell modulation depth (as in table1-l4-c2) between the 31 L4 C2 and 10 L4 outside cells. The paper states no alpha; 0.05 is used, the conventional level and consistent with the p values it calls significant (up to 0.019). Reproduced when p >= 0.05; the medians are reported.

claims.statement: L4 neurons, inside and outside C2, are more modulated by whisking phase than L5 neurons.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 6; Figure 2, figure supplement 1B
claims.quote: but both were significantly more phase modulated than L5 (p = 4.3e-5 and p = 0.012 respectively, Wilcoxon rank sum)
claims.criterion: Modulation depth per cell as in table1-l4-c2. Reproduced when both rank-sum tests give p < 0.05 with the L4 median higher; partially when one does.

claims.statement: Across L4 neurons, inside and outside C2, spike rate does not change between whisking and non-whisking periods.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 6; Figure 2D
claims.quote: There were no significant changes in firing rate between whisking and non-whisking across the L4 population (L4 inside C2, p = 0.75; L4 outside C2, p = 0.92)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test of per-cell whisking against non-whisking rate (the test named for L5 in the same sentence), each group apart, at alpha 0.05 (not stated; see phase-mod-l4-inside-outside). Reproduced when both p >= 0.05, partially when one is. Periods as in text-whisking-rates, with whisking read with and without touch epochs; the outcome is the one both give, else methods_underspecified. The median difference is reported.

claims.statement: L5 neurons fire modestly but significantly more during whisking than during non-whisking periods.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 6; Figure 2D
claims.quote: whereas L5 showed a modest, but significant increase with whisking (p = 0.019, Wilcoxon signed rank)
claims.criterion: As whisking-rate-l4-no-change, for the 11 L5 cells. Reproduced when p < 0.05 with the median of the per-cell differences (whisking minus non-whisking) positive, under both readings of whisking periods; the increase is the direction of the paired signed-rank test. The group medians are not the measure; Table 1 gives them (13.5 and 12.8 spikes/s) and they are shown only for comparison.

claims.statement: In L4 C2 neurons 70.6 +- 20.9% (mean +- s.d.) of spikes during exploration are coupled to touch, within an average of 14.9% of exploration time.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 8; Figure 3C
claims.quote: Over the L4 C2 population, 70.6% ± 20.9% (mean, s.d.) of spikes were coupled to touch in an average of 14.9% of exploration time
claims.criterion: Methods, Spikes accounted by active sensation. Exploration time is whisking epochs with touch epochs, leaving out touches >100 ms, within the sample epoch (Results, paragraph 7, "during whisking or touch in the sample epoch (exploration time)"). Each spike in exploration time is indexed by the time since the closest touch onset, less the cell's latency; y_ton(t_i) is the number of spikes within t_i of onset; the cutoff t_on is the first t_i where the increment falls below the 95th percentile of the increments of 1000 surrogate curves from shuffled spike times, curves smoothed by a degree-11 polynomial before differencing. The cutoff is the point where the curve levels off after its rise (Results, paragraph 7, "At some window size, the curve levels off ... This transition point defines the proportion of touch-coupled spikes"; Methods, "these curves rise steeply and then plateau"; the example cell's window is 8 to 40 ms), so t_on is the first t_i at which the smoothed increment, having been above the surrogates' 95th percentile at an earlier t_i, falls below it. A dip of the polynomial before the rise is not the cutoff; the literal search from t_i = 1 ms is shown as a variant only. The touch-coupled fraction is y_ton(t_on) over all exploration spikes; the time fraction is the time within [latency, latency + t_on] after touch onsets over exploration time. Open details, (1) the step of t_i, taken as 1 ms (the paper's bin for touch analyses); (2) the shuffle, read as (a) spike times drawn uniformly over exploration time or (b) the cell's spike times circularly shifted within each trial's exploration time; (3) "closest touch onset", read as (a) the nearest onset before the spike or (b) the nearest onset either side; (4) the range of t_i over which y_ton is built and fitted, which the paper does not give, read as (r100) 0 to 100 ms (the limit for prolonged touches) or (r200) 0 to 200 ms. All combinations of (2), (3) and (4) are run; reproduced when both values are within tolerance under all, methods_underspecified when they disagree.

claims.statement: L4 neurons outside C2 have far fewer touch-coupled spikes, 8.4 +- 13.3%, in 3.5% of exploration time.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 8; Figure 3C
claims.quote: L4 neurons outside of C2 had significantly less touch-evoked spikes, 8.4% ± 13.3% in 3.5% of exploration time (p = 6.53e-6, Wilcoxon rank sum)
claims.criterion: As fig3c-touch-spikes-l4c2, with its readings. The paper does not say how the touch window is placed for the six cells without a touch latency (latency-determinable). Table 1 gives this group a median of 3.6% and a range of 0 to 41.0%, so at most four of the 10 cells are at 0%, and those six were not all set to 0%. Readings, (a) the latency taken as 0 ms (window from touch onset) for cells without one; (b) the latency from the all-touch PCTH where the first-touch PCTH gives none, then (a) for any cell still without one. Both are run; the outcome is the one both give, else methods_underspecified. Setting those cells to 0% is shown as a variant. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance and the rank-sum test against L4 C2 gives p < 0.05 with the outside median lower.

claims.statement: L5 neurons have fewer touch-coupled spikes than L4 C2 neurons, 24.0 +- 18.6%, in 19.0% of exploration time.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 8; Figure 3C
claims.quote: L5 neurons in C2 also showed significantly less touch-evoked spikes, 24.0% ± 18.6% touch spikes in 19.0% of exploration time (p = 2.30e-5, Wilcoxon rank sum)
claims.criterion: As fig3c-touch-spikes-outside, for the 11 L5 cells.

claims.statement: In L4 C2 neurons 75.2 +- 19.0% of exploration spikes are coupled to touch or to whisking phase, within an average of 22.0% of exploration time.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 9; Figure 3D
claims.quote: Overall, for neurons in C2 75.2 ± 19.0% of spikes were coupled to touch or whisking phase in an average of 22.0% of exploration time
claims.criterion: After fig3c-touch-spikes-l4c2, the spikes not attributed to touch are indexed by the time to the closest preferred phase of a whisk cycle (preferred phase from the cosine fit; whisking epochs including those with non-monotonic phase, phase circular), y_whisk(t_i) built and its cutoff t_w found by the same shuffle rule (Methods), with the same start of the search (the first t_i at which the increment, having been above chance, falls below it). The fraction is (touch spikes + phase spikes) over exploration spikes; the time is the union of touch windows and windows of +-t_w around each cycle's preferred phase, truncated at cycle margins (Figure 3B legend), over exploration time. Open details as fig3c-touch-spikes-l4c2, plus (5) whether the phase window is +-t_w or t_w wide in total; all combinations are run, with the same rule for disagreement.

claims.statement: L4 neurons outside C2 have fewer touch or phase coupled spikes than L4 C2, 33.0 +- 30.2% in 16.9% of exploration time.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 9; Figure 3D
claims.quote: significantly more than outside of C2 (33.0 ± 30.2 in 16.9% of time; p = 2.88e-4)
claims.criterion: As fig3d-touch-phase-l4c2, with its readings; reproduced when both values are within tolerance and the rank-sum test gives p < 0.05 with the outside median lower.

claims.statement: L5 neurons have fewer touch or phase coupled spikes than L4 C2, 31.5 +- 16.4% in 26.1% of exploration time.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 9; Figure 3D
claims.quote: or in L5 (31.5 ± 16.4 in 26.1% of time; p = 2.96e-5, Wilcoxon rank sum)
claims.criterion: As fig3d-touch-phase-outside, for the 11 L5 cells.

claims.statement: Spikes coupled to whisking phase alone are 4.6 +- 8.7% in L4 C2, 23.8 +- 27.9% in L4 outside C2 and 7.6 +- 14.9% in L5.
claims.source: Results, L4 responses are temporally precise, paragraph 9; Figure 3D
claims.quote: Subtraction of the touch spikes from touch and phase spikes reveals that 4.6 ± 8.7% of spikes were purely phase coupled in L4 C2, vs 23.8 ± 27.9% outside of C2 and 7.6 ± 14.9% in L5
claims.criterion: Per cell, the touch or phase fraction less the touch fraction (fig3d-touch-phase-l4c2 and fig3c-touch-spikes-l4c2, same readings), then mean and s.d. per group. Reproduced when all three means are within tolerance and the L4 outside mean is the largest of the three.

claims.statement: Pooling the activity of only 15 L4 C2 neurons, integrated over 10 ms, is enough to detect 95% of touches.
claims.source: Results, Decoding touch, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
claims.quote: Pooling activity from only fifteen L4 neurons (out of approximately 1600 [ Lefort et al., 2009 ]) in C2 was sufficient to detect 95% of touches (integration time, 10 ms)
claims.criterion: Methods, Population decoding. Per neuron, touch-aligned responses from 30 ms before to 50 ms after each touch, leaving out touches with a second touch within 50 ms. For a population of N neurons drawn at random, 1000 responses per neuron drawn with replacement, each spike train causally integrated over 10 ms and pooled across neurons; at each time point a one-dimensional threshold decoder separates the pooled response from that in epochs without touch, the threshold chosen on half the data and performance measured on the other half; repeated to give 95% bounds. Open details, (1) the non-touch epochs, read as (a) the 30 ms before touch in the same responses or (b) 10 ms windows drawn from exploration time away from touch, under (a) with the sample taken, as the paper does not say which, as (a1) the 10 ms window ending at onset, (a2) the earliest full window (-30 to -20 ms) or (a3) all pre-touch windows; (2) the performance measure, read as (a) the fraction of touches detected at the best post-touch time point or (b) the percent correct over touch and non-touch samples, at the best post-touch time point, in both cases with the threshold that maximizes percent correct on the training half (the Methods' "optimal threshold", which they do not define further; no other criterion for it is in the paper); (3) whether the 1000 draws pair across neurons by touch (they cannot, as neurons were recorded apart; independent draws are used, as the Methods imply). The number of neurons where the mean performance first reaches 95% is found for each reading of (1) and (2); reproduced when it is within tolerance under all, else methods_underspecified with every result shown.

claims.statement: Touch detection by neurons from surrounding barrels, outside C2, is poor.
claims.source: Results, Decoding touch, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
claims.quote: Touch detection by neurons from surrounding barrels (>200 µm from the principal whisker) was poor
claims.criterion: As fig4a-touch-detection-c2, sampling from the 10 L4 outside cells (with replacement, as for C2). Reproduced when, under every reading, performance with 15 neurons is below that of C2 and its 95% bound excludes 95% detection; the Methods' note of "several-fold more information about touch in C2" is shown as the ratio of the population sizes needed for equal performance.

claims.statement: A naive Bayes decoder reading 200 L4 C2 neurons integrated over 10 ms decodes the time elapsed since touch with high precision, a minimum uncertainty of 0.55 ms (95% confidence) at 10 ms after touch onset.
claims.source: Results, Decoding touch, paragraph 1; Figure 4B; Figure 4, figure supplement 1
