claims.quote: a group of 200 neurons in C2, integrating in 10 ms windows after touch, also allowed decoding of elapsed time from touch with high precision (minimum 0.55 ms uncertainty with 95% confidence at 10 ms post-touch onset using a naïve Bayes decoder
claims.criterion: Methods, Population decoding. Responses sampled as fig4a-touch-detection-c2, each neuron's spike train integrated in a 10 ms sliding window; a multinomial naive Bayes classifier reports the most likely time since onset at each 1 ms time point, with the RMS time error from 100 bootstrap runs (Figure 4, figure supplement 1). Open details, (1) the uncertainty, read as (a) the RMS error, (b) the half width of the 95% bound of decoded time or (c) 1.96 times the RMS error; (2) train and test split, read as (a) half and half as for touch detection or (b) independent resampled sets for training and testing; (3) the times the decoder chooses among, which the paper does not give ("for every time point what was the most likely time elapsed from touch onset"), read as (c-all) every 1 ms over the sampled -30 to +50 ms response where a full window fits or (c-post) every 1 ms from onset on (the Results' "integrating in 10 ms windows after touch"); (4) the smoothing of zero counts in the likelihood, not given, read as add-one (Laplace) smoothing, a smaller pseudocount shown as a variant. Reproduced when the minimum over time points, at or near 10 ms after onset, is within tolerance under one reading of (1) for both readings of (2) and both of (3); the readings that match are said. Also shown, that the error falls with population size (Figure 4B inset).

claims.statement: Even 1000 L4 neurons give only a rough estimate of whisking phase, a resolution of 24 deg in C2 and 33 deg outside C2 at d' = 1 (76% correct discrimination).
claims.source: Results, Decoding touch, paragraph 2; Figure 4C
claims.quote: a large population of neurons (1000) was required to provide even a rough estimate of whisking phase (24° in C2, 33° outside at d′ = 1 performance, equivalent to 76% correct discrimination)
claims.criterion: Methods, Population decoding. Per neuron, spikes aligned to the phase of each whisk cycle with peak amplitude >2.5 deg, binned in 120 bins over -pi to pi; the cycles are the whisking cycles of Methods, Whisker analysis, as for phase tuning (whisking epochs lie outside touch epochs, "Whisking cycles during licking or within 70 ms after touch were excluded", and "Whisking epochs used for phase analysis had monotonic phase for a complete whisking cycle"); neurons drawn with replacement and their responses circularly shifted to give uniformly distributed preferred phases; a naive Bayes classifier discriminates the population response at two phases; the phase difference reaching 76% correct is found, median over 100 runs (Figure 4C legend). Open details, (1) the response per cycle, read as (a) the spike count in each phase bin of one cycle (Poisson or multinomial likelihood over cycles) or (b) the cycle-averaged rate per bin used as a Poisson mean; (2) the shifts, read as (a) random uniform shifts or (b) shifts that place preferred phases evenly; (3) bins with no spikes in the likelihood, which the paper does not treat, read as add-one (Laplace) smoothing of counts or a floor rate under (1)(b), the paper giving no value for either. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance and C2 is better than outside under all readings, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Touch response magnitude of L4 C2 neurons is strongly modulated by touch order, whisker velocity before touch and maximum curvature during touch, with mean modulation indices of 0.71 +- 0.25, 0.71 +- 0.27 and 0.72 +- 0.23.
claims.source: Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 2; Figure 5A-C
claims.quote: Touch response magnitude was highly modulated by each of the three variables (mean modulation index ... touch order, 0.71 ± 0.25; velocity, 0.71 ± 0.27; max curvature, 0.72 ± 0.23; mean ± std
claims.criterion: Figure 5 legend. Per L4 C2 cell, touches sorted by the property and split into 10 bins with equal numbers of touches; the mean spikes per touch in the cell's spike integration window (touch spike window) per bin; modulation index (max bin - min bin)/(max bin + min bin). Properties, order of the touch in its trial; whisker velocity at touch onset (d theta/dt); maximum curvature change during the touch. Open details, (1) velocity, read as (a) the velocity at the onset frame ("at touch onset", Figure 5A legend) or (b) the velocity in the frame before onset ("just before touch", Results; "pretouch velocity", Methods); (2) curvature, read as (a) max |Delta kappa| over the whole touch or (b) over 0 to 20 ms after onset (the window of the Methods for clustering); (3) touch order, where ties make equal bins impossible, read as (a) ranks with ties broken at random or (b) bins of whole order values as near equal as they can be. Reproduced when all three means are within tolerance under all readings, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Across cells, responsiveness to pre-touch velocity and to maximum curvature covary strongly (r = 0.80), and responsiveness to touch order is somewhat less correlated with both (r = 0.70 and 0.65).
claims.source: Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 2; Figure 5B-C
claims.quote: Responsiveness to pretouch velocity and max curvature covaried strongly (pairwise correlation coefficient 0.80, p = 4.3e-8), whereas touch order response was somewhat less correlated with velocity and curvature (correlation coefficients 0.70, 0.65, p = 1.0e-5, p = 8.2e-5)
claims.criterion: The paper does not say what is correlated. Readings, (a) Pearson correlation across the 31 L4 C2 cells of the modulation indices of fig5c-modulation-index (the reported p values are those of Pearson r with 29 degrees of freedom, e.g. r = 0.70 gives p near 1e-5); (b) Pearson correlation of the peak-normalized 10-bin tuning curves (Figure 5B) pooled over cells and bins. Reproduced when all three r are within tolerance with p < 0.05 under one reading, with velocity-curvature the largest; the readings that match are said.

claims.statement: The clustering of touches into five groups finds subsets with significantly less variability in touch properties than random samples of touches.
claims.source: Figure 6, figure supplement 1B legend
claims.quote: The procedure finds subset of points with significantly less behavioral variability than in the full dataset
claims.criterion: Methods, Analysis of spike count variance. Per L4 C2 cell, touches with inter-contact interval >250 ms; z-scored pre-touch velocity and maximum curvature change 0 to 20 ms after touch; OPTICS ordering; the run of N consecutive ordered touches with the smallest sum of pairwise distances is the first group, removed, and repeated for five groups, N being 20% of the touches (Figure 6, figure supplement 1A) and at least 20. Open details, (1) OPTICS parameters (minimum points, maximum radius), not given, read as (a) minimum points 5 with unbounded radius (the scikit-learn default) or (b) minimum points N; (2) inter-contact interval, read as (a) time since the previous touch offset or (b) since the previous onset; (3) N, read as 20% of the selected touches at the start, fixed for all five groups. The standard deviation of z-scored velocity in each group is compared with that of 1000 random samples of N touches; reproduced when, under all readings, the group standard deviation is below the 5th percentile of the random ones for the first group in most (>50%) cells.

claims.statement: Across L4 C2 neurons, the Fano factor following touch drops below one, lying close to the binomial limit (the theoretical minimum) for most cells.
claims.source: Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 4; Figure 6C-D
claims.quote: Across the population of neurons within C2 the FF following touch dropped below one, with the FF lying close to the binomial limit for most cells
claims.criterion: Figure 6C legend and Methods. Per cell and per touch group (fig6s1b, same readings), FF of spike counts in 10 ms windows starting 0 to 20 ms after touch in 1 ms steps; the minimum over windows per group, and the minimum across the five groups. Open details, (1) which minimum, read as (a) per group (Figure 6C red circles) or (b) across groups (blue circles); (2) "close", which the paper does not define, read as (a) the binomial limit 1 - m lies inside the cell's 95% resampling interval of the FF (1000 resamples, Methods) or (b) the FF lies nearer the binomial limit than the Poisson value 1. Reproduced when the population mean of the minimum FF is below 1 and, for more than half of the cells, the FF is close under the reading in force; every combination is run, the outcome being the one they all give, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: The low Fano factor after touch cannot be explained by a Poisson process with a 2.3 ms refractory period and rates matched to each neuron.
claims.source: Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 6; Figure 6D
claims.quote: Comparing the simulations with actual spike trains revealed that L4 neuron response precision could not be explained by the refractory period alone
claims.criterion: Methods, last paragraph, and Figure 6D. Per L4 C2 cell, spike trains simulated as a Poisson process with an absolute refractory period of 2.3 ms (the median minimum ISI) whose average touch response is matched to the data (Methods, "with average touch response matched to the data"), so the output PSTH, not the input rate, equals the cell's touch PSTH (1 ms bins), so the rate is raised to make up for the spikes the refractory period removes, as the free rate lambda(t) = r(t) / (1 - integral of r over [t - 2.3 ms, t)) of Berry and Meister (1998), the paper's cited method, or by adjusting the rate until the simulated PSTH matches; using the PSTH directly as the rate is not the paper's model and is shown as a variant only. One simulated train per real touch; FF computed as for the data in 10 ms sliding windows. Open details, (1) which touches, read as all >250 ms touches pooled, or per group as fig6cd; (2) the comparison, which the paper gives only as a figure, read as (a) the population mean data FF below the model's at the window of the data minimum, by more than the sum of the two s.e.m. (Figure 6D error bars), or (b) the per-cell data FF below the model's in more than half of the cells by a sign test at p < 0.05. Every combination is run; the outcome is the one they all give, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Counting spikes over the whole sample epoch, ignoring the millisecond structure of behavior, gives a very large Fano factor of 6.57 +- 5.41 (mean +- s.d. over L4 C2 cells).
claims.source: Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 7; Figure 6E, condition 1
claims.quote: Response variability was very large (FF = 6.57 mean ± 5.41 s.d.) when we ignored the millisecond time scale of behavior
claims.criterion: Figure 6E legend, condition 1. Per L4 C2 cell, FF across trials of the spike count while the pole is within reach; mean and s.d. over the 31 cells. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance and above 1.

claims.statement: Counting spikes in random 38 ms windows, as many per trial as there are touches, gives a Fano factor of 1.59 +- 0.49.
claims.source: Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 7; Figure 6E, condition 2
claims.quote: Integrating activity in time windows as wide as average touch response periods (38 ms) gave a FF of 1.59 ± 0.49
claims.criterion: Figure 6E legend, condition 2. Per cell, in each trial as many 38 ms windows at random times as the trial has touches; FF across all windows of the cell; mean over the 31 cells. Open detail, where windows are drawn, read as (a) within the sample epoch or (b) anywhere in the trial ("randomly sampling from the trial"); both are run with 100 random draws, the mean reported. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance under both, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Counting spikes in 38 ms windows aligned to touch onset (after a 6 ms latency) gives a Fano factor of 1.37 +- 0.74.
claims.source: Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 7; Figure 6E, condition 3
claims.quote: and FF of 1.37 ± 0.74 ( Figures 6E, 3 ) when aligned to touch onset
claims.criterion: Figure 6E legend, condition 3. Per cell, spike counts in the window 6 to 44 ms after each touch onset; FF across touches; mean over the 31 cells. Open detail, the touches, read as (a) all touches or (b) touches with inter-contact interval >250 ms; both are run, and the outcome is the one both give, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: A narrower 10 ms window after touch reduces the Fano factor to 0.73 +- 0.19.
claims.source: Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 7; Figure 6E, condition 4
claims.quote: Using a narrower touch window of 10 ms reduced the FF to 0.73 ± 0.19
claims.criterion: Figure 6E legend, condition 4. Per cell, the minimum over 10 ms windows starting 0 to 20 ms after touch onset (1 ms steps) of the FF across touches; mean over the 31 cells. Open details, (1) the touches, as fig6e-touch-38ms-ff; (2) the window starts, read as (a) 0 to 20 ms or (b) 0 to 10 ms so that windows lie within 0 to 20 ms. Every combination is run; the outcome is the one they all give, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Computed only across similar touches, the 10 ms Fano factor falls further to 0.54 +- 0.27, so that L4 responses to touch are almost noiseless.
claims.source: Results, Low spike count variability, paragraph 7; Figure 6E, condition 5
claims.quote: The FF was further reduced to 0.54 ± 0.27 when calculated only across similar touches
claims.criterion: Figure 6E legend, condition 5. As fig6e-touch-10ms-ff, within each of the five touch groups of fig6s1b-clusters-less-variable (same readings). Open detail, the per-cell value, read as (a) the minimum across the five groups (Figure 6C blue circles) or (b) the mean over groups of each group's minimum. Every combination is run; reproduced when the mean is within tolerance under all and, as the paragraph states, the five conditions of Figure 6E fall in order (1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5) under the same readings; else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: L4 neurons fire few spikes during whisker movements, on average fewer than 0.15 spikes per whisk cycle, which hinders decoding of whisking phase.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 7; Figure 4
claims.quote: their low spike rates during whisker movements (mean <0.15 spikes/whisk cycle) hinders efficient decoding of whisking phase from population activity
claims.criterion: Per L4 cell (inside and outside C2), spikes per whisk cycle over the whisking cycles used for phase analysis (amplitude >2.5 deg, monotonic phase, not during licking or within 70 ms after touch). Open detail, the population, read as (a) L4 C2 cells or (b) all 41 L4 cells, and the mean as (a) over cells or (b) over all cycles pooled. Reproduced when the mean is below 0.15 under all readings, else methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Mice licked early, during the delay epoch, on 13.3% +- 10% of trials, and these trials were not analysed.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2 (four trial types)
claims.quote: Trials in which the mice licked early during the delay epoch (13.3% ± 10%) were not analyzed
claims.criterion: The tolerance is the paper's stated spread. The paper does not say over what the mean and SD are taken. Readings (a) mean over imaged planes; (b) mean over sessions; (c) mean over mice; (d) all trials pooled. Denominator all trials with a lick or all trials of the session, both read. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance under one reading. If the dataset holds no early-lick trials, the claim cannot be tested.

claims.statement: Two-photon imaging covered 12 locations in 6 mice with 8.8 +- 2.6 planes per location, 105 planes in all, each imaged for 92 +- 26 trials at 73% +- 9% correct, 3 +- 1 planes per session.
claims.source: Results, Mapping Activity Using Two-Photon Calcium Imaging, paragraph 1; Figure 2E, 2F
claims.quote: For each mouse (n = 6), we collected data from 1 to 3 image locations (n = 12 locations in total, Figure 2E), each containing multiple (8.8 ± 2.6) image planes ... Each image plane (n = 105, Figure 2F and S2) was sampled at 14 Hz while mice performed the task for 92 ± 26 trials, with performance at 73% ± 9% trials correct ... allowing sequential imaging of 3 ± 1 planes per session (range 1–6
claims.criterion: Counts of mice, locations and planes are exact (tolerance 0, as they are counts of the recordings). Means take the paper's stated spread as tolerance. Trials per plane and percent correct are open as to which trials count; readings (a) the four analysed trial types (early lick and no-response excluded); (b) all trials of the plane. The Methods give 74% +- 9% for "Behavior performance during imaging", read as the same quantity. Reproduced when every value is within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Each imaged plane had on average 34 +- 13 CR, 36 +- 14 CL, 12 +- 5 ER and 10 +- 4 EL trials.
claims.source: Results, Mapping Activity Using Two-Photon Calcium Imaging, paragraph 3
claims.quote: average number of trials per imaged plane ... CR ... 34 ± 13, CL ... 36 ± 14; ER ... 12 ± 5, EL ... 10 ± 4
claims.criterion: Mean over the 105 planes of the number of trials of each type (early-lick trials excluded, convention T). Tolerances are the paper's stated spread. Reproduced when all four are within tolerance.

claims.statement: 15,431 neurons were imaged across 6 mice, 8,837 in ALM and 6,594 in MM.
claims.source: Results, Mapping Activity Using Two-Photon Calcium Imaging, paragraphs 2 and 3
claims.quote: Our sample (15,431 neurons across 6 mice) is therefore biased toward the active population
claims.criterion: Segmented cells (ROIs) over all planes. Area by readings A1 and A2 (convention A). Reproduced when the total and both area counts are within tolerance under one area reading; the reading that matches is the one used by the claims that split ALM and MM.

claims.statement: A large fraction of neurons distinguished between trial types, 23% in MM (1,523 of 6,594) and 31% in ALM (2,754 of 8,837).
claims.source: Results, Mapping Activity Using Two-Photon Calcium Imaging, paragraph 3
claims.quote: the activity of a large proportion of neurons distinguished between trial types in MM (23%, 1,523/6,594) ... and ALM (31%, 2,754/8,837
claims.criterion: The test is the Methods' 3-way ANOVA per time bin (convention M, p < 0.01 for any factor). The paper does not say how per-bin results make a neuron selective over the trial, nor over which window. Readings for the rule (R1) selective in at least one bin; (R2) selective in at least two consecutive bins; and for the window (W1) the task period 4.6 s before to 2.5 s after the go cue (the window of Figure 8F); (W2) the whole extracted window, 5 s before to 5 s after the go cue; (W3) trial start to the go cue plus 2.5 s. Each with time bins T1 and T2 and area readings A1 and A2. dF/F by reading V1 (convention T); V2 is reported. Reproduced when both counts and both fractions are within tolerance under one reading, and ALM has the higher fraction.

claims.statement: The selectivity of most neurons can be attributed to one of the three coefficients, especially early in the trial, so most neurons mainly encode one behavioural variable at a time.
claims.source: Results, Analysis of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 2; Figure S5 (not read)
claims.quote: The selectivity of most neurons can be attributed to one of the three coefficients, especially during the early part of the trial (Figure S5)
claims.criterion: Figure S5 was not read; written from the main text. Per time bin, among neurons trial-type selective at that bin (convention M), the fraction purely selective (one factor) and the fraction mixed. Reproduced when the purely selective fraction exceeds one half in every bin from trial start to the go cue; partially reproduced when it does in most of them (more than half of the bins) but not all. The fraction after the go cue is reported. This measure is fixed here, as the text gives none.

claims.statement: Different neurons coded for lick direction in different epochs, some during the sample and delay epochs before licking, some during the response epoch, and some after the mouse stopped consuming water.
claims.source: Results, Analysis of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 3; Figure 4A
claims.quote: Some neurons were selective during the sample and delay epochs, long before onset of licking ... Other neurons became selective during the response epoch ... Some neurons even represented licking direction after the animal stopped consuming water
claims.criterion: Pure lick-direction selectivity per bin (convention M). Reproduced when there are neurons purely lick-direction selective in the delay epoch, and other neurons first lick-direction selective after the go cue, and neurons lick-direction selective more than 2 s after the go cue. The paper gives no count or time for "stopped consuming water"; the lick times give the last lick of each trial, and lick-direction selectivity after the median last lick is reported as the reading of it. Counts of each group are reported.

claims.statement: Many object-location-selective neurons were selective during the sample epoch, and a subset coded object location mainly in the delay epoch after the pole was removed, some up to the end of the delay.
claims.source: Results, Analysis of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 4; Figure 4B
claims.quote: Many of these neurons were selective during the sample epoch when mice explored the object ... However, a subset of neurons coded object location primarily during the delay epoch, after the pole was removed ... Some of these neurons carried information about object location up to the end of the delay epoch
claims.criterion: Pure object-location selectivity per bin (convention M). Reproduced when (a) neurons are object-location selective in the sample epoch; (b) some neurons have most of their object-location-selective bins in the delay epoch; (c) some neurons are object-location selective in the last 0.5 s before the go cue. Counts of each group are reported.

claims.statement: Outcome-selective neurons typically became selective after the answer lick; some preferred correct and others error trials, and some kept the outcome long after the trial ended.
claims.source: Results, Analysis of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 5; Figure 4C
claims.quote: These neurons typically became selective after the answer lick. A subset of the outcome-selective neurons responded preferentially during correct trials ... whereas others responded strongly during error trials
claims.criterion: Pure outcome selectivity per bin (convention M). Reproduced when most outcome-selective neurons (more than half) have their first outcome-selective bin after the go cue, and both signs of gamma occur among them. The latest outcome-selective bins in the extracted window (up to 5 s after the go cue) are reported.

claims.statement: Most neurons with mixed selectivity were seen during the response epoch; a subset responded in only one trial type and a few switched the variable they coded during the trial.
claims.source: Results, Analysis of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 6; Figure 5
claims.quote: Most of these neurons with ‘‘mixed’’ selectivity were observed during the response epoch
claims.criterion: Mixed selectivity per bin (convention M). Reproduced when more than half of the neuron-bins of mixed selectivity fall after the go cue. Neurons purely selective for object location early and for outcome or lick direction later are counted and reported.

claims.statement: During the sample and early delay epochs, object location was represented mainly in MM.
claims.source: Results, Spatial Map of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 1; Figure 6B to 6D, 6H
claims.quote: During the sample and the early part of the delay epoch, representation of object location was prominent, mainly in MM
claims.criterion: Fraction of neurons purely object-location selective per time bin, in ALM and in MM (as Figure 6H and 6I), area by the reading that matched neuron-counts. Reproduced when the MM fraction exceeds the ALM fraction in most bins (more than half) from trial start to 2.2 s (the sample epoch and the first second of the delay; "early part" is not defined, and a window ending 2.7 s, the time of Figure 6D, the last panel the sentence cites, is also read). Figure 6 panels B to G are at 0.9, 1.5, 2.7, 3.9, 4.5 and 5.1 s after trial start (figure labels, in order); this is read from the extracted text, as the PDF could not be rendered.

claims.statement: Neurons selective for lick direction appeared first in the deep layers of ALM, early in the delay epoch.
claims.source: Results, Spatial Map of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 1; Figure 6D, 6E and 6H
claims.quote: Neurons selective for lick direction appeared first in the deep layers of ALM, early in the delay epoch
claims.criterion: Groups are ALM and MM, each split by depth (convention D, readings (D1) superficial against deep at 350 um; (D2) the three bins of Figure 6, 100-250, 250-400 and 400-620 um, with the deepest bin as deep). For each group, the fraction of neurons purely lick-direction selective per bin (Figure 6H). The text defines no onset for Figure 6; readings (F1) onset as convention O applied to the fraction; (F2) onset as convention O applied to mean |beta| (the measure used for the onset in Figure 8D), each with baselines O1 and O2. Reproduced when, under each reading, deep ALM has the earliest onset of all groups and that onset is in the delay epoch, no later than 2.7 s after trial start (the time of Figure 6D, the first panel the sentence cites for "early in the delay epoch").

claims.statement: Lick-direction selectivity, in number of neurons and strength, kept increasing and spread across ALM layers and to a minor extent into MM, peaking after the go cue.
claims.source: Results, Spatial Map of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 1; Figures 6F to 6I and S7 (not read)
claims.quote: Lickdirection selectivity, including number of neurons and the strength of coding, continued to increase and spread across ALM layers and to a minor extent into MM (Figure S7), reaching a maximum after the go cue
claims.criterion: Figure S7 was not read. Fraction of neurons purely lick-direction selective and mean |beta| (non-significant set to 0) per bin, in ALM and MM, each by depth (convention D). Reproduced when (a) in ALM both measures reach their maximum after the go cue; (b) the superficial ALM fraction at its maximum is above its value in the first half of the delay; (c) the MM fraction at its maximum is above its value in the delay epoch and below the ALM maximum. The paper does not say whether the MM value in the delay epoch is its mean over the delay bins or its maximum there; both are read, and (c) holds when it holds under one.

claims.statement: Outcome-selective neurons were seen only during the response epoch, scattered roughly uniformly through ALM and MM; mixed neurons were also seen mainly in the response epoch in both areas.
claims.source: Results, Spatial Map of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 2; Figure 6G to 6I
claims.quote: Outcome-selective neurons, which were observed only during the response epoch, were scattered approximately uniformly throughout ALM and MM
claims.criterion: Fraction of neurons purely outcome selective per bin in ALM and in MM. The paper gives no test; this measure is fixed here. Reproduced when (a) in both areas the largest fraction in any bin before the go cue is below one third of the largest fraction after it; and (b) the ALM and MM fractions averaged over the response epoch (go cue to 2.5 s after) differ by less than a factor of 1.5. The same is reported for mixed neurons.

claims.statement: Throughout the trial preparatory activity, as the fraction of lick-direction-selective neurons or the average coding coefficient, was most pronounced in ALM, while object location selectivity was mainly limited to MM.
claims.source: Results, Spatial Map of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 2; Figure 6H, 6I, S6 and S8 (not read)
claims.quote: Throughout the trial, preparatory activity, quantified either as fraction of lick direction-selective neuron (Figures 6H and 6I) or as average coding coefficient (Figures S6 and S8), was most pronounced in ALM, whereas object location related selectivity was mainly limited to MM
claims.criterion: Per bin, the fraction of purely lick-direction-selective neurons and mean |beta| (non-significant set to 0, convention M), and the same for object location and |alpha|, in ALM and MM. Reproduced when, in most bins (more than half) of the delay epoch, ALM is above MM on both lick-direction measures, and in most bins from trial start to the go cue MM is above ALM on both object-location measures; partially reproduced when only one of the two holds.

claims.statement: Optogenetic inactivation during the delay epoch affected lick direction more in ALM than in MM.
claims.source: Results, Spatial Map of Behavior-Related Activity, paragraph 2; Figure S9 (not read); Discussion, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Consistently, the effects of optogenetic inactivation during the delay epoch on lick direction were greater in ALM compared to MM
claims.criterion: Figure S9 and its methods were not read; the text gives only that VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice were used and, from Guo et al. (2014b), 1.5 mW average power. Measure, per site, the change in the fraction of lick-right (contralateral) responses under photoinhibition against control, on lick-right and lick-left trials. Reproduced when the bias is larger for ALM (2.5 mm anterior, 1.5 mm lateral) than for MM (1.5 mm anterior, 1.0 mm lateral). The test, the sites and the number of mice are not in the text read; no statistic can be named. The Discussion (paragraph beginning 'In previous experiments') attributes the inactivation to Guo et al. (2014b); whether Figure S9 shows those data or new ones is not in the text read.

claims.statement: In wide-field imaging, activity during the sample and early delay was most pronounced in MM, and spread forward and laterally to ALM as the delay progressed; after the response it rose across much of motor and somatosensory cortex.
claims.source: Results, Mapping Neural Activity Using Wide-Field Imaging; Figure 2B to 2D
claims.quote: During the sample and early parts of the delay epoch, activity was most pronounced in MM ... As the delay epoch progressed, activity spread forward and lateral to ALM ... Behavior-related activity therefore shifts from MM to ALM before the behavioral response
claims.criterion: Per mouse (5), dF/F0 per pixel with F0 the mean of the six frames before trial start, averaged over trials of each correct type (Methods, Wide field calcium imaging). Peak location (pixel of maximum dF/F0, averaged over CR and CL) in the sample epoch and in the last second of the delay, in stereotactic coordinates. Reproduced when the sample-epoch peak is nearer the MM centre and the late-delay peak nearer the ALM centre, in the mean over mice and in at least 3 of 5 mice. The paper's measure is the image itself; this measure is fixed here. The rise after the response across motor and somatosensory cortex is not judged; the response-epoch map is reported.

claims.statement: Early wide-field activity in MM was contralateral to the whiskers touching the object, and the later ALM activity was in both hemispheres.
claims.source: Results, Mapping Neural Activity Using Wide-Field Imaging; Figure S1 (not read)
claims.quote: contralateral to the whiskers touching the object (Figure S1) ... across both ALM hemispheres (Figure S1)
claims.criterion: Figure S1 was not read, and the main text describes a window over the left frontal cortex only; the bilateral imaging behind Figure S1 is not described in the text read. Reproduced when imaging of both hemispheres exists and MM activity in the sample epoch is larger in the hemisphere contralateral to the whiskers, and ALM activity at the end of the delay is present in both. Otherwise not testable from the text read.

claims.statement: In two-photon imaging, the peak of activity shifted from MM to ALM over the delay.
claims.source: Results, Mapping Activity Using Two-Photon Calcium Imaging, paragraph 3; Figure S4 (not read)
claims.quote: the peak of activity shifted from MM to ALM over the course of the delay epoch (Figure S4)
claims.criterion: Figure S4 was not read. Mean dF/F over all neurons and trials of the four types, per bin, in ALM and in MM; peak time of each. Reproduced when the MM mean peaks earlier than the ALM mean and the ALM mean is above its sample-epoch level at the end of the delay. The measure is fixed here. The paper defines neither term; readings for the sample-epoch level (L1) the mean over the sample-epoch bins, (L2) their maximum; for the end of the delay (E1) the last bin before the go cue, (E2) the mean over the last 0.5 s before it. Reproduced under one combination; all are reported. dF/F by reading V1 (convention T); V2 is reported.

claims.statement: IT neurons were found in both superficial and deep layers, PT neurons only in deep layers; 719 PT and 2,631 IT neurons were imaged in three mice.
claims.source: Results, Projection-Specific Coding, paragraph 1; Figure 8C
claims.quote: In three mice, we combined retrograde labeling of pyramidal tract (PT) (n = 719) and intratelencephalic (IT) (n = 2,631) neurons ... IT neurons were found in both superficial and deep layers, whereas PT neurons were exclusively in deep layers
claims.criterion: Labels as the dataset gives them. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance, no PT neuron is in a plane shallower than 350 um, and IT neurons occur in both depth groups (convention D).

claims.statement: In ALM the strongest lick direction selectivity was in the deep layers, where PT and IT neurons were intermingled.
claims.source: Results, Projection-Specific Coding, sentence beginning 'In ALM, the strongest lick direction selectivity'; Figures 8D and S10 (not read)
claims.quote: In ALM, the strongest lick direction selectivity was observed in the deep layers (Figures 8D and S10), where PT and IT neurons were intermingled
claims.criterion: Mean |beta| over neurons (non-significant set to 0) per bin, ALM deep against ALM superficial (convention D), with bootstrap SD (convention B). Figure 8D groups only the three labelled mice; readings (a) those three mice; (b) all six. Reproduced when the deep maximum over the trial exceeds the superficial maximum, and deep exceeds superficial in most bins (more than half) of the delay epoch.

claims.statement: During the delay epoch, ALM PT neurons showed a bias toward contralateral (lick right) selectivity.
claims.source: Results, Projection-Specific Coding, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 8D
claims.quote: A contra bias during the delay epoch was ... observed in PT neurons (Figure 8D), consistent with previous electrophysiological recordings
claims.criterion: Mean beta (signed, non-significant set to 0) of ALM PT neurons per bin over the delay epoch, with bootstrap SD (convention B); contra is lick right (beta > 0, convention M). Reproduced when the mean over the delay epoch is above zero by more than 2 bootstrap SD. The paper reports no test; the 2 SD bound is fixed here from the shading Figure 8D shows. dF/F by reading V1 (convention T); V2 is reported.

claims.statement: In ALM, lick direction selectivity (|beta|) was stronger and earlier in PT than in IT neurons, with an onset difference of 1.4 +- 0.6 s (p < 0.01, bootstrap).
claims.source: Results, Projection-Specific Coding, paragraph 2; Figure 8D
claims.quote: The magnitude of lick direction selectivity (jbj) appeared stronger and earlier in PT than in IT neurons (delta onset time; time when selectivity rose to >6 SD above baseline = 1.4 ± 0.6 s; p < 0.01, bootstrap
claims.criterion: Mean |beta| (non-significant set to 0) over ALM PT and over ALM IT neurons per bin; onset by convention O (baselines O1 and O2, onset rules S1 and S2, threshold from the baseline mean). The IT group is open, readings (I1) deep ALM IT, the neurons intermingled with PT; (I2) all ALM IT. The bootstrap is open, readings (H1) hierarchical over animals, planes and cells (convention B, as for Figure 8D); (H2) over cells. The +- is read as the bootstrap SD of the difference, and p as the fraction of resamples in which the PT onset is not earlier. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the difference is within tolerance, p < 0.01, and the PT maximum of mean |beta| exceeds the IT maximum.

claims.statement: The difference in onset of lick direction selectivity between PT and IT neurons was not detected in an electrophysiology dataset recorded under similar conditions (45 PT and 27 IT cells, Li et al., 2015).
claims.source: Results, Projection-Specific Coding, sentence beginning 'However, this difference in lick direction selectivity onset'; Discussion, paragraph beginning 'We analyzed neuronal selectivity'
claims.quote: However, this difference in lick direction selectivity onset was not detected in an electrophysiology dataset recorded under similar conditions (Li et al., 2015)
claims.criterion: The data are those of Li et al. (2015, Nature 519, 51-56), tagged PT and IT units in ALM; the paper does not say where they are deposited. A claim of absence with no test named in the text; the test of fig8d-pt-earlier-than-it (onset of mean |beta| by convention O, bootstrap over units, p < 0.01) is applied to it. The paper gives no method for these data beyond "the same analyses as imaging data" with "spike counts within 400 ms windows (in 100 ms steps)" (Methods, Electrophysiology data analysis, for its own units), so the details are readings. (1) Counts in 400 ms windows in 100 ms steps, as the paper's own spiking data. (2) Trials of the four types without photostimulation (the imaging trials had none, and photoinhibition changes selectivity), early-lick trials excluded by the early-lick record whatever the outcome record says (convention T); trial start is the onset of pole movement (sample-epoch onset), as in this paper's Methods, and time is taken from it, the go cue falling where the Li et al. task puts it. (3) Onset by convention O from trial start to the go cue, rules S1 and S2; baseline (O1) the windows wholly before trial start, (O2) the windows wholly within 0.5 s before trial start; a window is placed at its centre. (4) Units of all sessions pooled, as neurons are pooled for Figure 8D; bootstrap (H2) over units, as stated above, and (H1) hierarchical over animals, sessions and units, as convention B. Reproduced when no combination finds PT earlier at p < 0.01; partially reproduced when some do and some do not; the onset difference is reported either way.

claims.statement: The tagged units of dandiset 000010 (Li et al. 2015) are the 45 PT and 27 IT cells of the electrophysiology dataset the paper compares its imaging with.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'We analyzed neuronal selectivity'; dandiset 000010 version 0.220126.1905
claims.quote: (PT/IT cells; electrophysiology, 45/27; imaging, 719/2,631)
claims.criterion: Added by the author of attempt 000015-chen-2017-01 (protocol, Author step 4). The paper names Li et al. (2015) and no deposit; dandiset 000010 is that paper's data on DANDI. No identifier links its units to the paper's analysis, so records are matched by label and count only. Reproduced when the units table of version 0.220126.1905 labels exactly 45 units PT and 27 IT.

claims.statement: MM neurons showed strong object location selectivity in superficial and deep layers and in PT and IT cells, PT cells particularly in the early delay; neither PT nor IT neurons in MM showed prominent lick direction selectivity before licking.
claims.source: Results, Projection-Specific Coding, paragraph beginning 'ALM neurons displayed prominent lick direction selectivity'; Figure 8D; Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Object location selectivity was widespread in MM'
claims.quote: In contrast, MM neurons displayed strong object location selectivity in both superficial and deep layers, and in both PT and IT cells. PT neurons in MM also displayed strong object location selectivity particularly during the early delay period ... Neither PT nor IT neurons in MM displayed prominent lick direction selectivity before licking movement
claims.criterion: Mean |alpha| and mean |beta| (non-significant set to 0) per bin for the Figure 8D groups of MM (deep PT, deep IT, deep other, superficial IT, superficial other) and of ALM, with bootstrap SD (convention B). Reproduced when (a) every MM group has a maximum of mean |alpha| in the sample or early delay (trial start to 2.2 s) larger than that of the ALM group of the same depth and projection type (the paper contrasts ALM, "little object location selectivity", with MM); (b) MM PT mean |alpha| over the first second of the delay is the largest of the MM groups; (c) before the go cue, the MM PT and MM IT maxima of mean |beta| are below half the ALM deep maximum. Partially reproduced when (a) holds and (b) or (c) does not. The thresholds are fixed here; the paper gives none.

claims.statement: MM neurons were more active in posterior trials, when the pole was within reach of the whiskers, than in anterior trials.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'MM shows little preparatory activity'; Figure 8D
claims.quote: Neurons were more active in posterior trials, when the pole was within reach of the whiskers, than in the anterior location, when the pole was out of reach (Figure 8D
claims.criterion: Mean alpha (signed, non-significant set to 0) of MM neurons per bin over the sample epoch, with bootstrap SD (convention B); alpha > 0 is posterior preferring. Reproduced when the mean over the sample epoch is above zero by more than 2 bootstrap SD (bound fixed here). dF/F by reading V1 (convention T); V2 is reported.

claims.statement: Overall, neurons preferring error trials outnumbered those preferring correct trials.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'We also observed neurons representing trial outcome'; Figure 8D
claims.quote: Overall, neurons preferring error trials outnumbered neurons preferring correct trials (Figure 8D
claims.criterion: The paper cites Figure 8D, which shows mean signed gamma (non-significant set to 0), and gives no count or test. Readings (a) among neurons purely outcome selective at any bin from the go cue to 2.5 s after it, those whose gamma at their most significant bin is negative (error preferring) against positive, error preferring more numerous by a two-sided binomial test at p < 0.05 (test fixed here); (b) mean signed gamma over all neurons, averaged over the same window, below zero by more than 2 bootstrap SD (convention B; bound fixed here). Reproduced when both readings find error preference. dF/F by reading V1 (convention T); V2 is reported.

claims.statement: Coding is mainly determined by cortical location; cortical area (ALM against MM) and cell depth explain most of the variance of selectivity, more than projection type.
claims.source: Results, Projection-Specific Coding, paragraph 4; Figure 8E and 8F
claims.quote: Our results suggest that coding of PT and IT neurons is primarily determined by their location in the motor cortex ... Cortical area ... and cell depth ... explained the majority of response variability (Figures 8E and 8F
claims.criterion: Methods, variance of neuronal selectivity. Groupings area (ALM, MM; k = 2), depth (z < 350 against z >= 350 um; k = 2) and projection type (PT, IT, other; k = 3). For each grouping and coefficient (alpha, beta, gamma, |alpha|, |beta|, |gamma|, non-significant set to 0), SST(t) and SSB(t) over neurons; variance explained(t) = SSB/SST (Figure 8E); total variance explained = sum over t and the three absolute coefficients of SSB over the same sum of SST, t from 4.6 s before to 2.5 s after the go cue (Figure 8F). The neurons are open, readings (N1) the three labelled mice for all groupings; (N2) all six mice for area and depth, the three for projection type. Reproduced when total variance explained by area is the largest of the three (the Summary, "Cortical area was more predictive of neuronal selectivity than laminar location or axonal projection target") and area and depth together exceed projection type; partially reproduced when area and depth together exceed projection type but area is not the largest. Depth against projection type alone is reported. Bootstrap SD as convention B.

claims.statement: Of 567 single units recorded with silicon probes in left ALM and MM of 3 mice, 393 distinguished trial types, 115 in the sample, 182 in the delay and 309 in the response epoch.
claims.source: Results, Comparison with Extracellular Electrophysiology, paragraph 2; Methods, Electrophysiology data analysis
claims.quote: We recorded single units (n = 567, 3 mice) in the left ALM and MM under identical behavioral conditions as the imaging experiments. The spikes rates of 393 neurons distinguished trial types during either sample (n = 115), delay (n = 182), or response epoch (n = 309
claims.criterion: Units 297 in ALM (13 sessions) and 270 in MM (11 sessions) (Methods); the unit count is exact. The 3-way ANOVA of convention M on spike counts in 400 ms windows in 100 ms steps. How windows make an epoch selective is open, readings (R1) any window wholly inside the epoch with p < 0.01 for any factor; (R2) any window whose centre is inside the epoch; (R3) the ANOVA on the spike count of the whole epoch. The response epoch length is not given; readings 1.2 s and 2.5 s after the go cue (the end of the Figure 8F window). Whether the fast-spiking and intermediate units are included is open; readings all 567; the 558 left when the 9 intermediate units are excluded (Methods, "Units with intermediate values ... were excluded"); and the 486 putative pyramidal units. Reproduced when all values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: In the silicon probe recordings, object-location-selective neurons were most frequent in MM, lick-direction-selective neurons mainly in ALM, and outcome and mixed neurons numerous in both; most object location, lick direction and outcome selectivity fell in the sample, delay/response and response epochs.
claims.source: Results, Comparison with Extracellular Electrophysiology, paragraph 2; Figure 7D
claims.quote: The majority of object location-, lick direction-, and outcome-selective neurons were observed during sample, delay/response, and response epochs, respectively (Figure 7D). Neurons selective for object location were observed most frequently in MM; neurons selective for lick direction were mainly observed in ALM; neurons selective for outcome and mixed neurons were numerous in both ALM and MM
claims.criterion: Fraction of units purely selective for each factor, and mixed, per 400 ms window (100 ms steps), in ALM and MM (Figure 7D). Reproduced when (a) the object-location fraction peaks in the sample epoch and the time-averaged fraction is higher in MM than ALM; (b) the lick-direction fraction averaged over delay and response is higher in ALM than MM, and its peak is in the delay or response epoch; (c) the outcome fraction peaks in the response epoch and is above 5% in both areas there; (d) the mixed fraction is above 5% in both areas in the response epoch. The 5% level (above the 1% expected by chance at p < 0.01) is fixed here.

claims.statement: Whisker movements were similar across the four trial types, so neurons coding whisker movement were likely classed as non-selective.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'MM shows little preparatory activity'; Figure 1C
claims.quote: In our experiments, whisker movements were similar across trial types (Figure 1) and neurons encoding whisker movements were likely classified as ‘‘non-selective.’’
claims.criterion: A claim of absence for which the paper names no test. Whisker angle from the 1 kHz video, whisking amplitude per trial averaged over the sample epoch, compared across the four trial types by a one-way ANOVA per session at p < 0.05 (test fixed here). Reproduced when the test finds no difference in most sessions (more than half); the effect size is reported. Not testable if the dataset holds no whisker tracking.

claims.statement: Even in ALM, less than 20% of PT or IT cells displayed lick direction selectivity at any given time, and the onset timing was variable.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'We analyzed neuronal selectivity'; Figures 6, 8 and S10 (not read)
claims.quote: even in ALM, less than 20% of PT or IT cells displayed lick direction selectivity at any given time (Figures 6, 8, and S10), and the onset timing was variable
claims.criterion: Per bin, the fraction of ALM PT cells and of ALM IT cells that are lick-direction selective (convention M), over the extracted window. Which cells count is open, readings (a) purely lick-direction selective (as Figure 6); (b) beta significant, pure or mixed (as the coefficients of Figure 8D). The paper's number is a bound; tolerance 10% of it. Reproduced when the largest fraction of each group stays below 22% under one reading. The variability of onset is not judged.

claims.statement: The imaging dataset has 135 sessions from 4 mice (45, 48, 7 and 35 sessions), with on average 480 neurons per session, about 40 inhibitory, 330 excitatory and 100 unclassified; inhibitory neurons are 11% of the population.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Quantification and statistical analysis; Results, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Our simultaneous imaging and decision-making dataset includes 135 sessions from 4 mice (45, 48, 7, and 35 sessions per mouse). Median number of trials per session is 213, 253, 264, and 222, for each mouse. On average, 480 neurons were imaged per session, out of which ~40 neurons were inhibitory and ~330 were excitatory
claims.criterion: Mice are matched to the paper's mouse 1 to 4 by their session counts (45, 48, 7, 35). Neurons are the ROIs kept as good quality; counts per session from the ROI type labels. The session counts per mouse are compared as well; trials per session are counted (a) as all trials in the trial table and (b) as trials with a correct or incorrect choice, the paper not saying which. The inhibitory fraction is read (a) as inhibitory over all neurons and (b) as inhibitory over excitatory plus inhibitory. Reproduced when every value is within tolerance under one reading of each.

claims.statement: Choices depend strongly on stimulus rate, at chance at the 16 Hz boundary and more accurate for rates further from it.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1B
claims.quote: Decisions depended strongly on stimulus rate: performance was at chance when the stimulus rate was at the category boundary, and was better at rates further from the category boundary
claims.criterion: Figure 1B uses 10 mice; only the 4 imaged mice can be tested here, which is recorded as a deviation. Per mouse, trials of all sessions with a left or right choice; the fraction of "high" choices per stimulus rate, and a logistic regression of the high choice on rate (as the legend's glmfit). The paper gives no test; the fit's slope is the measure, as a positive slope is choice accuracy rising with distance from the boundary. Chance at 16 Hz holds by design (the Methods reward 16 Hz randomly) and the fraction of high choices at 16 Hz is reported. Reproduced when, in every mouse, the slope is positive at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Choice depends on current stimulus strength, on the previous trial's outcome and on the time since the previous trial; the effect of a previous success is stronger after a short ITI, and ITI has no significant effect after a failure.
claims.source: Figure S1B; Results, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Top left: strength of the sensory evidence affects the animal's choices: the stronger the evidence, the higher the impact. Top middle: Success of a previous trial also affects animal's decision; the effect is stronger when the previous success occurs after a short ITI (<7sec). Top Right: Same but for previous incorrect trials; the effect of ITI after a failure was not significant
claims.criterion: The model of STAR Methods eq. 1 per session (glmfit, binomial, logit), predicting a left choice. Stimulus strength as six bins of |rate - 16 Hz| of width 2 Hz (0-2, 2-4, ..., 10-12 Hz; code, behavior/trialHist_logisRegress_setVar.m with vec_ratesdiff = 0:2:12), signed by the side the rate favours; previous success and previous failure each split at an ITI of 7 s (code, vec_iti); trials with ITI over 30 s set aside (code). The ITI is the time from the previous choice to the current stimulus onset (Methods). The figure plots coefficients averaged over animals (10 mice; here 4) with SEM. The paper names no test; the two-tailed t-test of the Methods is used across mice, and across sessions per mouse as a second reading. Reproduced when the stimulus coefficients grow with strength (the largest bin above the smallest), the short-ITI success coefficient exceeds the long-ITI one significantly, and the two failure coefficients do not differ significantly (absence judged on that t-test).

claims.statement: Inferred spiking activity differs significantly between inhibitory and excitatory neurons throughout the trial, and in the bin just before the choice in every mouse.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 1G, H and I
claims.quote: The magnitude of inferred spiking activity was significantly different for inhibitory vs. excitatory neurons throughout the trial ( Figure 1G ; t-test, p<0.001). Just before the choice (97 ms, average of 3 frames), this difference was clear ( Figure 1H ) and significant for all mice ( Figure 1I , t-test; p<0.001)
claims.criterion: Correct trials (code, excInh_FRs.py). The bin 0-97 ms before the choice; activity averaged over trials per neuron. The paper does not say over what unit its t-test runs; the code (excInh_FRs.py) tests both, so the readings are (a) an unpaired two-tailed t-test across days of the day means (legend of 1I, mean +/- SEM across days) and (b) the same test on neurons pooled over days. The text does not say which cell type is higher; the direction is reported. Reproduced when p < 0.001 in every mouse, and for the example-mouse time course in every choice-aligned bin of at least one mouse under reading (a).

claims.statement: In an example session (285 excitatory and 29 inhibitory neurons), 24 excitatory (8%) and 5 inhibitory (17%) neurons were significantly choice selective just before the choice.
claims.source: Figure 2A legend
claims.quote: Data correspond to the 97 ms window preceding choice (285 excitatory and 29 inhibitory neurons) ... 5 inhibitory and 24 excitatory neurons (17% and 8%, respectively) were significantly choice selective
claims.criterion: The session is not named; it is the session with 285 excitatory and 29 inhibitory neurons, if exactly one has these counts. ROC as in the opening comment. The shuffle makes counts vary from run to run, like a random seed; as a standard choice the 50-shuffle procedure is repeated 20 times, and the claim is reproduced when the median count is within tolerance. Not testable if no session has these counts.

claims.statement: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons have a similar fraction of significantly choice-selective neurons just before the choice (median across mice 13% and 16%, about 43 excitatory and 6 inhibitory neurons per session); the difference is significant in mouse 4.
claims.source: Results, Individual excitatory and inhibitory neurons are similarly choice-selective, paragraph 1; Figure 2C
claims.quote: Importantly, excitatory and inhibitory neurons were similar in terms of the fraction of choice-selective neurons ( Figure 2B , C ; Figure S3B , C )
claims.criterion: ROC as in the opening comment, bin 0-97 ms before the choice (Methods). Per session the fraction of each cell type that is selective; per mouse the mean over sessions, then the median over the 4 mice. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, an unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse at p < 0.05 (Methods and code, ttest2). The paper reports a significant difference in mouse 4 only. Reproduced when the two medians are within tolerance and no significant difference is found in mice 1, 2 and 3; partially reproduced when only the t-tests hold. The per-session counts are read as the median across mice of the mean count per session. The normal-fit criterion is the code's; an empirical p from the 50 shuffles (two-sided, fraction of shuffles at least as far from 0.5) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The fraction of choice-selective neurons and the magnitude of choice selectivity increase gradually over the trial and peak just after the choice.
claims.source: Results, Individual excitatory and inhibitory neurons are similarly choice-selective, paragraph 1; Figure 2B and 2D
claims.quote: The fraction of choice-selective neurons ( Figure 2B ) and the magnitude of choice selectivity ( Figure 2D ) gradually increased over the trial, peaking just after the animal reported its choice
claims.criterion: ROC per 97 ms bin of the choice-aligned traces, as in the opening comment; per mouse the mean over sessions for each bin and cell type (the figure shows an example mouse, mean over 45 days). "Just after" is not fixed; readings are (a) the peak falls in the first bin after the choice (0-97 ms) and (b) it falls within 300 ms after the choice, the window the Methods give for the confirmation lick. Reproduced when, in at least the example mouse (the one with 45 sessions) and for both measures and both cell types, the earliest choice-aligned bin is below the bin before the choice and the peak lies in the window.

claims.statement: The magnitude and time course of choice selectivity are similar for excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: Results, Individual excitatory and inhibitory neurons are similarly choice-selective, paragraph 1; Figure 2D and 2E
claims.quote: as well as the magnitude and time course ( Figure 2D , E ) of choice selectivity
claims.criterion: Selectivity 2*|AUC-0.5| from correct trials (code), averaged over the neurons of each cell type per session, bin 0-97 ms before choice. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, an unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse at p < 0.05 (Methods; code choicePref_ROC_exc_inh_plotsAllMice.m, ttest2). Reproduced when no mouse shows a significant difference; partially reproduced when one mouse does; the mean difference per mouse is reported either way. For the time course the same test is shown per bin.

claims.statement: Restricted to excitatory and inhibitory neurons with the same spiking activity, choice selectivity is still similar, and the difference in mouse 4 of Figure 2C disappears.
claims.source: Results, Individual excitatory and inhibitory neurons are similarly choice-selective, paragraph 1; Figure S3D
claims.quote: D, ROC analysis restricted to those excitatory and inhibitory neurons that had the same spiking activity. Choice selectivity is still similar between the two cell types. Note that the significant difference observed for mouse 4 in Figure 2C is absent after controlling for the difference in spiking activity of inhibitory and excitatory neurons
claims.criterion: Matching as the Methods give for Figure S10D, E and as the code does (choicePref_ROC_exc_inh_plotsAllMice_sameFR.m) per session, the median activity over trials in the bin 0-97 ms before choice for each neuron, the range of medians cut into 50 bins, and only the neurons of both types in the bin that holds the most inhibitory neurons kept. A claim of absence, judged on the unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse at p < 0.05 (code, ttest2) on the session-mean selectivity and the session fraction selective. Reproduced when no mouse, mouse 4 included, shows a significant difference.

claims.statement: ROC on the window from 200 ms before to 300 ms after the choice gives a larger fraction of selective neurons, 21% of excitatory and 27% of inhibitory (median across mice), about 69 excitatory and 11 inhibitory neurons per session.
claims.source: Figure S3C
claims.quote: Fraction selective neurons at this time window (median across mice): excitatory: 21%; inhibitory: 27%, resulting in approximately 11 inhibitory and 69 excitatory neurons with significant choice selectivity per session
claims.criterion: As fig2bc-fraction-selective-similar, with activity averaged over the window before the ROC. The code (choicePref_ROC_exc_inh.m, aveAllTimes = -1) averages the bins from 2 before to 3 after the choice bin, 194 ms before to 291 ms after; readings are (a) that and (b) the frames from 200 ms before to 300 ms after the choice. Reproduced when all four values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Choice selectivity on correct and on error trials is positively correlated across neurons, so most neurons reflect the choice more than the stimulus, and within each mouse this correlation is very similar for excitatory and inhibitory neurons; it is weaker in mouse 4.
claims.source: Results, Individual excitatory and inhibitory neurons are similarly choice-selective, paragraph 2; Figure S3E
claims.quote: Importantly, however, within each subject, this correlation was very similar for excitatory vs. inhibitory neurons ( Figure S3E ), suggesting that the tendency for neurons to be modulated by the choice vs. the stimulus was similar in excitatory and inhibitory neurons
claims.criterion: Per session and neuron, AUC on correct trials and AUC on error trials (same left against right labels, bin 0-97 ms before choice); Pearson r across neurons per cell type; per mouse the mean r across sessions. Sessions need at least 10 error trials of each choice (the code's ROC threshold, applied to error trials; a reading). Reproduced when the mean r is positive for both types in every mouse, the excitatory and inhibitory means do not differ in any mouse by the paper's unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions at p < 0.05, and mouse 4 has the lowest mean r for at least one type.

claims.statement: Choice can be decoded from population activity well above chance, and inhibitory populations decode it as accurately as excitatory populations of the same size, in every mouse.
claims.source: Results, Choice is decoded with equal accuracy from both excitatory and inhibitory populations, paragraph 2; Figure 3B and 3C
claims.quote: Classification accuracy of inhibitory neurons was well above chance and was very similar to that of excitatory neurons ( Figure 3B , red and blue traces overlap; Figure S4 ... Similar classification accuracy for excitatory and inhibitory populations was observed in all subjects ( Figure 3C )
claims.criterion: Decoders as in the opening comment, correct trials, bin 0-97 ms before the choice, per session the accuracy averaged over the 50 repetitions (and over the 50 excitatory subsamples). Per mouse, accuracy is above chance when it exceeds the shuffled control by an unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions at p < 0.05. Equality is a claim of absence, judged on the paper's unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse (code, svm_excInh_trainDecoder_eachFrame_plots_sumAllMice.py, ttest_ind) at p < 0.05. Reproduced when in every mouse both cell types are above chance and do not differ; partially reproduced when they differ in one mouse. Mean accuracies are reported.

claims.statement: Accuracy of the all-neuron choice decoder grows after stimulus onset and peaks at the time of the choice.
claims.source: Results, Choice is decoded with equal accuracy from both excitatory and inhibitory populations, paragraph 1; Figure 3B
claims.quote: Classification accuracy gradually grew after stimulus onset and peaked at the time of the choice ( Figure 3B , black)
claims.criterion: All-neuron decoder trained and tested on each 97 ms bin of choice-aligned traces, correct trials; per mouse the mean over sessions. Figure 3B is one session; tested on the mouse means. "At the time of the choice" is read as (a) the peak in one of the two bins around the choice (97 ms before to 97 ms after) and (b) the peak within 300 ms of the choice. Reproduced when in every mouse the earliest choice-aligned bin is lower than the bin before the choice and the peak lies in the window.

claims.statement: In the decoder trained on all neurons, excitatory and inhibitory neurons receive weights of matched magnitude throughout the trial and with very similar distributions.
claims.source: Results, Choice is decoded with equal accuracy from both excitatory and inhibitory populations, paragraph 3; Figure 3D, E and F
claims.quote: The weight magnitudes of excitatory and inhibitory neurons were matched for the entire trial ( Figure 3D ), and the distributions of weights was very similar ( Figures 3E , F )
claims.criterion: All-neuron decoder at the best C, weights averaged over the 50 repetitions, each session's weight vector normalised to unit length (Methods); mean |w| per cell type per session at 0-97 ms before choice and per bin. Figure 3F marks a significant difference (star) in some mice that the text does not name. Judged on the paper's unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse at p < 0.05. Reproduced when no mouse differs, partially reproduced when one or two mice do, not reproduced otherwise; the pooled counts are compared with the expected values, and the mean |w| per mouse is reported.

claims.statement: A population of half excitatory and half inhibitory neurons decodes choice with accuracy similar to that of an excitatory population of the same size, so a mixed population offers no major advantage.
claims.source: Results, Choice is decoded with equal accuracy from both excitatory and inhibitory populations, paragraph 4; Figure 3H and 3I
claims.quote: Classification accuracy was similar for both decoders ( Figure 3H , I ), arguing that a mixed population offers no major advantage to decoding
claims.criterion: As the code (svm_excInh_trainDecoder_eachFrame.py, excInhHalf and allExc2inhSize) the mixed population is all n inhibitory neurons plus a random subsample of n excitatory neurons, and the control is 2n excitatory neurons, both over 50 subsamples; correct trials, bin 0-97 ms before choice. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse at p < 0.05. Reproduced when no mouse shows a significant difference between the two decoders in either direction; the difference per mouse is reported.

claims.statement: Excitatory and inhibitory populations are equally choice selective when decoders are trained on fluorescence traces.
claims.source: Results, Choice is decoded with equal accuracy from both excitatory and inhibitory populations, paragraph 2; Figure S5
claims.quote: Excitatory and inhibitory populations were equally choice selective even when the analysis was performed on raw calcium traces ( Figure S5 )
claims.criterion: As fig3bc-decoding-similar, with the CNMF denoised fluorescence traces (Figure S5A uses those of Figure 1D middle; code option do_Ctrace) in place of inferred spikes. The legend calls them fluorescence traces and the text raw calcium traces; readings are (a) the denoised traces and (b) Delta F/F traces. Same test and outcome rule.

claims.statement: Population activity is weakly informative about the previous trial's choice and about the stimulus category (the stimulus category weakly except in mouse 4), and excitatory and inhibitory populations are similarly selective for both.
claims.source: Results, Choice is decoded with equal accuracy from both excitatory and inhibitory populations, paragraph 5; Figure S6A and S6B
claims.quote: Excitatory and inhibitory populations were similarly selective for previous choice ( Figure S6A ). The population activity was also somewhat informative about whether the stimulus was above or below the category boundary ( Figure S6B ). Again, excitatory and inhibitory populations were similarly selective
claims.criterion: Decoders as in the opening comment. Stimulus category uses stimulus-aligned trials with equal numbers of left and right choices in each category (Methods). For previous choice the paper gives no alignment or window; readings are (a) choice-aligned traces, bin 0-97 ms before the choice, and (b) the first bins of the trial, before stimulus onset (the code's trialHistAnalysis option, which uses the ITI period). Above chance by the unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions against the shuffle; equality judged on the same test between cell types. Reproduced when, for both decoders, the all-neuron decoder is above chance in most mice and no mouse shows a significant excitatory to inhibitory difference; partially reproduced when one mouse does. The Figure S6B legend excepts mouse 4 from the weak stimulus-category signal, not from the excitatory to inhibitory comparison; the all-neuron accuracy per mouse is reported. The bin for stimulus category is (a) 0-97 ms before stimulus offset and (b) the bin of peak all-neuron accuracy; the paper fixes neither.

claims.statement: Population activity is strongly selective for trial outcome, reaching about 80% accuracy (median across mice) about 400 ms after the confirmation lick, with inhibitory neurons slightly more accurate than excitatory neurons after reward.
claims.source: Results, Choice is decoded with equal accuracy from both excitatory and inhibitory populations, paragraph 5; Figure S6C
claims.quote: Classification accuracy gradually increases and reaches 80% (median across mice) approximately 400ms after the animal confirms his choice (Figure S1A). Inhibitory neurons showed slightly higher selectivity for the outcome
claims.criterion: Outcome-aligned trials (aligned to the confirmation lick, the reward time), with equal numbers of left and right choice trials for each outcome (Methods); decoders otherwise as in the opening comment. The all-neuron accuracy at the bin containing 400 ms after the confirmation lick, mean over sessions per mouse, median over mice, within tolerance. Inhibitory above subsampled excitatory in every mouse (the text's "small but consistent difference"), in the mean over bins after the confirmation lick (the paper's "after reward delivery"); the end of the window is open, read as (a) 500 ms after the confirmation lick and (b) the end of the outcome-aligned traces. The paper gives no test for this difference; the unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse is reported. Reproduced when both hold.

claims.statement: Decoders trained on correct trials predict the choice on incorrect trials with high accuracy, slightly lower than on correct trials, and the reduction is similar for excitatory and inhibitory populations in every mouse.
claims.source: Figure S6D and S6E
claims.quote: Importantly, for all mice, the change in classification accuracy was quite similar for excitatory and inhibitory neurons (right), indicating that both populations reflect choice vs. stimulus to a comparable degree
claims.criterion: Decoders trained on correct trials at each bin and tested on held-out correct trials and on incorrect trials (code, testIncorr); bin 0-97 ms before choice. Accuracy on incorrect trials is high when above the shuffle by the unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse. The reduction (correct minus incorrect) of inhibitory and subsampled excitatory decoders is compared by the same test; a claim of absence. Reproduced when incorrect-trial accuracy is above the shuffle in every mouse and the reductions do not differ significantly in any mouse; mouse 4 should have the largest reduction for the all-neuron decoder.

claims.statement: Choice decoders lose accuracy at a similar rate away from their training time for excitatory and inhibitory populations, and their stability duration is indistinguishable.
claims.source: Results, Choice is decoded with equal accuracy from both excitatory and inhibitory populations, paragraph 6; Figure 4B, C and D; Figure S7A
claims.quote: This drop in accuracy occurred at a similar rate for excitatory and inhibitory populations ( Figure 4B ). To quantify this, we determined the time window over which classifier accuracy remained within 2 standard deviations of the accuracy at the training time ( Figure 4C ). This was indistinguishable for excitatory and inhibitory neurons ( Figure 4D ; Figure S7A )
claims.criterion: Decoders trained at each bin and tested at every bin on held-out trials (Methods), correct trials. For the decoder trained at 0-97 ms before choice, a test bin counts as stable when its accuracy is at least the accuracy at the training bin minus 2 standard deviations across the 50 repetitions (Methods and Figure 4C legend). The code (svm_excInh_trainDecoder_eachFrame_stabTestTimes_setVars_post.py) uses 2 standard errors (SD over the square root of the number of repetitions); since the Methods say standard deviations, the code's choice is shown as a variant. Stability duration is the number of stable bins times 97 ms (code, bins not required to be contiguous; contiguous bins around the training bin shown as a variant). Excitatory durations are averaged over the 50 subsamples. Sessions where the training-bin accuracy does not exceed the shuffle are left out (code, one-tailed t-test across repetitions; the code's alpha 0.001 and the Methods' general 0.05 are both readings). A claim of absence, judged on the code's test, an unpaired two-tailed t-test of the four mouse means (svm_excInh_trainDecoder_eachFrame_stabTestTimes_plots.py, ttest_ind across mice); the per-mouse test across sessions is shown as a variant. Reproduced when that test finds no difference.

claims.statement: The angle between decoders trained at different times shows a similar time course of stability for excitatory and inhibitory populations.
claims.source: Results, Choice is decoded with equal accuracy from both excitatory and inhibitory populations, paragraph 6; Figure S7C
claims.quote: An alternate method for assessing stability, computing the angle between the weights of pairs of classifiers trained at different time windows, likewise suggested that excitatory and inhibitory populations are similarly stable
claims.criterion: Angle in degrees between the weight vectors (averaged over repetitions) of decoders trained at each pair of bins, per session and cell type (excitatory over the 50 subsamples). The paper gives no summary or test; readings are (a) the mean angle over all pairs of bins and (b) the mean angle between the decoder at 0-97 ms before choice and each other bin. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse at p < 0.05. Reproduced when no mouse shows a significant difference.

claims.statement: In a model with non-selective inhibition, inhibitory neurons decode the choice less accurately than excitatory neurons for every ratio of excitatory-to-inhibitory to inhibitory-to-excitatory connection strength.
claims.source: Results, Modeling rules out decision circuits with non-selective inhibition, paragraph 2; Figure 5A; Figure S8
claims.quote: For this value (and indeed for all other values), inhibitory neurons had lower classification accuracy than excitatory neurons ( Figure 5A , bottom; Figure S8 , left), inconsistent with our experimental results
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. The linearised rate model of the STAR Methods with the printed parameters (sigma 1.25, delta 0.75, wEE 0.25, wII -2, wIE(0) 0.87, wEI(0) -0.87, c 0.1, NE 4000, NI 1000, n 50, h0 0.1), decoding accuracy Phi(sqrt(S/N)/2) from the input-averaged S/N, one network per point, the product wIE*wEI held at the reference while the ratio varies. The range of the ratio is not given; the range is read from Figure 5 if the PDF is supplied, otherwise 0.1 to 10 on a log scale (a standard choice). Reproduced when inhibitory accuracy is below excitatory at every value.

claims.statement: In signal-selective and SNR-selective models, inhibitory and excitatory neurons have matched decoding accuracy near the biologically plausible regime of equal excitatory-to-inhibitory and inhibitory-to-excitatory strengths; in all three models, accuracy rises faster for inhibitory than for excitatory neurons as the excitatory-to-inhibitory strength increases.
claims.source: Results, Modeling rules out decision circuits with non-selective inhibition, paragraphs 3 and 4; Figure 5B and 5C
claims.quote: In this circuit architecture, inhibitory and excitatory neurons had matched classification accuracy when the connection strength from excitatory to inhibitory neurons was about the same as the strength from inhibitory to excitatory ... Thus, in all panels of Figure 5 , classification accuracy increases faster for inhibitory neurons than excitatory ones as the excitatory to inhibitory connection strength increases
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. As fig5a-nonselective-model; signal-selective with rho 0.75 and the input split by population, averaged over 25 networks and 100 random picks of 50 neurons; SNR-selective with W_IE scaled by (r_j/NE)^4 and rescaled to the same mean. Reproduced when, for each model, the excitatory and inhibitory accuracy curves cross within a factor of 2 of a ratio of 1 (a reading of "about the same" and "near"), and when inhibitory accuracy rises faster than excitatory with the ratio in all three models.

claims.statement: The signal-selective model has the highest decoding accuracy of the three models at every connection-strength ratio and level of differential correlations, in both cell types.
claims.source: Results, Modeling rules out decision circuits with non-selective inhibition, paragraph 6; Figure S9
claims.quote: For all values of this parameter and in both cell types, signal-selective model has the highest classification accuracy for decoding the animal's choice
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. As fig5bc-selective-models-match, with differential correlations added as Sigma to Sigma + epsilon Delta h Delta h^T for epsilon 0, 0.25 and 0.5 (Figure S8 legend; which Sigma is garbled in the text, read as both Sigma_EE and Sigma_II, and as Sigma_EE only, two readings). The paper says "significantly" without a test; the claim is judged on the ordering. Reproduced when the signal-selective accuracy is highest at every ratio, epsilon and cell type.

claims.statement: Noise correlations are stronger between neurons with the same choice selectivity than between neurons with opposite selectivity, for excitatory-inhibitory, excitatory-excitatory and inhibitory-inhibitory pairs, significant in every mouse except mouse 3 for EE and II pairs; the same holds in the spontaneous pre-trial period.
claims.source: Results, Correlations are stronger between similarly tuned neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 6A; Figure S10A
claims.quote: Indeed, neurons with the same choice selectivity had stronger correlations ( Figure 6A )
