claims.criterion: As the Methods and code (imaging/corr_excInh_plots.m and corr_excInh_setVars.m) neurons are "ipsi" or "contra" preferring by the sign of AUC - 0.5 at 0-97 ms before choice (AUC from correct trials; significance not required); noise correlations from the same bin on trials with a choice, after subtracting each choice's mean response from its trials; Pearson r per pair; each neuron's r averaged over its partners of the given type and preference. Spontaneous correlations use the bin 0-97 ms before the initiation tone, without subtraction. The code tests same against opposite with an unpaired t-test on neurons pooled over sessions (ttest2); the across-session test (the legend's mean +/- SEM across days) is shown as a variant. Reproduced when same exceeds opposite significantly (p < 0.05) for EI pairs in all four mice and for EE and II pairs in mice 1, 2 and 4, and spontaneous correlations show the same pattern by the same test (the text's "the same correlation effects"; Figure S10A gives no test of its own); partially reproduced when this holds for at least two of the three pair types.

claims.statement: Inhibitory pairs have significantly higher noise correlations than excitatory pairs, with intermediate values for excitatory-inhibitory pairs, also for spontaneous correlations and for neurons matched in spiking activity.
claims.source: Results, Correlations are stronger between similarly tuned neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 6B and 6C; Figure S10B to S10E
claims.quote: Inhibitory pairs had significantly higher noise correlations compared to excitatory pairs ... This was true even when we restricted the analysis to inhibitory and excitatory neurons with the same inferred spiking activity ( Figure S10D , E ). Finally, similar to previous reports ... we found intermediate correlations for pairs consisting of one inhibitory neuron and one excitatory neuron ( Figure S10B , C )
claims.criterion: Per-neuron noise correlation as in fig6a-same-selectivity-correlations, averaged over partners of the same type (EE, II) or the other type (EI), bin 0-97 ms before choice; spontaneous as there; matched activity by the 50-bin "max bin" rule of the Methods. Readings for the test, an unpaired two-tailed t-test (Methods), are (a) across sessions per mouse on session means (Figure 6C, mean +/- SEM across days) and (b) on neurons pooled over sessions (code, utils/plotHist.m). Reproduced when II exceeds EE significantly in every mouse for noise, spontaneous and matched-activity correlations, with EI between them in the mean; the expected counts are matched by one mouse (the example mouse is not named).

claims.statement: Removing noise correlations by building pseudo populations increases choice decoding accuracy of the full population in every mouse.
claims.source: Results, Noise correlations limit decoding accuracy, paragraph 2; Figure 7A and 7B
claims.quote: In all mice, removing noise correlations resulted in a consistent increase in classification accuracy ( Figure 7B ; filled vs. open circles), establishing that noise correlations limit population accuracy in PPC
claims.criterion: All neurons, bin 0-97 ms before choice; neurons ranked by |AUC - 0.5| and added one at a time from the most selective (Methods); the AUC used for ranking is from all trials with a choice in the code (svm_excInh_trainDecoder_eachFrame.py), and from correct trials as a variant. Pseudo populations shuffle trial order independently for each neuron within left-choice and within right-choice trials (Methods). The change is pseudo minus real accuracy at the largest ensemble (Methods; code changeCA_shflTrsEachN). Trials are correct trials (as the other Figure 3 decoders); all trials with a choice is a second reading. Reproduced when the mean change across sessions is positive in every mouse and significant by the two-tailed t-test across sessions at p < 0.05, read as (a) a one-sample test of the per-session changes and (b) an unpaired test of pseudo against real accuracy, in every mouse.

claims.statement: During learning, choice decoding accuracy increases and correlates with behavioural performance across sessions, for all, excitatory and inhibitory populations (r = 0.55, 0.35, 0.32 in mouse 2 and 0.57, 0.63, 0.32 in mouse 3).
claims.source: Results, Selectivity increases in parallel in inhibitory and excitatory populations during learning, paragraph 1; Figure 8A, 8B and 8D
claims.quote: Classification accuracy of the choice decoder increased consistently as animals became experts in decision-making ( Figure 8A , left; Figure 8D , black), leading to a strong correlation between classifier accuracy and mouse performance over training ( Figure 8B , left)
claims.criterion: The 3 mice imaged through learning (by Figure S1C, mice 1, 2 and 4; the code's fni16, fni17, fni19). A decoder per session, bin 0-97 ms before choice. Trials are all outcomes in the code's learning script (svm_excInh_trainDecoder_eachFrame_beh_sumAllMice_plots.py, corrTrained = 0); readings are (a) all trials with a choice, balanced only by choice, and (b) equal numbers of correct and incorrect trials within each choice (the code's decodeChoiceEqCorrIncorr option). Performance is the fraction correct on easy trials (Figure 8B legend); easy as the code (svm_excInh_trainDecoder_eachFrame_stabAngles_setVars_behCA.py, thQStimStrength = [3]), the outermost of four equal bins of |rate - 16 Hz| on each side. The legend's "mouse 2" and "mouse 3" can be read as (a) the second and third of the three learning mice in the paper's numbering (mice 2 and 4) and (b) the paper's mice 2 and 3; the example mouse is the remaining one. Reproduced when in each learning mouse r is positive with p < 0.05 for all three populations and the six reported values are within tolerance under one reading of the mouse names; partially reproduced when only the signs and p-values hold.

claims.statement: The choice signal emerges progressively earlier in the trial as mice become experts, so the onset of above-chance decoding correlates negatively with performance (r = -0.60, -0.34, -0.38 in mouse 2 and -0.60, -0.27, -0.28 in mouse 3 for all, excitatory and inhibitory).
claims.source: Results, Selectivity increases in parallel in inhibitory and excitatory populations during learning, paragraph 1; Figure 8C and 8E
claims.quote: This resulted in a negative correlation between mouse performance and the onset of super-threshold decoding accuracy ( Figure 8C , left; Figure 8E , black)
claims.criterion: Decoders and mice as fig8ab-learning-accuracy, at every bin of choice-aligned traces. Per session and bin, accuracy against the shuffle by a t-test across the 50 repetitions; the onset is the start of the first run of significant bins lasting at least 500 ms (5 bins, code th1), in ms from the choice; sessions without such a run are left out (Methods). The Methods give p < 0.05; the code (svm_excInh_trainDecoder_eachFrame_plots.py) uses 0.001, shown as a variant. The code tests excitatory data against the inhibitory shuffle at one line (line 600); the excitatory shuffle is used, as the Methods describe. Reproduced when the correlation is negative with p < 0.05 for all three populations in each learning mouse and the six values are within tolerance under one reading of the mouse names; partially reproduced when only the signs and p-values hold.

claims.statement: The choice signal emerges at the same time in excitatory and inhibitory populations, and its magnitude and timing are matched for the two cell types throughout learning.
claims.source: Results, Selectivity increases in parallel in inhibitory and excitatory populations during learning, paragraph 1; Figure 8A to 8E
claims.quote: Importantly, the choice signal emerged at the same time in both populations, and its magnitude and timing was matched for the two cell types throughout learning ( Figure 8A - C , middle, right; Figure 8D - E , blue, red)
claims.criterion: Early and late days as the Methods give, by behavioural performance below the 20th or above the 80th percentile of all days; readings are (a) every day beyond the percentile (code, perc_thb = [20, 80]) and (b) only the run of days at the start (early) or end (late) of training beyond it (the Methods' "initial" and "last" days). Accuracy (bin 0-97 ms before choice) and onset of inhibitory and subsampled excitatory decoders in early and in late days. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's unpaired two-tailed t-test across days per mouse at p < 0.05. Reproduced when, in every learning mouse, neither accuracy nor onset differs between the cell types in early or late days, and late accuracy exceeds early accuracy for both types (Figure 8D) by the same test.

claims.statement: The learning-related increase in decoding accuracy remains when the number of trials is equal in every session.
claims.source: Results, Selectivity increases in parallel in inhibitory and excitatory populations during learning, paragraph 1; Figure S13C
claims.quote: This was not due to the presence of more correct trials in later sessions: an improvement in classification accuracy was clear even when the number of correct trials was matched for each session ( Figure S13C )
claims.criterion: Decoders trained on correct trials only (legend), with the same number of trials in every session of a mouse, the minimum over its sessions (code, same_HRLR_acrossDays). Late accuracy above early accuracy for all neurons by the unpaired two-tailed t-test across days at p < 0.05 in every learning mouse; early and late days as fig8de-learning-parallel.

claims.statement: Licking and running do not explain the learning-related changes; centre-spout licks before left and right choices are similar early and late in training, and decoding remains accurate in sessions where running did not differ between choices.
claims.source: Results, Selectivity increases in parallel in inhibitory and excitatory populations during learning, paragraph 2; Figure S12
claims.quote: Nonetheless, when we restricted our analysis to days in which running distance was indistinguishable for the two choices (0-97 ms before the choice, t-test, P>0.05), classifiers could still accurately predict the choice ( Figure S12D )
claims.criterion: Licks to the centre spout in the 250 ms before the choice, as a lick-rate trace per choice (the bin width is not given; 10 ms is a standard choice that cannot change the sign of a correlation much, shown with 1 ms as a variant); per session the Pearson r of the left-choice and right-choice traces; early against late days (as fig8de-learning-parallel) by the unpaired two-tailed t-test, a claim of absence. Running distance from the wheel encoder in the bin 0-97 ms before choice, left against right by a t-test per session; on sessions with P > 0.05, all-neuron accuracy above the shuffle. Reproduced when lick correlations do not differ between early and late days in any learning mouse and accuracy is above the shuffle in the selected sessions of every mouse.

claims.statement: Pairwise noise correlations are higher early in training than late, for all combinations of neuron types.
claims.source: Results, Selectivity increases in parallel in inhibitory and excitatory populations during learning, paragraph 3; Figure 8F
claims.quote: Pairwise correlations in neural activity were higher early in training, when mice were novices, compared to late in training, when mice approached expert behavior ( Figure 8F , unsaturated colors above saturated colors). This was observed for all combinations of neural pairs ( Figure 8F )
claims.criterion: Noise correlations as fig6bc-inhibitory-correlations-higher (EE, II, EI), early and late days as fig8de-learning-parallel. The paper gives no test; the Methods' two-tailed t-test (unpaired, across days per mouse) at p < 0.05 is used. Reproduced when early exceeds late significantly for all three pair types in every learning mouse; partially reproduced when early exceeds late in the mean for every type and mouse but not significantly in all.

claims.statement: Decoding accuracy of pseudo populations, which lack noise correlations, also increases significantly with training, so reduced noise correlations do not alone explain the improved accuracy.
claims.source: Results, Selectivity increases in parallel in inhibitory and excitatory populations during learning, paragraph 3; Figure S13A and S13B
claims.quote: Interestingly, a significant increase in the classification accuracy of pseudo populations was present ( Figure S13A , B )
claims.criterion: Pseudo populations as fig7-noise-correlations-limit-decoding, for all, subsampled excitatory and inhibitory decoders, bin 0-97 ms before choice, trials as fig8ab; early and late days as fig8de-learning-parallel. Reproduced when late exceeds early by the unpaired two-tailed t-test across days at p < 0.05 in every learning mouse for the all-neuron decoder, and in the same direction for both cell types.

claims.statement: The fraction of choice-selective neurons increases about threefold from early to late training, in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: Results, Selectivity increases in parallel in inhibitory and excitatory populations during learning, paragraph 3; Figure 8G
claims.quote: Indeed, the fraction of choice-selective neurons increased threefold during training, in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons ( Figure 8G )
claims.criterion: ROC as in the opening comment, bin 0-97 ms before choice; early and late days as fig8de-learning-parallel; per mouse the mean fraction over early and over late days. The ratio can be read (a) per mouse and cell type, then the mean over mice, and (b) on fractions pooled over the three mice. Reproduced when, for both cell types, the ratio is within tolerance under one reading and late exceeds early by the unpaired two-tailed t-test across days in every learning mouse (code choicePref_ROC_exc_inh_plotsAllMice.m, ttest2); partially reproduced when the increase is significant but the ratio outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons have similar temporal dynamics, with similar distributions of peak-activity times across the trial.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure S2
claims.quote: Diverse temporal dynamics were evident in both cell types ( Figure 1E , F ) and did not appreciably differ between the two ( Figure S2 )
claims.criterion: Per session, the fraction of neurons of each type whose trial-averaged activity peaks in each 100 ms window, traces aligned to each trial event and concatenated (Figure S2 and 1E legends); the alignment windows around each event are not given, and the windows used by the dataset's trial-segmented responses are used. The paper gives no test; the Methods' unpaired two-tailed t-test across sessions per mouse in each window, a claim of absence. With many windows, readings are (a) uncorrected p < 0.05 and (b) Bonferroni over windows. Reproduced when, in every mouse, the number of windows that differ is no more than expected by chance under (a) (binomial test at 0.05) and none differs under (b).

claims.statement: CNMF removes neuropil contamination as well as annulus subtraction; for an example component the two traces correlate with r = 0.96.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Neuropil Contamination removal; Figure S14
claims.quote: The comparison showed a very high degree of similarity between the two traces ( Figure S14 ; example component; r=0.96)
claims.criterion: Needs the raw movies; footprints binarised at 20% of their maximum, annulus at 3 pixels from the mask and 7 pixels wide, background subtracted, compared with the CNMF Delta F/F trace (Methods). The example component is not named; reproduced when the median r over components with annuli free of other sources is within tolerance (r cannot exceed 1, so the tolerance is the room to 1).

claims.statement: In GAD-Cre;Ai14 mice 98.2% of tdTomato neurons in PPC express GABA, and all GABA neurons express tdTomato.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Immunofluorescence staining for TdTomato and GABA; Figure S15
claims.quote: 98.2 % of tdTomato neurons expressed GABA, and all of the GABAergic neurons expressed tdTomato
claims.criterion: Needs the immunostained coronal sections (5 sections including PPC). Counts of tdTomato, GABA and double-labelled cells; tolerance is the room to 100%. Reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance and no GABA cell lacks tdTomato.

claims.statement: On high-contrast single-stimulus trials mice made 1.7 ± 2.5% incorrect choices and 10.1 ± 8.3% Misses (mean ± s.d. over 39 sessions of 10 mice).
claims.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraph 1; Fig. 1c,d
claims.quote: Their choices were most accurate for high-contrast single stimuli (i.e. when the other stimulus was absent; 1.7 ± 2.5% incorrect choices, i.e. turns in the wrong direction; 10.1 ± 8.3% Misses, i.e. failures to turn; mean ± s.d., n = 39 sessions, 10 mice)
claims.criterion: Trials with the high contrast on one side and zero on the other. Per session, the percentage of such trials with a turn to the wrong side, and with no turn (the task's recorded response, NoGo); the mean over the 39 sessions. Tolerances are the paper's s.d. over sessions. The paper does not say which trials enter. Readings (a) all trials of the session; (b) trials after dropping disengaged trials as in definition T. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading; the s.d. over sessions is reported as well.

claims.statement: With low-contrast single stimuli mice made 5.1 ± 6.4% incorrect choices and 29.8 ± 19.8% Misses.
claims.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraph 1
claims.quote: with low-contrast single stimuli (5.1 ± 6.4% incorrect choices; 29.8 ± 19.8% Misses)
claims.criterion: As fig1c-easy-performance, for trials with the low contrast on one side and zero on the other, under the same readings.

claims.statement: With competing stimuli of similar but unequal contrast (high against medium, medium against low) mice made 20.0 ± 7.9% incorrect choices and 13.9 ± 11.7% Misses.
claims.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraph 1
claims.quote: or with competing stimuli of similar but unequal contrast (20.0 ± 7.9% incorrect choices; 13.9 ± 11.7% Misses, on trials with high vs. medium or medium vs. low contrast)
claims.criterion: As fig1c-easy-performance, for trials with high against medium or medium against low contrast (either side), an incorrect choice being a turn towards the lower contrast, under the same readings.

claims.statement: Reaction times were longer in the harder conditions (low-contrast single stimuli and competing stimuli of similar contrast) than for high-contrast single stimuli.
claims.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraph 1; Fig. 1d
claims.quote: As expected, in these more challenging cases reaction times were longer ... multi-way ANOVA
claims.criterion: Reaction time is the movement onset (definition T, findWheelMoves3) minus stimulus onset on Left and Right choice trials. The paper names neither the factors of its multi-way ANOVA nor the trials. Readings of the factors (F1) condition class (high-contrast single, low-contrast single, competing similar contrasts) and session; (F2) condition class and subject; (F3) contrast and presence of a competing stimulus (the variables of the Fig. 1d legend) and session, the condition effect being that of either factor; readings of the trials (a) all Left and Right choice trials; (b) those of definition T (onset 125 to 400 ms). Reproduced when, under one reading, the condition factor has p < 1e-4 and the mean reaction time of the high-contrast single class is the shortest of the three.

claims.statement: Choice decoded from instantaneous wheel velocity is at chance (47.7%) 50 ms before detected movement onset and near perfect (94.6%) 50 ms after it.
claims.source: Methods, Training protocol, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 1q
claims.quote: The decoder performed essentially at chance 50 ms prior to movement onset (47.7%) compared to near perfect performance 50 ms after movement onset (94.6%)
claims.criterion: Velocity is the wheel position at t minus that at t - 10 ms (Methods), at times relative to the detected onset of Left and Right choice movements. The paper does not name the decoder. Readings (a) the sign of the velocity, a zero velocity counting as a guess (50%); (b) a logistic regression on velocity with 10-fold cross-validation over trials, per session. Accuracy is the mean over the 39 sessions (Extended Data Fig. 1q, s.d. across sessions). Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: On trials that ended in a Left or Right choice, mice turned the wheel within 400 ms of stimulus onset on 64.9 ± 14.0% (s.d.) of trials, nearly always (96.6 ± 3.4%) in the direction of their final choice.
claims.source: Methods, Training protocol, paragraph 1
claims.quote: turning the wheel within 400 ms of stimulus appearance (64.9 ± 14.0% s.d., n=39 sessions), nearly always in the same direction as their final choice (96.6 ± 3.4%)
claims.criterion: Per session, of trials whose recorded response is Left or Right, the percentage with a turn within 0.4 s of stimulus onset, and of those the percentage whose turn direction equals the recorded response; mean over the 39 sessions. The paper does not say what counts as "turning the wheel" here. Readings (a) the onset of a turn reaching 90 d.v.a. (the Left and Right Choice definition of the next sentence of the Methods); (b) any movement onset detected by findWheelMoves3, its direction that of the movement. Tolerances are the paper's s.d. over sessions. Reproduced when both are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: In the passive replay mice hardly ever turned the wheel; 94.1% ± 0.6% of passive trials with high-contrast stimuli had no movement.
claims.source: Results, Propagation of activity during the task, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In these passive trials the mice hardly ever turned the wheel (94.1% ± 0.6% of trials with high contrast stimuli had no movement)
claims.criterion: Passive replay presentations of a visual stimulus at the high contrast (on either side). The paper does not give the window or the spread. Readings of the window (a) -0.05 to 0.4 s from stimulus onset, the NoGo window of definition T; (b) 0 to 0.4 s; of the value (i) the mean over sessions; (ii) the pooled fraction. No movement is no detected wheel movement onset and no movement in progress in the window. The tolerance is the paper's stated spread. Reproduced when one reading is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Across 39 sessions in 10 mice with 92 probe insertions, 29,134 neurons were recorded (747 ± 38 per session, mean ± s.e.), 22,458 of them localized to one of 42 brain regions; the behaviour comprised 9,538 trials.
claims.source: Results, Brain-wide recording in visual behavior, paragraphs 2 and 3; Fig. 1c legend
claims.quote: Across all sessions we recorded from 29,134 neurons (n=747 ± 38 neurons per session, mean ± s.e.), of which 22,458 were localizable to one of 42 brain regions
claims.criterion: Counts of sessions, subjects and probes are exact. Neurons are units curated as single units. Readings of "neurons" (a) all such units; (b) those also with a trial firing rate of at least 0.1 Hz. Readings of "localizable" (i) neurons whose channel lies in one of the 42 regions of Extended Data Table 1; (ii) neurons of definition N. Readings of the trials (a) all trials; (b) trials kept after definition T. Reproduced when every count is within tolerance under one reading of each; partially reproduced when the exact counts hold and one other count does not.

claims.statement: Extended Data Table 1 gives, for each of the 42 regions, the number of recordings, mice, task-responsive neurons and neurons (for example MOs 19 recordings, 9 mice, 993 of 1,534 neurons responsive; MRN 11, 7, 722 of 857).
claims.source: Extended Data Table 1
claims.criterion: For each region of the table, the number of sessions with neurons of the region (definition N), the number of mice, the number of neurons and the number active during the task (definition N). Reproduced when the recordings and mice match exactly and the neuron counts are within 10% in at least 38 of the 42 regions; partially reproduced in 30 to 37 regions. The regions that differ are listed.

claims.statement: The 39 sessions are those of Supplementary Table 2, each with its subject, date, age and recorded areas (for example Cori 2016-12-14, 11 weeks, ACA, CA3, DG, LS, MOs, SUB, VISp), from the 10 subjects of Supplementary Table 1 with their sex and genotype.
claims.source: Supplementary Tables 1 and 2
claims.criterion: Each session of the table matched by subject and date. Reproduced when all 39 sessions are present, their subjects' sex and genotype match Supplementary Table 1, and the set of areas with neurons in each session matches the table in at least 35 sessions; partially reproduced when all sessions are present but the areas match in fewer.

claims.statement: 60.0% of neurons (13,466) were significantly modulated during the task; of these 74.3% consistently increased and 20.2% consistently decreased their activity.
claims.source: Results, Propagation of activity during the task, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2
claims.quote: A sizeable fraction of all neurons (60.0%, 13,466 neurons) had significant modulation of firing rate during the task. Most of these neurons (74.3%) consistently increased their activity during the task, but a sizeable minority (20.2%) consistently decreased
claims.criterion: Active during the task is any of the six tests of the Methods below 0.05/6, on trials T of the neurons localized to the 42 regions with a rate of at least 0.1 Hz (13,466 of 22,458 is 60.0%, and Extended Data Table 1 sums to these). The direction of a test against baseline is the sign of the code's effectSizes (kernelFitBasic.m); for the signrank tests 1, 2, 3 and 5 the count of positive minus negative trial differences, for the ranksum test 6 the rank sum of the post-reward rates minus its null value. Supplementary Fig. 1b counts a decrease as a higher baseline rate. The paper does not define "consistently". Readings (a) every test against baseline (1, 2, 3, 5, 6) with p below 0.05/6 has the same sign, test 4 being left out; (b) as (a) over the tests with p below 0.05. Reproduced when all four values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Statistically responsive neurons have higher baseline firing rates than other neurons (d' = 0.35 ± 0.04), while their spike amplitudes differ much less (d' = 0.10 ± 0.02).
claims.source: Supplementary Fig. 2 legend
claims.quote: Significant cells tend to have higher baseline firing rates ... while differences in spike amplitude are much smaller
claims.criterion: Values read from the supplement's Word file (the "±" is lost in the text). Baseline is the mean rate -0.2 to 0 s before stimulus onset; amplitude the mean spike waveform amplitude. The legend shows the cells per test (b to g) and gives one d' each; the paper does not say over what the ± is taken. Readings (a) significant on any of the six tests against the rest, the ± being a bootstrap s.e. over neurons; (b) the mean ± s.e. of the six per-test d' values. d' is the difference of means over the root mean of the two variances, a standard choice; the paper does not define it. Reproduced when both are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: When the mouse chose a contralateral stimulus, activity arose first in visual cortex and superficial superior colliculus and then spread to most regions; when it chose an ipsilateral stimulus, VIS and SCs were among the last areas to respond.
claims.source: Results, Propagation of activity during the task, paragraph 2; Fig. 2d,e
claims.quote: When a mouse successfully selected a visual stimulus contralateral to the recorded hemisphere, activity emerged first in classical visual regions such as visual cortex (VIS) and superficial superior colliculus (SCs), and soon spread to most of the remaining recorded regions ... VIS and SCs were now amongst the last areas to respond
claims.criterion: Correct contralateral (Right choice on a right stimulus alone) and correct ipsilateral trials (T, matched in contrast for d as in definition M). Per region the mean over responsive neurons of the normalized rate of the Methods (5 ms bins, causal half-Gaussian 0.02 s, trial mean, causal half-Gaussian 0.03 s, minus the baseline -0.02 to 0 s, divided by baseline + 0.5 sp/s). Responsive is open; readings (a) the display selection of the same Methods paragraph, a ranksum p < 0.0001 in at least three consecutive 0.1 s windows stepped by 0.005 s between task trials with stimuli and movements and those without both; (b) active during the task (definition N); (c) the Figs. 3 to 5 set. The paper defines no latency. Readings (L1) the first time after stimulus onset the region's trace reaches half its maximum in 0 to 0.4 s; (L2) the time of that maximum. Reproduced when, under one reading, on contralateral trials VISp (and the VIS group mean) and SCs fall in the earliest quarter of regions, and on ipsilateral trials both fall in the latest third. The quarter and the third are this file's reading of "first" and "amongst the last".

claims.statement: On Miss trials with a contralateral stimulus, activity appeared in a visual pathway of visual areas, basal ganglia and several midbrain structures but did not spread to the whole brain; on Miss trials with an ipsilateral stimulus there was essentially no activity.
claims.source: Results, Propagation of activity during the task, paragraph 2; Fig. 2f,g
claims.quote: activity was found in a “visual pathway” consisting of classical visual areas, basal ganglia, and several midbrain structures ... but failed to propagate globally. When the mouse missed an ipsilateral stimulus, essentially no activity was seen in the recorded hemisphere
claims.criterion: Fraction of neurons per region significantly activated (definition R, z > 4; readings Z1, Z2) on contrast-matched (M) correct contralateral Go trials and contralateral Miss trials, and on ipsilateral Miss trials. The visual pathway set is the VIS areas, LGd, LP, LD, SCs, CP, GPe, SNr, SCm, MRN, APN and ZI (the areas Fig. 3d and the Results name for vision); the rest are other regions. Reproduced when, under one reading, (i) on contralateral Miss trials the mean fraction over visual pathway regions exceeds that over other regions, (ii) the mean fraction over other regions is at least twice as large on contralateral Go as on contralateral Miss trials, and (iii) the pooled fraction on ipsilateral Miss trials is below half that on contralateral Miss trials. The thresholds are this file's reading of "failed to propagate globally" and "essentially no activity".

claims.statement: Neurons encoding the contralateral visual stimulus were found mainly in classical visual areas, common in visual cortex, thalamus and SCs, and occasionally in frontal cortex (MOs, ACA, PL), basal ganglia (CP, GPe, SNr) and midbrain nuclei (SCm, MRN, APN, ZI).
claims.source: Results, Globally distributed action coding, paragraph 3; Fig. 3d,f
claims.quote: Neurons encoding vision (i.e. requiring Vision kernels) were found in a pathway comprising primarily classical visual areas ... They were common in visual cortex (VIS) and thalamus, and superficial superior colliculus (SCs), but also were found occasionally in other structures such as frontal cortex (MOs, ACA, PL), basal ganglia (CP, GPe, SNr), and several midbrain nuclei (SCm, MRN, APN, ZI
claims.criterion: Kernel test K for the Contralateral Vision kernels, on neurons N (Figs. 3 to 5 set) and trials T; fraction per region of neurons passing analysis criteria, regions with fewer than 5 such neurons left out (Fig. 3d legend). Reproduced when more than half of all neurons requiring Contralateral Vision lie in the VIS areas, visual thalamus (LGd, LP, LD) and SCs; the regions with the five highest fractions are among these; and each of MOs, ACA, PL, CP, GPe, SNr, SCm, MRN, APN and ZI that is analysed has at least one such neuron. The half and the five regions are this file's reading of "primarily" and "common". Partially reproduced when the first two hold only.

claims.statement: Neurons encoding action (requiring the Action kernel) were found in all recorded regions, and most did not require a Choice kernel.
claims.source: Results, Globally distributed action coding, paragraph 3; Fig. 3e,g
claims.quote: In contrast, neurons encoding action (requiring an Action kernel) were spread throughout all recorded regions ... The great majority of neurons encoding action did not require an additional Choice kernel
claims.criterion: Kernel test K for the Action and the Choice kernels, as in fig3d-vision-localized. Reproduced when every analysed region (at least 5 neurons) has Action-requiring neurons and more than half of Action-requiring neurons do not require the Choice kernel; partially reproduced when at least 90% of regions have them.

claims.statement: The Focality index was 0.079 for choice, 0.069 for contralateral vision and 0.040 for action, with choice and vision each significantly more focal than action.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4f legend; Methods, Focality Index
claims.quote: This focality index was 0.079 for choice, 0.069 for visual kernels and 0.040 for action kernels; the differences between Choice and Move, as well as Contralateral Vision and Action, were statistically significant (p<0.05; bias-corrected bootstrap)
claims.criterion: F = sum of p_a squared over the square of the sum of p_a, p_a the fraction of neurons in region a requiring the kernel (kernel test K; Methods), over the 42 regions (the legend's floor of 0.0238 is 1/42). Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals, normal approximation with bootstrap bias and s.e. (MATLAB bootci "norm"); 2,000 resamples, a standard choice. The paper does not say what is resampled or how the difference is tested. Readings (B1) neurons resampled within each region; (B2) sessions resampled; (S1) the bootstrap interval of the difference (same resamples) excludes 0; (S2) the two intervals do not overlap. Reproduced when the three values are within tolerance and both differences are significant under one reading.

claims.statement: With Left and Right choice labels shuffled, 14 neurons (0.33%) passed the Choice kernel test, the false-positive rate of the test.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 5h legend; Methods, Estimation of false positive rate
claims.quote: A small number (14, 0.33%) of neurons are false positives in this shuffle test
claims.criterion: Each Left or Right choice trial gets the choice of another Left or Right trial drawn without replacement, and the whole kernel test K for Choice is rerun from the start (Methods). The fraction is of neurons entering the nested test (full-model VE at least 2%; 14 of about 4,240). The tolerance is two Poisson s.d. of a count of 14 (7.5 neurons), since 10% (1.4 neurons) is below the spread of one shuffle. Reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Choice-selective neurons were rare and found in frontal cortex (MOs, PL, MOp), basal ganglia (CP, SNr), higher-order thalamus, SCm, MRN and ZI, but not in VISp; 54 were in the midbrain (MRN, SCm, SNr, ZI) and 48 in the forebrain (MOs, PL, MOp, CP).
claims.source: Results, Forebrain and midbrain choice coding, paragraphs 1 and 3; Fig. 4b
claims.quote: These neurons were rare, and were found in frontal cortex (MOs, PL, and MOp), basal ganglia (CP, SNr), higher-order thalamus, motor-related superior colliculus (SCm), as well as two subcortical nuclei which unexpectedly contained neurons selective for choice (MRN and ZI ... but choice-selective neurons were not found in VISp
claims.criterion: Kernel test K for the Choice kernel, as in fig3d-vision-localized. The paper does not define higher-order thalamus; this file reads it as the thalamic regions other than the first-order relays LGd, VPL, VPM and MG. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance, VISp has no choice-selective neuron, each of MOs, PL, MOp, CP, SNr, SCm, MRN, ZI and one higher-order thalamic region has at least one, and the overall fraction of analysed neurons that are choice-selective is below 5% (this file's reading of "rare"). Partially reproduced when the regions hold but a count does not. The VISp count is reported with the count the 0.33% false-positive rate predicts.

claims.statement: The time course of choice decoding did not differ between frontal cortex, striatum and midbrain (two-way ANOVA on area and time, no effect of area and no interaction).
claims.source: Results, Forebrain and midbrain choice coding, paragraph 2; Fig. 4c; Methods, Population decoding
claims.quote: the time course of choice decoding could not be statistically distinguished between choice-selective regions in frontal cortex, striatum, and midbrain (two-way ANOVA on brain region and time, interaction p > 0.05
claims.criterion: Residual rates from the model without the Choice kernel (kernel test K, code determineResidualsWithout "moveLR"), Left against Right choice trials; an L1-regularized logistic regression on the residuals -0.05 to 0 s from movement onset of training trials; test trials' residuals at each time projected on its weights; the score is the mean projection on Left minus Right test trials (Methods). One population per area per recording; each score is divided by its area's mean across recordings at choice time (movement onset). A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-way ANOVA with factors time and area group (frontal, midbrain, striatum), at alpha 0.05. Time has 51 levels (50 d.f.). Open details, each a reading the notebook runs; (a) times -0.25 to 0 s from movement onset in 5 ms steps (the Choice kernel support and bin) or (b) -0.2 to 0.05 s; folds (a) 5-fold or (b) 10-fold over trials; L1 strength (a) chosen by inner cross-validation or (b) the library default. Reproduced when the interaction and area effects both have p > 0.05; not reproduced when either has p < 0.05. The F values and the effect sizes are reported.

claims.statement: In jPECC, visual cortex activity leads frontal cortex activity by about 40 ms in the period about 200 ms before movement, and visual cortex leads frontal cortex and midbrain at about 100 ms after stimulus onset.
claims.source: Fig. 4d legend; Extended Data Fig. 8d legend; Methods, jPECC analysis
claims.quote: population activity in visual cortex predicts that in frontal cortex following a ~40 ms lag, but only in the period ~200ms prior to movement
claims.criterion: jPECC as in the Methods and jPECC.m. Recordings with neurons of both groups (VIS, Frontal, Midbrain); spike counts in 10 ms bins, causal half-Gaussian of s.d. 25 ms, divided by baseline + 1 sp/s; per group and time bin PCA to 10 dimensions (fewer when either group has fewer neurons, the same number for both, jPECC.m); 10-fold over trials; CCA on training PCs with L2 regularization lambda 0.5 (rows lambda times identity appended, as jPECC.m); Pearson r of test projections on the first canonical pair, for each pair of time bins. Asymmetry index at t, the mean r along the slice from (t, t) to 50 ms of lead of the first group minus the mean along 50 ms of lead of the second; across recordings a t-test against 0 at each t, alpha 0.05 (the paper names no correction). Open; the baseline window, readings (a) -0.2 to 0 s and (b) -0.1 to 0 s before stimulus onset; the trials, readings (a) all trials T for stimulus alignment and Left and Right choice trials for movement alignment, (b) Left and Right choice trials for both. Reproduced when, under one reading, VIS leads Frontal at time points between -0.2 and -0.05 s from movement onset and VIS leads Frontal and Midbrain near 0.1 s after stimulus onset.

claims.statement: Population activity in midbrain and frontal cortex shows no consistent lead or lag.
claims.source: Results, Forebrain and midbrain choice coding, paragraph 2; Fig. 4d; Extended Data Fig. 8
claims.quote: it revealed no lag for activity correlations between frontal and midbrain areas
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the t-test across recordings of the Frontal-Midbrain asymmetry index against 0 at each time point (as fig4d-jpecc-vis-leads, same readings of the open details), alpha 0.05 uncorrected as the paper gives it. Reproduced when no time point from -0.25 to 0 s from movement onset is significant; not reproduced when any is. The mean index and the count of significant points are reported, with a Bonferroni variant.

claims.statement: Nearly all midbrain choice-selective neurons (53/54, 98%) preferred contralateral choices, while 19/48 (40%) forebrain ones preferred ipsilateral choices, significantly more than in the midbrain.
claims.source: Results, Forebrain and midbrain choice coding, paragraph 3; Fig. 4e-g
claims.quote: In midbrain (MRN, SCm, SNr, and ZI) nearly all choice-selective neurons (53/54, 98%) preferred contralateral choices ... with a sizeable proportion preferring ipsilateral choices (19/48, 40%, significantly more than in the midbrain
claims.criterion: Choice-selective neurons of fig4b-choice-regions. Preference is the choice with the higher model activity at movement onset relative to baseline (Fig. 4f,g legend, "estimated from the kernel model"). Open is the model activity. Readings (a) the Action kernel plus or minus the Choice kernel at lag 0 (kernels on baseline-subtracted rates); (b) the full model's prediction at movement onset averaged over Left and over Right choice trials. Reproduced when both percentages are within tolerance and a two-sided Fisher's exact test of the 2 by 2 table has p < 1e-5, under one reading.

claims.statement: Many midbrain choice-selective neurons (29/54, 54%) increased before one choice and were suppressed below baseline before the other, against 10/48 (21%) in the forebrain.
claims.source: Results, Forebrain and midbrain choice coding, paragraph 3; Fig. 4f,g
claims.quote: Many midbrain choice-selective neurons, moreover, exhibited directionally-opposed activity ... (10/48, 21% suppressed for non-preferred choice, significantly less than in the midbrain
claims.criterion: As fig4f-contralateral-preference, a neuron being suppressed when its model activity for the non-preferred choice at movement onset is below baseline (below 0 after the baseline subtraction), under readings (a) and (b). Reproduced when both are within tolerance and the two-sided Fisher's exact test has p < 1e-3, under one reading.

claims.statement: Neurons with significant detect probability (Go against NoGo for the same stimulus) around movement onset are found widely across regions, replicating the global action signal.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 7b legend; Methods, ccCP and Detect Probability analysis
claims.quote: Percentage of neurons in each area with significant Detect Probability measured around movement onset, replicating the finding from Fig 2d,e and Fig 3e that non-selective action signals are distributed widely
claims.criterion: ccCP algorithm of the Methods and choiceProbShuf.m, Go (Left or Right) against NoGo trials (T) within each of the 16 stimulus conditions, 2,000 within-condition label shuffles; a neuron is significant when its rank among shuffles puts it below 0.025 or above 0.975 (chance 5%, the dashed line of the legend). Sessions with fewer than 10 includable trials left out. NoGo trials take a movement time drawn from the Go trials (definition T). The window "around movement onset" is open; readings (a) -0.1 to 0.05 s (the pre-movement window of test 3); (b) -0.05 to 0 s (the choice decoding window). Regions are marked when the 95% binomial interval of the fraction (Clopper-Pearson, a standard choice) excludes 5%. Reproduced when at least three quarters of regions are marked above chance under one reading.

claims.statement: Neurons with significant choice probability around movement onset are restricted to frontal cortex, basal ganglia, midbrain and certain thalamic nuclei; six sessions were excluded for too few trials, holding 20.8% of the MOs choice-selective neurons of the kernel analysis.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 7c legend; Methods, ccCP and Detect Probability analysis
claims.quote: this analysis broadly replicates the finding from Fig 4b that choice selective neurons, around the time of movement onset, are restricted to frontal cortex, basal ganglia, midbrain, and certain thalamic nuclei
claims.criterion: As ed7b-detect-probability-widespread, for Left against Right choice trials within stimulus conditions; only conditions with both choices contribute. Reproduced when, under one reading, no VIS area and no hippocampal region (CA1, CA3, DG, SUB, POST) is marked above chance, at least one frontal, one basal ganglia (CP, GPe, SNr, ACB, LS) and one midbrain region is, and six sessions are excluded. Partially reproduced when the regional pattern holds and the session count does not.

claims.statement: Ipsilateral visual stimuli are hardly encoded, unlike contralateral ones.
claims.source: Methods, Determining individual neuron selectivity, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 5g
claims.quote: since the same argument should apply to Ipsilateral Vision correlates, and we found very little of such correlates
claims.criterion: Population decoding of the Methods (as fig4c-choice-timing) of contralateral against no contralateral stimulus, and ipsilateral against no ipsilateral stimulus, on residuals from the model without the tested Vision kernels, logistic regression on 0.05 to 0.15 s after stimulus onset; mean score per area. Same open readings as fig4c-choice-timing. Reproduced when the largest area mean for ipsilateral decoding is below a quarter of the largest for contralateral decoding under every reading. The counts of neurons requiring each kernel (test K) are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The kernels often explained a small fraction of cross-validated variance, even for neurons whose mean rates they predicted well (50.2% for the Fig. 3a neuron, 13.6% for the Fig. 3b neuron).
claims.source: Results, Globally distributed action coding, paragraph 2; Fig. 3c
claims.quote: The fraction of cross-validated variance the kernels explained was frequently small ... (50.2% for the neuron in Fig. 3a and 13.6% for the neuron in Fig. 3b
claims.criterion: Full-model cross-validated VE (kernel test K). Reproduced when the median VE over all analysed neurons is below 10% (this file's reading of "frequently small") and, if the two example neurons can be identified (the paper gives only their regions and rasters, Figs. 2a,b and 3a,b), their VE is within tolerance. When they cannot be identified the claim is judged on the median alone and the examples are reported as not identifiable.

claims.statement: More neurons were significantly activated by contralateral visual stimuli on Miss trials in the task than on passive trials with the same contrasts, and passive responses were weaker than those on Miss trials.
claims.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 1; Fig. 5b; Fig. 2h
claims.quote: more neurons were significantly activated by visual stimuli during the task (Miss trials), than in the passive trials
claims.criterion: Contrast-matched (M) Miss and passive trials; per region the fraction of neurons significantly activated (definition R, z > 4; readings Z1, Z2). Neurons are open; readings (a) neurons N of the Figs. 3 to 5 set; (b) all neurons of the 42 regions with a rate of at least 0.1 Hz. Passive trials with a wheel movement in -0.05 to 0.4 s are kept (the Methods drop none). Reproduced when, under one reading, the pooled fraction is larger on Miss than on passive trials, the excess (Miss minus passive) is positive in more than half the regions, and 34 sessions are kept.

claims.statement: Before the stimulus, neocortex and sensory thalamus were less active in the task than in the passive context, while basal ganglia and other subcortical choice areas were more active; VISp was lower and CP higher on Miss trials than on passive trials.
claims.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 1; Fig. 5a,c; Extended Data Fig. 9a; Methods, Engagement Index and pre-stimulus analyses
claims.quote: While neocortex and sensory thalamus showed a net decrease in pre-stimulus activity during task context, other regions ... showed a consistent increase
claims.criterion: Per region a nested ANOVA (Methods) on each neuron's mean rate 250 to 50 ms before stimulus onset, log10(x + 1 sp/s), trials with wheel movement in that window dropped. The factors are open, as the Methods and the Extended Data Fig. 9a legend disagree; readings (a) condition, session and neuron nested in session (Methods); (b) condition, session and subject (legend). Task trials are trials T; passive trials are open, readings (a) all passive replay events; (b) passive visual stimulus presentations. A region differs when the condition p < 0.0012 (0.05 over 42 regions). VISp and CP are compared as in Fig. 5a, the mean pre-stimulus rate over neurons on contrast-matched (M) Miss trials against passive trials, windows as the readings of ed6b-prestimulus-order; the paper gives no test for them. Reproduced when, under one reading, every differing neocortical region is lower in the task, every differing non-neocortical region other than visual thalamus (LGd, LP, LD) is higher, VISp is lower on Miss than on passive trials, and CP is higher.

claims.statement: Pre-stimulus firing in midbrain, basal ganglia and hippocampal regions is ordered Passive < Miss < Go, while in neocortical areas it is higher in Passive than in Miss and Go.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 6b legend
claims.quote: the pre-stimulus firing rate of midbrain, basal ganglia, and hippocampal regions is in the order Passive < Miss < Go; whereas pre-stimulus activity in neocortical areas instead is arranged as Passive > Miss and Go
claims.criterion: Per region the mean over neurons (N, Figs. 3 to 5 set) of the mean pre-stimulus rate on contrast-matched (M) Go, Miss and passive trials. The window is open; readings (a) -0.2 to 0 s (the engagement index window); (b) -0.25 to -0.05 s (the nested ANOVA window). Groups from utils/brainRegionGroups.m (midbrain MRN, SCm, SCs, APN, PAG; basal ganglia CP, GPe, SNr, ACB, LS; hippocampus POST, SUB, DG, CA1, CA3); neocortex as defined above. Reproduced when, under one reading, more than half the midbrain, basal ganglia and hippocampal regions show Passive < Miss < Go and more than half the neocortical regions show Passive above both Miss and Go.

claims.statement: Regions whose pre-stimulus rate differed between task and passive contexts showed similar differences between Go and Miss trials.
claims.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 2; Fig. 5d
claims.quote: Areas that showed differences in pre-stimulus firing rate between task and passive contexts also showed similar differences between Go and Miss trials
claims.criterion: Per region the mean over neurons of task minus passive and of Go minus Miss pre-stimulus rates (as ed6b-prestimulus-order, same readings), contrast-matched. The paper gives no test for Fig. 5d; the test used is the Pearson correlation across regions, the measure the paper reports for the companion comparison of Extended Data Fig. 7f. Reproduced when r > 0 with p < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: The pre-stimulus detect probability of each area correlated with its task minus passive difference (r = 0.48, p = 0.001), as the Go minus Miss difference does.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 7f legend
claims.quote: The pre-stimulus Detect Probability was correlated with the Engagement Index (i.e. Task-Passive difference) similarly to the Go-Miss difference (with r = 0.48, p=0.001; not shown)
claims.criterion: Per neuron the pre-stimulus DP (ccCP of Go against NoGo within stimulus conditions, minus 0.5); per area the mean over neurons; Pearson r across areas with the area's mean task minus passive pre-stimulus rate (as fig5d-go-miss-matches-task-passive). Windows as in ed6b-prestimulus-order, readings (a) and (b). Reproduced when r is within tolerance and p < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: An engagement index, the projection of pre-stimulus population activity onto the task minus passive difference vector, was higher on Go than on Miss trials consistently across recordings (mean difference 8.42 a.u., paired t-test p < 1e-4).
claims.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 2; Fig. 5f; Methods, Engagement Index and pre-stimulus analyses
claims.quote: This engagement index differed between Go and Miss trials consistently across recordings ... paired t-test
claims.criterion: Neurons of the regions that differ in fig5c-prestimulus-task-vs-passive, x_n the mean rate -0.2 to 0 s before stimulus onset on all task trials minus that on all passive trials, normalized to unit L2 norm per session; the index of trial i is x times the trial's pre-stimulus rate vector; per session the mean on Go minus the mean on Miss trials, with N trials per contralateral contrast, N the smaller of the Go and NoGo counts (Methods). Open; readings of task trials (a) trials T, (b) all task trials; of the contrast conditions (a) contralateral contrast > 0 (as definition M), (b) all four contralateral contrast levels, zero included. The tolerance of the neuron count is the paper's s.e. Reproduced when the paired t-test across sessions has p < 1e-4 with Go higher and the mean is within tolerance, under one reading; partially reproduced when the test holds and the mean does not.

claims.statement: The probability of a Go response rises with the engagement index on single trials.
claims.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 2; Fig. 5e
claims.quote: it was possible to predict whether an animal would respond to the stimulus on a given trial within the task context, by projecting pre-stimulus population activity onto a weight vector given by the difference of pre-stimulus activity in passive and task contexts
claims.criterion: Engagement index as in fig5f-engagement-index, z-scored; contrast-matched Go and Miss trials pooled over sessions; logistic regression of Go on the index (Fig. 5e legend). Open is the z-scoring, readings (a) within session, (b) over all trials. Reproduced when the slope is positive and its 95% interval excludes 0 under one reading.

claims.statement: The engagement index improves the prediction of Go responses beyond inter-trial interval, previous reward, pupil area and motion energy (deviance test, p = 1.5e-8).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9i legend; Methods, GLM prediction of P(Go) from pre-stimulus variables
claims.quote: The null hypothesis that engagement index had no additional effect on Go probability over all other variables was rejected using a deviance test (p=1.5e-8)
claims.criterion: Binomial GLM of Go against Miss on inter-trial interval, previous reward (0 or 1), pre-stimulus pupil area and motion energy (z-scored) and their squares, against the same model plus the engagement index, contrast-matched trials (Methods). Sessions with usable pupil video only (34 of 39 in the Methods). Open; the pre-stimulus window, readings (a) -0.2 to 0 s, (b) -0.25 to -0.05 s; pooling, readings (a) all sessions in one GLM, (b) one GLM per session with the deviances summed. Reproduced when the deviance test has p < 0.05 under one reading; p is reported against 1.5e-8.

claims.statement: The Go against Miss difference in engagement index persists on trials after rewards, after regressing out previous reward, and on trials after short and after long inter-trial intervals.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9c-f legend
claims.quote: c-f, Same plot after restricting to contrast-matched trials following rewards ... The effect persists in each case
claims.criterion: The index of fig5f-engagement-index on four trial sets; trials after a rewarded trial; all trials with each previous-reward group's mean subtracted; trials after short and after long inter-trial intervals. Open; the interval split, readings (a) median per session, (b) median over all trials; the test (Extended Data Fig. 9b says t-test), readings (a) paired t-test across sessions, (b) two-sample t-test over pooled Go and Miss trials. Reproduced when all four sets give Go higher with p < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: The engagement vector correlates better with the Go minus Miss vector than with the vectors of other behavioural variables, though not significantly for previous reward (p = 0.096).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9k legend
claims.quote: In each case we find that the correlation is greater for the Go-Miss vector (not reaching significance at alpha=0.05 level, however, for the comparison with the previous reward vector, p=0.096)
claims.criterion: Per recording, the Pearson correlation over neurons between the engagement vector (task minus passive pre-stimulus rate) and the Go minus Miss vector, and between the engagement vector and each other variable's vector. Open; each variable's vector, readings (a) the difference of pre-stimulus rates between trials above and below the variable's median (for previous reward, rewarded minus not); (b) each neuron's regression slope on the variable; the test across recordings, readings (a) paired t-test, (b) Wilcoxon signed-rank. Variables are pupil area, motion energy, inter-trial interval and previous reward. Reproduced when, under one reading, the Go-Miss correlation is larger on average for all four and the difference has p < 0.05 for pupil, motion energy and inter-trial interval.

claims.statement: The engagement index differs between Go and Miss trials even when computed from neurons that are otherwise not responsive in the task.
claims.source: Results, Distributed coding of task engagement, paragraph 1; Supplementary Fig. 3 legend
claims.quote: All neurons show a significant difference in Engagement Index between Go and Miss trials
claims.criterion: As fig5f-engagement-index, computed separately from all neurons, from task-responsive neurons (the Figs. 3 to 5 set) and from the others of the same regions. The p-values are only in the figure. Reproduced when the paired t-test gives Go higher with p < 0.05 for each set.

claims.statement: Probe tracks were localized with a lateral error of 39.3 um (median distance of DiI spots from the fitted track) and a longitudinal error of 88.7 um (median absolute deviation of held-out landmarks), with 15.1 ± 6.9 DiI spots per probe and a scaling of 1.08 ± 0.02.
claims.source: Methods, Anatomical targeting and probe localization, paragraphs 2 and 3
claims.quote: We quantified the lateral localization error by the median distance of the DiI spots from this common trajectory (39.3 μm)
claims.criterion: Needs the DiI spot coordinates in the atlas and the electrophysiological landmarks per probe (Methods); the trajectory by total least squares (Extended Data Fig. 2b), the longitudinal map by linear regression of landmarks, leave-one-landmark-out errors. Reproduced when all four values are within tolerance (the tolerances of the last two are the paper's s.d.).

claims.statement: Three subjects with high-density ECoG (two left, one right hemisphere) read aloud CV syllables made of 18 or 19 consonants followed by /a/, /i/ or /u/, each CV produced 15 to 100 times, with the microphone recorded with the ECoG at 3052 Hz.
claims.source: Methods, Subjects and Experimental Task, and Data acquisition and Signal Processing; Supplementary Table 1
claims.quote: Three native English speaking human subjects underwent chronic implantation of a high-density, subdural electrocortigraphic (ECoG) array over the left hemisphere (two subjects) or right hemisphere (one subject) ... composed of 18–19 consonants (19 consonants for two subjects, 18 consonants for one subject), followed by one of three vowels. Each CV was produced between 15 and 100 times
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the dataset holds three subjects with ECoG and audio, CV labels with 19, 19 and 18 consonants by three vowels (168 distinct CVs, Fig. 3c legend), at least 15 renditions of every CV and at most 100, and two left and one right hemisphere grids. Partially reproduced when it holds the three subjects but some counts differ; the counts found are reported. The sampling rate within 1 Hz of 3052 Hz (TDT rates are often printed rounded, e.g. 3051.76 Hz).

claims.statement: About 30 active vSMC electrodes were found per subject during syllable articulation, an electrode being active when its high-gamma z-score changed by more than 2 for any syllable.
claims.source: Results, vSMC Physiology During Syllable Production, paragraph 1
claims.quote: During syllable articulation, approximately 30 active vSMC electrode sites were identified per subject (~1200 mm 2 , change in z-score > 2 for any syllable)
claims.criterion: Per subject, vSMC electrodes whose mean Hg for any CV exceeds a z-score of 2 at any time in the epoch. OPEN, "change in z-score" read as (a) Hg above 2, (b) absolute Hg above 2 (increase or decrease). Reproduced when, under each baseline reading and one reading of the change, the mean count over subjects is within 27 to 33; partially reproduced when the mean is within tolerance under some baseline readings only. The ~1200 mm2 is not tested, as the paper does not say how it was measured; the counts per subject are reported.

claims.statement: In one subject, dorsal electrodes (e124, e108) were active for /b/ (lips), mid vSMC electrodes (e129, e133, e105) for /d/ (front tongue), and a more ventral electrode (e104) was most active for /g/ (back tongue).
claims.source: Results, vSMC Physiology During Syllable Production, paragraph 1; Figure 1c-e
claims.quote: Dorsally located electrodes (e.g. e124, e108; black) were active during production of /b/, which requires transient closure of the lips. In contrast, mid-positioned electrodes (e.g. e129, e133, e105; grey) were active during production of /d/ ... Amore ventral electrode (e.g. e104; red) was most active during production of /g/
claims.criterion: The paper does not say which subject Fig. 1 shows ("single subject brain", Fig. 1a legend) or how its electrodes are numbered. OPEN, the numbering; readings (a) the dataset's electrode index counted from 1, (b) counted from 0. The subject is the one in which all named electrodes are vSMC electrodes; each subject is tried. OPEN, the measure of activity for a syllable; readings (i) mean Hg at the paper's consonant time, -25 ms (Fig. 4a), (ii) peak mean Hg over the epoch (Fig. 1c-e shows the whole trace and says "most active"). Reproduced when, in one subject and numbering, e124 and e108 respond more to /ba/ than to /da/ and /ga/, e129, e133 and e105 respond more to /da/ than to /ba/ and /ga/, e104 responds more to /ga/ than to /ba/ and /da/, and the distance from the Sylvian fissure orders them /b/ electrodes above /d/ electrodes above e104; partially reproduced when the order holds but some named electrode prefers another syllable. Blocked as metadata_insufficient when no subject and numbering puts all named electrodes on vSMC.

claims.statement: Fricatives with different tongue-tip constriction locations (/th/, /s/, /sh/) engaged different electrodes; front-tongue consonants of different manner (/l/, /n/, /d/) engaged overlapping electrodes with different magnitudes; for /ja/, /ji/, /ju/ the activity was similar before the C-V transition, while a dorsal electrode was active during /u/ only.
claims.source: Results, vSMC Physiology During Syllable Production, paragraph 2; Figure 1f-h
claims.quote: Syllables with the same consonant followed by different vowels ( Fig. 1h, /ja/, /ji/, /ju/ ) revealed similar activity patterns preceding the CV transition. During vowel phonation, a dorsal electrode is clearly active during /u/ (black arrow), but not /i/ or /a/
claims.criterion: The paper calls these qualitative illustrations ("can be observed qualitatively") at electrodes it does not name, with no measure, window or test. Only the last part can be judged with the paper's own threshold. The Fig. 1h legend calls the dorsal electrode an "active lip electrode for /u/". The vowel time, +250 ms, is that of Fig. 4b. Reproduced when, in at least one subject, a vSMC electrode with a positive lips weight (claim fig2a-lips-dorsal) has mean Hg above a z-score of 2 (the activity rule of claim active-electrodes) at the vowel time, +250 ms, for /ju/ and below 2 for /ja/ and /ji/. The other parts are shown as traces and not judged (methods_underspecified for those parts).

claims.statement: Each articulator is represented across vSMC; the lip representation lies in dorsal vSMC and the tongue representation is spread over its ventral part.
claims.source: Results, Spatial Representation of Articulators, paragraph 1; Figure 2a
claims.quote: We found representations for each articulator distributed across vSMC ( Fig. 2a ). For example, the lip representation was localized to the dorsal aspect of vSMC, whereas the tongue representation was more distributed across the ventral aspect
claims.criterion: GLM of Methods Eq. 2, at each time and vSMC electrode, of the CVs' mean Hg on the four consonant articulators (Supplementary Figure 1d), by least squares. Electrodes kept when the mean over T_A of the "associated p-value" is below 0.05 for any articulator A (Methods). OPEN, which p-value; readings (a) the F-test of the whole model, (b) the t-test of articulator A's coefficient. W_iA is the mean of the weight over T_A (Methods Eq. 3); T_A is the subject's mean onset-to-offset window of significant partial correlations for A (claim fig3d-timing-sequence). OPEN, the measure of location, which the paper does not give; readings (a) the W-weighted mean dorsal-ventral distance from the Sylvian fissure over electrodes with positive weights, (b) the median dorsal-ventral distance of the top 10% of weights (the selection of Methods, Somatotopic map). The paper's finding is on the map averaged over subjects (Fig. 2a legend, "averaged over time and subjects"), so the electrodes of the three subjects are pooled. Reproduced when lips lie dorsal to tongue in the pooled data; the result per subject is reported (Supplementary Figure 2). The paper's maps are smoothed with a 2 mm uniform circular kernel and averaged over subjects; the maps are shown for comparison.

claims.statement: Across subjects the articulator representations are laid out from dorsal to ventral as larynx, lips, jaw, tongue and larynx, with a laryngeal representation at the dorsal end of vSMC as well as a ventral one.
claims.source: Results, Spatial Representation of Articulators, paragraph 2; Figure 2b; Discussion, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We found an overall somatotopic dorsal-ventral arrangement of articulator representations laid out in the following sequence: larynx (X), lips (L), jaw (J), tongue (T), and larynx (X)
claims.criterion: As in Methods, Somatotopic map. The W_iA maps of claim fig2a-lips-dorsal, per subject smoothed with a 2 mm uniform circular kernel in the (AP, DV) plane and averaged over subjects; the locations of the top 10% of weights for each articulator; then k = 4 nearest neighbours within 3 mm, mixed when no articulator holds more than 50%. OPEN, the grid on which maps are smoothed and averaged; a 1 mm grid is the standard choice, and 0.5 mm is shown as a variant. OPEN, the paper reads the sequence off Fig. 2b and gives no rule for it; the rule below is this file's reading and not the paper's. Reproduced when the DV positions of the top-10% points order as larynx (a dorsal group) above lips above jaw above tongue above larynx (a ventral group), read from the medians of each articulator's points with the larynx points split at the median DV of the lips and tongue points; partially reproduced when lips above jaw above tongue holds but the dorsal larynx group is absent. The 5% and 15% thresholds (Supplementary Figure 4) are shown as variants.

claims.statement: Electrodes with similar articulator representations lie closer together than chance; the mean spatial autocorrelation within 3 mm is 0.45 against 0.26 for permuted electrode positions.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 3a, b legend
claims.quote: The correlation values for the data (0.45 ± 0.03, mean ± s.e., 3 subjects x 4 articulators, n = 12) were significantly greater than for the randomized data (0.26 ± 0.02, mean ± s.d., 1000 randomizations for each subject; P < 10-3)
claims.criterion: Per subject and articulator, the smoothed W_iA map of claim fig2b-somatotopic- sequence; its normalized 2-D spatial autocorrelation; the mean within 3 mm of zero shift. Null by shuffling electrode locations within subject 1000 times before smoothing (Supplementary Methods). OPEN, the normalization of the 2-D correlation; readings (a) Pearson correlation of the overlapping parts at each shift, (b) the cross-correlation divided by its value at zero shift. Reproduced when the data's mean is within tolerance and above the 99.9th percentile of the null.

claims.statement: Each articulator's representation lies in a more consistent place across subjects than chance (mean cross-subject correlation within 3 mm 0.195 against 0.031).
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 3c, d legend
claims.quote: The correlation values for the data (0.195 ± 0.064, mean ± s.e., 3 subjects x 4 articulators, n = 12) were significantly greater than for the randomized data (0.031 ± 0.021, mean ± s.d., P < 10-3, 1000 iteration permutation test)
claims.criterion: As claim suppfig3b-spatial-clustering, with the cross-correlation of one articulator's maps between pairs of subjects (S1-S2, S2-S3, S1-S3). The right-hemisphere subject's AP axis is taken as the paper's coordinates give it (distance from the central sulcus, anterior positive), so no mirroring is needed. Reproduced when the data's mean is within tolerance and above the 99.9th percentile of the null.

claims.statement: Within each subject, adjacent articulator representations (larynx-tongue, tongue-jaw, jaw-lips) are spatially sequenced along the dorsal-ventral axis, with positive cross-correlation on one side of the diagonal (0.099) and negative on the other (-0.102), both beyond chance.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 3e, f legend
claims.quote: The correlation values for the above diagonal data were positive (0.099 ± 0.052, mean ± s.e., 3 subjects x 3 cross-articulator comparisons, n = 9) and significantly greater than for the randomized data ... the correlation values for the below diagonal data were negative (-0.102 ± 0.052, mean ± s.e., n = 9)
claims.criterion: As claim suppfig3b-spatial-clustering, cross-correlating larynx with tongue, tongue with jaw and jaw with lips within each subject; the mean over the 6 mm semicircles above and below the diagonal that the legend draws, the anterior-dorsal to posterior-ventral axis. Shifts above the dashed line are dorsal-posterior shifts (Supplementary Figure 3 legend). OPEN, which map of each pair (Larynx->Tongue, Tongue->Jaw, Jaw->Lips) is shifted against the other; swapping them swaps the two sides, so the sign change across the diagonal is judged on its size and the side found positive is reported. OPEN, the diagonal's exact angle; readings (a) 45 degrees, (b) the anisotropy axis of the mean autocorrelation of claim suppfig3b-spatial-clustering. Reproduced when the two means have opposite signs, the positive one within tolerance of 0.099 and the negative one within tolerance of -0.102, and both exceed the null's 99.9th percentile in magnitude.

claims.statement: The observed map is neither a perfect linear somatotopy nor random; the mean distance between electrodes preferring the same articulator (11.06 mm) and between those preferring different ones (15.11 mm) lie between the two null models.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 5b legend
claims.quote: The observed intra-articulator distances (11.06 ± 1.01 mm. mean ± s.e., n = 3188 pair-wise distances) and across articulator distances (15.11 ± 1.01mm, mean ± s.e., n = 4587 pair-wise distances) are both intermediate to these bounding values
claims.criterion: Electrodes of claim fig2a-lips-dorsal labelled by their largest W_iA (winner take all); Euclidean distances in the (AP, DV) plane between pairs of electrodes, within and across labels. OPEN, whether pairs are formed within subjects only or over the pooled electrodes of all subjects; both are run. The Methods do not describe how the linear somatotopy maps were made (the legend says "see Methods" and the Methods are silent), so the bounds are the legend's own values (linear 7.43 and 17.7 mm; random 14.08 and 14.07 mm). Reproduced when both observed means are within tolerance and lie strictly between the bounds; a random-scatter null, by permuting labels over the electrodes 1000 times, is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Single electrodes show a clear preferred articulator and also carry weights for other articulators.
claims.source: Results, Spatial Representation of Articulators, paragraph 2; Supplementary Figure 6
claims.quote: This analysis revealed clear preferred tuning for individual articulators at single electrodes (Fig. 2c, electrodes categorized according to the strongest articulator representation), and also demonstrated that single electrodes had functional representations of multiple articulators
claims.criterion: As in Methods (analysis of representational overlap) for the electrodes of claim fig2a-lips-dorsal. Electrodes grouped by their largest W_iA; for each, the positive weights as a percentage of their sum; the group means. Reproduced when, in every group, the preferred articulator has the largest mean percentage and at least one other articulator has a mean percentage above zero. The paper gives no number, so the group means are reported.

claims.statement: Articulator correlations follow a staggered sequence consistent across subjects; lip and tongue correlations begin well before sound onset, jaw and larynx align to the C-V transition, and the high and back tongue vowel features peak near the vowel midpoint (~250 ms).
claims.source: Results, Timing of Articulator Representations, paragraph 1; Figure 3a-d
claims.quote: lip and tongue correlations began well before sound onset ( Fig. 3a, c, d ); jaw and larynx correlations were aligned to the CV transition ( Fig. 3a, c, d ); high tongue and back tongue features showed high temporal specificity for the vowel phase, peaking near the acoustic mid-point of the vowels (~250 ms, Fig. 3b–d ). This sequence of articulator correlations was consistent across subjects
claims.criterion: Partial correlation (Methods Eq. 4), per vSMC electrode and time, of the CVs' mean Hg with each of the six articulator variables of Supplementary Figure 1d, the other five partialled out. For each articulator, electrodes whose peak rho exceeds the mean + 2.5 SD of rho over electrodes and time (Methods). OPEN, the set over which mean and SD are taken; readings for the subjects (per subject, or pooled) and for the articulators (all six together, or per articulator), all run. OPEN, the onset and offset, which the paper does not define; readings (a) the first and last times of the contiguous run around the peak above that threshold, (b) the same at half the peak, both run. One-way ANOVA across the six articulators of the timing values pooled over subjects. OPEN, which timing value the ANOVA uses; readings (a) onset, (b) peak. Acoustic onset per CV from the audio of the prototype rendition (Methods Eq. 1, cochlear spectrogram, "a thresholding procedure" on acoustic power whose threshold is not given; 10% of the prototype's peak power is a standard choice, which moves the onset by a few ms and is not expected to change the outcome). Where the dataset has no audio, the paper gives no other source for the onset; the dataset's hand-marked syllable start, averaged per CV, may stand in for it as a substitute recorded as a deviation (the paper transcribed the speech with WaveSurfer, Methods, Acoustic Analysis, but takes the onset from acoustic power), and the result against t = 0 is shown beside it. Reproduced when the ANOVA has p < 1e-10, the mean onsets of lips and tongue precede the mean acoustic onset, the mean onsets of jaw and larynx are later than those of lips and tongue, and the mean peaks of high and back tongue are within tolerance of 250 ms; partially reproduced when the ANOVA holds and two of the three order conditions hold. Counts per articulator are reported against the 211 total.

claims.statement: Onset latencies of the articulator model fit do not differ between electrodes just anterior and just posterior to the central sulcus (within 10 mm), nor across the guenon.
claims.source: Results, Timing of Articulator Representations, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure 7
claims.quote: we found no significant latency differences in those areas immediately anterior and posterior to the central sulcus (±10 mm), or across the geunon (a-b, P > 0.4, Rank-Sum test; n = 71 and n = 67 electrodes
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per electrode, the onset latency of the GLM R2 (Methods Eq. 2). OPEN, which electrodes; the paper does not say, and 71 + 67 is fewer than the 266 vSMC electrodes of Supplementary Figure 9; readings (a) the electrodes kept in claim fig2a-lips-dorsal, (b) all vSMC electrodes; both run and the counts reported. OPEN, the onset; readings (a) first time R2 is significant (F-test p < 0.05) in the run that holds its peak, (b) first time R2 exceeds the mean + 2.5 SD rule used for partial correlations. Electrodes within 10 mm anterior against within 10 mm posterior of the central sulcus. OPEN, what "across the geunon" compares; readings (a) electrodes on the guenon against those dorsal to it, (b) electrodes anterior against posterior to the guenon's midline; both run. How the guenon boundary is set is also open; the dataset's anatomical labels are used, and the comparison is blocked without them. Two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum at p < 0.05. Reproduced when neither comparison is significant under every onset reading; not reproduced when one is under every reading; the medians and counts are reported against 71 and 67.

claims.statement: The cortical state-space has nine spatial PCs in every subject, the eigenvalues falling fast up to the ninth and slowly after, together explaining about 60% of the variance.
claims.source: Results, Phonetic Organization of Spatial Patterns, paragraph 1; Methods, PCA and Cortical-State Space; Supplementary Figure 8
claims.quote: we used principal components analysis to transform the observed cortical activity patterns into a ‘cortical state-space’ (9 spatial PCs for all subjects, ~60% of variance explained
claims.criterion: PCA as in the header, per subject, on the vSMC electrodes. OPEN, the time range concatenated; readings (a) the epoch -500 to 750 ms, (b) the union of the early and late windows, -375 to 620 ms. Reproduced when, under each reading, the mean over subjects of the variance explained by nine PCs is within tolerance (methods_underspecified when the readings differ, as the header's rule for method readings says). The paper gives no measure of the inflection at the ninth eigenvalue, so the eigenvalue spectra are shown and not judged. Values per subject are reported. The Methods cite Supplemental Figure 6 for the eigenvalues; the figure is Supplementary Figure 8.
