claims.statement: Follow-up experiments at 34 degrees C confirmed the electrophysiological overlap between IT and ET neurons seen at room temperature.
claims.source: Results, "Distinct phenotypes of major families", paragraph 3; Extended Data Figure 6a-g
claims.quote: We confirmed the electrophysiological overlap between IT and ET neurons in follow-up experiments at 34 °C (Extended Data Fig. 6).
claims.criterion: The paper's family classifier (Fig. 3d) is applied to the 34 degree cells, as its code does it. Representation, the 17 features with four log-transformed, standardized, all 17 principal components scaled by the standard deviation of the first. Classifier, k = 10 nearest neighbours by Euclidean distance, leave-one-out, neighbours drawn from all cells with all features, the majority family among the neighbours; families scored are those present among Sst, Pvalb, IT and ET (NP is not used, as in the paper). Overlap is confirmed (reproduced) when at least 25% of ET cells are classified as IT or at least 25% of IT cells as ET, the paper's own threshold for "classified into wrong families" in Fig. 5a. Partially reproduced when the larger of the two is between 10% and 25%; not reproduced below 10%. Variants shown that do not decide the outcome are layer 5 cells only, a class-balanced kNN with IT subsampled to the number of ET cells, and a cross-validated logistic regression of IT against ET.

claims.statement: At 34 degrees C, the AP threshold showed a prominent difference between layer 5 IT and ET neurons.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 6e and its legend
claims.quote: The last panel additionally shows one feature that showed prominent difference at 34 °C.
claims.criterion: Two-sided Mann-Whitney U test between layer 5 IT and layer 5 ET cells at 34 degrees, the test the legend names, for each of the 17 features, without correction for multiple comparisons, as in the paper. Reproduced if the AP threshold has p < 0.05 and is among the three features with the smallest p; partially reproduced if p < 0.05 but it ranks lower; not reproduced if p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: The dandiset's recordings are the cells of the paper's published table of the 34 degree cohort, with the same t-type, layer and soma depth.
claims.source: Data availability; mini-atlas data/m1_patchseq_phys_temp_meta_data.csv
claims.quote: All preprocessed data (gene counts, electrophysiological and morphological features) and meta data are available at https://github.com/berenslab/mini-atlas ... https://dandiarchive.org/dandiset/000035 (physiological temperature) in NWB format.
claims.criterion: Cells are matched by the cell identifier stored in each file (cell_id) and the table's Cell column. The link holds (reproduced) if at least 95% of the dandiset's cells match and at least 95% of matched cells agree on t-type, on layer (the file's inferred layer against the layer the paper's code computes from soma depth and cortical thickness) and on soma depth. Partially reproduced if at least 95% match by identifier but agreement on a field is lower; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The electrophysiological features computed here from the dandiset's traces agree with the paper's published features for the same cells.
claims.source: Methods, "Extraction of electrophysiological features", paragraphs 1 and 12; mini-atlas data/m1_patchseq_phys_temp_ephys_features.csv
claims.quote: Twenty-nine electrophysiological properties of the neurons were automatically extracted based on the raw membrane voltage traces ... For all statistical analysis we used 17 features out of the extracted 29
claims.criterion: For each of the 17 features, Spearman correlation across matched cells between the value computed here and the published value. Reproduced if the correlation is at least 0.9 for at least 15 of the 17 features and at least 0.8 for all; partially reproduced if at least 0.8 for at least 12; not reproduced otherwise. The extraction here is a re-implementation of the paper's methods and code, so a disagreement may come from it; the notes say which.

claims.statement: For layer 5 Sst t-types, AP amplitude and AP width changed the most between room temperature and 34 degrees C, but the relative differences between t-types stayed roughly the same; AHP, input resistance, rebound and sag ratio changed little, and the relative differences between t-types stayed the same.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 6h and its legend
claims.quote: AP amplitude and AP width changed the most between conditions, but the relative differences between t-types stayed roughly the same. The other four shown features did not change much, and the relative differences between t-types stayed the same.
claims.criterion: Room-temperature values are the paper's published features of its main data set; 34 degree values are computed here from the dandiset. Cells are layer 5 Sst cells (the paper's code takes layer 5 from soma depth over cortical thickness, and leaves out excluded cells at room temperature); t-types with at least 5 cells in both conditions, as in the legend. For each of the six features, the shift is the median over those t-types of the difference of t-type medians (34 minus 25 degrees), divided by the standard deviation of the feature over all layer 5 Sst cells at room temperature. Part (i) holds if AP amplitude and AP width have the two largest absolute shifts. For each feature, the Spearman correlation across t-types between the t-type medians at the two temperatures; part (ii) holds if it is positive for all six features and its median over the six is at least 0.5. Reproduced if both parts hold, partially reproduced if one does, not reproduced if neither.

claims.statement: At physiological temperature, as at room temperature, morpho-electric properties of layer 5 Sst neurons varied continuously across the transcriptomic landscape, and the electrophysiological distance between Sst t-types correlated with their transcriptomic distance.
claims.source: Results, "Continuous phenotypic variation", paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 6i
claims.quote: Here we also found that morpho-electric properties varied continuously across the transcriptomic landscape ... We confirmed this effect in follow-up experiments at physiological temperature (Extended Data Fig. 6).

claims.statement: The dandiset's sessions can be matched to the 44 sessions the paper analysed (the results/main.parquet of the paper's code), and matched sessions agree on mouse, Cre line, area, depth and number of cells, and give the paper's per-trial ND.
claims.source: Code accessibility; results/main.parquet of github.com/wmayner/openscope-differentiation at commit 2d959bd
claims.criterion: Added by the author of attempt 000036-mayner-2022-01. Sessions are matched on mouse id and start time, the NWB session_start_time minus 7 hours being equal to the start_time of main.parquet to the millisecond (the session identifiers differ; the offset was found while preparing the attempt). The link holds (reproduced) when all 44 paper sessions match one dandiset session each, every matched session agrees on Cre line, area, depth and the number of cells with a dF/F trace, and the dandiset's dF/F gives the paper's unnormalised per-trial ND to a relative 1e-6 for at least 90% of trials when the trial start may move by -8 to +3 frames from where the NWB stimulus times put it. Partially reproduced when all sessions match but an agreement holds for fewer sessions or fewer trials; not reproduced when fewer than 44 sessions match. The unmatched dandiset sessions are listed, and the one that fits the excluded L5 AL session is named.

claims.statement: Data come from 45 two-photon sessions in nine mice (three per Cre line for L2/3, L4 and L5), 15 sessions per line and 9 per area over V1, LM, AL, PM and AM, with one L5 AL session excluded for recording problems.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1 and 2; Materials and Methods, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Data were collected from L2/3, L4, and L5 in each of five areas (V1, LM, AL, PM, and AM; Fig. 1 E ) across 45 experimental sessions (15 sessions per transgenic line; 9 sessions per area; 5 ± 1 sessions per mouse ... One imaging session in L5 of AL was excluded from our analyses because of technical problems with the two-photon recording
claims.criterion: Counts of sessions, subjects, Cre lines and targeted areas in the dataset. Counts are exact (a tolerance of 10% is under one unit). Reproduced when the dataset holds 45 sessions from 9 mice, 3 mice and 15 sessions per line, 3 sessions per layer and area pair; a dataset that holds only the 44 analysed sessions, the one missing being in L5 AL, also counts as reproduced, since the paper excluded that session (Results, paragraph 1); partially reproduced when it holds a subset of them that matches these counts in part. The sex of each mouse (L2/3 two males, L4 three, L5 one) and sessions per mouse (5 +/- 1) are reported. Whether the excluded L5 AL session can be identified (by its absence from the code's results/main.parquet) is reported.

claims.statement: 4018 cells were recorded over the 44 analysed sessions, 1683 in L2/3, 1781 in L4 and 554 in L5, with per layer and area totals from 62 (L4 AM) to 649 (L4 V1).
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 1-2
claims.criterion: Per session, the number of cells (ROIs) whose dF/F traces the dataset holds, summed per layer, per layer and area pair, and overall, over the 44 analysed sessions. Reproduced when the totals are within tolerance; the 15 layer and area totals of table-s1.csv (L2/3 V1 451, LM 353, AL 336, PM 259, AM 284; L4 V1 649, LM 456, AL 479, PM 135, AM 62; L5 V1 126, LM 185, AL 86, PM 76, AM 81) are compared and the number within 10% reported. If the dataset holds more ROIs than the paper used (for example invalid ROIs), the count after any validity flag the dataset gives is shown too.

claims.statement: Calcium indicator kinetics, measured as the half-life of an exponential fit to each cell's mean isolated-event-locked dF/F, do not differ across layers, areas or their interaction.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 1-3 legend
claims.quote: we found no layer × area interaction (likelihood ratio test; χ 2 (8) = 1.293, p = 0.996). We tested for main effects of layer and area in two further models and likewise found none
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests. Per cell, isolated L0 events (no other event in the window around it), the mean dF/F trace locked to them, an exponential a0 + a1 exp(-lambda t) fitted by least squares from the event to the end of the window, half-life ln 2 / lambda (legend; code fig_1-3.ipynb). LME models of half-life with session as random intercept, fitted by maximum likelihood, layer * area against layer + area; then layer + area against area alone, and against layer alone (code). Reproduced when none of the three likelihood ratio tests has p < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. The window has readings (a) 50 ms before and 100 ms after (legend, main) and (b) 50 and 100 samples (code, variant). Events come from the dataset if it holds L0 events; otherwise from the linked l0_analysis.py run on the dataset's dF/F. The median R2 of the fits and the lowest R2 (0.61 in the paper) are reported.

claims.statement: Unscrambled stimuli evoke higher ND than their phase-scrambled versions in L2/3 but not in L4 or L5, with a significant layer by stimulus category interaction.
claims.source: Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to excitatory cells in L2/3; Figure 3A
claims.quote: We fitted an LME model with stimulus category (unscrambled or scrambled), layer, and their interaction as fixed effects and found a significant interaction (likelihood ratio test, χ 2 (2) = 13.379, p = 0.00124). Post hoc tests showed that the unscrambled versus scrambled difference was specific to L2/3
claims.criterion: ND as in the opening comment for the 5 stimuli of the contrast over the 44 sessions; the layer model and post hoc tests as in the opening comment (Methods, LME models and Post hoc tests; code stats.ipynb). Reproduced when the likelihood ratio test has p < 0.05, the L2/3 post hoc test has adjusted p < 0.05, and the L4 and L5 tests do not; partially reproduced when L2/3 is significant and the interaction or the absence in L4 or L5 fails. Cohen's d per layer over pooled trials (code fig_3 notebook, effect_sizes) is compared with the expected value; the post hoc z values and CI bounds are reported.

claims.statement: The higher ND for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM, with a significant area by stimulus category interaction.
claims.source: Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM; Figure 3B
claims.quote: We fitted an LME model with stimulus category, area, and their interaction as fixed effects and found a significant interaction (likelihood ratio test, χ 2 (4) = 15.203, p = 0.00430). Post hoc tests showed that the unscrambled versus scrambled difference was specific to AL and AM
claims.criterion: As fig3a-layer-specific with area in place of layer. Reproduced when the likelihood ratio test has p < 0.05, the AL and AM post hoc tests have adjusted p < 0.05, and V1, LM and PM do not; partially reproduced when one of AL and AM is significant, or both are and another area is too. Cohen's d per area over pooled trials is compared with the expected values.

claims.statement: Over all 12 stimuli, naturalistic stimuli evoke higher ND than artificial ones in L2/3 and L5 (not L4) and in AL and AM (not V1, LM or PM), with significant interactions with layer and with area.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 3-1 legend
claims.quote: In this analysis, post hoc tests showed a significant effect also in L5; however, this contrast does not control for low-level stimulus characteristics and is thus harder to interpret
claims.criterion: As fig3a-layer-specific and fig3b-area-specific, on all 12 block stimuli (8 naturalistic, 4 artificial, as listed in the opening comment; 5280 trials; code stats.ipynb, Figure 3-1). Reproduced when both interactions have p < 0.05, L2/3 and L5 but not L4 are significant, and AL and AM but not V1, LM or PM are. The area chi2 is compared with the code's 22.213 and not with the legend's value, which repeats the layer test.

claims.statement: The L2/3, AL and AM specificity of the unscrambled against scrambled ND difference holds for nearly all choices of distance metric, state length, frequency spacing and spectral window.
claims.source: Extended Data Figures 3-2, 3-3 and 3-4 legends; Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM, paragraph 2
claims.quote: For nearly all other combinations of parameters, we likewise find that unscrambled stimuli elicit increased ND specifically in L2/3 of AL and AM
claims.criterion: ND recomputed for the 108 parameter sets of the code (main.ipynb), with state length 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5 and 10 s; Euclidean, city block and Chebyshev distance; linear or log-spaced frequency bins (code to_log_spacing); rectangular window without overlap (Fig. 3-2), Tukey (alpha 0.25) with 12.5% overlap (Fig. 3-3) and Kaiser (beta 14) with 50% overlap (Fig. 3-4), the windowed ones by scipy.signal.spectrogram rescaled to the FFT power as in spectral_differentiation.py. Then the layer and area models and post hoc tests of fig3a-layer-specific and fig3b-area-specific for each. A set agrees when both interactions have p < 0.05, L2/3 is the only significant layer and AL and AM are the only significant areas. The paper does not quantify "nearly all"; readings are at least 90% and at least 80% of the 108 sets. Reproduced when the share of agreeing sets meets the reading; the outcome is the one both readings give, and blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ. The share is also reported per window type, and for the looser rule that L2/3, AL and AM are each significant.

claims.statement: With locomotion and pupil diameter as covariates in the LME models, L2/3 of AL and AM remain the populations where ND is greater for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli, for nearly all parameter combinations.
claims.source: Extended Data Figures 3-5, 3-6 and 3-7 legends; Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Consistent with the simpler models, for nearly all parameter combinations, L2/3 of AL and AM emerged as the cell populations in which ND is greater for unscrambled versus scrambled stimuli
claims.criterion: As ext3-2-sensitivity with per-trial locomotion fraction and mean normalized pupil diameter added as fixed effects to the full and reduced models (code stats.ipynb, Figures 3-5 to 3-7). Same agreement rule and the same readings of "nearly all" (90% and 80% of 108 sets), crossed with the readings of artifact removal and pupil diameter named in the opening comment. The main parameter set (1 s, Euclidean, linear, rectangular) is reported on its own.

claims.statement: Spectral ND of L0 calcium events gives results similar to dF/F, with greater ND for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in L2/3 and in AL, while AM is at the threshold (p = 0.050).
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 3-8 legend
claims.quote: Results are similar to the main analysis on ΔF/F 0 traces shown in Figure 3
claims.criterion: ND as in the opening comment applied to the per-frame L0 event magnitudes in place of dF/F (code main.ipynb, events). The paper's stats code asserts that all 2200 trials enter the models (stats.ipynb, EXPECTED_NUMBER_OF_OBSERVATIONS); only its plotting notebook drops trials whose log ND is minus infinity. If any trial has zero event ND, it is dropped (no log exists), the number dropped is reported, and this is recorded as a deviation. Events from the dataset if it holds L0 events; otherwise from the linked l0_analysis.py on the dataset's dF/F. Models and tests as in fig3a-layer-specific and fig3b-area-specific. Reproduced when both interactions have p < 0.05, L2/3 is significant and L4 and L5 are not, AL is significant and V1, LM and PM are not; the AM result (adjusted p near 0.05 in the paper) is reported and not judged.

claims.statement: With the 200 ms after each L0 event removed from dF/F, ND remains greater for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in L2/3 and in AL, with significant interactions; AM is not significant (p = 0.0958).
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 3-9 legend
claims.quote: Results are similar to the main analysis shown in Figure 3 , indicating that our ND results are not driven solely by initial transients in the calcium response
claims.criterion: For each cell, the 6 dF/F samples starting at each frame with an L0 event set to missing and filled by linear interpolation (legend; code main.ipynb, TAU = 0.2 s), then ND and the models of fig3a-layer-specific and fig3b-area-specific. Events as in ext3-8-events-spectral. Reproduced when both interactions have p < 0.05, L2/3 is significant and L4 and L5 are not, and AL is significant and V1, LM and PM are not; the AM result is reported and not judged.

claims.statement: Part of the effect of stimulus category on ND is mediated by mean calcium event magnitude and part is direct (mediated 0.1351, direct 0.0951, proportion mediated 0.59).
claims.source: Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM, paragraph 4
claims.quote: We also analyzed whether the mean magnitude of calcium events (a proxy for firing rate) mediated the effect of stimulus category and found evidence for both mediated and direct effects
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the distance from each value to the nearer bound of its 95% CI, so every value within tolerance also lies inside the paper's interval. Data are the 5 contrast stimuli in the L2/3 AL and AM sessions only (6 sessions, 300 trials; code stats.ipynb, the subset the Methods do not name). Mediator per trial is the mean over cells and frames of the L0 event magnitudes (code main.ipynb, mean_magnitude); covariates are per-trial mean normalized pupil diameter and locomotion fraction. Mediator model mean_magnitude ~ category + pupil + locomotion + (1 | session) and outcome model log10 ND ~ mean_magnitude + category + pupil + locomotion + (1 | session), both by maximum likelihood, and R mediation::mediate with treatment category (Methods, Mediation analyses), 1000 quasi-Bayesian simulations (the package default), robustSE = TRUE and seed 803317503 as in the code. Reproduced when all three values are within tolerance and both the mediated and the direct effects have p < 0.05; partially reproduced when both effects are significant and a value falls outside. Readings of artifact removal and pupil diameter as in the opening comment.

claims.statement: Per-session permutation tests find ND greater for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in all 6 sessions of L2/3 AL and AM, in 8 of 15 L2/3 sessions, 1 of 15 L4 and 0 of 14 L5 sessions.
claims.source: Table 1; Results, Permutation tests for individual experimental sessions
claims.quote: In all sessions recorded from L2/3 of AL and AM, responses to unscrambled stimuli were significantly more differentiated than to scrambled stimuli ( p < 0.05)
claims.criterion: Counts are exact, since 10% of these counts is under one session. Per session, the difference in mean per-trial ND between the 20 unscrambled and 30 scrambled trials, with 20,000 random permutations of the category labels (Methods, Permutation tests). ND is log10 as in the code (table-1.ipynb); untransformed ND is a variant. p is the fraction of permuted differences greater than the observed (Methods) and, as a variant, greater than or equal with p <= 0.05 (code); significance at 0.05. Reproduced when all five counts match under the Methods rule; partially reproduced when the L2/3 AL and AM counts match and another differs by one session. The full 15-cell table is reported.

claims.statement: In L2/3 of AL and AM, the per-session effect size of unscrambled against scrambled ND is positively correlated with the fraction of time spent running (r = 0.896).
claims.source: Results, Arousal is correlated with effect size; Figure 4, top left
claims.quote: We found that in L2/3 of AL and AM, effect sizes were positively correlated with locomotion activity (Pearson’s r = 0.896; two-sided t test; t (4) = 4.030, p = 0.0157, 95% CI [0.308, 1.00]
claims.criterion: Tolerance is the distance to the nearer CI bound (the interval is [0.308, 1.00]). Per session, Cohen's d of per-trial log10 ND, 20 unscrambled against 30 scrambled trials, pooled SD (code fig_4.ipynb). Locomotion fraction is the share of all the session's 2p frames with |filtered velocity| >= 2.5 cm/s (Methods, Locomotion; code behavior_by_session). Pearson correlation over the 6 L2/3 AL and AM sessions, two-sided. Reproduced when r is within tolerance and p < 0.05 under both readings of artifact removal; partially reproduced when r is positive and within tolerance but p >= 0.05. Blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. The per-session values and the correlation over all 44 sessions (Fig. 4, bottom) are reported.

claims.statement: In L2/3 of AL and AM, the per-session effect size is positively but not significantly correlated with mean normalized pupil diameter (r = 0.716, p = 0.109).
claims.source: Results, Arousal is correlated with effect size; Figure 4, top right
claims.criterion: Tolerance is the distance to the nearer CI bound. Effect size as in fig4-locomotion-effect-size; pupil diameter per frame, normalized by its maximum within the 10 blocks, averaged over all the session's 2p frames (code). Reproduced when r is positive and within tolerance under every reading of pupil diameter (Methods semi-major axis; code 2*sqrt(area/pi) as a variant) and artifact removal; blocked as methods_underspecified when they disagree. The p-value is reported.

claims.statement: Within single L2/3 AL and AM sessions effect sizes are medium to very large (Cohen's d 0.57 to 1.25), while the effect over these sessions pooled is 0.34.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 6
claims.quote: while we observed medium to very large effect sizes within individual experimental sessions in L2/3 of AL and AM (Cohen’s d = 0.57–1.25), the overall effect was relatively subtle (Cohen’s d = 0.34)
claims.criterion: Per-session Cohen's d as in fig4-locomotion-effect-size; the pooled d over all 300 trials of the 6 sessions with pooled SD (code fig_4.ipynb). Reproduced when the six per-session values lie in the range widened by 10% of each bound (0.513 to 1.375), the extremes are within tolerance, and the pooled d is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Multivariate ND (mean distance to the centroid in an 8-dimensional UMAP embedding) is higher for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli specifically in L2/3.
claims.source: Results, Multivariate analysis also shows increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli; Figure 5A
claims.quote: The mean centroid distance was higher in response to unscrambled compared to scrambled stimuli ( Fig. 5 ), and this effect was specific to L2/3
claims.criterion: Per session, the dF/F of all cells over every 2p frame of the 50 trials of the 5 contrast stimuli, as a frames by cells matrix, reduced to 8 dimensions by UMAP with the parameters of umap-params.yml (n_neighbors 50, min_dist 0.5, Euclidean, spectral init, random_state 42; Methods, Multivariate differentiation). Per trial, the mean Euclidean distance of its frames to their centroid, log10 (code main.ipynb). Models and tests as in fig3a-layer-specific. Reproduced when the interaction has p < 0.05, L2/3 is significant and L4 and L5 are not. UMAP results depend on the library version; the version used is reported.

claims.statement: Multivariate ND is higher for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli specifically in AL and AM.
claims.source: Results, Multivariate analysis also shows increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli; Figure 5B
claims.quote: and areas AL and AM [area × stimulus category interaction ... likelihood ratio test, χ 2 (4) = 16.232, p = 0.00272
claims.criterion: Mean centroid distance as in fig5-multivariate-layer; the area model and tests of fig3b-area-specific. Reproduced when the interaction has p < 0.05, AL and AM are significant and V1, LM and PM are not.

claims.statement: Multivariate ND of L0 events is also higher for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in L2/3 and in AL and AM, and in V1 as well.
claims.source: Results, Multivariate analysis also shows increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli, paragraph 3; Extended Data Figure 5-1
claims.quote: The results of multivariate differentiation analysis of these data were consistent with our results using ΔF/F 0 traces (Extended Data Fig. 5-1 ), with the additional finding of significantly greater differentiation for unscrambled versus scrambled stimuli in L2/3 of V1 as well as AL and AM
claims.criterion: L0 event magnitudes summed in 1-s bins within the 5 contrast stimuli (Methods, Multivariate differentiation), then UMAP and mean centroid distance as in fig5-multivariate-layer, and the layer and area models of fig3a-layer-specific and fig3b-area-specific. Bins with no events are discarded before UMAP (Methods, main reading); the code keeps them (variant). Events as in ext3-8-events-spectral. The area model pools layers, so "L2/3 of V1" is tested as V1 in the area model and L2/3 in the layer model. Reproduced when both interactions have p < 0.05, L2/3 is the only significant layer, and V1, AL and AM are significant while LM and PM are not; partially reproduced when L2/3, AL and AM hold and V1 does not.

claims.statement: Stimulus category (unscrambled or scrambled) can be decoded accurately from most layers and areas, well above chance, without the layer and area specificity of ND.
claims.source: Results, Decoding analysis does not reveal layer or area specificity; Figure 6
claims.quote: Decoding performance was high for most areas and layers ( Fig. 6 ), in contrast to the unscrambled-scrambled difference in ND
claims.criterion: Per session, the 50 trials of the 5 contrast stimuli, each trial the dF/F of all cells over its frames flattened (trials truncated to the shortest), PCA keeping 99% of variance and shrinkage LDA (solver lsqr, shrinkage auto) in one pipeline, 5-fold stratified cross-validation without shuffling, mean balanced accuracy over folds (Methods, Decoding analyses; code main.ipynb). Chance is 0.5. The paper does not quantify "high" or "most"; "most" is read as more than half of the 15 layer and area populations, and "high" as a mean accuracy over the population's sessions of at least 0.75 and, second reading, at least 0.9. Reproduced when, under both readings, most populations are high and every layer and every area has a mean accuracy above 0.5; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. Per-session accuracies are reported. The paper reports no test of differences in decoding across layers or areas ("did not vary substantially", Abstract; "remarkably similar", Discussion), so the absence of specificity is shown, as accuracies by layer, area and pair, and is not judged.

claims.statement: Stimulus identity among all 12 stimuli can be decoded accurately from most layers and areas (chance 1/12).
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 6-1 legend; Results, Decoding analysis does not reveal layer or area specificity
claims.quote: Stimulus identity can be accurately decoded from most layers and areas using responses to all 12 stimuli
claims.criterion: As fig6-category-decoding with all 120 trials of the 12 stimuli and stimulus identity as the class (code main.ipynb). Chance is 1/12. Same readings of "most" and "high" (mean balanced accuracy at least 0.75, and at least 0.9); reproduced when both readings agree that most populations are high and every layer and area is above 1/12.

claims.statement: ND differs among the five continuous naturalistic clips, over all layers and areas.
claims.source: Results, Differences in ND among individual stimuli
claims.quote: We fitted an LME model with stimulus as a fixed effect and found it was significant (likelihood ratio test, χ 2 (4) = 32.115, p = 1.812e–6)
claims.criterion: Per-trial log10 ND of the snake, crickets, man writing, mousecam and conspecifics clips over all 44 sessions; log10 ND ~ stimulus + (1 | session) against log10 ND ~ 1 + (1 | session), maximum likelihood, likelihood ratio test (Methods, LME models; code fig_7,7-1.ipynb). Reproduced when p < 0.05 and chi2 is within tolerance; partially reproduced when p < 0.05 only.

claims.statement: The snake (predator) clip evokes higher ND than the conspecifics, crickets and man writing clips, and the mousecam clip higher ND than man writing.
claims.source: Results, Differences in ND among individual stimuli; Figure 7
claims.quote: revealed that the predator stimulus (a snake) evoked significantly higher differentiation than clips of conspecifics ... prey (crickets ... and a man writing ... The “mousecam” clip of movement through a wooded environment also evoked significantly higher differentiation than the clip of a man writing
claims.criterion: Pairwise differences of estimated marginal means from the model of fig7-stimulus-effect, emmeans(model, pairwise ~ stimulus) with Tukey adjustment, two-sided (Methods, Post hoc tests; code). The CIs are of the difference in log10 ND. Cohen's d of pooled per-trial log10 ND per pair (code). Reproduced when the four named pairs have adjusted p < 0.05 in the stated direction and the other six pairs do not (the Extended Data Fig. 7-1 legend speaks of "the four stimulus pairs identified as having significantly different levels of ND"); partially reproduced when three or more of the four hold. The estimated differences are checked against the CIs and reported.

claims.statement: Arousal alone does not account for the differences among continuous clips, with a mixture of direct and arousal-mediated effects; for the largest contrast, snake against man writing, there is evidence only for a direct effect of stimulus on ND, with locomotion or pupil diameter as mediator.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 7-1 legend
claims.quote: Notably, for the largest contrast (predator vs man writing), for both locomotion and pupil diameter we found evidence only for a direct effect
claims.criterion: Per-trial data of fig7-stimulus-effect. For each arousal variable as mediator with the other as covariate, mediator model mediator ~ stimulus + covariate + (1 | session) and outcome model log10 ND ~ mediator + stimulus + covariate + (1 | session), maximum likelihood, then mediation::mediate with treat.value snake and control.value man writing (Methods, Mediation analyses; code fig_7,7-1.ipynb, seed 803317503, 1000 simulations; the code negates pupil diameter, which changes only signs). Reproduced when, for both mediators, the direct effect has p < 0.05 and the mediated effect does not; partially reproduced when this holds for one. The other three significant pairs are reported. Readings of artifact removal and pupil diameter as in the opening comment.

claims.statement: Within L2/3 of AL and AM, mean ND per stimulus is positively correlated with stimulus differentiation across the 12 stimuli, but the noise stimulus is highly influential (Cook's D 2.318).
claims.source: Results, SD does not explain ND; Figure 8
claims.quote: Within L2/3 of AL and AM, the mean ND elicited by each stimulus was positively correlated with SD (Pearson’s r = 0.746, one-sided t test; t (10) = 3.542, p = 0.00267, 95% CI [0.393, 1.00]
claims.criterion: Tolerance of r is the distance to the nearer CI bound. SD per stimulus is ND as in the opening comment computed on the movie's pixel intensities (each pixel a cell, 30 frames/s, 1-s windows, Euclidean, median, no division by pixel count), after blurring each frame with a Gaussian whose half width at half maximum is the 8.92-degree RF radius (sigma per axis = radius in pixels / sqrt(2 ln 2), screen 120 x 95 degrees over 192 x 120 pixels, reflect mode; Methods, Spectral differentiation; code stimulus_properties.ipynb), then log10. Mean ND per stimulus is the mean of per-trial log10 ND over all trials of the 6 L2/3 AL and AM sessions (code fig_8.ipynb). Pearson correlation, one-sided (greater). Cook's D from the linear fit of mean ND on log SD. Reproduced when r is within tolerance with p < 0.05 and noise has the largest Cook's D, within tolerance. Movies from the dataset if it holds the stimulus frames; otherwise from the Zenodo deposit, a variant to record.

claims.statement: Without the noise stimulus the ND and SD correlation is weak and not significant (r = 0.258), and among the scrambled stimuli and their unscrambled counterparts there is no evidence of a relation (r = -0.378); so ND is not inherited from SD.
claims.source: Results, SD does not explain ND; Figure 8 legend
claims.quote: If we exclude this stimulus, we find a weaker correlation ( r = 0.258; one-sided t test; t (9) = 0.801, p = 0.222, 95% CI [–0.307, 1.00] ii ). Furthermore, there was no evidence of a relationship with ND when considering only the scrambled stimuli and their unscrambled counterparts
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests with the values of fig8-nd-sd-correlation. Pearson correlation of mean log10 ND on log10 SD over the 11 stimuli other than noise, one-sided (greater), and over the 5 contrast stimuli, two-sided. Reproduced when neither has p < 0.05; not reproduced when either does. Both r values are reported against the paper's (0.258 and -0.378).

claims.statement: ND in L2/3 of AL and AM is not explained by stimulus luminance, contrast or spectral energy.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 8-1 legend; Results, SD does not explain ND
claims.quote: We also did not find a relationship with stimulus luminance, contrast, or spectral energy
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Per stimulus, mean luminance is the mean pixel intensity and contrast the SD of pixel intensities of the unblurred movie; spectral energy is the sum of the energy spectral density of each pixel's intensity time series of the blurred movie after removing the DC component (legend; code stimulus_properties.ipynb). The paper names no test for this figure; readings are Pearson correlations of mean log10 ND (as in fig8-nd-sd-correlation) with each property over the 12 stimuli, (a) two-sided and (b) one-sided (greater), the tests of Fig. 8. DC removal has readings per-pixel mean (legend) and global mean (code). Reproduced when no correlation has p < 0.05 under any reading; not reproduced when one does under every reading; blocked as methods_underspecified when readings differ. All r values are reported.

claims.statement: The dataset holds 13 mice whose subject ids, sex, date of birth, imaged cell type (L2/3 or L5 pyramidal) and imaging plane (somata or distal apical dendrites) are as listed in Table 1.

claims.statement: Thirteen mice were imaged, three L2/3 dendritic, three L2/3 somatic, four L5 dendritic and three L5 somatic, each with at least three imaging sessions.

The duplicate, union and motion-border rules cannot be checked from the traces and are not tested.

claims.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 3

claims.criterion: The ROIs in each file (all are used, as in the paper's code). The sessions can be read as (a) the 33 sessions of the paper's analyses (local sessions 1 to 3 passing QC), (b) all sessions that passed QC, or (c) all 50 sessions. claims.statement: Matching produced 254 tracked ROIs in L2/3 dendritic planes, 261 in L2/3 somatic, 516 in L5 dendritic and 129 in L5 somatic, about 100 to 500 per plane and about 32 to 75% of the theoretical maximum number of trackable ROIs.

claims.criterion: A tracked ROI is one carrying a tracking index in the dataset; each mouse's count is the number of tracked ROIs in one of its three tracked sessions (equal across them). The totals are summed per plane over the 11 mice of the paper's analyses; this is the reading under which Table 2 gives these totals (mice 411400 and 412933, tracked on sessions 4 to 6, are left out); a sum over all 13 mice is shown as a variant. Tolerance 0 on the totals because they are counts of deposited indices. The theoretical maximum is not defined in the paper; readings are (a) per mouse, the smallest ROI count of its three tracked sessions, summed per plane, and (b) per mouse, the mean ROI count of those sessions, summed per plane. The range claim holds when, under one reading, the lowest and highest plane percentages are within tolerance. Reproduced when the four totals match and the range claim holds; partially reproduced when only the totals match.

claims.statement: The same imaging planes were recorded over three days and many ROIs could be identified in each day's recording, so that individual dendritic segments and somata can be followed over the three sessions.
claims.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 3

Reproduced when every tracked mouse's three sessions carry the same number of tracked ROIs and the tracking indices define one-to-one matches across the three sessions (each index appears once per session); not reproduced otherwise.

claims.criterion: The example mouse is the L5 somatic mouse with 47 tracked ROIs in Table 2 (411771, mouse_n 4 in the code's Fig. 8b panel). Count of tracked ROIs in its sessions in the dataset. Tolerance 0 because it is a count.

claims.statement: For the same L5 somatic mouse, two conflicting matches were removed from the union over session orderings.
claims.source: Figure 8b legend
claims.quote: enable two of the pairwise matches to be identified as conflicts and removed

claims.source: Figure 8b legend

The dataset holds only the final matches, and the repository's roi_tracking files give the fewest and most matches over orderings only for the two example mice (413663 and 411771). With those inputs only, the claim is blocked for lack of data for the other mice; the two examples' ranges (most minus fewest, also as a fraction of the final count) are reported. If the per-ordering counts of every mouse become available, reproduced when the median range over somatic mice is smaller than over dendritic mice, in absolute terms and as a fraction of the final count.

claims.statement: Gabor sequences are repeating 1.5-s sequences of five 300-ms images (A-B-C-D-G), each non-grey image holding 30 Gabor patches, with inconsistent sequences replacing D by U, whose mean orientation is shifted by 90 degrees (drawn from 90, 135, 180 and 225 degrees, against 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees for the other images).
claims.source: Methods, Visual stimulation, paragraphs 2 and 3
claims.quote: it consisted of repeating 1.5-second sequences, each comprising five consecutive images ( A-B-C-D-G ) presented for 300 ms each ... “Inconsistent” sequences were created by replacing D images with U images in the sequence ( A-B-C-U-G ) ... namely from {90°, 135°, 180°, 225°}
claims.criterion: From the stimulus parameter table of each session. Image durations from their start and stop times; the number of patches from the per-image parameters, if recorded (tolerance 0, a fixed design value). Reproduced when, in every session that holds the table, images follow the A-B-C-D/U-G order, last 300 ms +/- 10%, the mean orientations of A to D take only 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees, and U mean orientations take only 90, 135, 180 and 225 degrees and equal the sequence's mean orientation plus 90 degrees.

claims.statement: Visual flow is 105 white squares of 8 by 8 degrees moving at 50 degrees per second, in two consecutive periods (rightward and leftward) in random order, with 25% of squares reversed for 2 to 4 s during inconsistent flow.
claims.source: Methods, Visual stimulation, paragraph 4
claims.quote: The visual flow stimulus consisted of 105 white squares moving uniformly across the screen at a velocity of 50 visual degrees per second, with each square being 8 by 8 visual degrees in size.
claims.criterion: From the stimulus parameter table, where it records these values. Tolerance 0 on the number of squares because it is a design count. Reproduced when every session holding the table matches, and each session shows the two directions as two consecutive periods. Values the table does not hold are listed as untestable.

claims.statement: Each imaging session lasted 70 min, with 34 min of Gabor sequences and 17 min of visual flow in each direction, each stimulus period flanked by 30 s of grey screen.
claims.source: Methods, Visual stimulation, paragraph 1
claims.quote: optical imaging sessions always lasted 70 minutes, comprising 34 minutes of Gabor sequence stimulus and 17 minutes of visual flow stimulus in each direction. Each stimulus period was flanked by 1 or 30 seconds of grayscreen for the habituation and optical imaging sessions, respectively.
claims.criterion: From the stimulus table's start and stop times, per session. Reproduced when all three hold in every session; partially reproduced when they hold in at least 45 of 50.

claims.statement: Inconsistent sequences make up about 7% of Gabor sequences and 5% of visual flow time.
claims.source: Methods, Visual stimulation, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Inconsistent sequences, accounting for approximately 7% of the Gabor sequences and 5% of visual flow stimulus time, only occurred on optical imaging days, and not on habituation days.
claims.criterion: From the stimulus table, per session; the values compared are the means over sessions, and each session's value is reported. Gabor, the number of A-B-C-U-G sequences over all sequences; visual flow, the time with reversed squares over all visual flow time. Habituation sessions are not in the dataset (Table 2 lists imaging sessions only), so the absence of inconsistent stimuli during habituation is not tested.

claims.statement: Each session is divided into about 30 blocks, each of 30 to 90 s of consistent stimulus followed by 3 to 6 s (Gabor) or 2 to 4 s (visual flow) of inconsistent stimulus, in multiples of 1.5 s (Gabor) and 1 s (visual flow).
claims.source: Methods, Visual stimulation, paragraph 5
claims.quote: each 70-minute imaging session was broken up into approximately 30 blocks, each comprising 30–90 seconds of consistent sequences followed by several seconds of inconsistent sequences (3–6 seconds for Gabor sequence stimulus and 2–4 seconds for the visual flow stimulus)
claims.criterion: A block is a run of consistent stimulus ending with a run of inconsistent stimulus, from the stimulus table. The block count can be read as (a) per session, all stimuli together, (b) per stimulus (Gabor, and visual flow with both directions together), or (c) per stimulus and direction. Reproduced when, under one reading, the mean count is within tolerance and the consistent and inconsistent durations fall in the stated ranges (each widened by 10% of its bounds) for at least 95% of blocks.

claims.statement: Both somatic and dendritic ROIs responded clearly to the Gabor and visual flow stimuli, many with increased fluorescence at stimulus onset.
claims.source: Overview of data, paragraph 1; Figure 5
claims.quote: Both the somatic and dendritic ROIs showed clear responses to both the Gabor and visual flow stimuli, with many showing increased fluorescence responses to the onset of the stimuli (Fig. 5 ).
claims.criterion: Session 1 (local, passing QC; 11 mice), each line and plane. Selection as in the Figure 5 legend ("for the session") and the code (analysis/seq_analys.py get_sess_ex_traces, identify_gabor_roi_ns, identify_visflow_roi_ns), made within each mouse's session; the selected ROIs are then pooled over mice per line and plane (get_ex_traces_df, which draws 6 random examples from the pool for plotting; all selected ROIs are used here). Gabor, ROIs with SNR (claim fig7a-snr-above-1) above the session median; among them, those whose median pairwise correlation between individual sequence responses (each smoothed with a 4-point moving average), and the standard deviation and skew of their mean response, all exceed the 75th percentile of those ROIs; sequences are the -0.9 to 0.6 s window around D (consistent, panel a) or U (inconsistent, panel b) onset. Visual flow, per direction, the -2 to 2 s window around inconsistent flow onset; ROIs above the median SNR whose median pairwise correlation of post-onset responses and mean post-minus-pre difference exceed the 75th percentile. Traces are dF/F robust-scaled per ROI over the session ((x - median) / (95th - 5th percentile)), as in the code; unscaled dF/F is a variant. Reproduced when in all four planes the selection yields ROIs for the Gabor sequences and for each flow direction, and in each plane the mean over selected ROIs of their mean trace is higher after the reference onset (0 to 0.6 s for Gabor, 0 to 2 s for flow) than before it. Partially reproduced when this holds in at least two planes. Which Gabor panel enters the rule is not given by the paper (answer of 2026-10-22, questions/000037.yaml); the sentence cites Figure 5 as a whole, and the code selects panel a and panel b ROIs separately (get_sess_ex_traces, unexp 0 or 1). Readings are (a) panel a, (b) panel b, and (c) both panels, each required to hold. The outcome is the one all three readings give; methods_underspecified if they differ.

claims.statement: Responses to consistent and inconsistent stimuli differed clearly in the example ROIs.
claims.source: Overview of data, paragraph 1; Figure 5a versus b, and c and d
claims.quote: There were also clear differences in the responses to the consistent versus inconsistent stimuli as well (Fig. 5a versus b, and c & d).
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test and calls its examples randomly selected. Gabor, per plane, session 1, the ROIs selected as in fig5-example-responses; the selection can be read as (a) the panel a ROIs (selected on consistent sequences) or (b) the panel b ROIs (selected on inconsistent sequences). For the selected ROIs, the mean over ROIs of their mean trace after D onset and after U onset (0 to 0.6 s), with the SEM across ROIs as in the legend. A difference is clear when, at some time point in 0 to 0.6 s, the two mean traces differ by more than the sum of their SEMs (the plotted bands do not overlap). Reproduced when this holds in all four planes under both readings; partially reproduced when it holds in at least two planes under both; methods_underspecified if the readings disagree. For visual flow, the selection itself requires a larger response after inconsistent onset, so the comparison is circular and is reported, not judged.

claims.statement: Running velocity and pupil diameter were recorded in sessions 1 to 3 of all 11 mice, so their distributions can be shown per session across mice.
claims.source: Figure 6b legend
claims.quote: Data is stacked across all mice (11), with each mouse represented by a different shade of gray.
claims.criterion: The 33 sessions of the paper's analyses (local sessions 1 to 3 passing QC). A session counts when it holds a running velocity series in cm/s and a pupil diameter series in mm with finite values. Tolerance 0 because it is a count. Reproduced when all 33 sessions count; partially reproduced when at least 30 do.

claims.statement: ROI dF/F traces have a relatively high SNR, above 1.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 7a
claims.quote: These are shown in Fig. 7A , and demonstrate that our recordings have relatively high SNR (>1)
claims.criterion: SNR per ROI on its full-session unscaled dF/F trace, as in the Methods and the code (util math_util.calculate_snr). The values at or below the trace's median are mirrored about the median to form the noise sample; its mean and standard deviation define a normal distribution whose 95th percentile is the noise threshold; SNR is the mean of values above the threshold divided by the noise standard deviation. The 33 sessions of the paper's analyses, ROIs pooled over mice per line, plane and session (12 groups), as in the code. "SNR (>1)" can be read as (a) the median of each group above 1, (b) the 5th percentile of each group (the lower whisker) above 1, or (c) every ROI above 1. By this construction an ROI's SNR exceeds 1.645 whenever its median dF/F is at least 0, which bears on reading (c). These are readings of a reported number (docs/protocol.md, Reader, step 3), so the claim is reproduced when it holds under one reading; the notebook shows each and names those that hold.

claims.statement: ROI SNR is stable over the three days.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 7a
claims.quote: demonstrate that our recordings have relatively high SNR (>1) and that this is quite stable over days
claims.criterion: The SNR groups of fig7a-snr-above-1, compared across sessions 1 to 3 within each line and plane, as the boxplots of Figure 7a (notched, whiskers at the 5th and 95th percentiles, from the code). The paper defines no test. Stable can be read as (a) the notches of the three sessions overlap pairwise (matplotlib's notch, median +/- 1.57 IQR / sqrt(n), the code's plot) or (b) each session's median lies inside the interquartile range of every other session of the plane. Reproduced when all four planes are stable under both readings; partially reproduced when at least three are under both; methods_underspecified if the readings disagree.

claims.statement: The mean dF/F signal of ROIs is stable over days.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 7b
claims.quote: Similarly, the mean ΔF/F signal was stable over days (Fig. 7b ).
claims.criterion: Signal per ROI is the mean of its full-session dF/F values above the noise threshold of fig7a-snr-above-1, as the Figure 7b legend defines it and the code computes it (the last value returned by calculate_snr). Same groups, readings and decision as fig7a-snr-stable.

claims.statement: The distributions of pairwise ROI correlations are very similar for apical dendrite ROIs and somatic ROIs, which suggests the dendrites are not heavily over-segmented.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3; Figure 7c
claims.quote: The distributions of correlation coefficients were very similar for the apical dendrite ROIs and for the somatic ROIs (Fig. 7c ), suggesting that we were unlikely to be heavily over-segmenting the dendritic data.
claims.criterion: Pearson correlation of every pair of ROIs within a session, on full-session dF/F traces each smoothed with a centred 4-point moving average (Figure 7c legend; the code uses scipy.ndimage.convolve, mode mirror). The 33 sessions of the paper's analyses; pairs pooled over mice per line, plane and session, as in the code, which bins them in 40 bins of width 0.05 from -1 to 1. Similar is not defined; it is read as the dendritic and somatic distributions of the same line and session having medians, and 95th percentiles, that differ by less than (a) one bin (0.05) or (b) two bins (0.1). Reproduced when this holds for all six line and session comparisons under both readings; partially reproduced when it holds for at least four under both; methods_underspecified if the readings disagree. The fraction of pairs above 0.8 per group is reported.

claims.statement: About 0.01% of possible pairs of L2/3 dendritic ROIs have correlations above 0.8.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: To be more conservative, ROIs with correlations above 0.8 (e.g., approximately 0.01% of possible pairs of L2/3 dendrites)
claims.criterion: The correlations of fig7c-correlations-similar, L2/3 dendritic sessions. Tolerance 0.005 percentage points, the range of values that round to the stated one significant figure (0.005 to 0.015%), since the paper gives the value as approximate with one figure. Readings for the denominator are (a) all pairs pooled over the three sessions and the two analysed mice (413663 and 433414; 412933 is not included, its sessions 1 to 3 having failed QC, and its sessions 4 to 6 are outside the paper's analyses, as the code's Fig. 7c source data list only the first two), (b) the mean of the three per-session fractions, and (c) each of the three local sessions separately, pairs pooled over the two mice as Fig. 7c plots them; under (c) every session must be within tolerance, since the paper gives one value for L2/3 dendrites and names no session. Per-mouse sessions are not a reading the paper allows (answer of 2026-10-22, questions/000037.yaml). Above 0.8 is read as r > 0.8; r >= 0.8 (the code's histogram bin) is shown as a variant. Reproduced when one reading is within tolerance.

claims.statement: The per-ROI SNRs computed from the dataset agree with those in the source data of Figure 7a in the paper's repository.
claims.source: Figure 7a; paper_figures/dataset_paper/Fig7/data_files/panel_A.json at the commit above
claims.quote: These are shown in Fig. 7A
claims.criterion: Sessions matched by session id, ROIs by their order in the file. Reproduced when, in every one of the 33 sessions, the number of ROIs equals the source data's and at least 95% of ROIs have an SNR within 1% of the source value (the same computation on the same traces; 1% allows for numerical precision); partially reproduced when this holds in at least 30 sessions.

claims.statement: Mean dF/F responses across ROIs show distinct transients aligned to stimulus onsets (grey screen to stimulus) and offsets (stimulus to grey screen), which validates the temporal alignment of stimuli and recordings.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 5; Figure 9a and b
claims.quote: These ΔF/F traces show distinct transients that align with the stimulus onsets and offsets (Fig. 9 ), validating our temporal alignment, and demonstrating clear stimulus responses in the identified ROIs.
claims.criterion: The 33 sessions of the paper's analyses. As in the code (analysis/basic_analys.py get_stim_on_off_data), onsets are the ends of every grey screen period but the last, and offsets the starts of every grey screen period but the first; the text names transitions to and from Gabor sequences or visual flow, while the Figure 9a legend says "(Gabor sequence)", so the onsets and offsets can be read as (a) all transitions (text and code) or (b) Gabor transitions only. Window -2 to 2 s around each transition (code); per ROI, the mean trace over transitions; robust-scaled dF/F as in the code ((x - median) / (95th - 5th percentile) over the session), unscaled dF/F as a variant; then mean and SEM across ROIs pooled over mice per line, plane and session (12 groups). A group shows a transient when, at some time in 0 to 2 s, the mean trace differs from its mean over -2 to 0 s by more than k SEM at that time; k is not given and is read as 1 or 2. Reproduced when every group shows a transient at onset and at offset under all readings; partially reproduced when at least 9 of 12 groups do for both onset and offset under all readings; methods_underspecified if the readings give different outcomes.

claims.statement: Each session has three file versions; basic files are about 130 MB to 1.7 GB, the stimulus images add about 1.5 GB, and the motion-corrected stack adds about 45 GB.
claims.source: Data Records, Data organization, paragraph 2
claims.quote: amounting to about 130 MB to 1.7 GB per file. Adding the stimulus frame images increased the file sizes by about 1.5 GB each [I]. Further adding the motion corrected imaging stack increased the file sizes much more, by about 45 GB per file [S].
claims.criterion: Sizes from the archive's asset list, files identified by the naming convention of the paper (behavior+ophys, behavior+image+ophys, obj-raw_behavior+image+ophys). Added sizes are per session, [I] minus [B] and [S] minus [I]. MB and GB can be read as decimal or binary units; reproduced when, under one, all four values are within tolerance and every session has the three versions.

claims.statement: The basic files of the sessions 1 to 3 that passed QC are 33 files totalling about 15 GB.
claims.source: Usage Notes, paragraph 1
claims.quote: If only the basic data files for sessions 1 to 3 that passed quality control are needed, the total download size is approximately 15 GB for 33 files in total.
claims.criterion: Sessions 1 to 3 are local session numbers (Supplementary Table 1, as in the code's session table); passing QC as recorded in the dataset or Table 2. Tolerance 0 on the count because it is a count. Sizes from the asset list, decimal or binary GB as in file-sizes.

claims.statement: The recordings come from 11 rats and 27 sessions of 294 plus or minus 137 min, yielding 995 putative pyramidal cells and 126 putative interneurons.
claims.source: Results, Identification of brain states, paragraph 1; Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 1; Experimental Procedures
claims.quote: We recorded across different brain states from 11 rats ... Recordings from 27 sessions (294±137 min) ... This resulted in 995 putative pyramidal (pE) cells ... and 126 putative interneurons (pI)
claims.criterion: Counted over the files as deposited (22 files), with session duration from the first start to the last stop of the state table (the session's spike span is shown too). The spread given for duration is used as its tolerance. Reproduced when all five values are within tolerance, partially reproduced when at least three are, not reproduced otherwise. The counts in the 21 usable sessions are reported as well.

claims.statement: Median firing rates of pE cells are 0.76 Hz in WAKE, 0.69 Hz in nonREM and 0.88 Hz in REM; of pI cells 5.59, 4.69 and 4.25 Hz.
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 2; Figure 2A
claims.quote: Median rates (±SD) of putative pyramidal cells in each state were: WAKE: 0.76±1.53 Hz, nonREM: 0.69±0.86 Hz, REM: 0.88±1.33 Hz; and for putative interneurons were: WAKE: 5.59±7.25 Hz, nonREM: 4.69±5.62 Hz, REM 4.25±9.43 Hz.
claims.criterion: Each cell's rate over all epochs of a state in its session. Readings (a) WAKE without MAs, as defined above; (b) WAKE as every Awake epoch, MAs included. Reproduced when under one reading all six medians are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at least three are; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The distribution of pE firing rates is strongly positively skewed and spans three orders of magnitude, from 0.05 to 5 Hz.
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 2; Figure 2A
claims.quote: the distribution of per-cell mean firing rates for putative pyramidal neurons was strongly positively skewed ... spanning three orders of magnitude range from 0.05 Hz to 5 Hz (Figure 2A)
claims.criterion: On WAKE rates of pE cells (zero rates kept). Reproduced when the skewness of the rates in Hz is above 1 and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles lie within a factor of 2 of 0.05 Hz and 5 Hz. The range is read from a log axis ("three orders of magnitude"), so the tolerance is a factor on that scale, not 10% of each bound. Partially reproduced when only one of the two holds. The same numbers for nonREM and REM are reported.

claims.statement: The fraction of pE cells firing above 2 Hz is 19.2% in WAKE, 19.2% in REM and 8.8% in nonREM (chi-square, p < 1e-10).
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 2; Figure 2A
claims.quote: The right tail extended toward higher rates during WAKE and REM compared to nonREM (Figure 2A; fraction of >2 Hz neurons: WAKE= 19.2%; REM= 19.2%; nonREM= 8.8%; Chi-Square Test
claims.criterion: Rates as in fig2a-median-rates, reading (a). Chi-square tests on the 2 x 2 tables of cells above and below 2 Hz, nonREM against WAKE and nonREM against REM. Reproduced when the three fractions are within tolerance and both tests give p < 1e-10 with nonREM lower; partially reproduced when the tests hold but a fraction is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Per-cell nonREM and WAKE rates are highly correlated (R = 0.82), and the slope of their relation is below 1 (95% confidence interval 0.66 to 0.71), so state transitions act differently across the rate spectrum.
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 2; Figure 2B
claims.quote: Whereas nonREM and WAKE firing rates remained highly correlated on a per-cell basis (R = 0.82 ... the slope of this relationship significantly deviated from 1 (Figure 2B) ... (95% confidence interval of slope: 0.66 – 0.71)
claims.criterion: The slope is judged against the reported interval widened by 10% of each bound, 0.594 to 0.781 (given above as its centre and half width). Readings (a) log10 rates, cells with a zero rate in either state left out, OLS of nonREM on WAKE; (b) rates in Hz, all pE cells. Reproduced when under one reading R is within tolerance, the slope is in the widened interval and its 95% confidence interval excludes 1; partially reproduced when the slope is below 1 with its interval excluding 1 under some reading but the values miss. The reverse regression (WAKE on nonREM) is shown as a check on regression to the mean.

claims.statement: The burst index (fraction of spikes with inter-spike intervals under 15 ms) is highest in nonREM (median 11.8%), lowest in WAKE (4.0%), with REM (5.5%) slightly above WAKE (Kruskal-Wallis, p < 0.05).
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Burst index was highest during nonREM (median in nonREM = 11.8%) and lowest during WAKE (4.0 %), with REM (5.5 %) slightly higher than WAKE (p < 0.05; Kruskal-Wallis test).
claims.criterion: Per pE cell and state, intervals between consecutive spikes in the same epoch of that state; cells with fewer than 10 such intervals in a state are left out of it. Readings (a) the fraction of intervals under 15 ms; (b) the fraction of spikes with an interval under 15 ms to the previous or the next spike. Reproduced when under one reading the three medians are within tolerance, the order is nonREM > REM > WAKE, and a Kruskal-Wallis test across the three states gives p < 0.05; partially reproduced when the order and test hold but a median misses.

claims.statement: The average spike autocorrelogram of pE cells peaks near 8 ms in nonREM, with a smaller peak near 125 ms (theta) in REM and WAKE.
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
claims.quote: a large peak occurred at approximately 8ms inter-spike interval during nonREM, whereas smaller peaks were present at ~125 ms (i.e., theta frequency) during REM and WAKE (Figure 2C)
claims.criterion: Per pE cell and state, counts of spike-time differences at 1 ms resolution from 0 to 300 ms, pairs within the same epoch, divided by the cell's spike count in the state; averaged over cells with at least 100 spikes in the state. NREM peak is the argmax from 2 to 50 ms. The theta peak is the location of the maximum of the mean autocorrelogram smoothed with a 21 ms moving average between 60 and 250 ms, required to lie at least 3 ms inside that window. Reproduced when the nonREM peak is at 7 to 9 ms (8 ms plus or minus 10%, rounded to whole bins) and the theta peak in both REM and WAKE is within 112.5 to 137.5 ms; partially reproduced when one of the two parts holds.

claims.statement: The autocorrelogram of pE cells decays faster in nonREM than in WAKE and REM (decay fit exponent medians -1.35, -0.83 and -0.80; Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.05).
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
claims.quote: Time decay of the autocorrelograms of pyramidal neurons was significantly faster during nonREM compared to WAKE and REM (Figure 2C; decay fit exponent median nonREM = – 1.35, WAKE = – 0.83, REM = – 0.80; p < 0.05; Kruskal-Wallis test).

claims.statement: In nonREM, pairs of fast-firing pE cells are positively correlated, while pairs of one slow and one fast cell are negatively correlated.
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 5; Figure 2F
claims.quote: the fastest and slowest firing neurons tended to be positively correlated within groups, but were actually negatively correlated across groups (Figure 2F).
claims.criterion: Pearson correlation of spike counts in 100 ms bins over nonREM packets, for every pair of pE cells in the same session; mean correlation for each of the 21 combinations of six rate groups. Readings for the groups (a) WAKE-rate sextiles as above; (b) sextiles of the rate over the whole session. Reproduced when under one reading the mean correlation of group (6,6) pairs is positive and the largest of the 21, and that of (1,6) pairs is below zero by a two-sided one-sample t-test at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when only the (6,6) part holds.

claims.statement: Microarousals have a median duration of 15.9 plus or minus 3.3 s, occur 0.32 plus or minus 0.12 times per minute and occupy 9.1 plus or minus 3.5% of SLEEP (790 in total).
claims.source: Results, Identification of brain states, paragraph 2
claims.quote: There were a total of 790 MAs in our dataset (median duration = 15.9±3.3sec; frequency = 0.32±0.12 per minute; 9.1±3.5% of time in SLEEP).
claims.criterion: MAs derived from the state table as defined above; the paper's spreads are the tolerances. Readings (a) MAs inside SLEEP periods, frequency and fraction per session over SLEEP time, then averaged over sessions, median duration over all those MAs; (b) all MAs, pooled over sessions, frequency per minute of nonREM episode time. Reproduced when under one reading the three values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when two are. The total count is reported but not judged, as the dandiset holds 21 of 27 usable sessions.

claims.statement: The fraction of time occupied by MAs decreases over the course of nonREM episodes (R = -0.85, p < 1e-10).
claims.source: Results, Identification of brain states, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Over nonREM episodes the fraction of time occupied by MAs decreased (correlation versus normalized nonREM episode time: R = −0.85
claims.criterion: For each nonREM episode with at least one MA, the fraction of each of 10 normalized-time bins spent in MA. Readings (a) the mean fraction per bin over episodes, correlated with bin centre (10 points); (b) all episode bins pooled. Reproduced when under one reading R is within tolerance and p < 1e-10; partially reproduced when R is negative with p < 0.05 under some reading.

claims.statement: The duration of nonREM packets spans two orders of magnitude, with a median of 111 s.
claims.source: Results, Identification of brain states, paragraph 3
claims.quote: We found that the duration of packets was distributed over two orders of magnitude, with a median of 111 seconds.
claims.criterion: Readings (a) every Non-REM epoch; (b) Non-REM epochs inside SLEEP periods. Reproduced when the median is within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: The dataset holds 54 WAKE-SLEEP episodes (at least 7 min of WAKE followed by at least 20 min of SLEEP), an average of 2.0 per session, and sessions without one were discarded.
claims.source: Results, Identification of brain states, paragraph 3; Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 1; Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Sessions without full WAKE-SLEEP cycles (Supplementary Materials) were also discarded. ... We identified 54 WAKE-SLEEP episodes in our dataset, or an average of 2.0 episodes per neuron recorded (27 sessions)
claims.criterion: Cycles as defined above. Reproduced when the mean per session is within tolerance and every usable session has at least one; partially reproduced when one of the two holds. A variant that also accepts SLEEP ended by the end of the recording is shown.

claims.statement: The mean firing rate of pE cells declines over the course of SLEEP, restricted to nonREM (R = -0.11, p < 1e-3).
claims.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 1; Figure 3B
claims.quote: the arithmetic mean of the population firing rates of pE cells declined over the course of sleep using a test of correlation of spike rate versus time (Figure 3A–B; R = – 0.11
claims.criterion: Over the SLEEP periods of WAKE-SLEEP cycles. Readings (a) one point per nonREM packet at the normalized time of its midpoint, its population mean rate divided by the mean of these values over the period's packets; (b) 10 bins of normalized SLEEP time, Non-REM time only, bins with under 10 s of Non-REM dropped, normalized the same way. Reproduced when under one reading R is within tolerance and p < 1e-3; partially reproduced when R is negative with p < 1e-3 but outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The mean pE rate is lower in the last than in the first nonREM packet of SLEEP (1.04 plus or minus 1.20 against 0.88 plus or minus 0.91 Hz; Wilcoxon p < 0.02).
claims.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Comparison of the population discharge rates in the first and last nonREM packets of SLEEP episodes showed an overall mean rate decrease (1.04±1.20 Hz versus 0.88±0.91 Hz; p < 0.02; Wilcoxon test)
claims.criterion: Over cell and cycle pairs, first and last Non-REM epochs of each SLEEP period of a WAKE-SLEEP cycle. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance and a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives p < 0.02 with the last lower; partially reproduced when the test holds but a mean misses.

claims.statement: Comparing the same neurons in the first and last nonREM packets of SLEEP, the regression slope departs from 1 (95% confidence interval 0.827 to 0.880), as fast cells slow down and slow cells speed up.
claims.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 2; Figure 3D
claims.quote: we assessed spike rates of the same neurons in the first versus the last nonREM packets of SLEEP and found the slope of this correlation significantly departed from unity (slope 95% confidence interval 0.827–0.880)
claims.criterion: The interval widened by 10% of each bound is 0.744 to 0.968, given as centre and half width. Readings (a) log10 rates, OLS of last on first, pairs with a zero rate left out; (b) rates in Hz. Reproduced when under one reading the slope is in the widened interval and its 95% confidence interval excludes 1; partially reproduced when the slope is below 1 with its interval excluding 1 but outside the widened interval. The reverse regression and the same slope for two halves of one packet are shown as checks on regression to the mean; they do not change the outcome.

claims.statement: pE rates are lower in the 5 min of WAKE after SLEEP than in the 5 min before (p < 1e-6, Wilcoxon), with a decrease in the top three sextiles and an increase in the lowest.
claims.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 1; Results, Sleep sub-states induce differential lasting firing rate changes, paragraph 2; Figure 3E
claims.quote: the significantly decreased discharge rate of pE neurons in a 5-min post-sleep WAKE compared to a 5-min pre-sleep WAKE epoch ... a significant decrease firing in the top three sextile groups and an increase in the lowest sextile group (all ps < 0.05
claims.criterion: The last 300 s of the WAKE epoch before each cycle's SLEEP and the first 300 s of the Awake epoch that ends it (all of it when shorter). Readings for the unit of analysis (a) cell and cycle pairs; (b) per cell, the mean over its session's cycles. Population test, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank; sextile tests one-tailed Wilcoxon in the stated direction. Reproduced when under one reading the population decrease has p < 1e-6 and sextiles 4, 5 and 6 decrease and sextile 1 increases, each at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when the population decrease holds and at least two of the four sextile effects do.

claims.statement: Over SLEEP, restricted to nonREM, the fastest sextile decreases its rate while the slowest shows a marginal increase.
claims.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 2; Figure 3B
claims.quote: The mean spike discharge rate of highest-firing rate sextile groups significantly decreased over sleep whereas the activity of the lowest-firing rate sextile showed a marginal increase (Figure 3B; Pearson correlations versus normalized time).
claims.criterion: Readings (a) and (b) of fig3b-population-decline, per sextile. Reproduced when under one reading sextile 6 has R < 0 with p < 0.05 and sextile 1 has R > 0 (any p, as the paper calls it marginal); partially reproduced when only one of the two holds.

claims.statement: The coefficient of variation of pE firing rates decreases over the course of SLEEP (R = -0.05, p < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 2
claims.quote: the coefficient of firing rate variation also showed a significantly decreasing slope over the course of SLEEP (R = – 0.05; p < 0.01).
claims.criterion: CV across a session's pE cells of their rates at each point, readings (a) per packet and (b) 10 bins as in fig3b-population-decline, without normalization. The value of R depends on the binning, which the paper does not give, so it is not judged by tolerance. Reproduced when under one reading R < 0 with p < 0.01.

claims.statement: Within both nonREM episodes and nonREM packets, the fastest sextiles decrease their rates while the slowest increase.
claims.source: Results, Firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM episodes and packets, paragraph 5; Figure 4A and 4B, panel iv

claims.criterion: Time courses as defined above. Reproduced when sextile 6 has R < 0 and sextile 1 has R > 0, each at p < 0.05, in both episodes and packets; partially reproduced when this holds in one of the two, or when one sextile's direction holds in both.

claims.statement: The coefficient of variation of binned population rates decreases within nonREM episodes (R = -0.13) and packets (R = -0.12), both p < 1e-10.
claims.source: Results, Firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM episodes and packets, paragraph 5; Figure 4A and 4B, panel v
claims.quote: resulting in a decreasing coefficient of variation of binned population firing rates (Figure 4 A–B v; Repisode= −0.13 ... Rpacket= – 0.12
claims.criterion: CV across the session's pE cells of their rates in each bin, pooled. As the binning is not given, R is not judged by tolerance. Reproduced when R < 0 with p < 1e-10 in both episodes and packets; partially reproduced when in one.

claims.statement: The 15 ms burst index of pE cells increases within nonREM episodes (R = 0.09) and packets (R = 0.08), both p < 1e-10.
claims.source: Results, Firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM episodes and packets, paragraph 5; Figure 4A and 4B, panel vi

claims.criterion: In each bin, the fraction of intervals under 15 ms among the intervals of the session's pE cells whose two spikes lie in the same packet and whose later spike falls in the bin; pooled R against bin centre. Reproduced when R > 0 with p < 1e-10 in both episodes and packets; partially reproduced when in one.

claims.statement: Delta and sigma power increase over nonREM episodes and packets, while gamma power decreases over episodes but not over packets.
claims.source: Results, Firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM episodes and packets, paragraph 2; Figure 4A and 4B, panel i
claims.quote: Over nonREM episodes and packets, delta and sigma band power steadily increased (Trachsel et al., 1988), whereas gamma power decreased over episodes but not packets (Figure 4 A–B i).
claims.criterion: Log band power per bin minus its mean over the bins of the same packet or episode, pooled R against bin centre. Reproduced when delta and sigma have R > 0 with p < 0.05 in both episodes and packets, and gamma has R < 0 with p < 0.05 in episodes and p >= 0.05 or R >= 0 in packets; partially reproduced when the delta and sigma part holds and the gamma part does not.

claims.statement: Mean delta power within whole packets, normalized by nonREM delta power, is positively correlated with packet length (R = 0.31, p < 0.05).
claims.source: Results, Firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM episodes and packets, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Mean delta power within whole packets (normalized by nonREM delta power) was positively correlated with packet length (R = 0.31; p < 0.05).
claims.criterion: Per packet of at least 20 s, mean delta power over the packet divided by the mean over all Non-REM time of its session, against packet duration in s, pooled. Reproduced when R is within tolerance and p < 0.05; partially reproduced when R > 0 with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Per packet, the rate of the fastest sextile is negatively correlated with delta power (R = -0.28) and positively with gamma power (R = 0.44), and the rate of the slowest sextile is positively correlated with sigma power in the last 20 s of the packet (R = 0.25), all p < 1e-10.
claims.source: Results, Firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM episodes and packets, paragraph 6; Figure 4C and 4D
claims.quote: Per-packet firing rate of the top sextile group was negatively correlated with ... whole-packet delta power ... R= – 0.28 ... and gamma power (Figure 4D; R = 0.44 ... the bottom sextile group and sigma power in the last 20 sec of the packet (R = 0.25
