claims.criterion: Packets of at least 20 s. Group mean rate per packet and log band power, each z-scored over the packets of its session, pooled. Reproduced when all three R are within tolerance with p < 1e-10; partially reproduced when at least two have the stated sign with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: An intervening nonREM packet reduces the rates of the top two sextiles from one MA to the next (both p < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, Sleep sub-states induce differential lasting firing rate changes, paragraph 3; Figure 5B
claims.quote: Firing rates in the top two firing rate sextiles were significantly reduced by the intervening nonREM packet (both p < 0.01; Figure 5B, blue)
claims.criterion: Triplets of consecutive epochs MA, packet, MA. Change per pE cell and triplet is the rate in the second MA minus the first. Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank per sextile over cell and triplet pairs. Reproduced when sextiles 5 and 6 both have a negative mean change with p < 0.01; partially reproduced when one does. The per-cell mean over triplets is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: An intervening WAKE episode increases the rate of the fastest sextile from one nonREM packet to the next (24 triplets).
claims.source: Results, Sleep sub-states induce differential lasting firing rate changes, paragraph 4; Figure 5B
claims.quote: WAKE episodes increased the activity of the fastest-firing sextile group of pyramidal cells from nonREM packetn to packetn+1 (Figure 5B, black) ... uninterrupted nonREM-WAKE-nonREM triplets (n = 24)
claims.criterion: Triplets packet, WAKE, packet; change is the rate in the second packet minus the first; tests as in fig5b-nrem-between-ma. Reproduced when sextile 6 has a positive mean change with p < 0.05. The number of triplets is reported against the paper's 24.

claims.statement: An intervening MA increases the rates of slow-firing pE cells from one packet to the next and does not affect fast-firing cells.
claims.source: Results, Sleep sub-states induce differential lasting firing rate changes, paragraph 5; Figure 5B
claims.quote: MA epochs between packets did not affect fast-firing neurons but significantly increased the rate of slow-firing neurons from packetn to packetn+1 (Figure 5B, yellow).
claims.criterion: Triplets packet, MA, packet; tests as in fig5b-nrem-between-ma. Reproduced when sextile 1 has a positive mean change with p < 0.05 and sextile 6 has p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when sextile 1 increases but sextile 6 changes too.

claims.statement: An intervening REM episode decreases the rates of all sextiles from one packet to the next.
claims.source: Results, Sleep sub-states induce differential lasting firing rate changes, paragraph 5; Figure 5B
claims.quote: Finally, REM episodes decreased the spike rates from packetn to packetn+1 in all sextile groups (Figure 5B, red).
claims.criterion: Triplets packet, REM, packet; tests as in fig5b-nrem-between-ma. Reproduced when all six sextiles have a negative mean change with p < 0.05; partially reproduced when at least three do and none increases significantly.

claims.statement: Longer REM episodes produce a proportionally larger decrease of rates from one packet to the next (R = -0.22, p < 1e-2).
claims.source: Results, Sleep sub-states induce differential lasting firing rate changes, paragraph 5; Figure 5C
claims.quote: Longer REM episodes exerted a proportionally larger effect on rate changes from packetn to packetn+1 for all sextile groups (Figure 5C; R = – 0.22
claims.criterion: Triplets packet, REM, packet. Readings (a) per triplet, the fractional change of the pE population mean rate, (post - pre) / pre; (b) per cell and triplet, the fractional change, cells with a pre rate above 0. Reproduced when under one reading R is within tolerance with p < 0.01; partially reproduced when R < 0 with p < 0.01.

claims.statement: Sigma power in the last 20 s of a packet between two MAs correlates with a larger increase of the slowest sextile from one MA to the next (R = 0.181, p < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, Sleep sub-states induce differential lasting firing rate changes, paragraph 3; Figure 5C
claims.quote: sigma power in the last 20 seconds of nonREM packets was correlated with a greater increase in the lowest firing-rate sextile group in the MAn versus MAn+1 analysis (Figure 5C; R = 0.181, p < 0.01).
claims.criterion: MA, packet, MA triplets; log sigma power of the last 20 s of the packet z-scored over the session's packets; change of the sextile 1 mean rate from the first to the second MA. Reproduced when R is within tolerance with p < 0.01; partially reproduced when R > 0 with p < 0.01.

claims.statement: The increase of the slowest sextile's rate from one packet to the next is positively correlated with the change of delta power between the packets, regardless of the intervening state.
claims.source: Results, Sleep sub-states induce differential lasting firing rate changes, paragraph 5; Figure 5C
claims.quote: The increase of spike rate from packetn to packetn+1 in the slowest sextile group was positively correlated with the delta power change from packetn to packetn+1 (Figure 5C).
claims.criterion: Consecutive packets (any intervening epochs, within a nonREM episode or SLEEP period or not), each at least 20 s; change of the sextile 1 mean rate against the change of the session-normalized delta power (packet mean divided by the session's Non-REM mean). Reproduced when R > 0 with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Within WAKE the two fastest sextiles increase and the two slowest decrease their rates; within REM all sextiles except the fourth increase.
claims.source: Results, Firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM episodes and packets, paragraph 8 (Figure S5A and S5B)
claims.quote: entry into WAKE corresponded with an increase in firing rate of the highest sextile two groups and a drop in firing rate of the lowest two sextile groups (Figure S5A) ... During REM, all sextile groups except the fourth showed an increase in firing rate (Figure S5B)
claims.criterion: Time courses within WAKE epochs of at least 40 s and REM epochs of at least 20 s. The WAKE part holds when sextiles 5 and 6 have R > 0 and sextiles 1 and 2 R < 0, each at p < 0.05; the REM part when sextiles 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 have R > 0 at p < 0.05. Reproduced when both parts hold, partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: WAKE periods with more movement have a larger effect on the rate increase of the fastest sextile from one packet to the next (R = 0.43, p < 0.05).
claims.source: Results, Sleep sub-states induce differential lasting firing rate changes, paragraph 4; Figure 5C
claims.quote: Furthermore, WAKE periods with more movement had a proportionally larger effect (Figure 5C; R = 0.43; p < 0.05).

claims.statement: DOWN states have a median duration of 0.19 s and UP states 0.47 s.
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 4 (Figure S4A)
claims.quote: The durations of DOWN states of ‘slow oscillations’ showed a skewed distribution (median = 0.19s) and so did the UP states (median = 0.47s; Figure S4A).

claims.statement: Over SLEEP, the incidence of spindles (R = -0.093), UP states (R = -0.10) and DOWN states (R = -0.08) decreases and DOWN state duration increases, while spindle duration, frequency and amplitude do not change.
claims.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 3; Figure 3C
claims.quote: Incidence of spindles (1.94±0.39/min) decreased ... while spindle duration (0.52±0.32 sec), frequency (13.93±0.93 Hz) and amplitude (203.3±87.71 µV) did not change over SLEEP. Incidence of both UP states (R = – 0.10 ... and DOWN states (R = – 0.08 ... while the duration of DOWN states increased

claims.statement: Within packets the incidence of UP and DOWN states increases, UP states shorten and DOWN states lengthen, and spindle incidence and duration increase.
claims.source: Results, Firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM episodes and packets, paragraph 2 and 3; Figure 4A and 4B, panels ii and iii
claims.quote: The incidence of both UP states (R = 0.05 ... and DOWN states (R = 0.08 ... increased significantly within packets, whereas the duration of UP states decreased (R = – 0.02 ... and DOWN states increased (R = 0.07 ... and packets (R = 0.7 ... Spindle duration also increased

claims.statement: pE cells fire in stable sequences early in UP states, and the latency of a cell's first spike is negatively correlated with its firing rate.
claims.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 5; Figure 2D and 2E
claims.quote: pyramidal neurons fired in reliable spatiotemporal sequences during the early part of the UP state (<200 msec) and these stereotypical sequences remained stable across the entirety of sleep (Figure 2D). Additionally, the spike onset times of individual neurons in the sequences were negatively correlated with their firing rates (Figure 2E)

claims.statement: Within UP states, the fastest sextile and pI cells decrease and the slowest sextile increases from early to late SLEEP, and within packets the fastest sextile drops while pI cells increase.
claims.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 3; Results, Firing rate and LFP changes within nonREM episodes and packets, paragraph 7; Figure 3F and Figure 4E
claims.quote: the firing rates of the fastest sextile group and putative interneurons decreased later in sleep, whereas firing of the slowest sextile increased (Figure 3F) ... showed a drop in firing rate for the fastest sextile group ... an increase in firing rate of putative interneurons

claims.statement: Recordings were made in four rats, in eight novel exploration sessions, each a PRE sleep, a MAZE epoch on one of two linear tracks or a circular track, and a POST sleep.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure S1 (as cited in the text)
claims.quote: Simultaneous recordings of well-isolated CA1 pyramidal single units were performed in four rats ... exploration of one of two linear or a circular track (MAZE) ... preexperience sleep (PRE) and postexperience sleep (POST) ... (eight novel exploration sessions)
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the dandiset holds 4 subjects and 8 sessions, each with PRE, MAZE and POST epochs in this order, and the MAZE positions come from two linear tracks and one circular track.

claims.statement: The Bayesian decoder was built from 491 place cells over the eight sessions.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2
claims.quote: a spatial Bayesian decoder (2), constructed from the firing-rate vectors of place cells (n = 491 cells) during track running (eight novel exploration sessions)
claims.criterion: Place cells as defined in the opening comment. The 1 Hz threshold is a choice; 0.5 and 2 Hz are shown as variants and do not change the outcome.

claims.statement: Sequence scores (rZ) of candidate events are higher in POST sleep than in PRE sleep (replay).
claims.source: Figure 1C
claims.quote: Cumulative distribution of rZ for PRE, MAZE, and POSTevents, and 95% confidence intervals. ... Inset, mean ± SE of sequence scores in each condition. *P < 0.05; **P < 0.005; ***P < 0.0005 (Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by post hoc Tukey-Kramer tests).
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the mean rZ of POST events exceeds that of PRE events and the Tukey comparison on ranks after Kruskal-Wallis gives p < 0.05. Results per session are shown; partially reproduced when the pooled test holds but fewer than 5 of 8 sessions have a higher POST mean.

claims.statement: Sequence content is higher in MAZE immobility events than in PRE sleep events.
claims.source: Figure 1C; Figure 2C legend
claims.quote: the marked increase in sequence content observed in the MAZE and POSTepochs is driven by the recruitment of plastic cells
claims.criterion: As for fig1c-post-gt-pre, with MAZE events in place of POST events.

claims.statement: 216 neurons showed significant PCC scores in PRE or POST and were considered to contribute strongly to sequences.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2B
claims.quote: Neurons that showed significant PCC scores in either PRE or POST were considered to be strongly contributing to sequence formation (n = 216 neurons (Fig. 2B)
claims.criterion: Strongly contributing as defined in the opening comment. A false-positive rate for the PCC test is computed by repeating it with every rate map shifted, and shown.

claims.statement: Most neurons strongly contributing to PRE sequences (73%) also contributed to POST sequences.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2C as cited
claims.quote: Importantly, the majority of neurons strongly contributing to PRE (73%) also contributed to POST sequences (Fig. 2C and fig. S19)
claims.criterion: The fraction is pooled over sessions. Its chance level, the fraction of all place cells that are strongly contributing in POST, is shown.

claims.statement: The PRE to POST increase in sequence score is eliminated when the place fields of the 10 to 20% of cells with the highest dPCC are shuffled, and remains after shuffling the bottom 75%.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2D
claims.quote: Replay (POST > PRE) was eliminated after shuffling or removal of the top 10 to 20% of cells with the highest ΔPCC scores, whereas it remained after shuffling or removal of the bottom 75%
claims.criterion: Within each session the place cells are ranked by dPCC; the rate maps of the top or bottom X% (X = 10, 20, 50, 75) are circularly shifted by random amounts and PRE and POST events are decoded again. Replay is present when the mean POST rZ exceeds the mean PRE rZ with a one-sided rank-sum p < 0.05 (pooled over sessions). Reproduced when replay is absent after shuffling the top 10% or the top 20%, and present after shuffling the bottom 75%. Partially reproduced when only one of the two holds.

claims.statement: The PRE to POST increase in sequence content is attributable to a small number of plastic cells; removing them, unlike removing rigid cells, removes the increase.
claims.source: Figure 2E
claims.quote: The PRE to POST increase in sequence content is attributable to only a small number of plastic cells.
claims.criterion: Events are decoded again with plastic cells removed from the templates, and with rigid cells removed. Replay as in fig2d-shuffle-high-dpcc. Reproduced when replay is absent without plastic cells and present without rigid cells; partially reproduced when replay remains in both cases but the POST minus PRE difference without plastic cells is less than half of that without rigid cells.

claims.statement: Rigid and plastic neurons were similarly distributed along the track.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 3; fig. S2 as cited
claims.quote: Rigid and plastic neurons were similarly distributed along the track (fig. S2).
claims.criterion: The position of each cell's rate-map peak (in its direction of higher peak), as a fraction of the track length, is compared between rigid and plastic cells with a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 (the claim is of absence; the paper's test is not known, so this test is fixed here).

claims.statement: Plastic neurons had higher place-specific indices and fewer place fields than rigid cells.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 3A
claims.quote: Plastic neurons had higher place-specific indices and fewer place fields compared with rigid cells (Fig. 3A)
claims.criterion: Spatial information (Skaggs, bits per spike) and the number of place fields (contiguous runs of at least 3 bins at 1 Hz or more and at 20% of the peak or more), both from the rate map of the direction with the higher peak, compared with rank-sum tests. Reproduced when plastic cells have higher spatial information and fewer fields, each with p < 0.05; partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: Plastic but not rigid neurons increased their spatial specificity (in-field versus out-of-field firing ratio) steadily during the MAZE session.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 3B
claims.quote: plastic but not rigid neurons increased their spatial specificity steadily during learning (Fig. 3B and fig. S13)
claims.criterion: In-field bins are those of the cell's largest field on the whole-session map. For each cell the in-field over out-of-field rate is computed in the first and the last third of its running time; the change (last minus first, of the log ratio) is tested against 0 with a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test per group. Reproduced when plastic cells increase with p < 0.05 and rigid cells do not; partially reproduced when both increase; not reproduced when plastic cells do not.

claims.statement: Session-wide firing rates of rigid neurons were higher than those of plastic neurons.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 4A
claims.quote: Session-wide firing rates of rigid neurons were significantly higher compared with plastic neurons (Fig. 4, A and B, and figs. S14 and S15).
claims.criterion: Spike count over the whole recording duration, rank-sum test, p < 0.05 with the rigid median higher.

claims.statement: Ripple-related spiking, bursting and pairwise coactivation were higher in plastic than in rigid neurons.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 4A
claims.quote: Ripple-related spiking, bursting, and pair-wise coactivation were higher in plastic versus rigid neurons (Fig. 4A and figs. S14 to S16).
claims.criterion: Ripple-related spiking is the rate within PRE and POST candidate events over the session rate; bursting is the fraction of spikes with an inter-spike interval of 6 ms or less to a neighbour; coactivation is a cell's mean Pearson correlation of 100 ms spike counts with the session's other place cells over the whole session. Rank-sum tests. Reproduced when all three are higher in plastic cells with p < 0.05, partially reproduced for one or two, not reproduced for none.

claims.statement: In PRE sleep, coactivation was dominated by fast-firing neurons.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 4C
claims.quote: In PRE sleep, coactivity was dominated by fast-firing neurons, and these correlations remained unchanged into POST sleep.
claims.criterion: Place cells of each session are sorted by session firing rate and grouped into windows of 20% of the cells, stepped by 1% (as the legend states). For each window the mean pairwise Pearson correlation of 100 ms counts in PRE is computed; curves are averaged over sessions by window position. Reproduced when the Spearman correlation between window position and PRE coactivation on the averaged curve is above 0.5 and at least 5 of 8 sessions have a positive correlation.

claims.statement: Slow-firing neurons showed the strongest increases in coactivation from PRE to POST sleep.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 4C
claims.quote: In contrast, slow-firing neurons showed the strongest increases in coactivation from PRE to POST sleep (Fig. 4B).
claims.criterion: As in fig4c-pre-fast-coactivation, on POST minus PRE coactivation. Reproduced when the Spearman correlation on the averaged curve is below -0.5 and at least 5 of 8 sessions have a negative correlation.

claims.statement: Slow-firing cells showed the greatest replay, the partial correlation between RUN and POST coactivation accounting for PRE.
claims.source: Figure 4C legend
claims.quote: Moreover, it was the slow-firing cells that showed the greatest replay (partial correlation across coactivation values between RUN and POST, accounting for PRE).
claims.criterion: For each window, the partial correlation across its cell pairs between MAZE running and POST coactivation given PRE coactivation. Reproduced when the Spearman correlation on the averaged curve is below -0.5 and at least 5 of 8 sessions have a negative correlation.

claims.statement: Place cells divided into equal groups by sleep firing rate have medians of 0.39 Hz (low-rate) and 1.12 Hz (high-rate).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 6
claims.quote: we divided place cells into equal subgroups by either “off-line” sleep-firing rate or ripple-rate gain ... Low-rate neurons (median, 0.39 Hz) ... than high-rate cells (median, 1.12 Hz)
claims.criterion: Sleep firing rate is the rate over PRE and POST outside REM and awake periods, that is in non-REM sleep. The paper does not say whether the split is per session or pooled; the readings are (a) a median split within each session, (b) a median split of all place cells pooled. Reproduced when both medians are within tolerance under one reading. The rate over the whole of PRE and POST is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Low-rate neurons carried more spatial information per spike on the maze, and increased their within-ripple firing-rate gain from PRE to POST more than high-rate cells.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 6; fig. S16 as cited
claims.quote: Low-rate neurons (median, 0.39 Hz) contributed more spatial information per spike on the maze and displayed increased within-ripple firing-rate gains from PRE to POST sleep than high-rate cells
claims.criterion: Under the reading of rate-split-medians that matches (reading (a) if neither or both do), rank-sum tests of spatial information and of the change in gain (rate within candidate events over the epoch rate, POST minus PRE). Reproduced when low-rate cells are higher on both with p < 0.05, partially reproduced for one.

claims.statement: Slow-firing, but not fast-firing, neurons increased their contribution to sequences from PRE to POST sleep, in a decoding restricted to each group.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figure 4D
claims.quote: Slow-firing, but not fast-firing, neurons increased their contribution to neuronal sequences from PRE to POST sleep (Fig. 4D).
claims.criterion: Templates are restricted to the low-rate or the high-rate half (split as in figs16-low-rate-info-gain) and PRE and POST events decoded again. Replay as in fig2d-shuffle-high-dpcc. Reproduced when replay is present for low-rate cells and absent for high-rate cells; partially reproduced when present for both with a larger POST minus PRE difference for low-rate cells.

claims.statement: PRE to POST increases in sequence content were limited to cells with high ripple-specific recruitment (gain).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figure 4E
claims.quote: Conversely, PRE to POST increases in sequence content were limited to cells that showed a high degree of ripple-specific recruitment (gain) (Fig. 4E and figs. S20 to S22)
claims.criterion: Gain is the rate within PRE and POST candidate events over the PRE and POST rate; place cells are split at the session median. Decoding and replay as in fig4d-slow-sequences. Reproduced when replay is present for high-gain cells and absent for low-gain cells; partially reproduced when present for both with a larger difference for high-gain cells.

claims.statement: Of 206 mice that started training, 140 reached proficiency in the basic task and 98 in the full task.
claims.source: Results, opening section, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Out of 206 mice that started training, 140 achieved proficiency in the basic task, and 98 in the full task
claims.criterion: Counts of distinct mice under the paper's selection (project mice, criterion reached by 2020-03-23, code query_subjects), proficiency as P1 and P2 under each reading. A dataset that holds fewer mice is reported with the counts it holds; the claim is judged on the counts. P1 per the header (answers of 2026-10-22): trials completed are all trials; a mouse is proficient at the first session meeting the 1a or the 1b criteria, at any date (the pipeline's SessionTrainingStatus); 1b replacing 1a from 2019-09-12 (code text_trained1a_to_1b_sessions.py) is a variant.

claims.statement: Basic task training took 18.4 +- 13.0 days (s.d., n = 140 mice), from 3 days for the fastest mouse to 59 days for the slowest.
claims.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 2g
claims.quote: The average training took 18.4 ± 13.0 days (s.d., n = 140, Figure 2g )
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the number of training days (days with a session in the per-day summary the code reads) up to P1 (code figure2g_time_to_trained.py). The code's query branch counts days up to and including the P1 day, its CSV branch days before it; both readings are run. Mean and s.d. over the 140 mice (or those the dataset holds), and the minimum and maximum.

claims.statement: The number of days to basic task proficiency differed across laboratories; within-lab interquartile ranges ranged from 8 days (Lab 2) to 22 days (Lab 6).
claims.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 2g
claims.quote: The number of days needed to achieve basic task proficiency was different across laboratories ( Figure 2g , p<0.001, Kruskal-Wallis nonparametric test followed by a post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparisons test)
claims.criterion: Days per mouse as in fig2g-days-to-proficiency, under both of its readings. Kruskal-Wallis test across the seven labs (the code switches to a one-way ANOVA when the days pass scipy's normality test; shown as a variant). Reproduced when p < 0.001. Interquartile ranges per lab are pandas' default (linear) quantiles, as in the code.

claims.statement: Measured in trials, basic task training took 10.8 +- 8.6 thousand trials (s.d., n = 140), from one thousand for the fastest mouse to 43 thousand for the slowest; reaching 80% correct on easy trials took on average about 7.4 thousand trials.
claims.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 2, figure supplement 1
claims.quote: For mice that learned the task, the average training took 10.8 ± 8.6 thousands of trials (s.d., n = 140) ... The fastest learner met training criteria in one thousand trials, the slowest 43 thousand trials. To reach 80% on easy trials took on average ~7.4 thousand trials.
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the summed trial counts of the training days counted in fig2g-days-to-proficiency (code figure2g_time_to_trained.py), under both of its readings. The 7.4 thousand trials is printed by supp_figure2_performance_trials.py, and its method is followed. The 140 proficient mice, sessions (training days) with more than 100 trials, each mouse's easy-trial performance median-filtered over 3 sessions, training day counted from 0 at the mouse's first kept session, cumulative trials per mouse summed over its kept sessions; per training day, the mean over mice of performance and of cumulative trials; the value is the smallest mean cumulative trial count among training days whose mean performance exceeds 80%. Variant, shown only: the mean over mice of each mouse's cumulative trials at its first session above 80% correct on easy trials.

claims.statement: About 80% of mice that started training would learn the basic task within the 40 days usually allotted (Kaplan-Meier estimate over all 206 mice).
claims.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 4; Figure 2h
claims.quote: there was a 80% probability that mice would learn the task within the 40 days that were usually allotted, and when mice were trained for a longer duration, the success rate rose even further ( Figure 2h )
claims.criterion: Kaplan-Meier estimate (code figure2d_training_probability.py, lifelines) over all 206 mice that started training (Figure 2 legend, "Data in h is for all mice that started training (n = 206)"): time = number of sessions with status in_training or untrainable; event = the mouse's last status is neither, so mice still in training at the cutoff date are censored. The code leaves out mice still in training after the cutoff date; that is a variant. Without status labels in the dataset, time = training days to P1 for proficient mice and their total training days otherwise, with P1 as in the header (answer of 2026-10-22): "all contrasts introduced" in each of the three sessions (Appendix 1, table 1d) is the main reading, and the pipeline's check of the last session only (0% and 6.25% present) a variant. Reproduced when the cumulative proportion at day 40 is within the tolerance and higher at the last day than at day 40.

claims.statement: Contrast threshold and bias varied little during training; the threshold interquartile range slightly decreased from 12-29% in the first 10 training days to 11-23% thereafter, and the bias interquartile range went from -5.2 to 7.1% to -5.6 to 6.5%.
claims.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 2b,c
claims.quote: Estimates of contrast threshold did not vary much during training ( Figure 2b ), with an interquartile range that slightly decreased from 12–29% during the first 10 training days, and 11–23% thereafter. Likewise, bias did not vary much, with an interquartile range of −5.2% to 7.1% during the first 10 days to −5.6% to 6.5% thereafter ( Figure 2c ).
claims.criterion: Per-session psychometric threshold and bias of the 140 proficient mice, as plotted in Figure 2b,c (code figure2af_learning_curves_all_parameters.py): 50:50 sessions (the basic-task sessions with all their trials, header; answer of 2026-10-22) with more than 100 trials, threshold and bias only from sessions with six or more signed contrasts (legend: from the first session with 12% contrast), each mouse's series median-filtered over 3 sessions, training day counted from 0 at the mouse's first session (the code), so the first 10 training days are code days 0 to 9. The code does not print the interquartile ranges, so the pooling is open; readings (1) all session values pooled over mice within days 1-10 and after day 10, (2) as (1) without the median filter, each with "thereafter" as (a) days 11 to 40 (the plotted range) and (b) all later days. Reproduced when all eight bounds are within tolerance under one reading and the threshold range after day 10 is narrower than in days 1-10.

claims.statement: During training mice were not systematically biased to one side; absolute bias averaged 9.8 +- 12.1 (s.d.), and contrast threshold, which stabilized after about 10 sessions, averaged 17.8 +- 11.7%.
claims.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 2b,c
claims.quote: Mice across laboratories were not systematically biased towards a particular side and the absolute bias was similar across laboratories (9.8 ± 12.1 [s.d.] on average). Likewise, measures of contrast threshold stabilized after the first ~10 sessions, which was on average 17.8 ± 11.7% on average across institutions.
claims.criterion: Same per-session values and readings as fig2bc-threshold-bias-iqr. No code computes these numbers; the averaging is open, with readings (1) mean and s.d. over all session values pooled over mice (absolute bias over all days; threshold after day 10), and (2) mean of the seven lab means ("on average across institutions") with the s.d. over pooled values. Reproduced when the two means are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Variability in performance across mice decreased with training but did not disappear; between training days 15 and 40, mean easy-trial performance rose from 80.7% to 91.1% while its s.d. across mice fell from 19.1% to 10.1%.
claims.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 3; Figure 2, figure supplement 2
claims.quote: For example, between training days 15 and 40, when the average performance on easy trials of the mice increased from 80.7% to 91.1%, the variation across mice (s.d.) of performance on easy trials decreased from 19.1% to 10.1%.
claims.criterion: Easy-trial performance per mouse and training day for the 140 proficient mice. No code prints these four numbers. Readings (1) supp_figure2_performance_trials.py, which computes the mean and s.d. over mice per training day (behav_summary, behav_summary_std) from sessions with more than 100 trials, median-filtered over 3 sessions, training day counted from 0 at the first kept session, at training days 15 and 40 of that count (and at 14 and 39, if the text counts from 1); (2) the Figure 2a,d data (code figure2af: as (1) and only 50:50 sessions) at the same days; (3) the unfiltered per-day performance binned as in suppfig_variability_over_time.py (training_day strictly within 2 days of the bin centre) at days 15 and 39, the nearest bin to 40. Reproduced when the mean rises and the s.d. falls, with all four values within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: A Random Forests decoder applied to the change in easy-trial performance over the first five sessions predicted whether a mouse would be in the bottom quartile of learning speed with 53% accuracy (chance 25%), and misclassified a top-quartile mouse as bottom-quartile only 7% of the time.
claims.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 3
claims.quote: A Random Forests decoder applied to change in performance (% correct with easy, high-contrast stimuli) in the first five sessions was able to predict whether a mouse would end up in the bottom quartile of learning speed (the slowest learners) with accuracy of 53% (where chance is 25%). Conversely, the chance of misclassifying a fast-learning, top quartile mouse as a slow-learning, bottom quartile mouse, was only 7%.
claims.criterion: The repository at the cited commit holds no code for this analysis and the Methods do not describe it. Learning-speed quartiles from days to P1 (fig2g-days-to-proficiency; trials to P1, as in Figure 2, figure supplement 1c, is a further reading). Open details and the readings the text allows: features (a) the four session-to-session differences in easy-trial performance over sessions 1-5, (b) the five performances; labels (A) the four quartiles, (B) bottom quartile against the rest (chance 25% then the base rate); scikit-learn Random Forest with default settings and leave-one-out cross-validation, as for the lab classifiers in the Methods; accuracy read as (i) recall of the bottom-quartile class, (ii) overall four-class accuracy under (A), and (iii) precision of the bottom-quartile class. If the readings disagree on whether accuracy is near 53% and well above 25%, the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: At basic task proficiency, errors on easy (50% and 100%) contrasts were low, 9.5 +- 3.6%, with no significant difference across laboratories.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 3c
claims.quote: The lapse rates (i.e., the errors made in response to easy contrasts of 50% and 100%) were low (9.5 ± 3.6%, Figure 3c ) with no significant difference across laboratories.
claims.criterion: Per mouse, 100 minus the easy-trial performance over the pooled S1 trials (code figure3cde, perf_easy); mice with no valid trial duration are dropped, as in the code. Mean and s.d. over mice. The lab comparison is claim fig3cde-no-lab-difference-medians.

claims.statement: At basic task proficiency the contrast threshold was similar across laboratories at 14.3 +- 3.8 (s.d., n = 7 laboratories) and the response bias was small at 0.3 +- 8.4.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 3d,e
claims.quote: The slope of the curves, which measures contrast sensitivity, was also similar across laboratories, at 14.3 ± 3.8 (s.d., n = 7 laboratories, Figure 3d ). Finally, the horizontal displacement of the curve, which measures response bias, was small at 0.3 ± 8.4 (s.d., n = 7, Figure 3e ).
claims.criterion: Per mouse, psychometric threshold and bias fitted to the pooled S1 trials (code figure3cde). The code prints the mean and s.d. over mice (thres_mean, thres_std) while the text says n = 7 laboratories; readings (1) mean and s.d. over mice, (2) mean and s.d. over the seven lab means. The bias tolerance is 8.4/sqrt(7), the paper's s.d. over n = 7, because 10% of a value near zero is below any fitting precision.

claims.statement: At basic task proficiency, easy-trial performance, contrast threshold and bias did not differ in median across laboratories.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 3c-e
claims.quote: None of these measures showed a significant difference across laboratories, either in median (performance: p=0.63, threshold: p=0.81, bias: p=0.81, FDR corrected Kruskal-Wallis test)
claims.criterion: Per-mouse values from S1 as in fig3c-easy-errors-basic and fig3de-threshold-bias-basic. Kruskal-Wallis test across the seven labs for each variable, then Benjamini-Hochberg FDR over the six variables the code tests together (easy-trial performance, trial duration, trials per session, threshold, bias, trials per minute; code figure3cde). Reproduced when all three corrected p >= 0.05, not reproduced when any is below; the effect sizes are reported. The code's switch to ANOVA for normally distributed variables is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: At basic task proficiency, easy-trial performance, contrast threshold and bias did not differ in variance across laboratories.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 3c-e
claims.quote: or in variance (performance: p=0.09, threshold: p=0.57, bias: p=0.57, FDR corrected Levene's test)
claims.criterion: As fig3cde-no-lab-difference-medians, with scipy's Levene test (default, median-centred) and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR over the same six variables (code figure3cde). Reproduced when all three corrected p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: At basic task proficiency the median trial duration (stimulus onset to feedback) was 468 +- 221 ms, with some differences across laboratories.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 4; Figure 3, figure supplement 2a
claims.quote: The median time from stimulus onset to feedback (trial duration, a coarse measure of reaction time) was 468 ± 221 ms, showing some differences across laboratories ( Figure 3—figure supplement 2a , p=0.004, Kruskal-Wallis nonparametric test)
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the median of response time minus stimulus onset time over the pooled S1 trials, no-response trials left out (code figure3cde, reaction_time); the median and s.d. over mice (code rt_median, rt_std). Kruskal-Wallis across labs; the code FDR-corrects this p with the other five variables, the text does not say; readings uncorrected and corrected. Reproduced when the values are within tolerance and p < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: At basic task proficiency mice performed 719 +- 223 trials per session; the difference across laboratories was significant but only in one laboratory relative to the rest.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 4; Figure 3, figure supplement 2b
claims.quote: Mice on average performed 719 ± 223 trials per session ( Figure 3—figure supplement 2b ). This difference was significant (p<10 −6 , one-way ANOVA) but only in one laboratory relative to the rest.
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the mean number of trials over its S1 sessions (code figure3cde, n_trials); mean and s.d. over mice. One-way ANOVA across labs (code; the FDR correction it applies is a variant), then Tukey post hoc tests as in the code. Reproduced when the values are within tolerance, the ANOVA gives p < 1e-6, and the significant Tukey pairs all involve one lab. Partially reproduced when p < 0.05 but not below 1e-6, or the pairs involve more than one lab.

claims.statement: A Naive Bayes classifier could not identify a mouse's laboratory from its basic-task performance, threshold and bias; its accuracy was 0.12 +- 0.051 against a chance level of 0.11, and the 95% range of its distribution included chance.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 5; Figure 3f
claims.quote: Its mean accuracy was 0.12 ± 0.051, and a 95th percentile of its distribution included the chance level of 0.11 (mean of the null distribution).
claims.criterion: Lab classifier (shared definition) with scikit-learn GaussianNB on per-mouse easy-trial performance, threshold and bias from S1 (code figure3f_classifier_lab_membership_basic.py). The paper's test, from the code (figure3f_plot_classifier_basic.py), is that the classifier is not above chance when the 2.5th percentile of its 2000 accuracies is at or below the mean shuffled accuracy. Reproduced when that holds, not reproduced when the 2.5th percentile is above chance. The accuracy tolerance is the paper's stated s.d. of the subsample distribution. Subsample size per the Methods' rule (header, Lab classifier; answer of 2026-10-22): the lowest lab count over all datasets classified when it is below 8, the same for every classifier claim; 8 as in the code is a variant.

claims.statement: With the laboratory's time zone added as a feature, the classifier performed above chance and confused labs in the same time zone.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 5; Figure 3f; Figure 3, figure supplement 3b
claims.quote: If the classifier was given this variable during training and testing it performed above chance ( Figure 3f , Positive control ) and the confusion matrix showed clusters of labs located in the same time zone
claims.criterion: As fig3f-classifier-chance-basic with the lab's time zone as a fourth feature (the code's offsets, Europe 0, New York -5, Los Angeles -7, from the lab's location). Reproduced when the 2.5th percentile of the control accuracies is above the mean shuffled accuracy (the code also computes a 0.001th percentile, sig_control, shown as a variant) and the mean confusion matrix puts more off-diagonal mass on labs in the same time zone than on labs in others.

claims.statement: Random Forest and Logistic Regression classifiers also failed to predict laboratory membership from basic-task behavior.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 5; Figure 3, figure supplement 3d-i
claims.quote: Similar results were obtained with two other classifier algorithms ( Figure 3—figure supplement 3d–i ).
claims.criterion: As fig3f-classifier-chance-basic with scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier (100 trees, random_state 424242) and LogisticRegression (solver liblinear), as in the code. Reproduced when neither is above chance by the same rule.

claims.statement: The institutions named in the dandiset's files are the paper's seven laboratories, so that the code's lab numbers (Lab 1 to 7) and time zones can be given to the dataset's mice.
claims.source: Claims file header, code lab numbers and time zones (paper-behavior at commit edc4531)
claims.criterion: Each session's institution in the files is matched by name to the code's laboratories. Reproduced when the seven institutions match the seven laboratories one to one. Whether the session start times bear out the time zones (start hours shifted by the labs' offsets if they are in UTC, as stated) is reported. Added by the author of attempt 000045-ibl-2021-01 (protocol, Author, step 4) for fig3f-positive-control, whose time-zone feature comes from the paper's code by laboratory.

claims.statement: In the basic task, mouse choices were no more consistent within laboratories than across laboratories.
claims.source: Figure 3, figure supplement 1a legend
claims.quote: This averaged consistency was not significantly higher (p=0.73) than a null distribution generated by randomly shuffling lab assignments between mice and computing the average within-lab choice variability 10,000 times ( violin plot ). Therefore, choices were no more consistent within labs than across labs.
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the fraction of rightward choices at each signed contrast; per lab, the variance across mice at each contrast, its mean over contrasts, and the inverse (consistency); the mean over labs compared with 10,000 shuffles of lab labels across mice; p = fraction of shuffles above the data (legend; code suppfig_choicevariability_withinacrosslabs.py, where 50% contrast trials are dropped). Sessions per the legend, S1 ("same data as in Figure 3"); the code instead uses the P1 day and the two days after (days_from_criterion [0, 2]), shown as a variant. Reproduced when p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: In the full task, neither choice fractions nor the bias shift between blocks were more consistent within laboratories than expected by chance.
claims.source: Figure 3, figure supplement 1b,c legend; Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Within-lab choice consistency on the full task was not higher than expected by chance, p=0.25. ... Within-lab consistency in bias shift was not higher than expected by chance (p=0.31).
claims.criterion: As fig3s1a-choice-consistency-basic on S2 trials (legend "same data as in Figure 4"; code), with consistency computed per signed contrast and block before averaging (b), and for the bias shift (c) per mouse and contrast the fraction rightward in 20:80 blocks minus 80:20 blocks. Reproduced when both p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: With a looser proficiency criterion (80% correct on easy trials over three sessions, n = 150 mice), behavior was again consistent across laboratories; only the number of trials per session differed slightly, and a classifier failed to identify a mouse's laboratory.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 6; Figure 3, figure supplement 4
claims.quote: there was a small but significant difference in the number of trials per session across laboratories. All other measured parameters were similar.
claims.criterion: Sessions per the code (query_session_around_performance, suppfig_3-4a-f.py): for each mouse, the first three consecutive basic sessions each with more than 80% correct on easy trials; sessions with five or more signed contrasts kept; mice with three such sessions. Lab tests and FDR as in fig3cde-no-lab-difference-medians on the same six variables; Naive Bayes classifier on performance, threshold and bias as in fig3f-classifier-chance-basic (suppfig_classifier_lab_membership_perf.py). Reproduced when trials per session has corrected p < 0.05, the other five have p >= 0.05, and the classifier is not above chance.

claims.statement: In the first three sessions of the full task, bias in each block, contrast threshold in each block and performance on 100% contrast trials did not vary significantly across laboratories, and a classifier could not predict lab membership.
claims.source: Figure 3, figure supplement 5 legend; Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 6
claims.quote: Bias for each block prior did not vary significantly over labs (Kruskal-Wallis test, 20:80 blocks; p=0.96, 50:50 block; p=0.96, 80:20 block; p=0.89). ( b ) The contrast thresholds also did not vary systematically over labs (Kruskal-Wallis test, 20:80 block; p=0.078, 50:50 block; p=0.12, 80:20 block; p=0.17). ( c ) Performance on 100% contrast trials neither (Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.15).
claims.criterion: Per mouse and block, psychometric fits to the pooled trials of the first three full-task sessions, and performance on 100% contrast trials (legend; the code's correct_easy, which also counts any 50% contrast trials, is a variant). Sessions per the legend, the first three biased sessions from P1b, the first biased session on or after P1 (header; answer of 2026-10-22), with the code's P1b (first biased session with status trained_1b) a variant; the code (suppfig_variability_over_labs_first_biased.py) takes the biased sessions on training days 1 to 3 after P1b, and its classifier script days -1 to 3; both shown as variants. Kruskal-Wallis across labs for each of the seven variables, as the legend names it (the code corrects the seven p values with statsmodels' default Holm-Sidak method; variant). Naive Bayes classifier on the seven variables as in fig3f-classifier-chance-basic. Reproduced when all seven p >= 0.05 and the classifier is not above chance.

claims.statement: Mice incorporated the block priors into their choices from the first sessions of the full task.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 3, figure supplement 5a
claims.quote: Mice incorporated block priors into their choices already from the first sessions in which they were exposed to this full task
claims.criterion: Per-mouse bias in 80:20 and 20:80 blocks from the sessions of fig3s5-first-full-sessions (both readings). The paper reports no test for this; the test is the one the paper uses for the block effect on bias in Figure 4i (fig4i-bias-shifts-with-block), a Wilcoxon signed-rank test of bias in 80:20 against 20:80 blocks. Reproduced when bias is higher in 80:20 than in 20:80 blocks (median of paired differences) with p < 0.05. The median difference is also reported against the full-task proficiency threshold bias[80:20] - bias[20:80] > 5 (Appendix 1, table 1d), a criterion for counting mice and not a test, as a variant.

claims.statement: Mice that reached full task proficiency took 31.5 +- 16.1 days, or 20,494 +- 10,980 trials (s.d., n = 98), from the start of training; the fastest took 8 days (4691 trials), the slowest 81 days (61,316 trials).
claims.source: Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 2
claims.quote: For mice that reached full task proficiency, the average training from start to finish took 31.5 ± 16.1 days, or 20,494 ± 10,980 trials (s.d., n = 98). ... The fastest learner achieved proficiency in 8 days (4691 trials), the slowest 81 days (61,316 trials).
claims.criterion: Per mouse reaching P2, the last training-day number and the summed trials over training days up to and including the P2 day (code supp_queries.py, n_training_days = MAX(training_day), total_trials = SUM(n_trials_date)); mean, s.d., minimum and maximum over mice.

claims.statement: Block structure had the greatest effect on choices when sensory evidence was absent; the shift in rightward choices between 20:80 and 80:20 blocks was highest at 0% contrast in every laboratory, averaging 28.5%.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 4c-e
claims.quote: The average shift in rightward choices was invariably highest at 0% contrast, where rightward choices in the two blocks differed by an average of 28.5%.
claims.criterion: Per mouse, psychometric fits to the pooled S2 trials of the 20:80 and 80:20 blocks; the bias shift at each signed contrast is the fitted rightward choice percentage in 20:80 minus 80:20 (code figure4de_psychfuncs_biased.py; the Figure 4c legend reads it from the curves). Mean over mice at 0%. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance and, in each of the seven labs, the lab mean is highest at 0% contrast.

claims.statement: The bias shift at 0% contrast did not differ across laboratories more than within them.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 4d,e
claims.quote: This value did not significantly differ across laboratories any more than it differed within laboratories (one-way ANOVA F(6) = 1.345, p=0.2455, Figure 4d,e ).
claims.criterion: Per-mouse bias shift at 0% from fig4cd-biasshift-largest-at-zero; one-way ANOVA on lab (code, statsmodels ols and type 2 anova_lm). Reproduced when p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Block type did not significantly affect the contrast threshold.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 3; Figure 4f
claims.quote: Changes in block type did not significantly affect the contrast threshold (Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test, p=0.85, n = 98 mice, Figure 4f ).
claims.criterion: Per mouse, psychometric fits to the pooled S2 trials of 80:20 and of 20:80 blocks (code figure4fghi_variability_over_labs_full.py); scipy Wilcoxon signed-rank test of threshold in the two blocks. Reproduced when p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Block type changed lapse rates, which were higher on the left in 20:80 blocks and higher on the right in 80:20 blocks.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 3; Figure 4g,h
claims.quote: However, it did change the lapse rates, which were consistently higher on the left in the 20:80 blocks and on the right in the 80:20 blocks
claims.criterion: Fits as in fig4f-threshold-unchanged-by-block; left lapse gamma and right lapse lambda per block; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests between blocks. Reproduced when the left lapse is higher in 20:80 and the right lapse higher in 80:20 (median of paired differences) with p < 1e-6 and p < 1e-7; partially reproduced when the directions hold with p < 0.05 only.

claims.statement: Block type changed the overall bias consistently, with curves shifting left in 20:80 blocks and right in 80:20 blocks.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 3; Figure 4i
claims.quote: Finally, as expected there was a highly consistent change in overall bias, with curves shifting to the left in 20:80 trials and to the right in 80:20 trials
claims.criterion: Fits as in fig4f-threshold-unchanged-by-block; Wilcoxon signed-rank test of bias mu between blocks. Reproduced when mu is lower in 20:80 than in 80:20 blocks (median of paired differences) with p < 1e-16; partially reproduced when the direction holds with p < 0.05 only.

claims.statement: Threshold, lapses and bias in each block type showed no significant differences across laboratories.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 4f-i
claims.quote: An analysis of the psychometric curves showed highly consistent effects of block type, with no significant differences across laboratories ( Figure 4f–i ).
claims.criterion: The paper gives no test; the code (figure4fghi) runs the lab test (shared definition) on each of the eight per-block values (threshold, left lapse, right lapse, bias, in 80:20 and 20:80) and corrects the eight p values with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR. Reproduced when all eight corrected p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: A classifier trained on the full-task psychometric parameters could not predict the laboratory of individual mice above chance.
claims.source: Results, Performance in the full task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 3; Figure 4j
claims.quote: Just as in the basic task ( Figure 3 ), a classifier trained on these variables could not predict above chance the origin laboratory of individual mice above chance ( Figure 4j ).
claims.criterion: Lab classifier with GaussianNB on the eight per-block values of fig4fi-no-lab-difference from S2 (code figure4i_classifier_lab_membership_full.py); same rule as fig3f-classifier-chance-basic. Reproduced when not above chance.

claims.statement: In a logistic choice model fitted to each mouse, visual weights grew with contrast to above 3 at 100% contrast, while weights for past choices were much smaller and positive after both rewarded (basic 0.19, full 0.42) and unrewarded (basic 0.33, full 0.46) trials, indicating perseverance.
claims.source: Results, A probabilistic model reveals common strategies across mice and laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 5c,d,f,g
claims.quote: As expected, visual terms had large weights, which grew with contrast to reach values above 3 at 100% contrast. Weights for non-sensory factors were much lower ( Figure 5c,f , note different scale). Weights for past choices were positive for both rewarded (basic 0.19, full 0.42) and unrewarded previous trials (basic 0.33, full 0.46)
claims.criterion: Model per Methods (Probabilistic choice model, equations 2-4): logistic regression of choice (no-response trials left out) on signed indicators per nonzero contrast, the previous choice split by its outcome (r and u), a constant, and in the full task the block (+1 for 20:80, -1 for 80:20, 0 for 50:50); design matrix by patsy, fit by statsmodels Logit.fit_regularized with its defaults (code figure5_GLM_modelfit.py), per mouse and task. Sessions per the code: training days P1b-2 to P1b+3, split into basic and full by protocol; the Methods say three sessions per mouse, read as (b) the last three basic sessions before P1b and the first three full sessions. Contrasts per the Methods include 50%; the code drops 50% trials (variant). The paper does not say what is done for a mouse shown no 50% trials in the sessions used; readings (answer of 2026-10-22): (a) the Methods' model with W50 left out for that mouse, (b) the code's model, 50% trials dropped for every mouse ("only rarely present (should not be its own regressor)", figure5_GLM_modelfit.py, fit_glm). Means over mice of each weight. Reproduced when the 100% weight's mean exceeds 3 in both tasks, the visual weights increase with contrast, and the four history weights are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Previous choices influenced behavior more strongly in the full task than in the basic task, after both rewarded and unrewarded trials.
claims.source: Results, A probabilistic model reveals common strategies across mice and laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 5d,g
claims.quote: Indeed, previous choices more strongly influenced behavior in the full task, both after rewarded (t(125) = 10.736, p<10 −6 ) and unrewarded trials (t(125) = 4.817, p<10 −6 ).
claims.criterion: Per-mouse weights from fig5cf-glm-weights, mice with both fits; scipy ttest_rel of full against basic, NaN omitted (code figure5_GLM_plot.py). Reproduced when both t are positive with p < 0.05 (the code's num_star significance level). Note that t(125) = 4.817 gives a two-sided p of about 4e-6, above the printed bound of 1e-6; the t value, not the bound, is the reference.

claims.statement: The model predicted individual mouse choices well, with cross-validated accuracy of 81.03 +- 5.1% in the basic task and 82.1 +- 5.8% in the full task, similar across laboratories; mean condition numbers were 2.4 and 3.2.
claims.source: Results, A probabilistic model reveals common strategies across mice and laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 5, figure supplement 2c
claims.quote: Importantly, fitted weights and the model's predictive accuracy (unbiased: 81.03 + 5.1%, biased 82.1 + 5.8%) ( Figure 5—figure supplement 2 ) were similar across laboratories, suggesting an overall common strategy.
claims.criterion: Fits as in fig5cf-glm-weights with 5-fold cross-validation, folds shuffled (the code sets no seed; a standard seed is used and the spread over seeds shown). Accuracy readings: (1) the Figure 5, figure supplement 2c legend, the fraction of test trials where the predicted probability of the actual choice exceeds 50%; (2) the code, the mean predicted probability of the actual choice. Condition number of the design matrix (numpy cond), as in the code. "Similar across laboratories" is fig5s2-weights-similar-across-labs.

claims.statement: Fitted model weights and predictive accuracy were similar across laboratories.
claims.source: Results, A probabilistic model reveals common strategies across mice and laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 5, figure supplement 2
claims.quote: The model fit the mouse choices well and captured the relative importance of sensory and non-sensory information across mice and laboratories
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test; the code (figure5_GLM_plot.py) runs the lab test (shared definition, uncorrected) on each weight (6.25, 12.5, 25, 100, rewarded, unrewarded, bias, and block in the full task), pseudo-R2 and accuracy, per task. Reproduced when no test gives p < 0.05; partially reproduced when one or two of the up to 20 tests do; the p values are reported.

claims.statement: After correcting for slow fluctuations in decision bound, most mice used a win-stay lose-switch strategy, in both the basic and full tasks.
claims.source: Figure 5, figure supplement 1b legend; Results, A probabilistic model reveals common strategies across mice and laboratories, paragraph 3
claims.quote: When taking these slow state-changes into account, the majority of animals use a win-stay lose-switch strategy.
claims.criterion: Code suppfig_history_strategy.py: trials from training days P1b-2 to P1b+3, split by task; signed contrasts with fewer than 100 trials over all mice dropped; per mouse, task, previous choice and previous outcome a psychometric fit; the history shift = fitted rightward % at 0% contrast after a right choice minus after a left choice, separately after rewarded and unrewarded trials, from fits with more than 50 trials; the same with the next trial's choice and outcome; corrected shift = history shift minus next-trial shift (Lak et al., 2020a). Reproduced when, in each task, more than half the mice have a positive corrected post-reward shift and a negative corrected post-error shift.

claims.statement: After rewarded trials, choice updating was largest when the previous stimulus had low contrast and much smaller after high-contrast rewarded trials.
claims.source: Figure 5, figure supplement 1c legend
claims.quote: After rewarded trials, choice updating is largest when the visual stimulus was highly uncertain (i.e. had low contrast) but strongly diminished after more certain, rewarded trials.
claims.criterion: Corrected updating as in fig5s1b-win-stay-lose-switch, computed separately by the previous trial's absolute contrast (code suppfig_history_bycontrast.py; read only in outline here). The paper reports no test. Reproduced when, after rewarded trials, the mean corrected updating after 0% and 6.25% contrast exceeds that after 100% contrast in both tasks.

claims.statement: The session-ending criterion was not mandatory; 5,316 of 10,903 sessions ended earlier and 5,587 later, the latter continuing for a median of 19 +- 16 extra trials (m.a.d.).
claims.source: Results, Training progression in the basic task, paragraph 2; Figure 1, figure supplement 2
claims.quote: The criterion to end a session was not mandatory: some sessions were ended earlier (5,316/10,903 sessions) and others ended later (5,587/10,903 sessions). The latter sessions typically continued for an extra 19 ± 16 trials (median ±m.a.d., 5,587 sessions) longer.
claims.criterion: Code supp_queries.py: all mice that started training; per training day, an end criterion is met when a session that day has an end status (from the pipeline's SessionEndCriteriaImplemented table) or the day's summed session durations reach 90 minutes; extra trials = trials after the end-status trial. Without an end status in the dataset, it is recomputed from the three criteria of the Figure 1, figure supplement 2 legend (fewer than 400 trials in 45 min; over 400 trials and 90 min; over 400 trials and median reaction time over the last 20 trials above 5 times the session median), taking the first trial at which one is met.

claims.statement: Each imaging session recorded between 161 and 3,657 putative CA1 pyramidal cells.
claims.source: Results, Two-photon imaging of CA1 cells in morphed VR environments, paragraph 1; Methods, Two-photon imaging; Extended Data Fig. 1a,b
claims.quote: In each session, we were able to simultaneously image up to several thousands (range of 161–3,657) of putative CA1 pyramidal cells
claims.criterion: Count of cells (Suite2P regions kept as cells) per imaging session (Methods, Two-photon imaging). Which mice the range covers is not stated; Extended Data Fig. 1a,b plot R and F mice only, while the Methods speak of the whole study. Readings (a) every imaging session of R and F mice, (b) every imaging session of R, F and FD mice. Reproduced when, under a reading, the minimum and maximum fall within the range 161 to 3,657 widened by 10% of each bound.

claims.statement: The analyses of sessions 8 to N use 24 rare morph and 21 frequent morph sessions, holding 2,610 and 1,986 trials; the four decision mice contribute 2,460 trials.
claims.source: Figure 3c,d legend; Figure 6b,c legend; Extended Data Fig. 10g legend
claims.criterion: Sessions 8 and later per mouse (M1); trials are all imaged trials of those sessions. For the decision mice the paper does not say which sessions; read as (a) every imaged session and (b) sessions 8 and later. Reproduced when every count is within tolerance under a reading.

claims.statement: Before session 8, rare morph mice had fewer than 4% of trials with intermediate morph values, while frequent morph mice had 60%.
claims.source: Results, Two-photon imaging of CA1 cells in morphed VR environments, paragraph 4; Figure 1d,e
claims.quote: mice experienced very few trials with intermediate morph values (shared S ~ = 0.25 − 0.75 ) during the first 7 training sessions (<4% of trials with intermediate morph values before session 8 ... mice were frequently exposed to trials with intermediate morph values (60% of trials with intermediate morph values before session 8
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the fraction of all trials run in sessions 1 to 7 (imaged and not, M7) with S-tilde 0.25, 0.5 or 0.75. The paper does not say whether the fraction is pooled over mice or per mouse; readings (a) pooled over trials of the group, (b) every mouse. Reproduced when, under a reading, the rare morph fraction is below 4% and the frequent morph fraction is within 0.06 of 60%.

claims.statement: Place cells tiled the track in both conditions; 15,829 rare morph place cells (43% of recorded cells; 23% S-tilde = 0 and 21% S-tilde = 1 place cells) and 8,933 frequent morph place cells (30%; 11% and 10%).
claims.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 1
claims.quote: rare = 15,829 place cells across all S ~ values, 43% of recorded population, 23% of cells S ~ = 0 place cells, 21% of cells S ~ = 1 place cells; frequent = 8,933 place cells across all S ~ values, 30% of recorded population, 11% of cells S ~ = 0 place cells, 10% of cells S ~ = 1 place cells
claims.criterion: Methods, Place cell identification. Per session and separately for each S-tilde value, Skaggs spatial information of each cell over the 45 bins (M3) from the trial-averaged rate map and the occupancy of those trials; the code subtracts the global minimum of the map and adds 0.001 before the log (PlaceCellAnalysis.spatial_info), followed. Null from 1,000 shuffles, each circularly shifting the activity against position within every trial by a uniform random amount (utilities.make_pos_bin_trial_matrices, perm=True); a place cell has p = fraction of shuffles with SI at least the real SI at most 0.05. A cell is a place cell "across all S-tilde" if it is one for any S-tilde. Sessions 8 to N (M1); signal M2. Open details, (1) speed exclusion (M3 readings a and b); (2) the denominator, read as (a) all cells of the condition's sessions pooled, (b) the mean of per-session fractions. Reproduced when all eight values are within tolerance under one combination; partially reproduced when the counts or the fractions alone are.

claims.statement: A smaller proportion of recorded cells were place cells in the frequent morph than in the rare morph condition.
claims.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 4a
claims.quote: The proportion of recorded cells that were classified as place cells was smaller in the frequent morph compared to the rare morph condition
claims.criterion: The place cells of place-cell-fractions, under each of its readings. The paper reports no test. Reproduced when the frequent morph fraction (any S-tilde, and for S-tilde = 0 and = 1) is below the rare morph fraction under every reading; the per-mouse fractions are shown.

claims.statement: The fraction of cells that are place cells in both S-tilde = 0 and S-tilde = 1 trials (6.07% rare, 1.98% frequent) slightly exceeds the overlap expected of independent populations (4.78% and 1.06%), so the two extreme maps are largely independent (global remapping).
claims.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 4a
claims.quote: Specifically, 6.07% and 1.98% of recorded cells had significant spatial information in both environments for rare morph and frequent morph sessions, respectively (chance 4.78% and 1.06%, respectively; one-sample two-sided t -test of actual minus chance overlap, t =−4.87, P = 1.37×10 −5 , N = 45 sessions pooled across all mice)
claims.criterion: Place cells as in place-cell-fractions. Per session, actual overlap is the fraction of all cells that are place cells for both S-tilde = 0 and = 1; chance is the product of the two fractions (Results; code PlotAllPlaceCells, randovlp and actlovlp). The group values in the code are pooled; read as (a) pooled over cells and (b) the mean over sessions. Test, as the code runs it, scipy ttest_1samp of chance minus actual over all sessions of both groups (the order that gives the paper's negative t). Reproduced when the test gives p < 0.05 with actual above chance and the four values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when only the test holds. The 2020 code ran it on 47 sessions; the attempt reports its count.

claims.statement: Cells with place fields in both extreme environments (2,219 rare, 594 frequent) tended to cluster at the end points of the track and in the reward zone.
claims.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 4b,c
claims.quote: Cells with place fields in both extreme environments tended to cluster at the end points of the track and the reward zone
claims.criterion: Cells of edf4a-overlap-above-chance that are place cells in both. Location is the position bin of peak trial-averaged activity in S-tilde = 0 trials and in S-tilde = 1 trials (Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). The paper shows this only as scatter plots; it gives no region or test. The reward zone is 250 to 400 cm (Methods, Morphed environments); "end points" is read as (a) the first and last bin and (b) the first and last 50 cm. The reference is (a) the share of the track those regions cover and (b) the peak locations of all S-tilde = 0 place cells. Reproduced when, in both conditions, the share of overlap cells with peaks in the end points or reward zone exceeds the reference under every combination of readings; the counts are judged by their tolerances.

claims.statement: Rare morph place cells keep their map up to a threshold morph value (S about 0.25 to 0.5) and then switch coherently, while frequent morph place cells change gradually; the difference shows in the place-cell similarity matrices across S-tilde values.
claims.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 3; Figure 2e-h
claims.quote: In the rare morph condition, place cells maintained their representation until a threshold morph value ( S ≈ 0.25–0.50) and then coherently switched to a different representation ... This difference between conditions was also apparent in the normalized place cell population similarity matrices ( P < 0.0011, two-sided permutation test using animal identities (IDs), n = 12 mice)
claims.criterion: Methods, Place cell similarity matrices. Cells that are place cells for any S-tilde (place-cell-fractions), pooled over sessions 8 to N and mice of a condition. Per cell, the five trial-averaged rate maps (one per S-tilde, smoothed per M5), rows divided by their l2 norm, give a 5 x 5 cosine matrix; matrices are averaged over the cells of a condition and subtracted (rare minus frequent). For the z-scored version each cell's matrix is z-scored over its off-diagonal entries (Methods; the 2020 code z-scores jointly over all cells of a session, a variant). Mouse permutation test M12 on each entry, all cells of a mouse moving together, with the 6 rare and 6 frequent mice of the paper (the 2020 code counts R6 as frequent, mi<5, a variant). Reproduced when at least one off-diagonal entry of the z-scored difference lies outside the range of the 923 permuted differences, and at least one entry of the raw difference lies outside their 2.5 to 97.5 percentiles. The entries that do, with their signs, are reported.

claims.statement: In a nonlinear embedding (UMAP) of the morph-by-position activity of task-modulated cells, cells from rare morph and frequent morph mice can be told apart.
claims.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 5c
claims.quote: Rare and frequent morph cells were also separable using this approach.
claims.criterion: Methods, UMAP for dimensionality reduction. The Methods do not name the sessions; read as sessions 8 to N, the sessions of the remapping analyses (Results, Prior experience..., paragraph 1). Cells kept when the Euclidean distance between their mean S-tilde = 0 and S-tilde = 1 rate maps exceeds 99.9% of 1,000 shuffles of the S-tilde labels of those trials (the Methods report 18,230 cells kept, 150 of them dropped between the manifolds; the attempt reports its counts); maps binned by S into ten bins (edges not stated; read as ten equal bins over S from -0.1 to 1.1, a standard choice) and flattened (450 values per cell); UMAP (n_neighbors 100, correlation, min_dist 0.1, 3 dimensions; the code's min_dist 0.01 is a variant); DBSCAN into two manifolds (the code's min_samples 200, default eps), points outside both dropped; k-means with k = 10 in each; per cluster a new 10-dimensional UMAP (n_neighbors 20, min_dist 0.1, correlation); logistic regression with ridge penalty and balanced class weights (code default C = 1, 10-fold cross-validation, permutation_test_score) classifies rare against frequent cells; significant when accuracy exceeds all label shuffles. The number of shuffles disagrees, 100 in the Methods and 1,000 in the Extended Data Fig. 5c legend; both are run, and a cluster is significant under that reading when it exceeds all shuffles. The paper does not say how many clusters make the two "separable"; readings (a) most of the 20 clusters significant, (b) at least one. UMAP and k-means seeds are a standard choice. The outcome is the one all readings give.

claims.statement: Non-negative matrix factorization of single-cell trial-by-trial similarity matrices confirms discrete remapping in rare morph sessions and gradual remapping in frequent morph sessions.
claims.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 6
claims.quote: These findings were also confirmed using a second unsupervised approach ... non-negative matrix factorization
claims.criterion: Extended Data Fig. 6a legend. Per session 8 to N, each cell's trial-by-trial cosine similarity matrix (Methods, Single-cell trial-by-trial similarity matrices; maps smoothed per M5), upper triangle flattened, stacked over cells, factorised with rank 3; each factor reshaped into a trial-by-trial prototype and sorted by S. The paper judges the factors by eye and gives no measure. Read as follows (a reading, not from the paper, the same measure as fig3ab-block-versus-gradual-similarity). For each factor, average its prototype over S-tilde blocks (5 x 5, diagonal left out); for the factors whose largest block is (0, 0) or (1, 1), the step share of that extreme's row is the largest fall between neighbouring S-tilde values divided by the whole fall to the other extreme. Per session the mean over those factors, per mouse the mean over sessions. Reproduced when the across-mouse mean step share is higher for rare than for frequent morph mice and test M12 (2.5 and 97.5 percentiles) finds the difference. The 2020 code bins all sessions of a mouse into ten S bins with ranks 2 and 3 (SingleCellNMF), a variant.

claims.statement: Single-session population trial-by-trial similarity matrices show two blocks in the rare morph condition and a gradual transition between the extremes in the frequent morph condition.
claims.source: Results, Population similarity analyses reveal distinct remapping patterns visible at the level of single trials, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 3a,b; Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8
claims.quote: For the rare morph condition, a strong block diagonal structure in the trial-by-trial similarity matrices suggested clustering of morph values into two representations
claims.criterion: Methods, Population trial-by-trial similarity matrices. Per session, all cells' single trial rate maps (M2, M3, M5) concatenated per trial, rows l2-normalised, cosine matrix C; rows and columns binned by S-tilde, diagonal left out; binned matrices averaged over sessions per mouse. The paper judges the single sessions by eye and gives no measure of a block or of a gradual transition; the group comparison it tests is fig3f-zscored-difference-at-025, on which this claim depends. Read as follows (a reading, not from the paper). In the S-tilde = 0 row and in the S-tilde = 1 row of a mouse's binned matrix, the step share is the largest fall in similarity between neighbouring S-tilde values divided by the whole fall from the row's own extreme to the other extreme; two blocks give a share near 1, an even gradient one near 0.25. A mouse's value is the mean of its two rows. Reproduced when the across-mouse mean step share is higher for rare than for frequent morph mice and test M12 (2.5 and 97.5 percentiles) finds the difference; the per-mouse shares are shown.

claims.statement: In six named rare morph sessions, trials near S-tilde = 0.25 randomly take one extreme representation or the other, seen as checkerboard bands in the sorted similarity matrices.
claims.source: Results, Population similarity analyses reveal distinct remapping patterns visible at the level of single trials, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 7
claims.quote: checker-board dark bands were observed in the similarity matrices near S ~ = 0.25 , as if the matrix was missorted for R1 session 8, R2 session 13, R3 session 9, R4 session 11, R5 session 8 and R6 session 10
claims.criterion: The paper shows this by eye only. Read with the paper's own measure of which extreme a trial resembles, the whole-trial SF (M9). Reproduced when, in each of the six sessions named, the S-tilde = 0.25 trials include at least one trial with SF above 0.5 and at least one below 0.5. Session numbers follow the paper's numbering; how they map onto the dataset is the author's to show.

claims.statement: After z-scoring within session, trial-by-trial population similarity differs significantly between rare and frequent morph mice for S-tilde = 0.25 trials.
claims.source: Results, Population similarity analyses reveal distinct remapping patterns visible at the level of single trials, paragraph 3; Figure 3c-f
claims.quote: As predicted, group differences in trial-by-trial similarity were significant for S ~ = 0.25 trials after z -scoring within session similarity ( P < 0.05 two-sided mouse permutation test, n = 12 mice)
claims.criterion: Methods, Population trial-by-trial similarity matrices.
