Per session 8 to N, C as in fig3ab-block-versus-gradual-similarity; binned into the five S-tilde values (code PlotPopSimMats) as means over off-diagonal entries; the 25 binned entries z-scored within the session (Methods; the 2026 code z-scores the mouse means, a variant); averaged over sessions per mouse; rare minus frequent across-mouse means; permutation test M12 at the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of the 923 permuted differences. Reproduced when at least one entry of the S-tilde = 0.25 row is significant; the significant entries and their signs are reported.

claims.statement: Position-wise SF shows stable clustered representations along the whole track in rare morph mice and a spectrum in frequent morph mice; remapping happens soon after the trial starts and stays as the mouse runs.
claims.source: Results, CA1 representations show stable discrimination of morph values along the length of the track, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 4b-e
claims.quote: Plotting SF as a function of the position of the animal along the VR track revealed a clustering of stable representations across the entire length of the track for the rare morph condition ... Together, these results indicate that remapping rapidly occurred after the start of a new trial and remained stable as the animal traversed the virtual track.
claims.criterion: Position-wise SF (M9) for every trial of sessions 8 to N, averaged per S-tilde within session, then over sessions per mouse, then across mice with s.e.m. (Fig. 4d,e legends). The paper reads the curves by eye. Read as reproduced when (1) in both conditions the mean SF of S-tilde = 0 and of S-tilde = 1 differ by more than the sum of their s.e.m. in every bin after the first bin; (2) in rare morph mice the S-tilde 0.75 and 1.0 curves overlap within s.e.m. over most bins (Fig. 4d legend) while the S-tilde 0.25 curve stays nearer the S-tilde 0 than the S-tilde 1 curve; (3) in frequent morph mice the S-tilde 0.25 curve lies between the S-tilde 0 and 0.5 curves over most bins.

claims.statement: Delta D_KL of each session's Q estimate took the expected sign (negative for rare, positive for frequent) in 41 of 45 sessions and in every session of 9 of 12 mice; across mice, rare -0.88 +- 0.23 and frequent 0.50 +- 0.11 (mean +- s.e.m.), a significant difference.
claims.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 2; Figure 6a
claims.quote: This Δ D KL measure took the expected sign (rare sessions Δ D KL < 0 and frequent sessions Δ D KL > 0) in 41 out of 45 sessions, and it took the expected sign in every session from 9 out of 12 mice (across animal mean±s.e.m.: rare Δ D KL = −0.88 ± 0.23, frequent Δ D KL = 0.50±0.11; P <0.0011, two-sided animal permutation test, n = 12 mice)
claims.criterion: Per session 8 to N, SF (M9), Q (M10) and Delta D_KL (M11) against the ideal rare and frequent posteriors (M6 to M8); per-mouse mean over sessions; test M12. Tolerances are the paper's s.e.m. for the means and 10% for the counts. Reproduced when the test gives the observed difference outside the range of all permutations and all four values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the test and the signs hold but a value is outside. The code variants (likelihood widths of M8, the last-mouse group prior of M7, signal of M2) are shown and do not decide. The 2020 code printed rare -0.96 +- 0.31 and frequent 0.58 +- 0.14 (SFReg); no code for the 41 of 45 count or the test was found.

claims.statement: Q estimates pooled over all sessions and mice approximate the posterior of the matching condition (Delta D_KL rare -0.44, frequent 0.42).
claims.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 3; Figure 6b,c, left panels
claims.quote: Combining data from all sessions and all mice gave a robust approximation (Δ D KL ) of the posterior for both the rare morph and frequent morph conditions (rare Δ D KL = −0.44, frequent Δ D KL = 0.42
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the across-session Q estimate is the average of its session Q estimates, renormalised (Fig. 6b legend); the group Q sums the mouse Q estimates and renormalises (Methods, Estimating posterior distributions, "weighting mice equally"); Delta D_KL as M11. An alternative the Methods also allow (Reconstructing prior distributions, "pooled transformed SF values across all sessions for that mouse") is (b) per mouse one Q from all its trials pooled. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under a reading; partially reproduced when only the signs hold.

claims.statement: Priors reconstructed from each mouse's neural data alone are closer to the ideal prior of the mouse's own condition (Delta D_KL rare -0.46 +- 0.12, frequent 0.46 +- 0.07, mean +- s.e.m. across mice), a significant group difference.
claims.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 4; Figure 6b-d
claims.quote: A similar Δ D KL metric showed that the reconstructed priors are closer to the ideal prior from the correct condition than the ideal prior from the incorrect condition ( Fig. 6d ) (across animal mean±s.e.m.: rare Δ D KL = −0.46 ± 0.12, frequent Δ D KL = 0.46±0.07; P <0.0011, animal permutation test, n = 12 mice)
claims.criterion: Methods, Reconstructing prior distributions. Per mouse, transformed SF values of all sessions 8 to N pooled into one unnormalised Q (M10); R = sum over f-hat_h of Q(f_h | f-hat_h) divided by sum over f-hat_h of the likelihood P(f-hat_h | f_h) / Z(f-hat_h), Z the row sum of the unnormalised Q, then normalised; Delta D_KL = D_KL(P_rare prior || R) - D_KL(P_freq prior || R), in bits. The Methods formula writes Q in the second term; read as R, as the code computes it (SFReg, prior_post_reconstruction). Test M12 on the per-mouse values. Reproduced when the test puts the difference outside all permutations and both means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when only the test and signs hold.

claims.statement: The average MAP estimate of f_h for S-tilde = 0 trials is 11.08 under the rare and 10.64 under the frequent posterior, and for S-tilde = 1 trials 38.13 and 37.30.
claims.source: Methods, Estimating posterior distributions from population activity (Q estimates)
claims.quote: average rare morph MAP estimate for S ~ = 0 trials: f h = 11.08; average frequent morph MAP estimate for S ~ = 0 trials: f h = 10.64; average rare morph MAP estimate for S ~ = 1 trials: f h = 38.13; average frequent morph MAP estimate for S ~ = 1 trials: f h = 37.30
claims.criterion: Argmax over f_h of the group posteriors (M6 to M8) at the f-hat_h of each S-tilde = 0 or 1 trial, averaged over trials. Which trials is not stated; readings (a) all such trials of sessions 8 to N of both groups, (b) of each group's own sessions. Reproduced when all four are within tolerance under a reading. The code variants of M7 and M8 are shown.

claims.statement: The rare versus frequent remapping patterns were stable over sessions and emerged early in training (session 3) in most animals.
claims.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 9a-i
claims.quote: Of note, these remapping patterns observed in rare morph versus frequent morph conditions were stable over sessions and emerged early in training in most animals
claims.criterion: Delta D_KL (M9 to M11) of each mouse's session 3 (R6 has none, Extended Data Fig. 9c), and per session for sessions 3 and 8 to N (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). The ideal posteriors for session 3 are not stated; readings (a) the group posteriors of M8, (b) posteriors from the trials each mouse ran before session 3. "Most animals" is read as more than half of the 11 mice with a session 3. Reproduced when session 3 Delta D_KL has the expected sign (rare negative, frequent positive) in at least 6 of 11 mice under both readings, and in sessions 8 to N the sign of every mouse's per-session values is the same in most of its sessions.

claims.statement: For rare morph sessions, Q estimates are fit worse by the frequent, uniform, Gaussian and multimodal prior posteriors and by a uniform posterior than by the rare morph posterior.
claims.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 9j,k
claims.quote: Furthermore, a comparison of Q estimates to a number of other null model posteriors yielded poor fits to the data
claims.criterion: Per rare morph session 8 to N, the mean over f-hat_h (M11 rows) of D_KL(P || Q) for the rare posterior and for each null; Wilcoxon signed-rank of null minus rare over sessions (code NullModels4GrumpyPantsReviewer). Null priors not in the Methods, taken from the code (cell 3) on the M6 grid; uniform; Gaussian exp(-(x - 0.5)^2/0.2^2); multimodal, weights 1, 1, 10, 1, 1 at S 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 with exp(-d^2/0.08^2) bumps (in S, through M6); and a constant posterior. Each null posterior with the likelihood of M8. Reproduced when every one of the five tests gives p < 0.05 with the rare posterior closer. The 2020 code printed p = 4.68e-3 for the uniform prior, against 4.7e-4 in the legend.

claims.statement: For frequent morph sessions, Q estimates are fit worse by the rare, uniform, Gaussian and multimodal prior posteriors and by a uniform posterior than by the frequent morph posterior.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9l legend
claims.quote: Wilcoxon signed rank tests compare D KL for the frequent morph condition to D KL for all other posteriors in ( j )
claims.criterion: As edf9k-null-models-rare, for the frequent morph sessions 8 to N against the frequent posterior. Reproduced when all five tests give p < 0.05 with the frequent posterior closer.

claims.statement: Frequent morph mice trained to report whether S was above or below 0.5 by where they licked (FD1 to FD4) remapped like frequent morph mice without the task.
claims.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 6; Extended Data Fig. 10
claims.quote: The remapping patterns were similar to those observed in frequent morph mice that did not perform this task
claims.criterion: Extended Data Fig. 10f-h. SF, Q and Delta D_KL as in fig6a-dkl-sign and the prior reconstruction as in fig6d-prior-reconstruction, for FD mice; FD sessions are read as in session-and-trial-counts. The comparison is not stated; readings (a) the Q estimate pooled over FD mice has Delta D_KL > 0 (closer to the frequent posterior), (b) each FD mouse's reconstructed prior has Delta D_KL > 0. Reproduced when both readings hold; partially when one.

claims.statement: Well-trained mice ran steadily down the first half of the track and began licking as they approached the reward.
claims.source: Methods, Morphed environments, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 1c-g
claims.quote: Once the animals were well trained, they often ran consistently down the first half of the track and began licking as they approached the reward
claims.criterion: Lick rate in the 10 cm bins of M3 per trial, sessions 8 to N. Extended Data Fig. 1g bins trials by reward location (50 cm bins) and plots lick rate against position, with no test. Read as reproduced when, in the across-mouse mean for each reward-location bin, lick rate rises over the 50 cm before the reward location and its peak lies within 50 cm of the reward location, and per mouse the mean lick rate over 0 to 225 cm is below that over 250 to 400 cm. The running part of the statement is shown in no figure (Extended Data Fig. 1 shows licking only) and is not judged; mean speed by position is shown.

claims.statement: Of the stimulus features, the horizontal component of wall frequency f_h best predicts the first principal component of the variance across VR scenes.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2g legend; Results, Two-photon imaging of CA1 cells in morphed VR environments, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The horizontal component of wall frequency, f h , is the strongest predictor of the projection onto PC1.
claims.criterion: Extended Data Fig. 2a-g. Uses screenshots of the VR scene every 10 cm for the range of wall, tower and background morph settings, their per-channel FFT power spectra, PCA across settings, and single-predictor linear regressions onto PC1. These are renders of the Unity scenes, not recorded data. Reproduced when the f_h model has the lowest mean squared error of the single-feature models.

claims.statement: A Hebbian network with radial basis inputs and k-winners-take-all competition, trained on stimuli drawn from the rare or frequent morph prior, gives Q estimates that match the matching posterior.
claims.source: Results, Simple associative-learning mechanisms can approximate probabilistic inference in neural populations, paragraph 1; Figure 7b-f
claims.quote: model-derived SF values and Q estimates were good matches to the appropriate posterior distributions
claims.criterion: Methods, Hebbian learning model (the parameter list says "For Fig. 4", read as Fig. 7). M = 100 inputs with radial basis tuning exp(-(mu_j - f_h)^2/sigma^2) (the Methods drop the minus sign), sigma^2 = 4.11, centres tiling the stimulus axis; N = 100 outputs, K = 20, c_y = 0.01, sigma_y 0.01 N(0,1), sigma_S 2.74 N(0,1), eta = 0.1, tau = 0.001, W_max = 5, W initial U(0, 0.1). The Methods also list sigma_w 0.05 N(0,1) but place it in no equation; readings (a) added to each weight update, (b) left out; both are run. 1,000 training stimuli drawn from the group prior of M7; 50 models per condition (Fig. 7c legend). Not in the Methods, from the code (KWTA_EmpiricalPrior), testing on the 1,000-point grid of M6, SF centroids from test stimuli below 0.05 and above 0.9 units, the affine map on medians of [-0.1, 0.1] and [0.9, 1.1], then Q and Delta D_KL as M10 and M11. Seeds are a standard choice. Reproduced when the median Delta D_KL of the 50 rare-trained models is below 0 and that of the 50 frequent-trained models above 0 (Fig. 7f). The model uses no recorded activity; it needs only the trial morph values for the prior.

claims.statement: Priors reconstructed from the model's Q estimates are closer to the prior of the matching condition, though less closely matched than for the neural data.
claims.source: Results, Simple associative-learning mechanisms can approximate probabilistic inference in neural populations, paragraph 1; Figure 7g
claims.quote: These unsupervised reconstructions were quantitatively more similar to the prior of the matching condition, but the match between the reconstruction and the true priors was not as compelling as the match seen in the neural data.
claims.criterion: Models as in fig7-model-reproduces-remapping; R per model as in fig6d-prior-reconstruction, averaged over the 50 models (Fig. 7g legend, "Delta D_KL is for the averaged reconstructed prior"), in bits (the code's nats are a variant). Reproduced when the averaged reconstructed prior's Delta D_KL is negative for rare-trained and positive for frequent-trained models, and its magnitude is below the neural across-mouse mean magnitude of fig6d-prior-reconstruction in both conditions.

claims.statement: A simulated population that stochastically encodes samples from the rare or frequent morph posterior reproduces the recorded remapping patterns.
claims.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 6; Extended Data Fig. 3
claims.quote: Simulating neural populations that were designed to stochastically encode the posterior distributions also reproduced the remapping patterns described above
claims.criterion: Methods, Simulating a neural posterior distribution. Per trial, samples s from the group posterior (M8) at the trial's f-hat_h; neuron i has gamma activity with theta = 1 and kappa_i(s) = alpha exp(-(s - mu_i)^2/sigma^2) + beta, sigma = 4.11, alpha = 2, beta = 0, mu_i tiling f_h; 1,000 simulations (Extended Data Fig. 3g,h). The trials are those of the recorded sessions 8 to N (code TheoreticalSimMats uses a session's morph values and its cell count; the code's rbf_sigma 0.4, alpha 1 and beta 0.25 are a variant). Open, the samples per trial (Methods "several times", code 1) and the number of neurons, read as (a) one sample, the session's cell count, (b) 45 samples (one per position bin), 100 neurons. Reproduced when the z-scored rare minus frequent simulated similarity difference (Extended Data Fig. 3j) has the same sign as the recorded one (fig3f-zscored-difference-at-025) at every entry of the S-tilde = 0.25 row that was significant there, under both readings.

claims.statement: With reasonable assumed priors, the probabilistic inference framework reproduces the discrete and gradual remapping reported in earlier morphed-environment studies (Wills 2005, Colgin 2010 double and single location, Leutgeb 2005).
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figs. 1 to 4
claims.quote: making reasonable assumptions, we reproduced each of the conflicting findings from previous studies using our probabilistic inference framework
claims.criterion: A simulation with priors the authors propose for other laboratories' experiments (Supplementary Figs. 1 to 4; code WillsLeutgebColgin_models). It uses no data of this paper, so the dataset cannot test it; it is listed to cover the paper's findings.

claims.statement: The dataset's subjects and recording days are the paper's subjects S01 to S12 and the recording days the paper lists for each.
claims.source: Table 2; Methods, Data collection
claims.criterion: The days per subject in Table 2 are S01 days 3, 4, 5 and 7; S02 and S03 days 3 to 6; S05 days 3, 4 and 7; S04 and S06 to S12 days 3 to 7 (55 subject-days). The link holds (reproduced) when the dataset's subjects 01 to 12 have exactly these days in order. When it does not, the subjects are matched by their day sets where these are unique, and the mapping and any mismatch are reported; subjects whose day sets are identical cannot be told apart this way, so the event counts per subject (claim fig2-event-counts) are reported beside them.

claims.statement: Twelve subjects (8 male, 4 female, 29.4 +- 7.9 years) had on average 87.0 +- 12.9 surface electrodes; five also had 23.2 +- 12.1 depth electrodes; five were implanted in the right hemisphere and seven in the left.
claims.source: Methods, Subject information, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We analyzed opportunistic clinical recordings from 12 subjects (8 males, 4 females) during their clinical epilepsy monitoring. Subjects were (mean ± SD) 29.4 ± 7.9 years old ... resulting in 87.0 ± 12.9 total surface electrodes per subject (mean ± SD). In addition, five subjects had 23.2 ± 12.1 intracortical depth electrodes (mean ± SD). Electrodes were implanted primarily within one hemisphere for each subject (five right hemisphere, seven left hemisphere)
claims.criterion: Tolerances on the means are the SDs the paper states, as the protocol allows; the counts are exact. Surface electrodes are grid and strip electrodes, depth electrodes the rest (Extended Data Figure 1-1 legend). Values the dataset does not hold are reported as not testable.

claims.statement: Each subject contributed between 151 and 947 movement events (median 640 across subjects).
claims.source: Figure 2 legend
claims.quote: The total number of events for each subject was between 151 and 947 (median, 640 across subjects).
claims.criterion: Which events are counted is not fixed by the text. Readings are (a) all contralateral wrist movement events the dataset holds for a subject; (b) those left after dropping events marked false positive and ECoG segments with power below 0 dB or with 115-125 Hz power more than 3 SD above all segments (Methods, ECoG-event synchronization; the Figure 2 code reads its events from the spectral power files, which have these removed). Reproduced when all three values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: All ten behavioural and environmental features differ significantly across subjects.
claims.source: Results, Behavior during naturalistic movements, paragraph 3; Figure 2
claims.quote: All 10 metadata features significantly differed across subjects ( p < 0.001 for every feature, one-way Kruskal–Wallis test).
claims.criterion: For each of the ten features, a one-way Kruskal-Wallis test of the event values grouped by subject, on the events of claim fig2-event-counts (reading b, with reading a as a variant), reach angle folded as in the opening comment and day of recording as a number. Reproduced when p < 0.001 for all ten features; not reproduced otherwise, with every p reported.

claims.statement: Reach duration and reach magnitude vary little across subjects, with most reaches lasting under 2 s and covering under 200 pixels, and reach angle distributions tend to be bimodal with peaks near +90 and -90 degrees, with few side-to-side reaches.
claims.source: Results, Behavior during naturalistic movements, paragraph 3; Figure 2
claims.quote: Reach duration and reach magnitude show minimal intersubject variability, with most reaches lasting <2 s and covering <200 pixels ... For reach angle, the distributions tend to be bimodal, with peaks at ±90
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure for these words, so they are read as follows. "Most" is more than half of the events, judged in every subject and in the events pooled over subjects; reach duration in seconds and reach magnitude in pixels. Reach angle (folded to -90 to 90 degrees) is judged on a Gaussian kernel density with Scott's bandwidth, the seaborn kdeplot default the Figure 2 code uses, evaluated on -90 to 90; a subject is bimodal with peaks at +-90 when the density's two highest local maxima lie within 15 degrees of -90 and of +90 and the density at 0 degrees is below both. "Minimal intersubject variability" is read as the duration and magnitude parts holding in at least 10 of 12 subjects; the per-subject medians are reported. Reproduced when the duration and magnitude parts hold pooled and in at least 10 of 12 subjects, and the angle part holds pooled and in more than half of the subjects ("tend to"). Partially reproduced when one of the two parts holds.

claims.statement: Bimanual ratio and bimanual overlap are skewed toward unimanual movement of the contralateral arm, less so for subjects 02, 04 and 05, while the bimanual class is mostly bimanual.
claims.source: Results, Behavior during naturalistic movements, paragraph 4; Figure 2
claims.quote: For bimanual ratio and overlap features, the distributions are skewed toward unimanual movements of the contralateral limb, as expected from Extended Data Fig. 2-1 c , with less skew for subjects 02, 04, and 05. In contrast, the bimanual class categorical feature is primarily skewed toward bimanual movements
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure, so it is read as follows. Bimanual ratio (missing values 0.5, code) skewed toward unimanual when its median is below 0.5; bimanual overlap (seconds) skewed toward unimanual when its sample skewness (Fisher-Pearson) is positive; bimanual class mostly bimanual when more than half the events are bimanual. The paper's "less skew" for S02, S04 and S05 refers to both ratio and overlap, so it holds when each of the three is among the five subjects with the highest median bimanual ratio and among the five with the lowest overlap skewness; the two features are reported separately. Reproduced when the ratio and overlap parts hold pooled and in at least 9 of 12 subjects, the class part holds pooled and in more than half the subjects, and the S02, S04, S05 part holds; partially reproduced when some but not all of these hold.

claims.statement: Across all 12 subjects, the median displacement of the contralateral wrist after movement onset is substantially greater than that of the ipsilateral wrist, confirming that event detection mainly picked contralateral movements.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 2-1c legend; Results, Behavior during naturalistic movements, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Because we selected movement initiation events of the wrist contralateral to the hemisphere with implanted electrodes, the median contralateral wrist displacements (orange lines) across all 12 subjects are substantially greater than ipsilateral wrist displacements (gray lines).
claims.criterion: Per subject, the median over events of each wrist's displacement in pixels from its rest position, with events aligned at movement onset (Extended Data Figure 2-1b and c legends). The current code holds no script for this panel. The rest position is open; readings are (a) the mean position over -1.5 to -1 s, the behavioural baseline of the code (config.baseline_vals_movement; compute_wrist_radial_distance, used by archived figure code, takes the absolute change of the radial distance from the image origin over that baseline), and (b) the position at movement onset (the Methods' reach definition). Displacement is the Euclidean distance from the rest position. The window is 0 to 1.5 s, the end of the time axis of the archived plotting code (plot_behavior_traces). "Substantially greater" has no measure; the part holds in a subject when the peak of the contralateral median exceeds the peak of the ipsilateral median, and the ratio is reported. Event set as in fig2-event-counts reading b. Reproduced when this holds in all 12 subjects under both readings; partially when it holds in 10 or 11. Blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings give different outcomes.

claims.statement: Over all events, reach magnitude correlates with reach duration (r = 0.26) and onset speed (r = 0.56), reach duration with bimanual overlap (r = 0.48), and the bimanual features with one another (overlap and ratio 0.51, class and ratio 0.50, overlap and class 0.61).
claims.source: Results, Behavior during naturalistic movements, paragraph 5; Extended Data Figure 2-2
claims.quote: Reach magnitude positively correlates with reach duration ( r = 0.26) and onset speed ( r = 0.56) ... Reach duration is also positively correlated with bimanual overlap ( r = 0.48) ... overlap vs ratio, r = 0.51; class vs ratio, r = 0.50; and overlap vs class, r = 0.61
claims.criterion: Pearson correlation over the events of all 12 subjects pooled ("group-level"), on untransformed features in the units of Figure 2 (duration and overlap in seconds, magnitude in pixels, speed in pixels per second, missing bimanual ratios 0.5), as plot_feature_scattermatrix in the code computes it (pandas DataFrame.corr). Event set as in fig2-event-counts reading b, reading a shown as a variant. Reproduced when all six are within tolerance; partially when four or five are.

claims.statement: Reach counts were fairly even across recording days except for subjects 04, 05 and 09, each with one day holding most events, and events occurred mostly during waking hours.
claims.source: Results, Behavior during naturalistic movements, paragraph 3; Figure 2
claims.quote: The number of reaches detected across days of recording was fairly consistent, with the exceptions of subjects 04, 05, and 09, who each had 1 d representing most of the total events. As expected, detected movement events often occurred mostly during waking hours.
claims.criterion: "Most of the total events" is read as more than half. Reproduced when the subject's busiest day holds more than half of its events for S04, S05 and S09 and for none of the other nine subjects. Waking hours are not defined; they are read as 08:00 to 24:00, the two daytime bins of the paper's time-of-day feature, and the part holds when more than half of each subject's events fall in them. Partially reproduced when the day part holds for the three named subjects but also for one or two others, or when only one of the two parts holds. Event set as in fig2-event-counts reading b.

claims.statement: At the group level, low-frequency power decreases and high-frequency power increases at movement initiation in several cortical regions, as in controlled movement experiments.
claims.source: Figure 3; Results, Intracortical spectral power during naturalistic movements, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Generally, we find the expected pattern of low-frequency (∼4–30 Hz) spectral power decrease and high-frequency (∼50–120 Hz) power increases during movement initiation across multiple cortices ( Fig.
claims.criterion: Group spectrogram per region as the Methods and the code (plot_specs_group) make it. Per subject, the median over events of region power (spectral method of the opening comment); the mean over the 12 subjects; the group median over -1.5 to -1 s subtracted again (code). Masking as in the code (tfr_boot_sig_mask). Each subject's baseline time bins are shuffled within frequency, the median over subjects is taken, repeated to about 2000 values per frequency, two-sided percentile p, Benjamini-Hochberg over all frequency and time bins of the region at 0.05; non-significant values set to 0. "At movement initiation" is read two ways. (a) The mean of the masked values over 0 to 0.5 s, the window of the paper's banded analyses. (b) The time bin nearest 0 s. Reproduced when, under both readings, the masked mean over the 4-30 Hz bins is below 0 and over the 50-120 Hz bins above 0 in each of precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal. Partially reproduced when this holds in one or two of them. Blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: Spectral power changes are largest in precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal regions, and the three temporal regions show minimal movement-related changes.
claims.source: Results, Intracortical spectral power during naturalistic movements, paragraph 2; Figure 3
claims.quote: Spectral power deviations are largest in magnitude in precentral, postcentral, and inferior parietal regions, which are located in sensorimotor areas of the brain ... As expected, all three temporal cortical regions contain minimal movement-related spectral power fluctuations.
claims.criterion: On the masked group spectrograms of claim fig3-group-lfb-decrease-hfb-increase. The paper does not say how magnitude is measured. Readings are (a) the mean absolute masked value over all frequency bins and 0 to 0.5 s; (b) the same over the 4-30 Hz bins and, separately, over the 50-120 Hz bins, a region ranking high when it does in both; (c) as (a) over -0.5 to 0.5 s. Reproduced when, under every reading, precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal are the three largest of the eight regions and each temporal region is below all three. Partially reproduced when two of the three named regions are in the top three and the temporal part holds. Blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings give different outcomes.

claims.statement: Low-frequency power decreases are more spatially widespread than high-frequency increases and are also present in supramarginal and superior temporal regions.
claims.source: Results, Intracortical spectral power during naturalistic movements, paragraph 2; Figure 3
claims.quote: In addition, low-frequency power decreases appear more spatially widespread than high-frequency power increases and are also present in supramarginal and superior temporal regions.
claims.criterion: On the masked group spectrograms, over 0 to 0.5 s. Readings for "widespread" are (a) the number of regions with any significant negative bin in 4-30 Hz against the number with any significant positive bin in 50-120 Hz; (b) the count of significant negative 4-30 Hz bins against significant positive 50-120 Hz bins, summed over the eight regions and divided by the number of frequency bins in each range. Reproduced when, under both readings, the low-frequency count is larger, and supramarginal and superior temporal each have significant negative 4-30 Hz bins. Blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: In the precentral region every subject shows the low/high-frequency pattern, but amplitudes and frequency bands vary; subjects 03, 06, 07, 08 and 11 have increases up to 120 Hz, subjects 09 and 12 mainly at 60-80 Hz, and subjects 04 and 08 have narrower low-frequency decreases.
claims.source: Results, Intracortical spectral power during naturalistic movements, paragraph 3; Figure 4
claims.quote: For instance, the precentral region shows the same low/high-frequency power pattern for each subject ( Fig. 4 ), but the amplitudes and frequency bands of maximal power deviation differ widely across subjects. Subjects 03, 06, 07, 08, and 11 show increased power at high frequencies up to 120 Hz, while subjects 09 and 12 have increased power primarily between 60 and 80 Hz. For subjects 04 and 08, low-frequency power decreases occur across narrower frequency bands compared with the other subjects.
claims.criterion: Per subject, the unmasked median over events of precentral power (Figure 4 legend, no statistical masking), with the mean of that median over -1.5 to -1 s subtracted again, as plot_specs_single_region in the code does, averaged over 0 to 0.5 s (the window of the paper's banded analyses, Methods; Figure 4 itself shows whole spectrograms and fixes no window) to give a spectrum. The paper gives no measure, so the parts are read as follows. (1) Every subject has a negative mean over 8-32 Hz and a positive mean over 76-100 Hz. (2) For S03, S06, S07, S08 and S11 the 116 and 121 Hz bins are positive. (3) For S09 and S12 the largest value among the 56-121 Hz bins is at 61 to 76 Hz (bins within 60-80 Hz), and the mean over 101-121 Hz is below half of it. (4) The width of the decrease is the number of 1-46 Hz bins below half of the subject's most negative value; S04 and S08 are among the three subjects with the fewest. Reproduced when all four hold; partially when two or three hold. Part (1) failing in a subject is reported by subject.

claims.statement: Precentral LFB and HFB power in the 0.5 s after movement onset differs significantly across subjects.
claims.source: Results, Intracortical spectral power during naturalistic movements, paragraph 4; Figure 5; Table 1
claims.quote: For both frequency bands, spectral power significantly differed across subjects ( p < 0.001 for both bands, one-way Kruskal–Wallis test).
claims.criterion: Banded precentral power per event (opening comment; band mean as the main result, the code's median as a variant), all days pooled per subject. One-way Kruskal-Wallis test across the 12 subjects per band, as the Figure 5 notebook (pingouin kruskal). "Pooling over all electrodes" (Results) is the projection of all the subject's good electrodes onto the precentral region, as the code does. Reproduced when p < 0.001 in both bands.

claims.statement: Each subject's precentral band power lies in the 95% bootstrap interval Table 1 gives; LFB power is below baseline and HFB power above it for most subjects.
claims.source: Table 1
claims.criterion: Table 1 intervals (dB), LFB then HFB. S01 -1.87 to -1.29, 0.03 to 0.23; S02 -1.12 to -0.31, 0.07 to 0.64; S03 -2.11 to -1.73, 1.39 to 1.67; S04 -0.17 to 0.01, 0.32 to 0.52; S05 -0.7 to -0.38, 0.2 to 0.48; S06 -1.63 to -1.11, 2.02 to 2.37; S07 -0.84 to -0.51, 1.14 to 1.34; S08 -0.3 to 0.04, 0.36 to 0.63; S09 -0.57 to -0.08, -0.11 to 0.23; S10 -0.87 to -0.35, 0.01 to 0.3; S11 -2.3 to -1.86, 0.09 to 0.34; S12 -0.66 to -0.44, 0.06 to 0.2. The table does not say which statistic the interval is for. Readings are (a) the mean and (b) the median over the subject's events of banded precentral power. Band power is taken as the band mean (Methods) or the band median (code), giving four readings in all. Reproduced when, under one reading, the point estimate lies inside the paper's interval for all 24 subject and band pairs. Partially reproduced when it does for at least 18. The attempt's own 5000-replicate bootstrap intervals are shown beside the paper's.

claims.statement: Precentral band power differs significantly across recording days in LFB for subjects 03, 05, 06, 07, 08 and 11, and in HFB for subjects 03, 04, 07, 08 and 10, despite baseline subtraction.
claims.source: Results, Intracortical spectral power during naturalistic movements, paragraph 4; Figure 5; Table 2
claims.quote: We also found a significant effect of recording day in LFBs for subjects 03 ( p < 0.001, Kruskal–Wallis test), 05 ( p = 0.013), 06 ( p < 0.001), 07 ( p = 0.041), 08 ( p = 0.013), and 11 ( p < 0.001), as well as in HFBs for subjects 03 ( p = 0.002), 04 ( p < 0.001), 07 ( p < 0.001), 08 ( p = 0.004), and 10 ( p = 0.006).
claims.criterion: Per subject and band, a one-way Kruskal-Wallis test of banded precentral power across the subject's recording days, uncorrected, at p < 0.05 (Figure 5 legend; the notebook uses pingouin's uncorrected p). Band mean as the main result, band median (code) as a variant. The paper's pattern is the 11 significant pairs above and the 13 other subject and band pairs not significant. Reproduced when all 24 pairs agree; partially reproduced when at least 20 agree. Each p is reported, with the per-day 95% intervals of Table 2 for comparison.

claims.statement: Subtracting the -1.5 to -1 s baseline reduces the variability of band power across recording days, though clear variability remains.
claims.source: Results, Intracortical spectral power during naturalistic movements, paragraph 4; Extended Data Figure 5-1 legend
claims.quote: Baseline subtraction reduces the variation across recording days, as expected, but clear variability remains.
claims.criterion: The legend gives the measure, the SD across recording days of the average LFB (8-32 Hz) and HFB (76-100 Hz) power, with and without baseline subtraction. The figure could not be read and no code for it is in the repository, so what is averaged is open. Readings are (a) precentral region power, per subject, the SD across days of the day means of event band power; (b) the same per good electrode, pooled over electrodes and subjects. Without baseline means the 10*log10 band power with no subtraction. Reproduced when, under both readings and in both bands, the SD with baseline is below the SD without it for more than half of the units (subjects or electrodes). The paper gives no measure for "clear variability remains"; the Results tie it to the recording-day effects that persist after baseline subtraction (paragraph 4), so that part is judged by claim fig5-recording-day-effects finding a significant day effect in at least one subject, and the SDs with baseline are reported. Blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: Day-to-day changes in baseline-subtracted spectral power are small (about 1-2 dB) compared with spectral power without baseline subtraction (about 10-50 dB).
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 3
claims.quote: It is also worth noting that these day-to-day changes in ECoG spectral power are small in magnitude (±1–2 dB) relative to spectral power without any baseline values subtracted
claims.criterion: On precentral banded power, per subject and band, the day means of the event values. The day-to-day change is the largest absolute difference between a day mean and the subject's overall mean. It holds when every such change is at most 2.2 dB (2 dB widened by 10%). The level without baseline is the mean 10*log10 band power without subtraction. It depends on the voltage unit, which the paper does not state; readings are microvolts and volts. That part holds when the levels lie in 9 to 55 dB (10-50 dB widened by 10% of each bound) under one unit reading. Reproduced when both parts hold; partially when only the first does.

claims.statement: Regression models with the highest withheld R2 are mainly at electrodes over frontoparietal sensorimotor areas, for both bands.
claims.source: Figure 6b; Results, Modeling single-event spectral power with behavioral features, paragraph 2; Extended Data Figure 6-1
claims.quote: For both frequency bands, intracortical activity variability is best explained by the fit of our models to electrodes located in frontoparietal sensorimotor areas ( Fig. 6 b , Extended Data Fig. 6-1 ).
claims.criterion: Full-model withheld R2 per electrode and band (regression method of the opening comment). The paper shows this on brain maps and gives no measure. Each electrode is assigned to an area in one of two ways, (a) to the region of the eight with its largest projection weight, or (b) by projecting the electrode R2 values onto the eight regions with the projection weights, as for power, and averaging over subjects. Frontoparietal sensorimotor regions are precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal (the regions the Results call sensorimotor) with middle frontal and supramarginal. Under (a), the part holds when more than half of the electrodes with R2 > 0.05 are in these five regions and the median R2 of precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal electrodes exceeds that of temporal ones. Under (b), it holds when the three regions with the highest projected R2 are among the five frontoparietal ones. Reproduced when this holds in both bands under both readings. Blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: All regression models explain at most 25% of the variance of withheld single-event power.
claims.source: Results, Modeling single-event spectral power with behavioral features, paragraph 2
claims.quote: However, all R 2 scores are at most 0.25, indicating that even the best models cannot explain >75% of the variance in the withheld data.
claims.criterion: The largest split-averaged full-model withheld R2 over all good electrodes of all subjects in both bands (regression method of the opening comment). Reproduced when it is at most 0.275 (0.25 plus 10%). The value is also reported for the code's 80/20 split and median band power.

claims.statement: Reach angle and day of recording are the most informative features for single-event power, especially for low-frequency power.
claims.source: Figure 6c and legend; Results, Modeling single-event spectral power with behavioral features, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Among individual features, we find that reach angle and day of recording are the most informative ( Fig. 6 c ).
claims.criterion: Delta R2 per feature, electrode and band (opening comment), over electrodes with withheld R2 > 0.05 in that band, across all subjects. The summary across electrodes is the median, as the box plots of Figure 6c show (code). Reproduced when reach angle and recording day have the two largest median Delta R2 of the ten features in the LFB. The HFB ranking is reported, and the claim is partially reproduced when only one of the two is in the LFB top two. Shown as variants are the code's Delta R2 (shuffling test events too), the code's selection by LFB R2, the code's 80/20 split, and the code's inclusion of bad electrodes.

claims.statement: Reach angle is the feature most often retained by forward selection in sensorimotor regions, followed by reach duration, reach magnitude, bimanual ratio and bimanual overlap.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 6-2 legend; Results, Modeling single-event spectral power with behavioral features, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Reach angle is the feature most often retained, followed by reach duration, reach magnitude, bimanual ratio, and bimanual overlap.
claims.criterion: Per electrode and band, whether each feature is kept by forward selection (code feat_select_prob; a day or time-of-day one-hot column counts as 1/number of columns of that feature). The legend projects the retention probability onto the eight regions and averages across subjects; the code of this step is not in the repository. It is read as the projection-weighted mean over the subject's good electrodes, then the mean over subjects, as for power. The angle part holds when reach angle has the highest retention probability among the ten features in precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal for both bands. The legend does not say over which regions and bands its order of the next four features holds. Readings are (a) the retention probability averaged over the three sensorimotor regions and both bands and (b) the same over all eight regions; the order part holds when the features ranked second to fifth are reach duration, reach magnitude, bimanual ratio and bimanual overlap in that order. Reproduced when the angle part holds and the order part holds under both readings; partially reproduced when only the angle part holds. Blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings give different outcomes for the order part.

claims.statement: Upward reaches are associated with lower low-frequency power and higher high-frequency power, that is, a larger version of the average movement response.
claims.source: Figure 6d and legend; Results, Modeling single-event spectral power with behavioral features, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The coefficients for reach angle indicate that upward reaches are associated with decreased low-frequency power and increased high-frequency power compared with the average response.
claims.criterion: Reach angle coefficient (positive angle is upward, standardised feature), averaged over splits, over electrodes with withheld R2 > 0.05 in that band. Reproduced when the median coefficient is below 0 for LFB and above 0 for HFB; partially when it holds in one band. The code's selection by LFB R2 and its inclusion of bad electrodes are shown as variants.

claims.statement: Reach angle and day of recording have the largest coefficient magnitudes among the features, and the SD of the recording-day coefficients is large.
claims.source: Figure 6d and legend; Results, Modeling single-event spectral power with behavioral features, paragraph 2
claims.quote: In addition, both reach angle and day of recording have the largest coefficient magnitudes among behavioral features in the regression models ( Fig. 6 c ).
claims.criterion: Per electrode with withheld R2 > 0.05 in the band, the split-averaged coefficient of each continuous or binary feature, and for day and time of day the SD of their one-hot coefficients (Figure 6 legend, code). The Results cite Fig. 6c for this sentence, but the coefficients are in Fig. 6d, whose box plots show the signed coefficients (code). The paper does not say how magnitude is summarised across electrodes. Readings are (a) the median of the absolute coefficients and (b) the absolute value of the median coefficient, the box-plot centre. Reproduced when, under both readings, reach angle and recording day have the two largest values in both bands; partially when in one band. Blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings give different outcomes. Variants as for fig6c-angle-and-day-most-informative.

claims.statement: Of the recorded cells, 242 of 720 in the anterior thalamus and 111 of 357 in the PoS were classified as HD cells, 353 of 1077 in all.
claims.source: Methods, Head direction cells, paragraph 2; Results, first paragraph
claims.quote: 242 out of 720 recorded cells (41% on average) in the anterior thalamus, and 111 out of 357 (31%) cells in the PoS were classified as HD cells.
claims.criterion: HD cells are counted by the rule above in every session with position. The regions cannot be separated, so the pooled count and fraction are tested. The denominator can be read as (a) the units with at least one spike in the waking epoch, or (b) every row of the units tables in the sessions with position. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when one of them is. The thalamic split (242 of 720) and the PoS split (111 of 357) are blocked for lack of region labels; the count in the mice that appear to be thalamus only is shown as a variant and does not decide the outcome.

claims.statement: The firing rates of HD neurons are strongly correlated between waking and SWS and between waking and REM sleep.
claims.source: Figure 2a (ADn n = 215, PoS n = 62 cells)
claims.quote: First, the firing rates of HD neurons remained strongly correlated across brain states (Fig. 2a).
claims.criterion: For each HD cell in a session with sleep states, the mean rate in waking, SWS and REM. Pearson's r across cells of the waking rates against the SWS rates, and against the REM rates (the paper gives the r values only in figure insets). Reproduced when both r are at least 0.7 with p < 0.05; partially reproduced when both have p < 0.05 and either is below 0.7; not reproduced otherwise. The cell count is reported against the expected value but does not decide the outcome. Variants with log rates and per mouse are shown.

claims.statement: The pairwise correlations between HD neurons, within and across structures, are similar across brain states.
claims.source: Results, second paragraph; Figure 2b (ADn pairs n = 970, PoS pairs n = 92)
claims.quote: Second, the pairwise correlations between HD neuron pairs both within and across structures were robustly similar across states (Fig. 2b)
claims.criterion: For each pair of HD cells in a session with sleep states, both cells firing at 0.5 Hz or more (in every state as reading (a), in at least one state as reading (b)), the Pearson correlation of binned spike counts in each state, with 300 ms bins in waking and REM and 50 ms bins in SWS, as in Figure 3a. Pearson's r across pairs of the waking correlations against the SWS correlations, and against the REM correlations. Reproduced when both r are at least 0.7 with p < 0.05 under one reading; partially reproduced when both have p < 0.05 and either is below 0.7.

claims.statement: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal, estimated from the temporal profile of pairwise cross-correlograms, is about tenfold faster during SWS than during waking.
claims.source: Results, second paragraph; Figure 2e,f; Abstract ("accelerated tenfold")
claims.quote: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal, either estimated by a Bayesian decoder or from the temporal profile of pairwise cross-correlograms ... was approximately tenfold faster during SWS than during waking (Fig. 2e,f)
claims.criterion: The method of the paper's Methods (Estimation of angular velocity). For each pair the angular correlation of the two waking tuning curves as a function of offset; angular speed drawn from a chi-squared distribution with 3 degrees of freedom scaled to a mean v, with both directions of turning equally likely; the expected cross-correlogram at lag tau as the mean over speeds of the angular correlation at speed times tau. The observed cross-correlogram (10 ms bins, lags to 4 s, ratio to the value expected for independent firing) is fitted by scale times expected plus offset, with v found by a coarse grid and then a Nelder-Mead search. The paper does not say how expected and observed are put on one scale, so the free scale and offset are chosen here. Pairs as in fig2b reading (a), and a pair is kept when its fit in each state does not end at the edge of the search range. Reproduced when the median over pairs of the SWS to waking ratio is within tolerance; partially reproduced when it is outside but above 2 with SWS faster than waking in most pairs (sign test p < 0.05); not reproduced otherwise. The ratio is also given per mouse.

claims.statement: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal is similar during REM sleep and waking.
claims.source: Results, second paragraph; Figure 2e,f
claims.quote: Angular velocity of the internal HD signal was similar during waking and REM (Fig. 2e,f).
claims.criterion: The paper names no test, so "similar" is fixed here. With the pairs and fits of fig2f-sws-tenfold-faster, reproduced when the median over pairs of the REM to waking ratio lies between 0.67 and 1.5; not reproduced otherwise. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the log ratio against 0 is reported as well, with its effect size.

claims.statement: The zero-lag correlation between HD cell pairs falls with the offset of their preferred directions, positive below 60 degrees, negative above it and near zero at about 60 degrees, and this holds in waking, REM and SWS.
claims.source: Results, third paragraph; Figure 3a
claims.quote: Pairs of neurons with <60° offset showed positive correlations, pairs with >60° offset showed negative correlations, and pairs with approximately 60° offset were uncorrelated (Fig. 3a). The relationship between the 0-lag correlation and the preferred angular direction was preserved across brain states
claims.criterion: With the pair correlations of fig2b reading (a), and preferred directions from the waking tuning curves, the mean correlation in 10 degree bins of absolute offset (0 to 180), and the offset of its first crossing from positive to negative by linear interpolation, in each state. Reproduced when the crossing is within tolerance in all three states and the Pearson correlation of pair correlation with absolute offset is negative with p < 1e-6 in each; partially reproduced when the Pearson test holds in all three states and the crossing is within tolerance in one or two of them.

claims.statement: During waking, the observed correlations of HD cell pairs exceed those expected from independent rate-coded neurons for pairs with overlapping fields (0 plus or minus 15 degrees), and fall below them for pairs at about 60 degrees.
claims.source: Results, fourth paragraph; Figure 4a,b
claims.quote: However, correlations expected from independent rate-coded neurons could not fully account for the observed pairwise correlations of HD cells (Fig. 4a). ... were observed for neuron pairs with overlapping fields (0±15°), with a marked negative signal correlation at 60±15° offset (Fig. 4b,c)
claims.criterion: Waking only, following the Methods' formula. For each cell an intensity function, its waking tuning curve read at the head direction in 10 ms bins (expected spikes per bin); for each pair the mean cross-product of the two binned spike trains and of the two intensity functions at each lag, and the noise correlation as their difference averaged over lags from -50 to +50 ms. Pairs as in fig2b reading (a). Reproduced when the noise correlation is above 0 for pairs at 0 plus or minus 15 degrees and below 0 for pairs at 60 plus or minus 15 degrees, each by a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when one of the two holds. This criterion replaces one written before the first run, which put both cross-correlations on a Pearson scale (see the opening comment); that version is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The HD signal decoded with a Bayesian decoder from the HD cells faithfully tracks the head direction of the waking mouse.
claims.source: Methods, Bayesian reconstruction of head-direction; Figure 1c
claims.quote: These estimates faithfully tracked the head position in the waking mouse.
claims.criterion: In each session with at least 6 HD cells, a Poisson Bayesian decoder (10 ms bins, counts smoothed with a 300 ms s.d. Gaussian, flat prior, 6 degree angle bins) trained on tuning curves from one half of the waking epoch and tested on the other, both ways. The paper gives no number, so "faithfully" is fixed here as a median absolute error of 30 degrees or less. Reproduced when the pooled median error is 30 degrees or less and at least 80% of the sessions meet it; partially reproduced when the pooled median meets it and fewer sessions do. The paper decodes from one structure at a time; here the HD cells of a session are pooled.

claims.source: Results, first paragraph; Supplementary Figure 2b
claims.quote: ADn neurons exhibited peak rates almost three times higher than PoS cells (Supplementary Fig. 2b

claims.quote: HD signal was more strongly preserved in the ADn than in the PoS as shown by the stronger pairwise correlations in any brain state

claims.statement: Noise correlations of HD cell pairs are stronger in the ADn than in the PoS (p < 1e-9, Kruskal-Wallis).
claims.source: Results, fourth paragraph; Figure 4c
claims.quote: These signal correlations were stronger for ADn than PoS neurons

claims.quote: In the ADn, where noise correlations were highest for overlapping HD cells, the covariance-based OLE was approximately 50% better than the signal-based OLE (Fig. 4d,e), and significantly stronger than in the PoS

claims.quote: However, the HD signal extracted from ADn assemblies resulted in tuning curves more similar to actual HD fields than the HD signal decoded from PoS assemblies, in all brain states

claims.source: Results, fifth paragraph; Figure 5c to e

claims.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 6
claims.quote: The degree of synchrony decreased with the magnitude of difference between the preferred head directions of the neurons (Fig. 6b ... in all brain states (Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 7a).

claims.statement: Putative monosynaptic connections were found in 4.45% of 6960 ADn to PoS pairs and 0.35% of PoS to ADn pairs; among pyramidal PoS cells, 0.41% against 0.18% (p = 0.014).

claims.quote: revealed putative synaptic connections in a fraction of the pairs (4.45% of 6960 pairs from ADn to PoS, 0.35% from PoS to ADn ... (0.41% ADn-PoS pairs versus 0.18% PoS-ADn pairs

claims.quote: PoS HD cells that were post-synaptic to ADn HD cells shared the same preferred direction as their presynaptic neuron (Fig. 7d ... claims.statement: ADn HD cell spikes are associated with high-frequency oscillations of the PoS LFP.
claims.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 7c
claims.quote: ADn cell spiking was associated with high frequency LFP oscillations in the PoS (Fig. 7c)

claims.statement: A session holds about 40 control trials, 20 to 60 cooling trials and 20 to 80 recovery trials, 80 to 200 trials in all with a mean of 150.
claims.source: Results, MS cooling decreases hippocampal theta frequency and power, paragraph 2; STAR Methods, Electrophysiological Recordings
claims.quote: After a block of control trials (~ 40 trials) ... about 20 to 60 ‘cooling’ trials), followed by recovery trials (20 to 80) ... a total number of trials ranging from 80 to 200 (mean: 150 trials).
claims.criterion: Over BEH sessions. Reproduced when the mean number of trials is within tolerance, every session has 72 to 220 trials (80 to 200 widened by 10%), the median number of pre-cooling trials is 36 to 44, and the median numbers of cooling and of post-cooling trials fall within 18 to 66 and 18 to 88. Partially reproduced when the mean holds and one or two of the others fail.

claims.statement: MS cooling peaked about 60 s after its onset and lasted about 10 to 12 minutes.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Electrophysiological Recordings
claims.quote: The cooling typically peaked after about 60 sec after the cooling onset (suppl. fig. 1G) and lasted for about 10–12 minutes
claims.criterion: For the first cooling block of each TEMP session, onset is the first time the temperature falls 1 C below the median of the pre-cooling trials, and the minimum is the lowest temperature in the following 5 minutes. The duration is read two ways, (a) the time the temperature stays below 32 C, the threshold of the paper's code, and (b) the time from onset until the temperature is again within 1 C of the baseline. Reproduced when the median time to minimum is within tolerance and, under one reading, the median duration is within 9 to 13.2 minutes. Partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: Theta frequency decreased linearly with MS temperature (R = 0.81, P = 5.4e-48).
claims.source: Results, MS cooling decreases hippocampal theta frequency and power, paragraph 2; Figure 2G
claims.quote: Theta frequency decreased linearly with MS temperature (Figure 2g; down to 20° C; R = 0.81
claims.criterion: As the paper's code computes it. Each session's trials are aligned so that its first cooling trial is at position 65 of 200; trial theta frequency is the mean instantaneous frequency over frames above 30 cm/s; temperature is the trial mean. The series are averaged over sessions at each position, and R is the Pearson correlation of the two averaged series over the positions where both exist. Readings, (a) TEMP sessions, (b) BEH sessions with the dandiset's MS10 temperature curves included. Reproduced when, under one reading, R is within tolerance and P < 1e-10. Partially reproduced when R is positive with P < 0.05 under one reading but no reading is within tolerance. The correlation over single trials pooled across sessions is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Theta power also decreased with MS temperature, less tightly than frequency (R = 0.54, P = 1.2e-16).
claims.source: Results, MS cooling decreases hippocampal theta frequency and power, paragraph 2; Figure 2H
claims.quote: this relationship was more consistent across animals than the effect on theta power (R = 0.54
claims.criterion: As fig2g-theta-freq-temperature, with trial theta power (peak of the spectrogram, minus each session's mean over its aligned trials, as the code does), and the same readings. Reproduced when, under one reading, R is within tolerance and P < 1e-5, and R is lower than the frequency R of fig2g-theta-freq-temperature under the same reading. Partially reproduced when R is positive with P < 0.05 but outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The relationship of theta frequency with MS temperature was more consistent across animals than that of theta power.
claims.source: Results, MS cooling decreases hippocampal theta frequency and power, paragraph 2; Figure 2J
claims.quote: Theta frequency decreased linearly with MS temperature ... and this relationship was more consistent across animals than the effect on theta power
claims.criterion: Per animal, the R of the aligned series of fig2g and fig2h computed over that animal's TEMP sessions. Reproduced when every animal has a positive frequency R with P < 0.05, and the range (largest minus smallest) of the frequency R over animals is smaller than that of the power R. Partially reproduced when only one of the two holds.

claims.statement: Theta frequency and power were lower during MS cooling than before and after it.
claims.source: Figure 2I; Results, MS cooling decreases hippocampal theta frequency and power, paragraph 2
claims.quote: MS cooling induced fast and reversible change in the frequency and power of hippocampal theta oscillations (Figure 2d, e, f, i).
claims.criterion: Per BEH session, the mean over trials of theta frequency and of theta power in each state. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over sessions of cooling against pre and cooling against post, for frequency and for power. Reproduced when all four show cooling lower at P < 0.05; partially reproduced when the two frequency tests do and a power test does not.

claims.statement: During MS cooling LFP theta frequency decreased by 12%.
claims.source: Discussion, Theta phase organization of hippocampal cell assemblies, paragraph 5
claims.quote: During MS cooling, LFP theta frequency decreased by 12 %
claims.criterion: Readings, (a) the mean over BEH sessions of 100 (1 - cooling / pre) of the session means of trial theta frequency; (b) the same with the mean of pre and post as reference; (c) the same over all trials pooled. Reproduced when one reading is within tolerance; partially reproduced when every reading shows a decrease but none is within tolerance. The decrease of the LFP frequency within place fields is reported in fig4b-fp-flfp-decrease.

claims.statement: MS cooling increased choice errors about 3-fold, within each rat (P < 0.05 for all animals) and across all animals (P = 1e-6).
claims.source: Results, MS cooling increases behavioral errors, paragraph 1; Figure 6D and 6E
claims.quote: Overall, the number of memory errors increased approximately 3-fold, assessed either within rats (P < 0.05 for all animals) or across all animals
claims.criterion: Error rate is the percentage of error trials in a state, per BEH session. Readings of the ratio, (a) mean cooling rate over mean pre rate; (b) mean cooling rate over the mean of pre and post rates; (c) median over sessions of the per-session ratio of cooling to pre (sessions with a pre rate above 0). Wilcoxon signed-rank test of cooling against pre over sessions, and within each rat. Reproduced when, under one reading, the ratio is within tolerance, the test over sessions has P < 0.001, and every rat with at least 6 sessions has P < 0.05 (an exact signed-rank test cannot reach 0.05 with 5 sessions, so smaller rats are reported only). Partially reproduced when the increase is significant over sessions but the ratio or a rat fails.

claims.statement: The error rate after cooling did not differ from the error rate before it.
claims.source: Figure 6E (marked ns)
claims.quote: Choice errors shown as boxplots constructed from all sessions. ... ns = nonsignificant.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The figure marks one comparison as not significant; it is read as pre against post. Wilcoxon signed-rank test over BEH sessions of the post and pre error rates. Reproduced when P >= 0.05, not reproduced when P < 0.05; the median difference is given either way.

claims.statement: The worst memory performance occurred between trials 4 and 8 after the onset of cooling, when MS temperature reached its minimum.
claims.source: Results, MS cooling increases behavioral errors, paragraph 1; Figure 6C
claims.quote: The worst memory performance occurred between trials 4 and 8 after MS cooling, when the MS temperature reached its minimum
claims.criterion: The smoothed error series of the code (11-point Gaussian window) averaged over BEH sessions at each aligned position. The first cooling trial is trial 1 after onset. Reproduced when the maximum of the mean error series over trials 1 to 40 after onset falls at trials 4 to 8. The trial of the minimum of the mean temperature (TEMP sessions) is reported.

claims.statement: The incidence of errors correlated negatively with MS temperature (R = -0.35, P < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, MS cooling increases behavioral errors, paragraph 1; Figure 6F
claims.quote: The incidence of errors negatively and significantly correlated with temperature change (R = − 0.35; P < 0.01; all animals)
claims.criterion: The aligned series of the code (smoothed errors and trial temperature, averaged over sessions at each position). Readings, (a) positions 10 to 160 over TEMP sessions, the window of the code's correlation matrix; (b) all positions over TEMP sessions; (c) reading (a) with the MS10 temperature curves included. Reproduced when, under one reading, R is within tolerance and P < 0.01. Partially reproduced when R is negative with P < 0.01 under one reading and none is within tolerance. Per-animal R values are reported.

claims.statement: The incidence of errors correlated negatively with theta frequency (R = -0.35, P < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, MS cooling increases behavioral errors, paragraph 1; Figure 6G
claims.quote: The incidence of errors negatively and significantly correlated with ... theta frequency (R = − 0.35; P < 0.01; all animals)
claims.criterion: As fig6f-errors-temperature with trial theta frequency over BEH sessions. Readings, (a) positions 10 to 160; (b) all positions. Same rule.

claims.statement: The incidence of errors correlated less with theta power; only 2 of 5 animals had a significant correlation (R beyond -0.3, P < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, MS cooling increases behavioral errors, paragraph 1; Figure 6H and 6J
claims.quote: The incidence of errors negatively and significantly correlated with ... and less so with theta power (only 2 of 5 animals had significant R > − 0.3; P < 0.01)
claims.criterion: Per animal, the Pearson R of the smoothed error series and the theta power series, each averaged over that animal's BEH sessions at each aligned position (as the code's per-animal fits). An animal counts when R < -0.3 and P < 0.01. Reproduced when 2 animals count; partially reproduced when 1 or 3 do.

claims.statement: The incidence of errors did not correlate with the running speed of the rat (R about 0.1, P > 0.05 for all animals).
claims.source: Results, MS cooling increases behavioral errors, paragraph 1; Figure 6I and 6J
claims.quote: The incidence of errors negatively and significantly correlated with ... and not with the running speed of the rat (R ~ 0.1; P > 0.05 for all animals
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's per-animal correlations. Per animal, the Pearson R of the smoothed error series and the trial speed series, averaged over that animal's BEH sessions at each aligned position. Reproduced when no animal has P < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. R and P are given for every animal.

claims.statement: Running speed decreased relatively monotonically within a session.
claims.source: Results, Effects of MS cooling on single neuron properties, paragraph 3; Figure 4E and 6C
claims.quote: Running speed decreased relatively monotonically within session (Fig. 4e; see also Fig. 5c).
claims.criterion: Per BEH session, the Spearman correlation of trial mean speed with trial number. Reproduced when it is negative in at least 75% of sessions and the median over sessions is negative by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at P < 0.05; partially reproduced when it is negative in more than half of the sessions but below 75%.

claims.statement: Mean running speed was 87.3 +- 8.0 cm/s in control trials and 86.2 +- 9.9 cm/s during MS cooling.
claims.source: Results, MS temperature effects on theta time/phase compression of place cells sequences, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we combined trials before and after cooling into a single control group (mean running speed = 87.3±8.0). During MS cooling (mean running speed = 86.2±9.9)
claims.criterion: The tolerances are the paper's stated spreads. Mean over sessions of the session mean of trial speed. Readings, (a) all frames of the trials; (b) frames above 10 cm/s. Sessions are those of the code's Figure 5 list that are in the dandiset and have cooling states (15). Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Within-field and peak firing rates of place cells decreased moderately during MS cooling (11% and 12%; P < 1e-9 and P < 1e-11).
claims.source: Results, Effects of MS cooling on single neuron properties, paragraph 2 (Supplementary Figure 2)
claims.quote: Both within-field and peak firing rates of place cells decreased moderately during MS cooling (Suppl. Fig. 2; 11% and 12%
claims.criterion: Place fields of putative pyramidal cells in UNIT sessions. Within-field rate is the spike count over the time spent in the field on forward runs above 10 cm/s; peak rate is the maximum of the state's rate map within the field. Readings, (a) median over fields of the per-field percentage decrease; (b) ratio of the means over fields; (c) mean of the per-field percentage decrease. Wilcoxon signed-rank test over fields of cooling against pre. Reproduced when, under one reading, both decreases are within tolerance and both tests give P < 0.001; partially reproduced when both decreases are significant but no reading puts both within tolerance.

claims.statement: Firing rates of interneurons decreased during MS cooling by about 14%.
claims.source: Discussion, Theta phase organization of hippocampal cell assemblies, paragraph 5; Results, Effects of MS cooling on single neuron properties, paragraph 2
claims.quote: During MS cooling, LFP theta frequency decreased by 12 % and within-field firing rates of place cells decreased by a similar proportion (12%; interneurons 14%).
claims.criterion: Putative interneurons of UNIT sessions (see cooling.py), rate over frames of trials above 10 cm/s, cooling against pre. Readings, (a) median per-unit percentage decrease; (b) ratio of means. Reproduced when one reading is within tolerance and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over units gives P < 0.05; partially reproduced when the decrease is significant but outside tolerance.

claims.statement: MS cooling decreased both the oscillation frequency of place cells (fp) and the LFP theta frequency in their fields (fLFP) by about the same degree, and both recovered (fLFP 8.4, 7.7, 8.5 Hz; fp 10.6, 9.5, 10.4 Hz before, during and after; n = 365).
claims.source: Results, Effects of MS cooling on single neuron properties, paragraph 2; Figure 4B
claims.quote: MS cooling decreased both fp and fLFP, measured within the place fields of neurons, by approximately the same degree ... Both values recovered after cooling.
claims.criterion: The tolerances are the paper's stated spreads. Per place field and state, fp is the oscillation frequency of the field's spikes on forward runs above 10 cm/s (Methods and calc_trial_averages.m), and fLFP the mean instantaneous theta frequency at those spikes; fields need at least 50 such spikes in each state. Values are means over fields. Reproduced when all six means are within tolerance and both fp and fLFP are lower during cooling than pre by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over fields at P < 0.05; partially reproduced when both decreases are significant but a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: fp and fLFP were correlated across place fields before, during and after cooling (R = 0.61, 0.59 and 0.36; P < 1e-6 each).
claims.source: Figure 4C
claims.quote: Correlation between LFP theta frequency (fLFP) and place cell oscillation frequency (fp; Rpre = 0.61; Rcooling = 0.59; Rpost = 036
claims.criterion: Pearson R over the fields of fig4b-fp-flfp-decrease in each state. Reproduced when all three are within tolerance; partially reproduced when all three are positive with P < 0.05 and one or more is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: During MS cooling fp and fLFP decreased in parallel, so the difference fp - fLFP remained constant.
claims.source: Results, Effects of MS cooling on single neuron properties, paragraph 2; Discussion, Theta phase organization of hippocampal cell assemblies, paragraph 3
claims.quote: during MS cooling fp and fLFP decreased proportionally (i.e., fp–fLFP difference remained constant)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper names no test; its default paired test is used, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over fields of fp - fLFP during cooling against pre, at 0.05. Reproduced when P >= 0.05, not reproduced when P < 0.05; the median change is given.

claims.statement: fLFP and fp measured within place fields decreased linearly with MS temperature (fLFP R = 0.66, slope 0.071 Hz per C; fp R = 0.38, slope 0.09 Hz per C).
claims.source: Results, Effects of MS cooling on single neuron properties, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
claims.quote: The theta oscillation frequency of pyramidal neurons decreased linearly and paralleled the downward frequency shift of LFP theta oscillation (Fig. 4a; fLFP: R = 0.66, Slope = 0.071. fp: R = 0.38, slope = 0.09).
claims.criterion: As calc_trial_averages.m, for every place field of the TEMP sessions among UNIT sessions, windows of 20 consecutive trials stepped by one trial; in each window with more than 50 in-field spikes, fp, fLFP and the mean temperature at those spikes. Pearson R and least-squares slope over all windows pooled. Reproduced when all four values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when both slopes are positive with P < 0.05 and a value is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Place field size was highly correlated before and during MS cooling (R = 0.91).
claims.source: Results, Effect of MS cooling on place field features, paragraph 1; Figure 3C
claims.quote: Place field size does not change with MS cooling (R = 0.91).
claims.criterion: Field size in a state is the length of the contiguous run of bins around the field's peak where the state's rate map exceeds 10% of its peak within the field's bounds widened by 4 bins. Pearson R over fields. Reproduced when within tolerance; partially reproduced when R is 0.5 or more.

claims.statement: Place field size and fp were negatively correlated before, during and after cooling (R = -0.49, -0.40, -0.40; P < 1e-9).
claims.source: Figure 3D
claims.quote: Place field size continues to be inversely correlated with fp after MS cooling (Rpre = − 0.49; Rcooling = − 0.40; Rpost = − 0.40
claims.criterion: Pearson R over the fields of fig4b-fp-flfp-decrease of the state's field size (as fig3c-field-size-correlated) and fp. Reproduced when all three are within tolerance with P < 0.001; partially reproduced when all three are negative with P < 0.05.

claims.statement: Measured place field size correlated with the size predicted by SPF = v / (fp - fLFP) before (R = 0.55) and during (R = 0.54) cooling, and weakly after (R = 0.11).
claims.source: Results, Effect of MS cooling on place field features, paragraph 2; Figure 3E
claims.quote: We found a reliable and similar relationships between measured place field sizes and model-predicted sizes for trials before (R = 0.55), during (R = 0.54) and after (R = 0.11) MS cooling (Fig. 3e).
claims.criterion: v is the mean running speed at the field's spikes. Fields with fp - fLFP above 0.2 Hz. Reproduced when all three R are within tolerance; partially reproduced when pre and cooling are positive with P < 0.05.

claims.statement: The information content of place cell spikes was not altered by MS cooling (P > 0.26).
claims.source: Figure 3F; Results, Effect of MS cooling on place field features, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Information content of place cell spikes was also left unaltered by MS cooling (P > 0.26; Fig. 3f).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Bits per spike (PlaceCellInfo.m) of each place cell's map in each state; the paper's default paired test, Wilcoxon signed-rank over cells, for pre against cooling, cooling against post and pre against post. Reproduced when all three give P >= 0.05; not reproduced when any gives P < 0.05. Median changes are given.

claims.statement: The spatial scale of the population vector correlation of pyramidal cells was not affected by MS cooling.
claims.source: Results, Effect of MS cooling on place field features, paragraph 3; Figure 3H and 3I
claims.quote: Population vector correlation of pyramidal cells was not affected by MS cooling (Fig. 3g, h).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Per UNIT session and state, population vectors of the pyramidal cells' rate maps in each bin; the decorrelation curve is the mean correlation of vectors at bins d apart within a segment, and the scale is the first distance at which it drops below 0.5. The paper gives no test; its default paired test, a Wilcoxon signed-rank over sessions of pre against cooling, at 0.05. Reproduced when P >= 0.05.

claims.statement: The phase precession slope decreased slightly but significantly during MS cooling (P < 0.007 and P < 0.0003).
claims.source: Results, Effects of MS cooling on single neuron properties, paragraph 2; Figure 4D
claims.quote: The slope of the relationship between travel distance across the place field and phase advancement of spikes ... decreased slightly, but nevertheless significantly, during MS cooling (Fig. 4d).
claims.criterion: Per field and state, circular-linear regression of spike phase on position in the field. Readings, (a) the magnitude of the slope is smaller during cooling (flatter); (b) the signed slope is lower during cooling. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over fields of cooling against pre and against post. Reproduced when, under one reading, both comparisons give P < 0.05; partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: fp depended on running speed more strongly than fLFP, and fp during cooling was lower at all velocities.
claims.source: Results, Effects of MS cooling on single neuron properties, paragraph 3; Figure 4G and 4H
claims.quote: fp values during cooling were lower at all velocities (Fig. 4g) ... while speed exerted a relatively linear effect on fp, it had no or little effect on the frequency of fLFP
