claims.quote: Across the four datasets the mean correlation was positive (p=0.01, p=0.01, p=0.12, p=0.03) but only very modestly so (mean r = 0.21, 0.19, 0.06 and 0.13). Non-parametric correlations were similarly modest (mean Spearman's r = 0.20, 0.20, 0.06 and 0.11).
claims.criterion: Per neuron passing M6 (preparatory tuning > 5 spikes/s and peri-movement tuning at least 1.5 times the preparatory tuning, reading S1; S2 set aside, see the M6 answer), the Pearson and Spearman correlation over the 108 conditions between the preparatory rates and the peri-movement rates of M4, trials by M1 (reading T2; T1 set aside, see the M1 answer). The paper does not name the test of the mean against zero. Readings (P1) one-sample two-sided t-test of the r values; (P2) the same on Fisher z-transformed r; (P3) two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, both means are within tolerance and the test gives p < 0.05 with the mean positive; partially reproduced when the mean is positive with p < 0.05 under one combination but no combination puts both means within tolerance.

claims.statement: In the single-electrode datasets (monkeys A, B and J) the mean tuning correlation is 0.21, 0.19 and 0.06 (p = 0.01, 0.01 and 0.12), with mean Spearman correlations of 0.20, 0.20 and 0.06.
claims.source: Results, Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, paragraph 1; Figure 4A-C
claims.quote: Across the four datasets the mean correlation was positive (p=0.01, p=0.01, p=0.12, p=0.03) but only very modestly so (mean r = 0.21, 0.19, 0.06 and 0.13). Non-parametric correlations were similarly modest (mean Spearman's r = 0.20, 0.20, 0.06 and 0.11).
claims.criterion: As fig4d-mean-correlation-jarray, with the 10 spikes/s preparatory threshold, the speed task peri-movement window as in M4, and for monkey J the four 27-condition sets analysed as separate datasets (Methods, Task design). Reproduced per dataset the archive holds; blocked for datasets it does not hold.

claims.statement: The distributions of tuning correlations give little evidence (except perhaps weakly for monkey B) of one population with concordant tuning (r near 1) and another with opposing tuning (r near -1); most neurons have weakly correlated tuning, with a broad range of correlations centred near zero.
claims.source: Results, Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, paragraphs 3 and 4; Figure 4A-D
claims.quote: Even more disconcertingly, different neurons show markedly different relationships between preparatory and peri-movement activity, with a broad range of correlations centered near zero. ... Yet there is little evidence in Figure 4 (except perhaps weakly in panel B ) for one population of concordant tuning ( r ≈ 1) and another of opposing tuning ( r ≈ -1). Instead, most neurons have weakly correlated tuning.
claims.criterion: Per-neuron correlations from fig4d (and fig4abc for datasets the archive holds). A claim of absence judged by eye in the paper, which names no test and no threshold. Readings (U1) Hartigan's dip test of unimodality gives p >= 0.05; (U2) more neurons have |r| < 0.5 than have |r| >= 0.5. Reproduced when both hold, not reproduced when neither holds, and methods_underspecified when they disagree; the dip statistic and the share of |r| >= 0.8 are reported either way.

claims.statement: The correlation between preparatory tuning and peri-movement tuning measured at single time points begins to decline about 200 ms before movement onset and is near zero by movement onset.
claims.source: Results, Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, paragraph 2; Figure 4E and legend
claims.quote: The correlation with preparatory activity began to decline ∼200 ms prior to movement onset, and reached values near zero by movement onset ( Figure 4E ).
claims.criterion: Neurons as in fig4d. Per neuron, the M4 preparatory rates correlated over conditions with the rate at single times, smoothed with a 20 ms Gaussian (Figure 4E legend), every 10 ms from 400 ms before to 200 ms after movement onset; the mean over neurons at each time. The paper used rates spliced from go-cue and movement-onset locked averages, with the gap placed to minimise discontinuities (Supplemental Experimental Procedures); the placement is open. Readings (A1) movement-onset locked rates throughout; (A2) go-locked rates up to 100 ms after the go cue and movement-locked from 300 ms before onset, interpolated linearly in between where they overlap. The paper gives no test; "near zero" and "began to decline" are read as (i) the mean correlation at movement onset is not significantly above zero by the tests of fig4d (P1 to P3), and (ii) the mean correlation at movement onset is below that at 200 ms before onset, and more than half the drop from 400 ms before onset to onset happens after 200 ms before onset. Reproduced when (i) and (ii) hold.

claims.statement: In population averages sorted by each neuron's preparatory preference, the weak agreement between preparatory and peri-movement tuning dominates early, but the separation shrinks with time and shows little relation to preparatory tuning by movement onset.
claims.source: Results, Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, paragraph 3; Supplemental Figure 1 and legend
claims.quote: In population averages ( Supp. Fig. 1 ) the lack of correlation averages out and the means are dominated by the weak agreement between preparatory and peri-movement tuning. However, such effects grow dramatically smaller with time. By movement onset even population averages show little relationship with preparatory tuning ( Supp. Fig. 1 ).
claims.criterion: Neurons as in fig4d (Supplemental Figure 1 legend). Per neuron, the conditions with the strongest and weakest preparatory rate and two intermediate ones (open; read as the conditions at one third and two thirds of the rank order), each neuron's rates divided by its maximum rate, then averaged over neurons. The legend says only "normalizing each neuron's activity by its maximum rate (results were similar without normalization)" and does not say over what the maximum is taken (answered 2026-10-22). Readings (a) the maximum over all conditions and all plotted times; (b) the maximum over the four plotted conditions and plotted times. Both are run, and a combination of readings is one reading for the rule below. Separation is the strongest-minus-weakest average. The paper gives no threshold for "dramatically smaller"; readings (R1) separation at movement onset less than half its mean over the preparatory epoch; (R2) less than a quarter. Reproduced when the separation in the preparatory epoch is positive and the condition holds under one reading.

claims.statement: For every dataset the highest cross-validated PD performance in accounting for preparatory tuning is reached when the PD is expressed in the space built by PCA from the population peri-movement response, compared with task spaces and PCA-based kinematic and EMG spaces.
claims.source: Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 3; Figure 6A-D
claims.quote: For every dataset, the highest level of performance was achieved ... when PDs were expressed in the peri-movement space.
claims.criterion: J-array (and other datasets the archive holds). Trials by M1, reading T2 (T1 set aside, see the M1 answer). Neurons passing the preparatory part of M6 (S1; S2 set aside, see the M6 answer), regardless of peri-movement tuning (Methods, Correlations, last sentence). PD performance by M7 in (a) the peri-movement space (M5) for each k (M8, K1 and K2); (b) the kinematic space, PCA of a T-matrix of horizontal and vertical position, velocity and acceleration from 150 ms before movement onset, each variable scaled to unit range over times and conditions (Methods, PCA-based spaces), for each k; (c) every task space of M9 (V1, V2, G1, G2). EMG is not recorded for J-array. The end of the kinematic window is open ("until after the reach"); readings (W1) 800 ms after onset, as for the neural window; (W2) 600 ms, the longest reach duration in Figure 1 legend. The Methods say "each neuron contributed one kinematic variable"; readings (D1) the six variables once each; (D2) the six variables repeated in turn to make as many column blocks as there are neurons. Reproduced when, under every combination, the best mean performance over k of the peri-movement space exceeds the best of every other space; the outcome is methods_underspecified if the combinations disagree.

claims.statement: Considering each dimensionality separately, PD performance is almost always higher in the peri-movement space than in other spaces of the same dimensionality; for the maze task the 3-D endpoints and peak speed space does not perform well.
claims.source: Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 3; Figure 6A-D
claims.quote: Even if we consider each dimensionality individually, performance was almost always higher for the peri-movement space. An exception was that, among 3-dimensional spaces, the ‘targs+instr. spd.’ and ‘endpoints + max. spd.’ performed very well for the datasets collected using the speed task. The former is undefined for the maze task, but the latter did not perform well.
claims.criterion: Performances from fig6-peri-movement-space-best. Comparisons are each task space against the peri-movement space at the task space's dimensionality, and the kinematic space against the peri-movement space at each k. "Almost always" has no threshold in the paper. Readings (L1) all comparisons but at most one, the paper naming one class of exception (3-D spaces on the speed task); (L2) at least 90% of comparisons. "Did not perform well" for the 3-D endpoints + maximum speed space is read as below the 3-D peri-movement space. Reproduced on J-array when that space falls below the 3-D peri-movement space and the peri-movement space wins under L1 and L2; the outcome is methods_underspecified if L1 and L2 disagree.

claims.statement: PD performance in PCA-based spaces generally improves with dimensionality, peaks in a middle range, and declines beyond about 10 dimensions through over-fitting.
claims.source: Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 2; Figure 6A-D
claims.quote: Performance typically improved with dimensionality. ... Performance typically declined at dimensionalities >10, an indication of over-fitting.
claims.criterion: Peri-movement space mean performance over k = 1 to 14 (K1). The paper gives no test; "improved with dimensionality" and "declined at dimensionalities >10" are read as performance at the best k higher than at k = 1, the best k at 10 or below, and performance at k = 14 below that at the best k. Reproduced when all three hold.

claims.statement: Preparatory activity is moderately high-dimensional; depending on the dataset, 7 to 10 dimensions capture 90% of its variance across conditions.
claims.source: Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Estimating the upper limit of PD performance; Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 2
claims.quote: This T-matrix also allows us to estimate the dimensionality of preparatory activity ... depending on the dataset, 7-10 dimensions were required to capture 90% of the data variance.
claims.criterion: The c x n matrix of M4 preparatory rates (one row per condition, one column per neuron, not normalised, columns mean-centred), PCA, the smallest number of components whose cumulative variance reaches 90%. The range 7 to 10 widened by 10% of each bound gives 6.3 to 11, so 7 to 11 components. Which neurons enter is open; readings (N1) neurons passing the preparatory part of M6 (S1; S2 set aside, see the M6 answer); (N2) all neurons. Reproduced when the count is within the range under one reading.

claims.statement: Averaged over monkeys A, B and J (J-array excluded, no EMG), PD performance is highest in the peri-movement space at every dimensionality limit, the advantage grows with dimensionality, and task spaces are largely outperformed by the kinematic and EMG spaces, which are in turn outperformed by the peri-movement space.
claims.source: Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 5; Figure 6E and legend
claims.quote: Performance (averaged across neurons) was highest when the PD employed the space based on peri-movement neural activity. This performance differential increased at higher dimensionalities, indicating that the peri-movement space better captured higher-dimensional aspects of the data.
claims.criterion: Needs the speed task, the single-electrode J data and EMG; J-array is excluded by the paper. Limits of 3, 6 and 12 dimensions; for PCA-based spaces the best k up to the limit; only spaces defined for all three datasets (endpoints + maximum speed included, targets + instructed speed not); performance averaged over neurons, SE over neurons. The test behind the asterisks is not named; readings (Q1) paired t-test over neurons; (Q2) Wilcoxon signed-rank over neurons. The paper gives no threshold for "increased" or "largely"; they are read as the gap between the peri-movement space and the next best space being larger at the 12-dimension limit than at the 3-dimension limit, and the kinematic and EMG spaces each exceeding more than half of the task spaces at the 12-dimension limit. Reproduced when the peri-movement space is best under all three limits, no other space is significantly better, and both readings hold; blocked if the archive lacks those datasets.

claims.statement: A control space built from peri-movement responses in which each neuron's peri-movement pattern was inverted on a random half of the conditions performs poorly, so the trailing end of preparatory activity does not explain the peri-movement space's success.
claims.source: Results, Controls, paragraph 1; Figure 7A and legend
claims.quote: The PCA-based ‘shuffled-space’ performed poorly ( Figure 7A ); any contribution from the trailing end of preparatory activity (preserved despite shuffling) is insufficient to allow good performance.
claims.criterion: As fig6-peri-movement-space-best, with the T-matrix shuffled per neuron and condition with probability 0.5 (Figure 7A legend), activity kept up to 150 ms before movement onset and later activity reflected about the rate at that time (r'(t) = 2 r(-150 ms) - r(t)). The number of shuffles is not given; 10 shuffles with the mean performance reported and the spread shown, a standard choice. "Performed poorly" has no threshold; readings (H1) below the unshuffled peri-movement space at every k; (H2) H1 and its best over k below the best of the kinematic space. Reproduced when both hold; methods_underspecified when only H1 holds.

claims.statement: Moving the start of the peri-movement window from 150 ms before movement onset to movement onset costs little PD performance; at movement onset performance is 97% (monkey J) and 94% (monkeys A, B) of its original value.
claims.source: Results, Controls, paragraph 1; Figure 7B and legend
claims.quote: Finally, the start of the peri-movement window was 150 ms before movement onset but could be slid later in time with little decline in performance ( Figure 7B ). Even when the window began at movement onset ... performance was still at 97% (monkey J), and 94% (monkeys A, B) of its original value.
claims.criterion: As fig6-peri-movement-space-best, the peri-movement window starting at -150 ms and at 0 ms from movement onset, its end fixed; performance at the best k for each start (Figure 7B legend). "Monkey J" may mean (J1) the single-electrode J dataset only, which the archive may not hold, or (J2) both J datasets; under J2 the J-array ratio is compared with 0.97. Reproduced when a ratio the dataset can give is within tolerance.

claims.statement: The weak correlation between preparatory and peri-movement tuning does not depend on anterior-posterior recording location; regressing tuning correlation on AP location gives r = 0.20, p = 0.27 for J-array and no significant effect in any dataset.
claims.source: Results, Comparison of anterior versus posterior sites, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Regressing tuning correlation (as in Figure 4 ) against AP location yielded little or no effect: r =-0.05, p =0.82; r =-0.03, p =0.85; r =-0.07, p =0.52; and r =0.20, p =0.27 for the four datasets.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a linear regression (Pearson r and its p) of each neuron's tuning correlation (fig4d) on its AP location. Needs a per-unit AP location; for J-array, the electrode's position along the anterior-posterior axis of the arrays if the dataset gives it, else the array (PMd anterior, M1 posterior) as a two-level variant. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05; r reported either way.

claims.statement: The peri-movement space captures preparatory tuning at both anterior and posterior sites, with performance slightly better at anterior sites.
claims.source: Results, Comparison of anterior versus posterior sites, paragraph 1; Figure 7C and legend
claims.quote: The ability of the peri-movement space to capture tuning also held for both anterior and posterior sites ( Figure 7C ). ... Performance was slightly better at anterior sites
claims.criterion: As Figure 7C legend, a six-dimensional peri-movement space; neurons split at the median AP location (anterior at or above, posterior at or below); performance normalised by its upper limit, the performance of a PCA space from the preparatory activity of all neurons (Supplemental Experimental Procedures), and compared with random subdivisions of the same sizes. Whether the space for each half is built from that half only is open; readings (B1) from that half's neurons; (B2) from all neurons. Reproduced when normalised performance for both halves is above zero and within the spread of the random subdivisions or above it, and anterior is higher than posterior.

claims.statement: When the PD is measured on two random sets of 25 conditions, it is most stable in the peri-movement space, for every comparison space and all four datasets.
claims.source: Results, Stability of the PD, paragraph 2; Figure 7D and legend
claims.quote: Yet for every comparison, and for all four datasets, the PD was most stable when measured in the peri-movement space.
claims.criterion: Per neuron, 25 conditions drawn with replacement, PD fit by M7 regression (unit length), another 25 drawn, PD refit; consistency is the dot product of the two PDs, averaged over neurons (Results, Stability of the PD). The number of draws per neuron is not given; 100 draws averaged, a standard choice. Comparison spaces for the maze task (Figure 7D legend) endpoints + maximum speed (3-D), segment directions (6-D), the kinematic space at its best k from Figure 6 for this dataset; the peri-movement space at the same dimensionality as each. Reproduced when the peri-movement space has the higher mean consistency in every comparison.

claims.statement: In a simulated linear dynamical system (a harmonic oscillator held at 25 random initial states, then released), the preparatory to peri-movement tuning correlation of a unit is low (0.08), and a given preparatory rate can lead to opposing peri-movement patterns.
claims.source: Results, Tuning from a dynamical systems perspective, paragraph 2; Figure 8B-C and legend
claims.quote: The correlation of preparatory activity with peri-movement activity (averaged over the gray interval) was 0.08.
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. Two units, x(t+1) = W x(t) with W as printed in the Figure 8 legend, [[1, -2 pi/360], [2 pi/360, 1]] (the exact rotation shown as a variant), 25 random initial states. Open details, the distribution of initial states and the gray interval; readings (I1) uniform in [-1, 1] squared; (I2) standard normal; (J1) the first 360 steps after release; (J2) the first 180 steps. The seed is unknown, so the value is judged against the spread over 1000 draws of 25 states. Reproduced when 0.08 lies within the central 95% of that spread under one combination.

claims.statement: In the same simulated system, preparatory tuning is captured perfectly by a PD in the two-dimensional space found by PCA of the peri-movement activity.
claims.source: Results, Tuning from a dynamical systems perspective, paragraph 3; Figure 8D and legend; Supplemental Text
claims.quote: The PD points towards the pattern recruited by the activity of unit one (panel A ), and perfectly captures preparatory ‘tuning’.
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. As fig8-model-weak-correlation; PCA of the 25 x 2t matrix of peri-movement activity, k = 2, PD fit of unit 1's initial rates by M7 without cross-validation and with it. Reproduced when the fit is exact to numerical precision (R squared and leave-one-out performance above 0.999) under every reading.

claims.statement: Regression slopes of tp on ts are positive and less than one in every condition, so the animals estimated ts and their responses were biased toward the mean of the prior.
claims.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 3; Figure 1E and S1; Table S1
claims.quote: The regression slopes were positive, indicating that animals were able to estimate ts, and were less than unity, indicating that responses were biased toward to the mean of the prior (Figure 1E and S1, Table S1).
claims.criterion: For each prior, effector and direction (8 conditions), a weighted linear regression of tp on ts with each trial weighted by 1 over the variance of tp at its ts. Reproduced when all 8 slopes lie between 0 and 1 with 95% confidence intervals that exclude 0 and 1; partially reproduced when all 8 slopes lie between 0 and 1 but some interval includes 0 or 1; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: At the overlapping ts of 800 ms, biases were in opposite directions for the two priors (rank-sum test, p < 1e-43 in animal H over 17 sessions).
claims.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 3; Figure 1E; Table S2
claims.quote: The effect of the prior was most conspicuous at the overlapping ts for which biases were in opposite directions for the two prior conditions
claims.criterion: Trials with ts = 800 ms, pooled over effector and direction. Reproduced when the median of tp - 800 is negative for the Short prior and positive for the Long prior and a two-sided rank-sum test of tp between priors has p < 0.05. The paper's p value pools 17 sessions and is not expected here; the p value of this session is reported, and the test is shown per effector and direction.

claims.statement: Increments of tp between neighbouring ts are smaller at the extremes of the prior than near its mean, as the sigmoidal Bayesian estimator predicts (signed-rank test, p < 1e-11 in animal H).
claims.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 4; Figure 2E and 2F
claims.quote: Consistent with this prediction, tp increments at the extrema of the prior were smaller than increments near the mean
claims.criterion: For each of the 8 conditions, the mean tp at each of the 5 ts; the four increments between neighbours; increment at the extremes = mean of the first and last, in the middle = mean of the second and third. Reproduced when the middle increment exceeds the extreme one in most conditions and a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the 8 conditions has p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Biases are larger for the Long prior than for the Short prior, as scalar variability predicts; regression slopes are smaller for Long.
claims.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 4; Figure 2G and 2H
claims.quote: Third, due to scalar variability, biases for the Long prior should be larger than the Short prior condition (Figure 2G), which we confirmed empirically (Figure 2H, Table S1).
claims.criterion: With the slopes of beh-slopes, reproduced when the Long slope is below the Short slope in all 4 effector and direction datasets; partially reproduced for 3 of 4; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: A Bayesian observer model with scalar measurement and production noise fit to the behaviour captures the bias and the variance of tp in all conditions.
claims.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 4; Figure 2C and 2D; Table S3
claims.quote: Accordingly, fits of the model to behavior captured the bias and variance (Figure 2C,D) for both animals and across all experimental conditions (Figure S1, Table S3).
claims.criterion: The model fit per dataset (4 parameters). Across the 10 prior and ts conditions of a dataset, the R2 of the observed mean bias (tp - ts) by the model's predicted bias, and the Pearson correlation of the observed and predicted SD of tp. Reproduced when the bias R2 is at least 0.8 and the SD correlation is positive in all 4 datasets; partially reproduced when only one of the two holds in all 4; not reproduced otherwise. The fitted wm and wp are reported; Table S3 was not available for comparison.

claims.statement: About 30% of neurons were modulated by elapsed time (27% in monkey H) and more than 60% were sensitive to the prior (65% in monkey H), by a Poisson GLM of spike counts before Set compared by BIC.
claims.source: Results, Single-neuron response profiles, paragraph 3; Figure 3E; Methods, Generalized linear model
claims.quote: Results indicated that approximately 30% of neurons were modulated by elapsed time (27% Monkey H, 31% Monkey G), and more than 60% were sensitive to the prior condition (65% Monkey H, 62% Monkey G).
claims.criterion: Units as selected above. Counts in the 80 ms before each of the Short prior's ts values (480 to 800 ms after Ready), from every trial whose Set comes after that time (attrition), both priors. Full model log rate = prior + 5 time indicators + effector + direction; prior-dependent when its BIC is below that of the model without the prior. For ts dependence, a model per prior with that prior's 5 time indicators plus effector and direction against the model without the time indicators; ts-dependent when the BIC favours the full model in either prior. Reproduced when both fractions are within tolerance; partially reproduced when one is; not reproduced otherwise. The binomial 95% interval of each fraction is reported.

claims.statement: At the overlapping ts of 800 ms, firing rates differ between priors, with the largest difference during the support of the prior, between 480 and 800 ms after Ready.
claims.source: Results, Single-neuron response profiles, paragraph 3; Figure 3C and 3D
claims.quote: The influence of prior was most evident at the overlap ts of 800 ms (Figure 3C) ... many neurons had highly distinct firing rate patterns depending on the prior condition, with a maximum difference in firing rate during the support of the prior between 480 and 800 ms (Figure 3D).
claims.criterion: Per dataset, units as selected above, ts = 800 trials; per unit the difference of mean rates between priors in 160 ms bins from 320 ms before Ready to 640 ms after Set; the root mean square over units, averaged over the 4 datasets. Reproduced when the largest value falls in a bin within 480 to 800 ms after Ready and exceeds the 95th percentile of the largest value over 200 shuffles of the prior labels among ts = 800 trials; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Population activity is low dimensional; 3 to 4 principal components in the estimation epoch and 5 to 10 in the production epoch explain about 75% of the variance.
claims.source: Results, Geometry and dynamics of population activity, paragraph 2; Figure S3
claims.quote: For all datasets, the population activity in each epoch was relatively low dimensional: 3–4 principal components (PC) in the estimation epoch and 5–10 PCs in the production epoch explained nearly 75% of total variance (Figure S3).
claims.criterion: The number of components needed to reach 75% of the variance, per dataset and epoch. The ranges widened by 10% of each bound are 2.7 to 4.4 (3 or 4 components) in the estimation epoch and 4.5 to 11 (5 to 11) in the production epoch. Reproduced when all 8 values fall in their ranges; partially reproduced when at least 4 do; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Projections of estimation-epoch neural states onto the encoding axis match the Bayesian estimates from the model fitted to the behaviour (R2 = 0.993 for the Short prior, 0.996 for the Long prior, monkey H, Hand Left).
claims.source: Results, Encoding Bayesian estimate along curved trajectory, paragraph 1; Figure 4C
claims.quote: Neural projections onto u exhibited biases that matched the Bayesian model fitted to the behavior (R2 = 0.993 for the Short prior, 0.996 for the Long prior; Figure 4C)
claims.criterion: Weighted linear regression Xu = a + b te over the 20 ms time points of the prior's support, each point weighted by the number of trials it averages. The reported values can be read as (a) the Hand Left dataset, the representative condition of Figure 4C, or (b) the mean over the 4 datasets. Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance (R2 at least 0.894 and 0.896); partially reproduced when one is. The R2 for 1000 random unit vectors in the same PC space is shown as a reference.

claims.statement: Neural projections are better explained by the Bayesian model than by a linear function of ts with the same number of parameters, for both priors (signed-rank test on RMSE, p = 0.008 for each prior).
claims.source: Results, Encoding Bayesian estimate along curved trajectory, paragraph 1; Figure 4D top
claims.quote: Indeed, the neural projections were better explained by the Bayesian model than a linear model for both priors (signed-rank test for RMSE, p=0.008 for the Short prior, p=0.008 for the Long prior; Figure 4D).
claims.criterion: RMSE of the weighted fits Xu = a + b te and Xu = a + b ts, per dataset and prior. The paper's p = 0.008 is the smallest a signed-rank test gives over 8 datasets, so the Bayesian model was better in all 8. Reproduced when the Bayesian RMSE is lower in all 4 datasets for both priors; partially reproduced when it is for one prior; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: In the Long prior during the period matched to the support of the Short prior ("Short In Long"), there is no sigmoidal representation; the Bayesian model is not better than the linear one (signed-rank test, p = 0.74).
claims.source: Results, Encoding Bayesian estimate along curved trajectory, paragraph 1; Figure 4D top
claims.quote: As a negative control, we also analyzed neural data in the Long prior condition during a period temporally matched to support of the Short prior (“Short In Long” in Figure 4D) and found no evidence of sigmoidal representations
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Long prior states from 480 to 800 ms after Ready, an axis from the state at 480 to that at 800 ms, compared with the Short prior's te and with ts as above. Reproduced when a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the RMSE difference over the 4 datasets has p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The RMSE difference is reported per dataset.

claims.statement: Neural projections show more bias for the Long prior than for the Short prior, as a smaller regression slope of Xu on ts (signed-rank test, p = 0.008).
claims.source: Results, Encoding Bayesian estimate along curved trajectory, paragraph 2; Figure 4D bottom
claims.quote: the Long prior exhibited more bias than the Short prior as measured by slope of a regression line relating projections to ts (signed-rank test, p=0.008; Figure 4D).
claims.criterion: The slope of the weighted regression of Xu (spikes/s, in the shared PC space of the dataset) on ts (ms), per dataset and prior. Reproduced when the Long slope is below the Short slope in all 4 datasets; partially reproduced for 3; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Larger projections on the encoding axis at Set are followed by slower neural trajectories in the production epoch (Pearson correlation, rho Short = -0.74, rho Long = -0.51).
claims.source: Results, Controlling speed based on Bayesian estimate, paragraph 1; Figure 4E
claims.quote: For both conditions, larger projections along the encoding axis were associated with slower speeds across all conditions (Figure 4E; Pearson correlation, ρShort=−0.74 ... ρLong=−0.51
claims.criterion: Per prior, Xu at t = ts against the speed of the production trajectory of that ts, pooled over the 4 datasets (20 points). Reproduced when both correlations are within tolerance; partially reproduced when both are negative with p < 0.05 but at least one is outside tolerance, or when only one is within tolerance; not reproduced otherwise. Correlations within each dataset are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The initial speed of production trajectories (Set to Set + 400 ms) is biased toward the middle of the prior; its dependence on ts is shallower than the unbiased profile proportional to 1/ts (signed-rank test, p < 1e-3 over conditions and animals).
claims.source: Results, Controlling speed based on Bayesian estimate, paragraph 1; Figure 4F
claims.quote: The speed profile for each prior condition, however, demonstrated systematic biases with a central tendency: trajectories associated with shorter ts were slower than expected from an unbiased speed profile, and vice versa (Figure 4F
claims.criterion: Per dataset and prior, the mean step distance between Set and Set + 400 ms (trials with tp of at least 400 ms), the slope of its regression on ts, and the slope of the unbiased profile speed(middle ts) x middle ts / ts. Reproduced when the measured slope is shallower (less negative) than the unbiased one in most of the 8 dataset-priors and a two-sided signed-rank test of the difference has p < 0.05; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The speed of neural trajectories in the production epoch predicts the mean tp (Pearson correlation, rho Short = -0.58, rho Long = -0.52).
claims.source: Results, Controlling speed based on Bayesian estimate, paragraph 1; Figure 4G
claims.quote: we verified that the overall speed of dynamics throughout the production epoch was predictive of the resulting tp across both priors and across all experimental conditions (Figure 4G; Pearson correlation, ρShort=−0.58 ... ρLong=−0.52
claims.criterion: Per prior, the mean tp of each dataset and ts against the speed of that ts, pooled over the 4 datasets (20 points). Same rule as speed-vs-projection. The trial-by-trial correlation within each prior, effector and direction used by the Neural Latents Benchmark is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Instantaneous speed of neural trajectories in the full neural space is not modulated during the support of each prior (signed-rank test for zero regression slopes, p = 0.64 for Short, p = 0.08 for Long).
claims.source: Results, Alternative mechanisms (speed hypothesis); Figure 5B
claims.quote: for both prior conditions, speed remained unmodulated throughout the support of each prior (Figure 5b; signed-rank test for zero regression slopes during the support, p=0.64 for Short, p=0.08 for Long).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per dataset and prior, the distance between successive 20 ms states of the smoothed rates of all selected units, over the support of the prior (with attrition), regressed on time. Reproduced when a two-sided signed-rank test of the 4 slopes against zero has p >= 0.05 for each prior; not reproduced otherwise. With 4 datasets the test cannot reach p < 0.05; the slopes and their bootstrap intervals over trials are reported as the effect size.

claims.statement: In the first 200 ms after Set, trajectories for different ts run parallel; their distance to the middle ts trajectory does not change (signed-rank test for zero slopes, p = 0.92 for the shortest ts, p = 0.13 for the longest).
claims.source: Results, Alternative mechanisms (transient hypothesis); Figure 5D
claims.quote: Results indicated that neural trajectories for different ts in each prior evolved parallel to one another (signed-rank test for zero regression slopes relating the distance to time after Set, p=0.92 for the shortest ts, p=0.13 for the longest ts
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. PCA per dataset on Set to Set + 200 ms, both priors, at least 75% of variance; per dataset and prior the distance from the shortest and the longest ts trajectory to the middle ts trajectory at each 20 ms bin, regressed on time. Reproduced when a two-sided signed-rank test of the 8 slopes against zero has p >= 0.05 for both the shortest and the longest ts; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Aligned to the response, distances between trajectories for different ts decrease steadily up to movement initiation, without the converging then diverging pattern a ts-dependent threshold would produce.
claims.source: Results, Alternative mechanisms (threshold hypothesis); Figure 5F
claims.quote: However, the distance profile of neural trajectories did not show this converging-diverging pattern; instead, the distance between trajectories appeared to drop steadily throughout the production epoch, even near the time of motor initiation (Figure 5F
claims.criterion: PCA per dataset on Go - 800 ms to Go, both priors, keeping the components that explain 60% of the variance (the figure legend's value). Per dataset, prior and non-middle ts (32 curves), the distance to the middle ts trajectory at each 20 ms bin and the time of its minimum. The paper's test (one-tailed signed-rank, p = 1.5e-4) cannot be read unambiguously, so the criterion is fixed here. Reproduced when the median time of the minimum is in the last 40 ms before Go; partially reproduced when it is in the last 200 ms; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The variance across single trials of the GPFA neural state at Set projected on the encoding axis has an inverted-U profile over ts, lower at the extremes of each prior (one-tailed signed-rank test on quadratic coefficients, p = 0.0273, monkey H).
claims.source: Results, The curved manifold hypothesis captures the variance, paragraph 3; Figure 6C
claims.quote: The resulting variance profile of single-trial projections resembled an inverted U-shape on average, with a tendency for lower variances at the extrema of each prior (one-tailed signed-rank test on coefficients for quadratic term in polynomial fitting, p=0.0273
claims.criterion: GPFA (20 ms bins) per dataset on single trials from Ready to Set, both priors, units as selected above; the latent dimensionality chosen by 3-fold cross-validated log-likelihood from 4 and 8; orthonormalised latents. Per prior, u from the trial-averaged latents with attrition as above; each trial's latent state in its last bin before Set projected on u; Xu z-scored over the prior's trials; the variance at each ts; the quadratic coefficient of a polynomial fit of variance on ts. Reproduced when a one-tailed signed-rank test (coefficient below zero) over the 8 dataset-priors has p < 0.05; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The mean of the single-trial GPFA projections is sigmoidal (signed-rank test on increments, p = 0.0078) and has a higher slope for the Short prior (one-tailed signed-rank, p = 0.0625).
claims.source: Results, The curved manifold hypothesis captures the variance, paragraph 3; Figure 6D
claims.quote: the mean of the single-trial projections inferred from GPFA had a sigmoidal shape ... and higher slope for the Short prior
claims.criterion: With the GPFA projections of gpfa-variance-inverted-u, not z-scored. The mean Xu at each ts; increments as in beh-sigmoid-increments, compared by a two-sided signed-rank test over the 8 dataset-priors (sigmoidal when middle exceeds extreme with p < 0.05); the slope of mean Xu on ts per dataset and prior (higher for Short in all 4 datasets is the paper's p = 0.0625). Reproduced when both parts hold; partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: Recurrent neural networks trained on the two-prior task with scalar measurement noise behave like a Bayesian observer and show curved trajectories during the support of the prior, like DMFC.
claims.source: Results, Recurrent network models, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 7A to 7C and S7
claims.quote: we were able to build RNNs whose behavior was captured by a Bayesian observer model (Figure 7B) ... For instance, the network trajectories also exhibited curvature during the support of the prior (Figure 7C and S7).

claims.statement: In trained networks, compressing states along the encoding axis increases the regression to the mean of tp, and translating them shifts tp.
claims.source: Results, Recurrent network models, paragraph 4; Figure 7D and 7E
claims.quote: tp values exhibited progressively larger regression to the mean for larger compressive perturbations (Figure 7D), and underwent an overall upward or downward shift as a result of translation (Figure 7E).

claims.statement: The behavioural and neural results hold in monkey G as in monkey H.
claims.source: Results throughout; Figures 1 to 6 and S1 to S6

claims.statement: Over 10 sessions the recordings yielded 95.8 (SD 6.7) sorted neurons and 408 (SD 40.8) trials of the main finger task per session.
claims.source: Results, "Intracortical recordings during finger flexion", paragraphs 1 and 3
claims.quote: We recorded single and multineuron activity (95.8 ± standard deviation [SD] 6.7 neurons per session over 10 sessions) ... We repeated this online-control finger flexion task over multiple sessions (408 ± SD 40.8 trials/session over 10 sessions)
claims.criterion: The mean and SD of units per session match 95.8 and 6.7 to one decimal, and the mean and SD of trials per session match 408 and 40.8 to the nearest trial.

claims.statement: Online BCI classification of the cued finger was 86% accurate (SD 4% across sessions, weighted by trials) over 4016 trials in 10 sessions, against a chance level of 17%. No-Go trials of the first session are excluded because the classifier could not output No-Go that day.
claims.source: Figure 1b, Figure 1-figure supplement 3, Results, "Accurately decoding fingers from PPC single-neuron activity", paragraph 1
claims.quote: High classification accuracy during online control (86% ± SD 4% over 10 sessions; chance = 17%) (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 3)

claims.statement: Most (70%) of the online classification errors were middle-ring or ring-pinky confusions.
claims.source: Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 2; Figure 1b
claims.quote: The majority (70%) of the online classification errors were middle-ring or ring-pinky confusions (Figure 1b).

claims.statement: Offline classification of the cued finger from sorted firing rates in the window 0.5 to 1.5 s after the cue, with diagonal LDA and leave-one-out cross-validation within each session, was 92% accurate (SD 2% across sessions) over 4080 trials.
claims.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 4a, Results, "Accurately decoding fingers from PPC single-neuron activity", paragraph 1, Methods "Finger classification"
claims.quote: offline cross-validated classification (92% ± SD 2%; Figure 1—figure supplement 4a) demonstrated that the finger representations were reliable and linearly separable.

claims.statement: In the calibration task, offline cross-validated finger classification was 96% accurate (SD 3%) over 530 trials in nine sessions.
claims.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 4b, Results, "Accurately decoding fingers from PPC single-neuron activity", paragraph 1
claims.quote: During the calibration task, cross-validated classification was similarly robust (accuracy = 96% ± SD 3%; Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).

claims.statement: Most (89%) neurons were significantly tuned to at least one finger movement, by a two-tailed t-test of each finger's firing rate in the 0.5 to 1.5 s window against No-Go trials, p < 0.05 after FDR correction, with neurons below 0.1 Hz excluded and neurons pooled across sessions.
claims.source: Results, "Accurately decoding fingers from PPC single-neuron activity", paragraph 2, Figure 1-figure supplement 5, Methods "Single-unit tuning to finger flexion"
claims.quote: At the single-neuron level, most (89%) neurons were significantly tuned to individual finger-press movements (significance threshold: p < 0.05, FDR-corrected) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).

claims.statement: Linear regression could not decode the cue's screen coordinates from neural activity in the attempted-movement window; cross-validated r2 was close to 0 in every session.
claims.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 6a
claims.quote: Linear regression could not decode target location [x, y] coordinates from the neural activity during the attempted-movement period. Violin plot shows that cross-validated regression r2 values are close to 0 across sessions
claims.criterion: Cross-validated r2 at or below 0.05 for both coordinates in every session.

claims.statement: A diagonal LDA classifier could not classify the cue location from neural activity in the attempted-movement window.
claims.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 6b
claims.quote: A linear classifier (diagonal linear discriminant analysis [LDA]) could not classify the gaze location from neural activity during the attempted-movement period.
claims.criterion: Pooled cross-validated accuracy for the 12 cue locations lies inside the central 95% of accuracies obtained with shuffled location labels, while finger accuracy from the same features and classifier is far above its own shuffled range.

claims.statement: Fingers could not be classified from neural activity during the control task, in which the participant viewed the cues without attempting movements.
claims.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 6c
claims.quote: a linear classifier (diagonal LDA) could not classify finger movements from neural activity during passive observation (orange) of the finger press task.

claims.statement: In the session-averaged representational dissimilarity matrix (cross-validated Mahalanobis distance, window 0.5 to 1.5 s, No-Go excluded), the thumb is distinct, while the middle, ring and pinky fingers are close.
claims.source: Figure 2d and 2e, Results, "Finger representational structure matches the structure of able-bodied individuals", paragraph 3
claims.quote: For visual intuition, we also projected the representational structure to two dimensions in Figure 2e, which shows that the thumb is distinct, while the middle, ring, and pinky fingers are close in neural space.
claims.criterion: Every distance among the middle, ring and pinky fingers is smaller than every distance involving the thumb, in the session-averaged RDM.

claims.statement: The measured RDMs match the able-bodied PC-IP fMRI model better than the unstructured (pairwise-equidistant) model, by whitened unbiased cosine similarity (WUC), p = 5.7e-5.
claims.source: Figure 2f, Results, "Finger representational structure matches the structure of able-bodied individuals", paragraph 3
claims.quote: The measured representational structure matched the able-bodied representational structure significantly over the unstructured model (p = 5.7 × 10–5, two-tailed t-test) (Figure 2f)
claims.criterion: The bootstrap distribution over sessions of the WUC difference (able-bodied PC-IP minus unstructured) has its 95% interval above zero.

claims.statement: The measured RDMs match the able-bodied motor cortex (MC) fMRI model better than the able-bodied PC-IP fMRI model (p = 1.9e-6), and the WUC with the MC model is close to the noise ceiling.
claims.source: Figure 2-figure supplement 5a, Results, "Finger representational structure matches the structure of able-bodied individuals", paragraph 5
claims.quote: PC-IP BCI finger representations matched the able-bodied fMRI finger representational structure in the MC ... even better than that of able-bodied PC-IP (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). The WUC similarity with the MC RDM was close to the noise ceiling
claims.criterion: The bootstrap 95% interval of the WUC difference (MC minus PC-IP) is above zero, and the mean WUC with the MC model is at or above the lower noise ceiling minus 0.05.

claims.statement: Compared with the RDMs of individual able-bodied fMRI participants, participant NS's average PC-IP RDM was statistically typical (permutation test, p = 0.55).
claims.source: Results, "Finger representational structure matches the structure of able-bodied individuals", paragraph 4, Figure 2-figure supplement 4
claims.quote: When compared among the RDM distribution of individual able-bodied participants, participant NS's average PC-IP RDM was statistically typical (permutation shuffle test, p = 0.55)

claims.statement: The finger RDMs were consistent across sessions, with an average pairwise correlation between session RDMs of r = 0.90 (SD 0.04, min 0.83, max 0.99).
claims.source: Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 1
claims.quote: Indeed, participant NS's finger RDMs were largely consistent across different recording sessions (average pairwise correlation, excluding the diagonal: r = 0.90 ± SD 0.04, min 0.83, max 0.99).

claims.statement: Over sessions the model fit did not trend from the able-bodied model toward the unstructured model (session by model interaction t(6) = 0.50, one-tailed p = 0.32).
claims.source: Figure 3a, Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 1
claims.quote: However, we did not find conclusive evidence for a trend from the able-bodied model toward the unstructured model (linear-model session × model interaction: t(6) = 0.50, one-tailed t-test p = 0.32 ... (Figure 3a).
claims.criterion: In a regression of WUC on session index, model and their interaction, the interaction in the direction of the unstructured model is not significant (one-tailed p > 0.05).

claims.statement: The distances between the most confused finger pairs (middle-ring and ring-pinky) did not increase across sessions (one-tailed p > 0.99) or across runs within sessions (one-tailed p = 0.67).
claims.source: Figure 3b, Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 2, Methods "Measuring changes in the representational structure"
claims.quote: the middle-ring and ring-pinky distances did not increase over the course of the experiment (across sessions: t(8) = −4.5, one-tailed t-test p > 0.99 ... across runs within sessions: t(82) = −0.45, one-tailed t-test p = 0.67
claims.criterion: In a regression of the middle-ring and ring-pinky distances of per-run RDMs on finger pair, session index and run index, neither the session nor the run coefficient is significantly positive (one-tailed p > 0.05).

claims.statement: Across all finger pairs the inter-finger distances did not increase; they decreased slightly across sessions (t(8) = -4.0, two-tailed p = 0.004) and across runs within sessions (t(82) = -2.4, p = 0.019), with very small effect sizes (Cohen's f2 of 0.008 and 0.005).
claims.source: Figure 3-figure supplement 1, Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 2
claims.quote: Inter-finger distances instead decreased slightly (across sessions: t(8) = −4.0, two tailed t-test p = 0.004; across runs within sessions: t(82) = −2.4, two-tailed t-test p = 0.019), although the effect size was very small (across sessions: Cohen's f2 = 0.008 ...
claims.criterion: The session and run coefficients for all ten pairs are negative, and each Cohen's f2 is below 0.02.

claims.statement: In a time-resolved decomposition of the RDM into muscle and somatotopy component models, the muscle model emerged 170 ms before the somatotopy model (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test across sessions, p = 0.002).
claims.source: Figure 4e, Figure 4-figure supplement 2
claims.quote: RDA of the measured RDM over time shows an early fit to the muscle model and a late fit to the somatotopy model ... Difference in model start time (170 ms, Methods) was significant (p = 0.002, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

claims.statement: Among combinations of the hand-usage, muscle and somatotopy models, the hand usage plus somatotopy and muscle plus somatotopy combinations matched the data best.
claims.source: Figure 4-figure supplement 1, Results, "Finger representational structure is motor-like and then somatotopic", paragraph 3
claims.quote: Through a model selection procedure (Methods), we found that the hand usage + somatotopy and muscle + somatotopy model combinations matched the data best (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)

claims.statement: The able-bodied match and the representational dynamics hold when only well-isolated units (lowest third of L-ratio) are used.
claims.source: Figure 4-figure supplement 4c and 4d
claims.quote: showing that the measured RDMs match the able-bodied fMRI RDM significantly better than they match the unstructured model ... Representational dynamics analysis, repeated using only well-isolated units, shows an early fit to the muscle model and a late fit to the somatotopy model.

claims.statement: The layer 3/4 border sink of the DOWN-UP transition of non-REM slow oscillations (landmark b) lies slightly but significantly deeper than the early light-evoked sink (b') in the same mice, by 39 ± 49 um.
claims.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 2; Figure 1F
claims.quote: Sink b, associated with the “UP” state of slow oscillation during non-REM sleep, was slightly but significantly deeper than the light-evoked sink b′ in the layer 3/4 border (39 ± 49 μm
claims.criterion: Per mouse with light stimulation, the average CSD of DOWN-UP transitions (onsets from the UP and DOWN detection of the STAR Methods, as in buzcode DetectSlowWaves) and of light onsets, both as the second spatial difference of the LFP along the 64 sites (Figure 1D, 1E). The paper does not fix the time window or how a sink's depth is read from the map; the readings are the depth of the most negative CSD near the layer 3/4 border within (a) 0 to 100 ms after onset (the 100 ms pulse of the Results) and (b) 0 to 50 ms after onset (the early sink). Reproduced when, under a reading, b is deeper than b' with a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.05 and the mean difference is within tolerance (the paper's SD). CSD spatial smoothing is not given; none is applied (standard choice; it shifts a sink by less than a site).

claims.statement: The other CSD sinks and sources of slow oscillations (a, d, e) occur at the same depths as the corresponding light-evoked sinks and sources (a', d', e').
claims.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 2; Figure 1F
claims.quote: whereas the other sinks and sources occurred at the same depth as those seen with visual stimulation (p > 0.05, signed rank test)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test per landmark pair (a against a', d against d', e against e') at 0.05, with landmarks read as in fig1f-sink-b-deeper (sources as the most positive CSD near the stated depth). Reproduced when none of the three pairs differs at p < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. The mean differences are reported either way.

claims.statement: The distances between the five depth landmarks (the MUA power peak c and the CSD landmarks a, b, d, e) vary by less than 100 um from mouse to mouse.
claims.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 2; Figure 1G
claims.quote: Importantly, the distances between the five landmarks were consistent across animals and varied <100 μm from mouse to mouse ( Figure 1 G; n = 19)
claims.criterion: Landmark c is the depth of the peak of 500 Hz to 5 kHz power (Figure 1C, STAR Methods, Depth normalization); a, b, d, e are the DOWN-UP CSD landmarks as in fig1f-sink-b-deeper. "Varied" can be read as (a) the range (max minus min) across mice of each distance between adjacent landmarks, or (b) each mouse's deviation from the across-mouse mean distance. Reproduced when, under a reading, every adjacent-landmark distance varies by less than 110 um across the 19 mice.

claims.statement: Clustering the 64 sites by their pairwise gamma (30-100 Hz) coherence with a gradient-descent algorithm gives six clusters whose five boundaries are consistent across mice in normalized depth.
claims.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3; Figures 2A, 2B
claims.quote: the recording sites were clustered on the basis of their resulting cross-coherence matrix, resulting in six clusters whose five boundaries were consistent across animals when projected into normalized depth coordinates
claims.criterion: Coherence 30-100 Hz between all site pairs during waking (Figure 2A), clustered by the energy-gap rule of the STAR Methods (Gamma coherence and gradient descent clustering), from random starts, repeated (the paper says several times; 20 repeats is a standard choice) keeping the lowest energy. The paper does not say how the number of clusters reaches six (the algorithm merges to a local minimum). Readings are (a) the number of clusters at convergence, and (b) six clusters imposed. The boundary consistency test is unclear in what it compares; readings are (a) each boundary's normalized depth against the matching gamma IC boundary in the same mouse, and (b) each mouse's boundary depths against the across-mouse median. Reproduced when, under some reading, six clusters result in every mouse and no boundary differs at p < 0.05 by the signed-rank test.

claims.statement: The depth distribution of the six gamma coherence clusters corresponds roughly to the six cortical layers in each brain state and does not differ between states.
claims.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3; Figure 2B; Figure S2E
claims.quote: The depth distribution of the six gamma coherence clusters corresponded roughly to the six cortical layers in each brain state ( Figures 2 B and S2 ; p > 0.05, ANOVA for comparison across different states)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test as named, a one-way ANOVA across waking, non-REM and REM of each of the five boundary depths (19 mice per state), at 0.05. Reproduced when no boundary differs across states; not reproduced when any does. The STAR Methods (Statistical analysis) name "Kruskal-Wallis one-way analysis of variance" as the default test, so the word ANOVA may mean it; the Kruskal-Wallis result is shown as a variant. The boundary means per state are reported.

claims.statement: ICA of the 30-100 Hz LFP yields six main independent components whose spatial loadings are highly consistent across mice and whose depth distribution is related to the anatomical layers.
claims.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
claims.quote: ICA yielded six main independent components (ICs) that were highly consistent across animals (p < 0.001, Spearman’s correlation for ICs spatial loadings)
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the LFP band-passed 30-100 Hz, reduced by PCA to its first ten PCs, then runica (EEGLAB, Bell and Sejnowski; STAR Methods, Independent Component Analysis of LFPs); ICs ranked by variance explained, loadings as the inverse mixing matrix projected on depth. The paper does not say which six of the ten are the main ones or how ICs are matched across mice. Readings are (a) the six with the highest variance, matched by the depth of peak loading, and (b) the six whose loadings are confined in depth (not spread over all sites), matched likewise. The correlation test is (a) each mouse's loading against the across-mouse mean, or (b) all pairs of mice, in normalized depth. The brain state the ICA is run on is not given (Figure S2H compares IC variance across states, which suggests one decomposition per session); readings are the whole session and waking only. Reproduced when, under a reading, the median Spearman correlation is positive with p < 0.001 for each of the six ICs.

claims.statement: ICA removes volume-conducted currents, which account for 0.34 ± 0.11 of the V1 gamma LFP variance.
claims.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3
claims.quote: This method has the additional advantage of removing volume-conducted currents ( Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2012 ) that accounted for 0.34 ± 0.11 of V1 gamma LFP variance
claims.criterion: The paper does not say which components are volume conducted or how the fraction is formed. Readings are (a) the variance fraction of the components among the ten whose loadings are spread uniformly over depth (Fernandez-Ruiz et al. 2012), and (b) one minus the variance fraction of the six main ICs. Reproduced when, under a reading, the mean over mice is within tolerance (the paper's SD).

claims.statement: The three superficial gamma ICs have larger relative power than the three deep ones (0.14 ± 0.04 against 0.08 ± 0.03).
claims.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3; Figure 2D
claims.quote: The superficial gamma ICs had a significantly larger power compared with the deeper ones (top three versus bottom three; Figures 2 D and S4 ; 0.14 ± 0.04 versus 0.08 ± 0.03 relative power for ICs 1–3 versus 4–6
claims.criterion: Relative power is each IC's share of the variance of the band-passed (30-100 Hz) LFP, the "amount of variance they explain in the original data (relative power)" of the STAR Methods (Independent Component Analysis of LFPs), ICs numbered by depth from the surface. The six shares then sum to about 0.66 (3 x 0.14 + 3 x 0.08), which agrees with the 0.34 volume-conducted fraction of ica-volume-conduction-fraction. Values per mouse and IC pooled (57 against 57). Reproduced when both means are within tolerance (the paper's SD) and a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum gives p < 0.05 with ICs 1-3 larger.

claims.statement: Slow oscillation power (0.5-3 Hz) is dominant in non-REM sleep and largest in the deeper layers.
claims.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 1; Figures 3C, S3D
claims.quote: Slow oscillation power (0.5–3 Hz) was dominant in non-REM sleep ... especially in deeper layers
claims.criterion: Per mouse, state and site, LFP power in 0.5-3 Hz (Morlet wavelet, STAR Methods, Spectral analysis). State comparison on each mouse's mean over sites; layer comparison in non-REM on the mean over the sites of each of the six LFP layers (readings, (a) gamma coherence clusters, (b) depth bands of the six ICs). Reproduced when, under a reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test across states gives p < 0.05 with non-REM highest, and across layers p < 0.05 with the largest power in the deepest two layers.

claims.statement: In non-REM sleep the slow oscillation phase modulates gamma amplitude in superficial layers (69 ± 12 Hz, modulation index 2.7 ± 0.5 × 10^-3) and high gamma (>100 Hz) in deep layers (modulation index 2.3 ± 0.3 × 10^-3).
claims.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 1; Figure 3D, left
claims.quote: Slow oscillation was phase-coupled to gamma frequency power in superficial layers (69 ± 12 Hz; modulation index 2.7 ± 0.5 × 10 −3 ) and to the high-gamma (>100 Hz) band in deep layers
claims.criterion: Phase of the 1-3 Hz band in layer 6 during non-REM (Figure 3D legend; the Results give 0.5-3 Hz, a second reading), amplitude by Morlet wavelet on every site, Tort et al. (2008) modulation index with 18 phase bins of 20 degrees (the STAR Methods do not give the number of bins; 18 is the cited method's setting). Amplitude frequencies span 5 to 200 Hz, log spaced, as on the Figure 3D axis (read from the article PDF text, Document S2); the superficial peak is the frequency of largest index in 30-100 Hz on sites above landmark b, and the deep index the largest above 100 Hz on sites below landmark c. Reproduced when, under a reading, the peak frequency and both indices (mean over mice) are within tolerance (the paper's SD).

claims.statement: Slow gamma (30-60 Hz) dominates in superficial layers, most in waking, then REM, then non-REM sleep.
claims.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 1; Figures 3, S3B, S3D
claims.quote: Slow gamma oscillations (30–60 Hz) dominated in superficial layers, especially in the waking state followed by REM and non-REM sleep
claims.criterion: Mean 30-60 Hz power over superficial-layer sites (gamma coherence clusters 1-2, labelled L2 and L3 in Figures S3B and S3D, where the third of the six LFP layers is L4) per mouse and state. The test is not named; the Methods default for three groups is Kruskal-Wallis (reading a), and Figure S3E uses signed-rank tests between states (reading b, waking against REM and REM against non-REM). Reproduced when, under a reading, the order is waking > REM > non-REM in medians and the test gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The most prominent LFP pattern in the waking mouse is a 3-6 Hz oscillation with largest power in layer 4.
claims.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 2; Figure 3C, level b
claims.quote: The most prominent LFP pattern in the waking mouse was a 3–6 Hz oscillation with largest power in layer 4
claims.criterion: Mean-subtracted 3-6 Hz power in waking (STAR Methods, mean across channels subtracted per session) per mouse and layer (readings as in fig3c-slow-oscillation-nrem-deep). Reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis test across layers gives p < 0.05 and layer 4 (the layer containing landmark b) has the highest median.

claims.statement: In waking the 3-6 Hz rhythm is phase-coupled to a 15-25 Hz signal in multiple layers (22 ± 5 Hz, modulation index 4.8 ± 1.2 × 10^-4), to high gamma in superficial layers (90 ± 13 Hz, 2.7 ± 0.7 × 10^-4) and to the epsilon band (>100 Hz) in layer 5 (6.4 ± 1.8 × 10^-4).
claims.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 2; Figure 3D, right
claims.quote: The 3–6 Hz band was cross-frequency phase-coupled to a 15–25 Hz band signal in multiple layers (22 ± 5 Hz, modulation index 4.8 ± 1.2 × 10 −4 )
claims.criterion: Phase of the 3-6 Hz band recorded in layer 4 in waking (Figure 3D legend), amplitude on all sites, Tort modulation index as in fig3d-slow-oscillation-gamma-coupling. Whether waking means all waking or waking immobility (theta-low, where the rhythm occurs) is open; both are readings. Reproduced when, under a reading, all five values (means over mice) are within tolerance (the paper's SD).

claims.statement: The 3-6 Hz rhythm vanishes with movement; its power is negatively correlated with hippocampal theta power.
claims.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 3; Figure S2C
claims.quote: The antagonism between movement and the 3–6 Hz oscillation was quantified by the negative correlation between its power and the power of theta oscillation (p < 0.01, signed rank test; Figure S2 C)
claims.criterion: Per mouse in waking, the correlation of 3-6 Hz power (layer 4) with 6-9 Hz theta power (volume conducted, Results) over time (power-power comodulation, Figure S2C). The time base is not given; readings are the Morlet wavelet power time series of the STAR Methods (Spectral analysis), and the 10 s windows stepped by 1 s of the state scoring spectrogram (STAR Methods, Brain state scoring). Reproduced when, under a reading, the correlations are below zero by a signed-rank test against zero at p < 0.01.

claims.statement: Both principal cells and interneurons are strongly phase-locked to the trough of the layer 4 3-6 Hz rhythm.
claims.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 2; Figure 3F
claims.quote: Both principal cells and interneurons were strongly phase-locked to the trough of the layer 4-recorded 3–6 Hz rhythm
claims.criterion: Phases of spikes in waking on the 3-6 Hz layer 4 LFP (wavelet phase), units with Rayleigh p < 0.05 (Figure 3F legend). Reproduced when, for E cells and for I cells separately, the circular mean of the units' preferred phases lies within 90 degrees of the trough (180 degrees with peaks at 0) and the preferred phases are non-uniform by a Rayleigh test at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Visual stimulation blocks an ongoing 3-6 Hz rhythm, and the offset of a stimulus often induces a short rebound train of 3-6 Hz oscillation.
claims.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 3; Figure S2D (cited as S2I)
claims.quote: Visual stimulation also blocked an ongoing 3–6 Hz rhythm. However, the offset of visual stimulus often induced a short rebound train 3–6 Hz oscillation
claims.criterion: Wavelet amplitude of the layer 4 LFP around light pulses (Figure S2D, 400 ms pulses). The paper gives no test. Reproduced when the mean 3-6 Hz amplitude in the stimulus is below that of the 400 ms before onset, and that of the 500 ms after offset is above the pre-onset level, each across mice by a signed-rank test at p < 0.05 (the Methods' default paired test); the windows are open and the readings are the pulse duration and half of it.

claims.statement: The waking 3-6 Hz rhythm has spike and wave waveforms and a depth profile similar to the alpha rhythm in monkey V1.
claims.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 2; Figures 3A, 3B
claims.quote: in which the waveforms occasionally split into short “spike” and longer “wave” components with a depth profile distribution similar to the depth distribution of alpha waves (8–12 Hz) in monkey V1
claims.criterion: The comparison uses monkey data reproduced from Bollimunta et al. (2008) and the paper gives no measure of similarity. The mouse side can be shown (laminar 3-6 Hz traces, CSD profile, Figure 3E); the claim itself is recorded as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Clustering one session from each of the 19 mice yields 1,472 units, with 251 narrow-waveform putative interneurons and 1,075 wide-waveform putative principal cells.
claims.source: Results, Assignment of Neurons to Physiologically Defined Layers, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
claims.quote: Unit clustering was performed as described previously ( Fujisawa et al., 2008 ) using one session from each of the 19 mice, yielding a total of 1,472 units
claims.criterion: Units as sorted in the dataset; classes by the waveform rules of the STAR Methods (the opening comment), trough-to-peak latency from the mean waveform on the peak channel.

claims.statement: Short-latency CCG interactions identify 347 E and 100 I cells, and these agree with the waveform classes (97.4% of CCG-based E cells are waveform E cells; 98.0% of CCG-based I cells are waveform I cells).
claims.source: Results, Assignment of Neurons to Physiologically Defined Layers, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
claims.quote: Using these criteria, 347 and 100 units were classified as CCG-based E and I cells, respectively
claims.criterion: A unit is a CCG-based E (I) cell when it is the presynaptic unit of at least one significant peak (trough) by the monosynaptic rule of the STAR Methods (opening comment).

claims.statement: Fourteen of 15 optogenetically identified PV cells and 40 of 52 VGAT cells fall in the narrow-waveform inhibitory group.
claims.source: Results, Assignment of Neurons to Physiologically Defined Layers, paragraph 2; Figures 4D, 4E
claims.quote: Fourteen of 15 optogenetically identified PV cells (n = 11) and 40 of 52 VGAT cells were part of the inhibitory group defined by the spike waveform criterion
claims.criterion: Tagging by the STAR Methods rule (1 ms PSTH bins, mean of the two largest bins in 1-6 ms after the 10 ms pulse above the baseline mean plus 8 SD of -100 to 0 ms), in the 5 PV-Cre::Ai32 and 9 VGAT-Cre::Ai32 mice. The Methods give 500 pulses at each of three intensities (40, 70 and 100%) but not whether the PSTH pools them; readings are all pulses pooled, and each intensity separately with a unit tagged when any passes. The "(n = 11)" after 15 is unexplained; it is reported, not tested.

claims.statement: K-means clustering of the spike-gamma IC phase-coupling profiles of all units gives eight clusters that largely correspond to the anatomical cell body layers.
claims.source: Results, Assignment of Neurons to Physiologically Defined Layers, paragraph 3; Figures 5B, 5C
claims.quote: We therefore used the spike-gamma phase coupling profile of all units against the six ICs to perform K-means clustering ( STAR Methods ). This procedure yielded eight clusters
claims.criterion: Per unit, mean resultant length of spike phases on each of the six gamma ICs at 20 log-spaced wavelet scales from 30 to 100 Hz in waking (STAR Methods, Spectral analysis and Classification of units using spike-LFP phase coupling; Figure 5A is waking). K-means with the cityblock distance and the number of clusters by the silhouette criterion over 2 to 15 clusters (the range is not given; a standard choice). The paper does not say whether K-means runs on the coupling matrix or on its t-SNE embedding (Mahalanobis distance); both are readings. Nor does it say what the "matrix of spike-IC phase coupling" holds per unit; readings are the full profile (6 ICs x 20 scales, as plotted in Figure 5A) and one value per IC (the largest mean resultant length over the scales). Clusters are numbered by median normalized depth. Reproduced when, under a reading, eight clusters are optimal and their median depths increase in the order of Figure 5C with clusters 1-2 above landmark b, cluster 3 spanning b, clusters 4-6 around c, and 7-8 below d. If the silhouette favours another number, the eight-cluster solution is still used for the layer claims, and this claim is not reproduced. As K-means is random, ten repetitions with the lowest within-cluster sum are kept (standard choice).

claims.statement: Unit coupling to the gamma ICs is stratified in depth; above landmark b units couple to slow gamma, in deep layers coupling shifts toward fast gamma.
claims.source: Results, Assignment of Neurons to Physiologically Defined Layers, paragraph 3; Figure 5A; Figure S5
claims.quote: Around and above depth level b (i.e., layer 3/4 border; first three components), unit-IC coupling of both putative E and I neurons had a peak in the slow gamma range. In deep layers, unit-IC coupling shifted toward the fast gamma band
claims.criterion: Preferred frequency (largest mean vector length over the 20 scales) of each significantly modulated unit (Rayleigh p < 0.05). Reproduced when units above landmark b have a median preferred frequency in 30-60 Hz and units below landmark c a median above that of the superficial units, by rank-sum p < 0.05. The paper gives no test; the rank-sum is the Methods default for two groups. The reference IC for each unit is open; the readings are the IC of largest coupling and the IC of the unit's own depth.

claims.statement: Principal cell firing rates differ across layers; the fastest groups are in layers 5A and 5B and the slowest in the superficial layers.
claims.source: Results, Layer-Specific and Brain State-Dependent Features of Unit Firing, paragraph 1; Figure 6A
claims.quote: The fastest firing group corresponded to those in layers 5A and B ( Figure 6 , red and magenta groups), while the slowest ones were the superficial layers
claims.criterion: E cells by group (clusters 1-8). Firing rate in non-REM (Figure 6A legend) or over the whole session (the Results' "long-term mean firing rates"); both are readings. Reproduced when, under a reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p < 0.05, clusters 5 and 6 have the two highest medians, and clusters 1 and 2 the two lowest.

claims.statement: Deep-layer principal neurons fire more during waking than during non-REM sleep.
claims.source: Results, Layer-Specific and Brain State-Dependent Features of Unit Firing, paragraph 1; Figure 6B
claims.quote: Deep-layer neurons were significantly more active during waking compared with non-REM sleep
claims.criterion: Per E cell, rate in waking and in non-REM. The test is not named in the legend; readings are a signed-rank test on each cell's two rates (Methods default for paired data) and a rank-sum test (as in the Figure S6 legend for other state pairs). Deep groups are read as clusters 4-8 (layers 5 and 6) or clusters 5-8. Reproduced when, under a reading, each deep group has waking > non-REM at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when most of them do.

claims.statement: No such state dependence of firing rates is present in superficial neurons.
claims.source: Discussion, State Dependence of Firing Patterns and Interlaminar Interactions, paragraph 1; Figure 6B
claims.quote: Deep-layer neurons increased their excitability during waking ( Sakata and Harris, 2012 ), as quantified by their firing rates, whereas no such state dependence was present in superficial neurons
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the Figure 6B test at 0.05 for clusters 1 and 2 (layer 2/3), under each test reading of fig6b-deep-wake-higher (the paper does not name it; both are shown). Reproduced when neither group differs between waking and non-REM; not reproduced when either does. The median ratios are reported.

claims.statement: Superficial-layer principal neurons are the most bursty, followed by layer 6 and layer 4, while layer 5 neurons have the lowest burst indices.
claims.source: Results, Layer-Specific and Brain State-Dependent Features of Unit Firing, paragraph 2; Figure 6C
claims.quote: In general, superficial layer neurons exhibited more bursting behavior, followed by layer 6 and layer 4 neurons, while layer 5 neurons had the lowest burst indices
claims.criterion: The burst index is defined twice. Results, spikes in the 3-10 ms bins of the autocorrelogram divided by spikes in the 200-300 ms bin (reading a); STAR Methods, mean count in the 1.5-13.5 ms bins divided by mean count in the 200-300 ms bins (reading b). Bin width is not given (1 ms, a standard choice for reading b; reading a sums counts). Whole session. Reproduced when, under a reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test across the eight E groups gives p < 0.05 and the layer medians (pooling groups by layer) order as layer 2/3 > layer 6 > layer 4 > layer 5.

claims.statement: Deep layer 5 neurons show the strongest transient responses after the UP state onset (largest transient/steady firing ratio).
claims.source: Results, Layer-Specific and Brain State-Dependent Features of Unit Firing, paragraph 2; Figure 6D
claims.quote: By this measure, deep layer 5 neurons showed the strongest transient responses
claims.criterion: Index as the Results define it, peak rate in 0-200 ms divided by mean rate in 100-200 ms after UP onsets (DOWN-UP transitions). The PETH bin is not given; readings 5, 10 and 20 ms. Reproduced when, under a reading, Kruskal-Wallis across the eight E groups gives p < 0.05 and cluster 6 (L5b) has the highest median.

claims.statement: During the DOWN-UP transition layer 5B neurons fire first, followed by superficial and layer 6 neurons.
claims.source: Results, Layer-Specific and Brain State-Dependent Features of Unit Firing, paragraph 2; Figure 6E
claims.quote: During the DOWN-UP state transition, layer 5B neurons fired first, followed by superficial and layer 6 neurons
claims.criterion: Latency of spikes after DOWN-UP transitions; readings are (a) each cell's median latency of its first spike after each transition, and (b) the time of peak of its PETH in 0-300 ms. Reproduced when, under a reading, Kruskal-Wallis across the eight E groups gives p < 0.05 and cluster 6 has the shortest median latency.

claims.statement: Spike phase preference during the waking 3-6 Hz rhythm differs systematically across layers.
