claims.source: Results, Layer-Specific and Brain State-Dependent Features of Unit Firing, paragraph 2; Figure 6F
claims.quote: The distribution of spike firing latency during the 3–6 Hz rhythm of waking displayed characteristic laminar differences
claims.criterion: Preferred phase of each E cell on the layer 4 3-6 Hz LFP in waking. The test is not named; readings are Kruskal-Wallis on phases (Methods default) and a circular multi-sample test (Watson-Williams). Reproduced when, under a reading, the groups differ at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Phase locking to the 3-6 Hz rhythm is strongest in superficial layers and weakest in layer 6.
claims.source: Results, Layer-Specific and Brain State-Dependent Features of Unit Firing, paragraph 2; Figure 6G
claims.quote: The mean vector length of phase locking to the 3–6 Hz rhythm was strongest in the superficial layers and weakest in layer 6
claims.criterion: Mean resultant length of each E cell's spike phases on the layer 4 3-6 Hz LFP in waking. Reproduced when Kruskal-Wallis across the eight groups gives p < 0.05, one of clusters 1-2 has the highest median and one of clusters 7-8 the lowest.

claims.statement: Spike-gamma (30-100 Hz) coupling is stronger in waking than in non-REM in all layers except layer 5A.
claims.source: Results, Layer-Specific and Brain State-Dependent Features of Unit Firing, paragraph 2; Figure 6H
claims.quote: Spike-gamma (30–100 Hz) coupling was stronger in the waking animal compared with non-REM in all layers but layer 5A
claims.criterion: Mean resultant length of E cell spikes to gamma per state, two-sided rank-sum per group (legend). The reference is open; readings are the IC of the unit's own depth at its preferred frequency, and the largest coupling over the six ICs. Reproduced when, under a reading, waking > non-REM at p < 0.05 in each group but cluster 5, and cluster 5 does not differ.

claims.statement: The strongest spike-LFP coupling is in the 3-6 Hz band, followed by the slow gamma (30-60 Hz) band.
claims.source: Results, Layer-Specific and Brain State-Dependent Features of Unit Firing, paragraph 2; Figures S7A to S7D
claims.quote: The strongest spike-LFP coupling was observed in the 3–6 Hz band ( Figures 3 F and S7 ), followed by the slow gamma (30–60 Hz) band
claims.criterion: Per unit in waking, the frequency of largest mean resultant length (preferred frequency, STAR Methods) over log-spaced frequencies; the range is not given below 30 Hz (Figure S7 spans slow oscillation to gamma; 0.5 to 100 Hz is read). "Strongest" is read as (a) the histogram of preferred frequencies of significantly modulated units (Figures S7A, S7B) or (b) the mean modulation strength over units at each frequency (Figures S7C, S7D). Reproduced when, under a reading, the largest value falls in 3-6 Hz and the next in 30-60 Hz, among bands 0.5-3, 3-6, 6-15, 15-30, 30-60 and 60-100 Hz (standard bands; the S7C legend notes strong coupling below 2 Hz too, which reading (b) may show).

claims.statement: Of 102,332 potential neuron pairs, 525 putative excitatory and 323 putative inhibitory monosynaptic connections were identified.
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Of the 102,332 potential neuron pairs in all mice and sessions, we identified putative excitatory (E, n = 525) and inhibitory (I, n = 323) monosynaptic connections
claims.criterion: Detection by the STAR Methods rule (opening comment). The pair count can be read as ordered pairs within a session among (a) all units, or (b) E and I units only; and unordered pairs of each. Gaussian baseline unhollowed (Methods) and hollowed 0.6 (buzcode) are both run. Reproduced when, under a reading, all three counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Many connections are within the same layer (E-I 173 of 385, E-E 19 of 90, I-E 98 of 323), but there are also many cross-layer excitatory and inhibitory pairs.
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 1; Figures 7A, 7B, S8A
claims.quote: Although many identified excitatory connections were detected within the same layer (layers in these calculations refer to IC-based clusters) for both E-I ( Figures 7 A and 7B; n = 173 of 385 connections) and E-E (n = 19 of 90) pairs
claims.criterion: Pre and post cells typed E or I by waveform; same layer means the same one of the eight clusters, as the paper says layers here "refer to IC-based clusters" and Figure S8B numbers the IC-based clusters 1 to 8. The E-I total is given as 385 here and 392 two sentences later, and E-I plus E-E (475) falls short of 525; units not typed are the likely gap. Reproduced when each within-layer fraction is within 10% of the paper's (0.449, 0.211, 0.303).

claims.statement: Of the 172 putative excitatory connections of layer 2/3 pyramidal cells, 10 (5.8%) and 39 (22.7%) target layer 2/3 and layer 4/5/6 excitatory neurons, and 29 (16.9%) and 94 (54.7%) target layer 2/3 and layer 4/5 interneurons.
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 1; Figures 7E, 7G
claims.quote: Of the 172 putative excitatory connections of L2/3 pyramidal cells, 10 (5.8%) and 39 (22.7%) targeted L2/3 and L4/5/6 excitatory neurons, respectively, in addition to contacting 29 (16.9%) and 94 (54.7%) L2/3 and L4/5 interneurons, respectively
claims.criterion: Layer 2/3 is clusters 1-2; layers 4/5/6 clusters 3-8. "L4/5 interneurons" is read as (a) clusters 3-6 or (b) clusters 3-8 (the four shares sum to 100%, so layer 6 targets fall in this group). Reproduced when, under a reading, the total and all four shares are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Most presynaptic principal neurons have a single target in the recorded population, a few target several; an interneuron typically has one presynaptic partner, a few many, up to 16.
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 2; Figures 7B, 7C
claims.quote: A typical interneuron typically had one presynaptic partner, but a small fraction many, up to 16
claims.criterion: From the E-I connections, the count of targets per presynaptic E cell and of presynaptic E cells per I cell. Reproduced when the mode of both distributions is one and the largest convergence is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Almost half of E-I connections (168 of 392, 42.9%) have a reciprocal I-E connection, and reciprocal E-I-E connections are almost twice as frequent in layer 5 (60-70%) as in other layers.
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 2; Figure S8B (the text cites S7C)
claims.quote: Almost half of the E-I connections (168 of 392 [42.9%]) received reciprocal I-E connections when all layers were considered. Reciprocal E-I-E connections were almost twice more frequent in layer 5 (60%–70%) than in other layers
claims.criterion: For each E-I connection, whether the same I cell has a significant I-E connection back to the same E cell. Per cluster of the E cell (Figure S8B), the reciprocal fraction. The layer 5 range is 60 to 70%, widened by 10% of each bound to 54 to 77% (value and tolerance above). The text does not say whether the range spans the layer 5 clusters or describes layer 5 as a whole; readings are (a) each of clusters 4-6 in 54 to 77%, and (b) the fraction pooled over clusters 4-6 in 54 to 77%. "Almost twice" is taken as a ratio of at least 1.8 (2 less the default 10%) of the layer 5 fraction to that pooled over the other clusters. Reproduced when, under a reading, the overall fraction is within tolerance, the layer 5 range holds and the ratio is at least 1.8.

claims.statement: Spike transmission from layer 2/3 E cells to layer 5 I cells is weaker during non-REM sleep than during waking.
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 7D
claims.quote: We observed that spike transmission strength between layer 2/3 E cells and deep layer I and E cells became weaker during non-REM sleep compared with waking (L2/3 E cells to L5 I cells, p = 0.0012
claims.criterion: For the E-I connections from clusters 1-2 to I cells in clusters 4-6, transmission in waking and in non-REM from spikes in each state. The measure is named twice; readings are (a) the peak-to-baseline ratio of the CCG (Results; peak in +1.5 to +4 ms over the convolution predictor), and (b) the corrected spike transmission probability of English et al. 2017 (STAR Methods; excess counts over the predictor in +1.5 to +4 ms divided by presynaptic spikes, as in buzcode). Reproduced when, under a reading, waking > non-REM by a two-sided signed-rank test at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Spike transmission from layer 2/3 E cells to layer 4 I cells is weaker during non-REM sleep than during waking.
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 7E
claims.quote: L2/3 E cells to L4 I cells, p = 0.0010
claims.criterion: As fig7d-l23e-l5i-weaker-nrem, for I cells in cluster 3.

claims.statement: Spike transmission from layer 2/3 E cells to layer 5 E cells is weaker during non-REM sleep than during waking.
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 7H
claims.quote: L2/3 E cells to L5 E cells, p = 0.015; signed rank test
claims.criterion: As fig7d-l23e-l5i-weaker-nrem, for E-E connections to E cells in clusters 4-6.

claims.statement: E-E spike transmission among deep-layer principal cells (layer 5/6 to layer 5/6) is stronger during non-REM sleep than during waking.
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 3; Figures 7G, 7I
claims.quote: In contrast, putative E-E spike transmission in the deep layers (layer 5/6 to layer 5/6 principal cells) significantly increased during non-REM sleep compared with waking (p = 0.0061, signed rank test
claims.criterion: As fig7d-l23e-l5i-weaker-nrem, for E-E connections with both cells in clusters 4-8, with non-REM > waking.

claims.statement: Over all I-E pairs, spike suppression is stronger in waking than in non-REM sleep (dip 24.1% against 22.8% of the CCG baseline).
claims.source: Results, Within-Layer and Inter-layer Interactions among Neurons, paragraph 3; Figure S8F
claims.quote: When all I-E pairs were considered, spike suppression probability during waking was significantly stronger compared with non-REM (I-E dip wake, 24.1%; non-REM sleep, 22.8% relative to the CCG baseline
claims.criterion: For each I-E connection and state, the dip as (predictor minus CCG) over predictor at the deepest bin in +1.5 to +4 ms. Whether the reported values are means or medians over pairs is not said; both are readings. Reproduced when, under a reading, both values are within tolerance and waking > non-REM by a two-sided signed-rank test at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Connection strengths are skewed and lognormally distributed, a few strong connections mixed with many weak ones.
claims.source: Discussion, State Dependence of Firing Patterns and Interlaminar Interactions, paragraph 2; Figure S8C
claims.quote: The magnitude of both spike transmission probability and single neuron-induced excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) (in E-I and E-E connections) and IPSPs (I-E connections) showed a lognormal distribution
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test or measure of lognormality. The distribution of log transmission probabilities is shown with its skewness, as description; the claim is recorded as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Five neurons in four mice are specifically active during the DOWN state of non-REM slow oscillation, all in deep layer 6; four have bursty autocorrelograms and one is regular spiking.
claims.source: Results, DOWN State-Active Neurons, paragraph 1; Figures 8A, 8B
claims.quote: We found five neurons in four mice that were specifically and dominantly active during the DOWN state of non-REM slow oscillation ( Figures 8 A and 8B). All DOWN state-active neurons were found in deep layers 6
claims.criterion: The paper gives no rule for selecting these cells. Readings are (a) units whose mean rate within DOWN states exceeds their rate within UP states, and (b) units whose PETH around DOWN-UP transitions peaks before time zero and falls after it (Figure 8A). The tolerance is one neuron or one mouse, as 10% of the count is less than the smallest step. Reproduced when, under a reading, the counts are within tolerance and all the cells lie in clusters 7-8 or below landmark d.

claims.statement: The DOWN state-active neurons fire at 35.2 ± 23.1 Hz during DOWN states and 4.3 ± 3.1 Hz during UP states.
claims.source: Results, DOWN State-Active Neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 8B
claims.quote: These five neurons were not only active during the DOWN state but mainly silent during the UP state (35.2 ± 23.1 Hz during DOWN, 4.3 ± 3.1 Hz during UP; p < 0.016, rank sum test)
claims.criterion: For the cells of fig8-down-active-neurons, rate within DOWN and within UP intervals; mean over cells. Reproduced when both are within tolerance (the paper's SD) and a two-sided rank-sum test gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: DOWN state-active neurons are suppressed during light flashes, when other neurons respond, and during optogenetic activation of PV or VGAT neurons, after which they rebound about 30 ms later while other principal cells are still suppressed.
claims.source: Results, DOWN State-Active Neurons, paragraph 1; Figures 8C, 8D
claims.quote: During light flash presentation, their spiking activity was further reduced at the time when the remaining neurons robustly responded
claims.criterion: PSTHs around light flash onsets and around 10 ms blue pulses (PV-Cre and VGAT-Cre mice). The paper gives no test. Reproduced when, for each DOWN state-active cell recorded with the stimulus, the rate in the stimulus window (flash, the 100 ms after onset; blue pulse, 0-10 ms) is below its baseline (-100 to 0 ms, the Methods' tagging baseline), and the mean rebound at 30-50 ms after the blue pulse exceeds baseline while the mean of other E cells is below it. Windows are open beyond these; the readings use the 30 ms of the text and the pulse lengths of the Methods.

claims.statement: DOWN state-active neurons are inversely correlated with other principal cells and interneurons in both non-REM sleep and waking.
claims.source: Results, DOWN State-Active Neurons, paragraph 1; Figures 8E to 8H
claims.quote: Cross-correlation between the DOWN state-active cells and other principal cells showed an inverse correlation not only during non-REM but also in the waking animal
claims.criterion: Spike CCGs of each DOWN state-active cell with every other E and I cell of its session, per state. The paper gives no test or window; reading, the mean normalized CCG within ±50 ms (the scale of Figures 8E to 8H is not in the text, a standard choice) below the CCG at ±500 to 1000 ms. Reproduced when the mean over pairs is below baseline in both states for D-E pairs.

claims.statement: In the time discrimination task, subjects chose the frame that was shown first in 73% of trials when the two frames were separated by no boundary or by a soft boundary, and in 53% of trials, significantly fewer, when they were separated by a hard boundary.
claims.source: Figure 2a; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 3
claims.quote: subjects correctly identified which frame was shown first in 73 ± 7% and 73 ± 8% of trials when the two frames were separated by no boundary (NB) or a soft boundary (SB) ... subjects performed significantly worse when discriminating the order of frames separated by a hard boundary (HB) (Fig. 2a, red, HB: 53 ± 5%
claims.criterion: Besides the expected value, accuracy with no boundary and with a soft boundary must each be within 0.03 of 0.73, and accuracy across a hard boundary must be lower than both in paired tests over subjects (p < 0.05).

claims.statement: Reaction times in the time discrimination task were longer when the two frames were separated by a hard boundary (2.10 s) than by no boundary (1.62 s) or a soft boundary (1.59 s).
claims.source: Figure 2b; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Subjects also showed longer reaction times (Fig. 2b; HB: 2.10 ± 0.37 seconds; NB: 1.62 ± 0.28 seconds; SB: 1.59 ± 0.34 seconds; F (2, 57) = 14.25
claims.criterion: Besides the expected value, the reaction time across a hard boundary must be longer than with no boundary and with a soft boundary in paired tests over subjects (p < 0.05).

claims.statement: Confidence ratings in the time discrimination task were lower when the two frames were separated by a hard boundary (1.95 on a scale of 1 to 3) than by no boundary (2.52) or a soft boundary (2.59).
claims.source: Figure 2c; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 3
claims.quote: lower confidence ratings when discriminating the order of frames separated by a hard boundary (Fig. 2c; HB: 1.95 ± 0.45; NB: 2.52 ± 0.29; SB: 2.59 ± 0.23; F (2, 57) = 20.41
claims.criterion: Besides the expected value, confidence across a hard boundary must be lower than with no boundary and with a soft boundary in paired tests over subjects (p < 0.05).

claims.statement: Scene recognition accuracy did not differ between frames from clips with no boundary (76%), a soft boundary (75%) and a hard boundary (75%).
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 2a; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 4
claims.quote: the ability to recognize a frame as ‘old’ did not differ significantly between the types of boundaries preceding the frame (Extended Data Fig. 2a; NB: 76% ± 10%; SB: 75% ± 9%; HB: 75% ± 8%, F (2, 57) = 0.07, p = 0.94).
claims.criterion: Reproduced if a one-way ANOVA over the three kinds of clip, as in the paper, gives p > 0.05 and each mean over subjects is within 0.04 of the reported value.

claims.statement: Recognition accuracy for a target frame fell with the time between the frame and the boundary before it, for soft boundaries (r = -0.61) and hard boundaries (r = -0.44), but not for clips with no boundary (r = 0.085).
claims.source: Figure 2d-f; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Target frames presented shortly after a SB and HB were remembered better than those farther away from the boundary (Fig. 2e and 2f; SB: r = −0.61 ... recognition accuracy did not differ significantly as a function of time relative to NBs (Fig. 2d, Pearson correlation; NB: r = 0.085, p = 0.65).

claims.statement: 42 of 580 medial temporal lobe neurons (7.24%) were boundary cells, which changed their firing in the second after soft and hard boundaries but not in the middle of clips with no boundary; 2.11% were expected by chance.
claims.source: Figure 3a-c; Results, Medial temporal lobe neurons demarcate episodic transitions, paragraph 1; Methods, Boundary cell
claims.quote: 42/580 MTL neurons (7.24%; expected proportion by chance for all MTL neurons= 2.11%) were classified as boundary cells (Fig. 3c).
claims.criterion: Besides the expected value, the number of boundary cells must exceed the 95th percentile of the numbers found after shuffling the condition labels of the clips.

claims.statement: 36 of 580 medial temporal lobe neurons (6.20%) were event cells, which changed their firing in the second after hard boundaries but not after soft boundaries or in the middle of clips with no boundary; 2.26% were expected by chance.
claims.source: Figure 3e-g; Results, Medial temporal lobe neurons demarcate episodic transitions, paragraph 3; Methods, Event cell
claims.quote: 36/580 MTL neurons (6.20%; proportion expected by chance for all MTL neurons = 2.26%) were classified as event cells (Fig. 3g).
claims.criterion: Besides the expected value, the number of event cells must exceed the 95th percentile of the numbers found after shuffling the condition labels of the clips.

claims.statement: Boundary cells were most common in the parahippocampal gyrus (18 of 68 neurons, 26%, against 7% in the amygdala and 3.5% in the hippocampus), and event cells in the hippocampus (27 of 343, 7.9%, against 4.3% in the amygdala and 2.9% in the parahippocampal gyrus).
claims.source: Results, Medial temporal lobe neurons demarcate episodic transitions, paragraphs 1 and 3; Supplementary Table 4
claims.quote: The regions with the largest proportion of boundary cells were the parahippocampal gyrus (n= 18/68, 26.47%) ... The regions with the largest proportion of event cells were the hippocampus (n= 27/343, 7.87%)
claims.criterion: Reproduced if the parahippocampal gyrus has the highest proportion of boundary cells and the hippocampus the highest proportion of event cells of the three regions, each above the 95th percentile of its label-shuffling chance level. Partially reproduced if one of the two holds.

claims.statement: Boundary cells and event cells did not change their firing at clip onsets or offsets during encoding, nor at image onsets or offsets in the two memory tests.
claims.source: Figure 3d,h; Extended Data Figures 3 and 4; Results, Medial temporal lobe neurons demarcate episodic transitions, paragraphs 2 and 3
claims.quote: Boundary cells did not respond significantly to either clip or image onsets or offsets (p > 0.05; permutation t-test, Methods) ... event cells did not significantly change their firing rates following video clip onsets or offsets (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 3) during encoding, nor did they respond to image onsets or offsets
claims.criterion: Judged only if at least 10 boundary cells and 10 event cells are found under fig3c-boundary-cells and fig3g-event-cells; the dandiset does not say which neurons the paper put in each class.

claims.statement: 76 of 580 medial temporal lobe neurons (13.1%) changed their firing at clip onsets and 4 of 580 (0.7%) at clip offsets, and none of them was a boundary cell or an event cell.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 5; Results, Medial temporal lobe neurons demarcate episodic transitions, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Seventy six of 580 (13.1%, p = 0.01) and four of 580 (0.7%, p = 0.43) MTL cells changed their firing rate in response to clip onsets and clip offsets, respectively, but neither of these cells qualified as boundary cells or event cells (Extended Data Fig. 5).
claims.criterion: Reproduced if the fraction responding to clip onsets is within the tolerance and the fraction responding to clip offsets is not above the 5% expected by chance. Partially reproduced if only the first holds. The paper's test is one-tailed without saying in which direction; an increase in firing is tested.

claims.statement: Boundary cells responded to hard boundaries about 100 ms earlier than event cells; their firing peaked 197 ms after the boundary, against 301 ms for event cells.
claims.source: Figure 3i-j; Results, Medial temporal lobe neurons demarcate episodic transitions, paragraph 6
claims.quote: boundary cells responded to hard boundaries approximately 100 milliseconds earlier than event cells (Fig. 3i) ... boundary cells showed a peak at 197 ± 49 milliseconds, whereas event cells showed a peak at 301 ± 55 milliseconds (Fig. 3j, F (1, 76) = 274.78
claims.criterion: Judged only if at least 10 boundary cells and 10 event cells are found under fig3c-boundary-cells and fig3g-event-cells.

claims.statement: Of 405 neurons recorded outside the medial temporal lobe, 8 were boundary cells and 9 were event cells, so boundary responses are largely confined to the medial temporal lobe.
claims.source: Results, Medial temporal lobe neurons demarcate episodic transitions, paragraph 7; Supplementary Tables 2 and 4
claims.quote: We found 8/405 (1.96%) boundary cells and 9/405 (2.22%) event cells among the non-MTL group ... Thus, boundary responsive neurons are largely within the MTL

claims.statement: Boundary cells fired more after soft and hard boundaries during encoding when the frame that followed the boundary was later recognised than when it was forgotten; there was no such difference for clips with no boundary, for the time discrimination task, or for event cells.
claims.source: Figure 4a-c; Extended Data Figures 6 and 7; Results, Responses of boundary and event cells predict memory strength, paragraph 1
claims.quote: among boundary cells (n = 42) for frames preceded or followed by both SBs and HBs, but not by NBs ... the firing rate of boundary cells did not significantly predict performance in the time discrimination task ... the firing rate of event cells (n = 36) during encoding was not predictive of scene recognition memory

claims.statement: Event cells' spikes were locked more strongly to the phase of the theta-band local field potential after soft and hard boundaries when the temporal order of the clip was later remembered than when it was not; boundary cells showed no such effect.
claims.source: Figure 4e-h; Results, Responses of boundary and event cells predict memory strength, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The mean MRL across all event cells (n = 36) was significantly larger following both SB and HB but not NB if temporal order was later correctly remembered ... the strength of phase-locking of boundary cells neither predicted scene recognition memory success ... nor temporal order memory

claims.statement: The state of the population of all medial temporal lobe neurons changed abruptly in the first 300 ms after soft and hard boundaries, and only slowly in clips with no boundary, measured as the distance in principal-component space from the state at the boundary.
claims.source: Figure 5a-d; Results, Neural state shifts across boundaries reflect memory strength, paragraph 1
claims.quote: During NB video clips, the neural state exhibited only slow changes as a function of time ... In contrast, the neural state changed abruptly following SBs and HBs ... Plotting MDD as a function of time revealed an abrupt change within ~300 ms after the boundary for SB and HB video clips
claims.criterion: Judged on the distance from the state at the boundary, averaged over the second after the boundary, for each pseudo-trial. Reproduced if for both soft and hard boundaries it is larger than in clips with no boundary (one-sided permutation test over pseudo-trials, p < 0.05), and the same holds for the distance in the second after the boundary minus the distance in the second before it. Partially reproduced if both hold for only one of the two kinds of boundary.

claims.statement: The distance the population state travelled in the second after a boundary correlated positively with later recognition accuracy for soft (r = 0.65) and hard (r = 0.57) boundaries, and negatively with time discrimination accuracy for hard boundaries (r = -0.68).
claims.source: Figure 5i-j; Results, Neural state shifts across boundaries reflect memory strength, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The AUC MDD was positively correlated with recognition accuracy for frames following SBs and HBs, but not NBs ... the AUC MDD was negatively correlated with accuracy in the time discrimination task for HBs, but not for NBs or SBs

claims.statement: During scene recognition, population activity correlated with the activity during encoding shortly after the soft or hard boundary of the tested clip, for correctly recognised targets and for foils wrongly called old, but not for forgotten targets or correctly rejected foils.
claims.source: Figure 6a-h; Results, Neural context after boundaries reinstates during recognition, paragraphs 1, 2 and 4
claims.quote: were accompanied by a significant positive correlation between neural activity during the scene recognition and the encoding period shortly after SB/HB transitions ... no significant correlation for forgotten targets ... no significant correlation for correctly identified foils was observed ... strong correlations ... also occurred when a new image was incorrectly classified as seen before

claims.statement: The reinstated state was most similar to the state about 1.2 s after the boundary that preceded the tested frame, and 1.5 to 1.7 s before the tested frame itself was shown.
claims.source: Figure 6i; Results, Neural context after boundaries reinstates during recognition, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The reinstated neural context during retrieval was most similar to the neural context present during encoding approximately ~1.2s after the boundary that preceded the tested frame ... the point of time of maximal similarity preceded the time at which the later tested frame was shown by 1–1.5s

claims.statement: Reinstatement after soft and hard boundaries was stronger for old decisions made with high confidence than with low confidence.
claims.source: Figure 6j-m; Results, Neural context after boundaries reinstates during recognition, paragraph 3
claims.quote: the correlations following boundary transitions were significantly stronger in high- compared to low-confidence trials ... This difference was observed during both correctly remembered targets and falsely recognized foils

claims.statement: For foils wrongly called old, reinstatement was stronger when the foil was highly similar to its target; for correctly rejected foils it did not vary with similarity.
claims.source: Figure 6n-o; Results, Neural context after boundaries reinstates during recognition, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Correlations between encoding and scene recognition were significantly stronger for highly similar foils falsely recognized as old compared to low and medium similarity foils ... the extent of correlation for correctly rejected foils (true negatives) did not vary as a function of similarity

claims.statement: A total of 1,647 LS neurons were recorded from five animals, in 62 sessions.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 2G (N = 62 sessions)
claims.quote: We recorded a total of 1,647 LS neurons from five animals ... lateral septum (magenta; N = 62 sessions
claims.criterion: Units whose region label is ls, and the sessions holding at least one, over the five subjects. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance and five subjects hold LS units.

claims.statement: The hippocampal recordings hold 2,297 isolated CA1 units and 654 CA3 units (2,951 in all, Figure 3A).
claims.source: Results, first paragraph; Figure 3A legend
claims.quote: First, we examined the firing patterns of 1,587 place fields of 2,297 isolated CA1 units and 224 place fields of 654 CA3 units ... (N = 2,951 units, A)
claims.criterion: Units labelled hpc are counted as CA1 and units labelled ca3 as CA3. Reproduced when both are within tolerance; partially reproduced when only their sum is within 10% of 2,951.

claims.statement: Of the LS neurons, 840 fired at least 1.5 action potentials per trial on average.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; STAR Methods, position prediction analysis
claims.quote: We recorded a total of 1,647 LS neurons from five animals, of which 840 surpassed a minimum threshold of at least 1.5 action potentials per trial on average
claims.criterion: An LS unit passes when, in at least one condition with at least 10 trials, its spike count over those trials is at least 1.5 times the number of trials (makeFig2.m). Sessions without a hippocampal theta channel are counted too, as this criterion needs no LFP.

claims.statement: The majority of LS neurons (751 of 840, 89%) showed position encoding in their spike theta phase, compared with shuffled data, in at least one condition.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 2C and 2D
claims.quote: the majority of LS neurons showed a form of position encoding in their spike timing relative to the phase of theta oscillations ... (751/840,89%; two sample t test; p < 0.01) when compared to shuffled data, in at least one of the behavioral conditions
claims.criterion: A neuron counts when, in at least one included condition, its phase MSE is below the chance phase MSE by a two-sample t-test over the 10 splits at p < 0.01. The fraction is over active LS neurons in sessions with a theta channel.

claims.statement: Spike-phase decoding outperformed rate decoding of the rat's position for 786 of 840 LS neurons, 3,046 of 4,393 conditions, and 62 of 62 sessions.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figures 2F and 2G
claims.quote: Spike-phase-based decoding outperformed firing rate-based decoding of the rat’s position on the tracks (Figures 2F and 2G) whether we made the comparison at the level of LS neurons (N = 786/840; two-sample t test; p < 0.01), conditions (N = 3,046/4,393), or recording sessions (N = 62/62).
claims.criterion: A condition counts when its phase MSE is below its rate MSE by a two-sample t-test over the 10 splits at p < 0.01; a neuron counts when at least one of its conditions does; a session counts when its mean phase MSE over included LS conditions is below its mean rate MSE. The neuron tolerance is the distance to 100%, as 10% would pass any value above 84%. Reproduced when all three fractions are within tolerance; partially reproduced when phase is better than rate in more than half of neurons, conditions and sessions but a fraction is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Across LS neurons the spike-phase code is stronger than the rate code (two-sample t tests; N = 4,393 conditions, p < 1e-100; N = 62 sessions, p < 1e-10).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 2E
claims.quote: Across the population of LS neurons, we observed significantly stronger spike-phase coding when compared with models that utilized spike rate information (Figure 2E; two sample t tests; N = 4,393 conditions
claims.criterion: Two-sample t-tests of phase against rate MSE over included LS conditions and over sessions (session means). Reproduced when the phase MSE is lower in both with p below the paper's bounds (1e-100 and 1e-10); partially reproduced when lower in both with p < 0.05 but a bound is not reached.

claims.statement: The mean phase minus rate MSE is about -1,000 for LS conditions and -33 for hippocampal place fields, and -1,024 and -25 for LS and hippocampal sessions.
claims.source: Figure 2F and 2G legends
claims.quote: for all conditions for lateral septum (LS) cells (magenta; N = 4,393, mean = − 1,000) and hippocampal place fields (black; N = 1,820, mean = − 33) ... (black; N = 45 sessions, mean = − 25) and lateral septum (magenta; N = 62 sessions, mean = − 1,024)
claims.criterion: Session values are the mean over the session's included LS conditions, or its hippocampal place fields. Reproduced when all four are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the LS values are negative and larger in magnitude than the hippocampal ones at both levels but a value is outside tolerance. MSE depends on the number of position bins, which the paper gives only as about 1.5 cm.

claims.statement: For hippocampal place fields the distributions of rate and phase decoding errors are statistically equivalent (two-sample KS test; 1,820 place fields, p = 0.19; 45 sessions, p = 0.61).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1I
claims.quote: the distributions of mean squared errors for these two forms of encoding were statistically equivalent ... (Figure 1I; two-way Kolmogorov-Smirnov [KS] test; N = 1,820 place fields comparison p = 0.19; N = 45 sessions; p = 0.61)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Place fields are hippocampal cell and condition pairs with at least one field (place-field rule in lshpc.py); their phase and rate MSE are compared by a two-sample KS test, and so are the session means. Reproduced when neither test gives p < 0.05; not reproduced when either does. The mean difference is reported either way.

claims.statement: Only 5.3% (232 of 4,393) of LS rate maps showed place fields by the criteria applied to hippocampal units, where 31.7% (1,820 of 5,735) did.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4
claims.quote: only 5.3% (232/4,393) of LS ratemaps showed place fields, using the same criteria we applied to hippocampal units where 31.7% (1,820/5,735) of ratemaps displayed a place field.
claims.criterion: A rate map is an included cell and condition (at least 10 trials, 1.5 spikes per trial). Reproduced when both fractions are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the LS fraction is lower than the hippocampal one (chi-squared test, p < 0.05) but a fraction is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: 711 of 1,425 hippocampal neurons had at least one place field (1.27 fields per neuron on average); the median peak in-field rate was 8.5 Hz and the median field width 38 bins.
claims.source: STAR Methods, place field definition
claims.quote: Given these criteria, 711 of 1,425 HPC neurons had at least one place field with a mean of 1.27 ± 1.76 fields per neuron ... The median peak in-field firing rate was 8.5 ± 12 Hz, and the median field width was 38 ± 16 spatial bins (~57 cm).
claims.criterion: The neurons are hippocampal units passing the activity rule in at least one condition; a neuron has a field when any of its included conditions does. Peak rate and width are taken over all fields. Reproduced when all three are within tolerance; partially when one or two are.

claims.statement: The few LS rate maps with a place field were less stable across trials than CA1/CA3 place fields (median coefficient of variance 41.5 against 10; two-sample t test, p < 1e-20).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Those few LS ratemaps that did qualify as having a “place field” were significantly less stable across trials than CA1/CA3 place fields (median coefficient of variance = 41.5 for LS versus 10 for CA1/CA3 place fields; two sample t test
claims.criterion: The paper does not define the quantity. Readings, for the first field of each map, (a) the SD over trials of the rate at the field peak in Hz, as makeFig2.m computes; (b) that SD divided by the mean, in percent. Reproduced when, under one reading, both medians are within tolerance and LS is higher by a two-sample t-test at p < 1e-20; partially reproduced when, under one reading, LS is higher at p < 0.05 but a median is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Hippocampal place fields reach their peak information at smaller smoothing scales for phase than for rate (medians 15 and 29 bins; two-sample t test, p < 1e-40).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1E
claims.quote: The mean peak information rate occurred at consistently smaller spatial scales for phase “coding” compared to discharge frequency coding (Figure 1E; N = 1,820; two-sample t test
claims.criterion: Information as in the Methods (Olypher et al.) for each place field and smoothing of 1 to 50 bins. Values are discretized into 7 equal-width levels (rate over the map's range, phase over -pi to pi); P(k) is over all trials and bins, P(k|x) over trials at bin x, logs base 2; the peak information of a smoothing is the maximum over bins. The best smoothing is the argmax of the 5-point smoothed curve, and fields with a best smoothing of 49 or more are left out, as makeFig1.m does. Reproduced when both medians are within tolerance and the phase scale is smaller by a two-sample t-test at p < 1e-40; partially reproduced when it is smaller at p < 0.05 but a median is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: At smoothing below 6 cm (about one theta cycle) phase carries more spatial information than rate in hippocampal place fields, and above 10 cm rate carries more.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1G
claims.quote: For smoothing windows less than 6 cm ... the phase code carried significantly (two sample t test; p < 0.00001; N = 1,820 place fields) more spatial information than the firing rate code (Figure 1G), whereas at spatial scales larger than 10 cm the firing rate code was more informative.
claims.criterion: With the information of fig1e-phase-info-smaller-scale, the phase minus rate peak information per field for each smoothing. Fine smoothings are 2 and 3 bins (the first bin is skipped as in makeFig1.m), coarse ones 7 to 50 bins. Reproduced when the mean difference is positive at both fine smoothings with p < 1e-5 (two-sample t-test of phase against rate) and negative at p < 0.05 for at least 80% of the coarse smoothings; partially reproduced when only one of the two holds.

claims.statement: The strength of phase coding relative to rate coding increases with recording depth within the LS, within sessions and across animals.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figures 4A to 4D
claims.quote: Within single recording sessions in individual rats (Figures 4A and 4B) and across all animals (Figures 4C and 4D) the strength of phase coding, relative to rate coding, reliably increased as a function of recording depth within LS.
claims.criterion: The within-session part needs each unit's recording site, which the dandiset does not hold, so the test is across sessions. Per session the mean phase minus rate MSE over included LS conditions; per animal the Pearson correlation with the session's LS depth. Reproduced when r < 0 in every animal with at least four LS sessions and, with depth and value centred within animal, the pooled correlation is negative at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when the pooled test holds but not every animal.

claims.statement: The theta phase at the onset of LS phase fields varies with recording depth (DT5 r = 0.38, DT9 r = 0.25, DT2 r = 0.27; circular-linear correlation, p < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figure 4E
claims.quote: the phase onset for precession varied systematically and significantly with recording depth (DT5 r = 0.38, DT9 r = 0.25, DT2 r = 0.27; circular/linear correlation; p < 0.001).
claims.criterion: For each LS neuron with significant phase coding (fig2-ls-phase-vs-shuffle), in its significant condition with the lowest phase MSE, the circular mean phase of its spikes in the first 15 bins; correlated with the session's LS depth per animal (CircStat circ_corrcl). Reproduced when all three animals give p < 0.001 and r within tolerance; partially reproduced when all three give p < 0.001, or one or two do, with r outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Spike trains of hippocampal neurons predicted LS firing in 18.5% (2,087 of 11,264) of hippocampal-LS pairs, with a median optimal timescale of 25 ms.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 7; Figure 5D to 5F
claims.quote: Across 18.5% (2,087/11,264) of hippocampal-LS cell pairs examined, spike trains of hippocampal neurons reliably predicted the firing of action potentials in LS neurons ... the median optimal timescale for peer prediction was 25 ms (Figure 5F)
claims.criterion: Tested on a random sample of pairs, as all pairs do not fit the time limit. A pair is a hippocampal and an LS unit both active (1.5 spikes per trial) in the same condition, taken in that condition; each is kept with probability 0.01 (seeded). Spikes are counted in 1 ms bins inside the condition's trials. A Poisson GLM predicts the LS unit's counts from theta phase (sine, cosine and angle), position bin, speed and the hippocampal unit's spike train smoothed by a Gaussian of SD w, for w in 1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 75, 100 and 150 ms. The best w has the least deviance. Assembly strength is the reduction in deviance at the best w from the model without the hippocampal train, divided by the largest reduction over 10 shuffles of the hippocampal train's trial order (no trial kept with its own) at that w; an assembly has strength of at least 4. Reproduced when the 95% binomial interval of the fraction of assemblies overlaps 0.185 plus or minus 0.0185 and the median best w of the assemblies is within tolerance; partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: LS neurons that take part in at least one predictive assembly carry a stronger spatial phase code than those that do not (p < 1e-20).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 7; Figure 5G
claims.quote: LS neurons that participated in at least one predictive cell assembly were found to carry a more robust spatial phase code compared to neurons that were not part of a predictive assembly (Figure 5G; two sample t test

claims.statement: Theta phase coherence between LS and the CA3 pyramidal layer increases from the beginning to the end of the run, while coherence between LS and CA1 stays relatively flat.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 6C
claims.quote: LFP theta phase coherence between LS and CA1 pyramidal layer sites was relatively flat during the entire span of the tracks. In contrast, theta phase coherence between LS and CA3 pyramidal layer increased significantly from the beginning to the end of run (Figure 6C).
claims.criterion: Sessions with units labelled ca3 are CA3 sessions and sessions with units labelled hpc are CA1 sessions; the hippocampal channel is the theta channel. Coherence is the phase locking of the 4 to 12 Hz phase difference between the hippocampal and the LS channel in 150 ms windows moved in 50 ms steps, averaged in ten position segments per session over all trials. Per session the slope of coherence on segment. Reproduced when CA3 slopes are above zero (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p < 0.05) and above CA1 slopes (Mann-Whitney, p < 0.05); partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: Coupling between hippocampal theta phase and LS gamma amplitude increases along the run for both CA1 and CA3, and is stronger for CA3-LS than for CA1-LS.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 6D
claims.quote: Although the strength of coupling increased in both cases, it was significantly stronger for CA3-LS than for CA1-LS comparisons (Figure 6D).
claims.criterion: Per session and position segment, the circular-linear correlation between the 4 to 12 Hz phase of the hippocampal channel and the 50 ms RMS of the 40 to 200 Hz LS signal, with sessions grouped as in fig6c-ca3-coherence-increases. Reproduced when the session mean coupling is higher in CA3 than CA1 sessions (Mann-Whitney, p < 0.05) and the slopes on segment are above zero in both groups (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p < 0.05); partially reproduced when only the first holds.

claims.statement: CA3 place fields form progressively stronger gamma assemblies with LS along the track (r = 0.34) while CA1 coupling decreases (r = -0.11), and the two are anti-correlated (r = -0.88).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 6E
claims.quote: The functional coupling between CA1 place cells and LS neurons decreased somewhat (r = −0.11; p = 0.079; N = 260 pairs), while coupling between CA3 place cells and LS neurons significantly increased (r = 0.34; p = 0.006; N = 72 pairs)

claims.statement: The firing phases of ensembles of simultaneously recorded LS neurons read out position better than the firing phases or rates of an equal number of hippocampal neurons (p < 0.001 at 15 to 25 neurons).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure S7; STAR Methods, ensemble position prediction
claims.quote: the firing phases of ensembles of simultaneously recorded LS neurons (range: 1–53) provided a better readout of spatial position than either the firing phases or rates of an equivalent number of HPC neurons (Figure S7; two-sample t test; p < 0.001 at ensemble sizes of 15–25 neurons)
claims.criterion: Per session and condition with at least 15 included LS and 15 included hippocampal units, for ensembles of 15, 20 and 25 (as many as available), 10 random ensembles per region; features are the smoothed rate and phase of each unit, discretized into 20 levels; a Poisson naive Bayes decoder (mean level per unit and bin as rate) over 10 random 60/40 splits of the trial-by-bin samples; MSE averaged over splits. Reproduced when, at every ensemble size tested, LS phase MSE is lower than both hippocampal phase and rate MSE by two-sample t-tests at p < 0.001; partially reproduced when that holds at p < 0.05 or for one of the two comparisons.

claims.statement: Only 2.8% (125 of 4,393) of LS conditions showed a significant correlation between running speed and the rate of phase precession, and 10.7% of LS rate maps were modulated by running speed.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Only 125 of 4,393 LS conditions (2.8%) had significant correlations between running speed and the rate of phase precession ... only 10.7% of firing rate maps in LS were significantly modulated by running speed

claims.statement: LS rate maps have lower peak information rates than hippocampal place field maps (0.4 against 1.7 bits/cm; p < 1e-100).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4
claims.quote: LS action potential ratemaps had significantly lower peak information rates than hippocampal place field maps (average of 0.4 bits/cm versus 1.7 bits/cm; two-sample t test
claims.criterion: Information as in fig1e-phase-info-smaller-scale (7 equal-width levels over the map's range, Olypher et al.) on the trial-by-bin rate map of the place-field rule (Gaussian SD 4 bins); its peak over bins, divided by the session's bin size in cm (median trial path over 200 bins). LS maps are all included LS conditions; hippocampal maps are included hippocampal conditions with a place field. Sessions with positions in pixels (DT2) are left out. The paper does not say whether 0.4 and 1.7 are means or medians; both readings are shown. Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance and LS is lower by a two-sample t-test at p < 1e-100; partially reproduced when LS is lower at p < 0.05 but a value or the bound is not reached.

claims.statement: After maze rotation many LS neurons kept their phase precession related to distal room cues, so the phase shift is a spatial code.
claims.source: Discussion, Transmission and Utilization of the Hippocampal Spatial Map by LS Neurons, paragraph 2; Figure S6; STAR Methods, reference frame analysis
claims.quote: theta phase precession of many LS neurons retained their relation to distant room cues after the rotation of the maze, suggesting that the spike-phase shift is a spatial “code” (Figure S6)

claims.statement: In a spiking model, CA1 and CA3 inputs weighted dynamically as the measured assemblies give a rate-independent phase code in the LS neuron, which static or random weights, or the loss of theta sequences, do not.
claims.source: Figure 7; Results, paragraph 12
claims.quote: Thus, by dynamically weighting the outputs of CA3 and CA1 place fields at different positions, the assembly firing of the hippocampal output is transformed into a rate-independent phase code of that space in the LS

claims.statement: LS was recorded in 6 rats, with 1989 LS neurons; 37 recordings had CA1 and LS and 25 had CA3 and LS recorded simultaneously; LS HFO rates come from 89 recordings and CA1 ripple rates from 53.
claims.source: Results, first paragraph; Figure 1C legend; Figure 5B legend; STAR Methods, Experimental model and subject details
claims.quote: During initial recordings in LS (N = 6 rats) ... The dataset used for Figure 6 consists of 62 recordings with both CA1 and LS simultaneously recorded (N = 37) or CA3 and LS simultaneously recorded (N = 25)
claims.criterion: Counts from the files. Readings for a recording of a region are (a) a file with units labelled with that region, (b) a file with electrodes labelled with it; for LS neurons (a) all units labelled `ls`, (b) those with more than 50 spikes in high-power epochs (the phase-locking selection). For the HFO and ripple rate counts, the recordings with sleep states are a further reading (c). Reproduced when the animal count matches and all other counts are within tolerance under one reading each; partially reproduced when the animal count matches and at least three of the five other counts are.

claims.statement: Transient 120-180 Hz HFOs occur in LS in each of the 6 animals, with a robust increase in the firing probability of LS neurons at the events.
claims.source: Results, first paragraph; Figure 1A to C
claims.quote: we observed transient high frequency oscillations (HFOs) in the 120–180 Hz frequency range in each animal (Figure 1A, B) and an associated robust increase in the firing probability of LS neurons (Figure 1C)
claims.criterion: Per animal, the median instantaneous frequency of its LS HFOs is within 120 to 180 Hz, and the HFO-triggered spike probability of its LS neurons within +-10 ms of the event time, averaged over neurons, exceeds the probability at as many random times by more than 3 SEM across neurons (the figure's bounds). Reproduced when this holds in all 6 animals, partially reproduced in 3 to 5, not reproduced in fewer.

claims.statement: Across 6 animals, 29,955 LS HFO events were analysed.
claims.source: Figure 1C legend
claims.quote: Average power spectrum across all events (N = 6 animals, 29,955 events)
claims.criterion: Readings (a) events in all recordings with LS electrodes, (b) events in recordings with LS units. Reproduced when one reading is within tolerance.

claims.statement: On average 16% of LS neurons take part in a given HFO, firing an average of 0.23 spikes per event.
claims.source: Results, first paragraph (Figure S1A, B)
claims.quote: On average, 16% of LS neurons participated in any given event, firing an average of 0.23 spikes per event (Figure S1A, B)
claims.criterion: Spikes are counted between an event's start and stop. Readings (a) the mean over all events pooled, of the fraction of the recording's LS neurons with at least one spike, and the mean spike count over all neuron and event pairs; (b) the mean over recordings of the per-recording means. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when one is.

claims.statement: The vast majority of LS neurons (1840 of 1989, 92%) are significantly phase-locked to the 120-200 Hz band (Rayleigh P < 0.05), with a strong preference for the trough of each cycle.
claims.source: Results, first paragraph; Figure 1D, E; STAR Methods, Phase locking analysis
claims.quote: the vast majority of LS neurons (1840 of 1989; 92%) were significantly phase-locked to the 120–200 Hz frequency band, with a strong unimodal phase preference for the trough of each cycle (Figure 1D, E)
claims.criterion: Phase locking as in the Methods, on the recording's HFO detection channel. Readings for the denominator are (a) neurons with more than 50 spikes in high-power epochs, (b) all LS neurons. The trough preference holds when the circular mean of the preferred phases of significant neurons is within 45 degrees of the trough (180 degrees) and their Rayleigh test gives p < 0.05. Reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance under one reading and the trough preference holds; partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: LS HFOs are shorter than CA1 ripples from the same animals (27 +- 9 against 31 +- 14 ms; rank-sum P < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, first paragraph; Figure 1F
claims.quote: These events were significantly shorter in duration (27±9 vs 31±14 milliseconds) ... than CA1 ripples recorded from the same animals (Figure 1F, G; rank-sum test; P < 0.01)
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the paper's stated SDs. Events pooled over the animals with both LS and hippocampal channels. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance, LS HFOs are shorter and the rank-sum test gives p < 0.01; partially reproduced when LS HFOs are significantly shorter but a mean is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: LS HFOs are slower in frequency than CA1 ripples (147 +- 5.7 against 159 +- 8 Hz; rank-sum P < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, first paragraph; Figure 1G
claims.quote: These events were significantly ... slower in frequency (147±5.7 vs 159±8 Hz) than CA1 ripples recorded from the same animals (Figure 1F, G; rank-sum test; P < 0.01)
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the paper's stated SDs. As for fig1f-shorter-than-ripples, with the instantaneous frequency of the Methods.

claims.statement: LS HFOs show no significant correlation between event amplitude and peak frequency.
claims.source: Results, first paragraph; Figure 1H
claims.quote: However, they showed no significant correlation between event amplitude and peak frequency (Figure 1H)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper does not name its test; the test here is a Pearson correlation over all LS HFOs pooled, at p < 0.05. Reproduced when it finds no significant correlation, not reproduced when it does. The effect size (r) is reported either way, with Spearman and per-animal values as variants.

claims.statement: HFO events are seen only at recording sites within LS, not at sites in neighbouring structures.
claims.source: Results, second paragraph; Figure 2A to C
claims.quote: We only observed HFO events at recording sites that were confined to the LS (Figure 2A–C)
claims.criterion: In recordings with electrodes in regions other than LS and the hippocampus (cortex, corpus callosum, medial septum, fimbria), the 120-200 Hz power within +-20 ms of the LS HFO times in up to 30 min of all channels, divided by the power at random times, is compared between regions. Recordings with at least 20 HFOs in that block are used. Reproduced when the median ratio over LS channels exceeds the median ratio of every other non-hippocampal region in every such recording; partially reproduced when it does in most of them.

claims.statement: HFO power and the proportion of phase-locked neurons are highest in intermediate LS and taper towards its dorsal and ventral borders.
claims.source: Results, second paragraph; Figure 2D to F; Figure S1C, D
claims.quote: Both the power of HFOs and the proportion of phase-locked neurons were highest in the intermediate LS and tapered off as recordings approached either the dorsal or ventral border of LS

claims.statement: LS HFOs are travelling waves, posterior to anterior at 1.01 m/s (4 animals), medial to lateral at 0.53 m/s (1 animal) and dorsal to ventral at 2.19 m/s (4 animals).
claims.source: Results, second paragraph; Figure 3C
claims.quote: we estimated that the travel speed was 1.01 meters per second in the posterior-to-anterior direction (N = 4 animals), 0.53 meters per second in the medial-to-lateral direction (N = 1 animal), and 2.19 meters per second in the dorsal-to-ventral direction (N = 4 animals)

claims.statement: The co-activation of LS neuron pairs during HFOs (excess correlation) is not modulated by waking experience on a familiar maze (PRE against POST, rank-sum P = 0.36).
claims.source: Results, third paragraph; Figure 4B
claims.quote: It also suggested that the degree of co-activation observed is not modulated by waking experience in a familiar environment (Figure 4B; rank-sum test; P = 0.36; PRE vs POST)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a rank-sum test of PRE against POST excess correlations over all pairs, at p < 0.05. Pairs are LS neurons on different shanks in recordings with all three epochs. CCGs use 1 ms bins of the spikes inside LS HFOs (PRE, POST) or inside trials (BEHAV), normalized by the square root of the product of the spike counts, over +-400 ms, smoothed with Gaussian kernels of SD 5 ms and 200 ms (each divided by the kernel mass inside the window); the excess correlation is the difference of the two at zero lag. The jittered value moves every spike by a uniform +-200 ms before the CCG. A pair is kept when its CCG holds more than 5 spike pairs within +-200 ms in each epoch. Reproduced when the test finds no difference, not reproduced when it does; the effect size is reported either way.

claims.statement: Excess correlations during HFOs (PRE and POST) are higher than during maze traversal (rank-sum P < 0.001), and those of PRE and POST HFOs exceed chance from spikes jittered by +-200 ms (P < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, third paragraph; Figure 4B; Figure S3A
claims.quote: the excess correlations for HFOs during the PRE and POST epochs were much greater than expected by chance ... during LS HFOs there is a higher degree of co-activation than observed during behavior or expected given LS firing rates (rank-sum test; P < 0.001 for PRE vs BEHAV and BEHAV vs POST)
claims.criterion: Same pairs and measure as fig4b-pre-post-unchanged. Reproduced when PRE > BEHAV and POST > BEHAV by rank-sum p < 0.001 and PRE and POST exceed their jittered values by rank-sum p < 0.01; partially reproduced when one of the two comparisons holds.

claims.statement: Only 7 of 53 sessions have significantly different excess correlations in PRE and POST (rank-sum P < 0.01), three with PRE below POST and four with PRE above.
claims.source: Results, third paragraph
claims.quote: Only 7 out of 53 sessions had significantly different excess-correlation values for PRE and POST epochs (rank-sum test; P < 0.01), three where PRE was less than POST and four where PRE was greater than POST
claims.criterion: Per recording with at least 5 pairs, rank-sum test of PRE against POST at p < 0.01. Reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance and both directions occur; partially reproduced when the fraction is below 0.25 and both directions occur.

claims.statement: The temporal ordering of LS spike pairs during HFOs before and after the maze correlates with the ordering during traversal to a similar degree (P = 0.85).
claims.source: Results, fourth paragraph; Figure 4C
claims.quote: the spiking structure during HFOs prior to and after maze performance showed correlations with the spike ordering during maze traversal that were similar (Figure 4C; N = 53 recordings; Two-way T-test; P = 0.85)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The temporal bias of a pair is the sum of its normalized CCG over +1 to +200 ms minus that over -200 to -1 ms. Per recording with at least 10 pairs, the Pearson correlation over pairs of PRE with BEHAV biases, and of BEHAV with POST biases. The paper's test, a two-sample two-sided t-test of the two sets of correlations, at p < 0.05. Reproduced when it finds no difference, not reproduced when it does.

claims.statement: Cross-correlograms of LS pairs during HFOs correlate with those during traversal above chance up to about 20-fold temporal compression (P < 0.01), similarly for PRE and POST (P > 0.01 for all compression factors).
claims.source: Results, fourth paragraph; Figure 4D; Figure S3B
claims.quote: We found correlations significantly higher than chance (up to ~20-fold compression; P < 0.01) ... However, the strength of this compression was similar for HFOs recorded prior to, and after, maze traversal (P > 0.01 for all compression factors)
claims.criterion: For compression factors 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40 and 50, the unsmoothed 1 ms HFO CCG over +-120/c ms is interpolated to 241 points and correlated with the BEHAV CCG over +-120 ms. Chance is the same with the HFO CCG circularly shifted by a random lag. Per factor, actual against chance by a paired Wilcoxon test over pairs, and PRE against POST by rank-sum. Reproduced when both PRE and POST exceed chance (p < 0.01) at every factor up to 20 and PRE and POST do not differ (p > 0.01) at any factor; partially reproduced when they exceed chance up to at least 5 and one of the other parts fails.

claims.statement: Firing rates increase during post-behavior NREM sleep in CA1, CA3 and LS.
claims.source: Results, fifth paragraph (Figure S2A, B)
claims.quote: we observed a systematic increase in firing rates during post-behavior NREM sleep in CA1, as well as CA3 and LS populations
claims.criterion: Per unit, the firing rate in NREM within PRE and within POST, for units in recordings with sleep states and at least 60 s of NREM in each epoch. Per region (`hpc`, `ca3`, `ls`), a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, at p < 0.05, with the median POST/PRE ratio above 1. Reproduced when all three regions show the increase, partially reproduced when one or two do.

claims.statement: LS HFOs occur primarily during NREM sleep, and their rates are lower than those of hippocampal SPW-Rs.
claims.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 5A, B
claims.quote: we primarily observed HFO events during NREM sleep (Figure 5A) ... the overall rates of LS HFOs were significantly lower than hippocampal SPW-Rs (Figure 5B)
claims.criterion: Per recording with sleep states, the LS HFO rate in NREM and in WAKE, and the CA1 ripple rate in NREM where a hippocampal channel exists. Reproduced when the NREM rate exceeds the WAKE rate (Wilcoxon signed-rank over recordings, p < 0.05, median ratio above 1) and the LS HFO rate in NREM is below the CA1 ripple rate in the same recordings (Wilcoxon, p < 0.05); partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: LS HFOs are reliably coupled to CA1 ripples, with a median peak-to-peak lag of 6.4 +- 4.2 ms, CA1 leading LS.
claims.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 5D
claims.quote: Across recordings, we observed a reliable coupling of events across structures (Figure 5D) with a median peak-to-peak temporal lag of 6.4 ± 4.2 milliseconds (CA1 leading LS)
claims.criterion: Tolerance is the paper's stated spread. The lag is the LS HFO time minus the time of the nearest CA1 ripple within +-50 ms. Readings (a) the median over recordings of per-recording medians, (b) the median over all pairs pooled. Reproduced when the lag is within tolerance under one reading and the CA1-LS cross-correlogram peaks within +-25 ms above the mean of its flanks (100 to 200 ms) by more than 3 SD of the flanks, pooled over recordings.

claims.statement: HPC-LS coupling is stronger in NREM sleep than in waking; the fraction of LS HFOs within +-25 ms of a CA1 ripple is 0.3 in NREM and 0.15 in WAKE (P < 6.6e-6).
claims.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 5E and inset
claims.quote: HPC-LS coupling was significantly stronger during NREM sleep than during the waking immobile state ... the percentage of LS HFO events that occurred within ±25 milliseconds of a CA1 ripple (NREM = 0.3; WAKE = 0.15; P < 6.6e-6 two-way T-test; Figure 5E inset)
claims.criterion: Recordings with sleep states, a hippocampal channel and at least 10 LS HFOs in each state. Readings (a) the mean over recordings, (b) all HFOs pooled. NREM against WAKE by a two-sample two-sided t-test over recordings. Reproduced when NREM is higher with p < 0.001 and both values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when NREM is higher with p < 0.001 but a value is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: LS firing around CA1 ripples is higher during NREM than during waking.
claims.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 5F
claims.quote: This state-dependent coupling could also be observed ... in the SPW-R triggered LS firing rates (two-way T-test with Bonferroni correction; P < 0.001; Figure 5F)
claims.criterion: Per LS neuron in recordings with sleep states and a hippocampal channel, the firing rate within +-25 ms of CA1 ripple times, for NREM and WAKE ripples separately, in recordings with at least 20 ripples in each state. Paired two-sided t-test over neurons. Reproduced when NREM is higher with p < 0.001; the rate divided by the neuron's mean rate in the same state is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: CA1-LS phase coherence in the 120-180 Hz band around CA1 ripples does not differ from that of randomly jittered windows, so LS does not inherit the ripple wave by wave.
claims.source: Results, seventh paragraph; Figure 5F inset
claims.quote: phase coherence between HFOs and SPW-Rs was not significantly different from a shuffled distribution (Figure 5F inset)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the figure's bounds of +-3 SD. Per recording, the phase-locking value across ripples of the CA1 minus LS phase at the ripple time, and at 20 sets of times jittered by up to +-1 s. Averaged over recordings. Reproduced when the ripple value lies within the mean +-3 SD of the 20 jittered averages; not reproduced when it lies above.

claims.statement: Optogenetic activation of LS GABAergic neurons with a Gaussian light waveform induces local oscillations of about 140 Hz.
claims.source: Results, seventh paragraph; Figure 6
claims.quote: Using a Gaussian waveform of blue light (450 nm), mimicking the envelope of SPW-R-induced hippocampal excitation, local oscillations of ~140 Hz could be reliably induced (Figure 6C–E; S2)

claims.statement: The number of CA1 spikes in a SPW-R significantly predicts the number of spikes of 38% of LS neurons.
claims.source: Results, eighth paragraph; Figure 7D, E
claims.quote: For many LS neurons (38%), this measure significantly predicted the number of action potentials elicited in the postsynaptic LS neuron (Figure 7D, E)
claims.criterion: The paper does not state its model. Fixed here, for LS neurons in recordings with hippocampal units and at least 100 CA1 ripples, and with at least 20 spikes inside ripples in total. Per ripple, the LS neuron's spike count between ripple start and stop is predicted from the feature by a linear regression, scored by 5-fold cross-validated mean squared error (MSE); the feature is shuffled over ripples 100 times. Readings of "significant" are (a) the actual MSE below the 5th percentile of the shuffled MSEs, (b) a one-sample two-sided t-test of the shuffled MSEs against the actual one at p < 0.05, with the actual MSE lower. The chance rate is the same test applied to one shuffle against the others (the figure's red points). Reproduced when the percentage is within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when it is out of tolerance but above the chance rate (binomial p < 0.05) under that reading; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Brain state (WAKE or NREM) in which a SPW-R occurs significantly predicts the spike count of 26% of LS neurons.
claims.source: Results, eighth paragraph; Figure 7E
claims.quote: the rate of spiking for some LS neurons (26%) was significantly predicted by brain state (Figure 7E)
claims.criterion: As fig7e-ca1-spikes, with the state (NREM 1, WAKE 0) as the feature, over the ripples in those two states.

claims.statement: The duration of hippocampal SPW-Rs significantly predicts the spike count of about 20% of LS neurons.
claims.source: Results, eighth paragraph; Figure 7E
claims.quote: The duration of hippocampal events could also be used to significantly predict firing rates for ~20% of the LS neurons (Figure 7E)
claims.criterion: As fig7e-ca1-spikes, with the ripple duration as the feature.

claims.statement: The mean depth within the CA1 pyramidal layer of the neurons active in a SPW-R predicts the spike count of 23% of LS neurons.
claims.source: Results, eighth paragraph; Figure 7D, E; STAR Methods, Relative anatomical depth within CA1
claims.quote: For a set of LS neurons (23%), the recording depth of the active CA1 population correlated significantly with the number of action potentials elicited (Figure 7D, E)

claims.statement: The sequential content of SPW-Rs, by three replay scores, predicts the firing of only 7.9, 6.6 and 7.1% of LS neurons.
claims.source: Results, ninth paragraph; Figure 7D, E
claims.quote: The firing rates of only a minority of LS neurons—7.9, 6.6, and 7.1% respectively—could be significantly predicted by the sequential structure of hippocampal events captured by these methods (Figure 7D, E)

claims.statement: Template sequences extracted from SPW-Rs without supervision predict the firing of only 8.1% of LS neurons.
claims.source: Results, tenth paragraph; Figure 7E; Figure S5
claims.quote: we found that the percentage of LS neurons whose action potential firing could be significantly predicted with these templates was small (Figure 7E; 8.1%; P < 0.05)

claims.statement: All spike-content-independent ripple features predict LS firing above chance, while all spike-content-based features do not.
claims.source: Results, eleventh paragraph; Figure 7E, bottom row
claims.quote: all spike content-independent ripple features were significantly different from chance (left seven columns), while all spike content-based ripple features were not significantly different from chance (Figure 7E; right four columns; bottom row)

claims.statement: In a model HPC-LS circuit, forward, reverse and scrambled compressed sequences evoke nearly identical responses of the LS neuron.
claims.source: Results, twelfth paragraph; Figure 8C, D
claims.quote: By providing the model with temporally compressed forward, reverse, or scrambled replay events (Figure 8C), we observed that the response of the postsynaptic model LS neuron was nearly identical for all three event types (Figure 8D)

claims.statement: The paper made 19 paired spine Ca2+ imaging and HD-MEA recordings in 10 cultures, tested 20 spines (one per recording, two in one recording), and the recordings have a mean of 102 ± 43 sorted units each.
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraphs 1 and 2; Table 1
claims.quote: we conducted 19 paired spine Ca 2+ imaging and HD-MEA recording experiments in 10 different cell cultures ... based on 19 recordings with a mean of 102 ± 43 units per recording ... (in one of recordings two spines were chosen)
claims.criterion: Counts of recordings, cultures and spines are exact, as they describe the data collected. Units are the curated sorted units of each recording. The paper does not say over which set the mean and spread are taken or which SD is meant; Table 1 settles it, as 19 recordings (rows 9 and 10 counted once) with the population SD (ddof 0) give 101.6 ± 42.6, while 20 rows give 105.5 ± 44.8 and the sample SD gives 43.8. That reading is used, and the other is shown. The per-row unit counts of Table 1 are compared with the files as well, each within 10%.

claims.statement: For each of the 20 tested spines, the best-R (the Pearson R of the demixed spine trace with the convolved trace of its best-matching unit, outside network bursts) has the value given in Table 1, from 0.148 to 0.765.
claims.source: Table 1, column best_R; Figure 5(a)
claims.criterion: The pipeline of the opening comment, from the Methods 2.4 to 2.6 and notebook 1 of the code, with each detail cited there. Each spine is matched to its Table 1 row by culture and unit count; a spine's best-R matches when it is within 10% of the Table 1 value under at least one of the readings of the open details (p_thresh 96 to 99, hyperactive strategy (i) or (ii)), as the paper chose p_thresh per data set without reporting it. Every reading's value is shown. Reproduced when all 20 spines match; partially reproduced when 15 to 19 match; not reproduced otherwise. The lowess variant (frac 0.0002) and the code's default pair (97, (i)) are shown.

claims.statement: In the example recording of Figure 1(e), the best-R shows the largest increase over the next ordered R value among all units.
claims.source: Results, 3.1 Identifying the presynaptic unit of a dendritic target spine, last paragraph; Figure 1(e)
claims.quote: Moreover, the R value for the best-matching unit ( best-R ) shows the largest increase with respect to the next (ordered) R value among all units
claims.criterion: The paper does not say which recording is the example. For each spine, the R values of all units are sorted and the gap between best-R and the second R is compared with every other gap between consecutive sorted values. Reproduced when the first gap is the largest for at least one spine (the example is one of them); the number of spines for which it holds is reported. A claim about one unnamed example, so a weak test.

claims.statement: For each recording, simulated ground-truth connections of every unit give an F-score surface over the quantile pair (Q_test, Q_GT), whose maximum and optimal quantiles are those of Table 1 (max_F 0.485 to 0.870).
claims.source: Table 1, columns GT_Q, test_Q and max_F; Figure 4; Results, 3.3 Method validation and threshold optimization
claims.criterion: As in Results 3.3, Methods 2.8 and notebook 3 of the code. For every unit, 1'000 surrogates with the recording's noise and signal estimate (opening comment); for each surrogate the R with every unit's convolved trace over the kept frames; the test-Rs of unit i are the R of the surrogates of each surrogate's second-best unit with unit i's convolved trace (pooled over all 1'000 surrogates, imaging_tools.compute_test_r); the GT-Rs of unit i are the R of its own surrogates with its own trace. For each grid pair (100 values from 0 to 1, np.linspace rounded to 3 decimals, which gives the Table 1 quantiles), the threshold is the larger of the two quantiles; with unit i present, a surrogate whose best unit is i and whose best R passes is TP, else FN; with unit i removed, the best R of the other units passing is FP, else TN. F with beta 0.5, summed over all units. The Methods and the code disagree on a surrogate whose best unit is not i in the test with i present; the Methods count it FP if it passes and TN if not (main reading), the code counts it FN (variant). The noise estimate uses the background ROI of claim acceptance-9-of-20; for recording 3 (two spines) both spines' estimates are run. Each recording's max F matches when within 10% of Table 1; ties of the maximum are all reported, and Q_GT and Q_test match when one maximum lies within 10% of the Table 1 values. Reproduced when max F matches for at least 17 of the 19 recordings; partially for 10 to 16; not reproduced below. The quantiles are reported for each recording.

claims.statement: The simulated ground-truth test gives large F-scores across experiments, a mean maximum F-score of 0.692 ± 0.136 over 19 recordings with 1'000 surrogates per unit.
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We obtained typically large F -scores across experiments (mean = 0.692 ± 0.136 based on 19 recordings with a mean of 102 ± 43 units per recording and 1’000 generated surrogate spine Ca 2+ response traces per unit)
claims.criterion: Mean and population SD (ddof 0) over 19 recordings, recording 3 counted once; this is the reading that gives 0.692 ± 0.136 from Table 1 (20 rows give 0.697 ± 0.135). The ± is the sample spread, not an uncertainty of the mean, so the tolerance is 10% of each value. Under both readings of the classification of a misidentified surrogate (claim table1-optimal-thresholds).

claims.statement: The best-matching unit passed the acceptance test, and a monosynaptic connection was accepted, for 9 of the 20 spines (Table 1 rows 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 12 and 16).
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraph 1; Table 1, columns GT_thr, test_thr and accept?; Figure 5(a)
claims.quote: For 9 out of 20 spines, the best-matching unit passed the acceptance test, and a monosynaptic connection was confirmed
claims.criterion: The acceptance test of Results 3.2, Methods 2.7 and notebook 2, with 1'000 GT and 1'000 test surrogates (opening comment); accepted when best-R exceeds both thresholds. The quantiles are read two ways, (a) Table 1's GT_Q and test_Q for each spine, (b) the optimal quantiles found in claim table1-optimal-thresholds. The noise region is the background ROI held in the dataset, if it holds one; the paper says only that it was "close to the spine", so otherwise at least three background regions of at least the spine ROI's pixel count, without visible cell structure, are placed near the spine before any R is computed, and each is run. Each spine's GT_thr and test_thr are compared with Table 1 (10%). Reproduced when, under a reading, each spine's decision matches Table 1 (so 9 are accepted) for every noise region; partially reproduced when 17 to 19 decisions match; not reproduced otherwise. When noise regions or readings give different outcomes, the claim is methods_underspecified with every result shown. Rows 3, 6, 16 and 18 lie within 0.03 of a threshold in Table 1, so their decisions are also reported over five seeds.
