claims.statement: Accepted connections have larger best-R values than rejected ones (0.584 ± 0.149 against 0.331 ± 0.124; Mann-Whitney U = 12.0, n1 = 9, n2 = 11, P < 0.05).
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraph 2; Figure 5(b)
claims.quote: the accepted connections had significantly larger best-R values (0.584 ± 0.149) compared to the rejected ones (0.331 ± 0.124) (Mann-Whitney U =12.0, n 1 =9, n 2 =11, P <0.05)
claims.criterion: Over the spines as classified in claim acceptance-9-of-20 and their best-R from claim table1-best-r. Means and population SD (ddof 0), which give the reported ± from Table 1. The paper does not say whether the test is one- or two-sided; from Table 1, U = 12 is the smaller of the two U values and the two-sided p is 0.005, so both readings give P < 0.05 and both are shown. Reproduced when the means and U are within tolerance and the test gives P < 0.05 with the accepted group higher.

claims.statement: The best-R alone does not predict the outcome of the acceptance test; connections with R as high as about 0.6 were rejected, while an R of about 0.2 was enough for acceptance in another case.
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraph 2; Figure 5(b)
claims.quote: it is important to note that the value of the best-R alone was not a predictor for the outcome of the test. In fact, as one can see from figure 5(b) , the acceptance test rejected connections with R values as high as ~0.6, while in another case an R value of ~0.2 was enough for acceptance
claims.criterion: Settled by the expected values (Table 1 gives 0.602, row 17, and 0.217, row 3), with the further condition that the largest rejected best-R exceeds the smallest accepted one, so no best-R cut separates the two groups.

claims.statement: Connections were rejected in three scenarios, best-R below the test threshold only, below the GT threshold only, or below both, which shows the advantage of having two thresholds.
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraph 2; Figure 5(a)
claims.quote: we found that putative connections were rejected in three different scenarios ... The best-R was smaller than either one of the two thresholds or both thresholds
claims.criterion: The counts are not in the text; they are read from Table 1 (best_R against GT_thr and test_thr; rows 5, 8, 17, 18 below test only, row 13 below GT only, rows 7, 11, 14, 15, 19, 20 below both). Reproduced when each of the three scenarios occurs among the rejected spines of claim acceptance-9-of-20; the counts are reported against Table 1's, and a difference in count alone does not decide the outcome.

claims.statement: For some recordings the test threshold is larger than the GT threshold, and for others the reverse.
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraph 2; Figure 5(a)
claims.quote: Note that for some recordings the test threshold was larger than the GT threshold and vice versa for other recordings
claims.criterion: Over the 20 spines' thresholds from claim acceptance-9-of-20. Reproduced when at least one spine has test_thr above GT_thr and at least one the reverse. Table 1 has 15 and 5; the counts are reported.

claims.statement: Each recording's spike contrast (0.17 to 0.69) and ratio of spikes outside to inside network bursts (0.060 to 2.003) have the values given in Table 1.
claims.source: Table 1, columns OUT/IN ratio and spike contrast; Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraph 3
claims.criterion: Spike contrast from elephant 0.10.0 (Results 3.4), spike_contrast with its default parameters, over the recording's sorted spike trains. OUT/IN is the number of spikes outside network burst periods divided by the number inside, with the bursts of claim table1-best-r. The paper leaves open (a) which units enter, all sorted units or those kept after the hyperactive exclusion, (b) for OUT/IN, burst periods with or without the 0.1 s and 0.5 s extensions, and (c) the time span, the whole MEA recording or the span of simultaneous imaging. Every combination is run. A recording's value matches when within 10% of Table 1 under one combination; reproduced when both measures match for at least 17 of 19 recordings under one combination used for all; partially reproduced for 10 to 16; not reproduced below.

claims.statement: The network's spike contrast is negatively correlated with the maximum F-score of the recording (Spearman R = -0.737, P = 0.0002), so more synchronous networks give poorer classification.
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraph 3; Figure 5(c)
claims.quote: We found that both the spike contrast ( R =-0.737, P =0.0002, Spearman’s rank correlation, figure 5(c) ) ... of a network correlated with the classification performance as measured by the maximum F -score of the respective network
claims.criterion: Spearman rank correlation of spike contrast (claim table1-network-measures) with maximum F-score (claim table1-optimal-thresholds). The paper says it is per network, but Table 1 gives -0.737 (P = 0.00021) over its 20 rows, recording 3 counted twice, and -0.742 (P = 0.00027) over 19 recordings; both readings are run. Reproduced when R is within tolerance and P < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: The ratio of spikes outside to inside network bursts is positively correlated with the maximum F-score of the recording (Spearman R = 0.672, P = 0.0012).
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Performance evaluation on experimental data, paragraph 3; Figure 5(d) (the text cites figure 5(c) for both; the legend places this one in 5(d))
claims.quote: and the OUT/IN ratio ( R =0.672, P =0.0012, Spearman’s rank correlation, figure 5(c) ) of a network correlated with the classification performance as measured by the maximum F -score of the respective network
claims.criterion: As for claim fig5c-spike-contrast-vs-fscore, with the OUT/IN ratio. Table 1 gives 0.672 (P = 0.0012) over its 20 rows and 0.680 (P = 0.0014) over 19 recordings; both readings are run. Reproduced when R is within tolerance and P < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: The dandiset's recordings can be matched one to one to the recordings of Table S1, and the matched records agree on mouse, sex, mouse line and date.
claims.source: Table S1 (Supplemental Information)
claims.quote: Metadata for each afferent, including figure appearances.
claims.criterion: Records are matched by recording id, the NWB `identifier` without its "KS0" prefix (for example KS0240A to 240A); an identifier that ends in "_" is matched by its number alone when exactly one Table S1 recording has that number and mouse. Reproduced when all 60 files match a distinct Table S1 recording and at least 95% of matches agree on mouse id, sex, mouse line (ignoring spaces and case) and recording date; partially reproduced when at least 80% match and agree; otherwise not reproduced.

claims.statement: The initial dataset of 33 touch afferents comprises 54,647,500 video frames with simultaneous single-unit recordings, and the paper analyses 65,257,500 frames (2,175 min) in total.
claims.source: Results, Recording from Merkel and unidentified afferents during whisking and active touch, paragraph 3; STAR Methods, Quantification and Statistical Analysis
claims.quote: For our initial dataset (of 33 afferents), we obtained 54,647,500 frames of high-speed video with simultaneous single neuron recordings for analysis ... We report analysis of high-speed video comprising 65,257,500 frames (2,175 min) total
claims.criterion: Frames are trials times 2,500. The first value is summed over the 33 touch recordings of Table S1. For the total, the text allows these readings, in order (a) the 53 analysed afferents, (b) the 53 afferents and the 4 EMG sessions, (c) the 56 afferent recordings, (d) all 60 files. Reproduced when the first value and the total under one reading are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Identified Merkel afferents account for 823 minutes of the initial dataset and 846 minutes (25,365,000 frames) overall, against 999 minutes for unidentified afferents in the initial dataset.
claims.source: Results, Recording from Merkel and unidentified afferents during whisking and active touch, paragraph 3; STAR Methods, Quantification and Statistical Analysis
claims.quote: corresponding to 823 minutes total for identified Merkel afferents, and 999 minutes for unidentified afferents ... including 25,365,000 frames (846 min) from identified Merkel afferents
claims.criterion: Minutes are trials times 5 s, with Merkel identity from Table S1. "Overall" can be read as (a) the 17 analysed Merkel afferents or (b) all 20 identified Merkel afferents, including the 3 used only for Figure S1. Reproduced when all three values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when the first two are.

claims.statement: During non-whisking periods most afferents spiked at low rates (0.0 plus or minus 0.2 Hz, median and IQR, n = 33).
claims.source: Results, Recording from Merkel and unidentified afferents during whisking and active touch, paragraph 4; Figure 2C

claims.statement: All afferents responded with increased spike rates during whisker-pole contact (48.0 plus or minus 96.3 Hz, median and IQR, n = 33).
claims.source: Results, Recording from Merkel and unidentified afferents during whisking and active touch, paragraph 4; Figure 2C
claims.quote: All afferents responded with increased spike rates during touch (whisker-pole contact; 48.0 ± 96.3 Hz, median ± IQR, n = 33).
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the median is within tolerance and, by the Glossary rule, all 33 afferents are touch-sensitive (the 95% CI of the contact rate above and not overlapping the CIs of the non-whisking and the whisking-in-air rates). Partially reproduced when the median is within tolerance and at least 30 of 33 are touch-sensitive.

claims.statement: A subset of 13 of the 33 touch afferents (WT*) spiked especially strongly during whisking in air (19.1 plus or minus 58.2 Hz, median and IQR), and the other afferents divide into those sensitive to whisking and touch (WT) and to touch only (T).
claims.source: Results, Recording from Merkel and unidentified afferents during whisking and active touch, paragraph 4; Figure 2C; Glossary; Table S1
claims.quote: For a subset of WT afferents, spike rates during whisking in air were especially pronounced (Figure 2C, asterisks; 19.1 ± 58.2 Hz, median ± IQR; 13 of 33 afferents total
claims.criterion: Classes by the Glossary. Whisking-sensitive when the 95% CIs of the whisking-in-air and non-whisking rates do not overlap; WT when also touch-sensitive; WT* when WT, the whisking-in-air rate exceeds 1 Hz and at least 1,000 spikes were collected. The spike count can be read as (a) all spikes in the recording or (b) spikes during whisking in air. Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance and at least 30 of 33 afferents get the class (T, WT or WT*) Table S1 gives them; partially reproduced when the values are within tolerance but fewer classes agree.

claims.statement: Merkel and SA afferents responded to contact in a dramatically direction-selective manner, far more strongly to contacts in either the protraction or the retraction direction.
claims.source: Results, Active touch is encoded via sensitivity to moment and its rate of change, paragraph 1; Figure 3A, E, H, I
claims.quote: Merkel and SA afferents responded to contact by spiking in a slowly adapting and dramatically direction-selective manner, responding far more strongly to contacts in either the protraction or retraction direction
claims.criterion: Each contact (a run of contact frames) is protraction when its mean moment M0 is positive and retraction when negative (Figure 3F). For each Merkel or SA touch afferent (26, from Table S1), the mean contact rate in each direction, and the index (preferred minus non-preferred) over their sum. Reproduced when at least 80% of the 26 have an index of 0.5 or more (preferred rate at least three times the other); partially reproduced when at least half do. The RA afferents are shown for comparison and do not enter the criterion.

claims.statement: A full statistical model of ten mechanical and kinematic variables strongly predicted ongoing spike rate during touch (r = 0.71 plus or minus 0.16, mean and SD, n = 33).
claims.source: Results, Active touch is encoded via sensitivity to moment and its rate of change, paragraph 2; Figure 3D
claims.quote: A “full” model ... strongly predicted ongoing spike rate (r = 0.71 ± 0.16, mean ± SD, n = 33

claims.statement: Models fitted to moment or its rate of change alone explained spiking relatively poorly (r = 0.45 plus or minus 0.19 and 0.42 plus or minus 0.21).
claims.source: Results, Active touch is encoded via sensitivity to moment and its rate of change, paragraph 2; Figure 3D
claims.quote: Models fitted to moment or its rate of change alone explained spiking relatively poorly (r = 0.45 ± 0.19 and 0.42 ± 0.21, respectively; mean ± SD, n = 33

claims.statement: M0 and its rate of change together explained spiking (r = 0.63 plus or minus 0.20) better than any other pair of variables, and better than a model of M0, Fax and Flat (r = 0.48 plus or minus 0.19).
claims.source: Results, Active touch is encoded via sensitivity to moment and its rate of change, paragraph 2; Figure 3D; Figure S2C
claims.quote: However, M0 and ... together explained spiking (r = 0.63 ± 0.20, n = 33) better than any other pair of variables, and better than a more complex model fitted to M0, Fax, and Flat (r = 0.48 ± 0.19, n = 33
claims.criterion: All 45 pairs of the ten variables are fitted. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance, the M0 and M0 rate pair has the highest mean r of the 45 pairs, and it is above the M0, Fax and Flat model. Partially reproduced when the pair is among the three best pairs and above the M0, Fax and Flat model.

claims.statement: A simple viscoelastic model of moment and its rate of change predicted spike rates of Merkel and SA afferents during touch at levels comparable to the statistical model based on M0 and its rate of change (25 of 26 afferents fitted).
claims.source: Results, Active touch responses are predicted by a simple mechanical model, paragraph 2; Figure 4C; STAR Methods, Viscoelastic model
claims.quote: Remarkably, this mechanical model predicted spike rates at levels comparable to GAM statistical models (Figure 4C) ... In total, 25 of 26 (Merkel and unidentified SA) afferents were included
claims.criterion: The model of Eqs. M1 to M4 (q = 1,000, five fitted parameters, M0 scaled by the inverse of the 80th percentile of its absolute value), fitted by least squares between predicted rate and the spike rate smoothed by a Gaussian of sigma 4 ms on contact frames during whisking, for the 25 Merkel and SA touch afferents Table S1 marks as fitted. Performance is r as for the statistical models, on the same frames. Reproduced when the mean r of the viscoelastic model is at least the mean r of the M0 and M0 rate model minus 0.1; partially reproduced when it is at least that minus 0.2; otherwise not reproduced.

claims.statement: All 15 WT* afferents (13 touch WT* and 2 whisking-only) were dramatically modulated by whisk phase, with rates at non-preferred and preferred phases of 2.1 plus or minus 3.4 and 51.2 plus or minus 105.7 Hz (median and IQR).
claims.source: Results, Merkel and unidentified SA afferents encode whisk phase, paragraph 1; Figure 5A to C; Figure S3D
claims.quote: we found that all WT* afferents were also dramatically modulated by phase ... (Figure 5A–C; 2.1 ± 3.4 Hz vs 51.2 ± 105.7 Hz, respectively; median ± IQR; n = 15 total
claims.criterion: The 15 afferents are the touch afferents Table S1 marks WT* and the two whisking-only recordings (240A, 253A), as listed in Figure S3. Reproduced when both medians are within tolerance and every one of the 15 has a preferred-phase rate at least twice its non-preferred rate; partially reproduced when the medians are within tolerance and at least 12 of 15 do.

claims.statement: Across the population of WT* afferents, preferred phase spanned the whisk cycle.
claims.source: Results, Merkel and unidentified SA afferents encode whisk phase, paragraph 1; Figure 5D, E
claims.quote: Across the population of afferents, preferred phase spanned the whisk cycle (Figure 5D,E).
claims.criterion: Preferred phases of the 15 afferents of fig5-phase-modulation. Reproduced when they fall in at least three of the four quarter cycles of (-pi, pi] and a Rayleigh test does not find a single preferred direction (p > 0.05); partially reproduced when they fall in at least three quarters but the Rayleigh test is significant; otherwise not reproduced.

claims.statement: The preferred phase of each WT* afferent was largely invariant across whisk cycles of different amplitudes, frequencies and setpoints.
claims.source: Results, Merkel and unidentified SA afferents encode whisk phase, paragraph 1; Figure S3
claims.quote: Preferred phase of each afferent was largely invariant across whisk cycles of different amplitudes, frequencies and setpoints (Figure S3).
claims.criterion: For each of the 15 afferents and each of amplitude, frequency and setpoint, the whisking-in-air frames are split at the afferent's median of that variable, and a preferred phase is found in each half (30 equal-count bins). Reproduced when, for each of the three variables, the median over afferents of the absolute circular difference between the halves is below pi/4; partially reproduced when this holds for two of the three.

claims.statement: Statistical models fitted to whisker position, velocity, acceleration and jerk during whisking in air predicted phase tuning curves nearly perfectly (r = 0.97 plus or minus 0.04, n = 28), while single kinematic variables performed poorly.
claims.source: Results, Distribution of phase preferences mirrors tuning to inertial and muscle-specific stresses, paragraph 3; Figure S6A, B
claims.quote: While afferents typically showed poor sensitivity to single kinematic variables (position, velocity, acceleration or jerk ... combinations of three or more variables predicted phase tuning curves nearly perfectly ... r = 0.97 ± 0.04, mean ± SD, n = 28
claims.criterion: Models of the 15 combinations of the four variables fitted on whisking-in-air frames free of kinematic outliers. A predicted phase tuning curve is the mean predicted rate in each of 30 equal-count phase bins, compared by Pearson r with the observed curve. Tested on the 15 WT* afferents of fig5-phase-modulation, as the intact condition of the 13 progressive cutting recordings cannot be separated (see fig6-cut-eliminated). Reproduced when the full model's mean r is within tolerance and the mean r of each single-variable model is lower than that of the full model by at least 0.1; partially reproduced when only the first holds.

claims.statement: Preferred phases of all 28 WT* afferents spanned the whisk cycle, with a slight abundance in the retraction phase.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 6; Figure 7G
claims.quote: The distribution of preferred phases across our population of afferents spanned the whisk cycle, with a slight abundance during the retraction phase (Figure 7G).
claims.criterion: Needs the intact condition of the 13 progressive cutting recordings; see fig6-cut-eliminated.

claims.statement: Progressive whisker cutting eliminated spiking during whisking in air in 6 of 13 afferents (from 50.1 plus or minus 42.3 Hz intact to 0.9 plus or minus 0.7 Hz after the final cut, mean and SD).
claims.source: Results, Phase coding arises from external and internal stresses, paragraph 2; Figure 6B, E
claims.quote: Spiking during whisking in air was eliminated by this manipulation for a subset (6 of 13) of afferents (Figure 6B,E; from 50.1 ± 42.3 Hz for intact whisker, to 0.9 ± 0.7 Hz after final cut, mean ± SD
claims.criterion: Needs the cutting condition (intact, sham, cut 1 to 3) of each trial of the 13 progressive cutting recordings.

claims.statement: In 7 of 13 afferents self-motion responses remained after cutting (86.1 plus or minus 71.5 Hz intact against 70.3 plus or minus 58.5 Hz after the final cut).

claims.quote: Other afferents (7 of 13) showed self-motion responses that remained after cutting (Figure 6C–E; 86.1 ± 71.5 Hz for intact whisker vs 70.3 ± 58.5 Hz after final cut, mean ± SD, n = 7 SA)
claims.criterion: Needs the cutting condition of each trial; see fig6-cut-eliminated.

claims.statement: Cutting shortened the whisker to near its base (final length 0.37 plus or minus 0.43 mm, mean and SD, n = 13).
claims.source: Results, Phase coding arises from external and internal stresses, paragraph 2; Figure 6A
claims.quote: We repeated this process for up to three cuts, shortening the whisker eventually to near its base (Figure 6A; final length: 0.37 ± 0.43 mm, mean ± SD, n = 13)

claims.statement: After whisker trimming, phase tuning curves of the 7 afferents that kept spiking were correlated with intrinsic protractor or nasolabialis EMG (r = 0.66 plus or minus 0.27).

claims.quote: For those afferents that continued to spike after whisker trimming, the phase tuning curves were correlated with activation of either IP or NL muscles ... r = 0.66 ± 0.27, mean ± SD, n = 7 SA afferents

claims.statement: The spike rate lost after cutting was correlated with positive acceleration, negative acceleration or jerk (r = 0.71 plus or minus 0.19, n = 13).
claims.source: Results, Distribution of phase preferences mirrors tuning to inertial and muscle-specific stresses, paragraph 2; Figure 7E
claims.quote: These subtracted tuning curves were correlated with positive acceleration, negative acceleration or jerk (Figure 7E; r = 0.71 ± 0.19, mean ± SD, n = 13).

claims.statement: In 5 afferents recorded with the whisker already cut near its base, phase tuning was strongly correlated with intrinsic protractor or nasolabialis EMG (r = 0.76 plus or minus 0.06).
claims.source: Results, Distribution of phase preferences mirrors tuning to inertial and muscle-specific stresses, paragraph 2; Figure 7F
claims.quote: Phase tuning curves in these afferents were strongly correlated with EMG from either IP or NL muscles (Figure 7F; r = 0.76 ± 0.06, mean ± SD, n = 5).
claims.criterion: The best match is chosen between the intrinsic protractor and the nasolabialis phase curves, so the intrinsic protractor EMG is needed.

claims.statement: Motor unit activity of m. nasolabialis was phase modulated and correlated with negative whisker velocity (r = 0.93) and anti-correlated with positive velocity (r = -0.75) within whisk cycles.
claims.source: Figure S4F to H; Figure 7A
claims.quote: (H) Same as D, but for m. nasolabialis recording, showing high correlation with negative velocity within whisk cycles.
claims.criterion: The spike times of recording 11A (KSm11) are taken as the motor unit spikes, as Table S1 names it the extrinsic retractor recording. Phase curves are means over 30 equal-count phase bins of whisking frames (amplitude above 2.5 degrees); velocity is split into its positive part and the absolute value of its negative part. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the signs are as stated and the first is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Intrinsic protractor EMG was correlated with positive whisker velocity within whisk cycles (r = 0.94, 0.97 and 0.96 in three mice).
claims.source: Figure S4B to D; Figure 7A
claims.quote: Pearson correlation coefficients shown at right indicate that intrinsic protractor muscles and positive velocity were highly correlated within whisk cycles
claims.criterion: Needs the rectified EMG of recordings 7A, 8A and 9A.

claims.statement: The noise level of curvature estimates, curvature change during whisking in air as a percentage of that during contact, was 7.8 plus or minus 5.0% (mean and SD) across 33 sessions.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Video analysis, whisker baseline curvature; Figure S7
claims.quote: This quantifies how large curvature changes measured during whisking in air were as a percentage of those measured during contact ... Across 33 sessions, mean σk was 7.8 ± 5.0% (± SD
claims.criterion: Per touch recording, 100 times the mean absolute deltaKappa over frames with distance to the pole above 1 mm and amplitude above 2.5 degrees, divided by the mean over contact frames. Contact frames can be read as (a) contact = 1 and distance below 1 mm (the Glossary) or (b) contact = 1. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Identified Merkel afferents spiked at short latency (4.9 plus or minus 1.3 ms) and low jitter (SD of first-spike latency 0.91 plus or minus 0.29 ms) after brief light pulses.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Optogenetic identification; Figure S1C, D

claims.statement: Automatic contact classification agreed with manual curation for 99.5 plus or minus 0.2% of frames, with a false positive rate of 0.3 plus or minus 0.1%.

claims.quote: The overall rate of correct classification was 99.5 ± 0.2% (mean ± SD across 33 sessions) with a false positive rate of 0.3 ± 0.1%.

claims.statement: The dataset holds 15 mice, 115 sessions, 18,514 trials and 63,979,800 video frames, which is 88.9 hours of video.
claims.source: Methods, High-speed videography and whisker tracking, paragraph 2; Background & Summary, paragraph 5
claims.quote: The size of the dataset ... 15 mice, 88.9 hours, 115 sessions, 18,514 trials, 63,979,800 frames
claims.criterion: Mice are subject folders and sessions are NWB files. Tolerance 0 for the counts, as they are counts of deposited records, and 0.05 h for the hours, the rounding of the printed value. The paper does not define which trials and frames are counted. Readings for trials are (a) all rows of all trials tables, (b) rows with ignore_trial False. Readings for frames are (a) the frame counts of the raw video files, (b) the number of frames of the raw_whisker_position series (N_frames, Data Records), summed over sessions; hours are frames divided by 200 and by 3600 under each. Reproduced when mice and sessions match and trials and frames match exactly under one reading each; partially reproduced when mice and sessions match and trials and frames are within 10% under some reading; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Neural recordings from barrel cortex were made in 44 of the 115 sessions.
claims.source: Methods, Neural recordings during behavior, paragraph 1
claims.quote: For a subset (44/115) of the behavioral sessions that we report here, we also recorded neuronal activity in identified columns of the barrel cortex
claims.criterion: Count of NWB files whose name includes "ecephys" (Data Records, Directory structure) and, as a check, of files holding an "extracellular array recording" ElectricalSeries and a units table. Tolerance 0 because it is a count of deposited sessions. Reproduced when both counts are 44.

claims.statement: The dataset includes 33.8 hours of 64-channel neural recording at 30 kHz.
claims.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 5
claims.quote: includes 88.9 hours of behavioral video at 200 frames per second and 33.8 hours of 64-channel neural recording at 30 kHz
claims.criterion: The paper does not say which recording is timed. Readings are (a) the summed duration of the "extracellular array recording" timestamps in the NWB files (last minus first), (b) the summed duration of the main Open Ephys recordings under sourcedata/ (test recordings of a few seconds left out, Data Records, Raw data, neural acquisition files). Tolerance 0.05 h, the rounding of the printed value. Reproduced when one reading is within it; partially reproduced when one is within 10%. The channel count of the raw files (64) is checked; the NWB files exclude broken channels and may hold fewer.

claims.statement: In discrimination sessions convex shapes are rewarded on the right and concave on the left; in detection sessions either shape is rewarded on the right and catch trials with no shape on the left.
claims.source: Methods, Two behavioral tasks, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Shape discrimination mice were trained to lick right for convex shapes and left for concave shapes. Shape detection mice were trained to lick right for either shape (concave or convex) and to lick left on catch trials when no shape was presented at all
claims.criterion: From the trials table, rewarded_side against stimulus. A session is a detection session when any trial has stimulus "nothing" (Table 6, stimulus) or when its metadata names the task; otherwise discrimination, with the session metadata (experiment description) checked where it names the task. Reproduced when, over trials to analyse in every session, rewarded_side follows the rule of the session's task on every trial; partially reproduced when it does on at least 95% of trials in every session. All trials, including ignored ones, are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The stimulus "nothing" occurs only in the detection task.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, trials table, Table 6 (stimulus)
claims.quote: 'nothing' was only used in the detection task, not in the discrimination task
claims.criterion: Using the session metadata's task where it is given (experiment description or keywords), reproduced when no discrimination session holds a trial with stimulus "nothing". When the metadata do not name the task, the claim cannot be tested apart from task-rules (which uses "nothing" to assign the task) and is reported as such.

claims.statement: No mouse was trained on both tasks.
claims.source: Methods, Two behavioral tasks, paragraph 1
claims.quote: No mice were trained on both tasks
claims.criterion: Each session's task as assigned in task-rules. Reproduced when every mouse's sessions are all of one task.

claims.statement: The shape stops at one of three positions, close, medium or far.
claims.source: Methods, Two behavioral tasks, paragraph 2; Table 6 (servo_position)
claims.quote: The shape stopped at one of three different positions (close, medium, or far)
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the servo_position values over all trials with a shape (stimulus not "nothing") are exactly the set close, medium, far; not reproduced otherwise. The paper does not say that every session used all three, so the positions present in each session are reported and do not enter the outcome.

claims.statement: The response window opens 2 s after the servo motor starts moving the shape, which reaches its final position 0.8 to 0.4 s before the window opens, depending on the position.
claims.source: Methods, Two behavioral tasks, paragraph 3
claims.quote: which began exactly 2 seconds after the linear servo motor started moving the shape toward the mouse ... reached its final position between −0.8 s and −0.4 s, depending on whether the final position was close, medium, or far
claims.criterion: Testable only if the dataset records the time the motor starts or stops. The trial start_time is the synchronization pulse (Methods, Alignment of multiple data streams), which the paper does not place relative to motor onset, so it is not used as motor onset. When motor times exist, reproduced when the window opens 2 s (within one frame, 5 ms) after motor onset on at least 95% of trials and the motor stops between 0.8 and 0.4 s before it. The paper does not say which position arrives first, so the stop time per position is reported and its order is not judged. Otherwise blocked; the distribution of response_window_open_time minus start_time is reported for information.

claims.statement: The choice time is the first lick after the response window opens, and on spoiled trials with no lick it is set 45 s after the window opens.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, trials table, Table 6 (choice_time)
claims.quote: choice_time (float) The time of the choice lick, which is the first lick after the response window opened. On spoiled trials with no lick, this value is 45 seconds after the response window opened
claims.criterion: Lick times from the left, right and (where present) both lick series. For each non-spoiled trial, the first lick at or after response_window_open_time, compared with choice_time; its side compared with choice. For spoiled trials, choice_time minus response_window_open_time compared with 45 s. Licks and trial times are both aligned trial by trial, so a match within 5 ms (one frame, Methods, Alignment) counts. Reproduced when all of these hold on at least 99% of trials of each kind; partially reproduced at 95%. All trials are used, as the definition does not depend on ignore_trial.

claims.statement: The first lick in the response window decides the outcome; a choice on the rewarded side is correct, any other choice is an error, and a trial with no choice is spoiled.
claims.source: Methods, Two behavioral tasks, paragraph 4; Table 6 (outcome, choice)
claims.quote: Only the first lick (left or right) during the response window determined the trial outcome (correct or incorrect)
claims.criterion: From the trials table. Reproduced when on every trial outcome is "correct" exactly when choice equals rewarded_side, "error" when choice is the other side, and "spoil" exactly when choice is "nogo" (Table 6, choice); direct-delivery trials are shown apart, as their water does not depend on the choice. Partially reproduced when this holds on at least 99% of trials.

claims.statement: Correct licks were rewarded with water, and incorrect licks were punished with a timeout, typically 9 s long.
claims.source: Methods, Two behavioral tasks, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Correct licks were rewarded with water and incorrect licks were punished with a timeout, typically 9 seconds long
claims.criterion: Over trials to analyse. Reward is a reward time on the rewarded side between choice_time and stop_time; reproduced for this part when it occurs on every correct trial and on no error trial (partially when on at least 95% and at most 5%). The paper does not say how the timeout appears in the trial times. Readings are (a) the median over error trials of stop_time minus choice_time, (b) that median on error trials minus the same median on correct trials. The timeout part holds when the reading is within 0.9 s of 9 s. The claim is reproduced when the reward part holds and both readings hold, not reproduced when neither does, and blocked as methods_underspecified when they disagree, with both shown.

claims.statement: Every session began with 45 trials of Forced Alternation, which are non-random trials, before random trials.
claims.source: Methods, Session control and trial types to be dropped from analysis, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Even in fully trained mice, we found it best to begin every session with 45 trials of Forced Alternation, before switching to random trials
claims.criterion: By the trial field (trial number), since trials before the video began are left out of the table (Data Records, trials table). Reproduced when, in every session, every present trial numbered 0 to 44 has stim_is_random False; partially reproduced when that holds in more than half the sessions. The number of the first random trial in each session is reported.

claims.statement: A trial is marked ignore_trial when it is direct delivery, non-random, spoiled, optogenetic or otherwise munged.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, trials table, Table 6 (ignore_trial)
claims.quote: ignore_trial (bool) This is True if 'direct_delivery' is True, or 'stim_is_random' is False, or outcome is 'spoil', or 'optogenetic' is True, or the trial was otherwise munged
claims.criterion: Munged trials carry no flag of their own, so only one direction is tested. Reproduced when every trial with direct_delivery True, stim_is_random False, outcome "spoil" or optogenetic True has ignore_trial True. The number of trials with ignore_trial True and none of the four flags (the munged trials) is reported.

claims.statement: Each trial's stop time equals the next trial's start time, and the table's index is the trial number.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, trials table, Table 6 and the paragraph after it
claims.quote: stop_time (float) Stop time of the trial. (Equal to the start time of the next trial.) ... The index of this DataFrame is called "id" and is identical to the field "trial"
claims.criterion: Within each session, for consecutive rows, stop_time compared with the next start_time, and id with trial. Reproduced when both are equal (times within 1 ms) for every row; the last trial of a session is not compared.

claims.statement: Times in the NWB file are in a common video timebase in which frame F falls at exactly F/200 s.
claims.source: Methods, Alignment of multiple data streams, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Since the camera ran at 200 frames per second, frame F in the video is defined as occurring at exactly time F/200 in the common video timebase
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the timestamps of every processed whisker series and every pose series are integer multiples of 0.005 s (within 1e-6 s) and their spacing is 0.005 s except at gaps. Contact start and stop times are also checked against the 0.005 s grid.

claims.statement: Processed whisker timestamps have gaps, for instance during the 133 ms blackout at each trial start, because gaps longer than 4 frames (20 ms) were not interpolated.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, processing group processed_whisker_position, last paragraph
claims.quote: these timestamps will in general contain gaps, for instance during the 133 ms blackout synchronization pulse at the start of each trial. This is because we did not interpolate over gaps longer than 4 frames (20 ms)
claims.criterion: Two parts, per whisker and session. (1) Runs of consecutive frames with interpolated True are at most 4 frames long. (2) For each trial, the longest gap in the angle timestamps that begins within 0.2 s of start_time (missing time, gap minus one frame) is within 10% of 133 ms. The paper says "in general", so (2) is read as holding on more than half of trials for C1, C2 and C3. Reproduced when (1) holds everywhere and (2) holds; partially reproduced when one of them holds. C0 is reported apart, as it may be missing for long stretches.

claims.statement: Whisker bend is null on interpolated frames.
claims.source: Data Records, processed_whisker_position, Table 3 (bend)
claims.quote: This is null on interpolated frames
claims.criterion: Reproduced when, for every whisker and session, bend is NaN (or missing) on every frame with interpolated True. Bend values on non-interpolated frames that are NaN are counted and reported.

claims.statement: The neural data timestamps are regularly spaced in the common video timebase, at a rate near but not exactly 30 kHz.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, acquisition group extracellular array recording, last paragraph
claims.quote: The sampling rate is nearly 30 kHz, but not exactly, because it has been converted to the common video timebase used throughout the NWB file
claims.criterion: Per ecephys session, the rate is (number of samples minus one) over the span of the timestamps, and regular spacing is the spread of successive differences. Reproduced when every session's spacing is constant to within 1e-9 s (a linear map, Methods, continuous alignment), its rate differs from 30000 Hz by less than 1%, and it is not exactly 30000 Hz in at least one session.

claims.statement: The neural and video timebases are related by a linear fit whose residuals at the trial synchronization pulses are never more than one frame (5 ms).
claims.source: Technical Validation, Alignment data
claims.quote: In contrast the neural and video timebase were synchronized very well by a linear fit. Residuals were never more than a single frame (5 ms)
claims.criterion: Needs the pulse times in both streams, the neural from the analog input of the raw Open Ephys files under sourcedata/ (the sample at which it goes low), the video from the frame on which the raw video goes dark (Methods, Alignment). The paper gives no threshold for either detection. The input is read as low below half its range, and a frame as dark when its mean brightness is below half the session median; these are standard choices, not the paper's, and cannot change the outcome, as the paper says the video goes completely black and the input is a digital line. Detections are matched to trials by the intervals between trial starts (Methods, Alignment). A line is fit from neural to video pulse times per session. Reproduced when the largest absolute residual is at most 5 ms in every session; partially reproduced in more than 90% of sessions. When the raw files cannot give pulse times, blocked.

claims.statement: The behavioral (Arduino) timebase fit the other two timebases poorly, with residuals that varied slowly but predictably over the session, so behavioral events were aligned trial by trial.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Alignment data
claims.quote: We observed that the behavioral timebase was a poor fit to the other two timebases and that its residuals varied slowly but predictably over the session
claims.criterion: Needs trial start times in the behavioral (Arduino) timebase, which the Data Records do not list among the raw deposits (only video and Open Ephys files). If the dataset holds them, a line is fit from behavioral to video trial starts per session; reproduced when the largest residual exceeds one frame (5 ms), the bound the neural fit meets, in more than half the sessions. The paper gives no measure of "slowly but predictably"; the residuals are plotted against trial for every session and that part does not enter the outcome. Otherwise blocked.

claims.statement: Every unit in the dataset passed the objective quality criteria, among them at most 5% of inter-spike intervals below 3 ms and at most 20% of the recording below 5% of the mean firing rate.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Spike sorting
claims.quote: single units had to pass all of the following objective criteria ... ≤5% of the inter-spike intervals less than 3 ms; ≤1.5% change per minute in spike amplitude; ≤20% of the recording at <5% of the mean firing rate
claims.criterion: From the units table, as the NWB file holds only well-sorted single units (Data Records, Raw data, neural acquisition files). ISI part, the fraction of a unit's inter-spike intervals below 3 ms; holds when it is at most 5% for every unit. Firing-rate part, the fraction of time bins within obs_intervals whose rate is below 5% of the unit's mean rate; the paper gives no bin. Readings are (a) 60 s bins, the time unit of the amplitude criterion beside it, (b) one bin per trial (start_time to stop_time). It holds when the fraction is at most 20% for every unit. Reproduced when both parts hold under the readings run; not reproduced when the ISI part fails or the firing-rate part fails under both readings; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings of the firing-rate part disagree. The amplitude criteria need Kilosort amplitudes in microvolts and the detection threshold, which the paper does not give; they are reported where sourcedata/ allows and do not enter the outcome.

claims.statement: Each unit's depth is the depth of the electrode its neuron_channel indexes, and its layer is assigned from that depth.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, units table, Table 5
claims.quote: This is calculated by taking the depth of the electrode in the electrodes table which is indexed by the field "neuron_channel" for this unit ... This specifies the laminar location of the unit, based on its depth
claims.criterion: Per ecephys session. (1) A unit's depth equals the y of the electrodes row at index neuron_channel. (2) Layers are assigned by fixed boundaries (the paper uses ref. 26 and does not print them), so over all units of all sessions the depth ranges of the layers do not overlap and run from superficial to deep in the order L1, L2/3, L4, L5, L6 (whichever occur). Reproduced when both hold for every unit.

claims.statement: The NWB electrodes are ordered from superficial to deep, broken channels are excluded, the raw data columns follow the electrodes table, and the sites are 20 um apart over 1280 um.
claims.source: Methods, Ordering of neural data channels; Methods, Neural recordings during behavior, paragraph 4; Data Records, electrodes table
claims.quote: we ordered the channels in the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) file in order of the anatomical location of the corresponding recording site, from superficial to deepest. We excluded broken channels from the NWB file
claims.criterion: Per ecephys session. Reproduced when electrodes y increases strictly down the table, successive differences are multiples of 20 um (a larger step marks a broken channel), the number of rows is at most 64 and equals the number of data columns of the extracellular array recording, and the span of a full 64-site probe would be 63 steps of 20 um (1260 um between end site centres, which the paper's 1280 um, 64 x 20 um, includes). The location string of each electrode is checked to hold the five items Data Records lists.

claims.statement: Each recording session names the barrel column the probe was in, sampling typically C1, C2 and C3.
claims.source: Data Records, electrodes table, Table 4 (electrode_group); Methods, Neural recordings during behavior, paragraphs 2 and 3
claims.quote: Its "location" field specifies the barrel-related cortical column in which the recording device was inserted during this session
claims.criterion: Reproduced when every ecephys session's electrode group location names a barrel column (a row letter and arc number, or a straddler). The count of sessions per column is reported; the paper gives only a goal of sampling C1, C2 and C3 equally often, which is not judged.

claims.statement: Each unit has one observation interval, the start and stop of the neural recording, with its spike times in the common video timebase.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, units table, Table 5 (obs_intervals, spike_times)
claims.quote: In this dataset, there is only one contiguous chunk of data included per session, so the length of this list is one
claims.criterion: Reproduced when every unit has exactly one interval, all its spikes fall inside it, and the interval's start and stop equal the first and last raw neural timestamps of the session (within one sample), as Table 5 says it gives the start and stop of the neural recording; partially reproduced when the interval lies within that span but does not match its ends.

claims.statement: Each session holds pose tracking of four whiskers with eight markers each, whose pixel to millimetre conversion is the same for all markers within a session.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, processing group raw_whisker_position
claims.quote: It comprises four data interfaces, each of which is an ndx_pose.pose.PoseEstimation containing pose tracking data for one of the four whiskers that we tracked. In turn, each PoseEstimation comprises eight PoseEstimationSeries ... which is the same for all markers within a session but can vary across sessions
claims.criterion: Reproduced when every session has four PoseEstimation objects (C0 to C3) of eight series each, each series of shape (N_frames, 2), and one conversion value per session. Whether the conversion varies across sessions is reported.

claims.statement: The straddler whisker C0 rarely made contact with the shapes in most mice.
claims.source: Methods, Two behavioral tasks, paragraph 5
claims.quote: but this whisker rarely made contact with the shapes in most mice
claims.criterion: Per mouse, contact counts of each whisker over its sessions' trials to analyse. The paper gives no threshold for "rarely"; it is read as C0 making fewer contacts than each of C1, C2 and C3. Reproduced when this holds in more than half the mice. Each mouse's fraction of contacts made by C0 is reported.

claims.statement: Sessions with fewer than 90 trials to analyse were excluded.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Inclusion criteria
claims.quote: We also excluded sessions with fewer than 90 trials to analyze
claims.criterion: Readings for "trials to analyse" are (a) trials with ignore_trial False, (b) trials with stim_is_random True and outcome not spoil (the "random trials" of Methods, Session control). Reproduced when every session has at least 90 under both readings; not reproduced when a session has fewer under both; blocked as methods_underspecified when they disagree. The smallest count is reported.

claims.statement: Each included session has every whisker labeled in at least 95% of frames, and at most 2% of its contact events contain a frame with a missing label.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Inclusion criteria
claims.quote: we required that every whisker be labeled in ≥95% of the frames, that ≤2% of the contact events contained even a single frame with a missing label
claims.criterion: A frame is labeled for a whisker when it was not interpolated. The paper does not give the denominator or whether C0 counts. Readings for the frame fraction are (a) frames with interpolated False over the frames of the processed series, (b) frames with all eight markers in the raw pose series over the frames of the video. For contacts, a contact of a whisker has a missing label when any frame from start_time to stop_time is interpolated or absent from that whisker's processed series. Whiskers are (i) C0 to C3, (ii) C1 to C3, C0 "rarely made contact" and may not have been held to this. Reproduced when both thresholds hold in every session under every reading of each; not reproduced when they fail under all; blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise.

claims.statement: Contacts are stored per whisker as time intervals with start, stop, location in the frame and whisker angle.
claims.source: Data Records, NWB file, processing group identified_whisker_contacts
claims.quote: We have also added optional fields containing the location of each contact, expressed both as a Cartesian location within the frame and also as the angle of the whisker at the time of the contact
claims.criterion: Reproduced when every session has a contacts table for each tracked whisker that made contacts, with start_time not after stop_time on every row, a location (x and y) and an angle column.

claims.statement: Each NWB file holds the groups Table 1 lists, acquisition (neural recording and behavioral video), electrodes, processing, trials and units, with licks, rewards, raw and processed whisker position and whisker contacts under processing.
claims.source: Data Records, Annotated data in the NWB file, Table 1 and the sections after it
claims.quote: processing A group containing a ProcessingModule named "behavior". This includes processed data about behavioral events, whisker position, and whisker contacts
claims.criterion: The text names the processing data in two ways, as separate groups ("behavioral_events", "raw_whisker_position", "processed_whisker_position", "identified_whisker_contacts", each holding interfaces such as "whisker_C2") and, in Table 1, as one module "behavior". The paper's UsageNotes.ipynb (commit 33d610b) reads processing['behavior']['processed_position_whisker_C2'] and processing['behavior']['contacts_by_whisker_C2']. Reproduced when every file holds the contents of each section (licks left and right, rewards left and right, pose per whisker, angle, base, tip, bend and interpolated per whisker, contacts per whisker, the Table 6 columns of trials) under either naming, which is reported; ecephys files also the extracellular array recording, electrodes (Table 4) and units (Table 5 columns). Partially reproduced when a section's data are present under other names. The acquisition "behavioral video" holds a relative path to an existing video file.

claims.statement: The dataset has one folder per mouse with one NWB file per session, named sub-<mouse>_ses-<session>_behavior+image.nwb with "ecephys" added when neural data are present, the video of each session in a folder of the same name, and raw neural data under sourcedata.
claims.source: Data Records, Directory structure of the entire dataset
claims.quote: At the top level, there is one folder per subject ... Video files are stored in a directory with the same name as the corresponding NWB file. Finally, we also provide the raw neural data files in a directory called "sourcedata"
claims.criterion: From the dataset's file list. Reproduced when every NWB file is in its subject's folder and named as described, every session has a video in a folder named as its NWB file, and sourcedata/ holds Open Ephys files and Kilosort/Phy outputs for the ecephys sessions under sub-<mouse> folders; partially reproduced when one part fails for some sessions.

claims.statement: The raw videos are mkv files whose frame rate is set to 30 frames/s though the true rate is 200 frames/s, and most sessions are 640 x 550 pixels.
claims.source: Data Records, Raw data, video files; Methods, High-speed videography and whisker tracking, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Importantly, the frame rate of this video file is spuriously set to 30 frames per second, even though the true frame rate is 200 frames per second
claims.criterion: From the video file headers. Reproduced when every video is mkv (x264) with a nominal rate of 30 frames/s, and more than half the sessions are 640 x 550 (in either axis order); the frame count over 200 is compared with the span of the session's whisker timestamps and reported.

claims.statement: The mice were C57BL/6J, males and females in roughly equal proportion, and began training between postnatal days 90 and 180.
claims.source: Methods, Two behavioral tasks, paragraph 7
claims.quote: We purchased breeder mice from the C57BL/6 J strain ... Mice began behavioral training between postnatal days 90 and 180 ... We used males and females arbitrarily and in roughly equal proportion
claims.criterion: From subject metadata (sex, strain, date of birth) and session start times. Strain holds when every subject is C57BL/6J (any spelling). Age holds when every mouse's first session is at 90 days or older, as sessions came after training (the training start itself is not recorded). The paper sets no threshold for "roughly equal"; readings are (a) a two-sided binomial test of the sex counts against one half does not reject at p 0.05, (b) the minority sex is at least one third of the mice. Reproduced when strain, age and both sex readings hold; blocked as methods_underspecified when the two sex readings disagree; not reproduced otherwise. The counts are reported.

claims.statement: The mean distance between true and predicted marker labels is 2.8 pixels.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Validation of pose tracking data, paragraph 1
claims.quote: The simplest metric of tracking accuracy is the mean distance between the true label and the predicted label, which is 2.8 pixels in our case
claims.criterion: Needs the human-curated labels and the held-out predictions of the network (Technical Validation, doubly held-out cross validation), which the Data Records do not list among the deposits. The paper does not say over which curated datasets the mean is taken; readings are (a) curated dataset 1, (b) all five pooled. Reproduced when a reading is within tolerance; blocked when the labels are not in the dataset.

claims.statement: On curated dataset 1, 7433 randomly chosen typical frames, each type of tracking error (poorly traced, incorrectly classified, false positive, false negative) is below 0.2%.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Validation of pose tracking data, paragraphs 3 and 4; Fig. 2c
claims.quote: each type of error is nearly zero (<0.2%) on dataset 1, which is the only dataset representative of typical frames
claims.criterion: Error types as Technical Validation defines them (poorly traced, a tip or mean marker distance above 20 pixels; incorrectly classified; false positive; false negative), per whisker, on held-out predictions from the three-fold doubly held-out cross validation. Needs curated dataset 1 and the predictions, not among the listed deposits. Reproduced when all four rates are below 0.2%; blocked when the data are absent.

claims.statement: Error rates rise with each later set of challenge frames (curated datasets 2 to 5), and the most common error is the false negative.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Validation of pose tracking data, paragraph 4; Fig. 2c
claims.quote: Paradoxically, error rates increase with each subsequent set of challenge frames ... The most common type of error is the false negative
claims.criterion: As in tracking-error-dataset1, on curated datasets 1 to 5. The paper does not say whether "error rates" means each type or their total; readings are (a) the total of the four types, (b) each type. Reproduced when the rate rises from each set to the next and the false negative is the largest type in each set, under both readings; blocked as methods_underspecified when they disagree; blocked when the data are absent.

claims.statement: In the original study, shape discrimination mice compared the prevalence of contacts across whiskers, a computation enabled by tuning changes in barrel cortex, while shape detection mice responded to the total number of contacts across all whiskers and barrel cortex neurons kept their expected tuning.
claims.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 4 (findings of ref. 8)
claims.quote: We found that shape discrimination mice compared the prevalence of contacts across whiskers, a comparison computation enabled by tuning changes in the barrel cortex. In contrast, shape detection mice simply responded to the total number of contacts across all whiskers, and in that case barrel cortex neurons maintained their expected tuning
claims.criterion: A finding of ref. 8 (Rodgers et al. 2021, Neuron 109, 2308), restated here without any method; this paper gives no model, selection or test for it. Blocked as methods_underspecified under this claims file; a test needs the methods of ref. 8.

claims.statement: In earlier work on these data, barrel cortex represented sensory and motor variables in approximately orthogonal subspaces.
claims.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 4 (finding of ref. 10)
claims.quote: We have also reported that barrel cortex represents sensory and motor variables in approximately orthogonal subspaces, which could be useful for generalization to novel conditions
claims.criterion: A finding of ref. 10, restated here without any method; this paper gives no variables, model or measure of orthogonality for it. Blocked as methods_underspecified under this claims file; a test needs the methods of ref. 10.

claims.statement: Silicon probe recordings gave 1537 single units and 303 multi-units from 57 recording sessions.
claims.source: Results, "Sequence tiling of single-unit responses", paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 4a-d
claims.quote: We used silicon probes to record from multiple brain regions from both hemispheres (Fig. 2d) during the task, obtaining 1537 single-units and 303 multi-units (Methods; Extended Data Fig. 4a-e) from 57 recording sessions.
claims.criterion: Sessions are the 57 files described as ephys ALM, M1TJ, S1TJ, S1BF, M1B, S1L or ZZ. Units are classified by the two criteria of the Methods (a unit is multi when its ISI violation rate exceeds 1% or its contamination exceeds 15%). Reproduced when the session count is 57 and both unit counts are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the session count and the total (1840, 10%) match but the split does not; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The population analyses of Figure 3 use 8 S1TJ, 9 M1TJ, 13 ALM and 5 S1BF sessions.
claims.source: Figure 3b legend
claims.quote: S1TJ, n = 8 sessions; M1TJ, n = 9 sessions; ALM, n = 13 sessions; S1BF, n = 5 sessions for all Fig. 3 panels unless otherwise noted.
claims.criterion: Counted from the session descriptions; each file must also hold a units table and standard sequences in both directions. Exact counts are required, as they are counts of files.

claims.statement: Regressions used the simultaneously recorded units of each session, 32 plus or minus 13 units (mean and SD).
claims.source: Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 2
claims.quote: a weighted sum of instantaneous spike rates from simultaneously recorded units (32 ± 13 units; mean ± SD) plus the constant best predicted the value of a behavioral variable.
claims.criterion: Readings, (a) all units of the 35 Figure 3 sessions, (b) all units of the 57 recording sessions. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under a reading; partially when only the mean is.

claims.statement: Figure 3a averages 2684 trials of standard and backtracking sequences.
claims.source: Figure 3a legend
claims.quote: Time series of the behavioral variables (mean ± 99% bootstrap confidence interval; n = 2684 trials) for different sequence types.
claims.criterion: The number of trials chosen by the trial selection of the Methods (initiation time under 1 s, then the third most similar, at least 10, around the middle touch from -1 to 1 s) for each session, direction and trial type (standard, and backtracking where present) over the 35 sessions. Readings, (a) standard and backtracking trials, (b) standard trials only.

claims.statement: Tongue length L is decoded from population activity best in S1TJ and M1TJ and poorly in ALM and S1BF (R2 0.56, 0.42, 0.11 and 0.04).
claims.source: Figure 3b,c; Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 3
claims.quote: Overall, S1TJ and M1TJ had stronger coding of L and L' compared with ALM and the control region S1BF (Fig. 3b,c).
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the across-session SDs the figure prints. The order holds when the lower of the S1TJ and M1TJ means exceeds the higher of the ALM and S1BF means. Reproduced when the order holds and all four means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when only one of the two holds; not reproduced when neither does.

claims.statement: Tongue velocity L' is decoded best in S1TJ and M1TJ and poorly in ALM and S1BF (R2 0.35, 0.32, 0.07 and 0.01).
claims.source: Figure 3b,c; Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 3
claims.quote: Overall, S1TJ and M1TJ had stronger coding of L and L' compared with ALM and the control region S1BF (Fig. 3b,c).
claims.criterion: As for fig3c-length. L' is the time derivative of L, taken only where the tongue is out.

claims.statement: Tongue angle theta is encoded comparably in S1TJ, M1TJ and ALM, but not in S1BF (R2 0.59, 0.57, 0.54 and 0.12).
claims.source: Figure 3b,c; Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 3
claims.quote: S1TJ, M1TJ, and ALM, but not S1BF, all showed comparable encoding of θ (Fig. 3b,c).
claims.criterion: The pattern holds when the S1BF mean is below each of the other three and the three differ by less than 0.1 from each other (largest minus smallest). Reproduced when the pattern holds and all four means are within tolerance; partially when only one holds; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Sequence identity I is encoded most strongly in ALM, then progressively less in M1TJ, S1TJ and S1BF (R2 0.67, 0.42, 0.23 and 0.14).
claims.source: Figure 3b,c; Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 4
claims.quote: In ALM we found the strongest encoding of both I and τ (Fig. 3b,c). Encoding of I and τ became progressively weaker in M1TJ, S1TJ, and S1BF, respectively.
claims.criterion: The order holds when the means satisfy ALM > M1TJ > S1TJ > S1BF. Reproduced when the order holds and all four means are within tolerance; partially when only one holds; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Relative sequence time tau is encoded most strongly in ALM, then progressively less in M1TJ, S1TJ and S1BF (R2 0.60, 0.45, 0.17 and 0.08).
claims.source: Figure 3b,c; Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 4
claims.quote: In ALM we found the strongest encoding of both I and τ (Fig. 3b,c). Encoding of I and τ became progressively weaker in M1TJ, S1TJ, and S1BF, respectively.
claims.criterion: As for fig3c-identity. tau is the time from the middle touch.

claims.statement: Any pair of the five behavioural variables (L, L', theta, I, tau) is uncorrelated.
claims.source: Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 5b
claims.quote: Conveniently, any pair of these variables is uncorrelated (Extended Data Fig. 5b).
claims.criterion: Over the samples of the regression (selected standard trials, -0.5 to 0.5 s from the middle touch), the absolute Pearson correlation of each pair, averaged over the 35 sessions. The paper gives no threshold; reproduced when every pair is below 0.3 (a common bound for a weak correlation), partially when all but one pair are, not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Across regions, the summed variance explained by the five coding axes reached about half that of the top five principal components.
claims.source: Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 7; Extended Data Fig. 5e
claims.quote: Across regions, the sum of variance explained (VE) by the five coding axes reached about half that of the top five PCs (Methods; Extended Data Fig. 5e).
claims.criterion: The coding axes are the unit vectors of the elastic net weights; their VE is the variance of the projected normalised rates over the total variance, on -0.5 to 0.8 s around the middle touch of the selected standard trials. An axis with all weights zero has VE 0.

claims.statement: The five coding axes were largely orthogonal to each other.
claims.source: Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 7; Extended Data Fig. 5f
claims.quote: The five coding axes were largely orthogonal with each other (Extended Data Fig. 5f)
claims.criterion: The absolute cosine of each pair of coding axes, averaged over sessions where both are non-zero. Reproduced when every pair is below 0.3, partially when all but one or two are, not reproduced otherwise. The mean absolute cosine of random directions in the same sessions is shown as a reference.

claims.statement: After canonical correlation, ALM trajectories in the top three PCs correlate best with the theta, I, tau coding subspace (group 2), more than with L, L', theta (group 1) or all five variables with five PCs (group 3); in S1TJ and M1TJ the correlation is high only when the coding subspace includes L and L'.
claims.source: Figure 3d,e; Results, "Hierarchical population coding", paragraph 6
claims.quote: trajectories of the ALM population in the subspace of the top three PCs aligned (Fig. 3d) and correlated (Fig. 3e; group 2 in ALM) well with the trajectories in the subspace encoding θ, I, and τ ... M1TJ and S1TJ also showed a strong correlation but only when the coding subspaces included L and L'
claims.criterion: For each session, trial averages per direction of the decoded variables and of the PC projections on -0.5 to 0.8 s from the middle touch are concatenated; the mean canonical correlation is computed for group 1 (L, L', theta with PC1-3), group 2 (theta, I, tau with PC1-3) and group 3 (all five with PC1-5). Paired two-tailed permutation tests (sign flips over sessions) at p < 0.05 for five comparisons, the ones the figure marks; ALM 2 > 1 and 2 > 3; S1TJ 1 > 2 and 3 > 2; M1TJ 3 > 2. Reproduced when all five hold, partially for three or four, not reproduced for fewer.

claims.statement: ALM and M1TJ activity predicts whether the port backtracked from the initial missed lick on; S1TJ shows only an insignificant trend and S1BF no prediction.
claims.source: Figure 3f; Results, "Sequence branching signals in ALM, M1TJ", paragraph 2
claims.quote: ALM and M1TJ activity started to predict the presence or absence of backtracking during the initial missed lick (Fig. 3f). ... S1TJ populations showed only a statistically insignificant trend toward being able to distinguish backtracking from standard sequences ... As expected, S1BF populations showed no prediction.
claims.criterion: Sessions with backtracking in both directions. Standard and backtracking trials are selected as for Figure 3, and the two directions are balanced within each class by random subsampling. For each 15 ms bin from -0.15 to 0.4 s after the backtracking trigger (the middle touch), a linear SVM on the first 12 PCs of the normalised rates, 10-fold CV, balanced classes; the null is 20 label shuffles per session. A region decodes when its mean accuracy over sessions in 0.2 to 0.4 s exceeds the 95th percentile of the same mean over shuffles. Reproduced when ALM and M1TJ decode and S1TJ and S1BF do not; partially when ALM and M1TJ decode and S1TJ or S1BF also does, or when only one of ALM and M1TJ decodes; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: In the zigzag task, ALM population activity predicts the sequence identity (context) during subsequences with the same licking movements, across 6 sessions from 3 mice.
claims.source: Figure 4f,g; Results, "Context-dependent coding of subsequences", paragraph 2
claims.quote: Using population activity as a predictor, linear SVM classifiers (Methods) were able to predict the sequence identity, or context, in the example session (Fig. 4f) and across sessions and mice (Fig. 4g).
claims.criterion: The 6 files described as ephys ZZ. Trials with perfect execution (13 touches and no lick without a touch between the first and last touch). The four matched comparisons pair the seventh touch of one sequence with the third or eleventh touch of the other, which are at the same position and in the same direction of movement. For each 5 ms bin from -0.25 to 0.25 s, a linear SVM on 12 PCs, 10-fold CV, balanced classes, 20 label shuffles per session. A comparison decodes when the mean accuracy over sessions and bins exceeds the 95th percentile of the same mean over shuffles. Reproduced when all four decode, partially for one to three, not reproduced for none. The session and mouse counts are checked (6 and 3).

claims.statement: During the inter-trial interval, ALM populations encode the upcoming target position more strongly than the other regions.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 7e,f; Results, "ALM encodes upcoming sequences", paragraph 2
claims.quote: On average, ALM populations showed stronger encoding of TP (Extended Data Fig. 7e,f) compared to other regions.
claims.criterion: For each of the 35 sessions, the cross-validated R2 of an elastic net predicting the upcoming sequence direction from normalised rates in the second before the cue, over all standard trials. Reproduced when the ALM mean R2 is the highest and a one-sided Mann-Whitney test of ALM against each other region gives p < 0.05; partially when the ALM mean is the highest but not every test is significant; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: None of the regions, including ALM, encoded time or distance to the trial start during the inter-trial interval.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 7h; Results, "ALM encodes upcoming sequences", paragraph 2
claims.quote: None of the regions, including ALM, encoded time or a distance to trial start (Extended Data Fig. 7h)
claims.criterion: Same model as ed7f-target-position-alm, predicting the time to the cue over the 1 s before it. The paper gives no test; the claim of absence is reproduced when the mean R2 of every region is below 0.1 and not reproduced when any region's mean is 0.1 or more. The effect size is reported for each region.

claims.statement: Extended Data Fig. 4m counts 324 ALM, 233 M1TJ and 119 S1TJ neurons.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4m legend
claims.quote: Proportions of neurons from different clusters at different cortical depths. ... ALM (n = 324), M1TJ (n = 233) and S1TJ (n = 119).
claims.criterion: Neurons are units of the Figure 3 sessions of each region that pass the PETH activity threshold of the Methods (maximum of the 6 PETHs at least 10 spikes/s; PETHs over the selected trials in 0 to 0.5 s from the cue, -1 to 1 s from the middle touch and -0.5 to 0.7 s from the last consummatory touch, per direction). Readings, (a) single units, (b) single and multi-units. Reproduced when all three counts are within tolerance under a reading; partially when one or two are; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: More ALM neurons are tuned to sequence initiation than neurons of the other regions.
claims.source: Results, "Sequence tiling of single-unit responses", paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 4l
claims.quote: We observed that single-neuron responses tile the sequence progression (Fig. 2e-h, Extended Data Fig. 4k), with more ALM neurons tuned to sequence initiation (Extended Data Fig. 4l).
claims.criterion: For each active neuron (reading (a) of ed4m), the window holding the peak of its 6 PETHs. Reproduced when the fraction peaking in the initiation window is higher in ALM than in M1TJ and in S1TJ, each by Fisher's exact test at p < 0.05; partially when higher than both but significant for one; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: S1TJ and M1TJ contain more neurons modulated by individual licks than ALM.
claims.source: Results, "Sequence tiling of single-unit responses", paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 4n,o
claims.quote: S1TJ and M1TJ contained more neurons (e.g. cluster #7; Extended Data Fig. 4k,m) that show greater modulation by individual licks (Extended Data Fig. 4n,o).
claims.criterion: For each active neuron, the correlation of each mid-sequence PETH with its best fitting 6.5 Hz sinusoid, averaged over the two directions (r_avg). Reproduced when the median r_avg of S1TJ and of M1TJ each exceed ALM's with a one-sided Mann-Whitney p < 0.05; partially when one does; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: ALM contains neurons that fire during sequence execution and decrease firing abruptly when the tongue first contacts water, although licking continues.
claims.source: Results, "Reward modulation in ALM", paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 6a
claims.quote: ALM contained single neurons (Extended Data Fig. 6a) that fired actively during sequence execution but abruptly decreased firing upon tongue contact with water, even though mice continued with ~5 consummatory licks
claims.criterion: Over standard trials of the 13 ALM sessions, for each active ALM neuron, the rate in 0 to 0.5 s after the first touch at or after water delivery is compared with -0.5 to 0 s (Wilcoxon signed-rank over trials, p < 0.01). Reproduced when neurons that decrease outnumber those that increase (binomial test p < 0.05); not reproduced otherwise. M1TJ and S1TJ are shown for reference.

claims.statement: Expert mice completed the 7 port positions in about a second.
claims.source: Results, first section, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 1h
claims.quote: expert mice showed remarkable sequence execution speed, with the 7 positions completed in about a second (Extended Data Fig. 1h).
claims.criterion: Sessions are the recording sessions with standard sequences (ephys groups except ZZ) and the opto sessions (trials without light). Per mouse, the median over standard trials; the value is the median over mice. Readings, (a) from the first port-moving touch to the first touch at the last position, (b) from the cue to that touch. Reproduced when a reading is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Over training, 15 mice reduced their sequence initiation time and increased their sequence speed.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1l; Results, first section, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Learning curves for 15 individual mice (gray) and the mean (black) showing a reduction in sequence initiation time (left) in response to the auditory cue and an increase in sequence speed (right).
claims.criterion: Learning files (described as Data learning), standard trials, in session order. The first and last 100 standard trials of each mouse; initiation time is the cue to the first touch, sequence speed the mean over the six intervals of 1 over the time between port-moving touches. Reproduced when 15 mice are present and at least 12 of them show both a lower initiation time and a higher speed (medians), with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over mice at p < 0.05 for each; partially when only one of the two measures meets this; not reproduced otherwise. Files deposited twice are left out.

claims.statement: Mice reached proficiency in standard sequences after about 1500 trials of training.
claims.source: Results, first section, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 1l-n
claims.quote: Mice reached proficiency in standard sequences (Fig. 1e) after ~1500 trials of training (Methods; Extended Data Fig. 1l-n).
claims.criterion: The paper does not define proficiency. Readings, counting all trials of the learning files in session order, (a) the first trial at which the median sequence speed of a 100-trial bin (50% overlap) reaches 90% of the median over the mouse's last 500 learning trials, (b) the first bin whose median initiation time falls within 110% of the median over the last 500. The median over mice under a reading must be within tolerance.

claims.statement: Backtracking analyses used 7458 standard and 2695 backtracking sequences from 47 sessions of the 9 mice trained on backtracking.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2c,e legends; Methods, "Behavioural training", paragraph 4
claims.quote: The first 9 fully trained mice were used in backtracking related analyses ... n = 7458 standard and 2695 backtracking sequences from 47 total sessions.
claims.criterion: Sessions with backtracking trials ([1 2 3 1 4 5 6] or [5 4 3 5 2 1 0]). Readings, (a) all such non-learning files, (b) the same without the air and earplug control sessions, (c) as (b) without the opto efficiency sessions. Reproduced when all four values are within tolerance under a reading; partially when two or three are; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: After the port backtracked, mice took on average 1 to 2 missed licks before relocating it.
claims.source: Results, first section, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 2e
claims.quote: On average, it took 1 to 2 missed licks before mice quickly relocated the port (Extended Data Fig. 2e).
claims.criterion: Tolerance is the stated range 1 to 2 widened by 10% of each bound (0.9 to 2.2). The fourth interval runs from the middle touch to the next port-moving touch; a missed lick is a video lick starting in it with no touch onset within 12.5 ms of the lick. Sessions are those of Figure 3 with backtracking trials. Reproduced when the mean over backtracking trials is in range and exceeds that of standard trials (Mann-Whitney p < 0.05); partially when only the second holds; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: After the first lick that touched water, mice continued with about 5 consummatory licks.
claims.source: Results, "Reward modulation in ALM", paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 6b
claims.quote: ALM contained single neurons ... abruptly decreased firing upon tongue contact with water, even though mice continued with ~5 consummatory licks (Extended Data Fig. 6b)
claims.criterion: Standard trials of the 35 Figure 3 sessions. The first water lick is the first touch at or after water delivery; the bout continues while successive intervals are below 1.5 times the session's median inter-lick interval. Readings, (a) video licks after it, (b) touches after it, (c) as (a) counting the first water lick. Trials whose video ends during the bout are left out of (a) and (c). Reproduced when the median over trials is within tolerance under a reading.

claims.statement: Expert mice usually initiated sequences from the correct side without exploring the other side.
