Diagonal LDA (one variance per neuron, shared across classes) on Go-window firing rates of sorted neurons, one classifier per session and array, stratified 8-fold cross-validation, predictions on the held-out folds pooled over all trials of all sessions. Go window by O11. Readings O1 x O2. Reproduced when, under one reading, all three accuracies are within tolerance; partially reproduced when one or two are.

claims.statement: Most ten-finger classification errors confuse an adjacent finger of the same hand or the matching finger of the other hand (N-PPC 76%, J-PPC 66%, J-MC 68% of errors).
claims.source: Results, Decoding individual finger presses of either hand, paragraph 3; Figure 7c to 7e
claims.quote: The majority (N-PPC: 76%; J-PPC: 66%; J-MC: 68%) of classification errors were adjacent-finger-confusion or matching-across-hand-confusion
claims.criterion: From the pooled confusion matrices of tenfinger-decoding-accuracy. An error is adjacent when the predicted finger is on the same hand and next to the true one in the order thumb, index, middle, ring, pinky; matching when it is the same finger type of the other hand (Methods, Shared representations across hands, defines matching pairs). Reproduced when, under one reading, all three shares are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Matching right and left finger pairs are closer in neural distance than non-matching pairs, by 1.56 units in N-PPC (95% CI 1.33 to 1.78) and 4.30 in J-MC (2.74 to 5.46), but not conclusively in J-PPC (0.27, -0.17 to 0.64).
claims.source: Results, Compositional representation of finger and laterality, paragraph 1; Figure 8b; Supplementary Figures 9b and 10b
claims.quote: On average, matching right/left finger pairs were 1.56 distance-units (95% CI: [1.33, 1.78], Figure 8b ) closer to each other than non-matching fingers were. Matching fingers were also represented more similarly than non-matching fingers in J-MC (mean difference: 4.30, 95% CI: [2.74, 5.46]), but this result was not conclusive in J-PPC (mean difference: 0.27, 95% CI: [-0.17, 0.64])
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the distance from each value to the farther bound of its paper CI. Per session and array, cross-validated squared Mahalanobis distances between the ten conditions from Go-window firing rates, computed with rsatoolbox (Methods, Neural distance between fingers), normalized by the number of neurons; readings O3 x O4 (and O1). Matching pairs are the five different-hand same-finger pairs and non-matching the twenty different-hand different-finger pairs (Methods, Shared representations across hands); the elements of all sessions are pooled (Figure 8b legend), and the difference is the mean non-matching minus the mean matching, with its 95% CI by O5. Reproduced when, under one reading, the N-PPC and J-MC differences are positive with CIs excluding 0 and all three values are within tolerance, and the J-PPC CI includes 0 (the paper's own test for the J-PPC absence). Partially reproduced when the N-PPC and J-MC CIs exclude 0 with positive differences but a value is out of tolerance or the J-PPC CI excludes 0.

claims.statement: In N-PPC the inter-finger geometry is similar across hands, with the index finger relatively distinct from the middle and ring fingers in both hands.
claims.source: Results, Compositional representation of finger and laterality, paragraph 4; Figure 8a and 8d
claims.quote: We found that inter-finger vectors were similar across hands, with the index finger relatively distinct from the middle and ring fingers
claims.criterion: From the N-PPC distances of fig8b-matching-closer averaged over the 10 sessions (Figure 8a legend), read as the MDS of Figure 8d preserves them, limited to the index, middle and ring fingers as the Results limit them. The paper gives no measure of similarity across hands; the criterion reads it as the pattern the sentence names holding in both hands. Reproduced when, under one reading, in each hand the index-middle and index-ring distances both exceed the middle-ring distance. The MDS with Generalized Procrustes alignment (with scaling) across sessions, as the Methods describe, is shown.

claims.statement: Hand (left against right) decoders trained on four finger types generalize to the held-out finger type significantly above chance (p < 0.001, permutation test), with hand CCGP close to standard decoding accuracy, in N-PPC, J-MC and J-PPC.
claims.source: Results, Compositional representation of finger and laterality, paragraphs 5 and 6; Figure 8e; Supplementary Figures 8, 9e, 10e and 11
claims.quote: Consistent with this hypothesis, cross-condition hand-decoding generalization performance (hand CCGP) was significantly above chance (p < 0.001, permutation test). Furthermore, hand CCGP was close to the standard decoding accuracy
claims.criterion: As in Methods, Compositionality of finger representations, and the Supplementary Figure 8 legend. Per array, neurons of all sessions pooled into a pseudo-population (O6); Go-window firing rates; a two-class hand decoder (O7) trained on four finger-type pairs and tested on the held-out pair, CCGP averaged over the five folds. Null distribution from 1001 label shuffles; p is the fraction of shuffles whose CCGP reaches the observed one. Standard hand accuracy by stratified 8-fold cross-validation over all ten conditions. Reproduced when, under one reading, every array has p < 0.001 and CCGP close to standard accuracy by O9 (Figure 8e and Supplementary Figure 11 say hand CCGP matched standard accuracy in all three); partially reproduced when every p < 0.001 but closeness fails for an array. The CCGP and accuracy values are reported.

claims.statement: Finger-type decoders trained on one hand generalize to the other hand significantly above chance (p < 0.001), with finger-type CCGP close to standard decoding accuracy, in N-PPC and J-MC.
claims.source: Results, Compositional representation of finger and laterality, paragraphs 5 and 6; Figure 8e; Supplementary Figure 9e
claims.quote: The finger-type dimension also generalized across hands (p < 0.001), and finger-type CCGP was close to the standard decoding accuracy
claims.criterion: As fig8e-hand-ccgp, with a 5-class finger-type decoder trained on the right hand and tested on the left and the reverse, CCGP the mean of the two directions (Supplementary Figure 8 legend); chance 20%; standard accuracy by O8. Reproduced when, under one reading, both arrays have p < 0.001 and CCGP close to standard accuracy by O9; partially reproduced when both p < 0.001 but closeness fails for one.

claims.statement: J-PPC finger representations are less compositional; finger-type CCGP (36%) is above chance (p < 0.001) but much lower than within-hand accuracy (65%).
claims.source: Results, Compositional representation of finger and laterality, paragraph 6; Supplementary Figure 10e
claims.quote: Interestingly, J-PPC finger representations were less compositional. While above chance (p < 0.001), the finger-type CCGP (36%) was much lower than the within-hand accuracy (65%)
claims.criterion: As fig8e-finger-ccgp for J-PPC, with within-hand accuracy by O8 (a), which the Results name; O8 (b) is reported. Reproduced when, under one reading of O6 and O7, p < 0.001 and both values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when p < 0.001 and CCGP is below 0.9 of the within-hand accuracy but a value is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: Even at matched neural population size, J-PPC finger-type CCGP is lower than that of N-PPC and J-MC.
claims.source: Results, Compositional representation of finger and laterality, paragraph 6; Supplementary Figure 11
claims.quote: Even when accounting for differences in neural population size, finger-type CCGP for J-PPC was lower than finger-type CCGP for N-PPC and J-MC
claims.criterion: Neuron-dropping curves (Methods, Offline classification, on neuron-dropping curves, random subsets of neurons stacked across sessions) of finger-type CCGP per array, under the readings of fig8e-finger-ccgp. The number of random subsets per size (100) is a standard choice that cannot change the outcome. The grid of sizes is not given; sizes from 50 neurons in steps of 50 are a standard choice. Reproduced when, at every size up to the smallest of the three pooled populations (J-MC, about 260 neurons), the mean J-PPC finger-type CCGP is below the means of N-PPC and J-MC at that size.

claims.statement: In the contralateral alternating-cues task many neurons discriminate between finger conditions in the Go window (N-PPC 54%, J-PPC 30%, J-MC 78%), selective neurons differ from No-Go for about two fingers on average (2.1, 1.9, 2.7), and many have large effect sizes (eta2 > 0.14 in 40%, 25%, 64%).
claims.source: Results, Single-neuron modulation to individual finger presses, paragraph 2; Figure 4c to 4e; Supplementary Figures 2 and 3
claims.quote: A large portion of neurons (N-PPC: 54%; J-PPC: 30%; J-MC: 78%; Figure 4c ) discriminated firing rates across conditions (q < 0.05), and selective neurons were often selective for multiple finger movements (mean number of significant fingers, N-PPC: 2.1; J-PPC: 1.9; J-MC: 2.7). Moreover, many neurons discriminated between finger conditions with large effect sizes (percentage of neurons with η 2 > 0.14, N-PPC: 40%; J-PPC: 25%; J-MC: 64%
claims.criterion: As in Methods, Single-neuron selectivity. One-way ANOVA across the six conditions (five fingers and No-Go) of Go-window rates; FDR over the neurons of an array pooled across sessions (466, 308 and 278, per the legends of Figure 4c and Supplementary Figures 2c and 3c); Dunnett's test of each finger against No-Go, at 0.05; eta2 from the ANOVA. Both cue variants pooled. The paper does not say whether the number of significant fingers is averaged over discriminative neurons or over all neurons; readings (a) discriminative neurons, as "selective neurons" reads; (b) all neurons. Likewise the eta2 share is read (a) over all neurons, (b) over neurons with q < 0.05. Reproduced when, under one reading of each, all nine values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the three discriminative fractions are.

claims.statement: Slightly fewer PPC neurons are strongly tuned (q < 0.05 and eta2 > 0.14) during movement preparation (N-PPC 24%, J-PPC 23%) than during execution (N-PPC 43%, J-PPC 24%).
claims.source: Results, Single-neuron modulation to individual finger presses, paragraph 3; Figure 4e and Supplementary Figure 2e
claims.quote: slightly fewer PPC neurons had strong tuning (q < 0.05 and η 2 > 0.14) during movement preparation (N-PPC: 24%; J-PPC: 23%) than during movement execution (N-PPC: 43%; J-PPC: 24%)
claims.criterion: As fig4c-contra-discriminative, in the Delay window (200 to 700 ms after the Delay screen) and the Go window. Whether the FDR correction is applied per window or over both is not stated; readings (a) per window, (b) over both windows. The N-PPC Go value (43% with q < 0.05 and eta2 > 0.14) exceeds the 40% with eta2 > 0.14 of fig4c-contra-discriminative, so the two cannot share one denominator; readings of the denominator are (i) all neurons pooled over sessions, as the Methods pool single-neuron metrics; (ii) the mean over sessions of the per-session percentages, as the Figure 4c line shows. Reproduced when, under one reading, all four values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Contralateral finger movements (five fingers and No-Go) are classified offline well above the 17% chance level (N-PPC 86%, J-PPC 64%, J-MC 84%), and most errors are adjacent fingers (75%, 42%, 67%).
claims.source: Results, Classifying finger presses from neural activity, paragraph 1; Figure 5a; Supplementary Figures 4a and 5a
claims.quote: Classification accuracies substantially exceeded chance (N-PPC: 86%; J-PPC: 64%; J-MC: 84%; chance: 17%). The majority (N-PPC: 75%; J-PPC: 42%; J-MC: 67%) of errors misclassified an adjacent finger
claims.criterion: As tenfinger-decoding-accuracy, over six classes (T, I, M, R, P, No-Go) in the Go window. J-PPC 42% is called a majority in the text although below half; it is reproduced as a number. The paper does not say how errors involving No-Go enter the share; readings (a) all errors form the denominator and those involving No-Go are not adjacent; (b) only errors between two finger classes form the denominator. Reproduced when, under one reading of O1, O2 and these, all six values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the three accuracies are.

claims.statement: For N-PPC, cross-validated accuracy reaches 80% with about 40 training trials, about 70 neurons, and window durations of about 350 ms.
claims.source: Results, Classifying finger presses from neural activity, paragraphs 3 and 4; Figure 5b to 5d
claims.quote: Cross-validated accuracy increased with more training data, reaching 80% accuracy when training on about 40 trials (2.7 minutes) for N-PPC. Higher neuron counts provide more finger information and thus improved classification accuracy, reaching 80% accuracy at about 70 neurons for N-PPC
claims.criterion: As in Methods, Offline classification. Learning curve from subsets of each training fold; neuron-dropping curve from random subsets of neurons stacked across the 4 sessions; window sweep [200 ms, 200 ms + duration] after Go. Each value is the smallest training size, neuron count or duration at which mean accuracy reaches 80%. Step sizes and the number of random subsets (100) are standard choices. How stacked neurons of different sessions form trials is not stated; readings as O6. Reproduced when, under one reading, all three values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Finger movements are also decoded from PPC during the planning period, with lower accuracy than during execution (N-PPC 66%, J-PPC 61%, chance 17%).
claims.source: Results, Classifying finger presses from neural activity, paragraph 5; Figure 5e
claims.quote: Finger movements could also be decoded from PPC during the planning period ( Figure 5e )), although classification accuracy was lower (N-PPC: 66%; J-PPC: 61%; chance: 17%) than during movement execution
claims.criterion: As fig5a-contra-decoding in the Delay window. Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance and below the Go-window accuracies.

claims.statement: During online BMI control of right-hand fingers, participant N reached 86% accuracy (4016 trials over 9 sessions) and J 92% (1488 trials over 8 sessions), against 17% chance.
claims.source: Results, Brain-machine interface control of finger movements, paragraphs 3 and 4; Figure 6a and 6b
claims.quote: Confusion matrix for participant N (PPC), right-hand finger presses. 86% accuracy, 4016 trials over 9 sessions ... Confusion matrix for participant J (PPC+MC), right-hand finger presses. 92% accuracy, 1488 trials over 8 sessions
claims.criterion: Accuracy is the share of online trials whose decoded class (shown 1.5 s after the cue) equals the cued class, over all trials of the BMI runs (calibration runs without classifier output excluded). Reproduced when both are within tolerance and the trial and session counts match.

claims.statement: Retrospectively decoding J's BMI trials from a single array, with a classifier trained on earlier run-blocks, gives 83% (plus or minus 7%) from J-PPC and 87% (plus or minus 8%) from J-MC.
claims.source: Results, Brain-machine interface control of finger movements, paragraph 4; Supplementary Figure 6
claims.quote: We trained the linear classifier on earlier run-blocks [0, 1, …, M-1] and evaluated on run-block M, repeating for all run-blocks in each session. 83% +/- 7% accuracy (chance 17%), 1488 trials over 8 sessions ... Same as (a) using J-MC population activity. 87% +/- 8% accuracy (chance 17%), 1488 trials over 8 sessions
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the paper's spread. Diagonal LDA trained on run-blocks 0 to M-1 of a session and tested on block M, for every block, features by O10; accuracy pooled over the 1488 trials. Whether block 0 (the calibration run) is itself tested is not stated; it is not, as it has no earlier block to train on. Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Participant J controlled left-hand finger presses through the BMI with 94% accuracy (336 trials over 3 sessions).
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 7
claims.quote: Confusion matrix for participant J (PPC+MC), left-hand finger presses. 94% accuracy, 336 trials over 3 sessions
claims.criterion: As fig6-online-bmi, for the left-hand runs.

claims.statement: Of 87 mice entering the recording step, 61 passed session-level quality control and 58 resulted in NWB files; these 58 passive viewing experiments are the ones analysed.
claims.source: Results, A survey of visually evoked spiking, paragraph 2; Methods, Quality control for the Neuropixels recording session; Methods, Data processing pipeline
claims.quote: reducing the number of experiments analysed and presented here from 87 to 58
claims.criterion: Counts of sessions and of mice by genotype, from the session metadata. The tolerance is zero, not 10%, because these are counts of released sessions fixed by the release, as the Methods (Mice) give them. The pipeline failures before recording cannot be tested on released data and are not judged.

claims.statement: 284 of the 332 probes were mapped to the CCFv3.
claims.source: Methods, Neuropixels recordings, Probes; Methods, Ex vivo imaging quality control
claims.quote: In total, 284 out of 332 probes were mapped to the CCFv3
claims.criterion: A probe counts as mapped when its units carry CCF coordinates, as ExtDataFigure1/ExtDataFigure1jk.py counts it (has_ccf, a positive sum of anterior-posterior CCF coordinates over the probe's units passing the quality filters of that script). The tolerance on the two counts is zero for the reason given in methods-sessions-passing-qc. Open detail, which sessions the 332 probes come from; the text does not say, and the readings are (a) the 58 released experiments, (b) the 61 sessions passing quality control, of which only (a) can be counted on released data.

claims.statement: After quality filtering, 682 +/- 144 units were recorded per experiment, 119 +/- 48 per probe and 56 +/- 30 per visual area, with 6.1 +/- 1.1 visual areas sampled per experiment.
claims.source: Results, A survey of visually evoked spiking, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 1j, k
claims.quote: Overall, we recorded 682 ± 144 units per experiment, 119 ± 48 units per probe and 56 ± 30 units per visual area ( Extended Data Fig. 1j ), sampling 6.1 ± 1.1 visual areas per experiment
claims.criterion: Units filtered as the Extended Data Fig. 1j legend says (ISI violations < 0.5, amplitude cutoff < 0.1, presence ratio > 0.95), and as ExtDataFigure1jk.py does, also quality == good for the per-experiment and per-area counts but not for the per-probe count. Per experiment, all structures; per area, the eight areas V1, LM, RL, AL, PM, AM, LGN and LP, counting only areas with at least one unit; an area is sampled when it has at least one unit. Mean and SD (numpy std) across the 58 experiments, across probes, and across experiment-area pairs. The tolerance on the means is the stated spread, as the protocol asks; on the SD of units per experiment, 10%.

claims.statement: Units in the eight visual areas were highly visually responsive, 60% having a significant spatial receptive field within the monitor, against only 1.4% of units in the hippocampus (CA1, CA3 and dentate gyrus).
claims.source: Results, A survey of visually evoked spiking, paragraph 3; Fig. 1g
claims.quote: Units recorded in all eight cortical and thalamic visual areas were highly visually responsive, with 60% displaying significant spatial receptive fields within the boundaries of the monitor ... and found them in only 1.4% of units
claims.criterion: A receptive field is significant when the chi-square shuffle test of the Methods (Receptive field analysis; 1,000 location shuffles, spike counts over the 250 ms Gabor presentation) gives p < 0.01 (AllenSDK p_value_rf, Extended Data Fig. 4b legend). All non-noise units, with no quality filter, as Figure1/Figure1g.py loads them. The 60% is the pooled fraction over all units of the eight areas in all mice, as Figure1g.py computes it. The code does not compute the 1.4%; the readings are (a) pooled over all CA1, CA3 and DG units, (b) the mean across mice of each mouse's fraction (the quantity Fig. 1g plots). Reproduced when the 60% and, under one reading, the 1.4% are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Jitter-corrected CCGs during drifting gratings showed a significant sharp peak (within +/-10 ms and more than seven times the flank SD) for 16,119 of 2,089,890 possible cortical unit pairs, 0.96% +/- 0.13% per mouse in 25 mice.
claims.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 7b
claims.quote: yielding 16,119 pairs of units out of 2,089,890 possible pairs within the cortex ( Extended Data Fig. 7b ; 0.96% ± 0.13% per mouse, n = 25 mice)
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Cross-correlation analysis) give it. The 25 mice of the Functional Connectivity stimulus set (75 repeats per orientation); drifting gratings at 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees, 2 Hz, 0.04 cycles per degree, contrast 0.8; units of V1, LM, RL, AL, PM and AM with mean rate above 2 Hz from 50 to 500 ms after onset; CCG normalized by the triangular overlap and the geometric mean rate, computed per orientation and averaged over the four; jitter window 25 ms, the jittered CCG being the analytical expected value of ref. 77; a peak is significant when the maximum of the jitter-corrected CCG within +/-10 ms exceeds seven times the SD of the flanks at 50 to 100 ms from zero. Open details. The bin width is not stated; the example in Figure2/compute_ccg.ipynb uses 2,000 samples per 2 s presentation, so 1 ms, and no other reading is given by the text. The CCG window is not stated; the readings are (a) the 2 s presentation (the example's shape), (b) the 3 s of presentation and grey. The unit quality filter is not stated in the text (Extended Data Fig. 4b was not seen); the readings are (a) all non-noise units, (b) the filters of Extended Data Fig. 1j (ISI violations < 0.5, amplitude cutoff < 0.1, presence ratio > 0.95). Variant from the code, shown not judged, get_ccgjitter subtracts the CCG of one random jitter resample in place of the expected value. Reproduced when, under one reading, the three values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: In an example mouse, the CCG peak offsets between V1 and LM were shifted positive against the V1-V1 distribution (median 3.9 ms), so V1 units on average lead LM units.
claims.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 2; Fig. 2d
claims.quote: the peak offset distribution between V1 and LM showed a significant positive delay compared to the V1–V1 distribution ( Fig. 2d ; P = 2.6 × 10 −8 , two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test), indicating that V1 neurons ... lead LM neurons
claims.criterion: Sharp peaks as in fig2-sharp-peak-pairs, V1 as source and LM as target, a positive offset meaning V1 spikes lead. The example mouse is not identified in the paper or the code; the readings are each of the 25 mice. Reproduced when in at least one mouse the median V1 to LM offset is within tolerance and the two-sided rank-sum test against that mouse's V1-V1 offsets gives p < 0.05 with the V1-LM offsets higher. The result for every mouse is shown.

claims.statement: Across 25 mice, the CCG peak offset distributions between neighbouring cortical areas differ from the within-area distributions for V1-LM, LM-RL, RL-AL and PM-AM, but not for AL-PM.
claims.source: Methods, Cross-correlation analysis, last paragraph; Fig. 2e legend
claims.quote: All between-area distributions are significantly different from the within-area distributions at the 5% confidence level, except for AL–PM
claims.criterion: Neighbouring areas by the anatomical hierarchy order of the cortex (V1, LM, RL, AL, PM, AM), each pair compared with the within-area distribution of the lower area, as the Methods list them. Per mouse, a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test of the sharp peak offsets; p-values combined over the mice with Fisher's method (mice lacking either distribution left out, as the text does not say otherwise). Reproduced when V1-LM, LM-RL, RL-AL and PM-AM give combined p < 0.05 and AL-PM gives p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when four of the five pairs agree.

claims.statement: On average V1 units lead the units of the other cortical areas, while AM follows the other areas, placing AM at the top of the hierarchy.
claims.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 7c
claims.quote: On average, V1 units lead the activity of units in other areas ( Extended Data Fig. 7c , left column); by contrast, area AM follows other regions
claims.criterion: For each mouse and ordered pair of cortical areas, the median peak offset of the sharp peaks, averaged across mice (Extended Data Fig. 7c legend). Reproduced when the mean median offset is positive with V1 as source for each of the five other areas as target, and positive with AM as target for each of the five other areas as source; partially reproduced when this holds for at least eight of the ten pairs.

claims.statement: The matrix of pairwise directionality scores between cortical areas is correlated with the matrix of anatomical hierarchy score differences (Pearson r = 0.74 over 21 pairs).
claims.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 3; Fig. 2e, f
claims.quote: The matrix of pairwise directionality scores ( Fig. 2e ) between areas was very similar to the matrix of anatomical hierarchy score differences ( Fig. 2b ) (Pearson’s r = 0.74, P = 1 × 10 −4
claims.criterion: Directionality score DS = (C+ - C-)/(C+ + C-) for each source and target area, C+ and C- the numbers of sharp peaks with positive and negative lag (Methods, Directionality score; zero lags enter neither count). The anatomical difference is the target score minus the source score, from the scores in the opening comment, so that a source lower in the hierarchy gives a positive difference. In Figure2/comparison_anatomical_functional_connectivity_final.ipynb the anatomy matrix is row score minus column score, and in Figure2/ccg_distribution_model_final.ipynb the DS matrix has targets as rows ("To") and sources as columns ("From"). The 15 lower-triangle pairs and the 6 diagonal entries, each pair taken in the same orientation in both matrices, as the comparison notebook does (it prints r = 0.74, p = 1.47e-4). DS is computed from the sharp peak offsets pooled over the 25 mice, as ccg_distribution_model_final.ipynb does (it appends every mouse's offsets to one list per area pair) and as the Fig. 2e legend says ("from peak offset distributions across 25 mice"); the mean across mice of each mouse's DS is a variant. In that notebook an offset counts as positive when > -1 and negative when < -1 in its bin indexing; the author matches its own zero-lag convention to the Methods and shows the notebook's as a variant. Reproduced when r is within tolerance and p < 0.05. The precomputed DS matrix in data/processed_data/FFscore_grating_10.npy is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The physical layout of the areas does not account for the correlation between directionality and hierarchy in terms of average distance.
claims.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 7e
claims.quote: The spatial layout of areas could not account for this correlation in terms of average physical distance
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The legend shows Pearson and Spearman coefficients of the average 3D Euclidean distance between simultaneously recorded units of each pair of areas (CCFv3 coordinates) against their hierarchy score difference; their values are not in the text. The test is a Pearson correlation at p < 0.05 over the 21 pairs of Fig. 2f, the test the paper uses for every hierarchy correlation. Open detail, whether the difference is signed or absolute; the legend does not say, and both are run. Reproduced when the correlation is not significant; not reproduced when it is. r is reported either way.

claims.statement: The functional hierarchy is absent during spontaneous activity (30 min grey screen), which suggests it reflects activity driven by bottom-up input.
claims.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 7f, g
claims.quote: this organization was absent during spontaneous activity ( Extended Data Fig. 7f , g )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Jitter-corrected CCGs and sharp peaks as in fig2-sharp-peak-pairs, computed over the 30 min grey screen (Extended Data Fig. 7f legend); DS averaged across mice (Extended Data Fig. 7g legend). The paper names no test for the absence; the test it uses for the presence (Fig. 2f) is a Pearson correlation of DS against hierarchy score difference over the 21 pairs, and that test is applied at p < 0.05. Open detail, how the spontaneous period is cut into trials for the CCG; the text does not say, and the readings are segments of 2 s and of 3 s matching the grating trials. Reproduced when the correlation is not significant; not reproduced when it is. The number of sharp peaks per mouse and r are reported either way.

claims.statement: The measured functional network has a total hierarchy score of 0.89, close to a simulated ladder-like hierarchy with feedback (0.88), above a one-to-all (0.15) or three-level (0.38) network and below a strongly feedforward one (1.54).
claims.source: Methods, Network model simulation; Extended Data Fig. 8
claims.quote: The maximum difference of this trajectory (here between V1 and AM) is defined as the total hierarchy score (THS) of the network, which is 0.89 for the measured functional network in our data ... The resulting DS matrix showed a gradient very similar to the real data, with a THS equal to 0.88
claims.criterion: The mean DS from each source area to all target areas, and THS as the largest difference of these means across areas (Methods, Network model simulation). The DS matrix is that of fig2f-directionality-vs-anatomy (offsets pooled over mice), and the mean over targets includes the area's own diagonal entry, as Figure2/ccg_distribution_model_final.ipynb computes it (max minus min of np.mean(FF_score, axis=0) over the 6 x 6 matrix, printed as 0.8906). Reproduced when THS is within tolerance and lies between the one-to-all value 0.15 and the feedforward value 1.54, the comparison the Methods draw. The mean without the diagonal and the DS averaged across mice are shown as variants. The simulations need no data and are not rerun.

claims.statement: The mean time to first spike after a full-field flash in each area is correlated with its anatomical hierarchy score.
claims.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Fig. 3a to c
claims.quote: the mean visual latency of each area was correlated with its anatomical hierarchy score ( Fig. 3c ; Pearson’s r = 0.95, P = 0.00025)
claims.criterion: Time to first spike per trial is the first spike from 30 ms after flash onset, measured from onset; a unit's latency is the median over trials with a spike (Methods, Response latency; functions/time_to_first_spike.py). claims.statement: In the circular Kalman filter, an HD observation consistent with the current estimate increases certainty, while one that strongly conflicts with it (opposite direction) decreases certainty.
claims.source: Results, Circular Kalman Filtering, HD Observations, paragraph 1; Fig. 1 D and E
claims.quote: HD observations increase the observer’s certainty if they are confirmatory ... if HD observations strongly conflict with the current estimate (e.g., if they point in the opposite direction), they actually decrease certainty
claims.criterion: The update is the vector addition of Fig. 1 D and E and the observation term of Eq. 9 (kappa changes by kappa_z cos(z - mu) dt). In the code's circKF step (vM_Projection in circularFiltering.py, kappa_phi = 1, kappa_v = 1, dt = 0.01) the observation enters as that vector addition on the natural parameters, followed by the prediction step. Take a state with certainty kappa_t (any of 1, 2, 5) and apply one step with an HD observation at z = mu (confirmatory) and one at z = mu + pi (opposite). The paper fixes no single reliability for this; use the per-step reliabilities the Methods give, xi_fun_inv(gamma_z dt) for gamma_z = 1/s (Fig. 3E) and 10/s (Fig. 2H). Compare (a) the certainty right after the observation update with the certainty before it (the update of Fig. 1 D and E alone, before the prediction step), and (b) the certainty after the full step with the certainty after the same step with no observation (kappa_z = 0). Reproduced when, under both comparisons, every kappa_t and both reliabilities, the confirmatory observation gives higher and the opposite one lower certainty.

claims.statement: In a simulated Bayesian ring attractor of 80 neurons, the bump position tracks HD about as accurately as the circular Kalman filter, the bump amplitude tracks the filter's certainty, and when the visual cue is removed the amplitude decays toward its baseline.
claims.source: Results, Neural Network Implementation, paragraph 6; Fig. 2H
claims.quote: This network exhibits a spatially localized bump whose position tracks HD, with an accuracy similar to that of the circular Kalman filter itself ( Fig. 2 H ). Meanwhile, the amplitude of the bump accurately tracks the fluctuating HD posterior certainty in the circular Kalman filter ... When the visual cue is removed, the bump amplitude decays toward baseline
claims.criterion: Run Figure2h.ipynb as released (seed 42, T = 15, dt = 0.01, kappa_phi = 1, kappa_v = 2, N = 80, cue off from 5 to 10 s, information rate 15). The Methods give gamma_z = 10/s; run that as a second reading of the cue strength. Bump position and amplitude are decoded as in the Methods (x = A r, position arctan2(x2, x1), amplitude the vector length), with the notebook's scaling x = (2/N) A r, which puts the amplitude on the scale of kappa. The paper gives no number for "similar" or "accurately"; readings for both cue strengths: (a) the mean absolute circular difference between the network's and the circKF's HD estimates is smaller than the circKF's own mean absolute error to the true HD, over the whole run; (b) the Pearson correlation between bump amplitude and circKF certainty over the cue periods is at least 0.9. Decay: over the darkness period (5 to 10 s) the bump amplitude falls and ends closer to the baseline kappa* = 1 (Methods, Bayesian ring attractor) than it started. Reproduced when the decay holds and (a) and (b) hold under both cue strengths.

claims.statement: The Bayesian ring attractor tracks HD with the same accuracy as the circular Kalman filter when HD observations are reliable and with slightly lower accuracy when they are unreliable; in the unreliable regime its certainty stays near its baseline and overestimates the filter's certainty.
claims.source: Fig. 2I legend; Results, Neural Network Implementation, paragraph 7
claims.quote: The Bayesian ring attractor network tracks the true HD with the same accuracy ... if HD observations are reliable and, therefore, more informative but with slightly lower accuracy once they become less reliable, and therefore less informative. This drop co-occurs with an overestimate in the belief’s certainty
claims.criterion: From figure2i.npz as Figure2i.ipynb reads it, compare the circKF (vonMises_stats) and the Bayesian ring attractor (vonMises_q_stats) over the 23 information rates (0.01 to 100/s, kappa_v = 1, T = 20). Accuracy is the stored |m1|, certainty the mean final kappa. The paper names no rate that separates reliable from unreliable; readings for the reliable set: (a) rates of 1/s and above, (b) rates of 3/s and above. "Same accuracy" readings: the absolute difference is at most (i) 0.01 or (ii) 0.02 at every reliable rate. Reproduced when, under every combination, the accuracies are the same on the reliable set, the attractor's accuracy is below the circKF's at the lowest rates (0.01 to 0.1/s), and at those rates its mean certainty is above the circKF's.

claims.statement: A conventional ring attractor (fast decay to a fixed bump amplitude, with that amplitude optimized) is less accurate than the Bayesian ring attractor at every HD observation reliability, and reaches its accuracy only when observations are highly unreliable.
claims.source: Results, Bayesian vs. Conventional Ring Attractors, paragraphs 2 and 3; Fig. 3B
claims.quote: Even after this optimization of the conventional ring attractor, it does not rival the accuracy of the Bayesian ring attractor. The Bayesian attractor performs consistently better, regardless of the amount of information available to the network
claims.criterion: As in Figure3b,c,e,d_FigureS3.ipynb, the conventional attractor is the fixed-certainty filter (noUncert_stats) at the kappa* that maximizes the prior-weighted average accuracy (objective() with mean 0.5 and SD 1 over log rate, Methods, Performance measures, and Fig. 3B inset); the Bayesian ring attractor is vonMises_q_stats. Reproduced when the Bayesian attractor's accuracy is at least the conventional one's at every one of the 23 rates and strictly above it at every rate from 0.1/s to 10/s. The paper's "only once HD observations become highly unreliable" is checked as the difference being smallest at the lowest rates (0.01 and 0.03/s); reported, not judged.

claims.statement: The weight given to a new HD observation by the Bayesian ring attractor depends on both the observation's reliability and the current certainty and is close to that of the circular Kalman filter, deviating only for very uninformative observations; a conventional attractor weights observations by their reliability alone.
claims.source: Fig. 3C legend; Results, Bayesian vs. Conventional Ring Attractors, paragraph 3; SI Appendix, Fig. S3 legend
claims.quote: The update weight of the Bayesian attractor is close to optimal, visually indistinguishable from the circKF
claims.criterion: In the notebook, Fig. 3C plots the weight for a 90 degree observation as a map over the observation's and the posterior's informativeness and draws on it each model's mean certainty against information rate: circKF (vonMises_stats[0,:,2]) and Bayesian attractor (vonMises_q_stats[0,:,2]), both as Fisher information xi(kappa); the conventional attractor is a constant kappa*. Compute, at each of the 23 rates, the weight under the circKF's and under the attractor's mean certainty, with the per-observation reliability alpha = xi_fun_inv(rate x Delta t). The Methods and the code differ on the weight: readings (i) the Methods, w = (1/pi) tan^-1(alpha / kappa) with Delta t = 0.01 (10-ms observation, Fig. 3C legend and Methods); (ii) the notebook, w = arctan2(alpha, kappa) / (pi/2) with Delta t = 0.1. The paper gives no bound for "close"; readings: the absolute weight difference is at most (a) 0.02 or (b) 0.05 at every rate of 1/s and above. Reproduced when every combination holds and the largest difference falls at rates below 1/s (Fig. S3, "only deviates ... for very uninformative observations"). The conventional attractor's weight depending on reliability only follows from its constant kappa* and is not tested.

claims.statement: Across ring attractors with different bump decay speeds and baseline amplitudes, the best network has a slow decay (low beta) and performs about as well as the Bayesian ring attractor; performance drops as decay speed increases, which a larger baseline amplitude partly offsets.
claims.source: Results, Bayesian vs. Conventional Ring Attractors, paragraph 4; Fig. 3D
claims.quote: The network with the best performance overall had a slow bump decay speed (low β ), as expected ( Fig. 3 D and E ). While it featured similar performance to the Bayesian ring attractor, it had slightly different β and κ * parameters ... As the bump decay speed β increased further, performance dropped.
claims.criterion: figure3d.npz holds MSE_array, the prior-weighted average accuracy over the grid of kappa* (0.1 to 2.5) and beta (0.1 to 8), normalized by the particle filter reference as in the notebook. The Bayesian ring attractor is kappa* = 1, beta = 1/(kappa_phi + kappa_v) = 0.5 (Methods). The best network is the grid maximum. Reproduced when (1) the best beta is at most 1 (the scanned values above 1 are 2, 4 and 8); (2) the best network differs from (1, 0.5) in kappa* or beta; (3) the Bayesian attractor's normalized performance is within 10% of the best (the paper's "similar", default tolerance); (4) for beta above the best, the maximum over kappa* falls as beta rises; (5) for beta above the best, the kappa* that maximizes performance is at least the best network's kappa*.

claims.statement: In a network of 64 neurons with additive neural noise, inference accuracy drops below 70% of its noise-free value once the noise is large enough.
claims.source: Results, The Impact of Neural Noise on Inference Accuracy, paragraph 1; Fig. 3F
claims.quote: Indeed, simulating a network of 64 noisy neurons shows that, once the noise becomes sufficiently large, inference accuracy drops to below 70% of its noise-free value
claims.criterion: The paper states a bound, so no tolerance applies. The network without retuning keeps the kappa* and beta that are best at noise SD 0 (noretuning_MSE in the notebook). Normalization readings: (a) the notebook's, performance divided by the particle filter reference; (b) the legend's, performance divided by the same network's performance at noise SD 0. Range readings: (i) noise SD up to 10, the plotted range; (ii) up to 20, the largest simulated. Reproduced when the relative performance without retuning is below 70% at the largest noise SD under every combination.

claims.statement: Retuning the bump decay speed and baseline amplitude for each noise level reduces the drop in inference accuracy by about 35% compared with the network tuned for noise-free performance, and raises the signal-to-noise ratio.
claims.source: Results, The Impact of Neural Noise on Inference Accuracy, paragraph 3; Fig. 3F; SI Appendix, Fig. S4
claims.quote: Indeed, doing so reduced the drop in inference accuracy by about 35% when compared to the network tuned to optimize noise-free performance ( Fig. 3 D and F ) and also boosted the network’s signal-to-noise ratio
claims.criterion: From the notebook, retuned performance is the grid maximum at each noise SD (max_MSE), and the untuned one the noise-free optimum's value (noretuning_MSE); signal-to-noise as the notebook computes it (mean kappa over the weighted average, divided by sigma / sqrt(N/2), Methods). The drop is 100% minus relative performance, and the reduction is 1 minus the retuned drop over the untuned drop. The paper does not say at which noise level the 35% is taken; readings: (a) noise SD 10, the largest plotted; (b) noise SD 20, the largest simulated; (c) the mean of the reduction over noise SD 1 to 10. Each under the two normalizations of fig3f-noise-drop-below-70. These are readings of which number the 35% is, so the value part holds when the reduction is within 31.5 to 38.5% under at least one of them (every reading is shown). Reproduced when the value part holds and the retuned signal-to-noise ratio is at least the untuned one at every noise SD above 0. Fig. S4's statement that larger noise needs larger kappa* and beta is reported from the same grid, not judged.

claims.statement: Neural noise makes the bump position diffuse without bias and makes the bump amplitude drift upward and diffuse, which leads to overconfidence; for additive noise, a four-fold larger network halves the noise's effective SD.
claims.source: Results, The Impact of Neural Noise on Inference Accuracy, paragraphs 2 and 3; SI Appendix, section 5
claims.quote: First, it causes an unbiased random diffusion of μ t and, thus, an increasingly imprecise memory of the HD estimate. Second, it causes a positive drift and random diffusion of κ t
claims.criterion: The result is a derivation (SI Appendix, section 5); the Methods give the diffusion SD of kappa under additive noise as sqrt(sigma_nn^2 / N) per unit time. Test it with the code's RNN_filter_Run (with z=None added to its signature, see the code notes above) at the Bayesian ring attractor's parameters (kappa* = 1, beta = 0.5, tau = 1, so w_even = 1.5 and w_quad = 0.5 as in performance_scan_figure3f.py; stoch_corr 0, since it corrects for angular velocity input, which is absent here), with no HD input (I_ext = 0) and no angular velocity input (dy = 0), noise SD 1 and 2, N = 64 and 256, dt = 0.01, from a bump of amplitude 1, over 2,000 runs of T = 5. Reproduced when (1) the mean change of position is within 2 standard errors of 0 and its variance grows with time; (2) the mean amplitude at the end exceeds that of the noise-free run; (3) the SD of the one-step amplitude increments at N = 256 is half that at N = 64, within 10%. The run length, number of runs and starting amplitude are not given by the paper; they are standard choices that set only the precision.

claims.statement: The connectivity among EPG, Delta7 and PEN1 neurons in the hemibrain connectome resembles the connectivity of a network that implements the approximate circular Kalman filter, with shifted PEN1 to EPG projections and broad EPG to Delta7 to EPG inhibition.
claims.source: Fig. 4 B and C legends; SI Appendix, section 4A
claims.quote: The connectivity profile of a recurrent neural network (RNN) ( Fig. 2 D – F ) that implements an approximate circKF is strikingly similar to the connectivity of neurons in the Drosophila HD system.
claims.criterion: Fig. 4B legend: connections from hemibrain:v1.2.1, total synapse count per cell pair as the connection strength, neurons sorted by spatial position as a proxy for preferred HD, Delta7 to Delta7 omitted. The code does not hold this analysis. Sorting is open; readings: (a) by the protocerebral bridge glomerulus in the neuron's name (L9 to R9), (b) by the ellipsoid body or gall position in the name. Reproduced when, under both, (1) PEN1 to EPG connections are offset from the EPG to PEN1 connections, in opposite directions for left and right PEN1 neurons; (2) each Delta7 neuron receives EPG input from, and sends output to, EPG neurons at more than half of the sorted positions (broad inhibition, Fig. 4E).

claims.statement: A Drosophila-like multipopulation network, constrained by the connectome, tracks HD with an accuracy indistinguishable from the idealized Bayesian ring attractor across observation reliabilities.
claims.source: Results, Tuning a Biological Ring Attractor, paragraph 3; Fig. 4 G and H
claims.quote: We found that this network achieves a HD encoding accuracy which is indistinguishable from that of our idealized Bayesian ring attractor network ( Fig. 4 G and H ).
claims.criterion: From figure4g.npz as Figure4g,h.ipynb reads it, compare the Drosophila-like network (CX_stats) with the Bayesian ring attractor (vonMises_q_stats of the same file, same runs, dt = 0.001) at every information rate stored (the 23 rates of performance_scan_figure4g.py, since the notebook's glob over the empty data_raw/figure4g/ yields none). Readings for "indistinguishable": the absolute accuracy difference is at most (a) 0.01 or (b) 0.02 at every rate. Reproduced when both hold. The mean certainties (Fig. 4H) are reported, not judged.

claims.statement: The Bayesian ring attractor's inference accuracy depends little on its number of neurons.
claims.source: SI Appendix, Fig. S2 legend; Results, Neural Network Implementation, paragraph 6
claims.quote: Network inference performance is mostly independent of the number of neurons N in the Bayesian ring attractor network.
claims.criterion: figureS2.npz holds accuracy per information rate for N = 3, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 (the notebook's N_array), and vonMises_q_stats.npz the quadratic circKF reference. "Mostly" is not quantified; readings: for (a) N of 8 and more, (b) N of 16 and more, the accuracy is within 0.02 of the reference at every rate. Reproduced when both hold. The values for N = 3 and 4 are reported.

claims.statement: The paper predicts that the bump amplitude in the HD system is higher in the presence of reliable external HD cues, such as salient visual landmarks. The paper does not test this.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 7
claims.quote: Second, we predict that bump amplitude in the HD system should vary dynamically, with higher amplitudes in the presence of reliable external HD cues, such as salient visual landmarks.
claims.criterion: The paper gives the measure and nothing else. Bump amplitude is the length of the population vector of the activity's first Fourier component, ordered by preferred HD (Eq. 3; Methods, Simulation parameters, decoder A = (cos phi, sin phi)), in the EPG population that holds the HD bump (SI Appendix, section 4A). The paper does not say how cue reliability is set in an experiment, which activity signal (raw fluorescence or dF/F) feeds the decoder, the time windows, the unit of comparison or a test. Comparison as the paper's text allows: bump amplitude while the fly sees the more reliable cue against the less reliable cue, as the dataset labels them. Readings for the test: (a) per fly, mean amplitude higher with the more reliable cue in more than half of the flies; (b) a one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over flies, p below 0.05. Activity signal readings: (i) dF/F, (ii) raw fluorescence minus baseline. Reproduced when every combination finds higher amplitude with the more reliable cue; blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ. The second half of the prediction (a high bump amplitude makes the bump position less sensitive to new cues) has no measure in the paper and is not tested.

claims.statement: The experimental data are simultaneous patch-clamp and HD-MEA recordings of two cultured neurons, each stimulated with the eCode protocols repeated in four to six runs of about 200 s.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Methods 5.2, last paragraph, and 5.6.5
claims.quote: We acquired paired patch-clamp and extracellular signals from two cells of cortical cultures in embryonic rats ... The eCode protocols were repeated during four to six runs (each run lasted approximately 200 s)
claims.criterion: Count the neurons (NWB files) and, per neuron, the runs (the run label in the series names). Reproduced when there are two neurons, each with between 4 and 6 runs (widened by 10% of each bound, 3.6 to 6.6, so 4 to 6 runs), and the median run duration (first to last timestamp of a run's patch series) is within tolerance. The runs the paper's fits used are runs 1 to 5 of cell 1 and 3 to 6 of cell 2 (code, 0-export-to-nwb.ipynb); a dataset holding other runs is reported, not judged.

claims.statement: Each run applies the eCode protocols with the sweep numbers, step durations and amplitudes (in percent of the estimated rheobase) that the Methods list.
claims.source: Methods 5.2
claims.quote: IDthresh: The purpose of this protocol was to finely screen the current levels to correctly reestimate Irheo before processing. It consisted of 21 sweeps with a 270 ms square pulse of increasing amplitudes from 50% to 130% with step increments of 4%
claims.criterion: Per run, from the stimulus current series, count the sweeps of each protocol and measure step durations and amplitudes (current minus the pre-step holding level). The Methods give IDthres 21 sweeps of 270 ms, 50 to 130% by 4%; firepattern 2 sweeps of 3.6 s at 120 and 200%; IV 3 s steps; IDrest 11 sweeps of 1.35 s, 50 to 300% by 25%; APWaveform 50 ms pulses, 200 to 350% by 30%; HyperDepol 4 sweeps of 450 ms at -40 to -160% then 270 ms at 100%; sAHP 4 sweeps of 250 ms at 40%, 225 ms at 150 to 300% by 50%, 450 ms at 40%; PosCheops three ramps to 300% with up and down phases of 4, 2 and 1.33 s. The code's timings (ecodes_cell_timings in the feature notebooks) agree on every duration. For IV the Methods say 11 steps "from -140 to 20%" by 20%, which is 9 steps; the code's feature files list IV -140 to 60% (11 steps). Readings for IV (a) 11 steps, -140 to 60%; (b) 9 steps, -140 to 20%. The 100% scale is the IDthres scale (sweep k at 50 + 4k %), the rough rheobase from which the protocols were generated (Methods 5.6.5). Reproduced when, in every run of both cells, all eight protocols are present with these sweep counts and durations (within 10%) and every step amplitude is within 10% of its stated percentage of that scale (IV under either reading). Partially reproduced when counts and durations hold and amplitudes do not.

claims.statement: The holding current was set so that the read-out membrane potential was about -70 mV, which is about -84 mV after liquid junction potential correction.
claims.source: Methods 5.6.5, paragraph 1; Methods 5.2
claims.quote: the holding current was manually adjusted to obtain a resting membrane potential of around -70 mV (note that with LJP correction, this corresponds to -84 mV)
claims.criterion: Median membrane potential before the stimulus onset of each sweep (the code's ton, e.g. 400 ms for IDrest), median over sweeps per cell. The paper does not say whether the stored voltages are corrected for the junction potential. Readings (a) uncorrected, compared with -70 mV; (b) corrected, compared with -84 mV (tolerance 8.4 mV). Reproduced for a cell when its value matches under either reading; reproduced when it holds for both cells.

claims.statement: Only cells whose extracellular spikes were at least 50 uV were kept, so both recorded cells show extracellular spikes of 50 uV or more.
claims.source: Methods 5.6.5, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We discarded cells with extracellular spikes lower than 50 μV
claims.criterion: Template of each cell by the template method. The paper does not say how the spike amplitude was measured. Readings (a) the absolute negative peak on the largest channel; (b) the peak-to-peak amplitude on the largest channel. Reproduced when, for both cells, the amplitude is at least 50 uV under either reading.

claims.statement: The HD-MEA recorded more than 500 electrodes near the pipette simultaneously, out of at most 1024, at 20 kHz, and the patch signal was digitized at 20 kHz.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 2; Methods 5.6.2 and 5.6.5
claims.quote: The patch-clamp and the HD-MEA systems were synchronized so that we could simultaneously acquire the patch-clamp readout and the extracellular signals from more 500 electrodes in proximity of the patch pipette
claims.criterion: From the NWB electrodes table and series rates. Methods 5.2 says APWaveform was meant to be recorded "at high sampling rates (typically 200 kHz)", so the APWaveform patch series may be at 20 or 200 kHz. Reproduced when, for each cell, the number of recorded electrodes is above 500 and at most 1024, the MEA rate is 20 kHz, and the patch rate is 20 kHz for every protocol (APWaveform at 20 or 200 kHz).

claims.statement: The cultured cells were recorded between days in vitro 18 and 24.
claims.source: Methods 5.6.3, paragraph 2; Results 3.3, paragraphs 1 and 2
claims.quote: All experiments were conducted between days in vitro (DIVs) 18 and 24
claims.criterion: From the subject or session metadata, if they give the culture age or the plating date. The paper also writes "experiments performed between DIVs 18 and 21" (Results 3.3). Readings (a) 18 to 24; (b) 18 to 21. Reproduced when the age of both recordings lies in either range, widened by 10% of each bound.

claims.statement: In both cells the axon initial segment does not leave the soma but a dendrite (an axon-bearing dendrite).
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 6
claims.quote: Moreover, for both cells, the AIS did not originate directly from the soma but from one of the dendrites, which is termed an axon-bearing dendrite (ABD
claims.criterion: In each reconstructed morphology (SWC), the AIS is the path labeled "apic" (type 4, Methods 5.7.2). Reproduced when, in both cells, the first AIS point's parent is a dendrite point (type 3), not the soma (type 1).

claims.statement: The ground-truth model's rheobase, estimated with a 270 ms step, is 150 pA.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 4
claims.quote: All current amplitudes were computed with respect to the neuron's rheobase current (estimated using a 270 ms step). For our groundtruth model, the rheobase current was 150 pA
claims.criterion: The lowest amplitude of 270 ms steps that elicits a spike in the released ground-truth model, with the step series of the ground-truth notebook.

claims.statement: In the ground-truth model the action potential starts in the distal AIS and travels back toward the soma.
claims.source: Figure 3B; Results 3.2, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The AP is initiated at the distal end of the AIS and travels back toward the soma
claims.criterion: Simulate the released model with IDrest 300% (7-AIS-test.ipynb) and record the membrane potential at the soma, the middle and the distal AIS, as in Figure 3B; the code plots the average of the spike cutouts aligned on the somatic peaks. The paper does not say how the initiation site is read. Readings (a) the time the averaged AP crosses -20 mV (the code's eFEL threshold); (b) the time of the averaged AP peak. Reproduced when, under both readings, the distal AIS comes first, then the middle AIS, then the soma; with readings that disagree, methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: On the simulated 80-electrode MEA, the largest extracellular signal is on the electrode closest to the AIS.
claims.source: Figure 3A; Results 3.2, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The red trace depicts the signal with the largest amplitude, which appears on the electrode closest to the AIS
claims.criterion: The ground-truth template (repository fitting/extracellular/template.npy, or recomputed from the released model on the 20 by 4 probe at 50 um pitch). Reproduced when the channel with the largest peak-to-peak amplitude is the electrode nearest the AIS midpoint in the plane. The paper does not say which amplitude; the largest absolute negative peak is shown as well.

claims.statement: For the ground-truth model, the soma strategy uses 76 intracellular features; all adds 11 extracellular features (87), sections adds 33 (109), and single adds 77 (153).
claims.source: Table 1; Results 3.2, paragraph 6
claims.quote: A total of 76 intracellular features were extracted from these selected protocols ... the all strategy ... adds 11 extracellular features (total = 87). The sections strategy added 33 (three sections times 11 extracellular features), and the single strategy added 77 features
claims.criterion: Counted as the objectives of the evaluator per strategy (the code's "num features" cell in 3-compute-all-responses.ipynb). Tolerance 0 as these are counts fixed by design. The Methods 5.4 list "total of 79 features" for optimization; that count is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: On the ground-truth model, soma, all and sections give good intracellular fitness and single worse; single gives the best extracellular fitness and soma the worst.
claims.source: Figure 4A; Results 3.2, paragraph 7
claims.quote: While the soma, all, and sections strategies appeared to yield low scores (i.e., better fitness) for intracellular features, the single strategy produced solutions with worse intracellular fitness. Conversely, the single strategy yielded the best performance with respect to extracellular features, while the worst performance was achieved by using the soma strategy
claims.criterion: Fitting method, 10 seeds per strategy, intracellular and extracellular scores per seed. No test is reported. The paper shows box plots, so the medians over seeds are compared, with means as a variant. Reproduced when single has the highest intracellular median, single the lowest extracellular median and soma the highest extracellular median.

claims.statement: Over the ten seeds, the ground-truth fits reach intracellular scores of 62.8 +/- 13.6 for soma and 59.3 +/- 17.0 for all.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 3
claims.quote: (intracellular score: GT fitting: 62.8 ± 13.6 for soma and 59.3 ± 17.0 for all
claims.criterion: Fitting method, mean over the ten seeds; tolerances are the paper's stated spread (not named as SD or SEM; the SD over seeds is reported for comparison).

claims.statement: In validation, only the single strategy reproduces that the ground-truth model fires no spike in the depolarizing phase of HyperDepol -160% and one at HyperDepol -40%; soma, all and sections fire at -160%.
claims.source: Figure 4C; Results 3.2, paragraph 8
claims.quote: the soma, all, and sections strategies failed to reproduce the absence of spikes observed in the depolarization phase (second row: HyperDepol (−160%). Only the single ... strategy correctly did not generate a spike for HyperDepol (−160%) and did generate one for HyperDepol (−40%)
claims.criterion: Fitting method; for each strategy the seed with the lowest intracellular score (Figure 4C legend, and 3-compute-all-responses.ipynb). Spike count (eFEL, -20 mV) in the 270 ms depolarizing phase of HyperDepol -160% and -40%. Reproduced when the ground truth has 0 and at least 1 spikes, single matches both, and soma, all and sections each fire at -160%.

claims.statement: On validation protocols (86 intracellular features), the best solutions of the four strategies do not differ in intracellular feature scores.
claims.source: Figure 4B, left; Results 3.2, paragraph 8
claims.quote: No significant differences were ... detected across strategies (post hoc Mann-Whitney tests with Holm p-value correction)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Best-intracellular seed per strategy; validation protocols firepattern, HyperDepol, sAHP, PosCheops; feature score |GT - model| / (0.05 |GT|), a missing model feature set to 50 (4-optimization-performance.ipynb). Test as the paper names it, two-sided Mann-Whitney between strategies with Holm correction. The paper states no alpha and not which pairs; readings (a) soma against each other strategy (3 pairs), (b) all 6 pairs, each at alpha 0.05, the conventional level. Reproduced when no corrected p is below 0.05 under the reading in use; with two readings that disagree, methods_underspecified. The code runs a Conover post hoc test with Holm correction (scikit_posthocs.posthoc_conover); shown as a variant.

claims.statement: On extracellular features computed on all 80 electrodes (796 features), all three extracellular strategies score significantly better than the soma strategy.
claims.source: Figure 4B, right; Results 3.2, paragraph 8
claims.quote: All strategies making use of extracellular data significantly outperformed the soma strategy (post hoc Mann-Whitney tests with Holm p-value correction: soma VS all - p < 10−5, soma VS sections - p < 10−5, soma VS single - p < 10−5
claims.criterion: Best-intracellular seed per strategy; template from firepattern 120%; the 11 features on each of the 80 channels, invalid values left out; feature score |GT - model| / (0.05 |GT|), or |model| when GT is 0 (4-optimization-performance.ipynb). Two-sided Mann-Whitney, soma against each other strategy. The paper does not say over which pairs the Holm correction runs. Readings (a) the three soma comparisons; (b) all six pairs of strategies (as the code's Conover test does). Reproduced when, under both readings, each soma comparison has corrected p below 1e-5 with the other strategy's median score lower; partially reproduced when all three are below 0.05 but not all below 1e-5; with readings that disagree, methods_underspecified. The code's Conover test (scikit_posthocs.posthoc_conover, Holm) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The extracellular strategies fit the ground-truth template better on almost all electrodes, while the soma solution fails to capture the extracellular signals on many channels.
claims.source: Figure 4D; Results 3.2, paragraph 8
claims.quote: It is evident at first glance that the three extracellular strategies achieve a better fit for almost all electrodes, while the solution from the soma strategy ... failed to capture the complex dynamics of extracellular signals in many recording channels
claims.criterion: Templates from firepattern 120%, each channel normalized to its peak-to-peak (Figure 4D legend; the code divides by np.ptp of the absolute values, shown as a variant); per channel, the sum of absolute differences from the ground truth (the code's eap_dist, taken per channel). The legend names the seed with the best intracellular score, as the code does; the Results text says the best extracellular fit, shown as a variant. "Almost all" is not quantified. Readings (a) each extracellular strategy is closer than soma on more than half of the 80 channels; (b) on at least 72 of 80 (90%). Reproduced when the readings agree that each of all, sections and single is closer; with readings that disagree, methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Across the neuron, the all strategy gives lower AP waveform errors than the soma strategy at every tested location, and all extracellular strategies beat soma at every dendritic location.
claims.source: Figure 5; Results 3.2, paragraph 9
claims.quote: For all tested locations, the all strategy produces lower errors than the strategy. For all dendritic locations (both apical and basal), all extracellular strategies (all, single, sections) outperform the soma strategy
claims.criterion: Best-intracellular seed per strategy; firepattern 120%; APs detected at the soma, first and last left out, averaged at 8 locations (code positions, apical distal left and right, apical middle, apical proximal, basal left and right, AIS distal and proximal); amplitude, half-width, decay time and AHP by the code's compute_features; mean relative error of the four against the ground truth. The first sentence lacks a word ("than the strategy"); the reading is "than the soma strategy", the only one the next sentence allows. Reproduced when all is below soma at all 8 locations and all, single and sections are each below soma at the 6 dendritic ones; partially reproduced when only one of the two holds.

claims.statement: For both experimental cells, the soma strategy gives better intracellular scores and the all strategy better extracellular scores.
claims.source: Figures 7A and 8A; Results 3.3, paragraph 3
claims.quote: For both cell models, the application of the soma strategy yielded better intracellular scores, while the use of the all strategy resulted in better extracellular fitting
claims.criterion: Fitting method on each cell; features extracted from the dataset's patch recordings (runs as in recordings-two-cells-runs; BluePyEfe with the rheobase from IDthres. Methods 5.4 give the lowest amplitude triggering a spike in the majority of recordings, and an amplitude tolerance of 10%; these are the main result. The code (1-generate-experimental-features notebooks) sets the majority fraction to 0.4 for cell 1 and 0.2 for cell 2 and the tolerance to 30; shown as a variant) and the template method's template; morphology and model from the repository. 10 seeds each for soma and all. No test is reported; medians over seeds compared (box plots), means as a variant. Reproduced when, for both cells, soma has the lower median intracellular score and all the lower median extracellular score; partially reproduced when this holds for one cell.

claims.statement: Intracellular scores are 123.9 +/- 11.2 (soma) and 149.2 +/- 47.2 (all, one non-converging seed left out) for cell 1, and 152.8 +/- 9.22 (soma) and 177.6 +/- 20.4 (all) for cell 2, almost twice those of the ground-truth fits.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 3
claims.quote: cell 1 fitting: 123.9 ± 11.2 for soma and 149.2 ± 47.2 (excluding one seed that did not converge) for all; cell 2 fitting: 152.8 ± 9.22 for soma and 177.6 ± 20.4 for all
claims.criterion: As in fig78a-soma-intra-all-extra, mean over seeds; tolerances are the stated spread. Which seed "did not converge" is not said. Readings (a) the seed whose solution fires no spike (NaN template, dropped in 3-compute-all-responses_cell1.ipynb); (b) the seed with the highest intracellular score. Reproduced when all four values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: The experimental cell models of both strategies reproduce the main features of the spiking patterns of the validation protocols, except the soma model's PosCheops 300% response in cell 2, so including extracellular features does not keep the optimization from finding acceptable models.
claims.source: Figures 7B and 8B; Results 3.3, paragraphs 3 and 6
claims.quote: the models fitted on the experimental data could reproduce the main features of the intracellular spiking patterns of the validation protocols (panels B, with the exception of the PosCheops (300%) response for the soma strategy in cell 2
claims.criterion: The seed with the best intracellular score per strategy and cell (Figure 7B and 8B legends, and the code that makes the figures, 4-optimization-performance-cell1 and -cell2, best_intras; the 3-compute-all-responses notebooks also select the best extracellular seed for their own plots, shown as a variant). Validation protocols firepattern, HyperDepol, sAHP and PosCheops (Methods 5.4). "Main features" is not quantified. Readings (a) the model's spike count in each validation sweep lies within the range over the cell's runs; (b) the model's mean firing frequency (eFEL mean_frequency, one of the Methods 5.4 validation features) in each spiking sweep lies within that range. Reproduced when the readings agree that every model matches all its sweeps except the soma model of cell 2 on PosCheops 300%, which does not; partially reproduced when only that exception differs; with readings that disagree, methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: The simulated templates are qualitatively similar to the recorded ones, with mismatches mainly in cell 2, whose fits have higher extracellular scores than cell 1.
claims.source: Figures 7C and 8C, and 7A and 8A right; Results 3.3, paragraph 4
claims.quote: The worse fit of cell 2 with respect to cell 1 is also ... reflected by the overall higher extracellular scores
claims.criterion: Extracellular scores per seed as in fig78a-soma-intra-all-extra. The text cites "right box plots of panels B", which hold no box plots; panels A right are meant. Readings (a) the all strategy alone; (b) both strategies. Reproduced when the cell 2 median extracellular score is above the cell 1 median under both readings; with readings that disagree, methods_underspecified. The summed per-channel distance of normalized templates (eap_dist in the code) is reported for the best seed of each strategy and cell.

claims.statement: In the cell 2 all model, the template mismatch is explained by too small a somatic and too large an AIS contribution; the recorded positive upstroke near the basal dendrite coincides with the somatic negative current peak, and the initial negative phase with the AIS peak.
claims.source: Figure 10 legend; Results 3.3, paragraph 5
claims.quote: The upstroke of the experimental EAP close to the basal dendrite ... seems to coincide with the somatic negative peak ... The initial negative phase instead is time-locked to the AIS negative peak
claims.criterion: Best-intracellular cell 2 all model (Figure 10 legend and Results 3.3 name the all model; the code, 5-AP-dirstirbution-cell2.ipynb, passes the soma model's parameters, opt_results_validation["soma"], shown as a variant); transmembrane currents at the soma, the AIS and a basal dendrite (code, extra_recordings_from_positions with_currents, positions soma [0, 0, 0], basal [-92, 11, 0], AIS [-48, 5, 0] um, IDrest 250%, averaged over spike cutouts of 2 ms before and 5 ms after), aligned to the recorded template; the electrode near the basal dendrite and the one near the AIS are those nearest these positions (code, elec_idx_basal and elec_idx_ais). How the model and recorded time axes are aligned is not given; both are cut 2 ms before the peak, which is used. Reproduced when, on the electrode near the basal dendrite, the time of the recorded positive peak is nearer the somatic negative current peak than the AIS one, and the recorded initial negative peak nearer the AIS negative current peak than the somatic one. The electrode and dendrite location are those of Figure 10, which the text does not give by number; the 5-AP-dirstirbution-cell2 notebook positions are used.

claims.statement: The paper's data are the 50 sessions of Table 2, deposited on DANDI as dandiset 000037, with files named by subject and session ID. This claim checks whether dandiset 000336 holds any of those sessions.
claims.source: Data Records, paragraph 1 and Data organization; Table 2
claims.quote: The full dataset is publicly available in the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) format 24 on the DANDI Archive ( https://dandiarchive.org/dandiset/000037 )
claims.criterion: Sessions are matched by the subject ID and session ID of Table 2 (the naming convention of Data organization is sub-{subject ID}_ses-{session ID}, and the IDs may also be in the files' subject and session metadata). The link holds (reproduced) when dandiset 000336 holds the 33 sessions 1 to 3 that passed QC, the set the paper's figures use; partially reproduced when it holds some of the 50 sessions of Table 2; not reproduced when it holds none. When it holds none, every other claim in this file can only be tested on DANDI:000037.

claims.statement: 13 mice were imaged, 3 in L2/3-D, 3 in L2/3-S, 4 in L5-D and 3 in L5-S, 7 male and 6 female, each with at least three imaging sessions.
claims.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 3; Table 1; Data Records, Animal and recording session attributes, paragraph 1
claims.quote: 13 mice in total underwent imaging (L2/3-D: n = 3, L2/3-S: n = 3, L5-D: n = 4, L5-S: n = 3) with at least three optical imaging sessions recorded in each ... the dataset is well-split between male (7) and female (6) subjects
claims.criterion: Counts of subject records, so the tolerance is 0. Line and plane per mouse from the files' subject and imaging plane metadata (Cux2 is L2/3, Rbp4 is L5; plane depth as in Table 2), checked against Table 1, which gives the sex, date of birth, cell type and plane of each of the 13 subject IDs.

claims.statement: 50 imaging sessions were recorded from the 13 mice. Two mice have sessions that failed QC; the sessions 1 to 3 that passed QC are 33 files.
claims.source: Data Records, Animal and recording session attributes, paragraph 1; Table 2; Usage Notes, paragraph 1
claims.quote: data for 50 recording sessions total were gathered from 13 animals. Of these, two animals had at least one session that did not meet ... If only the basic data files for sessions 1 to 3 that passed quality control are needed, the total download size is approximately 15 GB for 33 files in total
claims.criterion: Counts of session records, tolerance 0. A session is one session ID of Table 2, with the QC status of Table 2 (the files may not carry it; Table 2 and mouse_df.csv of the paper's code give it). Table 2 lists failed sessions for 411400, 412933 and 440889, three mice, while the text says two; the readings are (a) mice whose sessions 1 to 3 include a failed session (411400 and 412933, the two left out of the paper's figures), or (b) any failed session (three mice). The count of 2 holds under reading (a); the count under (b) is reported.

claims.statement: After habituation each mouse had three 70-minute imaging sessions within three to six days, at most one per day.
claims.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 1; Fig. 2a
claims.quote: they underwent three 70-minute optical imaging sessions within a span of three to six days, with no more than one session occurring per day
claims.criterion: Session dates from the files' session start times, taken as local (Pacific) dates as in Table 2; start times stored in UTC can fall on the next day (the paper's code table mouse_df.csv gives 418779's sessions UTC dates 20181113 to 20181115 against Table 2's 20181112 to 20181114), so UTC dates are shown as a variant only. Two details are open. Which three sessions, (a) sessions 1 to 3 of each mouse as numbered in the paper's mouse_df.csv, or (b) the three tracked sessions (those with a nonzero tracked count in Table 2). What the span counts, (i) the days from the first session date to the third, or (ii) the calendar days inclusive. Reproduced when, under one pairing of readings, every mouse has its three sessions on distinct dates within a span of three to six days, and the session durations are within tolerance of 70 min. How a session's duration is measured is not stated; the readings are (x) first to last two-photon frame, and (y) the first stimulus onset to the last stimulus offset in the stimulus table, grey screen included. The spans and durations under every reading are reported.

claims.statement: Somata were imaged at 175 um (L2/3) and 375 um (L5) and distal apical dendrites at 50 to 75 um (L2/3) and 20 um (L5), at 30 Hz with 512 x 512 pixels over a 400 um field of view.
claims.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraphs 2 and 4; Table 2
claims.quote: two-photon calcium imaging was performed in either the cell body layer for somatic recordings (175 μ m depth for layer 2/3 and 375 μ m depth for layer 5) or in cortical layer 1 for distal apical dendritic recordings (50–75 μ m depth for layer 2/3 and 20 μ m depth for layer 5) ... Calcium fluorescence movies were recorded at 30 Hz with resonant scanners over a 400 μ m field of view with a resolution of 512 × 512 pixels
claims.criterion: From the imaging plane metadata (depth, rate) and the image dimensions. Image size is a count, tolerance 0. Depths are judged against Table 2, session by session, as exact values (they are targeted depths, recorded as metadata). Reproduced when every session's depth matches Table 2 and the rate and size are within tolerance.

claims.statement: 15 to 224 ROIs per session were retained in the somatic planes and 159 to 1636 in the dendritic planes.
claims.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 6; Table 2
claims.quote: In the somatic layers, 15–224 ROIs per mouse per session were identified and retained for analysis, compared to 159–1636 ROIs in the dendritic layers.
claims.criterion: A reported range, so it holds inside the range widened by 10% of each bound (13.5 to 246.4 somatic, 143.1 to 1799.6 dendritic). The ROI count of a session is the number of ROIs in its file (Table 2, "# ROIs"); the paper's code also drops ROIs with NaN or Inf values, and that count is shown as a variant. Which sessions is open, (a) the 33 sessions 1 to 3 that passed QC, as the code uses; (b) every session that passed QC; (c) all 50 sessions. Reproduced when, under one reading, the smallest and largest counts of each plane type fall within the widened range, and each session's count equals Table 2.

claims.statement: ROI matching across the three sessions gave 254 tracked ROIs in L2/3-D, 261 in L2/3-S, 516 in L5-D and 129 in L5-S, about 32 to 75% of the theoretical maximum.
claims.source: Methods, ROI tracking across sessions, paragraph 1; Table 2 ("# Tracked ROIs")
claims.quote: In total, the modified matching algorithm produced ~100–500 highly plausible matched ROIs per plane, i.e., ~32–75% of the theoretical maximum number of trackable ROIs (L2/3-D: n = 254, L2/3-S: n = 261, L5-D: n = 516, L5-S: n = 129)
