claims.criterion: Tracked ROIs are counted from the ROI tracking indices in the files, summed over the mice of a plane, for the 11 mice whose sessions 1 to 3 passed QC (the per-plane counts equal the sums of Table 2's tracked counts over those mice). These are counts of deposited indices, so the tolerance is 0. The theoretical maximum is not defined in the paper or the code. Readings, (a) per plane, the sum over mice of the smallest ROI count among the mouse's three sessions; (b) per plane, the sum over mice of the mean ROI count of its three sessions; (c) per mouse, the same as (a), giving one fraction per mouse. The range is a reported range, widened by 10% of each bound (28.8 to 82.5%). Reproduced when the four counts match and, under one reading, the smallest and largest fractions lie within the widened range; partially reproduced when the counts match and no reading puts the fractions in range.

claims.statement: In the example L2/3-D mouse, taking the union of matches over all session orderings and removing four conflicting matches gave 136 final matches; in the example L5-S mouse, removing two conflicts gave 47.
claims.source: Figure 8a and 8b legends
claims.quote: In this example, four pairwise matches were identified as conflicts and removed, yielding 136 final matches ... enable two of the pairwise matches to be identified as conflicts and removed, yielding 47 final matches
claims.criterion: The examples are mouse 6 (dendritic, plane "dend") and mouse 4 (somatic) of the paper's code (paper_organization.py, dendritic_roi_tracking_example and somatic_roi_tracking_example), which mouse_df.csv gives as subjects 413663 and 411771. Final matches are the tracked ROIs of their files, tolerance 0 as deposited counts. The conflict counts (4 and 2) come from the matching run over orderings, whose custom-modified code is not public (the repository holds only its outputs in roi_tracking/); they can only be tested by rerunning matching (see fig8-ordering-variation) and are reported, not judged, from such a rerun. Reproduced when both final match counts are exact.

claims.statement: The number of matched ROIs depends on the order in which sessions are aligned, and this variation is far smaller for somata than for dendrites.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 5; Figure 8a and 8b legends
claims.quote: The variation in number of matched ROIs across session orderings for somata was generally far less than that for dendrites due to their larger sizes and more regular shapes.
claims.criterion: Requires rerunning the matching on the ROI masks, which the files hold. The paper used a custom-modified version of github.com/AllenInstitute/ophys_nway_matching that is not public; the Methods give its one added rule, that dendritic matches must overlap by at least 10 to 20%. Open details and readings, the overlap threshold (a) 10% or (b) 20%; the measure of variation, (i) the range (largest minus smallest) of match counts over the six orderings divided by their mean, or (ii) the standard deviation over orderings divided by the mean. Run with the public package at a pinned commit and default parameters otherwise, over the six orderings of each tracked mouse's three sessions. Reproduced when, under every reading, the mean variation over the somatic mice is smaller than over the dendritic mice; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. Not testable if the public package cannot be run on these masks.

claims.statement: Each imaging session lasts 70 minutes, with 34 minutes of Gabor sequences and 17 minutes of visual flow in each direction, each stimulus period flanked by 30 s of grey screen.
claims.source: Methods, Visual stimulation, paragraph 1
claims.quote: optical imaging sessions always lasted 70 minutes, comprising 34 minutes of Gabor sequence stimulus and 17 minutes of visual flow stimulus in each direction. Each stimulus period was flanked by 1 or 30 seconds of grayscreen for the habituation and optical imaging sessions, respectively
claims.criterion: From the stimulus parameter table of each of the 33 analysed sessions (onset and offset times of each stimulus and of grey screen). The stimulus code fixes the same durations (run_generate_stimuli.py, gab_dur 34 min and sq_dur 17 min per visual flow block). Reproduced when every session's values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Inconsistent sequences are about 7% of Gabor sequences and 5% of visual flow time, in about 30 blocks per session, each 30 to 90 s of consistent stimulus followed by 3 to 6 s (Gabor) or 2 to 4 s (visual flow) of inconsistent stimulus.
claims.source: Methods, Visual stimulation, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Inconsistent sequences, accounting for approximately 7% of the Gabor sequences and 5% of visual flow stimulus time, only occurred on optical imaging days, and not on habituation days. In particular, each 70-minute imaging session was broken up into approximately 30 blocks, each comprising 30–90 seconds of consistent sequences followed by several seconds of inconsistent sequences
claims.criterion: From the stimulus parameter tables of the 33 analysed sessions. Gabor fraction, sequences whose fourth image is U over all sequences; visual flow fraction, the time with reversed squares over all visual flow time. Open, (a) the mean of per-session fractions, or (b) the fraction pooled over sessions. A block is a run of consistent stimulus followed by inconsistent stimulus; the stimulus code samples blocks separately within the Gabor period and within each visual flow period (stimulus_params.py, createseqlen). "30 blocks per session" is open, (i) per stimulus (Gabor blocks; visual flow blocks of both directions together), or (ii) all blocks of the session. Reproduced when, under one reading, both fractions and the block count are within tolerance and every consistent and inconsistent duration lies in the stated ranges.

claims.statement: Somatic and dendritic ROIs respond to both the Gabor and the visual flow stimuli, many with increased fluorescence at stimulus onset, and their responses differ between consistent and inconsistent stimuli.
claims.source: Overview of data, paragraph 1; Figure 5a to 5d
claims.quote: Both the somatic and dendritic ROIs showed clear responses to both the Gabor and visual flow stimuli, with many showing increased fluorescence responses to the onset of the stimuli ... There were also clear differences in the responses to the consistent versus inconsistent stimuli as well
claims.criterion: The paper shows randomly chosen example ROIs and runs no test. Session 1 of each of the 11 analysed mice, per plane (line and plane). Windows from the code (paper_organization.py) are 0.9 s before to 0.6 s after the onset of D or U images for Gabor sequences, and 2 s before to 2 s after the onset of inconsistent flow, for each flow direction. ROI selection, open, (a) all ROIs, or (b) the ROIs the Fig. 5 legends select (SNR above the session median, and the median pairwise correlation of single-sequence responses, smoothed with a four-point moving average, and the standard deviation and skew of the mean response for Gabor, or the inconsistent minus consistent mean response for flow, each above the session's 75th percentile). The response measure is the mean dF/F over 0 to 0.6 s after D against after U (Gabor), and over 0 to 2 s after against 2 s before inconsistent flow onset (flow), per ROI. The test is open, as the paper names none; the readings are (i) a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test across ROIs at p < 0.05, and (ii) the mean difference across ROIs exceeding twice its SEM (the legends plot mean and SEM). Reproduced when, under every reading pair, at least one stimulus in each of the four planes shows a consistent against inconsistent difference; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. The ROI-wise differences are reported for every plane, stimulus and reading. The first part of the statement (increased fluorescence at stimulus onset) is not judged here; it is tested, for grey screen to stimulus onsets, by fig9-onset-offset-transients.

claims.statement: Running velocity and pupil diameter were recorded in every analysed session, for the 11 mice whose data are shown aggregated in Fig. 6b.
claims.source: Overview of data, paragraph 2; Figure 6b legend; Methods, Running and pupil tracking
claims.quote: Histograms of aggregated running velocities ( top ) and pupil diameters ( bottom ), for each session. Data is stacked across all mice (11)
claims.criterion: A count of mice, tolerance 0. Reproduced when each of the 33 analysed sessions has a running velocity trace (cm/s) and a pupil diameter trace (mm) spanning the session. Running is median-filtered over five frames and frames with a single-frame change of at least 50 cm/s are dropped; pupil frames with a single-frame change of at least 0.05 mm are dropped (Methods, Running and pupil tracking); the code's pupil_run_histograms keeps missing data uninterpolated (rem_bad False). Histogram ranges are not judged.

claims.statement: ROI SNR is relatively high, above 1, in every plane and session, and stable over the three days.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 7a
claims.quote: demonstrate that our recordings have relatively high SNR (>1) and that this is quite stable over days
claims.criterion: SNR per ROI as in the Methods and calculate_snr (see the opening comment), on the unscaled dF/F trace of the whole session, all ROIs without NaN or Inf values, sessions 1 to 3 of the 11 analysed mice, ROIs pooled across mice within each line, plane and session (12 groups). "Above 1" is open, (a) the group median above 1 (the figure marks 1 as noise level on box plots of medians), or (b) the group 25th percentile above 1. "Stable over days" is open, as the paper gives no test, (i) within each plane, each session's median lies inside the 25th to 75th percentile box of each other session, or (ii) within each plane, each session's median is within 10% of the mean of the three session medians. Reproduced when every reading pair holds for all four planes; not reproduced when none does; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. Every group's median and quartiles are reported.

claims.statement: The mean dF/F signal of the ROIs is stable over days.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 7b
claims.quote: Similarly, the mean ΔF/F signal was stable over days
claims.criterion: The signal of an ROI is the mean of its dF/F values above the noise threshold used for SNR (Fig. 7b legend; calculate_snr, signal_mean). ROIs, sessions and groups as in fig7a-snr-high-stable. "Stable over days" has the readings (i) and (ii) of fig7a-snr-high-stable. Reproduced when both readings hold for all four planes; not reproduced when neither does; blocked as methods_underspecified when they disagree. Every group's median and quartiles are reported.

claims.statement: The distributions of pairwise ROI correlations are very similar for apical dendrite ROIs and for somatic ROIs, so the dendrites are unlikely to be heavily over-segmented.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3; Figure 7c
claims.quote: The distributions of correlation coefficients were very similar for the apical dendrite ROIs and for the somatic ROIs ... suggesting that we were unlikely to be heavily over-segmenting the dendritic data
claims.criterion: Pearson correlations over all ROI pairs of each session, from whole-session dF/F traces smoothed with a 4-sample rolling mean (Fig. 7c legend; get_correlation, rolling_win 4), ROIs without NaN or Inf values, sessions 1 to 3 of the 11 analysed mice, pooled across mice within each line, plane and session. Comparisons are dendritic against somatic within a line and session (six comparisons). The paper gives no measure of similarity. Its argument is that over-segmentation would give many highly correlated dendritic pairs, so the readings are (i) the dendritic median correlation lies inside the somatic 25th to 75th percentile range, and (ii) the dendritic 99th percentile does not exceed the somatic 99th percentile by more than 10% of the latter. Reproduced when both readings hold in all six comparisons; not reproduced when neither holds in most; blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise. Quantiles and the fractions of pairs above 0.8 are reported for every group.

claims.statement: About 0.01% of possible pairs of L2/3 dendritic ROIs have correlations above 0.8.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: ROIs with correlations above 0.8 (e.g., approximately 0.01% of possible pairs of L2/3 dendrites)
claims.criterion: Correlations as in fig7c-correlations-similar. The tolerance is half the last printed digit (values that round to 0.01% at one significant figure), since the paper writes "approximately" and the default 10% would demand more precision than it gives. The denominator is open, (a) pairs pooled over the L2/3-D sessions 1 to 3 of the analysed mice, (b) the mean of per-session fractions over those sessions, (c) session 1 only. Reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Mean dF/F traces show distinct transients aligned with the stimulus onsets and offsets (grey screen to stimulus and back), in every plane and session.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 6; Figure 9a and 9b
claims.quote: These ΔF/F traces show distinct transients that align with the stimulus onsets and offsets
claims.criterion: Onsets and offsets, windows and averaging as the code fixes them (see the opening comment; stimulus_onset_sess123 and stimulus_offset_sess123, pre 2 s, post 2 s, both stimuli), for sessions 1 to 3 of the 11 analysed mice, per line, plane and session (12 groups). Per ROI, the mean dF/F over 0 to 2 s after the event minus the mean over 2 s before. The paper gives no test and no sign for offsets. Readings, (i) the mean of this difference across ROIs exceeds twice its SEM in absolute value (the figure plots mean and SEM across ROIs), and (ii) a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test across ROIs at p < 0.05. Reproduced when both readings find a transient at onset and at offset in all 12 groups, partially reproduced when they agree that some groups lack one, blocked as methods_underspecified when they disagree. The Fig. 9a legend names the Gabor sequence onset only, while the text and the code use both stimuli; onsets of the Gabor stimulus alone are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: In prolonged open loop, fish cycle between passive epochs lasting 24.4 +/- 2.5 s and active epochs lasting 36.1 +/- 4.2 s (mean +/- SEM, n = 74 fish), swimming 29 +/- 6 times per active epoch.
claims.source: Figure 1H; Results, Withholding Visual Feedback during Swimming Induces Passivity, paragraph 3; STAR Methods, Futility-induced passivity behavioral analysis
claims.quote: Passive states (epochs when the animal did not swim for at least 5 s; Figures S1A and S1B) lasted 24.4 ± 2.5 s (mean ± SEM), and active states lasted 36.1 ± 4.2 s (n = 74; Figure 1H). ... the fish swam 29 ± 6 times (n = 74) during each epoch.
claims.criterion: The mean over fish of each fish's mean, in open loop. Readings, listed before the analysis; (a) epochs built from SwimIntervals by the Methods' rule; (b) the active and passive rows of the dandiset's ActivityStates table, over the whole recording, as the table does not say which condition they belong to; (c) as (a), with all epochs pooled over fish. Reproduced when, under one reading, all three values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when two are. The 12 fish here are a subset of the paper's 74.

claims.statement: In closed loop fish swim in discrete bouts about once per second (inter-swim interval 1.2 +/- 0.05 s, n = 74), and within active epochs of open loop the interval is 1.19 +/- 0.047 s against 24.4 s in passive epochs.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Futility-induced passivity behavioral analysis
claims.quote: Paralyzed fish in closed loop in our VR setup typically swam in discrete bouts, about once per second (1.2 ± 0.05 s, n = 74). ... (1.19 ± 0.047 s inter-swim-interval in active epochs versus 24.4 ± 2.5 s in passive epochs, n = 74, Figure S1B).
claims.criterion: Per fish the mean interval between successive bouts, then the mean over fish. The interval can be read as (a) start to start of successive bouts, or (b) end of one bout to the start of the next; and in closed loop as (i) intervals under 5 s, or (ii) all intervals. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when one is.

claims.statement: Fish spend much more time in the passive state when swimming produces no visual feedback (open loop) than in closed loop with a naturalistic gain, where passivity is rare.
claims.source: Figure 1J; Figure 1C to E; Results, Withholding Visual Feedback during Swimming Induces Passivity, paragraphs 3 and 4
claims.quote: Prevalence of the passive behavioral state depended on the motosensory gain ... As the gain approached 0 (i.e., open loop), fish gradually spent more and more time in the passive state.
claims.criterion: Per fish, the fraction of time in passive epochs (gaps of 5 s or more between bouts) in closed loop and in open loop. Reproduced when the open-loop fraction is higher by a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over fish at p < 0.05 and the median closed-loop fraction is below 10%; partially reproduced when only the test holds.

claims.statement: When switched from closed to open loop, fish first swim with higher vigor, then stop swimming.
claims.source: Figure 1C; Results, Withholding Visual Feedback during Swimming Induces Passivity, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In open loop, fish first swam with higher vigor, then stopped swimming for several to tens of seconds.
claims.criterion: For each switch from closed to open loop, the mean power (SwimIntervals) of the bouts from the switch to the first passive epoch, over the mean power of the bouts in the 30 s of closed loop before the switch. Per fish the median log ratio over switches. Reproduced when the log ratio is above 0 by a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over fish at p < 0.05. Switches with fewer than 3 bouts on either side are left out.

claims.statement: Before the switch to passivity the inter-swim interval increases progressively, and fish swim more vigorously and less frequently in the seconds before passivity.
claims.source: Figure 1I (n = 61 fish); Results, Withholding Visual Feedback during Swimming Induces Passivity, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Several seconds prior to passivity, fish swam more vigorously and less frequently and attempted to make larger amplitude turns (Figures 1I and S1C). ... Before the switch to passivity, inter-swim interval progressively increased, n = 61 fish
claims.criterion: For each passivity onset whose active epoch holds at least 10 bouts, the start-to-start intervals numbered back from the last one (k = 1 is the interval ending at the last bout) and the power of the bouts numbered back from the last. Per fish the mean at each k. Reproduced when the interval at k = 1 is longer than at k = 7 (one-sided Wilcoxon over fish, p < 0.05), the Spearman correlation between k and the mean over fish for k = 1 to 7 is negative, and the mean power of the last 3 bouts is higher than that of bouts 8 to 10 before onset (one-sided Wilcoxon over fish, p < 0.05). Partially reproduced when the interval part holds and the power part does not, or the reverse.

claims.statement: Whole-brain average neuronal activity is higher during active behavior than during passivity, and decays after passivity onset.
claims.source: Figure 2B and 2C; Results, Correlates of Passivity in Neuronal and Astrocytic Activity, paragraph 2
claims.quote: When animals switched from the active to the passive behavioral state, whole-brain average neuronal activity decreased ... Average neuronal Ca2+ decayed after passivity onset
claims.criterion: In the 8 files with processed neuronal traces, per fish the mean of the whole-brain neuronal signal over open-loop passive epochs minus that over open-loop active epochs. Reproduced when it is below 0 by a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over fish at p < 0.05. The change after onset (5 to 10 s after, minus 10 to 5 s before) is reported per fish.

claims.statement: Whole-brain average radial astrocyte calcium increases before passivity onset and peaks soon after it.
claims.source: Figure 2B and 2C (one example fish, 64 events); Figure 2G and 2I; Results, Correlates of Passivity in Neuronal and Astrocytic Activity, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Average neuronal Ca2+ decayed after passivity onset, while average glial Ca2+ increased before passivity onset and peaked soon after. ... This increase in glial Ca2+ started seconds before passivity onset
claims.criterion: In the 4 files with processed glial traces, per passivity onset the glial signal averaged over 1 to 4 s after onset minus its mean over 10 to 5 s before (the paper's reliability windows), and the mean over 2 to 0 s before onset minus the same baseline. Per fish, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over onsets. Reproduced when, in at least 3 of the 4 fish, both the after-onset increase and the before-onset increase have p < 0.05 and the peak of the onset-triggered average lies between 0 and 10 s after onset. Partially reproduced when only the after-onset increase holds in at least 3 fish. The number of onsets per fish is compared with the 64 events of the paper's example.

claims.statement: Whole-brain average neuronal and glial calcium are higher and fluctuate more strongly in open loop than in closed loop.
claims.source: Results, Correlates of Passivity in Neuronal and Astrocytic Activity, paragraph 2; Figure S2A
claims.quote: Both neuronal and glial Ca2+, averaged across the brain, were higher and fluctuated more strongly in open loop than in closed loop (Figure S2A).
claims.criterion: Per fish, the mean and the standard deviation of the whole-brain signal over open-loop time and over closed-loop time, leaving out the first 30 s after each switch. Neurons (8 fish); one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over fish for open above closed at p < 0.05. Glia (4 fish); open above closed in all 4 (a Wilcoxon test over 4 fish cannot reach p < 0.05). Reproduced when both measures hold for both cell types; partially reproduced when at least one measure holds for one cell type.

claims.statement: When fish in closed loop stop swimming because the stimulus stops moving, glial calcium signals are weaker than during futility-induced passivity.
claims.source: Figure 2H and 2M; Results, Correlates of Passivity in Neuronal and Astrocytic Activity, paragraph 3
claims.quote: When fish in a closed-loop protocol stopped swimming because the stimulus stopped moving, glial Ca2+ signals were weaker than during futility-induced passivity (Figure 2H).
claims.criterion: In the 4 files with processed glial traces, closed-loop pauses are gaps of 5 s or more between bouts that start in closed-loop time or in stationary-grating time with gain above 0. Response as in fig2c-glia-rise-at-passivity (1 to 4 s after onset minus 10 to 5 s before). Per fish, a one-sided Mann-Whitney test of closed-loop pause responses against open-loop passivity responses. Fish with fewer than 3 closed-loop pauses are left out; the claim is blocked (other) when fewer than 2 fish remain. Reproduced when the pause responses are smaller with p < 0.05 in every remaining fish; partially reproduced when they are smaller in median in every remaining fish.

claims.statement: Non-negative matrix factorization of neurons and radial astrocytes gives components consistent across fish; glial component 1, in the lateral medulla oblongata (L-MO), is the most reliable, rising before and peaking after passivity onset (n = 5 neuron fish, 6 glia fish).
claims.source: Figure 2D to 2G; Results, Correlates of Passivity in Neuronal and Astrocytic Activity, paragraph 3
claims.quote: We clustered the components into a set that occurred consistently across all fish ... identified a consistent subset of glial signals (Figure 2G, component 1). Calcium in astrocyte component 1 increased before and peaked after passivity onset

claims.statement: Of all brain regions, radial astrocytes in L-MO show the most consistent increases at passivity onset, with ramping signals before it.
claims.source: Figure 2K, 2L and 2M; Results, Correlates of Passivity in Neuronal and Astrocytic Activity, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Of all brain regions, L-MO radial astrocytes showed the most consistent increases in activity during passivity (Figure 2L) and showed ramping Ca2+ signals before passivity onset

claims.statement: Passive fish are less responsive to visual motion than active fish (p = 4.2e-7, n = 11).
claims.source: Figure 1K
claims.quote: Passive fish were less responsive to visual stimuli. ... In passive fish, response to motion was reduced.

claims.statement: Replaying in open loop the visual motion recorded in closed loop also induces passivity.
claims.source: Figure 1F
claims.quote: Futility-induced passivity also occurred when the stimulus seen in closed loop was replayed in open loop

claims.statement: Ablating radial astrocytes, or blocking their IP3 receptors, halves futility-induced passivity, while random neuronal ablation does not change it.
claims.source: Figure 4C, 4E and 4H; Results, Radial Astrocyte Activation Increases Passivity; Silencing Decreases Passivity, paragraphs 1 and 3
claims.quote: Ablated animals spent half as much time in the passive state as they did before ablation ... ablation of either a matched number of neurons in random locations ... did not affect futility-induced passivity ... This inactivation method also reduced futility-induced passivity

claims.statement: Activating radial astrocytes with TRPV1, CoChR or Opto-alpha1-AR suppresses swimming, and astrocyte activation drives GABAergic neurons at the edge of L-MO.
claims.source: Figure 5D, 5L, 5M and 5R; Results, Radial Astrocyte Activation Increases Passivity; Silencing Decreases Passivity, paragraphs 5 and 6; Results, Radial Astrocytes Drive Activity in GABAergic Neurons that Inhibit Swimming, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Thus, surges in Ca2+ in L-MO radial astrocytes alone appear sufficient to stop swimming. ... Both CoChR and Opto-a1-AR (Figure 5J) activation ... induced a drop in swim power ... L-MO radial astrocytes activate GABAergic neurons at the edge of L-MO

claims.statement: The neuronal population whose activity rises fastest before passivity overlaps the noradrenergic neurons of the medulla oblongata (NE-MO).
claims.source: Figure 6A
claims.quote: Population with the highest rate of increase overlaps with NE neurons

claims.statement: NE-MO activity precedes astrocyte activity at passivity, NE-MO ablation reduces passivity, and NE-MO stimulation activates radial astrocytes through alpha1B receptors.
claims.source: Figure 6B to 6N; Results, The Noradrenergic System Conveys Swim Failures to Radial Astrocytes, paragraphs 1 to 5
claims.quote: During futility-induced passivity, signals from NE neurons and glia were temporally coupled, with NE cell responses preceding astrocytic responses ... Ablating NE-MO with a two-photon laser greatly reduced time spent in passivity ... mediated by the a1B adrenergic receptor.

claims.statement: NE-MO neurons respond to swims without visual feedback, encoding sensory-motor mismatch.
claims.source: Figure 7A to 7G; Results, The Noradrenergic System Conveys Swim Failures to Radial Astrocytes, paragraphs 7 and 8
claims.quote: NE-MO responses were small or absent when fish swam with naturalistic feedback but large when they swam without feedback. ... Thus, NE-MO signals swim failures by encoding sensory-motor mismatch.

claims.statement: Radial astrocyte calcium grows with the number of consecutive failed swims and with the probability that a swim fails.
claims.source: Figure 7H to 7K; Results, Radial Astrocytes Integrate Evidence that Actions Are Futile, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Glial Ca2+ rose fastest when P = 0 (always futile), did not rise when P = 1 (always effective), and increased at intermediate rates for intermediate P ... Glial signals increased with number of failed bouts

claims.statement: The subjects and "Day" numbers that the paper's analysis code names for each experiment are sessions of the dandiset, so that the code's selection of sessions can be applied to it.
claims.source: Data and materials availability; README.md and functions/load.py of github.com/namboodirilab/ANCCR at commit cff4414; dandiset description (related resource "Subject and session information")
claims.criterion: Subject names are matched with "_" read as "-" (HJ_FP_M2 as HJ-FP-M2), and sessions by the number after "Day" in the file path, as load_dandi_url does. The link holds (reproduced) when every subject of the Matlab scripts' lists exists in the dandiset and every Day number from startday to endday (and each learnedday) of analysis/fig4/cumsum_pavlovian.m, analysis/fig4/cumsum_bgdrw_vs_extinction.m, analysis/fig5/intermediate_rsp_trialless.m, analysis/fig6/backpropagation_pavlovian.m, analysis/figS10/cue_acquisition.m and analysis/figS10/omission.m is a session of that subject of the task the script names (Pavlovian or Poisson), with the cue durations and reward schedule of the condition (2 s cue for Experiment 2, 8 s cue for Experiment 3, background rewards for Experiment 5, omitted rewards for Experiment 4, a 250 ms cue for Experiment 6). Partially reproduced when the subjects match and at least 90% of the listed days do; not reproduced otherwise. The spreadsheet named in the dandiset's description is compared with these lists where the author can pin a copy of it.

claims.statement: Animals were trained for 7 +/- 2.1 sessions of random rewards, 13.3 +/- 2.7 sessions of initial conditioning, 4.3 +/- 0.8 sessions with the 8 s cue, 8.1 +/- 2.5 sessions with background rewards and 2.6 +/- 0.8 sessions of extinction; in sequential conditioning, 5.6 +/- 2.4 (wild type) and 7.1 +/- 0.7 (DAT-Cre) sessions (mean +/- SD).
claims.source: Methods, Behavioral task, paragraphs 1 to 5
claims.quote: Animals were trained on Experiment 1 for 4-11 sessions (7 ± 2.1 sessions, mean ± std) ... (13.3 ± 2.7 sessions in total) ... (4.3 ± 0.8 sessions) ... (8.1 ± 2.5 sessions) ... (2.6 ± 0.8 sessions) ... (5.6 ± 2.4 and 7.1 ± 0.7 sessions for WT and DAT-Cre, respectively)
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the stated SDs. Sessions are counted per animal from the dandiset's session labels; for Experiments 2 to 5 the conditions are those of the code's Day ranges (startday to endday, which give these means and SDs; the 3 pre-condition sessions of Experiment 3 and the 1 before extinction are not counted). Experiment 1 counts the 12 s IRI random reward sessions of the 8 animals; Experiment 7 counts all sequential conditioning sessions after the random reward session. Reproduced when all seven means are within tolerance; partially reproduced for five or six.

claims.statement: In Experiment 1, 22.6 +/- 2.4% of rewards came less than 3 s after the previous reward and 5.7 +/- 0.1% had no lick before the next reward; both were excluded.
claims.source: Methods, Data analysis, Experiment 1, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we excluded rewards with less than 3 s IRI from the previous reward (22.6±2.4%) for the above analyses. Rewards without lick until the next reward (5.7±0.1%) were also excluded from analyses.
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the stated spreads. Per session, the fraction of rewards (the first of the session not counted as short) with IRI under 3 s, and the fraction with no lick before the next reward or the session end, as in analysis/fig3/corr_randomrewards.m (out_bgd, out_nolick), over the 12 s IRI sessions of the 8 animals. The paper does not say how the percentages are averaged; readings are (a) the mean over animals of each animal's mean over sessions, (b) the mean over all sessions pooled. Reproduced when both values fall within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: In experimentally naive mice given unpredicted sucrose, the dopamine response to reward increases with the number of rewards experienced, in every animal (Test 1).
claims.source: Figure 3D and 3E; Results, Tests 1 and 2, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Every animal showed an increasing sucrose response that reached a high positive asymptote.
claims.criterion: Methods, Data analysis, Experiment 1, and analysis/fig3/corr_randomrewards.m. Per animal, the 12 s IRI random reward sessions in order; rewards excluded when the IRI from the previous reward is under 3 s or no lick follows before the next reward (the first reward of a session is kept). Reward response is the AUC of dF/F from -0.5 to 1 s around the first lick after the reward minus the AUC from -2 to -0.5 s. Reward number is the reward's position among all of the animal's rewards, excluded ones counted (code). Pearson r between response and reward number over all the animal's sessions pooled; two-tailed one-sample t-test of the 8 values against 0. Reproduced when t > 0 with p < 0.05 and r > 0 in all 8 animals; partially reproduced when the t-test holds and r > 0 in fewer than 8.

claims.statement: The dopamine response to an unpredicted reward is positively correlated with the interval since the previous reward (Test 2).
claims.source: Figure 3G; Results, Tests 1 and 2, paragraph 5
claims.quote: The experimentally observed correlation between dopamine response to sucrose and the previous IRI was positive, thereby being consistent with ANCCR but not RPE.
claims.criterion: Rewards, exclusions and response as in fig3e-reward-response-increases. Per session, Pearson r between response and the previous IRI (the first reward of a session has none); per animal, the mean of r over its sessions; two-tailed one-sample t-test of the 8 means against 0 (analysis/fig3/corr_randomrewards.m). Reproduced when t > 0 and p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The positive correlation between reward response and previous IRI holds across sessions and does not change over the first 7 sessions.
claims.source: Figure S8K; Results, Tests 1 and 2, paragraph 5; Table S1
claims.quote: The correlation between dopamine response to a reward and the previous IRI remains positive across sessions.
claims.criterion: The per-session r of fig3g-response-iri-positive, for sessions 1 to 7 of each animal. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a linear regression of r on session number over the pooled sessions (the paper's n is 50). Reproduced when the slope has p >= 0.05 and the mean r over animals is above 0 in each of sessions 1 to 7 (legend; Results "consistently positive"); not reproduced when the slope is significant. Slope, its t and the per-session means are reported.

claims.statement: Total, consummatory and non-consummatory lick rates do not change across the first 7 random reward sessions.
claims.source: Figure S8B; Supplementary Note 3, point 1; Table S1
claims.quote: The lick rates generally remained constant across repeated sessions.
claims.criterion: Methods, Data analysis, Experiment 1, paragraph 2, and analysis/figS8/lick_rsp_randomrewards.m with functions/classifylicks.m. A lick bout is a run of licks less than 1 s apart; consummatory licks are those of the first bout after each reward (to its end, the next reward or the session end, as classifylicks.m). Per session, total rate = all licks over session duration; consummatory rate = consummatory licks over the summed consummatory bout durations; non-consummatory rate = the other licks over the rest of the session. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a linear regression of each rate on session number (1 to 7) over the pooled sessions. Reproduced when all three slopes have p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any is significant. Slopes and t are reported.

claims.statement: The consummatory lick rate after a reward is not correlated with the dopamine response to that reward.
claims.source: Figure S8C and S8D; Table S1
claims.quote: The consummatory lick rate is not correlated with dopamine reward response.
claims.criterion: analysis/figS8/lick_rsp_randomrewards.m. Per reward, consummatory licks after it divided by its consummatory bout length; reward response as in fig3e-reward-response-increases; rewards excluded when the IRI is under 3 s or the lick bout runs on from the previous reward (the code's separatebout test). Per animal, Pearson r over all its sessions pooled. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-tailed one-sample t-test of the 8 r against 0. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced otherwise. Mean r is reported.

claims.statement: Dopamine rises at the onset of consummatory lick bouts but falls slightly at the onset of non-consummatory (dry) lick bouts, so the rising reward response is not a general response to licking.
claims.source: Figure S8E; Table S1
claims.quote: The average lick bout onset response was positive for consummatory lick bouts (during sucrose consumption) but was slightly negative for dry lick bout onsets away from reward consumption.
claims.criterion: Legend of Figure S8E and analysis/figS8/lick_rsp_randomrewards.m. Consummatory onsets are the first licks after rewards; non-consummatory onsets are bout-onset licks (1 s rule) that are not consummatory. Per session, dF/F aligned to each onset from -3 to 6 s, z-scored with the mean and SD over onsets of each onset's mean dF/F from -1.5 to -0.5 s, averaged over onsets; per animal, the mean over sessions. The window in which the response is measured for the tests is given by neither the Methods, the legend nor the code; readings are the mean z over (a) 0 to 1 s, (b) -0.5 to 1 s (the Experiment 1 reward window), (c) 0 to 0.5 s from onset. Reproduced when, under every reading, the consummatory response is above 0, the non-consummatory response below 0 and their paired difference positive, each two-tailed at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Spontaneous baseline dopamine events, away from rewards and licks, do not change in size across random reward sessions.
claims.source: Figure S8F and S8G; Methods, Data analysis, Experiment 1, paragraph 3; Table S1
claims.quote: There was no change in the baseline dopamine activity across sessions.
claims.criterion: Methods, Experiment 1, paragraph 3, and analysis/figS8/baseline_activity_randomrewards.m. Peaks of dF/F found with a minimum distance of 50 samples, a minimum height of 20% of the mean of the top 5% of peaks of the animal's first session, and a minimum prominence of half that height (code). Peaks are kept when more than 0.5 s from any lick and more than 2 s from reward (Methods); the code instead drops peaks from 0 to 2 s after each first lick after reward, run as a variant. Per session, the mean peak size; per animal, Pearson r between session number and that mean. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-tailed one-sample t-test of the 8 r against 0. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced otherwise. Mean r is reported.

claims.statement: Across animals, the change of baseline dopamine activity over sessions is not correlated with the change of the reward response over sessions.
claims.source: Figure S8H; Supplementary Note 3, point 4
claims.quote: Dopamine baseline activity change across sessions is uncorrelated with dopamine reward response change across sessions.
claims.criterion: analysis/figS8/baseline_activity_randomrewards.m. Per animal, Pearson r between session number and the session mean reward response (rewards with IRI of 3 s or more, response as in fig3e-reward-response-increases), and the r of figs8g-baseline-unchanged. Table S1 gives no test; the code computes the Pearson correlation of the two over the 8 animals and its p. A claim of absence. Reproduced when that p >= 0.05; not reproduced otherwise. r and p are reported.

claims.statement: In a separate group of 6 mice, the non-consummatory lick rate depends on the session's mean IRI (6, 12 or 30 s) while the consummatory lick rate does not, so animals learn the average reward rate within at most two sessions.
claims.source: Figure S8L; Table S1
claims.quote: The non-consummatory exploratory licks made by the animals depended on the average IRI for a given session. Thus, animals learn the average reward rate of an environment within at most two sessions.
claims.criterion: analysis/figS8/lick_across_iri_randomrewards.m. Per session, consummatory and non-consummatory rates as in figs8b-lick-rates-constant; per animal and IRI, the mean of its two sessions (18 values). Linear regression of each rate on the IRI condition. The regressor is not given; readings are (a) the IRI in seconds, (b) the condition rank 1 to 3; both give the same sign. Reproduced when, under both, the non-consummatory slope is negative with p < 0.05 and the consummatory slope has p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when the non-consummatory part holds alone.

claims.statement: During initial cue-reward learning, the dopamine response to CS+ develops before anticipatory licking, and behavioral learning is much more abrupt than dopaminergic learning (Test 3).
claims.source: Figure 4C to 4F; Results, Tests 3-7, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Dopamine cue response considerably leads behavior across animals. ... Behavioral learning is much more abrupt than dopaminergic learning (paired t test for abruptness of change; t(6) = 9.06; two-tailed p = 1.0×10-4; paired t test for change trial; t(6) = -2.93; two-tailed p = 0.0263; n=7 animals)
claims.criterion: Methods, Data analysis, Experiments 2-5, paragraph 1, and analysis/fig4/cumsum_pavlovian.m (condition 1). Per animal, Experiment 2 sessions from startday to endday, CS+ trials in order. Lick measure, Methods, the lick rate in the 2 s from CS+ onset minus that in the 1 s before; the code counts licks from cue onset to the end of the trace (3 s), as a rate, minus the 1 s baseline rate, run as a variant. Dopamine, AUC from 0 to 2 s after CS+ onset halved minus the AUC from -1 to 0 s (smoothed traces, code). Trials used, the first round(1.5 x n) where n is the number of trials before the animal's learnedday (code). Cumulative sums of each, smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (sigma 2 trials, 10 wide, valid convolution) and divided by their last value; the distance of each point from trial 5 to the end minus 5 to the line from its first point to (end - 5, 1) (point2line.m). Abruptness is the largest distance and the change trial its position. Two-tailed paired t-tests over 7 animals. Reproduced when lick abruptness exceeds dopamine abruptness and the dopamine change trial is earlier than the lick change trial, each at p < 0.05. The paper's sign for the change trial (t = -2.93) and for abruptness (t = 9.06) cannot both be lick minus dopamine if dopamine leads; the direction is judged from the Results ("dopamine response to CS+ was evident long before animals showed anticipatory licking") and the sign of t is reported.

claims.statement: By the session at which behavior was acquired, the dopamine cue response had reached 93% of its value on the final session (about 100% relative to the mean of the last two sessions).
claims.source: Figure S10C; Supplementary Note 5, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Dopamine cue response reaches 93% of its response on the final session (~100% if normalized relative to average cue response on session n and n-1).
claims.criterion: analysis/figS10/cue_acquisition.m (the Methods give no measure for this panel). Per animal, Experiment 2 sessions from startday to endday; per session the mean over CS+ trials of the AUC of unsmoothed dF/F from 0 to 1 s after cue onset, without baseline subtraction (code); session x is the animal's learnedday, n the last session. The averaging is not stated; readings are (a) the mean over the 7 animals of each animal's ratio (code), (b) the ratio of the means over animals. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when one is. The Fig 4 baseline-subtracted 0 to 2 s measure is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: When the cue is lengthened from 2 s to 8 s (cue-reward delay 3 s to 9 s), animals change the timing of anticipatory licking abruptly, and this change is better fit by a changing model than by a constant one.
claims.source: Figure 4G to 4I; Results, Tests 3-7, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Behavior is learned abruptly by all animals, but the dopaminergic cue response shows little to no change. ... Paired t test for abruptness of change; t(6) = 22.92; two-tailed p = 4.52×10-7; one-sample t test for ΔAIC against a null of zero; t(6) = 7.49 for lick
claims.criterion: Methods, Experiments 2-5, paragraphs 1 to 3, and analysis/fig4/cumsum_pavlovian.m (condition 2). Per animal, the 3 sessions before startday and those up to endday; CS+ trials with at least one lick in cue and trace (others dropped); behavior is the median time from cue onset of the licks in cue and trace; dopamine as in fig4ef-dopamine-leads-behavior; trials used, the first round(1.9 x n), n the trials before startday. Abruptness from the cumulative sums as in fig4ef-dopamine-leads-behavior (for behavior, the cumulative sum of median lick time). Model comparison, from the code since the Methods' equations are lost from the text, changing model A(1 - 2^(-(x/L)^S)) + b, x the trial number, fitted by least squares to the per-trial values (not to the cumulative sums; code) with bounds A 0 to 9000, L n-10 to the number of trials, S 0 to 100, b 0 to 4000 for licks; constant model b; AIC = 2k + N ln(RSS) with N trials. The Methods name A, L and b as the free parameters, three, where the code fits four; k = 4 (code) is the main reading and k = 3 a variant. Delta AIC = AIC(constant) - AIC(changing), two-tailed one-sample t-test over 7 animals. Reproduced when lick abruptness exceeds dopamine abruptness at p < 0.05 and lick delta AIC is above 0 at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: After the cue-reward delay is lengthened, the dopamine cue response shows no significant change (Test 4).
claims.source: Figure 4G to 4I; Results, Tests 3-7, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Experimentally, we observed that while the animals learned the new delay rapidly, dopaminergic cue response showed no significant change (Fig 4 G-I).
claims.criterion: Trials and dopamine measure as in fig4hi-delay-change-behavior-changes; changing model bounds for dopamine A -2 to 50, L n-10 to the number of trials, S 0 to 10, b -10 to 10 (code). A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-tailed one-sample t-test of delta AIC = AIC(constant) - AIC(changing) for dopamine against 0, fitted to the per-trial values as for licks. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 or the mean delta AIC is below 0 (the constant model fits better, no change found); not reproduced when delta AIC is significantly above 0. Mean delta AIC is reported, with k = 3 as a variant.

claims.statement: After the delay change, there is no suppression of dopamine at the old reward time (3 s) in any animal, whereas omission of the reward in extinction does suppress dopamine at the reward time (Test 5).
claims.source: Figure 4J and S10B; Results, Tests 3-7, paragraph 2; Methods, Experiments 2-5, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Omission response is not negative with respect to pre-cue baseline for any animal after cue duration change but was negative during extinction.
claims.criterion: Methods, Experiments 2-5, paragraph 4, and analysis/figS10/omission.m. Per animal, the first session of Experiment 3 and the first extinction session (code day lists); CS+ trials; response is the AUC from 3 to 4 s after cue onset (Experiment 3) or 9 to 10 s (extinction, 1 s after the trace, the original reward time) minus the AUC from -1 to 0 s (Methods; the code divides the window AUC by 1000 and not the baseline, run as a variant); smoothed traces (code); cumulative sum over trials, its last value per session. Reproduced when the paired two-tailed t-test gives Experiment 3 above extinction at p < 0.05 and the Experiment 3 value is at or above 0 in all 7 animals and the extinction value below 0 (for extinction, the legend allows (a) in every animal or (b) on average; either suffices).

claims.statement: Behavioral learning of extinction is abrupt, much more so than the change of the dopamine cue response.
claims.source: Figure 4J to 4L
claims.quote: Across all animals, the dopaminergic cue response remains significantly positive despite abrupt behavioral learning of extinction (paired t test for abruptness of change; t(6) = 5.67; two-tailed p = 0.0013; paired t test for change trial; t(6) = -2.40; two-tailed p = 0.0531; n=7 animals).
claims.criterion: As fig4ef-dopamine-leads-behavior with analysis/fig4/cumsum_pavlovian.m condition 3, the session before extinction and those to endday, trials the first round(2.5 x n) with n the trials before extinction. Reproduced when lick abruptness exceeds dopamine abruptness at p < 0.05. The change-trial comparison is reported; it is not part of the finding.

claims.statement: The dopamine cue response remains significantly positive well after animals stop licking to the cue in extinction (Test 6).
claims.source: Figure 4J to 4L; Results, Tests 3-7, paragraph 3
claims.quote: As predicted by ANCCR but not RPE, dopamine cue response remained significantly positive well after animals cease to behaviorally respond to the cues (Fig 4J-L)
claims.criterion: Dopamine measure as in fig4ef-dopamine-leads-behavior, extinction sessions of the code's day lists. The paper reports no test for "significantly positive". Readings are (a) a two-tailed one-sample t-test over the 7 animals of the mean CS+ response in the last extinction session against 0; (b) the same over all CS+ trials after the lick change trial of fig4kl-extinction-abrupt-behavior; (c) per animal, a one-sample t-test over the trials of the last extinction session, positive at p < 0.05 in all 7. Reproduced when every reading gives a positive response at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: When unpredicted rewards are added during the ITI, the dopamine cue response stays positive but decreases faster over trials than during extinction (Test 7).
claims.source: Figure 4M to 4P; Results, Tests 3-7, paragraph 4
claims.quote: The dopamine cue response remained significantly positive but decayed across trials faster than during extinction (Fig 4M-P).
claims.criterion: analysis/fig4/cumsum_bgdrw_vs_extinction.m. Per animal and condition (Experiment 5, background rewards; Experiment 4, extinction), the 2 sessions before startday and those to endday; CS+ response as in fig4ef-dopamine-leads-behavior; 140 trials starting 50 trials before the condition starts; cumulative sum divided by the sum of the first 50. What the paired t-test compares is not in the Methods, legend or code; readings are (a) the normalized cumulative sum at trial 140, (b) its mean over the 90 trials after the change, (c) the mean post-change response divided by the mean of the 50 pre-change trials. Reproduced when, under every reading, background is below extinction at p < 0.05 (two-tailed paired t-test) and the mean background cue response over the 90 post-change trials is above 0 by a two-tailed one-sample t-test over animals at p < 0.05 (the paper gives no test for "remained significantly positive"; this one is set here).

claims.statement: In the trial-less task, the dopamine response to an intermediate cue (one arriving before the previous cue's reward) is positive but weaker than the response to the previous cue (Test 8).
claims.source: Figure 5C and 5D; Results, Test 8, paragraph 3
claims.quote: We did not observe any negative dopamine response to the intermediate cue regardless of how baseline was measured, and instead observed a positive but weaker response
claims.criterion: Methods, Data analysis, Experiment 6, and analysis/fig5/intermediate_rsp_trialless.m. Per animal, the Experiment 6 sessions from learnedday to endday (sessions after the animals lick in anticipation, Methods). An intermediate cue follows the previous cue by less than the mean cue-reward delay. Excluded (code), any cue of a run of three where both intervals are short; pairs 0.5 s apart or less; and intermediate cues 2.5 to 3 s after the previous cue (within 0.5 s of its reward, Methods). Cue response is the AUC from 0 to 0.5 s after the cue minus the AUC 0.5 s before the previous cue, for both cues of a pair (unsmoothed). Per session the mean over pairs, then the mean over sessions; the ratio intermediate over previous per animal; two-tailed one-sample t-test against 0. Reproduced when t > 0 at p < 0.05 and the mean ratio is below 1; partially reproduced when the ratio is positive but not below 1.

claims.statement: The dopamine response to the reward paired with an intermediate cue is larger than the response to the reward of the previous cue (the ratio is above 1).
claims.source: Figure 5D, right
claims.quote: and reward response (One sample t test against a null of one; t(6) = 2.95; two-tailed p value = 0.0256; n=7 animals)
claims.criterion: Pairs and baseline as in fig5d-intermediate-cue-positive. Reward response is the AUC from 0 to 0.5 s after the first lick after the reward (smoothed trace, code) minus the same baseline; rewards whose first lick follows the next reward are dropped (Methods; code). Per animal the ratio of session-averaged responses, intermediate over previous; two-tailed one-sample t-test against 1. Reproduced when the mean ratio exceeds 1 at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: With the baseline taken immediately before the intermediate cue and the response measured as a peak, the intermediate cue response is still positive.
claims.source: Figure S11D and S11E; Methods, Experiment 6, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Here, we measure baseline as the dopamine fluorescence immediately prior to the intermediate cue delivery, as opposed to the baseline prior to the first cue in Fig 5C, D. Cue response was defined as baseline subtracted peak response. The intermediate cue response was still positive.
claims.criterion: Sessions and pairs as in fig5d-intermediate-cue-positive. Response, the peak dF/F after each cue minus the dF/F immediately before it (Methods); the code holds no script for this panel. The peak window and the baseline are not fixed; readings are peak over (a) 0 to 0.5 s or (b) 0 to 1 s after the cue, each with baseline (i) the last sample before the cue or (ii) the mean over the 0.5 s before it. Ratio intermediate over previous per animal, two-tailed one-sample t-test against 0. Reproduced when every reading gives t > 0 at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: During initial cue-reward learning, dopamine activity does not shift backward from just before reward to the cue; the late (pre-reward) response does not differ from the early (cue) response in the first 100 trials (Test 9).
claims.source: Figure 6A and 6B; Results, Tests 9-11, paragraph 2; Supplementary Note 9
claims.quote: Our observations were not consistent with a backpropagating bump of activity and were instead consistent with an increase in cue response over trials of learning (Fig 6B)
claims.criterion: Methods, Experiments 2-5, paragraph 5, and analysis/fig6/backpropagation_pavlovian.m. Per animal, Experiment 2 sessions startday to endday, CS+ trials in order, the first 400. Early is the AUC from 0 to 1 s after cue onset and late from 2 to 3 s (the 1 s before reward). The Methods subtract a baseline (the 1 s before CS+ onset, the Experiments 2-5 baseline); the code does not, run as a variant. Both are divided by the mean early response over trials 351 to 400 (code, where the Methods say "last 50 trials"). The animal's value is the mean of late minus early over the first 100 trials over that normalizer. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-tailed paired t-test (one-sample on the differences) over 7 animals. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when late minus early differs significantly. The mean and t are reported.

claims.statement: In sequential conditioning without inhibition, the dopamine responses to CS2 and CS1 increase together early in learning (no difference in the first 50 trials) (Test 10).
claims.source: Figure 6C and 6D; Results, Tests 9-11, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Consistent with ANCCR, we experimentally found that cue2 and cue1 responses increased together early in learning prior to separating later in learning (Fig 6D).
claims.criterion: Methods, Experiment 7 analysis, and analysis/fig6/backpropagation_sequential.py. The 7 control animals; their sequential conditioning sessions in Day order; CS1 and CS2 the odd and even code-15 events; AUC from 0 to 1 s after each cue. The Methods subtract a baseline the code does not apply (variant); its window is not given, readings (i) the 1 s or (ii) the 1.5 s before CS1 (the Fig 6I baseline). The normalizer is the mean CS1 response over trials 151 to 200 (code; Methods "last 50 trials" of the first 200). Value per animal, the mean of CS2 minus CS1 over the first 50 trials over the normalizer (code). A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-tailed paired t-test over 7 animals. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced otherwise. The mean and t are reported.

claims.statement: Later in sequential conditioning, the CS2 response falls below the CS1 response (the two separate).
claims.source: Figure 6D, right; Results, Tests 9-11, paragraph 2
claims.quote: cue2 and cue1 responses increased together early in learning prior to separating later in learning
claims.criterion: Responses as in fig6d-cues-increase-together; per animal the mean CS2 response over trials 151 to 200 divided by the mean CS1 response over the same trials (code, Fig 6D right). The paper gives no test. Set here, reproduced when the mean ratio over the 7 animals is below 1 with a two-tailed one-sample t-test against 1 at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when the mean is below 1 without significance.

claims.statement: Optogenetic inhibition of VTA dopamine neurons strongly suppresses NAcc dopamine during the CS2-to-reward delay in DAT-Cre mice (to about -0.6 times the reward response on day 1) and reduces their reward response, compared with controls.
claims.source: Figure 6F and 6G; Results, Tests 9-11, paragraph 2; Supplementary Note 10
claims.quote: we first verified robust inhibition of mesolimbic dopamine release during the cue2→reward delay in the experimental group (~0.6 times the reward response on day 1 of conditioning)
claims.criterion: Methods, Experiment 7 analysis, and analysis/fig6/measure_inhibition_sequential.py. 6 DAT-Cre (M2 to M7) and 7 controls; the random reward session and the first conditioning session (the first two in Day order). Baseline, the mean AUC over the 0.5 s before CS1 (before the reward in the random reward session, code). Inhibition, the mean AUC from 1 to 1.5 s after CS2 onset minus baseline (the last 0.5 s before reward; the code's bins run from -0.5 to 1.5 s, the Methods' to 2 s; this bin is in both), divided by the reward response of the same session. Reward response, the mean AUC over 1 s after the first lick after reward minus baseline (Methods; the code's 0.5 s is a variant). Day 1 reward response over the random reward session's. Two-tailed two-sample t-tests. The ratio of a 0.5 s AUC to a 1 s AUC depends on the window lengths, and Supplementary Note 10 gives the -0.6 as the dopamine level at 1.5 s after inhibition onset relative to the reward response magnitude. The readings for the expected value are (a) the AUC ratio with the Methods' 1 s reward window, (b) the AUC ratio with the code's 0.5 s reward window (equal windows, as in measure_inhibition_sequential.py), (c) the ratio of mean dF/F levels (each AUC over its window length) with the 1 s reward window; the value holds if it matches under any of them. Reproduced when both tests give DAT-Cre lower at p < 0.05 and the DAT-Cre mean inhibition is within tolerance (10% of 0.6) under one reading; partially reproduced when the tests hold and the mean is outside tolerance under all.

claims.statement: Despite inhibition of dopamine from CS2 to reward, every DAT-Cre animal learns anticipatory licking and acquires a positive dopamine response to CS1, both increasing over sessions as in controls (Test 11).
claims.source: Figure 6I; Results, Tests 9-11, paragraph 2; Table S1
claims.quote: Consistent with ANCCR, we observed that every experimental animal learned the task and that mesolimbic dopamine acquired positive responses to cue1 in all experimental animals (Fig 6I).
claims.criterion: Methods, Experiment 7 analysis, and analysis/fig6/learnign_curve_sequential.py. Per animal, conditioning sessions in Day order, the first three and the last two. CS1 response, AUC from 0 to 1.5 s after CS1 minus AUC from -1.5 to 0 s, session mean, divided by the mean reward response of the first conditioning session (AUC 0 to 1.5 s after the first lick within 5 s of reward minus the same baseline). Licks, count from 0 to 3 s after CS1 minus count from -3 to 0 s, session mean. Per group, linear regression of the values on session position 0 to 4 pooled over animals (code). Reproduced when all four slopes are positive at p < 0.05 and, in each of the 6 DAT-Cre animals, the last session's CS1 response and licks are above 0; partially reproduced when the slopes hold but not every animal.

claims.statement: With inhibition, the CS1 dopamine response reaches a lower level in the last session than in controls.
claims.source: Figure 6I; Supplementary Note 10, paragraph 2; Table S1
claims.quote: mesolimbic dopamine acquired positive responses to cue1 in all experimental animals, albeit at a lower asymptote relative to the control group (Fig 6I)
claims.criterion: Last-session normalized CS1 response of fig6i-learning-despite-inhibition, controls against DAT-Cre, two-tailed two-sample t-test. Reproduced when DAT-Cre is lower at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In the last session, anticipatory licking does not differ between DAT-Cre and control animals.
claims.source: Figure 6I, right; Table S1
claims.criterion: Last-session licks of fig6i-learning-despite-inhibition. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-tailed two-sample t-test. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced otherwise. The difference is reported.

claims.statement: Anticipatory licking between CS1 and CS2, before inhibition starts, increases from the first to the last session (main effect of session), with no effect of genotype and no genotype by session interaction.
claims.source: Figure S12F; Table S1
claims.quote: Quantification of pre-CS2 anticipatory licks showing reward-seeking prior to CS2 (onset of dopamine neuron inhibition).
claims.criterion: Methods, Experiment 7 analysis (licks "from CS1 until ... CS2"), and analysis/fig6/learnign_curve_sequential.py. Per animal, the first and last conditioning sessions; licks from 0 to 1.5 s after CS1 minus licks in the 1.5 s before CS1, session mean. The code's baseline window is written in milliseconds on times in seconds (it starts 1500 s before CS1), run as a variant. Two-way mixed ANOVA, genotype between and session within, 6 DAT-Cre and 7 controls. Table S1 prints these p as one-tailed; the F-test p is used as is. Reproduced when the session effect is significant at p < 0.05 with more licks in the last session, and the genotype effect and interaction have p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Simulated ANCCR reproduces classic findings taken as support for RPE coding, including conditioned inhibition, blocking, overexpectation, trial-by-trial behavioral changes after dopamine inhibition at reward, and unblocking by dopamine activation.
claims.source: Figure 2D to 2I; Table S1
claims.quote: Simulations of ANCCR learning produces behavior consistent with conditioned inhibition (D), blocking (E), and overexpectation (F). ... H. Simulation of dopamine inhibition at reward time produces trial-by-trial changes in behavior (similar to (81)). I. Simulation of unblocking due to dopamine activation at reward during blocking (similar to (14)).
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. Parameters from Methods, Simulations, Previously reported experiments, and the scripts simulation/fig2/*.m at the commit read, with functions/calculateANCCR.m. Reproduced when each of the five tests has the sign of Table S1 at p < 0.05 over 20 iterations; partially reproduced for three or four.

claims.statement: In simulations of random rewards, TDRL RPE (CSC and microstimulus) predicts a reward response that decreases with experience and is negatively correlated with the previous IRI, while ANCCR predicts an increasing response positively correlated with the previous IRI.
claims.source: Figure 3B, 3C and 3F
claims.quote: C. Simulations confirming the intuitive reasoning from B for Test 1. ... F. Simulations confirming the intuitive reasoning from B for Test 2
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. simulation/fig3/randomreward.m with the Methods' parameters (Model 1 CSC and microstimulus, Model 2; 50,000, 20,000 and 2,000 trials; rewards with IRI under 3 s dropped; for Test 1 only trials up to 95% of a fitted Weibull asymptote). Reproduced when all six correlations have the reported sign at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In simulations of the trial-less task, TDRL RPE predicts a negative response to an intermediate cue relative to the previous cue, while ANCCR predicts a positive one; both predict a reward response ratio (intermediate over previous reward) above 1.
claims.source: Figure 5A and 5B; Results, Test 8, paragraphs 2 and 3
claims.quote: B. Confirmation of these intuitions based on simulations (Methods) (One sample t test against a null of zero; t(99) = RPE (CSC), -114.74; RPE (MS), -181.32; ANCCR, 322.53 ... Reward responses are predicted to be positive by both models (One sample t test against a null of one
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. simulation/fig5/poisson.m with the Methods' parameters (Model 2 pre-trained on Experiment 1; 1,000 cues per simulation, 100 repeats). Reproduced when the cue ratio is below 0 for both RPE models and above 0 for ANCCR, each at p < 0.05; the reward ratio above 1 at p < 0.05 for all three models is also required, and when the cue part holds without it the claim is partially reproduced.

claims.statement: With dopamine inhibited from CS2 to reward, TDRL RPE predicts a negative CS1 response and no learning, while ANCCR predicts a positive but reduced CS1 response.
claims.source: Figure 6H and S12A to S12C; Results, Tests 9-11, paragraph 2
claims.quote: With such strong inhibition, TDRL RPE predicted no behavioral learning in this experiment, and a strong negative cue1 dopamine response (Figs 6H, S12). In contrast, ANCCR predicted largely intact learning of cue1, but with slower behavioral learning and reduced cue1 response
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. simulation/fig6/serialcue.m and serialcue_rpe.m with the Methods' parameters (800 and 400 trials, inhibition -0.6 from CS2 to reward, lambda 0.95 for Fig 6). Reproduced when both models give a lower CS1 response with inhibition at p < 0.05, the RPE CS1 response with inhibition is below 0 and the ANCCR one above 0.

claims.statement: In simulations where cues arrive at exponential intervals and each is followed by reward at a fixed delay, ANCCR for the cue is significantly positive at every ratio of delay to inter-cue interval, while TDRL RPE is often lower than without an association.
claims.source: Figure S6A; Results, A retrospective causal learning algorithm, paragraph 2
claims.quote: However, across all ratios shown, contingency learning signals a significantly positive ANCCR for the cue, implying that the algorithm learns the cue-reward association without loss of generality.
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. simulation/figS6/timescale.m with the Methods' parameters (inter-cue interval 12 s, seven delays from 0.05 to 5 times it, T 5 times the IRI, exact means of eligibility traces, 100 repeats of 1,000 cues). The paper reports no test; set here, reproduced when at every ratio the cue ANCCR with the association is above 0 by a two-tailed one-sample t-test over the 100 repeats at p < 0.05, and above the value without the association. The TDRL comparison is reported.

claims.statement: Simulated ANCCR reproduces the timescale invariance of learning (trials to acquisition grow with the cue-reward delay only when the ITI is fixed, not when it is scaled with the delay), and TDRL does not.
claims.source: Figure S5C and S5D; Results, A retrospective causal learning algorithm, paragraph 2
claims.quote: C. Simulations demonstrating that TDRL cannot explain the timescale invariance, but that retrospective causal learning explains these results (Methods).
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. simulation/figS5/scaledITI_acquisition.m with the Methods' parameters (delays 3 to 10 s, ITI 30 s fixed or 10 times the delay, acquisition when the 30-trial moving average of the cue response crosses 0.6 for Model 2 and 0.08 for Model 1, 100 repeats). The paper reports no test; set here, over the 8 mean trials to acquisition per condition, a Spearman correlation with delay. Reproduced when, for Model 2, it is positive at p < 0.05 with fixed ITI and has p >= 0.05 with scaled ITI, and for Model 1 the scaled-ITI correlation is significant (not invariant). The reward probability simulation (rewardprobability_acquisition.m, Fig S5D) is reported.

claims.statement: Simulated ANCCR reproduces dopamine ramps when a series of cues predicts reward, and the changes of the ramp when the subject is teleported closer to reward or the cue speed changes.
claims.source: Figure S13A to S13D; Table S1
claims.quote: ANCCR signaling not only ramps up when a series of cues predicts reward, but also captures observed changes in dopamine activity when a subject was teleported to a moment closer to reward (A-B) or the speed of cue presentation changed (C-D).
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. simulation/figS13/ramping_teleport.m and ramping_speedchange.m with the Methods' parameters. These scripts were changed on 2023-05-10 ("codes for correction"), after the text read; both the version before (commit eca96a2, 2023-02-13) and the one at the commit read are run, and the outcome is stated for each. Reproduced when the five comparisons have the sign of Table S1 at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The calcium imaging data comprise 14 scans of one mouse, collected between P75 and P81, spanning a volume of about 1,200 x 1,100 x 500 um.
claims.source: Results, 2P calcium imaging, paragraph 1; Methods, 2P functional imaging
claims.quote: The dataset contains 14 individual scans, collected between postnatal day 75 (P75) and P81, spanning a volume of approximately 1,200 × 1,100 × 500 µm 3
claims.criterion: Count the distinct scans (session and scan index) and the distinct days on which they were recorded. The scan count is exact, as it is a count of files the paper lists. The ages are judged from the recording dates against the birth date of 19 December 2017 (Methods, Timeline); P75 to P81 (main text) and P75 to P80 (Methods timeline) are both readings the paper allows, and the claim holds when the dates fall within P75 to P81. The 6 days are the days of imaging of the 19 completed scans (Methods, 2P functional imaging); the 14 kept scans may span fewer, so a count of 6 or fewer days is consistent with the paper.

claims.statement: Eleven scans were imaged at 6.3 Hz with four depths (eight fields), two at 8.6 Hz with three depths (six fields) and one at 9.6 Hz with two depths (four fields); in the 11 scans the four planes span roughly 300 to 400 um.
claims.source: Methods, 2P functional imaging, paragraph 1; Results, 2P calcium imaging, paragraph 2
claims.quote: For 11 scans, imaging was performed at 6.3 Hz, collecting eight 620 × 1,100 μm fields per frame ... For 2 scans, imaging was performed at 8.6 Hz, collecting six 620 × 1,100 μm fields per frame ... For 1 scan, imaging was performed at 9.6 Hz, collecting four 620 × 1,000 μm fields per frame
claims.criterion: Per scan, the imaging rate, the number of fields and of distinct depths, from the dataset's imaging metadata. A scan matches a group when its rate is within 0.1 Hz of the group's (a standard choice, as the rates are printed to one decimal) and its number of depths is the group's; a field is one 620 um wide strip, and two fields per depth tile the field of view (Methods). The counts are exact. The depth span is the range from 300 to 400 um widened by 10% of each bound (270 to 440 um), as the protocol sets for a range. The paper does not say whether the range bounds every scan or describes the typical scan; the readings are (a) the span of each of the 11 scans lies in 270 to 440 um; (b) the median span of the 11 scans does.

claims.statement: In total 125,413 masks were segmented across the 14 scans, of which 115,372 were classified as somatic by a trained classifier (8.1% excluded).
claims.source: Results, 2P calcium imaging, paragraph 2; Methods, 2P functional imaging, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In total, 125,413 masks were generated across 14 scans, of which 115,372 were automatically classified as somatic masks by a trained classifier
claims.criterion: Count all segmented masks (units) over the 14 scans, and those the dataset marks as somatic. The paper does not say whether the dataset holds the non-somatic masks. The readings are (a) the dataset holds all masks with a somatic label, and both counts are tested; (b) it holds only the somatic masks, and only the 115,372 is tested, the total being untestable. The Methods' 8.1% does not equal 1 - 115,372/125,413 (8.0%); both are within the tolerance.

claims.statement: Consolidating masks imaged in more than one scan by their 3D position in the structural stack gives an estimated 75,909 unique functionally imaged neurons.
claims.source: Results, 2P calcium imaging, paragraph 4; Methods, 2P structural stack, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we estimate the functional imaging volume contains 75,909 unique functionally imaged neurons consolidated from 115,372 segmented somatic masks, with many neurons imaged in 2 or more scans
claims.criterion: The method is from the Methods (2P structural stack). Each scan field is registered into the structural stack and each somatic mask gets a 3D centroid; the closest 2 cells from different scans are grouped, iteratively, until all pairs are at least 10 um apart or a further join produces a mask taller than 20 um in z. The paper does not say how the height of a group is measured. The readings are (a) the range in z of the centroids in the group; (b) that range plus the z extent of one field's mask. It also does not say whether distances to a group are taken from its mean centroid or from its nearest member; the readings are (i) mean centroid, (ii) nearest member. The count is judged under each combination. If the dataset holds no stack coordinates for the masks, the claim cannot be tested from it.

claims.statement: The imaging volume is roughly 50% VISp and 50% higher visual areas (VISlm, VISrl and VISal), with each functional unit assigned an area from its position in the stack.
claims.source: Methods, Imaging site selection, paragraph 1; Methods, 2P structural stack, paragraph 3; Fig. 3a,d
claims.quote: This resulted in an imaging volume that was roughly 50% VISp and 50% higher visual area (HVA)
claims.criterion: The share of units labelled VISp among units with an area label. The paper's "roughly" gives no bound; 15 percentage points is set here, as 10% of 50 would read "roughly" more narrowly than the word allows. The paper does not say whether the share is of volume or of neurons, or which units count. The readings are (a) all somatic masks over the 14 scans; (b) one per unique neuron, when the dataset identifies them; (c) the area of the field of view. The claim holds when one reading is within the tolerance.

claims.statement: All scans drifted less than 10 um in z over the recording, and most less than 5 um.
claims.source: Methods, 2P structural stack, paragraph 2
claims.quote: All scans had less than 10-μm drift over the 1.5-h recording, and for most of them drift was limited to <5 μm
claims.criterion: The Methods say drift was found by sequential registration of sections of each scan into the structural stack; the length of a section and the registration of each are not given. The readings are (a) consecutive blocks of about 10 min (the stimulus blocks); (b) the two halves of the scan (the stimulus repeats one in each half). Drift is the range of the registered z of a field over the sections. Reproduced when every scan's drift is below 10 um and more than half of the scans are below 5 um, under one reading. If the dataset holds neither the stack nor the raw frames, the claim cannot be tested from it.

claims.statement: A two-channel structural stack (green GCaMP and red vasculature) of 1,412 x 1,322 x 670 um at 0.5 pixels per um was collected after Texas Red injection.
claims.source: Results, 2P calcium imaging, paragraph 3; Methods, 2P structural stack, paragraph 1
claims.quote: a 2-channel (green, red) 1,412 × 1,322 × 670 μm 3 (anteroposterior × mediolateral × radial depth) structural stack was collected at 0.5 pixels per μm
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the dataset holds the stack with two channels and its extent and resolution are within tolerance; the extent is the number of voxels divided by the resolution.

claims.statement: Each scan's stimulus lasted about 84 min and was made of 6 oracle clips of 10 s repeated 10 times (10 min), 144 unique natural clips of 10 s (24 min), 90 natural clips of 10 s shown twice (30 min), and 20 Trippy and 20 Monet2 seeds of 15 s each shown twice (10 min each).
claims.source: Methods, Stimulus composition; Results, Behavioural tracking and visual stimulation, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Each scan stimulus was approximately 84 min in duration and comprised
claims.criterion: Per scan, from the stimulus table, count the clips of each class and their repeats and sum the durations of the stimulus presentations. Counts are exact; the duration is the sum of trial durations (readings (a) trial start to trial end, as the stimulus table gives; (b) the nominal 10 s or 15 s per trial). Reproduced when all 14 scans match. The share of clips in each natural category (2 oracle, 48 unique and 30 repeated clips per category) is tested when the dataset names the category.

claims.statement: The oracle clips, the 90 twice-repeated clips and 10 of the 20 seeds of each parametric stimulus were the same in every scan; the 144 unique clips and the other 10 seeds differed between scans.
claims.source: Methods, Stimulus composition; Results, Behavioural tracking and visual stimulation, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The stimulus composition included a mixture of unique stimuli for each scan, some that were repeated across every scan, and some that were repeated within each scan
claims.criterion: Clips and seeds are identified by the stimulus identifiers the dataset gives (a condition hash, clip name or seed). Reproduced when the 6 oracle clips and 90 repeated clips occur in all 14 scans, 10 Monet2 and 10 Trippy seeds occur in all 14 scans, and the remaining clips and seeds each occur in one scan only. If the dataset gives no identifier for clips, the claim cannot be tested from it.

claims.statement: The six oracle clips were repeated in the same order ten times per scan.
claims.source: Results, Behavioural tracking and visual stimulation, paragraph 2
