claims.quote: 6 natural film stimuli clips totalling 1 min (oracle natural videos) were repeated in the same order 10 times per scan
claims.criterion: Per scan, find the 6 clips shown 10 times. The paper's code (Fig 3/panel_f/get_data.ipynb) takes each repeat as the 6 trials that follow the first oracle clip's onset in trial order. Reproduced when, in every scan, each of the 10 repeats shows the same 6 clips consecutively and in the same order.

claims.statement: Each scan was preceded by 0.15 to 5.5 min with the monitor on and followed by 8.3 to 21.2 min with the monitor off, to record spontaneous activity.
claims.source: Methods, Stimulus composition, last paragraph
claims.quote: Each scan was also preceded by 0.15–5.5 min with the monitor on, and followed by 8.3–21.2 min with the monitor off, in order to collect spontaneous neural activity
claims.criterion: Per scan, the time from the first imaging frame to the first stimulus onset, and from the last stimulus offset to the last imaging frame. Reproduced when every scan's values fall in the reported ranges widened by 10% of each bound (0.135 to 6.05 min and 7.47 to 23.32 min).

claims.statement: Each 15 s Monet2 block holds 16 equal periods of motion, one for each of 16 directions between 0 and 360 degrees, at 42.8 degrees per second.
claims.source: Methods, Global directional parametric stimulus; Fig. 3g legend
claims.quote: Each 15-s block consisted of 16 equal periods of motion along one of 16 unique directions of motion between 0–360° with a velocity of 42.8° s −1 at the nearest point on the monitor
claims.criterion: From the Monet2 trial table (directions and onsets per trial, as the code reads them in Fig 3/panel_g/get_data.ipynb). Reproduced when every Monet2 trial has 16 distinct directions in 0 to 360 degrees and periods within tolerance of 15 s / 16; the Fig. 3g legend gives 937 ms. The paper says the directions are unique, not that they are evenly spaced, so the spacing is reported and is not part of the outcome. The speed is checked only if the dataset gives it.

claims.statement: Neurons differ in how reliably they respond to the repeated oracle clips; units with high oracle scores give repeat-to-repeat responses that are consistent, and units with low scores do not.
claims.source: Fig. 3f; Results, Behavioural tracking and visual stimulation, paragraph 2; Methods, Oracle score
claims.quote: Raster of deconvolved calcium activity for three neurons to repeated stimulus trials (oracle trials; ten repeats of six sequential clips, with each repeat normalized independently). Rasters for high (top), medium (middle) and low (bottom) oracle scores
claims.criterion: The oracle score is, per unit, the jackknife mean of correlations between each oracle trial and the mean of the remaining trials (Methods, Oracle score), on the deconvolved trace interpolated at the scan's frame rate onto the oracle frames, with the unit's ms delay added to its frame times (code, Fig 3/panel_f/get_data.ipynb). The paper's code reads the score from a precomputed table, so the unit of a trial is open. The readings are (a) one trial is one repeat of the 6 clips, concatenated (10 trials); (b) each clip is scored apart over its 10 repeats, and the 6 scores are averaged. Units at the 99th, 79th and 34th percentiles of the score (the code's choices for the figure) are selected and their rasters shown. The paper's measure of repeat-to-repeat consistency is the oracle score itself (Results, paragraph 2; Methods, Oracle score), and it gives no other measure or test. Reproduced when, under both readings, the score can be computed for the units of the 14 scans and the scores of the three selected units are increasing from the 34th to the 99th percentile with the 99th percentile unit's score above 0, so that consistent and inconsistent units both occur. The mean pairwise Pearson correlation between single repeats of the 100 units nearest each percentile is shown as a variant; that measure is set here and is not the basis of the outcome.

claims.statement: Monet2 drives direction-tuned responses; neurons can be found preferring each of the 16 directions, and their trial-averaged responses peak at their preferred direction.
claims.source: Fig. 3g; Results, Behavioural tracking and visual stimulation, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Trial-averaged raster (central 500 ms of trial-average raster for each direction, out of 937 ms) of deconvolved calcium activity for 80 neurons in 40 Monet2 trials (16 randomly ordered directions) grouped by preferred direction (5 neurons per direction
claims.criterion: From the code (Fig 3/panel_g/get_data.ipynb). Per unit, the deconvolved trace is interpolated, with its ms delay, at 6.3 Hz over each direction period less (15/16 - 0.5)/2 s at each end (the central 500 ms), and averaged over the 40 Monet2 trials. The code takes the preferred direction from a von Mises fit (pipeline_radtune.VonFit, method 3, direction) and the 5 units per direction bin with the highest von_pred_adv, among units in nda.ScanInclude; the fit is not described in the paper and its code is not in the repository. The readings are (a) the preferred direction is the direction with the highest mean response over the central window; (b) the peak of a von Mises function fitted to the 16 mean responses. Reproduced when, under both readings, every one of the 16 directions is preferred by at least 5 units (the figure's 5 per direction). The paper gives no measure or test of tuning strength. Two choices set here, not from the paper, that do not decide the outcome, are the following. The 5 units shown per direction are those with the highest ratio of the response at the preferred direction to the mean over all directions; and a split-half check (preferred direction from the first 20 trials, response from the last 20) of whether their response at the preferred direction exceeds the mean at the other 15 is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Treadmill velocity, and the pupil position and diameter from video of the left eye, were recorded throughout each scan.
claims.source: Results, Behavioural tracking and visual stimulation, paragraph 1; Methods, Eye and face camera; Methods, Treadmill
claims.quote: Treadmill rotation (single axis) and video of the left eye were captured throughout the scan, yielding locomotion velocity, eye movements and pupil diameter data
claims.criterion: Reproduced when all 14 scans hold treadmill velocity and pupil position and diameter covering the imaging period (from the first to the last imaging frame, gaps within it allowed as the Methods say untracked frames are stored as NaN), with every scan's treadmill rate in 51.3 to 110 Hz (the range widened by 10% of each bound) and the eye camera rate within tolerance. The share of eye frames with a pupil fit is reported per scan; the paper gives no value for it.

claims.statement: The binary flip code of the photodiode signal, used to align stimulus and behaviour clocks, was recovered for 89% of trials.
claims.source: Methods, Stimulus alignment
claims.quote: The encoded binary signal was reconstructed for 89% of trials
claims.criterion: Needs the raw photodiode signal at 10 MHz, or a per-trial flag of whether the code was read. The decoding is given only in outline (a sine convolution and local peak detection on a three-level signal), so if the dataset holds the raw signal the claim is tested with each of (a) a flag stored by the pipeline, if present, and (b) a decode of the three-level signal by peak detection, and holds when one reading is within tolerance. If the dataset holds only the aligned stimulus times, the claim cannot be tested from it.

claims.statement: Experts manually matched 19,181 functional ROIs from 14 scans to 15,439 individual EM neurons.
claims.source: Results, Functional–structural co-registration, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we used the results of the transform to guide a group of experts to manually match 19,181 functional ROIs from 14 scans to 15,439 individual EM neurons
claims.criterion: The match table is CAVE table coregistration_manual_v4 (Methods, Assigning manual matches), matched to the dataset's units by session, scan index and unit id, as the Fig. 6k code does. The paper gives no materialization version for the counts; the readings are (a) the version its code uses, 1181; (b) the latest public version. Reproduced when, under one reading, the counts are within tolerance. The share of the table's ROIs found in the dataset is reported; the paper gives no value for it, so it is not part of the outcome. Counting the EM identifiers the dataset itself holds in its plane segmentation columns is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Units independently matched to the same EM neuron in two scans have higher signal correlation than each matched unit with the nearest unmatched unit in the other scan, more clearly for units with oracle score above 0.2.
claims.source: Results, Functional–structural co-registration, paragraph 2; Methods, Evaluating manual matches; Extended Data Fig. 4f–h
claims.quote: ROIs with at least moderate visual responses that are independently matched to the same neuron across multiple scans have higher signal correlations than adjacent neurons
claims.criterion: From the Methods (Evaluating manual matches). For every EM neuron matched to at least two scans, the signal correlation is the Pearson correlation between trial-averaged responses to the oracle stimuli of the matched unit in scan A and the matched unit in scan B; the two controls are the matched unit in scan A with the nearest unit in scan B not matched to the neuron, and the converse. The paper does not define nearest (in which space) or how a neuron matched in more than two scans contributes. The readings for nearest are (a) nearest by 3D centroid in the structural stack; (b) nearest in the same field in 2D. Pairs are all pairs of scans for the neuron, a choice set here, as the paper's scan A and scan B fix no rule. The paper reports no test; reproduced when, under both readings, the matched correlation exceeds both control correlations for more than half of the pairs, and the median difference is larger when both matched units have oracle score above 0.2 than over all pairs. A two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of matched against control is reported.

claims.statement: The fiducial-based automatch assigns 84,198 functional ROIs to 37,364 EM neurons with 83% precision against manual matches; dropping the bottom 30% of separation scores gives 90% precision with 59,934 ROIs and 31,042 neurons.
claims.source: Results, Functional–structural co-registration, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 5
claims.quote: This method (referred to as the fiducial-based automatch table) resulted in 84,198 functional ROIs matched to 37,364 EM neurons. Considering all matches, this method achieved 83% precision relative to manual matchers, but filtering out matches in the bottom 30% of separation scores yields 90% precision, while still including 59,934 functional ROIs and 31,042 EM neurons
claims.criterion: Precision as the Methods define it (Evaluating automatch tables). Both tables are first restricted to rows where the functional unit or the EM neuron was attempted by the manual matchers; true positives are rows in both tables, false positives rows only in the automatch. Separation scores are turned into percentiles and the threshold is a minimum (Methods). The paper does not say how attempted is decided; the readings are (a) the unit or the neuron occurs in the manual table; (b) the unit's scan field was attempted, any unit of a scan in the manual table. Reproduced when all values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: The vessel-based automatch, without fiducials, assigns 75,856 functional ROIs to 34,712 EM neurons with 84% precision; dropping the bottom 30% of separation scores gives 90% precision with 53,248 ROIs and 28,233 neurons.
claims.source: Results, Functional–structural co-registration, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 5
claims.quote: This table (referred to as the vessel-based automatch table) contains 75,856 functional ROIs matched to 34,712 EM neurons. Remarkably, this fiducial-free method performed as well as the fiducial-based method, achieving 84% precision with manual matches
claims.criterion: As for fiducial-automatch, with the same readings of attempted.

claims.statement: Keeping only the matches on which both automated methods agree gives 89% agreement with manual matches, with 60,091 ROIs and 29,620 EM neurons.
claims.source: Results, Functional–structural co-registration, paragraph 5; Methods, Generating the fiducial-vessel agreement automatch table
claims.quote: this hybrid automated table achieves 89% agreement with no additional filtering, yielding 60,091 functional ROIs and 29,620 EM neurons
claims.criterion: The two automatch tables merged on session, scan_idx, field, unit_id and target_id (Methods); agreement is precision as in fiducial-automatch, with the same readings of attempted.

claims.statement: A co-registration transform built from 2,934 expert-matched fiducials (1,994 somata and 942 blood vessels) has an average residual of 3.8 um; the staged transform lowers the residual from about 10 um to 5.6, 4.6, 3.9, 3.5, 3.1 and 2.9 um.
claims.source: Results, Functional–structural co-registration, paragraph 1; Methods, Co-registration Transform
claims.quote: In the first step, we generated a co-registration transform using a set of 2,934 expert-matched fiducials ... The average residual was 3.8 μm
claims.criterion: Count the released fiducials by kind. The paper gives the total as 2,934 but its parts sum to 2,936, so the tolerance of 2 admits both readings of the total and no other count. The 3.8 um is not tied to a stage of the Methods' transform, whose stages give 10, 5.6, 4.6, 3.9, 3.5, 3.1, 2.9 and 0.003 um. The readings are (a) the leave-one-out residual of the full transform (Methods); (b) the residual after the first thin plate spline step of the third group (n = 3, 3.9 um, within tolerance). Reproduced when, applying the released transform to the released fiducials, one reading gives a value within tolerance.

claims.statement: The block was cut into 27,972 sections of 40 nm, 26,652 were imaged by five autoTEMs, and an 800 um region of sections 7,931 to 27,904 was processed, split into two subvolumes of about 35% and 65% of the sections.
claims.source: Results, The EM volume, paragraphs 1 and 2
claims.quote: The tissue sample was trimmed and sectioned into 27,972 serial sections (nominal thickness 40 nm) ... A total of 26,652 sections were imaged by 5 customized automated TEMs
claims.criterion: The released imagery and its metadata give the sections of each subvolume (7,931 to 14,815 and 14,816 to 27,904). The processed region is 27,904 - 7,931 + 1 sections. Counts of sections cut and imaged are reported if the released metadata give them.

claims.statement: Automated detection found 524 million synaptic clefts (186 million in subvolume 35, 337 million in subvolume 65), with 96% precision and 89% recall against 8,611 manually annotated synapses in 70 subvolumes, and 98% partner assignment accuracy on 191 held-out synapses.
claims.source: Results, Automated reconstruction, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 1
claims.quote: We automatically detected and associated a total of 524 million synaptic clefts across both subvolumes ... We manually identified synapses in 70 small subvolumes ( n = 8,611 synapses) distributed across the dataset, giving the automated detection an estimated precision of 96% and recall of 89%
claims.criterion: Counts from the released synapse tables. Precision and recall can be tested only if the manual annotations of the 70 test subvolumes are public; the paper does not say how a detection is matched to a manual synapse, so if they are, the readings are (a) overlap of the cleft with the annotation point; (b) cleft centroid within 100 nm of the point.

claims.statement: Nuclei were automatically segmented in subvolume 65, 144,120 in all.
claims.source: Results, Automated reconstruction, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Nuclei were also automatically segmented ( n = 144,120) within subvolume 65

claims.statement: An SVM on nucleus features detects neurons with 96.9% precision and 99.6% recall, predicting 82,247 neurons in subvolume 65, of which 69,957 have well-segmented somata; a multilayer perceptron separates excitatory from inhibitory neurons with 97% accuracy (96% precision and 94% recall for inhibitory calls).
claims.source: Methods, Cell classification
claims.quote: This model predicted 82,247 neurons detected within the larger subvolume ... We estimate from this test that the classifier had an overall accuracy of 97% with an estimated 96% precision and 94% recall for inhibitory calls
claims.criterion: Counts from the released tables. The accuracies rest on manual labels (a 100 um column and 350 further sampled cells) that the paper does not say are released; they are tested only if those labels are public.

claims.statement: The released segmentation holds 1,046,656 proofreading edits as of 16 September 2024; 1,433 neurons have proofread axons, 85 excitatory neurons have fully proofread axons and dendrites, and 1,188 excitatory neurons have proofread dendrites.
claims.source: Results, Proofreading, paragraphs 1 to 3
claims.quote: The released segmentation now contains all 1,046,656 edits of the proofreading that had occurred as of 16 September 2024
claims.criterion: Neurons with proofread axons are rows with status_axon true in proofreading_status_and_strategy (Methods). The readings for the version are (a) 1181, as the code uses; (b) the version nearest after 16 September 2024. The 85 and 1,188 are groups of other studies that the table may not label; they are tested only if a released table names them.

claims.statement: Comparing proofread with automated dendrites, 99% of inputs assigned to a postsynaptic soma in the automated segmentation were correct.
claims.source: Results, Proofreading, paragraph 3; Results, Integrated analysis, paragraph 5
claims.quote: From the proofread dendrites, we determined that 99% of inputs were correct when assigned to a postsynaptic soma in the automated segmentation
claims.criterion: For neurons with status_dendrite true, the input synapses on the root before proofreading against those on the proofread root; precision is the share of pre-proofreading inputs that remain. The tolerance is 1 point, as the 10% rule would allow values above 100%. The paper does not say which root counts as before proofreading; the readings are (a) the root at the earliest materialization in which the nucleus occurs; (b) the root before the first edit in the edit history.

claims.statement: The longest proofread excitatory axon measures 18.9 mm with 2,483 synaptic outputs; inhibitory axons range from 1.1 to 32.3 mm in length with a mean of 2,754 outputs (range 99 to 14,019).
claims.source: Results, Proofreading, paragraph 3
claims.quote: the longest excitatory axon measuring 18.9 mm with 2,483 synaptic outputs and inhibitory axons ranging from in length from 1.1 to 32.3 mm with a mean of 2,754 synaptic outputs (range 99–14,019)
claims.criterion: Axon length from the skeleton of each neuron with a proofread axon, axon compartment only. The paper does not say how length or the axon compartment is obtained; the readings are (a) the released skeletons' axon labels; (b) NEURD's axon split. The inhibitory range is judged as a range widened by 10% of each bound.

claims.statement: The automated segmentation had 7,050 objects merging 17,753 neurons; after manual and automated splitting the total of individually segmented neurons is 84,035, and NEURD made more than 164,000 edits.
claims.source: Results, Proofreading, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 3
claims.quote: there were 7,050 segmented objects consisting of a total of 17,753 neurons that were merged together (based on nucleus segmentation) ... bringing the total number of individually segmented neurons to 84,035
claims.criterion: A neuron is individually segmented when its root id holds one neuronal nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 3 uses nucleus_ref_neuron_svm). The before counts (7,050 and 17,753) are tested only if the first materialization is public.

claims.statement: Between 60% and 95% of the output synapses of proofread axons map to postsynaptic targets with a known soma, depending on cell type and location.
claims.source: Fig. 6f; Results, Integrated analysis, paragraph 5
claims.quote: between 60 and 95% of those outputs can be accurately mapped onto their postsynaptic targets with a known soma location, depending on the cell type and its spatial location in the volume
claims.criterion: For each neuron with a proofread axon, the fraction of its output synapses whose postsynaptic root holds exactly one nucleus. The range is widened by 10% of each bound (54 to 100%, as a fraction cannot pass 100%). The paper says the fraction depends on cell type and location but not what the range bounds; the readings are (a) the fraction of every neuron with a proofread axon lies in the widened range; (b) the mean fraction of each cell class (the colours of Fig. 6f) does. Reproduced when one reading holds; the share of neurons in the range is reported.

claims.statement: For the example proofread L2/3 VISp pyramidal cell, 74.5% (1,053 of 1,412) of its output synapses are onto objects with a single nucleus (275 onto inhibitory, 662 onto excitatory and 116 onto unclassified cells), 359 onto orphan fragments, and 365 onto functionally matched cells.
claims.source: Fig. 6g,h; Results, Integrated analysis, paragraphs 5 and 6
claims.quote: For this particular proofread neuron, 74.5% (1,053 out of 1,412 synapses) are onto objects with a single nucleus (as determined from automated detection), with 275 synapses onto cells classified as inhibitory, 662 synapses onto cells classified as excitatory, and 116 synapses onto cells whose soma did not pass classification quality control
claims.criterion: Output synapses of nucleus 294657's root, excluding autapses, merged with the nucleus table on the postsynaptic root (code). The code does not count classes; the class table is not named, and the readings are (a) aibs_metamodel_mtypes_v661_v2, as the Fig. 7 code uses; (b) the cell class table the Methods' classifier fills (Cell classification). Matched cells are those in coregistration_manual_v4.

claims.statement: The oracle responses of the example cell's functionally co-registered postsynaptic targets can be retrieved from the functional data and set beside the presynaptic cell's.
claims.source: Fig. 6k; Results, Integrated analysis, paragraph 6
claims.quote: By filtering the synaptic targets with functionally matched neurons (Fig. 6k ), one can further identify which targets have been matched to the functional experiments (365 out of 1,412) and use DataJoint to query the functional data or read NWB files deposited in the DANDI data archive
claims.criterion: From the code (Fig 6/panel_k/get_data.ipynb). The targets of nucleus 294657 are matched to units in coregistration_manual_v4; per target nucleus, the scan with the highest oracle score is kept, and targets are sorted by summed synapse size. Each unit's oracle trace is averaged over the 10 repeats at 6.3 Hz and min-max normalized. Reproduced when the presynaptic cell and every matched target nucleus of the table have units with oracle trials in the dataset; any target not found is listed. The figure carries no finding beyond this; no response measure is compared.

claims.statement: From 94 proofread excitatory axons one can query 69,962 output synapses, onto 20,112 distinct neuron somata.
claims.source: Discussion, Importance of functional connectomics, paragraph 3
claims.quote: from just 94 proofread excitatory axons, one can query 69,962 output synapses, which map to 20,112 distinct neuron soma in the volume
claims.criterion: The paper does not say which 94 axons. The readings are (a) excitatory neurons with strategy_axon axon_fully_extended; (b) those with fully or partially extended axons whose count is 94 at some public version. Reproduced when one reading gives 94 axons (tolerance 9) and both counts within tolerance.

claims.statement: The outputs of proofread neurons, more than 900,000 synaptic connections, show differences in interlaminar communication between excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: Fig. 7a–c; Results, Cell types, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Examining the output of proofread neurons, which includes more than 900,000 synaptic connections between neurons, reveals key differences in the interlaminar communication between excitatory and inhibitory neurons
claims.criterion: From the code. Presynaptic neurons are those with strategy_axon axon_partially_extended, axon_fully_extended or axon_interareal; postsynaptic cells are those with a unique entry in aibs_metamodel_mtypes_v661_v2; soma depth from the minnie_ds transform. The code's edge list sums to 812,686 synapses onto typed cells, short of "more than 900,000". The readings of the count are (a) synapses onto typed cells, as plotted; (b) all output synapses of those neurons, typed or not. The paper reports "more than 900,000", a lower bound, so the count holds when it is at least 810,000 (900,000 less 10%), with no upper limit. The paper names the differences only in the figure and gives no measure or test of them. Reproduced when the count holds under one reading; the difference part of the claim is recorded as methods_underspecified. The share of each panel's synapses whose presynaptic and postsynaptic somata lie in the same layer (layer bounds from layer_bounds_v3.npy, code) is shown as a description for E to E, E to I and I to E; that measure is set here.

claims.statement: Seven layer 3 pyramidal cells can be followed through their first-order excitatory and inhibitory targets to the second-order excitatory targets of those inhibitory cells, grouped by inhibitory targeting type (DTC, PTC, ITC, STC).
claims.source: Fig. 7d; Results, Cell types, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we can follow a collection of layer 3 pyramidal neurons and compare their first-order (direct) connectivity onto excitatory cell types and inhibitory neurons as well as the second-order (two-hop) connectivity of those inhibitory neurons that are targeted by the layer 3 cells
claims.criterion: The paper names no finding beyond the display. Reproduced when the seven cells' first and second order synapse counts recomputed from CAVE (version 1181) agree with the repository's csv files to within 10% per cell and type.

claims.statement: The two tasks elicited up to 24 movement conditions, with an average of 16 to 17 conditions per session.
claims.source: Results, BMI to study neural population control of movement, paragraph beginning "To study control of diverse movements"; Methods, Neuroprosthetic tasks
claims.quote: Our tasks elicited up to 24 conditions of movement (with an average of 16–17 conditions per session)
claims.criterion: A condition is a task (co, cw, ccw) and target pair, with cw and ccw labelled as in the shared method. The range 16 to 17 widened by 10% of each bound (14.4 to 18.7) decides. The paper does not say what makes a condition count; readings, (a) conditions with at least one rewarded trial; (b) conditions with at least one (command, condition) tuple of 15 or more occurrences. The mean is over all 13 sessions; per-monkey means are reported. Reproduced when the mean lies in 14.4 to 18.7 under one reading.

claims.statement: Each analysed command was used regularly (15 or more times) in several conditions, about 7 on average, typically 5 to 10.
claims.source: Results, BMI to study neural population control of movement, paragraph beginning "Importantly, the BMI enabled us"; Figure S1B; Methods, Conditions that used a command regularly
claims.quote: Each individual command was used with regularity during multiple conditions (on average ~7 conditions, Figure S1B)
claims.criterion: Per session, for each of the 32 commands (magnitude bins 0 to 3), the number of conditions with 15 or more occurrences, counting commands with at least two such conditions, as the Results say and the Figure S1B code does (plot_fr_diffs.py 2797-2870). The code plots one box per session and computes no average; readings of the average, (a) the mean over all commands of all sessions pooled; (b) the mean of the session means. Reproduced when one reading is within 6.3 to 7.7 and the median over commands lies within 5 to 10 widened by 10% (4.5 to 11) (Methods, "Typically, an individual command is used regularly in 5–10 conditions").

claims.statement: The same command is used within command subtrajectories that differ between conditions more than expected from subsampling the condition-pooled subtrajectories (normalized distance 1.920 for Monkey G and 2.342 for Monkey J).
claims.source: Figure S1D legend
claims.quote: Condition-specific command subtrajectories are overall significantly different from the condition-pooled command subtrajectory: Monkey G [J]: p-value < 0.001 for 9/9 [4/4] sessions, p-value < 0.001 pooled over sessions (mean of command subtrajectory distances = 1.920 [2.342]
claims.criterion: As in Methods, Comparing command subtrajectories, and the code (plot_fr_diffs.py 2425-2717). For each tuple with 15 or more occurrences, of a command used in at least two conditions, the condition's average command subtrajectory (x and y command, bins -5 to +5 around each occurrence, occurrences within 5 bins of a trial's start or end left out) and the average over the matched condition-pooled set; distance is the L2 norm of the 2 x 11 difference. 1000 bootstrap subsamples of the condition's size from the matched pool give the null; distances are divided by the bootstrap mean. The Statistics Summary names the behavior-preserving shuffle for Figures S1D and S1E, but that shuffle permutes activity and leaves commands unchanged, so it gives no null for command distances; the subsampling of the Methods section and the legend is the test. Session and pooled tests as in the shared method. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance and the session tests give p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and pooled p < 0.001 in each monkey; partially reproduced when the tests hold and a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The same command is followed by next commands that differ between conditions more than expected from subsampling (normalized distance 1.676 for Monkey G and 2.178 for Monkey J).
claims.source: Figure S1E legend
claims.quote: Condition-specific next commands are overall significantly different from the condition-pooled next command: Monkey G [J]: p-value < 0.01 for 9/9 [4/4] sessions, p-value < 0.001 for 8/9 [4/4] sessions, p-value < 0.001 pooled over sessions (mean of next command distances = 1.676 [2.178]
claims.criterion: As figs1d-command-subtrajectories-differ, with the average command in the bin after each occurrence (occurrences in a trial's last bin left out) in place of the subtrajectory, and the 2-dimensional Euclidean distance (Methods, Comparing command subtrajectories, last paragraph; plot_fr_diffs.py 3513-3525). Reproduced when both means are within tolerance, the session tests give p < 0.01 in all sessions and the pooled tests p < 0.001; partially reproduced when the tests hold and a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Neural population activity issuing a given command differs between conditions more than expected from shuffled data, by 10% to 200% on session averages (normalized distance 1.222 for Monkey G and 1.724 for Monkey J), in every session.
claims.source: Results, The same command is issued by different neural activity patterns in different movements, paragraph 2; Figure 3D; Table S1
claims.quote: Overall, neural activity issuing a given command significantly deviated across conditions relative to the shuffle distribution (Figure 3B–E). Distances averaged within-session ranged from 10% to 200% larger than shuffle distance
claims.criterion: Per tuple (15 or more occurrences), the decoder-null population distance between the condition's mean activity and the matched condition-pooled mean, divided by the mean of its null distribution (Methods, Condition-specific neural activity distances); the session value is the mean over tuples. Null readings (a) and (b) and commands-counted readings (a) and (b) of the shared method. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, both monkey means are within tolerance, every session mean lies within 1.1 to 3.0 widened by 10% of each bound (0.99 to 3.3), and the session and pooled tests give p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and in both pooled tests. Partially reproduced when the tests hold and a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Single-neuron activity issuing a given command differs between conditions more than expected from shuffled data, aggregating over (command, condition, neuron) tuples, in every session.
claims.source: Figure 3B legend; Table S1 (row 3B)
claims.quote: Distance was significantly greater than shuffle distance aggregating over all (command, condition, neuron) tuples: Monkey G [J]: p-value < 0.001 for 9/9 [4/4] sessions, p-value < 0.001 pooled over sessions.
claims.criterion: Per (command, condition, neuron), the absolute difference between the condition's mean rate and the matched condition-pooled mean; the session value is the mean over tuples and neurons, and the monkey value the mean over sessions. Table S1 gives no unit; the code prints these numbers in Hz, not divided by the shuffle (plot_fr_diffs.py 1766-1773), and the shuffle means printed (1.004 for G, 0.745 for J) are consistent with that. Readings of the null as in the shared method. Reproduced when the session and pooled tests give p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and in both pooled tests, and both means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Distances exceed the shuffle for about 30% (Monkey G) and 70% (Monkey J) of individual (command, condition) tuples, about 65% and 90% of commands aggregated over conditions, and about 40% and 80% of neurons aggregated over tuples.
claims.source: Results, The same command is issued by different neural activity patterns in different movements, paragraph 2; Figure 3E
claims.quote: Distances were significantly larger than shuffle distances for a large fraction of individual (command, condition) tuples (~30% for Monkey G, ~70% for Monkey J), individual commands (~65% for G, ~90% for J) when aggregating over conditions, and individual neurons (~40% for G, ~80% for J)
claims.criterion: Significance is p < 0.05 against the null (distance above its 95th percentile). Tuples, population distance per tuple. Commands, the mean over a command's conditions of its population distances against the same mean over the null (Methods, Activity distances pooling over conditions). Neurons, the mean over tuples of a neuron's absolute distance against the same mean over the null. The fractions are per session and the reported value is the mean of session fractions (plot_fr_diffs.py 2109); the pooled fraction over all items is a second reading. For neurons the Methods aggregate over all tuples with 15 or more observations, and the code's plotted fraction over the tuples significant at the population level; both are readings. Null and commands-counted readings as in the shared method. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all six values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at least four are and every fraction is above the 0.05 chance level.

claims.statement: A linear dynamics model fit on all conditions predicts, on held-out data, the activity issuing a given command from the previous activity better than shuffle dynamics, and generalizes to left-out commands and left-out conditions.
claims.source: Figure 4C legend; Results, Invariant dynamics predict the different neural activity patterns used to issue the same command, paragraph beginning "On the level of single time points"; Table S1 (rows 4C)
claims.quote: Full dynamics, command left-out dynamics, and condition left-out dynamics all predicted neural activity significantly better than shuffle dynamics. For each model: Monkey G [J]: p-value < 0.001 for 9/9 [4/4] sessions, p-value < 0.001 for sessions pooled.
claims.criterion: Prediction of x_t from x_{t-1} and c_t by Gaussian conditioning (shared method), on held-out folds for the full model; for the left-out models, one model per command bin (32) or per condition, trained without the bins issuing that command (Figure S4A legend, activity that transitions to and from the command is left out; the code drops bins whose command at t or t-1 is that command, generalization_plots.py 940-1080) or without that condition, and tested on the left-out bins. R2 pooled over neurons on the collated predictions, per session; the monkey value is the mean over sessions. Significance, R2 above the 95th percentile of the shuffle models' R2 (Table S1 gives 0.130 for G and 0.196 for J), and pooled as in the shared method. Shuffle-model ridge readings as in the shared method. Reproduced when every model beats the shuffle with p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and in the pooled tests, and the six R2 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and some R2 values are outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The dynamics model predicts the condition-specific average activity for a command, of single neurons and of the population, with lower error than shuffle dynamics.
claims.source: Figure 4D and 4E legends; Table S1 (rows 4D, 4E)
claims.quote: The full dynamics model predicted individual neuron activity better than shuffle dynamics, aggregating over all (command, condition, neuron) tuples (Monkey G [J]: p-value < 0.001 for 9/9 [4/4] sessions, p-value < 0.001 for pooled sessions).
claims.criterion: For each tuple, the full model's prediction (conditioned on the command) averaged over the tuple's bins, against the tuple's mean activity; single-neuron error is the absolute difference per neuron, population error the L2 norm in the decoder-null space (Methods, Predicting condition-specific activity). Aggregated per session over tuples (and neurons), then over sessions, against the same aggregate for each shuffle model; significant when below the 5th percentile of the shuffle (Table S1 gives 1.359 for G and 1.454 for J, and 0.99 of the shuffle mean for the population). Which tuples are aggregated is open; readings, (a) all tuples with 15 or more observations (legend, "all"); (b) only tuples significant in fig3d-population-distance (the code's only_sig_cc=True, plot_pred_fr_diffs.py 1119-1132). Reproduced when, under one reading, both errors are below the shuffle with p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and in the pooled tests, and the four values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and a value is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Invariant dynamics predict 20% to 40% of the condition-specific component of neural activity (the part not explained by the command alone), significantly more than shuffle dynamics.
claims.source: Results, Invariant dynamics predict the different neural activity patterns used to issue the same command, paragraph beginning "The invariant dynamics model also predicted"; Figure 4F; Table S1 (row 4F)
claims.quote: It predicted 20–40% of the condition-specific component of neural activity
claims.criterion: Per tuple, the true component is the tuple's mean activity minus the mean of the command-only prediction, and the predicted component the dynamics prediction (conditioned on the command) minus the same; R2 of predicted against true components over tuples, in decoder-null coordinates as the code does (plot_pred_fr_diffs.py 1079-1081; Methods, Predicting condition-specific component). Shuffle R2 is about 0 (Table S1, -0.006 G and -0.016 J). Tuples, readings (a) and (b) of fig4de-condition-specific-activity-predicted. Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance, every session value lies within 0.2 to 0.4 widened by 10% (0.18 to 0.44), and the tests give p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and pooled.

claims.statement: The dynamics model predicts the condition-specific activity better than shuffle dynamics for the vast majority of (command, condition) tuples, commands and neurons.
claims.source: Results, Invariant dynamics predict the different neural activity patterns used to issue the same command, paragraph beginning "The invariant dynamics model also predicted"; Figure 4G
claims.quote: The model predicted neural activity for the vast majority of commands, conditions, and neurons (Figure 4G), revealing that dynamics were indeed invariant.
claims.criterion: Per session, the fraction of tuples whose population prediction error is below the 5th percentile of the shuffle models' errors; of commands, by the error averaged over the command's conditions; of neurons, by the error averaged over tuples (Methods, Predicting condition-specific activity; denominators all tuples with 15 or more observations, plot_pred_fr_diffs.py 980-988). The paper gives no number; "majority" is read at its least, a fraction above 0.5. Reproduced when the mean of session fractions is above 0.5 for all three in both monkeys; partially reproduced when it holds for some of the six; the values are reported.

claims.statement: The fitted dynamics are low-dimensional, with 2 to 4 eigenvalues per session whose decay time exceeds the 0.1 s bin (2 to 5 for decoder-null dynamics), and decay to a fixed point with little rotation (mean frequency about 0.1 Hz for Monkey G and 0 Hz for Monkey J).
claims.source: Results, Invariant dynamics predict the different neural activity patterns used to issue the same command, paragraph beginning "We found that the dynamics were low-dimensional"; Figure S3B and S3C legends
claims.quote: The dimensionality of the full dynamics matrix (decoder-null dynamics matrix) ranged from 2-4 (2-5) when considering the eigenvalues that had timescales greater than the BMI update’s timescale of 0.1 seconds.
claims.criterion: Per session, A fit on all pairs with the session's ridge parameter (the code refits in-sample, plot_pred_fr_diffs.py 1791-1921); for each eigenvalue, decay time -0.1 s / ln|lambda| and frequency |angle(lambda)| / (2 pi 0.1 s) (Methods, Dimensionality and eigenvalues). Dimensionality is the number of eigenvalues with decay time above 0.1 s, conjugate pairs counted as two. The code first keeps the eigenvalues that make up 99% of the summed |lambda|; the count without that step is a variant. Decoder-null dynamics fit on activity projected into the decoder-null space. Reproduced when every session's dimensionality is 2 to 4 (decoder-null 2 to 5), the Monkey G mean frequencies are within tolerance (S3C gives them as "~0.1 (~0.06) Hz") and every Monkey J long-timescale eigenvalue is real (0 Hz). Partially reproduced when the counts hold and the frequencies do not.

claims.statement: The full dynamics model, its command and condition left-out versions, and dynamics restricted to the decoder-null space all predict the next neural activity from the current activity better than shuffle dynamics.
claims.source: Figure 5C legend; Results, Invariant dynamics align with the decoder, propagating neural activity to issue the next command, paragraph 3; Table S1 (rows 5C)
claims.quote: All models predicted next neural activity significantly better than shuffle dynamics. For each model, Monkey G [J]: p-value < 0.001 for 9/9 [4/4] sessions, p-value < 0.001 for sessions pooled.
claims.criterion: Prediction A x_{t-1} + b without the command, on held-out folds (Methods, Predicting next neural activity); decoder-null dynamics fit on activity projected into the decoder-null space with the session mean of the decoder-space part added back (Methods, Decoder-null dynamics model). R2 pooled over neurons per session, mean over sessions; significance against the 95th percentile of the shuffle models (Table S1, 0.055 G and 0.053 J) and pooled as in the shared method. Shuffle-model ridge readings as in the shared method. Reproduced when every model beats the shuffle with p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and pooled, and the eight R2 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and some values are outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The full dynamics model predicts about 4 dimensions of neural activity (dynamics eigenvectors) more accurately than the rest.
claims.source: Results, Invariant dynamics align with the decoder, propagating neural activity to issue the next command, paragraph 3; Figure 5D
claims.quote: the full dynamics model was low-dimensional (Figure S3B) and predicted ~4 dimensions more accurately than the rest of neural activity (Figure 5D)
claims.criterion: Per session, held-out predictions and true activity projected onto each eigenvector of A (Methods, Predicting next neural activity; the code uses the fold-0 A, splits complex pairs into real and imaginary parts and projects with the pseudo-inverse, generalization_plots.py 2116-2195), R2 per dimension, sorted. The paper gives no rule for which dimensions count as predicted "more accurately than the rest"; readings, (a) the number with R2 above the session's pooled R2 of the full model (fig5c-next-activity); (b) the number with R2 above the session's 95th percentile of shuffle R2 for all activity. "~4" is read as 3 to 5. Reproduced when, under one reading, the median over sessions is 3 to 5 in each monkey; the sorted R2 curves are shown.

claims.statement: The full dynamics model and its command and condition left-out versions predict the next command from the current activity better than shuffle dynamics, while decoder-null dynamics give no prediction of it.
claims.source: Figure 5E legend; Results, Invariant dynamics align with the decoder, propagating neural activity to issue the next command, paragraph 3; Table S1 (rows labelled 5D)
claims.quote: All models except decoder-null dynamics predicted next command significantly better than shuffle dynamics.
claims.criterion: Predicted next command K (A x_{t-1} + b) against the true command, R2 pooled over the x and y components (Methods, Predicting next command; generalization_plots.py 2744-2768), per session and averaged. Shuffle 95th percentiles in Table S1 are 0.266 (G) and 0.188 (J). The decoder-null tolerance is half the printed precision of "0.0", as its prediction of the command is a constant by construction. Shuffle-model ridge readings as in the shared method. Reproduced when the full and command left-out models beat the shuffle with p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and pooled, the condition left-out model beats it pooled in both monkeys, the decoder-null model does not beat it in any session, and the R2 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and some values are outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The dynamics model predicts the condition-specific average next command better than shuffle dynamics, aggregated over tuples, and for the majority of (command, condition) tuples.
claims.source: Figure 5F legend; Results, Invariant dynamics align with the decoder, propagating neural activity to issue the next command, paragraph 3; Table S1 (row labelled 5E)
claims.quote: The full dynamics model predicted condition-specific next command better than shuffle dynamics, aggregating over all (command, condition) tuples (Monkey G [J]: p-value < 0.001 for 9/9 [4/4] sessions, p-value < 0.001 for pooled sessions).
claims.criterion: Per tuple, the average of K (A x_{t-1} + b) over the tuple's bins against the average true next command; error the L2 norm; significant when below the 5th percentile of the shuffle models' errors (Methods, Predicting condition-specific next command; Table S1 gives 5.38 for G and 9.240 for J). The unit of the error is not given; the command's own units (those of the decoder's velocity update) are used. Session and pooled aggregates as in the shared method. Reproduced when the aggregate tests give p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and pooled, the mean of session fractions of significant tuples is above 0.5 in each monkey ("majority"), and both errors are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and the error values or the fractions do not.

claims.statement: The dynamics model predicts whether the next command turns clockwise or counterclockwise relative to the condition-pooled next command, and the angle of the turn, better than shuffle dynamics.
claims.source: Results, Invariant dynamics align with the decoder, propagating neural activity to issue the next command, paragraph 4; Figure 5H; Table S1 (rows labelled 5G)
claims.quote: Specifically, the dynamics model predicted whether the turn would be clockwise or counter clockwise (Figure 5H left) and the angle of turn (Fig 5H right) better than shuffle dynamics.
claims.criterion: Per tuple, the signed angle from the matched condition-pooled mean next command to the condition's mean next command, true and predicted (sign from the cross product; Methods, Analysis of predicted command angle; pred_fwd.py 356-428). Sign accuracy is the fraction of tuples with matching sign, against the 95th percentile of the shuffle (Table S1, 0.541 G, 0.480 J); angle error is the mean absolute difference of the two angles in degrees, against the 5th percentile of the shuffle (26.415 G, 12.636 J). Reproduced when both measures beat the shuffle with p < 0.001 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions and pooled, and the four values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and some values are outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Adding previous neural activity (invariant dynamics) to a model that encodes the command, cursor state, target and task significantly improves the held-out prediction of neural activity.
claims.source: Figure S5B legend; Results, Invariant dynamics predict the different neural activity patterns used to issue the same command, paragraph beginning "On the level of single time points"
claims.quote: Incorporating invariant neural dynamics (cyan) significantly improves upon predictions from the model with all task-relevant variables
claims.criterion: Behavior-encoding model, activity at t given the command, cursor position and velocity at t-1, target position and a categorical target and task variable (Methods, Estimation of behavior-encoding models), predictors z-scored, ridge with cross-validated parameter, 5 folds; the same model plus x_{t-1}. Held-out R2 pooled over neurons. One pair per session, as the Methods say ("session was paired") and the code does (plot_pred_fr_diffs.py 192); the paper's N (18 and 8) counts the two R2 values of each of the 9 and 4 sessions, as its p-values are those of a paired t-test with 8 and 3 degrees of freedom (T = -7.182 gives p = 9.4e-05 with 8; T = -5.141 gives p = 0.0143 with 3). Reproduced when a paired t-test gives p < 0.05 in each monkey with the model with dynamics higher.

claims.statement: A recurrent switching linear dynamical system (rsLDS) does not predict neural activity better than the linear ridge dynamics model.
claims.source: Results, Invariant dynamics predict the different neural activity patterns used to issue the same command, paragraph beginning "We found that the dynamics were low-dimensional"; Figure S5F legend
claims.quote: Notably, a non-linear dynamics model (a recurrent switching linear dynamical system52) did not out-perform these simple linear dynamics
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test. rsLDS from the ssm package (github.com/lindermanlab/ssm), "recurrent_only" transitions, Gaussian dynamics and emissions, latent dimension set to the number of neurons (legend; the code uses neurons minus 1, single_subspace=True, after dropping neurons below 0.5 Hz and mean-subtracting), fit by Laplace EM, structured mean field, 10 iterations; number of discrete states K from 1 to 5; 5 folds by trial; one-step prediction of the next bin's activity (rebuttal_train_rslds_plot_model_R2.ipynb cells 7 to 9; generate_models.py 1849-2193). Reproduced when, for every K, the mean over sessions of the rsLDS held-out R2 is not above the ridge model's in each monkey; the R2 values are reported. The code leaves out Monkey G sessions 2 and 4; all sessions and the code's subset are shown.

claims.statement: The residual of the dynamics model is larger early in the trial than late, consistent with large input at movement start.
claims.source: Figure S3F legend
claims.quote: The residual is larger in the early trial period than the late trial period.
claims.criterion: Residual of the held-out prediction x_t - (A x_{t-1} + b), its L2 norm divided by the square root of the number of neurons per bin. Trial length set to the session's median trial time; early and late are the first and last thirds of it; per trial the mean residual norm in each epoch; trials shorter than the median left out. LME (statsmodels mixedlm) of residual on epoch with session as group (legend; util_fcns.run_LME). Reproduced when the late-minus-early effect is negative with p < 0.05 in each monkey. The code's grouping mixes Monkey J trials into the Monkey G model (plot_pred_fr_diffs.py 3013); the per-monkey test is the main one.

claims.statement: Dynamics models trained without all commands of one angle bin, or of one magnitude bin, still predict the left-out activity (given the command) better than shuffle dynamics.
claims.source: Figure S4B legend
claims.quote: All commands in a particular angular bin are left out and predicted significantly better than shuffle dynamics
claims.criterion: As fig4c-dynamics-predict-activity-given-command, with one model per angle bin (8) or magnitude bin (4) left out of training (Methods, Generalization of invariant dynamics). Shuffle 95th percentiles are 0.130 (G) and 0.196 (J). Reproduced when the pooled tests give p < 0.001 in each monkey, the session tests hold in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions, and the R2 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and some values are outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Dynamics models trained without whole classes of conditions (vertical, horizontal or diagonal targets, both tasks) still predict the left-out activity better than shuffle dynamics.
claims.source: Figure S4G legend
claims.quote: All neural activity in a particular set of left-out conditions is left out and predicted significantly better than shuffle dynamics.
claims.criterion: Classes as in the Methods (targets at 90 and 270, 0 and 180, and the two diagonals, both tasks, cw and ccw together); the code defines them by condition index per monkey (generalization_plots.py 1161-1164), which is the reading used, the Methods' "45 and 215 degrees" being taken as the 45 and 225 degree diagonal. Prediction given the command, as in fig4c. Reproduced when every class beats the shuffle with p < 0.001 pooled in each monkey, in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions, and the R2 values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Across pairs of conditions issuing the same command, the dynamics-predicted distance between average activity correlates with the true distance, for single neurons and for the population.
claims.source: Figure S6C and S6D legends; Results, Invariant dynamics predict the different neural activity patterns used to issue the same command, paragraph beginning "Finally, the dynamics model preserved structure"
claims.quote: Dynamics-predicted distances across condition-pairs are significantly correlated with true distances
claims.criterion: For each command and pair of conditions each with 15 or more occurrences, the true distance between the two conditions' mean activity and the distance between the dynamics model's predictions (conditioned on the command), per neuron (absolute difference, Hz) and for the population (decoder-null L2 norm divided by the square root of the number of neurons, Methods, Analysis of activity issuing a given command), with pairwise command matching as in the code (plot_pred_fr_diffs.py 1464-1788). scipy linregress per session and on data pooled over sessions. Reproduced when every session and the pooled regression give p < 0.001 with positive slope and the pooled r values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Across pairs of conditions, the distance between activity patterns issuing the same command correlates with the distance between the command subtrajectories, and the dynamics model's predicted distances keep this relationship.
claims.source: Results, The same command is issued by different neural activity patterns in different movements, paragraph 2; Figure S6G legend
claims.quote: Over all commands, command subtrajectory distance across a condition-pair is significantly correlated with population activity distance
claims.criterion: For commands used in more than five conditions, each pair of conditions with 15 or more occurrences; neural distance is the decoder-null population distance between the two conditions' mean activity (true, or predicted by the dynamics model), behavior distance the L2 norm of the difference of their command subtrajectories (Methods, Correlating neural distance with behavior). statsmodels mixedlm of neural on behavior distance with a random intercept per command and session (plot_pred_fr_diffs.py 2335-2760). Reproduced when, in each monkey, the pooled slope is positive with p < 0.001 for both true and predicted distances.

claims.statement: Across pairs of conditions, the dynamics-predicted distance between the next commands that follow the same command correlates with the true distance.
claims.source: Figure S6K legend; Results, Invariant dynamics align with the decoder, propagating neural activity to issue the next command, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Dynamics-predicted distance between next commands across a condition-pair is significantly correlated with the true distance
claims.criterion: For each command and pair of conditions, the distance between the two conditions' mean next commands, true and predicted by K (A x_{t-1} + b) (pred_fwd.py 701-931); scipy linregress per session and pooled. Reproduced when the pooled regressions give p < 0.001 with positive slope, at least 8 of 9 G and 4 of 4 J sessions are significant, and both r values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: In an optimal feedback control model that drives the recorded decoders, a neural population with the fitted invariant dynamics needs significantly less input to perform the tasks than one with no dynamics.
claims.source: Figure 6C legend; Results, An OFC model reveals that invariant dynamics reduce the input, paragraph 4; Table S2
claims.quote: These simulations revealed that the population required significantly less input in the Full Dynamics Model than in the No Dynamics Model (Figure 6C).
claims.criterion: Simulation as in Methods, Optimal feedback control model and simulation. Per session, A and b of the full dynamics model; finite-horizon LQR with terminal cost on cursor position and velocity only and input cost the identity (the code's Q_f = 100, R = I, LQR/ behavior_co_obs.py 2194-2220), horizon 40 bins (center-out) or 20 + 20 through a waypoint 6 cm from the obstacle (obstacle); 20 trials for each of 24 conditions; initial state the fixed point; isotropic neural noise with variance equal to the mean per-neuron variance of the noiseless No Dynamics simulation; No Dynamics Model A = 0 with b kept. Input magnitude per trial is the L2 (Frobenius) norm of the N x T input matrix, averaged over a condition's 20 trials. Wilcoxon signed-rank paired over the 24 conditions per session; LME (statsmodels mixedlm) of magnitude on model with session as group. Reproduced when, in each monkey, the full model's input is lower with LME p < 0.05 and the Wilcoxon gives p < 0.05 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions. Noise is random; the seed is a standard choice.

claims.statement: When the model's invariant dynamics are restricted to the decoder-null space, the input needed is not different from a population with no dynamics.
claims.source: Figure 6D legend; Table S2
claims.quote: There was no significant difference in input magnitude between Decoder-null Dynamics (pink ‘D’) and No Dynamics (black ‘ND’) when pooling across sessions (Monkey G [J] p-value > 0.05) and on individual sessions
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests. As fig6c-dynamics-reduce-input with the decoder-null dynamics model (fit on activity projected into the decoder-null space), each against its own No Dynamics Model with the decoder-null offset. Reproduced when the LME gives p >= 0.05 in each monkey and the Wilcoxon p >= 0.05 in every session; not reproduced when the LME, or the Wilcoxon in any session, finds a difference; the effect size is reported either way.

claims.statement: In the OFC simulations, activity issuing the same command differs between conditions more than shuffle with the fitted full dynamics, but not without dynamics or with decoder-null dynamics.
claims.source: Figure 6G and 6H legends; Results, An OFC model reveals that invariant dynamics reduce the input, paragraph 5; Table S2
claims.quote: The population activity distances for (command, condition) tuples were significantly larger than shuffle in the Full Dynamics Model but not in the No Dynamics Model (Figure 6FG).
claims.criterion: On the simulations of fig6c and fig6d, commands discretized and tuples of 15 or more occurrences as for the recorded data; per tuple the decoder-null population distance (as in fig3d) and the mean of its null. The Methods compare each model with its own behavior-preserving shuffle (Methods, Simulated activity issuing a given command) and do not give the number of shuffles for the simulations; the code draws condition-sized subsamples of the matched pool (LQR/analyze_lqr.py 177-326). Readings, (a) behavior-preserving shuffle of the simulated activity, 1000 shuffles as for the recorded data; (b) the code's subsampling. Per session, Mann-Whitney U of observed distances against the tuples' null means; per monkey, LME of distance on source (simulation or shuffle) with session as group. Reproduced when the full model's distances exceed the null in each monkey (LME p < 0.05; Mann-Whitney p < 0.05 in at least 8 of 9 G and 3 of 4 J sessions) and, as claims of absence on the same tests, the No Dynamics models (of both comparisons) and the Decoder-null model give LME p >= 0.05 in each monkey, and Mann-Whitney p >= 0.05 in every session (Figure 6G and 6H legends). Partially reproduced when the full model's effect holds and an absence does not.

claims.statement: For Monkey J, a time-invariant linear map of neural activity accounts for 99.6, 99.6, 99.5 and 99.8% of the variance of the point process filter's command in the four sessions.
claims.source: Methods, Command definition, Monkey J
claims.quote: for all four analyzed sessions, neural activity mapped through could account for 99.6, 99.6, 99.5, and 99.8 percent of the variance of the command respectively
claims.criterion: Per session, the least-squares matrix (no intercept) from 5 ms spike counts to the PPF's velocity update over all rewarded trials of both tasks, and its in-sample variance accounted for, 1 minus the summed squared residual of x and y over the summed squares of the demeaned update (generate_models.py 3044-3103). The tolerance is the distance to 99%, the threshold the code asserts (generate_models_utils.py 512-513), as 10% of the value would admit any fit. Reproduced when every session accounts for at least 99% and the four values are within 0.5 percentage points of those reported. Needs the PPF update or its parameters; blocked when the dataset has neither.

claims.statement: The data come from 459 sessions of 139 mice recorded in 12 laboratories.
claims.source: Abstract; Methods, Inclusion criteria, Sessions and insertions, paragraph 4
claims.quote: recorded with 699 Neuropixels probes across 139 mice in 12 laboratories ... After applying these criteria, a total of 459 sessions, 699 insertions and 621,733 neurons remained

claims.statement: 699 Neuropixels insertions yielded 621,733 units, an average of 889 per probe.
claims.source: Abstract; Results, Recordings, paragraph 1; Methods, Inclusion criteria, Sessions and insertions, paragraph 4
claims.quote: we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes ... This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe.

claims.statement: Stringent quality metrics identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, an average of 108 per probe.
claims.source: Results, Recordings, paragraph 1; Methods, Inclusion criteria, Neurons and brain regions, paragraph 1
claims.quote: we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.
claims.criterion: A unit is well-isolated when its ibl_quality_score is 1 (all three metrics passed). The data check also tests that the score equals the fraction of the three metrics (median amplitude above 50 uV, noise cutoff below 20, sliding refractory period pass) that each unit passes.

claims.statement: The main analyses use a canonical dataset of 201 regions with at least 2 sessions of 5 well-isolated neurons and at least 20 neurons in total, 62,857 neurons.
claims.source: Results, Neural analyses, paragraph 1; Methods, Inclusion criteria, Neurons and brain regions, paragraph 1
claims.quote: a canonical dataset of 201 regions for which we had at least 2 sessions with 5 well-isolated neurons each and at least 20 well-isolated neurons after pooling all sessions (for a total of 62,857 neurons
claims.criterion: Regions are Beryl regions of each unit's peak channel, void and root left out, with the inclusion steps applied in the order of the code's meta/inclusion_info.py. The count at each step is compared with that file's table.

claims.statement: The probes covered 279 brain areas.
claims.source: Abstract
claims.quote: The probes covered 279 brain areas in the left forebrain and midbrain and the right hindbrain and cerebellum.

claims.statement: The 139 mice were 94 male and 45 female.
claims.source: Results, Behavioural task, paragraph 1; Methods, Animals
claims.quote: We trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task

claims.statement: On the day of recording the mice were aged 13 to 178 weeks (mean 44.96, median 27.0) and weighed 16.1 to 35.7 g (mean 23.9, median 23.84).
claims.source: Methods, Animals
claims.quote: Mice were aged 13–178 weeks (mean 44.96 weeks, median 27.0 weeks) and weighed 16.1–35.7 g (mean 23.9 g, median 23.84 g) on the day of electrophysiological recordings.
claims.criterion: Age is session start minus date of birth; weight is the subject weight in each file. Readings, one value per mouse, (a) at its first recording session, (b) at its last, or (c) one value per session. Age and weight are judged separately; each holds when its four values are within tolerance under one reading. Reproduced when both hold, partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: The insertions used Neuropixels 1.0 probes of versions 3A (109) and 3B2 (586), and Neuropixels 2.4 probes (4).
claims.source: Methods, Materials and apparatus, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Neural recordings were made using Neuropixels probes, either v.1.0 (3A or 3B2, n = 109 and n = 586 insertions, respectively) or v.2.4 (n = 4 insertions)
claims.criterion: The files name probes by imec model; NP1010 (no PXI port or slot, as 3A probes were recorded with an FPGA) is read as 3A, PRB_1_4_0480_1 with or without the _C suffix as 3B2, and NP2010 as the 2.x probes. The counts are of insertions over sessions.

claims.statement: Recorded sessions lasted on average 645 trials (median 602, range 401 to 1,525).
claims.source: Results, Behavioural task, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Recorded sessions lasted on average 645 trials (median of 602, range of 401–1,525).

claims.statement: Receptive-field mapping after the task (504 of 699 insertions) found a relatively small fraction of cells with significant receptive fields, with large fractions in VISp, VISl and SCs.
claims.source: Results, Representation of visual stimulus, paragraph 9; Methods, RF mapping; Supplementary Fig. 5
claims.quote: Overall, we found a relatively small fraction of cells with significant RFs (Supplementary Fig. 5). The regions with large fractions tended to be classical visual regions (VISp, VISl and SCs).

claims.statement: After training, mice made correct choices on 81.4 +/- 0.4% (mean +/- s.d.) of trials.
claims.source: Results, Behavioural task, paragraph 2
claims.quote: After training, they made correct choices on 81.4 ± 0.4% (mean ± s.d.) of the trials
claims.criterion: The tolerance is the paper's stated spread. Readings (a) mean over mice of each mouse's percent correct over all its trials; (b) the same over analysed trials (first movement time 0.08 to 2 s and complete events); (c) mean over sessions of all trials; (d) all trials pooled. Reproduced when one reading is within tolerance. The spread is reported as s.d. and s.e.m.

claims.statement: On 0% contrast trials mice were rewarded on 58.7 +/- 0.4% (mean +/- s.e.m. across mice) of trials, better than chance (t138 = 20.18, P = 5.2e-43).
claims.source: Results, Behavioural task, paragraph 2; Fig. 1d legend
claims.quote: On 0% contrast trials, in which no visual information was provided, mice gained rewards on 58.7 ± 0.4% (mean ± s.e.m) of trials, significantly better than chance
claims.criterion: One value per mouse, pooled over its sessions; one-sample t-test against 50% with 138 degrees of freedom. Readings (a) all 0% contrast trials, (b) analysed 0% contrast trials. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: 22.8% of first wheel-movement times occurred under 80 ms after stimulus onset.
claims.source: Fig. 1c legend
claims.quote: A total of 22.8% first wheel-movement times occurred under 80 ms (not shown).
claims.criterion: First movement time is the first movement minus stimulus onset. Readings, (a) over all trials of the 459 sessions, a trial without a first movement counting as not early; (b) over trials with both times; (c) mean over sessions of (b).

claims.statement: Mice performed better and faster on trials with high visual contrast.
claims.source: Fig. 1d; Results, Behavioural task, paragraph 2
claims.quote: they made correct choices on 81.4 ± 0.4% (mean ± s.d.) of the trials, performing better and faster on trials with high visual stimulus contrast (Fig. 1d).
claims.criterion: Per mouse, pooled over sessions, the percent correct and the median first movement time at each of the five contrasts, over trials with a response. Reproduced when, across mice, percent correct at 100% is higher than at 0% and median first movement time at 100% is shorter than at 0% (Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.05 each), and the median over mice of percent correct rises with contrast at every step; partially reproduced when only one of the two measures holds.

claims.statement: Towards the end of the sessions, performance decreased and first wheel-movement times increased.
claims.source: Fig. 1e,f; Results, Behavioural task, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Towards the end of the sessions, performance decreased and first wheel-movement times increased (Fig. 1e,f).
claims.criterion: Per mouse, pooled over sessions, the percent correct on non-zero contrast trials and the median first movement time over the last 50 trials of each session against trials 51 to 300 before the end. Reproduced when the end has lower percent correct and longer first movement times (Wilcoxon signed-rank across mice p < 0.05 each); partially reproduced when one holds.

claims.statement: After a block switch, mice took around 5 to 10 trials to adjust their behaviour, as shown by the fraction of correct choices on 0% contrast trials after the switch.
claims.source: Fig. 1g; Results, Behavioural task, paragraph 2
claims.quote: After a block switch, mice took around 5–10 trials to adjust their behaviour to the new block, as revealed by the fraction of correct choices made on 0% contrast trials after the switch (Fig. 1g).
claims.criterion: Switches between biased blocks; on 0% contrast trials at positions 1 to 40 after the switch, the fraction of choices matching the stimulus side (which follows the new block), per position pooled over each mouse's sessions and averaged over mice. Fit p(n) = a - b exp(-(n - 1) / tau). Readings (a) tau, (b) the trials to cover 90% of the change, 1 + tau ln 10. Reproduced when one reading lies within 4.5 to 11 trials (5 to 10 widened by 10%).

claims.statement: For all contrast values mice chose the side of the block's likely stimulus more often, responding right more often in right blocks than in left blocks.
claims.source: Fig. 1h; Results, Behavioural task, paragraph 2
claims.quote: That is, for all contrast values, mice tended to answer left more often on left blocks than right blocks (Fig. 1h).
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the fraction of right choices at each of the nine signed contrasts in right blocks (p_left 0.2) and left blocks (p_left 0.8), over trials with a response. Reproduced when the right-block fraction is higher at all nine contrasts (median difference above 0 and Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.05 across mice); partially reproduced at 6 to 8 contrasts.

claims.statement: The visual stimulus side, decoded from the first 100 ms after stimulus onset, was represented in a narrower set of regions than choice or feedback, with strong signatures in visual cortex such as VISp.
claims.source: Fig. 4a,i; Results, Representation of visual stimulus, paragraph 2; Discussion, paragraph 4
claims.quote: the activity of neurons in the primary visual cortex (VISp) could be used to predict the stimulus side (Fig. 4i) ... The visual stimulus (Fig. 4) was represented (before movement) in a more restricted manner.
claims.criterion: Decoding of stimulus side on non-zero contrast analysed trials, null from pseudo-sessions, over the tested regions (see the opening comment). Reproduced when VISp is significant and fewer tested regions are significant for stimulus than for choice and than for feedback; partially reproduced when only one of the two holds. The agreement of each region's significance with the paper's table region_info.csv is reported, and does not decide.

claims.statement: Choice, decoded from the 100 ms before the first wheel movement, was represented in a larger number of regions than the visual stimulus, with strong effects in hindbrain regions such as GRN.
claims.source: Fig. 5a,i; Results, Representation of choice, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The decoding analysis suggested a representation of choice (left versus right upcoming action) in a larger number of brain regions than the representation of the visual stimulus ... The strongest effect sizes were observed in the hindbrain (GRN, VII, PRNr and MARN)
claims.criterion: Decoding of choice on analysed trials, null from synthetic sessions of an action-kernel model fitted per session, over the tested regions. Reproduced when GRN is significant and more tested regions are significant for choice than for stimulus; partially reproduced when only one holds.

claims.statement: Whether the trial was correct could be decoded from the 200 ms after feedback onset in nearly all recorded regions, almost perfectly in many.
claims.source: Fig. 6a,i; Results, Representation of feedback, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Using the neural responses in the 200 ms after feedback onset, we were able to decode whether the trial was correct from nearly all recorded brain regions (Fig. 6a,f). In many regions, decoding was almost perfect.
claims.criterion: Decoding of feedback on analysed trials, null from synthetic sessions, over the 10 tested regions. Reproduced when at least 9 tested regions, including IRN, are significant; partially reproduced for 6 to 8; not reproduced below 6. The number of region-sessions with a balanced accuracy above 0.9 is reported.

claims.statement: Single-cell tests controlling for choice and block found few stimulus-selective neurons (0.5% of all neurons); even in the regions with the largest fractions, such as visual cortex, the fraction did not exceed about 10%.
claims.source: Fig. 4b; Results, Representation of visual stimulus, paragraph 4
claims.quote: with 0.5% of all neurons correlated with a stimulus side (Fig. 4b) ... However, even in the regions that contained the largest fractions of responsive neurons (such as the visual cortex), this fraction did not exceed about 10%.
claims.criterion: Over the neurons of the tested and latency regions (14 regions). Reproduced when no region exceeds 11% and at least 10 of the 14 regional fractions are within 0.02 of the paper's region_info.csv value. The 0.5% of all neurons cannot be tested on a set of regions chosen this way, and the pooled fraction is reported. The paper's false-positive rate for the selection, 0.001 x 0.05 = 5e-5, is checked with a null run (pseudo-session stimulus sides and blocks); if the 95% interval of the null fraction excludes 1/3 to 3 times 5e-5, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: More neurons responded to choice than to the visual stimulus (4% of all neurons), with the largest fractions in hindbrain, midbrain and thalamic regions.
claims.source: Fig. 5b; Results, Representation of choice, paragraph 3
claims.quote: More single neurons significantly responded to choice than to the visual stimulus (Fig. 5b,f). That is, firing rates of 4% of all neurons ... The largest fractions of neurons that significantly responded to choice were in the hindbrain, cerebellar, midbrain and thalamic regions
claims.criterion: Over the same 14 regions. Reproduced when the pooled choice fraction is higher than the pooled stimulus fraction (binomial test on the neurons selective for exactly one, p < 0.05) and the regional choice fractions correlate with region_info.csv (Spearman, p < 0.05). The same false-positive check applies, with synthetic choices.

claims.statement: The latency of the stimulus trajectory separation ordered the visual regions as LGd < VISp, which is about equal to LP, < VISpm < VISam, at about 34, 42, 42, 57 and 78 ms.
claims.source: Fig. 4d,l,m; Results, Representation of visual stimulus, paragraph 7
claims.quote: A spatiotemporally finely resolved view of latency differences was obtained, such that LGd < VISp ≈ LP < VISpm < VISam (latencies of around 34, 42, 42, 57 and 78 ms, respectively
claims.criterion: Trajectories over all canonical sessions of each region, 0 to 150 ms after stimulus onset. Latency as the Methods define it, the first time the distance reaches 70% of its range; the code's added condition that this time be significant point-wise is a variant. Reproduced when the order holds (LGd below both VISp and LP, both below VISpm, VISpm below VISam, and VISp and LP within 10 ms of each other) and all five values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when only one of the two holds.

claims.statement: The early visual wave was followed by later stimulus encoding in the MRN, SCm, PRNr, IRN and GRN, with latencies of about 100 to 120 ms.
claims.source: Fig. 4d,l,m; Results, Representation of visual stimulus, paragraph 7
