claims.quote: finding that ADN axons and visual axons are mostly restricted to the boundaries of the heading and landmark clusters, respectively (Fig. 5I), although there is some overlap with the alignment cluster boundary
claims.criterion: An LDA model trained on the soma features and their GMM classes (Methods, Clustering of RSC soma responses) projects the axon features (same Gaussian fits, Methods, Clustering of axonal responses) onto its first two discriminants; each soma class has a 95% ellipse (Methods; read as the 95% region of a bivariate normal fitted to the class's points). Axons as in fig4-axons-light-on-shape, readings (a) and (b). "Mostly" is read as more than half. Reproduced when, under a reading, more than half of ADN axons lie inside the heading ellipse and more than half of visual axons inside the landmark ellipse; partially reproduced when only one holds. The shares inside the alignment ellipse are reported.

claims.statement: When only the visual cues rotate (no proprioceptive or somatosensory input), the visual contributions to tuning are retained, but heading-cell responses are strongly degraded.
claims.source: Results, A functional class of RSC neurons coregisters visual and heading signals, paragraph 4; Figure 5J, K
claims.quote: We found that the visual contributions to tuning were retained in visual cue only rotation, but the loss of proprioceptive and somatosensory information strongly degraded the heading cell responses
claims.criterion: Neurons matched between a standard-rotation and a visual-cue-only recording (Figure 5K legend), classed in the standard recording. The paper gives neither the number of recordings nor a measure or test. Readings, (a) the fraction of cells of each class that pass the heading-selection test in the visual-only recording; (b) the peak-to-trough range of the class's mean aligned light-on tuning curve (light-on shifts from the standard recording) in visual-only relative to standard rotation. Reproduced when, under a reading, landmark cells keep a bimodal light-on curve in visual-only rotation (flip score of the class mean above 0) and heading cells lose more than landmark cells (lower fraction or lower relative range). Blocked if the dataset holds no visual-cue-only recordings.

claims.statement: Decoding heading from all tuned RSC cells within single 100 ms frames is accurate in the light-on condition despite the symmetric cues (mean decoder accuracy 0.82, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.86).
claims.source: Results, Contributions of distinct classes to representation of heading, paragraph 1; Figure 6A
claims.quote: When sampling across all the classes, the heading network shows remarkable accuracy, even in the presence of symmetric visual cues (mean decoder accuracy = 0.82, 95% CI = [0.78, 0.86]
claims.criterion: The decoding method of the opening comment, sampling from all three classes. Tolerance is the half-width of the paper's 95% CI. Reproduced when a reading of the decoder gives a mean within tolerance; every reading is reported.

claims.statement: In the light-off condition the decoder's accuracy from all tuned cells drops (mean 0.44, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.54; p = 7.6e-3 against light-on) but stays above chance.
claims.source: Results, Contributions of distinct classes to representation of heading, paragraph 1; Figure 6A, bottom
claims.quote: When transitioning from light-on to light-off, there is a drop in the performance of the decoder, although the performance remains above chance ... (mean decoder accuracy = 0.44, 95% CI = [0.34, 0.54], p = 7.6 × 10−3
claims.criterion: As fig6a-population-light-on, light-off trials. Above chance means the 95% interval excludes chance (Methods), under either chance reading (0.18 or 0.10). Reproduced when, under a decoder reading, the mean is within tolerance, the interval excludes chance and the bootstrapped t-test of light-on against light-off gives p < 0.05 with light-off lower.

claims.statement: Heading cells alone decode heading accurately in both light-on (0.61, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.66) and light-off (0.44, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.52) conditions, with no significant difference between them (p = 0.11).
claims.source: Results, Contributions of distinct classes to representation of heading, paragraph 2; Figure 6B, top
claims.quote: We found that heading cells were able to accurately decode in both light-on (mean decoder accuracy = 0.61, 95% CI = [0.56, 0.66]) and light-off conditions (mean decoder accuracy = 0.44, 95% CI = [0.36, 0.52]), suggesting that they contribute to the heading signal in both conditions (p = 0.11
claims.criterion: The decoding method of the opening comment on heading cells only. The values are judged under each decoder reading; reproduced when a reading puts both within tolerance and both intervals exclude chance. The absence of a light difference is judged on the paper's bootstrapped t-test alone, not significant when p >= 0.05; the claim is not reproduced if p < 0.05 under the reading that matches the values.

claims.statement: Landmark cells decode heading very well in light-on (0.80, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.84) but fall to chance in light-off (0.20, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.27; p = 8.0e-4).
claims.source: Results, Contributions of distinct classes to representation of heading, paragraph 2; Figure 6B, middle
claims.quote: landmark cells have very high decoder performance in the light-on condition (mean decoder accuracy = 0.80, 95% CI = [0.75, 0.84]), with an overrepresentation of decoder errors at 180°, which immediately plummets to chance levels in the light-off condition (mean decoder accuracy = 0.20, 95% CI = [0.14, 0.27]; p = 8.0 × 10−4
claims.criterion: The decoding method on landmark cells only; tolerances from the paper's intervals (the larger half-width). Reproduced when, under a decoder reading, both means are within tolerance, the light-on against light-off p < 0.05, and the light-off interval includes chance. Under the 0.10 chance reading the paper's own light-off interval excludes chance; the outcome under each chance reading is reported.

claims.statement: Alignment cells decode between heading and landmark cells, better in light-on (0.71, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.76) and fairly accurately in light-off (0.51, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.59), with no significant difference (p = 0.54).
claims.source: Results, Contributions of distinct classes to representation of heading, paragraph 2; Figure 6B, bottom
claims.quote: alignment cells show decoder performance that is between that of heading and landmark cells, taking advantage of improved decoding from the visual cues in the light-on condition (mean decoder accuracy = 0.71, 95% CI = [0.66, 0.76]), but retaining fairly accurate heading in the light-off condition (mean decoder accuracy = 0.51, 95% CI = [0.43, 0.59], p = 0.54
claims.criterion: The decoding method on alignment cells only. Reproduced when, under a decoder reading, both means are within tolerance, the light-on mean lies between those of heading and landmark cells, and the light-off interval excludes chance. The absence of a light difference is judged on the bootstrapped t-test alone (p >= 0.05); the claim is not reproduced if p < 0.05 under the reading that matches the values.

claims.statement: Decoding from landmark cells in light-on gives an overrepresentation of 180 degree errors from the symmetric cues, while heading cells show no preponderance of 180 degree errors.
claims.source: Results, Contributions of distinct classes to representation of heading, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 6B
claims.quote: As expected based on their tuning curves, heading cells did not exhibit a preponderance of 180° errors, suggesting they do not represent visual information directly
claims.criterion: Light-on decoder errors of the class decoders, under each decoder reading. The paper gives no measure; the measure is the share of frames with an absolute error within 18 degrees of 180 (the paper's accuracy window, moved to 180), against its share of 0.10 under uniform errors. Reproduced when that share exceeds 0.10 for landmark cells and is no more than 0.10 for heading cells.

claims.statement: In light-on, heading cells alone decode worse than the whole tuned population, so alone they may not give an optimal representation of instantaneous heading.
claims.source: Results, Contributions of distinct classes to representation of heading, paragraph 2; Figure 6B, right (the text cites "Fig. 6C, right", but the class comparison is the right panel of Figure 6B by its legend); Table S1
claims.quote: Since their decoder performance is lower than the population in the light-on condition, heading cells alone may be insufficient for ... providing an optimal representation of instantaneous heading
claims.criterion: Table S1, which holds the class comparisons (linear mixed-effects models, Figure 6 legend), was not read (supplement missing), so the model is open. Readings, (a) the 95% bootstrap intervals of light-on accuracy for heading cells and for all tuned cells do not overlap; (b) a linear mixed-effects model of per-trial light-on decoder error with class (heading or total) as fixed effect and, as random intercept, (i) recording or (ii) mouse (Statistical information, mixed models control for cells within the same animal) gives p < 0.05 with heading cells worse. Reproduced when a reading holds under a decoder reading.

claims.statement: For unipolar 600 ns pulses and for bipolar 600+600 ns pulses with every second phase amplitude, a train of 5 pulses at 1 Hz evoked YP uptake that increased with the local electric field strength.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
claims.quote: A train of 5 pulses applied at 1 Hz evoked YP uptake proportionally to the local electric field strength ( Fig. 2A ), along with a strong dependence on the 2 nd phase amplitude.
claims.criterion: YP per ROI along bb' as defined in Methods 2.5, with the field of each ROI from the model (opening comment). For each of the five second phase amplitudes (0, 25, 50, 75, 100%), the dish values at the ROI with the strongest field are compared with those at the ROI with the weakest field by the paper's two-sided Student's t-test (Methods 2.5), read (a) paired across dishes and (b) unpaired. Reproduced when YP is higher at the strongest field with p < 0.05 for all five amplitudes; partially reproduced for three or four; not reproduced otherwise. When readings (a) and (b) give different outcomes the claim is methods_underspecified. The paper reports no test for this finding; the strongest against weakest ROI comparison is the file's reading of "proportionally", with the test taken from Methods 2.5. The Spearman correlation of mean YP with field across ROI is reported for each amplitude as a description.

claims.statement: Although the panels of Fig. 2A look similar, their vertical scale goes from 1200 a.u. for unipolar pulses down to only 250 a.u. for bipolar pulses with a 75% second phase.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
claims.quote: note the difference in the vertical scale, which is varied from 1200 a.u. for unipolar pulses to only 250 a.u. for 75% bipolar pulses
claims.criterion: The numbers are axis limits, not measured values, so they bound the data. With YP in the units of the dataset's fluorescence images, reproduced when the largest mean plus s.e.m. over ROI is at most 1200 a.u. for unipolar pulses and at most 250 a.u. for 75% bipolar pulses, and the largest unipolar mean exceeds 250 a.u. (so that the unipolar data could not fit the 75% scale). If the images are not in the units the paper measured (for example rescaled on export), only the ratio of the two largest means is reported and the claim is blocked on the absolute values.

claims.statement: YP uptake increased exponentially with the field strength, and the second phase did not change the slope of the exponential fits on a semi-log scale.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 2B and its legend
claims.quote: YP uptake increased exponentially with the electric field, and the presence of the 2nd phase did not change the apparent slope of exponential fits when plotted on a semi-log scale
claims.criterion: As the Fig. 2B legend says, mean YP per ROI is fitted with an exponential function of field, YP = A exp(kE), leaving out low-signal ROI. The legend's cutoff is "less than 6-8 kV/cm"; readings 6, 7 and 8 kV/cm are each run. Grapher's fitting method is not given; readings are (a) nonlinear least squares on linear YP and (b) linear regression of log YP on field. The exponential is judged adequate when it fits better than a straight line (lower residual sum of squares on linear YP) for at least four of five amplitudes; the paper gives no such test, so this rule is the file's and is named as such. For the slope (a claim of absence, with no test reported), the paper's test, a two-sided t-test at p < 0.05, compares the slope k of each bipolar amplitude with the unipolar slope, using (i) per-dish fits compared by an unpaired t-test and (ii) the fits to the means with the slope standard errors. Reproduced when no bipolar slope differs from the unipolar slope at p < 0.05 and the exponential is adequate; not reproduced when any slope differs. Slopes and their ratios to the unipolar slope are reported under every reading; when the readings disagree the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: The strongest inhibition of YP uptake, to about 20% of the uptake after unipolar pulses, was reached with a second phase of 50 to 75% of the first (p < 0.01).
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 2; Figure 2C and its legend
claims.quote: The maximum inhibition of YP uptake, down to ~20% of the unipolar pulses, was achieved with the 2 nd phase set to 50-75% of the first one (p<0.01, Fig. 2C ).
claims.criterion: As the Fig. 2C legend says, for each selected field strength the mean YP for each amplitude is expressed as percent of the unipolar mean at that field. The paper names 6.7, 8.7 and 15.1 kV/cm and does not list the other selected values; all ROI with fields from 8.7 to 15.1 kV/cm are used. Reproduced when the lowest of the 50% and 75% values is below the 25% and 100% values at every such field, the percent is within 18 to 22%, and the 50 or 75% dish values differ from the unipolar dish values by an unpaired two-sided t-test at p < 0.01. Which "~20%" is meant is open; readings are (a) the mean percent over the fields from 8.7 to 15.1 kV/cm for the better of 50 and 75%, and (b) the lowest percent at any of those fields. Which comparison carries p < 0.01 is open; readings are (i) 50% and 75% against unipolar and (ii) 50% and 75% against 25% and 100%, each on raw YP and on dish values divided by the unipolar mean. Reproduced when the values and the test hold under one reading of each; partially reproduced when the ordering and test hold but the percent is outside tolerance under every reading.

claims.statement: Between 8.7 and 15.1 kV/cm the degree of inhibition by the second phase did not depend on the field strength.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
claims.quote: The degree of inhibition showed no dependence on the electric field strength between 8.7 and 15.1 kV/cm.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Bipolar YP of each dish is divided by the unipolar mean at the same ROI field (Fig. 2C legend, unipolar as 100%). For each bipolar amplitude, the values at 8.7 kV/cm are compared with those at 15.1 kV/cm, and every pair of ROI fields in the range is compared, by the paper's two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 (Methods 2.5), which the paper does not say is paired or unpaired, so it is run (a) paired across dishes and (b) unpaired. Reproduced when the 8.7 against 15.1 comparison shows no difference for any amplitude under both; not reproduced when it does under both; methods_underspecified when (a) and (b) disagree. The other pairs and the size of each difference are shown as variants.

claims.statement: Inhibition was weaker at 6.7 kV/cm than at the higher field strengths, with p < 0.01 for the 50% bipolar pulses and p < 0.05 for the 100% bipolar pulses.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
claims.quote: However, inhibition was weaker at 6.7 kV/cm (p<0.01 compared to the higher electric field strengths for 50% bipolar pulses, and p<0.05 for 100% bipolar pulses).
claims.criterion: Bipolar YP as percent of the unipolar mean at the same field, per dish, as in fig2c-inhibition-flat-above-8-7. For 50% and for 100% bipolar pulses, the value at the ROI closest to 6.7 kV/cm is compared with the higher fields (ROI from 8.7 to 15.1 kV/cm) by a two-sided Student's t-test. "Compared to the higher electric field strengths" allows two readings, (i) against each higher field ROI and (ii) against the dish values of all higher field ROI pooled; either suffices. The test is not said to be paired, so each is run (a) paired and (b) unpaired, and the outcome is the one (a) and (b) both give (methods_underspecified when they differ). Reproduced when the percent at 6.7 kV/cm is higher than at every higher field, with p < 0.01 for 50% and p < 0.05 for 100%; partially reproduced when it is higher at every field but the tests hold for only one amplitude.

claims.statement: Uptake rose with field strength and with pulse number for both uni- and bipolar pulses, almost linearly with the number of pulses, so that plots for 5, 10 and 15 pulses look alike when the y-axis is scaled to 800, 1600 and 2400 a.u.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 3A to C
claims.quote: Increasing the pulse number increased YP uptake almost linearly [ 15 ]. Therefore, YP uptake plots for 5, 10, and 15 pulses appeared almost identical when plotted with the y-axis scaled proportionally (to 800, 1600, and 2400 a.u., respectively).
claims.criterion: Mean YP per ROI along bb' for each pulse type and number, ROI below the paper's background cutoff (7 to 8 kV/cm, Results 3.2; readings 7 and 8) left out. The ratios are taken (a) as the mean over ROI of the ratio of means, and (b) as the ratio of the 2nd degree polynomial fits the paper used (Fig. 3 legend) averaged over the included field range. The expected 2 and 3 are read from the axis limits 800, 1600 and 2400 a.u. and "almost linearly"; the paper prints no ratio. Reproduced when both ratios are within tolerance for unipolar and for bipolar pulses; partially reproduced when they are for one pulse type. The paper does not fix the measure, so the outcome is the one (a) and (b) both give, and methods_underspecified when they differ.

claims.statement: The relative efficiency of 50% bipolar pulses was the same for 5, 10 and 15 pulses and did not depend on the field strength.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 2; Figure 3D and its legend
claims.quote: The plots for 5, 10, and 15 pulses nearly overlapped, showing that within the studied limits cancellation of electroporation by adding a 50% opposite polarity phase did not depend on the pulse number or the electric field strength.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, for which the paper reports no test. As the Fig. 3 legend says, mean YP against field is fitted with a 2nd degree polynomial for each pulse type and number, and the bipolar fit is divided by the unipolar fit, over fields above 7 to 8 kV/cm (readings 7 and 8). The paper's test, a two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05, is applied to dish values of bipolar YP divided by the unipolar mean at the same ROI, (i) between pulse numbers at each ROI (unpaired) and (ii) between the lowest and highest included ROI for each pulse number (paired). Reproduced when no comparison of pulse numbers differs at any ROI and no field comparison differs; not reproduced otherwise. The fitted ratio curves and their range are reported.

claims.statement: Bipolar 300+300 and 600+600 ns pulses with a 50% second phase gave 20 to 25% of the uptake of the respective unipolar pulses, independent of the field strength.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 4A to D
claims.quote: Electroporation by 300+300 and 600+600 ns pulses was at 20-25% of the respective unipolar pulses and did not depend on the electric field strength.
claims.criterion: The reported range 20 to 25% is widened by 10% of each bound, to 18 to 27.5%. The ratio is that of the fits of bipolar and unipolar mean YP against field (Fig. 4 legend, "either exponential or polynomial"; the legend does not say which for which duration, so three readings are run, (a) exponential for all, (b) 2nd degree polynomial for all, as in Fig. 3, and (c) for each curve the one with the lower residual sum of squares). Fields are those above the background cutoff stated for Fig. 3 (7 to 8 kV/cm, readings 7 and 8; the Fig. 4 legend refers to Fig. 2 and the text and states no cutoff of its own). Reproduced when, for both durations, the ratio stays in 18 to 27.5% over the included field range; partially reproduced when its mean over the range does but it leaves the range somewhere. The outcome is the one the fit readings all give; methods_underspecified when they differ. The field dependence is judged as in fig3d-cancellation-independent-of-number, between the lowest and highest included ROI.

claims.statement: Bipolar 1200+1200 ns pulses cancelled more at moderate field strengths, reducing YP uptake to a tenth of unipolar pulses.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 4D
claims.quote: However, longer 1200+1200 ns pulses were somewhat more efficient at cancellation at moderate electric field strengths, reducing the YP fluorescence 10-fold ( Fig. 4D ).
claims.criterion: Ratio of the fits of bipolar and unipolar mean YP against field, as in fig4ac-ns-bipolar-20-25pct. "Moderate" is not defined; readings are (a) the lowest value of the ratio curve over the included field range and (b) the ratio at the middle of that range; either suffices, as they read the paper's word. Reproduced when the value is within tolerance under one of them and is below the 300 and 600 ns ratios at the same field. The fit readings of fig4ac-ns-bipolar-20-25pct must all agree on the outcome; methods_underspecified when they differ.

claims.statement: A 50% second phase also reduced uptake by 50, 100 and 500 us pulses, to 30 to 50% of the unipolar effect, a weak but highly significant cancellation (p < 0.01).
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 4E to H
claims.quote: Cancellation by these longer pulses was relatively weak (to 30-50% of the unipolar pulse effect) but highly significant (p<0.01).
claims.criterion: The reported range 30 to 50% is widened by 10% of each bound, to 27 to 55%. For each of the three durations, the ratio of the fits of bipolar and unipolar mean YP against field (Fig. 4 legend, fit readings as in fig4ac-ns-bipolar-20-25pct) over the field range where uptake is measurable, and an unpaired two-sided t-test of bipolar against unipolar dish YP at each ROI. The paper gives no cutoff for measurable uptake with microsecond pulses (Fig. 3's 7 to 8 kV/cm does not apply to their lower field range); this is open, and the notebook shows the ratio at every ROI with positive unipolar mean YP. "To 30-50%" is read (i) as the ratio's mean over that range and (ii) as the ratio staying in the range throughout; either suffices. Reproduced when, for all three durations, the ratio is in 27 to 55% and bipolar YP is lower than unipolar YP at p < 0.01 at most ROI with measurable uptake; partially reproduced for one or two durations. Which comparison the paper's single p < 0.01 covers is not given; "most ROI" is the file's reading of it.

claims.statement: For microsecond pulses, cancellation was stronger at lower field strengths.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 4H
claims.quote: The trend for more efficient cancellation at the lower electric field strengths persisted throughout the microsecond range ( Fig. 4H ).
claims.criterion: The ratio of the bipolar and unipolar fits (Fig. 4 legend) for 50, 100 and 500 us pulses. Reproduced when the ratio rises from the lowest to the highest field with measurable uptake for all three durations; partially reproduced for one or two. The paper gives no test for this trend; dish ratios at the lowest and highest such ROI are compared by a paired two-sided t-test and reported.

claims.statement: Along the line from anode to cathode, YP uptake was nearly symmetrical for 300 and 600 ns pulses.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 4; Figure 5A and B
claims.quote: YP uptake data measured along the aa' line was nearly symmetrical for 300- and 600-ns pulses ( Fig. 5A , B ).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. ROI along aa' (Methods 2.3 and 2.5, Fig. 5 legend), in the Fig. 4 dishes; each anodic ROI is paired with the cathodic ROI at the same distance from the centre. YP at the two sides is compared by the paper's two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 at each distance, for uni- and bipolar 300 and 600 ns pulses. The paper does not say whether the test is paired, so it is run (a) paired across dishes and (b) unpaired. Reproduced when no distance shows a difference under both; not reproduced when one does under both; methods_underspecified when (a) and (b) disagree. The size of the anode over cathode ratio is reported at each distance.

claims.statement: For 50 to 500 us pulses, YP uptake was significantly stronger on the anodic side (p < 0.01), and for 1200 ns unipolar pulses marginally stronger there.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 4; Figure 5C to F
claims.quote: At 1200 ns, the effect of unipolar pulses appeared marginally stronger at the anodic side ( Fig. 5C ), and still longer 50-500 μs pulses showed significantly stronger YP uptake (p<0.01) at the anodic site.
claims.criterion: ROI along aa', paired by distance from the centre as in fig5-ns-symmetric-along-aa. Reproduced when, for each of 50, 100 and 500 us unipolar pulses, anodic YP exceeds cathodic YP with p < 0.01 (two-sided t-test, run paired and unpaired; the outcome is the one both give, methods_underspecified when they differ) at one or more distances, and the 1200 ns unipolar anodic mean exceeds the cathodic mean at most distances. Bipolar pulses are reported as well; the text does not say whether its p < 0.01 covers them.

claims.statement: Unipolar 600 ns pulse trains at 10 to 500 kHz were as efficient as at 1 Hz, while at 833 kHz uptake was 2 to 3 times higher across the field range.
claims.source: Results 3.4, paragraph 1; Figure 6A and D
claims.quote: Unipolar pulses at 10 to 500 kHz showed the same efficiency as at 1 Hz ( Fig. 6A , D ). ... YP uptake after 833 kHz exposure was 2-3 fold higher than at other frequencies throughout the studied range of the electric field strengths.
claims.criterion: The reported range 2 to 3 is widened by 10% of each bound, to 1.8 to 3.3. Mean YP per ROI along bb' for each repetition rate. The fold is the 833 kHz mean over the mean of each other rate at the same ROI, over ROI with uptake above background. For "the same efficiency" (a claim of absence), each rate from 10 to 500 kHz is compared with 1 Hz at each ROI by the paper's unpaired two-sided t-test at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the fold is in 1.8 to 3.3 at every such ROI and no 10 to 500 kHz rate differs from 1 Hz; partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: Bipolar 600+600 ns pulse trains at all kHz rates were less efficient than at 1 Hz, barely above background, the difference being largest (2.5 times) at the highest field.
claims.source: Results 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 6B and E
claims.quote: In contrast, the efficiency of bipolar pulses at all kHz frequencies was less than at 1 Hz, and the electroporative uptake of YP was just marginally above the background level ( Fig. 6B , E ). The difference between 1 Hz and kHz-rate trains was maximum (2.5 times) at the highest electric field strength.
claims.criterion: Mean YP per ROI along bb'. Reproduced when the mean at every kHz rate (10 kHz to 833 kHz) is below the 1 Hz mean at the ROI with the strongest field, the largest 1 Hz over kHz ratio over ROI is at that ROI, and that ratio is within tolerance. "The difference between 1 Hz and kHz-rate trains" is read (a) against the mean over all kHz rates and (b) against each kHz rate; one reading suffices.

claims.statement: At 833 kHz and 12 to 15 kV/cm, bipolar pulses had only 3 to 4% of the effect of unipolar pulses, about a 30-fold reduction, the strongest cancellation in the study.
claims.source: Results 3.4, paragraph 3; Figure 6C and F
claims.quote: At 12-15 kV/cm, the effect of bipolar pulses at 833 kHz was only 3-4% of the effect of unipolar pulses (~30-fold reduction).
claims.criterion: The reported range 3 to 4% is widened by 10% of each bound, to 2.7 to 4.4%. The ratio is that of the fits of bipolar and unipolar mean YP against field at 833 kHz (Fig. 6 legend, "either exponential or polynomial"; fit readings as in fig4ac-ns-bipolar-20-25pct, whose outcomes must agree, methods_underspecified when they differ). The ratio of means at each ROI is shown as a variant. Reproduced when the ratio is within 2.7 to 4.4% at the fields from 12 to 15 kV/cm, and lower than the ratio at every other repetition rate.

claims.statement: Fitting the cathodic pole response to the first unipolar pulse gave a charging time constant of 200 ns and a maximum polarization of 31% emission change (425 points, r = 0.93, p < 0.0001), and the discharge after it a time constant of 520 ns from 31.5% (425 points, r = 0.85, p < 0.0001).
claims.source: Results 3.5, paragraph 2; Figure 7 (dotted lines, top panel)
claims.quote: The best fit for membrane charging with an exponential function (using the first pulse in the unipolar pulse train) yielded the time constant of 200 ns and the maximum membrane polarization at 31% emission change (425 datapoints, correlation coefficient 0.93, p<0.0001). The best fit for the discharging portion of the curve yielded the same initial polarization (31.5% emission change) but, unexpectedly, a 2.5 times larger time constant of 520 ns
claims.criterion: FluoVolt emission at the cathode-facing pole of the 18 cells given unipolar pulses, scaled to whole-cell emission, the two trials of each cell averaged, as percent difference from the mean of the 40 points before the pulse (Methods 2.6). A single exponential (Fig. 7 legend) is fitted to the first pulse (0 to 600 ns, charging, A(1 - exp(-t/tau))) and to the interval from its end to the next pulse (600 to 1200 ns at 833 kHz, discharge, A exp(-t/tau)). The 425 datapoints are about 18 cells times 24 time steps of 25 ns, so the readings are (a) per-cell points pooled (the reading the count supports) and (b) the trace averaged over cells. Reproduced when all four values are within tolerance under one reading and both correlations have p < 0.0001.

claims.statement: Bipolar pulses caused the same initial polarization as unipolar ones during the first phase, followed by a faster discharge and an overshoot into the opposite polarity.
claims.source: Results 3.5, paragraph 1; Figure 7
claims.quote: Bipolar nsEP caused the same initial polarization during the first phase of the pulse, followed by a faster discharge and an overshoot into the opposite polarity.
claims.criterion: Cathodic pole traces as in fig7-charging-time-constant, for the 17 bipolar and 18 unipolar cells. Reproduced when (i) at the end of the first phase (600 ns) the bipolar and unipolar cell values do not differ by the paper's two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 (Methods 2.5; unpaired, as they are different cells), a claim of absence judged on that test, with the paper's error bar gap rule (Methods 2.5) shown as a variant; (ii) after the first phase the bipolar trace returns to the resting level sooner than the unipolar trace; and (iii) during the second phase (600 to 1200 ns) the bipolar mean goes below the resting level, its minimum differing from zero by a two-sided one-sample t-test across cells at p < 0.05 (the Methods 2.5 test and threshold applied to this point, a reading of the file, as the paper reports no test here).

claims.statement: With 600 ns unipolar pulses at 833 kHz, each pulse charged the membrane to the same peak, with no stepwise build-up; the pulses merged into a continuous sawtooth polarization.
claims.source: Results 3.5, paragraph 3; Figure 7
claims.quote: Although charging by the subsequent pulses in unipolar pulse trains started with the partially charged membrane, it reached the same peak potential. A stepwise build-up of the peak membrane potential ... did not occur in our experiments with 833-kHz, 600-ns unipolar pulses.
claims.criterion: Cathodic pole traces of the unipolar cells as in fig7-charging-time-constant. The peak of each of the five pulses (the value at the end of each pulse) is compared with the first by the paper's two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 (a claim of absence). The paper does not say whether it is paired; it is run (a) paired across cells and (b) unpaired, and methods_underspecified when they disagree. Reproduced when no later peak differs from the first and the trace between pulses stays above the resting level (the minimum before each of pulses 2 to 5 differs from zero by a two-sided one-sample t-test across cells at p < 0.05, the Methods 2.5 test applied here by the file); not reproduced when a later peak differs from the first at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In the worst case tested, trains of 5 bipolar pulses (second phase 50%) at 1 Hz heated the sample to no more than 30 degrees C; at 833 kHz heating exceeded 30 degrees C but never reached 44 degrees C, and stayed close to 30 degrees C along the bb' line.
claims.source: Methods 2.4, paragraph 2; Figure 1E
claims.quote: Pulses applied at 1 Hz (the repetition rate used in all but one sets of experiments) caused only modest heating, not exceeding 30 °C. At a high repetition rate of 833 kHz, heating exceeded 30 °C but never reached the next transition point of 44 °C and remained close to 30 °C (green to blue transition) along the bb' line
claims.criterion: Measured with thermochromic liquid crystal sheets photographed with a camera (Methods 2.4). Reproduced when the photographs show no blue at 1 Hz, and at 833 kHz no return to black (44 degrees C) and no more than the green to blue transition along bb'. The dandiset is not meant to hold these photographs.

claims.statement: For high-frequency bursts of nsEP, a stronger electric field enhanced bipolar cancellation.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 1; Figure 6C and F
claims.quote: For high-frequency nsEP bursts, stronger electric field enhanced cancellation ( Fig. 6C , F ).
claims.criterion: The ratio of the fits of bipolar and unipolar mean YP against field (Fig. 6 legend, fit readings as in fig4ac-ns-bipolar-20-25pct, whose outcomes must agree, methods_underspecified when they differ) for each kHz repetition rate (10 to 833 kHz), over the ROI with unipolar uptake above background (the paper gives no cutoff for Fig. 6; the Fig. 3 cutoff of 7 to 8 kV/cm is used, readings 7 and 8). "High-frequency" is not defined; readings are (a) 833 kHz only and (b) every kHz rate; either suffices. Reproduced when the ratio falls from the lowest to the highest included field. The paper reports no test; dish ratios (bipolar YP over the unipolar mean at the same ROI) at the lowest and highest included ROI are compared by an unpaired two-sided t-test and reported.

claims.statement: After excluding cross sections near the edge of the imaging volume, each of the 14 PVS segments yields between 54 and 451 normal cross sections, about 0.8 um apart.
claims.source: Methods, Creating normal cross sections
claims.quote: This resulted in between 54 and 451 different cross sections for each of the 14 PVS segments that were included in the subsequent analysis. The average distance between normal planes was approximately 0.8 μ m.
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4 of the opening comment, one slice per centerline point. The claim holds under a reading when the fewest and most cross sections per segment lie in the range 54 to 451 widened by 10% of each bound, and the mean spacing is within tolerance. Every combination of readings of P1, P2 and P4 is run.

claims.statement: Where a high signal-to-noise 2D time-averaged image was acquired, the 3D segmentation at the matching depth overlaps the 2D segmentation by at least 70% of the union area, for both PVS and vessel.
claims.source: Methods, Image Segmentation, last paragraph; Figure 2 legend
claims.quote: To consider the segmentation successful, at least 70% of the area had to overlap in both PVS and vessel ... The 3D segmentation and 2D segmentation match over 70% which gives confidence that 3D segmentation is accurate.
claims.criterion: Overlap as Equation 1, the area of the intersection over the area of the union of the 2D and 3D segmentations at the depth that minimizes their difference, after aligning the fields of view (the registration of Boster et al., reference 31, is not described here). The 2D segmentations must come with the data, since the paper's thresholds for them are not given. Reproduced when every validated segment has overlap of at least 0.70 for both PVS and vessel. The 70% is the paper's acceptance threshold, so no tolerance applies.

claims.statement: PVS area increases with vessel area only approximately; the least-squares line of PVS area on vessel area over all cross sections has slope 1.05 (95% CI 0.973 to 1.12) and R2 of 0.158.
claims.source: Results, Area ratio, paragraph 1; Figure 5A
claims.quote: The area of the PVS generally increases with the area of the vessel, but the trend is only approximate, as evidenced by the low R 2 value of the fit line (0.158). The slope of the fit line is 1.05, (95% confidence interval 0.973, 1.12).
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P5, segmented areas of every retained cross section pooled over the 14 segments, ordinary least squares of PVS area on vessel area (Figure 5A legend). The slope tolerance is the larger half-width of the paper's 95% CI; the R2 tolerance is 10%. Open, whether the line has an intercept. Readings (a) with intercept, (b) through the origin (the Results compare the slope with the area ratio). Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The PVS-to-vessel area ratio of the segmentation varies widely across cross sections; its distribution peaks at 1.12, its median is 1.88 and its IQR is 1.79 (25th percentile 1.21, 75th 3.00), so the ratio varies by more than 100%.
claims.source: Results, Area ratio, paragraph 1; Figure 5E; Table 2
claims.quote: There is considerable variation in the area ratio, and the interquartile range of the segmented area ratio is 1.79 ( Table 2 ), a value on the same order as the median value of 1.88, meaning that the area ratio varies by more than 100%. The peak value of 1.12
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P5 and P7, the ratio of every retained cross section pooled over the 14 segments. Reproduced when, under one combination of the readings of P1, P2, P4, P5, P6 (when P5 reading b) and P7, all five values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the median and IQR are within tolerance but the peak is not.

claims.statement: Variation in PVS area is much larger between PVS segments than along the length of a single segment.
claims.source: Results, Area ratio, paragraph 2; Figure 5B and 5C
claims.quote: From Figure 5 , it is clear that the variation in PVS area is much larger between segments of PVS than along the length of a single PVS segment. We quantified this difference by plotting the median PVS area from each segment and the interquartile range of each segment
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4, per segment the median and IQR of segmented PVS area (Figure 5B and 5C). The paper compares these by eye and gives no measure. Readings of "much larger" from what the figure shows (a) the IQR of the 14 segment medians is larger than the median of the 14 within-segment IQRs; (b) the range of the 14 segment medians is larger than the largest within-segment IQR. Reproduced when both readings hold, not reproduced when neither holds; otherwise methods_underspecified. All 28 values are shown.

claims.statement: The peak of the segmented area ratio distribution ranges from 0.6 to 11.43 across the 14 locations, and in all but one location the ratio's variation along the vessel lies within 30% of the peak, so variation between segments dominates.
claims.source: Results, Area ratio, paragraph 2; Additional File 3 (Additional File 4 in the list)
claims.quote: The peak of the area ratio distribution ranges from 0.6 to 11.43 across the different locations. Although their area ratio varies along the length of each vessel, in all but one case, this variation occurs within 30% of the peak
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P5 and P7, applied per location. Open, what "variation within 30% of the peak" measures. Readings (a) the 25th and 75th percentiles both lie within 30% of the peak value; (b) the IQR is at most 30% of the peak value; (c) the IQR is at most 60% of the peak value (30% each side); (d) all non-outlier values (outliers as the Methods define them, the values the per-location plots show) lie within 30% of the peak. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the two peaks and the count are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Of the three fits, the polynomial fit matches the segmentation's area ratio most closely in 73% of cross sections, the spline fit in 19% and the ellipse fit in 8%, and its distribution matches the segmentation's best.
claims.source: Results, Area ratio, paragraph 3; Figure 5D and 5E
claims.quote: The distribution of the PVS-to-vessel area ratio in segmentations is matched most closely by the polynomial fit ( Figure 5E ), and the value of the area ratio in segmentations is matched most closely by the polynomial fit in 73% of cases ( Figure 5D ) ... the ellipse fit gives the closest match in only 8% of cases ... The spline fit gives the closest match in 19% of the cases
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P6 and P9. Per cross section, the fit whose area ratio has the smallest absolute difference from the segmentation's (Figure 5D, "best predicted"). Every combination of the readings of P5, P6 and P9 (ellipse region) is run. Reproduced when, under one combination, the three shares are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the polynomial share is the largest and above 50% but the shares are not all within tolerance.

claims.statement: The area ratio distribution peaks at 1.21 for the polynomial fit (close to the segmentation's 1.12), 2.08 for the ellipse fit, which does not narrow at the ends, and 1.48 for the spline fit, whose ratio varies little because it scales with vessel size alone.
claims.source: Results, Area ratio, paragraph 3; Table 2; Figure 5E
claims.quote: The peak of the area ratio distribution for the polynomial fit is 1.21, similar to the peak of the segmentation distribution of 1.12 ... has a significantly higher peak of 2.08 because it does not narrow at the ends. The spline fit gives the closest match in 19% of the cases and has a peak of 1.48
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P7 and P9, fit areas over the vessel area under each reading of P5 for the fits. The paper reports no test for "significantly higher". Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the order of the peaks (ellipse above spline above polynomial) holds and the spline IQR is the smallest of the three.

claims.statement: The hydraulic resistance per unit length of the segmented PVS is well predicted by a power law in PVS area (R2 = 0.944), with exponent -1.75 (95% CI -1.763 to -1.737), close to the -2 of a shape scaled in size alone.
claims.source: Results, Hydraulic Resistance, paragraph 2; Figure 6A
claims.quote: The hydraulic resistance can be reasonably predicted with a power-law fit as a function of the PVS area alone (R 2 = 0.944). The exponent in the power law fit is −1.75 (95% confidence interval −1.763, −1.737)
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4 and P8 on the segmented PVS, area from the segmentation (P5), all retained cross sections pooled. The exponent tolerance is the half-width of the paper's 95% CI. Open, how the power law is fit. Readings (a) least squares of log resistance on log area, R2 on the log scale; (b) nonlinear least squares of resistance on area, R2 on the linear scale. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, both values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the R2 is within tolerance and the exponent lies between -2 and -1.5.

claims.statement: The distribution of segmented PVS hydraulic resistance per unit length over all cross sections peaks at 1.73e15 Pa s/m^4, with a median of 3.84e15 Pa s/m^4.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 4; Conclusion; Table 2; Figure 6B
claims.quote: Here, we report the distribution of hydraulic resistances for thousands of PVS cross sections, with its peak at 1.73×10 15 Pa· s/m 4
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4, P7 and P8. Open, beyond P7, whether the 20 bins are even on a linear or a logarithmic scale of resistance (the paper says evenly spaced and the values span two orders of magnitude). Readings (a) linear, (b) logarithmic. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, both values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the median is and the peak is not.

claims.statement: Variation in resistance is much larger between locations than along each PVS; the per-location peaks range from 3.23e14 to 1.98e16, and in 65% of vessels all the variation lies within 37% of the peak.
claims.source: Results, Hydraulic Resistance, paragraph 2; Figure 6B; Additional File 5
claims.quote: it is evident that the variation between locations is much larger than that along the PVS at each location. The peak of hydraulic resistance distributions ranges from 3.23×10 14 to 1.98×10 16 across different locations, whereas, in 65% of the vessels, all the variation occurs within 37% of the peak of the distribution
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4, P7 and P8, per location. Open, what "all the variation" measures. Readings (a) the 25th and 75th percentiles lie within 37% of the peak; (b) all non-outlier values (outliers as the Methods define them) lie within 37% of the peak; (c) the IQR is at most 37% of the peak. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the two peaks and the share are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The distribution of hydraulic resistance of the polynomial fit matches that of the segmentation most closely, followed by the ellipse fit, and the polynomial fit is the best match for the majority of cross sections; the distribution peaks are 1.44e15 (polynomial), 7.06e14 (ellipse), 1.07e16 (spline) and 1.32e15 (optimal annulus) Pa s/m^4.
claims.source: Results, Hydraulic Resistance, paragraph 2; Figure 6B and 6C; Table 2. The Results sentence cites Figure 5B, which is the resistance distribution of Figure 6B
claims.quote: Figure 5B shows that the distribution of hydraulic resistances for the polynomial fit matches that of the segmentation most closely, followed by the ellipse fit
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P9. The optimal annulus resistance from Equation 3 with the segmentation's area ratio K and the fitted vessel radius R1; the printed equation is garbled and is read, from Tithof et al. (reference 18) and its units, as R = mu 6.67 K^-1.96 / R1^4. The Discussion confirms this reading, since with the paper's viscosity, K = 1.4 and R1 = 23 um it gives the 8.7e15 Pa s/m^4 the paper quotes from Tithof et al. (reference 35). Per cross section the best match is the model with the smallest absolute difference in resistance from the segmentation (Figure 6C). Open, which models compete in Figure 6C (its legend says "each model"; Figure 5D leaves out the annulus because its area ratio is the segmentation's, which does not apply to resistance). Readings (a) ellipse, polynomial and spline fits, (b) the three fits and the optimal annulus. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the polynomial fit is the best match for more than half the cross sections and the four peaks are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the polynomial is the best match for the largest share but the peaks are not all within tolerance.

claims.statement: The resistance distribution of the optimal elliptical annulus is very similar to that of the ellipse fit, and both tend to underestimate the resistance of the segmented PVS.
claims.source: Results, Hydraulic Resistance, paragraph 3; Figure 6B
claims.quote: The distribution of resistances for the optimal elliptical annulus is very similar to that of the ellipse fit ... Though both the ellipse fit and annulus tend to underestimate the resistance of the PVS
claims.criterion: As in fig5b-polynomial-closest-resistance. "Tend to underestimate" has no measure in the paper; readings (a) the median of the per-cross-section ratio of fit (or annulus) resistance to segmented resistance is below 1, (b) the peak and the median of the fit's (or annulus's) resistance distribution are below the segmentation's (Table 2 has ellipse 7.06e14 and 1.55e15, annulus 1.32e15 and 2.49e15, segmentation 1.73e15 and 3.84e15). "Very similar" has no measure either, and the paper's own Table 2 values are not within 10% of each other (annulus over ellipse, 1.87 for the peaks and 1.61 for the medians), so a 10% closeness test would fail the paper's own numbers; the Optimal model section also says the annulus is more similar to the segmentation than the ellipse fit is. Similarity is therefore judged against the paper's numbers, the annulus-over-ellipse ratios of peak and median within 10% of 1.87 and 1.61. Reproduced when, under one reading, both underestimate and the two ratios are within tolerance; partially reproduced when only the underestimation holds.

claims.statement: The spline fit's resistance is considerably larger than the segmentation's, its distribution peak about 5 times larger, despite a larger area ratio, because the spline PVS narrows rapidly away from the vessel.
claims.source: Results, Hydraulic Resistance, paragraph 3; Figure 6B inset
claims.quote: The resistance for the spline fit is considerably larger than that of the segmentation (distribution peak is 5 times larger)
claims.criterion: Peaks as in the claims it depends on. Table 2 gives 1.07e16 over 1.73e15, a ratio of 6.2, which the text calls 5; readings (a) the text's 5 with 10% tolerance, (b) Table 2's 6.2 with 10% tolerance. Reproduced when the ratio is within tolerance under one reading and the median spline resistance exceeds the median segmented resistance.

claims.statement: In a representative cross section, the polynomial fit's velocity profile resembles the segmentation's, the ellipse fit gives much higher velocities and the spline fit much lower; these trends are generally consistent across cross sections.
claims.source: Results, Hydraulic Resistance, paragraph 4; Figure 7 legend
claims.quote: In this example case, the velocity profile for the polynomial fit is similar to the velocity profile in the segmentation, whereas the ellipse fit results in much higher velocities, and the spline fit results in much lower velocities.
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P9, velocity from the Poisson solution at a pressure gradient of 500 Pa/m (Methods). The representative cross section is not identified, so the claim is tested over all cross sections, as the text's "generally consistent in all cross sections" allows. Open, the velocity measure. Readings (a) maximum velocity, (b) mean velocity (flow rate over area). Reproduced when, under one reading, in more than half the cross sections the ellipse fit is faster than the segmentation, the spline fit slower, and the polynomial fit closer to the segmentation than either.

claims.statement: The fitted vessel radius distribution peaks at 28 um.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 2; Results, Characteristics of the typical PVS shape, paragraph 2; Figure 8A and 9C
claims.quote: We approximated the cross-sectional shape of the vessel as a circle and found that the peak of the vessel radius distribution is 28 μ m
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4, P6 and P7. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the peak is within tolerance. Table 3 gives an R1 peak of 64.9 um, which disagrees; it is not used (opening comment).

claims.statement: The ellipse fit shows an elongated, eccentric PVS with the vessel slightly below its center; R1 peaks at 28 um and R3 at 35 um, R3/R1 at 0.80, R2/R1 at 2.89, R3/R2 at 0.398, the vertical offset Ov at 0.24, and the horizontal offset Oh is centered near zero with a much wider distribution than Ov.
claims.source: Results, Characteristics of the typical PVS shape, paragraphs 2 to 5; Figure 8A, 8C, 8D, 8E and 8F
claims.quote: the distribution of R 1 , the vessel radius, is similar to that of R 3 , the minor axis length (distribution peaks at 28 μ m and 35 μ m, respectively, see Figure 8A ), and the ratio between them ( R 3 / R 1 ) is generally close to 1 (distribution peaks at 0.80, Figure 8E )
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4, P6, P7 and P9 (ellipse). Open, the units of Ov and Oh, printed without units. Readings (a) offsets over R1, (b) over R3, (c) in um. Ov positive when the vessel is below the ellipse center, as the text reads it. Oh "centered around zero" and "much wider" are read as the median of Oh within one Ov peak value of zero and the IQR of Oh at least twice the IQR of Ov. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all values are within tolerance and the Oh conditions hold; partially reproduced when the ratios R3/R1, R2/R1 and R3/R2 are within tolerance and the rest is not.

claims.statement: The PVS usually consists of two mostly or entirely disconnected lobes on either side of the vessel; the polynomial fit's HC (top of PVS above top of vessel) peaks at zero, and when the lobes connect the channel is narrow, usually less than 0.5 R1.
claims.source: Results, Characteristics of the typical PVS shape, paragraph 2; Figure 9C; Table 3
claims.quote: The distribution peaks at zero ( Figure 9C ), suggesting that the top of the vessel is most often very nearly aligned with the top of the PVS and that the PVS is often separated into two lobes. Even when the two sides are connected, the channel connecting them is quite narrow, usually less than 0.5 R 1 .
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4, P6, P7 and P9 (polynomial). A 10% tolerance on a value near zero is meaningless; the tolerance is one tenth of R1 (0.1 in HC/R1), the scale of the paper's 0.5 R1 statement; this is a choice and is recorded as a deviation. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the peak of HC/R1 is within 0.1 of zero and, among cross sections with HC greater than zero, more than half have HC below 0.5 R1.

claims.statement: The PVS is about twice as wide as the vessel radius and asymmetric about the vessel; the short-side width WS/R1 peaks near 1.1, the long-side width WL/R1 near 1.9, and WS/WL near 0.5.
claims.source: Results, Characteristics of the typical PVS shape, paragraphs 3 and 5; Figure 9E; Table 3
claims.quote: The short side is significantly shorter than the long side (distribution peaks of 1.1 and 1.9, respectively, Figure 9E ) and for the ratio between them, W S / W L , the distribution peaks at approximately 0.5, indicating that the two PVS sides are typically asymmetric
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4, P6, P7 and P9 (polynomial). The Results also say WS/R1 peaks at 1.85, which Table 3 and the sentence quoted give for WL/R1; Table 3 is followed. The paper reports no test for "significantly shorter", and WS is by definition no longer than WL. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the three peaks are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The PVS widths on the left and right sides of the vessel do not differ significantly.
claims.source: Results, Characteristics of the typical PVS shape, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Since there was no statistically significant difference between the left and right sides, we report the distribution of the short ( W S ) and long ( W L ) sides of each cross section.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence whose test the paper does not name. Widths W of the polynomial fit on each side (P9), left and right fixed by the direction along the centerline (P3). Readings (a) Wilcoxon signed-rank test on paired left and right widths over all cross sections, (b) two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the two distributions, (c) Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the per-segment median left and right widths (14 pairs); alpha 0.05. Reproduced when no reading finds a difference, not reproduced when all do, otherwise methods_underspecified. The median difference and its sign are shown for each.

claims.statement: The PVS is tallest next to the vessel and narrows far from it; the heights H1/R1, H2/R1 and H3/R1 peak at 1.34, 0.792 and 0.307, so H1 is about 4 times H3.
claims.source: Results, Characteristics of the typical PVS shape, paragraph 6; Figure 9A; Table 3
claims.quote: the distributions of heights of the PVS, H 1 , H 2 , and H 3 , peak at 1.34, 0.792, and 0.307, respectively, indicating that the PVS is larger closer to the vessel and smaller at the ends of the PVS. H 1 , the height of the PVS close to the vessel, is 4 times larger than H 3
claims.criterion: Pipeline P1 to P4, P6, P7 and P9 (polynomial), heights per side; open, whether each cross section contributes both sides or their mean. Readings (a) both sides pooled, (b) mean of the two sides. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the three peaks are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the order H1 above H2 above H3 holds for the peaks and medians but the values are not within tolerance.

claims.statement: The bottom edge of the PVS is most often concave; the distribution of (H2 - H3)/(H1 - H2) peaks at 0.108, below the value of 1 that separates concave from convex.
claims.source: Results, Characteristics of the typical PVS shape, paragraph 7; Figure 9F
claims.quote: The peak of the curvature distribution is 0.108, showing that the PVS is most often concave
claims.criterion: As fig9a-heights-taper, with the same readings. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the peak is within tolerance and more than half the values are below 1; partially reproduced when only the second holds.

claims.statement: Chronic recordings were made from 17 adult mice (12 males, 5 females) electroporated at E13.5 (n = 4), E14.5 (n = 3), E15.5 (n = 6) and E16.5 (n = 4).
claims.source: Results, In vivo recordings from birthdated CA1 pyramidal neurons, paragraph 1; Methods, Implantation and recording, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Chronic recordings were performed from n = 17 freely moving adult mice (12 males, 5 females; age 3–6 months; electroporated at: E13.5, n = 4; E14.5, n = 3; E15.5, n = 6; E16.5, n = 4)
claims.criterion: Mice are the distinct subject ids of the dandiset; sex from the files' subject metadata; birthdate from the subject id prefix (e13 is E13.5), the only place the files hold it. Reproduced when the counts of mice, of each sex and of each birthdate all match exactly (counts of animals carry no measurement error, so the tolerance is zero). Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The recordings comprise 92 sessions lasting 113.7 to 475.6 min (median 309.1 min), each including a homecage period of sleep and wake.
claims.source: Methods, Implantation and recording, paragraph 2
claims.quote: All recordings (92 sessions ranging in duration from 113.7 min to 475.6 min; median duration = 309.1 min) included a homecage period of sleep and wake.
claims.criterion: A session is a processed (behavior+ecephys) file; its duration is the end of its last sleep-state or ripple interval (the files' clocks start at 0). The paper gives two session counts, 92 (Methods) and 96 (the per-birthdate session counts of Figure 1e, and the Figure 7f legend); the count is judged under either reading, within 10%. The range holds when every duration lies within 113.7 to 475.6 min widened by 10% of each bound (102.3 to 523.2 min). Reproduced when the count (either reading), the median and the range all hold. Partially reproduced when the durations hold and the count does not. Not reproduced when the durations do not hold. Each session must also hold sleep states including non-REM sleep.

claims.statement: SPW-Rs were detected with duration limits of 20 to 200 ms, and their median duration across all recordings was 36.4 ms.
claims.source: Figure 2b legend; Methods, SPW-R detection
claims.quote: SPW-R duration limits were set to be between 20 and 200 ms. ... White dotted lines indicate the median duration of SPW-Rs across all recordings (36.4 ms).
claims.criterion: Durations from the Ripples tables of all processed files. Readings for "median across all recordings", listed before the analysis; (a) the median over all ripples pooled; (b) the median of the per-session medians. Reproduced when the median is within tolerance under one reading and every ripple lies within 20 to 200 ms. Partially reproduced when only one of the two holds. Not reproduced when neither does.

claims.statement: The dataset includes 9,471 well-isolated units, 7,411 putative pyramidal cells and 2,060 putative interneurons.
claims.source: Methods, Unit isolation and classification; Extended Data Figure 2a
claims.quote: The dataset includes a total of 7,411 well-isolated putative pyramidal cells and 2,060 putative interneurons ... for isolated units (n = 9,471)
claims.criterion: Units are the rows of the units tables of all processed files. The fraction of putative pyramidal cells uses this attempt's rule (session mean rate at most 5 Hz), as the files hold no cell type; it is reported as a check of the rule, and the outcome rests on the count. Reproduced when the count is within tolerance. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Nine mice (E13.5 n = 2, E14.5 n = 2, E15.5 n = 2, E16.5 n = 3) ran a spatial alternation task on a familiar figure-eight maze, and a cohort of three mice also explored novel environments.
claims.source: Results, SBD pyramidal neurons exhibit overlapping place tuning, paragraphs 1 and 3; Methods, Behavior, paragraphs 1 and 2
claims.quote: A subset of n = 9 mice (E13.5, n = 2; E14.5, n = 2; E15.5, n = 2; E16.5, n = 3) was trained on a spatial alternation task in a figure-eight maze ... a subset of n = 3 mice (Supplementary Table 1) that underwent in utero electroporation was exposed to novel environments
claims.criterion: Mice with figure-eight trials and mice with a second maze recording are counted from the trials tables. The paper calls the novel-environment cohort separate; its code (ratemap_remap.m) leaves out two mice, e15_13f1 and e16_3m2, from the familiar-maze analysis, so the third novel mouse is also in the nine. Readings; (a) disjoint cohorts, 12 mice with maze data, 9 of them at the stated birthdates and 3 with novel recordings; (b) the code's reading, the maze mice without e15_13f1 and e16_3m2 are the nine at the stated birthdates, and 3 mice have novel recordings. Reproduced when one reading matches exactly. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: On the figure-eight maze each trial was 205 cm long, position was tracked at 30 Hz, and animals ran at least ten trials along each arm in every session.
claims.source: Methods, Behavior, paragraph 1
claims.quote: The length of each trial was 205 cm. ... at a frame rate of 30 Hz ... Animals were required to run at least ten trials along each arm (at least twenty trials total) within each session.
claims.criterion: Trial length is the median over familiar figure-eight trials of the largest linearized position inside the trial; tracking rate is 1 over the median interval of the position timestamps. Trials per arm are counted in every familiar figure-eight recording under two readings of "along each arm"; (a) the visited arm; (b) the expected arm. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance and every session has at least ten trials per arm under one reading. Partially reproduced when the values hold and every session has at least 20 trials but some session has fewer than ten on one arm. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The novel-environment cohort of three mice made 16 novel environment explorations in six distinct environments (two linear tracks, three open fields and one figure-eight maze).
claims.source: Results, SBD pyramidal neurons exhibit overlapping place tuning, paragraph 3; Methods, Behavior, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Altogether, we obtained n = 16 novel environment explorations across animals. Six distinct novel environments were employed: two linear tracks, three open fields and one figure-eight maze.
claims.criterion: A novel exploration is a maze recording other than the first of its session, with trials and position. Reproduced when 3 mice and 16 (within tolerance) explorations are found. Partially reproduced when 3 mice are found with fewer explorations. Not reproduced otherwise. The kinds of environment are read from the track length and the x-y extent, and reported.

claims.statement: Population firing-rate vectors at the same linearized position decorrelate between left and right trials once the animal leaves the common stem of the figure-eight maze (median correlations stem 0.93, turn 1 0.412, arm 0.372, turn 2 0.394).
claims.source: Figure 5e
claims.quote: Population firing rate vectors at linearized positions along the maze decorrelated between left and right trial types as soon as animals exited the common stem segment of the maze (Fig. 5e).
claims.criterion: Sessions are the familiar figure-eight recordings of the nine maze mice (all maze mice except e15_13f1 and e16_3m2, as in ratemap_remap.m). In each session and each 1 cm bin of the 205, the Pearson correlation across putative pyramidal cells of their left-trial and right-trial rates; bins pooled over sessions by segment (stem bins 1-74, turn 1 75-111, arm 112-185, turn 2 186-205). Kruskal-Wallis test across the four segments. Reproduced when all four medians are within tolerance and the test gives p < 0.05 with the stem highest. Partially reproduced when the stem median exceeds each of the other three and the test gives p < 0.05, but a median is outside tolerance. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Individual pyramidal neurons preserve their theta-related firing rates between the familiar and novel environments (Spearman rho = 0.7378, n = 2,544 neurons).
claims.source: Figure 6c, top
claims.quote: Individual pyramidal neurons preserved their theta-related firing rates across environments
claims.criterion: Putative pyramidal cells of the sessions with a novel exploration; for each, the firing rate while running at 5 cm/s or faster in the familiar figure-eight trials and in the novel maze trials. Spearman correlation over cells with both rates. Reproduced when rho is at least 0.664 (the lower end of the tolerance; a stronger correlation supports preservation more) with p < 0.05. Partially reproduced when rho is positive with p < 0.05 but below 0.664. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Pairwise spatial ratemap correlations between pyramidal neurons are higher in novel environments (median 0.048) than in the familiar environment (median -0.045).
claims.source: Figure 6c, bottom
claims.quote: pairwise analysis revealed systematically higher spatial ratemap correlations in novel environments (Fig. 6c)
claims.criterion: All pairs of putative pyramidal cells in the sessions of the three novel-environment mice (the paper's pairs each include one light-responsive neuron, which cannot be identified here). claims.statement: DLS dopamine fluctuations are significantly negatively correlated with translational velocity at short timescales (under 10 s), and the correlation reverses and becomes positive at longer timescales, for both dLight transient rates and binned amplitudes.
claims.source: Results, Relating DLS dopamine to spontaneous behavior, paragraph 2; Figure 1e
claims.quote: These dopamine fluctuations (measured as both dLight transient rates and average binned amplitudes) were only weakly correlated with many aspects of movement kinematics ... but were significantly negatively correlated with translational velocity at short timescales (<10 s); this correlation reversed and became positive at longer timescales
claims.criterion: Per session, the z-scored dLight and the 2D speed are averaged (amplitude) or the rate of upward crossings of 1.96 is taken (transient rate) in non-overlapping bins of 0.25 to 59.75 s in 0.5-s steps, bins with fewer than the modal number of frames dropped, and Pearson r taken per session, then averaged over sessions. The null is 100 shuffles of the binned dLight within each session; a mean r outside the 2.5 to 97.5 percentiles of the shuffled means is significant. "At short timescales" can be read as (a) at every timescale below 10 s, or (b) at the shortest timescale (0.25 s). For one measure the claim holds when, under a reading, the mean r is significantly negative and at some timescale of 10 s or more it is significantly positive. Reproduced when it holds for both measures; partially reproduced for one.

claims.statement: Average syllable-associated dLight amplitudes differ across syllables (Kruskal-Wallis H = 209.29, P < 1e-25, n = 518 mouse-syllable pairs).

claims.quote: Right, z-scored average syllable-associated waveforms, sorted by peak fluorescence ... Kruskal–Wallis H test on average syllable-associated fluorescence amplitudes
claims.criterion: Per mouse and named syllable, the mean syllable-associated dLight over all instances in the mouse's sessions; a Kruskal-Wallis test across the 37 syllables. Reproduced when P < 1e-25 and both values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when P < 0.05 but the P or a value misses; not reproduced when P >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Random forest classifiers cannot predict which syllable is being expressed from the coincident dLight peak amplitude or waveform.

claims.criterion: Instances of the 37 named syllables are subsampled to 1,000 per syllable (seeded), and a random forest (100 trees) is trained with stratified fivefold cross-validation on (i) the peak amplitude alone and (ii) the 0 to 0.3 s waveform and its derivative. Chance is 1/37. The paper gives no accuracy; "unable to predict" is taken as held-out accuracy below twice chance (0.054). Reproduced when both feature sets are below it; partially reproduced when one is. Accuracy with shuffled labels is reported as the null.

claims.statement: Syllables associated on average with more DLS dopamine in an experiment tend to be used more.

claims.criterion: Per experiment, the mean syllable-associated dLight of instances longer than 0.3 s is z-scored across syllables; per mouse and syllable this value and the syllable count are averaged over experiments, keeping syllables with at least 100 instances in the mouse. A Huber regressor (epsilon 1.05) predicts count from dLight with fivefold cross-validation repeated 20 times; r is the Pearson correlation of held-out predictions with the data, and its null is 200 fits with dLight shuffled. Reproduced when r > 0 with one-sided shuffle P < 0.05.

claims.statement: Mice string together less predictable sequences after syllables associated with more dopamine; average syllable-associated dLight correlates positively with the entropy of the syllable's outgoing transitions.

claims.criterion: As for fig2b-dlight-usage-across-syllables, with the Shannon entropy (nats) of each syllable's outgoing transition probabilities per experiment, averaged per mouse and syllable, in place of the count. Reproduced when r > 0 with one-sided shuffle P < 0.05.

claims.statement: When an instance of a syllable coincides with a higher-amplitude dopamine transient, that syllable is used more over the following minutes.
claims.source: Results, Dopamine predicts future syllable use and sequencing, paragraph 2; Figure 2c-g
claims.quote: if a given instance of a syllable coincided with a relatively high amplitude dopamine transient, that syllable was then used more over the next several minutes
claims.criterion: Per experiment and named syllable, for each instance its syllable-associated dLight and the count of the same syllable among the next n syllables, for n = 10 to 390 in steps of 20 (instances without n following syllables dropped). Pearson r is taken within each of five equal time segments of the session and averaged, then averaged over experiments per mouse and syllable, then over mouse-syllable pairs. The null is 100 shuffles of dLight within experiment, syllable and segment; one-sided P is the fraction of shuffled means at or above the observed one. Reproduced when the mean r is positive with P < 0.05 at every n from 10 to 190 (about two minutes); partially reproduced when it is so at n = 10 but not throughout; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Brief (250 ms) Opto-DA does not change movement at the moment of stimulation; no comparison between stimulation and catch trials in any mouse is significant.

Stimulation trials are pulse onsets; catch trials are online target onsets in the same sessions with no pulse within the next 0.5 s, aligned 0.17 s after onset (the median latency to stimulation). Per trial, the mean 2D speed from 0 to 1 s after alignment minus the mean over the preceding 1 s. Per Opto-DA mouse, a one-sided Mann-Whitney U test of stimulation above catch, P < 0.05 uncorrected as the legend gives. Reproduced when no Opto-DA mouse is significant; not reproduced when any is. Holm-corrected results and controls are shown as variants.

claims.criterion: Pulse trains (pulses under 50 ms) are grouped into stimulations by gaps over 1 s. Trials as in fig3l-no-kinematic-effect, with speed from 0 to 3 s after alignment. Per mouse, a one-sided Mann-Whitney U test of stimulation above catch. Reproduced when each of the three Opto-DA mice with 3-s sessions is significant (P < 0.05); partially reproduced when one or two are; not reproduced when none is. Controls are reported.

claims.statement: CA1 pyramidal neurons were recorded and probed in four CaMKIIa-Cre::Ai32 mice, 822 pyramidal neurons in all, 43.3 plus or minus 8.37 per session.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we recorded and probed large numbers of CA1 pyramidal neurons simultaneously in freely moving ... n = 822 pyramidal neurons in four mice; 43.3 ± 8.37 pyramidal neurons per session
claims.criterion: Putative pyramidal cells (baseline-epoch rate below 5 Hz), each session counted once. The paper does not say which sessions it used; the readings are (a) all sessions, (b) the sessions whose epochs name the uLED stimulation protocol. Reproduced when, under one reading, all three values are within tolerance (the per-session tolerance is the paper's standard deviation); partially reproduced when the mice and the per-session mean match but the total does not.

claims.statement: uLEDs were driven with 20 ms pulses at random sites with randomly variable 20 to 40 ms offsets, so that the stimulation of each site recurred at about 0.3 to 0.6 s intervals.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 2; Figure 1C
claims.quote: μLEDs were activated (0.02 to 0.1 μW, 20 ms duration) with randomly variable (20 to 40 ms) offsets so that stimulation of each site reccurred at ~0.3- to 0.6-s intervals
claims.criterion: Over the stimulation epochs of the two sessions with pulse times. Reproduced when the median pulse duration is within tolerance, the median offset between the end of one pulse and the start of the next (any uLED) lies within 18 to 44 ms (the range widened by 10% of each bound), and the median interval between successive pulses of each uLED with at least 1000 pulses lies within 0.27 to 0.66 s. Partially reproduced when the duration holds but one of the other two does not.

claims.statement: Of 822 pyramidal neurons, 611 responded to light from the uLEDs.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 2; Figure 1E
claims.quote: Of 822 neurons, 611 responded unequally to the three neighboring μLEDs
claims.criterion: Fraction of putative pyramidal cells in the two sessions with pulse times that pass the three-way test for at least one uLED. Readings of which pulses are tested are (a) the home-cage PreStim epoch, (b) all stimulation epochs (PreStim, Maze and PostStim). Reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Light-induced spike responses of individual pyramidal cells decreased during sharp-wave ripples (n = 485 neurons, P < 1e-55, Wilcoxon paired signed-rank test).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 3; Figure 1, F to I
claims.quote: light-induced spike responses in individual pyramidal cells decreased during SPW-Rs (ΔRate; Fig. 1, F to I).
claims.criterion: Light-responsive putative pyramidal cells of the two sessions, over the home-cage stimulation epochs (PreStim and PostStim). For each cell, the light rate in its light windows and the control rate in control windows, each split by whether the window overlaps a deposited ripple interval. Readings of the response are (a) the rate difference, light minus control (Hz), (b) the ratio light over control. Reproduced when, under one reading, the response inside ripples is lower than outside them by a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05 with a negative median difference. The paper's p-value cannot be reached with the few cells of two sessions and is not part of the criterion; cells with no control spikes inside ripples are left out of reading (b).

claims.statement: The firing-rate change of pyramidal neurons during SPW-Rs is negatively correlated with their baseline firing rate (rho = -0.19, P < 1e-7).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 3 (figure S10)
claims.quote: the negative correlation between firing-rate change during SPW-R and baseline firing rates of neurons
claims.criterion: Every putative pyramidal cell of every session with at least 50 deposited ripples in its first epoch. Baseline rate is the rate in the first epoch; the SPW-R change is measured in the same epoch, inside the deposited ripple intervals against outside them. Readings of the change are (a) log2 of the ratio of the rate inside to the rate outside (cells with no spikes inside ripples left out), (b) the difference inside minus outside (Hz). Reproduced when, under one reading, rho is within tolerance and p < 1e-7. Partially reproduced when rho is negative with p < 0.05 under one reading but no reading meets the full criterion. The tolerance is the half-width of the 95% interval of a Spearman rho at the paper's n of 822, since the paper gives no interval and 10% of 0.19 is below the sampling error.

claims.statement: During track running, the light-induced rate gain is largest at the trough of the theta cycle (P < 1e-6, Wilcoxon test).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4; Figure 2, A and B
claims.quote: We observed a gain at the trough of the theta cycle, the phase corresponding to the strongest synchrony of pyramidal neurons (Fig. 2A)
claims.criterion: Light-responsive putative pyramidal cells of the two sessions, Maze epoch, during laps. Theta phase from the LFP channel with the largest ripple power (6 to 10 Hz, Hilbert), taken at the middle of each light or control window. Gain is light rate minus control rate in the trough half of the cycle (phase beyond +-90 degrees from the peak) and in the peak half. Reproduced when the gain in the trough half is higher by a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05. The gain in six 60-degree bins is shown as a variant.
