claims.statement: More than half of the pyramidal neurons were place cells, 73% of light-responsive and 71% of non-responsive neurons, with no difference between them (P = 0.90, chi-squared test).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4 (figure S11)
claims.quote: more than half of the pyramidal neurons were classified as place cells [73% and 71% of light-responsive and nonresponsive neurons, respectively; P = 0.90, χ2 test
claims.criterion: Putative pyramidal cells of the two sessions, place cells by the control maps of the Maze epoch. The absence of a difference is judged on the paper's test, a chi-squared test of the 2 x 2 table (with Yates' correction, scipy's default) at p >= 0.05. Reproduced when that test finds no difference and both fractions are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the test finds no difference but a fraction is outside tolerance; not reproduced when the test finds a difference.

claims.statement: The light-induced rate increase is higher within than outside the place field (n = 553 place fields, P < 1e-115, Wilcoxon test).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4; Figure 2, C to E
claims.quote: The induced rate increase was higher within than outside the place field (Fig. 2E and fig. S12).
claims.criterion: Every control place field of a light-responsive putative pyramidal cell in the two sessions. Gain is light rate minus control rate, each from unsmoothed counts over time while the animal is inside the field's bins, and outside them in the same running direction. Reproduced when in-field gain exceeds out-of-field gain by a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05 with a positive median difference.

claims.statement: The in-field gain is positively correlated with the out-of-field firing rate (rho = 0.17, P < 1e-5) and with the home-cage firing rate of the neuron (rho = 0.25, P < 1e-7).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4 (figure S12)
claims.quote: This in-field gain was positively correlated with both the out-of-field firing rate and the home-cage firing rate of the neuron
claims.criterion: Over the place fields of fig2e-infield-gain. Out-of-field rate is the control rate outside the field in the same direction; home-cage rate is the rate in the first epoch. Reproduced when both rho values are within tolerance, partially reproduced when one is. The tolerance is the half-width of the 95% interval of rho at the paper's n of 553, as the paper gives no interval. Whether p reaches the paper's values is reported, not judged.

claims.statement: Light responses in the home cage before the track were stronger in place cells than in non-place cells (P < 1e-4, Kruskal-Wallis test).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 5; Figure 3A
claims.quote: Light responses in place cells, tested in the home cage before the track, were significantly stronger than in non-place cells
claims.criterion: Every putative pyramidal cell of the two sessions with at least one tested uLED. The response is the largest, over its tested uLEDs, of the rate during the pulse minus the rate before it (Hz) in the PreStim epoch. Reproduced when place cells have the higher median and a Kruskal-Wallis test gives p < 0.05. The z-scored response is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Optogenetic depolarization revealed place fields in the majority of non-place cells, 289 of 417 (69.3%).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 5; Figure 3, B and C
claims.quote: optogenetic depolarization revealed place fields in the majority of non-place cells (Fig. 3, B and C; 69.3%, 289 of 417
claims.criterion: Non-place putative pyramidal cells of the two sessions with a light map field (same field rule as the control maps) in at least one direction. Readings of the denominator are (a) light-responsive non-place cells, with light maps from the uLEDs each responds to, (b) all non-place cells, with light maps from every uLED with at least 1000 pulses. Reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: The spatial location of light-induced spikes matches that of spikes without stimulation, both for place fields of place cells (P < 1e-40) and for unmasked place fields of non-place cells, whose sparse control spikes form ghost fields (P < 1e-10).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 5; Figure 3, C and E
claims.quote: We found a robust correlation between the spatial location of induced place field spikes and the sparse spikes of non-place cells in the absence of stimulation (Fig. 3, C and E
claims.criterion: For each field (control fields of light-responsive place cells; light fields of light-responsive non-place cells, reading (a) of fig3c-unmasked-fields), the peak bin of the control map and of the light map in the same direction. Reproduced when the two peak positions are positively correlated (Pearson, p < 0.05) in both groups; partially reproduced when in one. The paper's test (chi-squared against 500 shuffles) is not described in the main text; a test against shuffled cell pairings is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Place fields during light stimulation were more stable between the first and second halves of the session than during control epochs, for both true place fields and unmasked place fields (P < 1e-9 and P < 1e-19, two-way ANOVA).
claims.source: Figure 3F
claims.quote: Place fields during light stimulation were more stable for both true place fields and unmasked place fields
claims.criterion: Per field direction as in fig3e-ghost-fields, stability is the Spearman correlation of the map from laps 11 to 60 with the map from laps 71 to 120, as in the legend, computed for the light map and for the control map. Reproduced when, in both groups, light stability exceeds control stability by a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when in one group. A two-way ANOVA (stimulation by group) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Spatial information of control and light-stimulated epochs is correlated, and the light-boosted increase is stronger for unmasked place fields of non-place cells than for place cells (P < 1e-15, Kruskal-Wallis test).
claims.source: Figure 3G
claims.quote: Correlation of spatial information (Bits/spike) between control and light-stimulated epochs ... Light-boosted effect was stronger for unmasked place fields of non-place cells than for place cell place fields
claims.criterion: Skaggs spatial information (bits per spike) of the control and light maps per direction, for the two groups of fig3e-ghost-fields. Reproduced when control and light information are positively correlated (Spearman p < 0.05) in both groups and the increase (light minus control) is larger for non-place cells than for place cells by a Kruskal-Wallis test at p < 0.05. Partially reproduced when only one part holds.

claims.statement: Cofiring of place cell pairs during SPW-Rs in the home cage is positively correlated with their spatial overlap on the track (P < 1e-27), while pairs of a place cell and a non-place cell show no such relationship (P = 0.11).
claims.source: Figure 4C (legend); Main text, paragraph 7; Figure 4, B and C
claims.quote: SPW-R cofiring was positively correlated with spatial overlap in place cell pairs ... but not in pairs with place and non-place cell (non-PC) partners (P = 0.11).
claims.criterion: Pairs of putative pyramidal cells within each of the two sessions. Cofiring is the Pearson correlation of spike counts per deposited ripple over the ripples of the home-cage epochs without stimulation (BaselinePre and BaselinePost); spatial overlap is the Spearman correlation of the two cells' control maps, both directions joined. Part 1 holds when Spearman rho of cofiring against overlap is positive with p < 0.05 over place cell pairs. Part 2 is a claim of absence judged on the paper's test, Spearman correlation at p < 0.05 over place and non-place pairs; it holds when that test finds no correlation. Reproduced when both parts hold, partially reproduced when one does, not reproduced when neither.

claims.statement: With light-induced spikes, the relationship between SPW-R cofiring and spatial overlap appears for pairs that include non-place cells (P < 1e-5, Spearman correlation).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 7; Figure 4, C and D (legend panel D)
claims.quote: during optogenetic stimulation, the relationship between cofiring during SPW-Rs and spatial overlap was revealed for unmasked place fields of non-place field pairs (Fig. 4C).
claims.criterion: Pairs of a place cell and a non-place cell, both light-responsive, within each session. Cofiring as in fig4c-swr-cofiring-place-pairs; spatial overlap from the two cells' light maps, both directions joined. Reproduced when Spearman rho is positive with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Stronger light (three intensities) decreased the light-induced response during SPW-Rs, increased the in-field gain of place cells several-fold, and increased the in-field gain of unmasked fields (Figure 1J, Figure 2F, Figure 3D; Friedman tests).
claims.source: Figure 1J, Figure 2F, Figure 3D; Main text, paragraphs 3 and 4
claims.quote: Increasing Vm depolarization decreased the light-induced response during SPW-Rs (Fig. 1J) ... Increasing depolarization of Vm by stronger light intensity increased the in-field gain several-fold (Fig. 2F).
claims.criterion: Needs the light intensity of each pulse at three levels.

claims.statement: Intracellular recordings in which the membrane potential was varied reproduce the decreased gain during SPW-Rs (five cells in anesthetized rats and five in head-fixed mice, P = 0.002).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 3; Figure 1, K to M
claims.quote: more directly by intracellular experiments, in which Vm was systematically varied (Fig. 1, K to M), reproducing the effect seen with optogenetic Vm depolarization (Fig. 1I)
claims.criterion: Needs the intracellular recordings.

claims.statement: During SPW-Rs, excitatory neurons increased their firing rates more than inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 3 (figure S9)
claims.quote: During sharp-wave ripples (SPW-Rs), excitatory neurons increased their firing rates more than inhibitory neurons (fig. S9)
claims.criterion: Needs the classification of units into pyramidal cells and interneurons.

claims.statement: Decoding of position is most accurate from light-boosted spikes of place cells, and light-induced spikes of non-place cells predict position better than control spikes of place cells (P = 0.001, Tukey test).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 6; Figure 3H
claims.quote: The root mean squared error of the decoded position was highest for the sparse non-place cell spikes and lowest for light-boosted spikes of place cells. The induced spikes of non-place cells more accurately predicted the mouse's position on the track
claims.criterion: Needs the decoder, its bins and its cross-validation, which are in the supplement.

claims.statement: ICA assemblies of place cells in the home cage show higher spatial correlation than chance, mixed assemblies of place and non-place cells do not, and with unmasked place fields they reach the level of place-cell assemblies.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 7; Figure 4, E and F
claims.quote: Assembly members of place cells, but not of mixtures of place and non-place cells, showed higher spatial correlation than chance (Fig. 4E). However, when spikes of unmasked place fields were considered, they expressed spatial correlation at the level of real place cells
claims.criterion: Needs the assembly detection settings (bin size, significance of components) and the chance level, which are in the supplement.

claims.statement: Sequential firing of place cells is correlated with spike sequences during SPW-Rs, and the fraction of SPW-Rs with significant trajectories increases when unmasked place fields are included in the template (P < 1e-4, Friedman test).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 7; Figure 4, G and H
claims.quote: Sequential firing of place cells was correlated with spike sequences during SPW-Rs (Fig. 4G) ... The fraction of SPW-R events with significant virtual track trajectories increased when unmasked place fields were also included for the construction of the place field sequence template
claims.criterion: Needs the Bayesian decoding and shuffle procedure, which are in the supplement.

claims.statement: Correct response rates were 90.2 +/- 7.8% for IN and 93.1 +/- 4.3% for OUT trials, and the rate of correct responses decreased with set size, from 98.5% (set size 4) to 90.5% (6) and 84.7% (8), a significant effect in a permuted repeated-measures ANOVA over 36 sessions.
claims.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 2; Figure 1B
claims.quote: The average correct response rates were 90.2 ± 7.8% for IN and 93.1 ± 4.3% for OUT. The rate of correct responses decreased with set size from a set size of 4 (98.5% correct responses) to set sizes of 6 (90.5%) and 8 (84.7%)
claims.criterion: All trials of the 36 sessions. The IN and OUT tolerances are the SD the paper gives; the others are 10%. Open, how percentages are formed; readings (a) the mean of per-session percentages (Fig. 1B shows sessions), (b) trials pooled over sessions. The ANOVA has set size as the within factor and session as the unit (F with 2 and 70 degrees of freedom); its permutation scheme is not given, and the reading is set-size labels shuffled within each session, 4999 permutations (P = 0.0002 as 1/(n + 1), Methods, Statistics). Reproduced when, under one reading, all values are within tolerance, the order 4 above 6 above 8 holds and the ANOVA has P < 0.05.

claims.statement: Across all sessions the working memory capacity (Cowan's K) averaged 6.8 letters.
claims.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Across all sessions, the capacity averaged 6.8 [Cowan's K , (correct IN rate + correct OUT rate − 1) × set size]
claims.criterion: K = (correct IN rate + correct OUT rate - 1) x set size, per session, as the Results define it, averaged over the 36 sessions. Open, which set size and rates enter; readings (a) K at set size 8 from the set size 8 rates, (b) the maximum of K over the three set sizes, (c) the rates pooled over all set sizes multiplied by 8, the largest set size, (d) the mean of K over the three set sizes. Reproduced when one reading is within tolerance.

claims.statement: The mean response time of correct trials (1630 trials) increased with workload, by 48 ms per item, a significant effect in a permuted repeated-measures ANOVA.
claims.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 2; Figure 1C
claims.quote: The mean response time (RT) for the correct trials (1630 trials) increased with workload (48 ms per item; permuted repeated-measures ANOVA, F 2,2007 = 21.10, P = 0.0002; Fig. 1C )
claims.criterion: RT relative to probe onset (Fig. 1C legend), correct trials. Table S2 (Fig. 1c) names the test a permutation ANOVA with n the number of trials (1630) and df = (2, 2007), so the ANOVA is run on trials with set size as factor (one-way, permuted set-size labels). The F has 2007 error degrees of freedom, which does not fit the 1630 trials; its F is reported. Open, how 48 ms per item is obtained; readings (i) the slope of a line fit over all correct trials, (ii) the mean over sessions of per-session slopes, (iii) the slope over the three set-size means, (iv) the difference between set sizes 8 and 4 divided by 4. Open, per-session value for reading (ii), mean RT (the text) or median RT (Fig. 1C). Reproduced when RT rises with set size, the ANOVA has P < 0.05, and under one reading the slope and the trial count are within tolerance. The F value is reported, not judged, since its degrees of freedom cannot be matched to a stated design.

claims.statement: Correct IN/OUT decisions were made faster than incorrect ones (1.36 +/- 0.64 s against 1.87 +/- 1.21 s).
claims.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Correct IN/OUT decisions were made more rapidly than incorrect decisions (1.36 ± 0.64 s versus 1.87 ± 1.21 s, respectively; permutation t test, t = 5.06, P = 5.0 × 10 −5 )
claims.criterion: RT relative to probe onset. The tolerances are the SDs the paper gives. Readings (a) all trials pooled, mean +/- SD over trials, unpaired permutation t test; (b) per-session means, paired over sessions with at least one error. The permutation t test as in Methods, Statistics (2000 permutations; the printed P implies more, which only moves the minimum P). Reproduced when, under one reading, both means are within tolerance and correct RT is shorter with P < 0.05.

claims.statement: 1526 neurons were recorded (51 +/- 35 per session), 676 in hippocampus, 449 in entorhinal cortex and 401 in amygdala.
claims.source: Results, Single-unit electrophysiology, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We recorded the activity of 1526 (51 ± 35 per session) neurons from the hippocampus ( n = 676), entorhinal cortex ( n = 449), and amygdala ( n = 401) across all microelectrodes
claims.criterion: Counts of sorted units over all sessions, a unit seen in several sessions counted once per session (Results, same paragraph). The counts are exact, since they describe the deposited units; a difference is reported with its size. Hippocampus is the hippocampal head and body electrodes (AH and PH in the data descriptor's Table 1), entorhinal cortex EC, amygdala A. Open, the sessions in the per-session mean (1526 over 36 sessions is 42); readings (a) all 36 sessions, (b) sessions with at least one unit.

claims.statement: The mean firing rate of all neurons was 2.55 +/- 3.30 Hz; the percentage of interspike intervals below 3 ms was 1.58 +/- 4.18%, and the ratio of the peak of the mean waveform to the SD of the noise was 3.28 +/- 1.56.
claims.source: Results, Single-unit electrophysiology, paragraph 1; Methods, Spike detection and single-unit identification; fig. S1
claims.quote: The percentage of ISI below 3 ms was 1.58 ± 4.18%, and the ratio of the peak amplitude of the mean waveform to the SD of the noise was 3.28 ± 1.56
claims.criterion: Over all 1526 units. The tolerances are the SDs the paper gives. Open, the time base of the firing rate; readings (a) spikes over the total duration of the task trials, (b) over the whole session. Open, the noise SD of the SNR; readings (a) the mean over samples of the deposited waveform SD, (b) the waveform SD at the first samples of the 2 ms window. Reproduced when, under one reading, all three means are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Neurons with higher firing during maintenance than fixation (maintenance neurons) occurred in all three areas, most frequently in hippocampus, where 20.6% of the recorded neurons were maintenance neurons.
claims.source: Results, Single-unit electrophysiology, paragraph 2; Figure 2B; table S2 (Fig. 2b)
claims.quote: We identified maintenance neurons in all recorded areas ( Fig. 2B ); however, they occurred most frequently within the hippocampus (χ 2 1 = 47.30, P = 6.1 × 10 −12 ), where 20.6% of all recorded neurons were maintenance neurons (permutation test against scrambled data, P = 0.002)
claims.criterion: Correct trials. A maintenance neuron has a higher firing rate in maintenance (-3 to 0 s) than in fixation (-6 to -5 s) (fig. S2 legend) by a permutation t test (Results; Methods, Statistics), on per-trial rates, paired and unpaired as named in the opening comment, P < 0.05. Per area, the count is compared with a null from shuffling the maintenance and fixation labels within each trial and rerunning the selection ("permuted labels", Fig. 2 legend; the labels are not named, and the period labels are the only labels of this selection), at both numbers of repetitions. The chi-square has 1 degree of freedom; readings (a) a 2 x 2 table of hippocampus against entorhinal cortex and amygdala pooled, without continuity correction, (b) the same with Yates correction. Reproduced when, under one reading of each open detail, the hippocampal percentage is the highest of the three areas and within tolerance, the chi-square has P < 0.05, and the hippocampal count exceeds the null at P < 0.05; partially reproduced when hippocampus is highest and significant but the percentage is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: During maintenance, 15% of hippocampal maintenance neurons (21 neurons) increased their firing rate with workload (set size 4 against set sizes 6 and 8), a significant percentage against scrambled data; the percentage was not significant in entorhinal cortex or amygdala.
claims.source: Results, Single-unit electrophysiology, paragraph 2; Figure 2C; table S2 (Fig. 2c)
claims.quote: During maintenance, a subset of maintenance neurons in the hippocampus (15%, 21 neurons; permutation test against scrambled data, P = 0.002) increased their firing rates systematically with workload (set size 4 versus set sizes 6 and 8; Fig. 2C )
claims.criterion: Maintenance neurons from fig2b-maintenance-neurons-hippocampus, correct trials, maintenance -3 to 0 s. The test of load dependence is not named; readings (a) a permutation t test of per-trial maintenance rates, set size 4 against 6 and 8 (Methods, Statistics, for two distributions), (b) a cluster-based nonparametric permutation test on the firing rate over the maintenance period, 500 ms bins at 20 ms steps (Fig. 2A legend; Methods, Statistics, for firing rates), each at P < 0.05 with the rate higher for 6 and 8. The null shuffles set size labels across trials and reruns the test ("permuted labels", Fig. 2 legend), at both numbers of repetitions. Reproduced when, under one reading, the hippocampal count is within tolerance and significant at P < 0.05 and neither other area is significant; partially reproduced when hippocampus is significant but the count is outside tolerance or another area is significant too.

claims.statement: Neurons firing specifically after the probe letter (probe neurons) occurred in all areas, most prominently in entorhinal cortex, where 9% of neurons (41) were probe neurons.
claims.source: Results, Single-unit electrophysiology, paragraph 3; Figure 3E; table S2 (Fig. 3e)
claims.quote: We identified probe neurons in all areas and, most prominently, in the entorhinal cortex (χ 2 1 = 23.16, P = 1.5 × 10 −6 ; Fig. 3E ), in which 9% of neurons were probe neurons (41 neurons; permutation test against scrambled data, P = 0.001)
claims.criterion: Correct trials. A probe neuron has a higher firing rate after the probe than in encoding (-5 to -3 s) and than in maintenance (-3 to 0 s), each by a permutation t test at P < 0.05 (Results, same paragraph). The probe window is not given; readings (a) 0 to 1 s after probe onset, (b) probe onset to the button press of each trial (the probe is shown until the response, Methods, Task), (c) -500 to 0 ms relative to the button press, the window used for retrieval decoding (Fig. 4F legend). Paired and unpaired as in the opening comment. Null and chi-square readings as in fig2b-maintenance-neurons-hippocampus, with entorhinal cortex against the other two areas. Reproduced when, under one reading, entorhinal cortex has the highest percentage, its count is within tolerance, the chi-square has P < 0.05 and the entorhinal count exceeds the null at P < 0.05.

claims.statement: Peak firing of probe neurons was higher when aligned to probe onset than when aligned to the button press (5.47 +/- 4.97 Hz against 4.28 +/- 4.37 Hz), so their firing reflects the probe stimulus more than movement preparation.
claims.source: Results, Single-unit electrophysiology, paragraph 4; Figure 3A and 3B
claims.quote: Aligning the response with the probe stimulus onset resulted in significantly higher peak firing rates (mean for all probe neurons, 5.47 ± 4.97 Hz versus 4.28 ± 4.37 Hz; permutation t test, t 75 = 4.40, P = 0.0005
claims.criterion: All probe neurons of fig3e-probe-neurons-entorhinal (76 by the reported degrees of freedom and by 8 neurons being 10.5%). Per neuron, the maximum of the trial-averaged rate in 200 ms bins at 20 ms steps (Fig. 3 legend) after each alignment; the tolerances are the SDs the paper gives; paired permutation t test over neurons (Methods, Statistics). Open, the window of the maximum; readings (a) 0 to 1 s after the alignment event, (b) 1 s before to 1 s after it. Reproduced when, under one reading, the probe-aligned peak is higher with P < 0.05 and both means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the direction and test hold but a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Only a few probe neurons reflected the decision (8 neurons, 10.5% of probe neurons, IN against OUT), and only one showed workload dependence.
claims.source: Results, Single-unit electrophysiology, paragraph 4; Figure 3A to 3D
claims.quote: However, only a small number of probe neurons (eight neurons, 10.5% of probe neurons) reflected the subject's decision (IN versus OUT; Fig. 3 , A and B), and only one neuron showed workload dependence
claims.criterion: Probe neurons from fig3e-probe-neurons-entorhinal. IN against OUT, and set size 4 against 6 and 8, by a cluster-based nonparametric permutation test at P < 0.05 on the rate in 200 ms bins at 20 ms steps after probe onset (Fig. 3A and 3C legends). The time range tested is not given; readings (a) 0 to 1 s after probe onset, (b) 0 to 2 s. Reproduced when, under one reading, both counts are within tolerance (a count of one may be 0 to 2, as 10% of one neuron cannot be judged); partially reproduced when one holds.

claims.statement: The first three demixed principal components of the population firing rates explained 44.7% of the variance and separated set sizes 4, 6 and 8, with three angles of 120 degrees in the dPC2-dPC3 plane; the first 15 components explained 79%.
claims.source: Results, Attractors in neural population dynamics, paragraph 1; Figure 4A; fig. S3
claims.quote: We formed a three-dimensional space from the first three demixed principal components (dPCs 1, 2, and 3, explaining 44.7% of the variance; Fig. 4A , fig. S3, and movie S1). dPCA distinguished between workloads 4, 6, and 8.
claims.criterion: dPCA (Kobak et al. 2016) of all neurons, correct trials, trial-averaged per set size, from spikes in 2 ms bins smoothed with a 1000 ms Gaussian kernel and z-scored to the fixation period (Methods, dPCA of firing rates), with time and set-size marginalizations, components ordered by explained variance. Open, the scale of the z-score; readings (a) mean and SD of the fixation rate, (b) fixation mean and SD over the whole trial. Open, the dPCA regularization; readings (a) the toolbox's cross-validated lambda, (b) none. Angles are those at the centroid between the three set-size points of the dPC2-dPC3 projection, averaged over maintenance. Reproduced when, under one reading, both variances and all three angles are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the set sizes separate (all pairwise maintenance distances exceed those of label-shuffled dPCA runs) but a value is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: In the dPCA state space, the speed of the population trajectory was highest during encoding and lowest during maintenance, lower than in each other trial period, including fixation.
claims.source: Results, Attractors in neural population dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure 4B
claims.quote: The speed was highest during encoding, when maintenance neurons ramped up their firing. By contrast, speed was lowest during maintenance (permutation t test against the other trial periods, P = 0.0005)
claims.criterion: The dPCA of fig4a-dpca-workload-separation, first 15 dPCs (Fig. 4 legend). Speed V(t) as Methods equation 2 with step 20 ms, averaged over set sizes and over each period; 200 runs of dPCA on neural trajectories subsampled at 20% with replacement (Methods). Periods fixation -6 to -5 s, encoding -5 to -3 s, maintenance -3 to 0 s; the retrieval window is not given; readings (a) 0 to 1 s after probe onset, (b) 0 to 2 s. Permutation t test of the per-run maintenance speeds against each other period. Open, the number of runs; the Methods give 200 dPCA runs and table S2 (Fig. 4b, 4c) gives n = 2000 "nr of runs"; both are run. Reproduced when, under one reading, maintenance speed is below each other period with P < 0.05 and encoding speed is the highest; partially reproduced when maintenance is lowest but encoding is not highest.

claims.statement: The pairwise distance between the trajectories of different set sizes was larger during maintenance than during encoding, and the largest of the trial periods.
claims.source: Results, Attractors in neural population dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure 4C
claims.quote: Analyzing the pairwise distance between trajectories that corresponded to different set sizes, we found that the distances during maintenance were larger than during encoding (permutation t test, P = 0.0005; Fig. 4C )
claims.criterion: As fig4b-speed-lowest-maintenance, with distance from Methods equation 1 between each of the three pairs of set-size trajectories, averaged over pairs and over each period, 200 or 2000 subsampled runs (as there). Reproduced when, under one reading, maintenance distance exceeds encoding distance with P < 0.05 and is the largest of the four periods; partially reproduced when it exceeds encoding only.

claims.statement: During encoding of high-workload trials (set sizes 6 and 8), hippocampal neurons, but not entorhinal or amygdala neurons, predicted whether the subject would later respond correctly, with a median decoding accuracy of 80%.
claims.source: Results, Decoding of information during the trial, paragraph 2; Figure 4D
claims.quote: For the encoding period (−5 to −3 s), we found that the activity of hippocampal neurons, but not neurons in other areas, could be used to decode whether the subject would later reply correctly or incorrectly in the trial. The median decoding accuracy was 80% (permutation test against scrambled data, P = 0.002; Fig. 4D )
claims.criterion: Pseudopopulation decoding with a support vector machine as in the NDT toolbox (Methods, Neural decoding): spikes in 1 ms bins smoothed in a 1500 ms window, classified at 250 ms steps, 500 resampling runs, trials of set sizes 6 and 8 (Fig. 4D legend), units from sessions with at least five incorrect responses, five cross-validation splits; null from 500 runs with scrambled labels; Bonferroni over 12 tests. Populations hippocampus, entorhinal cortex and amygdala. Open, the smoothing window shape; readings (a) a 1500 ms boxcar (NDT binning), (b) a Gaussian. Open, feature normalization; readings (a) z-score per neuron on training data (NDT's usual preprocessing), (b) none. Open, the SVM kernel; the reading is NDT's default linear kernel. Open, how "median accuracy" is taken; readings (a) median over resampling runs of the accuracy averaged over the 250 ms steps inside -5 to -3 s, (b) median over runs and steps together. Reproduced when, under one reading, hippocampus is above the null at corrected P < 0.05 with median within tolerance and neither other area is significant; partially reproduced when hippocampus holds and another area is significant too.

claims.statement: During maintenance, workload (set size 4 against 6 and 8) could be decoded from hippocampal neurons with a median accuracy of 80%, but not from neurons of the other areas.
claims.source: Results, Decoding of information during the trial, paragraph 2; Figure 4E
claims.quote: For the maintenance period, we found that the workload (set size 4 versus set sizes 6 and 8) of each trial could be decoded from hippocampal neurons but not from neurons in the other areas (permutation test against scrambled data, P = 0.002; Fig. 4E ). The median decoding accuracy was 80%.
claims.criterion: As fig4d-encoding-decodes-correct, with correct trials, labels set size 4 against 6 and 8, all units, ten cross-validation splits, and the maintenance period -3 to 0 s. Open, class balance; readings (a) equal numbers of trials per class drawn for each neuron (NDT's requirement), (b) all trials. Reproduced when, under one reading, hippocampus is above the null at corrected P < 0.05 with median within tolerance and neither entorhinal cortex nor amygdala is significant; partially reproduced when hippocampus holds and another area is significant too.

claims.statement: Excluding any one subject changed the hippocampal workload decoding accuracy to a value in the range 71 to 81%.
claims.source: Results, Decoding of information during the trial, paragraph 2
claims.quote: To ensure that some subjects did not drive the results, we performed a leave-one-out analysis. The exclusion of any subject changed the decoding accuracy to a value in the range [71 to 81%].
claims.criterion: The decoder of fig4e-maintenance-decodes-workload rerun nine times, each without the hippocampal units of one subject. Reproduced when all nine accuracies lie in 71 to 81% widened by 10% of each bound (63.9 to 89.1%), under a reading of fig4e that reproduced.

claims.statement: Workload decoding from hippocampal maintenance neurons alone was little different from decoding from all hippocampal neurons, while excluding the maintenance neurons reduced the accuracy to 71%.
claims.source: Results, Decoding of information during the trial, paragraph 2; Figure 4E
claims.quote: We also performed the same analysis using only maintenance neurons; there was little difference in the decoding accuracy between the use of only maintenance neurons and the use of the whole population of hippocampal neurons. Conversely, the exclusion of maintenance neurons reduced the prediction accuracy to 71%.
claims.criterion: The decoder of fig4e-maintenance-decodes-workload on (i) hippocampal maintenance neurons only and (ii) hippocampal neurons other than maintenance neurons. "Little difference" is not quantified; it is judged with the protocol's default tolerance, the maintenance-neuron median within 8 percentage points (10% of the 80% accuracy) of the all-hippocampus median, with (i) significant against its scrambled null (Fig. 4E legend, "Sufficient decoding was possible"). Reproduced when both parts hold and (ii) is within tolerance and below the all-hippocampus median.

claims.statement: The decoder did not distinguish trials of set size 6 from set size 8.
claims.source: Results, Decoding of information during the trial, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The decoder did not distinguish between trials of set sizes 6 and 8, which points to a ceiling effect
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper reports no separate test; the decoding test of the Methods is used, as in fig4e-maintenance-decodes-workload, with labels set size 6 against 8, hippocampal neurons, maintenance period, against 500 scrambled-label runs at P < 0.05 (the Bonferroni correction of the Methods covers the 12 tests of Fig. 4D to 4F, which do not include this one). Reproduced when the accuracy is not above the null; not reproduced when it is. The median accuracy is reported either way.

claims.statement: During retrieval (500 ms before the button press), neurons in all recorded areas predicted the IN or OUT response; with all neurons the median decoding accuracy reached 90%.
claims.source: Results, Decoding of information during the trial, paragraph 2; Figure 4F
claims.quote: For the retrieval period, we found that neurons from all areas encoded whether the subject would later reply by pressing the IN or OUT button in the trial (permutation test against scrambled data, P = 0.002; Fig. 4F ). The median decoding accuracy reached 90% if firing from all neurons was included
claims.criterion: As fig4d-encoding-decodes-correct, with correct trials, labels IN against OUT, a 500 ms window ending at the button press (Fig. 4F legend, -500 to 0 ms; Methods, a narrow 500 ms window), ten cross-validation splits, populations hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, amygdala and all neurons. Reproduced when, under one reading, each of the four populations is above its null at corrected P < 0.05 and the all-neuron median is within tolerance; partially reproduced when some but not all areas are significant.

claims.statement: Ranking the first 200 neurons of each region by their dPCA loading, hippocampal neurons had higher loadings than entorhinal and amygdala neurons at each rank except the first three, where entorhinal neurons had the highest loading.
claims.source: fig. S3d legend
claims.quote: For each rank, hippocampus (cyan) had a higher loading than entorhinal cortex (magenta) (paired Wilcoxon test P < 10-33) and amygdala (yellow), except for the first three ranks
claims.criterion: The dPCA of fig4a-dpca-workload-separation. The legend names both dPC3 (title) and dPC2 (text); readings (a) dPC2, (b) dPC3. Open, the loading; readings (i) the absolute decoder weight of the neuron, (ii) the signed weight. Per region the 200 largest, sorted; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test of hippocampus against entorhinal cortex over the 200 ranks. Reproduced when, under one reading, hippocampus is higher with P < 0.05 and higher than amygdala at most ranks.

claims.statement: In subject 1, scalp EEG power during the last 2 s of maintenance was higher for set size 8 than for set size 4 at Pz (8.5 to 16 Hz) and at Fz (8 to 12.5 Hz); this workload-dependent power increase did not appear in the other subjects.
claims.source: Results, Electrophysiology of cortico-hippocampal functional coupling, paragraph 2; Figure 5B and 5C; fig. S5; table S1
claims.quote: the scalp EEG power increased during maintenance for a high workload (set size 8), with a peak within the 8- to 12-Hz alpha range over parietal cortex ( Fig. 5 , A and B). This workload-dependent EEG power increase extended to frontal electrode Fz ( Fig. 5C ). While this power increase is known from healthy subjects for the same or similar task ( 5 , 6 ), it did not appear in the other subjects of our study group (fig. S5 and table S1)
claims.criterion: Last 2 s of maintenance, scalp EEG re-referenced to averaged mastoids, multitaper spectra (+/- 2 Hz smoothing, seven tapers; Methods, Frequency spectra), trials of set size 8 against 4, cluster-based nonparametric permutation test over frequency (P < 0.05). Open, the frequency range tested; readings (a) 4 to 30 Hz (the time-frequency range in Methods), (b) 1 to 40 Hz. Subject 1 reproduced when Pz and Fz each have a significant cluster of higher set size 8 power overlapping 8.5 to 16 Hz and 8 to 12.5 Hz respectively. "Other subjects": table S1 gives EEG workload dependence as no for subjects 2 to 8 and decrease for subject 9, on the channels of fig. S5, which are not named in the text (the legend cites table S7, which does not exist); the reading is the scalp electrode of each subject's maximal PLV (table S1), the columns table S1 sets side by side, with Pz and Fz shown as a variant. Reproduced when subject 1 holds and none of subjects 2 to 9 has a significant increase, as the text says; partially reproduced when subject 1 holds and another subject has an increase.

claims.statement: In subject 1, theta-alpha power (7.5 to 10 Hz) in the left hippocampal iEEG increased with workload during maintenance.
claims.source: Figure 5G and 5H; Results, Electrophysiology of cortico-hippocampal functional coupling, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Theta-alpha power (7.5 to 10.0 Hz) in the left hippocampal iEEG increased with workload during maintenance.
claims.criterion: Subject 1, the left hippocampal bipolar channel of the maximal PLV pair (table S1), last 2 s of maintenance, multitaper spectra as in fig5-subject1-eeg-power-workload, normalized to fixation power (Fig. 5H legend), set size 8 against 4, cluster-based test at P < 0.05. Reproduced when a significant cluster of higher set size 8 power overlaps 7.5 to 10 Hz. Table S1 also lists iEEG workload dependence as increase for subjects 1 and 6 and no for the others; this is reported for all subjects.

claims.statement: In subject 1, the average firing rate of the five hippocampal maintenance neurons was higher for high workload (set size 8 against 4) during encoding and maintenance.
claims.source: Figure 5I; Results, Electrophysiology of cortico-hippocampal functional coupling, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The average firing rate of maintenance neurons in this subject was higher for a high workload during encoding and maintenance ( n = 5 hippocampal neurons with more than 100 spikes during both encoding and maintenance)
claims.criterion: Subject 1, hippocampal maintenance neurons from fig2b-maintenance-neurons-hippocampus with more than 100 spikes in encoding and in maintenance. Their average rate over time, set size 8 against 4, cluster-based nonparametric permutation test at P < 0.05. Open, the unit of the test; readings (a) trials, with the per-trial rate averaged over the five neurons, (b) neuron-trial pairs. Reproduced when, under one reading, the count is 5 and significant clusters of higher set size 8 rate fall in both encoding and maintenance.

claims.statement: In subject 1, the task increased the phase locking value (PLV) between hippocampal iEEG and scalp EEG at Pz in the alpha band during the last 2 s of maintenance; this PLV was higher for set size 8 than 4 (9.0 to 12.0 Hz) and maximal at occipitoparietal electrodes. The PLV to Fz was also higher for set size 8 (8.5 to 10 Hz).
claims.source: Figure 5D, 5E and 5F; Results, Electrophysiology of cortico-hippocampal functional coupling, paragraph 3; fig. S4
claims.quote: The WM task enhanced the hippocampal-cortical PLV specifically in the 8–10 Hz alpha range and during the maintenance period ( Fig. 5D and fig. S4). The PLV increased with workload ( Fig. 5E ) and was highest at occipitoparietal electrode sites ( Fig. 5F ).
claims.criterion: The PLV method of fig6-plv-all-subjects for subject 1. Reproduced when the maximal PLV pair is the left hippocampus with Pz, its PLV in the last 2 s of maintenance exceeds that in encoding (method of fig6-plv-maintenance-over-encoding, the golden bar of Fig. 5) in bins overlapping 8 to 10 Hz, its workload difference (set size 8 minus 4) exceeds the 95th percentile of the label-shuffled null in bins overlapping 9.0 to 12.0 Hz, the scalp electrode with the highest alpha PLV to that hippocampal channel is parietal or occipital, and the hippocampus-Fz workload difference is significant in bins overlapping 8.5 to 10 Hz; partially reproduced when the Pz parts hold and the Fz part does not.

claims.statement: All subjects showed a significant hippocampal-scalp PLV peak during maintenance (set size 8), with individual frequency bands whose lower bound lay in the theta-alpha range and which extended up to 17.5 Hz (median band limits 6.0 to 11.5 Hz).
claims.source: Results, Cortico-hippocampal low-frequency coupling in the group of subjects, paragraph 1; Figure 6A to 6H; table S1
claims.quote: All subjects showed a significant PLV peak for at least one pair of signals recorded from a scalp electrode and a hippocampal channel (table S1). The frequency band of the maximal significant PLV indicated individual differences
claims.criterion: Per subject, every pair of a hippocampal bipolar iEEG channel (deepest contacts of each hippocampal macroelectrode) and a scalp electrode. Last 2 s of maintenance, 2-s epochs, set size 8, multitaper spectra (+/- 2 Hz, seven tapers, the spectra of Methods, Frequency spectra, which the PLV section says it uses), PLV as Methods equation 3. Significance per frequency bin against the 95th percentile of 200 PLVs with trials of one channel permuted (one-tailed). The pair and band of the highest significant PLV are kept (table S1); the individual band is the contiguous run of significant bins around the peak. Open, the frequency range searched; readings (a) 4 to 30 Hz, (b) 1 to 40 Hz. Trials as in the opening comment. Reproduced when, under one reading, all nine subjects have a significant pair and both median band limits are within tolerance; partially reproduced when all nine are significant and the medians are not.

claims.statement: Table S1 gives for each subject the scalp electrode of maximal PLV, its peak frequency and the maximal PLV (subject 1 Pz 10.5 Hz 0.72; 2 F3 7 Hz 0.40; 3 F3 12 Hz 0.43; 4 F3 14 Hz 0.85; 5 P3 5.5 Hz 0.60; 6 O1 7.5 Hz 0.50; 7 O1 7.5 Hz 0.64; 8 O1 11.5 Hz 0.57; 9 O1 8 Hz 0.69), with the hippocampal electrode in the left hemisphere for subjects 1 to 6 and the right for 7 to 9.
claims.source: table S1
claims.criterion: From fig6-plv-all-subjects. Reproduced when, under one reading, at least seven of the nine subjects have the same scalp electrode, hippocampal hemisphere, and maximal PLV within tolerance; partially reproduced for four to six. Peak frequencies are reported against the table.

claims.statement: During maintenance, PLV in the individual frequency band was higher for set size 8 than set size 4 in eight of nine subjects (range 5.5 to 16.5 Hz, median band limits 7.8 to 10 Hz).
claims.source: Results, Cortico-hippocampal low-frequency coupling in the group of subjects, paragraph 2; Figure 6A to 6H; table S1
claims.quote: During maintenance, the PLV was increased for high workload in eight of nine subjects in the individual frequency band (set size 4 versus set size 8; permutation test, P = 0.05; range, 5.5 to 16.5 Hz; median band limits, 7.8 to 10 Hz; Fig. 6 and table S1)
claims.criterion: The pair of fig6-plv-all-subjects per subject. PLV for set size 8 minus PLV for set size 4, against the 95th percentile of 200 differences with the epochs randomly assigned to the two set sizes (Methods, Phase-locking value). A subject counts when at least one bin inside the individual band is significant. Table S1 lists subject 3 as not significant. Reproduced when, under one reading, eight subjects count (seven or nine is partially reproduced) and both medians and the range (5.5 to 16.5 Hz widened by 10% of each bound) hold.

claims.statement: The PLV during the last 2 s of maintenance exceeded the PLV during encoding in eight of nine subjects, so hippocampal-cortical connectivity in the theta-alpha range increased specifically during maintenance.
claims.source: Results, Cortico-hippocampal low-frequency coupling in the group of subjects, paragraph 2; Figure 6A to 6H; table S1
claims.quote: the PLV during maintenance exceeded the PLV during encoding in eight of nine subjects ( Fig. 6 and table S1)
claims.criterion: The pair of fig6-plv-all-subjects per subject. PLV in the last 2 s of maintenance minus PLV in encoding (-5 to -3 s), against the 95th percentile of 200 differences with epochs randomly assigned to the two periods (Methods). Open, which trials; readings (a) set size 8 trials, where the PLV was selected, (b) all set sizes pooled. A subject counts when a bin in the individual band is significant. Table S1 lists subject 4 as not significant. Reproduced when, under one reading, eight subjects count; partially reproduced for seven or nine.

claims.statement: In the majority of subjects, iEEG and EEG power in the individual frequency band did not differ during maintenance, which suggests that the PLV differences came from phase consistency.
claims.source: Results, Cortico-hippocampal low-frequency coupling in the group of subjects, paragraph 1; table S1
claims.quote: In the majority of the subjects, there were no differences in the iEEG or EEG power in the individual frequency band during maintenance, which suggests that the differences in PLV were primarily a result of the differences in phase consistency.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Table S1 reports it as workload dependence (set size 8 against 4) of EEG and of iEEG power, so that is the comparison: per subject, the channels of the maximal PLV pair, last 2 s of maintenance, multitaper spectra as in fig5-subject1-eeg-power-workload, cluster-based permutation test at P < 0.05 over the individual band. Reproduced when at least five of nine subjects show no significant difference for EEG and at least five for iEEG; not reproduced otherwise. Table S1 has two of nine with an EEG difference (subjects 1 and 9) and two with an iEEG difference (subjects 1 and 6); the per-subject results are reported against it.

claims.statement: Across subjects, maximal PLV increased from the anterior to the posterior end of the hippocampal axis (34 electrode pairs, R2 = 0.118), and PLV to posterior sites (y < -20 mm) was higher than to anterior sites.
claims.source: Figure 6I; Results, Cortico-hippocampal low-frequency coupling in the group of subjects, paragraph 3
claims.quote: For the subject group, there was a gradual increase in the PLV from the anterior end to the posterior end of the hippocampal axis during maintenance ( R 2 = 0.118, P = 0.0467) and the PLV to posterior sites ( y < −20 mm) was higher than to anterior sites (permutation t test, t = 2.09, P = 0.0405)
claims.criterion: Per subject, the scalp electrode of the maximal PLV pair, paired with every hippocampal bipolar channel; for each, the maximal PLV in the subject's individual band during maintenance, set size 8 (as in fig6-plv-all-subjects), plotted against the MNI y coordinate of the hippocampal contact (Fig. 6I). Open, the coordinate of a bipolar channel; readings (a) the deepest contact, (b) the midpoint of the two contacts. The fit's P from a permutation of PLV values over positions (2000 permutations; table S2 gives 32 degrees of freedom). Reproduced when, under one reading, there are 34 pairs, the slope is positive (PLV higher posteriorly) with P < 0.05 and R2 within tolerance, and posterior sites exceed anterior sites by an unpaired permutation t test at P < 0.05; partially reproduced when the direction and one of the two tests hold.

claims.statement: There was no evidence that the PLV differed between left and right hippocampus.
claims.source: Results, Cortico-hippocampal low-frequency coupling in the group of subjects, paragraph 3; Figure 6I
claims.quote: There was no evidence that the PLV differed between the left and right hippocampus.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper names no test here; Methods, Statistics, give the permutation t test for comparing two distributions, which is used: the 34 maximal PLV values of fig6i-plv-posterior-gradient, left against right channels, unpaired, P < 0.05. Reproduced when the test is not significant; not reproduced when it is. The difference of means is reported either way.

claims.statement: The increase in PLV did not differ significantly between hippocampal channels inside and outside the seizure onset zone.
claims.source: Results, Recordings in the epileptogenic zone, paragraph 1; table S1
claims.quote: When comparing hippocampal channels within and outside the seizure onset zone (SOZ) (table S1), the increase in the PLV was not significantly different between the non-SOZ electrodes and SOZ electrodes.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, with the permutation t test of Methods, Statistics, unpaired, P < 0.05. SOZ membership from the deposited SOZ electrode list (table S1 marks the maximal-PLV hippocampal channel as SOZ in subjects 3 and 4). Open, which increase; readings (a) set size 8 minus set size 4, (b) maintenance minus encoding, each the maximum in the individual band. Open, which channels; readings (a) all hippocampal channels paired with the maximal-PLV scalp electrode, as in Fig. 6I, (b) the nine maximal-PLV pairs. Reproduced when no reading finds a significant difference; not reproduced when a reading does. Effect sizes are reported for every reading.

claims.statement: The rates of clinically relevant high-frequency oscillations were not affected by performing the task.
claims.source: Results, Recordings in the epileptogenic zone, paragraph 1
claims.quote: The rates of clinically relevant HFOs were not affected by the performance of the task.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence for which the paper names neither the HFO detector nor the test nor the comparison. It cites reference 27 (Fedele et al. 2017, Sci Rep 7, 13836) for the detector; that paper is not under paper/ and was not read. The comparison is not given; the readings the text allows are (a) per-channel HFO rates in the task periods (encoding, maintenance) against fixation, (b) rates in trials of set size 8 against set size 4. The test is then the permutation t test of Methods, Statistics, at P < 0.05, the paper's general test for two distributions. Reproduced when no reading finds a significant difference in any channel group (SOZ, non-SOZ); not reproduced when one does. Without the detector of reference 27 (a question to a reader) the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Maintenance neurons showed significant spike-field coherence to the local field potential, but not to the iEEG or scalp EEG, and for all frequency bins the percentage of neurons with spike-field coherence was higher during maintenance than during encoding.
claims.source: Results, Spike-field coherence, paragraph 1; fig. S6b; Figure 5J
claims.quote: We found significant spike-field coherence to the LFP but not to the iEEG or the scalp EEG. For all frequency bins, the percentage of neurons with spike-field coherence was higher during maintenance than during encoding (fig. S6).
claims.criterion: Maintenance neurons of fig2b-maintenance-neurons-hippocampus with at least 100 spikes in both periods (fig. S6b legend gives N = 94). Pairwise phase consistency, the P-hat-2 estimator of Vinck et al. 2012 (FieldTrip ppc2), between each neuron's spikes and the LFP of the same microwire; maintenance is the last 2 s (fig. S6a), encoding -5 to -3 s. Significance per frequency bin against the 95th percentile of 200 PPCs with the spike trials permuted (Methods, Spike-field coherence). Open, the frequency range; readings (a) 4 to 30 Hz, (b) 1 to 40 Hz. Open, the spectral estimate around each spike; the reading is FieldTrip's spike-triggered spectrum with a window of a fixed number of cycles, and the cycle number is a further open detail, run at 3 and 5 cycles. Reproduced when, under one reading, the maintenance percentage exceeds the encoding percentage in every frequency bin and the percentages for iEEG and scalp EEG are no higher than the 5% expected by chance (the paper does not say how "not to the iEEG or the scalp EEG" was judged; this is the reading of its per-bin 95th percentile threshold); partially reproduced when the maintenance percentage is higher in most bins. The LFP of the microwires is not among the data listed by the data descriptor; if the dataset lacks it, the LFP parts are blocked and the iEEG and scalp EEG parts are run.

claims.statement: Performance was almost perfect at set sizes 1 (98% correct) and 2 (99%) and fell at 4 (88%) and 6 (73%), a significant effect of set size in a permuted repeated-measures ANOVA over 16 sessions; average performance was 89%.
claims.source: Results, 3.1 Task and behavior, paragraph 1; Figure 1b; Discussion 4.1, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The partici- pants showed almost perfect performance at set size of 1 (98% correct responses) and 2 (99 %), and a decrease at 4 (88%) and 6 (73%) ( Fig. 1 b, permuted repeated-measures ANOVA, F 3,45 = 89.79, p = .0002, 16 ses- sions)
claims.criterion: All trials of the 16 sessions. The paper does not say how percentages are pooled; readings (a) trials pooled over sessions and (b) the mean of per-session percentages. The ANOVA has set size as the within factor and session as the subject (F with 3 and 45 degrees of freedom, Results 3.1); its permutation scheme is not given, and the reading is set-size labels shuffled within each session, 4999 permutations (from p = .0002 as 1/(N+1), Methods 2.6). Reproduced when, under one reading, the five percentages and the F value are within tolerance, the order 1 and 2 above 4 above 6 holds, and the ANOVA has p < .05.

claims.statement: Across sessions the median working memory capacity was 3.2 by Pashler's K (range 2.2 to 5) and 3 by Cowan's K (range 1.9 to 4.5), so participants held at least 3 squares and set sizes 4 and 6 exceeded capacity.
claims.source: Results, 3.1 Task and behavior, paragraph 1; Figure 1b; Table 1
claims.quote: Across all sessions, the median memory capacity according to Pashler ( K P ) was 3.2 (range 2.2–5). According to Cowan's K ( K C ) me- dian memory capacity was 3 (range 1.9–4.5)
claims.criterion: Per session and set size, hit rate is the fraction of change trials answered "different" and false alarm rate the fraction of no-change trials answered "different" (the usual reading of the formulas in Methods 2.2, which do not define them). KP = (H - FA) N / (1 - FA) and KC = (H - FA) N; capacity is Kmax = max over set sizes of KP (Figure 1b legend). Open, the unit of the median. Readings (a) per participant, the mean over that participant's sessions as in Table 1 (13 values) and (b) per session (16 values); the text says "across all sessions", while the Table 1 values give 3.23 under (a). Open, how KC is reduced to one value; readings (i) max over set sizes, as for KP, and (ii) KC at set size 6. Reproduced when, under one reading, both medians are within tolerance and both ranges are inside the reported ranges widened by 10% of each bound.

claims.statement: Table 1 gives, per participant, the number of sessions, the memory capacity Kmax (2.41, 2.25, 3.04, 3.00, 2.87, 3.88, 3.00, 3.23, 3.58, 3.81, 5.00, 3.83, 4.50 for participants 1 to 13) and the number of neurons (33, 36, 106, 85, 29, 96, 48, 150, 23, 62, 11, 57, 73).
claims.source: Table 1
claims.criterion: Neurons counted per participant over all sessions. Kmax per session computed as in behavior-capacity (Kmax = max over set sizes of KP, Table 1 legend) and averaged over a participant's sessions (Methods 2.2). Reproduced when every neuron count and every Kmax value is within tolerance (for the three two-session participants the per-session values are also shown); partially reproduced when the neuron counts hold and some Kmax values do not.

claims.statement: Mean response time on correct trials (2678 trials) increased with set size, by 118 ms per item, a significant effect in a permuted repeated-measures ANOVA over 16 sessions.
claims.source: Results, 3.1 Task and behavior, paragraph 1; Figure 1c
claims.quote: The mean response time (RT) for the correct trials (2678 trials) increased with set size ( Fig. 1 c, 118 ms/item, permuted repeated-measures ANOVA, F 3,45 = 48.47; p = .0002, 16 sessions)
claims.criterion: Response time from test array onset (Figure 1c legend), correct trials. The ANOVA as in behavior-accuracy-by-set-size, on per-session values. Open, the per-session value; readings (a) mean RT (the text) and (b) median RT (Figure 1c). Open, how 118 ms/item is obtained; readings (i) the slope of a line fit of per-session values on set size, averaged over sessions, (ii) the slope of a line fit over all correct trials pooled, (iii) the slope of a line fit of the four set-size means. Reproduced when RT rises with set size, the ANOVA has p < .05, and under one reading the slope, the F value and the trial count are within tolerance.

claims.statement: 809 neurons were recorded, 454 in hippocampus, 209 in entorhinal cortex and 146 in amygdala, 50 plus or minus 25 (range 11 to 96) per session.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 Neuronal firing, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We recorded the ac- tivity of 809 neurons from the hippocampus (Hipp, n = 454), entorhi- nal cortex (Ent, n = 209), and amygdala (Amg, n = 146) across all microelectrodes. We recorded 50 ± 25 (range 11–96) neurons per ses- sion.
claims.criterion: Hippocampus is the hippocampal head and body sites (AH and PH, Table 1), entorhinal cortex EC and amygdala A. Reproduced when all values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Over all neurons, 0.79 plus or minus 1.54% of inter-spike intervals were shorter than 3 ms, most neurons were below 0.5%, and the peak signal-to-noise ratio of the mean waveform was 3.81 plus or minus 0.82.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 Neuronal firing, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Over all neu- rons, the percentage of inter-spike intervals (ISI) shorter than 3 ms was 0.79 ± 1.54%. The majority of neurons had short ISI percentages less than 0.5%. ... SNR waveform peak over all neurons was 3.81 ± 0.82.
claims.criterion: ISI percentage per neuron, mean and SD over neurons. Open, which spikes; readings (i) the whole recording and (ii) spikes within trials only (the paper does not say); "majority" means more than half of the neurons below 0.5%. SNR is the peak amplitude of the mean waveform over the standard deviation of the noise (Results 3.2); the noise is not defined. Readings (a) the standard deviation of the single-spike waveforms around their mean, averaged over samples, and (b) a noise level stored with the unit by the spike sorter, if the data hold one. Reproduced when, under one reading, the ISI values and the majority hold and the SNR values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the ISI values hold only.

claims.statement: The median (IQR) firing rate over all neurons was 1.09 (0.52 to 2.43) Hz over the trial, 1.12 (0.54 to 2.56) Hz during fixation, 1.10 (0.53 to 2.50) Hz during encoding, 1.09 (0.54 to 2.51) Hz during maintenance and 1.02 (0.49 to 2.45) Hz during test.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 Neuronal firing, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We identified the firing rate over all neurons as median (inter-quartile range, IQR) 1.09 (0.52–2.43) Hz throughout the trial du- ration. Median (IQR) firing rate over all neurons was 1.12 (0.54–2.56) Hz during fixation, 1.10 (0.53–2.50) Hz during encoding, 1.09 (0.54– 2.51) Hz for maintenance and 1.02 (0.49–2.45) Hz during test.
claims.criterion: Per neuron, the spike count in the period divided by its duration, averaged over trials; median and quartiles over the 809 neurons. Open, which trials; readings (a) correct trials (the paper's default for subsequent analyses) and (b) all trials, since this paragraph comes before that default is stated. Open, the extent of "throughout the trial"; readings (i) from fixation start to test array offset (fixation, encoding, maintenance and test periods joined) and (ii) from the warning signal to the end of the inter-trial interval. Reproduced when, under one reading, all five medians are within tolerance and their quartiles are within 10% of the printed ones.

claims.statement: Maintenance neurons, firing more during maintenance than during fixation, were found in all three regions, 55 of 454 in hippocampus, 21 of 209 in entorhinal cortex and 16 of 146 in amygdala, each a significant proportion.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 Neuronal firing, paragraph 4; Figure 2c
claims.quote: These maintenance neurons were defined by their higher firing rates during the maintenance period than during the fixation period ... Maintenance neurons were found in the hippocampus, the amygdala and the entorhinal cortex (per- mutation t-test, p < .05, Fig. 2 b, c).
claims.criterion: Correct trials. Per neuron, the firing rate in the maintenance period (0.9 s from memory array offset) against the fixation period (900 ms before memory array onset), permutation t-test (Methods 2.3, 2.6), p < .05 with a higher maintenance mean; readings (a) paired and (b) unpaired, as in the opening comment. Counts per region from Figure 2c. Significance of each region's count by the permutation test against scrambled labels (Figure 2c legend), period labels shuffled within trials, 499 repetitions. Reproduced when, under one reading, the three counts are within tolerance and each region's count has p < .05.

claims.statement: Among maintenance neurons, a significant number increased firing with workload in hippocampus (10 of 55, 18%) and entorhinal cortex (5 of 21, 24%), and a significant number decreased firing with workload in hippocampus (6 of 55, 11%); in entorhinal cortex 2 decreased and in amygdala 1 increased, not significant.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 Neuronal firing, paragraph 5; Figure 2d
claims.quote: we found a significant number of maintenance neurons that showed an increase in firing with workload in the hippocampus (10/55 = 18%, permutation test against scrambled labels, p = .002, Fig. 2 d) and entorhinal cortex (5/21 = 24%, permutation test against scrambled labels, p = .002). We also found a significant number of maintenance neurons that showed a decrease in firing rate with workload in the hippocampus (6/55 = 11%, permutation test against scrambled labels, p = .002).
claims.criterion: Within the maintenance neurons of fig2c-maintenance-neurons, correct trials, maintenance period firing of low workload (set sizes 1 and 2) against high workload (4 and 6) trials. The per-neuron test is not named; readings (a) the permutation t-test of Methods 2.6 on per-trial maintenance rates, unpaired, p < .05, direction from the sign of the difference, and (b) the cluster-based nonparametric permutation test over time used for the example neuron in Figure 2a, a neuron counting when a significant cluster falls in the maintenance period. Significance of each count by shuffling set-size labels across trials within the session, rerunning the per-neuron test, 499 repetitions. Reproduced when, under one reading, the three named counts are within tolerance and each has p < .05, and the entorhinal decrease and amygdala counts are not significant; partially reproduced when two of the three named counts hold with p < .05.

claims.statement: More hippocampal neurons were classified as maintenance neurons on correct trials than on incorrect trials (55 of 454, 12%, against 30 of 454, 7%).
claims.source: Results, 3.2 Neuronal firing, paragraph 6
claims.quote: There were more of these hippocam- pal neurons for correct trials vs incorrect trials (55/454 = 12% vs. 30/454 = 7%, permutation test against scrambled labels, p = .002).
claims.criterion: The maintenance neuron selection of fig2c-maintenance-neurons run separately on correct trials and on incorrect trials of each session. Open, whether trial numbers were equalized; readings (a) all correct and all incorrect trials (the count 55 equals the count of Figure 2c, which points to this reading) and (b) correct trials randomly subsampled to the number of incorrect trials in the session, count averaged over 100 subsamples (the paper does not mention equalizing; 100 is a standard choice). Significance by shuffling correct and incorrect labels across trials within each session and recounting the difference, 499 repetitions. Reproduced when, under one reading, both counts are within tolerance and the difference has p < .05; partially reproduced when the correct count exceeds the incorrect count with p < .05 but the counts are out of tolerance.

claims.statement: Test neurons, firing more after the test array than during encoding and maintenance, made up 46 of 809 neurons (6%), half the number of maintenance neurons, and were found in all regions (17 of 454 in hippocampus, 19 of 209 in entorhinal cortex, 10 of 146 in amygdala).
claims.source: Results, 3.2 Neuronal firing, paragraph 7; Figure 3b
claims.quote: These test neurons were defined based on increased firing only during the presentation of the test array relative to encoding and maintenance (permutation t-test, Fig. 3 a). With a rate of 46/809 = 6%, these were half the number of maintenance neurons ( Fig. 3 b).
claims.criterion: Correct trials, permutation t-test with a higher test-period mean at p < .05. The Methods and Results define the comparison differently; readings (a) test against maintenance only (Methods 2.3), (b) test against encoding and test against maintenance, both significant (Results 3.2), and (c) test against encoding and maintenance joined. The test period is the 2 s of the test array (Methods 2.2); paired and unpaired as in the opening comment. Significance of each region's count as in fig2c-maintenance-neurons. The Methods come first, so reading (a) is the main one; reproduced when, under (a), or under (b) or (c) if (a) fails, the four counts are within tolerance and each region has p < .05. Which readings match is reported.

claims.statement: Demixed PCA of the population separated set sizes 1, 2, 4 and 6; dPCs 2, 3 and 4 explained 36% of the variance (significant against scrambled labels), the separation appeared early in the trial, and the first 15 dPCs explained 81.4% of the variance.
claims.source: Results, 3.3 Neuronal population analysis, paragraph 1; Figure 4a
claims.quote: dPCA clearly distinguished between set sizes 1, 2, 4, and 6. For better visualization we formed a three-dimensional space from three demixed principal components (dPCs 2, 3 and 4, explaining 36% of the variance, permutation test against scrambled labels, p = .002, Fig. 4 a). ... we included the first 15 dPCs that explain 81.4% of the signal variance
claims.criterion: Method from Methods 2.4. All 809 neurons pooled across sessions, correct trials, trial-averaged rates per set size from 1 ms bins smoothed with a Gaussian kernel over a 1000 ms window, minus each neuron's mean fixation rate; dPCA (Kobak et al. 2016) with time and set-size marginalizations, components ordered by explained variance. Open and named readings. Kernel width; (a) a 1000-sample MATLAB gausswin window (SD 200 ms) and (b) a window of plus or minus 3 SD (SD 167 ms). Regularization; (c) none and (d) the toolbox's cross-validated lambda. Time span; fixation onset to test array offset. The p = .002 test is read as set-size labels shuffled across trials, dPCA refit, 499 repetitions, comparing the variance of dPCs 2 to 4. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, both variance values are within tolerance, the set-size variance exceeds the shuffled null at p < .05, and the four set-size trajectories are distinct during maintenance. The early separation and the 90 degree angles in the dPC3-dPC4 plane are shown and not judged (the paper gives no measure for either).

claims.statement: Multidimensional speed in the 15-dPC space was highest during encoding and lowest during maintenance, lower than in encoding and test.
claims.source: Results, 3.3 Neuronal population analysis, paragraph 1; Figure 4b
claims.quote: Multidimensional speed was highest during encoding, when maintenance neurons ramped up their firing. Speed was lowest during maintenance (permutation t-test against encoding and test periods, p = .0005).
claims.criterion: dPCA as in fig4a-dpca-separates-set-sizes, run 500 times, each on a 20% subsample with replacement of the neural firing rate trajectories (Methods 2.4). Open, what is subsampled; readings (a) neurons and (b) trials. Speed is the Euclidean norm of the time derivative of the trajectory in the first 15 dPCs, averaged over set sizes and over time in each period, one value per period per run (the paper does not define speed beyond "rate of change over time"; this combination over set sizes and time is a reading, not the paper's). Maintenance against encoding and against test by permutation t-test (Methods 2.6) on the 500 values per period. Reproduced when, under one reading, maintenance speed is below encoding and test with p < .05 for both, and encoding is the highest of the four periods. The figure shows fixation speed near maintenance speed; that comparison is not claimed.

claims.statement: The pairwise distance between set-size trajectories was larger during maintenance than during encoding, and the largest of all periods, consistent with attractors during maintenance.
claims.source: Results, 3.3 Neuronal population analysis, paragraph 1; Figure 4c
claims.quote: Analysing the pairwise distance between trajecto- ries that corresponded to different set sizes, we found that the distances during maintenance were larger than during encoding (permutation t- test, p = .0005, Fig. 4 c).
claims.criterion: The runs of fig4b-speed-lowest-in-maintenance. Distance is the Euclidean distance in the first 15 dPCs between the trajectories of each of the six pairs of set sizes, averaged over pairs and over time in each period (the averaging is a reading; the paper and the Figure 4c legend say only "pairwise distance between all possible pairs"). Reproduced when, under one reading, maintenance distance exceeds encoding distance with p < .05 by permutation t-test and is the largest of the four periods; partially reproduced when only the first holds. The comparison with test (starred in Figure 4c) is shown.

claims.statement: During maintenance, workload (set sizes 1 and 2 against 4 and 6) was decoded from all neurons pooled with median accuracy 87.5%, above chance; leaving out any one participant gave accuracies with IQR 85.7 to 87.6%.
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Decoding of information during the trial, paragraph 1; Figure 4d
claims.quote: For the maintenance periods, we found that the workload (set size 1, 2 vs. set sizes 4, 6) of each trial could be decoded with median decoding accuracy of 87.5% when all neurons were pooled ( Fig. 4 d, permuta- tion test against scrambled labels, p = .001). In a leave-one-out anal- ysis, the exclusion of any participant resulted in decoding accuracy in the IQR [85.7–87.6%]
claims.criterion: From Methods 2.5. Correct trials, labels low (1, 2) and high (4, 6) workload; per neuron, spike counts in a 1000 ms window (1 ms bins); pseudo-population of all neurons; SVM as in the NDT toolbox, trained and tested separately for each window, windows centred every 100 ms; 20 cross-validation splits, 500 resampling runs; accuracy is the median over runs; null from 1000 runs with shuffled labels; p Bonferroni-corrected for 4 groups (threshold .0125). Open and named readings. Which window is "maintenance"; (a) the window centred on the middle of the maintenance period (1.25 s after memory array onset, nearest 100 ms centres 1.2 and 1.3 s) and (b) the median over windows centred inside the maintenance period. Trials per label in the pseudo-population; the paper gives 145 to 169 training trials (95%), read as (c) the largest equal number per label available in every session and (d) the session's own trial count, with each session's neurons resampled to it. Features; (e) z-scored per neuron as in common NDT use and (f) raw counts. SVM kernel; linear (the NDT libsvm default; the paper says nothing). Leave-one-out repeats the analysis without each participant's neurons, 13 values. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the accuracy is within tolerance with p < .0125 and the leave-one-out quartiles are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Workload was decoded during maintenance from hippocampal neurons (75%) and entorhinal neurons (80%) but not from amygdala neurons.
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Decoding of information during the trial, paragraph 1; Figure 4d
claims.quote: When pooling neurons from the three anatomical re- gions separately, decoding accuracy was significant for the hippocam- pus (75%, Fig. 4 d column 3) and for the entorhinal cortex neurons (80%, Fig. 4 d column 5), but not for neurons in the amygdala.
claims.criterion: The decoder and readings of fig4d-decode-workload-all, on each region's neurons. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, hippocampus and entorhinal accuracies are within tolerance with p < .0125 and amygdala has p of .0125 or more (the paper's corrected threshold; the amygdala accuracy, near 62% in Figure 4d, is reported); partially reproduced when two of the three regions match.

claims.statement: Trial-wise performance (correct against incorrect) could not be decoded from MTL firing in any group (all 55%, hippocampus 55%, entorhinal 55%, amygdala 50%; p from .40 to .56).
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Decoding of information during the trial, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Decoding accuracy for the prediction of trial-wise performance (cor- rect vs. incorrect trials) was not significant (All MTL: 55%, p = .45, Hipp: 55%, p = .40, Ent: 55%, p = .44, Amg: 50%, p = .56). We could not decode performance with neural firing in the MTL.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. The decoder of fig4d-decode-workload-all with labels correct and incorrect, all set sizes, maintenance window, null from 1000 shuffled runs, Bonferroni over 4 groups. Open, how the few incorrect trials are balanced; the reading is equal trials per label set to the smallest number of incorrect trials in any session, all neurons kept. Reproduced when no group reaches p < .0125; not reproduced when any does. Accuracies are reported either way.

claims.statement: In amygdalae outside the SOZ, delta power (1-4 Hz) is lower during AVERSIVE than during NEUTRAL sequences, and the reduction lasts through the AVERSIVE sequence.
claims.source: Results 2.1, paragraph 1; Figure 1B
claims.quote: In nSOZ amygdalae, DELTA band power was consistently reduced throughout the duration of the AVERSIVE sequence (Fig. 1B)
claims.criterion: The iEEG power method of the opening comment (Methods 4.8 and 4.11), run under each reading listed there (z-scoring, amygdala set, cluster statistic, mixed model or the unpaired t-test variant). Reproduced when, under the mixed model, at least one cluster with AVERSIVE below NEUTRAL has permutation p < 0.05 and the AVERSIVE mean delta power is below the NEUTRAL mean over the 24 s block, under every reading of the open details; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. The Results say "throughout the duration" and Discussion 3.1 says the suppression "lasted for most of the AVERSIVE sequence"; no number is given in the main text (the abstract says "lasting up to 18 s"). "Most" is read as more than half of the 24 s block, and the claim is partially reproduced when the significant clusters cover less than half of it. The extent of the clusters is reported, and compared with the 18 s of the abstract.

claims.statement: High gamma power (above 60 Hz) is higher during AVERSIVE than during NEUTRAL sequences in the first 2 s of the sequence.
claims.source: Results 2.1, paragraph 1; Figure 1C
claims.quote: The HGP was enhanced in response to aversive stimuli during the first 2 s of the AVERSIVE sequence presentation (Fig. 1C, unpaired t-tests, corrected for multiple comparisons using random permutations, p < 0.05)
claims.criterion: As fig1b-delta-decrease, for HGP. Reproduced when a cluster with AVERSIVE above NEUTRAL with permutation p < 0.05 lies within, or begins within, the first 2 s after sequence onset, under every reading of the open details; the cluster's start and end are reported.

claims.statement: No AVERSIVE against NEUTRAL difference is found in the theta, alpha, beta and gamma (30-60 Hz) bands.
claims.source: Results 2.1, paragraph 1; bands in Methods 4.8
claims.quote: Since no effect was observed in the other spectral bands (see Methods 7.8), in the following we focus on DELTA power and HGP
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the mixed model with cluster-based permutation of Methods 4.11 (p < 0.05), run on theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-15 Hz), beta (15-30 Hz) and gamma (30-60 Hz) as in fig1b-delta-decrease. Reproduced when no band has a cluster with p < 0.05; not reproduced when any does; the cluster p-values and extents are reported. The "Methods 7.8" the Results cite is not in the text, so the test cannot be checked against it.

claims.statement: Across the 14 amygdalae, the DELTA modulation index and the HGP modulation index are negatively correlated.
claims.source: Results 2.1, paragraph 2; Figure 1D
claims.quote: MI and HGP-MI were negatively correlated across all amygdalae
claims.criterion: MI per amygdala as in table2-mi-values (Methods 4.11), each reading of the MI window. Reproduced when r is within tolerance and p < 0.05 under every reading; partially reproduced when r is negative with p < 0.05 but outside tolerance. The Spearman r of the printed Table 2 values is reported as well.

claims.statement: Among the 7 amygdalae outside the SOZ, the stronger the HGP enhancement (HGP MI), the stronger the reduction of DELTA power (more negative DELTA MI).
