claims.source: Results 2.1, paragraph 2; Table 2
claims.quote: Specifically for amygdalae not included in the SOZ, we observed that the stronger the HGP enhancement, the stronger the reduction in DELTA power (Table 2)
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test or number for this. Correlations are Spearman's (Methods 4.11), so the reading is the Spearman r between DELTA MI and HGP MI over the 7 nSOZ amygdalae of table2-mi-values (amygdalae 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12), under each reading of the MI window. Reproduced when r is negative under every reading; its p is reported, and so is the r of the printed Table 2 values.

claims.statement: The modulation indices of DELTA and HGP for each of the 14 amygdalae are as printed in Table 2.
claims.source: Table 2, columns Modulation index (MI) of iEEG, DELTA and HGP
claims.criterion: MI = AVERSIVE minus NEUTRAL time-averaged z-scored power envelope over the temporal clusters where the conditions differ significantly (Methods 4.11, Table 2 legend), with the preprocessing and the readings of the opening comment. Tolerance is 10% of each value, and 0.005 (half the last printed digit) where 10% is smaller, as the table rounds to two decimals. Reproduced when, under one reading, all 28 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the signs of all 28 agree; the number within tolerance is reported for every reading.

claims.statement: DELTA power is reduced (negative MI) in 12 of the 14 amygdalae, whether inside or outside the SOZ.
claims.source: Results 2.1, paragraph 3; Table 2
claims.quote: DELTA power was reduced in 12 of 14 amygdalae (negative MI in Table 2), irrespective of whether the amygdalae were within the SOZ or not
claims.criterion: Count of negative DELTA MI over the 14 amygdalae of table2-mi-values, under each reading of the MI window. Reproduced when the count is 11 to 13 (12 with 10%) under every reading and amygdalae with negative MI are found both inside and outside the SOZ.

claims.statement: All 7 amygdalae outside the SOZ have a positive HGP MI, while the response is absent in amygdalae within the SOZ (6 of 7 negative).
claims.source: Results 2.1, paragraph 3; Table 2 and its legend
claims.quote: All amygdalae outside SOZ showed a positive HGP-MI in response to AVERSIVE videos, while this response was absent in amygdalae within the SOZ (p 1⁄4 0.009)
claims.criterion: Counts from the HGP MI of table2-mi-values, under each reading of the MI window; counts of 7 amygdalae have no room for a 10% tolerance, so they must match. The test behind p = 0.009 is not named; readings are (a) Wilcoxon rank-sum of HGP MI, nSOZ against SOZ; (b) unpaired t-test of HGP MI (the test the Results name for Fig. 1C); (c) Fisher's exact or chi-square test of the counts of positive MI. Reproduced when both counts match and the difference has p < 0.05 under one of the readings; each reading's p is reported.

claims.statement: The HGP MI, but not the DELTA MI, distinguishes amygdalae within the SOZ from those outside it.
claims.source: Figure 1E legend
claims.quote: HGP but not DELTA distinguishes between amygdalae within SOZ and outside SOZ (p 1⁄4 0.019, not corrected)
claims.criterion: The legend names no test. Readings are (a) Wilcoxon rank-sum and (b) unpaired t-test, of the MI of table2-mi-values, nSOZ against SOZ, uncorrected, threshold p < 0.05 (Methods 4.11). Reproduced when, under a reading, HGP MI differs with p < 0.05 and DELTA MI does not; the DELTA part is a claim of absence judged on the same test. Not reproduced when HGP does not differ or DELTA does under every reading; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: HGP enhancement indicates amygdalar functional integrity (outside the SOZ) with sensitivity 7/7 (100%), specificity 6/7 (86%) and accuracy 13/14 (93%).
claims.source: Results 2.1, paragraph 3; Methods 4.11, paragraph 4
claims.quote: With sensitivity (7/7 1⁄4 100% CI [66–100]%), high specificity (6/7 1⁄4 86% CI [42 99]%) and accuracy 93% (13/14, CI [66–99]%), HGP enhancement indicated amygdalar functional integrity
claims.criterion: The effect is HGP enhancement, a positive HGP MI (Methods 4.11 define TP as the effect in a nSOZ amygdala, FP in a SOZ amygdala, FN its absence in nSOZ, TN its absence in SOZ). Methods 4.11 say the effect was "either HGP enhancement in the first 2 s or sustained delta decrease"; the Results apply it to HGP, which is followed here. Counts must match (no tolerance on counts of 7). The 95% confidence intervals used "the binomial distribution"; the exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval is the reading, and its bounds are reported beside the printed ones.

claims.statement: The HGP response is more specific than the DELTA response for indicating amygdalar dysfunction within the SOZ, by a chi-square test that is not significant (p about 0.2).
claims.source: Figure 1F legend
claims.quote: The HGP response exceeds the DELTA response in specificity when indicating the amygdala’s dysfunction within SOZ (p~0.2 HGP 5/5 DELTA 1/5, chi2-test)
claims.criterion: The paper does not say which amygdalae form the printed counts 5/5 and 1/5, and no subset of Table 2 is named that gives them. Readings are (a) the specificity counts as in Methods 4.11 over the 7 SOZ amygdalae, HGP effect absent (HGP MI not positive) against DELTA effect absent (DELTA MI not negative), compared with a chi-square test of the 2 by 2 table; (b) the printed counts 5/5 against 1/5 in a chi-square test. Reproduced when HGP specificity exceeds DELTA specificity under reading (a); the chi-square p of both readings is reported against the printed p about 0.2. Blocked as methods_underspecified if the readings disagree on which is more specific.

claims.statement: In the left amygdala of Participant 4, the BOLD time course is negatively correlated with DELTA power and positively correlated with HGP over the video sequence.
claims.source: Results 2.2, paragraph 2; Figure 2A and 2C; Table 2, amygdala 6
claims.quote: BOLD response and DELTA power were negatively correlated during presentation of video sequence (correlation of BOLDDELTA time-courses r 1⁄4 �0.48 p < 0.01), while BOLD and HGP were positively correlated (correlation BOLD-HGP Spearman’s r 1⁄4 0.41 p < 0.01)
claims.criterion: Methods 4.10. The iEEG power envelope (Methods 4.8) is smoothed, down-sampled to the 1.5 s BOLD time points and smoothed over 5 time points (7.5 s), then correlated (Spearman) with the BOLD time course of the amygdala VOI over the video sequence. The BOLD time course is outside data, the clinical fMRI of the patient (Methods 4.6), for which the paper names no deposit. The smoothing before down-sampling and the 5-point window shape are not given; the 1 s smoothing of Methods 4.8 and a boxcar are used, standard choices. Whether the iEEG and BOLD time courses are aligned at sequence onset with no lag is not stated beyond the smoothing that "takes into account the time-lag"; no lag is the reading. Methods 4.10 say the correlation is made "at the single trial level"; whether that is one correlation over the whole sequence of single trials or one per trial, averaged, is not stated. Readings are (i) the whole video sequence, (ii) per trial and averaged. Reproduced when both r are within tolerance with p < 0.01 after FDR under one reading.

claims.statement: Across amygdalae with BOLD, DELTA power and BOLD are negatively correlated in 4 of 5 nSOZ amygdalae, while HGP and BOLD are positively correlated in 3 of 5 nSOZ and 1 of 4 SOZ amygdalae.
claims.source: Results 2.2, paragraph 3; Table 2; Figure 2C
claims.quote: DELTA power and BOLD responses showed a negative correlation in 4/5 nSOZ amygdalae, while the correlation of HGP and BOLD was positive in the 3/5 the nSOZ amygdalae and 1/4 SOZ amygdalae (Table 2, Fig. 2C)
claims.criterion: The correlation of fig2-participant4-bold-correlations, for each of the 9 amygdalae with BOLD in Table 2 (patients 1 R, 2 L, 2 R, 3 L, 4 L, 7 L, 7 R, 8 L, 9 R), p-values FDR corrected across them (Table 2 legend; the family is not given, readings (a) the 9 tests of one band, (b) all 18 tests). Counts of 5 or fewer must match. The Table 2 legend states 5/5 positive BOLD-HGP correlations, which the table's own values do not support; the Results' 3/5 and 1/4 are the claim.

claims.statement: The Spearman correlations of BOLD with DELTA power and with HGP for each of the 9 amygdalae with BOLD are as printed in Table 2.
claims.source: Table 2, columns Correlation BOLD vs. DELTA and BOLD vs. HGP, r
claims.criterion: The correlation of fig2-participant4-bold-correlations for each amygdala, under each of its readings. Tolerance is 10% of each value, and 0.005 (half the last printed digit) where 10% is smaller. Reproduced when, under one reading, all 18 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the signs of all 18 agree; the number within tolerance is reported for every reading. The printed p-values (FDR corrected) are reported beside the computed ones.

claims.statement: The two nSOZ amygdalae without a significant HGP-BOLD correlation have a very low HGP MI.
claims.source: Results 2.2, paragraph 3; Table 2 (amygdalae 10 and 12)
claims.quote: the two nSOZ amygdalae that did not show a significant correlation between HGB and BOLD, had a remarkably low MI for HGP (MI < 0.05, Table 2)
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the nSOZ amygdalae without a significant positive HGP-BOLD correlation in table2-bold-correlations-group are the two with the lowest HGP MI among the 5 nSOZ amygdalae with BOLD, both MI at most 0.055 (Table 2 prints 0.04 and 0.05, so "MI < 0.05" is read as below 0.05 within the rounding of the table, with the 10% tolerance).

claims.statement: Spike sorting gave 50 putative neuron clusters from 9 amygdalae, of which 41 had a firing rate above 1 Hz and were analysed.
claims.source: Results 2.3, paragraph 1; Methods 4.9
claims.quote: We identified 50 putative clusters of neurons (Niediek et al., 2016) from 9 amygdalae and included those with firing rate >1 Hz (N 1⁄4 41 neurons) in further analysis
claims.criterion: Mean firing rate over the recording (the whole task) above 1 Hz. The paper does not give the interval over which the 1 Hz rate is taken; readings (a) all trials, (b) the whole recording, as the dataset allows. Table 1 lists clusters in 8 amygdalae of 6 patients and the abstract says 5 participants; the number of amygdalae and patients with units is reported against all three. The dataset may hold only the clusters above 1 Hz (the data descriptor applies the same 1 Hz rule), in which case 50 cannot be tested.

claims.statement: All 41 neurons fire more during AVERSIVE than during NEUTRAL sequences (FRV 0.26 plus or minus 0.15).
claims.source: Results 2.3, paragraph 2; Figure 3A
claims.quote: All 41 clusters of neurons increased their firing rate during the AVERSIVE condition (Firing Rate Variation, FRV 1⁄4 0.26 �0.15)
claims.criterion: FRV per neuron is the AVERSIVE minus NEUTRAL mean firing rate over the whole time interval of firing (Methods 4.11), under readings (a) the 24 s blocks, (b) the 26 s trials. Tolerance is the stated spread (0.15). Reproduced when every neuron has FRV > 0 and the mean is within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when the mean is within tolerance and most neurons have FRV > 0. "FRV" is called Firing Rate Variation here and Firing Rate Variability in Methods 4.11; it is the same measure.

claims.statement: The neurons' firing rose gradually and stayed enhanced throughout the AVERSIVE sequences, not as an immediate response at onset.
claims.source: Results 2.3, paragraph 2; Figure 3A
claims.quote: Contrary to our expectation of an immediate spiking onset, the neurons increased their firing gradually and sustained enhanced firing throughout the AVERSIVE video sequences
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure or test for this. Population AVERSIVE minus NEUTRAL firing rate across the 41 neurons, time-locked to sequence onset, in 100 ms bins smoothed over 1 s (Fig. 3A legend). The test is open; readings are (a) the difference averaged over the first 2 s is smaller than over 2 to 24 s (gradual), with the difference positive in each of the twelve 2 s bins of the block (sustained); (b) the time of the difference's first peak is later than 2 s and the difference stays positive to 24 s. Reproduced when both readings agree it holds, not reproduced when both agree it does not, blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise. The curve is shown either way.

claims.statement: Across neurons, the correlation of firing rate with macro-electrode HGP does not differ between the AVERSIVE and NEUTRAL conditions.
claims.source: Results 2.3, paragraph 3; Figure 3B, lower boxplot
claims.quote: Across all neurons, the covariation of neuronal firing with HGP was not significantly different between the two experimental conditions (Spearman’s r 1⁄4 0.17 ... �0.28 in AVERSIVE, 0.18 �0.18 in NEUTRAL; Wilcoxon paired test, p > 0.05)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test of per-neuron Spearman r (AVERSIVE against NEUTRAL) at p < 0.05. HGP is the bipolar macro channel of the neuron's amygdala (Methods 4.8 envelope). Open time base, readings (a) 100 ms bins smoothed over 1 s (Fig. 3A legend), (b) 1.5 s with 5-point smoothing (Methods 4.10), (c) 15 s smoothing (Fig. 3D legend); and (i) concatenated blocks of the condition, (ii) per block and averaged. Reproduced when the test finds no difference, not reproduced when it does; the effect size is reported for every reading. Tolerances on the means are the stated spreads.

claims.statement: Across neurons, the correlation of firing rate with microwire high gamma power (muHGP) is higher in the AVERSIVE than in the NEUTRAL condition.
claims.source: Results 2.3, paragraph 3; Figure 3B, upper boxplot
claims.quote: the covariation of neuronal firing with μHGP was higher during AVERSIVE than during NEUTRAL conditions (Spearman’s r 1⁄4 0.51 �0.18 during AVERSIVE, 0.43 �0.16 during NEUTRAL; Wilcoxon paired test, p < 0.01)
claims.criterion: As fig3b-firing-hgp-no-condition-difference, with HGP from the microwire signal of the neuron's own microwire (the paper says muHGP is recorded "locally at the level of the microwires"; which microwire, the neuron's own or a neighbour, is not stated, reading (a) its own, (b) the mean over the bundle). The paper does not give the microwire LFP filtering; the high gamma method of Methods 4.8 is the reading. Needs the continuous microwire signals. Reproduced when the Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives p < 0.01 with AVERSIVE higher under every reading, and the means are within the stated spreads.

claims.statement: Across neurons, the spatial synchronization index (SSI) is strongly positively correlated with the firing rate variability (FRV).
claims.source: Results 2.3, paragraph 4; Figure 3C; Figure 4A
claims.quote: We found a strong positive correlation across all participants between the SSI and FRV (Spearman’s r 1⁄4 0.78, p < 1e-7)
claims.criterion: SSI per neuron is the mean Spearman correlation of its firing rate with each neuron of the same amygdala on a different microwire (Methods 4.11, Fig. 3C legend); FRV as in fig3a-firing-increase-aversive. The firing rate time base and the span (whole session) are open, readings (a) 100 ms bins smoothed over 1 s, (b) 15 s smoothing, over the whole session. Reproduced when r is within tolerance and p < 1e-7 under one reading, and r > 0 with p < 0.05 under every reading; partially reproduced when r > 0 with p < 0.05 under every reading but no reading gives the value.

claims.statement: Across neurons, the ongoing firing rate correlates positively with muHGP (0.27), HGP (0.19) and BOLD (0.23), and the correlation is lowest with HGP.
claims.source: Results 2.3, paragraph 5; Figure 3D and its inset
claims.quote: Across all neurons and participants, the ongoing firing rate positively correlated with μHGP (Spearman’s r 1⁄4 0.27 �0.15), HGP (Spearman’s r 1⁄4 0.19 � 0.17) and BOLD (Spearman’s r 1⁄4 0.23 �0.20) ... Across all recording modalities, the correlation of the firing rate and other measures was lowest with HGP (Wilcoxon’s paired test, p < 1e-2)
claims.criterion: Per neuron, Spearman r of the firing rate with each measure over the video sequence, 15 s smoothing (Fig. 3D legend) as reading (a), the Methods 4.10 time base (1.5 s, 5 points) as reading (b). The HGP part uses the dataset alone and is judged by itself; muHGP needs the microwire signals and BOLD the outside fMRI data. "Lowest with HGP" is read as two Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, HGP against muHGP and HGP against BOLD, each p < 0.01. Reproduced when the three means are within their stated spreads and both tests hold; partially reproduced when only the parts testable on the data available hold, which the notes say.

claims.statement: The per-neuron correlation of firing rate with HGP is described by both FRV and SSI in a multiple linear regression.
claims.source: Results 2.4, paragraph 1; Figure 4B
claims.quote: We found that the co-modulation between neuronal firing and HGP is described by both FVR and SSI (Fig. 4B, r 1⁄4 0.59, p < 1e-4)
claims.criterion: Dependent variable the per-neuron Spearman r of firing rate with HGP (as in fig3d-firing-correlations-modalities), independent variables FRV and SSI (Methods 4.11). The paper does not say what r is; readings (a) the multiple correlation R of the least-squares fit, (b) Spearman r of fitted against observed values. "Described by both" is read as both coefficients with p < 0.05; the paper gives no signs, so the signs are reported. Reproduced when the model p < 1e-4, r is within tolerance under one reading, and both coefficients hold.

claims.statement: The per-neuron correlation of firing rate with BOLD is described by FRV but not by SSI.
claims.source: Results 2.4, paragraph 1; Figure 4C
claims.quote: while the co-modulation between neuronal firing and BOLD is described by FRV (Fig. 4C, Spearman’s r 1⁄4 0.69, p < 1e-4), but not SSI
claims.criterion: As fig4b-regression-firing-hgp, dependent variable the per-neuron Spearman r of firing rate with BOLD. Reproduced when the model p < 1e-4, r is within tolerance under a reading, the FRV coefficient has p < 0.05 and the SSI coefficient p >= 0.05 (the absence judged at the paper's threshold, p < 0.05, Methods 4.11).

claims.statement: Across neurons, the correlation of firing with HGP is positively correlated with the correlation of firing with BOLD.
claims.source: Results 2.4, paragraph 2; Figure 4D
claims.quote: Fig. 4D displays the covariation of neuronal firing with BOLD (x-axis) and HGP (y-axis) (Spearman’s r 1⁄4 0.72, p < 1e-3)
claims.criterion: Per-neuron correlations of fig3d-firing-correlations-modalities, under each of its readings. Reproduced when r is within tolerance and p < 1e-3 under one reading and r > 0 with p < 0.05 under every reading.

claims.statement: The neural analyses use 93,881 layer 2/3 neurons from 141 sessions of 8 mice, parcellated into V1 (14,373), PM (9,564), AM (14,974), MM (9,885), RSC (23,036) and A (22,049).
claims.source: Results, Calcium imaging of neural activity across posterior cortex, paragraph 1; STAR Methods, Area parcellation
claims.quote: assigned coordinates to 93,881 layer 2/3 neurons imaged from 141 sessions of 8 mice ... we obtained 14,373 neurons in V1, 9,564 neurons in PM, 14,974 neurons in AM, 9,885 neurons in MM, 23,036 neurons in RSC, and 22,049 neurons in area A
claims.criterion: Counted over layer 2/3 cell-body sources in sessions above 65% correct (STAR Methods, Classification of the sources), with area labels from the paper's parcellation (STAR Methods, Area parcellation). The number of mice is exact (tolerance 0, a count of subjects); the others take the default 10%. If the dataset gives no area labels the area counts are untestable and the claim is judged on the totals.

claims.statement: Performance is high before a rule switch, typically falls below chance after it, and recovers gradually to high accuracy by the end of the block.
claims.source: Results, Mice learned flexible cue-choice associations, paragraph 2; Figure 1D; Figure S1B
claims.quote: Their behavioral performance was high before rule switches and typically dropped below chance after switches before gradually recovering to high accuracy by the end of a block, without signs of anticipating rule switches
claims.criterion: From the STAR Methods, Task performance analysis, on sessions with overall fraction correct above 0.5 and visually guided trials excluded. Each block's outcomes are fit with the sigmoid of the Methods (reward rate as L over one plus exp of minus (t - t0) over k, plus b) by minimizing cross-entropy; initial and end performance are the fitted values at the first and last trial. The parameter constraints are not given; a standard choice (L and b keeping the rate within 0 to 1, k positive) is used, which should not change the outcome. Reproduced when, over switches (hierarchical bootstrap, mice then switches), the mean fitted initial performance after a switch is below 0.5 and the mean fitted end performance is above 0.7 (the Methods' bound for a recovered switch) and above the initial performance (two-tailed p < 0.05). Partially reproduced when the fall and recovery hold but the initial value is not below 0.5.

claims.statement: The strategy LSTM predicts the mouse's choices in held-out sessions with 80.2% ± 5.1% accuracy (mean ± SD).
claims.source: Results, Decision-making strategy varied, paragraph 1; STAR Methods, LSTM model
claims.quote: The LSTM accurately predicted a mouse's choices in held-out sessions (80.2% ± 5.1%, mean ± SD)
claims.criterion: The LSTM of the STAR Methods (16 units, leave-one-session-out per mouse), with its stated hyperparameters. How accuracy is scored is not said; the standard reading is used, a choice predicted correct when the model's probability for the actual cue gives more than 0.5 to the actual choice. The tolerance is the reported SD, the paper's stated spread. Open, with readings run in turn. (a) The SD is over sessions or (b) over mice; (c) sessions are all behavioral sessions or (d) those above 0.65 correct, which the Methods use for the later analyses. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance under any reading.

claims.statement: The LSTM predicts choices better (higher log likelihood) than the best reinforcement learning model (model 4, separate learning rates for rewarded and unrewarded trials).
claims.source: Figure S1H
claims.quote: Log likelihood of the LSTM was greater than the RL model (p = 5.95 × 10-22, Wilcoxon signed rank test)
claims.criterion: Session-averaged held-out log likelihood (log base 2) of the LSTM and of RL model 4 of the STAR Methods (Q learning with decay, separate learning rates for rewarded and unrewarded trials, choice perseverance, bias and lapse), both leave-one-session-out per mouse, on the 216 sessions. Reproduced when the LSTM is higher with a Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.05. The form of the lapse term is garbled in the text; the standard mixture (one minus lambda times the softmax plus lambda over two) is used.

claims.statement: Before a switch mice show little choice bias and follow the rule; after a switch the probability of the actual choice falls near chance, bias-following rises moderately, and rule-following then recovers gradually.
claims.source: Results, Decision-making strategy varied, paragraph 2; Figure 1I
claims.quote: On average, prior to a rule switch, mice performed with little choice bias and followed the correct rule ... After a rule switch, the randomness of choices increased rapidly, as seen by near chance levels of the model's probability of the actual choice, and bias-following increased moderately. Then, rule-following recovered gradually for the new rule belief
claims.criterion: Strategy variables from the LSTM (shared method), aligned to switches, on the 265 switches of Figure 1I (switches with end performance above 70%, sessions above 0.65 correct). The windows are not given; the readings are the 10 and the 20 trials before and after the switch (20 is the window the Methods use for trajectory correlation). Reproduced when, under every reading, (1) rule-following before the switch is above zero, (2) probability of actual choice in the first window after the switch is lower than before and within 0.1 of 0.5 at its minimum, (3) bias-following after is higher than before, and (4) rule-following after the first window rises toward its pre-switch level by the end of the block; each comparison by hierarchical bootstrap (mice then switches), two-tailed p < 0.05. The 0.1 margin for near chance is a choice of this file, as the paper gives none; the value is reported.

claims.statement: Visually guided trials do not update rule belief more than normal trials in the 30 trials after a switch (0.013 ± 0.0055 against 0.0080 ± 0.0023; p = 0.34).
claims.source: STAR Methods, Decision-making strategy variables, last paragraph
claims.quote: The rule update per trial was 0.013 ± 0.0055 for visually guided trials and 0.0080 ± 0.0023 for normal trials (difference = 0.0052 ± 0.0057, p = 0.34, hierarchical bootstrap mean ± SEM, n = 265 switches)
claims.criterion: Delta rule belief per trial toward the current rule (signed so that positive is toward the new rule), averaged over the 30 trials after each switch, compared by hierarchical bootstrap (mice then switches), two-tailed. A claim of absence. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, as the paper's test found; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The difference is reported either way. Tolerances are the reported SEMs.

claims.statement: Inhibiting RSC or PPC lowers task performance compared with control trials and with S1 inhibition; the RSC against PPC difference is not significant (p = 0.058).
claims.source: Results, Photoinhibition of posterior cortical areas, paragraph 1; Figure 1L
claims.quote: Inhibiting either RSC or PPC led to markedly lower task performance compared to control trials or trials in which part of primary somatosensory cortex (S1) was inhibited
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Analysis of photoinhibition experiments. Fraction correct on target trials against control trials within session, by the modified hierarchical bootstrap (10,000 samples of session means, mice then sessions, averaged within mouse then across mice). Reproduced when RSC and PPC are each below control and below S1 with two-tailed p < 0.05. The RSC against PPC difference is reported.

claims.statement: Inhibition of PPC and RSC decreases rule-following compared with control trials and with S1 inhibition; bias-following increases, strongly in a subset of mice.
claims.source: Results, Photoinhibition of posterior cortical areas, paragraph 2; Figure 1M; Figure S1K
claims.quote: PPC and RSC inhibition decreased rule-following compared to control trials and S1 inhibition
claims.criterion: The strategy LSTM with one input per inhibition target (STAR Methods, LSTM model), target trials against control trials within session by the modified hierarchical bootstrap of the photoinhibition Methods. Reproduced when rule-following is lower than control for RSC and PPC and lower than for S1, each with two-tailed p < 0.05. Bias-following changes are reported, with the number of mice whose increase exceeds 0.2 (the paper finds 3 for RSC and 1 for PPC).

claims.statement: Across sessions, the change in rule-following under RSC or PPC inhibition is not correlated with the change in bias-following.
claims.source: Figure S1M
claims.quote: Pearson correlation 0.18 (p = 0.10 vs. zero) for RSC and -0.03 (p = 0.74) for PPC
claims.criterion: Per session, target minus control for rule-following and for bias-following; the Pearson correlation across sessions tested against zero. A claim of absence. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 for both RSC and PPC; not reproduced when either is p < 0.05. The r values are reported.

claims.statement: Running trajectories of choice-matched trials become less correlated with one another after a rule switch.
claims.source: Results, Running trajectories reflected the within-trial dynamics, paragraph 1; Figure 2C
claims.quote: This variability in running trajectories increased following a rule switch
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Running trajectory correlation analysis. Velocities binned on a grid of maze positions, Pearson correlation of each pair of choice-matched trials averaged over the three velocities, each trial's mean against the session's mean over all choice-matched pairs, aligned to switches; mean over the 20 trials before against the 20 trials after. The position grid is not given; the readings are 20 and 11 equal bins of the maze (the counts the paper uses for its position bases and decoders). Reproduced when, under both, Delta trajectory correlation is lower after than before with a hierarchical bootstrap (mice then switches, 10,000 samples) two-tailed p < 0.05; the paper reports no test, and this is its default.

claims.statement: Dynamic choice crosses threshold sooner on trials with higher rule-following or bias-following.
claims.source: Results, Running trajectories reflected the within-trial dynamics, paragraph 3; Figure 2F
claims.quote: As expected, the latency to dynamic choice crossing a threshold was shorter on trials with higher rule- or bias-following
claims.criterion: Latency is the time from trial onset at which dynamic choice reaches 0.9 on left trials or 0.1 on right trials, divided by the session's mean trial duration (STAR Methods, Modeling of dynamic choice); n = 85,463 trials in the paper. The strategy bins of the figure are not given in the text; the readings are 5 and 10 quantile bins of each strategy variable, and the Spearman correlation over trials. Reproduced when latency falls with rule-following and with bias-following under every reading (Spearman rho below zero, and the highest bin shorter than the lowest by hierarchical bootstrap, mice then trials, two-tailed p < 0.05). The duration tolerance is the reported SD.

claims.statement: With high rule-following, choice commitment starts near chance and rises during the maze; with low rule-following it stays low until late; with high bias-following it is high from trial onset.
claims.source: Results, Running trajectories reflected the within-trial dynamics, paragraph 3; Figure 2G; Figure S2L
claims.quote: On trials with high rule-following, choice commitment started near chance but increased rapidly during maze traversal ... when rule-following was low, choice commitment was low until late in the trial ... when mice followed a bias, choice commitment was high at trial onset
claims.criterion: Choice commitment is the log likelihood (base 2) of the reported choice under dynamic choice at each position (STAR Methods, Modeling of dynamic choice). Tested as in Figure S2L (its Methods are in the legend). Per session, choice commitment at each maze position bin is regressed on rule-following, bias-following and local reward rate (fraction correct over the adjacent 9 trials); coefficients are averaged by hierarchical bootstrap over 216 sessions. Reproduced when the bias-following coefficient is above zero in the first position bin and the rule-following coefficient is near zero there (two-tailed p >= 0.05 against zero, or smaller than a tenth of the bias coefficient; the paper says only "near zero", and the tenth is a bound this file sets), and the rule-following coefficient in the last stem bin is above zero and above its first-bin value (p < 0.05). The number of position bins is not given; 11 equal bins (the paper's decoder bins) and 20 are both run.

claims.statement: Cue-biased running varies across mice and sessions and is not correlated with task performance or with the time course of dynamic choice.
claims.source: Results, Running trajectories reflected the within-trial dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure S2H, S2I, S2K
claims.quote: this behavior was variable across mice and sessions and was uncorrelated with task performance and the time course of dynamic choice
claims.criterion: Strength of cue-biased running is the session-averaged log likelihood of the cue under cue-biased running (STAR Methods, Modeling of dynamic choice). The paper reports no test; Figure S2I shows per-mouse regression lines. A claim of absence, with the readings (a) Pearson correlation of session cue decoding against session fraction correct, pooled over sessions, and (b) the per-mouse regression slopes tested against zero across mice. Reproduced when neither finds a correlation at p < 0.05; mixed results are reported as such. The sign of the roll-velocity coefficient of the logistic cue decoder (first 25% of the stem, 10-fold) is reported per session to show the variation of Figure S2K. The part on the time course of dynamic choice is shown only in Figure S2G (choice decoding over the maze in 7 quantile bins of cue decoding strength, 216 sessions), with no test or measure; those curves are reported and that part is not judged.

claims.statement: The GLM explains a fraction 0.25 ± 0.17 (mean ± SD) of the Poisson deviance of single neurons on held-out test data.
claims.source: Results, Calcium imaging of neural activity, paragraph 2; Figure 3I; Figure S3E
claims.quote: The GLM explained a substantial amount of moment-to-moment variability in a neuron's activity (fraction of Poisson deviance explained: 0.25 ± 0.17, mean ± SD
claims.criterion: GLM as in the opening comment, over the 93,881 neurons, test data (20% of trials). The tolerances are 10%. The SD is the spread over neurons, not the uncertainty of the mean, so it is not used as the mean's tolerance.

claims.statement: 42,998 neurons have test fraction deviance explained above 0.2 (V1 7,775, PM 4,934, AM 6,878, MM 3,991, RSC 10,329, A 9,091); 68,532 pass a threshold of 0.1.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Generalized Linear Models, Fitting procedure; Figure S3D
claims.quote: 42,998 neurons were selected, including 7,775 neurons in V1, 4,934 neurons in PM, 6,878 neurons in AM, 3,991 neurons in MM, 10,329 neurons in RSC, and 9,091 neurons in area A
claims.criterion: Counted from the GLM fits of fig3i-glm-fit, under both lambda readings and both orders of the drift exclusion (opening comment).

claims.statement: Fraction explained deviance on the CV held-out data differs very little from that on the test data (0.0010 ± 0.0006, mean ± SEM), so encoding measured on CV held-out data is not inflated by overfitting.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Quantification of fraction explained deviance (without re-fitting); Figure S3E
claims.quote: We confirmed that the difference in the fraction explained deviance evaluated on the CV held-out data and test data was sufficiently small (0.0010 ± 0.0006, mean ± SEM
claims.criterion: Mean over neurons of the CV held-out minus the test fraction deviance explained; SEM over neurons. The tolerance is the reported SEM. Which neurons enter (all 93,881 or the 42,998 well-fit) is not said; both are reported, and the claim is reproduced when either is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Area A has higher encoding of instantaneous movement and lower encoding of task variables than every other area, and V1 has higher task-variable encoding than every other area.
claims.source: Results, Distinct encoding gradients, paragraph 1; Figure 3M
claims.quote: the encoding of task variables exhibited an anterior-posterior gradient with highest strength in V1, intermediate in RSC, and lowest in area A, whereas movement encoding strength exhibited a gradient in the opposite direction
claims.criterion: Encoding strength (opening comment) of the group of all movement variables and the group of all task variables over the whole trial, per well-fit neuron, averaged per area by hierarchical bootstrap (mice then neurons, 1,000 samples). Reproduced when A is above every other area for movement and below every other area for task variables, and V1 above every other area for task variables, each with two-tailed p < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg over the area pairs. Partially reproduced when the ordering holds but some pair is not significant. The same test at the 0.1 fit threshold (Figure S8K) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Cue encoding during stem traversal is strongest in V1 (higher than every other area), strong in AM and PM, weaker in RSC and weakest in A (lower than every other area).
claims.source: Results, Distinct encoding gradients, paragraph 2; Figure 3O; Figure S4K
claims.quote: Encoding of the visual cue identity was strongest in V1 and neighboring areas AM and PM, weaker in RSC, and weakest in area A
claims.criterion: Encoding strength of cue in the stem epoch per well-fit neuron, area means by hierarchical bootstrap. Reproduced when V1 is above and A below every other area (two-tailed p < 0.05, Benjamini-Hochberg over pairs), and the means of AM and PM exceed that of RSC.

claims.statement: Cue decoded from populations of about 100 nearby neurons follows the same gradient as single-neuron cue encoding.
claims.source: Results, Distinct encoding gradients, paragraph 2; Figure 3Q
claims.quote: which was corroborated with decoding of these variables from the activity of ~100 simultaneously recorded neurons
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Trial phase-specific logistic decoders. Simultaneously imaged neurons split into spatially adjacent, non-overlapping groups of about 100 (all layer 2/3 neurons, no fit selection), PCA to 90% variance, logistic regression with elastic net (10% L1) in 11 position bins with 5-fold CV, performance as log likelihood (base 2); 974 decoders in the paper. How the elastic net strength is chosen is not said; the readings are the lambda of minimum CV deviance and the one-SE lambda (the two that MATLAB lassoglm returns). How groups of about 100 are formed is not said; the readings are k-means on neuron positions with k equal to the session's neurons over 100, and a grid of equal-count tiles. Which of the 11 position bins enter a decoder's value in Figure 3Q is not said; the readings are the bins in the stem and all 11 bins. Reproduced when, under every reading, the decoder means per area (by centroid) rank V1 highest and A lowest, with V1 above A at two-tailed p < 0.05 (hierarchical bootstrap, mice then decoders).

claims.statement: Encoding of decision-making strategy variables, with their interactions, is moderate and does not differ between areas, except AM against A.
claims.source: Results, Distinct encoding gradients, paragraph 3; Figure 3R; Figure S4L
claims.quote: Variables related to the decision-making strategy, including their interactions with other task variables, collectively exhibited a moderate encoding strength distributed evenly across posterior cortex
claims.criterion: Encoding strength of the group of all strategy variables and their interactions over the full trial, area means by hierarchical bootstrap, two-tailed tests for the 15 area pairs with Benjamini-Hochberg at FDR 0.05, as the legend states. A claim of absence for 14 pairs. Reproduced when no pair other than AM against A is significant after correction; not reproduced when any other pair is. The AM against A result and all differences are reported.

claims.statement: The previous trial's outcome is encoded much more strongly than its cue or choice, and evenly over space.
claims.source: Results, Distinct encoding gradients, paragraph 3; Figure S4P to S4S
claims.quote: The previous trial's outcome was much more strongly encoded than the previous trial's cue or choice
claims.criterion: Encoding strength of previous outcome, previous cue and previous choice in the stem epoch per well-fit neuron. The paper reports no test. Reproduced when the mean over all well-fit neurons of previous outcome exceeds both others with hierarchical bootstrap two-tailed p < 0.05 (the Methods' default test); the paper's sentence is about posterior cortex as a whole, so the same comparison per area is reported, not judged. Evenness is reported as the area means; it is not judged, as the paper gives no test for it.

claims.statement: During stem traversal, dynamic choice is encoded more than reported choice in all areas, most in RSC (above V1, PM and A, not different from AM and MM), while reported choice encoding is not above zero.
claims.source: Results, Encoding of dynamic choice was enriched in RSC, paragraph 1; Figure 4A, 4B
claims.quote: during traversal of the maze stem, encoding of dynamic choice was distributed across all areas but enriched in RSC and adjacent medial areas, accounting for a substantial amount of neural activity compared to near-zero encoding of reported choice
claims.criterion: Encoding strength of dynamic choice and of reported choice in the stem epoch, area means by hierarchical bootstrap. Reproduced when (1) dynamic exceeds reported in all six areas, (2) RSC exceeds V1, PM and A, each two-tailed p < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg, and (3) reported choice is not above zero in any area at p < 0.05 (a claim of absence, on the paper's bootstrap test). RSC against AM and MM is reported.

claims.statement: In the feedback period/ITI, reported choice is encoded more than dynamic choice in all areas, and RSC encodes reported choice more than every other area.
claims.source: Results, Encoding of dynamic choice was enriched in RSC, paragraph 1; Figure 4C
claims.quote: In contrast, during the feedback and ITI periods, we observed greater encoding of reported choice than dynamic choice
claims.criterion: Encoding strength in the feedback period/ITI epoch (the 16 temporal bins after the maze end), area means by hierarchical bootstrap. Reproduced when reported exceeds dynamic in all six areas and RSC exceeds each other area for reported choice, two-tailed p < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg.

claims.statement: Population decoders trained on reported choice are more related to dynamic choice (partial correlation 0.35 ± 0.02) than to reported choice (0.14 ± 0.02), a difference of 0.21 ± 0.02.
claims.source: Results, Encoding of dynamic choice was enriched in RSC, paragraph 2; Figure 4D
claims.quote: Partial correlations were greater for dynamic choice than reported choice, revealing that even decoders trained to predict reported choice were more closely related to dynamic choice
claims.criterion: Reported-choice decoders as in fig3q-cue-decoding (same decoder readings), stem traversal frames, held-out predictions; partial Spearman correlations per decoder; bootstrap over decoders (hierarchical, mice then decoders). Tolerances are the reported SEMs. Reproduced when the difference is above zero with p < 0.05 and the three values are within tolerance under a reading; partially reproduced when only the sign and test hold.

claims.statement: From populations of about 100 neurons, dynamic choice is decoded better (Spearman 0.59 ± 0.02) than reported choice (0.26 ± 0.02), both above chance.
claims.source: Figure S5F
claims.quote: Decoding of both dynamic and reported choice was above chance (p < 10-3, bootstrap), but decoding of reported choice was less accurate than dynamic choice
claims.criterion: Decoders as in fig3q-cue-decoding; Spearman correlation of held-out predictions with true values over stem frames. Tolerances are the reported SEMs. Reproduced when both exceed zero and dynamic exceeds reported (p < 0.05) and the values are within tolerance under a reading.

claims.statement: In all areas except V1 and A, dynamic choice is encoded more than roll velocity during stem traversal.
claims.source: Figure S5I
claims.quote: For all areas except V1 and area A, the mean fraction explained deviance for dynamic choice was greater than roll velocity, which controls left-right movements in the maze (AM: p = 0.006; PM, MM and RSC: p < 10-3)
claims.criterion: Encoding strength in the stem epoch of dynamic choice and of roll velocity (its linear term; reading two adds its pairwise interactions with the other velocities), paired per neuron, area means by hierarchical bootstrap. Reproduced when dynamic choice exceeds roll velocity in PM, AM, MM and RSC at two-tailed p < 0.05. V1 and A are reported.

claims.statement: With past and upcoming movement added to the GLM, dynamic choice encoding drops but stays above zero in all areas and higher in RSC than in V1, PM and A.
claims.source: Results, Encoding of dynamic choice was enriched in RSC, paragraph 3; Figure S5M
claims.quote: Encoding of dynamic choice in models with movement history was significantly greater than zero in all 6 areas (p < 10-3), and was higher in RSC compared to V1, PM and area A (p < 10-3)
claims.criterion: The alternative GLM of the Methods (Design matrix) with velocities and accelerations on 5-df b-splines shifted every 1/3 s over 2 s past and future, no pairwise movement interactions. Reproduced when dynamic choice encoding in the stem is lower than in the main model in all areas, above zero in all areas, and higher in RSC than V1, PM and A, each two-tailed p < 0.05 by hierarchical bootstrap.

claims.statement: Maze position is encoded in all areas, most strongly in RSC (above V1, PM and A, not different from AM and MM).
claims.source: Results, Encoding of dynamic choice was enriched in RSC, paragraph 4; Figure 4F, 4G
claims.quote: Encoding of maze position was present in all areas, but strongest in RSC, with a similar medial-to-lateral gradient as choice encoding
claims.criterion: Encoding strength of trial phase (maze position) in the stem epoch, area means by hierarchical bootstrap. Reproduced when every area is above zero and RSC exceeds V1, PM and A at two-tailed p < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg. RSC against AM and MM is reported.

claims.statement: RSC is most active in the maze stem and least active in the feedback period/ITI, when area A is more active.
claims.source: Results, Encoding of dynamic choice was enriched in RSC, paragraph 4; Figure 4H
claims.quote: RSC was also most active in the maze stem and least active during feedback and ITI periods, when area A was more active
claims.criterion: Deconvolved activity z-scored per neuron, averaged per neuron in each epoch (Figure 4H). Over what the z-score is taken is not said; the session is the standard reading. Which neurons enter is not said; the readings are all 93,881 and the well-fit 42,998. The sentence allows two comparisons, both run. (a) Between areas, RSC's mean in the stem exceeds every other area's and in the feedback period/ITI is below A's. (b) Within RSC, its mean in the stem exceeds its means in the arms and in the feedback period/ITI, its feedback period/ITI mean is the lowest of the three, and in the feedback period/ITI A's mean exceeds RSC's. Each comparison by hierarchical bootstrap, two-tailed p < 0.05 (the Methods' default test; the legend gives none). Reproduced when the comparisons hold under every reading.

claims.statement: Cue and movement have the highest mutual information between encoding strength and area, yet their equivalent random fractions are above 0.75 and equivalent jitters near 0.6, closer to fully distributed than fully modular.
claims.source: Results, Encoding of most variables is highly distributed, paragraph 2; Figure 5E, 5F; Figure S6A
claims.quote: Cue and movement were the two variables with the highest mutual information between encoding strength and posterior cortical area. However, their equivalent random fractions were greater than 0.75 ... Similarly, their equivalent jitters were near 0.6
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Quantification of distributedness. Active neurons per epoch (epoch-averaged null deviance above trial-averaged null deviance), 1,000 sampled per area, encoding strength ranked, mutual information with area label (scikit-learn mutual_info_classif) normalized by the fully modular model, repeated 1,000 times; the equivalent random fraction and jitter are the nearest neighbours on the model curves (100 values from 0.01 to 1; 491 values from 0.1 to 5; 100 simulations each). Epochs are stem for cue, whole trial for movement. For a whole-trial variable the active-neuron rule (epoch-averaged above trial-averaged null deviance) cannot select anyone as written; the readings are all well-fit neurons and all neurons. Reproduced when cue and movement have the two highest normalized MI of the variables tested, both random fractions exceed 0.75 and both jitters are within 10% of 0.6. Whether the active-neuron pool is the well-fit neurons or all neurons is not said; the counts (20,202 stem, 12,719 feedback) match the well-fit pool, which is used, with all neurons as a variant.

claims.statement: Maze position and choice are even more distributed (equivalent random fraction near 0.9), and decision-making strategy is the most distributed (near 1).
claims.source: Results, Encoding of most variables is highly distributed, paragraph 2; Figure 5E
claims.quote: The encoding of maze position and choice were even more distributed than cue and movement, with equivalent random fractions near 0.9. All other variables were also highly distributed, with decision-making strategy being the most distributed (random fraction near one)
claims.criterion: As fig5e-cue-movement-distributed; maze position and dynamic choice in the stem, reported choice and outcome in the feedback period/ITI, strategy over the whole trial (the Methods name stem for position and dynamic choice, feedback for reported choice and outcome; the strategy epoch is not named, so stem and whole trial are both run). Which "choice" the sentence means is not fixed; dynamic choice (stem) and reported choice (feedback) are both reported, and the claim holds when either is within tolerance and above cue and movement. Reproduced when the values are within tolerance and strategy has the highest random fraction.

claims.statement: Neurons in V1, A and RSC are typically decoded to their own areas from their encoding profiles, while neurons in AM and MM are decoded across all of posterior cortex.
claims.source: Results, Single-neuron encoding profiles confirm functional gradients, paragraph 1; Figure 6A, 6B
claims.quote: Neurons in V1, A, and RSC were typically predicted to reside in their actual areas of origin, indicating that these neurons had distinctive encoding profiles, in contrast to neurons from AM and MM that were predicted to reside in all sites across posterior cortex
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Decoding anatomical locations. Encoding profile is the mean fraction explained deviance of the 11 variable groups over 6 epochs; 241 logistic decoders on a 0.15 mm grid, Gaussian targets (sigma 0.15 mm), Tensorflow, Adam (0.01), L2, leave-one-mouse-out; outputs divided by sampling density and normalized per neuron. The L2 strength is not given; the readings are the values of the GLM's lambda grid chosen by leave-one-mouse-out loss, and the grid's middle value 1e-3. For each area, the average decoded distribution over its neurons; the measure is the fraction of its mass inside the area's own territory divided by the fraction of decoder sites inside it. The paper shows Figure 6B as maps only and gives no measure; this ratio is a choice of this file. Reproduced when, under every reading, V1, A and RSC each have a higher ratio than both AM and MM.

claims.statement: Non-negative factorization of the decoded locations is dominated by three factors (reconstruction error 33.8% ± 3.1% with three, 55% with one), forming spatial gradients peaking in V1, RSC and A.
claims.source: Results, Single-neuron encoding profiles confirm functional gradients, paragraph 2; Figure 6D; Figure S6I; STAR Methods, Non-negative matrix factorization
claims.quote: Strikingly, these factors formed three distinct spatial gradients that dominated the anatomical organization of encoding with peaks in V1, RSC and A, respectively
claims.criterion: scikit-learn NMF of the 42,998 by 241 prediction matrix for k = 1 to 10; reconstruction error is the Frobenius norm of the residual over that of the data. The tolerance for three factors is the reported bootstrap SEM. Reproduced when the errors are within tolerance, the improvement flattens from four factors (the gain from 3 to 4 is smaller than from 2 to 3), and the three factors' decoder scores peak inside V1, RSC and A, one each. NMF initialization is a standard choice (scikit-learn default).

claims.statement: Cue weighs most in factor 1, maze position and choice in factor 2, and movement in factor 3.
claims.source: Results, Single-neuron encoding profiles confirm functional gradients, paragraph 2; Figure S6G
claims.quote: cue was greatest in factor 1, maze position and choice were greatest in factor 2, and movement was greatest in factor 3
claims.criterion: Each factor's profile is the score-weighted mean of the location decoders' coefficients (STAR Methods, Non-negative matrix factorization). Factors are numbered by their peak (V1, RSC, A). Reproduced when, across the three factors, cue's weight is highest in the V1 factor, position's and dynamic choice's in the RSC factor, and movement's in the A factor, in the stem epoch.

claims.statement: The number of principal components needed for 70% of variance is 8, 6 and 3 for GLM coefficients, encoding strengths and decoded locations, and 35, 23 and 16 for 95%.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Analysis of dimensionality of encoding across neurons versus encoding across cortical space
claims.quote: The number of principal components needed to explain 70% of the variance in the three matrices was 8, 6, and 3, respectively, and further, 35, 23, and 16 principal components were needed to explain 95% of the variance
claims.criterion: PCA of the three matrices of the Methods over the well-fit neurons. Whether columns are standardized first is not said; centred only and z-scored are both run. The claim is reproduced when every count is within tolerance under a reading, and partially when the ordering (coefficients > strengths > locations) holds at both levels.

claims.statement: Correlations in single-neuron encoding strength between cue, dynamic choice and movement are similar across areas and close to zero; only A differs for cue against movement.
claims.source: Results, Conjunctive structure of encoding, paragraph 2; Figure 7D to 7F
claims.quote: Strikingly, the correlations in encoding between pairs of cue, choice, and movement variables were similar across areas, despite major differences in the encoding strengths of these variables between areas ... In addition, the correlation coefficients were close to zero
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Correlation between encoding of pairs of variables. Fraction null deviance (re-fitting) in the stem, local spatial mean subtracted (smoothed map, SD 150 um), active neurons only, Pearson correlation per area, bootstrap (mice then neurons). A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test as written, a two-tailed comparison of two unpaired bootstrap samples per area pair at p > 0.05 (no correction is stated; Benjamini-Hochberg is shown as a variant). Reproduced when no pair differs for cue and dynamic choice or for dynamic choice and movement, and for cue and movement only pairs involving A differ; every r is reported, and near zero is judged as |r| < 0.2, a bound this file sets, as the paper gives none.

claims.statement: A neuron's area is decoded well from encoding strengths, poorly from encoding correlations, and barely better from both than from strengths alone.
claims.source: Results, Conjunctive structure of encoding, paragraph 3; Figure 7G, 7H
claims.quote: Although decoding based on encoding correlations allowed above-chance performance, it was poor relative to decoding from encoding strengths alone. Further, decoding with both encoding correlations and encoding strengths was barely improved from decoding with encoding strengths alone
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Decoding of area. Spatial-mean-subtracted, z-scored encoding strengths of 11 variables for active neurons in the stem; interaction terms are their pairwise products; one-against-others scikit-learn LogisticRegression, leave-one-mouse-out, auROC on held-out mice; Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The paired samples of the test are not named; the reading is the 8 held-out mice (the legend gives mean ± SEM over the leave-one-mouse-out procedure). No parameters are given for LogisticRegression; its defaults (L2, C = 1) are the reading. Reproduced when strengths beat correlations in at least five of six areas (p < 0.05) and strengths plus correlations is not better than strengths after Benjamini-Hochberg in any area.

claims.statement: Cue and choice decoders trained at one maze position lose accuracy when tested at other positions.
claims.source: Results, Flexible, high-dimensional representations, paragraph 1; Figure 8C, 8D
claims.quote: decoders trained to predict cue or choice at one maze position degraded in accuracy when tested at other maze positions
claims.criterion: Decoders of fig3q-cue-decoding, one per position bin, tested at every other bin; cue on sessions with cue offset at 0.76 of the maze, positions with cue present (698 decoders in the paper) scored as log likelihood (base 2), dynamic choice on 974 decoders scored as Spearman correlation (Figure 8C, 8D legends). Reproduced when performance falls with train-test distance (mean at the largest distance below that at zero distance, hierarchical bootstrap two-tailed p < 0.05) for both variables in every area.

claims.statement: Shattering dimensionality for conjunctions of cue, choice, position, movement and rule belief is well above chance and similar across areas, and nearly identical to that of populations drawn from all areas.
claims.source: Results, Flexible, high-dimensional representations, paragraph 2; Figure 8F, 8G; Figure S8A to S8C
claims.quote: Shattering dimensionality for all conjunctions in all areas was well above chance, and interestingly, shattering dimensionality for each conjunction was similar across posterior cortex ... Almost all differences between areas were not statistically significant and fell within a range of < 10% classification accuracy for each conjunction
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Quantification of shattering dimensionality. Pseudo-populations of 1,000 neurons per area by hierarchical bootstrap (1,000 samples), all layer 2/3 neurons, stem frames, trial samples split 50-50 (test capped at 30), standardized on training data, linear SVC on every marginally balanced dichotomy, 10 splits, with the bins and C values of the Methods (C = 1.0 for cue and position, 0.1 otherwise). Conjunctions as listed in the Methods (cue or choice by 10 position bins, cue by 3 rule-belief bins by 6 position bins, cue by choice by 4 position bins, 6 quantile bins per velocity axis); the exact set in Figure 8G is shown only in the figure. Whether "choice" is dynamic choice (binned in 2) or reported choice is not fixed except for Figure S8A (dynamic); both are run. Reproduced when every conjunction in every area is above 0.5, the spread of area means per conjunction is under 0.10, and no area pair differs after Benjamini-Hochberg except RSC against A for cue by dynamic choice by position (a claim of absence on the paper's test).

claims.statement: GLMs fit with L2 regularization perform slightly worse on test data than with group lasso (difference -0.0175 ± 0.0052), and the main encoding results hold with L2.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Quantification of fraction explained deviance (without re-fitting); Figure S8D to S8J
claims.quote: The performance of the models on test data was worse on average than those with group lasso (difference in fraction of explained deviance
claims.criterion: The GLM refit with an L2 penalty in place of group lasso (the code's elastic_net with l1_ratio 0), lambda chosen as in the main fit. The Methods print -0.0175 and the legend 0.018 for the same difference; the Methods' signed value is used. Tolerance is the reported SEM. Reproduced when the difference is within tolerance and below zero at p < 0.05, and the gradients of fig3m-movement-task-gradient and fig3o-cue-gradient keep their ordering with L2.

claims.statement: With a looser fit threshold (fraction deviance explained above 0.1, 68,532 neurons), the area differences in movement, task, cue, choice, position and strategy encoding are the same.
claims.source: Results, Calcium imaging of neural activity, paragraph 2; Figure S8K to S8O
claims.quote: for subsequent analyses, we focused on well fit neurons although results were robust to this criterion
claims.criterion: The tests of the claims it depends on, repeated on neurons above 0.1. Reproduced when each of them gives the same outcome as on the 42,998 neurons; the legend of Figure S8N reports RSC above V1, PM and A at p < 0.05 for position, and S8O strategy pairs at p > 0.04, not significant after correction.

claims.statement: At maze positions where cue and reported choice are equally decodable from running, single neurons encode dynamic choice more than cue-biased running in all areas except V1 and PM, and population decoders decode dynamic choice better than cue-biased running in all areas.
claims.source: Figure S5L; Results, Encoding of dynamic choice was enriched in RSC, paragraph 3
claims.quote: For single neuron encoding magnitudes, dynamic choice was greater than cue-biased running (p < 10-3) for all areas except V1 and PM. For population decoding performance, dynamic choice was greater than cue-biased running (p < 10-3) for all areas
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Analysis of dynamic choice and cue-biased running at matched positions. Per session, trial-averaged LSTM log likelihood of reported choice and of cue over maze position; thresholds spaced by 0.1 over the session's range; at each threshold the positions where each reaches it. Single neurons, fraction explained deviance of dynamic choice and of cue-biased running at the matched positions; decoders, logistic decoders as in fig3q-cue-decoding on the three closest timepoints around the matched positions, scored as Spearman correlation; both averaged over threshold levels, then per area by hierarchical bootstrap. Which crossing counts when a curve reaches a threshold more than once is not said; the readings are the first crossing and the last. Reproduced when, under every reading, dynamic choice exceeds cue-biased running at two-tailed p < 0.05 in AM, MM, RSC and A for single neurons and in all six areas for decoders. V1 and PM single-neuron results are reported.

claims.statement: In the two-dimensional encoding embedding, area distributions overlap; their centroids are offset, but many neurons lie closer to the centroid of another area than to that of their own area.
claims.source: Results, Single-neuron encoding profiles confirm functional gradients, paragraph 3; Figure 6H; Figure S6L
claims.quote: Although the centroids of the distributions (i.e. most typical encoding profiles) were offset from one another, many neurons were functionally closer to the centroid of a different area than to the centroid of the area where they resided
claims.criterion: STAR Methods, Linear embedding of single neuron encoding properties. PCA of the coefficients of the 241 location decoders; each well-fit neuron's encoding profile projected on the first two components; area centroids as the mean of the area's neurons. For each area, the fraction of its neurons whose Euclidean distance in the embedding is smaller to some other area's centroid than to their own. The paper gives no number for "many"; reproduced when this fraction exceeds 0.25 in every area, a bound this file sets. The fractions are reported, and the same measure in the full encoding space (where the dendrogram's centroids are taken) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The proportion of cells with grid structure depended on layer. Most well-separated layer II cells were grid cells (66 of 108), against a smaller proportion in layers III (78 of 223), V (17 of 110) and VI (42 of 186).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 2; Fig. 1D; table S1A
claims.quote: The proportion of cells with a sinusoidal modulation was layer-dependent (Fig. 1D and table S1). Whereas most well-separated layer II cells had strongly periodic firing fields, only a smaller proportion of the deeper neurons had such characteristics
claims.criterion: All cells of all 17 rats, grouped by layer; a grid cell has gridness above 0, the paper's criterion (SOM, Autocorrelation of rate maps), with readings O1 to O3. The paper reports no test of the layer difference. Reproduced when the layer II fraction is above 0.5 and above that of each deeper layer, and the four fractions are within tolerance. Partially reproduced when the order holds but a fraction is outside tolerance. The fractions need every sorted cell of a layer as the denominator; if the dataset holds grid cells only, the claim cannot be tested.

claims.statement: Grid cells with tessellating firing fields were found in all four principal cell layers of MEC (II, III, V and VI).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 2; Fig. 1, A and B; table S1A
claims.quote: Grid cells with tessellating firing fields (7) were observed in all principal cell layers (Fig. 1, A and B).
claims.criterion: Grid cells as in layer2-grid (gridness above 0, readings O1 to O3). Reproduced when at least one grid cell is found in each of layers II, III, V and VI.

claims.statement: Among deeper-layer cells with periodic firing, the range of gridness did not differ from that of layer II cells.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 2; Fig. 1D
claims.quote: however, the range of Bgridness[ among those cells was not different from that of the layer II cells
claims.criterion: A claim of absence for which the paper names no test and no level. Cells are the grid cells of each layer (gridness above 0, readings O1 to O3). The readings of the test are (a) a two-sided Mann-Whitney test of gridness, layer II against layers III to VI pooled; (b) a Kruskal-Wallis test across the four layers; each at p < 0.05, the level the paper uses for its other comparisons. Reproduced when no reading finds a difference; not reproduced when all do; methods_underspecified when they disagree. The median and range of gridness per layer are reported either way.

claims.statement: All 203 grid cells had stable periodic firing patterns within and between trials.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 3; figs. S1 and S2
claims.quote: All 203 neurons that passed this criterion had stable periodic firing patterns both within and between trials (figs. S1 and S2).
claims.criterion: Grid cells as in layer2-grid. Between trials, the paper's measure is the spatial correlation of the two trials' rate maps, bin by bin (SOM, Analysis of place fields; fig. S2), for cells recorded in two trials. The paper gives no threshold for "stable" and does not define stability within a trial. Readings for stable between trials are (a) a positive map correlation with Pearson p < 0.05; (b) gridness above 0 in each trial's map. Within a trial the readings are (a) the same tests on the maps of the first and second halves of each trial; (b) on the maps of odd and even minutes, as the head-direction Methods split a trial. Reproduced when every grid cell passes under every reading; partially reproduced when at least 90% do; methods_underspecified when the readings disagree on these outcomes. The count of grid cells is checked only if the dataset holds all sorted cells.

claims.statement: In every layer grid spacing increased with distance from the postrhinal border, by a factor of 1.5 to 2 over the sampled range, with the densest spacing (about 35 to 40 cm) near the border; the correlations (0.46 to 0.94) were significant in every layer and did not differ between layers.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 3; fig. S3
claims.quote: Irrespective of layer, the scale of the grid in these cells increased by a factor of 1.5 to 2 from the dorsalmost to the ventralmost recording location, such that cells near the postrhinal border had the densest spacing (È35 to 40 cm) ... The correlations between distance from the ... postrhinal border on the one hand and spacing and field size on the other were significant in all layers (spacing, 0.46 e r e 0.94; field size, 0.44 e r e 0.94; all, P G 0.005)
claims.criterion: Grid cells of each layer, spacing as in the SOM (median distance from the centre to the six inner peaks of the autocorrelogram, readings O1 and O2), against the distance of the recording site from the postrhinal border, from the histology (SOM, Histology; fig. S3). Reproduced when, in every layer, Pearson r is positive with p < 0.005 and within tolerance, and the ratio and near-border spacing are within tolerance. Partially reproduced when every layer's correlation is positive and significant but a number is outside tolerance. The paper does not say how the ratio is formed; readings are (a) per layer, the mean spacing at the most ventral recording location over that at the most dorsal; (b) the values of the regression line at those two locations. Near the border means the cells at each layer's most dorsal location. The fig. S3 legend adds that there was no significant difference between layers, with no test named; readings are (a) pairwise comparisons of the correlations by Fisher's z, (b) the layer by distance interaction in a linear model of spacing, each at p < 0.05. That part is reported, and it is judged as an absence; if a reading finds a difference the claim is at most partially reproduced. Needs the recording sites' distances from the postrhinal border.

claims.statement: In every layer grid field size increased with distance from the postrhinal border (0.44 ≤ r ≤ 0.94, all P < 0.005), with the smallest fields (about 500 cm2) near the border.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 3; fig. S3
claims.quote: cells near the postrhinal border had the densest spacing (È35 to 40 cm) and the smallest firing fields (È500 cm2) (fig. S3)
claims.criterion: Grid cells of each layer against the distance of the recording site from the postrhinal border. The paper does not define field size. Readings are (a) the area of the central peak of the autocorrelogram, as contiguous pixels above the r = 0.10 threshold the SOM uses for peaks; (b) the mean area of the firing fields of the rate map, as contiguous bins above 20% of the cell's peak rate, a common definition that this paper does not give. Reproduced when, under a reading, r is positive with p < 0.005 in every layer, each r within the widened range and the field size of the cells at each layer's most dorsal location within tolerance; methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. Needs the recording sites' distances from the postrhinal border.

claims.statement: In all layers the spatial phase of nearby grid cells was distributed (their vertices were offset), while grid orientation was consistent across simultaneously recorded cells.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 3, last sentence; fig. S2 legend
claims.quote: In all layers, the phase of the grid was distributed, i.e., the vertices of most nearby grid cells were offset relative to each other, but the orientation of the grids was consistent across all simultaneously recorded cells.
claims.criterion: Pairs of grid cells recorded simultaneously (same rat and trial), orientation as in the SOM, compared modulo 60 degrees. The paper gives no measure of phase offset and no threshold for either part. Orientation is consistent when the within-session pairwise differences are smaller than the differences between sessions of different rats (the fig. S2 legend ascribes the broad range of orientations to differences between rats), by a one-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05; this test is a standard choice, not the paper's. Phase is distributed when, for most pairs (more than half), the peak of the rate-map crosscorrelogram nearest the centre is displaced from the centre; readings for displaced, standard choices since the paper gives none, are (a) by more than one fifth of the grid spacing, (b) by more than the 3 cm bin. The paper does not say whether the between-rat differences are taken within a layer; fig. S2 shows orientation per layer and ascribes the range to rats, but names no pool, so the readings are (a) pairs of sessions of different rats in the same layer, (b) in any layers (answer of 2026-10-20). Reproduced when both parts hold under every reading, the readings O1 to O3 included, in each layer with at least one simultaneous pair.

claims.statement: No head-direction cells were found in layer II, whereas a large proportion of the cells in layers III to VI had directional preferences (273 of 385 cells, counting conjunctive cells).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4; Fig. 2E; table S1B
claims.quote: No head-direction cells were found in layer II (Fig. 2E). In contrast, a large proportion of the cells in layers III to VI had directional preferences (273 of 385 cells) (Fig. 2E).
claims.criterion: Cells of the nine two-LED rats only; head-direction cells by the SOM criteria with readings O1 and O4; directional cells are head-direction cells plus conjunctive cells (220 + 53 = 273, table S1B). Reproduced when no layer II cell passes and the fractions are within tolerance; partially reproduced when no layer II cell passes and the deeper fraction is above 0.5 but a number is outside tolerance. The fractions need every sorted cell as denominator; if the dataset holds grid cells only, only the layer II part can be tested, and the claim is at most partially reproduced.

claims.statement: Beneath layer II, head-direction cells were usually recorded together with grid cells.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4; fig. S6
claims.quote: Beneath layer II, grid cells were colocalized with head-direction cells ... Head-direction cells were usually encountered together with grid cells (fig. S6).
claims.criterion: Two-LED rats, layers III to VI, cell classes as in hd-layers and layer2-grid. The paper does not fix the unit of colocalization or what "usually" means. Readings of the unit are (a) the recording session (rat, location and trial); (b) the tetrode within a session. The head-direction cells are the pure head-direction cells of table S1B (answer of 2026-10-20); fig. S6 counts "grid cells, head-direction cells and grid x head-direction cells" as three classes, and table S1B and the speed paragraph use "head-direction cells" for the 220 pure ones. The cell they are found with is another cell of the unit, as fig. S6 counts each cell in one class. The paper's classes allow two readings of that cell, (a) a pure grid cell, the class fig. S6 calls grid cells; (b) a grid or conjunctive cell, since conjunctive cells meet the grid criterion. Reproduced when, under every reading, more than half of the units holding a head-direction cell also hold such a cell; methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: The breadth of directional tuning did not differ between layers III, V and VI (mean U2 18.2, 25.2 and 18.3; mean angular standard deviation 55.9, 52.2 and 58.2 degrees; P > 0.05).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4; fig. S4
claims.quote: The breadth of tuning was not significantly different between layers III, V, and VI (mean U2 values, 18.2, 25.2, and 18.3, respectively; mean angular standard deviations, 55.9-, 52.2-, and 58.2-; P 9 0.05) (fig. S4).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence; the paper names the level (P > 0.05) but not the test. Readings of the test are (a) a one-way ANOVA across the three layers, the test the paper uses for its slope comparison; (b) a Kruskal-Wallis test; each on U2 and on angular standard deviation. Readings of the cells are (a) pure head-direction cells; (b) head-direction and conjunctive cells together. Angular standard deviation from the mean vector length r (SOM, Analysis of head-direction cells, citing Batschelet, S8); the SOM calls it "the angular standard deviation of the mean vector" and the fig. S2 and S4 legends "the circular standard deviation", so the paper allows (a) Batschelet's angular deviation, sqrt(2(1 - r)), and (b) his circular standard deviation, sqrt(-2 ln r), both in degrees (answer of 2026-10-20). Reproduced when no reading finds a difference at p < 0.05; not reproduced when all do; methods_underspecified when they disagree. The means are reported and compared with tolerance either way; a reproduced absence with means outside tolerance is partially reproduced. Fig. S4 gives 388 cells for layers III to VI, the main text 385.

claims.statement: The entire range of head directions was represented by the preferred directions of head-direction cells in each of layers III, V and VI.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4; Fig. 2F
claims.quote: The entire range of head directions was represented in all three layers (Fig. 2F).
claims.criterion: Head-direction and conjunctive cells of each layer; preferred direction as the bin of peak rate (SOM, Analysis of head-direction cells). The paper gives no measure of coverage. Readings are that each (a) 30-degree, (b) 60-degree or (c) 90-degree sector of the circle holds the preferred direction of at least one cell of the layer. Reproduced when all readings hold in all three layers; not reproduced when none does in some layer; otherwise methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Preferred directions of simultaneously recorded head-direction cells in the same area were widely distributed; in most ensembles of five or more cells (8 of 12) they showed no significant clustering.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4; Fig. 2G; fig. S5
claims.quote: When several head-direction cells were recorded simultaneously in the same area, their peak firing directions were widely distributed (Fig. 2G and fig. S5).
claims.criterion: As in fig. S5, every session with 5 or more simultaneously recorded head-direction cells; the directions of the cells' mean vectors (the test uses angles only; the rate is the vector length of the plot) tested for clustering with Watson's one-sample U2 test of uniformity at p < 0.05, against the critical value for the number of cells. Whether conjunctive cells count is not stated; readings are (a) pure head-direction cells, (b) with conjunctive cells. Reproduced when, under a reading, fewer than half of the ensembles show significant clustering; the counts are compared with the expected values. methods_underspecified when the readings disagree on this.

claims.statement: Directional tuning curves were always stable across the two trials (circular correlation r = 0.84, P < 0.001).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Directional tuning curves were always stable across trials (circular correlation, r 0 0.84, P G 0.001).
claims.criterion: Head-direction and conjunctive cells recorded in both trials of the same session. The paper does not say what was correlated. Readings are (a) across cells, the circular-circular correlation of the preferred direction in trial 1 with that in trial 2; (b) per cell, the Pearson correlation of the two trials' 60-bin tuning curves, averaged over cells, with the significance of that mean tested against 0 by a one-sample t-test (a standard choice). Reproduced when, under a reading, r is within tolerance with p < 0.001; methods_underspecified when one reading reproduces and another fails.

claims.statement: In head-direction cells, firing rose from a low background rate (typically below 0.5 Hz) to a high maximum rate (5 to 40 Hz) when the rat's head faced the cell's range of directions.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 4, second sentence; Fig. 2D; fig. S4
claims.quote: In these neurons, firing increased from a low background rate (typically G 0.5 Hz) to a high maximum rate (5 to 40 Hz) whenever the rat_s head faced a certain range of directions (Fig. 2D, fig. S4, and table S1).
