claims.criterion: Head-direction cells of the two-LED rats, by the SOM criteria with readings O1 and O4; whether conjunctive cells are included is open, readings (a) pure head-direction cells, (b) with conjunctive cells. Peak rate is the rate in the bin with the highest rate of the unsmoothed 60-bin tuning curve (SOM, Analysis of head-direction cells). The paper does not define the background rate or "typically"; readings, standard choices, are (a) the rate in the lowest bin of the tuning curve, (b) the mean rate over the bins more than 90 degrees from the preferred direction; "typically" is read as the median over cells. Reproduced when, under a reading, the median background rate is below 0.55 Hz (the paper's bound of 0.5 Hz widened by 10%) and at least 90% of the cells have peak rates from 4.5 to 44 Hz; methods_underspecified when readings disagree.

claims.statement: The proportion of grid cells with conjunctive head-direction tuning depended on layer (66% in layer III, 90% in layer V, 28% in layer VI, none in layer II); the difference was significant across all four layers and across layers III to VI.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 5; table S1B
claims.quote: The proportion of grid cells with conjunctive properties was layer-dependent (table S1). The largest proportion was encountered in layers III and V, where 66% and 90% of the grid cells had dual response properties, respectively. In layer VI, the proportion was 28%. No conjunctive cells were observed in layer II. Differences between layers were significant (all four cell layers, c(3) 0 28.4, P G 0.001; layers III to VI, c(2) 0 6.2, P G 0.05)
claims.criterion: Two-LED rats; grid cells (gridness above 0) and conjunctive cells (grid and head-direction criteria) by the SOM, readings O1 to O4. The paper does not give the table its chi-square was run on, and the counts of table S1B do not yield 28.4 and 6.2 under the obvious tables. Readings are (a) conjunctive against non-conjunctive grid cells per layer, the proportion the text describes; (b) conjunctive cells against all other cells per layer. Reproduced when, under a reading, both chi-square tests are significant (p < 0.001 for four layers, p < 0.05 for layers III to VI) and the four fractions are within tolerance; partially reproduced when no layer II cell is conjunctive and the four-layer test is significant but a fraction or the three-layer test fails. Layer V holds 10 grid cells in the paper, so its fraction is coarse.

claims.statement: Grid cells and head-direction cells formed overlapping populations; the joint distribution of gridness and directional tuning was continuous, with some grid cells directionally tuned and some head-direction cells having grid structure.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 5; Fig. 3, A to E; fig. S7
claims.quote: Grid cells and head-direction cells formed overlapping populations. The 2D distribution of gridness and directional tuning was continuous, such that some grid cells were directionally tuned and some head-direction cells had grid correlates (Fig. 3, A to D, and fig. S7).
claims.criterion: Two-LED rats, all cells, gridness against Watson U2 (log scale) as in Fig. 3E. The paper gives no test of continuity. Reproduced when conjunctive cells exist (cells passing both criteria) and, under readings O1 to O4, the cells passing either criterion form no separate clusters; the last part is read as the absence of a gap, along each axis, wider than a quarter of that axis's range among them, a standard choice and not the paper's.

claims.statement: Directional tuning of conjunctive cells did not differ from that of pure head-direction cells (mean U2 18.0 against 19.4, P > 0.05).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 5; Fig. 3, D and E
claims.quote: The degree of directional tuning in cells that met selection criteria for both gridness and directionality was not significantly different from that of pure headdirection cells (mean U2 values, 18.0 and 19.4, respectively; P 9 0.05) (Fig. 3, D and E).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence; the paper names the level but not the test. Readings are (a) a two-sided t-test, (b) a two-sided Mann-Whitney test, of U2 in conjunctive against pure head-direction cells, at p < 0.05. Reproduced when no reading finds a difference; not reproduced when all do; methods_underspecified when they disagree. A reproduced absence with means outside tolerance is partially reproduced.

claims.statement: Cells with different degrees of gridness and directionality always responded as a coherent ensemble to rotation of a polarizing cue card; in the example (layer VI, Fig. 3F and fig. S8), a grid cell and four head-direction cells were recorded together, the head-direction cells all rotated 90 degrees with the card, and the grid cell's map is shown following it.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 5; Fig. 3F; fig. S8
claims.quote: Cells with different degrees of gridness and directionality always responded as a coherent ensemble during environmental manipulations such as the rotation of a polarizing cue card (Fig. 3F and fig. S8) (22).
claims.criterion: The cue-rotation sessions of the five rats tested (small circular box, card rotated 90 degrees and back). The paper gives no measure of rotation. For each cell, the rotation from the standard trial to the rotated trial is the angle that maximizes (a) for grid structure, the correlation between the rotated standard rate map and the rotated-trial map, in 6-degree steps; (b) for head-direction tuning, the correlation of the 60-bin tuning curves under circular shift. Coherent means all cells of a session rotate by the same angle; readings of "the same" are within (a) 18 degrees (three tuning bins) and (b) 30 degrees of each other. Reproduced when every session with two or more cells is coherent under both readings; methods_underspecified when they disagree. The rotation of each session relative to the 90 degrees of the card is reported.

claims.statement: Regression showed a consistent positive speed-rate relation in nearly all grid cells (141 of 150), head-direction cells (153 of 220) and conjunctive cells (45 of 53).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 6; Fig. 4, A and B
claims.quote: Yet, regression analyses showed a consistent positive speed-rate relation in nearly all grid cells (141/150 cells, P G 0.001), headdirection cells (153/220 cells, P G 0.001) and grid ... head-direction cells (45/53 cells, P G 0.001), suggesting that a substantial proportion of the network expressed information about how fast the animal was moving (Fig. 4B).
claims.criterion: Per cell, speed and firing rate in 1-s bins over the trial, unsmoothed, all bins kept including those outside firing fields, and a linear regression of rate on speed (SOM, Velocity tuning). Which cells count is open, with readings (a) a cell counts when the slope is positive with P < 0.001, the per-cell reading of the main text's "141/150 cells, P < 0.001"; (b) a cell counts when the slope is positive, as the Fig. 4B legend says ("Nearly all ... had positive slope values"), the P < 0.001 then being a test of the count across cells that the paper does not name; under (b) the count is also tested against half the cells by a one-sided binomial sign test at p < 0.001, a standard choice. Grid cells are the 150 grid cells that are not conjunctive (203 - 53), which include the grid cells of the single-LED rats; head-direction and conjunctive cells from the two-LED rats. Open details, each with readings. Speed in a 1-s bin is (a) the path length of the tracked positions over the bin, (b) the distance between the positions at the start and end of the bin; positions are (a) the 15-point mean-filtered positions of the place-field Methods, (b) the raw tracked positions. Trials as O1. The significance of the relation is that of (a) the regression slope, (b) Pearson's r, (c) Spearman's rank correlation, which the SOM reports gave nearly identical values. Two kinds of reading (answer of 2026-10-20). The counting readings (a) and (b) and the three significance measures are readings of the reported number, what "141/150 cells, P < 0.001" counts; for a given set of method details the outcome is the best of them. The speed measure, the positions, the trials (O1) and the cell classes (O1 to O4, as in layer2-grid and hd-layers) are method details, and the outcome must be the same under every combination of them. For each combination of method details, the claim is reproduced when, under some reading of the number, all three fractions are within tolerance; partially reproduced when no reading reproduces it but under some reading the grid and conjunctive fractions exceed the head-direction fraction and all exceed one half. The claim takes that outcome when every combination of method details gives it; methods_underspecified when they disagree.

claims.statement: The slope of the speed-rate regression was steeper for conjunctive cells and grid cells than for head-direction cells, and did not differ between conjunctive and grid cells.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 6; Fig. 4B
claims.quote: The slope of the regression line was steeper for conjunctive cells and grid cells than for headdirection cells EF(2,422) 0 5.5, P G 0.005; conjunctive versus head-direction, P 0 0.009; grid versus head-direction, P 0 0.01; conjunctive versus grid, P 0 0.60; Tukey HSD test).
claims.criterion: Slopes from the regressions of the speed claim, all 423 cells, with its readings. One-way ANOVA of slope on cell class and Tukey HSD (main text). Reproduced when the ANOVA has p < 0.005, Tukey gives conjunctive and grid each steeper than head-direction at p < 0.05 and conjunctive against grid p > 0.05. Partially reproduced when the ANOVA is significant at p < 0.05 and one of the two comparisons with head-direction is significant. The printed F(2,422) has one more error degree of freedom than 423 cells in three groups allow (420); the degrees of freedom are reported.

claims.statement: The intercept of the speed-rate regression was positive in all cells but one (422 of 423), and mean rates at the lowest speeds (0 to 3 cm/s) were about 2.3 to 2.5 Hz in each cell class, so firing persisted during brief stops.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph 6; Fig. 4C
claims.quote: The yintercept of the regression line was positive in 422 out of 423 cells (Fig. 4C). Average rates at the lowest velocity (0 to 3 cm/s) were 2.26 T 0.03 Hz (grid cells), 2.50 T 0.02 Hz (headdirection cells) and 2.39 T 0.05 Hz (grid ... head-direction cells).
claims.criterion: Regressions and readings as in the speed claim. The tolerances on the rates are the paper's printed spread, whose kind (SEM or SD) is not stated. The paper does not say how the average was taken; readings are (a) the mean over cells of each cell's mean rate in the 1-s bins with speed from 0 to 3 cm/s; (b) the mean over all such bins of all cells of a class pooled. Reproduced when, under a reading, the fraction is within tolerance and the three rates are within their tolerances; partially reproduced when the fraction holds and the rates are within 10% of the printed values.

claims.statement: In both monkeys accuracy falls as the number of objects grows, yet stays far above the chance of saccading to a random stimulus object for two- and three-object stimuli.
claims.source: Results, Task, Behavior, and Hypotheses, paragraph 1; Figure 1b
claims.quote: Animals learned the task and exhibited variable reaction times, with error rates increasing as the number of objects grew ... However, performance remained far above chance for two- and three-object stimuli
claims.criterion: Per monkey, the fraction correct (T2) of completed trials (T1) for 1, 2 and 3 objects; chance is 1/n, as the Fig. 1b legend defines it. Reproduced when, for both monkeys, the fraction falls from 1 to 2 to 3 objects and the 2- and 3-object fractions lie above 1/2 and 1/3. The paper gives no test; "far above" is not given a number, so the margin is reported and not judged. Which trials form the figure is open: (a) Triangle trials on the triangle only, as the paper's figures/figure_1/performance/performance.ipynb plots; (b) Triangle and Ring trials pooled, as the legend says (the Ring has no 3-object trials). Each reading is run under both correctness radii of T2. For reference, that notebook printed, for reading (a) with the code's radius, P 0.953, 0.93, 0.692 and E 0.928, 0.759, 0.561 for 1, 2, 3 objects; these are reported against, not used to judge.

claims.statement: Reaction times, from cue onset to the response saccade, vary from trial to trial, with trials faster than 180 ms counted as broken fixation.
claims.source: Results, Task, Behavior, and Hypotheses, paragraph 1; Figure 1c legend
claims.quote: Animals learned the task and exhibited variable reaction times
claims.criterion: Per monkey, reaction times (T3) of completed trials, correct and incorrect apart, as in figures/figure_1/reaction_times/reaction_times.ipynb, which bins them from 100 to 600 ms and shows 150 to 500 ms. Trials with a saccade earlier than 180 ms after cue onset are left out as broken fixation (Fig. 1c legend). Which trials form the figure is open, as for fig1b-performance-load: (a) Triangle trials on the triangle, as the notebook plots; (b) Triangle and Ring trials pooled, as the legend says; both are run. The paper fixes no measure of variability. Reproduced when the distribution of each monkey is not degenerate (interquartile range above one 10 ms bin) and its median lies inside the plotted 150 to 500 ms range; these cut-offs are the agent's reading of "variable" and are recorded as such. The histograms, quartiles and the share of trials under 180 ms before the cut are reported.

claims.statement: A common error is a saccade to the location of a non-target stimulus object, reporting the cued identity at the wrong location.
claims.source: Discussion, Position-identity binding, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 1
claims.quote: A common error in our task occurs when the monkey reports the identity of an object at the wrong location ( Extended Data Fig. 1 ), consistent with misbinding in working memory
claims.criterion: Completed Triangle trials on the triangle with 2 or 3 objects, per monkey. Each response is assigned to the triangle vertex within the correctness radius (T2), as in load_triangle_data.py (response_location), and counted by target location and response location as in Extended Data Fig. 1. Among incorrect trials, the share whose response lies at a non-target object's vertex. The paper gives no number for "common"; two readings are run, (a) these responses are the largest class of errors (against responses at an empty vertex or at no vertex), and (b) they are more than half of the errors. Reproduced when both readings hold for both monkeys and both set sizes, not reproduced when neither does; when the readings give different outcomes the claim is methods_underspecified, with the shares reported.

claims.statement: The Triangle dataset holds 4,688 neurons, 2,937 in DMFC and 1,751 in FEF, from 24 sessions, 10 from Monkey P and 14 from Monkey E.
claims.source: Results, The Triangle Dataset, paragraph 1; Methods, Neurophysiology, last paragraph
claims.quote: We recorded 4,688 well-isolated neurons (2,937 from DMFC and 1,751 from FEF) in the Triangle dataset across 24 sessions
claims.criterion: Sessions are the counts stated in Methods, Neurophysiology, so no tolerance. Unit counts take the default 10%. Which units are counted is open: (a) good and mua units with delay-phase rate above 1 Hz on Triangle trials, which is how figures/figure_2/selectivity/selectivity.ipynb printed 4688, 2937 and 1751; (b) as (a) and also stable for at least 500 trials (T5, Methods); (c) good units only, reading "well-isolated" literally. Reproduced when all five values match under one reading. DMFC is probe s0, FEF the V-probes.

claims.statement: The Ring dataset holds 3,051 neurons, 1,712 in DMFC and 1,339 in FEF, from 22 sessions, 10 from Monkey P and 12 from Monkey E.
claims.source: Results, Replication of the Results with the Ring Dataset, paragraph 1; Methods, Neurophysiology, last paragraph
claims.quote: We recorded 3,051 well-isolated neurons (1,712 from DMFC and 1,339 from FEF) across 22 neurophysiology sessions
claims.criterion: As triangle-unit-counts, with the same three readings, on Ring trials. The paper's Ring notebooks list 20 sessions (10 per monkey); the session dates found are reported against both counts.

claims.statement: Neurons are typically active in both the stimulus and the delay phase, and a unit's spatial preference is similar across the two phases.
claims.source: Results, The Triangle Dataset, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 2a and 2b
claims.quote: We found that neurons were typically active in both stimulus and delay phases ( Extended Data Fig. 2 )
claims.criterion: Triangle units (T5), per monkey. Panel a, the stimulus-phase (0 to 1000 ms after stimulus onset) against the delay-phase mean rate (T4) per unit; panel b, per unit and triangle location, the 1-object mean rate at that location divided by the unit's mean over locations, stimulus phase against delay phase, for DMFC and FEF apart, as the legend defines it. The paper gives no test. Readings of "typically active in both": (a) the Pearson and (b) the Spearman correlation across units of panel a's rates is positive at p < 0.05, for both monkeys; (c) more than half of the units, all above 1 Hz in the delay phase by T5, are also above 1 Hz in the stimulus phase (the Methods' activity threshold applied to the other phase). Panel b is judged by readings (a) and (b) per monkey and area. Reproduced when all three readings hold for panel a in both monkeys and (a) and (b) hold for at least three of the four panel b plots; not reproduced when none hold; methods_underspecified when they differ. The second half of the statement is read from the title of the panel b legend, "Correlation in spatial selectivity across stimulus and delay phases"; the three-of-four rule is the agent's reading. The correlations and shares are reported.

claims.statement: Single-trial delay-phase activity carries information about object positions and identities, decoded above a shuffled-label control.
claims.source: Results, The Triangle Dataset, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 3a and 3b
claims.quote: We also found that neural activity contained information about object positions and identities ( Extended Data Fig. 3a-b )
claims.criterion: As the Extended Data Fig. 3 legend and figures/supp_fig_decoding/ fix it, on the three Triangle sessions with the most units entering the models (T7; the code's analysis notebook uses Perle 2022-05-31, 2022-06-01 and 2022-06-04): a linear decoder (MSE loss to a one-hot target, L1 weight 0.003, SGD at learning rate 0.01, 10,000 steps, config_1_triangle.py) from single-trial rates of the stimulus and delay phases, ten 80/20 train/test splits, against the same with shuffled labels. Panel a decodes the location or identity of 1-object trials; panel b, on 2-object trials, the absent location or identity. The paper sets no rule for "above control"; readings (a) the neural accuracy exceeds the shuffled accuracy in all ten splits; (b) the mean neural accuracy exceeds the shuffled mean by more than two standard deviations of the shuffled splits. Reproduced when, under both readings, delay-phase position and identity decoding of panel a are above control in all three sessions; panel b is reported, with the legend's 66% mark.

claims.statement: The coding axes of a two-object decoder come out nearly orthogonal even for synthetic data with no slot structure, so decoder orthogonality does not diagnose slots.
claims.source: Methods, Decoding Analyses, paragraphs 1 and 4; Extended Data Fig. 3c
claims.quote: However, we found that this orthogonality resulted even on synthetic data that was specifically not Slot-like. In other words, orthogonality of these decoding subspaces is not diagnostic of object slots.
claims.criterion: The 2-object decoder of Methods, Decoding Analyses (two linear decoders and a per-trial assignment sigma pressed to be binary; figures/supp_fig_decoding/modeling/models.py, LinearModel2Objects) fitted on 2-object trials of the three Triangle sessions of ext3ab-decoding and of the three Ring sessions with the most units entering the models (the Extended Data Fig. 3 legend picks three sessions from each dataset; the code's run_2_ring.py uses Perle 2022-06-09, 2022-06-10 and 2022-06-11), and on the Receptive Field and Orthogonal synthetic datasets built from them as Methods describe; angles between corresponding columns of W0 and W1 for each location, over ten bootstraps, stimulus and delay phases. The paper gives no threshold for "orthogonal". Reproduced when the angles for the neural data and for the Receptive Field data are both centred near 90 degrees, read as (a) a median between 75 and 105 degrees and (b) a median within 10 degrees of the Orthogonal dataset's median; both cut-offs are the agent's. Not reproduced when neither reading holds; methods_underspecified when they differ.

claims.statement: Delay-phase position and identity AUCs on 1-object trials span a wide range across units.
claims.source: Results, The Triangle Dataset, paragraph 1; Figure 2b
claims.quote: A Receiver Operating Characteristic analysis of firing rates in the delay phase revealed a wide range of selectivities for position and identity across neurons ( Fig. 2b )
claims.criterion: Position and identity AUC (T6) of every Triangle unit (T5) per monkey, with significance at p < 0.05 as the legend shades it. The paper gives no number for "wide". Reproduced when, for both monkeys and both features, the AUCs run from near 0.5 (lowest decile below 0.6) to high values (highest decile above 0.7), with both significant and non-significant units present; the deciles are reported under both p-value methods of T6. These cut-offs are the agent's reading of "wide range" and are recorded as such.

claims.statement: In the Triangle dataset, pairs of neurons with similar 1-object tuning have positive noise correlations on 2-object trials, and dissimilarly tuned pairs negative ones.
claims.source: Results, The Triangle Dataset, paragraph 2; Figure 2d
claims.quote: Pairs of neurons with similar selectivities on 1-object trials tended to have positive noise correlations on 2-object trials ... Conversely, dissimilarly tuned pairs of neurons tended to have negative noise correlations.
claims.criterion: Pairs of simultaneously recorded Triangle units, per monkey, delay-phase rates (T4). Main method, Methods, Noise Correlations: signal correlation is the correlation across the 9 1-object conditions of the two units' mean rates, pairs dropped unless each condition has at least 3 trials; noise correlation is the mean over the 18 2-object conditions (identity included) with at least 3 shared trials of the across-trial correlation. Variant, the paper's figures/figure_2/noise_correlations/run_compute_triangle.py: per pair and per triple of two 1-object conditions and their 2-object composite, the signal correlation from the two 1-object conditions with trials shuffled between units, the noise correlation on the composite, units above 1 Hz, rows kept with more than 5 trials in each condition. As in plot_noise_vs_signal_correlation.ipynb, signal correlation is cut into 6 bins with edges at linspace(-0.8, 0.8, 7), ends open, and the mean noise correlation per bin is shown with its 95% confidence interval. The paper gives no test. Reproduced when, for both monkeys, the bin of highest signal correlation has a mean noise correlation above zero and the lowest bin one below zero, each with a 95% interval excluding zero; partially reproduced when only the rise from the lowest to the highest bin holds (non-overlapping intervals). Both methods are run; when they differ the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: On the Triangle dataset the Gain model has a higher cross-validated model likelihood than the Slot and Switching models, in 88% of sessions and in every session with at least 100 simultaneously recorded units.
claims.source: Results, Modeling Results, paragraph 1; Figure 4a
claims.quote: Across sessions, the Gain model had a higher cross-validated likelihood than the Slot and Switching models ( Fig. 4a ). This held for 88% of sessions, including all sessions with at least 100 simultaneously recorded units.
claims.criterion: Models fitted and compared as T7 on all 24 Triangle sessions. A session's winner is the model of highest mean model likelihood over its splits. The test behind the brackets is, in model_comparison.ipynb, an independent two-sample t-test (scipy ttest_ind) between two models' session-by-split likelihoods, per monkey; the legend marks p < 0.05 while the notebook draws brackets at p < 0.01, and both thresholds are reported. Reproduced when Gain's mean likelihood exceeds both others' for both monkeys with t-test p < 0.05, and the two expected shares hold. "At least 100 units" is read as at least 100 modeled units (T7); the notebook's > 100 is shown as a variant. Unit stability threshold of T5 (500 against 200 trials) is run both ways. The paper's notebook printed 12 of 14 sessions for E and 10 of 10 for P. A full refit is the test; the bracket pattern of the figure could not be read (no PDF).

claims.statement: The Gain model's advantage holds in DMFC alone, in FEF alone, and in single neurons alone.
claims.source: Results, Modeling Results, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 6
claims.quote: The results were consistent across both DMFC and FEF ( Extended Data Fig. 6 )
claims.criterion: As fig4a-gain-best-triangle, restricted as the Extended Data Fig. 6 legend fixes it to 8 Triangle sessions (the four with the most units from each monkey), refitted with units from DMFC only (probe s0), FEF only (V-probes), and good units only (unit_filters.py qualities). Reproduced when, in each of the three restrictions, Gain has the highest mean model likelihood and differs from each other model by the t-test of fig4a at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when this holds in two of three.

claims.statement: Letting slots be arbitrary linear subspaces (the General Slot model) does not change the model comparison; Gain still wins.
claims.source: Results, Slot hypothesis, paragraph 1; Methods, General Slot Model; Extended Data Fig. 5
claims.quote: we found that relaxing this assumption and allowing the slots to be linear subspaces in neural activity space does not qualitatively change our results ( Extended Data Fig. 5 )
claims.criterion: As fig4a-gain-best-triangle on the 24 Triangle sessions with the General Slot model (configs/neural/triangle_slot.py, 2 slots) in place of the disjoint Slot model. Reproduced when Gain's mean likelihood exceeds General Slot's and Switching's for both monkeys at t-test p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Applied to synthetic spike trains sampled from each fitted model, the full fitting and comparison pipeline recovers the generating model, Slot, Switching or Gain.
claims.source: Results, Modeling Results, paragraph 3; Methods, Validation Using Synthetic Data; Figure 4b
claims.quote: This analysis confirmed that our model comparison reliably recovered the ground truth for each of the Slot, Switching, and Gain models ( Fig. 4b )
claims.criterion: As Methods, Validation Using Synthetic Data, with phys_modeling/synthetic_datasets and configs/synthetic: the ten Triangle sessions with the most units (five per monkey), one shared split, each model at its stopping step sampled as Poisson spikes with kappa 0; kappa and stopping step re-tuned; models refitted; model likelihood as T7 but over 300 neuron-trial pairs. The number of new splits is open: two (Methods) or five (seeds 3 to 7 in figures/figure_4/model_comparison/identifiability.ipynb); both are allowed, the run states which. Reproduced when, for each of the three generating models, that model has the highest mean likelihood and beats each other model by the t-test of fig4a at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Two slots give the best cross-validated likelihood for the Slot model on both datasets and both monkeys.
claims.source: Methods, Slot Model, paragraphs 1 and 2
claims.quote: Through hyperparameter sweeping, we found that N slots = 2 provided the best cross-validated performance on both the Triangle and Ring dataset for both monkeys.
claims.criterion: As Methods, Slot Model, paragraph 2: for each monkey and dataset, 4 random sessions, N slots of 1, 2, 3 and 4, two random splits each, mean test log-likelihood. Reproduced when 2 is best on average in all four monkey and dataset combinations. The random sessions are drawn with a fixed seed and named.

claims.statement: For most sessions the best temporal smoothness kappa lies inside the sweep, is broadly the same across models, and is lower in sessions with more units.
claims.source: Methods, Tuning the Temporal Smoothness and Training Steps, paragraphs 1 and 2; Extended Data Fig. 11
claims.quote: We found that for most sessions, cross-validated likelihood was maximized for a value of κ somewhere in the middle of our sweep. Furthermore, this optimal value of κ was broadly consistent across models.
claims.criterion: From the kappa sweeps of T7 on the Triangle sessions. Reproduced when (i) in more than half of sessions and models the best kappa is neither 0 nor 200 ms; (ii) per session the best kappas of the three models span at most 60 ms (three sweep steps) in more than half of sessions; (iii) the Spearman correlation across sessions of unit count and best kappa is negative, per model. The unit count is the number of modeled units (T7), the count the code's figures colour sessions by; the count of all units (T5) is shown as a variant. The paper gives no numbers for (ii) and (iii); the 60 ms span is the agent's reading of "broadly consistent" and is reported with the full table. Reproduced when (i), (ii) and (iii) hold; partially reproduced when (i) and (iii) hold and (ii) does not.

claims.statement: The Gain model's per-trial gains are spread across objects and do not pick one object per trial.
claims.source: Results, Gain model predictions for behavioral errors and reaction times, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 7c
claims.quote: These gains were distributed across the objects and did not sparsely select one object per trial ( Extended Data Fig. 7 )
claims.criterion: Gains (T8) of the fitted Gain models on 3-object Triangle trials, per monkey and object location, as Extended Data Fig. 7c plots them (figures/supp_fig_attn_distribution/attention_distribution.ipynb). The paper fixes no measure of sparsity. Readings, both run; (a) the share of trials with one gain above 0.9 and the other two below 0.1; (b) the same with 0.8 and 0.2. Reproduced when under both readings fewer than half of trials are one-object selections, for both monkeys. The Slot and Switching attention values of panels a and b are shown for comparison.

claims.statement: On 3-object Triangle trials, performance is higher when the target object's neurally inferred delay gain is higher (R = 0.35 for Monkey P, 0.26 for Monkey E).
claims.source: Figure 4c legend; Results, Gain model predictions for behavioral errors and reaction times, paragraph 1
claims.quote: The regression is significantly positive for both monkeys ( R = 0. 35±0. 04, p < 10 −9 for Monkey P; R = 0. 26±0. 04, p < 10 −7 for Monkey E) ... Strikingly, performance was higher for objects with higher delay-phase gains ( Fig. 4c )
claims.criterion: As figures/figure_4/attention_behavior/performance_reaction_time.ipynb: completed 3-object Triangle trials with a gain (T8); for each session, split and target location, the mean target gain and the mean performance (T2); Pearson R and its p across these points per monkey (the notebook had 300 points for P and 420 for E); the ± is the standard deviation of R over 1000 bootstrap resamples of the points. Reproduced when R lies within the paper's ± of the value and p is below the paper's bound, for both monkeys; partially reproduced when R is positive with p < 0.05 in both but outside tolerance. Both correctness radii (T2) are run.

claims.statement: On correct 3-object Triangle trials, the residual target gain is negatively correlated with residual reaction time (R = -0.14 for Monkey P, -0.04 for Monkey E).
claims.source: Figure 4d legend; Results, Gain model predictions for behavioral errors and reaction times, paragraph 1
claims.quote: The regression slope is significantly negative for both monkeys ( R =− 0. 14±0. 016, p < 10 −10 for Monkey P; R =− 0. 04±0. 015, p = 0. 007 for Monkey E) ... residual gains were negatively correlated with residual reaction times ( Fig. 4d )
claims.criterion: Correct completed 3-object Triangle trials. Within each group of trials with the same stimulus (locations and identities), cue (target) and session, the target gain is de-meaned and scaled to variance 1 and the reaction time (T3) de-meaned, as the legend says; Pearson R across trials per monkey, ± as in fig4c-gain-performance-triangle. Order of steps is open: (a) gains averaged over the ten splits, then normalized (legend); (b) normalized within each split, then averaged per trial (performance_reaction_time.ipynb). claims.statement: The relations of attention to accuracy and reaction time are weaker for the Slot and Switching models than for the Gain model.

Panel a's statistics are garbled in the text (only "−4 for Monkey P; −10 for Monkey E" survives), so panel a is reported without expected values. The paper's own panel c values exceed the Gain model's R for performance, so "weaker" can only be read on reaction time and on panel b and d significance; the claim is judged on the reaction-time relation. Reproduced when the expected values hold within the paper's ± and the Gain model's reaction-time R (fig4d) is more negative than the Slot's and the Switching's for both monkeys; the performance comparison is reported. The legend calls panel b "not significant for either monkey" while printing p = 0.034 for Monkey P; recorded as printed.

claims.statement: Both monkeys perform well on the Ring dataset, with reaction-time variability like that on the Triangle dataset.
claims.source: Results, Replication of the Results with the Ring Dataset, paragraph 1; Figure 5a and 5b; Extended Data Fig. 9a and 9b (the Results cite "Extended Data Fig. 8a-b", but the per-monkey Ring figure is the ninth Extended Data legend)

The paper gives no number. Reproduced when the 2-object fraction correct is above chance (1/2) for both monkeys and each monkey's Ring reaction-time interquartile range is within a factor of 1.5 of its Triangle one; the factor is the agent's reading of "similar" and the ranges are reported. For reference, the paper's notebook printed P 0.958 and 0.903, E 0.945 and 0.756 for 1 and 2 objects with the code's radius.

claims.statement: Ring neurons in DMFC and FEF show a variety of spatial receptive fields and diverse delay-phase position and identity selectivities, as in the Triangle dataset.

claims.quote: These neurons showed a variety of spatial receptive fields in both DMFC and FEF ( Fig. 5c ; Extended Data Fig. 9c ) and diverse selectivities to position and identity in delay-phase firing rates ( Fig. 5d ), similar to the Triangle dataset
claims.criterion: Position and identity AUC (T6) of Ring units, judged as fig2b-selectivity-range. Tuning curves as Methods, Ring Dataset Tuning Curves (256 points on the ring, 100 bootstraps of 100 1-object trials, Gaussian kernel of 2.4 degrees); "variety" is judged by the preferred angles of units with significant position AUC, reproduced when in each area they fall in all three 120-degree sectors.

claims.statement: In the Ring dataset, noise correlation rises with signal correlation, as in the Triangle dataset.
claims.source: Results, Replication of the Results with the Ring Dataset, paragraph 1; Figure 5e; Extended Data Fig. 9d

claims.criterion: As Methods, Ring Dataset Signal and Noise Correlations (the Methods call it Fig. 5c), on pairs of Ring units: trials embedded in 6 dimensions (x and y of each fruit, 0 when absent); signal correlation on 1-object trials between one unit's rate and the other's on the nearest-neighbour trial. The noise correlation is open between (a) the Methods' wording, per 2-object trial the correlation of the two units over its 10 nearest-neighbour trials, averaged over trials, and (b) the paper's figures/figure_5/noise_correlations/run_compute_ring.py, each trial's rate minus the mean of its 10 neighbours, one Pearson correlation of these residuals across trials. Pairs kept with at least 50 1-object and 200 2-object trials (noise_correlations.ipynb); 8 bins of signal correlation with edges at linspace(-s, s, 9), s 0.8 for P and pooled, 0.3 for E. The paper gives no test. Reproduced when, per monkey, the mean noise correlation of the highest bin exceeds that of the lowest with non-overlapping 95% intervals; when the readings differ the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: On the Ring dataset the Gain model again has higher model likelihood than the Slot and Switching models, for both monkeys.

claims.statement: About 227 interneurons were imaged per mouse (226.6 ± 27.3, mean ± std over 16 mice), and 121.0 ± 28.4 per mouse were assigned a putative subtype.
claims.source: Results, Fast, targeted in vivo calcium imaging in 3D and post hoc molecular identification of CA1 INs, paragraph 1
claims.quote: total of 3626 INs in 16 mice, 226.6 ± 27.3 INs per mouse, mean ± std ... 1936 were assigned to a putative IN subtype identity (121.0 ± 28.4 per mouse, mean ± std)
claims.criterion: The tolerance is the paper's standard deviation over mice, since one mouse is compared with the spread across mice. Imaged interneurons are the ROIs in the files. Two readings of "assigned a subtype" are allowed, the ROIs labelled with one of the six subtypes of Figures 1 to 6, and all ROIs not labelled UNIDENTIFIED (which adds the label NOTHING).

claims.statement: The layer distribution of each subtype along the CA1 depth axis is consistent with earlier anatomical studies.
claims.source: Figure 1F
claims.quote: The overall proportion (Figure S1) and layer distribution of each of these subtypes was consistent with previous studies (Figure 1F)

claims.statement: The majority of interneurons were positively correlated with running velocity, and about 10% were negatively correlated, across all subtypes (156 negative and 1429 positive in Figure 2D).
claims.source: Results, Locomotion-state-dependent activity of molecularly identified IN subpopulations during spatial navigation, paragraph 1; Figure 2C, 2D
claims.quote: found that the majority of INs were positively correlated with velocity ... we also observed that ~10% of cells exhibited negative correlations, present across all subtypes (Figure 2C)
claims.criterion: The correlation of each ROI is the paper's (the signed Pearson r of largest absolute value over lags from -5 to +5 s), averaged over the sessions in which the ROI was imaged. Readings of the denominator allowed are all imaged ROIs and the ROIs in the six subtypes. The claim holds if more than half the ROIs are positive and the fraction negative is within the tolerance under either reading.

claims.statement: Negatively correlated cells were significantly enriched in CCKC, where nearly half of cells were more active during immobility.
claims.source: Results, Locomotion-state-dependent activity of molecularly identified IN subpopulations during spatial navigation, paragraph 1; Figure 2B, 2C
claims.quote: Negatively correlated cells were significantly enriched in CCKC, where nearly half of cells showed increased activity during immobility (Figure 2B, 2C)
claims.criterion: The fraction of CCKC with a negative correlation is at least 0.35, and higher than in the other five subtypes pooled with a one-sided Fisher exact test at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The correlation with velocity differs between the six subtypes (one-way ANOVA, p < 1e-10, with Tukey's post hoc test).
claims.source: Figure 2C legend
claims.quote: Pearson’s correlation coefficients of ΔF/F traces and velocity ... One-way ANOVA
claims.criterion: One-way ANOVA across the six subtypes at p < 0.05. The paper's p-value comes from seven mice and is not expected here. Tukey's test is shown.

claims.statement: IvC/NGFC were less modulated by locomotion than other subtypes.
claims.source: Results, Locomotion-state-dependent activity of molecularly identified IN subpopulations during spatial navigation, paragraph 1; Figure 2C
claims.quote: We also found that IvC/NGFC were less modulated by locomotion, consistent with previous results
claims.criterion: Two readings of "less modulated" are allowed, a lower correlation and a lower absolute correlation. Either holds if IvC/NGFC are lower than PVBC, SomC, BiC and AAC pooled (CCKC are left out, as their correlations are mixed in sign), with a one-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Negatively correlated cells were enriched in stratum oriens and positively correlated cells in stratum pyramidale.
claims.source: Figure 2D legend
claims.quote: Negatively correlated cells are more dorsal in stratum oriens than positively correlated cells, which are closer to stratum pyramidale

claims.statement: The activity of positively correlated cells followed changes in velocity by up to several seconds, while the activity of negatively correlated cells was more tightly linked in time to changes in velocity.
claims.source: Results, Locomotion-state-dependent activity of molecularly identified IN subpopulations during spatial navigation, paragraph 1 (Figure S2)
claims.quote: while the activity of positively correlated cells generally followed changes in velocity by up to several seconds, the activity of negatively correlated cells was more tightly linked in time to changes in velocity
claims.criterion: The lag is the one at which the correlation peaks (negative when activity lags velocity). The claim holds if the median lag of positively correlated ROIs is negative and the absolute lags of negatively correlated ROIs are smaller than those of positively correlated ROIs, with a one-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05. All imaged ROIs are used, as the claim is made regardless of subtype.

claims.statement: Run-start and run-stop responses show that immobility-triggered activation is specific to CCKC.
claims.source: Results, Locomotion-state-dependent activity of molecularly identified IN subpopulations during spatial navigation, paragraph 1 (Figure S2)
claims.quote: we calculated the average run-start and run-stop responses for each cell (Figure S2), which further detailed the unicity of immobility-triggered activation of CCKC
claims.criterion: The run-stop response (mean dF/F in the 3 s after the event minus the 3 s before) is positive on average for CCKC, and higher in CCKC than in the other five subtypes pooled with a one-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05. Events must be separated by "several seconds"; 5 s is used, and 3 s and 10 s are shown as variants.

claims.statement: A deep network classified PV-expressing, SOM-expressing, CCK and IvC/NGFC cells from dF/F, velocity and depth with accuracies of 64, 71, 60 and 59%.
claims.source: Results, Decoding of IN molecular identity with a machine-learning approach, paragraph 1 (Figure S3)
claims.quote: a 4-class problem consisting of, PV-expressing INs, SOM-expressing INs, CCKC, and IvC/NGFC. The classification showed higher accuracy (64%, 71% 60% and 59%, respectively)

claims.statement: During sharp-wave ripples PVBC were generally strongly modulated while most SomC were not.
claims.source: Figure 3D
claims.quote: PVBC were generally strongly modulated ... while most SomC were not

claims.statement: AAC and BiC showed bimodal modulation during sharp-wave ripples, and all subtypes but CCKC and IvC/NGFC split into a modulated and a non-modulated group.
claims.source: Figure 3E, 3F
claims.quote: AAC and BiC showed prominent bimodal profiles (Figure S4), with some cells strongly modulated during SWRs but others remaining silent ... All subtypes but CCKC and NGFC separated into 2 distinct groups

claims.statement: 17.5 ± 6.4% (mean ± sem over 6 mice, 3 sessions each) of interneurons, blind of subtype, passed the test for significant spatial selectivity.
claims.source: Results, Spatially selective activity dynamics of CA1 INs during head-fixed spatial navigation, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: spatially-selective INs (blind of subtype, 17.5 ± 6.4% in total passed the threshold, mean ± sem, n = 6 mice, 3 sessions per mouse)
claims.criterion: The fraction of imaged ROIs selected in each session, averaged over the three sessions. Two readings of the rule are allowed, with the peak above 100% dF/F and without the peak rule (in case the paper's dF/F was scaled differently). The claim holds if either is within the tolerance, the paper's sem.

claims.statement: 12.7 ± 8.3% of interneurons (mean ± sem) had negative spatial selectivity, slightly fewer than had positive selectivity.
claims.source: Results, Spatially selective activity dynamics of CA1 INs during head-fixed spatial navigation, paragraph 1 (Figure S5)
claims.quote: The fraction of negative spatially modulated cells was also slightly lower (blind of subtype, 12.7 ± 8.3%, mean ± sem, n = 6 mice, 3 sessions per mouse) than the fraction of positive spatially modulated cells
claims.criterion: The fraction of imaged ROIs with a negative field in each session, averaged over the three sessions, within the paper's sem.

claims.statement: Position decoded from the small subset of spatially selective interneurons was about as accurate as from all interneurons, and more accurate than from as many randomly chosen interneurons or with position shuffled.
claims.source: Figure 4D
claims.quote: Decoding accuracy originates mainly from spatially modulated cells, although they represent only a small fraction of all recorded interneurons
claims.criterion: Per session, a linear SVM decodes the position bin from lap-wise tuning curves, leaving one lap out. The selected subset is the cells with a positive field under the peak rule where a session has at least 5 of them, and otherwise without the peak rule. The claim holds in a session if the error from the subset is at most 1.25 times the error from all ROIs, below the mean error of 10 random subsets of the same size, and below the error with dF/F shifted circularly against position. It holds overall if it holds in at least two of the three sessions.

claims.statement: BiC had a higher probability than other subtypes of being spatially modulated again in other sessions.
claims.source: Figure 4E, bottom
claims.quote: BiC have a higher probability to stay spatially modulated on different sessions
claims.criterion: Needs at least 5 BiC imaged; otherwise blocked.

claims.statement: The selectivity index of spatially selective cells did not differ between subtypes (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.35).
claims.source: Figure 4F
claims.quote: SomC have a subset of cells with sharp fields but the mean is not different from that of the other subtypes (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.35)
claims.criterion: One-way ANOVA across subtypes of the selectivity index of cells with a positive field (averaged over the sessions in which a cell was selected), using the subtypes with at least 3 such cells. Selection follows the rule of fig4d-decoding (the peak rule unless it gives too few cells). Not found (p >= 0.05) is reproduced. If fewer than two subtypes have 3 cells, blocked.

claims.statement: Spatially selective PVBC had a more stable within-session recruitment (odd-even lap correlation of tuning curves) than spatially selective SomC.
claims.source: Results, Spatially selective activity dynamics of CA1 INs during head-fixed spatial navigation, paragraph 1; Figure 4H
claims.quote: spatially-selective PVBC displayed a significantly more stable within-session recruitment than spatially-selective SomC (Figure 4H)
claims.criterion: Needs at least 5 spatially selective PVBC and 5 SomC (selection as in fig4d-decoding); otherwise blocked. Holds if PVBC have the higher mean odd-even correlation and an unpaired t-test gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Within-session stability of tuning curves differed between subtypes, PVBC showing the highest and CCKC the lowest odd-even correlations.
claims.source: Results, Spatially selective activity dynamics of CA1 INs during head-fixed spatial navigation, paragraph 2 (Figure S6A, S6B)
claims.quote: While there were differences in within session stability across molecularly defined IN subtypes, with PVBC and CCKC showing the highest and lowest within-session correlations, respectively
claims.criterion: All imaged ROIs of each subtype, regardless of spatial selectivity, each ROI's correlation averaged over sessions. Holds if PVBC have the highest and CCKC the lowest mean among subtypes with at least 5 cells.

claims.statement: Tuning curve correlations of the same cells after 1 hour and after 24 hours were lower than within-session correlations, and still higher than chance.
claims.source: Results, Spatially selective activity dynamics of CA1 INs during head-fixed spatial navigation, paragraph 2 (Figure S6I)
claims.quote: Tuning curve correlations after both 1 hour and 24 hours were significantly lower than the within-session correlations across all IN subtypes ... correlations at later time points (1h and 24h) were still significantly higher than chance levels
claims.criterion: The same-day pair of sessions stands in for 1 hour and the pairs two days apart for 24 hours. The ROI with the same index is taken as the same cell, as the dandiset describes. Lower is a paired Wilcoxon test against the within-session correlation of the earlier session at p < 0.05. Chance is the mean correlation with cell identities shuffled; two readings are allowed, shuffling among all ROIs and shuffling within subtype. Above chance is p < 0.05 over 1000 shuffles. Both are tested on the ROIs in the six subtypes, and must hold for the same-day pair and for both two-day pairs.

claims.statement: Interneuron tuning curves decorrelated on exposure to a novel belt, more than with the passage of time, and context could be decoded from population activity.
claims.source: Figure 5B, 5C, 5D
claims.quote: INs displayed a significant decorrelation in their spatial tuning upon exposure to belt B (Figure 5B). This remapping could not be explained simply by the passage of time

claims.statement: PVBC, SomC, BiC and AAC decreased their activity in the first laps on a novel belt; CCKC were not modulated.
claims.source: Figure 5F, 5H
claims.quote: we observed a significant decrease in IN activity for the first several laps in context B for PVBC, SomC, BiC, and AAC subtypes (Figure 5F, H). CCKC were not modulated by the context change

claims.statement: In goal-oriented learning, SomC and BiC had higher reward modulation indices than other subtypes.

claims.quote: On average, SomC and BiC had significantly higher RMI values than the other subtypes, reflecting a preferential reward-related modulation (Figure 6D)

claims.statement: After the reward zone moved, SomC and BiC activity increased at the old zone above chance, and this decreased over the session.
claims.source: Figure 6G, 6H
claims.quote: observed a significant increase from chance level only in SomC and BiC (Figure 6G, S7) ... SomC and BiC activity levels gradually decreased and increased in the old and current reward zones, respectively (Figure 6H)

claims.statement: VIP+/CCK+ and VIP+/M2R+ cells were negatively correlated with velocity, and all ISI subtypes positively.
claims.source: Figure 7C
claims.quote: We observed that all ISI subtypes were positively correlated with velocity ... VIP+/CCK+ INs all exhibited negative velocity correlations and were more active during immobility ... all VIP+/M2R+ cells were activated during immobility (Figure 7C)

claims.statement: VIP+/CR- cells and type III ISIs were less correlated with SomC and BiC than with PV+ cells.
claims.source: Figure 7H, 7I
claims.quote: the activity dynamics of VIP+/CR− cells and Type III ISIs, but not Type I ISIs, were significantly less correlated with SomC and BiC than with perisomatic-targeting PV+ INs (PVBCs and AACs) (Figure 7H, 7I)

claims.statement: The human L1 patch-seq dataset has 250 cells passing transcriptomic quality, 194 with electrophysiology passing quality control and 71 reconstructed; by subclass, 96 LAMP5, 35 MC4R, 33 PAX6, 15 L1 VIP and 15 other cells have electrophysiology.
claims.source: Results, L1 patch-seq pipeline and transcriptomic references, paragraph 4; Table S2
claims.quote: All cells were filtered for transcriptomic (n=250) and electrophysiological quality (n=194), and a subset of neurons (n=71) with sufficient cell labeling were imaged at high resolution
claims.criterion: Counts of dandiset cells in the primary set P (strict L1 set, AIBS, long-square features extracted) that belong to one of the ten L1 t-types (homology_type set), overall and by homology_type; this is Table S2's "ephys cell count", as summarize() in l1_cross_species.ipynb cells 8 and 9 computes it over combined_l12, which drops cells without a homology_type. Reproduced when every count is within its tolerance. The 250 and 71 counts need transcriptomes and reconstructions and are not tested here; the count of dandiset files not in P is reported.

claims.statement: In transcriptomic reference data, many human L1 t-types form separated clusters while mouse L1 t-types vary more continuously, suggesting stronger transcriptomic specialization in human L1.
claims.source: Results, L1 patch-seq pipeline and transcriptomic references, paragraph 1; Figure 1A
claims.quote: many human t-types formed separated clusters, with others clustered in groups of related t-types, whereas mouse L1 t-types showed more continuous variability
claims.criterion: The paper shows this with UMAP projections and reports no test or measure for the contrast. A reading named here, not the paper's test, uses the paper's transcriptomic d' (Methods, Discriminant analysis, NB d' on the reference data, as used for Fig. 1B); reproduced when the median pairwise d' among human L1 t-types exceeds that among mouse L1 t-types.

claims.statement: Ten human and eight mouse L1 t-types are defined from the references; grouping human t-types with d' below 2.2 forms three subclasses, leaving three t-types ungrouped.
claims.source: Results, L1 patch-seq pipeline and transcriptomic references, paragraph 1; Figure 1B; Methods, Subclasses and cross-species homology
claims.quote: we identified 10 L1 t-types in human and 8 in mouse ... This formed three subclasses, with three t-types remaining ungrouped
claims.criterion: Tolerances are zero because these are counts of categories that define the taxonomy; a 10% tolerance would admit no other integer. L1 t-types are those making up more than 5% of L1 cells or with more than 50% of the type in L1 dissections (Methods); subclasses group t-type pairs with NB-discriminant d' < 2.2 (Methods).

claims.statement: Cross-species matching of mouse t-types to human subclasses gives four homology-driven subclasses; two human L1 t-types (SST BAGE2, VIP PCDH20) are homologous to deeper-layer mouse types and are left out.
claims.source: Results, L1 patch-seq pipeline and transcriptomic references, paragraph 3; Figure 1D
claims.quote: These matches resulted in four homology-driven subclasses (called subclasses hereafter) with proportions largely comparable across species ... Two additional human L1 t-types (SST BAGE2 and VIP PCDH20) were excluded from cross-species L1 subclasses because of their homology to t-types found in deeper layers, but not L1 of mouse neocortex

claims.statement: Subclass proportions in the L1 patch-seq data differ between human and mouse for every subclass except L1 VIP, PAX6 being the notable difference.
claims.source: Figure 1E legend; Results, L1 patch-seq pipeline and transcriptomic references, paragraph 3
claims.quote: All cross-species proportion differences (except L1 VIP) significant at FDR-corrected p<0.001, one vs. rest Fisher’s exact tests
claims.criterion: As l1_proportions.ipynb cells 47 and 48 (fisher_test_all). Human cells of the strict set with soma in L1 (strict_l1, layer 1, border cells left out); mouse patch-seq cells with layer_ccf or layer_lims 1 from the full mouse metadata; categories LAMP5, MC4R, PAX6, L1 VIP, other L1 t-types and deeper t-types (cells with no homology_type). For each category a two-sided Fisher's exact test of species against in category or not; Benjamini-Hochberg across categories. Reproduced when every category but L1 VIP has FDR p < 0.001 and L1 VIP does not.

claims.statement: Compared with snRNA-seq, patch-seq sampled fewer SST BAGE2 and more PAX6 CDH12 and VIP TSPAN12 cells; MERFISH proportions did not differ from patch-seq.
claims.source: Results, L1 patch-seq pipeline and transcriptomic references, paragraph 6; Figure S2A
claims.quote: patch-seq had fewer SST BAGE2 cells and more PAX6 CDH12 and VIP TSPAN12 compared to snRNA-seq (p<0.05, False discovery rate or FDR-corrected Fisher’s exact test). MERFISH had intermediate proportions of SST BAGE2 with no significant differences compared to patch-seq (p>0.18)

claims.statement: Marker gene expression by t-type correlates strongly between patch-seq and the snRNA-seq reference (r = 0.84).
claims.source: Figure S1D legend; Results, L1 patch-seq pipeline and transcriptomic references, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Correlation of marker gene expression between patch-seq and snRNA-seq reference (r=0.84, p<10-18)

claims.statement: Human L1 subclasses differ in electrophysiology, notably in sag and initial firing rate (Kruskal-Wallis, FDR-corrected p < 1e-7).
claims.source: Results, Morpho-electric diversity in human L1, paragraph 1; Figure 2C
claims.quote: Electrophysiologically, subclasses were distinguished by subthreshold properties such as sag ... as well as several suprathreshold properties including firing rate ... Electrophysiological and morphological features distinguishing L1 subclasses (KW test, FDR-corrected p<10−7 for electrophysiology
claims.criterion: As l1_subclass_distinctness.ipynb cells 8 and 10 (run_kw_dunn), which wrote Data S2. Cells in P of the four core subclasses; features with more than 40% non-missing values among l1_type cells of P; per feature a Kruskal-Wallis test across subclasses, epsilon2 = H/(n-1), Benjamini-Hochberg across features; Dunn's post hoc tests on significant features, FDR across pairs (Methods and legend; the code's cell 10 runs pairwise Mann-Whitney tests instead, posthoc='mw_full', shown as a variant). Sag is IPFX sag at the hyperpolarizing sweep closest to -100 mV; initial firing rate is first_isi_inv_hero (inverse first ISI at rheobase + 40 pA), as Fig. 2C plots (O1). Reproduced when both have FDR p < 1e-7; partially reproduced when both have FDR p < 0.05 but not both below 1e-7.

claims.statement: LAMP5 cells show small sag and adaptation, PAX6 cells minimal sag and a high initial firing rate, while MC4R and L1 VIP cells show strong sag.
claims.source: Results, Morpho-electric diversity in human L1, paragraph 2; Figure 2B and 2C
claims.quote: Their electrophysiological phenotype was relatively undistinguished, with firing-rate adaptation and sag present but small ... along with minimal sag and high initial firing rate at the onset of response to depolarizing current injection ... MC4R cells had extremely compact ball-like axonal arbors, along with strong sag ... with a consistent stellate-like dendrite morphology and high sag
claims.criterion: On the cells and features of fig2c-subclass-ephys-differences. Reproduced when (i) the median sag of MC4R and of L1 VIP each exceeds that of LAMP5 and of PAX6, (ii) PAX6 has the lowest median sag of the four, and (iii) PAX6 has the highest median first_isi_inv_hero. Not reproduced otherwise. Dunn's FDR-corrected p for each pair is reported; the paper states the ordering in words and reports no pairwise values in the text read.

claims.statement: Spike adaptation properties are strongly and inversely related to sag across human L1 cells (R2 = 0.74).
claims.source: Results, Morpho-electric diversity in human L1, paragraph 1; Figure S3A legend
claims.quote: Spike adaptation properties showed a strong inverse relationship with sag across the dataset (Fig. S3A)
claims.criterion: As l1_subclass_distinctness.ipynb cells 8, 16 and 17. Cells in P with l1_type (the five groups, other included); OLS of upstroke_adapt_ratio on sag with HC3 errors (run_regressions). Reproduced when R2 is within tolerance and p < 1e-13, and cells with more sag show less change of spike upstroke from the first to the third spike. The ratio's order is open (O1); the direction is judged on the change, whichever order the ratio has, and the slope's sign is reported with the order used.

claims.statement: Within the LAMP5 subclass, sag and initial firing rate decrease from the NMBR to the DBP to the LCP2 t-type.
claims.source: Results, Morpho-electric diversity in human L1, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
claims.quote: Within the LAMP5 subclass, sag and initial firing rate decreased from the NMBR t-type to DBP to LCP2 t-types ... Spearman correlation FDR-corrected p<10−3
claims.criterion: As l1_subclass_distinctness.ipynb cell 59. All LAMP5 cells of the strict L1 set (the code does not restrict to P), t-type coded in the order LCP2, DBP, NMBR; Spearman correlation of each feature whose name has no "3" with that code (run_correlations), Benjamini-Hochberg across features. Reproduced when sag and first_isi_inv_hero each have FDR p < 0.001 and a positive Spearman rho with that code (values decreasing from NMBR to DBP to LCP2). If the dandiset lacks the Amsterdam and Szeged LAMP5 cells the code includes, the test runs on what it holds and the notes say so; the same test on P alone is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Human L1 subclasses differ morphologically in vertical orientation of axons and dendrites, axon extent and shape, and dendrite branching (Kruskal-Wallis, FDR p < 1e-3).
claims.source: Results, Morpho-electric diversity in human L1, paragraph 1; Figure 2D
claims.quote: Morphologically, subclasses were distinguished by vertical orientation of axons and dendrites, axon extent and shape, and dendrite branching

claims.statement: No electrophysiological feature of human L1 cells differs with donor medical condition, sex or age after FDR correction.
claims.source: Results, Morpho-electric diversity in human L1, paragraph 3; Figure S6A and S6B legends
claims.quote: AP width (upper right) was the only significant electrophysiology feature (MW p=0.03, NS after FDR correction)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests. As l1_metadata_effects.ipynb cells 50 and 51 (medical condition), 99 and 100 (sex), 108 to 110 (age) and the Methods (Statistical analysis of variability). Cells of the strict L1 set with l1_type, AIBS and long-square features extracted; features with more than 40% non-missing values. Medical condition as epileptic or not (code's epileptic(), from the medical_conditions column) and sex, each by two-sided exact Mann-Whitney tests; age by Spearman correlation, where the code (run_correlations, default filter_dropouts) first drops features with fewer than 5 values above 1; Benjamini-Hochberg across features within each variable. The code takes condition, sex and age from LIMS donor records; the public table's medical_conditions, donor_sex and donor_age columns stand in for them. Reproduced when no feature has FDR p < 0.05 for any of the three; not reproduced when any does. The smallest uncorrected p and its feature are reported for each.

claims.statement: Cells from tumor patients have higher dendritic branching than cells from epilepsy patients, not explained by brain area or subclass.
claims.source: Results, Morpho-electric diversity in human L1, paragraph 3; Figure S6A
claims.quote: with the exception of higher dendritic branching in cells from tumor patients compared to epilepsy patients

claims.statement: Some electrophysiological features of human L1 cells, including input resistance, vary with brain region; sparsely sampled regions either match MTG or have larger input resistance.
claims.source: Results, Cross-species differences in L1, paragraph 2; Figure S6C
claims.quote: We also explored dependence of L1 interneuron morpho-electric properties on brain region within our human data and found moderate effects on a set of features including dendrite extent and input resistance (Fig. S6C). The other features of Fig. S6C (sag_peak_t, downstroke_rheo, avg_rate_max) are reported.

The ANOVA follows O2, readings (a) and (b). Features as Fig. 3D plots them, sag, rheobase_i and peak_deltav_ramp (AP height). claims.statement: The human versus mouse electrophysiological differences found against VISp are replicated against mouse TEa, so they are not regional.

The features shown are the distinct top features by r (select_distinct, Spearman threshold 0.8), ranked by (a) the effect against TEa, as the Fig. 3E legend says ("Features selected by largest effect size against TEa"), or (b) the effect against VIS, as the code does (cell 22). claims.statement: In nucleated patches, mouse L1 neurons (only LAMP5 cells were sampled in mouse) have much higher A-type K+ conductance than human, with comparable D-type conductance.

claims.criterion: The paper reports no test for this panel. Conductance per the Methods (Voltage clamp experiments) from the nucleated-patch sweeps, IKA as total minus current after a step to -20 mV, IKD as that current minus the sustained current, conductance with EK = -100 mV, divided by patch surface area. Which step gives each cell's value is not fixed; readings (a) the +70 mV step, (b) the maximum over steps. Compared with the paper's cross-species test, two-sided Mann-Whitney (Methods). Reproduced when, under both readings, mouse A-type density is higher at p < 0.05 and D-type does not differ at p < 0.05. Needs the nucleated-patch sweeps in the dandiset, the patch diameters (measured from images, Fig. 3F) and mouse LAMP5 recordings whose deposit the paper does not name; the claim is blocked for whichever is missing.

claims.statement: Human and mouse L1 subclasses have a similar amount of morpho-electric variability but along different features; sag and spike shape adaptation vary in human but little in mouse, while ISI adaptation and AHP vary in mouse.
claims.source: Results, Cross-species differences in L1, paragraph 4; Figure 3G
claims.quote: we found that the two species had a similar amount of variability (number of significantly different features and their effect size) but varied along different sets of features (Fig. 3G). The most distinct features in human, like sag and spike shape adaptation, showed little variability in mouse, and unlike in human, mouse subclasses varied physiologically in ISI adaptation and spike after-hyperpolarization (AHP) properties
claims.criterion: Electrophysiology only. As l1_subclass_distinctness.ipynb cells 10 and 37. Human, the set of fig2c-subclass-ephys-differences; mouse, VISp cells of the strict mouse set with l1_type and features more than 40% non-missing; per species a Kruskal-Wallis test per feature across subclasses, epsilon2 = H/(n-1), Benjamini-Hochberg. Reproduced when (i) sag and upstroke_adapt_ratio have FDR p < 0.05 in human and a smaller epsilon2 in mouse, and (ii) at least one ISI adaptation feature (isi_adapt_ratio, adapt_mean or adapt_hero) and one AHP feature (fast_trough_deltav_rheo, fast_trough_deltav_hero, trough_slowdeltav_rheo, trough_slowdeltav_hero or ahp_delay_ratio_hero) have FDR p < 0.05 in mouse and a larger epsilon2 than in human. "Similar amount" is not defined by the paper; the count of FDR significant features and their mean epsilon2 are reported for both species and called similar when each mouse value is within 10% of the human one, a reading named here, not part of the outcome.

claims.statement: MC4R (rosehip) cells are distinguished from the rest of human L1 by strong sag and by irregular firing (Mann-Whitney, FDR p < 1e-4).
claims.source: Figure 4B legend; Results, Rosehip cells, paragraph 1

claims.criterion: As l1_rosehip.ipynb cell 6. AIBS cells of the strict L1 set, in group against all other cells of that set; two-sided exact Mann-Whitney per feature (run_twosamp), Benjamini-Hochberg across all features. Features of Fig. 4B, sag and ir_late_mean (irregularity ratio, O1). The group is read as (a) the MC4R subclass, as the code does, or (b) each MC4R t-type in turn, as the legend's "MC4R t-types" allows. Reproduced when, under a reading, both features have FDR p < 1e-4 with the group higher.

claims.statement: Both rosehip t-types have strong sag, but only ADARB2 MC4R fires irregularly, with stronger and faster sag than SST CHRNA4.
claims.source: Results, Rosehip cells, paragraph 1; Figure 4B

Cells of P grouped as LAMP5, SST CHRNA4, ADARB2 MC4R, PAX6, L1 VIP (other left out); Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn's tests on the seven pairs the code lists (each MC4R t-type against LAMP5, PAX6 and L1 VIP, and CHRNA4 against ADARB2), Benjamini-Hochberg across pairs. Reproduced when (i) ADARB2 MC4R has a higher ir_late_mean than SST CHRNA4 with FDR p < 0.05, (ii) SST CHRNA4's ir_late_mean does not exceed LAMP5's, PAX6's or L1 VIP's with FDR p < 0.05, (iii) both MC4R t-types have a higher median sag than LAMP5 and PAX6, and (iv) ADARB2 MC4R has a higher median sag and faster sag than SST CHRNA4. The paper does not define "faster"; readings (a) shorter median sag_peak_t (time to the sag peak), (b) shorter median sag_tau (Table S1, "rapid time constant"); when they give different outcomes the claim is methods_underspecified with both shown. The Dunn p for every pair is reported.

claims.statement: PAX6 TNFAIP8L3 cells are distinguished from all other human L1 cells by a high initial firing rate at rheobase and an after-depolarization following the last spike.

claims.statement: Pairwise electrophysiological distinctness (d') of human L1 t-types is smaller within subclasses than between them; the only within-subclass pair with high d' is LAMP5 NMBR against LAMP5 LCP2.
claims.source: Results, Cross-modality relationships of L1 subclasses and t-types, paragraph 1; Figure 6A
claims.quote: The resulting t-type similarity matrices (Fig. 6A) showed comparable subclass structure in both electrophysiology and transcriptomics, with smaller d’ values within subclass blocks and higher values outside ... The single within-subclass pair with a high d’ was LAMP5 NMBR and LAMP5 LCP2
claims.criterion: As l1_dprime.ipynb cells 9 to 13 and cluster_pairs.py. Cells of P; t-types with at least 5 cells (code) or at least 4 (legend, "Groups with N<4 excluded"), both run; features more than 80% non-missing; RobustScaler, KNN imputation, per-feature LocalOutlierFactor < -20 set missing, KNN imputation again; for each t-type pair a random forest (scikit-learn defaults, class_weight balanced_subsample) scored by 5-fold stratified cross_val_predict probabilities; d' = sqrt(2) times the inverse normal of the ROC AUC, AUC of 1 replaced by (n-1)/n. Random seeds are a standard choice (unset in the code); the matrix is reported for the seed used. "High" is not fixed; readings (a) d' >= 2.2, the Methods' threshold for grouping t-types, (b) d' above the median between-subclass d'. Reproduced when, under both readings, NMBR-LCP2 is the only within-subclass pair that is high and the mean within-subclass d' is below the mean between-subclass d'. Within-subclass pairs are those inside LAMP5, MC4R and PAX6 (other is not a subclass, as get_distances in the code treats it).

claims.statement: Electrophysiological and transcriptomic d' of human L1 t-type pairs are correlated (Pearson r = 0.59, p = 0.00016).
claims.source: Results, Cross-modality relationships of L1 subclasses and t-types, paragraph 1; Figure 6B
claims.quote: d’ metrics were highly correlated between modalities, demonstrating that cell types with distinctive transcriptomes have similarly distinctive electrophysiological properties (Pearson r=0.59, p=0.00016
claims.criterion: As l1_dprime.ipynb cells 49 to 51 and 83. Electrophysiology d' from fig6a-ephys-dprime-subclass-structure (code reading, at least 5 cells); patch-seq transcriptomic d' from the zero-inflated negative binomial discriminant (Methods) on the human MTG marker genes, over t-types of l1_type cells; Pearson r over the t-type pairs present in both matrices. The input scale is open; readings (a) CPM, as the Methods say for d' analyses, (b) log(CPM+1), as the code passes. The number of folds differs; readings (i) 5, as the Methods give for the d' cross-validation, (ii) 4, as the code passes (cell 51). Reproduced when, under every combination of these readings, r is within tolerance and p < 0.05. The ZINB curve fits (zinb_human.h5) are not public; they are refitted as the Methods describe (phi by spline, pi by sigmoid against the NB mean) and the notes say so.

claims.statement: Subclasses are more transcriptomically distinct in human than mouse, and in mouse the VIP subclass is highly distinct in all modalities while the others are less so.
claims.source: Results, Cross-modality relationships of L1 subclasses and t-types, paragraph 1; Figure 6C
claims.quote: These results confirmed the generally higher transcriptomic distinctness of subclasses in human and show that in mouse the VIP subclass was highly distinct in all modalities, with other subclasses generally less distinct

claims.statement: Two-cluster Gaussian mixtures on the best pair of electrophysiological features recover each subclass with F1 scores of 0.81 (LAMP5), 0.69 (MC4R), 0.89 (PAX6) and 0.5 (all others).
claims.source: Results, Cross-modality relationships of L1 subclasses and t-types, paragraph 2; Figure 6D legend
claims.quote: F1 scores ... LAMP5 0.81, MC4R 0.69, PAX6 0.89, all others 0.5
claims.criterion: As clustering_classification.ipynb cells 16 to 21 and clustering.py. Cells of P with l1_type and soma in L1; features more than 60% non-missing; Yeo-Johnson power transform and KNN imputation (the legend confirms Yeo-Johnson); L1 VIP and other merged as "all others". For each group, every single feature and every pair, a 2-component Gaussian mixture (k-means init, 5 inits) fitted to the unlabelled data, the component holding most of the group's cells taken as the group, F1 against the labels; the best subspace (1 or 2 features) is kept. Preprocessing follows O3; readings (a) and (b). Random seed 0 as the code sets. Reproduced when, under both readings, all four F1 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when three are.

claims.statement: A multi-class classifier assigns human L1 subclasses from electrophysiology with 82% cross-validated accuracy, balanced across subclasses.
claims.source: Results, Cross-modality relationships of L1 subclasses and t-types, paragraph 2; Figure S8A
claims.quote: A multi-class classifier evaluated by cross-validation on the primary dataset had 82% accuracy balanced across subclasses
claims.criterion: As clustering_classification.ipynb cells 26 to 35 and 44 to 45, and the Methods (Clustering and classification). Cells of the strict L1 set in the four core subclasses with soma in L1, AIBS and long-square features extracted; logistic regression with balanced class weights after RobustScaler and KNN imputation, preprocessing per O3; repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation (scikit-learn defaults, 10 repeats). The number can be read several ways, each run; features (a) those more than 50% non-missing at every site (cell 45), (b) the site-aligned subset (cell 35, see figs8b-classifier-holdout); score (i) accuracy, as the code prints, (ii) balanced accuracy, the mean diagonal of the row-normalized confusion matrix, as the text's "balanced across subclasses" allows. Reproduced when any reading is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Trained on the primary dataset with site-dependent features excluded, the classifier reaches 81% accuracy on held-out cells recorded at other sites.
claims.source: Results, Cross-modality relationships of L1 subclasses and t-types, paragraph 2; Figure S8B
claims.quote: After excluding features for which the distributions strongly differed from the primary dataset, we found comparable classification performance (81%, Fig. S8B)
claims.criterion: As clustering_classification.ipynb cells 26 to 38 and the Methods. Features more than 50% non-missing at every site; a one-way ANOVA (OLS, HC3) of each on site (AIBS, Amsterdam, Szeged), features with p < 0.05 or R2 > 0.05 excluded (Methods; the code keeps p > 0.05 and R2 < 0.05, the same rule); classifier as figs8a-classifier-cv fitted on all AIBS cells; scored on the Amsterdam and Szeged cells of the four core subclasses with soma in L1. Score readings (i) accuracy, as the code prints, (ii) balanced accuracy. Reproduced when either is within tolerance. The held-out cells are part of the paper's recordings; if the dandiset does not hold them the claim is blocked data_missing.

claims.statement: At a 180 degree change of field direction (near the base electrodes), paired-pulse trains give less YP uptake than single-pulse trains, 2-fold less at 1 Hz and 20-fold less at 833 kHz.
claims.source: Results, 2.1, paragraph 3; Figure 2
claims.quote: Maximum cancellation was expectedly observed at the 180° vector change, reducing YP uptake compared to single-pulse trains 2-fold at 1 Hz and as much as 20-fold at 833 kHz
claims.criterion: From the Figure 2 legend and Results 2.1, per ROI along the bisecting line, the paired-pulse YP value as % of the single-pulse value in the same ROI, at each frequency, under normalization readings (i) and (ii), with each ROI's angle under the angle readings of the opening comment. The fold value is 100 divided by that %. "At the 180 degree vector change" is read as (1) the ROI of largest angle (nearest the base) or (2) the ROI of lowest mean value ("maximum cancellation"); these are readings of the reported numbers and a value holds when it matches under any of them with either normalization. Reproduced when both values hold, under each background reading; blocked as methods_underspecified when background readings (a) and (b) give different outcomes.

claims.statement: Cancellation weakens as the angle is reduced, and paired and single pulses become equally effective at about 160 degrees at 1 Hz and about 130 degrees at 833 kHz.
claims.source: Results, 2.1, paragraph 3; Figure 2
claims.quote: Cancellation weakened as the angle was reduced, and at about 160° (1 Hz) or 130° (833 kHz), the effects of paired-pulse trains became the same as those of single-pulse ones
claims.criterion: Measure as in fig2-180-cancellation. The crossover is the largest angle at which the mean paired-pulse value reaches 100%, found by linear interpolation between neighboring ROIs. The paper does not say how it was located; interpolation is a standard choice that cannot move the angle by more than one ROI spacing. The weakening of cancellation is shown by the value rising from below 100% at 180 degrees to 100% at the crossover and is not tested apart. Reproduced when both angles are within tolerance under one normalization reading at least, under each background reading; blocked as methods_underspecified when background readings (a) and (b) give different outcomes.
