SST subclass reconstructions, morphology features z-scored; for each DBC, the fraction of its 5 nearest SST neighbours (feature space and a default umap-learn embedding) that are DBCs. Reproduced when the mean fraction is at least twice the DBC share of SST reconstructions in both spaces. The hedged separation by t-type is not judged; the fraction of each DBC's DBC neighbours of its own t-type is reported.

claims.statement: The analyses of PRF at constant 200 us pulse duration rest on 1,050 S1 RSUs, 247 S1 FSUs, 913 POm RSUs and 106 POm FSUs, and the 3000 Hz and 30 Hz sessions of Figure 4 on 312 and 148 S1 RSUs, 54 and 61 S1 FSUs, 233 and 189 POm RSUs, and 17 and 43 POm FSUs.
claims.source: Figure 4 legend; Figure 6 legend
claims.quote: There are 312 RSUs and 54 FSUs recorded from S1, 233 RSUs and 17 FSUs recorded from POm for PRF 3,000 Hz. There are 148 RSUs and 61 FSUs recorded from S1 and189 RSUs and 43 FSUs recorded from POm for PRF 30 Hz
claims.criterion: Units and cell types by Method S (opening comment), readings K1 and K2, counted per session and condition. Each count is matched when it is within tolerance under one reading. Reproduced when at least 10 of the 12 counts match, partially reproduced for 6 to 9, not reproduced below 6. The per-condition counts the Results give for Figures 6 to 9 are reported alongside. This claim checks the selection that the other claims use.

claims.statement: With tFUS at 3000 Hz PRF and 60% DC targeting S1, S1 RSUs increase their firing during sonication.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
claims.quote: RSUs from S1 (n = 312, p = 3.13 × 10−7) and POm (n = 233, p = 0.0003) were both activated during 3,000 Hz PRF sonication
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 RSUs of the 3000 Hz 60% DC sessions. Kruskal-Wallis across the pre-stimulus and the post-onset 67 ms windows to 268 ms, then the 0 to 67 ms window against baseline, one-tailed for an increase. Reproduced when the post hoc test gives corrected p < 0.01 under every reading.

claims.statement: With 3000 Hz PRF tFUS on S1, POm RSUs are activated during sonication, synchronized with S1 RSUs.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4B
claims.quote: RSUs from S1 (n = 312, p = 3.13 × 10−7) and POm (n = 233, p = 0.0003) were both activated during 3,000 Hz PRF sonication
claims.criterion: As fig4-s1-rsu-timelocked-3000, for POm RSUs of the same sessions. Reproduced when the 0 to 67 ms window is significantly above baseline (corrected p < 0.01) under every reading.

claims.statement: After 3000 Hz PRF sonication, S1 RSUs, POm RSUs and S1 FSUs show delayed activation from about 134 ms.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4A and 4B
claims.quote: Postsonication activations were presented for S1 RSUs (p = 5 × 10−18), POm RSUs (p = 0.0007), and S1 FSUs (n = 54, p = 4.03 × 10−8) from 134 ms
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), 3000 Hz 60% DC sessions. The paper says the activations start from 134 ms but not which window its p-values come from; the readings are the 134 to 201 ms window and the 201 to 268 ms window. Reproduced when, under one of these windows and every reading of Method S, each of the three groups is significantly above baseline (one-tailed, corrected p < 0.01); partially reproduced when two of the three are.

claims.statement: With 30 Hz PRF and 0.6% DC, S1 RSUs show an inhibitory response just after sonication (67 to 134 ms).
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4A, right
claims.quote: At 30 Hz PRF, the S1 RSUs showed an inhibitory response after sonication (67–134 ms, n = 148, p = 0.0029)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 RSUs of the 30 Hz 0.6% DC sessions, window 67 to 134 ms against baseline, one-tailed for a decrease. Reproduced when corrected p < 0.01 under every reading.

claims.statement: With 30 Hz PRF, POm RSUs show delayed excitatory activity at 134 to 268 ms.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4B legend
claims.quote: POm RSUs expressed delayed excitatory activities (n = 189, p = 2 × 10−9)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), POm RSUs of the 30 Hz 0.6% DC sessions. The legend places the activity at 134 to 268 ms; the readings are the 134 to 201 ms window, the 201 to 268 ms window, and one 134 ms window from 134 to 268 ms. Reproduced when, under one window and every reading of Method S, the increase over baseline has corrected p < 0.01.

claims.statement: S1 FSUs show no time-locked response to 3000 Hz PRF, and S1 FSUs at 30 Hz and POm FSUs at both PRFs show no activity change.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: There was no activity change among S1 FSUs (n = 61) to 30 Hz PRF and POm FSUs to both PRFs (3,000 Hz, n = 17; 30 Hz, n = 43)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, Method S (opening comment): the post hoc one-tailed Wilcoxon test against baseline at corrected p < 0.01 in each 67 ms window from 0 to 268 ms (for S1 FSUs at 3000 Hz, the 0 to 67 ms window only, as the Results limit it to time-locked responses), testing both an increase and a decrease. Reproduced when no window is significant for S1 FSUs at 30 Hz, POm FSUs at 3000 Hz, POm FSUs at 30 Hz, and S1 FSUs at 3000 Hz during sonication; not reproduced when any is. The mean normalized rates are reported either way. The readings of Method S apply as in the other claims.

claims.statement: In sham sessions without tFUS, S1 and POm RSUs and FSUs show no time-locked and no delayed (201 to 268 ms) change.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 5A
claims.quote: In sham condition (no tFUS), S1 neurons and POm neurons showed no time-locked (S1 RSUs: n = 31, p = 1.0; S1 FSUs: n = 53, p = 0.55; POm RSUs: n = 67, p = 1.0; POm FSUs: n = 67, p = 1.0) and delayed
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, Method S (opening comment), sham sessions aligned on their trial event times: one-tailed post hoc Wilcoxon test against baseline at corrected p < 0.01 in the 0 to 67 ms and 201 to 268 ms windows, for the four groups, testing both an increase and a decrease (the paper states no change and not the tail). Reproduced when none of these tests is significant; not reproduced when any is. The unit counts are reported against the expected values; they do not decide the claim.

claims.statement: With tFUS steered to the cingulate cortex (CG1) at 3000 Hz PRF, S1 and POm RSUs and FSUs show no time-locked and no delayed (201 to 268 ms) change.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 5B
claims.quote: In control condition (tFUS targeted at CG1), S1 neurons and POm neurons showed no time-locked (S1 RSUs: n = 12, p = 1.0; S1 FSUs: n = 34, p = 1.0; POm RSUs: n = 55, p = 1.0; POm FSUs: n = 42, p = 0.33) and delayed responses
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged as fig5-sham-no-response on the CG1 control sessions, both tails. Reproduced when none of the tests is significant at corrected p < 0.01; not reproduced when any is.

claims.statement: At constant 200 us pulse duration, time-locked responses of S1 RSUs are elicited only by the high PRFs (1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz), with the highest level at 1500 Hz (123.34 +/- 4.3%), and S1 RSU responses during sonication differ across PRFs.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6A
claims.quote: time-locked S1 RSUs’ responses could only be elicited from high PRFs: 1,500 Hz (n = 284, p = 2.74 × 10−6 compared with baseline), 3,000 Hz (n = 312, p = 3.13 × 10−7), and 4,500 Hz (n = 152, p = 0.0028), among which 1,500 Hz evoked highest response level of 123.34 ± 4.3%
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 RSUs of the five PRF sessions at 200 us pulse duration, window 0 to 67 ms. Kruskal-Wallis across the five PRFs at p < 0.01; one-tailed post hoc tests against baseline for an increase at corrected p < 0.01. Tolerance on the mean is the paper's stated SEM. Reproduced when, under every reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test is significant, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz are significant and 30 and 300 Hz are not, and the highest mean is at 1500 Hz; partially reproduced when the significance pattern holds but the highest mean is elsewhere or out of tolerance.

claims.statement: Delayed responses (201 to 268 ms) of S1 RSUs appear at PRFs above 30 Hz and are highest at 4500 Hz (148.39 +/- 5.41%), and differ across PRFs.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6A legend
claims.quote: The delayed responses (201–268 ms) of RSUs could be observed at PRFs higher than 30 Hz and the highest response occurred at 4,500 Hz (148.39 ± 5.41%)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), as fig6a-s1-rsu-timelocked-high-prf, window 201 to 268 ms. Reproduced when, under every reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test across PRFs has p < 0.01, 300, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz are significantly above baseline and 30 Hz is not, and the highest mean, at 4500 Hz, is within tolerance; partially reproduced when the significance pattern holds and the mean does not.

claims.statement: S1 FSUs show no time-locked response to any PRF, and delayed responses only at PRFs higher than 1500 Hz, highest at 4500 Hz (158.75 +/- 10.75%).
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6B
claims.quote: FSUs did not show time-locked responses to any PRFs and only presented delayed responses at PRFs higher than 1,500 Hz, with the highest response level at 4,500 Hz (158.75 ± 10.75%)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 FSUs of the PRF sessions at 200 us pulse duration. "Higher than 1,500 Hz" can be read as (a) 3000 and 4500 Hz or (b) 1500 Hz and above. Reproduced when, under every reading of Method S, no PRF is significantly above baseline at 0 to 67 ms, the delayed responses at 201 to 268 ms are significant for exactly the PRFs of (a) or of (b), the Kruskal-Wallis across PRFs at 201 to 268 ms has p < 0.01, and the 4500 Hz mean is the highest and within tolerance; partially reproduced when all but the mean hold.

claims.statement: Time-locked responses of POm RSUs are elicited by 1500 and 3000 Hz PRFs, and POm RSU responses during sonication differ across PRFs.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6C
claims.quote: time-locked responses (Fig. 6B) from POm RSUs could be elicited by 1,500 Hz (n = 153, p = 0.003) and 3,000 Hz PRFs (n = 233, p = 0.0003)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), POm RSUs of the PRF sessions at 200 us pulse duration, window 0 to 67 ms. Reproduced when, under every reading, the Kruskal-Wallis across PRFs has p < 0.01 and 1500 and 3000 Hz are significantly above baseline while 30, 300 and 4500 Hz are not; partially reproduced when 1500 and 3000 Hz are significant and another PRF is too.

claims.statement: Delayed responses (201 to 268 ms) of POm RSUs are induced by PRFs from 1500 Hz up and are highest at 1500 Hz (141.68 +/- 2.38%).
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6C legend
claims.quote: the delayed responses (201–268 ms) of POm RSUs were induced by PRFs higher than 1,500 Hz and were highest (141.68 ± 2.38%) at 1,500 Hz
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), POm RSUs, window 201 to 268 ms. The sentence says "higher than 1,500 Hz" and that the highest response is at 1500 Hz, so the reading taken is 1500 Hz and above (Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 2, says the delayed activities of POm RSUs were inclined to 1500 Hz); 3000 and 4500 Hz alone is shown as a variant. Reproduced when, under every reading of Method S, the Kruskal-Wallis across PRFs has p < 0.01, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz are significantly above baseline while 30 and 300 Hz are not, and the highest mean is at 1500 Hz within tolerance; partially reproduced when the significance pattern holds and the mean does not.

claims.statement: POm FSUs show no time-locked response to any PRF relative to baseline, and delayed responses only to 4500 Hz.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6D legend
claims.quote: The FSUs did not show any time-locked responses and only expressed the delayed responses to 4,500 Hz (n = 26, p = 4.2 × 10−6)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), POm FSUs of the PRF sessions at 200 us pulse duration. Reproduced when, under every reading, no PRF is significantly above baseline at 0 to 67 ms, only 4500 Hz is significantly above baseline at 201 to 268 ms, and the Kruskal-Wallis across PRFs at 201 to 268 ms has p < 0.01. The 30 against 1500 Hz comparison during sonication is reported.

claims.statement: At 3000 Hz PRF, S1 RSU time-locked responses depend on DC and are elicited at 30% and 60% DC; delayed responses appear at 6, 30 and 60% DC.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 4; Figure 7A
claims.quote: with 3,000 Hz PRF, the time-locked responses of S1 RSUs were dependent on DCs which can be elicited with DC of 30% (n = 194, p = 3.38 × 10−6) and 60% (n = 312, p = 5.96 × 10−6). Delayed activities of RSUs were found at 6% (n = 56, p = 0.001), 30% (n = 194, p = 9.64 × 10−32), and 60% (n = 312, p = 1.38 × 10−15)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 RSUs of the 3000 Hz sessions at DC 0.6, 6, 30, 60 and 90% (pulse durations 2, 20, 100, 200 and 300 us). Reproduced when, under every reading, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, exactly 30 and 60% are significantly above baseline at 0 to 67 ms, and exactly 6, 30 and 60% at 201 to 268 ms; partially reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis tests hold and the significant DCs include those named with at most one other.

claims.statement: At 3000 Hz PRF, delayed responses of S1 FSUs are elicited by 6, 30 and 60% DC, the same range as S1 RSUs.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 4; Figure 7B
claims.quote: Delayed responses of FSUs could be elicited by 6% (n = 22, p = 1.29 × 10−8), 30% (n = 49, p = 2.32 × 10−11), and 60% (n = 54, p = 2.38 × 10−8) DCs (Fig. 7B), which were the same range of S1 RSUs
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 FSUs of the 3000 Hz DC sessions, window 201 to 268 ms. Reproduced when, under every reading, exactly 6, 30 and 60% DC are significantly above baseline; partially reproduced when these three are and one other DC is too. The 0.6 against 30% comparison is reported.

claims.statement: At 3000 Hz PRF, POm RSU time-locked responses do not depend on DC and are highest at 60% (106 +/- 0.77%); their delayed responses depend on DC and are activated at DCs of 6% and above.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 4; Figure 7C legend
claims.quote: The POm RSUs’ time-locked responses did not show DC dependence and were highest at 60% (106 ± 0.77%; Fig. 7C). Delayed responses could be activated by DC higher than 6% (6%, n = 22, p = 1.55 × 10−6; n = 7, p = 0.001; 60%, n = 233, p = 1.28 × 10−6; 90%, n = 18, p = 0.006)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), POm RSUs of the 3000 Hz DC sessions. The sentence lists 6% under "higher than 6%" and gives one entry without its DC (n = 7), which by its place is read as 30%; the reading taken is 6, 30, 60 and 90% significant. Reproduced when, under every reading of Method S, the Kruskal-Wallis across DCs at 0 to 67 ms has p >= 0.01 and at 201 to 268 ms p < 0.01, the 60% mean at 0 to 67 ms is the highest and within tolerance, and 6, 30, 60 and 90% are significantly above baseline at 201 to 268 ms; partially reproduced when the two Kruskal-Wallis results hold and the rest does not in full.

claims.statement: At 3000 Hz PRF, POm FSUs show no time-locked response against baseline but higher activity at 30% DC than at 0.6% and 6% during sonication, and delayed responses at 30, 60 and 90% DC.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 4; Figure 7D
claims.quote: There was no time-locked responses of POm FSUs compared with baseline while 30% DC showed higher activities compared with 0.6% (p = 0.0001) and 6% DC (p = 0.0003). The delayed activities of POm FSUs occurred at 30% (n = 18, p = 0.003), 60% (n = 17, p = 0.005), and 90% (n = 52, p = 6.8 × 10−5) DCs
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), POm FSUs of the 3000 Hz DC sessions; between-DC post hoc tests are one-tailed two-sample Wilcoxon tests on units' normalized rates (W1 only, as units differ between sessions), Bonferroni over (B1) the 10 pairs among the five DCs or (M2) the 15 pairs among them and baseline, as the count is not given. Reproduced when, under every reading, no DC is significantly above baseline at 0 to 67 ms, 30% exceeds 0.6% and 6% there, and 30, 60 and 90% are significantly above baseline at 201 to 268 ms; partially reproduced when two of these three parts hold.

claims.statement: At 30 Hz PRF, S1 RSUs show time-locked responses to 6, 30 and 90% DC and delayed responses to 90% DC, with DC-dependent activity during and after sonication.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 4; Figure 8A
claims.quote: With 30 Hz PRF stimulation (Fig. 8A), the S1 RSUs showed time-locked responses to DC of 6% (n = 81, p = 1.19 × 10−8), 30% (n = 61, p = 0.001), and 90% (n = 66, p = 2.17 × 10−6) and delayed responses to 90% DC (n = 66, p = 1.5 × 10−24)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 RSUs of the 30 Hz sessions at DC 0.6, 6, 30, 60 and 90% (pulse durations 0.2, 2, 10, 20 and 30 ms). Reproduced when, under every reading, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, exactly 6, 30 and 90% are significantly above baseline at 0 to 67 ms and exactly 90% at 201 to 268 ms; partially reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis tests hold and the significant DCs include those named with at most one other.

claims.statement: At 30 Hz PRF, 90% DC induces a time-locked increase in S1 FSUs, and S1 FSUs show delayed responses only to 90% DC; their responses depend on DC during sonication but not after.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 4; Figure 8B legend
claims.quote: 90% DC with 30 Hz PRF induced positive time-locked response in S1 FSUs (Fig. 8B; n = 28, p = 4.57 × 10−11). Like S1 RSUs, S1 FSUs only showed delayed responses to 90% DC (n = 28, p = 0.007) with 30 Hz PRF
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 FSUs of the 30 Hz DC sessions. Reproduced when, under every reading, 90% DC is significantly above baseline at 0 to 67 ms and is the only DC significantly above baseline at 201 to 268 ms, and the Kruskal-Wallis across DCs has p < 0.01 at 0 to 67 ms and p >= 0.01 at 201 to 268 ms (the legend's "no difference", judged on the paper's test); partially reproduced when the two 90% results hold and a Kruskal-Wallis result does not.

claims.statement: At constant 60% DC, only 30 Hz PRF differs from the other PRFs in its effect on S1 RSUs during sonication, while postsonication activity is highest at 4500 Hz.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 4; Figure 9A
claims.quote: only 30 Hz PRF showed different effects to other PRFs (300 Hz, p = 0.008; 1,500 Hz, p = 0.006; 3,000 Hz, p = 0.007; 4,500 Hz, p = 0.0003) on S1 RSUs during sonication, while postsonication activities preferred 4,500 Hz
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 RSUs of the 60% DC sessions at the five PRFs (pulse durations 20 ms, 2 ms, 400, 200 and 133 us). Between-PRF post hoc tests are one-tailed two-sample Wilcoxon tests on units' normalized rates. The Bonferroni count is not given and is open, (B1) the 10 pairs among the five PRFs or (M2) the 15 pairs among them and baseline. The direction of the 30 Hz difference is not stated; both tails are reported and the one the data show is used. Reproduced when, under every reading of N1, N2 and K1, K2, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, 30 Hz differs from each other PRF at corrected p < 0.01 at 0 to 67 ms while no pair of the other four does, and the 4500 Hz mean at 201 to 268 ms is the highest; partially reproduced when 30 Hz differs from at least three of the four.

claims.statement: At constant 60% DC, S1 FSUs respond to 1500 Hz PRF during sonication and prefer 4500 Hz postsonication.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 4; Figure 9B
claims.quote: S1 FSUs responded to 1,500 Hz PRF (n = 48, p = 3.35 ×10−6) during sonication and preferred 4,500 Hz post sonication (n = 18, p = 5.84 × 10−10; Fig. 9B)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), S1 FSUs of the 60% DC sessions. Reproduced when, under every reading, 1500 Hz is significantly above baseline at 0 to 67 ms, 4500 Hz is significantly above baseline at 201 to 268 ms with the highest mean there, and both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01; partially reproduced when the two significant responses hold and the rest does not.

claims.statement: With 3000 Hz PRF and 60% DC, the directional correlation from S1 RSUs to POm RSUs and from POm RSUs to S1 FSUs increases during sonication; postsonication, the correlation from S1 RSUs to POm FSUs and from POm RSUs to S1 RSUs decreases.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 10A
claims.quote: When 3,000 Hz PRF was applied, S1 RSUs showed an increased correlation to POm RSUs during sonication (p = 0.01). At the same period, POm RSUs showed enhanced correlation to S1 FSUs (p = 0.02)
claims.criterion: Method D (opening comment), pairs within the 3000 Hz 60% DC sessions, four directions (S1 RSU to POm RSU, S1 RSU to POm FSU, POm RSU to S1 RSU, POm RSU to S1 FSU). The postsonication window is not given; the readings are each 67 ms window from 67 to 268 ms. Reproduced when, under every reading of Method D and of the cell types, S1 RSU to POm RSU and POm RSU to S1 FSU are significantly above prestimulation at 0 to 67 ms (one-tailed, p < 0.05) and the other two directions are not, and, in one postsonication window, S1 RSU to POm FSU and POm RSU to S1 RSU are significantly below prestimulation; partially reproduced when the during-sonication part holds alone. The numbers of pairs are reported.

claims.statement: With 30 Hz PRF, the directional correlation from S1 RSUs to POm FSUs increases and that from POm RSUs to S1 FSUs decreases during sonication.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 10B legend
claims.quote: When delivering 30 Hz ultrasound, S1 RSUs to POm FSUs higher correlated (p = 0.0058), while POm RSUs showed decreased correlation to S1 FSUs during sonication (p = 0.0058)
claims.criterion: Method D, pairs within the 30 Hz 0.6% DC sessions, window 0 to 67 ms against prestimulation. Reproduced when, under every reading, S1 RSU to POm FSU is significantly higher and POm RSU to S1 FSU significantly lower (one-tailed, p < 0.05); partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: At constant 200 us pulse duration, the S1 RSU to POm RSU correlation change during sonication does not depend on PRF, though 1500 Hz gives a higher change than 30 Hz.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 10C
claims.quote: When applying tFUS with constant 200 μs PD, varying the DC and PRF, the correlation did not show PRF-dependent change. A total of 1,500 Hz PRF did show a higher correlation change compared with 30 Hz PRF (Fig. 10C; p = 0.02)
claims.criterion: Method T (opening comment), S1 RSU and POm RSU pairs of the five PRF sessions at 200 us pulse duration. The absence of PRF dependence is judged on the paper's test: reproduced in that part when the Kruskal-Wallis across PRFs has p >= 0.05. The 1500 against 30 Hz part holds when the one-tailed Wilcoxon test (W1, as pairs differ between sessions) gives p < 0.05 with 1500 Hz higher. Reproduced when both parts hold under D1 and D2 and K1 and K2; partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: At constant 60% DC, the S1 RSU to POm RSU correlation change during sonication depends on PRF, with a preference for 1500 and 3000 Hz.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 10D
claims.quote: Then we fixed the DC to 60% and varied PRF. Unlike the neuronal responses (Fig. 9), the correlation showed the preference to 1,500 and 3,000 Hz
claims.criterion: Method T, S1 RSU and POm RSU pairs of the 60% DC sessions at the five PRFs. Reproduced when, under D1 and D2 and K1 and K2, the Kruskal-Wallis across PRFs has p < 0.05 and the two largest changes are at 1500 and 3000 Hz, by the mean and by the median change (the paper does not say which it compares); partially reproduced when the test holds and only one of the two is among the two largest.

claims.statement: The S1 RSU to POm RSU correlation change depends on DC at 30 Hz PRF, changing most at middle DCs (6, 30, 60%), and does not depend on DC at 3000 Hz PRF.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 10E and 10F
claims.quote: For 30 Hz PRF (Fig. 10E), the correlation tended to change most at a middle range (6, 30, 60%) and respond less to lower (e.g., 0.6%) and higher DC (e.g., 90%). For 3,000 Hz PRF, the pathway correlation showed DC independence (Fig. 10F)
claims.criterion: Method T, S1 RSU and POm RSU pairs of the 30 Hz and of the 3000 Hz DC sessions. Reproduced when, under D1 and D2 and K1 and K2, the Kruskal-Wallis across DCs at 30 Hz has p < 0.05 with the changes at 6, 30 and 60% each above those at 0.6 and 90%, by the mean and by the median change (the paper does not say which), and the Kruskal-Wallis across DCs at 3000 Hz has p >= 0.05 (the absence judged on the paper's test); partially reproduced when one PRF's result holds.

claims.statement: Auditory cortex neurons respond to tFUS on S1 in a PRF-dependent way, time-locked to 1500 and 3000 Hz and postsonication to 30, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz, with the least response to 300 Hz.
claims.source: Results, Auditory confound on CTC pathway modulation using tFUS, paragraph 1; Figure 11B (legend labels it C)
claims.quote: During sonication, the AC neurons showed time-locked responses to 1,500 Hz (n = 107, p = 9.9 × 10−5) and 3,000 Hz PRF (n = 104, p = 1.98 × 10−7). Postsonication, neuronal responses were activated by 30 Hz (n = 83, p = 1.77 × 10−20), 1,500 Hz, (n = 107, p = 1.36 × 10−5), 3,000 Hz (n = 104, p = 4.47 × 10−13), and 4,500 Hz (n = 100, p = 1.66 × 10−40)
claims.criterion: Method S (opening comment), AC units of the auditory-confound group (S1 and AC probes), all cell types together as the paper reports AC neurons without a split. The paper does not say which DC goes with each PRF here ("varying combination of PRFs and DCs"); the readings are the 200 us pulse duration series and the 60% DC series. Reproduced when, under one series and every reading of Method S, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, exactly 1500 and 3000 Hz are significantly above baseline at 0 to 67 ms, and exactly 30, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz at 201 to 268 ms; partially reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis tests hold and at least four of the six named responses are significant. The PRF with the lowest mean postsonication response is reported (the legend names 300 Hz).

claims.statement: With 30 Hz PRF on S1, the directional correlation from AC neurons to S1 RSUs increases during sonication and lasts about 150 to 200 ms, and the correlation from AC neurons to S1 FSUs changes too.
claims.source: Results, Auditory confound on CTC pathway modulation using tFUS, paragraph 2; Figure 11C legend
claims.quote: During tFUS sonication with 30 Hz PRF, the correlation from 878 paired AC neurons to S1 RSUs significantly increased (p = 0.0014) which lasting for ∼150 ms (left)
claims.criterion: Method D, AC units to S1 RSUs and to S1 FSUs of the 30 Hz sessions of the auditory-confound group. The legend says the increase lasts about 150 ms and the Results about 200 ms; it holds when the windows from 0 ms up to 134 ms or up to 201 ms are each above prestimulation. The paper is self-contradictory on AC to S1 FSUs (the legend says it decreased during and right after sonication, the Results that the same synchronization is found), so that part is reported and does not decide. Reproduced when, under every reading of Method D, AC to S1 RSU is significantly above prestimulation (one-tailed, p < 0.05) at 0 to 67 ms and in the next window; partially reproduced when only the 0 to 67 ms window is. The legend's 1,421 AC and S1 RSU pairs, and the 878 pairs, are reported against the counts found.

claims.statement: With 3000 Hz PRF on S1, the directional correlation between AC neurons and S1 RSUs does not change, and AC neurons and S1 FSUs show only a postsonication change at about 200 to 300 ms.
claims.source: Results, Auditory confound on CTC pathway modulation using tFUS, paragraph 2; Figure 11D legend
claims.quote: However, when delivering 3,000 Hz PRF ultrasound energy to S1, auditory neurons did not show directional correlation change with S1 RSUs. The correlation change of AC neurons with S1 FSUs only occurred ∼200–300 ms
claims.criterion: Method D, AC units and S1 RSUs and FSUs of the 3000 Hz sessions of the auditory-confound group. The absence for S1 RSUs is judged on the paper's test: no 67 ms window from 0 to 268 ms differs from prestimulation at one-tailed p < 0.05 in either direction, for AC to S1 RSU. The S1 FSU part holds when AC to S1 FSU (or S1 FSU to AC, as the legend calls the change bidirectional) differs from prestimulation in the 201 to 268 ms window or the 268 to 335 ms window and in no window before 201 ms. Reproduced when both parts hold under every reading; partially reproduced when the S1 RSU part holds alone. The legend's 1,714 and 1,016 pairs are reported.

claims.statement: The study recorded 36 patients in 44 sessions, with 1,454 single neurons (360 hippocampus, 496 amygdala, 204 pre-SMA, 188 dACC, 206 vmPFC) and 1,922 microwire LFP channels (586, 421, 283, 325 and 307).
claims.source: Methods, Patients and Spike sorting; Results, Hippocampal PAC is modulated by WM load, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We isolated 360 neurons in the hippocampus, 496 in the amygdala, 204 in the pre-SMA, 188 in the dACC and 206 in the vmPFC. Of the LFP channels, 586 channels were in the hippocampus, 421 in the amygdala, 283 in the pre-SMA, 325 in the dACC and 307 in the vmPFC
claims.criterion: Counts from the units and LFP electrode tables, with areas merged across hemispheres as condenseAreas.m does. Tolerance is 0 because these are counts of the recordings the dataset is said to hold, not estimates. Reproduced when every total and every per-area count matches exactly; partially reproduced when all are within 2%.

claims.statement: Patients responded more slowly in load 3 than in load 1 trials (1.46 s against 1.33 s).
claims.source: Results, Main, paragraph 3; Figure 1d
claims.quote: the participants responded slower (1.46 s versus 1.33 s; t 43 = 6.42, P < 0.001)
claims.criterion: RT is response time minus probe onset (Fig. 1d legend; code). Per session the median RT of correct trials in each load, as NWB_QA_graphs.m computes it; the values are the means over sessions; the paired permutation t-test over 44 sessions (G2). The per-session mean RT of correct trials is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Patients were less accurate in load 3 than in load 1 trials (91.60% against 95.71%).
claims.source: Results, Main, paragraph 3; Figure 1d
claims.quote: less accurately (91.60% versus 95.71%; t 43 = −4.45, P < 0.001) in load 3 trials compared with load 1 trials
claims.criterion: Per session the percentage of correct trials (response_accuracy) in each load; means over sessions; paired permutation t-test over 44 sessions (G2).

claims.statement: Mean accuracy was 93.66 +/- 7.04% (s.d. over sessions), and 78.34 +/- 20.09% of errors were false negatives.
claims.source: Results, Main, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Mean accuracy was 93.66 ± 7.04% (mean ± s.d.; 78.34 ± 20.09% of all errors were false negatives)
claims.criterion: Tolerance is the s.d. the paper reports. A false negative is an incorrect response to a match probe (probe_in_out = 1). Sessions without errors are left out of the second mean.

claims.statement: Across all recorded channels, PAC during maintenance was strongest between theta phase (3-7 Hz) and the amplitude of a low (30-55 Hz) and a high (70-140 Hz) gamma band.
claims.source: Results, Hippocampal PAC is modulated by WM load, paragraph 1; Figure 2a
claims.quote: PAC was strongest between the phase in the theta range (3–7 Hz) and the amplitude in two different gamma-frequency bands ... a lower (30–55 Hz) and a higher gamma range (70–140 Hz)
claims.criterion: Comodulogram as in cfc_tort_comodulogram.m (Methods, PAC; O1, O2) on the -0.5 to 3 s epochs of subsampled correct trials of both loads, cut to 0 to 2.5 s, phase centres 2 to 14 Hz (2 Hz bandwidth), amplitude centres 30 to 150 Hz in 5 Hz steps (bandwidth twice the phase centre), 18 bins, z-scored against 200 trial-shuffled surrogates; averaged over channels (1,917 in the paper). Reproduced when the largest mean z lies at a phase centre of 4 or 6 Hz, and the amplitude profile at those phase centres has a local maximum within 30 to 55 Hz and another within 70 to 140 Hz.

claims.statement: 137 of 586 hippocampal channels showed significant theta-high-gamma PAC; the proportions of such channels in the hippocampus, amygdala and vmPFC exceeded the trial-shuffled null, while pre-SMA and dACC had few such channels.
claims.source: Results, Hippocampal PAC is modulated by WM load, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 2b
claims.quote: For theta to high-gamma PAC, 137 out of 586 hippocampal channels showed significant PAC across all correct trials from both load conditions
claims.criterion: A channel has significant PAC when its mean z-scored MI over theta and high gamma (O3), from all subsampled trials of both loads, exceeds 1.64 (Methods, PAC). The amygdala, vmPFC, pre-SMA and dACC counts are the n of the load tests (Fig. 2c legend; t129, t39, t4, t13). Reproduced when the hippocampal, amygdala and vmPFC proportions exceed the 99th percentile of their surrogate null (O4) and the counts are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the three exceed the null and a count is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: In the 137 hippocampal channels with significant PAC, theta-high-gamma PAC was weaker in load 3 than in load 1 trials.
claims.source: Results, Hippocampal PAC is modulated by WM load, paragraph 1; Figure 2c (left)
claims.quote: This comparison revealed significantly weaker theta–high-gamma PAC in load 3 compared with load 1 trials ( t 136 = −4.26, P < 0.001
claims.criterion: Per significant hippocampal channel, the mean z-scored MI over theta and high gamma (O3) in load 1 and in load 3 (equal trial counts, O2), each z-scored against 200 surrogates of its own load; paired permutation t-test over channels; Benjamini-Hochberg over the five areas' p-values. Reproduced when the corrected p < 0.05 with load 1 higher.

claims.statement: Theta-high-gamma PAC did not differ between loads in the amygdala, vmPFC, pre-SMA or dACC channels with significant PAC.
claims.source: Results, Hippocampal PAC is modulated by WM load, paragraph 2; Figure 2c (middle and right)
claims.quote: theta–high-gamma PAC did not differ significantly between the two load conditions in neither of these two areas (Fig. 2c ; t 129 = 1.43, P = 0.38, Bayes factor (BF) 01 = 1.40; and t 39 = 0.16, P = 0.87, BF 01 = 5.84, respectively)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The test of fig2c-hippocampus-load in each of the four areas, FDR corrected over five areas. Reproduced when no area has corrected p < 0.05; not reproduced when any has. The mean load difference of each area is reported.

claims.statement: Averaging significant PAC channels within each patient, hippocampal PAC was again stronger in load 1 than in load 3, and no other area showed a load difference.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2b legend
claims.quote: Only in the hippocampus again, PAC was stronger for load 1 as compared to load 3 (n = 23 patients, p = 0.0049), observable in almost each single patient. No significant differences were found between the load conditions in other regions
claims.criterion: Per patient (sessions of one patient pooled), the mean over significant channels of each load's z-scored theta-high-gamma MI; paired permutation t-test over patients per area. Reproduced when the hippocampus gives p < 0.05 with load 1 higher and no other area gives p < 0.05; partially reproduced when the hippocampus holds and another area also differs.

claims.statement: Theta-low-gamma (30-55 Hz) PAC did not differ between loads in any region.
claims.source: Results, Hippocampal PAC is modulated by WM load, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 2c
claims.quote: For PAC involving the low gamma band (30–55 Hz), there were no significant differences between the load conditions in any of the regions
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. As fig2c-hippocampus-load with low gamma (amplitude centres 30 to 55 Hz, O3) both for channel selection and for the load test (the paper's n are 148, 155, 10, 22 and 48 channels). The legend names no correction, so the test is run uncorrected; the FDR-corrected result is shown as a variant. Reproduced when no area has p < 0.05; not reproduced when any has.

claims.statement: Split into slow (2-5 Hz) and fast (5-9 Hz) theta, PAC differed between loads only in the hippocampus and only with high gamma, most strongly for fast theta (t116 = -3.05, p = 0.0015; slow theta, t147 = -2.31, p = 0.0163).
claims.source: Supplementary Table S1; Supplementary Discussion, Related work on role of theta
claims.quote: PAC differed significantly only in the hippocampus and only for high gamma power combined with either low or high theta frequency bands, with the strongest differences in the fast theta band
claims.criterion: The phase bands are not mapped to centre frequencies in the text. Readings are (a) slow theta as phase centres 2 and 4 Hz and fast theta as 6 and 8 Hz of the comodulogram; (b) bands filtered directly at 2-5 Hz and 5-9 Hz. Channels are selected per band combination, as the differing n of Table S1 show. Reproduced when, under one reading, of the area and band tests (19 in Table S1, since pre-SMA had no significant fast theta to high gamma channel) only the two hippocampal high-gamma tests give p < 0.05, both with load 1 higher.

claims.statement: In the hippocampus, stronger single-trial theta-high-gamma PAC went with faster RTs, while no such relation held in the amygdala or vmPFC.
claims.source: Results, Hippocampal PAC is modulated by WM load, paragraph 2; Figure 2f; Supplementary Table S2
claims.quote: In the hippocampus, faster RTs were associated with stronger single-trial estimates of TG-PAC
claims.criterion: Correct trials of the significant PAC channels; RT ~ 1 + PAC + load + PAC*load + (1|patientID) + (1|patientID:channelID), normal response (Table S2), single-trial PAC under each reading of O5. Reproduced when, under the readings, the hippocampal PAC term is negative with p < 0.05 and the amygdala and vmPFC terms have p >= 0.05; methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: The hippocampal load effect on PAC was not explained by theta or gamma power, theta waveform asymmetry, theta-gamma phase-phase coupling, preferred phase or PAC peak frequency.
claims.source: Results, Hippocampal PAC is modulated by WM load, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 3b, c, d, g, h
claims.quote: we tested whether the differences in hippocampal PAC between loads could be explained by changes in power, theta waveform shape, cross-frequency phase–phase coupling, preferred phase or PAC peak frequency but did not find evidence for any of those factors
claims.criterion: A claim of absence over the 137 channels, each with a two-sided paired permutation t-test between loads (Extended Data Fig. 3 legend, panels b, c, d, h). Theta (3-7 Hz) and gamma (70-140 Hz) power on the PAC trials, the paper's bands; the power estimate is not stated, and readings are (a) the mean squared Hilbert amplitude from the PAC filters of O3, (b) the Welch spectrum of the 0 to 2.5 s window averaged over each band; peak-to-trough and rise-to-decay asymmetry from the bycycle toolbox with its default settings (the paper gives none); theta-high-gamma phase-phase coupling as the n:m phase locking value of refs 73 and 83 (the ratio is not given; readings are the ratio of the band centres, 5 to 105 Hz, and the ratio of each phase and amplitude centre pair of O3, averaged); the load difference of preferred phase tested against zero, by a test the paper does not name (the legend's t-tests cover panels a-f and h, not g), with readings (a) a V test of the per-channel differences against 0, (b) a two-sided permutation t-test of the differences wrapped to -180 to 180 degrees against 0; the peak frequency from a comodulogram with 0.5 Hz phase steps. Reproduced when none of the tests gives p < 0.05; partially reproduced when one does; not reproduced when more do. The asymmetries are also tested against 0.5.

claims.statement: The distribution of gamma amplitude over theta phase was wider (lower kappa) in load 3 than in load 1 across hippocampal PAC channels.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3a legend
claims.quote: Across all PAC channels, kappa was significantly lower in load 3 compared to load 1 (n = 137 channels, t(136) = −3.7453, p = 0.0001) trials
claims.criterion: Kappa is the von Mises concentration estimated (circ_kappa) from the 18-bin distribution of high-gamma amplitude over theta phase, bins weighted by their normalized amplitude; the estimator is not named, and circ_kappa of the CircStat toolbox is the standard choice. Paired permutation t-test over channels.

claims.statement: 110 of the 137 hippocampal PAC channels (80.29%) showed theta-high-gamma nesting, and PAC remained lower in load 3 than load 1 in those channels.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3e legend
claims.quote: 110 of the 137 significant PAC channels (80.29%) in the hippocampus showed nesting between high gamma and theta. When testing PAC between the load conditions after removing channels that did not show significant nesting, PAC was still significantly lower in load 3 than 1 (n = 110; t(109) = −4.10; p = 0.0001)
claims.criterion: Nesting as in the Methods (PAC, last paragraph) after Vaz et al.; a local maximum is a sample of the averaged raw waveform larger than both neighbours. Reproduced when the load test holds in the nested channels and the count is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Raw (not z-scored) theta-gamma MI was also larger in load 1 than in load 3 in the hippocampal PAC channels.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3f legend
claims.quote: Raw theta-gamma PAC was significantly larger in load 1 compared to load 3 (n = 137; t(136) = −4.0264, p = 0.0001)

claims.statement: The slope of the log-log power spectrum did not differ between load 1 and load 3 trials in hippocampal channels.
claims.source: Methods, LFP preprocessing
claims.quote: The slope of log–log power spectra did not differ significantly between load 1 and load 3 trials in hippocampal channels ( n = 586 channels; mean slope −1.7526 ± 0.3902 versus −1.7517 ± 0.3928, t 585 = −0.86, P = 0.39)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The frequency range and the spectral estimate for the slope are not given. Readings are a linear fit of log power on log frequency of the Welch spectrum of the 0 to 2.5 s maintenance window over (a) 2 to 150 Hz; (b) 30 to 150 Hz. Tolerance is the reported s.d. Reproduced when the paired permutation t-test gives p >= 0.05; not reproduced when it gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Category neurons were found above chance in the hippocampus (89, 24.72%), amygdala (181, 36.49%) and vmPFC (37, 17.96%), but not in the pre-SMA and dACC.
claims.source: Results, Category cells support WM maintenance, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 4a
claims.quote: We identified such cells at numbers higher than expected by chance within the hippocampus (89 neurons (24.72%)), amygdala (181 neurons (36.49%)) and vmPFC (37 neurons (17.96%)) but not within the pre-SMA and dACC
claims.criterion: Selection as in NWB_calcSelective_SB.m, which matches the Methods. Spike rate 0.2 to 1.0 s after the onset of every encoding picture and of the probe, all trials; category is the first digit of the picture ID; a permutation one-way ANOVA over categories (statcond, 2,000 permutations) with p < 0.05, then an unpaired permutation t-test (2,000) of the category with the highest mean rate against all other presentations with two-sided p < 0.1 (one-sided 0.05). Chance by shuffling category labels across presentations 500 times; significant above the 99th percentile. The pre-SMA and dACC counts are from Extended Data Fig. 4b. Reproduced when the three areas exceed the 99th percentile, pre-SMA and dACC do not, and the counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: MTL category neurons stayed above baseline during maintenance in both preferred and non-preferred trials, and fired more when their preferred category was held in memory.
claims.source: Results, Category cells support WM maintenance, paragraph 1; Figure 3b
claims.quote: Category neurons ( n = 270) remained active (preferred (pref.) versus baseline (bsl), P = 0.0001; non-preferred (non-pref.), P = 0.0001) and retained their selectivity during the maintenance period, with FRs higher for preferred compared with non-preferred categories ( P = 0.001)
claims.criterion: Hippocampal and amygdala category neurons pooled; per neuron the mean maintenance rate over correct preferred trials (G4), over correct non-preferred trials, and the mean baseline rate over all correct trials (G3); paired permutation t-tests over neurons, under both readings of O6 (for b the baseline is 0% by definition, so the first two tests are one-sample tests against zero). Reproduced when all three tests give p < 0.05 with maintenance above baseline and preferred above non-preferred under both readings.

claims.statement: Persistent and selective maintenance activity of category neurons held in the hippocampus and amygdala separately, but vmPFC category neurons returned to baseline and did not differ between preferred and non-preferred trials.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4b legend
claims.quote: The activity of category neurons in the vmPFC (right) during the delay period was not significantly larger than that during baseline ... Also, their FRs did not differ significantly between when the preferred and the non-preferred category of a cell was maintained in WM (t(36) = 1.03, p = 0.32, BF 01 = 3.47)
claims.criterion: The tests of fig3b-persistent-activity per area. Reproduced when, in the hippocampus and amygdala, all three tests give p < 0.05 in the paper's direction, and in the vmPFC none does (the vmPFC part is a claim of absence on the same tests); partially reproduced when one of the two parts holds.

claims.statement: In preferred trials, MTL category neurons fired more during maintenance in load 1 than in load 3, while no load effect appeared in non-preferred trials.
claims.source: Results, Category cells support WM maintenance, paragraph 2; Figure 3c; Extended Data Fig. 5a
claims.quote: The activity of category neurons in the MTL was modulated by load, with FRs higher in load 1 than in load 3 in preferred trials ( t 269 = 2.65, P = 0.004; Fig. 3c ), but not in non-preferred trials ( t 269 = −1.46, P = 0.14
claims.criterion: Per neuron the mean maintenance rate in correct preferred load 1 and correct preferred load 3 trials (G4), and the same for non-preferred trials; paired permutation t-tests, both readings of O6. Reproduced when the preferred test gives p < 0.05 with load 1 higher and the non-preferred test gives p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when only the first holds.

claims.statement: MTL category neurons fired more during maintenance in correct than in incorrect trials.
claims.source: Results, Category cells support WM maintenance, paragraph 2; Figure 3d
claims.quote: FRs were higher in correct as compared to incorrect trials across both load conditions ( t 245 = 2.43, P = 0.02
claims.criterion: Per neuron the mean maintenance rate over correct and over incorrect trials of both loads. The trials are not specified; readings are (a) all trials; (b) preferred trials only.
