claims.criterion: Counts are exact. Sessions are counted when they are stage 5 or 6, have at least 100 rewards with at least 20% at each port, and belong to a mouse with at least 10 such sessions (STAR Methods). The number of dandiset sessions that pass, and the number in the dandiset, are both reported; a mismatch with 381 is reported with the sessions that differ. The 500 stage 5 and 6 sessions and the 18 excluded mice are checked only if the dandiset holds them.

claims.statement: Mice that reached proficiency took 21 +/- 8 training sessions to reach stage 5.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Training and inclusion criteria, last paragraph
claims.quote: Mice that reached proficiency took 21 ± 8 training sessions to reach stage 5
claims.criterion: Tolerance is the paper's stated spread (it does not say SD or SEM). Testable only if the dataset holds the training sessions before stage 5 with their stage; the count per mouse is the number of sessions before the first stage 5 session.

claims.statement: In stage 6, responses to distractors of the untrained modality were below 10%, with no discernible change in task performance.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Training and inclusion criteria, Stage 6
claims.quote: There was no discernible change in task performance, and response rates to the distractors were <10%
claims.criterion: The paper does not say whether the rate is per mouse, per session or pooled. Readings are (a) pooled over all stage 6 distractor trials of each mouse, (b) mean over stage 6 sessions of each mouse, (c) pooled over all mice. The paper does not say whether the bound holds per mouse or overall. Reproduced when every mouse with stage 6 sessions is below 0.10 under (a) or (b), or the overall rate is below 0.10 under (c); the readings met are reported. "No discernible change" is not tested (no measure given).

claims.statement: Cross-validated GLM-HMMs fit separately to each of the 13 mice gave between 3 and 5 states per mouse.
claims.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Figure S2
claims.quote: we fit GLM-HMMs separately to each of the 13 mice that reached proficiency on the sensory discrimination task (8 auditory and 5 visual task performers). While there was diversity in the best number of states across subjects (3–5 states
claims.criterion: Models fit as in M1 and M2, states counted under both readings of O1. A reported range, so the claim holds when every mouse's number of states lies in 3 to 5 (the range widened by 10% of each bound) under one reading. The counts per mouse are shown for each reading. The model this claim selects is the one the later claims use.

claims.statement: For the example mouse, a 4-state GLM-HMM was selected; it predicted 78% of choices against 70% for a one-state model.
claims.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 5; Figure 1G
claims.quote: A one-state GLM-HMM, equivalent to assuming stationary performance during training, correctly predicted the choice of the example mouse on 70% of trials, while the best-fit 4-state GLM-HMM correctly predicted 78% of choices
claims.criterion: The example mouse is subject BW046, a visual-task mouse (Figure1.py and 7_example_mouse_decoding.py name it). Accuracy computed as in fig2d-prediction-accuracy. Reproduced when the three values are within tolerance under one reading of O1.

claims.statement: Six stereotyped performance states emerged across mice. Every mouse had an optimal and a disengaged state and at least one sub-optimal state (bias left or right, avoid left or right).
claims.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Figure 2A
claims.quote: Each subject exhibited both optimal (state 1) and disengaged (state 2) states, along with at least one additional sub-optimal performance state
claims.criterion: States labelled as in M3. Reproduced when all 13 mice have an optimal and a disengaged state and at least one other state, and each other state matches one of the four sub-optimal templates. The counts of mice with each sub-optimal type, as Figure 2A labels them (Figure2.py), are bias left 6, avoid right 4, bias right 5, avoid left 5; they are compared and reported but do not decide the claim, as they rest on random fits.

claims.statement: Mice spent the largest proportion of trials in the optimal state (around half), more than in the disengaged, sub-optimal or indeterminate states; 13.1% +/- 1.6% of trials were indeterminate.
claims.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Figure 2B
claims.quote: Subjects spent the largest proportion of trials in the optimal performance state ... and only 13.1% ± 1.6% of trials were in an indeterminate state
claims.criterion: Per mouse, trials of sessions in which the optimal state occurs (M5, Figure2.py), pooled; fractions in optimal, disengaged, sub-optimal (pooled) and indeterminate. Tolerance is the paper's SEM. Reproduced when the indeterminate fraction is within tolerance and the optimal fraction is larger than each other fraction by two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests at p < 0.05 over the 13 mice.

claims.statement: Epochs of the optimal state lasted longer than disengaged and sub-optimal epochs (about 37 against about 15 trials), and the median transition between discrete states took 3.4 +/- 0.3 trials.
claims.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Discussion, paragraph beginning "Here, we used recently implemented GLM-HMMs"; Figure 2C
claims.quote: Additionally, epochs of the optimal state lasted longer than those of sub-optimal states ... and the median transition time between discrete states (dwell time in indeterminate states) was 3.4 ± 0.3 trials
claims.criterion: Epochs are runs of consecutive trials in one discrete state within a session (flex_hmm.get_dwell_times, called as plot_dwell_times in Figure2.py). That function records a dwell one trial longer than the run for every epoch but a session's last, and one trial shorter for the last; the dwell is read both as (x) the run length and (y) the code's count. The indeterminate dwell is the number of trials from the end of one discrete epoch (or the session start) to the start of the next, zero for a direct transition (Figure2.py, first trial minus the previous epoch's last_trial); a disengaged epoch of more than 40 trials that ends a session is left out (Figure2.py). Per mouse, the median dwell of each state type (the first length at which its cumulative distribution exceeds 0.499, as Figure2.py). The 3.4 is the mean over mice of the median indeterminate dwell. The Discussion's 37 and about 15 can be read as (a) the mean over mice of the per-mouse median dwell, (b) the mean over mice of the per-mouse mean dwell, (c) the mean over all epochs pooled; for the 15, disengaged and sub-optimal are each compared. Reproduced when optimal dwell exceeds disengaged and sub-optimal dwell by two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests at p < 0.05, the 3.4 is within tolerance, and the 37 and 15 are within tolerance under one reading of (a) to (c) with (x) or (y).

claims.statement: The best-fit GLM-HMM predicted 75.7% +/- 1.7% of choices, a 10.8% +/- 1.3% improvement over a one-state (static performance) model.
claims.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Figure 2D
claims.quote: the best-fit GLM-HMM correctly predicted 75.7% ± 1.7% of choices, a significant 10.8% ± 1.3% improvement over the classical static-performance assumption
claims.criterion: As 6_predictive_accuracy.py. Per mouse, 5 folds; each fold holds out a contiguous block of 20% of the trials of every session (StratifiedKFold on session index, fold order permuted per session). On the training trials, concatenated, a one-state model and a model with the mouse's selected number of states are fit (5 initializations, the best by test log-likelihood kept). For each test trial, the state is the most likely next state from the transition matrix given the most likely state of the posterior over the preceding test trials (the initial distribution for the first), and the predicted choice is the most likely choice of that state's GLM. Accuracy is the mean over folds. Tolerances are the paper's SEMs. The improvement can be read as (a) percentage points, (b) relative to the one-state accuracy. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading (and O1) and the best model is better by a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05 (O4; the rank-sum is shown).

claims.statement: The probability of being in the optimal state follows an inverted-U function of pupil diameter, highest at intermediate diameters, in nearly all mice.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 2; Figure 3C; Figure S3
claims.quote: The inverted-U relationship was found in nearly all subjects, and the pupil diameter that gave the highest probability for being in the optimal state was calculated for each
claims.criterion: As 4_optimal_pupils.py and Figure3.py, on sessions of M5. Discrete-state trials are binned by pupil diameter (0.02 of the session maximum); P(optimal) per bin with more than 5 trials (low bins merged into the first such bin). The polynomial degree (1 to 7) is the elbow of the mean 5-fold test r2 against degree (largest height above the line from degree 1 to degree 7); the final polynomial is fit to all bins and the optimal pupil is the maximum of the fit on a 0.001 grid within the data range. The paper defines no per-mouse test of the shape. Readings are (i) the fit's maximum lies inside the data range with lower fitted values at both ends (Figure S3 legend), (ii) the quadratic term of a degree-2 fit is negative (the sign Figure S8 uses for an inverted U). "Nearly all" is not defined; readings are (a) at least 12 of 13 mice, (b) at least 11 of 13. Reproduced when (b) holds under (i) or (ii); the counts under every reading are shown.

claims.statement: The optimal pupil diameter is smaller in mice performing the auditory task than in those performing the visual task.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 2; Figure 3D
claims.quote: Subjects performing the auditory task had significantly smaller optimal pupil sizes than those performing the visual task
claims.criterion: Optimal pupils per mouse from fig3c-inverted-u-pupil. Reproduced when the auditory median is below the visual median and a two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Across mice, aligned to each mouse's optimal pupil, the probability of the optimal state is an inverted U and the probability of the disengaged state a U of pupil diameter; this holds also on trials when the mice were stationary.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 3; Figure 3E
claims.quote: we found a prominent U relationship between the probability of being in the disengaged state and pupil diameter ... These relationships were maintained when considering only trials where the mice were stationary
claims.criterion: P(state) per 0.02 pupil bin as in fig3c-inverted-u-pupil, shifted by each mouse's optimal pupil and averaged over mice (Figure3.py). The paper reports no test. Read here as the shape the text names, tested on the mean curve over bins with data from at least half the mice. A second-order polynomial fit to the mean curve has a negative quadratic term for optimal and a positive one for disengaged, with the vertex inside the range (the sign Figure S8 uses for these shapes). The stationary subset has no threshold in the paper. Readings are (a) locomotion speed of exactly zero, (b) locomotion speed below 0.02 m/s (the lowest bin of FigureS3_S4.py). Reproduced when both shapes hold on all trials and on the stationary subset under one reading; partially reproduced when they hold on all trials only.

claims.statement: Second-order cross-validated regression fits of optimal-state probability are poorer for face motion energy (r2 0.49 +/- 0.08) and locomotion speed (0.44 +/- 0.07) than for pupil diameter (0.72 +/- 0.03).
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 4; Figure S4
claims.quote: pupil diameter: r 2 = 0.72 ± 0.03; face motion energy: r 2 = 0.49 ± 0.08, Wilcoxon signed-rank test vs. pupil: p = 0.04, locomotion speed: r 2 = 0.44 ± 0.07, Wilcoxon signed-rank test vs. pupil: p = 0.002
claims.criterion: For pupil, the mean over 5 folds of the test r2 of a degree-2 polynomial fit to binned P(optimal), as 4_optimal_pupils.py computes it (trials split by KFold, bins with more than 2 training or 3 test trials). The same for face motion energy and locomotion speed, with bins under both readings of O5. Tolerances are the paper's SEMs. Reproduced when the three values are within tolerance and both measures are below pupil by two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests at p < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: Optimal-state probability peaks at intermediate values of the movement index, an inverted U similar to pupil diameter (cross-validated r2 0.63 +/- 0.06, not different from pupil).
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 5; Figure 3F; Figure S5D
claims.quote: Using this combined movement index, a clear inverted-U pattern emerged, showing that optimal performance state occupancy peaked at intermediate levels of uninstructed movement, similar to that of pupil diameter (regression of movement index vs. optimal state, cross-validated r 2 = 0.63 ± 0.06
claims.criterion: Movement index as M4; r2 as in figs4-r2-individual-movement under both readings of O5. Inverted U as in fig3e-u-disengaged-pupil (negative quadratic term of a degree-2 fit to the mean P(optimal) curve over 0.25 bins of Figure3.py, vertex inside the range). The paper's "similar to" is judged by its test, a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test against pupil r2. Reproduced when r2 is within tolerance under one reading, the shape holds, and that test gives p >= 0.05; the difference in r2 is reported either way.

claims.statement: The probability of the disengaged state is a U-shaped function of the movement index.
claims.source: Figure 3F legend
claims.quote: There is a marked U-shaped relationship between both pupil diameter and movement index and the probability of being in the disengaged state
claims.criterion: As Figure3.py, sessions of M5. P(disengaged) per 0.25 movement-index bin from -5 to 5 (bins with more than 5 discrete-state trials), averaged over mice. The paper reports no test. Read, as in fig3e-u-disengaged-pupil, as the shape the text names, on the mean curve over bins with data from at least half the mice; a second-order polynomial fit to it has a positive quadratic term with the vertex inside the range. Reproduced when that holds. The bin coverage rule and the fit are chosen here, not by the paper.

claims.statement: The absolute difference from the optimal pupil diameter is smaller in the optimal state (7%) than in the disengaged (12.6%) and sub-optimal (9%) states.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 5
claims.quote: These correlations translate to a significant decrease in the absolute difference from the calculated optimal pupil diameter during optimal state occupancy as compared to sub-optimal or disengaged states (optimal: 7% ± 0.3%, disengaged: 12.6% ± 1%, sub-optimal: 9% ± 0.5%
claims.criterion: Per trial, the absolute difference between pupil diameter and the mouse's optimal pupil (STAR Methods, Determining optimal pupil diameters); per mouse, the mean in each state (sub-optimal pooled); no code computes these, so the sessions are read both ways of O3. Tolerances are the paper's SEMs. Reproduced when the three values are within tolerance under one reading and the optimal state is lower than each other by two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Raw face motion energy tends to be larger in the optimal state (0.48 a.u.) than in the disengaged (0.43) and sub-optimal (0.44) states.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 5
claims.quote: a trend toward larger raw face motion energy during optimal state occupancy (optimal: 0.48 ± 0.02 a.u., disengaged: 0.43 ± 0.3 a.u., sub-optimal: 0.44 ± 0.03 a.u.; opt. vs. dis. p = 0.06, opt. vs. sub. p = 0.04
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the mean face motion energy at stimulus onset in each state (M4), with sessions read both ways of O3. Tolerances are the paper's SEMs, except for disengaged, where the printed SEM of 0.3 is larger than the value and reads as a misprint, so 10% is used. Reproduced when the three values are within tolerance under one reading and the optimal mean is the largest, with the optimal against sub-optimal two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05; the optimal against disengaged p is reported.

claims.statement: Raw locomotion speed does not differ between optimal, disengaged and sub-optimal states (0.14 m/s in each).
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 5
claims.quote: but no significant differences in raw locomotion speed (optimal: 0.14 ± 0.02 m/s, disengaged: 0.14 ± 0.2 m/s, suboptimal: 0.14 ± 0.02 m/s; opt. vs. dis. p = 0.84, opt. vs. sub. p = 1
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests, two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over mice at p < 0.05 of per-mouse mean speeds at stimulus onset, optimal against disengaged and against sub-optimal (pooled), sessions both ways of O3. Reproduced when neither test finds a difference; not reproduced when either does. Tolerances are the SEMs, except for the printed 0.2 for disengaged (larger than the value, read as a misprint, 10% used). The differences are reported either way.

claims.statement: The 10-trial variability of pupil diameter, face motion energy and locomotion speed is lower in the optimal state than in the disengaged and sub-optimal states.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 6; Figure 4A
claims.quote: For all arousal measures recorded−pupil diameter, face motion energy, and locomotion speed−we found significantly reduced variability during optimal performance state occupancy as compared to sub-optimal or disengaged states
claims.criterion: As Figure4.py, on all sessions (M5). Per mouse, the mean over trials of each state of the 10-trial standard deviation (M4) of each measure; sub-optimal pooled. Reproduced when for all three measures the optimal mean is lower than the disengaged and the sub-optimal means by two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests at p < 0.05 (six tests); partially reproduced when all six differences have that sign and at least four tests pass.

claims.statement: Variability of the measures decreases on entering the optimal state and increases on leaving it.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 6; Figure 4B
claims.quote: Strikingly, this decrease in variability predicts transitions into and out of the optimal state
claims.criterion: As Figure4.py, all sessions. Optimal epochs with a dwell above 9 as flex_hmm.get_dwell_times counts it (see fig2c-dwell-times; a run of at least 9 trials for an epoch that is not a session's last, at least 11 for the last); entries from a non-optimal discrete state and exits to one. For each, the 10-trial standard deviation over the 10 trials before and 10 after the boundary; per mouse, the mean over transitions. The commented test in Figure4.py compares, per mouse, position 10 (the last trial before entry, or the last optimal trial) with position 20 (the tenth trial after), two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank over mice. Reproduced when all three measures decrease at entry and increase at exit, and the four comparisons the figure marks significant (pupil exit, face entry, locomotion entry and exit) give p < 0.05; partially reproduced when all six changes have the stated sign and fewer tests pass.

claims.statement: The correlation between pupil diameter and the movement index is lower during the optimal state than during the disengaged and sub-optimal states.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 7; Figures 4C and 4D
claims.quote: During optimal state epochs, the correlation between pupil diameter and the movement index is significantly reduced across subjects
claims.criterion: As Figure4.py, all sessions. Per mouse and state (sub-optimal pooled), the Pearson r between movement index and pupil diameter over the state's trials. Reproduced when the optimal r is lower than the disengaged and the sub-optimal r by two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The correlations of pupil diameter with face motion energy and with locomotion speed are also reduced during the optimal state.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 7; Figure S6B and S6D
claims.quote: This decrease in correlation is also seen when considering individual measures of face motion energy and locomotion speed
claims.criterion: As FigureS6.py, sessions of M5. Per mouse and state, Pearson r of pupil with face motion energy and with locomotion speed. The legend does not say which pairs are marked. Reproduced when, for both pairs of measures, the optimal r is lower than the disengaged r or the sub-optimal r by a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when this holds for one pair. The face-locomotion correlation (S6F) is reported.

claims.statement: For every mouse, support vector machines on the value and 10-trial variability of the measures predict the performance state above chance, with 88.2% +/- 1.8% accuracy for optimal against disengaged and 77.7% +/- 2% for optimal against sub-optimal states.
claims.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 1; Figures 5B and 5C
claims.quote: We found that for all subjects, performance states could be significantly predicted using the recorded arousal measures with high accuracy (opt. vs. dis. = 88.2% ± 1.8%; opt. vs. sub. = 77.7% ± 2%
claims.criterion: As 5_decoding.py and Figure5.py, sessions of M5. For each mouse, optimal against each other state separately (13 disengaged and 19 sub-optimal classifications), only when the two classes give more than 30 trials. Equal numbers of trials per class, at most 1500, sampled at random; features min-max scaled; RBF SVC (scikit-learn defaults); 5-fold KFold; accuracy is the mean over folds and over 1000 runs. Features are the six of the Methods (pupil, face motion energy, locomotion speed and their 10-trial SDs). Two code variants are shown, the "All measures" points of Figure5.py and FigureS7.py, which are 5_decoding.py condition 0 (all eight features, with the movement index and its SD shuffled in the training set only), and the eight features unshuffled (condition 13). The null is 1000 runs with all training features shuffled across trials (the code's surrogate; the Methods say class labels are permuted, which is the same up to pairing); z is the mean over runs of (accuracy minus null mean) over null SD. The Methods give no significance threshold; Figure5.py draws a dashed line at z = 1.98. Readings are (a) z > 1.98 (that line), (b) z > 1.645, (c) accuracy above the 95th percentile of the null. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance (the paper's SEMs) and every classification is significant under one reading.

claims.statement: Pupil diameter (value and variability) is the best single raw measure for state classification, better than face motion energy and only slightly better than locomotion speed.
claims.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 2; Figure S7
claims.quote: Pupil diameter (value and trial-to-trial variability) was the best individual raw measure for state classification
claims.criterion: Classifiers as fig5c-state-classification. The Results cite Figure S7 as a whole for p = 0.0039 and 0.106; the Figure S7B legend gives p = 0.004 and 0.14 for the shuffling comparison, so the Results values may come from S7A or from another run of S7B. Readings are (a) Figure S7A, keeping only one measure's value and SD (code conditions shuffling all other features), (b) Figure S7B, shuffling one measure's value and SD (with the movement index, as 5_decoding.py conditions 6 to 8), comparing the drop. The quantity compared can be (i) accuracy or (ii) z-score. Reproduced when, under one reading, pupil exceeds face motion energy by a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05 over the 32 classifications and exceeds locomotion speed on average.

claims.statement: The movement index is the best predictor of performance state, encoding more information about states than pupil diameter.
claims.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 2; Figure 5C
claims.quote: Interestingly, we found that the best predictor of performance state was the computed movement index incorporating face motion energy and locomotion speed, which encoded more information about states compared to pupil diameter
claims.criterion: Classifiers as fig5c-state-classification on the eight features of 5_decoding.py, keeping either the pupil value and SD or the movement index value and SD and shuffling all others in the training set (Figure 5C legend). In 5_decoding.py the movement-index condition (shuffle_schedule [1,2,3,4,5]) also keeps the pupil value unshuffled; that is shown as a variant. In the final Figure5.py (idx = [0,1,2,3,4,5]) the legend label "Movement index" falls on condition 1 (face and locomotion shuffled, pupil and movement index kept), while a superseded line (idx = [0,5,2]) names condition 5; condition 1 is shown as a further variant. The quantity compared can be (i) accuracy or (ii) z-score. Reproduced when the movement index exceeds pupil by a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05 over the 32 classifications under one of (i) and (ii).

claims.statement: In linear regressions of state probability on the measures, the quadratic weights of pupil diameter and of locomotion speed are negative for the optimal state and positive for the disengaged state, as are the weights of their 10-trial SDs, while face motion energy weights center on zero.
claims.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 3; Figure S8A
claims.quote: weights for the quadratic terms fit to predict optimal state probability were negative for pupil diameter across mice ... and the weights were positive when fit to disengaged state probabilities ... This was also true for quadratic terms of locomotion speed, while face motion energy had weights centered around zero across subjects
claims.criterion: As FigureS8.py, sessions of M5. Per mouse, OLS of each state's posterior probability per trial on min-max scaled features (constant, pupil, face, locomotion, their squares and pairwise products, their 10-trial SDs, and the triple product), the design min-max scaled again. The paper reports no test for "across mice" and "consistently". Readings are (a) a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the 13 weights against zero at p < 0.05 with the stated sign (the paper's test family, M6), (b) the median weight over mice has the stated sign; "centered around zero" is the test of (a) at p >= 0.05. Reproduced when this holds for the pupil and locomotion quadratic and SD weights in the optimal (negative) and disengaged (positive) fits, and the face quadratic and SD weights do not differ from zero; partially reproduced when the pupil terms hold and others do not.

claims.statement: With the movement index, the quadratic movement weight is negative for the optimal state, and the pupil-by-movement interaction is the only consistent weight for sub-optimal states (0.42 +/- 0.11), differing from its weight for the optimal state (-0.95 +/- 0.21).
claims.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 3; Figure S8B
claims.quote: the only consistently weighted feature across fits to sub-optimal state probabilities was the interaction between pupil diameter and the movement index ( Figure S8B ; 0.42 ± 0.11), which was also significantly different than weights fit to optimal state probability (−0.95 ± 0.21
claims.criterion: As FigureS8.py (second model). Per mouse, OLS of each state's posterior probability on min-max scaled constant, pupil, movement index, their squares and product, the pupil SD and the movement SD index, the design min-max scaled again. Each sub-optimal state of each mouse is one fit (the code pools them all). Tolerances are the paper's SEMs. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance, the two sets differ by a two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test at p < 0.05, and the mean quadratic movement weight of the optimal fits is negative.

claims.statement: The inter-trial interval is long enough that trial-evoked responses do not carry over; correlations of the measures at trial start with the prior ITI are weak and centered on zero, and evoked pupil responses do not differ across performance states.
claims.source: Figure S1C and S1D
claims.quote: Correlations between all measures at the start of a trial and prior inter trial intervals are weak and centered around zero across mice. (D) Average evoked pupil responses of mice are not significantly different across performance states
claims.criterion: As FigureS1.py, all sessions. Per mouse, Pearson r between each measure at stimulus onset (pupil from the trial's pupil trace at onset, face motion energy and locomotion speed as M4) and the preceding ITI, taken as the difference between consecutive trial start times within a session; trials with any value missing are dropped. The paper gives no threshold for "weak and centered around zero"; readings, chosen here and not from the paper, are (a) median r over mice with absolute value below 0.1, (b) below 0.2, each with a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero at p >= 0.05. The ITI part holds when it holds for all three measures under one reading. The evoked pupil response is defined by FigureS1.py as follows. From onset to 2.5 s after, the largest rise and the largest fall of pupil diameter from its onset value, keeping the one of larger absolute size, signed; per mouse, the median over the trials of each state. The absence across states is judged on the paper's test, a Kruskal-Wallis test over mice of these medians. For the groups, FigureS1.py plots optimal, disengaged, sub-optimal (pooled) and indeterminate in the panel whose legend gives p = 0.54, so the test is run on those four groups, as the paper's test of absence; the three discrete states alone are shown as a variant. Reproduced when the four-group test gives p >= 0.05 and the ITI part holds; the effect sizes are given either way.

claims.statement: The movement index is equally correlated with face motion energy and with locomotion speed, and highly correlated with both in each mouse.
claims.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 4; Figure S5B and S5C
claims.quote: we combined these two measures into a single continuous measure of uninstructed movement levels termed the “movement index,” which is equally correlated with each measure
claims.criterion: Per mouse, Pearson r of the movement index (M4) with face motion energy and with locomotion speed over the trials of M5 (Figure3.py). The sum of two z-scores has equal correlation with each term by construction, so the test is that the two r agree to 0.01 in every mouse. "Highly correlated" has no threshold in the paper; readings are (a) both r above 0.7 in every mouse, (b) both above 0.5. Reproduced when the r agree and (b) holds; the reading met is reported.

claims.statement: In the simulations, 1 kV applied to one electrode gives about 1.8 kV/cm in the center of the small array and 0.8 kV/cm in the center of the large array. The field near the energized electrode is about 4-fold higher (7 and 3.5 kV/cm per kV). Energizing one diagonal gives no field in the center.
claims.source: Methods 2.3, paragraph 4; Figure 3
claims.quote: For example, applying 1 kV to one electrode produced the electric field of approximately 1.8 kV/cm and 0.8 kV/cm in center of the small and large arrays ... The electric field strength was about 4-fold higher near the energized electrode (7 kV/cm and 3.5 kV/cm per 1 kV applied, for the small and large arrays, respectively) Note that energizing either electrode diagonal produced no electric field in the center of the array
claims.criterion: The values are outputs of the paper's Sim4Life finite-element model (Methods 2.3, built as in the paper's reference 15). The paper names no public deposit of the model or its field maps. The claim is tested only if the dataset holds the simulated field maps. Then reproduced when the four values are within tolerance and the center field for diagonal energizing is zero. A field model built by the author is not the paper's and is not a test. Without the maps the claim is blocked as data_missing.

claims.statement: Sham-exposed cells gain no YP fluorescence over the 10 min of imaging. Cells given pulses show a gradual rise in YP signal from the first frame after exposure.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 2; Figure 4
claims.quote: Sham-exposed cells showed no gain in YP fluorescence during the 10 min of observation. In contrast, cells treated by electric pulses displayed gradual increase in YP signal, starting from the image frame taken immediately after nsEP exposure.
claims.criterion: Per cell F minus F0, where F0 is the mean of the six frames before the pulse at 57 s (Methods 2.2). A claim of absence for sham, judged with the paper's test (Methods 2.4, a two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05), here one-sample against zero at the end of recording (O7, both readings). Reproduced when sham F minus F0 does not differ from zero, and every pulsed group's mean exceeds sham at the first frame after 57 s and keeps rising (end value above the first-frame value). The sham effect size is given either way.

claims.statement: A single 600-ns pulse at 15 kV/cm gives the strongest YP uptake, 126 +/- 14 a.u. (n = 25 cells) by the end of recording.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 2; Figure 4
claims.quote: A single 600-ns pulse at 15 kV/cm caused by far the strongest YP uptake, reaching 126±14 a.u. (n=25) by the end of recording.
claims.criterion: Tolerance is the paper's s.e. F minus F0 per cell (Methods 2.2), mean over cells, at the end of recording under either reading of O7. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance under one reading, the group has 25 cells (n is checked as reported), and the mean exceeds each other group's.

claims.statement: Bipolar signals that start with the same pulse cause much weaker uptake (p < 0.001). By the end of recording the 4-phasic signal reaches 20.8 +/- 2.0 a.u., the 8-phasic 6.9 +/- 1.6 a.u., and the 8-phasic with 5-us delays 25.4 +/- 2.8 a.u.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 2; Figure 4
claims.quote: Bipolar signals started with exactly the same pulse (600 ns, 15 kV/cm) but caused significantly weaker effects (p<0.001). By the end of recording, YP signal reached only 20.8±2.0 a.u. for the 4-phasic signal; 6.9±1.6 a.u. for the 8-phasic signal; and 25.4±2.8 a.u. for the 8-phasic signal with 5-μs delays between phases.
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the paper's s.e. Per cell F minus F0 at the end of recording (O7, both readings). Each bipolar group is compared with the unipolar group by an unpaired two-sided Student's t-test (Methods 2.4), in its equal-variance form, which is what Student's t-test names. The Welch form is shown as a variant only. Reproduced when, under one reading, all three means are within tolerance and all three tests give p < 0.001.

claims.statement: The 8-phasic signal with no delays causes about 20-fold weaker electroporation than a single unipolar pulse. The 4-phasic signal and the delayed 8-phasic signal cancel 4 to 5-fold.
claims.source: Figure 4 legend; Results 3.1, paragraph 2; Results 3.4, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Note that applying the 8-phasic bipolar signal with no inter-phase delays caused about 20-fold weaker electroporation than a single unipolar pulse
claims.criterion: Ratio of group means at the end of recording (O7, both readings). For the "4-5-fold" of Results 3.4 the range widened by 10% of each bound is 3.6 to 5.5. The paper's own means give 18.3 for the 8-phasic signal, 6.1 for the 4-phasic and 5.0 for the delayed 8-phasic. So the 4-phasic ratio printed in Results 3.1 already falls outside the 4 to 5 range. The main test is therefore the 8-phasic ratio, plus the ordering of cancellation (8-phasic strongest, the other two weaker). Reproduced when the 8-phasic ratio is within 18 to 22 and is the largest of the three. Partially reproduced when the ordering holds but the ratio is outside tolerance. Both of the other ratios are reported against 3.6 to 5.5.

claims.statement: Without rotation, the control of 40 unipolar trains from e1 causes much stronger electroporation throughout the array than 40 Packet 2 packets started from e1. The uptake after trains follows the field strength distribution and falls with distance from e1.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 5A
claims.quote: The lack of cancellation caused a much stronger electroporation throughout the array, and the distribution of YP uptake expectedly followed the electric field strength distribution in Fig. 3C .
claims.criterion: YP intensity along the e1 to e3 diagonal (Fig. 5A legend), Packet 2 at 6.4 kV, 40 packets against 40 trains, n = 4 to 5 dishes. Measured at three places the text names, the e1 end (outermost ROI), the center (O1) and the e3 end, each under O4 (a) and (b). Reproduced when the train mean exceeds the packet mean at all three places with unpaired two-sided t-tests at p < 0.05 (Methods 2.4), and the train profile falls with distance from e1 as the field does (Results 3.2), read as the e1-end value above the center value by the same test. The paper gives no test of the profile's shape, so the full train profile is shown. The outcome is the one all readings give; otherwise methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Without rotation, Packet 2 enhances electroporation in the center of the array despite the weakening of the field with distance from e1. Uptake near e1 still stays stronger than in the center.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 5A
claims.quote: In contrast, Packet 2 enhanced electroporation in the center of the array, despite gradual weakening of the electric field with distance from e1. However, the bipolar cancellation only partially offset the electric field weakening, and electroporation near e1 remained stronger than in the center.
claims.criterion: The 40-packet profile along the e1 to e3 diagonal (Fig. 5A). "Enhanced in the center" is read as a central peak, the center value (O1) above the lowest value between the center and the e1 end. Reproduced when, under all readings of O1 and O4, the center exceeds that trough and the e1-end value exceeds the center, each by a two-sided t-test at p < 0.05 over dishes (Methods 2.4; paired and unpaired, O6). When readings differ, methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: With rotation (1P x 40), Packet 2 smears the effect at the perimeter and brings out a remote effect in the center. The same rotation of unipolar trains (1T x 40) leaves a void of electroporation in the center.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 2; Figure 5B
claims.quote: Rotation with Packet 2 “smeared” the electroporation effect at the perimeter and emphasized the remote effect in the center. This remote effect contrasted with a void of electroporation in the center when the pulse train was applied in the same manner instead of the packet.
claims.criterion: Profiles averaged across both diagonals (Fig. 5B legend), n = 4 to 5. Reproduced when, under all readings of O1, O2 and O4, the 1P x 40 center value exceeds its lowest value between center and periphery, and the 1T x 40 center value is below its most peripheral value. The paper gives no measure of a "void", so whether the 1T x 40 center is the lowest point of its profile is reported but not required. Each comparison uses a two-sided t-test at p < 0.05 (Methods 2.4, O6).

claims.statement: Normalized to the most peripheral ROI (100%), rotated Packet 2 and rotated trains show sharply different spatial distributions. The packet's center is relatively high and the trains' center is relatively low.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 2; Figure 5C
claims.quote: The striking difference in the spatial distribution of electroporation between the CANCAN and control treatments is appreciated best by comparing the normalized fluorescence data, when the emission intensity in the most peripheral (closest to the electrode) ROI is taken as 100% ( Fig. 5C ).
claims.criterion: The paper prints no number for Fig. 5C. Same data as Fig. 5B, as % of the most peripheral ROI (O2, O3). Reproduced when the normalized center (O1) for 1P x 40 exceeds that for 1T x 40 by an unpaired two-sided t-test at p < 0.05 (Methods 2.4), under all readings. The normalized center values are reported, and whether the 1P x 40 value is above 100%.

claims.statement: Raising the total number of rotated Packet 2 packets from 4 to 20 and 40 strongly raises YP uptake throughout the array. A central peak is discernible for every treatment.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6A
claims.quote: Increasing the total number of applied packets from 4 to 20 and 40 profoundly enhanced the electroporative YP dye uptake throughout the electrode array ( Fig. 6A ). The peak of electroporation in the center was clearly discernable for all tested treatments.
claims.criterion: 1Px4, 5Px4 and 10Px4 (Fig. 6 legend), n = 3 to 4. The paper does not give the array or the voltage. Reproduced when, at the periphery (O2) and the center (O1), the means rise in the order 4 < 20 < 40 packets with 4 against 40 significant by an unpaired two-sided t-test at p < 0.05 (Methods 2.4), and each treatment's center exceeds the lowest value between center and periphery, under all readings of O1, O2 and O4.

claims.statement: The center is almost twofold brighter than the periphery for 1Px4. It is about the same as the periphery for 5Px4 and 10Px4.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6B
claims.quote: Its brightness was almost twofold higher than at the periphery for a single packet was applied 4 times from different directions, or about the same as at the periphery for the rotation of 5 and 10 packets ( Fig. 6B ).
claims.criterion: Center (O1) as a fraction of the most peripheral ROI (O2), normalized as O3, under O4. "Almost twofold" is taken as 2 with the default 10% tolerance. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all three values are within tolerance. Partially reproduced when the 1Px4 value is within tolerance and the others are not. All combinations are shown.

claims.statement: For all three packet numbers, the least affected area (between the center and the electrodes) shows about 2-fold lower fluorescence than the center.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6
claims.quote: Interestingly, the least affected area of the cell monolayer (between the center and the electrodes) showed about 2-fold lower fluorescence intensity than in the center for all the treatments.
claims.criterion: The minimum is the lowest value of the profile between the center and the most peripheral ROI. Readings are (a) the lowest single ROI of the mean profile; (b) the minimum of the LOESS fit (O5). Center as O1, background as O4. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the ratio is within tolerance for all three treatments.

claims.statement: The central peak becomes narrower with more packets.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6
claims.quote: Also, the central peak appeared narrower (sharper) with increasing the number of packets.
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure of peak width. Readings are (a) full width at half height of the central peak above the lowest value between center and periphery, on the mean profile; (b) the same on the LOESS fit (O5); (c) the distance between the two troughs flanking the center. Reproduced when, under all readings, the width falls from 1Px4 to 5Px4 to 10Px4. Partially reproduced when 10Px4 is narrower than 1Px4 under all readings but the order is not monotonic. When readings disagree, methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Raising the first-pulse amplitude from 2.4 to 5.6 kV (1Px4, small array) raises YP fluorescence about equally everywhere. It rises 15.5 times at the most peripheral point, 16.2 times half-way to the center and 16.8 times in the center.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 7A
claims.quote: For example, when the first pulse amplitude was increased from 2.4 to 5.6 kV ... YP fluorescence increased 15.5 times at the most peripheral point; 16.2 times half-way to the center; and 16.8 times in the center ( Fig. 7A ).
claims.criterion: Ratios of mean intensities (n = 3) at the most peripheral ROI (O2), the ROI half-way between it and the center, and the center (O1). Background is O4. Background subtraction can change ratios this large, so both readings are run. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all three ratios are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Normalized to the most peripheral ROI, profiles for different amplitudes fully overlap. The amplitude changes the degree of electroporation but not its spatial distribution. This holds for rotation of multiple packets (10Px4) and for the larger array.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 2; Figures 7B, 7C and 7D; Discussion, paragraph 5
claims.quote: When the YP emission was normalized to the most peripheral ROI, the data for different nsEP amplitudes fully overlapped ( Fig. 7B ). ... The findings held true for rotating multiple packets and when using the larger array ( Fig. 7C and D ).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged with the paper's test (Methods 2.4), an unpaired two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05, n = 3 per voltage. For each panel pair (A/B small array 1Px4; C/D large array 10Px4), the normalized values (O2, O3) of the lowest and the highest voltage are compared at the center and at half-way. Reproduced when no comparison reaches p < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. The differences in percentage points are given either way, and all voltage pairs are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Packets 1, 2 and 3 at 4 kV, rotated one cycle, give the same YP uptake in the center (215 to 235 a.u.).
claims.source: Results 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8A
claims.quote: All packets produced the same YP uptake in the center (215–235 a.u.)
claims.criterion: The reported range 215 to 235 widened by 10% of each bound is 193.5 to 258.5 a.u. Center as O1, background as O4, n = 3 to 4. A claim of absence for differences, judged with unpaired two-sided t-tests at p < 0.05 (Methods 2.4) between each pair of packets. Reproduced when the three means are inside 193.5 to 258.5 under one reading and no pair differs at p < 0.05. Not reproduced when a pair differs. Effect sizes are given either way.

claims.statement: Packets 1 and 3 cause much more YP uptake near the electrodes (250 to 350 a.u.) than Packet 2 (about 120 a.u.), p < 0.01.
claims.source: Results 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8A
claims.quote: but Packets 1 and 3 caused drastically more YP uptake near the electrodes (250–350 a.u. vs ~120 a.u. for packet 1, p<0.01, Fig. 8A )
claims.criterion: The text prints "~120 a.u. for packet 1". Since Packets 1 and 3 are the 250 to 350 group, ~120 a.u. must be Packet 2, and it is read so. The range 250 to 350 widened by 10% of each bound is 225 to 385. Most peripheral ROI as O2, background as O4. Reproduced when, under one reading, Packets 1 and 3 are inside 225 to 385, Packet 2 is within tolerance, and each of Packets 1 and 3 exceeds Packet 2 by an unpaired two-sided t-test at p < 0.01.

claims.statement: The normalized center YP emission is 183% of the periphery for Packet 2, but 83% for Packet 3 and 74% for Packet 1.
claims.source: Results 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8B
claims.quote: The superiority of Packet 2 for CANCAN targeting is highlighted by the drop of normalized YP emission in the center from 183% for Packet 2 to 83% and 74% for Packets 3 and 1, respectively ( Fig. 8B ).
claims.criterion: Center (O1) in % of the most peripheral ROI (O2), normalized as O3, background as O4. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all three values are within tolerance. Partially reproduced when the order (Packet 2 above 100%, Packets 1 and 3 below 100%) holds but a value is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: With the large array lifted 1, 2 and 3 mm above the monolayer, YP emission near the electrodes falls 2.4, 6.4 and 9 times, against electrodes touching the cells. In the center it falls only 1.02, 1.4 and 3.8 times.
claims.source: Results 3.5, paragraph 1; Figure 9A
claims.quote: Specifically, YP emission near the electrodes decreased 2.4, 6.4, and 9 times with 1-, 2- and 3-mm gaps (as compared to electrodes being in the same plane with cells); in the center, it decreased just 1.02, 1.4, and 3.8 times, respectively.
claims.criterion: Ratios of mean intensities (n = 3 to 4) at 0 mm over each gap. "Near the electrodes" is the most peripheral ROI (Fig. 9B legend, "measurements most distant from the center"; O2). Center as O1, background as O4. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all six ratios are within tolerance. Partially reproduced when every near-electrode ratio exceeds the center ratio at the same gap but some values are outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The faster fading of the effect near the electrodes raises targeting efficiency (center over periphery) to as much as 600% for the 2-mm gap. In the images, electroporation is confined almost entirely to the center when the electrodes are above the monolayer.
claims.source: Results 3.5, paragraph 1; Figures 9B and 9C
claims.quote: Such disproportionally faster fading of the effect near electrodes boosted the CANCAN targeting efficiency (measured as a ratio of the effect in the center and at the periphery) to as much as 600% for the 2-mm gap ( Fig. 9B ).
claims.criterion: Center (O1) in % of the most peripheral ROI (O2), normalized as O3, background as O4. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the 2-mm value is within tolerance and is the largest of the four distances. The 0, 1 and 3 mm values are reported.

claims.statement: Per session, 137 to 256 PMd and 55 to 93 M1 neurons were isolated in Monkey C and 66 to 121 PMd and 26 to 51 M1 neurons in Monkey M; neurons above 5 Hz, pooled over all CF and VR sessions, number 918 in M1 and 2221 in PMd.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Neural recordings, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Across all sessions, we isolated between 137 - 256 PMd and 55 - 93 M1 neurons for Monkey C, and 66 - 121 PMd and 26 - 51 M1 neurons for Monkey M ... Pooled across all monkeys and CF and VR sessions, this gave a population of 918 M1 and 2221 PMd neurons
claims.criterion: Units as sorted in the data, per area and session, for the 9 CF and 7 VR sessions. Each per-session count must lie in its monkey's range widened by 10% of each bound. The 5 Hz rule is the trial-averaged mean rate over all trials of the session (Methods do not say which trials; reading as stated). Reproduced when all ranges and both pooled counts hold; partially reproduced when the ranges hold and a pooled count does not.

claims.statement: On exposure to the curl field the monkeys made large reach direction errors that shrank gradually until behavior stabilized, and mirror-image after-effects appeared at the start of Washout.
claims.source: Results, Curl field adaptation involves widespread ..., paragraph 1; Figure 2C and 2D
claims.quote: Within each session, the monkeys exhibited large errors upon exposure to the CF, which were gradually reduced until behavior stabilized ... Further evidence of adaptation was revealed by behavioral after-effects (mirror image errors) that occurred upon return to normal reaching during the Washout epoch
claims.criterion: Error as M1 (movement onset per O10), CW sessions sign-flipped. The paper gives no test. Per session, the mean error of the Early block, of the Late block (O1 readings) and of the first eight Washout trials (Figure 5 legend). Reproduced when, across the 9 CF sessions, the Early mean exceeds the Late mean in at least 8 sessions and is greater by a two-sided paired t-test at p < 0.05, and the first eight Washout trials have a mean error of opposite sign to the Early Force error in at least 8 sessions. The thresholds of 8 of 9 sessions and the t-test are the reader's operational reading of "large errors ... gradually reduced" and are recorded as a deviation; the session medians are shown.

claims.statement: In VR sessions behavioral errors were similar in magnitude and time course to those of CF sessions, with large initial errors in Rotation and strong after-effects in Washout.
claims.source: Results, PMd to M1 mapping is unchanged throughout adaptation to a visuomotor rotation, paragraph 2; Figure 7B and 7C
claims.quote: In many respects, adaptation during the CF and VR sessions was quite similar. Behavioral errors were similar in magnitude and time course
claims.criterion: As fig2d-cf-behavioral-adaptation for the 7 VR sessions (Rotation in place of Force). Reproduced when the VR sessions meet the same rule and a two-sided two-sample t-test of per-session Early errors, VR against CF, gives p >= 0.05 (no test is given by the paper for "similar"; this reading is recorded as a deviation and the medians of both are shown).

claims.statement: In a representative CF session, the pairwise covariance of neurons in the Force and Washout blocks correlated with Baseline values at r of at least 0.85 in M1 and at least 0.93 in PMd.
claims.source: Results, Models to study adaptation-related changes ..., paragraph 2; Figure S2E
claims.quote: representative session ... Pearson's correlation with Baseline values r ≥ 0.85 for M1 and r ≥ 0.93 for PMd
claims.criterion: Method from STAR Methods, Single neuron covariance. Neurons above 1 Hz; spikes in 10 ms bins from target presentation to target acquisition; five blocks (Baseline split in two, Force split in two, Washout); in each block trials averaged per target; covariance between all pairs of neurons; Pearson r between each block's covariances and the Baseline covariances (Figure S2D legend, the two Baseline halves compared with each other and the Force and Washout blocks with the full Baseline). The representative session is the Monkey C session of Figures S2 and S6A, which the paper does not name; every CF session is computed. Open (deviation) whether the diagonal (variances) enters the correlation; both are run. Open (deviation) which neurons the r values pool, since the Results call them a representative session and the Figure S2E legend says "all combinations of neurons recorded in each of the nine CF sessions"; readings (a) one session at a time, (b) the pairs of all nine CF sessions pooled into one correlation per block. Reproduced when, under reading (a), at least one CF session has all its block r values at or above 0.85 - 0.085 in M1 and 0.93 - 0.093 in PMd, or, under reading (b), the pooled block r values meet the same bounds.

claims.statement: Across all CF sessions the similarity of the covariance between Baseline and the Force and Washout blocks resembled that between random subsamples of Baseline, so the covariance structure did not change with adaptation.
claims.source: Results, Models to study adaptation-related changes ..., paragraph 2; Figure S3A
claims.quote: Across all sessions, the differences in covariance strongly resembled those obtained from random subsamples of Baseline data for which the covariance structure should be unchanged
claims.criterion: Covariance as figs2-covariance-preserved-example; the reference distribution from random subsamples of Baseline trials, compared with each other, 100 times per session (STAR Methods, Single neuron covariance; the subsample size is not given, read as two random halves of Baseline compared with each other, as in Figure S2D). The paper gives no test. Reading recorded as a deviation; reproduced when, in each area, the median over sessions of the Force 1, Force 2 and Washout r values lies inside the range of the pooled Baseline-split r values, and partially reproduced when that holds for one area only. The distributions are shown.

claims.statement: In VR sessions as well, the changes in neural activity preserved the population covariance structure.
claims.source: Results, PMd to M1 mapping is unchanged throughout adaptation to a visuomotor rotation, paragraph 2; Figure S3B (the Results cite it as Figure S2B, which shows CF example neurons; the VR covariance summary is Figure S3B)
claims.quote: Additionally, changes in neural activity preserved the population covariance structure
claims.criterion: As figs3a-covariance-like-baseline-split for the 7 VR sessions (Rotation blocks in place of Force).

claims.statement: In every session the PMd manifold had more dimensions than the M1 manifold (median 14 against 8.5).
claims.source: Results, Models to study adaptation-related changes ..., paragraph 3; Figure 3B
claims.quote: In all sessions, the PMd manifold contained more dimensions than did the M1 manifold ... M1 median, 8.5; PMd median, 14
claims.criterion: Dimensionality by the method adapted from Machens et al. 2010 (STAR Methods, Dimensionality reduction, paragraph 2) on rates as M2; noise from differences between random pairs of trials to the same target, 1000 repetitions, 99% limit of each noise eigenvalue; threshold rule and data as O9, window as O3. Over all 16 sessions (Figure 3B legend, "all sessions from both monkeys"). Reproduced when, under one reading, PMd exceeds M1 in every session and both medians are within tolerance; partially reproduced when PMd exceeds M1 in every session and a median is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: With random subsamples of equal, fixed numbers of neurons, estimated dimensionality fell for small samples but PMd stayed higher-dimensional than M1 for every neuron count tested.
claims.source: Figure S4D legend; STAR Methods, Dimensionality reduction, paragraph 2
claims.quote: With decreasing neuron counts, we began to underestimate the apparent dimensionality. However, critically, PMd (red) was consistently higher dimensional than M1 (black) for all tested neuron counts
claims.criterion: As fig3b-pmd-higher-dimensional, on random subsamples of 40, 50, 60 and 70 neurons per area and all neurons (the counts on the Figure S4D axis), mean over sessions. Number of subsamples per size not given; standard choice of 100 (cannot change the sign of the comparison in expectation). Sessions with fewer neurons than a size are left out of that size (open; deviation). Reproduced when the PMd mean exceeds the M1 mean at every size.

claims.statement: Single neurons contributed to both output-potent and output-null subspaces; the null/potent index was centered on zero with virtually no neurons near -1 or 1.
claims.source: Figure S4C legend; STAR Methods, Output-potent and output-null subspaces, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The distribution of neurons was centered around zero and virtually no neurons had a null/potent index close to -1 / 1, indicating that the output-potent and output-null subspaces captured population-wide features
claims.criterion: Index per PMd neuron from the product of the PCA loading matrix and V (M2, M3, O7) as (sum of absolute potent weights - sum of absolute null weights) / (sum of both). "Magnitude" is read as the sum of absolute values; the sum of squares is the second reading. Reproduced when the mean index over neurons lies between -0.1 and 0.1 and fewer than 1% of neurons have an absolute index above 0.9 (the reader's reading of "centered" and "virtually no", recorded as a deviation); the shuffled control is shown.

claims.statement: In the CF sessions pooled, the number of M1 or PMd neurons with significant GLM fits was 214 for M1-M1, 338 for PMd-PMd, 170 for PC-M1, 144 for Pot-M1 and 97 for Null-M1; the Basic model was significant for 522 of 918 M1 and 612 of 2221 PMd neurons.
claims.source: Figures 3C and S5E (cell counts in the panels); STAR Methods, Selecting cells with significant GLM predictions
claims.quote: This reduced the pool of candidate cells to 522 of 918 (57%) in M1 and 612 of 2221 (28%) in PMd
claims.criterion: Selection as M6 with M2 to M5; readings O3, O6, O8. The Basic counts are read as over all CF and VR sessions (the denominators 918 and 2221 are the pooled counts); the per-model counts are over the nine CF sessions (Figure 3C legend, "pooled across nine sessions"). Reproduced when, under one reading, all seven counts are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at least four are.

claims.statement: Pot-M1 and Null-M1 had similar cross-validated accuracy within the end-of-Force training trials.
claims.source: Results, Output-potent activity in PMd consistently predicts M1 neurons ..., paragraph 2; Figure S5E
claims.quote: Both models had similar accuracy when evaluated within the end-of-Force training trials using ten-fold crossvalidation
claims.criterion: Cross-validated rpR2 of the selected cells for Pot-M1 and Null-M1 in the CF sessions (M6). The paper gives no test for "similar"; the test it uses for rpR2 distributions is the two-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov test at p = 0.01 (M8), taken here. A claim of absence; reproduced when that test does not find a difference, with medians of both shown.

claims.statement: The rpR2 distributions of the within-area models M1-M1 and PMd-PMd did not differ between Early and Late Force trials (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 0.72 and p = 0.19).
claims.source: Figure 3E (p-values in the panel); Results, Curl field adaptation is not associated ..., paragraph 2
claims.quote: M1-M1 and PMd-PMd had similar distributions during Early and Late
claims.criterion: Per selected cell, rpR2 of the trained model (M6) on the Early and on the Late block (O1; rpR2 computed over the block's bins together), pooled over the nine CF sessions; two-sided two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (M8) at p = 0.01. A claim of absence; reproduced when the test is not significant for both models under every reading, not reproduced when it is significant for either; p-values and medians shown.

claims.statement: Model error of M1-M1 and PMd-PMd did not differ between Early and Late Force; the local models generalized throughout CF adaptation.
claims.source: Figure 3G (legend "No effects were significant (two-sample t-test)"); Results, Curl field adaptation is not associated ..., paragraph 2
claims.quote: We found that both within-area models ( M1 -M1, PMd -PMd) generalized well, predicting the adaptation-related changes in single-neuron spiking nearly equally well in both blocks
claims.criterion: Model error as M7 (O1, O5), Early against Late, two-sided two-sample t-test at p = 0.01 (M8), per model. A claim of absence, judged on this test; reproduced when neither model differs, not reproduced when either does; the mean errors are shown.

claims.statement: Null-M1 generalized significantly worse in Early than in Late Force, while Pot-M1 generalized well in both blocks.
claims.source: Figure 4D legend (Results cite it as Figure 4E); Results, Output-potent activity in PMd consistently predicts M1 neurons ..., paragraph 2
claims.quote: The Pot -M1 model generalized well throughout learning, making accurate predictions in Early Force as well as Late Force ... However, the Null -M1 model generalized significantly worse in the Early block than in the Late block
claims.criterion: Model error as M7 (O1, O5), Early against Late, two-sided two-sample t-test at p = 0.01 (M8), with subspaces from M3 (O7). Reproduced when, under every reading, Null-M1 has a significantly larger Early error and Pot-M1 has no significant difference; partially reproduced when the Null-M1 effect holds and Pot-M1 also differs; not reproduced when Null-M1 does not differ. Readings that disagree block the claim.

Whether 685 is counted before or after that exclusion is not said; both counts are shown and either may match. The degrees of freedom of the Figure 4e cluster tests (78, 73, 50, 52, 111, 140, 167) imply 80, 75, 52, 54, 113, 142 and 169 neurons, 685 in total. Those of Extended Data Figure 8d imply 613 untagged, 39 BLA-NAc and 32 BLA-CeA neurons, 684 in total; the Methods exclude one BLA-CeA neuron from every analysis except basal firing, so that exclusion does not explain the gap of one. These counts are reported.

claims.statement: In the CRISPR group, untagged BLA neurons and BLA-CeA neurons have lower basal firing rates than in controls, while BLA-NAc neurons do not differ.

claims.quote: Both non-tagged BLA neurons and the BLA-CeA neurons showed significantly lower basal firing rates (in Hz) in the CRISPR group compared to the control group

claims.statement: BLA-NAc and BLA-CeA neurons are identified by short-latency responses to light at the end of each session.

claims.quote: At the end of each session, we optogenetically photoidentified BLA-NAc and BLA-CeA neurons based on previously reported photoresponse latencies
claims.criterion: The Methods' rule (Analysis for in vivo recordings). PSTHs of 1 ms bins 50 ms around light onset, z-scored against the 50 ms before it; a unit is photo-responsive when it has a significant excitation (z above 1.98) within 6 ms of onset, no significant response 7 to 50 ms after onset with a 6 ms moving average, and no significant response in the fake session. Its projection (BLA-NAc or BLA-CeA) is that of the mouse's Cav2-Cre injection. Which light pulses enter the PSTH is not fixed; readings are (a) all pulse onsets of the 1, 10 and 100 Hz trains and the onset of the 1 s light, (b) the 1 Hz pulses only. When the dataset holds the authors' tag labels they are used and the recomputed labels are compared with them. Reproduced when the identified counts are within 10% of 39 BLA-NAc and 32 BLA-CeA neurons (counts read from the degrees of freedom of Extended Data Figure 8d and 8j) under one reading.

claims.statement: The CRISPR group has smaller proportions of neurons excited or inhibited by each of the three CSs, but the response magnitude of the responsive neurons does not differ from controls.

claims.quote: CRISPR mice showed overall reduced proportions, but not responsive amplitudes of excited and inhibited neurons to all three cues relative to the control group
claims.criterion: PSTHs of 20 ms bins for 1 s before and after CS onset, z-scored against the 1 s before onset; a response is significant at a z-score of plus or minus 1.98 (Methods). How the threshold is applied is not fixed; readings are (a) the mean z-score over 0 to 1 s, (b) any 20 ms bin in 0 to 1 s. The paper gives no test for the proportions; reproduced when, under every reading, the CRISPR proportion of excited and of inhibited neurons is lower for all three CSs, and the amplitude comparison (two-tailed unpaired t-test, the paper's default) finds no difference at p < 0.05 for any of the six cue and direction groups.

claims.statement: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of BLA responses to the sucrose, neutral and shock CSs gives seven functional clusters.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT amplify BLA representation, paragraph 1; Figure 4d
claims.quote: we clustered BLA neurons into seven functional groups based on their responses across all task events using unsupervised hierarchical clustering
claims.criterion: As the Methods give it (Functional hierarchical clustering). Per neuron, 20 ms PSTHs from 1 s before to 1 s after CS onset, z-scored with the mean and SD of the 1 s baseline, smoothed in time with a Gaussian-weighted moving average of smoothing factor 0.85 (MATLAB smoothdata), the sucrose, neutral and shock CS traces concatenated; all neurons of both groups clustered together. Ward linkage with correlation distance; cut at 35% of the maximum linkage distance. Ward on a correlation distance is not standard, so the readings are (a) Ward linkage on the correlation distance matrix, (b) Ward linkage with Euclidean distance on rows centred and scaled to unit norm (equivalent to correlation). Reproduced when one reading gives seven clusters.

claims.statement: Within the task-relevant clusters, the CRISPR group has smaller responses to the sucrose and shock CSs than controls, while neutral-CS responses are largely unchanged.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT amplify BLA representation, paragraph 1; Figure 4e
claims.quote: the CRISPR-cKO decreased the proportions of CS-responsive neurons and attenuated the magnitude of neural responses to Sucrose and Shock CSs within each task-relevant cluster
claims.criterion: Clusters from fig4d-seven-clusters. Per neuron the response is the mean z-score in a window after CS onset; the window is the shaded region of Figure 4e, not given in the text, and the readings are (a) 0 to 1 s, (b) 0 to 0.5 s. Per cluster and CS, a two-tailed unpaired t-test of CRISPR against control neurons. The paper's cluster numbering cannot be recovered from the text, so clusters are judged as a set. The paper found 7 of the 14 sucrose and shock tests significant, each with a smaller absolute response in CRISPR, and 1 of 7 neutral tests. Reproduced when, under every reading, at least 5 of 14 sucrose and shock tests have p < 0.05 with a smaller absolute response in CRISPR and at most 2 of 7 neutral tests do; partially reproduced when 3 or 4 do.

claims.statement: In the CRISPR group, smaller proportions of BLA-NAc neurons fall in the clusters that preferentially encode positive valence (clusters 1 and 3), and smaller proportions of BLA-CeA neurons in those that preferentially encode negative valence (clusters 2 and 4), than in controls.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 8i
claims.quote: The proportion of BLA-NAc neurons in cluster 1 and 3 which preferentially encode positive valence was less in the CRISPR group compared to the control group
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test. Clusters from fig4d-seven-clusters; the paper's numbering cannot be recovered from the text, and the legend names which clusters encode positive or negative valence without defining it. Reading, a cluster encodes positive valence when its mean z-scored response over 0 to 1 s after CS onset (as in fig4e-cluster-responses-attenuated) is higher to the sucrose CS than to the shock CS, and negative valence when the reverse. Reproduced when the fraction of BLA-NAc neurons in positive-valence clusters and the fraction of BLA-CeA neurons in negative-valence clusters are both lower in CRISPR than in control.

claims.statement: In controls BLA-NAc neurons are excited and BLA-CeA neurons inhibited by the sucrose CS; the CRISPR-cKO removes the BLA-NAc excitation and the BLA-CeA inhibition.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT amplify BLA representation, paragraph 1; Figure 4f-g; Extended Data Figure 8j
claims.quote: BLA-NAc and BLA-CeA population in the CRISPR group showed significantly reduced excitation and inhibition to the sucrose CS compared to the control group, respectively
claims.criterion: Response per neuron as in fig4e-cluster-responses-attenuated (z-scored 20 ms PSTH, windows (a) 0 to 1 s, (b) 0 to 0.5 s). Extended Data Figure 8j measures a "valence encoding pattern" the text does not define; its tests are recorded but not run. Reproduced when, under every reading, the BLA-NAc sucrose response is lower and the BLA-CeA sucrose response higher (less negative) in CRISPR than in control, each with p < 0.05 by a two-tailed unpaired t-test, and the control BLA-NAc mean is above zero and the control BLA-CeA mean below zero. The neutral and shock CS comparisons are reported.

claims.statement: In control mice BLA-NAc neurons are predominantly excited by the sucrose CS and BLA-CeA neurons by the shock CS.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT amplify BLA representation, paragraph 1; Figure 4f-g
claims.quote: we replicated our previous reports in control mice showing that BLA-NAc and BLA-CeA neurons are predominantly excited by Sucrose CS and Shock CS, respectively
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test. Control mice only, responses as in fig4fg-projector-sucrose-responses. "Predominantly excited" is read as (a) the population mean response to that CS is positive and larger than to the other CS, (b) the proportion of neurons significantly excited (z above 1.98, as in ed8fg-fewer-responsive-neurons) is larger for that CS than for the other. Reproduced when both hold for both populations under every reading.

claims.statement: Population trajectories of the CRISPR group are shorter for all three CSs, and the distance between sucrose and shock trajectories is smaller, than in controls.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT amplify BLA representation, paragraph 2; Figure 5a
claims.quote: trajectories in the CRISPR group showed significant decreases in total trajectory length and trajectory distance between sucrose and shock trials compared to the controls
claims.criterion: As the Methods give it (Neural trajectory analysis). Per neuron, mean firing rates in 20 ms bins from -1 to 1 s around each CS onset (raw rates, as the legend says). Control neurons randomly subsampled to the number of CRISPR neurons. One PCA for both groups, with the same coefficients for every projection. The text does not say how a single PCA spans two sets of neurons; readings are (a) the two groups' neuron-by-time matrices, of equal neuron count, are stacked along time, so each component weights neuron slots shared by the groups (the reading that lets the same coefficients serve both groups and the cross-group decoder of Figure 5b-c), (b) all neurons of both groups are variables and each group's trajectory uses its own neurons with the other group's entries set to zero. Components explaining 95% of variance; length as the sum of Euclidean distances between adjacent bins; distance between the sucrose and shock trajectories as the bin-by-bin Euclidean distance summed over bins (a mean gives the same comparison). Statistics over leave-one-mouse-out iterations with the PCA coefficients fixed, two-tailed unpaired t-test. The random subsample and the neuron pairing are not fixed and could change the outcome, so each reading is run over 20 random subsamples and the fraction of them reaching p < 0.05 reported. Reproduced when, under every reading, the median subsample gives a shorter CRISPR length for all three CSs and a smaller CRISPR sucrose to shock distance, each with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: A linear SVM decodes sucrose against shock trials from BLA population activity above label-shuffled chance in both control and CRISPR groups, with no significant difference between the groups.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT to the BLA mediates passive-active behavioral strategies, paragraph 2; Figure 5b
claims.quote: We found that BLA neurons from both control and CRISPR groups could decode the trial type compared to label-shuffled trials, when the SVM classifier was trained and tested within-group
claims.criterion: As the Methods give it (Support Vector Machine classifier). Single-trial activity projected on the global PCA coefficients of fig5a-trajectories-reduced, first 10 PCs as features, linear SVM, 5-fold cross-validation (80% train, 20% test), sucrose trials subsampled to the shock count 50 times per fold, AUC of the ROC; the same with training labels shuffled. Open details, each run. The neurons were not recorded together, so a single "trial" of the population is a pseudo-trial; readings are (a) trial k of a type for every neuron, up to the smallest trial count, (b) one trial drawn at random per neuron for each pseudo-trial. Time, (i) features from activity averaged over 0 to 1 s after CS onset (the legend's "averaged neural activity of each trial"), (ii) AUC per 20 ms bin, averaged over 0 to 1 s (the Methods' "as a function of time"). Statistics on the 5 fold AUCs by one-way ANOVA with Holm-Sidak comparisons. Reproduced when, under every reading, both within-group AUCs exceed their shuffled AUCs at p < 0.05 and control against CRISPR has p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: A decoder trained on CRISPR data decodes control data, but a decoder trained on control data performs significantly worse on CRISPR data.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT to the BLA mediates passive-active behavioral strategies, paragraph 2; Figure 5c
claims.quote: SVM decoder performance significantly dropped when the model was trained on the control data and tested on the CRISPR data, compared to trained on the CRISPR data and tested on the control data
claims.criterion: As fig5b-within-group-decoding, training on one group's pseudo-trials and testing on the other's, in the shared PC space of reading (a) of fig5a-trajectories-reduced (reading (b) gives disjoint features for the two groups, so cross-group decoding is run under (a) only). Reproduced when, under every remaining reading, trained-on-CRISPR AUC exceeds trained-on-control AUC at p < 0.05 and both exceed shuffled. The statistics section's effect sizes, read as the first condition minus the second, run the other way (trained on control tested on CRISPR is 0.4769 above shuffled, trained on CRISPR tested on control 0.1662 above, a gap of 0.31), so its labels and the text disagree. The direction of the Results and the legend is judged; the opposite result is reported and the disagreement recorded as a deviation.

claims.statement: CRISPR mice make more port entries at baseline and in the late sucrose-trial period, have a lower baseline-normalized port entry response to the sucrose CS, and freeze more to the shock CS relative to baseline.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT to the BLA mediates passive-active behavioral strategies, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 8e
claims.quote: showed significantly enhanced baseline port entries and reduced port entry specificity during sucrose trials, compared to the control group
claims.criterion: Last discrimination-task session. Port entry probability with 500 ms bins over 25 s before and after CS onset, z-scored against the 25 s baseline (Methods). Baseline is the 25 s before CS onset; the late window is 10 to 25 s after sucrose delivery as the statistics say; the window of the z-scored comparison is not given, readings (a) 0 to 10 s and (b) 0 to 25 s after CS onset. Freezing in shock trials by the Methods' velocity rule (below 0.3 cm/s) during the CS. The text does not say how freezing was z-scored; readings are (c) against the freezing fraction in the 20 s before CS onset across the session's shock trials, (d) against the 30 s before CS onset (the video segment of Measurement of fear behavior). Reproduced when the four significant comparisons have p < 0.05 in the stated directions under every reading (two-tailed unpaired t-test across mice).

claims.statement: Unsupervised trial-by-trial clustering of pose-derived behavior gives seven clusters for sucrose trials and five for shock trials, which separate passive and active strategies.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT to the BLA mediates passive-active behavioral strategies, paragraph 3; Figure 5d-e and 5g-h; Methods, Unsupervised trial-based classification of behaviors
claims.quote: Following watershed segmentation, we obtained seven clusters for sucrose trials and five clusters for shock trials
claims.criterion: As the Methods give it.
