Pose of head, electrode, ears and tail from DeepLabCut; eight measures (velocity, distance to port, direction, direction relative to port, and the change of each) for 300 frames (20 s at 15 fps) after CS onset; tsfresh 0.16.0 features (about 6000); PCA, t-SNE on the top 30 PCs (Extended Data Figure 8k), a kernel density over the t-SNE map (seaborn kdeplot), local maxima as markers for a watershed; sucrose and shock trials separately. The paper's pose estimates or its trained network are needed; if the dataset holds neither, a new network would be the agent's choice and the claim is blocked. t-SNE perplexity, the kernel bandwidth and the random seed are not given; they change the cluster count, so the defaults of scikit-learn and seaborn are used with several seeds and the counts reported. Reproduced when the default settings give 7 and 5 clusters for most seeds.

claims.statement: Control mice show more active-strategy trials than CRISPR mice in both sucrose and shock trials.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT to the BLA mediates passive-active behavioral strategies, paragraph 3; Figure 5f and 5i
claims.quote: We found that control mice preferred active behavioral strategies during both sucrose and shock trials ... CRISPR-cKO abolished this behavioral preference to active strategies
claims.criterion: Clusters from fig5dh-behavior-clusters labelled passive or active as the Figure 5 legend defines them, sucrose clusters by low or high change in distance moved toward the port after CS onset, shock clusters by high freezing with low darting or low freezing with high darting. The split is not given; readings are (a) clusters above or below the median of the cluster means, (b) above or below the mean over all trials. Shock clusters matching neither pattern are left out. Darting is not defined in the text and freezing in this task is read by the Methods' 0.3 cm/s rule. Per mouse the fraction of active trials; two-tailed unpaired t-test. Reproduced when, under every reading, control mice have a higher fraction for both trial types with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: BLA responses to the CSs are larger in active trials, and the CRISPR-cKO reduces the responses of untagged BLA neurons in active trials for both sucrose and shock CSs.
claims.source: Results, NT inputs from the PVT to the BLA mediates passive-active behavioral strategies, paragraph 3; Extended Data Figure 8o and 8s
claims.quote: Finally, we observed predominant BLA neural responses to CSs during the active behavioral trials, which were diminished by the
claims.criterion: Response per neuron and trial type as in fig4e-cluster-responses-attenuated, computed separately over active and passive trials, with trial numbers matched between the two (Methods). The unit of the ANOVA is not given (its degrees of freedom exceed the neuron counts); readings are (a) neuron by state values, (b) trial by neuron values. Two-way ANOVA of group by state with Holm-Sidak comparisons. Reproduced when, under every reading, untagged neurons in active trials respond less in CRISPR than in control at p < 0.05 for both CSs. The first part of the statement (larger responses in active trials) has the paper's support only in the sucrose-CS state effect; the state effects are reported for both CSs.

claims.statement: Bath-applied NT (10 nM) enhances EPSCs in BLA-NAc neurons and suppresses them in BLA-CeM neurons, and an NTSR1 antagonist abolishes the difference.
claims.source: Results, The temporal dynamics of NT are critical for valence assignment, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 9f-g
claims.quote: At a concentration of 10 nM, NT significantly enhanced EPSCs in BLA-NAc neurons and suppressed EPSCs in BLA-CeM neurons

claims.statement: Pre-incubation with NT (10 nM) reduces STDP-induced LTP in BLA-NAc neurons but not in BLA-CeM neurons.
claims.source: Results, The temporal dynamics of NT are critical for valence assignment, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 9k-l
claims.quote: STDP-induced LTP in the presence of NT (10 nM) 10–50 minutes after induction was reduced in BLA-NAc neurons, but unchanged in BLA-CeM neurons compared with the ACSF control

claims.statement: Intra-BLA NTSR1 antagonist before conditioning enhances tone-sucrose learning and does not change freezing in tone-shock conditioning.
claims.source: Results, The temporal dynamics of NT are critical for valence assignment, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 10b-c
claims.quote: NTSR1 antagonist delivered in the BLA 15 minutes before the conditioning session enhanced reward learning but had no effects on punishment learning

claims.statement: Ntsr1 CRISPR-cKO in BLA-CeA neurons, but not BLA-NAc neurons, reduces port entry to the sucrose CS; global BLA Ntsr1 cKO before acquisition impairs tone-sucrose learning, while cKO after acquisition does not affect recall.
claims.source: Results, The temporal dynamics of NT are critical for valence assignment, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 10k and 10o
claims.quote: we found that CRISPR-cKO of Ntsr1 gene in the BLA suppressed reward learning

claims.statement: The Kiloscope records thousands of neurons at once in a freely behaving mouse; in the mouse with the best expression EXTRACT gave 2,948 footprints.
claims.source: Main text, page 546, paragraph 3; Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 1
claims.quote: The second design, the Kiloscope, provides cellular resolution imaging across a 4.8 × 3.6 mm FOV in a device weighing only 1.4 g, allowing us to simultaneously record from thousands of neurons in a freely behaving mouse ... For the mouse with the best calcium indicator expression, this extraction yielded 2,948 footprints
claims.criterion: The count is the number of footprints EXTRACT returned for the one session, as the Methods report it (NoRMCorre, then EXTRACT with a minimum cell-finding SNR of 2). Reproduced when the count is within tolerance and the footprints were recorded together in a session of free exploration of the maze.

claims.statement: In the mouse with the most footprints, manual curation leaves 2,382 putative neurons.
claims.source: Main text, page 548, paragraph 2; Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 6a
claims.quote: In the data from the mouse with the most footprints, manual curation using the same criteria described above yielded 2,382 footprints.
claims.criterion: The curation was made by eye (Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 1) and cannot be redone from the paper. The claim is tested by counting the footprints marked as curated, if the data mark them; otherwise it cannot be tested.

claims.statement: The Kiloscope was used in four mice, and more than a thousand neurons were recorded at once in more than one of them; EXTRACT gave 2,948, 401, 1,029 and 112 footprints.
claims.source: Main text, page 548, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 6b to 6d
claims.quote: we used the microscope to record in four freely moving mice and were able to simultaneously record more than a thousand neurons in cortex in multiple mice ... We then analyzed the data using EXTRACT and extracted 2,948, 401, 1,029 and 112 footprints in these mice.

claims.statement: The Featherscope recorded hundreds of neurons in juvenile songbirds; curation gave 177, 46 and 225 footprints in three birds.
claims.source: Main text, page 548, paragraph 1 (continuing from page 547); Extended Data Fig. 5
claims.quote: and extracted 177, 46 and 225 manually curated footprints that exhibited the spatial profile and temporal fluctuations characteristic of neuronal calcium signals in cortex

claims.statement: Birds carrying the Featherscope sang 3,861 to 23,545 syllables per day, within the normal range.
claims.source: Main text, page 547, paragraph 2; Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Implanted birds sang between 3,861 and 23,545 syllables per day, within the normal range and far exceeding the minimum amount needed for analysis of neural activity
claims.criterion: Per bird, the maximum over days of the number of syllables sung in a day (Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 3). A reported range, so reproduced when the three values lie in the range widened by 10% of each bound (3475 to 25900).

claims.statement: The activity of almost all LMAN footprints during song shows the sparse random bursting seen in earlier recordings of LMAN.
claims.source: Main text, page 548, paragraph 1; Fig. 2c and 2d
claims.quote: The activity patterns of almost all footprints recapitulate the sparse random bursting seen in previous observations of LMAN activity during song (Fig. 2c,d)
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure of sparse bursting and no count of the footprints that show it; the claim cannot be judged by a method the paper fixes (methods_underspecified).

claims.statement: The Kiloscope's field of view is 4.8 x 3.6 mm (about 4 mm in the abstract).
claims.source: Abstract; main text, page 546, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The second design, the Kiloscope, provides cellular resolution imaging across a 4.8 × 3.6 mm FOV
claims.criterion: The field of view is the imaging frame's width and height in pixels times the object-plane pixel size. The paper does not state the pixel size. The code uses 5.94 um per pixel for the Kiloscope (sf3/widefield/analysis.m, on 808 x 608 pixel frames) and 5.35 um per pixel for the Kiloscope bead images (f2+sf4/wf_analysis_secondorder.m); the main text's 0.13 pixels = 0.7 um implies about 5.4 um. A pixel size stored with the data is used when there is one; otherwise both code values are readings, and the claim is reproduced when both sides are within tolerance under a reading.

claims.statement: The two microscopes weigh 1.4 g (Kiloscope, large field of view) and 1.0 g (Featherscope, 1.0 mm field of view).
claims.source: Abstract; main text, page 546, paragraph 3; Methods, Optics and construction, paragraph 9
claims.quote: Using this light path, we designed two microscopes: one optimized for FOV (~4 mm FOV; 1.4 g), and the other optimized for weight (1.0 mm FOV; 1.0 g).

claims.statement: The Featherscope's resolution (FWHM of the bead PSF) is about 4 um at the centre of the field of view and 7 um at the edges.
claims.source: Main text, page 547, paragraph 1 (continuing from page 546); Fig. 1e
claims.quote: center of its FOV, which decreases to 7 μm at the edges and is limited by the astigmatism of the GRIN lenses (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b)
claims.criterion: As in f2+sf4/feather_analysis_secondorder.m, each bead region at its listed slice (the most focused, Methods, Imaging performance characterization) is fitted with a rotated 2D Gaussian with the code's second-order pixel correction at 1.68 um per pixel, and FWHM is 2.355 times each axis's width. Radial distance is from the code's centre (row 273, column 400), and beads are grouped to the nearest of 0, 100, ..., 500 um; centre is the 0 um group and edge the 500 um group. Which width is "resolution" is open. The readings are (a) the median major-axis FWHM, (b) the median minor-axis FWHM (the box plots of Fig. 1e), (c) the mean major-axis FWHM, (d) the mean minor-axis FWHM (the code's error bar plot, one curve per axis). Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under a reading.

claims.statement: The Kiloscope's resolution (FWHM of the bead PSF) is about 4 um at the centre of the field of view and about 5 um at the edges.
claims.source: Main text, page 547, paragraph 1; Fig. 1f
claims.quote: The Kiloscope has a resolution of approximately 4 μm at the center of its FOV, which decreases to about 5 μm at the edges and is limited by the sensor pixel size
claims.criterion: As for fig1e-featherscope-psf, with f2+sf4/wf_analysis_secondorder.m (5.35 um per pixel, centre at row 259, column 420, groups 0, 250, ..., 1500 um; edge is the 1500 um group), and the same four readings.

claims.statement: Both microscopes have field curvature small enough for typical imaging depths.
claims.source: Main text, page 547, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 1c and 1f
claims.quote: Both microscope designs have sufficiently small field curvature for typical imaging depths (Extended Data Fig. 1c,f).
claims.criterion: The paper gives no bound on field curvature and no typical imaging depth, so no method it fixes decides the claim (methods_underspecified). The height of best focus against radius (the Slice column, over the 100 um stack of the Methods) is reported for both microscopes.

claims.statement: Images of a USAF 1951 target resolve elements of 2.19 um line width with the Featherscope and 4.38 um with the Kiloscope, and 2.2 um with Kiloscope optics on a sensor with 1.4 um pixels.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1b, 1e and 4b
claims.quote: The line widths of the largest and smallest elements visible in the inset are 3.91 μm and 2.19 μm, respectively ... The line widths of the largest and smallest elements visible in the inset are 6.96 μm and 4.38 μm, respectively ... The smallest element in group 7 is resolvable and has a linewidth of 2.2 μm.

claims.statement: For the Featherscope, the axicon correction optics give a flat signal profile across the field of view, where total vignetting (optical vignetting with Gaussian illumination) makes the signal fall toward the edges.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2b; Methods, Coupling optics, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Total vignetting (yellow) illustrates the decrease in fluorescent signal caused by the combination of optical vignetting and a Gaussian-shaped excitation light profile. The curve with correction optics (blue) illustrates the flat signal intensity profile that can be achieved with an axicon pair that increases the excitation intensity at the edges of the field of view.
claims.criterion: Radial profiles as sf3/feather/analysis.m computes them (1.68 um per pixel, centred on the intensity-weighted centre, 1 um radial bins, moving median of 3 bins, normalized to the 99th percentile); the corrected profile is the axicons image, total vignetting the reference image, optical vignetting the led image. The paper gives no measure of flatness. The edge radius is open; the readings are 0.5 mm (half the 1.0 mm field of view) and 0.45 mm. Reproduced when, under both, the corrected profile at the edge radius is higher than the total vignetting profile and its fall from the centre is smaller. The profiles are shown.

claims.statement: For the Kiloscope, the axicon correction optics give a flat signal profile across the field of view, where total vignetting makes the signal fall toward the edges.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2c
claims.quote: c, same as in (b) but for the Kiloscope.
claims.criterion: As for ed2b-featherscope-flat-illumination, with sf3/widefield/analysis.m (5.94 um per pixel, moving median of 10 bins). The edge radius readings are 1.8 mm (half the 3.6 mm side) and 2.0 mm (the code's plotted range).

claims.statement: The onboard analog-to-digital converter records test tones with a root-mean-square residual of 0.2% of full scale.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3
claims.quote: The time series deviates from a pure tone with a root-mean-square residual of 0.2% of the full scale, calculated using the full bandwidth of the recorded signal.

claims.statement: Lateral shifts of the image due to the mouse's movement are small, with a root-mean-square displacement of 0.13 pixels (0.7 um).
claims.source: Main text, page 548, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 7
claims.quote: Lateral shifts of the image due to mouse motion were small (root-mean-square displacement of 0.13 pixels or 0.7 μm (Extended Data Fig. 7).
claims.criterion: Displacements are those NoRMCorre estimates on the raw imaging video of the session (Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 7 plots horizontal and vertical displacement of the field of view over time). The NoRMCorre settings are not given; rigid registration (one shift per frame, as plotted) with NoRMCorre's defaults is a standard choice. How the root mean square is formed is open. The readings are (a) the root mean square of the 2D shift's length about the mean shift, (b) the same about zero shift, (c) the root mean square over both axes' shifts about their means. Microns use the pixel sizes of abstract-kiloscope-fov. Reproduced when the value in pixels is within tolerance under a reading.

claims.statement: Linear SVM decoders trained on half of the data decode the mouse's combined quadrant and movement direction on the other half at an accuracy at least three times chance, above that of decoders trained on shuffled data.
claims.source: Main text, page 549, paragraph 1; Fig. 2i and 2j; Methods, Data analysis, paragraphs 4 and 5
claims.quote: We trained a support vector machine (SVM) model on half of the data and used the other half to decode the mouse's combined position and movement direction, with the resulting accuracy at least three times chance level (Fig. 2j, P < 0.001, Monte Carlo sampling of n = 1,000 shuffled datasets).
claims.criterion: Eight classes, the four quadrants by two directions (Fig. 2i), and the common method above with lambda 3.2e-7. The decoding matrix is the average of 200 fits (quadrant_direction_decoding.m). The null is 1,000 decoders trained on their own shuffles (Methods, paragraph 5), each giving a median accuracy; p is the fraction of null values at or above the real median accuracy. The code holds no null for this panel, so how many fits make one null decoder is open. The readings are (n1) one fit per shuffle, (n2) the average matrix of 200 fits per shuffle, as for the real matrix (subset_sweep.m averages its shuffled decoders over the same number of fits as its real ones). The p-value is judged under both; when they disagree on p < 0.001, the claim is methods_underspecified. Chance is 1/8 (the code sets white at 1/Nclass). Which accuracy must reach three times chance is open. The readings are (a) the median of the diagonal at least 0.375, (b) every diagonal element at least 0.375. Reproduced when p < 0.001 and the accuracy holds under a reading; partially reproduced when p < 0.001 and the median of the diagonal exceeds 1/8 but neither reading holds.

claims.statement: Decoding accuracy depends on the number of footprints used, with P at or below 2.7 x 10^-4 (Mann-Whitney U) for every decoder size from 2 to 2,048 footprints.
claims.source: Main text, page 549, paragraph 1; Fig. 2k; Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 5
claims.quote: The accuracy of the decoder depended on the number of footprints used (Fig. 2k, P ≤ 2.7 × 10−4 for all decoder sizes, Mann–Whitney U).
claims.criterion: As subset_sweep.m does it, with the common method above (quadrant and direction labels, lambda 6.75e-8 as in the code). For each size 2^1 to 2^11, 64 random subsets of footprints; for each subset, the average decoding matrix of 100 fits and its median accuracy, then the same subset after the shuffle, again 100 fits. What the Mann-Whitney U compares is open. The readings are (a) original against shuffled at each size, (b) original at each size against original at the next size. Reproduced when, under a reading, every two-sided test has p at or below 2.7e-4 and the median of the original accuracies at 2,048 footprints exceeds that at 2; partially reproduced when every test has p < 0.05 and the medians rise.

claims.statement: Decoders built from the 32 footprints closest to a point decode quadrant and direction with accuracies that differ substantially across the field of view.
claims.source: Main text, page 549, paragraph 1; Fig. 2l; Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Notably, footprints in different regions of the FOV yielded substantially different decoding accuracies (Fig. 2l).
claims.criterion: Map points every 5 image pixels over rows 1 to 608 and columns 140 to 700 (the code's grid, subregion_map_quaddir.m); a point is used when at least 32 footprints lie within 270 um (Methods). A footprint's position is not given in the Methods; the code takes the first pixel (in column order) at which the footprint's spatial weight equals 1, its peak, and that is used, with the centroid shown as a variant. At each point, the 32 footprints nearest to it; its value is the median accuracy of the average matrix of 10 fits (code), with quadrant and direction labels and lambda 6.75e-8 (code). The null is 1,000 decoders trained on shuffled data from 32 randomly chosen footprints (Methods). Points are significant at Benjamini-Hochberg 5% over all used points. Open details and their readings. Pixel size for the 270 um radius, 5.94 um (45 pixels) or 5.35 um (50 pixels, the code's radius); random footprints drawn anew for each null decoder, or one draw for all; each null decoder one fit, or the average matrix of 10 fits as at the points; p as the fraction of null values at or above the point's value, or that count plus one over 1,001. "Substantially different" is read as (i) significant and non-significant used points both present, and (ii) the values of the used points spanning at least 0.108 (the 0.18 to 0.30 range of the Fig. 2l colour bar, less 10%). Reproduced when at least one point is significant and (i) and (ii) hold under every combination of readings; not reproduced when they fail under every combination; otherwise methods_underspecified, with every result shown. The code's choice of 64 footprints within 50 pixels is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The correlated activity in each NMF component is driven by footprints spread across the field of view.
claims.source: Main text, page 549, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 8; Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Note that the correlated activity visible in each component is driven by footprints from across the FOV (Extended Data Fig. 8).
claims.criterion: The traces of the curated footprints (Fig. 2h; extract_curated.mat in the code) are factored by NMF into eight components (Methods), with multiplicative updates, 4 replicates and tolerances 1e-7 (ridgeline_nmf_grouping.m); each footprint goes to the component in which its weight ranks highest among footprints (same script). Footprints of a component are active in its event when their maximum within 25 s of the event time exceeds half their maximum over the recording (single_component_raster.m). The event times are open. The code lists eight times (820, 770, 990, 700, 400, 420, 1000 and 410 s) for components whose numbering a new NMF run does not reproduce. The readings are (a) the time of each component's largest temporal weight, (b) the code's eight times, each assigned one to one to the component with the largest temporal weights at those times. "From across the FOV" has no measure in the paper, and none is in the code. The plain reading used is that each event's active footprints lie in all four quarters of the field of view (split at the midlines of the extent of all footprint positions, taken as for fig2l-local-decoding-map). Reproduced when every component's event meets it under both event readings; not reproduced when some event fails it under both; otherwise methods_underspecified. The maps of active footprints (the code's Extended Data Fig. 8b, footprints thresholded at 10% of their maximum) and their counts are shown.

claims.statement: Position within the maze can be decoded with octant resolution from the activity, above decoders trained on shuffled data.
claims.source: Main text, page 549, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 9a and 9b
claims.quote: We used the same approach to decode even more fine-grained position information (Extended Data Fig. 9, P < 0.001, Monte Carlo sampling as in Fig. 2j).
claims.criterion: Eight classes, the eight octants (each side of the loop halved, direction not coded; Extended Data Fig. 9a), with the common method above and lambda 6.75e-8. The decoding matrix is the average of 200 fits (octant_decoding.m). The null is as in fig2-quadrant-direction-decoding, 1,000 decoders on their own shuffles, with the same two readings (n1) and (n2). Reproduced when the real median accuracy exceeds every null value (p < 0.001) and exceeds chance (1/8) under both; not reproduced when it fails under both; otherwise methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Decoders built from the 32 footprints closest to a point decode octant position significantly in parts of the field of view, with accuracy that varies across it.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9c; Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 5
claims.criterion: As fig2l-local-decoding-map, with octant labels, the average matrix of 40 fits per point (subregion_map_octant.m; a null decoder is one fit or the average of 40) and the same open details and readings, except (ii). The paper gives no colour bar for this map in its text and no measure of how much the accuracy varies, so no span threshold is set; the claim is judged on (i) and the span of the used points' values is reported. Reproduced when at least one point is significant and (i) holds under every combination of readings; not reproduced when it fails under every combination; otherwise methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Some footprints have activity localized to subregions of the maze.
claims.source: Main text, page 549, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 10
claims.quote: An examination of individual neural firing rate maps yielded footprints whose activity was localized to subregions of the maze (Extended Data Fig. 10).
claims.criterion: The paper selected footprints by eye "for large-scale structure in their receptive fields" (Extended Data Fig. 10 legend), a rule that cannot be redone. The maps are as in place_cells.m. Frames with speed above its 80th percentile; a footprint is active in a frame when its trace exceeds 1% of its maximum; the plotted value is the fraction of time active at each location, smoothed with a Gaussian of 10 video pixels. The code also computes, per footprint, the entropy of its mean activity over 100 bins of linear position between the 1st and 99th percentiles, and sorts footprints by the peak of the smoothed map. Neither the paper nor the code sets a threshold or a test for "localized", and the paper's selection by eye cannot be redone, so the claim cannot be judged by a method the paper fixes (methods_underspecified). The maps and the entropy and peak of every footprint are reported, with the code's 12 selected footprints (ifig in place_cells.m, indices into the curated set) when the data's footprint order can be matched to the curated set.

claims.statement: In a probabilistic atlas built from 10 young-adult NeuroPAL worms, the positional variability of cell bodies differs across neuron types.
claims.source: Results, Variability in Neuronal Cell Body Positions, paragraph 2; Figures 2C and 2D
claims.quote: This map revealed different positional variability across neuron types
claims.criterion: The atlas is fit on all 10 worms, head and tail, as in the shared method above; a neuron's positional variability is the standard deviation of its atlas positional covariance along each of the three principal axes of the atlas means (the axes Methods S1 Figure 6.1 plots, major and minor axes of position). The paper gives no test or threshold. The one difference it quantifies is OLLR against OLLL, over a factor of two (claim fig2c-ollr-more-variable-than-olll), so the claim is reproduced when, along at least one axis, the largest per-neuron standard deviation is more than twice the smallest within the head and within the tail. The distribution of per-neuron standard deviations is reported.

claims.statement: In the head atlas, OLLR shows over twice the positional variability of OLLL along the anterior-posterior axis.
claims.source: Figure 2C legend
claims.quote: OLLR exhibits over twice the positional variability of OLLL in its anterior-posterior axis
claims.criterion: Head atlas fit on all 10 worms as in the shared method. The anterior-posterior axis is the major axis of the atlas means (Methods S1 Figure 6.1 legend; the CELL_ID code aligns positions to it by principal components, AutoId.major_axis_align). "Positional variability" can be read as (a) the standard deviation of the neuron's positional distribution along that axis, (b) its variance, or (c) the anterior-posterior extent of the 50% contour within the 2-D plane Figure 2 slices (left-right or dorsal-ventral view, the conditional distribution in that plane). Reproduced when the OLLR to OLLL ratio exceeds 2 under any reading; all three are reported.

claims.statement: Unsupervised identification of neurons against the statistical atlas of NeuroPAL colors and positions is 86% accurate in the head and 94% in the tail, cross-validated.
claims.source: Results, Semi-automated Neuronal Identification, paragraph 2; Figures 7B and 7C; Methods S1 section 6.3, Figure 6.4
claims.quote: Accuracy was 86% for the head and 94% for the tail.
claims.criterion: Leave-one-out over the 10 worms (Methods S1 Figure 6.4 legend), head and tail apart. For each held-out worm, the atlas is fit on the other 9 (Algorithm 4) with 6-D features (position in um and the three landmark colors); the held-out worm is identified by Algorithm 5 and the Hungarian assignment (equation 4.18), and a neuron is correct when its assigned identity is its annotation. Open details, each run. Which neurons are identified, (a) the hand-annotated neurons, (b) the automatic detections of claim ms1-detection-accuracy matched to annotations within 3 um, unmatched annotated neurons counted wrong. Start of the alignment, Algorithm 5 initializes it at the identity on the positions as given (the Methods, main result); the CELL_ID code (AutoId.global_alignment) first aligns the worm's major axis and searches rotations about it (theta from 0 to 2 pi in steps of 0.25, both orientations, 10 alternations, color regression with ridge 1e5), shown as a variant. Colors, the dandiset's stored per-neuron colors if it holds them, and the Methods S1 Figure 6.2 readout recomputed from the images if it holds images. These are method details; the outcome is the one they give together, and differing outcomes block the claim as methods_underspecified. The reported numbers can be read as (i) the mean over held-out worms of per-worm accuracy or (ii) the accuracy over all neurons pooled, and as (1) per-neuron identity or (2) identity at class level for left/right pairs (Methods S1 footnote 1 scores midline pairs such as RMFL/R by class but does not list them; class level for every left/right pair is the upper bound of that rule). The number is matched when it falls within tolerance under any of these readings.

claims.statement: Accuracy depends on neuron density; it is high for all tail ganglia and lower for the dense ventral ganglion of the head.
claims.source: Results, Semi-automated Neuronal Identification, paragraph 2; Figures 7B and 7C legend
claims.quote: Accuracy largely depended on neuron density; for example, our pipeline achieved high accuracy for all tail ganglia but lower accuracy for the much denser ventral ganglion in the head.
claims.criterion: The per-neuron results of fig7bc-identification-accuracy (the Methods reading, and each other reading as a variant), grouped by ganglion. Ganglion membership is taken from the dandiset if it records it, else from the CELL_ID neuron tables (Data/NeuroPAL) or the ganglion lists of the GUI; the head ganglia are those of Methods S1 Figure 6.8 (anterior and posterior pharynx, anterior, dorsal, lateral, ventral and retrovesicular ganglia) and the tail ganglia pre-anal, dorso-rectal and lumbar. Reproduced when every tail ganglion has a higher accuracy than the head's ventral ganglion; the rank of the ventral ganglion among head ganglia and the ganglion densities are reported.

claims.statement: Manually annotating eight neurons, chosen by the software as the least certain, raises head identification accuracy above 90% on average.
claims.source: Results, Semi-automated Neuronal Identification, paragraph 2; Figure 7B; Methods S1 section 6.5, Figure 6.9
claims.quote: Adding eight manual annotations, on average, brings the head accuracy above 90%
claims.criterion: In the leave-one-out runs of fig7bc-identification-accuracy (head), the neuron whose row of the Sinkhorn probability matrix is closest to uniform is annotated with its true identity, the likelihoods are updated as CELL_ID does (AutoId.update_log_likelihood sets the annotated neuron's row to the minimum except its true identity at the maximum) and the assignment recomputed (AutoId.update_id, without re-alignment); repeated eight times. "Closest to uniform" is open, read as (a) the highest entropy of the row and (b) the lowest top probability (the code's ranking, AutoId.add_to_image); a method detail, both run. The accuracy after eight annotations can be read as over all neurons with the annotated ones counted correct, or over the unannotated neurons only; matched under either. Reproduced when the mean over held-out worms exceeds 90%.

claims.statement: Annotating the most uncertain neurons first raises identification accuracy much faster than annotating neurons in random order, in head and tail.
claims.source: Methods S1, section 6.5, Figure 6.9
claims.quote: Figure 6.9 shows that following this strategy, the accuracy increases much faster ... than by a random recommendation
claims.criterion: As in fig7b-eight-labels-above-90, for 1 to 50 annotations in the head and 1 to 16 in the tail (the ranges of Figure 6.9), against the same procedure with neurons chosen at random (the mean of 100 random orders per held-out worm, a standard choice that should not change the outcome). Reproduced when, in head and tail, the mean accuracy over worms with the most uncertain neurons first is above the random curve at most annotation counts and its mean over the range is higher; both curves are shown.

claims.statement: Restricted to neuron positions without color, automated identification accuracy drops to 50% in the head and 68% in the tail, showing the gain from NeuroPAL's colors.
claims.source: Results, Semi-automated Neuronal Identification, paragraph 3; Methods S1 section 6.3, Figure 6.5
claims.quote: When we restricted the model to assign identities only on the basis of location, automated accuracy dropped to 50% for the head and 68% for the tail
claims.criterion: As fig7bc-identification-accuracy, with every reading listed there, but with the atlas and the held-out worm restricted to the three position coordinates ("using only position information", Methods S1 Figure 6.5 legend). Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading and each is below the full model's accuracy under the same reading.

claims.statement: The automatic neuron detection (matching pursuit) reaches 80% accuracy in the head and 88% in the tail, at 191 and 44 detections, with precision and recall both about 90% in the head and 93% in the tail.
claims.source: Methods S1, section 6.2, Figure 6.3
claims.quote: As shown in figures 6.3 our algorithm reaches the accuracy of 80% in head and 88% in tail. This occurs when we find K = 191 and K = 44 neurons in head and tail in which case we get similar precision and recall values that are both equal to 90% and 93% in head and tail respectively.
claims.criterion: Needs the images. Detection as Methods S1 sections 2 and 3 describe and CELL_ID implements it (Preprocess.zscore_frame, Preprocess.filter_gut_lysosomes, AutoDetect.detect, with a 1.5 um exclusion radius), run for K = 191 (head) and K = 44 (tail) on each of the 10 worms. Detections are matched one to one to the hand annotations by the Hungarian algorithm on distances, with distances over 3 um set to infinity (section 6.2); accuracy is TP / (TP + FP + FN), precision TP / (TP + FP), recall TP / (TP + FN). The values are the means over the 10 worms (Figure 6.3 plots means and standard deviations). The detection bounds that the GUI takes from its preferences (minimum eigenvalue of the Gaussian shape and the size thresholds of the gut and lysosome filter) are not given in the paper; the CELL_ID defaults at d9f5df9 are used and named as a deviation. Blocked if the dandiset holds no images.

claims.statement: The identification's confidence is calibrated; per-neuron confidence and accuracy largely agree in head and tail.
claims.source: Methods S1, section 6.4, Figure 6.8
claims.quote: Figure 6.8 shows that confidence and accuracy ... are largely in good agreement, as desired
claims.criterion: From the leave-one-out runs of fig7bc-identification-accuracy, per atlas neuron, the mean over held-out worms of the Sinkhorn probability of the assigned identity (confidence) and the fraction of worms in which it is correct (accuracy), with left/right midline pairs scored by class as in footnote 1 of Methods S1 section 6.4. The paper gives no measure of agreement and no threshold; "largely in good agreement" is open. Two readings, each run, (a) a positive Spearman correlation between per-neuron confidence and accuracy with p < 0.05 and (b) a mean absolute difference between confidence and accuracy under 10 percentage points (a standard choice, not from the paper). Reproduced in head and tail when both readings agree that it holds; when they disagree the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified. The reliability plot is shown.

claims.statement: Using the atlas of neuron positions from the 10 worms to define neighbors, NeuroPAL's designed color map leaves 3.5% of neighboring neuron pairs below the color discrimination margin.
claims.source: Methods S2, section 4.3, paragraph 1
claims.quote: NeuroPAL, which comprehensively identifies all neuron types, exhibited a theoretical color violation of 3.5%.
claims.criterion: Neighbors are pairs whose positional covariance ellipses, at 95% probability mass, include each other (Methods S2 section 2; Optimal_Coloring computeProbAdjacency.m, 1000 samples per neuron, seed 1), from the head and tail atlases fit on all 10 worms. Colors are the NeuroPAL colors of Optimal_Coloring data.mat (NeuroPAL_colors), normalized to sum to one per neuron as find_optimal_colors.m does; the margin is 1/3. The Methods define the violation rate as the share of neighboring pairs whose color distance is below the margin (section 4.3); the code reports the mean shortfall below the margin over neighboring pairs (find_optimal_colors.m); the Methods measure is the main result and the code's is a variant. Whether the 3.5% pools head and tail is not said for NeuroPAL itself; the solver runs of Methods S2 section 4.2 use the 235 head and tail neurons together, and Methods S2 Figure 1A shows head and tail with one value, so pooled is the main reading; head and tail apart are reported as variants, and the number is matched under any of them. The outside inputs are the NeuroPAL colors from the code repository.

claims.statement: The optimal-coloring algorithm, using WormBase reporters, finds NeuroPAL alternatives with 1.7% color violations with 39 reporters and 10.5% when restricted to 3 reporters.
claims.source: Results, An Optimal-Coloring Algorithm for Other Tissues and Model Organisms, paragraph 3; Figures 7D and 7E; Methods S2 Figure 1
claims.quote: In our simulations, we achieve color violations of 1.7% when using 39 reporters and 10.5% when restricting the solution to only 3 reporters
claims.criterion: Adjacency as in ms2-neuropal-color-violations. The Brain Atlas reporter table of Optimal_Coloring data.mat (1192 reporters, 654 unique), 3 colors, margin 1/3, solved with optimal_color_solver.m; the best of 10,000 runs for the roughly 40-reporter case (sparsity 100, Methods S2 Figure 3 legend) and of 7,500 runs for the 3-reporter case (Methods S2 Figure 1 legend), both with 3 colors at 3 intensities (Figure 7 legend; Methods S2 Figure 1 panel labels, Colors=3 Intensities=3 Reporters=39 and Reporters=3). The sparsity giving 3 reporters is not stated; the reading is the sparsity whose solutions use 3 reporters after the code's Otsu threshold. Violations as in ms2-neuropal-color-violations (Methods measure, code measure as a variant). Reproduced when the best solutions are within tolerance; the solver is stochastic and fewer runs may be used if the full number cannot run, which is recorded as a deviation.

claims.statement: A transgene of 41 reporter-fluorophore fusions gives a stereotyped color map with which every neuron of the C. elegans hermaphrodite can be identified, each distinguishable from its neighbors by color.
claims.source: Results, Empirical Assembly of NeuroPAL, paragraph 2; Figure 1E
claims.quote: The final transgene, composed of 41 different reporter-fluorophore fusions, allowed us to unambiguously assign identities to every neuron in C. elegans based on a stereotyped color map
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset. The 10 annotated worms bear on it only through the atlas claims above (fig7bc-identification-accuracy and ms2-neuropal-color-violations).

claims.statement: The NeuroPAL expression pattern is stable and stereotyped, except that four neuron classes (AVL, RIM, RIS and PVW) vary in brightness.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal Color Verification and Phenotypic Assessment of NeuroPAL Strains, paragraph 1
claims.quote: A minor exception was four neuron classes that exhibited variable brightness (AVL, RIM, RIS, and PVW).
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset; the paper's scoring of hundreds of animals is not given as data. The color covariance of these four classes in the 10-worm atlas may be reported as context and does not decide the claim.

claims.statement: Of the NeuroPAL integrants, otIs669 (OH15262) is the brightest, and otIs670 (OH15263) has locomotion and chemotaxis closest to wild type.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal Color Verification and Phenotypic Assessment of NeuroPAL Strains, paragraph 2; Figures S1A to S1G; Table S2
claims.quote: The brightest integrant was otls669 (strain OH15262). The integrant with locomotion and chemotactic behavior closest to wild-type, otls670 (strain OH15263), is less bright
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: Metabotropic acetylcholine, glutamate and GABA receptors are expressed in 97% of all neurons; 70% express GARs, 54% MGLs and 89% GBBs.
claims.source: Results, Expression Maps for All Metabotropic Neurotransmitter Receptors, paragraph 2; Figure 4C
claims.quote: we find that these receptors are expressed in 97% of all neurons ... 70% express GARs, 54% express MGLs, and 89% express GBBs
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: Every postsynaptic partner of every GABA-releasing neuron expresses a GABA-B receptor, whereas only 60% express a GABA-A receptor.
claims.source: Results, Expression Maps for All Metabotropic Neurotransmitter Receptors, paragraph 3; Figures 4B and 4G
claims.quote: We found that every postsynaptic partner of every GABA-releasing neuron expresses one of the two GABA B receptors. In contrast, only 60% of postsynaptic partners of GABAergic neurons express any of the seven GABA A receptors
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset. Figure 4D's legend notes that one polyadic synapse from AVF brings the GABA-B count to just under 100%.

claims.statement: 76% of postsynaptic partners of cholinergic neurons express GAR receptors and 66% of postsynaptic partners of glutamatergic neurons express MGL receptors; metabotropic receptors can take part in 75% of all synaptic connections from neurotransmitter-releasing neurons.
claims.source: Results, Expression Maps for All Metabotropic Neurotransmitter Receptors, paragraph 3; Figure 4D; Discussion, paragraph 3
claims.quote: 76% of the postsynaptic partners of cholinergic neurons express GAR receptors, and 66% of the postsynaptic partners of glutamatergic neurons express MGL receptors
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: Many receptor-expressing neurons have no presynaptic partner releasing the cognate transmitter (31% of GABA-A and 37% of GABA-B expressing neurons; 3% of GAR and 10% of MGL expressing neurons), and 92% of neurons express GABA receptors while 10% release GABA, suggesting widespread extrasynaptic signaling.
claims.source: Results, Expression Maps for All Metabotropic Neurotransmitter Receptors, paragraph 4; Figure 4E
claims.quote: 31% of GABA A and 37% of GABA B receptor-expressing neurons have no presynaptic GABAergic partner. Moreover, we found 92% of all neurons express GABA receptors, and yet only 10% of neurons release GABA.
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset. The sentence giving 3% and 10% pairs GAR and MGL with "glutamatergic and cholinergic neurons, respectively", the reverse of the receptors' ligands; the cognate reading (GAR with cholinergic, MGL with glutamatergic) is the one Figure 4E's legend describes.

claims.statement: Sensory neurons are the most prominent recipients of the putative extrasynaptic communication.
claims.source: Results, Expression Maps for All Metabotropic Neurotransmitter Receptors, paragraph 4; Figure 4F
claims.quote: Notably, sensory neurons appear to be the most prominent recipients of extrasynaptic communication
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: In pag-3 null mutants the NeuroPAL color codes of VA and VB motor neurons are absent, and the AVE and PVR interneurons change color.
claims.source: Results, Uncovering Determinants of Cell Fate, paragraph 1; Figures 5A and 5B
claims.quote: As predicted, the color codes that identify the VA and VB cell types in NeuroPAL are absent in pag-3 mutants ... Unexpectedly, we also found color changes in the AVE and PVR interneurons caused by pag-3 mutation.
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset. The p-values are recorded as the paper's significance standard (p or q of at most 0.05 after correction, STAR Methods); the values are in Table S5.

claims.statement: A pag-3 fosmid reporter is expressed in neurons not previously reported, including AVE and PVR.
claims.source: Results, Uncovering Determinants of Cell Fate, paragraph 1; Figure 5C
claims.quote: By checking a fosmid-based reporter, we discovered pag-3 expression in neurons that had gone previously unidentified, including AVE and PVR
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: In eor-1 null mutants the dorsal and ventral RME neurons lose all blue NeuroPAL color and UNC-25/GAD reporter expression but keep the panneuronal label, while RMEL/R are unchanged and UNC-47/VGAT expression is not affected.
claims.source: Results, Uncovering Determinants of Cell Fate, paragraph 2; Figures 5E to 5G
claims.quote: The dorsal and ventral RME neurons (RMED/V) lost all their blue coloring but retained their panneuronal label ... In contrast, the left and right RME neurons (RMEL/R) exhibited no changes in their color codes.
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: NaCl (160 mM) evokes left/right asymmetric responses in the ASE neurons, with ASER increasing its calcium.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Activity Imaging of Gustatory and Olfactory Responses, paragraph 3; Figure 6D
claims.quote: NaCl evoked stereotyped left/right (L/R) asymmetric responses in the two ASE neurons. However, ASER exhibited an increase in [Ca 2+ ] upon NaCl presentation
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset. The paper's test (STAR Methods, Analysis of brainwide imaging data) is a two-tailed unpaired t test for asymmetry, at p of at most 0.05.

claims.statement: 2-butanone and 2,3-pentanedione evoke stochastically asymmetric responses in the AWC ON/OFF pair.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Activity Imaging of Gustatory and Olfactory Responses, paragraph 4; Figure 6D
claims.quote: 2-butanone and 2,3-pentanedione evoked stochastically asymmetric responses in the AWC ON/OFF neuron pair
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: NaCl evokes significant responses in six interneurons with no previously known function, AIN, AVF, AVH, AVJ, I2 and MI.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Activity Imaging of Gustatory and Olfactory Responses, paragraph 3; Figures 6C to 6F
claims.quote: In particular, we detected significant NaCl responses in six interneurons with no previously known function ... AIN, AVF, AVH, AVJ, I2, and MI.
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset. Responding neurons are those significant (q of at most 0.05) by a two-tailed paired t test of the stimulus period against the equal period before it, FDR q-values (Storey 2002), with up to 42 left/right neuron pairs or 21 single neurons from 21 heads (STAR Methods, Analysis of brainwide imaging data).

claims.statement: Odors evoke responses across many sensory and interneurons but with more inhibitory (decreasing calcium) activity than NaCl.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Activity Imaging of Gustatory and Olfactory Responses, paragraph 4; Figure 6C
claims.quote: We found that odors also evoked responses in a large set of both sensory and interneurons, throughout the brain, but exhibited more inhibitory activity (decreasing [Ca 2+ ]) than seen for NaCl
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: The sets of responding neurons overlap but differ by stimulus; ASJ is excited by NaCl and inhibited by both odors, and RIC is excited only by 2,3-pentanedione.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Activity Imaging of Gustatory and Olfactory Responses, paragraph 4; Figures 6C to 6F
claims.quote: For example, the ASJ sensory neurons were excited by NaCl but inhibited by both odors, whereas the RIC interneurons were excited solely by 2,3-pentanedione.
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: In the tail, PVQ is significantly excited by 2,3-pentanedione, and sensory and interneurons show significant post-stimulus responses to all three stimuli.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Activity Imaging of Gustatory and Olfactory Responses, paragraph 4; Table S6
claims.quote: In the tail, the PVQ interneurons were significantly excited upon presentation of 2,3-pentanedione, while a mix of sensory and interneurons exhibited significant post-stimulus responses
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset. Post-stimulus responses are those whose stimulus mean exceeds the pre-stimulus mean and whose post-stimulus mean exceeds the stimulus mean by a one-tailed paired t test, FDR corrected at q of at most 0.05, over 21 tails (STAR Methods, Analysis of brainwide imaging data).

claims.statement: Both salt and odors elicit responses across the pharyngeal nervous system.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Activity Imaging of Gustatory and Olfactory Responses, paragraph 4; Figure 6F
claims.quote: Surprisingly, both salt and odors elicited responses across the pharyngeal nervous system
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: In many animals AVF shows robust cyclical activity of about 0.3 Hz throughout the recording, regardless of stimuli, similar to the strain's crawling frequency.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Activity Imaging of Gustatory and Olfactory Responses, paragraph 5; Figures S1G and S1H
claims.quote: the pair of AVF interneurons displayed robust cyclical activity for the entire 4-min recording, irrespective of delivery of gustatory or olfactory stimuli. The frequency of this activity was ~0.3 Hz
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset. Figure S1H counts peaks per 4-minute interval in traces median filtered at 0.5 s, from five OH16230 worms.

claims.statement: Pairwise neuronal correlations are similar across individuals for a given stimulus, but each stimulus produces its own brainwide correlation pattern.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Neuronal Dynamics and Connectivity, paragraph 1; Figures 6G to 6I, S2C to S2E
claims.quote: We found similar stimulus-specific neuronal correlations across individuals, but each stimulus generated its own brainwide correlation pattern
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: Functional correlations between neurons correspond poorly to synapse counts; R squared is 2.8% (head) and 1.7% (tail) for electrical and 0.5% (head) and 1.5% (tail) for chemical connectivity.
claims.source: Results, Whole-Brain Neuronal Dynamics and Connectivity, paragraph 2; Figures 6J and 6K
claims.quote: We found low Pearson correlation between these functional and structural matrices. For electrical connectivity, R 2 = 2.8% in the head and R 2 = 1.7% in the tail, and for chemical connectivity, R 2 = 0.5% in the head and R 2 = 1.5% in the tail
claims.criterion: Not tested on the dandiset.

claims.statement: The two deposited mice are the mice of the same names in the paper's per-mouse source data, with the same shock group, and the freezing computed from the dandiset's freezing intervals agrees with the per-mouse freezing the paper reports for them.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 9b and 9c; source-data repository denisecailab/RetrospectiveMemoryLinkingData_2024
claims.criterion: Records are matched by the mouse name (subject_id in the files, Mouse in the CSV files). The session descriptions name the context of each recall session. Freezing is read in two ways, (a) the percentage of MotionSeries frames that fall inside a freezing interval and (b) the summed duration of the freezing intervals over the duration of the MotionSeries. Reproduced when both mice are found, their shock amplitude in the files matches the source data's group, and all four values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when two or three are; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: In the calcium imaging and EEG/EMG experiment, high-shock mice froze more during aversive recall than low-shock mice (t7 = 8.99, p = 0.020).
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 9b
claims.quote: High-shock mice froze more during Aversive recall than low-shock mice
claims.criterion: The dandiset holds one mouse per group, so the paper's t-test cannot be run. Freezing as in source-data-link reading (a), in Recall1 (the aversive context). Reproduced when the high-shock mouse (Ca_EEG2-1) freezes more than the low-shock mouse (Ca_EEG3-4) and the per-30-s-bin freezing of the two sessions (10 bins each) differs by a two-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when only the direction holds; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: During offline periods, hippocampal population bursts occur more often than expected from shuffled neuronal activity, so CA1 neurons fire in a more coordinated way than chance.
claims.source: Results, Neutral ensemble recruited into population bursts, paragraph 1; Extended Data Figure 3l and 3m
claims.quote: True burst frequencies were greater than shuffled burst frequencies in every mouse ... suggesting that during the offline period, hippocampal CA1 neurons fire in a more coordinated manner than would be expected from shuffled neuronal activities
claims.criterion: In each of the three deposited offline recordings, burst frequency (events per minute) of the population trace, compared with 1000 surrogates in which each cell's trace is circularly shifted by an independent random offset and the population trace is recomputed and z-scored as for the data. Reproduced when the true frequency exceeds the 95th percentile of the surrogates in all three recordings; partially reproduced when it exceeds the surrogate mean in all three but the 95th percentile in fewer; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The mean population activity during offline periods is more right-skewed than in shuffled data, showing brief burst-like activations that need coordinated activity of groups of neurons.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 3n and 3o
claims.quote: The true skew was greater than the shuffled skew in every mouse ... supporting the idea that the mean population activity undergoes brief burst-like activations requiring the coordinated activity of groups of neurons
claims.criterion: As offline-bursts-above-shuffle, with the skewness of the population trace (scipy.stats.skew) in place of the burst frequency, and the same thresholds for the three outcomes.

claims.statement: Offline population bursts coincide with the mouse briefly slowing down about 1 s before the burst and resuming its movement about 1 to 2 s later.
claims.source: Figure 2d and 2e; Extended Data Figure 6e; Results, Co-reactivation occurs more during wake, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Mice showed a robust and brief slowing down around 1 s before each burst event, before increasing locomotion back up around 2 s later.
claims.criterion: Movement is the magnitude of the telemetry ActivitySignal (the absolute value, averaged in 100 ms bins), the only movement measure in the offline files. Time zero of a burst is read two ways, (a) the frame of peak population activity and (b) the first frame of the event. For each burst with both windows inside the recording, the mean movement from 1 s before to time zero is compared with the mean from 5 s to 3 s before, by a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test (lower before the burst). Reproduced when p < 0.05 in all three offline recordings under one reading; partially reproduced when it holds in one or two; not reproduced otherwise. The mean movement trace from 5 s before to 5 s after time zero is shown, with the same windows around random times as a reference.

claims.statement: After a strong (high-shock) aversive experience, during wake in the offline period the overlap ensemble co-bursts more with the neutral ensemble than with the aversive ensemble (t4 = 4.94, P = 0.016).
claims.source: Figure 5c (left); Methods, "Ensemble co-participation analysis"
claims.quote: Left, wake high-shock mice had higher co-bursting of overlap × neutral than overlap × aversive
claims.criterion: Tested on the one deposited high-shock mouse (Ca_EEG2-1) and its one deposited offline recording after aversive encoding (the first of 24). A burst is assigned the sleep state of its peak frame. Two readings of wake, (a) wake and quiet wake together and (b) wake alone, and two readings of a co-participation, (i) both ensembles participate, whatever the third does, and (ii) both participate and the third does not. Over the wake bursts, the percentage with overlap and neutral co-participation (OxN) and with overlap and aversive co-participation (OxA). Reproduced when OxN > OxA under one reading and an exact McNemar test across those bursts gives p < 0.05; partially reproduced when OxN > OxA under one reading without that; not reproduced when OxN <= OxA under every reading.

claims.statement: Fear spreads from an aversive context to a neutral context experienced 2 days before (retrospective linking) but not to one experienced 2 days after (prospective), with no difference in aversive recall between the groups.
claims.source: Figure 1a to 1c; Results, Retrospective memory linking across days, paragraph 1
claims.quote: There was no difference in freezing in the aversive context between groups ... In the retrospective group, mice froze more in the neutral context compared with in the novel context ... in the prospective group, there was no difference in freezing between the neutral and novel contexts

claims.statement: High-shock mice froze more than low-shock mice in the aversive context, and froze more in the neutral than in the novel context, while low-shock mice did not.
claims.source: Figure 1d to 1f
claims.quote: Mice froze more in the aversive context after receiving a high shock versus low shock ... High-shock mice froze more in the neutral versus novel contexts ... and low-shock mice froze no differently

claims.statement: In high-shock mice, aversive recall freezing correlates with the strength of retrospective memory linking (R2 = 0.45, P = 0.016), but not in low-shock mice.
claims.source: Figure 1g
claims.quote: Aversive memory strength was correlated with the strength of retrospective memory linking in high-shock mice ... but not in low-shock mice

claims.statement: Chemogenetic inhibition of the hippocampus in the 12 h after aversive encoding prevents retrospective memory linking and leaves the aversive memory intact.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 1l to 1p; Results, Retrospective memory linking across days, paragraph 3
claims.quote: We found that this prevented retrospective memory linking (that is, selective freezing in the neutral context compared with in the novel context) while leaving the aversive memory intact

claims.statement: A cocaine experience also drives retrospective memory linking to a neutral context experienced 2 days before.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 2g to 2i; Results, Retrospective memory linking across days, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we also found evidence that a highly salient, appetitive experience (that is, cocaine exposure) also drove retrospective memory linking to a neutral context memory formed 2 days before

claims.statement: Cells active during aversive encoding are reactivated offline and preferentially during aversive recall.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 3e to 3k; Results, Offline reactivation of a past neutral ensemble, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we found that the ensemble of cells active during aversive encoding was reactivated offline and preferentially reactivated during aversive memory recall

claims.statement: During offline 2 the neutral ensemble is less active than the aversive and overlap ensembles in low-shock mice but no differently active in high-shock mice.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 4f
claims.quote: The Neutral ensemble was less active than the Aversive and Overlap ensembles ... In high-shock mice ... these three ensembles were no differently active from each other

claims.statement: During offline 1 a greater percentage of the neutral ensemble participates in bursts than of the remaining ensemble, in both shock groups.
claims.source: Figure 3c
claims.quote: During offline 1 in the low- and high-shock groups, a greater percentage of the neutral ensemble participated in bursts than the remaining ensemble

claims.statement: During offline 2 the neutral ensemble preferentially participates in bursts relative to the remaining ensemble in high-shock mice (t7 = 4.88) but not in low-shock mice.
claims.source: Figure 3d to 3f
claims.quote: High-shock mice showed higher neutral ensemble participation relative to the remaining ensemble ... low-shock mice showed no difference in ensemble participation

claims.statement: During burst periods the overlap ensemble participates independently in more bursts than the aversive and neutral ensembles, with no difference between shock groups.
claims.source: Figure 4b and 4c
claims.quote: During burst periods, the overlap ensemble participated independently in more bursts than the aversive ensemble ... and more than the neutral ensemble ... but there was no difference in participation across low- versus high-shock mice

claims.statement: In the one-hour offline experiment, high-shock mice show more overlap-neutral than overlap-aversive co-bursting during bursts (t7 = 4.95), low-shock mice do not, and there is no such difference outside bursts.
claims.source: Figure 4e and 4f; Extended Data Figure 4k to 4o
claims.quote: Overlap ensemble preferentially co-participated with the neutral ensemble (N) rather than with the aversive ensemble (A) ... whereas in the low-shock group, there was no difference in overlap ensemble participation with the neutral and aversive ensembles

claims.statement: The overlap ensemble is enriched in putative inhibitory neurons identified by chemotagging.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 5; Extended Data Figure 6b and 6c
claims.quote: Here, the Overlap ensemble comprised a larger fraction of the inhibitory neuron population than any of the other ensembles ... the Overlap ensemble was composed more of inhibitory neurons than the other ensembles were

claims.statement: Without a shock, overlap-neutral co-bursting does not exceed overlap-aversive co-bursting and no memory linking occurs.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 8d, 8f and 8g; Results, Co-bursting of the overlap and neutral ensemble, paragraph 4
claims.quote: the co-bursting of the overlap and neutral ensembles was not different from the co-bursting of the overlap and aversive ensembles during the offline period ... these mice showed no differences in freezing in the neutral versus novel contexts during recall

claims.statement: Neural activity during neutral and aversive encoding is highly discriminable, with no difference between low- and high-shock mice.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 7; Results, Co-bursting of the overlap and neutral ensemble, paragraph 4
claims.quote: We found that the neural activity patterns for neutral and aversive contexts were highly discriminable. There were no differences between the low- and high-shock groups during encoding

claims.statement: In the calcium imaging and EEG/EMG experiment, high-shock mice froze more in the neutral than in the novel context (t4 = 4.02, p = 0.03), while low-shock mice did not.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 9c
claims.quote: High-shock mice froze more during Neutral vs Novel recall ... whereas low-shock mice froze no differently in Neutral vs Novel recall

claims.statement: During NREM and REM sleep, overlap-neutral and overlap-aversive co-bursting do not differ in either shock group.
claims.source: Figure 5c (middle and right)
claims.quote: Middle, for NREM, there was no difference in high-shock ... or low-shock ... co-bursting. Right, for REM, there was no difference in high-shock ... or low-shock ... co-bursting

claims.statement: In low-shock mice, overlap-neutral and overlap-aversive co-bursting during wake do not differ (t3 = 1.20, P = 0.32).
claims.source: Figure 5c (left)
claims.quote: low-shock mice had no difference in co-bursting between these ensembles

claims.statement: Mice wearing a Miniscope sleep normally, the intermittent recording scheme captures the time spent in each state, and sleep structure is not changed by neutral or aversive encoding.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 9d to 9g and Extended Data Figure 10; Results, Co-reactivation occurs more during wake, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We first validated that mice could wear the Miniscope without disruptions to their sleep ... We confirmed that our calcium recording scheme reliably captured all sleep states ... There were no differences in sleep features ... after the neutral or aversive encoding compared to pre-experiment sleep

claims.statement: The overlap ensemble is reactivated more during neutral recall than during novel-context exposure in high-shock mice compared with low-shock mice (t12 = 3.2, P = 0.007).
claims.source: Figure 6a; Extended Data Figure 4q to 4s; Results, Ensemble co-reactivation in neutral context recall, paragraph 2
claims.quote: the cells that were active during both neutral and aversive encoding (overlap ensemble) were reactivated more during neutral recall than novel-context exposure in the high-shock but not the low-shock group

claims.statement: In high-shock mice the neutral encoding-to-recall population correlation is lower than in low-shock mice and lower than the aversive encoding-to-recall correlation.
claims.source: Figure 6b
claims.quote: During neutral recall in high-shock mice, population activity vectors were less correlated with the average neutral encoding population vector than aversive recall activity was with the average aversive encoding population vector ... Neutral encoding-to-recall correlations were also lower in high- versus low-shock mice

claims.statement: For the pooled alarm pheromone stimuli, separate logistic curves for young and old ants fit better than a single curve, and old ants leave the nest faster.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1C; Table S1, row "Pooled alarm pheromone stimuli"
claims.quote: For the pooled alarm pheromone stimuli, the preferred model incorporated separate curves for young and old ants, with old ants responding faster
claims.criterion: From the Methods, Table S1 and alarm_behavior_calculations.py (commit 1aef6bc). For each trial of the three alarm stimuli and each time point from -10 to 60 s in 10 s steps, the proportion of young ants outside the nest (young outside over the colony's young, as the code computes it; the Methods' "by the total number within the arena" is settled by the code) and the same for old ants. The logistic Y = YM*Y0/((YM-Y0)*exp(-K*x)+Y0) of Table S1 is fit by least squares to all per-trial points, once shared (3 parameters) and once per age (6), and compared by the extra sum-of-squares F test; the residual degrees of freedom should be 314. Prism's starting values are not given; any start that converges is a standard choice. Reproduced when separate curves are preferred at p < 0.05, old ants are faster, and the six parameters are within tolerance. "Faster" is not defined; readings (a) K old above K young, (b) the old curve above the young curve at every time from 0 to 60 s. Partially reproduced when the test and direction hold but a parameter is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: For the vehicle control a single curve for young and old ants is preferred, so the two ages have similar baseline behavior.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1C right; Table S1, row "Vehicle control"
claims.quote: For the vehicle control, a single curve for young and old ants was the preferred model (extra sum-of-squares F test), indicating similar baseline behavioral patterns
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. As in fig1c-old-faster-alarm, but on the pentane trials and with the quadratic Y = B0 + B1*X + B2*X^2 the Methods and Table S1 give. Reproduced when the extra sum-of-squares F test gives p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. F, p and the fitted parameters are reported either way.

claims.statement: The three alarm stimuli (4-methyl-3-heptanone, 4-methyl-3-heptanol and the 9:1 blend) make the ants leave the nest in a similar manner; one curve fits all three.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1B; Table S1, row "Alarm pheromone stimuli, comparing stimuli"
claims.quote: all three alarm pheromone stimuli caused ants to leave the nest in a similar manner, so these samples were pooled for analyzing effects of age
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per trial and time point (-10 to 60 s), the proportion of all ants outside the nest; the logistic of Table S1 fit shared and per stimulus; extra sum-of-squares F test (residual degrees of freedom 151). Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; F, p and the parameters are reported either way.

claims.statement: For 4-methyl-3-heptanone alone, separate curves for young and old ants are preferred, with old ants above young.
claims.source: Figure S1 and legend; Table S1, row "4-methyl-3-heptanone, comparing age"
claims.quote: For 4-methyl-3-heptanone, a model with separate curves was preferred.
claims.criterion: As fig1c-old-faster-alarm, on the 4-methyl-3-heptanone trials only. Reproduced when separate curves are preferred at p < 0.05 and old ants are faster under at least one of the two readings of fig1c-old-faster-alarm. The legend states no direction for this stimulus; the direction is read from Table S1, where YM and Y0 are higher for old ants (0.921 and 0.662 against 0.830 and 0.534) while K is nearly equal (0.097 against 0.095), so reading (b) is the one Table S1 supports. The fitted parameters are reported.

claims.statement: For 4-methyl-3-heptanol and for the blend, single curves for both ages are preferred, though the trends are similar to 4-methyl-3-heptanone.
claims.source: Figure S1 and legend; Table S1, rows "4-methyl-3-heptanol" and "Blend, comparing age"
claims.quote: For 4-methyl-3-heptanol and the blend, similar trends were observed, but single curve models were preferred
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, as fig1c-old-faster-alarm on each stimulus. Reproduced when both tests give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when either gives p < 0.05. The direction of the fitted curves is reported.

claims.statement: Total GCaMP6s fluorescence in the AL of dissected brains does not differ between young and old ants.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2A and 2B
claims.quote: Total fluorescence intensity did not differ with age, and calcium responses measured by changes in GCaMP6s fluorescence should therefore be comparable between the two age cohorts
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. From the Methods (Confocal microscopy), a sum Z-projection of each brain's GCaMP6s channel, a rectangle around each AL, and its integrated intensity (Fiji Measure); Welch's t test of young against old. The ROI rectangles and n are not given (n is printed in Figure 2B only); readings for the sample (a) each AL a value, (b) the mean of a brain's two ALs. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 under the paper's test (the outcome both readings give; if they differ, both are shown and the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified).

claims.statement: The mean calcium response across the entire AL to each alarm pheromone does not differ between young and old ants, at 3% or at 48%.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 2C and 2D
claims.quote: we observed no effect of age on mean calcium response across the entire AL for either of the two tested concentrations
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Peak response maps as in the shared methods; per trial, the mean pixel value inside a single ROI around the AL boundary defined on a max Z-projection of raw fluorescence (Methods); per ant, the mean over its three trials of the odor; Welch's t test young against old for each of the four pheromone and concentration cells. The AL outline was drawn by hand; it is taken from the raw max projection by a threshold, a standard choice, and the result is also shown with the outline shrunk and grown by 5 pixels. Reproduced when all four tests give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any gives p < 0.05. The cohort means are reported. The 32-plane projection of the macro is a variant.

claims.statement: At 48%, 4-methyl-3-heptanone activates a few more glomeruli in young than in old ants (medians of 4 against 2 responding ROIs), while the count for 4-methyl-3-heptanol does not differ with age.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 2E
claims.quote: While there was no significant difference for 4-methyl-3-heptanol, 4-methyl-3-heptanone activated a few more glomeruli in young ants than in old ants (medians of 4 versus 2 responding ROIs)
claims.criterion: From the Methods (Image processing). For each 48% ant, ROIs of the size and shape of single glomeruli that respond in at least two trials, from the peak response maps; per ROI and trial the mean peak fold change; an ROI responds to an odor when its mean over that odor's trials is >= 0.2. The ROIs were drawn by hand; here they are the connected regions of a trial's map at >= 0.2 that recur, overlapping, in at least two trials of any odor, split at glomerulus size, a choice the paper does not fix, so the counts are also compared ant by ant with Data S2. This ROI procedure is a choice made here, not the paper's; when its outcome differs from the outcome the paper's counts in Data S2 give, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, with both shown. Motion-artifact trials under both readings of the shared open details. Wilcoxon rank-sum test (R defaults) of young against old per pheromone. Reproduced when 4-methyl-3-heptanone gives p < 0.05 with young higher and medians within tolerance, and 4-methyl-3-heptanol gives p >= 0.05. Partially reproduced when the direction and the 4-methyl-3-heptanol result hold but the medians or the significance do not.

claims.statement: Alarm pheromones are represented sparsely at both ages; only a small fraction of the roughly 500 AL glomeruli respond to them.
claims.source: Results, paragraphs 4 and 5; Figure 2C and 2E
claims.quote: Calcium responses to 4-methyl-3-heptanone and 4-methyl-3-heptanol were sparse at both tested ages ... Out of the ~500 glomeruli in the ant AL, only a small fraction responded to alarm pheromones in young and/or old ants
claims.criterion: The paper gives no threshold for "sparse" or "small fraction". On the 48% counts of fig2e-heptanone-breadth-falls, readings (a) every ant's count for each alarm pheromone is at most 5% of 500 (25 ROIs), (b) at most 10% (50 ROIs). Reproduced when both readings hold; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, with the counts shown.

claims.statement: The alarm pheromone response averaged over the six focal glomeruli does not differ between young and old ants.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure S2A
claims.quote: The mean of responses across these six glomeruli did not differ with age
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per ant and pheromone, the AUC of each focal glomerulus (shared methods, both fold-change readings), the mean over the glomeruli identified in that ant (Figure S2A legend; some ants lack one), Welch's t test of young against old. Reproduced when both tests give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when either gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In glomeruli G1 to G4 alarm pheromone responses tend to weaken with age; the decline is significant only for 4-methyl-3-heptanone in G2.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 3B; Figure S2B
claims.quote: For G1–G4, we observed a trend toward weaker responses with increasing age, which was statistically significant for responses to 4-methyl-3-heptanone in G2
claims.criterion: Per ant, the AUC of G1 to G4 for each pheromone at 48% (shared methods, both fold-change readings); Welch's t test of young against old for each of the eight pairs. Reproduced when G2 with 4-methyl-3-heptanone gives p < 0.05 with young higher and the other seven give p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when G2 holds and one or more of the others also reaches p < 0.05. The sign of the young minus old mean is reported for all eight, for the trend.

claims.statement: PGb and PGa respond significantly more strongly to alarm pheromones in old than in young ants; PGa does not respond to 4-methyl-3-heptanone.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 3C and 3D
claims.quote: The patterns in PG b and PG a were quite different, with significantly stronger calcium responses in old ants compared to young ants
claims.criterion: Per ant, the AUC of PGb and PGa for each pheromone at 48% (shared methods, both fold-change readings); Welch's t test of young against old. Which pairs Figure 3D marks significant cannot be read from the text; readings (a) PGb for both pheromones and PGa for 4-methyl-3-heptanol, (b) PGb for at least one pheromone and PGa for 4-methyl-3-heptanol. Reproduced when, under a reading, each of its pairs gives p < 0.05 with old higher; not reproduced when no reading holds. PGa's 4-methyl-3-heptanone AUC is reported.

claims.statement: PGb and PGa responses to alarm pheromones do not differ between 60-day-old ants and the 90-day-old ants of the earlier study, so the change occurs between 14 and 60 days.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figure 3C and 3D
claims.quote: We found no significant differences between 60- and 90-day-old ants
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. The 90-day values are the earlier study's data, DANDI 000467 (Hart et al. 2023, Cell 186, 3079), named in the key resources table; this paper does not say which of those ants, odors and concentrations enter Figure 3C and 3D, nor whether their AUC was recomputed. Readings (a) the 000467 ants given the two pheromones at the same 48% concentration, AUC computed here as for 000773; (b) the per-ant values the earlier paper or Data S2 publishes. Welch's t test of 60 against 90 days for PGb with each pheromone and PGa with 4-methyl-3-heptanol. Reproduced when all give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any gives p < 0.05.
