claims.statement: At 48%, 3-hexanone and isopropanol evoke broad AL responses in young but not old ants; mean peak responses across the AL fall more than 9-fold (3-hexanone) and more than 57-fold (isopropanol) with age.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 7; Figure S3A and S3B
claims.quote: Mean peak calcium responses across the AL declined dramatically with age for 3-hexanone (>9-fold decline) and isopropanol (>57-fold decline)
claims.criterion: Whole-AL mean peak fold change per ant as in fig2d-whole-al-alarm-no-age-effect; Welch's t test of young against old per odor. Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with young higher and the ratios of cohort means exceed 8.1 and 51.3; partially reproduced when the tests hold but a ratio is lower. The ratio is unstable when the old mean is near zero; the cohort means are reported with it.

claims.statement: The age decline of whole-AL responses is specific to 3-hexanone and isopropanol at 48%; ethylpyrazine, ethanol and propionic acid at 48%, and all five general odorants at 3%, show no age effect.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 7; Figure S3B
claims.quote: an effect that was specific to these two odorants when presented at 48% concentration
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, with the measure of fig2d-whole-al-alarm-no-age-effect. Reproduced when all eight tests give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Age does not change the number of glomeruli activated by ethylpyrazine, ethanol or propionic acid at 48%.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 7; Figure S3C
claims.quote: we found no effect of age on the number of activated glomeruli for ethylpyrazine, ethanol, or propionic acid
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Responding-ROI counts as in fig2e-heptanone-breadth-falls; Wilcoxon rank-sum test (R defaults) per odorant. Reproduced when all three give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: 3-hexanone excites all six focal glomeruli in young ants and PGb, PGa and G4 in old ants; isopropanol excites all but G1 in young ants only; propionic acid excites G4 at both ages; no other general odorant excites a focal glomerulus.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 8; Figure S4A
claims.quote: We found that 3-hexanone activated all six glomeruli in young ants as well as activating PG b , PG a , and G4 in old ants, while isopropanol activated five of the focal glomeruli (all except G1) in young ants only ... Additionally, propionic acid activated G4 in young and old ants, while none of the other general odorants activated any of the six focal glomeruli
claims.criterion: Per ant, the AUC of each focal glomerulus for each general odorant at 48% (shared methods, both fold-change readings); for each age, glomerulus and odorant (60 cells), a one-sided one-sample t test that the mean AUC exceeds zero (Figure S4A legend), at p < 0.05 uncorrected as the figure marks it. Reproduced when exactly the 16 cells above are significant; partially reproduced when the text's pattern for 3-hexanone and isopropanol holds but cells for the other odorants differ; not reproduced otherwise. All mismatches are listed.

claims.statement: Responses to 3-hexanone and isopropanol decline significantly with age in five of the six focal glomeruli (3-hexanone in all but PGb, isopropanol in all but G1).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 4; Figure S4B
claims.quote: Directly comparing calcium responses across age cohorts showed that responses to 3-hexanone and isopropanol each significantly declined with age in 5 out of 6 glomeruli (3-hexanone, all except PG b ; isopropanol, all except G1)
claims.criterion: Per ant, the AUC of each focal glomerulus for 3-hexanone and isopropanol at 48% (shared methods, both fold-change readings); Welch's t test of young against old. Reproduced when the ten pairs above give p < 0.05 with young higher and 3-hexanone in PGb and isopropanol in G1 give p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when at least four of the five glomeruli per odorant decline significantly.

claims.statement: In young ants propionic acid gives a very small negative deflection in G2 and G3 that declines in amplitude with age; its responses in G4 tend to fall with age, not significantly.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 4; Figure S4B
claims.quote: We also found that, in young ants, propionic acid produced a very small negative deflection in G2 and G3 that declined in amplitude with age ... Propionic acid responses in G4 also tended to decrease with age, but the difference was not statistically significant
claims.criterion: Per ant, the AUC for propionic acid at 48% in G2, G3 and G4 (shared methods, both fold-change readings); Welch's t test of young against old. Reproduced when the young mean AUC is below zero in G2 and G3, both tests give p < 0.05 with the old mean nearer zero, and G4 gives p >= 0.05 with the old mean below the young.

claims.statement: In PGb, 3-hexanone responses of old ants have a lower peak but decline more slowly than those of young ants; the AUC over frames 9 to 14 is larger in young ants and over frames 35 to 40 larger in old ants.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 10; Figure S4C and S4D
claims.quote: responses to 3-hexanone in PG b had a lower peak amplitude but then declined more slowly in old versus young ants
claims.criterion: Per ant, the PGb fold-change trace for 3-hexanone at 48% (shared methods, both fold-change readings), the mean of its three trials (Figure S4C legend), summed over frames 9 to 14 and over frames 35 to 40 (the legend's "AUC", whose plotted scale is that of a sum). Reproduced when frames 9 to 14 give young above old and frames 35 to 40 old above young, each by Welch's t test at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: In PGb and PGa, responses to alarm pheromones rise with age while responses to general odorants fall or stay absent; no general odorant response rises with age in any focal glomerulus.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figures 3, 4 and S4B
claims.quote: Whereas alarm pheromone responses increased with age specifically in PG b and PG a , general odorant responses showed overall similar patterns across all six glomeruli, either with no responses or decreasing responses with age
claims.criterion: Reproduced when fig3d-pg-stronger-old is reproduced, PGb or PGa has at least one general odorant with a significant decline in fig4-general-odorants-decline, and none of the 30 glomerulus and general odorant Welch's t tests at 48% gives p < 0.05 with old higher.

claims.statement: Recording amplifier saturation after a 0.2 ms pulse lasts about 0.14, 0.24, 0.26 and 0.30 ms at 5, 25, 50 and 100 uA, increasing with amplitude.
claims.source: Results, Orthogonal multi-Neuropixels recordings, paragraph 3; Figure 1L
claims.quote: saturation persisted for approximately 0.14 ± 0.00 ms at 5 μ A, 0.24 ± 0.01 ms at 25 μ A, 0.26 ± 0.01 ms at 50 μ A, and 0.30 ± 0.01 ms at 100 μ A ( Figure 1L , one-way ANOVA, F = 105.62, p < 0.001)
claims.criterion: Needs the raw AP band, which the paper says is not in the NWB. Method from figure1.ipynb (cells 22 to 26), as the Methods give none - cathodal trials (first 75) aligned to the artifact onset found on channel 0, samples above 1100 uV counted per trial and channel and converted to ms at 30 kHz, averaged over trials, outlier channels (|z| >= 1) replaced by their neighbours' mean, averaged over channels to one value per probe; one-way ANOVA (scipy f_oneway) across the four amplitudes. Reproduced when the four means are within tolerance and the ANOVA has p < 0.001.

claims.statement: Saturation duration increases with amplitude, and polarity does not significantly change it.
claims.source: Results, Orthogonal multi-Neuropixels recordings, paragraph 3; Figure S1B
claims.quote: despite increases in saturation with amplitude (two-way ANOVA, F = 236.04, p < 0.001), and polarity alone did not significantly change saturation duration ( F = 2.48, p = 0.09)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-way ANOVA of saturation duration (as in fig1l-saturation-amplitude) on amplitude and polarity; figure1.ipynb cell 34 uses ols('value ~ amplitude * C(polarity)') with type II sums of squares. Reproduced when the polarity effect has p >= 0.05 and the amplitude effect p < 0.001; the polarity effect size is reported.

claims.statement: The spatial extent of the evoked potential, both superficial and deep to the stimulation source, increases with amplitude (superficial about -424, -683, -742 and -744 um; deep about 510, 591, 662 and 712 um at 5, 25, 50 and 100 uA).
claims.source: Results, Evoked potential spatial extent increases sub-linearly with amplitude, paragraph 3; Figure 2G
claims.quote: Both the superficial and deep distance from stimulation increased with amplitude ( Figure 2G , superficial ... p = 0.002, linear mixed-effects model
claims.criterion: Needs the raw AP band, which the paper says is not in the NWB; the code's intermediate EP_boundaries_w_array_distances_curated.pkl holds the boundaries it computed (an outside input for the author to judge). Method, STAR Methods (Algorithmically determining the spatial extent) - trials aligned by threshold detection of the saturating artifact, 0.3 to 3 ms window, per sample the median over the saline channels outside the brain subtracted (Methods say the first 20 such channels, figure2.ipynb cell 8 uses 15; the code's 15 is a variant), mean over trials, the 1 ms sample, extent on each side where the potential returns to 20 uV. Where the Methods are silent the code is followed - Gaussian smoothing over channels (sigma 2), peak taken past channel 30 and kept only if above 40 uV, the boundary moved two channels inward. Distance is Euclidean CCF distance, negative superficial. Cathodal values. The model, from the Methods - recording as random intercept, maximum likelihood, Wald z test of the amplitude term; the fixed effects are polarity, amplitude, boundary type and probe identity "and their interactions", which the Methods do not list, so the readings are (a) these main effects with amplitude x polarity and amplitude x boundary type, (b) the full factorial; amplitude is (i) numeric or (ii) categorical. The code has no mixed model (its OLS ANOVA 'distance ~ C(polarity) * amplitude', cell 20, is shown as a variant). The printed values were read as per-amplitude means; the code's cell 16 prints SDs cumulative over amplitudes and its 100 uA superficial mean (-743.84) is pooled over all four, and cell 17 gives per-amplitude means (-424, -725, -812, -750; 510, 605, 747, 888), so both the per-amplitude and the cumulative means are computed. Reproduced when under one reading the amplitude effect has p < 0.05 and the means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the effect holds and the means do not.

claims.statement: The increase in spatial extent with amplitude is sublinear and poorly fit by a linear regression (superficial R2 = 0.02, deep R2 = 0.17), unlike the linear growth of the point-source model.
claims.source: Results, Evoked potential spatial extent increases sub-linearly with amplitude, paragraph 3; Figure 2G; Figure S2F
claims.quote: the increase in spatial extent of the biologically observed evoked potential was sublinear and poorly fit by linear regression (superficial R 2 = 0.02 and deep R 2 = 0.17)
claims.criterion: Extents as in fig2g-extent-increases, cathodal. As in figure2.ipynb cells 16 to 18, scipy linregress of the individual probe extents (CCF distance) on amplitude, pooled over amplitudes, one fit per side. The code's cell 16 prints linear R2 0.02 superficial and 0.16 deep (its quadratic deep fit gives 0.17); the Figure S2F legend gives, for peak-aligned distance, cathodal R2 0.02 dorsal and 0.20 ventral. Both distance types are run, CCF as the main reading. Tolerance 0.05 in R2 (10% of 0.02 is below the precision printed). Reproduced when both R2 are within tolerance and the step from 50 to 100 uA in mean extent is smaller than the step from 5 to 25 uA on each side (sublinear).

claims.statement: Spatial extents do not differ across polarities.
claims.source: Results, Evoked potential spatial extent increases sub-linearly with amplitude, paragraph 3; Figure 2I; Figure S2E
claims.quote: Notably, spatial extents did not differ across polarities ( Figures 2J and S2E , linear mixed-effects model, p = 0.151
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the mixed model of fig2g-extent-increases (each of its readings), polarity term. Reproduced when the polarity effect has p >= 0.05 under the readings; not reproduced when it is significant. The Results (p = 0.151) and the legends (p = 0.495, radial extent at 50 uA in Figure 2I) give two values; both the model over all amplitudes and the 50 uA comparison are run. The code's OLS is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Probe trajectory affects spatial extent, with larger extents on probe C, which stays in cortex, than on probes A and B, which cross the white matter into subcortical areas.
claims.source: Results, Evoked potential spatial extent increases sub-linearly with amplitude, paragraph 4; Figure 2H
claims.quote: we observed probe trajectory had a significant effect on average spatial extent, most notably with an increase in spatial extent for probe C ( Figure 2H , probe A vs. probe C: p < 0.001, probe B vs. probe C: p < 0.001
claims.criterion: Absolute extents (superficial and deep) as in fig2g-extent-increases, with probe identity (A, B, C) as a fixed effect in the same mixed model and readings, probe C as reference. Reproduced when probe C has the largest mean absolute extent and both contrasts have p < 0.05. The code (figure3.ipynb cell 15) fits an OLS of probe B against probe C only and finds no main effect (p = 0.72); it is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: For all polarities, the maximum evoked potential and its area under the curve at 1 ms increase nearly linearly with amplitude.
claims.source: Results, Evoked potential spatial extent increases sub-linearly with amplitude, paragraph 2; Figure S2G and S2H
claims.quote: For all polarities, both the maximum evoked potential and AUC increased nearly linearly ( Figures S2G and S2H
claims.criterion: Needs the raw AP band. Per probe, the maximum and the area under the curve between the two boundaries of the 1 ms profile (as in fig2g-extent-increases); linear regression on amplitude per polarity, with the R2 of the S2G and S2H legends (cathodal 0.16 and 0.23, anodal 0.04 and 0.07, bipolar 0.20 and 0.23) compared at a tolerance of 0.05. Reproduced when for every polarity both slopes are positive with p < 0.05 and the cathodal R2 are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The evoked-potential volume, the convex hull of the six extents on the three probes, tends to increase sublinearly with amplitude (cathodal 0.31, 0.43 and 0.61 mm3 at 25, 50 and 100 uA), with no significant main effect of amplitude or polarity.
claims.source: Results, Anisotropic volumetric profile of the induced electrical field, paragraph 1; Figure 3C
claims.quote: trended to increase sublinearly with stimulation amplitude ( Figure 3C ; cathodal polarity ... 0.31 ± 0.20 mm 3 , −50 μ A: 0.43 ± 0.19 mm 3 , −100 μ A: 0.61 ± 0.22 mm 3 ; linear R 2 = 0.259
claims.criterion: Needs the raw AP band. Methods - the four recordings with all six extents (jlh31, jlh32, jlh34 and jlh48 in the code), CCF coordinates of the six boundary points, scipy ConvexHull volume; 25, 50 and 100 uA. Two-way ANOVA of volume on amplitude and polarity (code, ols('volume ~ C(polarity) * amplitude'), type II). The code's typo in figure2.ipynb cell 39 (a_up_cff) reuses an earlier recording's probe A point when that point is missing; the corrected and the code's points are both computed. Reproduced when the cathodal means and R2 are within tolerance and neither main effect has p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Evoked potentials extend broadly within cortex but are compressed ventrally at the corpus callosum; along probe C, which stays in cortex, they extend beyond a fitted isotropic sphere, and along probe B, which crosses into white matter, they are truncated relative to it.
claims.source: Results, Anisotropic volumetric profile of the induced electrical field, paragraph 2; Figure 3D and 3E
claims.quote: when probes remained in cortex (probe C, Figure 3E ), responses extended beyond the symmetric fit, whereas when probes traversed into subcortical white matter (probe B, Figure 3E ), responses were truncated relative to the sphere
claims.criterion: Needs the raw AP band. Methods (Isotropic spherical fits, Convex-hull comparison) - for each recording and cathodal amplitude, the fixed-centre sphere radius r_L2 = mean distance of the six points from the stimulation contact; the signed difference between each measured point's distance and r_L2 stands for the hull deviation along that direction. Reproduced when, averaged over the four recordings and three cathodal amplitudes, the deep point of probe C lies outside the sphere (positive) and the deep point of probe B inside it (negative). The tessellated point-to-facet deviation of the Methods is computed as well and must agree in sign.

claims.statement: Anisotropy strength averages 0.493 +- 0.288 across amplitudes and polarities and does not vary with amplitude or polarity.
claims.source: Results, Anisotropic volumetric profile of the induced electrical field, paragraph 3; Figure 3F and 3G
claims.quote: Across all amplitudes and polarities, anisotropy strength averaged 0.493 ± 0.288 and did not vary systematically with stimulation amplitude or polarity
claims.criterion: Needs the raw AP band. Methods (Anisotropy metrics) - for each recording and condition, least-squares fit d_i = a + b.u_i of each point's distance on its unit direction from the stimulation contact, AS = norm(b)/a. Two-way ANOVA of AS on polarity and amplitude (code, figure3.ipynb cells 31 to 35, 'anisotropy_strength ~ C(polarity) * C(amp_abs)', type II). The legend names three polarities; the code (cell 35) groups monopolar against bipolar (polarity 1 df), which gives the printed F = 2.81 and 0.143; both groupings are run. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance and neither main effect has p < 0.05 (the absence part judged on that ANOVA).

claims.statement: The centre of mass of the evoked-potential volume is displaced from the stimulating contact (displacement greater than zero), with a dorsal component of 105 +- 46 um away from the corpus callosum that does not reach significance.
claims.source: Results, Anisotropic volumetric profile of the induced electrical field, paragraph 3; Figure 3H
claims.quote: The displacement magnitude exceeded zero (one-sample t test vs. 0, p = 0.02), indicating anisotropy. The dorsal (superficial) component averaged 105 ± 46 μ m away from the corpus callosum and, while directionally consistent, did not reach significance (one-sample t test vs. 0, p = 0.1095)
claims.criterion: Needs the raw AP band. Methods (Center-shift direction metric) - centre of mass is the mean of the six boundary points; displacement is centre of mass minus the stimulation contact, in CCF. Tolerance is the stated spread (46 um, n = 4). What is tested is open; readings (a) per recording, the displacement averaged over conditions, one-sample t test of its magnitude and of its DV component against 0 (n = 4), as figure3.ipynb cell 28 does; (b) the free-centre sphere shift per condition and recording pooled, per axis, as cell 45 does. Reproduced when under one reading the magnitude test has p < 0.05, the DV component is dorsal and within tolerance.

claims.statement: First-spike latencies after a pulse are bimodal, with an early peak, a pause at a median of 1.95 ms across parameters and a broader peak from about 2.5 ms, which sets the 2 ms direct window.
claims.source: Results, Evoked spiking is sparse and increases in density with amplitude, paragraph 3; Figure 4D; Figure S3B
claims.quote: the distribution of first-spike latencies, which exhibited a bimodal shape: an early peak immediately after stimulation, followed by a brief pause occurring at a median value of 1.95 ms across parameters
claims.criterion: As in figure4_figure5_figure6.ipynb cells 20 to 23 (the Methods give no procedure) - first spike after each pulse for all good units, pooled per polarity and amplitude, histogram in 0.1 ms bins over 0 to 15 ms (Figure 4D legend), trough is the minimum bin between 0.5 and 5 ms; median over the conditions (the code takes the four cathodal amplitudes). Reproduced when the median trough is within tolerance and the histogram has a higher bin before the trough and after it.

claims.statement: Gaussian mixtures of first-spike latencies give amplitude-specific direct windows (0.68, 1.14, 1.22 and 1.47 ms at 5, 25, 50 and 100 uA cathodal), and the proportion of direct responders does not differ from that of the 2 ms window.
claims.source: Results, Evoked spiking is sparse and increases in density with amplitude, paragraph 3; Figure S3C and S3D
claims.quote: create a direct response window for each amplitude (5 μA: 0.68 ms; 25 μA: 1.14 ms; 50 μA: 1.22 ms, and 100 μA: 1.47 ms, Figure S3C ); there was no statistical difference in the overall proportion of direct responders compared to the 2-ms window used
claims.criterion: Not in the code. Methods (Gaussian mixture models) - first-spike latencies 0 to 15 ms per condition (only conditions with at least 200), one-dimensional GMM by maximum likelihood; the Methods say both "4 Gaussian components" and selection by minimum BIC, so the readings are (a) k = 4 fixed (as the S3C legend, k = 4) and (b) k chosen by BIC up to 4; the window is the crossover of the posteriors of the two earliest components. Responders per recording with each window (nDRP > 0.15, baseline window 7 to 5 ms before onset for 2 ms; for the GMM windows the baseline length is open, readings (i) a baseline as long as the window, (ii) the 2 ms baseline), compared by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across 9 recordings with FDR correction (S3D legend). Reproduced when under one reading the four windows are within tolerance and no comparison has adjusted p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Direct responders are sparse and mostly lie within the average boundaries of the evoked potential (33.3%, 74.1%, 88.2% and 100% at 5, 25, 50 and 100 uA), with more outside at 5 uA.
claims.source: Results, Evoked spiking is sparse and increases in density with amplitude, paragraph 4; Figure 4F
claims.quote: Direct responders were sparse and generally constrained within the average boundaries of the evoked potential (33.3% for 5 μ A, 74.1% for 25 μ A, 88.2% for 50 μ A, and 100% for 100 μ A
claims.criterion: Cathodal direct responders (nDRP > 0.15) pooled over recordings; a responder is within when its signed distance (norm_distance) lies between the mean superficial and mean deep extents of the evoked potential at that amplitude (fig2g-extent-increases; the code reads them from EP_distances.pkl, an outside input for the author to judge). The code (figure4_figure5_figure6 cell 27) gives 0.483, 0.765, 0.889 and 1.0 over all responders, and its RS-only count (cell 54) gives 0.333, 0.741, 0.882 and 1.0, the printed numbers. Readings (a) all responders, (b) RS responders only. Reproduced when under one reading the four fractions are within tolerance and the 5 uA fraction is the lowest.

claims.statement: The spatial extent of direct responders stays relatively constant across amplitudes (1180 +- 559, 884 +- 652, 965 +- 451 and 522 +- 313 um), with no significant amplitude effect.
claims.source: Results, Evoked spiking is sparse and increases in density with amplitude, paragraph 4; Figure 4H and 4I
claims.quote: the spatial extent of single-unit responders remained relatively constant across amplitudes (5 μ A: 1180 ± 559 μ m, 25 μ A: 884 ± 652 μ m, 50 μ A: 965 ± 451 μ m, and 100 μ A: 522 ± 313 μ m, One-way ANOVA, F = 1.265, p = 0.312)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. As in figure4_figure5_figure6 cell 30 - per recording and cathodal amplitude, extent = |minimum| + maximum of the responders' signed distances (norm_distance); one-way ANOVA of these per-recording extents across the four amplitudes. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; the means are compared with tolerance and reported (the code prints 868 +- 671 um at 50 uA).

claims.statement: Higher amplitudes bring direct responders closer to the stimulation site (mean distance 426, 300, 137 and 146 um at 5, 25, 50 and 100 uA), driven by 5 against 50 and 5 against 100 uA.
claims.source: Results, Evoked spiking is sparse and increases in density with amplitude, paragraph 4; Figure 4H
claims.quote: Stimulation amplitude significantly decreased the average distance from stimulation of responsive units ... one-way ANOVA, F = 4.15, p = 0.007), driven specifically by differences between 5 μ A and 50 μ A and between 5 μ A and 100 μ A (post hoc Tukey tests: 5 vs. 50 μ A, p = 0.015; 5 vs. 100 μ A, p = 0.019
claims.criterion: As in figure4_figure5_figure6 cell 32 - signed distance (norm_distance) of cathodal direct responders pooled over recordings, one row per responder and amplitude; one-way ANOVA across amplitudes and Tukey HSD. Reproduced when the ANOVA and both named Tukey contrasts have p < 0.05 and the four means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold and the means do not.

claims.statement: 5 and 100 uA recruit distinct spatial populations of direct responders; the other pairs the paper reports (5-25, 25-50, 25-100 and 50-100 uA) do not differ after correction.
claims.source: Results, Evoked spiking is sparse and increases in density with amplitude, paragraph 4; Figure 4H and 4I
claims.quote: Further, 5 μ A and 100 μ A recruited distinct spatial populations (pairwise two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, corrected for six comparisons using the Holm-Šidák procedure
claims.criterion: The distance distributions of fig4h-distance-decreases, scipy ks_2samp for the six pairs, Holm-Sidak correction (code, cells 34 and 35). Reproduced when 5 against 100 uA has adjusted p < 0.05 and the 5-25, 25-50, 25-100 and 50-100 pairs do not; partially reproduced when only the first part holds. The paper prints no value for 5 against 50 uA; it is reported and not judged.

claims.statement: The proportion of direct responders among units within the evoked potential is small and increases with amplitude (0.014, 0.020, 0.031 and 0.030), so fewer than 5% of neurons are directly activated.
claims.source: Results, Evoked spiking is sparse and increases in density with amplitude, paragraph 5; Figure 4I
claims.quote: The proportion of responders within the evoked potential increased with amplitude (5 μ A: 0.014 ± 0.12, 25 μ A: 0.020 ± 0.14, 50 μ A: 0.031 ± 0.172, and 100 μ A: 0.030 ± 0.170; linear ANOVA, F = 5.41, p = 0.020
claims.criterion: The printed spreads equal the SD of a 0/1 indicator (sqrt(p(1-p))), so the proportion is the mean of a responder indicator over units pooled across recordings, and the "linear ANOVA" an OLS of that indicator on amplitude. These numbers are not printed by the code; its nearest cell (figure4_figure5_figure6 cell 37) uses nDRP > 0.10, the 100 uA boundaries and raw distance and gets 0.019 to 0.037. Readings (a) units within the amplitude's own mean evoked-potential boundaries on norm_distance, nDRP > 0.15, amplitude numeric; (b) as (a) with the 100 uA boundaries; (c) as (a) with raw CCF distance. Cathodal; boundaries as in fig4f-responders-within-ep. Reproduced when under one reading the four proportions are within tolerance, all below 0.05, and the slope on amplitude is positive with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Among units responsive at any amplitude (99 units), direct response probability increases with amplitude (0.12, 0.14, 0.19 and 0.23), so higher amplitude both recruits more neurons and raises their spiking probability.
claims.source: Results, Evoked spiking is sparse and increases in density with amplitude, paragraph 5; Figure 4J
claims.quote: among responders, direct-response probability increased with amplitude (5 μ A: 0.12 ± 0.20, 25 μ A: 0.14 ± 0.21, 50 μ A: 0.19 ± 0.25, and 100 μ A: 0.23 ± 0.31; F = 12.78, p = 0.0004, Figure 4J )
claims.criterion: Units with nDRP > 0.15 at any cathodal amplitude and a value at all four (code, figure4_figure5_figure6 cell 39). The test is named a one-way ANOVA; the code fits ols('norm_prob ~ amplitude') with amplitude numeric (F = 12.78, 1 df). Readings (a) the code's regression, (b) a one-way ANOVA with amplitude categorical, (c) a repeated-measures ANOVA over units. Reproduced when under one reading p < 0.05 with nDRP rising with amplitude and the means and unit count are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Broader windows (5 and 10 ms) give more responsive units than the 2 ms window (0.092 and 0.175 at 100 uA), and their amplitude dependence is stronger.
claims.source: Results, Evoked spiking is sparse and increases in density with amplitude, paragraph 6; Figure S3E
claims.quote: As expected, broader windows increased the proportion of responsive units (0.092 ± 0.01 for the 5 ms window and 0.175 ± 0.01 for the 10 ms window at 100 μ A, FDR-corrected p < 0.001, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests
claims.criterion: Not in the code. Per recording, the proportion of units with nDRP > 0.15 in windows of 2, 5 and 10 ms after onset, cathodal (mean and SEM over 9 recordings, S3E legend). The baseline window is open for the longer windows; readings (a) a 2 ms baseline as in spike_probability called with the longer window (the code's function keeps it 2 ms long, ending 3 ms plus the window before onset), (b) a baseline as long as the window, ending 3 ms before onset. Paired Wilcoxon tests across recordings with FDR correction. Reproduced when under one reading both 100 uA proportions are within tolerance and exceed the 2 ms proportion with adjusted p < 0.05, and the increase from 5 to 100 uA is larger for the 5 and 10 ms windows than for 2 ms. With 9 recordings the smallest two-sided exact Wilcoxon p is 0.0039, so p < 0.001 cannot be matched across recordings; this is recorded and the claim is judged at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Clustering the direct responders by response probability across amplitude gives six clusters, broadly dose-dependent (58.6% of responders) or amplitude-selective, responding almost only at one amplitude (19.2% at 5 uA, 15.2% at 25 uA, 7.1% at 100 uA).
claims.source: Results, Stimulation amplitude and polarity tune unit-specific recruitment, paragraph 1; Figure 5A to 5C; Figure S5A
claims.quote: Hierarchical clustering produced six clusters ( Figure S5A ; cophenetic correlation coefficient (CCC) = 0.702, mean silhouette score = 0.352) that were broadly either dose-dependent or amplitude-selective. Surprisingly, while 58.6% of direct responders exhibited dose-dependent increases in response probability
claims.criterion: The 99 responders of fig4j-drp-increases. Ward linkage, dendrogram cut with maxclust at k = 6 (Methods; code cells 71 to 75). Features - the Methods say "normalized feature vectors"; the code uses the four cathodal nDRP values unscaled. Readings (a) nDRP as the code, (b) each unit's vector divided by its maximum. A cluster is amplitude-selective when its mean nDRP peaks at one amplitude and is below half that peak at every other; otherwise dose-dependent (the paper labels clusters by eye; the code's cluster sizes 15, 19, 40, 13, 7 and 5 give 58 of 99 in the three rising clusters). Reproduced when under one reading the CCC and silhouette are within tolerance and the cluster fractions match within tolerance in some assignment of clusters to the labels; partially reproduced when six clusters include both kinds but the fractions differ.

claims.statement: Clustering responders by their response to cathodal, anodal and bipolar pulses shows a polarity bias - 69.1% are polarity-specific, preferring bipolar (27.7%), anodal (23.6%) or cathodal (17.7%) pulses; smaller groups are dose-selective but polarity-agnostic (10.9%), cathodal-phase-led (12.7%) or monopolar-only (3.3%).
claims.source: Results, Stimulation amplitude and polarity tune unit-specific recruitment, paragraph 2; Figure 5D to 5F; Figure S5B
claims.quote: revealed a striking polarity bias: 69.1% of directly activated units were polarity-specific, preferring bipolar (27.7%, Figure 5F , i ), anodal (23.6%, Figure 5F , ii ), or cathodal (17.7%, Figure 5F , iii ) stimulation
claims.criterion: As in the code (cells 77 to 81) - units with nDRP > 0.15 in any polarity and amplitude; features are per polarity the maximum nDRP over amplitudes, divided by the unit's maximum over polarities; Ward linkage, maxclust k = 6. The legend gives n = 99 units, while the code's population is 220 units (its cluster sizes 61, 52, 39, 28 and 24 give the printed 27.7, 23.6, 17.7, 12.7 and 10.9%); readings (a) the code's population, (b) the 99 cathodal responders of fig4j-drp-increases. A cluster prefers a polarity when its mean normalised response is highest for it and below half for both others (a labelling rule not from the paper, which labels clusters by inspection of Figure 5F; the outcome rests on the fractions matching in some assignment of clusters to the labels). Reproduced when under one reading CCC and silhouette are within tolerance and the three polarity-specific fractions are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Direct responders stay sparse for both FS and RS units across amplitudes, with a main effect of amplitude but no effect of waveform class or interaction.
claims.source: Results, Cell type correlates with direct activation distance distributions, paragraph 1 (the text cites Figure 6I; the panels are Figure 5I and 5J)
claims.quote: The proportion of direct responders remained sparse across amplitudes for both FS ... and RS neurons ... with a significant main effect of amplitude but no effect of waveform class or interaction
claims.criterion: Not in the code. The spreads are those of a 0/1 indicator, so the proportions are means of a responder indicator (nDRP > 0.15) over FS or RS units pooled across recordings, cathodal; two-way ANOVA of the indicator on amplitude and waveform class. Readings (a) all FS and RS units, (b) units within the evoked potential as in fig4i-proportion-within-ep; amplitude (i) categorical or (ii) numeric. The full values are FS 0.032, 0.035, 0.030, 0.040 and RS 0.013, 0.033, 0.039, 0.037. Reproduced when under one reading the proportions are within tolerance and the waveform and interaction terms have p >= 0.05 (absence on the paper's test) and amplitude p < 0.05.

claims.statement: FS direct responders lie closer to the stimulation site than RS responders, and higher amplitude brings both closer.
claims.source: Results, Cell type correlates with direct activation distance distributions, paragraph 2; Figure 5I and 5J
claims.quote: FS responders were clustered significantly closer to the stimulation site than RS responders (two-way ANOVA, F waveform = 8.04, p = 0.005)
claims.criterion: As in the code (figure4_figure5_figure6 cell 57) - signed distance (norm_distance) of cathodal direct responders classed FS or RS, ols('value ~ C(amplitude) * C(cell_type)'), type II. Reproduced when the waveform and amplitude terms have p < 0.05 with the FS mean below the RS mean over amplitudes; the per-amplitude means (FS 205, 203, -2, 60; RS 567, 337, 208, 185 um) are compared with tolerance and reported (the FS values near zero cannot take a 10% tolerance and are reported only).

claims.statement: FS responders lie almost entirely within the evoked potential even at low amplitude (75%, 83.3%, 100%, 100%), while only 33% of RS responders do at 5 uA, rising with amplitude.
claims.source: Results, Cell type correlates with direct activation distance distributions, paragraph 2; Figure 5I and 5J
claims.quote: FS responders were almost entirely constrained within the evoked-potential boundary, even at low amplitudes (75.0% for 5 μ A; 83.3% for 25 μ A; 100% for 50 μ A; and 100% for 100 μ A). In contrast, only 33.0% of RS responders were within the evoked potential at 5 μ A
claims.criterion: As fig4f-responders-within-ep, split by waveform class (code cell 54). Reproduced when the four values are within tolerance and FS fractions are at or above RS fractions at every amplitude.

claims.statement: In the 10 ms after a pulse, the firing of FS and RS cortical units differs at every amplitude.
claims.source: Results, Cell type correlates with direct activation distance distributions, paragraph 3; Figure S6B
claims.quote: we observed pronounced differences in spiking between waveform classes across amplitudes that evolved with stimulation strength (Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests at each amplitude
claims.criterion: From the S6B legend and the code (figure4_figure5_figure6 cells 62 to 67), the Methods being silent. Per recording, cortical good units (CCF name containing "area") of each class, first 75 cathodal trials; spikes of all units of the class pooled, counted per trial in bins, averaged over trials and divided by the number of units of the class (the "normalised firing rate"); the bins from 0 to 10 ms of every recording's FS PSTH pooled as one sample and of every RS PSTH as the other; scipy ks_2samp at each amplitude, Holm-Sidak adjusted over the four. Bin width - the legend says 2 ms, the code uses 1 ms (pre 5 ms, post 10 ms); both are run. Reproduced when under one bin width all four adjusted p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Spiking modulation after a single pulse increases with amplitude for cortical units (12.60, 13.37, 15.11, 20.21) but stays about constant for subcortical units (12.27, 12.60, 12.08, 13.48), differing between them at 50 and 100 uA.
claims.source: Results, Single pulse electrical stimulation leads to extensive circuit response, paragraph 1; Figure 6C
claims.quote: The magnitude of spiking modulation ( STAR Methods ) increased with amplitude for cortical units ... but remained relatively constant for subcortical units
claims.criterion: The modulation index MI = (r_resp - r_base)/(r_resp + r_base + eps) per bin. The sources disagree on its window - the Methods give a response window of 500 to 1000 ms with 5 ms bins, the Figure 6C legend a 500 ms window aligned to onset with 5 ms bins, and the code (figure7 cell 28) 0 to 500 ms in 10 ms bins with the baseline the median rate from 1000 to 500 ms before onset. The "magnitude of modulation" is not defined in the paper; the code takes the trapezoid area of |MI| over bins (unit spacing), one value per unit, mean +- SD over units. As that area scales with the number of bins, the printed values are reached only with the code's 10 ms bins; readings (a) code, 0 to 500 ms, 10 ms bins, (b) legend, 0 to 500 ms, 5 ms bins, (c) Methods, 500 to 1000 ms, 5 ms bins, each with the code's baseline. Units good and stable, first 75 cathodal trials, regions as the code's classify_region (cortical when the CCF name contains "area"). Two-way ANOVA ols('AUC ~ Amplitude_mag * C(Region)'), type II, amplitude numeric; cortical against subcortical per amplitude by t test, Student's (text) and Welch's (code) both run. Reproduced when under reading (a) the four values are within tolerance and under every reading the region, amplitude and interaction terms have p < 0.001, cortex grows more with amplitude than subcortex, and the 50 and 100 uA comparisons have p < 0.001.

claims.statement: At 100 uA higher visual areas, beyond the reach of direct activation, are more modulated than subcortical units (15.82 against 13.48) although both lie at similar distances from the stimulation site.
claims.source: Results, Single pulse electrical stimulation leads to extensive circuit response, paragraph 1; Figure 6D; Figure S8A
claims.quote: Higher visual areas (HVAs) exhibited responses at higher amplitudes (magnitude of modulation = 15.82 ± 9.97) that were significantly different from those of subcortical units (magnitude of modulation = 13.48 ± 7.70) at 100 μ A (Tukey HSD, p = 0.004
claims.criterion: Magnitude of modulation as in fig6c-modulation-cortex (its readings). Groups by the Figure 6 legend - HVA is LM, AM and PM (the code's figure7 cell 39 takes any CCF name with "layer" and not "primary", which also takes dentate gyrus and superior colliculus layers; shown as a variant), subcortical is hippocampus (CA1, subiculum, dentate gyrus) and superior colliculus, V1 the primary visual area. Tukey HSD over V1, HVA and subcortical at 100 uA cathodal; Mann-Whitney U test of Euclidean distances to the stimulation contact, HVA against subcortical. Reproduced when under reading (a) the two values are within tolerance and, under the legend's groups, HVA exceeds subcortical with Tukey p < 0.05 and the distance test has p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: The proportion of cortical units in the circuit response grows with amplitude (0.14, 0.21, 0.52, 0.79), so more than half are recruited at the higher amplitudes; subcortical units respond less but also increase (0.08, 0.09, 0.17, 0.35).
claims.source: Results, Single pulse electrical stimulation leads to extensive circuit response, paragraph 2; Figure 6E; Figure S7C
claims.quote: Further, the proportion of cortical neurons participating in this circuit response increased with amplitude (5 μ A: 0.14 ± 0.05, 25 μ A: 0.21 ± 0.08, 50 μ A: 0.52 ± 0.26, and 100 μ A: 0.79 ± 0.21; F amplitude = 175.18, p < 0.001), such that at the highest amplitudes, over half of all recorded cortical units were recruited
claims.criterion: Circuit responder - ZETA test (zetapy getZeta) on spike times in a 300 ms window after onset, p < 0.05 (Methods; code assign_zeta_sig on zetascores300ms). Per recording and region, the fraction of good stable units that respond, cathodal for the values. Regions by the code's map_region_to_group (cortical V1 and A, LM, RL, PM, AM; subcortical the other in-brain regions except optic radiation, corpus callosum and retrosplenial). The "multivariate ANOVA" is in the code ols('Value ~ Amplitude * C(Polarity) * C(Region)'), type II, amplitude numeric. The cached zetascores are an outside input; ZETA is recomputed from the dataset and the two are compared. Reproduced when the six proportions are within tolerance, the cortical value at 50 and 100 uA is above 0.5, and the amplitude and region terms have p < 0.001; partially reproduced when the trend and tests hold but some values are out of tolerance (ZETA is a resampling test).

claims.statement: Response timing shows no propagating wave - time to peak inhibition and to peak rebound excitation do not correlate with distance from the stimulation site.
claims.source: Results, Single pulse electrical stimulation leads to extensive circuit response, paragraph 3; Figure 6F
claims.quote: This was confirmed statistically by the absence of a relationship between distance from stimulation and time to peak inhibition ( Figure 6F , ii ; Pearson r = 0.09) or time to peak rebound excitation ( Figure 6F , iii ; Pearson r = −0.03)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, Pearson correlation of signed distance (negative dorsal) with time to peak, each at p < 0.05. Units and peaks from the code (figure7 cells 20 to 23) - cortical units that are circuit responders at 50 uA cathodal; MI in 5 ms bins over 0 to 500 ms; Gaussian smoothing (sigma 2.5 ms); peaks by find_peaks with prominence 0.2, width at least 4 ms, latency at least 20 ms, time by the local centre of mass over +-6 ms; inhibitory peaks on -MI. The code leaves out jlh39 and jlh49; with and without them both run. Text and legend swap the two r values; both peaks are tested. Reproduced when neither correlation has p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Direct response probability is slightly but significantly higher on high than on low cortical-state trials at every cathodal amplitude.
claims.source: Results, Single pulse electrical stimulation leads to extensive circuit response, paragraph 4; Figure S9B
claims.quote: DRP was slightly higher during high cortical states across stimulation amplitudes
claims.criterion: Not in the code. Per recording and cathodal condition, trials split at the median of the population spike count in the 500 ms before onset (Methods; S9A legend); per unit DRP within each half; paired Wilcoxon across units, FDR over amplitudes. Open, with readings - the population counted (a) all good units, (b) cortical units; the measure (i) DRP, (ii) nDRP; units (x) all good units, (y) direct responders. Reproduced when under one reading high exceeds low at all four amplitudes with adjusted p < 0.05 and the 5 and 100 uA values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the direction and tests hold but the values do not.

claims.statement: After a pulse the population's dimensionality drops (participation ratio and effective dimensionality fall), even as firing rate fluctuates, with a brief rise in effective dimensionality within 20 ms at 5, 25 and 50 uA.
claims.source: Results, Single pulse electrical stimulation leads to extensive circuit response, paragraph 5; Figure 6G
claims.quote: the response window was associated with a pronounced reduction in neural dimensionality, as reflected by decreases in both PR and effective dimensionality
claims.criterion: Methods (Dimensionality calculation) - for all cortical neurons of a recording, firing rate in 2 ms bins; per bin the neuron covariance across trials, PR = (sum of eigenvalues)^2 / sum of squared eigenvalues, and the number of PCA components for 95% of variance. From the code (figure7 cell 69) where the Methods are silent - first 75 cathodal trials, bins from -200 to +500 ms, each recording's trace divided by its median over pre-stimulus bins, averaged over recordings; epochs early 0 to 10 ms, middle 12 to 150 ms, late 170 to 300 ms (cell 52). Cortical units are those whose region contains "area" (the code's "layer" filter, which takes dentate gyrus and superior colliculus units, is a variant). Bin width - the Methods and the code use 2 ms, the Figure 6G legend says 5 ms; both are run. The paper reports no test. Reproduced when under one bin width, at every amplitude, the mean normalised PR and effective dimensionality in the middle epoch are below 1, and at 5, 25 and 50 uA the normalised effective dimensionality rises above 1 within 0 to 20 ms ("small transient increases"; open, readings (a) its mean over 0 to 20 ms, (b) its largest bin in 0 to 20 ms); partially reproduced when only the reduction holds.

claims.statement: Mice learned to detect high-contrast static gratings over 1353.8 +- 496.8 rewarded high-contrast trials and 14802 +- 5154 total trials.
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 2; Figure 7D
claims.quote: Mice successfully learned to detect high-contrast static gratings (>30% contrast) over an average of 1353.8 ± 496.8 rewarded high-contrast trials and 14802 ± 5154 total trials
claims.criterion: Behaviour data, which the paper does not name among its deposits. Methods (Quantifying task learning) - d' from high-contrast (> 30%) rewarded trials, hits with reaction time 0.15 to 0.6 s, false positives outside; "learned" when d' is stable above 0. The code (figure8) counts trials until a sustained rolling d' above -0.3 and is the variant that gives the printed numbers. Tolerance is the stated spread over 4 mice. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance under one of the two definitions.

claims.statement: Mice generalized from gratings to the moving-circle stimulus before electrical testing (d' 2.35 +- 0.30), comparable to high-contrast gratings (1.62 +- 0.92).
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 2; Figure 7E
claims.quote: These mice generalized detection of static gratings to the moving-circle stimulus before testing electrical stimulation, achieving a sensitivity index of d ′ = 2.35 ± 0.30, comparable to their performance on high-contrast grating stimuli ( d ′ = 1.62 ± 0.92, p = 0.113)
claims.criterion: Behaviour data. d' for high-contrast gratings and moving circles at the start of Phase 3 (Figure 7E legend), d' = Z(H) - Z(F) with F the catch-trial lick rate (Methods); the extent of "the beginning of phase 3" is open, readings (a) each mouse's first Phase 3 session, (b) the code's selection (figure8 cells 10 and 11). Tolerance is the SEM over 4 mice. Reproduced when both are within tolerance, both exceed 0 by one-sample t test at p < 0.05, and the paired test has p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Mice detect single pulses at similar rates across amplitudes (d' 0.37, 0.32, 0.36 and 0.45 at 5, 25, 50 and 100 uA); amplitude has no significant effect.
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 4; Figure 7G
claims.quote: Mice detected single pulses of electrical stimulation at similar rates across amplitudes ( d ′ for 5 μ A: 0.37 ± 0.04, 25 μ A: 0.32 ± 0.14, 50 μ A: 0.36 ± 0.06, and 100 μ A: 0.45 ± 0.14; F amplitude = 1.74, p = 0.21
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a one-way ANOVA of per-mouse d' on amplitude (categorical), p >= 0.05. d' per mouse and amplitude = Z(hit rate) - Z(catch lick rate), single pulses of Phase 3, trials removed where the 10-trial rolling false-alarm or lapse rate exceeds 0.7 (Methods). The code (figure8 cell 22) pools catch trials per mouse, applies no correction, and fits ols('Dprime ~ Amplitude') with amplitude numeric (F = 1.749, 13 df, 100 uA from 3 mice); shown as a variant. Tolerance is the SEM over mice.

claims.statement: Single pulses are detected above chance (average d' 0.37 +- 0.06).
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 4; Figure 7H
claims.quote: and above chance levels (average pulse d ′ = 0.37 ± 0.06; one-sample t test compared to d ′ = 0, p = 0.001
claims.criterion: d' as in fig7g-no-amplitude-effect, all single pulses pooled per mouse; one-sample t test against 0 over 4 mice. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance and p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Anodal-leading pulses are marginally more detectable than cathodal-leading pulses (d' 0.44 against 0.33).
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 4; Figure S10C
claims.quote: Anodal-leading waveforms were marginally more detectable than cathodal-leading waveforms (anodal d ′ = 0.44 ± 0.06, cathodal d ′ = 0.33 ± 0.09; paired t test, p = 0.028
claims.criterion: d' per mouse and polarity as in fig7g-no-amplitude-effect; paired t test. In the code one mouse's anodal d' is undefined and dropped, so the test has 3 pairs; readings (a) the mice with a defined d' for both, (b) all 4 mice with rates clipped to 1/(2N) and 1 - 1/(2N). Reproduced when under one reading anodal exceeds cathodal with p < 0.05 and both means are within tolerance.

claims.statement: High-frequency trains (100 to 300 Hz, 10 to 50 pulses) are detected better than single pulses (d' 0.66 against 0.37), with no significant difference by frequency.
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 4; Figure 7H; Figure S10D
claims.quote: yielded higher detection sensitivity than single pulses ( d ′ = 0.66 ± 0.11 vs. 0.37 ± 0.06; paired t test, p = 0.019). Within stimulation trains, detection sensitivity did not differ significantly by frequency
claims.criterion: d' per mouse for train trials and for single pulses as in fig7g-no-amplitude-effect; paired t test; one-way ANOVA of d' across 100, 200 and 300 Hz (unevenly sampled; the code has 4, 2 and 3 mice). Reproduced when trains exceed pulses with p < 0.05, the train mean is within tolerance, and the frequency ANOVA has p >= 0.05 (absence on the paper's test).

claims.statement: Detection of visual stimuli increases with contrast for gratings and moving circles, emerges at 4% contrast for gratings and 2% for circles, and single pulses perform like 2 to 4% contrast while trains perform near 8%.
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 4; Figure 7I

Single pulses of electrical stimulation performed comparably to visual contrasts between 2% and 4%, whereas stimulation trains performed near the level of an 8% visual contrast
claims.criterion: d' per mouse and contrast for Phase 3 gratings and moving circles as in fig7g-no-amplitude-effect; ANOVA of d' on contrast per class (named one-way; the code fits contrast as numeric, both run); one-sample t tests against 0 per contrast. Tolerance is the SEM over mice. Reproduced when both contrast effects have p < 0.05, the lowest significant contrast is 4% for gratings and 2% for circles (p < 0.05), and the single-pulse d' lies between the d' of the two classes at 2% and 4% (lowest to highest of the four) and the train d' within the SEM of the 8% values; partially reproduced when the contrast effects hold but the equivalences do not.

claims.statement: Within sessions, electrical stimulation becomes less detectable across trials (slope -0.004 per trial).
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 5; Figure 7J
claims.quote: Within individual sessions, electrical stimulation became less detectable across trials (mixed linear model regression
claims.criterion: Behaviour data. From the code (figure8 cells 36 and 37), the Methods being silent - per session, single-pulse electrical trials in order; d' in a rolling window of 15 trials with log-linear correction (H + 0.5)/(N + 1), F the mouse's overall catch rate; mixedlm('Dprime ~ Trial', groups = Mouse), REML. Reproduced when the slope is negative with p < 0.05 and slope and intercept are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Detection of electrical stimulation does not improve across sessions.
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 6; Figure S10F
claims.quote: We observed no evidence of such learning: detection performance did not increase across sessions (ordinary least-squares regression, R 2 = 0.01, F = 1.12, slope = −0.004, p slope = 0.29
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test - OLS of per-session d' on session index (code, figure8 cells 40 and 41, log-linear corrected d' over all electrical trials of a session, sessions from the first with electrical stimulation, 117 sessions). Reproduced when the slope is not positive with p < 0.05; slope and p reported.

claims.statement: Reaction times fall with contrast for both visual classes, while reaction times to electrical stimulation are like those to low-contrast visual stimuli.
claims.source: Results, Single pulses of electrical stimulation are weakly detected, paragraph 5; Figure S10E (the text cites S10F)

claims.criterion: The paper's tests are said to be in Table S1, which is not in the text read, so the test is open. Hit reaction times per trial, Phase 3, per class and contrast or amplitude. Readings (a) Spearman correlation of per-mouse median reaction time with contrast, (b) one-way ANOVA of per-mouse median reaction time on contrast; each per visual class, decrease at p < 0.05. The electrical stimulation part holds when the per-mouse median electrical reaction time lies within the range of the medians at 2 to 8% contrast. Reproduced when both readings give a decrease for both classes and the electrical part holds; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: The passive identity dataset holds 81 OB-p, 84 mPFC-p and 1978 untagged neurons from 10 mice; the concentration dataset 87 OB-p, 102 mPFC-p and 2232 untagged neurons from 10 mice; the Go/NoGo dataset 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p tagged) with, per session, 95 +/- 2 OB-p, 87 +/- 8 mPFC-p and 1690 +/- 35 untagged neurons.

Per session (mean ± SD), we recorded 95 ± 2 OB-p, 87 ± 8 mPFC-p, and 1690 ± 35 untagged neurons
claims.criterion: Counts of suite2p cells (iscell) by tag, per experiment, as the code's load_experiment builds them. The Go/NoGo tolerances are the paper's SD. "Per session" is read as (a) the total over all mice of one task day, averaged over task days 1 to 3, or (b) the same over days 0 to 3; for OB-p and mPFC-p, only the mice tagged for that target count. Reproduced when all values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when the identity and concentration counts are and the Go/NoGo counts are not.

claims.statement: OB-p and mPFC-p mice do not differ in the number of jGCaMP7f neurons or of co- labeled jGCaMP7f/tdTomato neurons.
claims.source: Figure S2B legend
claims.quote: Quantification of jGCaMP7f and co-labeled jGCaMP7f/tdTomato-expressing neurons in OB-p and mPFC-p mice. (OB-p, N = 9; mPFC-p, N = 10. Unpaired two-tailed t-test
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per mouse, the number of suite2p cells and of red (tdTomato-tagged) cells, with an unpaired two-tailed Student t-test of OB-p against mPFC-p mice for each count. The legend does not say which session gives a mouse's count when a mouse was imaged more than once; readings are (a) each mouse's first imaging session and (b) its mean over sessions. The legend also leaves open whether the co-labeled measure is a count or a share of the mouse's jGCaMP7f neurons; readings are (c) the count and (d) the percentage of jGCaMP7f neurons. Reproduced when neither test has p < 0.05 under the readings; not reproduced when either has p < 0.05 under all readings. The mouse counts per group are reported against 9 and 10.

claims.statement: An MLP trained on normalized fluorescence traces pooled across the identity and Go/NoGo datasets classifies OB-p against mPFC-p neurons with F1 scores of 0.688 (OB-p) and 0.557 (mPFC-p).

claims.quote: The MLP achieved F1 scores of 0.688 (OB-p) and 0.557 (mPFC-p)
claims.criterion: Inputs as for the transformer (Methods, Preprocessing), trials from 1 s before to 15 s after odor onset (70 frames), L = 5 subsamples of M = 20 trials per neuron, the identity passive and Go/NoGo datasets, within-animal split 0.8/0.1/0.1 of neurons, averaged over the seeds 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46. The MLP's architecture and training hyperparameters are in Table 8, which is missing from the text; until it is supplied the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified. Whether untagged neurons are a third class in training (Figure 1F colors them) is open; readings are (a) two classes, OB-p and mPFC-p only, and (b) three classes, with F1 reported for OB-p and mPFC-p.

claims.statement: A transformer classifier on single-neuron calcium traces decodes projection target with F1 0.759 (OB-p) and 0.744 (mPFC-p) when neurons from all animals are split, and 0.754 (OB-p) and 0.623 (mPFC-p) when one OB-p and one mPFC-p animal are held out.
claims.source: Results, Temporal structure of activity predicts OB-p vs mPFC-p identity, paragraph 1; Figure S3B
claims.quote: which improved test performance to 0.759 (OB-p) and 0.744 (mPFC-p) ( Figure S3B ) ... Performance remained high ... 0.754 OB-p; 0.623 mPFC-p
claims.criterion: As in the Methods (Projection decoding analysis with a transformer model). Identity passive and Go/NoGo datasets; trials from 1 s before to 15 s after odor onset (70 frames); L = 5 subsamples of M = 20 trials per neuron; patches of 2 frames embedded in 128 dimensions; a ViT encoder with a class token; trial latents average-pooled; majority vote over subsamples; Adam with cosine decay. Within-animal split 0.8/0.1/0.1 over seeds 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46; across-animal over 6 held-out OB-p/mPFC-p pairs (Table 6) with seeds 42, 43, 44. The depth, heads, learning rate, epochs and batch size (Table 5) and the held-out pairs (Table 6) are missing from the text; until they are supplied the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified. Classes as in mlp-projection-f1 (readings a and b).

claims.statement: Attention rollout on correctly classified neurons puts the informative epochs early after odor onset (about 0 to 3 s) for OB-p neurons and later in the trial for mPFC-p neurons.

claims.quote: informative epochs cluster early after odor onset (around 0-3 s) for OB-p neurons, but later in the trial for mPFC-p neurons
claims.criterion: From the transformer of transformer-projection-f1, attention rollout (Abnar and Zuidema 2020) of the class token over patches, averaged over trials per correctly classified subsample, averaged over 10 seeds, OB-p minus mPFC-p (Figure 1G legend), on the identity dataset. Reproduced when the difference is positive over most of 0 to 3 s after odor onset and negative over most of the time after 3 s. Blocked with the transformer while Table 5 is missing.

claims.statement: The transformer's penultimate-layer embeddings separate OB-p from mPFC-p neurons, with little clustering by animal or dataset.

claims.quote: which separated OB-p and mPFC-p well with minimal clustering by animal or dataset
claims.criterion: The paper shows PCA plots and gives no measure of separation, so the claim can be judged only by inspecting the same plots (PCA of neuron embeddings, seed 42, colored by label, animal and dataset). It is blocked with the transformer while Table 5 is missing; if run, it is reported as plots without an outcome beyond what they show.

claims.statement: Lifetime sparseness does not differ significantly between OB-p, mPFC-p and untagged neurons in the identity dataset.
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure 2B
claims.quote: Odor responses in PCx were generally sparse on the single cell level, with no significant differences in lifetime sparseness between groups
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Per neuron, lifetime sparseness over the 8 odors of its trial- averaged binarized activity (0 to 5 s window), 81 OB-p, 84 mPFC-p and 1978 untagged neurons. The text names no test here; the test the paper uses for the other single-cell comparisons of Figure 2 is the two-sided Mann-Whitney U test with Bonferroni correction, taken here over the 3 pairs. Reproduced when no pair has corrected p < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. Medians are reported.

claims.statement: Mutual information between binarized activity and odor identity does not differ between OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, but is lower for OB-p than untagged neurons (p = 0.012).

claims.quote: Mutual information did not differ significantly between projection sub-populations, but was lower for OB-p neurons than for untagged neurons (p = 0.012)
claims.criterion: Per neuron, mutual information between its binary activity per trial (0 to 5 s window) and the odor (8 odors). Two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction over the 3 pairs. Reproduced when OB-p against mPFC-p has corrected p >= 0.05 and OB-p is lower than untagged with corrected p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Population sparseness per trial differs only between OB-p and untagged populations (p = 1.26 x 10^-5).
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure 2D

claims.criterion: Population sparseness per pseudo-population trial (8 odors by 8 trials, 64 per group) over all cells of the group, from their binary activity on that trial (0 to 5 s). Two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests over the 3 pairs, Bonferroni corrected. Reproduced when only OB-p against untagged has corrected p < 0.05. The direction is reported (the paper does not state it).

claims.statement: A higher proportion of OB-p than mPFC-p neurons responds to odorants.
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 2
claims.quote: with OB-p neurons responding in a significantly higher proportion than mPFC-p neurons (two-sided Mann–Whitney U test with Bonferroni corrected p-values, p = 5.79 × 10⁻ 7 )
claims.criterion: The proportion of active cells (Methods, Metrics derived from response binarization) per trial, 0 to 5 s window. Readings of the sample are (a) per pseudo- population trial over all cells of the group (64 values per group) and (b) per neuron, the proportion of trials it is active (mean binarized activity). Two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, Bonferroni corrected over the 3 pairs. Reproduced when OB-p exceeds mPFC-p with corrected p < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: OB-p populations contain higher fractions of both unreliable and reliable responsive cells per trial (10.97% and 1.54%) than mPFC-p populations (8.71% and 0.25%).
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure 2E
claims.quote: OB-p populations contained higher fractions of both unreliable and reliable cells (10.97% and 1.54%, respectively) than mPFC-p populations ( Figure 2E , 8.71% and 0.25%
claims.criterion: Methods, Reliability analysis. A cell responds on a trial when its mean normalized fluorescence 0 to 5 s after onset exceeds its baseline mean plus 2.33 baseline SDs; a cell is reliable if it responds on more than half of its odor trials, unreliable otherwise; per trial, the percentage of the group's cells that respond and are reliable, and that respond and are unreliable. Open details are the baseline window, read as (a) the 4 s before onset (the Methods' baseline for active responses) or (b) the whole 5 s pre-odor baseline; whether the baseline mean and SD are per trial or pooled over the cell's trials, read as (c) per trial or (d) pooled; and whether "more than half" counts over all odor trials or per odor, read as (e) all odor trials or (f) any odor. Trials are pseudo- population trials (64). Two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests of OB-p against mPFC-p, Bonferroni corrected. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the four percentages are within tolerance and both tests have corrected p < 0.05 with OB-p higher; partially reproduced when both directions and tests hold but the values do not. Which trials are the samples is also open (the legend gives only neuron counts); readings are (g) pseudo- population trials (64) and (h) each mouse's own trials, pooled by group.

claims.statement: In the 30 Hz data OB-p neurons reach their first calcium peak after odor onset sooner than mPFC-p neurons; OB-p and untagged neurons do not differ.
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 3; Figure 2F
claims.quote: OB-p neurons exhibited shorter latencies to reach the first peak of calcium activity following odor onset compared to mPFC-p neurons
claims.criterion: Fast (30 Hz) dataset. Peaks found on normalized fluorescence per trial with the Methods' minimum criteria (width 100 ms, distance 1 s, height 0.5, prominence 0.25), read as scipy.signal.find_peaks arguments, ignoring the first and last second of each trial; latency is the time of the first peak after odor onset. Whether a latency is per trial (all trials with a peak) or per neuron (median over trials) is open; the sizes of the p- values suggest per trial, and both are run, (a) per trial and (b) per neuron. Two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests, Bonferroni corrected over the 3 pairs. Reproduced when OB-p is shorter than mPFC-p with corrected p < 0.05 under one reading, and, under that reading, OB-p against untagged has corrected p >= 0.05 (the statement's claim of absence, on the same test); the "= 1" is not required.

claims.statement: OB-p neurons have more calcium peaks at early time points after odor onset than mPFC-p neurons.
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 3; Figure 2G and Figure S4A to S4C
claims.quote: OB-p neurons also had more peaks during earlier time points than mPFC-p neurons
claims.criterion: Peaks as in fig2f-latency, counted per trial in time bins aligned to odor onset and averaged per neuron. The paper gives no bin width, no window for "earlier" and no test. Readings of "earlier" are (a) 0 to 2 s (the odor pulse) and (b) 0 to 3 s (the early epoch of Figure 1G). Reproduced when the mean number of peaks per trial in that window is higher for OB-p than mPFC-p under both readings; the counts are reported. The OASIS deconvolved- event version (Figure S4) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Odor identity decoded from 5 s windows reaches similar accuracy in size-matched OB- p and mPFC-p pseudo-populations, above chance and slightly below untagged.
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 4; Figure 2H
claims.quote: both OB-p and mPFC-p pseudo-populations reached similar accuracy levels, significantly above chance but slightly lower than the untagged population ( Figure 2H ; two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.398)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence for OB-p against mPFC-p, on the paper's test. Linear SVM, 8 odors, mean normalized fluorescence per cell in the window, 5-fold cross-validation, 75- cell pseudo-populations, 200 train/test repeats (Figure 2H legend, right). The window is 0 to 5 s in the legend and 1 to 5 s in the Methods; both are run, (a) 0 to 5 s and (b) 1 to 5 s. Reproduced when the two-sided Mann-Whitney U test of the 200 OB-p against the 200 mPFC-p accuracies has p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The mean accuracies are reported against chance (12.5%) and against untagged. If the two windows disagree the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In an early window (0 to 2 s) OB-p pseudo-populations decode odor identity better than mPFC-p pseudo-populations.
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 5; Figure 2I
claims.quote: we found that OB-p pseudo-populations outperformed mPFC-p pseudo-populations ( Figure 2I , two-sided Mann-Whitney U test with p = 2.15 × 10⁻ 30 )
claims.criterion: As fig2h-identity-decoding-5s with a 0 to 2 s window. Reproduced when OB-p accuracy exceeds mPFC-p with two-sided Mann-Whitney U p < 0.05 over the 200 repeats.

claims.statement: With a sliding window, odor identity decoding accuracy peaks earlier for OB-p than for mPFC-p pseudo-populations.
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 5; Figure 2J
claims.quote: SVM classification using a sliding window for odor responses revealed that decoding accuracy for OB-p neurons peaked earlier than for mPFC-p neurons
claims.criterion: Linear SVM on mean normalized fluorescence in consecutive windows across the trial, trained and tested on the same window, 75-cell pseudo-populations, 100 repeats. The window is 250 ms in the Figure 2J legend and 500 ms in the Methods; at 4.53 Hz a 250 ms window holds one or two frames. Both are run, (a) 250 ms and (b) 500 ms. No test is given. Reproduced when the time of the peak of the mean accuracy curve is earlier for OB-p than for mPFC-p under both readings; the times and the 95% intervals of the peak time over repeats are reported.

claims.statement: Late in the trial, mPFC-p pseudo-populations keep low but above-chance identity decoding that exceeds OB-p decoding.
claims.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 5; Figure 2K
claims.quote: mPFC-p pseudo-populations maintained low but above-chance identity decoding that exceeded OB-p decoding later in the trial
claims.criterion: From the same-window accuracies of fig2j-identity-decoding-peaks-earlier (the diagonal of Figure 2K). "Later in the trial" is not bounded; it is read as after odor offset, (a) 2 to 15 s and (b) 5 to 15 s after onset. Reproduced when, under both readings, the mPFC-p mean accuracy over the window exceeds 12.5% and exceeds the OB-p mean, with repeats as samples (one-sample one-sided t-test against 12.5% and two-sided Mann-Whitney U, p < 0.05, the tests the paper uses for decoding elsewhere).

claims.statement: Similar fractions of OB-p and mPFC-p neurons are tuned to odor identity, but OB-p neurons more often show significant effects of concentration and identity by concentration interactions, which are rare in mPFC-p neurons.
claims.source: Results, Odor concentration is robustly encoded in OB-p but not mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 3B and 3C
claims.quote: Across time, similar fractions of OB-p and mPFC-p neurons were significantly tuned to odor identity ( Figure 3B ) ... By contrast, OB-p neurons were more likely to show significant main effects of concentration, as well as identity × concentration interactions
claims.criterion: Concentration dataset. Per neuron, a two-way ANOVA (identity, 3 odors, by concentration, 3 levels, with interaction) on mean normalized fluorescence in the first 5 s of odor presentation over trials (Figure 3B legend), p < 0.05 per term; the fraction of neurons significant per term per group. The time-resolved version (Figure 3C) uses sliding windows of unstated width, read as (a) 500 ms and (b) 1 s steps of the same width. The paper gives no test of the fractions. Reproduced when, in the 0 to 5 s analysis, the OB-p fractions for concentration and for interaction both exceed the mPFC-p fractions, and the OB-p minus mPFC-p difference for identity is smaller in absolute size than that for concentration; the time courses are reported.

claims.statement: OB-p pseudo-populations decode odor concentration more accurately and earlier than mPFC-p and untagged pseudo-populations, while mPFC-p decoding stays close to chance.
claims.source: Results, Odor concentration is robustly encoded in OB-p but not mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 3D and 3E
claims.quote: OB-p pseudo-populations reached higher concentration classification accuracy and did so earlier in the trial than both mPFC-p and untagged pseudo-populations, whereas mPFC-p ensembles supported only weak concentration decoding that remained close to chance
claims.criterion: Per odor, a linear SVM decoding the 3 concentrations from mean normalized fluorescence in sliding windows (250 ms in the Figure 3D legend, 500 ms in Figure 3E and the Methods; both run), 75-cell pseudo-populations, 100 repeats, accuracies averaged over the 3 odors; chance 33.3%. No test is given. Reproduced when the peak mean accuracy of OB-p exceeds those of mPFC-p and untagged, the OB-p peak time is earlier than both, and the mPFC-p peak mean accuracy is below the midpoint between chance and the OB-p peak, under both window readings. The midpoint is a reading of "close to chance", recorded as such; the paper gives no bound.

claims.statement: Pairwise concentration decoding (low against medium, medium against high, low against high) is strongest and most sustained in OB-p ensembles, intermediate in untagged neurons and weakest in mPFC-p neurons.
claims.source: Results, Odor concentration is robustly encoded in OB-p but not mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 3; Figure S5G
claims.quote: concentration decoding was again strongest and most sustained in OB-p ensembles, intermediate in untagged neurons, and weakest in mPFC-p neurons
claims.criterion: As fig3de-concentration-decoding, with binary SVMs for each pair of concentrations per odor (chance 50%), averaged over odors, same-window accuracies. Read as the mean same-window accuracy over 0 to 15 s after onset per group. Reproduced when the order OB-p > untagged > mPFC-p holds for all three pairs under both window readings.

claims.statement: Across the three concentrations, response sparseness and the fraction of active cells change only modestly in all three populations.
claims.source: Results, Odor concentration is robustly encoded in OB-p but not mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 2; Figure S5A to S5D
claims.quote: overall response sparseness and the fraction of active cells changed only modestly in all three populations ( Figure S5 )
claims.criterion: Per concentration (0.1%, 1%, 10% in the Figure S5 legend), the percentage of active cells (binarized, 0 to 5 s) and lifetime sparseness per neuron over the 3 odors, population sparseness per subject (Figure S5D). The paper gives no test and no bound for "modestly"; the values per population and concentration are reported and the claim is judged only on whether no population shows a monotonic change of more than half its value at 0.1% across the range, a reading of "only modestly" recorded as such.

claims.statement: Go/NoGo performance improves across training days, with no difference between OB- p and mPFC-p labelled mice, reaching 73.7% correct trials on day 3.
claims.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4C
claims.quote: Behavioral performance improved as training progressed, with no significant difference between OB-p and mPFC-p labelled mice ... with, on average, 73.7% correct trials (hit and correct rejection) on day 3
claims.criterion: Per mouse and task day (1 to 3), percent correct = (hits + correct rejections) / scored CS trials, with hits as relabeled in the Methods (reward within 10 s after the delay), excluding bad trials. A one-way repeated-measures ANOVA on days, and a mixed ANOVA (days within, projection between). Reproduced when F and the day 3 mean are within tolerance, the day effect has p < 0.05 in both ANOVAs and projection and interaction have p >= 0.05. The Methods give the 10 s relabeling for neural analyses, so whether it applies to behavioral accuracy is open; readings are (a) hits as scored (lick in the reward window) and (b) hits as relabeled. Whether the NWB outcome labels already apply the relabeling is the author's to check. Reproduced when the conditions hold under one reading; both are reported.

claims.statement: Anticipatory licking in response to the rewarded odorants increases across training.
claims.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4C right and Figure S6
claims.quote: an increase in anticipatory licking in response to the rewarded odorants
claims.criterion: Lick rate on CS+ trials before the reward window opens. "Anticipatory" is read as (a) the delay, 2 to 5 s after odor onset, and (b) odor and delay, 0 to 5 s. The paper gives no test. Reproduced when the mean over mice of the CS+ lick rate is higher on day 3 than on day 1 under both readings; per-mouse values are reported.

claims.statement: In expert mice (day 3), OB-p pseudo-populations decode odor identity above chance in all four task phases, peaking early (delay) and declining later, whereas mPFC-p pseudo-populations are near chance early and improve later in the trial.
claims.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 4D, 4E and 4F
claims.quote: odor identity decoding in OB-p pseudo-populations was greater than chance across all 4 task phases ... Decoding accuracy peaked during early trial phases (delay phase after odor exposure), but declined later in the trial (action) ... In contrast, mPFC-p pseudo-populations performed near chance during early trial phases, but decoding accuracy increased later in the trial
claims.criterion: Day 3, 4 odors (chance 25%), linear SVM per task phase (trained and tested on the same phase), 85-cell pseudo-populations from 4 OB-p and 3 mPFC-p mice, 100 repeats; aggregate readings (a) mean and (b) maximum over the phase. One-sample one-sided t-tests against 25% over the 100 accuracies, Bonferroni over 4 phases.
