Reproduced when, under one aggregate reading, OB-p is above chance in all 4 phases with its highest mean accuracy in the delay phase and lower in act-late than in delay, and mPFC-p has its two lowest mean accuracies in odor and delay and its highest in act-early or act-late. The Figure 4F legend's OB-p against mPFC-p differences in every phase are reported with two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (the paper's test for such comparisons in Figure 4H).

claims.statement: Generalized odor valence can be decoded above chance from a general PCx (any-p) pseudo-population in all task phases in expert mice.
claims.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 4; Figure 4G and Figure S8H
claims.quote: We found that odor valence could be decoded with high accuracy from a general PCx pseudo-population across all phases
claims.criterion: Day 3. Generalized valence (Methods) trains on one CS+/CS- pair and tests on the other, all 4 permutations, accuracy averaged over them; any-p pseudo-populations of 85 cells sampled from tagged and untagged cells of all 7 mice, 100 repeats, per task phase; aggregate readings (a) mean and (b) maximum. One-sample one-sided t-tests against 50%, Bonferroni over 4 phases. Reproduced when all 4 phases have corrected p < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: In expert mice OB-p pseudo-populations encode generalized valence in the odor and delay phases but fall to chance in the action phases, while mPFC-p pseudo-populations encode valence in the later but not the earliest phase; the two differ in all four phases.
claims.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 5; Figure 4H
claims.quote: OB-p pseudo-populations accurately encoded odor valence during early phases of the trial (odor exposure, delay), but that decoding accuracy decreased to chance level later in the trial (action) ... In contrast, mPFC-p pseudo-populations encoded odor valence during later but not early phases of the trial
claims.criterion: As fig4g-valence-any with OB-p and mPFC-p pseudo-populations. Reproduced when, under one aggregate reading, OB-p is above 50% (corrected p < 0.05) in odor and delay and not in act-late; mPFC-p is not above 50% in odor and is above in delay, act-early and act- late; and the two-sided Mann-Whitney U test of OB-p against mPFC-p accuracies has corrected p < 0.05 in all four phases. Partially reproduced when the pattern of above-chance phases holds and the between-group tests hold in two or three phases. The text's act-early OB-p result (p = 0.00141, above chance) is reported alongside.

claims.statement: Restricted to correct trials, OB-p pseudo-populations encode valence well early and much less later, mPFC-p pseudo-populations encode it more accurately late than early, and the two differ in all four phases.
claims.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraphs 6 and 7; Figure 4I and 4J
claims.quote: OB-p pseudo-populations accurately encoded odor valence during early phases of the trial but much less so later ... mPFC-p pseudo-populations encoded odor valence late in correct trials more accurately than early ... For all four task phases, these projection pseudo-populations performed differently from one another at decoding valence for correct trials
claims.criterion: Day 3, correct trials only (hits and correct rejections). Which valence scheme Figure 4I and 4J use is open, since the legend says generalized valence in correct trials is in Figure S8E and S8G; the reading is valence (unconstrained) for correct trials (Methods, the fifth classifier), with the generalized scheme as the subject of figs8-generalized-valence-correct. 85 cells, 100 repeats, aggregate readings (a) mean and (b) maximum. Reproduced when, under one reading, OB-p mean accuracy is higher in odor and delay than in act-early and act-late, mPFC-p is higher in act-early and act-late than in odor and delay with odor not above 50% (corrected p >= 0.05), and OB-p against mPFC-p differs (two-sided Mann-Whitney U, Bonferroni, p < 0.05) in all four phases.

claims.statement: Generalized valence decoding in correct trials differs between OB-p and mPFC-p pseudo-populations in the odor and act-early phases but not in the delay and act-late phases.
claims.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 7; Figure S8E, S8G and S8K
claims.quote: We also observed significant differences with generalized valence decoding performance in correct trials between projection pseudo-populations during odor and act-early phases
claims.criterion: Day 3, correct trials, generalized valence (4 permutations), 85 cells, 100 repeats, aggregate readings (a) mean and (b) maximum. Reproduced when, under one reading, the two-sided Mann-Whitney U test of OB-p against mPFC-p has corrected p < 0.05 in odor and act-early and corrected p >= 0.05 in delay and act-late; the direction in each phase is reported.

claims.statement: Longitudinal tracking across the three Go/NoGo sessions follows 46 OB-p and 41 mPFC-p neurons in 4 OB-p and 3 mPFC-p tagged mice.
claims.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 1; Methods, Longitudinal tracking
claims.quote: we longitudinally tracked identified neurons across three Go/NoGo sessions and followed 46 OB-p and 41 mPFC-p neurons in 4 OB-p–tagged and 3 mPFC-p–tagged mice
claims.criterion: Cells with one tracking identifier present in all four sessions (day 0 to 3) and red in at least 3 of them (code criterion min_3_sessions), counted per projection. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance; the counts under the code's other criteria (min_1_session, first_4_sessions, all_sessions) are reported.

claims.statement: Tracked OB-p and mPFC-p neurons do not differ in the average slope of their session-averaged normalized fluorescence across the three Go/NoGo days.
claims.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 2; Figure S10D
claims.quote: there was no significant difference in the average slope between OB-p and mPFC-p neurons
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test. For each tracked neuron and each combination of odor valence (CS+, CS-) and task phase (4), the mean normalized fluorescence over the phase and over that valence's trials on each of days 1 to 3, and the least-squares slope over days; a mixed ANOVA with the combination (8 levels) within neurons and projection between. Reproduced when the projection effect has p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The interaction is reported against p = 0.0031.

claims.statement: Changes in lifetime sparseness across sessions show no clear effect of projection target.
claims.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 2; Figure S10E
claims.quote: We similarly quantified changes in lifetime sparseness across sessions and did not observe a clear effect of projection target
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Per tracked neuron, task phase and day, lifetime sparseness over the 4 odors of binarized activity in that phase; slope over days 1 to 3; a mixed ANOVA with phase within and projection between. Reproduced when the projection effect has p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Tracked OB-p neurons show a higher coefficient of variation of session-averaged fluorescence across days than mPFC-p neurons.
claims.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 5C
claims.quote: OB-p neurons typically showed higher fluorescence CV across days than mPFC-p neurons ( Figure 5C, D ). A mixed ANOVA on CV within combinations of odors and task phases revealed a significant effect of projection target (p = 0.0127)
claims.criterion: Per tracked neuron and combination, the coefficient of variation (SD over mean) of the session-averaged normalized fluorescence over days 1 to 3; a mixed ANOVA with the combination within neurons and projection between. Open details are the combination, read as (a) valence (CS+, CS-, as plotted in Figure 5C) by phase, 8 levels, and (b) odor (4) by phase, 16 levels; and the treatment of means near zero or negative (normalized fluorescence is centred near zero), read as (c) SD over the absolute mean and (d) SD over the mean. Reproduced when, under every combination of readings, the projection effect has p < 0.05 with OB-p higher (by median CV); when readings disagree, methods_underspecified. The per-condition Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction (Figure S10F) are reported.

claims.statement: Identity decoding transfers across sessions comparably in tracked OB-p and mPFC-p ensembles, whereas generalized valence decoding transfers better in mPFC-p ensembles, especially across distal sessions.
claims.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 4; Figure 5E and Figure S11
claims.quote: When decoding odor identity, transferability across dissimilar sessions was comparable between OB-p and mPFC-p ensembles ... whereas mPFC-p ensembles maintained higher valence decoding accuracy, particularly for generalized valence across distal sessions
claims.criterion: Per mouse, a linear SVM on its tracked projection neurons, trained on one (day, phase) and tested on another, for days 1 to 3 and the 4 phases (Figure 5D); same-phase and adjacent-phase pairs only; transfers grouped as within session, proximal (consecutive days) and distal (day 1 and day 3). Open details, which could change the outcome. The samples of the Mann-Whitney test, read as (a) every qualifying accuracy entry of every mouse and (b) per mouse means; the folds for train and test within one session, read as 5- fold stratified cross-validation; aggregate readings mean and maximum. Two-sided Mann- Whitney U tests of OB-p against mPFC-p entries per group, Bonferroni over the 3 groups. Reproduced when, under one reading, identity has corrected p >= 0.05 for proximal and distal, and generalized valence has mPFC-p higher with corrected p < 0.05 for distal.

claims.statement: The temporal structure of valence coding across sessions is more stable in tracked mPFC-p than OB-p ensembles, while odor identity coding is not.
claims.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 5; Figure 5F and Figure S12B
claims.quote: These analyses revealed that the temporal structure of valence coding was consistently more stable in mPFC-p than in OB-p ensembles
claims.criterion: From the per-mouse transfer matrices of fig5e-transferability, each 4 by 4 transfer block (train day, test day) flattened, and Pearson correlations between pairs of blocks (Methods, Decoding with tracked neurons). Open details are which blocks are paired, read as (a) all pairs of the 9 blocks and (b) pairs sharing the training day; and the samples, read as (c) every correlation of every mouse and (d) per mouse means. Two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests of OB-p against mPFC-p correlations, Bonferroni over the 4 schemes. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, valence, generalized valence and correct-trial valence each have mPFC-p higher with corrected p < 0.05 and odor identity has corrected p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: The differences in timing of identity and valence encoding between OB-p and mPFC- p ensembles increase over the course of learning.
claims.source: Discussion, Functional specializations of projection neurons align with those of their target areas, paragraph 1; Figure S7A and Figure S9
claims.quote: Notably, these differences increased over the course of learning
claims.criterion: As in the Figure S7A and S9 legends. Per projection and task phase, accuracies of 50 size-matched pseudo-populations per day are sampled and the slope of accuracy over days 1 to 3 is fitted, 1000 times; a null from day-shuffled data; two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction of observed against null slopes, for identity and generalized valence. The paper gives no test of the difference itself; the claim is read as reproduced when the slopes are significantly positive (corrected p < 0.05, above the null) for OB-p in the odor or delay phase and for mPFC-p in an action phase, for identity or generalized valence. Aggregate readings mean and maximum.

claims.statement: A single 600-ns unipolar pulse at 15 kV/cm caused by far the strongest YP uptake in single CHO cells (126 +/- 14 a.u. at the end of recording, n = 25), while bipolar signals starting with the same pulse caused significantly weaker uptake (4-phase 20.8 +/- 2.0, 8-phase 6.9 +/- 1.6, 8-phase with 5-us delays 25.4 +/- 2.8 a.u.; p < 0.001); sham caused no gain.
claims.source: Results, 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: Sham-exposed cells showed no gain in YP fluorescence during the 10 min of observation ... A single 600-ns pulse at 15 kV/cm caused by far the strongest YP uptake, reaching 126±14 a.u. (n=25) by the end of recording. Bipolar signals started with exactly the same pulse (600 ns, 15 kV/cm) but caused significantly weaker effects (p<0.001). By the end of recording, YP signal reached only 20.8±2.0 a.u. for the 4-phasic signal; 6.9±1.6 a.u. for the 8-phasic signal; and 25.4±2.8 a.u. for the 8-phasic signal with 5-μs delays between phases
claims.criterion: Per cell, F-F0 at the last image (600 s), F the mean intensity in a ROI drawn around the cell and F0 the mean of the six images before the pulse; F-F0 is what Methods 2.2 calls the background-corrected emission, and no other subtraction is named. Tolerances are the paper's s.e. Reproduced when the four group means are within tolerance and each bipolar group is below the unipolar group by a two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.001; partially reproduced when the order and the tests hold but some means fall outside tolerance. The sham group is reported and not judged, as the paper gives no value or test for it. Whether the t-test is the test used for single cells is open (Methods 2.2 names none); a Welch t-test is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The 8-phase bipolar signal caused about 20-fold weaker electroporation than the single unipolar pulse, and was the most efficient at cancellation; the 4-phase and delayed 8-phase signals cancelled 4 to 5 fold.
claims.source: Results, 3.1, paragraph 1; Results, 3.4, paragraph 1; Figure 4 legend
claims.quote: Note that applying the 8-phasic bipolar signal with no inter-phase delays caused about 20-fold weaker electroporation than a single unipolar pulse
claims.criterion: Ratios of group mean F-F0 at 600 s, as in fig4-bipolar-cancellation. Reproduced when the 8-phase ratio is within 18 to 22 and is the largest of the three, and the other two ratios are within 3.6 to 5.5. The paper's own end values give 18.3, 6.1 and 5.0, so the 4-phase ratio of Section 3.4 does not match its Section 3.1 numbers; the ratio from the paper's means is reported beside the range.

claims.statement: Packet 2 applied 40 times from e1 caused much weaker electroporation throughout the large array than 40 unipolar trains from e1, and enhanced electroporation in the center, but electroporation near e1 stayed stronger than in the center.
claims.source: Results, 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 5A
claims.quote: The lack of cancellation caused a much stronger electroporation throughout the array ... In contrast, Packet 2 enhanced electroporation in the center of the array, despite gradual weakening of the electric field with distance from e1. However, the bipolar cancellation only partially offset the electric field weakening, and electroporation near e1 remained stronger than in the center
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header, along the e1-e3 diagonal (Fig. 5A legend), first pulse 6.4 kV, n = 4 to 5 dishes. Reproduced when (i) the train profile exceeds the packet profile at the e1 end, the center and the e3 end by two-sided Student's t-tests at p < 0.05; (ii) "enhanced electroporation in the center" holds under either reading the text allows, (a) the packet profile has a central local maximum, the center above the minimum between center and e1 by a t-test at p < 0.05, or (b) the center over the e1-end value is higher for the packet than for the train, by a t-test on per-dish ratios at p < 0.05; and (iii) the packet value at the e1 end exceeds the packet center value. Partially reproduced when two of the three hold.

claims.statement: Rotating the first-energized electrode with Packet 2 (1Px40) emphasized the remote effect in the center of the array, while the same rotation with the pulse train (1Tx40) left a void of electroporation in the center.
claims.source: Results, 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 5B and 5C
claims.quote: Rotation with Packet 2 “smeared” the electroporation effect at the perimeter and emphasized the remote effect in the center. This remote effect contrasted with a void of electroporation in the center when the pulse train was applied in the same manner instead of the packet
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header, both diagonals averaged (Fig. 5B legend), normalized as in Fig. 5C, n = 4 to 5 dishes. Reproduced when the normalized center of 1Px40 exceeds that of 1Tx40 by a two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05, the 1Px40 center exceeds the minimum of its profile between center and electrodes, and the 1Tx40 profile has its minimum at the center (the paper gives no other definition of the void).

claims.statement: Increasing the total number of rotated Packet 2 packets from 4 (1Px4) to 20 (5Px4) and 40 (10Px4) profoundly enhanced YP uptake throughout the electrode array.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6A
claims.quote: Increasing the total number of applied packets from 4 to 20 and 40 profoundly enhanced the electroporative YP dye uptake throughout the electrode array
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header, in a.u., n = 3 to 4 dishes per treatment (Fig. 6 legend). "Throughout" is read at the periphery, the center and the minimum between them. Reproduced when at all three places the mean is ordered 4 < 20 < 40 packets and 40 exceeds 4 by a two-sided Student's t-test on per-dish values at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when the order holds at all three places and the test at one or two.

claims.statement: The central peak was almost twofold brighter than the periphery for 1Px4, and about the same as the periphery for 5Px4 and 10Px4.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6B
claims.quote: Its brightness was almost twofold higher than at the periphery for a single packet was applied 4 times from different directions, or about the same as at the periphery for the rotation of 5 and 10 packets
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header, normalized as in Fig. 6B. Tolerances are 10% of the value, as the paper gives no spread; "almost twofold" is read as 200%, so a value from 180% to 200% fits the words best and is reported as such. Reproduced when all three values are within tolerance under one combination of the header's readings; partially reproduced when 1Px4 is within tolerance and above both other treatments.

claims.statement: For all packet numbers the central peak was clearly discernible, and the least affected area of the monolayer, between the center and the electrodes, showed about 2-fold lower intensity than the center.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6A and 6B
claims.quote: The peak of electroporation in the center was clearly discernable for all tested treatments ... Interestingly, the least affected area of the cell monolayer (between the center and the electrodes) showed about 2-fold lower fluorescence intensity than in the center for all the treatments
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header. The least affected area is the minimum of the mean profile between the center and the most peripheral ROI, on each side; readings (t1) the mean of the two sides and (t2) each side. Reproduced when the ratio is within 1.8 to 2.2 for all three treatments; partially reproduced when it is within tolerance for one or two and above 1 for all.

claims.statement: The central peak appeared narrower (sharper) with increasing number of packets.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6
claims.quote: Also, the central peak appeared narrower (sharper) with increasing the number of packets
claims.criterion: The paper defines no width measure (the Discussion names width, or sharpness, of the remote peak as a parameter without a definition). Readings (w1) full width of the central peak at half of its height above the least affected area (the minima of fig6-trough-half-of-center); (w2) the distance between the two minima on either side of the center. Each on the mean normalized profile, with LOESS variants as in the header. Reproduced when, under a reading, width decreases from 4 to 20 to 40 packets; partially reproduced when 40 is narrower than 4 but 20 is out of order.

claims.statement: With 1Px4 in the small array, raising the first-pulse amplitude from 2.4 to 5.6 kV raised YP fluorescence 15.5 times at the most peripheral point, 16.2 times half-way to the center and 16.8 times in the center.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 7A
claims.quote: when the first pulse amplitude was increased from 2.4 to 5.6 kV ... YP fluorescence increased 15.5 times at the most peripheral point; 16.2 times half-way to the center; and 16.8 times in the center
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header, ratios of mean a.u. profiles, n = 3 dishes. Half-way is the ROI nearest half the distance from the center to the most peripheral ROI. Reproduced when all three ratios are within tolerance; partially reproduced when one or two are.

claims.statement: Normalized to the most peripheral ROI, the profiles for different nsEP amplitudes fully overlapped, in the small array with 1Px4 and in the large array with 10Px4, so NG-CANCAN targeting did not depend on amplitude within the range studied.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 7B and 7D
claims.quote: When the YP emission was normalized to the most peripheral ROI, the data for different nsEP amplitudes fully overlapped ... The findings held true for rotating multiple packets and when using the larger array ( Fig. 7C and D ). Overall, our results show that NG-CANCAN targeting of electroporation does not depend on nsEP amplitude
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 (Methods 2.4), on per-dish normalized values (n = 3), at the center and half-way places of fig7ab-amplitude-scales-uptake. Reproduced when no pair of amplitudes differs at either place, in each array; not reproduced when any pair does, with the arrays reported apart. The largest difference in percentage points is reported either way, and the paper's error-bar rule (a gap longer than the error bars, Methods 2.4) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Remote targeting, at least within the limits studied, did not depend on array size; the authors infer that findings from small arrays can be extrapolated to larger inter-electrode distances.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 4; Figure 7
claims.quote: The electric field distribution and strength achieved within each array at a given pulse voltage were obviously different, but the remote targeting, at least within studied limits, did not depend on either the electric pulse amplitude or array size ( Fig. 7 )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 (Methods 2.4), on per-dish normalized center values (n = 3 per group, Fig. 7 legend), small array (Fig. 7B) against large array (Fig. 7D), at each first-pulse voltage the two share and pooled over voltages. Reproduced when the test finds no difference, not reproduced when it does; the difference in percentage points is given either way. The paper names no comparison measure, and Fig. 7 compares arrays under different protocols (1Px4 small, 10Px4 large), which Fig. 6 shows changes the normalized center; this confound is reported with the result. Comparing whole normalized profiles on a distance scaled to each array's measured half-diagonal is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: At 4 kV and one rotation, Packets 1, 2 and 3 produced the same YP uptake in the center (215 to 235 a.u.), but Packets 1 and 3 caused much more uptake near the electrodes (250 to 350 a.u.) than Packet 2 (about 120 a.u., p < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8A
claims.quote: All packets produced the same YP uptake in the center (215–235 a.u.), but Packets 1 and 3 caused drastically more YP uptake near the electrodes (250–350 a.u. vs ~120 a.u. for packet 1, p<0.01, Fig. 8A )
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header, a.u., near the electrodes being the most peripheral ROI. The sentence says "~120 a.u. for packet 1", which contradicts its own clause; it is read as Packet 2, as Fig. 8B and the Discussion imply. Reproduced when the centers fall in 193.5 to 258.5 a.u., Packets 1 and 3 near the electrodes in 225 to 385 a.u., Packet 2 in 108 to 132 a.u., and Packets 1 and 3 each exceed Packet 2 near the electrodes by a two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.01; partially reproduced when the order and tests hold but values fall outside the ranges.

claims.statement: Normalized YP emission in the center was 183% for Packet 2, against 83% for Packet 3 and 74% for Packet 1.
claims.source: Results, 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8B
claims.quote: The superiority of Packet 2 for CANCAN targeting is highlighted by the drop of normalized YP emission in the center from 183% for Packet 2 to 83% and 74% for Packets 3 and 1, respectively
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header, normalized as in Fig. 8B. Reproduced when all three are within tolerance under one combination of readings; partially reproduced when Packet 2 is highest and above 100% but some values fall outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The bipolar signal with the strongest cancellation between two electrodes (8-phase, Fig. 4) gave the most efficient remote targeting in the quadrupole (Packet 2, Fig. 8).
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 3; Figures 4 and 8
claims.quote: Three packets for CANCAN targeting were designed to produce three types of bipolar signals near electrodes and we showed that, indeed, the strongest bipolar cancellation has led to the most efficient remote targeting ( Figs. 4 and 8 )
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the signal with the largest unipolar-over-bipolar ratio in Fig. 4 (8-phase) matches the packet with the highest normalized center in Fig. 8 (Packet 2).

claims.statement: With the large array lifted 1, 2 and 3 mm above the monolayer, YP emission near the electrodes fell 2.4, 6.4 and 9 times, and in the center only 1.02, 1.4 and 3.8 times, relative to electrodes touching the monolayer.
claims.source: Results, 3.5, paragraph 1; Figure 9A
claims.quote: Specifically, YP emission near the electrodes decreased 2.4, 6.4, and 9 times with 1-, 2- and 3-mm gaps (as compared to electrodes being in the same plane with cells); in the center, it decreased just 1.02, 1.4, and 3.8 times, respectively
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header, a.u., 10Px4 with Packet 2 at 6.4 kV, n = 3 to 4 dishes; near the electrodes is the most peripheral ROI (Fig. 9B legend, "measurements most distant from the center"). Reproduced when all six ratios are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at each gap the near-electrode ratio exceeds the center ratio but some values fall outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The faster fading near the electrodes raised targeting efficiency (center over periphery) to as much as 600% with a 2-mm gap, and electroporation was restricted almost entirely to the center with the electrodes above the monolayer.
claims.source: Results, 3.5, paragraph 1; Figure 9B and 9C
claims.quote: Such disproportionally faster fading of the effect near electrodes boosted the CANCAN targeting efficiency (measured as a ratio of the effect in the center and at the periphery) to as much as 600% for the 2-mm gap ( Fig. 9B )
claims.criterion: Profile method of the header, normalized as in Fig. 9B. Reproduced when the 2-mm value is within 540 to 660% and is the largest of the four gaps (0 to 3 mm, "as much as"); partially reproduced when it is within tolerance but another gap is higher. The second part of the statement rests on the sample images of Fig. 9C and is not judged on its own.

claims.statement: In the Sim4Life simulation, 1 kV on one electrode gives about 1.8 kV/cm (small array) and 0.8 kV/cm (large array) in the center and about 4-fold more near the energized electrode (7 and 3.5 kV/cm), while energizing a diagonal gives no field in the center.
claims.source: Methods, 2.3, paragraph 3; Figure 3
claims.quote: applying 1 kV to one electrode produced the electric field of approximately 1.8 kV/cm and 0.8 kV/cm in center of the small and large arrays ... The electric field strength was about 4-fold higher near the energized electrode (7 kV/cm and 3.5 kV/cm per 1 kV applied, for the small and large arrays, respectively) Note that energizing either electrode diagonal produced no electric field in the center of the array
claims.criterion: A simulation, not recorded data. It needs the Sim4Life model of the arrays (needle diameter 1.5 mm, large-array diagonal 8.4 mm; the small array's geometry, the medium conductivity and the solution depth are not given here and are said to follow reference 15, Pakhomov et al. 2021, doi:10.1016/j.bioelechem.2021.107876). The paper deposits no model, so the claim is tested only if such a model is supplied; how far from the electrode "near" is measured is open. Reproduced when the four values are within tolerance and the center field with a diagonal energized is below 1% of the single-electrode center field.

claims.statement: In MNAV the produced vectors match the actual vectors in direction and magnitude; performance is quantified by the slope of the regression of v_p on v_a.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 4 (The monkeys learned to perform MNAV); Figure 1b,c
claims.quote: The produced vectors ( v p ) quantified in terms of temporal distance (magnitude) and direction (sign) closely matched the actual vectors separating the start and target landmarks
claims.criterion: Per recorded session and monkey, ordinary least squares regression of signed v_p on signed v_a over all MNAV trials with no exclusion (Methods, Bayesian model of behaviour, last paragraph, says Fig. 1b,c slopes include all trials); the code (mnav_ec_fig1.m, get_tatp, lines 242 to 266) drops only trials without a recorded production (0.01 < |tp| and tp < 99 s), followed, and fits both all trials (black line) and validtrials_mm trials only (red line); the valid-only fit is a variant. "Closely matched" is judged against the paper's own performance criterion, a regression slope of 0.8 (Methods, Performance criterion). Reproduced when, in each monkey, the median session slope is at least 0.8 and every slope is positive; partially reproduced when that holds in one monkey only. Fig. 1c pools behavioural sessions with at least 400 successful MNAV trials (code cp.mintrial_in_session), most of them training sessions; the recorded sessions are a subset, and the result is reported for the sessions the dataset holds, with that subset named as a deviation.

claims.statement: After training on 15 start and target pairs, the monkeys performed the 15 held-out pairs with high performance from the first generalization session.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 1d,e
claims.quote: we found that they were able to readily generalize with high performance from the very first session
claims.criterion: Per monkey, the regression slope of v_p on v_a (all trials) on the held-out pairs in the first generalization session (monkey A sequence 1, monkey M sequence 2, code mnav_ec_fig1.m lines 24 to 25). Reproduced when that slope is at least 0.8, the training criterion of the Methods. The generalization sessions preceded the recordings (Methods, Electrophysiology, paragraph 1), so the test needs behavioural sessions the paper describes but may not have deposited; whether the dataset holds them is the author's to find.

claims.statement: A substantial fraction of EC neurons have significantly periodic activity during mental navigation, 37% (231/614) in monkey A and 36% (311/864) in monkey M, and the proportion per session ranged from 0% to 45% depending on recording site.
claims.source: Results, Neural signatures, paragraph 2; Figure 2c,d
claims.quote: Across sessions, the proportion of neurons with a significant PI ranged from 0% to 45% depending on the recording site in the posterior EC, with an overall average of 37% (231/614) and 36% (311/864) in monkeys A and M, respectively
claims.criterion: PI and classification as in the opening comment. A neuron counts as periodic when it is periodic in either direction (code count_ramp_periodicity_leftright, line 4550); the denominator is all units of the monkey (614 and 864). Each combination of the open readings (classification rule a or b, surrogate durations, Methods or code lag range) is run. Reproduced when, under the readings, both counts are within tolerance and every session's proportion lies in 0 to 49.5% (the reported range widened by 10% of its upper bound); partially reproduced when one of these three conditions fails and the others hold. The 0.37 printed for A is 231/614 = 0.376; the counts are the expected values.

claims.statement: Across neurons with significant PI, the lag of the peak PI was at or near 0.65 s, the temporal distance between landmarks.
claims.source: Results, Neural signatures, paragraph 2; Figure 2d; Extended Data Fig. 2a
claims.quote: across neurons with significant PI, the peak lag was at or near 0.65 s, which matches the temporal distance between consecutive landmarks
claims.criterion: Periodic neurons and periodicity as in fig2-periodic-proportion, per monkey and direction (Extended Data Fig. 2a shows the two directions). "Near" is read with the 100 ms window centred on 0.65 s that the paper uses for periodicity at 0.65 s (Results, paragraph 4, on Extended Data Fig. 2c), hence the tolerance of 0.05 s. Reproduced when the median periodicity is within 0.60 to 0.70 s in every monkey and direction; partially reproduced when in some. The mode, in 50 ms bins (a plotting choice), is reported as well.

claims.statement: Eye position (horizontal and vertical) and joystick position during the navigation epoch show no periodicity; their PI at 650 ms is below chance.
claims.source: Results, Neural signatures, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 3a-c
claims.quote: Complementary analyses revealed no such periodicity in the monkeys' eye and hand (joystick) movements
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The signals are treated as the firing rates are for the PI (opening comment), per trial between joystick onset and 500 ms before offset; the code for this figure is not in the repository (mnav_ec_fig2.m line 450 says it is to be copied in), so the bootstrap is open. Readings: (a) 100 resamples of the pooled trials with replacement, full size; (b) 100 subsamples of one third of the trials without replacement, as in the code's peak-phase bootstrap. Open, what "chance" is, two readings from the legend: (a) the threshold of two SD above the GP surrogate PI at 650 ms; (b) the mean GP surrogate PI at 650 ms. Open, any smoothing of the eye and joystick signals (the paper gives none); the PI rate smoothing is used. The paper's test is the one-tailed t-test (df 99) of the 100 bootstrap PIs at 650 ms against chance, with the alternative that PI is below chance. Reproduced when, for each of the three signals, that test finds PI below chance at p < 0.0001 (the legend's P << 0.0001); not reproduced when, for any signal, PI at 650 ms is significantly above chance by the same test with the opposite tail at p < 0.05; partially reproduced otherwise. The three mean PIs are compared with the expected values and reported either way.

claims.statement: In periodic neurons the PI at 0.65 s is significantly stronger during the mental navigation epoch than during the inter-trial interval, in both monkeys and both directions.
claims.source: Results, Neural signatures, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 2b
claims.quote: The PI was significantly stronger during the mental navigation epoch (Extended Data Fig. 2b ), which suggests that the periodic activity was specific to mental navigation
claims.criterion: Code get_overall_PI (mnav_ec_fig2.m lines 4267 to 4473): per direction, periodic neurons whose navigation PI at the 650 ms lag exceeds the threshold; for each, the PI at 650 ms minus its mean PI from the first lag at which PI is positive, in navigation and in the ITI. ITI segments longer than 4 s (Methods, NTS, main reading; the code's cp.spontdur_iti_thres of 4.3 s is a variant), processed as the navigation epoch, each cut to the median navigation tp (code lines 3708 to 3713). Open, where in the ITI the segment starts (the code's alignment of its ITI tensor is not shown); readings, from the start of the ITI or ending at the next trial's start. The legend's direction labels (right and left) are matched to the code's direction 1 (ta > 0, which the code labels JS left) and 2 by both readings of the label. Reproduced when the one-tailed paired t-test gives p < 0.0001 with navigation higher in all four monkey and direction groups; partially reproduced when in two or three. Neuron counts are compared with the degrees of freedom.

claims.statement: Neurons significantly periodic at 0.65 s had a lower PI on error trials than on correct trials, suggesting weaker periodicity contributed to larger errors.
claims.source: Results, Neural signatures, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 2c
claims.quote: Neurons that were significantly periodic within a 100-ms window centred at 0.65 s had a lower PI during error trials (Extended Data Fig. 2c ), suggesting that weaker periodicity contributed to committing larger errors
claims.criterion: PI at 650 ms as in ed2b-pi-navigation-above-iti. Error trials, Methods (MNAV): trials with more than one attempt, the first attempt analysed; the code uses succ == 0 of any attempt with |tp| > 1.8 s (line 3691), a variant. Distance at least 3 landmarks in both. Neurons, open between the Results' words (periodicity within 0.60 to 0.70 s) and the code (PI at the 650 ms lag above threshold, lines 4414 to 4417); both are run. Reproduced when, under the readings, correct-trial PI exceeds error-trial PI by a one-tailed paired t-test at p < 0.0001 in all four monkey and direction groups; partially reproduced in two or three.

claims.statement: The first local peak of activity before joystick offset is centred close to -0.65 s and differs from a null distribution built by random phase shifts of the same spikes.
claims.source: Results, Neural signatures, paragraph 3; Figure 2e
claims.quote: The first peak preceding the joystick offset was centred close to -0.65 s and differed significantly from a null distribution generated by applying random phase shifts to the same spiking data (KS test, P << 0.0001)
claims.criterion: Methods, Quantification of the phase of local bumps, and code lines 4600 to 4939. Trials, from the code: one direction, distance 4 or 5, the code's valid trials (first-attempt trials not flagged as lapses; Methods, Bayesian model, describe the lapse mixture), trials with low rate in -1.5 to -0.5 s dropped, at least 25 trials. Per neuron, the trial-averaged rate of a random subsample of one third of the trials (code), the highest local maximum in the one-second window before joystick offset (Methods, main reading; the code's -1 to -0.1 s, lines 4735 to 4752, is a variant; peaks by findpeaks with prominence 0.05 on the min-max normalised window); 100 subsamples (Fig. 2e legend and Methods; the code uses 1,000, a variant). Null, each trial circularly shifted by a random length. Per neuron the two-sample KS test of bootstrap against null, and the mode of the bootstrap phases. Across periodic neurons whose KS test gives p < 0.001 (Methods), the median of the modes. Open, what the KS P << 0.0001 of Fig. 2e and the Results tests, two readings: (a) per neuron, reported as the number of neurons tested with p < 0.0001; (b) the pooled bootstrap first-peak phases of all tested neurons against the pooled null. Reproduced when that median is within -0.70 to -0.60 s per monkey (the 100 ms window of ed2c, the paper's own for "at 0.65 s") and the KS test gives p < 0.0001 under reading (b), or for more than half of the tested neurons under reading (a); partially reproduced when one monkey meets it. The code's Fig. 2f uses direction 1 for M and 2 for A; both directions are run for both monkeys and that choice shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The second and third local peaks before joystick offset are centred near multiples of 0.65 s.
claims.source: Results, Neural signatures, paragraph 3; Figure 2e,f; Extended Data Fig. 4a,b
claims.quote: We extended this analysis to earlier times in the navigation epoch and found that these were centred near multiples of 0.65 s
claims.criterion: As fig2e-first-peak-near-065. The second peak is the highest local maximum in the 1 s window before the first, the third in the 1 s window before the second (Methods and Fig. 2e legend). Reproduced when the medians of the second and third peak modes lie within 0.05 s of -1.30 and -1.95 s per monkey; partially reproduced when the second peak meets it and the third does not, or in one monkey only.

claims.statement: For trials of the same desired distance, the periodicity of EC neurons is significantly longer (lower frequency) on overshoot trials (top tertile of produced vector) than on undershoot trials (bottom tertile).
claims.source: Results, Neural signatures, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 4c,d
claims.quote: We found a small but significant increase in the periodicity (that is, lower frequency) for the top tertile compared to the bottom tertile
claims.criterion: Extended Data Fig. 4d legend and code lines 2180 to 2508 and 496 to 604. Periodic neurons; correct (first-attempt) MNAV trials of distance 3, per direction; trials sorted by timing error (code |tp| - |ta|), bottom and top tertiles; each neuron's periodicity computed on each tertile as in the opening comment (the code's variant uses the window 0.1 s to tp - 0.4 s and lags 100 to 1,090 ms); neurons with fewer than 15 trials in a tertile dropped; neurons with periodicity 0 or above 1 s dropped (code). Rank-sum test of overshoot against undershoot periodicities across neurons. Reproduced when, in both monkeys, overshoot periodicity is larger with rank-sum p < 0.05; partially reproduced in one monkey. A printed Z of -3.3 gives p near 0.001, not below 0.0001, so the paper's bound is not used as the threshold; the paper's p bound is recorded as printed. The code assigns the left-direction list where the right is tested (lines 2259 to 2264), a bug not followed.

claims.statement: Single EC neurons encode temporal distance in their firing rate before joystick onset, before joystick offset, or, in a small number, at both.
claims.source: Results, Ramping, paragraph 1; Figure 3b
claims.quote: Some neurons encoded distance at joystick onset, others at joystick offset, and a small number of neurons had a representation of distance at both onset and offset
claims.criterion: Cross-validated R2 (Methods, Cross-validated R2; code mnav_ec_fig3.m lines 1353 to 1508): correct MNAV trials, mean rate in the window, trials split at random into halves, a linear fit of rate on ordinal distance 1 to 5 on the training half scored on the held-out half, 50 splits averaged (code), each distance subsampled to the smallest count (code). Positive coding is mean R2 > 0 (code rsqthres = 0, R2 below -1 dropped). Open, the window: (a) 100 ms before onset and offset (Results); (b) 200 ms before (Methods, Cross-validated R2); the code's time-warped windows (-200 to -100 ms before onset, -400 to -300 ms at offset) are a variant. Neurons with at least 10 trials per distance in both directions (code), direction 1 (code line 93). Reproduced when, under each reading and in each monkey, the proportions of neurons with positive coding at onset only and at offset only each exceed the proportion with positive R2 under the shuffled regressor (code line 1519), and the proportion coding at both is smaller than each of the two; partially reproduced when that holds under some readings only.

claims.statement: At the population level distance is encoded weakly before joystick onset and robustly and linearly before joystick offset; offset R2 exceeds onset R2 in both monkeys.
claims.source: Results, Ramping, paragraph 1; Figure 3d
claims.quote: By contrast, population neural states in both monkeys had a robust linear relationship with distance before joystick offset
claims.criterion: Targeted dimensionality reduction (Methods; code mnav_ec_fig3.m lines 1264 to 1487): pseudo-population of each monkey's neurons with at least 10 correct trials per distance in both directions, direction 1 (code); rates centred per neuron; regression of rate on ordinal distance on a random half of the trials; the axis is the coefficient vector at the time of largest norm; held-out half projected onto it; R2 of a linear fit of the mean projection on distance 1 to 5; 50 resamples. The code denoises with the principal components holding 80% of the training variance before the regression; the Methods do not mention it; both are run. Windows: Methods, -200 to 0 ms before onset and -500 to -300 ms before offset (main); code, -200 to -100 ms and -400 to -300 ms on time-warped bins (variant). Reproduced when, in each monkey, offset R2 exceeds onset R2 with a two-sided rank-sum p < 0.0001 over the 50 resamples under the readings run; partially reproduced in one monkey.

claims.statement: Near joystick offset the distance effect on the mean firing rate is significantly larger than that on the slope of the firing rate.
claims.source: Results, Ramping, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 4e
claims.quote: A direct comparison of the two indicated that the distance effect due to the firing rate is significantly larger than that due to the slope of the firing rate
claims.criterion: Four-way ANOVA (distance, start landmark, target landmark, direction) on correct trials, run on the mean rate and on the slope of a line fitted to the rate, per neuron; the distance F-statistics compared. The code loads this result precomputed (mnav_ec_fig3.m line 149), so windows come from the paper, which gives three: (a) Methods, rate -500 to -300 ms and slope -550 to -250 ms before offset; (b) Extended Data Fig. 4 legend, rate in the last 200 ms and slope in the last 300 ms; (c) Results, Ramping, paragraph 3, rate and slope both in -550 to -250 ms. Neurons with at least 10 trials in each of the 30 conditions, taken from the code's landmark ANOVA (line 1777), since the code for this analysis is not in the repository. Test: two-sample t-test (legend); the code's paired test on differences is a variant. Reproduced when, in both monkeys and under all window readings, rate F exceeds slope F at p < 0.0001; partially reproduced in one monkey.

claims.statement: Significantly less variance of firing rate near joystick offset is explained by the start or the target landmark than by distance.
claims.source: Results, Ramping, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 4f,g
claims.quote: We found that significantly less variance of the neural firing rate near joystick offset was explained by either the start or the target landmark compared with distance
claims.criterion: Four-way ANOVA with distance (absolute), start landmark, target landmark and direction (Methods; code mnav_ec_fig3.m line 1166), per neuron with at least 10 correct trials in each of the 30 conditions; F-statistics of distance and of start (target) landmark compared across neurons with a significant effect (p < 0.05) of either. Open, the window: (a) -500 to -300 ms before offset (Methods); (b) the last 200 ms (legend); the code's -400 to -300 ms is a variant. Open, the test: (a) t-test on the differences of F (Methods, and code line 1202, paired); (b) two-sample t-test (legend). Reproduced when distance F exceeds both landmark F at p < 0.0001 in both monkeys under all readings; partially reproduced when under some.

claims.statement: The structure of pairwise cross-correlations among simultaneously recorded periodic neurons is conserved between the mental navigation epoch and the ITI (monkey A r = 0.84, monkey M r = 0.86).
claims.source: Results, Ramping, paragraph 5; Figure 3e; Extended Data Fig. 5b
claims.quote: Notably, the structure of correlations across the pairs was similar between the two periods
claims.criterion: Code mnav_ec_fig3.m lines 226 to 451 and 677 to 860, and Extended Data Fig. 5b legend. One session per monkey; the code uses its fifth monkey A session and first monkey M session in its session list, whose order is not shown; open, the readings are the chronological fifth (A) and first (M) session, and each session holding at least 20 periodic neurons. Neurons: the most periodic by PI score, (a) 20 (Fig. 3e legend) or (b) 25 (code line 741 and Extended Data Fig. 5a). 20 neurons give 190 pairs, the count in the Results and r(188) for monkey A; 294 pairs (r(292)) for monkey M match neither 20 nor 25 neurons (190 or 300 pairs), so the M pair count is open and is reported. Rates smoothed as for the PI, linearly detrended, cross-correlation normalised to 1 at lag 0, averaged over trials; MNAV first-attempt trials of distance above 3 from onset to 500 ms before offset; ITI segments longer than 4 s, the first 3 s (code). Per pair, the mean cross-correlation over lags -5 to 5 ms; Pearson r across pairs between MNAV and ITI. Per session reading, reproduced when, for each monkey, r is within tolerance and p < 0.0001 under one neuron reading; partially reproduced when r is positive and p < 0.0001 but out of tolerance. The outcome is the one all session readings give; when they differ, the claim is methods_underspecified with every session shown. The degrees of freedom (188, 292) are compared with the pair counts.

claims.statement: The conserved correlation structure generalizes to the inference epoch, error trials and both directions of movement.
claims.source: Results, Ramping, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 5a-c
claims.quote: This finding was robust and generalized to all task epochs, including the inference epoch (during start and target landmark presentation but before mental navigation), error trials and for both directions of movement
claims.criterion: As fig3e-xcorr-conserved-iti, with the MNAV pair values correlated against those of the inference epoch (first image onset -0.2 to 1.2 s, code lines 792 to 793), error trials (first attempt of multi-attempt trials, Methods) and each direction separately. Extended Data Fig. 5c tests Pearson correlation at p < 0.05 with Bonferroni correction across lags. Reproduced when every comparison gives a positive r with p < 0.05 at lag 0 after Bonferroni correction over the lags tested (-900 to 900 ms, code lines 433 to 451), in both monkeys; partially reproduced when most do.

claims.statement: Many EC neurons have a Fano factor that is periodic at about 0.65 s: 55% (341/614) in monkey A and 43% (378/864) in monkey M.
claims.source: Results, The behaviour of the monkeys, paragraph 4; Figure 4h; Extended Data Fig. 8
claims.quote: The proportion of neurons with a periodic Fano factor was 43% (378/864) in monkey M and 55% (341/614) in monkey A
claims.criterion: Extended Data Fig. 8 legend and code mnav_ec_fig2.m plot_fanofactor, lines 991 to 1180. Correct MNAV trials with |tp| at least 2.3 s, one direction, at least 12 trials (code); spike counts in 200 ms windows stepped by 30 ms from joystick onset (code); Fano factor (variance over mean across trials) bootstrapped 100 times; Poisson null from the mean rate, 100 times (legend); each Fano time course linearly detrended, autocorrelated to 1.6 s and its PI computed as in the opening comment. Selection, open: (a) legend, PI significantly above the null by a two-sample t-test at p < 0.0001/20 in the 300 to 900 ms lag window (the code's window is 400 to 900 ms, a variant); (b) code ffgridness650, PI at 650 ms against the null by a one-tailed Welch t-test at alpha 0.01 (line 1135). Open, direction: a neuron counts if it qualifies in (i) either direction or (ii) direction 1. Denominator all units. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, both counts are within tolerance and the periodicities of the selected neurons have a median within 0.60 to 0.70 s; partially reproduced when the median holds and the counts do not. Every combination is shown; the code does not compute the counts.

claims.statement: The periodic Fano factor is not a by-product of firing-rate periodicity; it is also present in neurons whose firing rate is not periodic.
claims.source: Results, The behaviour of the monkeys, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 8c,f
claims.quote: This periodicity was not a by-product of the underlying periodicity of firing rates, and was also evident in neurons with non-periodic activity
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test or count for this finding. The neurons are those not periodic in firing rate (fig2-periodic-proportion, either direction) that have a periodic Fano factor (fig4h-periodic-fano-factor, same readings). The code has a one-sided binomial test of cell counts against 5% chance with all units as the denominator (mnav_ec_fig2.m lines 445 to 448, counts 99/614 and 74/864, not labelled and not in the paper); reading it as this test, the count is compared with 5% of all units (main) and, as a variant, with 5% of the non-periodic neurons. Reproduced when p < 0.05 in both monkeys under the readings for which fig4h is run; partially reproduced in one. The counts are reported and compared with 99 and 74 for information only.

claims.statement: Most EC neurons show a motor-related response before joystick offset, 77% (477/614) in monkey A and 70% (607/864) in monkey M, including most non-periodic neurons (81%, 368/452, in A and 89%, 432/481, in M).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 10 legend; Discussion, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Overall, the majority of neurons in both monkeys showed such motor-related response, 77% (477/614) in monkey A and 70% (607/864) in monkey M
claims.criterion: Code mnav_ec_fig2.m lines 3966 to 4006 and 422 to 443: direction 1, first-attempt trials of distance at least 3 with |tp| > 1.5 s, at least 6 trials; unsmoothed mean rate in tp - 1 to tp - 0.6 s and in tp - 0.4 to tp - 0.1 s after joystick onset; 200 bootstrap means of each, compared by a two-sample t-test at p < 0.0001 (legend and code); the code's test is two-sided (ttest2, line 4000), so a decrease also counts, followed; counting increases only is a variant. Non-periodic, PI score at or below threshold with more than 15 trials (code). Reproduced when all six counts are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the four proportions are each above 50%. The code's direction (1 only) against either direction is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: A Bayesian observer model whose timing variability grows sublinearly, as with resets at multiples of 0.65 s, fits the monkeys' behaviour better than a scalar-variability model without resets.
claims.source: Results, The behaviour of the monkeys, paragraph 6; Figure 4g
claims.quote: Fitting these two models to the monkeys' behaviour, we found that the model with intermediate resets was significantly better than the one without resets at capturing behaviour
claims.criterion: Methods, Bayesian model of behaviour; mnav_ec_fig4.m lines 1124 to 1184. Fig. 4g compares the code's models 10 and 12 (bls_offset_noncounter_oa and bls_offset_counter_oa_atp, line 1126 and get_mdl_names), whose functions are not in the repository; the repository holds only models 1 and 2 (utilities/bls_offset_counter_nonuniformPrior_self.m and bls_offset_noncounter_nonuniformPrior_self.m), which are used here, and what the oa and atp variants change is open. Per session, both models (measurement noise wm, production noise wp, offset b; reset model with SD proportional to the square root of the interval, no-reset model proportional to it) fit by maximum likelihood (fminsearch from [0.5, 0.5, 0]) to |v_p| against |v_a| of correct MNAV trials, with the code's prior (linear in the interval, c = 0.5846, m = -0.1026, over 0.65 to 3.25 s). The Methods exclude lapses with a Gaussian against uniform (0 to 3 v_p) mixture before fitting; the code has none; Methods main, no exclusion a variant. Per session, model error is the absolute difference between the data's and the model's summed squared bias plus variance across distances (code line 118). Paired t-test of no-reset against reset error across sessions. Reproduced when, in each monkey, the reset model has lower error with p < 0.0001. The code's paired t-test leaves out the first session (line 1184; its ttest2 at line 1133 is a variant), so the degrees of freedom imply 79 and 103 sessions, more than the 17 and 15 recorded, so the paper's fit used behavioural sessions beyond the recordings; the test is run on the sessions the dataset holds, and a smaller n is named as a deviation.

claims.statement: In the model, Hebbian plasticity from grid-cell modules to a landmark unit selectively strengthens inputs from the cells whose periodicity and phase match the external landmarks, so that the internal drive alone reproduces the landmark input when it is removed.
claims.source: Results, The behaviour of the monkeys, paragraph 2; Figure 4a,b; Extended Data Fig. 6a-c
claims.quote: In the presence of external landmarks, synapses were modified such that CAN inputs mimicked the external input, and when the external input was extinguished, the CAN drive alone was able to emulate that external drive
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. The code's utilities/gc1d_init_oja.m and the Methods (Oja's rule, learning rate below 1e-7, weights centred per module) with an external input at 0.65 s periodicity and four phases. Reproduced when, after learning, the grid cell with the largest weight onto the landmark unit belongs to the module of matching periodicity and its phase is within one unit spacing of the landmark phase for every phase tested.

claims.statement: The CAN model without landmarks shows scalar variability, its SD growing linearly with temporal distance, while the model with endogenous landmarks shows subscalar variability, with a power-law exponent below 1.
claims.source: Results, The behaviour of the monkeys, paragraph 5; Figure 4c,d
claims.quote: We verified this sublinearity by nonlinear regression in which the standard deviation and mean had a power-law relationship with an exponent of less than unity
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. gc_CAN_model_simulation.m and utilities/gc1d_*.m: two rings of 364 units, landmarks at states 60 to 300 in steps of 60, velocity 0.42 with landmarks and 0.35 without, Weber fraction 0.8 (Fig. 4c loads wm8), 50 simulations; times to reach each landmark state; 1,000 bootstrap SD and mean; s.d. = a mean^b + c fitted per bootstrap; one-tailed t-test of b against 1. The no-landmark velocity, Methods (CAN model), main reading: set by a grid search done separately for each of the five base intervals so that the mean time to reach each distance equals that of the landmark model (Extended Data Fig. 6e); the script's single wolm_speed of 0.35 (line 20) is a variant. Reproduced when b < 1 at p < 0.0001 with landmarks and the no-landmark model's b is not significantly below 1. The script's own wm = 0.05 and file name disagree with Fig. 4c; Fig. 4c's values are used.

claims.statement: In the CAN model with endogenous landmarks, the Fano factor of individual units fluctuates periodically with a periodicity of 0.65 s, and the periodicity of the Fano factor follows that of unit activation across a range of velocities.
claims.source: Results, The behaviour of the monkeys, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 6d
claims.quote: As expected by the presence of reset events, the Fano factor of individual units fluctuated periodically with a periodicity of 0.65 s
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data. Methods (Fano factor of CAN model units): 50 simulations under noisy velocity input, mean and variance of each unit across simulations, then the PI procedure of the opening comment on the Fano factor and on the activation time series. Code mnav_ec_fig4.m lines 293 to 345: each unit's Fano time course linearly detrended, ACG to 2,000 lags, PI at lags 1 to 1,600, periodicity the lag of maximum PI below 750; the code loads its simulations precomputed (ff_fr_dense_sampled_speed_wm2), so they are run afresh with the model of fig4d-model-subscalar-variability. Velocities, Extended Data Fig. 6d, a range around 42 a.u. whose values the paper does not give; open, a standard grid is used and named. Reproduced when, at the velocity whose unit-activation periodicity is 0.65 s, the median Fano-factor periodicity across units lies within 0.60 to 0.70 s (the 100 ms window the paper uses for "at 0.65 s"), and Fano and activation periodicities rise together across velocities (positive Spearman correlation, p < 0.05, a standard choice); partially reproduced when one of the two holds.

claims.statement: The relative phases of cell to cell cross-correlations of periodic EC neurons are more tightly clustered than predicted for grid cells by the CAN model.
claims.source: Results, The behaviour of the monkeys, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 5e-g
claims.quote: we found a significantly tighter clustering of the relative phase distribution of cell–cell cross-correlation in our data, which differs from what is predicted for GCs in rodents
claims.criterion: Extended Data Fig. 5e-g legend. Per pair of simultaneously recorded periodic neurons (fig3e-xcorr-conserved-iti selection), the lag of the peak of the mean cross-correlation in the navigation epoch, and the same for pairs of model units (fig4d-model-subscalar-variability, landmark model). The paper names no test and no measure of clustering; both are open. Readings, spread taken as the SD of the peak lags or as their interquartile range, each compared between monkey and model pairs by a two-sample test of spread (Levene test, a standard choice). Reproduced when, in both monkeys, the spread is smaller than the model's at p < 0.05 under every reading; partially reproduced in one monkey. The outcome rests on choices the paper does not make, which is recorded as a deviation.

claims.statement: Inhalation durations appear bimodal, and a Gaussian-mixture and hierarchical clustering of inhalation waveforms sorts them into slow and fast inhalations; fast inhalations are shorter and have steeper airflow changes than slow ones.
claims.source: Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 1; Figure 1C; STAR Methods, Inhalation clustering
claims.quote: Since the distribution of inhalation durations appeared bimodal, we developed a semi-unsupervised method that sorted inhalations into slow and fast depending on their airflow rate waveforms ... Fast inhalations had shorter duration and steeper changes in airflow rate than slow inhalations.
claims.criterion: Per STAR Methods, Analysis of the breathing signal and Inhalation clustering (the code does not hold this step). Breathing signal band-passed 0.5 to 50 Hz, smoothed with a Gaussian of SD 25 ms; peaks at local minima, peaks closer than 65 ms to the next dropped; onset and offset at the zero crossings around the peak. Waveforms of 100 ms centred on the peak, normalised by their 2-norm, PCA to the fewest PCs explaining 98% of variance, GMM (full covariance, regularisation 0.05, 15 replicates, 10,000 iterations) with the number of clusters by the Calinski-Harabasz index, centroids merged by a correlation-distance hierarchical dendrogram into two clusters, the one with shorter mean inhalation length named fast. Where the dataset gives slow and fast labels, they are compared with this output (fraction of agreement reported). Reproduced when, in every mouse, the fast class has a shorter median inhalation length and steeper negative and positive inhalation slopes (10% to 90% of peak amplitude, Methods) than the slow class, and the leave-one-mouse-out accuracy is within tolerance. Open, and named as readings, is how the dendrogram is cut when it gives three clusters ("two clusters were similar and stemmed from the same branch" was decided by visual inspection) - (a) merge the two clusters sharing the nearest parent; (b) cut the dendrogram at two clusters. Which eight mice formed the cross-validation is not stated; all awake mice with breathing are used, and the eight-mouse sets are a variant when the count differs.

claims.statement: PCx population activity encodes the inhalation phase; a cross-validated support vector regression predicts the phase above a shuffle null in individual mice.
claims.source: Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 3; Figures 1E and S1A
claims.quote: Hence, PCx activity encoded the phase and speed of each inhalation (Figures 1E and 1F; Figures S1A and S1B).
claims.criterion: Per STAR Methods, Inhalation phase decoding. Firing rates from spikes smoothed with a Gaussian of SD 20 ms, downsampled to 10 ms bins; mice with at least 20 PCx neurons; PCs up to a cumulative explained variance above 0.5 (at least two); phase in [0, 1] linearly from onset to offset of each sorted inhalation; non-overlapping epochs of 30 s of concatenated inhalation periods, all ordered pairs of epochs as train and test; SVR with scikit-learn defaults (RBF kernel); score the squared Pearson correlation, averaged over pairs; null from shuffling the phase array before prediction. Reproduced when in every mouse the R2 exceeds the 95th percentile of its null; partially reproduced when that holds in most mice. The number of shuffles is not given; 1000 is used, a standard choice that does not change the outcome.

claims.statement: The inhalation speed (fast against slow) can be decoded above chance from the mean firing rate in the first 180 ms of inhalation in individual mice.
claims.source: Figure S1B; Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Decoding the inhalation speed (fast versus slow) using the mean firing rate in the early 180 ms of inhalation in individual mice.
claims.criterion: Per STAR Methods, Inhalation speed decoding, and decoding_of_inh_type_control.m and decoding_of_inh_type_control_single_mice.m. Odorless inhalations, 180 ms spike counts, a sample of 400 inhalations balanced between slow and fast, linear SVM (libsvm through the Neural Decoding Toolbox), 10-fold cross-validation, z-scoring with training-set statistics, 100 resampling runs and 100 draws of inhalations. Whether 400 is the total or the count per class is open; readings (a) 200 slow and 200 fast, (b) 400 of each. Reproduced when in every mouse the mean accuracy minus one SD exceeds the 50% chance level (the panel shows mean and SD with the chance line).

claims.statement: Of 660 PCx neurons in six mice, 31.1% (205) reliably respond to at least one odor concentration.
claims.source: Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 3; Figure 1H legend
claims.quote: Of the recorded neurons, 31.1% reliably responded to at least one odor concentration (205 of 660 neurons; six mice).
claims.criterion: Neurons of the six mice with 0.01 and 0.1% concentrations, kept as in STAR Methods, Spike sorting and inclusion criteria (above 0.5 Hz). A neuron is odor-responsive when, for any odor at 0.01 or 0.1%, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Figure 1H legend) is significant at p < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment; the code (fig1_H_I_mech_induced_change_olf_resp.m) adjusts across the odor-concentration tests of each neuron and calls the neuron responsive if any adjusted p < 0.05. The paired values of the signed-rank test are not stated, and the code loads them precomputed ("odorStatistics_wholeStimulus", a "greater" test). Readings (a) per trial, the spike count over the whole 5 s odor period against the same-length period before odor onset, one-sided (odor greater); (b) as (a), two-sided; (c) per trial, the mean 180 ms inhalation response during the odor against the mean over odorless inhalations of that trial, one-sided. Reproduced when one reading gives counts within tolerance.

claims.statement: In 72.2% of odor-responsive neurons (148 of 205) the response amplitude during inhalation depends on how fast the animal inhales, more than expected by chance.
claims.source: Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 3; Figures 1H and 1I
claims.quote: Strikingly, how fast an animal inhaled influenced the response amplitude during inhalation in 72.2% of those neurons (148 of 205 neurons; Figures 1G–1I).
claims.criterion: Per the Figure 1H legend and fig1_H_I_mech_induced_change_olf_resp.m. For every odor-responsive neuron and every odor and concentration (0.01, 0.1%) for which its adjusted p < 0.05, the mean firing rate in 180 ms after onset of each fast and each slow odor inhalation; two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, fast against slow, at p <= 0.01. A neuron counts when any of its responses differs. Figure 1I compares the count of differing responses with a null from 1000 shuffles of the slow and fast labels; reproduced when the counts are within tolerance and the observed number of differing responses exceeds the 95th percentile of the shuffle null (the paper gives no p-value for Figure 1I); whether it exceeds every shuffle is reported. The odor-inhalation window follows the Methods (0 to 5 s), with the code's 0.4 to 5 s as a variant.

claims.statement: A faster inhalation increases 37.3% of odor responses and decreases 19.2% of them.
claims.source: Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 3; Figure 1H
claims.quote: The impact of a faster inhalation was not uniform across odor responses: 37.3% of the odor responses increased with a rapid inhalation, whereas 19.2% decreased in amplitude.
claims.criterion: As in fig1_H_I_mech_induced_change_olf_resp.m, over the same responses as fig1hi-sniff-changes-responses, one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests at p <= 0.005 each way (fast greater; fast smaller), as fractions of all tested responses. A variant takes the sign of the mean difference among the responses that differ in the two-sided test at p <= 0.01.

claims.statement: The sniff-driven variability in odor responses is already significant in the first 70 ms of an inhalation.
claims.source: Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 3; Figure S1C
claims.quote: This sniffdriven variability in odor responses was already significant during the first 70 ms of an inhalation (Figure S1C).
claims.criterion: As fig1hi-sniff-changes-responses with the 70 ms window after inhalation onset (Figure S1C legend; two-sided rank-sum at p < 0.01; null from 1000 label shuffles). "Significant" is read as the observed fraction of differing responses exceeding the 95th percentile of the shuffle null; reproduced when it does.

claims.statement: Regular-spiking (putatively excitatory or feedforward inhibitory) and fast-spiking (putatively feedback inhibitory) neurons show similar effects of inhalation speed on their odor responses.
claims.source: Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 3; Figure S1D
claims.quote: After sorting neurons into regular spiking (RS; putatively excitatory or feedforward inhibitory) and fast spiking (FS; putatively feedback inhibitory), we observed similar effects of the inhalation speed in both types (Figure S1D).
claims.criterion: RS and FS units per STAR Methods, Spike sorting and inclusion criteria, k-means (squared Euclidean, 10,000 iterations, 2,500 replicates) per mouse on trough-to-peak latency, waveform asymmetry (p2 - p1)/(p2 + p1) and mean firing rate, the cluster with higher rate, shorter latency and larger asymmetry named FS. Per mouse and type, the fraction of responses enhanced by a fast inhalation, by a slow inhalation, and sniff invariant (rank-sum, p < 0.01, as in the legend). The paper reports no test. Readings for "similar" (a) for each of the three fractions, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test of RS against FS over the six mice gives p >= 0.05; (b) the same with a Mann-Whitney test. Reproduced when all three fractions pass under a reading and both types have a nonzero fraction of responses changed by speed.

claims.statement: Across odor-responsive neurons, the absolute response change caused by a slow-to-fast switch in inhalation (at 0.01%) is larger than that caused by a tenfold increase in concentration (0.01 to 0.1%, slow inhalations).
claims.source: Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 4; Figure 1J
claims.quote: On average, sniffs caused a response amplitude change bigger than that caused by a 10-fold increase in odor concentration in the odor-responsive neurons (Figure 1J).
claims.criterion: As fig1_J_slow_to_fast_change_vs_01_to_1.m. Pairs are odor-responsive neurons with an odor for which either concentration is responsive (adjusted p < 0.05). Per pair, mean rate at 0.01% fast minus 0.01% slow, and 0.1% slow minus 0.01% slow, in 180 ms after inhalation onset; absolute values compared by a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test (the legend). Reproduced when the sniff change is larger (higher median) at p < 0.0001; partially reproduced when p < 0.05 only. The code's tests (two-sided rank-sum and paired t test) are reported as variants.

claims.statement: Concentration discriminability (CDI) of single neurons is lower when slow and fast inhalations are mixed than when computed within one inhalation speed.
claims.source: Results, Sniffing causes unstable odor responses in the PCx, paragraph 4; Figure 1L
claims.quote: Combining responses from slow and fast inhalations decreased the CDI compared with responses observed during uniform inhalation speeds (Figure 1L).
claims.criterion: Per STAR Methods, Concentration discrimination index. For each pair of fig1j-sniff-change-larger-than-concentration, CDI = abs(1 - 2*auROC) of 180 ms spike counts at 0.01% against 0.1%, from equal-size random samples of inhalations for the two concentrations, 100 draws averaged, for slow, fast and mixed inhalations. The within-speed value is the mean of the slow and fast CDI (fig1_L_CDI_svmAcc_typeSpecific_vs_mix.m). Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test of within against mixed; reproduced when mixed is lower at p < 0.0001, partially when p < 0.05 only. The sample size per draw and the make-up of the mixed sample are not given (the code loads the CDI precomputed). Readings (a) the sample size is the smallest count over slow and fast at both concentrations, and the mixed sample is half slow and half fast; (b) the same size, mixed sample drawn at random from all inhalations; (c) per set, the smaller count of the two concentrations. The code's tests (rank-sum, Kolmogorov-Smirnov) are variants.

claims.statement: A regularised Poisson GLM with inhalation speed, concentration and their interaction explains 91.9% of the variance in the mean spike count during the first 180 ms of odor inhalation across neurons.
claims.source: Results, PCx neurons randomly mix olfactory and non-olfactory inputs during inhalations, paragraph 2
claims.quote: This model explained 91.9% of the variance in the mean number of spikes generated during the first 180 ms of odor inhalation across all neurons.
claims.criterion: The GLM fits of fig2c-interaction-small. How the variance is computed is not stated. Readings (a) R2 between predicted and observed mean spike counts per neuron-odor pair and condition (4 concentrations by 2 speeds), pooled over all pairs; (b) the mean over pairs of the same R2 within each pair; (c) the deviance explained of each fit on single inhalations, averaged over pairs. Reproduced when one reading is within tolerance.

claims.statement: In the GLM, the interaction between inhalation speed and concentration has a small effect on the odor response, while the inhalation-speed (non-olfactory) term has a larger additive or subtractive effect.
claims.source: Results, PCx neurons randomly mix olfactory and non-olfactory inputs during inhalations, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
claims.quote: The GLM analysis revealed that the interaction between inhalation speed and concentration response had a small effect on the odor response amplitude during an inhalation (Figure 2C). Instead, the non-olfactory input had a more significant additive or subtractive effect (Figure 2C).
claims.criterion: Per STAR Methods, Encoding models, and GLM_model.m with fig2_C_D_GLM_coeff.m. All kept neurons of the four concentration-series mice, each odor separately. Spike count in the 180 ms after inhalation onset; regressors I (fast 1, slow 0), C (0 odorless, 0.33, 0.66, 1 for 0.01, 0.1, 1%) and I*C; Poisson GLM with glmnet elastic net, alpha 0.95, the penalty at lambda_1se of 10-fold cross-validation (nFold = min(smallest class - 3, 10)), as the code settles; inhalations resampled to equal numbers per speed and concentration 100 times and coefficients averaged. Reproduced when the median absolute interaction weight is below the median absolute inhalation-speed weight, over all pairs. The 95th percentile of each absolute weight is reported (the figure's whiskers).

claims.statement: The signs of the inhalation-speed and concentration weights can differ within a neuron, so that a fast inhalation can raise or lower a response regardless of how the neuron responds to a higher concentration; the combination is heterogeneous across neurons.
claims.source: Results, PCx neurons randomly mix olfactory and non-olfactory inputs during inhalations, paragraph 3; Figure 2D
claims.quote: Importantly, the sign of the weight for the non-olfactory input and the odor concentration factors could differ in the same neuron (Figure 2D). The non-olfactory input caused by a fast inhalation could increase or decrease the odor response amplitude regardless of how the neuron responded to a higher concentration of that odor.
claims.criterion: The weights of fig2c-interaction-small. Reproduced when neuron-odor pairs with nonzero weights lie in all four sign quadrants of inhalation against concentration weight, including both opposite-sign quadrants. The Pearson correlation of the two weights (as fig2_C_D_GLM_coeff.m computes it) and the count per quadrant are reported.

claims.statement: RS and FS neurons both show a heterogeneous distribution of inhalation-speed and concentration sensitivities.
claims.source: Results, PCx neurons randomly mix olfactory and non-olfactory inputs during inhalations, paragraph 3; Figures S2A and S2B
claims.quote: We similarly found a heterogeneous distribution of non-olfactory sensitivities in RS and FS neurons (Figures S2A and S2B).
claims.criterion: The criterion of fig2d-mixed-sensitivities applied to RS and FS neurons separately, with RS and FS as in figs1d-rs-fs-similar.
