claims.statement: Spike waveform features (asymmetry and trough-to-peak delay) cannot predict a neuron's inhalation-speed weight, concentration weight, or both, with any of three models.
claims.source: Results, PCx neurons randomly mix olfactory and non-olfactory inputs during inhalations, paragraph 3; Figure S2C; STAR Methods, Prediction of encoding properties from waveforms
claims.quote: In none of the 9 cases, the predictive model could extract a significant relationship (as measured by the cross-validated R2 of the regression) between the spike waveform and the encoding parameters.
claims.criterion: Per STAR Methods, standardised features; elastic-net linear model (95% ridge, 5% lasso, penalty by nested 10-fold CV), KNN regressor (k by nested CV), 1000 bagged trees (minimum leaf 5); 10-fold CV over cells; targets a, b, and a and b jointly. The Methods do not say which weights (GLM or linear model) are the a and b used, nor what makes an R2 significant. Readings for the weights (a) the GLM weights of fig2c-interaction-small; (b) the linear-model weights of fig5ef-correlated-subpopulations. Readings for significance (i) cross-validated R2 not above 0; (ii) R2 not above the 95th percentile of a null from shuffling the targets across cells (1000 shuffles). Reproduced when no model and target is significant under each reading.

claims.statement: Restricting the GLM analysis to the first 70 ms of inhalation gives similar results.
claims.source: Results, PCx neurons randomly mix olfactory and non-olfactory inputs during inhalations, paragraph 3; Figure S2D
claims.quote: Finally, restricting the analysis to the early 70 ms of inhalation also gave similar results (Figure S2D).
claims.criterion: The criteria of fig2c-interaction-small and fig2d-mixed-sensitivities with spike counts in the 70 ms after inhalation onset; reproduced when both hold.

claims.statement: In tracheostomized anesthetized mice, 57.1% of PCx neurons (144 of 252) encode the rate of artificial nasal airflow, 117 with positive and 27 with negative slopes.
claims.source: Results, A mechanosensory input signals the nasal airflow rate to the PCx, paragraph 2; Figure 3C
claims.quote: We found that 57.1% of neurons displayed mechanosensory responses, meaning that they encoded the airflow rate.
claims.criterion: As fig3_C_artificial_inhalation_expriment.m. Single units above 0.1 Hz in olfactory areas (OLF, EPd, PIR) more than 50 um from an area border. Per pulse, firing rate in (0, 500] ms after pulse onset minus (-500, 0] ms; responses z-scored over all pulses of the unit; linear regression on the airflow rank (1 to 5); tuned when the slope p <= 0.01 (t test of the slope, as the legend says). Reproduced when all four counts are within tolerance; partially when the tuned count is but the split by sign is not. If the dataset lacks the anatomical labels, all units are used and the count of 252 is compared.

claims.statement: Faster artificial airflow shortens response latency without significantly changing the order in which neurons are activated.

claims.statement: After bulbectomy, 15.7% of PCx neurons still fire more during fast sniffs than normal inhalations, against 29.7% in control mice.

Pseudo-population of the four mice, odor inhalations of both odors at three concentrations, balanced per speed and concentration, 180 ms counts; PCA on z-scored responses; for each of the first 15 PCs, linear SVM (10-fold CV, 100 resamples, 100 draws) per odor for speed and concentration. Read from mean and SD as the figure shows - "high accuracy" or "decoded" as mean minus one SD above chance (50% speed, 33.3% concentration, 25% identity of four odors), "could not" as chance within mean plus or minus one SD. Per odor and for 100 pseudo-population samples, LDA (eigen solver, Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage) on spike counts for concentration within fast, within slow, and for speed; first column of the scalings; angles transformed to 90 - |90 - Q| (the notebook takes |90 - angle|, the complement; the Methods form is used and the notebook's shown as a variant). Reproduced when the mean slow-fast concentration angle is below the mean concentration-speed angle for both odors. The number of neurons per sample is not given; readings (a) all 464 neurons with inhalations resampled, as the notebook's input file name suggests; (b) 143 neurons drawn at random, the size used elsewhere in Figure 5.

The gap between cis and trans is reported.

Selection per STAR Methods, |b| between |a*tan(pi/12)| and |a*tan(5*pi/12)|, positive when a and b share sign, negative otherwise, uncorrelated as their union; the code (fig5_H_I_high_correlated_sub_units.m) uses a lower bound |a|*(pi/4 - pi/6), close to tan(pi/12), shown as a variant. claims.statement: Over 20 consecutive 10 ms bins of an inhalation, concentration decoding within and across inhalation speeds is similar for mechanosensitive and sniff-insensitive neurons.

Readings (a) population by time bin on trans accuracies of the resamples; (b) population by time bin on cis and trans accuracies pooled. claims.statement: In a population simulated from the fitted coefficients, an inhalation-driven concentration change makes concentration decoding across inhalation speeds worse than within speed as the change grows, and adding the mechanosensory input restores decoding of the true concentration for any change.
claims.source: Results, Airflow information affords tolerance to flow-dependent concentration fluctuations, paragraph 1; Figures 6B and 6C; STAR Methods, Simulation of sniff-induced concentration changes
claims.quote: Consistently, decoders trained on the responses during slow and fast inhalations classified the odor concentration worse than decoders trained using only one inhalation speed as the simulated influence of the airflow on the concentration increased (Figure 6C). However, supplementing this population with mechanosensory responses was sufficient to reduce ambiguity and retrieve the actual concentration for any DIC (Figures 6B and 6C).
claims.criterion: Simulated per STAR Methods, R = Poisson(a I + b Cn) with Cn = log(Ce + k I Ce), Ce 0.01, 0.1, 1%, k from 0 to 1, a and b the linear-model coefficients of fig5ef-correlated-subpopulations, a set to 0 for the population without mechanosensory input. The Methods do not say which neurons are simulated, how negative rates are handled or how many events are drawn; the code (simulation_effect_of_inh_on_con_lrModel_exponential.ipynb with coeff_for_simulation.m) settles these and is followed for them - it simulates only neurons whose a or b is significant (linear-model ANOVA p-value averaged over resamples, p <= 0.01), draws 100 events per speed and concentration, adds the fitted intercept, and when a neuron has negative rates shifts them up by the minimum plus 0.025; it uses 20 k values from 0 to 1, 500 simulations and a 10-fold linear SVC (C 1). The code also adds the change as k*b*C*I on the 0.33/0.66/1 scale in place of the Methods' log form; that form is a variant. A variant simulating all neurons is shown. Reproduced when, without mechanosensory input, the mixed-speed decoder's accuracy falls below the within-speed decoders' as k grows (lower at k = 0.7 by more than one SD), and with it the mixed-speed accuracy stays within one SD of within-speed accuracy at every k.

Reproduced when a reading holds for every pair and both classifiers.

claims.statement: In the presence of synaptic blockers, CTZ increases spiking of ChR2(C128S)-expressing neurons, and 590 nm light, which closes the step-function opsin, abolishes that spiking.
claims.source: Figure 6c; Results, Interluminescence-mediated activation of postsynaptic neurons requires opsins, paragraph 1
claims.quote: 590 nm light completely abolished spiking initiated by CTZ
claims.criterion: Two-tailed Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank tests on 5 s counts (Fig. 6c legend). The legend does not say which counts each test pairs. Readings, (a) SB + CTZ is before against after adding SB + CTZ, and green light is before against after the 590 nm light; (b) green light is before SB + CTZ against after the 590 nm light. Reproduced when SB + CTZ gives p < 0.05 with counts higher after, and green light gives p < 0.05 with counts lower after, under the reading the source data's columns support. The Results print p = 0.0001 and the legend p < 0.0001 for green light; either matches.

claims.statement: With the non-functional opsin ChR2(C128S)-E97R-D253A in postsynaptic neurons, CTZ does not increase spiking in the presence of synaptic blockers.
claims.source: Figure 6f; Results, Interluminescence-mediated activation of postsynaptic neurons requires opsins, paragraph 1
claims.quote: In cultures expressing inactive ChR2(C128S)-E97R-D253A in postsynaptic neurons, CTZ generated bioluminescence, but no increase in spiking
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's two-tailed Mann-Whitney test of 5 s counts after SB alone against after SB + CTZ (Fig. 6f legend). Reproduced when p >= 0.05; the median difference is reported.

claims.statement: In co-cultures, blue light and CTZ increase spiking of the postsynaptic population without changing activity of the presynaptic cortical neurons, and only electrodes that respond to blue light respond to CTZ.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 3d, 3e; Results, Interluminescence requires connections between pre- and postsynaptic neurons, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Blue light LED stimulation (which directly activates the postsynaptic Opsin) or CTZ addition (which depends on ongoing spontaneous presynaptic activity) by contrast, increased spiking in ChR2(C128S) expressing postsynaptic neurons but without a change in the activity of cortical presynaptic neurons
claims.criterion: Shown by representative recordings with no measure or test. Reproduced when, in co-culture recordings, CTZ raises 5 s spike counts on postsynaptic electrodes and not on presynaptic ones, and no electrode without a blue-light response responds to CTZ. The presynaptic electrodes' counts are not in the Supplementary Data as described, and the recordings are not deposited.

claims.statement: Co-cultures with intact connections fire synchronously across the two populations with a short delay; cutting the connections disrupts the inter-population synchrony.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 2; Methods, Un-cut vs Cut experiment
claims.quote: Representative example of MEA recording of a mature (DIV21) co-culture (i) showing synchronicity in spontaneous intra-population firing activity, but a strongly disrupted inter-population synchronicity
claims.criterion: Shown by representative recordings with no measure or test. The recordings are not deposited.

claims.statement: CTZ infusion causes a rise in bioluminescence over barrel cortex in both Opsin (+) and Opsin (-) mice.
claims.source: Figure 7b; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In both Opsin (+) mice and Opsin (−) control mice CTZ presentation caused a rise in bioluminescent light production
claims.criterion: The bioluminescence time series of the in vivo pipeline (see the opening comment), for the five imaged mice (2 Opsin (+), 3 Opsin (-), as in the Fig. 7b legend), under ROI readings (o2a) and (o2b). The paper reports no test. Reproduced when, in every imaged mouse, the mean over 0 to 1200 s after onset exceeds the mean over the 180 s before onset by more than the upper bound of the bootstrapped 95% confidence interval of the baseline mean (1 s frames as samples, 10000 resamples as a standard choice, two-sided bound). The Methods give this rule for an electrode contact exceeding baseline, not for the bioluminescence signal; its use here is a choice of this file, and the mean after and before onset are shown for each mouse.

claims.statement: In Opsin (+) mice broad-band gamma oscillations emerge with CTZ, and similar changes are not seen in Opsin (-) mice despite bioluminescence.
claims.source: Figure 7c; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In Opsin (+) mice, we observed robust, broad-band gamma oscillation emergence that initiated with CTZ presentation ... In contrast, similar changes were not observed in the Opsin (−) control group, despite robust bioluminescent photon output
claims.criterion: Fig. 7c is a group spectrogram averaged over all contacts. From the in vivo pipeline, the group mean over contacts and mice of P (dB) over 30 to 100 Hz (the Methods' gamma band) and 0 to 1200 s after onset. Reproduced when the Opsin (+) value is above 0 dB and above the Opsin (-) value. The paper gives no threshold for "not observed"; the per-mouse values are reported. Readings (o1) and (o2) are run; the outcome is the one all readings give, and when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, with every result shown.

claims.statement: The gamma increase is seen on about half of the contacts in Opsin (+) mice (15.7 +/- 10.1 SD contacts per mouse) against 2.7 +/- 2.5 in Opsin (-) mice.
claims.source: Figure 7d; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 3
claims.quote: were evident on ~half of all electrode contacts in the Opsin (+) group (Fig. 7d : Opsin (+) = 15.7 ± 10.1 SD electrodes/mouse; Opsin (−): M = 2.7 ± 2.5 SD
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the SDs the paper states. A contact exceeds baseline when its mean gamma power (dB) over 0 to 1200 s after onset is above the bootstrapped 95% confidence interval of the mean of its baseline (Methods, Statistical analysis), with the baseline as the 1 s spectrogram steps of the 180 s before onset and 10000 resamples as a standard choice. Open, with the readings run. The band, (a) 30 to 100 Hz (Methods) or (b) 80 to 100 Hz (Fig. 7d legend). The bound, (a) the upper end of a two-sided 95% interval or (b) a one-sided 95th percentile. Plus (o1) and (o2). Reproduced when both means are within tolerance and the Opsin (+) mean is higher. The outcome is the one all readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, with every result shown.

claims.statement: The gamma increase in Opsin (+) mice is localised to the more superficial and granular layers of the cortical depth.
claims.source: Figure 7d; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 3
claims.quote: These Interluminescence gamma increases were localized to more superficial and granular layers across the neocortical depth
claims.criterion: Fig. 7d shows depth profiles of gamma power (dB) across contacts; the paper gives no layer boundaries and no test. Per contact, the Opsin (+) group mean over mice of gamma power (dB) over 0 to 1200 s after onset, ordered by contact depth from the probe map. Open, with the readings run. The band, (a) 80 to 100 Hz (Fig. 7d legend) or (b) 30 to 100 Hz (Methods). The split, (a) the upper half of the kept contacts against the lower half, or (b) the upper two thirds against the deepest third (the probe spans about 790 um from the surface, so its deepest part lies below the granular layer). Reproduced when the upper part has the higher mean under every reading.

claims.statement: Across electrodes, gamma power relative to baseline is higher in Opsin (+) than in Opsin (-) mice (mean 0.53 +/- 0.86 SD against -0.10 +/- 0.24 dB; medians 0.34 and -0.17).
claims.source: Figure 7e; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Analysis of each metric at the mouse or electrode level showed significantly higher values for the Opsin (+) group (Fig. 7e Mean gamma (dB) power across electrodes: Opsin (+) Mean = 0.53 ± 0.86 SD, Median = 0.34; Opsin (−) Mean = −0.10 ± 0.24 SD, Median = −0.17; KS test p < 0.0001; 1-tailed Mann–Whitney U test U = 4163, n 1 = n 2 = 75, p < 0.0001
claims.criterion: Gamma power from the in vivo pipeline, 30 to 100 Hz (Methods). The KS test is on all contact by time-bin by animal values of each group pooled (1 s spectrogram steps over 0 to 1200 s); the Mann-Whitney test, one-tailed (Opsin (+) greater), is on the 75 time-averaged contact values of each group (Methods, Statistical analysis). Means tolerate the stated SDs, medians 10%. Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 in the stated direction and the four values are within tolerance under every combination of readings (o1) and (o2) (when the readings give different outcomes, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, with every result shown); partially reproduced when the tests hold and the values do not. Fig. 7d's band (80 to 100 Hz) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Across electrodes, gamma events after CTZ are more numerous in Opsin (+) than in Opsin (-) mice (mean 213.60 +/- 139.53 SD against 139.28 +/- 72.97; medians 222 and 149).
claims.source: Figure 7e; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Mean gamma event number across electrodes: Opsin (+) Mean = 213.60 ± 139.53 SD, Median = 222; Opsin (−) Mean = 139.28 ± 72.97 SD, Median = 149; KS test p < 0.0001; 1-tailed Mann–Whitney U test U = 3609.50, n 1 = n 2 = 75, p < 0.0001
claims.criterion: Gamma events from the in vivo pipeline, counted per contact over the 1200 s window, under readings (o1), (o2), (o3) and (o4). The time bins of the pooled KS test for events are not given. Readings, (a) event counts per 1 s bin, (b) the per-contact totals. The Mann-Whitney test is one-tailed on the 75 per-contact counts of each group. Means tolerate the stated SDs, medians 10%. Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with Opsin (+) higher and the four values are within tolerance under every combination of readings (when the readings give different outcomes, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, with every result shown); partially reproduced when the tests hold and the values do not.

claims.statement: At the mouse level, gamma power relative to baseline is higher in Opsin (+) than in Opsin (-) mice (mean 1.16 +/- 1.09 SD against 0.03 +/- 0.18 dB), with every Opsin (+) mouse above every Opsin (-) mouse (U = 9).
claims.source: Figure 7e; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Mean gamma power across mice Opsin (+) Mean = 1.16 ± 1.09 SD, Median = 0.88; Opsin (−) Mean = 0.03 ± 0.18 SD, Median = 0.09; 1-tailed Mann–Whitney U test U = 9, n 1 = n 2 = 3, p < 0.05
claims.criterion: Each mouse's value is the 85th percentile of its 25 time-averaged contact values (Methods, Statistical analysis), with the percentile under readings (o6) and alignment under (o1) and (o2). Means tolerate the stated SDs, medians 10%. With 3 against 3 mice, U = 9 means complete separation, and its exact one-tailed p is 1/20 = 0.05, so the test is judged by U. Reproduced when U = 9 with Opsin (+) higher and the four values are within tolerance under every combination of readings (when the readings give different outcomes, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, with every result shown); partially reproduced when U = 9 and the values are not.

claims.statement: At the mouse level, gamma events are more numerous in Opsin (+) than in Opsin (-) mice (mean 327.25 +/- 45.58 SD against 199.33 +/- 36.08), with complete separation (U = 9).
claims.source: Figure 7e; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Mean gamma event number across mice Opsin (+) Mean = 327.25 ± 45.58 SD, Median = 304.25; Opsin (−) Mean = 199.33 ± 36.08 SD, Median = 203.75; 1-tailed Mann–Whitney U test U = 9, p < 0.05
claims.criterion: As fig7e-gamma-power-mice, on the per-contact gamma event counts, under readings (o1) to (o4) and (o6).

claims.statement: Across electrodes, MUA rises more from baseline in Opsin (+) than in Opsin (-) mice (mean 37.14 +/- 45.50 SD against 13.71 +/- 21.44 percent; medians 15.49 and 8.96).
claims.source: Figure 7f; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Opsin (+) Mean = 37.14 ± 45.50 SD, Median = 15.49; Opsin (−) Mean = 13.71 ± 21.44 SD, Median = 8.96; KS test p < 0.0001; 2-tailed Mann–Whitney U test U = 3899, n 1 = n 2 = 75, p < 0.0001
claims.criterion: MUA from the in vivo pipeline under readings (o1), (o2) and (o5); the KS test on all 1 s bins over 0 to 1200 s of each group pooled, the two-tailed Mann-Whitney test on the 75 time-averaged contact values of each group (Methods). Means tolerate the stated SDs, medians 10%. Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with Opsin (+) higher and the four values are within tolerance under every combination of readings (when the readings give different outcomes, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, with every result shown); partially reproduced when the tests hold and the values do not.

claims.statement: At the mouse level the MUA difference is not significant (mean 77.72 +/- 47.40 SD against 27.15 +/- 18.38 percent; U = 9, p > 0.05, two-tailed), though Opsin (+) mice show MUA increases higher than, or equal to, the highest Opsin (-) values.
claims.source: Figure 7f; Results, Interluminescence in vivo, paragraph 4
claims.quote: MUA differences were significant when analyzed at the electrode, but not the mouse, level ... Mean MUA (percent change from baseline) across mice: Opsin (+) Mean = 77.72 ± 47.40 SD, Median = 52.15; Opsin (−) Mean = 27.15 ± 18.38 SD, Median = 27.24; 2-tailed Mann–Whitney U test U = 9, p > 0.05
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test on each mouse's 85th percentile of time-averaged contact MUA (Methods), under readings (o1), (o2), (o5) and (o6). With 3 against 3 mice the smallest two-tailed exact p is 0.1, so this test cannot reach p < 0.05; the absence part holds whatever the data, and the claim is judged on U and the values. Reproduced when U = 9 with Opsin (+) higher and the four values are within tolerance under every combination of readings (when the readings give different outcomes, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, with every result shown); partially reproduced when U is 7 or 8, or U = 9 and the values are not within tolerance.

claims.statement: PoSub units split into 1,835 putative excitatory cells and 427 putative FS cells by firing rate and waveform, and 1,602 excitatory cells (87%) were HD cells with HD information above 0.2 bits per spike; the vertical recordings gave 931 units from 14 mice and the parallel ones 1,999 units from 18 mice.
claims.source: Results, High-density recordings in the PoSub of freely moving mice, paragraph 1; Methods, Spike sorting and unit classification, and HD tuning curves and tuning metrics
claims.quote: The probe was implanted either vertically ( n = 931 units from 14 mice, range ... or parallel to PoSub cell layers ( n = 1,999 units from 18 mice ... PoSub units were subdivided into putative excitatory cells ( n = 1,835) and putative PoSub-FS cells ( n = 427) based on mean firing rate and waveform shape ... were classified as PoSub-HD cells (>0.2 bits per spike, n = 1602, 87% of excitatory cells
claims.criterion: Classification as fixed in the opening comment (Methods). The 0.4 ms trough-to-peak cut is the main reading and the code's 0.35 ms a variant; the HD threshold is read as 0.2 bits per spike (Results, Methods and code) and as the 99th percentile of the excitatory cells' time-reversed HD information (Methods' definition). The fraction can be 87% (Results) or 85% (Methods, "85% of putative excitatory cells"); either value within tolerance counts. Unit counts are over all units of each probe orientation as the dandiset's metadata gives it. The dandiset holds 31 of the 32 sessions, so a count below the paper's by one session's cells is reported as such. If the dandiset carries its own cell-type labels, they are compared with the recomputed classes and both counts are shown.

claims.statement: Putative excitatory PoSub cells carry more HD information than their time-reversed controls, and HD information across all PoSub cells is bimodal.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2b,c
claims.quote: Distribution of HD information carried by tuning curves of putative excitatory cells in PoSub ( n = 1835; Wilcoxon signed rank test vs time-reversed control, z = 37.1
claims.criterion: As in Duszkiewicz2024_Figure_BasicProperties.m, log10 HD information of each excitatory cell against that of its time-reversed control, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, paired by cell. The paper reports z = 37.1 and no p-value. Reproduced when p < 0.05 with the real median above the control median. The bimodality of Extended Data Fig. 2c is shown, not judged.

claims.statement: The HD information carried by PoSub-FS cell tuning curves is higher than that of their time-reversed controls.
claims.source: Results, Tuning of PoSub-FS cells is stable and anchored to landmarks, paragraph 1; Figure 2a
claims.quote: at the population level, the quantity of HD information conveyed by PoSub-FS cells was significantly higher than that of the time-reversed control
claims.criterion: As in Duszkiewicz2024_Figure_BasicProperties.m, log10 HD information of each FS cell against its time-reversed control, Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Fig. 2a legend, n = 427, z = 17.9, no p-value printed). Reproduced when p < 0.05 and the median of the real values is above that of the controls. The median HD information of PoSub-HD cells (the dashed line of Fig. 2a) is reported alongside.

claims.statement: The animal's HD can be decoded accurately from PoSub-FS cell spiking with a Bayesian decoder built on their tuning curves, and decoding error falls as more FS cells are used.
claims.source: Results, Tuning of PoSub-FS cells is stable and anchored to landmarks, paragraph 1; Figure 2b; Extended Data Fig. 2e
claims.quote: The information contained in PoSub-FS cell tuning curves was sufficient to accurately decode the animal's HD from PoSub-FS cell spiking activity
claims.criterion: The Methods do not describe this decoder; Duszkiewicz2024_GetBayesianDecoding.m settles it. Tuning curves (360 bins, 3 degree smoothing) from the first half of the square epoch at speed above 2 cm/s; spike counts in 100 ms bins smoothed with a Gaussian of 2 bins s.d.; one-dimensional Bayesian decoding (Poisson) over the second half of the epoch, all times; error as the absolute angular difference from the real HD, median per session; the same with time-reversed tuning curves gives the chance level. Reproduced when the mean over the sessions (32 in the paper) of the FS decoder's median error is below the chance level (the mean of the control medians, as Extended Data Fig. 2e draws it) and the Pearson correlation across sessions between the number of FS cells and the median error is negative with p < 0.05 (Extended Data Fig. 2e, Pearson, n = 32). The HD-cell decoder's error is shown for comparison.

claims.statement: The tuning of PoSub-FS cells is preserved between the square and triangular arenas, as it is for PoSub-HD cells.
claims.source: Results, Tuning of PoSub-FS cells is stable and anchored to landmarks, paragraph 2; Figure 2c; Extended Data Fig. 2j
claims.quote: the tuning of PoSub-FS cells was stable within a single exploration epoch (Extended Data Fig. 2h ) and independent of the enclosure geometry (Fig. 2c ), reflecting the properties of canonical PoSub-HD cells
claims.criterion: Sessions with a triangle epoch. Selection from Figure_Stability.m, FS cells with rate above 10 Hz and HD cells with rate above 0.5 Hz in both arenas. The triangle tuning curves of each session are shifted back by the circular mean rotation of its HD cells (the lag of maximum square-triangle cross-correlation), as the Methods say; then the Pearson correlation at zero lag of each cell's square and triangle curves, against the same for time-reversed curves, Wilcoxon signed-rank (Fig. 2c, n = 264 FS cells, z = 14.0; Extended Data Fig. 2j, n = 1,013 HD cells, z = 27.6; no p-values printed). Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with real correlations above the controls. Curves smoothed at 3 degrees (Methods); the code's 2 degrees is a variant.

claims.statement: Tuning curves of PoSub-FS and PoSub-HD cells computed from the two halves of the square-arena epoch are correlated above their time-reversed controls.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2h,i
claims.quote: PoSub-FS cell tuning curve correlation across two halves of the square arena epoch
claims.criterion: As in Figure_Stability.m and GetHdTuning_xval.m, tuning curves from the two halves of the movement epoch, zero-lag Pearson correlation per cell against the time-reversed halves, Wilcoxon signed-rank (FS n = 427, z = 17.8; HD n = 1,602, z = 34.7; no p-values printed). Reproduced when both give p < 0.05 with real correlations higher. Smoothing at 3 degrees (Methods), 2 degrees (code) as a variant.

claims.statement: In a cue rotation task PoSub-FS cell tuning curves follow the rotated distal landmark together with PoSub-HD cells.
claims.source: Results, Tuning of PoSub-FS cells is stable and anchored to landmarks, paragraph 2; Figure 2d-f
claims.quote: PoSub-FS cell tuning curves followed the rotated distal landmark in concert with PoSub-HD cells
claims.criterion: Per the Methods (Analysis of HD cell realignment after cue rotation) and Figure_CueRotation.m. Rotation epochs kept when the decoder error over the next 200 s exceeds 45 degrees and the animal moved (mean speed at least 2 cm/s) in the preceding epoch; realignment ends at 0.99 of a fitted sigmoid; per FS cell the mean absolute difference between its rotation and the mean rotation of the session's HD cells, against the time-reversed control, Wilcoxon signed-rank (n = 99 FS cells, z = 8.25, no p-value printed). Reproduced when p < 0.05 with real differences smaller than control. The Methods' exclusion reads "(1) ... and (2)"; it is read as excluding epochs that fail either condition and, as a second reading, both. The code (Duszkiewicz2024_GetSigmoids_CueRotation.m) uses another rule, run as a variant. It excludes an epoch when the change in circular mean decoder error from the previous epoch is below 45 degrees, or the circular variance of the error (converted with rad2deg) exceeds 10, or the mean absolute angular head velocity is below 10; it has no speed condition.

claims.statement: ADN-HD cells have broader tuning curves than PoSub-HD cells.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 1; Figure 3c
claims.quote: In mice, ADN-HD cells tend to have broader HD tuning curves than PoSub-HD cells
claims.criterion: Width as in the opening comment (code). Mann-Whitney U test of PoSub-HD against ADN-HD widths (n = 1,602 and 97, z = 11.4, no p-value printed). Reproduced when p < 0.05 with the ADN median wider. ADN-HD cells are classified by Duszkiewicz2024_GetCellTypes_ADN.m.

claims.statement: Fourier power of tuning curves decays quickly with frequency, and the first ten components hold on average 98% of the total power.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Across the cell population, the Fourier power decayed rapidly as a function of frequency. Hence, for clarity, we focused our analysis on the relative power of the first ten Fourier components that contained, on average, 98% of the total power
claims.criterion: The tolerance is 0.02 because a fraction cannot exceed 1, so 10% of the value would not test it. "The cell population" is read as (a) PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cells pooled (the dandiset) and (b) each of the two separately; ADN-HD cells, when available, as a variant. Power is read as (a) the squared modulus of the complex coefficient (code, and the Parseval check of Extended Data Fig. 3e) and (b) the root mean square of the sine and cosine projections (Methods' words). Reproduced when one population reading under each power reading is within tolerance.

claims.statement: The average Fourier signatures of PoSub-FS, PoSub-HD and ADN-HD populations differ, with ADN-HD cells having more power at low and less at high components than PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cells, which are alike.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 3; Figure 3e; Extended Data Fig. 3f
claims.quote: the Fourier signature of ADN-HD cells was different from both PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cells, with higher power at low frequencies and lower power at higher frequencies
claims.criterion: As in Figure_Fourier.m, a repeated-measures ANOVA (fitrm and ranova) of the ten normalized powers with cell type as the between-subjects term; the component by cell type interaction. The code enters cell type as a numeric covariate (PoSub-FS 1, PoSub-HD 2, ADN-HD 3), which is what gives the paper's degrees of freedom (9, 19116) for 2,126 cells; a categorical factor would give (18, 19107). The numeric coding is the main reading and the categorical factor a variant. The paper does not say which components are "low" and "high"; the readings are (a) the ADN-HD mean signature above both PoSub means at component 1 and below both summed over components 3 to 10, and (b) the ADN-HD cumulative signature (Fig. 3e inset) above both PoSub cumulative signatures at every component from 1 to 9. Reproduced when p < 0.05 and the direction holds under both readings. Both power readings (squared modulus, code; root mean square, Methods) are run. The same ANOVA on PoSub-FS and PoSub-HD only, which the dandiset alone allows, is shown as a variant and not judged.

claims.statement: Individual PoSub-HD cell Fourier spectra are closer to the average PoSub-FS signature than ADN-HD cell spectra are.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 3; Figure 3f
claims.quote: we found that the average Fourier signature of the PoSub-FS cell population was often indistinguishable from the Fourier signatures of individual PoSub-HD cells
claims.criterion: KL divergence between each HD cell's ten-component spectrum and the mean PoSub-FS spectrum, Mann-Whitney U of PoSub-HD against ADN-HD. Readings, all run, for what the paper leaves open or states against its code. Divergence direction, D_KL(sigma_i || S) (Methods) and D_KL(S || sigma_i) (code). Power, squared modulus (code) and root mean square (Methods). Reproduced when p < 1e-9 with the PoSub-HD median smaller under every reading; partially reproduced when p < 0.05 with PoSub-HD smaller under every reading but p is not below 1e-9 in all. PoSub-HD cells are all HD cells (n = 1,602); the shipped code's multipeak filter is the Extended Data Fig. 3k control.

claims.statement: The smaller distance of PoSub-HD than ADN-HD spectra from the PoSub-FS signature holds after excluding multipeaked HD cells, after excluding noisy clusters, and with a 10 cm/s speed threshold; ADN-HD cells have higher multipeak scores than PoSub-HD cells.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 3j,k
claims.quote: the similarity between PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cell Fourier signatures on a population level was preserved when the analysis was limited to HD cells with a single receptive field. Additionally, it was preserved when a threshold was applied to keep only the best isolated unit clusters or when a higher velocity threshold was used to compute tuning curves
claims.criterion: The Fig. 3f test under each control, with the readings of fig3f-posub-hd-closer-to-fs. Multipeak score as the Methods define it, the mean of the normalized curve outside its peak (plus or minus the width from the maximum), cells kept below 0.05 (code, Figure_Fourier.m); expected n = 789 and 69, z = 10.4. Contamination score, spike autocorrelogram at plus or minus 100 ms in 1 ms bins, value at 0.1 ms over the highest value, clusters kept at or below 0.2; n = 1,472 and 83, z = 5.91. Speed above 10 cm/s; n = 1,602 and 97, z = 6.46. Multipeak scores, Mann-Whitney U, n = 1,602 and 97, z = 4.25. No p-values are printed. Reproduced when all four tests give p < 0.05 in the paper's direction under every reading.

claims.statement: Compared with time-reversed controls, the PoSub-FS spectrum has higher power for the first three Fourier components only.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 4; Figure 3g
claims.quote: Compared to controls, the spectrum of PoSub-FS cells showed higher power for the first three Fourier components only
claims.criterion: As in Figure_Fourier.m, ten normalized powers of each FS cell and of its time-reversed curve; repeated-measures ANOVA with condition and component as within factors (the interaction); then a Wilcoxon signed-rank test per component with p multiplied by 10. The code divides the printed z by 10, which is why the legend's z values are small; the test's own z is reported too. Reproduced when the interaction has p < 0.05 and components 1, 2 and 3, and no other, are significantly higher than control after correction. Both power readings are run.

claims.statement: Of the 427 PoSub-FS cells, 231, 141 and 55 have their highest power in the first, second and third Fourier component, proportions similar to the relative mean power of those components.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 4; Figure 3h; Extended Data Fig. 4a legend
claims.quote: The proportions of recorded PoSub-FS cells with the highest relative power in each of the first three Fourier components were similar to the relative mean power for the population
claims.criterion: The counts are those of Extended Data Fig. 4a (n = (231, 141, 55)), each cell assigned to the largest of its first three powers (code, highComp; the power reading does not change the assignment). "Similar" is not defined; the readings are (a) the three proportions are in the same order as the mean relative powers of components 1 to 3 renormalized over those three, and (b) each proportion is within 10% of its renormalized mean power. Reproduced when the counts are within tolerance and both readings hold under both power readings; partially reproduced when the counts hold and only one reading does.

claims.statement: Fourier signatures are far more variable among PoSub-FS cells than among HD cells of the same region, so individual FS cells are narrowly tuned in Fourier space.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 3g
claims.quote: while the shape of Fourier signatures was largely uniform among HD cells from the same brain region, it was highly variable among PoSub-FS cells
claims.criterion: Distance of each cell's spectrum from its own population's mean spectrum. The legend says "statistical distance" and its abbreviations name D_KL; the code (Figure_Fourier.m, ftDist) uses the Euclidean distance over the ten components for the ANOVA and the tests. Both are run, with both power readings. The part the dandiset holds is FS against PoSub-HD, Mann-Whitney U, p multiplied by 3 (legend z = 5.71, a third of the test's z as the code divides it; no p printed). Reproduced when that test gives p < 0.05 with FS distances larger under every reading. The ANOVA and the comparisons with ADN-HD (z = 3.40 and 0.45) are run when the figshare ADN data are used and are reported.

claims.statement: Phases of the Fourier components are correlated with each other in individual HD cells but random relative to each other in PoSub-FS cells.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 3l
claims.quote: In contrast, the Fourier components of individual PoSub-FS cells had random phases relative to each other
claims.criterion: As in Figure_Fourier.m, phase of each component as the angle of the complex coefficient; circular correlation (circ_corrcc) between twice the first phase (mod 2 pi) and the second phase, and between three times the first phase and the third phase, across cells (Extended Data Fig. 3l, 1,602 PoSub-HD and 427 PoSub-FS cells). The FS part is a claim of absence judged on that test at p < 0.05. Reproduced when both PoSub-HD correlations are significant and neither FS correlation is; the coefficients are reported either way. ADN-HD cells are a variant when their data are used.

claims.statement: Tuning curve auto-correlograms of FS cells with the highest power in the second component peak at 180 degrees, and those with the highest power in the third at 120 and 240 degrees, above controls.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 6; Extended Data Fig. 4a
claims.quote: Auto-correlograms of tuning curves for cells with maximum power for the second component showed a second maximum at 180°, reflecting their twofold radial symmetry. For cells with maximum power in the third component, auto-correlograms peaked at 120° and 240°
claims.criterion: Cross-validated auto-correlograms as the Methods and GetTuningAutocorr_xval.m give them (z-scored curves from the two halves of the movement epoch, Pearson correlation at each circular shift). As in Figure_Fourier.m, the value at 180 degrees (row 181) for twofold cells and at 120 degrees (row 121) for threefold cells, each against the same value from the time-reversed curves; the code tests no value at 240 degrees, which is shown and not judged. Test, Wilcoxon signed-rank (legend, n = 141 and 55; no statistic printed); the code's Mann-Whitney U (ranksum) is a variant. Reproduced when both give p < 0.05 with real values higher.

claims.statement: In a joint Isomap embedding of tuning curve auto-correlograms, PoSub-HD cells lie nearer the centre of the PoSub-FS distribution than ADN-HD cells.
claims.source: Results, Equivalence of PoSub-HD and FS cell tuning in Fourier space, paragraph 6; Extended Data Fig. 4c,d
claims.quote: The distribution of PoSub-HD cells occupied the center of the PoSub-FS cell distribution while that of ADN-HD cells was closer to the periphery
claims.criterion: As in the Methods and Figure_Fourier.m, Isomap (12 neighbours, 2 dimensions) on the cross-validated auto-correlograms of all FS, PoSub-HD and ADN-HD cells together; Euclidean distance of each HD cell to the mean FS position; Mann-Whitney U of PoSub-HD against ADN-HD (n = 1,602 and 97, z = 4.26, no p printed). Reproduced when p < 0.05 with PoSub-HD distances smaller.

claims.statement: In simulation, random linear combinations of HD-tuned inputs preserve the input population's average Fourier spectrum, and the proportions of outputs dominated by the first three components converge to those of PoSub-FS cells when the s.d. of the weights exceeds their mean.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cell tuning reveals key circuit properties, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 4a-d,g; Extended Data Fig. 5
claims.quote: random connectivity preserved the Fourier spectrum of the input population ... This convergence emerged for weight distributions in which the standard deviation (s.d.) exceeded the mean of the weights
claims.criterion: A result of simulation, not of the recordings. It can be tested only by rerunning a simulation the paper does not fully specify (input tuning widths, number of inputs, the log-normal weight parameters, 30 simulations per point); the author reports it as not testable from the dataset unless the simulation code is found.

claims.statement: Putative synaptic weights from PoSub-HD to PoSub-FS cells, estimated from spike train cross-correlograms, are heavy-tailed with an s.d. larger than their mean, in the range where simulations predict the radial symmetries of FS tuning.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cell tuning reveals key circuit properties, paragraph 2; Figure 4e,f; Extended Data Fig. 2f,g
claims.quote: The distribution was heavy-tailed (Fig. 4f ), with the ratio of s.d. and mean input weight (i.e. coefficient of variation), in the range where in silico simulation predicted the emergence of radial symmetries
claims.criterion: Detection from the Methods (Detection of monosynaptic connections) with details from GetSpikeCrosscorrs.m, GetSynapticPairs.m and Figure_SynapticConnections.m. Cross-correlograms in 0.2 ms bins over plus or minus 50 ms (Methods; the code's plus or minus 25 ms is a variant), baseline from convolution with a partially hollowed Gaussian of about 4 ms s.d. (cch_conv, window 41 bins), upper bound the 99th percentile of the Poisson distribution at the largest predicted count within 0 to 2 ms, at least two consecutive bins above it; HD cell as reference with the peak at positive lag, latency above 0.5 ms, no peak at negative lag. Weight as the code's strZ, peak minus prediction over the square root of the prediction (the ratio strR is a variant). The paper prints no CV in the text; Figure 4g and the sentence above make the threshold s.d. greater than the mean. Reproduced when the CV of the weights over all putative HD-to-FS connections exceeds 1 and their skewness is positive.

claims.statement: A model fit to the PoSub-FS tuning statistics gives near-Gaussian weights from ADN-HD inputs and heavy-tailed weights from PoSub-HD inputs, so that FS tuning is best explained by flat, high-rate ADN input and HD-modulated, low-rate PoSub input.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cell tuning reveals key circuit properties, paragraph 3; Figure 4h; Supplementary Methods, Fourier spectrum simulations, Model fitting
claims.quote: established that PoSub-FS cell-like outputs are best explained by flat, high firing rate inputs from ADN-HD cells and low firing rate, HD-modulated inputs from PoSub-HD cells
claims.criterion: The fit uses the recorded FS, PoSub-HD and ADN-HD tuning curves (the ADN curves only on figshare) and three losses minimized with Adam (learning rate 0.0001, 200,000 steps), the first two scaled by 0.25 of their left-hand side, ADN inputs expanded tenfold by circular shifts (Supplementary Methods). The input numbers and initial values are not given. The author reports it as not testable unless the fitting code is found; a reimplementation would rest on the author's choices.

claims.statement: Light over ADN in VGAT-Cre mice with ArchT in TRN raises the firing of ADN-HD cells but not of non-HD thalamic cells, without broadening ADN-HD tuning curves.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells receive directionally uniform thalamic input, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 7b-d
claims.quote: Targeted illumination of ADN (inactivating the inhibitory presynaptic terminals of the TRN neurons) resulted in a net increase of the firing rates of ADN-HD cells but not of untuned neurons (non-HD cells) recorded in the same sessions
claims.criterion: Light ON, the 240 one-second pulses; OFF, the 4 s before each pulse onset (Methods; offStart = 4 in Figure_Optogenetics.m). Cells with rate above 0.5 Hz in ON, OFF and baseline (code). Modulation as the ON over OFF rate (code, optoRes); ADN-HD against non-HD, Mann-Whitney U (n = 52 and 75, z = 6.57, no p printed), reproduced when p < 0.05 with ADN-HD higher and ADN-HD median above 1. Width (1 degree bins, 3 degree smoothing) before and during light is a claim of absence judged on the legend's Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05; the code's rank-sum test is a variant.

claims.statement: Thalamic disinhibition raises the firing rates of PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cells in ArchT mice; the rise of FS cells is larger than in control-virus mice.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells receive directionally uniform thalamic input, paragraph 3; Figure 5b; Extended Data Fig. 7e,f
claims.quote: Similarly to the upstream ADN-HD cells, PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cells increased their firing rates
claims.criterion: Opto sessions of PoSub, cells and ON and OFF epochs as in ed7-adn-disinhibition; modulation as the ON over OFF rate (code); ArchT against control, Mann-Whitney U (Extended Data Fig. 7f; PoSub-FS n = 47 and 38, z = 4.99; PoSub-HD n = 83 and 89, z = 1.69; no p printed). The paper's z for PoSub-HD corresponds to a two-tailed p of about 0.09. Reproduced when the FS test gives p < 0.05 with ArchT higher and the ArchT medians of both FS and HD cells exceed 1 and exceed the control medians. If the dandiset lacks the control sessions, only the ArchT medians and a Wilcoxon signed-rank of per-pulse ON against OFF rates (the Methods' light-modulation test) can be shown, and the claim is partially testable.

claims.statement: Thalamic disinhibition preserves the HD tuning of PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cells.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells receive directionally uniform thalamic input, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 7g-j
claims.quote: increased their firing rates (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 7e,f ) while preserving their HD tuning
claims.criterion: Two claims of absence judged on the legends' tests at p < 0.05. PoSub-HD tuning curve width, baseline against high gain, Wilcoxon signed-rank (Extended Data Fig. 7i, z = 0.30; the legend's n = 52 is read as the ArchT PoSub-HD cells, 83 in Fig. 5, as Figure_Optogenetics.m selects them, and the count found is reported; the code's rank-sum test is a variant). PoSub-FS baseline against high-gain tuning curve correlation (6 degree bins, no smoothing, all 47 ArchT FS cells, as Figure_Optogenetics.m computes rTC), ArchT against control, Mann-Whitney U (Extended Data Fig. 7j, n = 47 and 38, z = 1.14). Reproduced when neither test finds a difference; the effect sizes are reported.

claims.statement: Thalamic gain modulates PoSub-HD cell tuning multiplicatively and PoSub-FS cell tuning additively, so that FS cells receive thalamic input that is uniform across directions.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells receive directionally uniform thalamic input, paragraph 4; Figure 5c-e; Extended Data Fig. 8a,b
claims.quote: The modulation of PoSub-HD cells was purely multiplicative ... In contrast, modulation of PoSub-FS cell tuning was exclusively additive
claims.criterion: Per the Methods (Gain modulation analysis, experiment) and Figure_Optogenetics.m. ON and OFF tuning curves in 6 degree bins, unsmoothed, without speed threshold, both divided by the maximum of the OFF curve; linear fit of ON on OFF (polyfit), slope the multiplicative and intercept the additive factor. ArchT cells excluded, by the Methods, when they show neither a significant light modulation (Wilcoxon signed-rank of per-pulse ON against preceding OFF rates, p < 0.05) nor a significant ON-OFF tuning correlation (Pearson, p < 0.05). The sentence reads "did not show ... and did not show", so the readings are (a) exclusion when both fail and (b) when either fails; the code (c) excludes on the correlation alone. The paper excluded 1 of 47 FS cells and no other cells. Tests, Mann-Whitney U, ArchT PoSub-HD against PoSub-FS (Fig. 5e, additive z = 7.72, multiplicative z = 5.99; legend n = (83, 52), read as 83 and 46); each against control (Extended Data Fig. 8a, HD additive z = 1.57, multiplicative z = 6.80; 8b, FS additive z = 4.16, multiplicative z = 0.36; no p printed). Reproduced when, under every reading, HD multiplicative factors exceed FS ones and FS additive factors exceed HD ones (p < 0.05), HD multiplicative and FS additive factors exceed control (p < 0.05), and HD additive and FS multiplicative factors do not differ from control (p of 0.05 or more). Partially reproduced when the HD against FS comparisons hold and the control comparisons cannot be run or do not all hold.

claims.statement: Simulations of noisy gain on real FS tuning curves show that multiplicative gain would be detectable at the FS cells' tuning correlations, and the FS data are best explained by additive gain.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells receive directionally uniform thalamic input, paragraph 4; Methods, Gain modulation analysis, simulations; Extended Data Fig. 8c,d
claims.quote: These simulations allowed us to establish that multiplicative gain is indeed detectable in tuning curves with correlation values similar to those observed experimentally in PoSub-FS cells and that our experimental results in PoSub-FS cells are best explained by significant additive gain
claims.criterion: Per the Methods and Duszkiewicz2024_Figure_GainSimulation.m. ArchT FS baseline curves; simulated high-gain curves with no gain, with multiplicative gain (times 1.2) or additive gain (plus 20% of the curve's maximum) before Gaussian noise titrated to the observed distribution of baseline-high-gain correlations; factors computed as for the data; each simulation's factor distributions against the control group's, Mann-Whitney U (n = 46 and 38). Reproduced when the multiplicative simulation's multiplicative factors differ from control (p < 0.05) and the additive simulation's factors match the data's pattern (additive differs, multiplicative does not). The noise seed is a standard choice.

claims.statement: ADN-HD cells show multiplicative factors like those of PoSub-HD cells and larger additive factors.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells receive directionally uniform thalamic input, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 8e,f
claims.quote: this high degree of multiplicative modulation largely reflected the modulation of the upstream ADN-HD cells
claims.criterion: Factors as in fig5e-hd-multiplicative-fs-additive. ADN-HD against PoSub-HD, Mann-Whitney U (multiplicative z = 0.55, additive z = 5.07; no p printed). Reproduced when the multiplicative factors do not differ (p of 0.05 or more, a claim of absence on the paper's test) and the additive factors do (p < 0.05, ADN higher, as the Extended Data Fig. 8 title says ADN-HD cells show a mixture of both).

claims.statement: GLM cross-coupling of PoSub-HD pairs, PoSub-FS pairs and PoSub-HD to PoSub-FS pairs is preserved between wakefulness and REM sleep, less for FS pairs than for HD pairs.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells are coupled to the PoSub-HD ring manifold, paragraph 2; Figure 6a-c
claims.quote: Similarly, PoSub-FS cell pairs also preserved their coupling across WAKE and REM, albeit to a smaller degree than PoSub-HD cell pairs (Fig. 6a-c , middle). Notably, the coupling of the two cell populations to each other was also preserved across WAKE and REM
claims.criterion: Sessions with at least 100 s of REM (Methods). GLM per the Methods and GetGLM_Forward.m and GetGLM_Reverse.m. Spike counts in 100 ms bins smoothed with a 100 ms s.d. Gaussian; the population rate (all units) smoothed alike and z-scored; cell B's train z-scored; Poisson GLM (log link) of cell A on population rate and cell B within WAKE (the square epoch) or REM; the coefficient at lag 0 averaged with the reversed pair's; pairs with fit warnings removed. Pearson correlation across pairs of WAKE against REM coefficients for HD-HD, FS-FS and HD-FS pairs (n = 34,270, 2,492 and 8,992; no r or p in the text). Reproduced when all three correlations are positive with p < 0.05 and the FS-FS r is below the HD-HD r. The HD-FS count is read as either ordering of the pair (code, both ordered sets) or one per pair; Extended Data Fig. 9d gives 18,992, so both counts are shown.

claims.statement: The polarity of the GLM coupling within a pair depends on the similarity of the two cells' HD tuning, during both WAKE and REM.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells are coupled to the PoSub-HD ring manifold, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 9d
claims.quote: Predictably, the polarity of the cross-coupling coefficient depended on the HD tuning relationship within each cell pair during both WAKE and REM
claims.criterion: As in Figure_GLMRemWake.m, Pearson correlation across pairs between the zero-lag tuning curve correlation and the lag-0 coupling coefficient, for HD-FS and FS-FS pairs, in WAKE and in REM (n = 18,992 and 2,492). Reproduced when all four correlations are positive with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: HD tuning curves of PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cells computed from the virtual HD of the WAKE ring manifold are equivalent to those computed from the real HD.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells are coupled to the PoSub-HD ring manifold, paragraph 3; Figure 7a,b; Extended Data Fig. 10e
claims.quote: The HD tuning curves of both PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cells computed using virtual HD values during WAKE were equivalent to those computed using real HD values
claims.criterion: Per the Methods (Visualization and analysis of the ring manifold). HD cell spikes over the whole square epoch in 200 ms bins, smoothed with a 400 ms s.d. Gaussian, square root; Isomap with 12 neighbours and 3 dimensions; virtual HD the four-quadrant arctangent of the first two dimensions, its direction chosen by the smaller circular variance of the difference from real HD, its origin by the mean offset of maximum cross-correlation over HD cells; real and virtual tuning curves in 1 degree bins, 3 degree smoothing, real HD downsampled to 200 ms. Zero-lag Pearson correlation of each cell's real and virtual curves against the time-reversed Isomap angle control, Wilcoxon signed-rank (HD n = 1,602, z = 34.7; FS n = 427, z = 17.9; no p printed). Reproduced when both give p < 0.05 with real correlations higher.

claims.statement: Population vectors of PoSub-HD cells lie on a ring during WAKE, farther from the centre of the manifold than shuffled vectors, and the ring has the same radius during REM.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 10b,d; Figure 7c legend
claims.quote: Distance of population vectors to the center of the manifold ( d ) is the same during WAKE and REM
claims.criterion: Per the Methods and the Isomap scripts, distance of each point to the manifold centre, normalized to the mean distance of the real projection; shuffles by shifting each cell's binned train by a random number of bins. Mean distance real against shuffled, Wilcoxon signed-rank across sessions (n = 32, z = 4.79), reproduced when p < 0.05 with real larger. REM against subsampled WAKE in the joint embedding is a claim of absence on the legend's Wilcoxon signed-rank (n = 26, z = 0.17), reproduced when p is 0.05 or more. The shuffle and subsampling seeds are standard choices.

claims.statement: During REM sleep the HD tuning of PoSub-HD and PoSub-FS cells can be estimated from the virtual HD of the ring manifold alone and matches their WAKE tuning.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells are coupled to the PoSub-HD ring manifold, paragraph 4; Figure 7c,d; Extended Data Fig. 10f
claims.quote: Notably, HD tuning of PoSub-FS cells could also be accurately estimated during REM based solely on the virtual HD obtained from the HD ring attractor manifold
claims.criterion: Sessions with at least 100 s of REM. WAKE population vectors randomly subsampled to the number of REM vectors, Isomap on both together, virtual HD as in fig7b-wake-isomap-tuning; tuning curves in 6 degree bins with 6 degree smoothing. Cells with REM rate above 0.5 Hz (HD) or above 10 Hz (FS), as Figure_IsomapREM.m selects them (expected n = 1,148 and 317). Zero-lag Pearson correlation of WAKE and REM curves against the time-reversed control, Wilcoxon signed-rank (HD z = 29.2, FS z = 10.4; no p printed). The WAKE curve is read as the WAKE Isomap curve (legend) and as the real-HD WAKE curve (the code's cc_WkRem); both are run. Reproduced when, under both readings, both tests give p < 0.05 with real correlations higher.

claims.statement: Along a Neuropixel probe crossing pRSC and PoSub, HD tuning of excitatory cells rises in a step at the functional border between the two regions.
claims.source: Results, High-density recordings in the PoSub of freely moving mice, paragraph 1; Figure 1a-c
claims.quote: We first established the functional border between PoSub and posterior retrosplenial cortex (pRSC) using a Neuropixel linear electrode array
claims.criterion: The paper reports no measure, test or border position for the step, and the code places no border. HD information of excitatory cells against probe depth, with the running average of Duszkiewicz2024_Figure_SingleRec_NPX.m (mean HD information in 50 um depth bins from 0 to -2.5 mm, empty bins interpolated, Gaussian smoothing of 2 bins s.d.). Reproduced when the running average rises in a single step from low values at the pRSC end of the probe to high values at the PoSub end, as Fig. 1b shows it; the profile is shown, and since no test is given the judgement is qualitative and is reported as such.

claims.statement: TRN sends denser inhibitory projections to ADN than to the other rostral thalamic nuclei.
claims.source: Results, PoSub-FS cells receive directionally uniform thalamic input, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 6
claims.quote: The ADN is strongly innervated by inhibitory afferents from the thalamic reticular nucleus
claims.criterion: Anatomy (ImageJ intensity of GFP in ROIs per nucleus) on images the paper does not deposit. Not testable from the dataset.

claims.statement: In the three sessions the monkeys performed 768, 824 and 745 trials (L, X, Y), of which 717, 788 and 688 were successful and 685, 752 and 637 were analyzed.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Table 2
claims.quote: during these sessions the monkeys performed from 745 to 824 total trials, of which from 688 to 798 were performed successfully, with from 637 to 752 trials being retained for analysis
claims.criterion: Counts per session from the trial records; analyzed trials are successful trials not preceded by an error trial (Methods, Behavioral Task). The text gives 798 as the largest success count and Table 2 gives 788 for monkey X; the table's 788 is used, and 798 is a second reading of that count. The exact counts are reported. Reproduced when all nine are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the analyzed counts are within tolerance and some other count is not.

claims.statement: The median duration from movement onset to contact differs among the monkeys (255, 235 and 335 ms for L, X and Y; Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.001), giving 52, 48 and 68 normalized samples from M to C.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Table 2
claims.quote: The duration of the epoch from movement onset to peripheral object contact, which we refer to as the reach-to-grasp epoch, differed among the three monkeys ... with medians ranging from 235 to 335 ms
claims.criterion: Movement time from onset (common methods, both readings) to contact, over the analyzed trials. The paper prints the bound as "P <10-3" with a garbled glyph; it is read as P < 0.001. Table 2's footnote does not say whether the median and quartiles are over analyzed or all successful trials; readings (a) analyzed trials, (b) all successful trials (the Fig. 5 legend speaks of "all successful trials"). Reproduced when, under one reading, the three medians are within tolerance and a Kruskal-Wallis test across monkeys gives p < 0.001. The sample counts follow from the medians at 200 Hz and are reported.

claims.statement: Monkey L successfully reached to, grasped and manipulated the coaxial cylinder at the 45 degree location in 28 trials of its session.
claims.source: Figure 2 legend; Results, Temporal Trajectories of Individual Joint Angles, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Each frame shows data from 28 successfully performed trials in which monkey L reached to, grasped, and manipulated the coaxial cylinder at the 45° location
claims.criterion: Analyzed trials (common methods) of session L20120928 with that object and location. The legend says "successfully performed"; readings (a) analyzed trials, (b) all successful trials. Reproduced when either count is within tolerance.

claims.statement: In monkey L's movements to the coaxial cylinder at 45 degrees, the distal forearm speed has a bell-shaped profile, ShoulderIER moves monophasically from one position to another, and ElbowFlex first increases and then decreases.
claims.source: Results, Temporal Trajectories of Individual Joint Angles, paragraph 2; Figure 2
claims.quote: although the speed of the distal forearm point showed the conventional bell-shaped profile, the trajectories of individual joint angles showed a variety of temporal patterns. Only ShoulderIER showed a monophasic transition from one angular position to another. The elbow flexion/extension (ElbowFlex) angle first increased and then decreased
claims.criterion: The trials of fig2-trial-count-coax-45, time-normalized (common methods), the mean trajectory over trials from M to C. The paper gives no measure for these shapes, so they are read as follows (open, a reading of the words). Bell-shaped is a single interior maximum of the mean distal forearm speed; the distal forearm point is the point 1.1 cm deep to the five distal forearm markers (Methods), and the mean of the five markers is a variant. Monophasic is a mean ShoulderIER whose derivative keeps one sign from M to C. ElbowFlex is read as a mean whose maximum lies inside the epoch with a rise before it and a fall after it. Reproduced when all three hold; partially reproduced when two hold.

claims.statement: In the same movements, the ThumbFlex, four MCP, ThumbMCP, IndexPIP, MiddlePIP, RingPIP and ThumbAbAd angles extend (decrease) first, pause or slightly reverse near the middle of the epoch, near the time of peak transport speed, then extend again, and keep extending, opening the hand, until just before contact.
claims.source: Results, Temporal Trajectories of Individual Joint Angles, paragraphs 2 and 3; Figure 2
claims.quote: All of these angles initially decreased (extended), paused or slightly reversed near the middle of the reach-to-grasp epoch, and then decreased again, apparently separating the time course of hand opening into two phases ... all of these latter joints continued to extend (decreasing values), opening the hand, until immediately prior to peripheral object contact
claims.criterion: The trials of fig2-trial-count-coax-45, the mean time-normalized trajectory of each of the ten angles the paper lists (ThumbFlex, the four MCP, ThumbMCP, IndexPIP, MiddlePIP, RingPIP and ThumbAbAd; LittlePIP is not in this list, the paper puts it with the angles that decrease, increase and decrease again). No measure is given, so the words are read as follows (open). A pause is a local minimum of the extension speed (the negative of the mean angle's derivative), or a reversal to positive derivative, between 25% and 75% of normalized time; its time is compared with that of peak distal forearm speed. Extension until just before contact is the mean angle's minimum lying at or after 80% of normalized time. Reproduced when both hold for at least 8 of the 10 angles; partially reproduced for 5 to 7.

claims.statement: For ArmPS in monkey L, the location effect rises until about midway between onset and contact and then declines to small but still significant values before contact; the object effect stays small until shortly before the midpoint and then rises until contact, when it accounts for almost all the variance; the interaction is significant but small throughout.
claims.source: Figure 4; Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 2
claims.quote: After movement onset (M), the main effect of location (red) increased until approximately midway between movement onset and peripheral object contact (C) and thereafter decreased, reaching small but still significant values prior to contact. In contrast, the main effect of object (blue) remained small until shortly before the midpoint and then rose progressively until contact, at which time the object effect accounted for almost all of the variance in ArmPS angle
claims.criterion: ANOVA effect sizes and significance as in the common methods, ArmPS, session L20120928, each sum of squares reading. "Approximately midway" and "almost all" are not given numbers; they are read as a location peak between 30% and 70% of normalized time, and an object eta2 at C of at least 0.9 (the default 10% tolerance on all of the variance, 1.0). Reproduced when, under every sum of squares reading, the location peak lies in that window, location eta2 at C is below its peak and significant, object eta2 at C is at least 0.9, object eta2 is below location eta2 at 30%, and the interaction eta2 is below both main effects at C and significant at some time from M to C. Partially reproduced when the order of the location peak and the object rise holds but a number does not. Readings that disagree make the claim blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Across the 22 angles in all three monkeys, the largest location effects are in the shoulder and wrist angles and the largest object effects in the digit angles.
claims.source: Figure 5; Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 3
claims.quote: As expected, the largest effects of location were found in proximal joints, appearing as prominent red traces in shoulder and wrist angles, while the largest effects of object were found in the joints of the hand
claims.criterion: ANOVA effect sizes from the common methods, each monkey. Reproduced when, in each monkey, the angle with the largest peak location eta2 from M to C is a shoulder or wrist angle (Table 1 groups Shoulder and Wrist), and the angle with the largest peak object eta2 is one of the 15 digit angles. The mean peak location eta2 over shoulder and wrist angles, and over digit angles, is reported, and likewise for object. Partially reproduced when this holds in two monkeys.

claims.statement: For a given angle, location and object effects both typically become significant early in the movement, close to movement onset, and evolve concurrently, with small but significant interaction effects.
claims.source: Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraphs 3 and 5; Figure 5
claims.quote: For any given joint angle, although location and object effects differed in magnitude, both typically attained significance early in the course of the present movements and evolved concurrently, with small but significant interaction effects (cyan traces) present as well
claims.criterion: ANOVA significance from the common methods. For each angle and monkey, the first normalized time at or after M where the location effect is significant, and the same for object and interaction. "Early" is not given a number; read as at or before 30% of normalized time, the paper's early sample point. Reproduced when, in each monkey, both location and object first become significant by 30% in more than half of the 22 angles ("typically"), and the interaction is significant at some time from M to C in more than half. Partially reproduced when this holds in two monkeys.

claims.statement: ShoulderIER is dominated by location effects with little or no object effect.
claims.source: Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 4; Figure 5
claims.quote: ShoulderIER was dominated by location effects with little or no object effect
claims.criterion: Qm of ShoulderIER (Eq. 2), each monkey. A Qm of 1 is a location effect with no object effect (Methods); the paper gives no bound for "little or no object effect", and it is read (a reading, not fixed by the paper) with the default 10% tolerance as Qm of at least 0.9. Reproduced when Qm is at least 0.9 at both the 30% and 90% points in all three monkeys, and partially reproduced when Qm exceeds 0.5 at both points in all three but is below 0.9 somewhere.

claims.statement: ShoulderAbAd and ShoulderFlex both have clear object effects, in some cases beginning early in the reach.
claims.source: Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 4; Figure 5
claims.quote: The other shoulder angles, ShoulderAbAd and ShoulderFlex, both had clear object effects, however, in some cases beginning quite ... early in the reach-to-grasp
claims.criterion: ANOVA significance from the common methods. "Quite early" is not given a number and is read as by 30% of normalized time, the paper's early sample point (a reading). Reproduced when the object effect of both angles is significant at some time from M to C in all three monkeys, and is significant by 30% of normalized time in at least one angle and monkey. Partially reproduced when the object effect is significant for both angles in two monkeys.

claims.statement: ElbowFlex shows little location effect and a large object effect in each of the three monkeys.
claims.source: Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 4; Figure 5; compare Discussion, Effects of Object on Proximal Joint Angles, paragraph 1
claims.quote: the ElbowFlex angle showed surprisingly little location effect and instead had a large object effect in each of the three monkeys
claims.criterion: ANOVA effect sizes from the common methods. The paper describes ElbowFlex in two ways, so two readings are listed. (a) The Results, object effect larger than location effect in each monkey, judged as mean object eta2 from M to C above mean location eta2 in all three. (b) The Discussion ("substantially larger than location effects in monkey L and similar in magnitude to location effects in monkeys X and Y"), judged as mean object eta2 above mean location eta2 in L, and the ratio of the two means between 0.5 and 2 in X and Y (the bounds of "similar" are a reading, not fixed by the paper). Fig. 6A's Qm of 0.55 and 0.54 at 90% in X and Y agrees with (b). Reproduced when either reading holds; the means and ratios are reported.

claims.statement: The wrist angles ArmPS, WristRU and WristFlex each have location and object effects of comparable magnitude.
claims.source: Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 4; Figure 5
claims.quote: The wrist angles, ArmPS, WristRU, and WristFE, each had location and object effects of comparable magnitude
claims.criterion: ANOVA effect sizes from the common methods; the text's WristFE is WristFlex. The paper gives no bound for "comparable"; it is read as a ratio of peak object eta2 to peak location eta2 from M to C between 0.5 and 2 (a reading, not fixed by the paper). Reproduced when this holds for the three wrist angles in all three monkeys; partially reproduced when it holds for at least 6 of the 9 angle-monkey pairs. The ratios are reported.

claims.statement: In all joint angles of the hand object effects predominate, with small location effects in some, particularly in monkey L; object effects in proximal joints are somewhat more marked than location effects in distal joints.
claims.source: Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 4; Figure 5
claims.quote: In all joint angles of the hand, object effects predominated. Nevertheless, small location effects were present in some, particularly in monkey L ... Overall, object effects in proximal joints were somewhat more marked than location effects in distal joints
claims.criterion: ANOVA effect sizes from the common methods; hand angles are the 15 digit angles. The paper gives no measure; predominate is read as peak object eta2 above peak location eta2 from M to C (a reading). The paper uses "proximal" both for shoulder and wrist (paragraph 3) and for shoulder and elbow as against the wrist and digits (paragraph 5), so proximal angles have two readings, (a) the four shoulder and elbow angles, (b) these and the three wrist angles; distal angles are the 15 digit angles in both. Reproduced when this holds for all 15 digit angles in all three monkeys, the mean over digit angles of peak location eta2 is largest in monkey L, and the mean peak object eta2 of the proximal angles exceeds the mean peak location eta2 of the 15 digit angles, pooled over monkeys, under either reading of proximal. Partially reproduced when the first part holds for at least 40 of the 45 angle-monkey pairs.

claims.statement: Location effects generally become large early in the movement and object effects later, typically peaking only in the second half; in the shoulder, location effects keep rising through the reach, while in the wrist and digits they rise, peak and decline as object effects increase.
claims.source: Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 5; Figure 5
claims.quote: location effects generally became large early in the course of these movements, while object effects generally became large later, typically reaching their maxima for a given joint only in the second half of the movements. In the shoulder joints, location effects typically continued to increase throughout the reach-to-grasp; but in the more distal joints of the wrist and digits, location effects typically rose initially, peaked, and then declined as the object effects increased
claims.criterion: ANOVA effect sizes from the common methods. For each angle and monkey, the normalized times of the location and object peaks from M to C. "Typically" is read as more than half of the angles. Reproduced when, in each monkey, (1) the object peak lies after 50% for more than half of the 22 angles, (2) the object peak is later than the location peak for more than half of the 22 angles, (3) the location peak lies after 90% for at least two of the three shoulder angles, and (4) the location peak lies before 90% and location eta2 at C is below the peak, for more than half of the 18 wrist and digit angles. "Typically", the 90% bound for "continued to increase" and "peaked, and then declined" are readings, not fixed by the paper. Partially reproduced when (1) and (2) hold in all monkeys and (3) or (4) fails.

claims.statement: Interaction effects, while often significant, are typically small; for no joint angle does the interaction effect account for more variance than either main effect.
claims.source: Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 6; Figure 5
claims.quote: Third, interaction effects, while often significant, typically were small. For no joint angle did the interaction effect account for more variance than either the location effect or the object effect
claims.criterion: ANOVA effect sizes from the common methods. The sentence allows two readings; the Discussion adds that rarely was an interaction larger than both main effects. (a) For every angle and monkey, the peak interaction eta2 from M to C is below the larger of the two peak main effects. (b) For every angle and monkey, at no sample from M to C is the interaction eta2 above both main effects at that sample. Reproduced when either reading holds for all 66 angle-monkey pairs; partially reproduced when it holds for at least 60. The number of pairs and samples where the interaction exceeds one or both main effects is reported.

claims.statement: At the 30% point Qm varies widely across angles, while at the 90% point only the three shoulder angles in each monkey, ElbowFlex in X and Y (0.55, 0.54) and WristRU in Y (0.56) have Qm above 0.5; all other angles have Qm below 0.5.
claims.source: Figure 6A; Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 7
claims.quote: Figure 6A shows that, at the 30% time point, different joint angles had a wide variety of Qm ratios, but by the 90% time point only a few joint angles, particularly all three shoulder angles in each of the three monkeys, had Qm ratios ... 0.55 and 0.54, respectively) and WristRU in monkey Y (0.56). At the 90% time point, all other joints had Qm ratios
claims.criterion: Qm (Eq. 2) at the 30% and 90% points (common methods), each sum of squares reading. Reproduced when, at 90%, the angles with Qm above 0.5 are exactly the nine shoulder angle-monkey pairs plus ElbowFlex in X and Y and WristRU in Y, the three values are within tolerance, and at 30% each monkey has Qm values on both sides of 0.5. Partially reproduced when the nine shoulder pairs are above 0.5 and at most three of the other 57 pairs fall on the other side of 0.5 from the paper. Readings that disagree make the claim blocked as methods_underspecified.
