claims.statement: Qx is below 0.4 for the large majority of angles at both 30% and 90%; at 30% only WristFlex and ThumbFlex in monkey X and ThumbFlex in monkey Y exceed 0.4, none in monkey L, and at 90% all are below 0.4.
claims.source: Figure 6B; Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 8
claims.quote: At the 30% time point, only monkey X showed Qx ratios ... in two joints angles, WristFlex and ThumbFlex, indicating substantial location ... object interactions early in the movement. In monkey Y only ThumbFlex had a large Qx. In monkey L no joint angles had a large Qx at the 30% time point. By the 90% time point, all Qx ratios were
claims.criterion: Qx (Eq. 3) at the 30% and 90% points (common methods), each sum of squares reading. Reproduced when the set of angle-monkey pairs with Qx above 0.4 at 30% is exactly WristFlex and ThumbFlex in X and ThumbFlex in Y, and no pair exceeds 0.4 at 90%. Partially reproduced when at most three of the 132 pair-time values fall on the other side of 0.4 from the paper. Readings that disagree make the claim blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Averaged over the 22 angles at the 30% point, location effects are as large as or larger than object effects (location/object/interaction, L 0.22/0.08/0.05, X 0.15/0.16/0.05, Y 0.12/0.11/0.04).
claims.source: Figure 7; Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 9
claims.quote: At the 30% time point, location effects were as large as, or somewhat larger than, object effects (location/object/ interaction: monkey L: 0.22/0.08/0.05; monkey X: 0.15/0.16/ 0.05; monkey Y: 0.12/0.11/0.04)
claims.criterion: Mean over the 22 angles of eta2 (Eq. 1) for each effect at the 30% point, under every sum of squares reading and both placements of the maximum SSError (common methods). The tolerance is the default 10%, tight for two-decimal values; the values printed to two decimals are compared after rounding. The sum of squares type and the SSError placement are method details the paper leaves open, so the outcome is the one all combinations give. Reproduced when all nine values are within tolerance under every combination; partially reproduced when, under every combination, location is at least object minus 0.01 in every monkey and some value misses tolerance. Combinations that give different outcomes make the claim blocked as methods_underspecified. The values under every combination are shown.

claims.statement: By the 90% point object effects are substantially larger on average than location effects in all three monkeys (location/object/interaction, L 0.12/0.52/0.07, X 0.13/0.44/0.04, Y 0.20/0.36/0.08).
claims.source: Figure 7; Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 9
claims.quote: By the 90% time point, still prior to contact with the object, object effects were substantially larger on average than location effects in all three monkeys (location/ object/interaction; monkey L: 0.12/0.52/0.07; monkey X: 0.13/ 0.44/0.04; monkey Y: 0.20/0.36/0.08)
claims.criterion: As fig7-mean-eta-30, at the 90% point. Reproduced when all nine values are within tolerance under every combination of readings; partially reproduced when, under every combination, mean object eta2 exceeds mean location eta2 in all three monkeys and some value misses tolerance. Combinations that give different outcomes make the claim blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Averaged over angles, location and object effects begin to appear at about the same time; after the 30% point object effects grow more than location effects, which decline somewhat in L and X and stay about constant in Y; the proportions stay about constant after contact; interaction effects stay small.
claims.source: Figure 7; Results, Effects of Location and Object on Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 9
claims.quote: Main effects of location and of object began to appear at approximately the same time on average ... Thereafter, object effects grew more than location effects, which actually declined somewhat in monkeys L and X, although remaining relatively constant in monkey Y ... The ratio of location, object, and interaction effects then remained relatively constant after peripheral object contact
claims.criterion: Mean eta2 over the 22 angles as a function of normalized time (common methods). The paper gives no measure for these words; they are read as follows (open). Begin to appear is the first sample at or after M where the mean exceeds 0.05; the two times are compared, and "approximately the same" is a difference of at most 10% of normalized time. Growth from 30% to 90% is larger for object than location in each monkey. Location at 90% is below location at 30% in L and X, and not below it in Y (the paper's own values for Y rise from 0.12 to 0.20, so "relatively constant" is read as not declining). Constant after contact is Qm of the mean eta2 values staying within 0.1 of its value at C over the samples after C. The interaction mean is below both main effect means from 30% to C. Reproduced when all parts hold in all monkeys; partially reproduced when the growth part holds and another fails.

claims.statement: Location given the object is best predicted by shoulder angles, which reach nearly 100% before contact, then by wrist angles, which match shoulder angles early but fall below them by the midpoint; digit angle groups exceed chance early, become less accurate than proximal groups shortly after onset, and still carry some location information just before contact.
claims.source: Figure 8A; Results, LDA of Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 2
claims.quote: In predicting location, shoulder joint angles (blue) were easily dissociated for different locations of a given object, reaching nearly 100% correct before peripheral object contact. Wrist angles (red) were next most strongly predictive of location. In the first part of the movements, wrist angles predicted location as accurately as shoulder angles in all three monkeys ... Nevertheless, note that just prior to peripheral object contact (C), wrist joints and even digit joints still had some degree of discriminable information on location
claims.criterion: LDA of location given object, from the common methods, each prior and interval reading. Nearly 100% is read with the default 10% tolerance as at least 90% correct; "the first part of the movements" as the 30% point and "by the temporal midpoint" as the 50% point (readings, not fixed by the paper). In each monkey, (1) shoulder accuracy at least 90% at some sample from 90% to C; (2) the mean accuracy over the samples from 50% to C orders shoulder above wrist, and wrist above each digit group; (3) the shoulder and wrist 95% intervals overlap at the 30% point and wrist upper bound is below shoulder accuracy at the 50% point; (4) each digit group's interval lower bound is above chance at the 30% point and at the 90% point; chance is the mean of 1/(locations available) over objects. Reproduced when all parts hold in all three monkeys under every reading; partially reproduced when (1) and (2) hold in all monkeys. Readings that disagree make the claim blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Object given the location is predicted similarly by all five angle groups, each reaching near 100% correct before contact in all three monkeys, including the shoulder angles.
claims.source: Figure 8B; Results, LDA of Joint Angles as a Function of Time, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In all three monkeys, all five joint-angle groups reached levels of object prediction close to 100% correct prior to peripheral object contact
claims.criterion: LDA of object given location, from the common methods, each prior and interval reading. Close to 100% is read with the default 10% tolerance as at least 90% correct. Reproduced when each of the five groups reaches at least 90% at some sample from 90% of normalized time to C, in all three monkeys, under every reading; partially reproduced when this holds for at least 12 of the 15 group-monkey pairs. Readings that disagree make the claim blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: At the 90% point in monkey L, index finger flexion varies modestly with location for the perpendicular and coaxial cylinders but little for the button and sphere, and hand configuration varies more with object than with location.
claims.source: Figure 9; Results, Hand Configurations and Reach Trajectories, paragraphs 1 and 2
claims.quote: Modest variation in the degree of index finger flexion is evident depending on location for the perpendicular and coaxial cylinders, but relatively little if any variation in index finger flexion was present for the button or sphere ... A modest degree of locationdependent variation in hand configuration again can be appreciated, although more variation in hand configuration depended on object
claims.criterion: As in Fig. 9 (legend and Results), session L20120928, the 90% point, marker positions averaged over successful trials of each location-object combination, translated and rotated to co-register the five hand markers. The paper gives no measure of spread; the following is a reading (open). Location spread per object is the mean distance of the four index finger markers' combination means from their mean over locations; object spread per location likewise over objects, using all 20 digit markers, compared with location spread using all 20 digit markers. Reproduced when index location spread is larger for each cylinder than for each of button and sphere, and mean object spread exceeds mean location spread. Partially reproduced when one of the two holds. If the dataset holds joint angles and not markers, the across-location SD of mean IndexMCP and IndexPIP per object is used instead, as a variant.

claims.statement: Distal forearm point trajectories vary mainly with location, but at a given location they also depend on the object from early in the reach, with little overlap between objects by the end; at contact the point is typically highest for the sphere, intermediate for the coaxial cylinder and lowest for the button.
claims.source: Figure 10; Results, Hand Configurations and Reach Trajectories, paragraphs 3 and 4; Discussion, Effects of Object on Proximal Joint Angles, paragraph 1
claims.quote: At any given location, however, the trajectory of the distal forearm point through space depended to some extent on the object to which the hand was being transported, beginning quite early in the reach ... by the time of peripheral object contact, the distal forearm point typically was positioned highest for the sphere (orange), intermediate for the coaxial cylinder (cyan), and lowest for the button (violet) at any of the locations sampled
claims.criterion: Distal forearm point from the distal forearm markers in earth-fixed coordinates (as the Results say), successful trials, normalized time. Fig. 10 does not name the monkey; readings (a) monkey L (as Figs. 3 and 9), (b) each monkey. The paper gives no measure here (its quantitative support is Fig. 8B); the following is a reading (open). The LDA of object given location of the common methods, run on the point's three coordinates; reproduced when its accuracy interval lower bound exceeds chance by the 30% point and accuracy reaches at least 90% at C, and the mean up coordinate at C is ordered sphere above coaxial cylinder above button at more than half of the locations where all three were presented. Partially reproduced when one of these holds. Under reading (b) the result per monkey is reported and the claim judged on L.

claims.statement: The elbow point trajectory, set by shoulder rotation alone, also varies mainly with location and to some extent with object from early in the reach.
claims.source: Results, Hand Configurations and Reach Trajectories, paragraph 4 (plots not illustrated)
claims.quote: These plots likewise demonstrated variation depending primarily on location, but also depending to some extent on the object, beginning early in the reach
claims.criterion: The elbow point estimated as in the Methods (from the three upper arm and three proximal forearm markers, 1.7 cm deep), the same reading and measure as fig10-forearm-trajectory-object, without the vertical ordering, and with a location LDA given object on the same coordinates. "Primarily on location" is read (a reading, the paper gives no measure) as the comparison of accuracies above chance below. Reproduced when object classification given location exceeds chance by the 30% point and, at C, location accuracy given object minus its chance level exceeds object accuracy given location minus its chance level. The monkey is not named; judged on L with the others reported.

claims.statement: Late in the reach, location-dependent differences in hand shape are minor compared with object-dependent differences in distal forearm position, as the lower accuracy of predicting location from digit angles compared with the high accuracy of predicting object from shoulder angles confirms; grasp shape is comparatively invariant to location.
claims.source: Discussion, Effects of Location on Distal Joint Angles, paragraph 2; Figure 8; Abstract
claims.quote: The late location-dependent differences in hand shape (Fig. 9) overall seemed relatively minor compared with the objectdependent differences in distal forearm position (Fig. 10). This impression was confirmed by the lower prediction accuracies of location from digit joint angles compared with the high prediction accuracy of object from shoulder joint angles (Fig. 8)
claims.criterion: LDA from the common methods, each prior and interval reading. The paper compares percent correct and does not name the time; "late" is read as the 90% point (the time of Fig. 9) and as C, two readings of the text. Reproduced when, in each monkey, the object accuracy given location from shoulder angles exceeds the location accuracy given object from each of the three digit groups, at the 90% point or at C; partially reproduced when this holds in two monkeys. Accuracy above chance for each is reported as well. Prior and interval readings that disagree make the claim blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Of 1881 MEC neurons recorded in nine mice, 103 were classified as grid cells from their open arena firing, 11.4 +- 17.4 grid cells per mouse, 0.4 to 9.5% of each mouse's neurons.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Supplementary file 1
claims.quote: we identified 103/1881 neurons as grid cells (11.4±17.4 grid cells/mouse, range 0.4–9.5%, Supplementary file 1 )
claims.criterion: Units and grid cells as in the opening comment (Methods, Spike sorting and Analysis of neural activity in the open arena; exclusions from vr_grid_population_level_plots.py). The counts are matched within tolerance; the per-mouse range holds inside 0.36 to 10.45%. The preprocessing repo's classification (grid score and spatial information above mean + 2.326 SD of the shuffles) is shown as a variant. Whether grid cells are counted once per session or once per recording day is not said; the paper counts units per session (Supplementary file 1 gives 1881 cells over 215 sessions), and that is the reading used.

claims.statement: Per mouse, the numbers of cells, sessions, trials per session and grid cells are as in Supplementary file 1, in total 1881 cells and 215 sessions, with most grid cells from M11 (53) and M14 (26).
claims.source: Supplementary file 1
claims.criterion: Cells, sessions and grid cells per mouse counted as in grid-cell-count. Reproduced when the listed totals are within tolerance and, for each of the nine mice, the number of sessions is within 10% of the table (M1 11, M3 26, M6 21, M7 23, M10 16, M11 35, M12 21, M13 25, M14 37).

claims.statement: Grid cells had field sizes of 7.5 +- 3.3 cm and grid spacing of 72.5 +- 13.7 cm.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1
claims.quote: These grid cells had field sizes of 7.5±3.3 cm and grid spacing of 72.5±13.7 cm
claims.criterion: The Methods do not define field size or grid spacing. The preprocessing repo (PostSorting/open_field_grid_cells.py) fixes them; grid spacing is the median distance from the autocorrelogram centre to the six ring fields times the bin size, and field size is sqrt(area of the central autocorrelogram field in bins x bin size) / pi. That is used. Means over the 103 grid cells (grid-cell-count), matched within tolerance; the SDs are reported.

claims.statement: At the session level, 68 of 103 grid cells had periodogram peaks within 0.05 of an integer spatial frequency (task-anchored), 32 had peaks elsewhere (task-independent) and 3 had no peak above the false alarm threshold (aperiodic), over 61 sessions with 233 +- 135 trials per session.
claims.source: Results, Grid cells exhibit either task-anchored or task-independent firing, paragraph 2; Figure 2D-E
claims.quote: We found that 68 of 103 grid cells had peaks in their periodograms within 5% of an integer multiple of the spatial frequency of the track repetition ... By contrast, 32 of 103 grid cells had periodograms with peaks at frequencies outside 5% ... were rare (3/103)
claims.criterion: Session-level class as in the opening comment (Methods; vr_grid_cells.get_lomb_classifier with the field shuffle threshold). The counts are matched within tolerance (the 10% rule makes the aperiodic count exact; it is reproduced at 3 and the count is reported otherwise). The false alarm threshold uses random shuffles; the counts are shown for the run made.

claims.statement: Among non-grid cells, the proportion with session-level task-anchored firing was similar to that of grid cells, task-independent periodic firing was rarer and aperiodic firing was more common.
claims.source: Results, Grid cells exhibit either task-anchored or task-independent firing, paragraph 2; Figure 2E
claims.quote: When we carried out similar analyses for non-grid cells, we found that the proportion of neurons with task-anchored firing was similar, but task-independent periodic firing was rarer, while aperiodic firing neurons were more common
claims.criterion: Session-level classes for grid (G) and non-grid (NG) cells as in fig2-session-level-classes. The paper reports no test. "Rarer" and "more common" are judged by direction, NG TI percentage below G and NG aperiodic percentage above G. The paper does not fix how "similar" is judged; the readings are (a) the G against NG difference in TA percentage is smaller in absolute value than both the TI and the aperiodic differences, (b) a two-sided Fisher exact test of TA against other classes between G and NG is not significant at 0.05. Reproduced when both directions hold and "similar" holds under both readings; if the readings disagree the claim is methods_underspecified. Percentages are reported.

claims.statement: Session-level task-anchored grid cells had higher spatial information scores on the track than task-independent grid cells.
claims.source: Figure 2F; Results, Grid cells exhibit either task-anchored or task-independent firing, paragraph 3
claims.quote: These differences manifest as substantially higher spatial information scores, but similar average firing rates, for grid cells with session-level task-anchored firing compared with task-independent firing
claims.criterion: Per grid cell, spatial information (bits/s) of the whole-session track rate map. As CompareGroups.Rmd does, lmer(log(SI) ~ class + (1 | mouse/session)) compared with the null model by anova, then emmeans pairs (default Tukey adjustment). Reproduced when the class effect has p < 0.05 and the TAG against TIG contrast is significant at 0.05 with TAG higher.

claims.statement: Mean firing rates on the track did not differ between session-level task-anchored and task-independent grid cells.
claims.source: Figure 2F; Results, Grid cells exhibit either task-anchored or task-independent firing, paragraph 3
claims.quote: These differences manifest as substantially higher spatial information scores, but similar average firing rates
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test as in CompareGroups.Rmd, lmer(log(mean track rate) ~ class + (1 | mouse/session)) and the emmeans TAG against TIG contrast (Tukey adjusted). Reproduced when that contrast has p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The ratio of group means is reported either way.

claims.statement: Periodogram peak power and peak width did not differ between task-anchored and task-independent grid cells.
claims.source: Figure 2F; Results, Grid cells exhibit either task-anchored or task-independent firing, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Features of the periodogram such as peak power and peak width did not differ between task-anchored grid cells and task-independent grid cells
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests as in CompareGroups.Rmd, lmer(peak power ~ class + (1 | mouse/session)) untransformed and lmer(log(peak width) ~ class + (1 | mouse/session)), each with the emmeans TAG against TIG contrast. Peak width is not defined in the Methods; the code (add_peak_width in vr_grid_population_level_plots.py) is followed. Reproduced when both contrasts have p >= 0.05; not reproduced when either has p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Aperiodic grid cells had much lower mean firing rates than task-anchored or task-independent grid cells, suggesting their lack of periodicity reflects inactivity.
claims.source: Figure 2F; Results, Grid cells exhibit either task-anchored or task-independent firing, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The aperiodic grid cells had much lower mean firing rates than the task-anchored grid or task-independent grid cells suggesting that their apparent lack of periodicity reflects inactivity
claims.criterion: As in fig2f-firing-rate-similar (CompareGroups.Rmd). Reproduced when the class effect has p < 0.05 and both the TAG against AG and TIG against AG contrasts are significant at 0.05 with AG lower; partially reproduced when only one contrast is.

claims.statement: For 26.2% of grid cells (27/103) the trial-level classification was consistently task-anchored or task-independent on more than 85% of trials, whereas for 73.8% (76/103) no single coding scheme accounted for more than 85% of trials.
claims.source: Results, Grid cells switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing, paragraph 2; Figure 3F
claims.quote: For 26.2% of grid cells (27/103) the classification was consistently (>85% of trials) task-anchored or task-independent ( Figure 3F ), whereas for 73.8% of grid cells (76/103) no single coding scheme accounted for more than 85% of trials
claims.criterion: Trial-level classes as in the opening comment. The paper's text leaves two choices open, and all four combinations are run. The proportion is either (a) of rolling windows, as add_rolling_stats computes it, with the code's >= 0.85, or (b) of trial labels with > 0.85, as the text says. The stable modes are either (i) TA or TI, as the first sentence says, or (ii) TA, TI or aperiodic, as "no single coding scheme" and Figure 3-figure supplement 4 allow. Reproduced when the counts are within tolerance under any combination.

claims.statement: Grid cells classified as task-anchored at the session level were biased towards high proportions of task-anchored trials, and session-level task-independent cells towards high proportions of task-independent trials, though many varied between trials.
claims.source: Results, Grid cells switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing, paragraph 2; Figure 3F
claims.quote: Grid cells identified as having task-anchored firing in our initial session-level analysis ( Figure 2 ) were biassed towards high proportions of task-anchored trials
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test. Proportions of a session in each mode under readings (a) windows and (b) trials, as in fig3f-switching-within-session. Reproduced when, under both readings, the median TA proportion of TAG cells exceeds that of TIG cells and the median TI proportion of TIG cells exceeds that of TAG cells. The medians and histograms are reported.

claims.statement: Within grid cells, spatial information was higher on trials classified as task-anchored than on trials classified as task-independent.
claims.source: Figure 3G; Results, Grid cells switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing, paragraph 3
claims.quote: This difference was associated with substantially lower spatial information scores for trials with task-independent firing, while mean firing rates were similar
claims.criterion: For each grid cell, spatial information (bits/s) over TA trials and over TI trials, with the larger set randomly subsampled to the size of the smaller (Methods, Analysis of neural activity during the location memory task). The code (add_spatial_information_during_position_and_distance_trials) draws the trial numbers from the rolling window centres, so a trial can be drawn more than once; the Methods' trial labels are the main reading and the code a variant. As Compare_by_trial.Rmd does, lmer(log(SI) ~ mode + (1 | mouse/session)) against the null model by anova. Reproduced when p < 0.05 with SI higher on TA trials.

claims.statement: Mean firing rates of grid cells were similar on task-anchored and task-independent trials.
claims.source: Figure 3G
claims.quote: whereas the average firing rate was similar between task-anchored and task-independent trials (right)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test as in Compare_by_trial.Rmd, lmer(log(rate) ~ mode + (1 | mouse/session)) against the null model, with the same trial subsets as fig3g-trial-spatial-information. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The ratio of means is reported.

claims.statement: Grouping grid cells by a stable mode over trials (more than 85%), stable task-anchored cells had higher spatial information than stable task-independent cells while mean firing rates did not differ, as with the session-level grouping.
claims.source: Figure 3-figure supplement 4A-B; Results, Grid cells switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Conclusions from this analysis are similar to those of Figure 2F
claims.criterion: As CompareGroups_StableCats.Rmd does, cells with a TA proportion > 0.85 form TA, with a TI proportion > 0.85 form TI. The proportion is of trial labels, as the legend says (">85% of trials"); the code's proportion of rolling windows is a variant and is shown. The third group is open. The legend reads it as stable aperiodic cells, while the code puts every other grid cell in it ("None"); both are run. lmer(log(SI) ~ group + (1 | mouse/session)) and lmer(log(rate) ~ group + (1 | mouse/session)), emmeans pairs. Reproduced when, under both third-group readings, the SI TA against TI contrast is significant at 0.05 with TA higher and the firing rate contrast has p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Grid cells spent more of a session in task-independent periodic firing than non-grid cells; the distributions of task-anchored, task-independent and aperiodic epochs differed between grid and non-grid cells.
claims.source: Figure 3-figure supplement 5B; Results, Grid cells switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing, paragraph 2
claims.quote: For non-grid cells, consistent with session-level analyses, we again found that a sub-population showed task-anchored firing at a trial level, while task-independent periodic firing was substantially less common than in the grid cell population
claims.criterion: Per cell, the proportion of the session in each mode, under readings (a) windows (the code's rolling:proportion_encoding columns, which plot_proportion_of_session_encoding_mode plots) and (b) trial labels. Two-sample KS tests (scipy ks_2samp) of grid against non-grid cells per mode. No code was found for this test. Reproduced when, under a reading, the TI test has p < 0.05 with grid cells higher and the other two tests also have p < 0.05; partially reproduced when only the TI test does.

claims.statement: Periods of task-anchored or task-independent firing extended in blocks across multiple trials, with a distribution of block lengths that differed from that of trial-shuffled data.
claims.source: Figure 3-figure supplement 6B; Results, Grid cells switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing, paragraph 3
claims.quote: among all grid cells periods of task-anchored or task-independent firing extended in blocks across multiple trials, with the distribution of block lengths substantially different to that generated by shuffled data
claims.criterion: As vr_grid_cells.add_rolling_stats_shuffled_test and get_block_lengths_any_code do, per grid cell, runs of identical rolling window classes, excluding aperiodic runs, with lengths divided by the number of windows in the session; shuffled data reorder the trials of the rate map once per cell, recompute the periodograms and classify with the same adjusted threshold. KS test of pooled data against pooled shuffled block lengths (plot_rolling_lomb_block_lengths_vs_shuffled). Reproduced when p < 0.05 and the data have fewer blocks than the shuffled data (longer blocks). The shuffle is random; the result of the run made is reported.

claims.statement: The percentage of beaconed trials in a session did not affect how often grid cells showed task-anchored coding.
claims.source: Figure 3-figure supplement 7B
claims.quote: The percentage of beaconed trials did not have a significant effect on the occurrence of task-anchored coding
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test as the legend gives it, binomial GLMMs (logit) with and without percentage of beaconed trials as a fixed effect, random effects of mouse, session and neuron, compared by likelihood ratio. No code for it is in the repository. The response is not stated. The readings are (a) per trial, TA (1) against any other class (0), and (b) per trial, TA against TI with aperiodic trials dropped. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 under the reading run; if the readings give different outcomes the claim is methods_underspecified. The fitted slope is reported.

claims.statement: Simultaneously recorded grid cells agreed strongly in their trial-by-trial firing mode, with agreement greater between grid cell pairs than between pairs involving non-grid cells, whose agreement was more variable and lower on average.
claims.source: Figure 4D-E; Results, Grid cells switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Agreement was greater between grid cell pairs than between pairs involving non-grid cells
claims.criterion: Agreement of a cell pair is the fraction of trials with the same trial-level class, over each unordered pair of cells in a session, aperiodic trials included (Methods; generate_agreement_dataframe). The pairwise contrasts have the denominator degrees of freedom of the agreement_analysis.Rmd model on differences, lmerTest lmer(diff ~ comp + (1 | mouse/session)) with emmeans, where diff is a pair's agreement minus the mean of its 10 shuffled agreements. The shuffle splits the trial classes of one cell into runs and reorders them at random. That model is the main reading, and the notebook's lmer on raw agreement is a variant. The printed T values are all negative although G-G is reported higher, so the sign is taken from the text. Reproduced when the G-G estimate exceeds both NG-NG and G-NG with p < 0.05 for both contrasts.

claims.statement: For grid-grid, non-grid-non-grid and grid-non-grid pairs, agreement in firing mode differed from that of shuffled trial classifications.
claims.source: Figure 4E legend
claims.quote: Agreement in the firing mode between each combination of grid (G) and non-grid (NG) cells and corresponding scores for the shuffled data (lower), and the difference between the shuffled and actual scores
claims.criterion: As agreement_analysis.Rmd (mod_fit) does, per pair type, glmmTMB beta models of agreement with and without a shuffled (0/1) fixed effect, pairs with agreement exactly 0 or 1 dropped, compared by anova. The notebook fits two random-effect structures, which are the two readings. They are (a) session nested in mouse and (b) cell j nested in cell i nested in session nested in mouse; the Methods do not say which was reported. Reproduced when all three pair types have p < 0.05 under both readings; if the readings differ the claim is methods_underspecified. The direction of each difference (data against shuffled) is reported.

claims.statement: The drop in spatial information when the grid population was task-independent, relative to when it was task-anchored, was greater for grid cells than for non-grid cells, which kept similar spatial information.
claims.source: Figure 4F; Results, Grid cells switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Non-grid cells also differed from the grid cell population in that their activity maintained similar spatial information between trials when grid cells were task-anchored versus when they were task-independent
claims.criterion: In each session with grid cells, the grid consensus class per trial is the mode of the grid cells' trial classes. With two disagreeing cells, the Methods pick one at random; the code (add_spatial_imformation_during_dominant_modes) takes scipy's mode, which resolves ties to task-anchored; the Methods are the main reading and the code a variant. Equal numbers of consensus TA and TI trials are drawn at random, and spatial information is computed for every cell on each set. The measure is diff = (SI_TA - SI_TI) / SI_TA. As GridvsNonGrid.Rmd does, lmer(diff ~ grid_cell + (1 | mouse/session)) against the null model, and emmeans of each group tested against zero. Reproduced when the group effect has p < 0.05, the grid mean is above zero with p < 0.05, and the non-grid mean has p >= 0.05 against zero.

claims.statement: In sessions with stable grid codes, the proportion of hit trials on cued (beaconed) trials was similar whether grid firing was task-anchored or task-independent.
claims.source: Figure 6B; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 2
claims.quote: On cued trials the spatial organisation of stopping behaviour ( Figures 5C vs D and 6A ) and the proportion of hit trials ( Figure 6B ) was similar for both groups
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Stable sessions are those with a grid cell having one mode, TA or TI, on > 85% of its trials (Figure 6 legend); the code's >= 0.85 of rolling windows (generate_long_form_for_R_by_session) is a variant and is shown. One cell represents a session (drop_duplicate_sessions keeps the first in table order, which sets the class of a session holding both a stable TA and a stable TI cell; both assignments are shown if such a session exists). Trials are those not rejected; hit = 1, try and run = 0. As behaviour_analysis_grid_cells_stable_sessions.Rmd does, glmer(hit ~ class + (1 | mouse/session) + (0 + class | mouse/session), binomial logit, bobyqa) against the null model on beaconed trials. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. Hit percentages per class are reported (per session, then averaged over mice, as Figure 6B plots).

claims.statement: In sessions with stable grid codes, the proportion of hit trials on non-beaconed and probe trials was substantially reduced when grid firing was task-independent.
claims.source: Figure 6B; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 2
claims.quote: while the proportion of hit trials was substantially reduced ( Figure 6B )
claims.criterion: Sessions, trials and model as in fig6b-stable-beaconed-similar, fitted to non-beaconed and probe trials separately. Reproduced when both have p < 0.05 with the TI hit proportion lower; partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: In sessions with stable grid codes, stopping on non-beaconed and probe trials was spatially organised around the reward zone when grid activity was task-anchored, but largely not when it was task-independent; on cued trials it was similar in both.
claims.source: Figure 6A; Figure 5C-D; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 2
claims.quote: on non-beaconed and probe trials stopping behaviour was clearly spatial when grid activity was task-anchored, but spatial organisation was largely absent when grid activity was task-independent
claims.criterion: Stable sessions as in fig6b-stable-beaconed-similar (trial reading main, window reading a variant), one cell per session within each class as plot_stop_histogram_for_stable_cells_averaged_over_cells selects them, stop density relative to the uniform shuffled baseline per session (Methods; SD 1 cm smoothing, the code's 2 bins as a variant), averaged over sessions with SEM. The paper gives no measure of "spatial". The readings are (a) the mean baseline-subtracted density in the reward zone (90 to 110 cm) is above zero by more than its SEM across sessions, (b) the maximum of the averaged profile between 30 and 170 cm lies in the reward zone. Reproduced when, under both readings, non-beaconed and probe trials are spatial for TA and not for TI, and beaconed trials are spatial for both. If the readings differ the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Over all sessions, at the trial level, the proportion of hits on beaconed trials was similar whether grid cells were task-anchored or task-independent.
claims.source: Figure 6D; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: On cued trials the spatial organisation of stopping behaviour ( Figures 5E–F – 6C ), and the proportion of hit trials ( Figure 6D ), was similar irrespective of whether grid cell fields were task-anchored or task-independent
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. One row per grid cell and trial; rejected trials and trials classed aperiodic or unclassified dropped; hit = 1, try and run = 0. As behaviour_analysis_grid_cells.Rmd does, glmer(hit ~ class + (1 | mouse/session/cell) + (0 + class | mouse/session/cell), binomial logit, bobyqa) against the null model, beaconed trials. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. Hit percentages per class are reported, per cell then averaged over sessions and mice as plot_percentage_hits_for_remapped_encoding_cells_averaged_over_cells does.

claims.statement: Over all sessions, at the trial level, the proportion of hits on non-beaconed trials was reduced when grid firing was task-independent.
claims.source: Figure 6D; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: and the proportion of successful trials was reduced compared with when grid firing was task-anchored ( Figure 6D )
claims.criterion: Model as in fig6d-epochs-beaconed-similar, non-beaconed trials. Reproduced when p < 0.05 with the TA coefficient positive (more hits when task-anchored).

claims.statement: On probe trials the proportion of hits was lower when grid firing was task-independent, though the paper's test for probe trials was not significant.
claims.source: Figure 6D; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: On average, spatial stopping behaviour was reduced on non-beaconed and probe trials during which grid firing was task-independent ( Figure 6C ), and the proportion of successful trials was reduced
claims.criterion: Model as in fig6d-epochs-beaconed-similar, probe trials. The text states a reduction and the legend's test is not significant, so the claim is judged on direction. Reproduced when the mean hit percentage for TI is below that for TA (per cell, then session, then mouse, as the figure code averages) and the GLMM coefficient for TA is positive. The p-value is reported.

claims.statement: Over all sessions, spatial stopping on non-beaconed and probe trials was reduced on trials when grid firing was task-independent, while on cued trials it was similar.
claims.source: Figure 6C; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: On average, spatial stopping behaviour was reduced on non-beaconed and probe trials during which grid firing was task-independent ( Figure 6C )
claims.criterion: Per grid cell, baseline-subtracted stop density over its TA trials and over its TI trials (rejected trials dropped), averaged across cells with weights equal to the cell's fraction of trials in that mode times 1 / (grid cells in its session) (Methods, Analysis of behaviour; get_session_weights). The readings for "spatial" are those of fig6a-stable-stop-density, and "reduced" means the TA reward zone mean exceeds the TI mean. Reproduced when, under both readings, non-beaconed and probe trials show TI below TA and beaconed trials are spatial for both. If the readings differ the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Task-anchored firing occurred on a greater proportion of non-beaconed and probe hit trials than task-independent firing, but on a smaller proportion of run trials.
claims.source: Figure 6E; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 4
claims.quote: task-anchored firing occurred on a greater proportion of non-beaconed and probe trials that were hits compared with task-independent firing, but on a smaller proportion of run trials
claims.criterion: Per grid cell and outcome (hit, try, run), the percentage of that outcome's trials that are TA among TA and TI trials, averaged with weights (fraction of the trial type's trials with that outcome) x 1 / (grid cells in the session), over cells having all three outcomes (get_percentage_from_rolling_classifier_column). As behaviour_analysis_hit_try_run.Rmd does, glmer(TA ~ outcome + (1 | mouse/session/cell) + (0 + outcome | mouse/session/cell), binomial) against the null model per trial type. Reproduced when, for non-beaconed and probe trials, the weighted TA percentage is above 50% for hits and below 50% for runs, and the non-beaconed model has p < 0.05. Hit, try and run follow the Methods (95th percentile of hit trials' reward zone speeds); the code's 95% normal interval (add_hit_miss_try) is a variant and is shown.

claims.statement: The odds ratio for reward on task-anchored relative to task-independent trials was close to 1 when cues were available but much larger without cues.
claims.source: Figure 6F; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 4
claims.quote: the odds ratio for receipt of reward on task-anchored versus task-independent trials was close to 1 when cues were available, but was much larger in the absence of cues
claims.criterion: Odds ratios and their p-values from the full models of fig6d (exponentiated fixed effect of task-anchored against task-independent, as sjPlot tab_model reports, Wald p) per trial type (Methods, Statistical analyses). The odds ratio values appear only in the figure, which was not available. Reproduced when the non-beaconed odds ratio is above 1 with p < 0.05 and is larger than the beaconed odds ratio, and the beaconed p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: The differences in outcome between task-anchored and task-independent trials were not associated with differences in running speed profiles.
claims.source: Figure 6-figure supplement 1B; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The differences in outcomes between task-anchored versus task-independent trials were not associated with differences in running speed profiles
claims.criterion: Speed in 1 cm bins per trial, Gaussian SD 2 cm (Methods), per trial type and outcome, split by the grid cell's trial class, with trials used once per simultaneously recorded grid cell (legend; plot_speed_profiles_between_p_and_d_groups). The paper reports no test. It plots the mean with SD across trials, and that is the reading here. Reproduced when, for every trial type and outcome with both classes present, the TA mean profile lies within the TI mean +- 1 SD over the track and the TI mean lies within the TA mean +- 1 SD.

claims.statement: Classifying trials by correlation with a template of task-anchored firing also gave similar performance on cued trials but impaired performance on uncued trials when grid cells were not task-anchored.
claims.source: Figure 6-figure supplement 2F-H; Results, Task-anchored coding by grid cells is selectively associated with successful path integration-dependent reward localisation, paragraph 4
claims.quote: also indicated a similar behavioural performance on cued trials, but impaired performance on uncued trials when grid cells were in a task-independent mode
claims.criterion: Template is the mean smoothed rate map over the cell's Lomb-Scargle TA trials; each trial's Pearson correlation with it at >= 0.5 is TA+, otherwise TA- (Methods; add_rolling_stats_by_trial_number_using_alternative_classification, add_alternative_classification). The Methods discard units with < 15% TA trials; the code instead labels all their trials TA- and keeps them, a variant. Aperiodic trials are dropped. Model as behaviour_analysis_grid_cells_altmethod.Rmd, as in fig6d-epochs-beaconed-similar with the TA+/TA- class. Reproduced when beaconed p >= 0.05 and non-beaconed p < 0.05 with fewer hits on TA- trials.

claims.statement: Units are sorted into fast spiking units (FSU) and regular spiking units (RSU) by k-means clustering of the initial phase and after-hyperpolarization phase durations of their action potentials; in one animal's recordings this gave 28 FSU and 32 RSU, 60 in total.
claims.source: Figure 3B and 3C; Methods 2.5
claims.quote: K -means clustering of detected neurons from one animal's recordings, showing 28 fast spiking units (FSU) and 32 regular spiking units (RSU), for 60 total.
claims.criterion: The header's cell type method. The paper does not name the animal, nor whether its "recordings" are one session or all of its sessions; the readings are R1, the units of one session, and R2, the units of all of one animal's sessions in one series. Reproduced when, under one reading, some animal gives all three counts within tolerance and the two clusters separate on both features (the FSU cluster has the shorter median initial phase and after-hyperpolarization phase). Partially reproduced when the clusters separate as stated but no animal matches the counts. When the dataset carries the paper's labels (K0), the agreement of K1 and K2 with them is reported.

claims.statement: RSUs show time-locked responses to tFUS, an increase in firing rate during the 67 ms of stimulation, in both awake and anesthetized recordings.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 4C and 4E
claims.quote: We observed time-locked responses from RSU in both awake and anesthetized recordings, with an observable increase in firing rate during tFUS stimulation
claims.criterion: Figure 4 shows single examples at 1500 Hz PRF, 30% DC and reports no group test. The paper's group test of a time-locked response is the comparison with sham (Results 3.2 and 3.3), so the claim is judged on it. RSU time-locked responses (0 to 67 ms) of the 1500 Hz, 200 us sessions against the sham sessions of the same state, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum, p < 0.05, with the 1500 Hz mean above the sham mean and above 100%. Reproduced when this holds in both states under every reading; partially reproduced when in one state only. The units whose PSTH rises in 0 to 67 ms are counted per state.

claims.statement: FSU delayed responses to tFUS at 1500 Hz PRF begin later in awake rats (mean onset 0.51 s, spread 0.14 s) than under anesthesia (0.24 s, spread 0.08 s), and the onset distributions differ significantly by a Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 4H and 4I
claims.quote: In the anesthetized model, these delayed responses had an average onset latency of 0.24 s ± 0.08 s, while in the awake model they had an average onset latency of 0.51 s ± 0.14 s ... Comparing the distributions using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, we found that delayed response onset times varied significantly between awake and anesthetized models
claims.criterion: The header's latency method (readings S1/S2, D1/D2, L1/L2, Q1/Q2, T1/T2), FSU only. The paper does not say whether the spread is an SD or an SEM; it is used as the tolerance. Reproduced when, under every reading, both means are within tolerance and a two-sided rank-sum test of awake against anesthetized latencies gives p < 0.001 with the awake values later. Partially reproduced when the test holds with the awake values later but a mean is outside tolerance. Not reproduced when the test fails or the direction is reversed.

claims.statement: Awake FSU delayed-response onset latencies have a wider spread than anesthetized ones and appear to have two peaks.
claims.source: Results 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 4H
claims.quote: The awake model had a wider variance of onset latencies, and appears to have two peaks
claims.criterion: Latencies as in fig4hi-fsu-delayed-latency. Reproduced when the SD of the awake latencies exceeds that of the anesthetized latencies under every reading. The paper gives no test of bimodality ("appears to have two peaks"), so the peaks do not decide the outcome; the histogram in the paper's 35.7 ms bins and its local maxima are shown.

claims.statement: In awake rats PRF is a significant factor for RSU time-locked responses; 30 Hz and 300 Hz PRF give lower responses than every higher PRF (so 30 Hz is also below 300 Hz), 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz do not differ, and sham differs from every PRF but 30 Hz.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 5A
claims.quote: Examining the time-locked response from RSU in the awake model using Kruskal–Wallis ANOVA, we find that PRF is a significant factor ... Post hoc tests show that 30 Hz and 300 Hz PRF induced responses lower than all higher PRFs ... The sham condition was significantly different than all but the 30 Hz condition ... 1500 Hz, 3000 Hz, and 4500 Hz showed no significant differences
claims.criterion: The header's group test, awake batch 1 PRF series, RSU, 0 to 67 ms; the sham is the awake batch 2 sham. Six parts, each at corrected p < 0.05 - (1) the Kruskal-Wallis is significant; (2) 30 Hz is below each of 300, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz; (3) 300 Hz is below each of 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz; (4) no pair among 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz differs; (5) sham differs from 300, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz; (6) sham does not differ from 30 Hz. Part (2) includes 300 Hz because 300 Hz is one of "all higher PRFs" for 30 Hz, and Results 3.2 says the only difference under anesthesia is that 30 Hz and 300 Hz do not differ. Reproduced when all six hold under every reading; partially reproduced when (1) and at least four others hold; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Under anesthesia RSU time-locked responses depend on PRF as in the awake model, the only difference being that 30 Hz and 300 Hz do not differ significantly.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 5C
claims.quote: The anesthetized model had similar statistical results, with the only difference being that no significant difference was observed between 30 Hz and 300 Hz PRF levels
claims.criterion: As fig5a-rsu-time-locked-prf-awake, on the anesthetized batch 1 PRF series with the anesthetized batch 2 sham, with part (2) read as 30 Hz below each of 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz (not 300 Hz), and a seventh part, that 30 Hz and 300 Hz do not differ (corrected p >= 0.05). Reproduced when all parts hold under every reading; partially reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis and at least five others hold; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Anesthesia is a significant factor in the RSU time-locked response by two-way ANOVA, and it lowers the average magnitude of RSU responses.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 1; Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Although these results demonstrate'
claims.quote: Two-way ANOVA additionally finds that anesthesia is a significant factor in the time-locked response from RSU ... Anesthesia was observed to decrease the average magnitude of RSU responses
claims.criterion: The header's two-way ANOVA (A1 and A2) on RSU time-locked responses of the batch 1 PRF series. Reproduced when the anesthesia effect has p < 0.01 and the anesthetized mean, over all PRF levels, is below the awake mean, under every reading. Partially reproduced when the effect has 0.01 <= p < 0.05 with that direction. Per-PRF means of each state are shown.

claims.statement: FSU time-locked responses show no significant differences across PRF levels, in either the awake or the anesthetized model.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 5B and 5D
claims.quote: FSU in both the awake and the anesthetized model show no significant differences due to PRF levels
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the header's Kruskal-Wallis on FSU time-locked responses (0 to 67 ms) across the five PRF levels of the batch 1 series (G1), in each state at 0.05, with post hoc rank-sum tests at Bonferroni-corrected 0.05. Reproduced when no Kruskal-Wallis and no post hoc pair is significant in either state; not reproduced when any is. The effect sizes (the range of group medians) and the G2 test are shown.

claims.statement: Awake RSU delayed responses (0.5 to 1 s) depend on PRF, are highest at 1500 Hz and 3000 Hz with lower responses at both lower and higher PRFs, and every PRF is significantly higher than sham.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 2; Figure 5E
claims.quote: RSUs in the awake rats had highest responses to 1500 Hz and 3000 Hz ... with a decrease at both higher and lower frequencies, and all conditions found to be significantly higher than sham
claims.criterion: The header's group test, awake batch 1 PRF series and awake sham, RSU, 0.5 to 1 s. Parts at corrected p < 0.05 - (1) the Kruskal-Wallis is significant; (2) each of 1500 and 3000 Hz is higher than each of 30, 300 and 4500 Hz; (3) each PRF is higher than sham. The paper does not say whether 1500 and 3000 Hz must each beat every other level, so (2) is also read as R2, the two highest means are those of 1500 and 3000 Hz and each is significantly above 30 Hz and 4500 Hz. Reproduced when (1), (3) and (2) hold under one of the readings of (2), under every other reading; partially reproduced when (1) and (3) hold without (2), or (1) and (2) without (3).

claims.statement: Awake FSU delayed responses depend on PRF, are strongest at 4500 Hz, differ between 30 Hz and the three highest PRFs and between 300 Hz and the two highest, and at 30 Hz and 300 Hz are not significantly higher than sham.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 2; Figure 5F
claims.quote: FSUs in the awake model show the strongest responses to 4500 Hz PRF, with significant differences between 30 Hz and the highest three PRFs, and 300 Hz and the highest two PRFs ... 30 Hz and 300 Hz were not found to be significantly higher than sham
claims.criterion: The header's group test, awake batch 1 PRF series and awake sham, FSU, 0.5 to 1 s. Parts - (1) the Kruskal-Wallis is significant; (2) the 4500 Hz mean is the highest; (3) 30 Hz differs from 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz; (4) 300 Hz differs from 3000 and 4500 Hz; (5) neither 30 Hz nor 300 Hz is significantly higher than sham. Significance at corrected p < 0.05. Reproduced when all hold under every reading; partially reproduced when (1) holds with at least three of the others; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Under anesthesia PRF is a significant factor for the delayed responses (0.2 to 0.7 s) of both RSUs and FSUs, which broadly prefer higher PRFs.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 2; Figure 5G and 5H
claims.quote: PRF was found to be a significant factor for RSU and FSU in both awake and anesthetized settings ... Both RSUs and FSUs in the anesthetized rats had similar sensitivity as their time-locked responses, broadly preferring higher PRFs
claims.criterion: The header's Kruskal-Wallis on the anesthetized batch 1 PRF series, 0.2 to 0.7 s, for RSU and FSU separately (G1). "Broadly preferring higher PRFs" is read as the mean of 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz pooled exceeding that of 30 and 300 Hz pooled, the split the paper uses for time-locked responses (Results 3.2 paragraph 1). Reproduced when, for both cell types, the Kruskal-Wallis has p < 0.05 and the higher PRFs have the higher mean, under every reading; partially reproduced when this holds for one cell type.

claims.statement: Anesthesia is a significant factor in the delayed response for both RSUs and FSUs by two-way ANOVA, and it lowers the average response magnitude.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 2; Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Although these results demonstrate'
claims.quote: Using two-way ANOVA, we found that anesthesia is a significant factor in the delayed response for both RSU ... and FSU
claims.criterion: The header's two-way ANOVA (A1 and A2) on delayed responses of the batch 1 PRF series, each state's own window. Reproduced when, under every reading, the anesthesia effect has p < 0.001 for RSU and p < 0.01 for FSU, and in each cell type the anesthetized mean over all PRF levels is below the awake mean (Discussion, "an average decrease in response magnitude" for FSU). Partially reproduced when both effects have p < 0.05 with that direction but a bound is missed, or when one cell type holds.

claims.statement: In the five rats recorded awake and anesthetized in the same week, time-locked responses to the low PRF and 1500 Hz differ significantly in both states, with a reduced response under anesthesia.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 3; Figure 6A to 6D
claims.quote: In analysis of the time locked responses, we observed significant differences in response to 300 Hz PRF and 1500 Hz PRF stimulation in both awake and anesthetized conditions ... but with a reduced response under anesthesia
claims.criterion: Batch 2 on-target sessions; the low PRF is the one the dataset records (30 Hz in Methods 2.3, 300 Hz here). The text does not name the cell type; the Figure 6 legend says panels A to D repeat Figure 5A, 5B, 5E and 5F, and the time-locked RSU panel is the one where the Figure 5 PRF effect holds, so the claim is judged on RSU, 0 to 67 ms; FSU and the delayed windows are shown as variants. In each state, low PRF against 1500 Hz by two-sided rank-sum, Bonferroni-corrected over the pairs of the groups (G1, the two PRFs; G2, with the sham). Reduced under anesthesia is judged, as no test is named, by the anesthetized mean being below the awake mean; the paper does not say at which PRF, so the readings are M1, at each of the two PRFs, and M2, over both PRFs pooled; the rank-sum p of each is shown. Reproduced when the PRF difference has corrected p < 0.05 in both states and the reduction holds under M1 or M2, under every other reading; partially reproduced when the PRF difference holds in one state.

claims.statement: Awake RSU mean responses, time-locked and delayed, rise with ISPTA up to around 60 mW/cm2 and then decline.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 4; Figure 6E and 6G
claims.quote: We observe that RSU's in both their time-locked and delayed responses initially increase till around 60 mW cm −2 , after which the response declines.
claims.criterion: Means of the awake batch 1 PRF series RSU responses (Figure 5A and 5E values) against the ISPTA of each PRF given in Methods 2.3. Results 3.2 paragraph 4 also says the 1500 Hz (30.13 mW/cm2) mean is the highest time-locked one, so the peak is read as the mean at 1500 or 3000 Hz. Reproduced when, for both windows, the highest mean is at 1500 or 3000 Hz, the means rise from 30 Hz to that peak, and the 4500 Hz mean is below the peak, under every reading. Partially reproduced when this holds for one window. No test is reported; the SEM of each mean is shown.

claims.statement: Awake FSUs show no time-locked response, and their delayed response increases almost linearly with ISPTA.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 4; Figure 6F and 6H
claims.quote: FSU's show no time-locked response, and their delayed response increases almost linearly with I SPTA .
claims.criterion: Means of the awake batch 1 PRF series FSU responses against ISPTA. The paper gives no measure of "no time-locked response" beyond the absence of a PRF effect, so that part takes the outcome of fig5bd-fsu-time-locked-no-prf for the awake state. The delayed part holds when the five delayed means increase with ISPTA (Spearman rho = 1 over the five points); "almost linearly" has no threshold in the paper, so the Pearson r of the means against ISPTA is reported and does not decide. Reproduced when both parts hold under every reading; partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: Among PRFs, 1500 Hz gives the highest mean RSU time-locked response in awake rats, although not significantly above 3000 and 4500 Hz.
claims.source: Results 3.2, paragraph 4; Figure 5A
claims.quote: Although it is not statistically significant, we found that 1500 Hz produces the highest mean time-locked response
claims.criterion: Means of awake batch 1 PRF series RSU responses, 0 to 67 ms. Reproduced when the 1500 Hz mean is the highest of the five under every reading; the corrected rank-sum p of 1500 Hz against 3000 and 4500 Hz is shown.

claims.statement: Awake RSU time-locked responses at 1500 Hz PRF are significantly lower at 6% DC than at 60% DC (and, by the Figure 7A legend, than at 30% DC), and every DC is significantly higher than sham.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 7A and its legend
claims.quote: Time-locked responses from RSUs showed a significantly lower response to 6% DC than those to 60%, with all conditions significantly higher than sham
claims.criterion: The header's group test on the awake batch 1 DC series (6, 30, 60%) with the awake sham, RSU, 0 to 67 ms. Parts at corrected p < 0.05 - (1) the Kruskal-Wallis is significant; (2) 6% is below 60%; (3) each DC is above sham; (4) 6% is below 30% (Figure 7A legend, "6% DC results in a significantly lower response than 30% or 60%"). Reproduced when all hold under every reading; partially reproduced when (1) and at least one of the others hold.

claims.statement: By mean values 60% DC gives the strongest RSU time-locked response, though it is only significantly higher than 6%.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 7A
claims.quote: Based on mean values, 60% DC appears to produce the strongest time-locked response, although it is only statistically significantly higher than the 6% condition.
claims.criterion: Means of awake DC series RSU responses, 0 to 67 ms. Reproduced when the 60% mean is the highest of the three under every reading; the corrected rank-sum p of 60% against 30% is shown.

claims.statement: FSUs show no time-locked response across DC levels; no significant differences are observed.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 7B
claims.quote: no time-locked response was observed as in the PRF study
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the header's Kruskal-Wallis on FSU time-locked responses across 6, 30 and 60% DC (G1) at 0.05, with post hoc rank-sum tests at Bonferroni-corrected 0.05. Reproduced when none is significant; not reproduced when any is. The group medians and the G2 test are shown.

claims.statement: Awake RSU delayed responses prefer 30% DC over 6% and 60%, all three DCs differ (Figure 7C legend), and at 60% DC they do not differ from sham.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 7C and its legend
claims.quote: Delayed responses however preferred 30% DC over 6% and 60% ... and 60% DC showed no significant difference from sham
claims.criterion: The header's group test on the awake DC series with the awake sham, RSU, 0.5 to 1 s. Parts - (1) the Kruskal-Wallis is significant; (2) 30% is above 6% and above 60%; (3) 60% does not differ from sham; (4) 6% and 60% differ (Figure 7C legend, "Significantly different responses are observed between all DCs"). Significance at corrected p < 0.05. Reproduced when all hold under every reading; partially reproduced when (1) and (2) hold without (3) or (4), or (1) and (3) with 30% above one of the two.

claims.statement: Awake FSU delayed responses are significantly higher at 60% DC than at 6%, and at 6% DC they do not differ from sham.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 7D
claims.quote: Delayed responses from FSUs showed a significantly higher response to 60% DC over 6% ... with 6% DC found to be not significantly different from sham
claims.criterion: The header's group test on the awake DC series with the awake sham, FSU, 0.5 to 1 s. Parts - (1) the Kruskal-Wallis is significant; (2) 60% is above 6% at corrected p < 0.05; (3) 6% does not differ from sham. Reproduced when all hold under every reading; partially reproduced when (1) and (2) hold without (3).

claims.statement: The off-target sham at 1500 Hz PRF produced no significant response, so the activation is not attributed to an auditory or skull-conduction confound.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'One potential confound'; Methods 2.3
claims.quote: In this study we additionally performed a sham condition delivering ultrasound off target to the front of the skull, and did not observe any significant response.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper names no test of the sham against baseline; its only tests involving sham compare it with on-target conditions (Results 3.2, 3.3), and those are judged in their own claims. The Methods tests (Kruskal-Wallis with post hoc rank-sum) have no baseline group. What the sham is compared with is therefore open, and this file names no reading the text supports; the sham's mean normalized rates for RSU and FSU in each window and state are to be shown, and the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In the 3000 Hz PRF (60% DC) sessions 312 RSUs and 54 FSUs were recorded from S1 and 233 RSUs and 17 FSUs from POm; in the 30 Hz PRF (0.6% DC) sessions 148 RSUs and 61 FSUs from S1 and 189 RSUs and 43 FSUs from POm.
claims.source: Figure 4 legend
claims.quote: There are 312 RSUs and 54 FSUs recorded from S1, 233 RSUs and 17 FSUs recorded from POm for PRF 3,000 Hz. There are 148 RSUs and 61 FSUs recorded from S1 and189 RSUs and 43 FSUs recorded from POm for PRF 30 Hz.
claims.criterion: Units with more than 2000 spikes in the 3000 Hz, 200 us and the 30 Hz, 200 us sessions of the S1 and POm rats, typed as in the header (K1 or K2, P1 or P2). Reproduced when, under one reading, all eight counts are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the total per area and condition is within 10% under one reading but the RSU/FSU split is not; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: S1 RSUs are activated during sonication (0 to 67 ms) with 3000 Hz PRF, 60% DC tFUS aimed at S1.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
claims.quote: RSUs from S1 (n = 312, p = 3.13 × 10−7) and POm (n = 233, p = 0.0003) were both activated during 3,000 Hz PRF sonication
claims.criterion: The header's method, 3000 Hz PRF with 200 us PD, S1 RSUs, window 0 to 67 ms against baseline, one-tailed (greater), Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01. Reproduced when this holds under every reading; not reproduced when it fails under every reading. The mean normalized rate is reported.

claims.statement: POm RSUs are activated during sonication with 3000 Hz PRF tFUS aimed at S1, in synchrony with S1 RSUs.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4B
claims.quote: RSUs from S1 (n = 312, p = 3.13 × 10−7) and POm (n = 233, p = 0.0003) were both activated during 3,000 Hz PRF sonication
claims.criterion: As fig4a-s1-rsu-time-locked-3000, for POm RSUs in the same sessions.

claims.statement: After 3000 Hz PRF sonication S1 RSUs, POm RSUs and S1 FSUs show delayed activation from 134 ms.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4A and 4B
claims.quote: Postsonication activations were presented for S1 RSUs (p = 5 × 10−18), POm RSUs (p = 0.0007), and S1 FSUs (n = 54, p = 4.03 × 10−8) from 134 ms.
claims.criterion: The header's method, 3000 Hz sessions. The paper does not say which bin "from 134 ms" the p-values belong to; the readings are the 134 to 201 ms bin and the 201 to 268 ms bin, and a group is counted as activated when either bin is significant (greater, p < 0.01 corrected). Reproduced when all three groups are activated under every method reading; partially reproduced when one or two are; not reproduced when none is.

claims.statement: With 30 Hz PRF (0.6% DC), S1 RSUs show an inhibitory response after sonication (67 to 134 ms) and POm RSUs show delayed excitatory activity (134 to 268 ms).
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4 legend
claims.quote: At 30 Hz PRF, the S1 RSUs showed an inhibitory response after sonication (67–134 ms, n = 148, p = 0.0029) and POm RSUs expressed delayed excitatory activities (n = 189, p = 2 × 10−9).
claims.criterion: The header's method, 30 Hz, 200 us sessions. S1 RSUs, 67 to 134 ms, one-tailed (less); POm RSUs, the 134 to 201 or the 201 to 268 ms bin (the legend gives 134 to 268 ms), one-tailed (greater); p < 0.01 corrected. Reproduced when both hold under every reading; partially reproduced when one does; not reproduced when neither does.

claims.statement: S1 FSUs show no time-locked response to 3000 Hz PRF, S1 FSUs show no activity change to 30 Hz PRF, and POm FSUs show no change to either PRF.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: There was no activity change among S1 FSUs (n = 61) to 30 Hz PRF and POm FSUs to both PRFs (3,000 Hz, n = 17; 30 Hz, n = 43).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test as the header gives it (post hoc one-tailed two-sample Wilcoxon against baseline, Bonferroni, p < 0.01), in every 67 ms bin from 0 to 268 ms, in both tails; for S1 FSUs at 3000 Hz only the 0 to 67 ms bin. Reproduced when no bin is significant for any of the four groups; not reproduced when any is. The test sample is B1 or B2 as the header names (two-sample, as the paper says); B3 is shown as a variant. The mean normalized rates are reported either way.

claims.statement: In sham sessions (no tFUS), S1 and POm RSUs and FSUs show no time-locked and no delayed (201 to 268 ms) activity change.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 5A
claims.quote: In sham condition (no tFUS), S1 neurons and POm neurons showed no time-locked (S1 RSUs: n = 31, p = 1.0; S1 FSUs: n = 53, p = 0.55; POm RSUs: n = 67, p = 1.0; POm FSUs: n = 67, p = 1.0)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence on the paper's test (header method; 0 to 67 ms and 201 to 268 ms against baseline, one-tailed greater, Bonferroni, p < 0.01), in the sessions without tFUS, with sonication onset taken as the trial times the sessions carry. Reproduced when no group is significant in either window; not reproduced when any is. Unit counts are compared with expected separately and do not decide the outcome.

claims.statement: With 3000 Hz PRF tFUS aimed at CG1, S1 and POm RSUs and FSUs show no time-locked and no delayed (201 to 268 ms) activity change.
claims.source: Results, Synchronizing neuronal responses to tFUS in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 5B
claims.quote: In control condition (tFUS targeted at CG1), S1 neurons and POm neurons showed no time-locked (S1 RSUs: n = 12, p = 1.0; S1 FSUs: n = 34, p = 1.0; POm RSUs: n = 55, p = 1.0; POm FSUs: n = 42, p = 0.33) and delayed responses (201–268 ms, S1 RSUs: p = 1.0; S1 FSUs: p = 0.10; POm RSUs: p = 0.32, POm FSUs: p = 1.0).
claims.criterion: As fig5a-sham-no-change, in the sessions with tFUS aimed at CG1.

claims.statement: The PRF series (PD 200 us) comprises 1050 RSUs and 247 FSUs from S1 and 913 RSUs and 106 FSUs from POm.
claims.source: Figure 6 legend
claims.quote: The comparison of neuronal responses for sorted 1,050 RSUs (A) and 247 FSUs (B) recorded from S1 was conducted using Kruskal–Wallis ... The comparison of neuronal responses for sorted 913 RSUs (C) and 106 FSUs (D) recorded from POm was conducted using Kruskal–Wallis.
claims.criterion: Units with more than 2000 spikes in the 30, 300, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz sessions with 200 us PD, of the S1 and POm rats, typed as in the header. Reproduced when all four counts are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when the area totals are within 10% but the split is not.

claims.statement: With constant 200 us PD, time-locked S1 RSU responses are elicited only by high PRFs (1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz), the highest at 1500 Hz (123.34 +/- 4.3%), and the during-sonication response differs across PRFs.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6A
claims.quote: time-locked S1 RSUs’ responses could only be elicited from high PRFs: 1,500 Hz (n = 284, p = 2.74 × 10−6 compared with baseline), 3,000 Hz (n = 312, p = 3.13 × 10−7), and 4,500 Hz (n = 152, p = 0.0028), among which 1,500 Hz evoked highest response level of 123.34 ± 4.3%
claims.criterion: The header's method on the PRF series, window 0 to 67 ms. Reproduced when, under every method reading, the Kruskal-Wallis across PRFs has p < 0.01, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz are each above baseline (one-tailed, corrected p < 0.01), 30 and 300 Hz are not, and 1500 Hz has the highest mean normalized rate; partially reproduced when the three high PRFs are significant but the rest does not hold. The mean (+/- SEM) at 1500 Hz is compared with expected; the tolerance is the paper's SEM.

claims.statement: Delayed (201 to 268 ms) S1 RSU responses occur at PRFs above 30 Hz, the highest at 4500 Hz (148.39 +/- 5.41%), and are PRF dependent.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6A
claims.quote: The delayed responses (201–268 ms) of RSUs could be observed at PRFs higher than 30 Hz and the highest response occurred at 4,500 Hz (148.39 ± 5.41%).
claims.criterion: The header's method on the PRF series, window 201 to 268 ms. Reproduced when, under every method reading, the Kruskal-Wallis has p < 0.01, 300, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz are each above baseline (one-tailed, corrected p < 0.01), 30 Hz is not, and 4500 Hz has the highest mean; partially reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis and the highest PRF hold but not every PRF above 30 Hz is significant.

claims.statement: S1 FSUs show no time-locked response to any PRF and delayed responses only at PRFs above 1500 Hz, highest at 4500 Hz (158.75 +/- 10.75%), PRF dependent postsonication.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6B
claims.quote: FSUs did not show time-locked responses to any PRFs and only presented delayed responses at PRFs higher than 1,500 Hz, with the highest response level at 4,500 Hz (158.75 ± 10.75%).
claims.criterion: The header's method on the PRF series. "Higher than 1,500 Hz" can be read as (a) 3000 and 4500 Hz, or (b) 1500 Hz and above. Reproduced when, under every method reading, no PRF is above baseline in 0 to 67 ms (a claim of absence on the paper's test, one-tailed, corrected p < 0.01), the postsonication Kruskal-Wallis has p < 0.01, the PRFs of reading (a) or of reading (b) are exactly those significant in 201 to 268 ms, and 4500 Hz has the highest mean. Partially reproduced when the absence of time-locked responses and the highest PRF hold but the set of significant PRFs matches neither reading.

claims.statement: POm RSUs show time-locked responses to 1500 and 3000 Hz PRF and delayed responses at PRFs from 1500 Hz, highest at 1500 Hz (141.68 +/- 2.38%); both windows are PRF dependent.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6C
claims.quote: time-locked responses (Fig. 6B) from POm RSUs could be elicited by 1,500 Hz (n = 153, p = 0.003) and 3,000 Hz PRFs (n = 233, p = 0.0003). However, the delayed responses (201–268 ms) of POm RSUs were induced by PRFs higher than 1,500 Hz and were highest (141.68 ± 2.38%) at 1,500 Hz.
claims.criterion: The header's method on the PRF series. The Results cite Fig. 6B for this panel but the legend places POm RSUs in panel C; it is read as Fig. 6C. The text says delayed responses occur at PRFs "higher than 1,500 Hz" and are highest at 1500 Hz, so the set is read as 1500 Hz and above. Reproduced when, under every method reading, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, 1500 and 3000 Hz are above baseline in 0 to 67 ms and 30, 300 and 4500 Hz are not, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz are above baseline in 201 to 268 ms and 30 and 300 Hz are not, and 1500 Hz has the highest postsonication mean. Partially reproduced when the time-locked part holds and the delayed part does not, or the reverse.

claims.statement: POm FSUs show no time-locked response to any PRF (though 30 and 1500 Hz differ from each other) and a delayed response only to 4500 Hz; postsonication activity is PRF dependent.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 6D
claims.quote: The FSUs did not show any time-locked responses and only expressed the delayed responses to 4,500 Hz (n = 26, p = 4.2 × 10−6).
claims.criterion: The header's method on the PRF series. Reproduced when, under every method reading, no PRF is above baseline in 0 to 67 ms (absence on the paper's test), only 4500 Hz is above baseline in 201 to 268 ms, and the postsonication Kruskal-Wallis has p < 0.01. The 30 against 1500 Hz comparison (direction not given, so both tails are reported) is reported and does not decide the outcome.

claims.statement: At 3000 Hz PRF, S1 RSU time-locked responses depend on DC and occur at 30% and 60%; delayed responses occur at 6%, 30% and 60%.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 3; Figure 7A
claims.quote: with 3,000 Hz PRF, the time-locked responses of S1 RSUs were dependent on DCs which can be elicited with DC of 30% (n = 194, p = 3.38 × 10−6) and 60% (n = 312, p = 5.96 × 10−6). Delayed activities of RSUs were found at 6% (n = 56, p = 0.001), 30% (n = 194, p = 9.64 × 10−32), and 60% (n = 312, p = 1.38 × 10−15).
claims.criterion: The header's method on the 3000 Hz sessions with PD 2, 20, 100, 200 and 300 us (0.6, 6, 30, 60, 90% DC). Reproduced when, under every method reading, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, exactly 30% and 60% are above baseline in 0 to 67 ms, and exactly 6, 30 and 60% are above baseline in 201 to 268 ms; partially reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis tests hold and the significant set differs by one DC in one window.
