claims.statement: At 3000 Hz PRF, S1 FSUs show delayed responses at 6%, 30% and 60% DC, the same range as S1 RSUs, and 0.6% differs from 30% postsonication.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 3; Figure 7B
claims.quote: Delayed responses of FSUs could be elicited by 6% (n = 22, p = 1.29 × 10−8), 30% (n = 49, p = 2.32 × 10−11), and 60% (n = 54, p = 2.38 × 10−8) DCs (Fig. 7B), which were the same range of S1 RSUs.
claims.criterion: The header's method on the 3000 Hz DC series, window 201 to 268 ms. Reproduced when, under every method reading, exactly 6, 30 and 60% are above baseline (one-tailed, corrected p < 0.01) and 0.6% and 30% differ (one-tailed, p < 0.01; the legend gives no direction, so both tails are run and either is accepted, and the direction is reported); partially reproduced when the set differs by one DC.

claims.statement: At 3000 Hz PRF, POm RSU time-locked responses show no DC dependence (highest at 60%, 106 +/- 0.77%), while delayed responses are DC dependent and occur at DCs of 6% and above.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 3; Figure 7C
claims.quote: The POm RSUs’ time-locked responses did not show DC dependence and were highest at 60% (106 ± 0.77%; Fig. 7C). Delayed responses could be activated by DC higher than 6% (6%, n = 22, p = 1.55 × 10−6; n = 7, p = 0.001; 60%, n = 233, p = 1.28 × 10−6; 90%, n = 18, p = 0.006).
claims.criterion: The header's method on the 3000 Hz DC series. The text lists 6% under "higher than 6%", and one entry (n = 7) has no DC; it is read as 30%, the only DC from 6 to 90% missing from the list. Reproduced when, under every method reading, the Kruskal-Wallis across DCs in 0 to 67 ms has p >= 0.01 (absence on the paper's test), 60% has the highest mean in that window, the Kruskal-Wallis in 201 to 268 ms has p < 0.01, and 6, 30, 60 and 90% are above baseline in 201 to 268 ms while 0.6% is not. Partially reproduced when the time-locked part holds and the delayed set differs by one DC. The paper's n of 233 at 60% equals the 3000 Hz count of Fig. 4 while the panel total is 286, so the per-DC counts are reported.

claims.statement: At 3000 Hz PRF, POm FSUs show no time-locked response against baseline, though 30% DC is higher than 0.6% and 6% during sonication; delayed responses occur at 30%, 60% and 90%.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 3; Figure 7D
claims.quote: There was no time-locked responses of POm FSUs compared with baseline while 30% DC showed higher activities compared with 0.6% (p = 0.0001) and 6% DC (p = 0.0003). The delayed activities of POm FSUs occurred at 30% (n = 18, p = 0.003), 60% (n = 17, p = 0.005), and 90% (n = 52, p = 6.8 × 10−5) DCs
claims.criterion: The header's method on the 3000 Hz DC series. Reproduced when, under every method reading, no DC is above baseline in 0 to 67 ms (absence on the paper's test), the Kruskal-Wallis in 0 to 67 ms has p < 0.01 with 30% greater than 0.6% and 6% (one-tailed, p < 0.01), and exactly 30, 60 and 90% are above baseline in 201 to 268 ms. Partially reproduced when two of these three parts hold.

claims.statement: At 30 Hz PRF, S1 RSUs show time-locked responses at 6%, 30% and 90% DC and a delayed response at 90%; both windows are DC dependent.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 3; Figure 8A
claims.quote: With 30 Hz PRF stimulation (Fig. 8A), the S1 RSUs showed time-locked responses to DC of 6% (n = 81, p = 1.19 × 10−8), 30% (n = 61, p = 0.001), and 90% (n = 66, p = 2.17 × 10−6) and delayed responses to 90% DC (n = 66, p = 1.5 × 10−24).
claims.criterion: The header's method on the 30 Hz sessions with PD 200 us, 2, 10, 20 and 30 ms (0.6, 6, 30, 60, 90% DC). Reproduced when, under every method reading, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, exactly 6, 30 and 90% are above baseline in 0 to 67 ms, and only 90% is above baseline in 201 to 268 ms; partially reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis tests hold and the significant set differs by one DC in one window.

claims.statement: At 30 Hz PRF, 90% DC induces a time-locked increase in S1 FSUs and the only delayed S1 FSU response; FSU responses are DC dependent during sonication but not postsonication.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 3; Figure 8B
claims.quote: Moreover, 90% DC with 30 Hz PRF induced positive time-locked response in S1 FSUs (Fig. 8B; n = 28, p = 4.57 × 10−11). Like S1 RSUs, S1 FSUs only showed delayed responses to 90% DC (n = 28, p = 0.007) with 30 Hz PRF.
claims.criterion: The header's method on the 30 Hz DC series. Reproduced when, under every method reading, the Kruskal-Wallis in 0 to 67 ms has p < 0.01, 90% is above baseline in both windows, no other DC is above baseline in 201 to 268 ms, and the Kruskal-Wallis in 201 to 268 ms has p >= 0.01 (absence on the paper's test). Partially reproduced when the 90% responses hold and one of the other parts does not.

claims.statement: At constant 60% DC, during sonication only 30 Hz PRF differs from the other PRFs in S1 RSUs, and postsonication activity is highest at 4500 Hz; both windows are PRF dependent.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 3; Figure 9A
claims.quote: only 30 Hz PRF showed different effects to other PRFs (300 Hz, p = 0.008; 1,500 Hz, p = 0.006; 3,000 Hz, p = 0.007; 4,500 Hz, p = 0.0003) on S1 RSUs during sonication, while postsonication activities preferred 4,500 Hz
claims.criterion: The header's method on the 60% DC sessions (PD 20 ms, 2 ms, 400 us, 200 us and 133 us at 30, 300, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz). The paper does not give the direction of the 30 Hz difference; both tails are run and the one in which the four tests agree is used. Reproduced when, under every method reading, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, 30 Hz differs from each other PRF in 0 to 67 ms (one-tailed, p < 0.01, in one direction for all four), no pair among 300 to 4500 Hz differs at p < 0.01, and 4500 Hz has the highest mean in 201 to 268 ms. Partially reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis tests and one of the two other parts hold.

claims.statement: At constant 60% DC, S1 FSUs respond to 1500 Hz PRF during sonication and prefer 4500 Hz postsonication; both windows are PRF dependent.
claims.source: Results, tFUS parameters on affecting neuronal activities of CTC pathway, paragraph 3; Figure 9B
claims.quote: S1 FSUs responded to 1,500 Hz PRF (n = 48, p = 3.35 ×10−6) during sonication and preferred 4,500 Hz post sonication (n = 18, p = 5.84 × 10−10; Fig. 9B).
claims.criterion: The header's method on the 60% DC sessions. Reproduced when, under every method reading, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, 1500 Hz is above baseline in 0 to 67 ms, 4500 Hz is above baseline in 201 to 268 ms and has the highest mean there; partially reproduced when one of the two baseline comparisons holds.

claims.statement: With 3000 Hz PRF, 60% DC, the directional correlation from S1 RSUs to POm RSUs and from POm RSUs to S1 FSUs increases during sonication, while the other two directional correlations do not change then; postsonication, S1 RSU to POm FSU and POm RSU to S1 RSU correlation decreases.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 10A and its legend
claims.quote: With 3,000 Hz PRF, 60% DC stimulation, S1 RSUs showed enhanced correlation to POm RSUs during sonication (Fig. 10A) ... POm RSUs showed an increased correlation to S1 FSUs during sonication ... Postsonication, we found the correlation from S1 RSUs to POm FSUs and POm RSUs to S1 RSUs significantly decreased
claims.criterion: The header's dSTTC method on the 3000 Hz, 200 us sessions, cross-area pairs in each session. During sonication is the first bin from 0 ms; postsonication is read as any of the bins from the end of sonication to 268 ms (the paper names no bin). Reproduced when, under every dSTTC reading (D1, A1/A2, W1/W2, S1/S2) and every cell-type reading, S1 RSU to POm RSU and POm RSU to S1 FSU are above prestimulation in the first bin (one-tailed, p < 0.05), S1 RSU to POm FSU and POm RSU to S1 RSU are not significant in that bin in either tail (the legend's "the other directional correlation did not show significant change during sonication", judged on the paper's test), and S1 RSU to POm FSU and POm RSU to S1 RSU are below prestimulation in some postsonication bin (one-tailed, p < 0.05). Partially reproduced when the two during-sonication increases hold and another part does not, or one increase holds. The number of pairs of each type is reported.

claims.statement: With 30 Hz PRF, S1 RSU to POm FSU directional correlation increases and POm RSU to S1 FSU correlation decreases during sonication.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 1; Figure 10B
claims.quote: When delivering 30 Hz ultrasound, S1 RSUs to POm FSUs higher correlated (p = 0.0058), while POm RSUs showed decreased correlation to S1 FSUs during sonication (p = 0.0058).
claims.criterion: The header's dSTTC method on the 30 Hz, 200 us sessions, the first bin from 0 ms. Reproduced when, under every dSTTC reading (D1, A1/A2, W1/W2, S1/S2) and every cell-type reading, S1 RSU to POm FSU is above prestimulation and POm RSU to S1 FSU below it (one-tailed, p < 0.05); partially reproduced when one holds.

claims.statement: With constant 200 us PD, the S1 RSU to POm RSU correlation change during sonication shows no PRF dependence overall, though 1500 Hz gives a higher change than 30 Hz.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 10C
claims.quote: When applying tFUS with constant 200 μs PD, varying the DC and PRF, the correlation did not show PRF-dependent change. A total of 1,500 Hz PRF did show a higher correlation change compared with 30 Hz PRF (Fig. 10C; p = 0.02).
claims.criterion: STTC (header) between S1 RSUs and POm RSUs, in the first bin from 0 ms, normalized to the prestimulation bin (S1 or S2), in the PRF series, under every STTC reading (A1/A2, W1/W2, S1/S2) and every cell-type reading. The absence is judged on the paper's test, a Kruskal-Wallis across the five PRFs at 0.05. Reproduced when, under every reading, that test has p >= 0.05 and the one-tailed Wilcoxon of 1500 Hz greater than 30 Hz has p < 0.05; partially reproduced when only one of the two holds. The dandiset's stored STTC values are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: At constant 60% DC, the S1 RSU to POm RSU correlation change is PRF dependent, with a preference for 1500 and 3000 Hz.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 10D
claims.quote: Then we fixed the DC to 60% and varied PRF. Unlike the neuronal responses (Fig. 9), the correlation showed the preference to 1,500 and 3,000 Hz (Fig. 10D).
claims.criterion: As fig10c-sttc-constant-pd, on the 60% DC sessions. Reproduced when, under every reading, the Kruskal-Wallis across PRFs has p < 0.05 and 1500 and 3000 Hz have the two highest changes, by mean (M1) or by median (M2), the header's two readings of the group summary; partially reproduced when the test holds and one of the two is among the two highest.

claims.statement: At 30 Hz PRF, the S1 RSU to POm RSU correlation change depends on DC, changing most at middle DCs (6, 30, 60%) and less at 0.6% and 90%.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 10E
claims.quote: For 30 Hz PRF (Fig. 10E), the correlation tended to change most at a middle range (6, 30, 60%) and respond less to lower (e.g., 0.6%) and higher DC (e.g., 90%).
claims.criterion: As fig10c-sttc-constant-pd, on the 30 Hz DC series. The paper does not say whether "change most" means the largest increase or the largest change in either direction; the readings are the signed change and its size (the absolute difference under S1, the absolute distance of the ratio from 1 under S2), each summarized by mean (M1) or median (M2). Reproduced when, under every reading, the Kruskal-Wallis across DCs has p < 0.05 and each of 6, 30 and 60% has a larger change than both 0.6% and 90%; partially reproduced when the test holds and the order holds for two of the three middle DCs.

claims.statement: At 3000 Hz PRF, the S1 RSU to POm RSU correlation change does not depend on DC.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 2; Figure 10F
claims.quote: For 3,000 Hz PRF, the pathway correlation showed DC independence (Fig. 10F).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence on the paper's test, a Kruskal-Wallis across the five DCs of the 3000 Hz series at 0.05, on STTC as in fig10c-sttc-constant-pd. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 under every reading; not reproduced when p < 0.05 under every reading. The medians are reported.

claims.statement: The PRFs that elicit stronger local S1 RSU responses are more likely to also activate the CTC pathway, so pathway modulation is PRF dependent.
claims.source: Results, tFUS elicited correlation change in CTC pathway, paragraph 3; Discussion, The feedback and feedforward cortico-thalomo-cortical circuits, paragraph 2
claims.quote: our results demonstrate that this pathway modulation is PRF dependent. To be more specific, the PRFs that could elicit stronger local neuronal responses were more likely to also activate CTC pathway activity.
claims.criterion: The paper gives no test. The Discussion (The feedback and feedforward cortico-thalomo-cortical circuits, paragraph 2) states it as "S1 RSUs' preference for 1,500 and 3,000 Hz, and the POm highest responses as well as the strongest correlation change were induced by the same PRF range", so it is read as a shared range, not a shared single PRF, in the PD 200 us series of Figs. 6A and 10C. Reproduced when, under every reading, the PRF with the highest mean S1 RSU response in 0 to 67 ms and the PRF with the highest STTC change (M1 or M2) are both 1500 or 3000 Hz; not reproduced otherwise. The Spearman correlation of the two PRF orders, and the same comparison on the 60% DC series (Figs. 9A and 10D), are reported and decide nothing.

claims.statement: AC neurons in the S1-AC rats show time-locked responses to 1500 and 3000 Hz PRF and postsonication responses to 30, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz, both PRF dependent, least at 300 Hz.
claims.source: Results, Auditory confound on CTC pathway modulation using tFUS, paragraph 1; Figure 11A and 11B
claims.quote: During sonication, the AC neurons showed time-locked responses to 1,500 Hz (n = 107, p = 9.9 × 10−5) and 3,000 Hz PRF (n = 104, p = 1.98 × 10−7). Postsonication, neuronal responses were activated by 30 Hz (n = 83, p = 1.77 × 10−20), 1,500 Hz, (n = 107, p = 1.36 × 10−5), 3,000 Hz (n = 104, p = 4.47 × 10−13), and 4,500 Hz (n = 100, p = 1.66 × 10−40).
claims.criterion: The header's spiking method on all AC units (more than 2000 spikes, not typed) in the PRF series with 200 us PD; the Fig. 11 legend calls the panel C, read as B. Windows 0 to 67 and 201 to 268 ms. The postsonication window of Fig. 11 is not stated; 201 to 268 ms is used as in Figs. 5 to 9, and the 67 to 134 and 134 to 201 ms bins are shown. Reproduced when, under every method reading, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.01, exactly 1500 and 3000 Hz are above baseline during sonication, exactly 30, 1500, 3000 and 4500 Hz are above baseline postsonication, and 300 Hz has the lowest mean normalized rate in at least one of the two windows (the legend's "least responses to tFUS 300 Hz PRF" names no window); partially reproduced when the sets differ by one PRF in one window or the 300 Hz part fails.

claims.statement: With 30 Hz PRF, the directional correlation from AC neurons to S1 RSUs increases during sonication and lasts about 150 to 200 ms.
claims.source: Results, Auditory confound on CTC pathway modulation using tFUS, paragraph 2; Figure 11C legend
claims.quote: During tFUS sonication with 30 Hz PRF, the correlation from 878 paired AC neurons to S1 RSUs significantly increased (p = 0.0014) which lasting for ∼150 ms (left).
claims.criterion: The header's dSTTC method, AC neurons as source and S1 RSUs as target, in the 30 Hz, 200 us sessions of the S1-AC rats. The legend says the increase lasts about 150 ms and the Results about 200 ms; both are named and either is accepted. Reproduced when, under every dSTTC reading (D1, A1/A2, W1/W2, S1/S2) and every cell-type reading, the first bin from 0 ms is above prestimulation (one-tailed, p < 0.05); the bins that stay significant are reported for the duration. The legend's 1421 is read two ways, as the AC and S1 RSU pairs of the 30 Hz sessions (its words) or as all AC and S1 pairs of those sessions (as the 1714 of panel D is); the count matches when it fits either. The legend reports the AC to S1 FSU correlation decreasing during and right after sonication, while the Results say the synchronization "could also be found on AC neurons to S1 FSUs"; this part is shown in both tails and does not decide the outcome.

claims.statement: With 3000 Hz PRF, AC neurons show no directional correlation change with S1 RSUs, and their correlation with S1 FSUs changes only about 200 to 300 ms after onset.
claims.source: Results, Auditory confound on CTC pathway modulation using tFUS, paragraph 2; Figure 11D legend
claims.quote: However, when delivering 3,000 Hz PRF ultrasound energy to S1, auditory neurons did not show directional correlation change with S1 RSUs. The correlation change of AC neurons with S1 FSUs only occurred ∼200–300 ms.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence for AC to S1 RSU, judged on the paper's test (one-tailed two-sample Wilcoxon of each bin from 0 to 268 ms against prestimulation, both tails, p < 0.05) in the 3000 Hz, 200 us sessions of the S1-AC rats. Reproduced when no bin is significant for AC to S1 RSU and, for AC to S1 FSU, the first bin from 0 ms is not significant and a bin within about 200 to 300 ms (201 to 268 or 268 to 335 ms under W1; 200 to 250 or 250 to 300 ms under W2) is, in either tail (the legend calls the change bidirectional); partially reproduced when the absence holds and the FSU timing does not. Not reproduced when an AC to S1 RSU bin is significant. Under every dSTTC reading (D1, A1/A2, W1/W2, S1/S2) and every cell-type reading.

claims.statement: Low PRF (30 Hz) induces a direct auditory confound by enhancing AC to S1 correlation during sonication, while high PRF (3000 Hz) shows less auditory confound on time-locked modulation.
claims.source: Results, Auditory confound on CTC pathway modulation using tFUS, paragraph 2
claims.quote: These results indicate that low PRF would induce direct auditory confound by enhancing the correlation between auditory and S1 neuronal activities, while high PRF showed less auditory confound on time-locked neuronal modulation.
claims.criterion: Reproduced when fig11c-ac-to-s1-30hz and fig11d-ac-to-s1-3000 are both reproduced; partially reproduced when one is.

claims.statement: The units the paper analysed can be found in the dandiset, and the dandiset's spike times and trials reproduce the per-unit peri-movement activity the paper's code stored.
claims.source: Data Availability; Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.0cfxpnvxm, Gaia_Analy.mat and Isis_Analy.mat
claims.quote: Data and code can be found at https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.0cfxpnvxm.
claims.criterion: Records are matched by file name (session_id), channel id and sort letter of the curated units. For the 394 records the paper's code keeps (not VLp, no missing SDF), the link holds (reproduced) when at least 90% are found in every file they span and, for matched unit-directions with at least 10 valid trials, the SDF computed from the dandiset correlates with the stored SDF at r > 0.9 for at least 90%. Partially reproduced when 50 to 90% of the records are found or match; not reproduced below 50%. Trial counts and the location labels of the matched units are reported.

claims.statement: 209 single units met the criteria to be included as GPi neurons (105 in NHP G, 104 in NHP I) and 185 as VLa neurons (66 and 119).
claims.source: Results, Basic approach, database, and activity at rest, paragraph 5; Table 1
claims.quote: a total of 209 single units met the criteria to be included as GPi neurons and 218 as VLa neurons (Table 1).
claims.criterion: Units under the dandiset rule, counted by area. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance. The Results text gives 218 VLa units where Table 1 gives 185; both readings are checked for VLa. Counts per animal are reported, and, as variants, the count of distinct channel and sort letter combinations per day (treating them as one neuron, an assumption) and the count of the paper's list found in the dandiset.

claims.statement: The resting firing rate of GPi neurons (mean 70.1 spikes/s) is significantly higher than that of VLa neurons (13.5 spikes/s), and the rates are consistent between the two animals.
claims.source: Results, Basic approach, database, and activity at rest, paragraph 5; Table 1
claims.quote: the resting firing rate of GPi neurons was significantly higher than that of VLa neurons ... and those rates and the differences between neural populations were highly consistent for the two animals
claims.criterion: Rest rate per unit-direction as the mean SDF from -1500 to -301 ms around movement onset (Fig2_3_S8_S9.m), averaged over unit-directions. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance and a rank sum test finds GPi higher (p < 0.05). Per animal values are reported.

claims.statement: Action potentials of GPi neurons are shorter than those of VLa neurons (trough to peak 0.24 against 0.50 ms; rank sum p = 1e-33).
claims.source: Results, Basic approach, database, and activity at rest, paragraph 5; Table 1
claims.quote: Also, as expected, the action potentials of GPi neurons were short in duration as compared with those of VLa neurons
claims.criterion: Width as the time from the trough to the following peak of the mean waveform on the unit's channel in the dandiset's 200 Hz high-pass filtered trace, from the spikes in one stored chunk (about 3.2 s) per unit. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance and GPi widths are smaller (rank sum p < 0.05); partially reproduced when only the difference holds.

claims.statement: The firing rate of most units ramps during the start-position hold period (97% of GPi and 98% of VLa units with a significant linear trend); slopes are distributed symmetrically around zero, without a difference between GPi and VLa (rank sum p = 0.29).
claims.source: Results, Basic approach, database, and activity at rest, paragraph 6; Fig 2A
claims.quote: The mean firing rate of most single units showed small but significant ramps during the start-position hold period ... 97% and 98% of GPi and VLa cells, respectively). ... For both GPi and VLa unit populations, the observed slopes were distributed symmetrically around zero
claims.criterion: A unit has a significant slope when the 95% CI of the OLS slope of its mean SDF over the control period excludes zero in at least one direction (Fig2_3_S8_S9.m). Reproduced when both fractions are within tolerance and the slopes of GPi and VLa do not differ by a rank sum test (p >= 0.05). The mean slopes (paper -0.05 and -0.14 spikes/s2) are reported.

claims.statement: Nearly all units change their discharge around movement for at least one direction (GPi 99%, 206 of 209; VLa 88.1%, 163 of 185 in Table 1, 94% in the text).
claims.source: Results, Movement-related increases in firing are common in both GPi and VLa, paragraph 1; Table 1
claims.quote: Nearly all single units showed a significant peri-movement change in discharge for at least one direction of movement, with slightly fewer VLa units responding (99% of GPi neurons and 94% of VLa neurons; p = 0.02, chi-squared test).
claims.criterion: A unit is responsive when an increase or a decrease is detected for at least one direction. Reproduced when both fractions are within tolerance; VLa is read as 88.1% (Table 1) or 94% (text, tolerance 9.4), and either reading counts.

claims.statement: Monophasic increases are the most common form of response in both GPi and VLa (48.7% and 65.3% of responses), and increases make up most detected changes (61.5% and 68.8%, biphasic responses counted twice), more than decreases (chi-squared p = 1.2e-17).
claims.source: Results, Movement-related increases in firing are common in both GPi and VLa, paragraph 3; Table 1; Fig 2B
claims.quote: Monophasic increases were the most common form of response both in GPi and in VLa (48.7% and 65.3% of responses detected, respectively; Table 1). ... increases in firing were also more common than decreases both in GPi and in VLa (61.5% and 68.8% of changes, respectively
claims.criterion: Over unit-directions with a response. Reproduced when monophasic increase is the most common of the four forms in both areas, increases exceed 50% of changes in both areas, and all four values are within tolerance. Partially reproduced when the order holds (increases most common in both) but a value is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Monophasic changes are more common in VLa than in GPi (88.9% against 66.7% of responses; chi-squared p = 2.8e-12), and polyphasic responses more common in GPi.
claims.source: Results, Movement-related increases in firing are common in both GPi and VLa, paragraph 2; Table 1
claims.quote: Monophasic changes in firing ... were the most common change detected in both GPi and VLa, amounting to 66.7% and 88.9% of all responses detected, respectively. Monophasic responses were more common in VLa than in GPi
claims.criterion: Over unit-directions with a response, a chi-squared test of monophasic against polyphasic by area. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance and VLa is higher with p < 0.05; partially reproduced when only the significant difference holds.

claims.statement: The mean integrated change in firing over the peri-movement epoch is positive in both GPi and VLa (3.89 and 1.75 spikes), significantly different from zero.
claims.source: Results, Movement-related increases in firing are common in both GPi and VLa, paragraph 4; Table 1
claims.quote: This inclination toward increases was confirmed quantitatively by integrating changes in firing rate from baseline across the peri-movement epoch individually for each neuron. The mean of this integrated change was positive both for GPi and VLa
claims.criterion: Over unit-directions (Fig2_3_S8_S9.m). Reproduced when both means are positive with a signed rank test against zero at p < 0.05 and both are within tolerance; partially reproduced when both are significantly positive but a value is outside tolerance. Table 1 gives the unit as "sp x 10^3"; the code divides the summed rate deviation in spikes/s at 1 ms by 1000, which gives spikes, and that is the reading used.

claims.statement: Peri-movement changes begin later in GPi than in VLa (median onsets -47 and -90 ms; rank sum p = 2.4e-5).
claims.source: Results, Response onset latencies in GPi and VLa are incompatible with gating and rebound, paragraph 1; Fig 3A
claims.quote: on average, GPi changes in discharge began later than those in VLa (median onset times: -47 and -90 ms for GPi and VLa populations, respectively
claims.criterion: All detected increases and decreases pooled per area (Fig2_3_S8_S9.m, "ALL RESPONSES"). Reproduced when GPi onsets are later than VLa onsets by a rank sum test (p < 0.05) and both medians are within tolerance; partially reproduced when only the significant difference holds.

claims.statement: GPi decreases lag behind VLa increases (median onsets -27 and -88 ms; rank sum p = 4.9e-4), against the gating prediction.
claims.source: Results, Response onset latencies in GPi and VLa are incompatible with gating and rebound, paragraph 1; Fig 3B
claims.quote: the distribution of GPi decreases lagged in time behind that of VLa increases (median onset times: -27 and -88 ms for GPi and VLa populations, respectively
claims.criterion: As fig3a-vla-leads-gpi, on GPi decreases against VLa increases.

claims.statement: VLa decreases precede GPi increases (median onsets -108 and -62 ms; rank sum p = 0.01).
claims.source: Results, Response onset latencies in GPi and VLa are incompatible with gating and rebound, paragraph 1; Fig 3C
claims.quote: VLa decreases did not follow but rather preceded GPi increases (median onset times: -62 and -108 ms for GPi and VLa populations, respectively; z = 2.58, p = 0.01, rank sum test; Fig 3C).
claims.criterion: As fig3a-vla-leads-gpi, on VLa decreases against GPi increases.

claims.statement: Comparing every GPi response with every VLa response, 96% of comparisons conflict with gating (178,846 of 187,154); only 4% have a GPi onset 0 to 50 ms before the VLa onset with the opposite sign.
claims.source: Results, Response onset latencies in GPi and VLa are incompatible with gating and rebound, paragraph 2
claims.quote: A large preponderance of these comparisons (96%, n = 178,846 of 187,154 comparisons) directly conflicted with the gating hypothesis because of the relative timing or signs of the responses
claims.criterion: Every detected GPi change against every detected VLa change; a comparison fits gating when the GPi onset precedes the VLa onset by 0 to 50 ms and the signs are opposite. Reproduced when the conflicting fraction is within tolerance.

claims.statement: A majority of GPi neurons (109 of 206) and some VLa neurons (56 of 179) respond significantly more strongly to one movement direction.
claims.source: Results, Movement-related increases in firing are common in both GPi and VLa, paragraph 5; Materials and methods, Spike sorting and detection of peri-movement discharge, paragraph 8
claims.quote: the majority of GPi neurons (109 out of 206) and some VLa neurons (56 out of 179) showed significantly stronger responses to one of the movement directions
claims.criterion: For responsive units, trial spike counts in the 300 ms from the unit's earliest detected onset compared between left and right trials (rank sum p < 0.005, Methods). Reproduced when both fractions are within tolerance; partially reproduced when GPi is directional more often than VLa (chi-squared p < 0.05) but a value is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Short-time-scale spike-to-spike correlations between simultaneously recorded GPi and VLa units are rare (3.5% of 427 pairs over whole recordings, 2.2% of 183 at rest, 5.2% of 172 during movement) and their peaks are not larger than those of jittered controls (p = 0.975, 0.675 and 0.998).
claims.source: Results, Correlated activity in GPi-VLa cell pairs is rare and unbiased, paragraph 1; Fig 4A-F; Table 2
claims.quote: only 3.5% of the CCFs showed any statistically significant modulation (15 of 427 cell pairs; ... the overall distribution of the peak absolute correlation values was not greater than the distribution of control peak absolute correlations
claims.criterion: A claim of absence judged on the paper's test, the one-sided permutation test of the KS statistic of peak absolute CCFs (0 to 10 ms) against jittered controls (Fig4_S10to13.m). Reproduced when p >= 0.05 in all three periods; not reproduced when p < 0.05 in any. Pairs are GPi and VLa units of the dandiset rule in the same file, with at least 100 spikes each in the period. The fraction of significant pairs, its binomial test against 5%, and the signs of the significant peaks are reported.

claims.statement: Trial-to-trial noise correlations between GPi and VLa are rare (5.4% of 332 pairs at rest, 7.2% of 372 during movement), not different from shuffled controls (p = 0.07 and 0.388), and equally often positive and negative.
claims.source: Results, Correlated activity in GPi-VLa cell pairs is rare and unbiased, paragraph 5; Fig 4G-H; Table 2
claims.quote: We found that the overall distribution of noise correlations was not significantly different from the control distribution (Fig 4G and 4H; p = 0.07 during rest, p = 0.388 during movement; permutation test).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence judged on the paper's test, the one-sided permutation test of the KS statistic of the absolute noise correlations against trial-shuffled controls. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 in both periods; not reproduced when p < 0.05 in either. Noise correlations are computed per pair and target on 500 ms spike counts in the rest and movement windows, with the Methods' exclusions; the fraction outside the 2.5 to 97.5 percentiles of the pooled shuffles and its sign balance are reported, counted (a) over pair-targets and (b) over pairs.

claims.statement: At rest, GPi burst onsets, burst offsets and pause onsets are each followed by a small, slow decrease of the population VLa firing rate.
claims.source: Results, VLa activity decreases with bursts and pauses in GPi activity, paragraphs 1 and 2; Fig 5A-C; Table 2
claims.quote: Small but significant transient decreases in VLa population spike rate were evident following both the onsets and offsets of bursts. ... a deceleration in VLa activity was also associated with pauses in GPi activity (Fig 5C).
claims.criterion: Bursts and pauses detected outside the task by the Poisson surprise method (Methods); VLa SDF (10 ms kernel) averaged around each event per pair, pairs with noisy baselines left out as the Methods say; population average over pairs. Its control is the same average with the events shifted by random offsets of 2 to 20 s within rest, 400 times, with the 2.5 and 97.5 percentile band widened so that 5% of controls cross it anywhere in 0 to 300 ms. Reproduced when the population average falls below the band within 0 to 300 ms after the event for all three event types; partially reproduced for one or two. The onset of the decrease (paper 119, 95 and 50 ms) and the per-pair fractions of significant changes are reported.

claims.statement: Reaction times do not differ between the animals or reach directions; movement durations are longer for reaches to the right target, and NHP G moves more slowly than NHP I.
claims.source: Results, Task performance, paragraph 1; S2 Fig
claims.quote: Reaction times did not differ significantly between the two animals ... or between the two reach directions ... Movement durations were longer for reaches to the more-distant, right target than to the left ... NHP G moved more slowly overall compared with NHP I
claims.criterion: Per file and direction, the median reaction time and movement duration of valid trials; a two-way ANOVA (animal, direction, interaction). Reproduced when the reaction time has no significant animal or direction effect (p >= 0.05) and the movement duration has both, right longer and G slower (p < 0.05). Partially reproduced when the movement duration part holds and the reaction time part does not, or the reverse.

claims.statement: Agonist EMG activity begins well before movement onset, at similar times in both animals (-123 and -135 ms).
claims.source: Results, Task performance, paragraph 1; S3 Fig
claims.quote: reach-related changes in agonist muscle EMG began well before the overt onset of movement as detected mechanically and those onset latencies were similar for the two animals (-123 and -135 ms in NHP G and I, respectively; S3 Fig).

claims.statement: Thalamic neurons inhibited by GPi stimulation lie dorsal and anterior to neurons excited by SCP stimulation, with a narrow border between VLa and VLp.
claims.source: Results, Basic approach, database, and activity at rest, paragraph 2; Fig 1A-B; S1 Fig
claims.quote: thalamic neurons inhibited by GPi stimulation ... were always encountered at locations that were dorsal and anterior to neurons excited by SCP stimulation ... In most cases a narrow border (<0.5 mm) separated the deepest GPi-inhibited neuron and the dorsal-most SCP-excited cell

claims.statement: In a model thalamocortical cell with N converging GPi inputs, post-spike inhibition grows with GPi synchrony c and shrinks with convergence N, approximately as ((N - 1)/N)c + 1/N.
claims.source: Results, Simulations suggest GPi-VLa communication scales with GPi synchrony and convergence, paragraph 1; Fig 6B-C
claims.quote: Results showed a clear growth of the post-spike inhibition of VLa with increasing c ... the post-spike inhibition of VLa decreased in magnitude as the number of converging GPi neurons (N) increased. Average correlations ... were approximately proportional to [(N - 1)/N]c + 1/N

claims.statement: Eyes stimulation was applied on 27 days per stimulated area (OFC, dmPFC and ACCg), 15 per area from monkey L and 12 per area from monkey T, and Mouth stimulation on 5 days per area from monkey T.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Closed-loop microstimulation protocol, paragraph 1; Figure 1B legend
claims.quote: In our main experiments (Eyes stimulation; n = 15 per area from monkey L and n = 12 per area from monkey T)
claims.criterion: Counts of days, so no tolerance; a day counts when it holds stimulation and sham trials of the named experiment and area. The code's day lists (S2_Gaze_Stats_Basic_Behaviors_Combined.m) give the dates of the 81 Eyes stimulation days. Reproduced when every count matches; partially reproduced when the Eyes counts match and the Mouth days are not in the dataset.

claims.statement: Each day held on average 10 live social gaze sessions (9 to 11) and 5 non-social control sessions (4 to 8) for monkey L, and 15 social (14 to 15) and 5 control sessions for monkey T, each 300 s long.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Experimental setup, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Each data collection day consisted of a total of alternating 10 live social gaze sessions and 5 non-social control sessions on average for monkey L (9-11 social and 4-8 control sessions across all days) and alternating 15 live social gaze sessions and 5 non-social control sessions on average for monkey T (14-15 social and 5 control sessions across all days). Each session lasted 300 sec.
claims.criterion: Over the Eyes stimulation days. The reported ranges (9 to 11, 4 to 8, 14 to 15, 5) are checked as ranges widened by 10% of each bound. Reproduced when all means and ranges hold.

claims.statement: In the live social gaze condition, the total numbers of microstimulations and of shams per day were comparable across the three stimulated areas and between the two monkeys.
claims.source: Results, opening section, paragraph 2; Figure 1E legend
claims.quote: The total number of microstimulations (and shams) received per day was comparable across the three stimulated regions and comparable between the two animals both in the social gaze and non-social control conditions (Fig. 1E, live social gaze condition, all p > 0.90
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per day, the number of microstimulation trials and of sham trials of the social sessions, counted as in S1_Total_Number_of_Stim_Combined.m (the trials kept for analysis). Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, two-sided, between each pair of areas for both monkeys combined and for each monkey, and between the monkeys for each area, 12 tests for stimulations and 12 for shams, each set FDR-corrected (Benjamini-Hochberg; the code calls dsp3.fdr, an outside package). Reproduced when no corrected p is below 0.05; the smallest corrected p is reported, and whether all exceed 0.90.

claims.statement: In the non-social control condition the numbers of microstimulations and shams per day were also comparable across areas and between monkeys.
claims.source: Results, opening section, paragraph 2; Figure S1D legend
claims.quote: Fig. S1D, non-social control condition, all p > 0.10
claims.criterion: As fig1e-stim-counts-comparable, on the control (RDM) sessions. Reproduced when no FDR-corrected p is below 0.05; whether all exceed 0.10 is reported.

claims.statement: The stimulated monkeys made significantly more fixations per day on the partner's Eyes than on the non-eye Face, for days of all three stimulated areas.
claims.source: Results, opening section, paragraph 2; Figure S1E
claims.quote: The total number of fixations on partner's Eyes per day was significantly higher than fixations on non-eye Face for all three stimulated brain regions (Fig. S1E, top, all p < 10−4, Wilcoxon signed rank, two-sided, FDR-corrected)
claims.criterion: Per day, the number of M1 fixations in the Eyes ROI and in the non-eye Face ROI (whole Face minus Eyes) over the social sessions, compared with a two-sided signed-rank test over the 27 days of each area, FDR-corrected (Benjamini-Hochberg, dsp3.fdr) over the 15 day-count tests of S3_Stats_ROI_number_duration_final.m (By_region_total_number_p_correct, both monkeys combined; Eyes against non-eye Face and Eyes against RDM for each area, and the rank-sum tests between areas for Eyes, non-eye Face and RDM). The Methods say "total number ... for each day"; the code takes the mean over the day's sessions of the per-session count. Readings (a) the day's total and (b) the mean per session; they give the same ranks only when session numbers are equal. Reproduced when, under each reading, Eyes exceed non-eye Face with corrected p < 0.05 for all three areas; the p-values are compared with 10^-4.

claims.statement: The number of fixations on the partner's Eyes per day was comparable to the number of fixations on the RDM stimulus, for days of all three areas.
claims.source: Results, opening section, paragraph 2; Figure S1E
claims.quote: the total number of fixations on partner's Eyes per day was comparable to fixations on the RDM stimulus for days involving the three stimulated regions (Fig. S1E, top, all p > 0.30)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per day, M1 fixations in the Eyes ROI in social sessions against fixations in the RDM ROI in control sessions, paired by day, two-sided signed-rank test per area, FDR-corrected as in figs1e-eyes-more-than-face, under the same two readings of the day count. Reproduced when no corrected p is below 0.05 under the paper's reading (a); reading (b) is shown as the code's variant.

claims.statement: After OFC microstimulations, compared with shams, the stimulated monkey's fixations in the 1.5 s post-gaze epoch were more clustered around the partner monkey.
claims.source: Results, Closed-loop microstimulations of OFC facilitate momentary social attention in the spatial dimension, paragraph 2; Figure 2A
claims.quote: Specifically, microstimulations of OFC led to more clustered subsequent gaze fixations around the partner monkey (Fig. 2A
claims.criterion: From the Methods (Fixation density map): fixations of the post-gaze epoch assigned to 1-degree squares of a 40 by 40 degree grid centred on the partner's Eyes ROI, counts summed per day for stimulation and for sham trials, the stimulation minus sham difference averaged over days per area, monkey T's maps flipped horizontally. The normalisation is given two ways, and both are run: (1) the Methods, each day's maps z-scored over grid squares before the difference; (2) the code (S1_Gaze_Fixation_Heatmap.m), the difference divided by the day's total count of stimulation and sham fixations. The paper reads the map by eye and gives no measure of "more clustered"; the readings named are (a) the averaged difference summed over squares inside the whole Face ROI is positive, and (b) the same inside the Eyes ROI. The claim is reproduced when the OFC map is positive under every reading and normalisation, not reproduced when it is negative under all, and blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ. dmPFC and ACCg values are reported alongside.

claims.statement: OFC microstimulations decreased the social gaze distance, the mean distance of the stimulated monkey's fixations in the post-gaze epoch from the centre of the partner's Eyes, compared with shams; the effect held in each monkey.
claims.source: Results, Closed-loop microstimulations of OFC facilitate momentary social attention in the spatial dimension, paragraph 3; Figure 2C legend
claims.quote: microstimulations of OFC significantly decreased the average distance of one's own gaze positions in space relative to partner's Eyes during the post-gaze epoch, compared to shams (Fig. 2C, p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank, two-sided
claims.criterion: Social gaze distance per trial and per day as in the opening comment (STAR Methods, Gaze distance analyses; S3_Basic_Gaze_Matrices_Combined.m, S1_Gaze_Results_Combined.m and S2_Gaze_Stats_Basic_Behaviors_Combined.m), day means of stimulation trials against day means of sham trials, two-sided signed-rank test over OFC days. The outcome is judged on the Methods reading of the fixations (M1-only and mutual events); the code's M1-only reading is shown as a variant (opening comment). Reproduced when the combined test gives p < 0.001 with the median day difference (stimulation minus sham) negative, and each monkey's test gives p < 0.05 in the same direction; partially reproduced when the combined test gives p < 0.05 in that direction but a monkey's does not or the combined p is not below 0.001. The p-values are compared with the reported ones.

claims.statement: Microstimulations of dmPFC or ACCg did not change social gaze distance.
claims.source: Results, Closed-loop microstimulations of OFC facilitate momentary social attention in the spatial dimension, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
claims.quote: By contrast, we did not observe such stimulation effect on social gaze distance for dmPFC (Fig. 2C, p = 0.361) or ACCg (Fig. 2C, p = 0.374)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, as in fig2c-ofc-social-gaze-distance for dmPFC and ACCg days. Reproduced when neither test gives p < 0.05; the median day differences and p-values are reported.

claims.statement: The OFC effect on social gaze distance was stronger for fixations in the hemifield contralateral to the stimulated hemisphere; it was significant for contralateral fixations, not for ipsilateral ones, and the contralateral effect exceeded the ipsilateral one.
claims.source: Results, Closed-loop microstimulations of OFC facilitate momentary social attention in the spatial dimension, paragraph 3; Figure 2E legend
claims.quote: Notably, the observed stimulation effect of OFC was more pronounced for gaze fixations in the contralateral visual field of the stimulated brain hemisphere (Fig. 2D–E; contralateral: p < 0.001; significant statistics for individual animals are reported in the figure legend; ipsilateral: p = 0.068; contralateral vs. ipsilateral: p = 0.026, Wilcoxon signed rank, two-sided)
claims.criterion: Fixations split by hemifield as in the opening comment (S1_Get_data_gaze_Lynch.m and _Tarantino.m), social gaze distance per trial and day computed within each hemifield. The effect of a day is the stimulation minus sham difference of day means. Tests from the Methods: signed-rank of stimulation against sham per hemifield, and signed-rank of the contralateral effect against the ipsilateral effect paired by day (the code holds no script for this last test; the pairing by day follows from the Methods' "Wilcoxon signed rank test ... between hemifields"). Days without fixations in a hemifield are left out of that test. Reproduced when the contralateral test gives p < 0.05 with negative median effect, the ipsilateral test gives p >= 0.05, and the contralateral against ipsilateral test gives p < 0.05 with the contralateral effect more negative. Partially reproduced when only the contralateral effect holds. Per-monkey values are reported and compared.

claims.statement: For dmPFC and ACCg there was no stimulation effect on social gaze distance in either hemifield, and no difference between hemifields.
claims.source: Results, Closed-loop microstimulations of OFC facilitate momentary social attention in the spatial dimension, paragraph 3; Figure 2E
claims.quote: Again, no such effect was observed in either hemifield for dmPFC (Fig. 2E, contralateral: p = 0.501; ipsilateral: p = 0.149; contralateral vs. ipsilateral: p = 0.230) or ACCg (Fig. 2E, p = 0.442; p = 0.517; p = 0.564)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests as in fig2e-ofc-contralateral for dmPFC and ACCg. Reproduced when none of the six tests gives p < 0.05; effects and p-values are reported.

claims.statement: In the non-social control condition, microstimulations of none of the three areas changed the distance of fixations from the centre of the RDM stimulus.
claims.source: Results, Closed-loop microstimulations of OFC facilitate momentary social attention in the spatial dimension, paragraph 4; Figure 2F
claims.quote: Crucially, these stimulation effects of OFC were exclusively observed in the live social gaze condition ... and not in the non-social gaze control condition using the RDM stimulus with no behavioral meaning to monkeys (Fig. 2F, OFC
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Non-social gaze distance as social gaze distance with the centre of the RDM ROI in place of the Eyes (STAR Methods, Gaze distance analyses, last sentence; S1_Dot_Results_Combined.m), on control-session trials, signed-rank over days per area. Reproduced when no area gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In the non-social control condition there was no stimulation effect in either hemifield, and no hemifield difference, for any area.
claims.source: Results, Closed-loop microstimulations of OFC facilitate momentary social attention in the spatial dimension, paragraph 4; Figure 2G-H
claims.quote: The absence of stimulation effect for the RDM stimulus was also found when gaze fixation locations were split by hemifield for OFC (Fig. 2G–H; contralateral: p = 0.097; ipsilateral: p = 0.249; contralateral vs. ipsilateral: p = 0.442), dmPFC (p = 0.374; p = 0.517; p = 0.773) or ACCg (p = 0.532; p = 0.943; p = 0.171)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests, as fig2e-ofc-contralateral on control-session trials with distances to the RDM centre. The hemifield split uses the same reference as the code uses for social sessions, center_roi_m2_face (S1_Get_data_dot_Lynch.m and _Tarantino.m; opening comment). Reproduced when none of the nine tests gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The OFC decrease of social gaze distance also held within 2 s and within 3 s after the trial for both monkeys combined and for monkey L, not for monkey T.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Gaze distance analyses, paragraph 1
claims.quote: In fact, the effect was present and lasted longer beyond 1.5 sec in one of the stimulated monkeys (within 2 sec after trial onset
claims.criterion: As fig2c-ofc-social-gaze-distance with the window [0, 2) s and [0, 3) s (the code's alternative call basic_gaze_matrices(GazeData, 0, 3)). Reproduced when, for both windows, the combined and monkey L tests give p < 0.05 with stimulation below sham and the monkey T test gives p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when the combined tests hold.

claims.statement: OFC microstimulations did not change the number of fixations within the partner's Eyes or whole Face in the post-gaze window, in either monkey, for windows of 1.5, 2 or 3 s.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Gaze distance analyses, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Following OFC microstimulations, unlike more clustered subsequent gaze fixations around another social agent, we did not observe any change in the total number of fixations within partner's Eyes (within 1.5 sec
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests. Per trial, the number of M1 fixations starting in the window and lying in the Eyes ROI, or in the whole Face ROI (Eyes, Mouth and the rest of the face), counting M1-only events as the code does (fixation_m1_eye_number and fixation_m1_wholeface_number in S3_Basic_Gaze_Matrices_Combined.m, which use M1-only events); day means per trial type; signed-rank test over OFC days for each monkey. Readings for the events counted are (a) M1-only events, as the code, (b) M1-only and mutual events. Reproduced when no test gives p < 0.05 under the code's reading (a); reading (b) is shown.

claims.statement: With OFC microstimulations the stimulated monkey spent more time looking within the partner's whole Face in the post-gaze epoch (48.9 ms more than with shams, both monkeys combined), and more weakly within the Eyes; dmPFC and ACCg showed no such effect.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Gaze distance analyses, paragraph 2
claims.quote: With OFC microstimulations, the monkeys spent more time looking within the partner's whole Face (p = 0.003, stim minus sham difference = 48.9 msec for both monkeys combined; p = 0.008, diff = 66.6 msec for monkey L and p = 0.129, diff = 39.5 msec for monkey T)
claims.criterion: Per trial, the summed duration of M1 fixations starting in [0, 1.5) s and lying in the whole Face ROI or in the Eyes ROI (fixation_m1_wholeface_totalduration and fixation_m1_eye_totalduration in the code, M1-only events, 0 when none); day means per trial type; signed-rank test over days. How "diff" is taken is not stated; the readings are (a) the median over days of the stimulation minus sham day means, (b) the mean over days of that difference. Reproduced when the OFC whole Face test gives p < 0.05 with stimulation longer, dmPFC and ACCg give p >= 0.05, the OFC Eyes test gives p < 0.05, and under one reading the OFC whole Face differences fall within tolerance. Partially reproduced when the tests hold and no reading matches the numbers.

claims.statement: When microstimulations were triggered by looking at the partner's Mouth (or at an RDM stimulus at the Mouth location), none of the three areas changed social or non-social gaze distance, in either hemifield.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Gaze distance analyses (Mouth stimulation); Results, Closed-loop microstimulations of OFC facilitate momentary social attention in the spatial dimension, paragraph 4
claims.quote: On the day level, none of the three brain regions had any microstimulation effect on social gaze distance (OFC
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Social gaze distance on Mouth stimulation days as in fig2c-ofc-social-gaze-distance with the centre of the partner's Mouth ROI (same size as the Eyes ROI without padding), and non-social distance to the centre of the RDM ROI at the Mouth location; signed-rank over the 5 days per area, both hemifields and each hemifield. The code in the repository holds no Mouth-stimulation script; the trial handling of the Eyes analysis is used. Reproduced when no test gives p < 0.05. If the dataset does not hold the Mouth stimulation days the claim cannot be tested.

claims.statement: For contralateral fixations, the OFC stimulation effect on social gaze distance was significantly more negative in Eyes stimulation than in Mouth stimulation, but not for ipsilateral fixations or both hemifields combined; the difference was stronger using monkey T's Eyes days only.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Gaze distance analyses (Mouth stimulation)
claims.quote: For fixations in the contralateral hemifield, microstimulation effect (stimulation minus sham) of OFC led to significantly smaller social gaze distance in Eyes stimulation compared to Month stimulation (p = 0.009), while no effect was observed for fixations in the ipsilateral hemifield (p = 0.724) or when both hemifields combined (p = 0.799)
claims.criterion: From the Methods. The OFC effect per day is the stimulation minus sham difference of day-mean social gaze distance. 5 days are drawn with replacement from the 27 OFC Eyes days (or the 12 of monkey T) 1,000 times, the median effect of each draw is taken, and the 1,000 medians are compared with the median effect of the 5 OFC Mouth days. The p-value is not defined in the paper and no code holds it; the readings are (a) the fraction of bootstrap medians at or above the Mouth median (one-sided, Eyes smaller), (b) twice the smaller tail fraction (two-sided). The seed is a standard choice and is recorded. Reproduced when, under a reading, the contralateral p values are below 0.05 and the ipsilateral and combined ones are not, for both the all-days and the monkey-T comparisons; the outcome follows the rule for several readings.

claims.statement: OFC microstimulations decreased the inter-looking interval, the latency of the stimulated monkey to look back at the partner's whole Face within 5 s after the trial, compared with shams; dmPFC and ACCg microstimulations did not.
claims.source: Results, Microstimulations of OFC also promote momentary social attention in the temporal dimension, Inter-looking interval, paragraph 1; Figure 3B legend
claims.quote: Microstimulations of OFC decreased this inter-looking interval (Fig. 3B, p = 0.035, Wilcoxon signed rank, two-sided; see Fig. S3A for an alternative visualization). However, we did not observe such stimulation effect for dmPFC (Fig. 3B, p = 0.792) or ACCg (Fig. 3B, p = 0.291)
claims.criterion: From the Methods (Gaze latency analyses) and S1_Gaze_M1_Latency_Combined.m. Per trial, the time from the trial sample to the start of the first M1-only or mutual whole Face event that starts after it and within 5,000 samples (5 s); no such event leaves the trial out (NaN). Day means per trial type, ignoring NaN; signed-rank over days. Reproduced when OFC gives p < 0.05 with stimulation shorter and dmPFC and ACCg give p >= 0.05; per-monkey values are reported (the paper finds neither significant alone).

claims.statement: The inter-looking interval did not change with stimulation in the non-social control condition, for any area.
claims.source: Results, Microstimulations of OFC also promote momentary social attention in the temporal dimension, Inter-looking interval, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Further, this reduction of inter-looking interval from OFC microstimulations was specific to social attention as no effect was observed in the non-social gaze condition
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, as fig3b-ofc-inter-looking-interval on control sessions with the corresponding whole Face ROI and M1 events only (S1_Dot_M1_Latency_Combined.m). Reproduced when no area gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: On 41% of microstimulation and sham trials per day on average, the stimulated monkey did not look back at the partner's whole Face within the 5 s window.
claims.source: Results, Microstimulations of OFC also promote momentary social attention in the temporal dimension, Inter-looking interval, paragraph 1
claims.quote: the stimulated monkey did not look back at the partner's whole Face during the examined time window on 41% of microstimulation and sham trials per day on average
claims.criterion: Per day, the fraction of analysed social-session trials (stimulation and sham together) whose inter-looking interval is NaN, averaged over days. The days averaged over are not stated; the readings are (a) all 81 Eyes stimulation days, (b) the 27 OFC days. Reproduced when a reading falls within tolerance.

claims.statement: With all trials of each area pooled across days, OFC microstimulations still decreased the inter-looking interval, while dmPFC and ACCg did not.
claims.source: Results, Microstimulations of OFC also promote momentary social attention in the temporal dimension, Inter-looking interval, paragraph 1; Figure S3B legend
claims.quote: Nevertheless, when we combined all trials for each stimulated region, we still observed similar results to the day-level analysis above (Fig. S3B, OFC
claims.criterion: Trial inter-looking intervals as in fig3b-ofc-inter-looking-interval, stimulation trials against sham trials of all days of an area pooled, rank-sum test (S3_Gaze_M1_Latency_Across_Trials.m). Reproduced when OFC gives p < 0.05 with stimulation shorter and dmPFC and ACCg give p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: At the day level, microstimulations did not significantly reduce the reciprocation latency in any area; on 86% of trials per day on average there was no sequence of the partner looking at the stimulated monkey followed by the stimulated monkey looking back.
claims.source: Results, Reciprocation latency, paragraph 1; Figure S3C legend
claims.quote: On the day level, microstimulations did not seem to greatly reduce such reciprocation latency (Fig. S3C–D, OFC
claims.criterion: Reciprocation latency per trial from S1_Gaze_ITI_Combined.m ("all_face" events): whole Face events of M1 and of M2 that start in the 5 s after the trial, mutual events counted for both; for each run of consecutive M2 events followed by an M1 event, the time from the start of the run's first M2 event to the start of that M1 event; the trial's value is the mean over such sequences, NaN when there is none. Day means per trial type ignoring NaN; signed-rank over days. A claim of absence for the tests: reproduced when no area gives p < 0.05. The 86% is the per-day fraction of analysed trials with NaN, averaged over days, under the readings (a) all 81 days, (b) the 27 OFC days; it is reported against its tolerance and is part of the claim.

claims.statement: With trials pooled across days, OFC microstimulations decreased the latency of the stimulated monkey to reciprocate the partner's gaze to his face; dmPFC and ACCg did not.
claims.source: Results, Reciprocation latency, paragraph 1; Figure 3D legend
claims.quote: When combining all trials for each stimulated region, we observed that microstimulations of OFC decreased reciprocation latency (Fig. 3D, p = 0.011, Wilcoxon rank sum, two-sided). We again did not observe such stimulation effect for dmPFC (Fig. 3D, p = 0.777) or ACCg (Fig. 3D, p = 0.368)
claims.criterion: Trial reciprocation latencies as in figs3c-reciprocation-day-level-none, stimulation trials against sham trials of all days of an area pooled, NaN trials left out, rank-sum test (S3_Gaze_ITI_Across_Trials.m). Reproduced when OFC gives p < 0.05 with stimulation shorter and dmPFC and ACCg give p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Microstimulations in none of the areas changed the partner monkey's social gaze distance, inter-looking interval or reciprocation latency.
claims.source: Results, Microstimulations do not change momentary social attention in the unstimulated animal, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Therefore, we did not find any evidence that the social gaze behaviors of the unstimulated monkey were altered on a short timescale during social gaze interactions.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests (signed-rank over days per area). M2 social gaze distance: M2 fixations starting in [0, 1.5) s, distance to the centre of M1's Eyes ROI (m2_distance_to_eyes in the code). M2 inter-looking interval, from the Results: the latency between the first and second M2 whole Face events within 5 s after the trial. M2 reciprocation latency, from the Results: the latency of M2 to look at M1's whole Face within 5 s after the trial when M2 was being looked at by M1. The code in the repository has no script for the two M2 latencies; whether the latency is taken from the trial time or from the start of the M1 look is open for the reciprocation latency, readings (a) from the start of the M1 whole Face event, (b) from the trial time. Reproduced when no test gives p < 0.05 under every reading.

claims.statement: Microstimulations did not change the relative causal strength of gaze between the monkeys in any area.
claims.source: Results, Do microstimulations of OFC also lead to longer timescale modulation of social gaze exchanges?, paragraph 1; Figure S4A legend
claims.quote: We did not observe stimulation effect on the magnitudes of relative causal strength (OFC ... dmPFC ... ACCg
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Relative causal strength per trial from the causal decomposition analysis of Yang, Peng and Huang (2018; code at github.com/accyang/causal-decomposition-analysis) of the moment-by-moment social gaze distance of M1 (to M2's Eyes centre) and of M2 (to M1's Eyes centre), in 10 ms bins (S1_Gaze_Binned_Distance_Combined.m), over the post-gaze epoch; the trial value is the mean over IMFs of the M1-to-M2 relative causal strength (S2_Gaze_Get_CDI.m). Trials are excluded when either monkey has more than 1 s of continuous NaN samples or when the ends of a smoothed gap are more than 20 degrees apart (Methods). Open, with no source: the smoothing used to fill gaps between fixations, and the decomposition's noise level, ensemble size and other settings. The output folder name cd_output_null_02_1000_150_100_10 suggests noise 0.2, 1,000 ensembles and 150 bins (1.5 s); this is taken as reading (a), and reading (b) is the defaults of the Yang et al. code with the same 150 bins. Linear interpolation over gaps is the gap filling under both, named as a standard choice that the paper does not fix. Day means per trial type, signed-rank over days per area. Reproduced when no area gives p < 0.05 under each reading.

claims.statement: Neither trial type nor time epoch (first 45 against next 45 stimulations) changed the relative causal strength in any area.
claims.source: Results, Do microstimulations of OFC also lead to longer timescale modulation of social gaze exchanges?, paragraph 1; Figure S4B legend
claims.quote: We did not observe effect of microstimulation trial type or time epoch on relative casual strength (OFC
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests. Epochs as in epoch-days-76-of-81; day means of relative causal strength for stimulation and sham trials in each epoch; the paper does not list the comparisons; the readings are (a) the four pairs that differ in one factor (stimulation against sham within each epoch, early against late within each trial type), (b) all six pairs of the four groups. Reproduced when no test gives p < 0.05 under each reading.

claims.statement: 76 of the 81 days had at least 90 microstimulations and entered the epoch analysis; the five excluded were 1 OFC day of monkey L and, of monkey T, 1 OFC, 2 dmPFC and 1 ACCg day.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Inter-individual gaze dynamics analyses, paragraph 2
claims.quote: 76 out of 81 days had at least 90 stimulations. The 5 days excluded from further analysis were 1 day from monkey L with OFC microstimulations, 1 day from monkey T OFC, 2 days from monkey T dmPFC, and 1 day from monkey T ACCg.
claims.criterion: A count of days with named composition, so no tolerance; the code (S1_Gaze_Time_Epoch.m) names the excluded days, 08122019 (L, OFC), 12222021 (T, OFC), 11052021 and 12172021 (T, dmPFC), 11042021 (T, ACCg). Stimulations are counted (a) among the analysed trials (first trial of each run and trials in the last 5 s dropped), as the code counts them, or (b) among all stimulations delivered. Reproduced when a reading gives 76 days with the named composition.

claims.statement: For OFC, the slope of the fitted relation between social gaze distance and relative causal strength did not differ between the early and late epochs, for both hemifields combined, contralateral or ipsilateral fixations.
claims.source: Results, Do microstimulations of OFC also lead to longer timescale modulation of social gaze exchanges?, paragraph 1; Figure 4C; Figure S4C-D
claims.quote: we correlated social gaze distance and relative causal strength (STAR Methods) and found the slope of this fitted correlation comparable between early and late epochs for OFC (Fig. S4C, both hemifields combined: p = 0.757; Fig. 4C, contralateral: p = 0.882; Fig. S4D, ipsilateral: p = 0.098)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. From the Methods and S3_Gaze_Correlation_by_Epoch.m. For each day and epoch, an ordinary least squares fit (fitlm) of relative causal strength on social gaze distance (in degrees) over the stimulation trials of the epoch; distance is the trial mean over fixations in the post-gaze epoch, overall, contralateral or ipsilateral. Late against early slopes, signed-rank over OFC days. Reproduced when no test gives p < 0.05, under each reading of figs4a-causal-strength-no-stim-effect.

claims.statement: For dmPFC, the slope of the relation between contralateral social gaze distance and relative causal strength was larger in the late than in the early epoch (p = 0.054, at the margin), and significantly so for both hemifields combined; not for ipsilateral fixations, and not for ACCg.
claims.source: Figure 4C legend; Figure S4C-D legends
claims.quote: For dmPFC, the slope of this fitted correlation was stronger for the late epoch than early epoch (p = 0.054 for both monkeys combined; p = 0.048 for monkey L and p = 0.625 for monkey T)
claims.criterion: Slopes as in ofc-slope-unchanged-by-epoch for dmPFC and ACCg days. Reproduced when the dmPFC contralateral test gives p at most 0.0594 (the reported 0.054 widened by 10%, the protocol's default tolerance; the paper marks it "p ≈ 0.05") with late slopes larger (median late minus early positive), the dmPFC both-hemifields test gives p < 0.05 in the same direction, and the dmPFC ipsilateral and the ACCg tests give p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when the direction holds and only some of these do. Results under each reading of the causal decomposition are shown.

claims.statement: Against a null from shuffling the order of each day's 90 stimulations, the dmPFC increase of the contralateral slope from early to late epoch was significant (p = 0.015), not for both hemifields combined or ipsilateral fixations.
claims.source: Results, Do microstimulations of OFC also lead to longer timescale modulation of social gaze exchanges?, paragraph 2; Figure 4D legend; Figure S4E-F legends
claims.quote: However, the slope of this fitted correlation for dmPFC was stronger for the late epoch than early epoch, specifically for gaze fixations in the contralateral hemifield (Fig. 4D; p = 0.015, permutation test
claims.criterion: From the Methods, the Figure 4D and S4E legends, S1_Gaze_Time_Epoch.m and S3_Gaze_Correlation_by_Epoch.m. The real statistic is the median over days of the late minus early slope (S3_Gaze_Correlation_by_Epoch.m). Null, from the Methods: within each day the 90 stimulation trials are permuted 1,000 times and split into the first 45 and the next 45, slopes refitted, and for each permutation the median over days of the slope difference is taken. The repository does not build this null: S3_Gaze_Correlation_by_Epoch.m loads a precomputed Decomp_Temporal_shuffled file whose causal strength field is named causal_m1m2_eyes_null, so whether the null also uses causal strengths from a null decomposition is open; the Methods construction above, with the real causal strengths carried with their trials, is used. The p-value computation is not in the repository; the readings are (a) one-sided in the direction of the real median, the fraction of null medians beyond it, as the code computes the permutation p of Fig. 5G (S6_Gaze_Saccade_Kinematics_Combined.m), (b) two-sided, twice that fraction. Reproduced when dmPFC contralateral gives p < 0.05 with a positive real median and the both-hemifields and ipsilateral tests give p >= 0.05; the outcome follows the rule for several readings, and per-monkey values are reported. (The Figure S4F legend prints a "* p < 0.05" key while the Results give p = 0.455; the Results value is used.)

claims.statement: For dmPFC, the slope of the relation between social gaze distance and relative causal strength was on average positive in both epochs, so that the closer the stimulated monkey looked to the partner, the more his gaze was led by the partner.
claims.source: Results, Do microstimulations of OFC also lead to longer timescale modulation of social gaze exchanges?, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Specifically, the slope of this examined correlation on average was positive in both early and late epochs for gaze fixations in both hemifields for dmPFC
claims.criterion: Slopes as in ofc-slope-unchanged-by-epoch, dmPFC days. "On average" is read as the mean over days, with the median as a second reading. "In both hemifields" is read as (a) the slope with both hemifields combined, (b) the contralateral and the ipsilateral slopes each. Reproduced when the average slope is positive in both epochs under every reading; the outcome follows the rule for several readings. No test is reported for this sign.

claims.statement: Microstimulations of OFC or dmPFC did not change the duration of the Eyes fixation that triggered the trial.
claims.source: Results, Microstimulation effects of OFC and dmPFC are not driven by low-level properties of saccades, paragraph 1; Figure 5A
claims.quote: Importantly, the observed effects of OFC and dmPFC microstimulations were not driven by any change in the duration of current looking to partner's Eyes that triggered a microstimulation or sham (Fig. 5A, OFC
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per trial, the duration of the M1 Eyes event in progress at the trial time; day means per trial type; signed-rank over days. Readings for the events (the code for this panel is not among the scripts read) are (a) M1-only and mutual Eyes events, (b) M1-only events. Reproduced when neither area gives p < 0.05 under each reading.

claims.statement: Pupil size did not differ between microstimulation and sham trials in any 10 ms bin of the 700 ms after trial onset, for any area.
claims.source: Results, Microstimulation effects of OFC and dmPFC are not driven by low-level properties of saccades, paragraph 1; Figure 5B legend
claims.quote: No difference was observed for pupil size between the two trial types throughout the 700-msec period following trial onset for any of the three stimulated regions.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. From the Methods and stim/S5_Pupil_Size.m. Trials where M1's gaze stays within the partner's whole Face ROI for the whole 700 ms after the trial; M1 pupil size averaged over trials per day and type in 10 ms bins; signed-rank per bin over days, uncorrected. Reproduced when no bin of any area gives p < 0.05; the number of bins below 0.05 is reported.

claims.statement: The numbers of microsaccades and macrosaccades in the post-gaze epoch did not differ between microstimulation and sham trials for OFC or dmPFC.
claims.source: Results, Microstimulation effects of OFC and dmPFC are not driven by low-level properties of saccades, paragraph 1; Figure 5C-D
claims.quote: number of microsaccades (Fig. 5C, OFC
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Saccades detected by the unsupervised clustering method of Otero-Millan et al. (2014); a saccade lying strictly within a fixation interval (EyeMMV) is a microsaccade, any other a macrosaccade (Methods). Counts per trial in the post-gaze epoch, day means per type, signed-rank over days. If the dataset holds no saccade events, the detection must be run with the Otero-Millan code (outside software) and the claim is with_inputs for that run. Reproduced when no test gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Microstimulations of OFC or dmPFC did not change macrosaccade peak velocity, the slope of peak velocity on amplitude, or that slope by saccade direction.
claims.source: Results, Microstimulation effects of OFC and dmPFC are not driven by low-level properties of saccades, paragraph 1; Figure 5E-H
claims.quote: macrosaccade peak velocity (Fig. 5E, OFC
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests. From the Methods and S6_Gaze_Saccade_Kinematics_Combined.m. The first macrosaccade of each trial's post-gaze epoch; day mean peak velocity per type, signed-rank. Per day, a linear fit of peak velocity on amplitude for stimulation and for sham trials, the slope difference tested against zero by signed-rank; the permutation test shuffles the trial labels 1,000 times within each day and gives the fraction of shuffled median differences beyond the real median, on its side, as the code does. Direction groups II, IC, CI and CC by the hemifields of start and end, signed-rank against zero per group. Reproduced when no test gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Mice trained on RI60 accept more shocks in the shock probes than mice trained on RR20 (main effect of schedule, F1,43 = 6.37, p < 0.05; schedule by time interaction, F1,43 = 4.54, p < 0.05), and RI60 mice accept more shocks on the late probe than on the early one (p < 0.01).
claims.source: Results, A random interval schedule of reinforcement promotes punishment-resistant reward-seeking, paragraph 2; Figure 1D
claims.quote: We observed a significant main effect of schedule (RI60 vs RR20) on the number of shocks mice were willing to receive on the shock probes ... after extended RI60 training, mice increased the number of shocks they were willing to receive
claims.criterion: Mice of the fiber photometry experiment with both probes. A two-way mixed ANOVA (schedule between mice, probe within) on shock counts. Reproduced when the schedule main effect and the interaction both have p < 0.05 with RI60 higher, and a paired t-test of late against early in RI60 mice has Bonferroni-corrected (x2) p < 0.01. Partially reproduced when the RI60 increase holds but the schedule effect or the interaction does not. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: RI60-trained mice take longer to complete the omission probe than RR20-trained mice (unpaired t-test, p < 0.05; n = 20 and 7).
claims.source: Results, A random interval schedule of reinforcement promotes punishment-resistant reward-seeking, paragraph 3; Figure 1E
claims.quote: RI60-trained mice took longer to complete the omission probe than RR20-trained mice
claims.criterion: Omission completion time per mouse (the 50th reward, or 60 min). Reproduced when the RI60 mean exceeds the RR20 mean with an unpaired t-test p < 0.05; partially when the direction holds with p >= 0.05; not reproduced when RR20 is longer.

claims.statement: Among RI60 mice, shocks received on the late probe and omission completion time are not significantly correlated (r = 0.42, ns).
claims.source: Results, A random interval schedule of reinforcement promotes punishment-resistant reward-seeking, paragraph 5; Figure 1F
claims.quote: We found that these two measures were not significantly correlated
claims.criterion: Absence claim. Pearson correlation over RI60 mice with both measures. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; r is reported either way.

claims.statement: RI60 mice are split by their shock probe counts into 9 punishment resistant (PR), 9 delayed punishment resistant (DPR) and 18 punishment sensitive (PS) mice, by the rule in the Methods (DPR when the count rises by more than 85%; otherwise PR when the early count exceeds 13).
claims.source: Figure 2A; STAR Methods, Behavioral Analysis, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Mice in the top quartile of changers (who increased the number of shocks received by greater than 85%) were classified as delayed punishment resistant (DPR; n=9) ... with mice receiving more than 13 shocks on the first probe classified as punishment resistant (PR; n=9) and those earning fewer as punishment sensitive
claims.criterion: The counts are those of the labels stored in the dandiset's RI60 fiber photometry mice. Reproduced when the counts match and the rule, applied to the dandiset's probe counts, gives the stored label for every mouse with both probes. Partially reproduced when the counts match and the rule agrees for at least 80% of those mice. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: There is an interaction of phenotype and probe on shocks received (p < 0.0001), and only DPR mice receive significantly more shocks on the late probe than the early one.
claims.source: Results, Three punishment-related phenotypes emerge with extended RI60 training, paragraph 1; Figure 2B
