claims.statement: Normalized to the periphery, the central peak is almost twofold for 1Px4 and about the same as the periphery for 5Px4 and 10Px4; the trough between center and electrodes is about twofold lower than the center for all treatments; the central peak becomes narrower with more packets.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6B
claims.quote: Its brightness was almost twofold higher than at the periphery for a single packet was applied 4 times from different directions, or about the same as at the periphery for the rotation of 5 and 10 packets ( Fig. 6B ). Interestingly, the least affected area of the cell monolayer (between the center and the electrodes) showed about 2-fold lower fluorescence intensity than in the center for all the treatments. Also, the central peak appeared narrower (sharper) with increasing the number of packets.
claims.criterion: Values from dish means, under the readings of the opening comment. "Almost twofold" is taken as 200% with the 10% tolerance, so it holds from 180% to 220%. The paper does not define the width of the central peak. Readings, (a) the full width of the normalized mean profile at half the height of the peak above the trough, (b) the distance between the troughs on either side of the center. The narrowing holds when the width decreases from 1Px4 to 5Px4 to 10Px4; it is judged under both readings, and blocked as methods_underspecified if they disagree. Reproduced when the values are within tolerance and the narrowing holds; partially when only some of them hold.

claims.statement: On the small array with 1Px4, raising the first pulse amplitude from 2.4 to 5.6 kV increases YP fluorescence 15.5 times at the most peripheral point, 16.2 times half-way to the center and 16.8 times in the center.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 7A
claims.quote: when the first pulse amplitude was increased from 2.4 to 5.6 kV (and the amplitude of the other pulses in the packet was increased proportionally, see Fig. 2C ), YP fluorescence increased 15.5 times at the most peripheral point; 16.2 times half-way to the center; and 16.8 times in the center ( Fig. 7A ).
claims.criterion: Ratios of the 5.6 kV mean to the 2.4 kV mean over dishes (n = 3), in a.u. "Half-way to the center" is the ROI at half the distance from the center to the most peripheral ROI; the paper does not say whether background is subtracted from the a.u. values, and none is, as in the Methods. Reproduced when all three ratios are within tolerance under a reading of the opening comment (ROI count, diagonals, center ROI, raw or LOESS); partially when one or two are.

claims.statement: Normalized to the most peripheral ROI, the profiles for different first pulse amplitudes fully overlap, so the spatial distribution of electroporation, and NG-CANCAN targeting, does not depend on amplitude within the studied range.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 7B
claims.quote: In contrast, changing nsEP amplitude affected the degree of electroporation but not its spatial distribution ( Fig. 7 ). ... When the YP emission was normalized to the most peripheral ROI, the data for different nsEP amplitudes fully overlapped ( Fig. 7B ).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper names one test, the two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 (Section 2.4), and reads significance from the error bar gap. Small array, 1Px4, every voltage of Fig. 7A and 7B (n = 3 dishes each). The normalized values at the center ROI and at the half-way ROI, the positions the paper reports in this paragraph, are compared between every pair of voltages, with no correction, as the paper applies none. Reproduced when no pair differs at p < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. The differences and their p-values are reported either way, and a test over all ROIs is shown as a variant. The voltages other than 2.4 and 5.6 kV are printed only in the figure, which was not read; the attempt takes them from the dataset.

claims.statement: The independence of the normalized distribution from amplitude also holds when rotating multiple packets (10Px4) on the larger array.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 7C and 7D
claims.quote: The findings held true for rotating multiple packets and when using the larger array ( Fig. 7C and D ). Overall, our results show that NG-CANCAN targeting of electroporation does not depend on nsEP amplitude, at least within the studied amplitude range.
claims.criterion: As fig7b-targeting-independent-of-amplitude, on the large array with 10Px4 (Fig. 7C and 7D, n = 3), with the same test, positions and rule. The rise of a.u. values with voltage at the three positions (the "degree of electroporation") is reported as well.

claims.statement: Remote targeting, within the studied limits, depends neither on pulse amplitude nor on array size, so findings from small arrays can be extrapolated to larger inter-electrode distances.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 5; Figure 7
claims.quote: the remote targeting, at least within studied limits, did not depend on either the electric pulse amplitude or array size ( Fig. 7 ). We infer that findings from small electrode arrays can be extrapolated to larger inter-electrode distances.
claims.criterion: The paper's evidence is Fig. 7, where the small array received 1Px4 and the large array 10Px4; Fig. 6B shows that the packet number alone changes the normalized center value, so no comparison in the paper isolates array size, and the paper names no test for it. The claim is judged as the Discussion rests it, on amplitude independence in both arrays. Reproduced when fig7b-targeting-independent-of-amplitude and fig7cd-holds-for-large-array are both reproduced. The normalized profiles of the two arrays, on distance as a fraction of the half diagonal, are shown side by side, with the packet confound stated.

claims.statement: Packets 1, 2 and 3 (4 kV, 1Px4) produce the same YP uptake in the center (215 to 235 a.u.), but Packets 1 and 3 cause much more uptake near the electrodes (250 to 350 a.u.) than Packet 2 (about 120 a.u.), p < 0.01.
claims.source: Results, 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8A
claims.quote: All packets produced the same YP uptake in the center (215–235 a.u.), but Packets 1 and 3 caused drastically more YP uptake near the electrodes (250–350 a.u. vs ~120 a.u. for packet 1, p<0.01, Fig. 8A ).
claims.criterion: The text reads "~120 a.u. for packet 1", which contradicts the same sentence; it is read as Packet 2, the packet with the lower uptake near electrodes in the rest of Section 3.4 and in Fig. 8B. "Near the electrodes" is the most peripheral ROI. Reproduced when the values are in their ranges and Packets 1 and 3 each exceed Packet 2 at the most peripheral ROI with p < 0.01 by the two-sided Student's t-test. The "same" center uptake is a claim of absence, judged by the same test at p < 0.05 for each pair of packets at the center ROI; it holds when no pair differs, and the differences are reported.

claims.statement: Normalized to the most peripheral ROI, YP emission in the center drops from 183% for Packet 2 to 83% for Packet 3 and 74% for Packet 1, so the packet with the strongest bipolar cancellation targets best.
claims.source: Results, 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8B
claims.quote: The superiority of Packet 2 for CANCAN targeting is highlighted by the drop of normalized YP emission in the center from 183% for Packet 2 to 83% and 74% for Packets 3 and 1, respectively ( Fig. 8B ).
claims.criterion: Under the readings of the opening comment; the readings of normalization are (a) the ratio of the mean center value to the mean peripheral value over dishes, (b) the mean over dishes of each dish's normalized center value. Reproduced when all three values are within tolerance under a reading.

claims.statement: Raising the large array 1, 2 and 3 mm above the monolayer reduces YP emission near the electrodes 2.4, 6.4 and 9 times but in the center only 1.02, 1.4 and 3.8 times, raising the targeting efficiency (center over periphery) to as much as 600% at 2 mm.
claims.source: Results, 3.5, paragraph 1; Figure 9A and 9B
claims.quote: Specifically, YP emission near the electrodes decreased 2.4, 6.4, and 9 times with 1-, 2- and 3-mm gaps (as compared to electrodes being in the same plane with cells); in the center, it decreased just 1.02, 1.4, and 3.8 times, respectively. Such disproportionally faster fading of the effect near electrodes boosted the CANCAN targeting efficiency (measured as a ratio of the effect in the center and at the periphery) to as much as 600% for the 2-mm gap ( Fig. 9B ).
claims.criterion: Ratios of dish means (n = 3 to 4) at the most peripheral ROI ("near the electrodes", the Fig. 9B legend's "measurements most distant from the center") and at the center ROI. The 600% is read as the normalized center value for 2 mm, which the paper calls the largest ("as much as"); it should be the largest of the four gaps. Reproduced when all values are within tolerance under a reading of the opening comment; partially when the center ratios are below the electrode ratios at every gap but some values are out of tolerance.

claims.statement: With the electrodes above the monolayer, electroporation is restricted almost exclusively to the center of the array.
claims.source: Results, 3.5, paragraph 1; Figure 9C
claims.quote: YP fluorescence images in Fig. 9C show that electroporation is restricted almost exclusively to the remote target (center) when electrodes are placed above the cell monolayer.
claims.criterion: The paper shows this with sample images and gives no measure. Judged on the ROI profiles of Fig. 9A, for the 1, 2 and 3 mm gaps. Reproduced when, for each gap, the center ROI is the maximum of the mean profile and exceeds the most peripheral ROI by the Methods' two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05; partially when this holds for some gaps.

claims.statement: A single unipolar 600-ns pulse at 15 kV/cm causes the strongest YP uptake of all treatments in single CHO cells, reaching 126 +/- 14 a.u. (n = 25) by the end of recording.
claims.source: Results, 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: A single 600-ns pulse at 15 kV/cm caused by far the strongest YP uptake, reaching 126±14 a.u. (n=25) by the end of recording.
claims.criterion: Per cell, F-F0 as in Section 2.2 (ROI mean intensity minus the mean of the six images before the pulses), at the last image of the 600-s series; the group mean over cells. Tolerance is the paper's s.e. Reproduced when the unipolar mean is within tolerance and is the highest of the five groups.

claims.statement: Bipolar signals starting with the same pulse cause significantly weaker uptake than the single pulse (p < 0.001), reaching 20.8 +/- 2.0 a.u. (4-phase), 6.9 +/- 1.6 a.u. (8-phase) and 25.4 +/- 2.8 a.u. (8-phase with 5-us delays) by the end of recording.
claims.source: Results, 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: Bipolar signals started with exactly the same pulse (600 ns, 15 kV/cm) but caused significantly weaker effects (p<0.001). By the end of recording, YP signal reached only 20.8±2.0 a.u. for the 4-phasic signal; 6.9±1.6 a.u. for the 8-phasic signal; and 25.4±2.8 a.u. for the 8-phasic signal with 5-μs delays between phases.
claims.criterion: F-F0 per cell at the last image, as in fig4-unipolar-strongest; tolerances are the paper's s.e. Section 2.2 says F-F0 was used for statistical analyses but names no test; the only test the Methods name is the two-sided Student's t-test (Section 2.4), so each bipolar group is compared with the unipolar group by that test on per-cell values, and this choice is recorded as open. Reproduced when all three means are within tolerance and all three tests give p < 0.001; partially reproduced when the tests hold but a mean falls outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Sham-exposed cells show no gain in YP fluorescence over the 10 min of observation.
claims.source: Results, 3.1, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: Sham-exposed cells showed no gain in YP fluorescence during the 10 min of observation.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper names no test for it (Section 2.2 names none); its only named test is the two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 (Section 2.4), applied here as a one-sample test of per-cell F-F0 at the last image against 0, which is the same as a paired test of F against F0. That this is the test is open and recorded as such. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; the mean F-F0 and its s.e. are reported either way.

claims.statement: The 8-phase bipolar signal causes about 20-fold weaker electroporation than a single unipolar pulse identical to its first phase, while the 4-phase and the delayed 8-phase signals cancel only 4 to 5-fold.
claims.source: Results, 3.1, paragraph 1, and 3.4, paragraph 1; Figure 4 legend
claims.quote: the other two types of bipolar signals which were less efficient at cancellation (4–5-fold, Fig. 4 ). ... Note that applying the 8-phasic bipolar signal with no inter-phase delays caused about 20-fold weaker electroporation than a single unipolar pulse
claims.criterion: Ratios of group means of F-F0 at the last image. The 8-phase ratio is reproduced within 18 to 22. Section 3.4 gives 4 to 5-fold for the other two, but the paper's own means (126/20.8 = 6.1 and 126/25.4 = 5.0) give 6.1 for the 4-phase signal, so the 4 to 5 range (widened to 3.6 to 5.5) is judged and the paper's own ratios are reported beside it. Reproduced when the 8-phase ratio is within tolerance and both other ratios are within the widened range; partially reproduced when only the 8-phase ratio is.

claims.statement: Without rotation, the unipolar control trains from e1 cause much stronger electroporation throughout the array than 40 Packet 2 applications from e1, and the uptake with trains follows the electric field strength.
claims.source: Results, 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 5A
claims.quote: The lack of cancellation caused a much stronger electroporation throughout the array, and the distribution of YP uptake expectedly followed the electric field strength distribution in Fig. 3C.
claims.criterion: Profiles along the e1 to e3 diagonal, as in the Fig. 5A legend; per dish, intensity per ROI in a.u.; mean over dishes per ROI. The paper reports no test for this finding; the Methods' test is the two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 on dish values (Section 2.4). "Throughout" allows two readings, (a) trains higher at every ROI, by the t-test at each ROI, (b) trains higher in the per-dish mean over all ROIs, by the t-test on those means. The trains profile must also decline from e1 toward the center (it follows the field of Fig. 3C). Reproduced when both readings hold, not reproduced when neither does, and blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ; outcomes under each reading are reported.

claims.statement: Packet 2 without rotation enhances electroporation in the center of the array despite the weakening field, but uptake near e1 remains stronger than in the center.
claims.source: Results, 3.2, paragraph 1; Figure 5A
claims.quote: In contrast, Packet 2 enhanced electroporation in the center of the array, despite gradual weakening of the electric field with distance from e1. However, the bipolar cancellation only partially offset the electric field weakening, and electroporation near e1 remained stronger than in the center.
claims.criterion: The 40 Packets profile along the e1 to e3 diagonal (Fig. 5A). The paper gives no number. Reproduced when the center ROI exceeds the lowest ROI between e1 and the center (a central peak), and the ROI closest to e1 exceeds the center ROI. Which ROI is the center (the single ROI at distance 0, or the mean of the two ROIs flanking 0 when none sits at 0) is open; both are shown.

claims.statement: Rotating the first-energized electrode with Packet 2 (1Px40) makes electroporation in the center exceed that at the perimeter, while the same rotation of control trains leaves a void of electroporation in the center.
claims.source: Results, 3.2, paragraph 2; Figure 5B and 5C
claims.quote: Rotation with Packet 2 “smeared” the electroporation effect at the perimeter and emphasized the remote effect in the center. This remote effect contrasted with a void of electroporation in the center when the pulse train was applied in the same manner instead of the packet.
claims.criterion: Profiles averaged across both diagonals (Fig. 5B legend), normalized to the most peripheral ROI as 100% (Fig. 5C). Which peripheral ROI is open; readings (a) the mean of the ROIs closest to each electrode, (b) each diagonal end separately. Reproduced when, under a reading, the 1Px40 center is above 100% and the 1T x 40 center is below 100%, and the two differ by a two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 over dishes.

claims.statement: Increasing the total number of rotated Packet 2 applications from 4 to 20 and 40 strongly increases YP uptake throughout the array.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6A
claims.quote: Increasing the total number of applied packets from 4 to 20 and 40 profoundly enhanced the electroporative YP dye uptake throughout the electrode array
claims.criterion: Profiles in a.u. for 1Px4, 5Px4 and 10Px4, mean over dishes per ROI. Readings of "throughout" as in fig5a-trains-stronger-throughout, (a) at every ROI, (b) in the per-dish mean over ROIs. The paper reports no test; the Methods' test (Section 2.4) is applied to the 4 against 40 difference, at each ROI under (a) and on the means under (b). Under each reading the claim holds when uptake rises from 4 to 20 to 40 packets and the 4 against 40 difference is significant at p < 0.05. Reproduced when both readings hold, not reproduced when neither does, blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ. The paper does not say which array or amplitude Fig. 6 used; this does not change the comparison.

claims.statement: The central peak is almost twofold higher than the periphery for 1Px4, and about equal to the periphery for 5Px4 and 10Px4; the least affected area between center and electrodes is about 2-fold lower than the center for all treatments.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6B
claims.quote: Its brightness was almost twofold higher than at the periphery for a single packet was applied 4 times from different directions, or about the same as at the periphery for the rotation of 5 and 10 packets ( Fig. 6B ). Interestingly, the least affected area of the cell monolayer (between the center and the electrodes) showed about 2-fold lower fluorescence intensity than in the center for all the treatments.
claims.criterion: Normalized profiles as in Fig. 6B; peripheral ROI readings as in fig5bc-rotation-focuses-center. "Almost twofold" is read as 200% with the 10% tolerance, and values from 180% to 200% are counted within it. The minimum is the lowest ROI between the center and an electrode, on each side; readings (a) the lower of the two sides, (b) their mean. Reproduced when all values hold under one reading; partially reproduced when the 1Px4 value holds and others do not.

claims.statement: The central peak becomes narrower (sharper) as the number of packets increases.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 6
claims.quote: Also, the central peak appeared narrower (sharper) with increasing the number of packets.
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure of width. Readings, each on the normalized profiles of Fig. 6B, (a) the distance between the two minima flanking the center, (b) the full width of the central peak at half its height above the flanking minima. Reproduced when width falls from 1Px4 to 5Px4 to 10Px4 under both readings; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Raising the first-pulse amplitude from 2.4 to 5.6 kV (small array, 1Px4) increases YP fluorescence about 16-fold at all locations, 15.5 times at the most peripheral point, 16.2 times half-way to the center and 16.8 times in the center.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 7A
claims.quote: when the first pulse amplitude was increased from 2.4 to 5.6 kV ... YP fluorescence increased 15.5 times at the most peripheral point; 16.2 times half-way to the center; and 16.8 times in the center
claims.criterion: Ratio of the mean over dishes at 5.6 kV to that at 2.4 kV, in a.u., at the ROI closest to the electrodes, the ROI half-way between it and the center, and the center ROI. Peripheral and center readings as in fig5bc-rotation-focuses-center. Whether the a.u. values are background-subtracted is not stated; both raw and background-subtracted ratios are shown, with background taken from an image region without cells or from sham dishes, if the data hold either. Reproduced when all three ratios are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Normalized to the most peripheral ROI, the profiles for different amplitudes fully overlap, in the small array with 1Px4 and in the large array with 10Px4, so targeting does not depend on nsEP amplitude within the range studied.
claims.source: Results, 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 7B and 7D
claims.quote: When the YP emission was normalized to the most peripheral ROI, the data for different nsEP amplitudes fully overlapped ( Fig. 7B ). ... The findings held true for rotating multiple packets and when using the larger array ( Fig. 7C and D ).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper reports no test for it; the Methods' test is the two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05 over dishes (Section 2.4). The text concludes that targeting does not depend on amplitude, and Section 3.3, paragraph 1, defines targeting efficiency as the ratio of the effect in the center to that near the electrodes, so the measure judged is the normalized center value. In each array it is compared between every pair of amplitudes. Reproduced when no comparison is significant; not reproduced when any is. The effect sizes, and the same tests at the half-way ROI and at every ROI ("fully overlapped" read as whole profiles), are shown as variants.

claims.statement: Remote targeting does not depend on array size, so findings in small arrays can be extrapolated to larger inter-electrode distances.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 5; Figure 7
claims.quote: the remote targeting, at least within studied limits, did not depend on either the electric pulse amplitude or array size ( Fig. 7 ).
claims.criterion: The paper supports this with Fig. 7 only, where the small array was tested with 1Px4 and the large with 10Px4, so size and packet number are confounded. Reproduced when fig7bd-targeting-independent-of-amplitude holds in both arrays; the normalized center values of the two arrays are reported, with the confound named.

claims.statement: Packets 1, 2 and 3 (4 kV, 1Px4) produce the same YP uptake in the center of the array, 215 to 235 a.u.
claims.source: Results, 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8A
claims.quote: All packets produced the same YP uptake in the center (215–235 a.u.)
claims.criterion: Mean over dishes of the center ROI per packet, in a.u. (center readings as in fig5a-packet-center-peak-e1-stronger; one diagonal or the mean of both, as Fig. 8 does not say, both shown). Each packet's value should lie in 193.5 to 258.5 a.u. The equality is a claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.05, between each pair of packets. Reproduced when all three values are in range and no pair differs; partially reproduced when no pair differs but a value is out of range. The paper does not say which array Fig. 8 used; the author reports which the data show, and the a.u. values are judged as they are.

claims.statement: Packets 1 and 3 cause much more YP uptake near the electrodes (250 to 350 a.u.) than Packet 2 (about 120 a.u.), p < 0.01.
claims.source: Results, 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8A
claims.quote: but Packets 1 and 3 caused drastically more YP uptake near the electrodes (250–350 a.u. vs ~120 a.u. for packet 1, p<0.01, Fig. 8A ).
claims.criterion: The text says "~120 a.u. for packet 1", which contradicts the Packets 1 and 3 range in the same sentence and Fig. 8B; it is read as Packet 2. Near electrodes is the most peripheral ROI; readings (a) the mean of the ROIs closest to each electrode, (b) the ROI closest to e1, and one diagonal or both as in fig8a-equal-center-uptake. Reproduced when, under one reading, Packets 1 and 3 lie in 225 to 385 a.u., Packet 2 in 108 to 132 a.u., and each of Packets 1 and 3 exceeds Packet 2 by a two-sided Student's t-test at p < 0.01; partially reproduced when the tests hold and the values do not.

claims.statement: Normalized to the most peripheral ROI, YP emission in the center is 183% for Packet 2 and drops to 83% for Packet 3 and 74% for Packet 1.
claims.source: Results, 3.4, paragraph 2; Figure 8B
claims.quote: The superiority of Packet 2 for CANCAN targeting is highlighted by the drop of normalized YP emission in the center from 183% for Packet 2 to 83% and 74% for Packets 3 and 1, respectively ( Fig. 8B ).
claims.criterion: Normalization as the Methods give it, per profile to its most peripheral ROI. Open readings, all shown, (a) normalize each dish then average, (b) normalize the mean profile; peripheral ROI and diagonals as in fig8a-more-uptake-near-electrodes. Reproduced when all three values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when Packet 2 is the highest and above 100% while Packets 1 and 3 are below 100%, without all values in tolerance.

claims.statement: Raising the large array 1, 2 and 3 mm above the monolayer reduces YP emission near the electrodes 2.4, 6.4 and 9 times, but in the center only 1.02, 1.4 and 3.8 times.
claims.source: Results, 3.5, paragraph 1; Figure 9A
claims.quote: Specifically, YP emission near the electrodes decreased 2.4, 6.4, and 9 times with 1-, 2- and 3-mm gaps (as compared to electrodes being in the same plane with cells); in the center, it decreased just 1.02, 1.4, and 3.8 times, respectively.
claims.criterion: Ratios of the mean over dishes at 0 mm to that at each gap, in a.u., at the most peripheral ROI and at the center ROI (readings as in fig8a-more-uptake-near-electrodes and fig5a-packet-center-peak-e1-stronger). Reproduced when all six ratios are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when, at every gap, the peripheral decrease exceeds the center decrease but some ratio is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: The gap boosts targeting efficiency, the ratio of the center to the periphery, to as much as 600% at 2 mm.
claims.source: Results, 3.5, paragraph 1; Figure 9B and 9C
claims.quote: Such disproportionally faster fading of the effect near electrodes boosted the CANCAN targeting efficiency (measured as a ratio of the effect in the center and at the periphery) to as much as 600% for the 2-mm gap ( Fig. 9B ).
claims.criterion: Normalized as in Fig. 9B (% of the ROI most distant from the center); normalization readings as in fig8b-packet2-best-targeting. Reproduced when the 2-mm value is within tolerance under one reading and is the highest of the four distances.

claims.statement: In freely behaving mice engaging in aggression, rSLDS fits show an integration dimension x1 with a longer time constant than the orthogonal dimension x2, an approximate line attractor.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1n and 1o; Results, Line attractor for observing aggression, paragraph 1
claims.quote: revealed an approximate line attractor under both conditions, exhibiting ramping and persistent activity aligned and maintained across both performed and observed attack sessions
claims.criterion: For each mouse, an rSLDS with 2 latent dimensions fit to the engaging session (number of states by fivefold cross-validation, Methods, or 3 states with the sample code's settings; both readings run). The cvR2 of each fit is reported; no mouse is excluded by the Methods' 70% rule, since the paper reports n = 5 in both conditions while the mean observation cvR2 it gives (67.2%) is below 70%. Time constants from the eigenvalues of each state's dynamics matrix as the sample code computes them; x1 is the dimension with the larger time constant in the state that holds the slow dynamics (the state with the largest time constant). Reproduced when the x1 time constants exceed the x2 time constants across the 5 mice by a two-tailed unpaired Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05. The line attractor score, log2 of the largest over the second largest time constant (Methods), is reported per mouse.

claims.statement: In the same mice observing aggression, rSLDS fits also show an x1 dimension with a longer time constant than x2.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1p and 1q; Results, Line attractor for observing aggression, paragraph 1
claims.quote: revealed an approximate line attractor under both conditions
claims.criterion: As ed1n-engaging-x1-slower, on the observation sessions.

claims.statement: In freely behaving mice, average x1 activity differs between sniffing the SW mouse and observing the SW mouse attack a BALB/c intruder.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1m
claims.quote: Average activity in the x 1 dimension during sniffing of the SW mouse, vs observing the SW mouse a BALB\c intruder (n = 4 mice, *p = 0.0286, Two-tailed Mann Whitney U -test
claims.criterion: The legend is garbled and the panel was not read, so the direction is not fixed from the text. Per mouse, the mean of the x1 projection of the observation session over frames annotated as sniffing the SW mouse and over frames annotated as observing attack. Reproduced when a two-tailed unpaired Mann-Whitney test over mice gives p < 0.05; the direction is reported. The legend's n of 4 (of 5 mice) is not explained; all mice with both annotations are used and the count is reported.

claims.statement: The activity of x1 neurons during observed attack bouts does not differ from their activity during engaged attack.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3c
claims.quote: comparison of the activity during observing attack bouts and engaging in attack (n = 5 mice, p = 0.42, Two-tailed Mann-Whitney U -test
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per mouse, the mean activity of the x1 neurons of each condition during attack bouts (observed or engaged). Reproduced when a two-tailed Mann-Whitney test over mice gives p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The difference is reported either way. Which neurons are x1 neurons is not fixed beyond the rSLDS weights; the readings are the five neurons with the largest absolute x1 weight (as in Fig. 1i) and the neurons the dataset marks as x1, if it does.

claims.statement: Over the full interaction, autocorrelation half-widths of x1 neurons are similar when observing (25 +/- 0.8 s) and engaging in aggression (20 +/- 1.7 s).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3e
claims.quote: mean achw during observation: 25 ± 0.8s, mean achw during engagement: 20 ± 1.7s, n=5 mice, p = 0.125
claims.criterion: Autocorrelation per neuron as in Methods equations 7 and 8 (the sample code's autocorr_matlab). The half-width is not defined beyond its name; the reading is the first lag at which the autocorrelation falls to 0.5 or below, in seconds at 10 Hz. Per mouse, the mean over x1 neurons (readings of x1 neurons as in ed3c). The "full interaction" is not bounded in the paper; readings are the whole session and the span from the first intruder entry to the last removal. Expected values within tolerance, and, as a claim of absence, a two-tailed test over mice with p >= 0.05, run as an unpaired Mann-Whitney test and as a paired signed-rank test (header, Tests; the printed 0.125 is an exact signed-rank value).

claims.statement: Aligned to removal of the last intruder, autocorrelation half-widths of x1 neurons are similar when observing (14 +/- 1 s) and engaging (11 +/- 1.6 s).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3f
claims.quote: mean achw during observation: 14 ± 1s, mean achw during engagement: 11 ± 1.6s, n = 5 mice, p = 0.187
claims.criterion: As ed3e-achw-full-session, on activity from the removal of the last intruder to the end of the session (the paper does not give the window's end; the session end is the only reading the legend allows), with both test readings (the printed 0.187 is the exact signed-rank value 0.1875 at n = 5).

claims.statement: A decoder trained on x1 activity during observation separates observed attack bouts from non-attack bouts better than shuffled controls.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3g
claims.quote: A SVM decoder was trained on data from integration dimension activity to separate bouts of observing attack from non attack bouts. Right: Quantification of the decoder accuracy performance (n = 5 mice, p = 0.0079
claims.criterion: As the Methods describe (Decoding behaviour from integration dimension). Attack bouts separated by less than 5 s merged into trials, classes balanced; a one-dimensional threshold on the normalized x1 signal fit by a linear SVM on training frames and scored on held-out frames; shuffles assign the behaviour labels randomly to bouts, 20 times, and 1,000 times per mouse for the significance test (Methods). The Methods report accuracy "on data from all other trials for each mouse" without giving the split further; the readings are training on one trial and testing on all others, leave-one-trial-out, and fivefold over trials. Reproduced when decoder accuracy exceeds shuffled accuracy across mice by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The decoder trained on observing attack decodes engaged attack from x1 activity better than shuffled data, so x1 encodes a similar variable in both conditions.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3h; Results, Line attractor for observing aggression, paragraph 1
claims.quote: could be reliably used to decode from held-out data instances of both observation of and engagement in attack, suggesting that this dimension encodes a similar internal state variable under both conditions
claims.criterion: The decoder of ed3g-decode-observed-attack applied to the engaging session's x1 signal (frames of attack against all others); the paper does not say whether the engaging session is projected with the observation model's weights or its own; both readings run. Reproduced when accuracy exceeds that of the shuffled decoder across mice by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Around 70% of the neurons that contribute to the line attractor overlap between observing and engaging in aggression.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4c; Results, Line attractor for observing aggression, paragraph 1
claims.quote: suggesting that a highly overlapping set of neurons (70%) contributes to line-attractor dynamics during observing or engaging in attack
claims.criterion: The paper does not say how a neuron is counted as contributing, or the denominator. Readings for contributing are (a) the top five neurons by absolute weight, as in Fig. 1i, and (b) the neurons the dataset marks as x1 neurons, if it does. Readings for the overlap are the shared fraction of (i) the observation set and (ii) the engagement set. Reproduced when one reading gives a mean within tolerance.

claims.statement: The x1 weight vector during observation is more aligned with the x1 weight vector during engagement than with the x2 weight vector.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4d
claims.quote: rSLDS weights of the x 1 dimension during observation were compared to model weights of the x 1 and x 2 dimensions during engagement using a dot product of the two weight vectors. (n = 5 mice, ***p = 0.0079
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the dot product of the observation x1 weight vector with the engagement x1 vector and with the engagement x2 vector, over neurons present in both sessions. The paper does not say whether vectors are normalized or signs aligned; the readings are the raw dot product and the absolute dot product of unit vectors. Reproduced when x1-x1 exceeds x1-x2 across mice by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05 under one reading.

claims.statement: During the solitary baseline, x2 neurons show more frequent spontaneous calcium transients than x1 neurons (2.3 against 1.6 events).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4g; Results, Line attractor for observing aggression, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we did see a slightly but significantly higher frequency of spontaneous calcium transients in x 2 neurons
claims.criterion: A transient is a crossing above 1.5 standard deviations of the z-scored activity (legend) during the 5 min baseline at the start of the session (Methods, Behaviour annotations). The paper does not say per what time the frequency is, which session's baseline, or which model's x1 and x2 neurons are used; readings are events per baseline and per minute, and the engaging and observing sessions' baselines and models. Reproduced when x2 exceeds x1 across mice by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05; the values are compared with the expected ones under each reading.

claims.statement: Baseline transient amplitude (0.58 against 0.71 z) and decay constant (1.7 against 2.3 s) do not differ between x1 and x2 neurons.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4h and 4i; Results, Line attractor for observing aggression, paragraph 2
claims.quote: We did not detect a difference in amplitude or decay constant (tau) between x 1 and x 2 neurons
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, two-tailed over mice for each measure, run as an unpaired Mann-Whitney test and as a paired signed-rank test (header, Tests; the printed 0.188 is the exact signed-rank value 0.1875 at n = 5); reproduced when neither measure gives p < 0.05. Transients as in ed4g-x2-more-spontaneous. The decay constant fit is not described; the reading is an exponential fit to the mean transient from its peak.

claims.statement: In head-fixed mice observing aggression, rSLDS fits to 2P data show an x1 dimension with longer time constants than x2.
claims.source: Figure 1e; Results, Line attractor for observing aggression, paragraph 4
claims.quote: during observation of aggression by the head-fixed mice, rSLDS analysis identified an integration dimension with slow dynamics ( x 1 ) aligned to an approximate line attractor, and an orthogonal dimension with faster dynamics ( x 2 )
claims.criterion: As ed1n-engaging-x1-slower, on the 2P observation sessions, with the sample code's 2P settings (2 states) as the second reading. Methods add that 2P flow fields were fit with an input term for the presence of the BALB/c intruder; fits with and without that input are both run. The legend's P is read from its star key (four stars, P < 0.0001), the only test in the figure besides panel m.

claims.statement: The line attractor score is positive across the 9 head-fixed mice.
claims.source: Figure 1f
claims.criterion: Score = log2 of the largest time constant over the second largest (Methods, Calculation of line attractor score) of each mouse's fit. The paper gives no threshold; the readings are (a) the mean over mice above 0 and (b) every mouse above 0. Reproduced when both hold; partially reproduced when only (a) holds.

claims.statement: The experimentally observed network time constants of the integration dimension lie in a range of about 50 to 200 s.
claims.source: Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 5
claims.quote: could yield network time constants ( τ n ) in the experimentally observed range (~50–200 s
claims.criterion: A reported range; reproduced when the x1 time constants of the 9 mice lie within 50 to 200 s widened by 10% of each bound (45 to 220 s); partially reproduced when the median lies inside. The paper does not say which fits the range comes from; readings are the 2P observation fits (9 mice) and these together with the miniscope fits. The expected value is the midpoint and is not itself tested.

claims.statement: The x1 and x2 dimensions are nearly orthogonal, with a subspace angle of 88.1 +/- 0.87 degrees across 9 mice.
claims.source: Methods, Dynamical system models of neural data, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we initially confirmed the orthogonality of these dimensions by computing the subspace angle between them (88.1 ± 0.87°, n = 9 mice)
claims.criterion: The angle between the two columns of C (the stored factor weights), per mouse, averaged over the 9 2P mice.

claims.statement: rSLDS models of miniscope data explain 84.7% of variance during engagement and 67.2% during observation of aggression (cross-validated R2).
claims.source: Methods, Dynamical system models of neural data, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Models fit to miniscope data during engagement of aggression obtained a cvR 2 = 84.7 ± 0.03%, while the same model explains 67.2 ± 0.02% of variance in data obtained from observation of aggression
claims.criterion: Fivefold cross-validation, training on four portions and testing on the fifth (Methods). The printed spreads (0.03% and 0.02%) are read as fractions (3 and 2 percentage points), the only reading that fits a spread over 5 mice, and are used as tolerances. The paper does not say whether the portions are contiguous blocks or random frames, or how R2 is taken (neural activity predicted from inferred latents); readings are contiguous blocks and random frames. The Methods also require 70% cvR2 before downstream use, which the observation value does not meet; this is reported.

claims.statement: Neurons contributing to x1 have longer autocorrelation half-widths than those contributing to x2 in head-fixed observation.
claims.source: Figure 1l and 1m; Results, Line attractor for observing aggression, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Neurons contributing to the integration dimension displayed more persistence than those aligned with the faster dimension
claims.criterion: Five neurons per dimension per mouse (45 each over 9 mice, legend of Fig. 1l), the five with the largest absolute weight on that dimension (Fig. 1i). ACHW as in ed3e-achw-full-session, on the observation session. Per-mouse means compared by a two-tailed test, unpaired Mann-Whitney and paired signed-rank (header, Tests; 0.0078 at n = 9 is an exact value of both); reproduced when x1 exceeds x2 at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Only a small fraction of neural activity is explained by the head-fixed observer's movements, and the variance explained does not differ between x1 and x2 neurons.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 5a-e; Results, Line attractor for observing aggression, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Importantly, only a small fraction of the neural activity could be explained by movements of the observer mouse
claims.criterion: GLM of each neuron on the first ten principal components of 500 motion SVDs at lags up to 10 s, ridge, tenfold cross-validation, cvR2 (Methods). The Methods call the ten features "binary" without saying how they are binarized; readings are the continuous components and components thresholded at their median. Reproduced when the median cvR2 over neurons is below 0.1 (the paper gives no value; "small fraction" read as under 10% of variance, a reading named here and reported with the full distribution) and a two-tailed test of per-mouse x1 against x2 means gives p >= 0.05, run as an unpaired Mann-Whitney test and as a paired signed-rank test (header, Tests; the printed 0.8125 is an exact signed-rank value at n = 7). Needs the face videos or their SVDs.

claims.statement: Photostimulation of five x1 neurons with four pulses at 20 s ISI produces integration in the x1 dimension, with ISI activity rising with each pulse and not returning to baseline.
claims.source: Figure 2c and 2d; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 2
claims.quote: optogenetic reactivation of cohorts of five individual x 1 neurons yielded robust integration of activity in the entire x 1 dimension-weighted population, as evidenced by progressively increasing peak activity during the 20 s ISI after each consecutive pulse
claims.criterion: The x1 projection of the x1-activation session (sample code). Per mouse, the mean over baseline and over each ISI under readings Wa and Wb; Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's correction under readings Ca and Cb (header). Reproduced when, under one reading, at least three Dunn comparisons give p < 0.05 and the mean over mice rises from the first to the third ISI. Partially reproduced when the rise holds but fewer comparisons are significant.

claims.statement: x1 photostimulation moves the population activity vector progressively along the line attractor; the state-space distance from the initial point grows with each pulse, both at the end of stimulation and at the end of each ISI.
claims.source: Figure 2e-h; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 3
claims.quote: This revealed that the x 1 perturbations resulted in progressive, stable on-manifold movement along the attractor with each consecutive stimulation, as measured by the increase in both metrics
claims.criterion: State = (x1 projection, x2 projection) of the x1-activation session. Euclidean distance from t_initial to t_stim-end (onset + 2 s) and to t_post-stim (the frame before the next onset; for the last pulse, onset + 21 s). t_initial is not fixed beyond "during the baseline period"; readings are the mean baseline state and the last baseline frame. What the distances are compared with is not given; readings are (a) each pulse against the distances of baseline frames from t_initial and (b) each pulse against the first. Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's correction. Reproduced when, under one reading, the mean distance rises from pulse 1 to pulse 3 for both metrics and three of four comparisons give p < 0.05 for each metric, as the legends report.

claims.statement: Photoactivated x1 neurons reach peak activity comparable to their peak during observation of aggression.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 7d-f; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Activated x 1 neurons exhibited activity levels comparable to their response during observation of aggression
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per mouse, the mean over the five targeted x1 neurons of their peak z-score during observation and during the activation session; reproduced when a two-tailed Mann-Whitney test gives p >= 0.05. The difference is reported.

claims.statement: x1 activation with an 8 s ISI also produces integration in the x1 dimension.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 8a; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Similar results were obtained using an 8 s ISI
claims.criterion: As fig2d-x1-integration, on the 8 s ISI x1-activation session (onsets at frames 140, 240, 340, 440). Reproduced when, under one reading, three of four comparisons give p < 0.05 and the mean rises from the first to the third ISI.

claims.statement: x1 integration scales with laser power, being larger with 5 mW than with 1 mW per neuron.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 8e and 8f; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 2
claims.quote: This activity also scaled with different laser powers
claims.criterion: Per mouse and period (baseline and each ISI, readings Wa and Wb), the mean x1 projection at 1 mW and at 5 mW; per period, a two-tailed Mann-Whitney test. Reproduced when three of the four ISIs give 5 mW higher at p < 0.05 under one reading (the legend's four values have three below 0.05; the fourth is read as the baseline or one ISI).

claims.statement: Given the same pulsed input, the rSLDS model fit to observation data also integrates along x1, as in the data.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 8c; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Providing the same (digital optogenetic) input to the fit rSLDS model also resulted in integration by the model along the x 1 dimension, similar to that observed in the data
claims.criterion: The paper does not say how the input enters the model. Readings are (a) the input weight learned for the BALB/c-presence input of the observation fit (Methods, flow fields fit with input terms) driven by a 2 s pulse at each stimulation onset; (b) a pulse added to x1 at each onset, of the size of the first evoked x1 response. The model is simulated forward from the baseline state with its discrete states. Reproduced when the simulated x1 at the end of each ISI rises from the first to the third ISI in at least 6 of the 8 mice under one reading; the cross-validated R2 against the data (about 85%, Methods) is reported.

claims.statement: x1 stimulation does not evoke appreciable activity in the x2 dimension.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 8g-i; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Importantly, x 1 stimulation did not evoke appreciable activity in x 2 dimension neurons
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. The x2 projection of the x1-activation session, per mouse means of baseline and ISIs (Wa, Wb), Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's correction (Ca, Cb). Reproduced when no comparison gives p < 0.05 under the reading used for fig2d-x1-integration; the size of each difference is reported.

claims.statement: Photostimulation of five x2 neurons does not produce integration; x2 activity is transient and decays to baseline during each ISI.
claims.source: Figure 2i-k; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Importantly, activation of x 2 neurons did not lead to integration
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. As fig2d-x1-integration, on the x2 projection of the x2-activation session; reproduced when no Dunn comparison gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: With an 8 s ISI, x2 activation also produces no integration in x2.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 8b; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 4
claims.quote: we observed stimulus-locked transient activity in the x 2 dimension followed by a decay back to the baseline during the ISI period, across stimulation paradigms
claims.criterion: As fig2k-x2-no-integration, on the 8 s ISI x2-activation session.

claims.statement: x2 activation has little effect on x1 activity; in the paper's test two of four comparisons are not significant (P = 0.276) and two are (P = 0.0072 and 0.03).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 8j-l; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 4
claims.quote: with little to no effect on x 1 neurons
claims.criterion: The x1 projection of the x2-activation session, tested as fig2d-x1-integration. The paper's own test finds two significant comparisons, so the claim is judged against that pattern. Reproduced when, under one reading, at most two comparisons give p < 0.05 and the mean ISI x1 response is smaller than under x1 activation (fig2d-x1-integration) in every ISI. The legend reports n = 8, though Fig. 2k has 7 mice with x2 activation; the number found is reported.

claims.statement: x2 activation moves the population vector transiently off the attractor during each pulse, after which it relaxes back near its initial location.
claims.source: Figure 2l-o; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 4
claims.quote: we observed that x 2 neuron activation caused transient off-manifold movements of the PAV orthogonal to the attractor axis during each pulse ... After each stimulus, the PAV relaxed back into the attractor, near to the initial location that it occupied before the stimulus
claims.criterion: As fig2gh-x1-moves-along-attractor, on the x2-activation session. Reproduced when, under one reading, at least three of four stimulation-end comparisons give p < 0.05 and at most one ISI-end comparison does (the legends' pattern), and the mean ISI-end distance is smaller than the mean stimulation-end distance.

claims.statement: Integration of pulses saturates after the third pulse; a model with a finite attractor fits the x1 response better than an infinite one.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9a-d; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 3
claims.quote: we found that integration of optogenetic stimulation pulses saturated in the x 1 dimension after the third pulse, suggesting that the line attractor occupies a finite portion of the neural state space
claims.criterion: The two models are described only by their predictions (further pulses add no ramp once the system reaches a point, against each pulse adding the same step). Readings are (a) a step model fit to the x1 trace whose cumulative level is capped at a fitted maximum, against the same model uncapped; (b) the mean ISI levels compared directly, saturation being ISI4 not above ISI3 while ISI3 is above ISI2. Reproduced when under (a) the capped model has lower mean square error in the whole trace and after the third pulse by Mann-Whitney across mice at p < 0.05, or under (b) the pattern holds across mice.

claims.statement: x2 stimulation after x1 has moved the system along the attractor perturbs it off the line, after which it relaxes to the position reached after x1 stimulation and not to baseline.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9e-i; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 4
claims.quote: This x 2 perturbation also resulted in transient off-manifold movements of the PAV orthogonal to the line attractor, followed by relaxation to the position occupied after the previous x 1 stimulation
claims.criterion: In the combined session, the distance from baseline of the state after each stimulation (the legend's "activity distance from baseline after each photostimulation"). Reproduced when the state after x2 stimulation remains farther from baseline than the baseline state (Dunn p < 0.05 for the post-x1 point) and does not differ from the state before x2 stimulation (p >= 0.05). The time points are not given; readings are the frame before the next onset and the mean over each ISI (Wa).

claims.statement: Activating randomly selected neurons that are not weighted by either dimension does not produce activity along x1 or x2.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9j-n; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 4
claims.quote: activation of randomly selected neurons that were not weighted by either dimension did not produce activity along either the x 1 or x 2 dimension
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. As fig2d-x1-integration on the x1 and on the x2 projection of the random-activation session; reproduced when no comparison gives p < 0.05 in either.

claims.statement: Activating x1 or x2 ensembles does not change the head-fixed mouse's movements.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 5f-j; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Activation of either ensemble did not result in overt changes in the behaviour of the head-fixed mouse
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per mouse, the mean of each of the top five motion SVDs before and during stimulation; reproduced when no two-tailed Mann-Whitney test gives p < 0.05. Needs the face videos or their SVDs.

claims.statement: x1 and x2 neurons are not spatially clustered; distances within and between the two groups do not differ.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 6i-k; Results, Holographic activation shows integration, paragraph 1
claims.quote: did not observe spatial clustering of x 1 or x 2 neurons
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per mouse, the mean pairwise distance within x1, within x2 and between x1 and x2 neurons, from cell centroids; reproduced when no Dunn comparison gives p < 0.05. Which neurons count as x1 and x2 is read as in ed3c-x1-activity-observe-vs-engage.

claims.statement: A linear SVM cannot separate x1 from x2 neurons by position better than shuffled labels.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 7a-c
claims.quote: Accuracy of SVM decoder trained on data versus shuffled control (n=10 mice, p=0.156
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Linear SVM on cell positions per FOV, shuffles by random assignment of identity, 20 repeats, mean accuracy (Methods, Spatial cluster decoder). The cross-validation is not given; readings are leave-one-out and fivefold. Reproduced when the two-tailed Mann-Whitney test of accuracy gives p >= 0.05. The n of 10 mice is more than the 9 of Fig. 1; the number found is reported.

claims.statement: Photostimulation through the GRIN lens is spatially confined; the response of a reference cell is close to zero when the spiral is 15 um from its soma.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 6d-h
claims.quote: Note that at 15 µm the average response in the reference cells is close to zero
claims.criterion: Per reference cell (17 cells), the mean response at each offset from the soma. Reproduced when the mean at 15 um is below 10% of the mean at 0 um (the paper gives no value; "close to zero" read as under a tenth of the on-soma response, a reading named here). Needs the calibration recordings.

claims.statement: Non-targeted x1 neurons outside 50 um of the targeted cells integrate during group x1 activation.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 10a-c; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 1
claims.quote: even after excluding the targeted x 1 neurons themselves as well as potentially off-target neurons located within a 50 µm radius of the targeted cell ... we observed integration in the remaining x 1 neurons
claims.criterion: In the x1-activation session, x1 neurons that are not targeted and lie more than 50 um from every targeted cell; their weighted average activity (weights from the x1 factor), tested as fig2d-x1-integration. Reproduced when at least one ISI exceeds baseline at p < 0.001 under one reading and the mean rises from the first to the third ISI.

claims.statement: Integrated activity of targeted x1 neurons is decoded better from non-targeted x1 neurons (about 80% variance explained) than from non-targeted x2 or random neurons (about 40%).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 10d-g; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Decoding from non-targeted x 1 neurons can explain significantly more variance (80% versus 40%) than non-targeted x 2 or randomly selected neurons (n = 8 mice, *p = 0.01, ***p = 0.0003
claims.criterion: A support vector machine decoder (legend) predicting the mean activity of the targeted x1 neurons from non-targeted neurons. Not given and named as open, with readings, are the regression form (linear support vector regression), the number of neurons in each set (equal to the smaller set, random subsets of the same size for the random set), and the validation (fivefold over contiguous blocks). Reproduced when x1 exceeds both x2 and random by Dunn's test at p < 0.05 and the values are within tolerance; partially when the order holds without the values.

claims.statement: Responses of non-targeted neurons to single x1 neuron stimulation are mostly positive.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 10h and 10i; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 2
claims.quote: These experiments revealed a slowly decaying elevation of activity during the ISI period in non-targeted x 1 neurons after each pulse of activation (Fig. 3b,d ) that was mostly positive
claims.criterion: A neuron's response is positive or negative when its mean response after photostimulation is 1.5 standard deviations above or below its baseline (legend of Extended Data Fig. 10h). The post-stimulation window is not given; readings Wa and Wb. Reproduced when positive responders outnumber negative responders, pooled over the unitary x1 stimulation sessions (the legend reports fractions of non-targeted neurons, not a count of mice); the count per mouse is reported.

claims.statement: Putative follower x1 neurons lie on average 139 +/- 35 um from the targeted cell, 11% within 50 um, and their response is not positively correlated with distance.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 10j-n; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Notably, the strength of functional connectivity was not positively correlated with the distance from the targeted photostimulated cell
claims.criterion: A putative follower is a non-targeted x1 neuron that responded to stimulation of a single targeted x1 neuron, by the 1.5 SD rule of the legend of Extended Data Fig. 10h (ed10hi-responses-mostly-positive). The Methods (Terminology) define putative followers as lying outside 50 um, which cannot give the legend's 11% within 50 um; here responders at any distance are counted, the only reading that allows that number. Expected values within tolerance, and the correlation of response with distance (the legend's regression line) not positive at p < 0.05. The paper gives no test; the reading is a Pearson test, named here.

claims.statement: Excluding neurons within 50 um of the targeted cell does not change the follower response to single x1 neuron stimulation.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 10o and 10p; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 2
claims.quote: was still observed even after excluding neurons in a 50 µm zone surrounding the targeted neuron
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per mouse and ISI, the mean response of non-targeted x1 neurons with and without the exclusion; reproduced when no Dunn comparison gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The response of non-targeted x1 neurons scales with the number of targeted x1 neurons, larger with five than with one.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 10q and 10r; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 2
claims.quote: revealed that the response strength of the non-targeted x 1 neurons scaled with the number of targeted x 1 neurons
claims.criterion: Per mouse and ISI (Wa, Wb), the mean x1 projection over non-targeted x1 neurons in the one-neuron and the five-neuron sessions, compared per ISI by Dunn's test. Reproduced when five exceeds one in all four ISIs at p < 0.05 under one reading; partially when in two or three.

claims.statement: Stimulating single x1 neurons raises the activity of non-targeted x1 neurons, with a slowly decaying elevation during the ISI.
claims.source: Figure 3a, 3b and 3d; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 2
claims.quote: These experiments revealed a slowly decaying elevation of activity during the ISI period in non-targeted x 1 neurons after each pulse of activation
claims.criterion: The average z-scored activity of non-targeted x1 neurons in the unitary x1 sessions, per mouse (averaged over its targeted neurons), tested as fig2d-x1-integration. Reproduced when, under one reading, three of four comparisons give p < 0.05, as the legend reports.

claims.statement: Stimulating single x1 neurons does not raise activity in non-targeted x2 neurons.
claims.source: Figure 3c and 3e; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 3
claims.quote: we observed little activity in non-targeted x 2 neurons after activation of unitary x 1 or x 2 neurons
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. As fig3d-single-x1-drives-x1 on non-targeted x2 neurons; reproduced when no comparison gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Stimulating single x2 neurons gives a trend toward rising activity in non-targeted x1 neurons that the text calls not statistically significant.
claims.source: Figure 3f-i; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 3
claims.quote: While there was a trend to a gradual increase in activity in non-targeted x 1 neurons after repeated activation of unitary x 2 neurons (Fig. 3f–h ), that increase was not statistically significant
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, as fig3d-single-x1-drives-x1 on non-targeted x1 neurons in the unitary x2 sessions. Reproduced when no comparison gives p < 0.05. The legend itself reports one comparison at P = 0.0316 against the text's "not statistically significant"; the attempt reports which comparisons reach 0.05.

claims.statement: Stimulating single x2 neurons does not raise activity in non-targeted x2 neurons.
claims.source: Figure 3g and 3j; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Quantification of activity in non-targeted x 2 neurons after targeting of single x 2 neurons (NS)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. As fig3d-single-x1-drives-x1 on non-targeted x2 neurons in the unitary x2 sessions; reproduced when no comparison gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: About 36% of x1-to-x1 pairs have influence scores above the highest x1-to-x2 pair (a z-score of about 0.6), a relatively dense functional ensemble.
claims.source: Figure 4a; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 4
claims.quote: we considered the percentage of x 1 → x 1 pairs that had influence scores higher than the highest x 1 → x 2 pair, which had a z score of around 0.6 ... The fraction of x 1 → x 1 pairs above this threshold was around 36%
claims.criterion: Influence score = the average evoked z-scored activity of each non-targeted photoactivated neuron after photostimulation of a single targeted cell (Results). The averaging window is not given; readings Wa and Wb pooled over the four ISIs. The legend counts 99 pairs from 7 mice; the pair counts found are reported. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: In purely excitatory spiking networks, only relatively sparse integration subnetworks (around 8 to 12%) with slow synaptic time constants (around 20 s) give network time constants of 50 to 200 s; fast glutamatergic networks fail over the same densities.
claims.source: Figure 4c-f; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 5
claims.quote: we found that only artificial networks based on relatively sparse connectivity (around 8–12%) and slow synaptic time constants (around 20 s) could yield network time constants ( τ n ) in the experimentally observed range (~50–200 s; Fig. 4c,e (red shading)). By contrast, networks with fast glutamatergic connectivity failed to do so over the same range of connection densities
claims.criterion: A simulation as the Methods give it (Mechanistic modelling), 1,000 neurons, a 200-neuron subnetwork, weights U(0, 1/N) and U(0, 1/Np), tau_n = tau_s / (1 - lambda_max). Reproduced when, at tau_s = 20 s, tau_n falls in 50 to 200 s (widened 10%, 45 to 220 s) for some density between 8% and 12% (widened, 7.2% to 13.2%), and at tau_s of 0.6 s or less no stable density in the simulated range of 0 to 20% (legend of Fig. 4c) gives tau_n of 45 s or more. Uses no recorded data.

claims.statement: With fast feedback inhibition, a network with slow transmission (20 s) and the measured 36% density integrates pulsed input like the data, while a fast glutamatergic network (100 ms) does not.
claims.source: Figure 4g-l; Results, Line-attractor neurons form ensembles, paragraph 6
claims.quote: networks simulated with a long τ s (20s) and dense σ (36%) could integrate digital optogenetic stimulation in a manner like that observed experimentally ... By contrast, purely glutamatergic networks ( τ s = 100 ms) were unable to integrate at the observed timescales given the measured connectivity density
claims.criterion: The Methods network with inhibition (tau_I 50 ms, g = 1, g_inh 5 or 10, and 1 by the Methods or 1.25 by the legend of Fig. 4h, both run), four smoothed input pulses at 20 s ISI to a random 25% of neurons, Euler steps of 1 ms, noise N(0,1)/5. The pulse width and the calcium kernel are not given (readings 2 s, as in vivo, and an exponential kernel of 1 s decay as a standard choice that cannot change whether activity integrates). Reproduced when the subnetwork's mean rate at the end of each ISI rises from the first to the third ISI at tau_s 20 s and does not at tau_s 0.1 s, for one of the g_inh values. Uses no recorded data.

claims.statement: Across mice, the x1 time constant during observation correlates strongly with the functional connectivity among x1 neurons measured as the AUC of non-targeted x1 neurons after the third pulse (R2 = 0.87).
claims.source: Figure 5g; Results, Attractor stability ties to connectivity, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The strength of this correlation was higher after the third stimulus ( r 2 = 0.87) compared with after the first stimulus ( r 2 = 0.59)
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the x1 time constant of its observation fit (the "intrinsic leak rate" over the whole session, Methods; readings are the largest time constant over states and the x1 time constant of the state occupied after BALB/c removal) and the AUC of the average z-scored activity of non-targeted x1 neurons in its unitary x1 sessions after the third pulse (readings Wa and Wb for the window). Pearson R2 and its p-value over 8 mice. Reproduced when R2 is within tolerance and p < 0.001 under one reading; partially when p < 0.05 with a positive slope.

claims.statement: The correlation is weaker after the first stimulus (R2 = 0.59) than after the third.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 12c and 12d; Results, Attractor stability ties to connectivity, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The strength of this correlation was higher after the third stimulus ( r 2 = 0.87) compared with after the first stimulus ( r 2 = 0.59)
claims.criterion: As fig5g-time-constant-vs-connectivity, after the first pulse. Reproduced when R2 is within tolerance and below the third-pulse R2 under the same reading. The Extended Data Fig. 12b legend gives r2 0.87 for x2 neurons after the third stimulus, which conflicts with the Results and with Fig. 12e-h; it is not used.

claims.statement: The rate of ramp-up along x1 does not correlate with functional connectivity among x1 neurons (r2 = 0.01).
claims.source: Figure 5f; Extended Data Fig. 12b-d; Results, Attractor stability ties to connectivity, paragraph 2
claims.quote: By contrast, there was no correlation between functional connectivity and the rate of ramp-up, suggesting that the latter might be driven by extrinsic inputs to the VMHvl
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a linear correlation over 8 mice. The rate of ramp-up is not defined; readings are (a) the slope of a linear fit to x1 from BALB/c entry to the x1 maximum while the intruder is present and (b) the x1 rise over the first 10 s after entry divided by 10 s. AUC after the third pulse as in fig5g. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 under the reading used; r2 is reported.

claims.statement: The time constant does not correlate with the influence of targeted x1 neurons on non-targeted x2 neurons, so the relation is specific to the x1 subnetwork.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 12e-h; Results, Attractor stability ties to connectivity, paragraph 2
claims.quote: the correlation between attractor stability and functional connectivity was specific to neurons in the integration ( x 1 ) subnetwork, and did not hold when rSLDS time constants were compared with the influence strength of targeted x 1 neurons on x 2 cells
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. As fig5g-time-constant-vs-connectivity with non-targeted x2 neurons, for AUC and average z-score after the first and the third pulse (the four panels e to h). The legend gives no test; the Pearson test of fig5g is used. Reproduced when none of the four correlations gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The striatal recordings that pass the locomotion criteria number 42 from 12 Vglut2 mice, 22 from 6 Calb1 mice, 47 from 10 Anxa1 mice, 74 from 14 DAT mice and 75 from 14 Aldh1a1 mice.
claims.source: Figure 2f legend; Extended Data Figure 6b,c legends; Methods, Analysis of signaling during locomotion, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Vglut2 mice = 12, n = 42 recordings; Calb1 mice = 6, n = 22 recordings; Anxa1 mice = 10, n = 47 recordings; DAT mice = 14, n = 74 recordings ... Aldh1a1 mice = 14, n = 75 recordings
claims.criterion: Recordings are selected by the locomotion criteria in the file's opening comment. Reproduced when all five recording counts are within tolerance, partially reproduced when three or four are, not reproduced otherwise. Mouse counts are reported against the legend (12, 6, 10, 14, 14) and the Methods (12, 6, 9, 14, 14), which differ for Anxa1.

claims.statement: The striatal recordings in the reward analysis number 28 (Vglut2), 17 (Calb1), 51 (Anxa1) and 63 (DAT), and in the air puff analysis 29, 17, 57 and 69.
claims.source: Figure 4d and 4f legends; Methods, Criteria for recording inclusion, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Vglut2 mice = 11, n = 28 recordings; Calb1 mice = 8, n = 17 recordings; Anxa1 mice = 8, n = 51; DAT mice = 11, n = 63 recordings ... Vglut2 mice = 12, n = 29 recordings; Calb1 mice = 8, n = 17 recordings; Anxa1 mice = 8, n = 57 recordings; DAT mice = 11, n = 69 recordings
claims.criterion: Recordings are selected by the stimulus criteria in the file's opening comment. Reproduced when all eight counts are within tolerance, partially reproduced when five to seven are, not reproduced otherwise. Mouse counts are reported against the legends.

claims.statement: Cross-correlations between dF/F and acceleration show a trough at positive lags for Calb1 and Vglut2 axons (transients after decelerations) and a peak at positive lags for Anxa1 axons (transients after accelerations).
claims.source: Figure 2d,f; Results, Genetic subtypes show different signaling patterns during locomotion, paragraph 2
claims.quote: cross-correlations between calcium ΔF/F traces (ΔF/F traces) and acceleration revealed a deep trough at positive time lags for Calb1+ and Vglut2+ axons (indicative of calcium transient peaks after decelerations), but a large peak at positive lags for Anxa1+ axons
claims.criterion: For each recording, the cross-correlation over running periods (1 s of lags, smoothed over 5 lags, as the code does) is integrated over lags 0 to 1 s. Reproduced when the integrals are negative for Vglut2 and Calb1 and positive for Anxa1, each by a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against 0 at p < 0.05 after multiplying by 3; partially reproduced when this holds for two of the three subtypes. The same is shown for the 405 nm control, and per mouse.

claims.statement: Calb1 transients follow decelerations with a shorter lag than Vglut2 transients; the trough of the cross-correlation is at 0.42 s for Vglut2 and 0.17 s for Calb1 on average (P = 1e-6).
claims.source: Figure 2i legend
claims.quote: Timing analysis showing the lag of the trough in the ΔF/F-acceleration cross-correlations for each recording from Calb1 and Vglut2 ... Mean Vglut2 = 0.42, Calb1 = 0.17
claims.criterion: The lag of the minimum of each recording's smoothed cross-correlation between 0 and 1 s (Methods); the code's report, 0.02 s later, is a variant. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance and a two-sided rank-sum test of Vglut2 against Calb1 gives p < 0.05 after multiplying by 3 (the legend states a Bonferroni correction; the code prints the uncorrected value, also shown); partially reproduced when Vglut2 lags are significantly longer but a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: In a PCA of the cross-correlations of all Vglut2, Calb1 and Anxa1 striatal recordings, PC1 explains 64.2% and PC2 20.1% of the variance (84.3% together).
claims.source: Figure 2j,k; Results, Genetic subtypes show different signaling patterns during locomotion, paragraph 3
claims.quote: finding that the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) explained 84.3% of the variance in the cross-correlations (64.2% PC1 and 20.1% PC2)
claims.criterion: Uncentered PCA (as the Methods and code state) of the smoothed cross-correlations of the Vglut2, Calb1 and Anxa1 recordings, with MATLAB's sign convention (the largest loading of each component positive). Reproduced when both values are within tolerance, partially reproduced when one is.

claims.statement: The PC1/PC2 angles of the cross-correlations separate the subtypes, with mean angles of 141 degrees for Vglut2, 208 for Calb1 and 239 for Anxa1 (P = 2e-7 V-C, 4e-11 V-A, 2e-4 C-A).
claims.source: Figure 2l; Results, Genetic subtypes show different signaling patterns during locomotion, paragraph 3
claims.quote: the decomposition of each recording along these PCs revealed distributions that were well separated between the subtypes (Fig. 2k,l; mean PC1/PC2 angles ... = 141° for Vglut2+, 208° for Calb1+ and 239° for Anxa1+
claims.criterion: Angles of the PC1 and PC2 scores, each divided by its standard deviation over all selected recordings of the five groups, in 0 to 360 degrees, as the code does. Pairwise two-sided rank-sum tests on the angles with the circle opened at 45 degrees, multiplied by 3. Reproduced when the three means are within tolerance and the three tests give p < 0.05; partially reproduced when the order Vglut2 < Calb1 < Anxa1 of the means holds and at least two tests give p < 0.05 but a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Triggered averages on large accelerations and decelerations average 135 +/- 77 accelerations and 138 +/- 101 decelerations per recording (mean +/- s.d.).
claims.source: Methods, Analysis of signaling during locomotion, paragraph 6 (Figure 2g)
claims.quote: Triggered averages were the result of averaging 135 ± 77 accelerations and 138 ± 101 decelerations (mean ± s.d.) per recording (Fig. 2g).
claims.criterion: The acceleration and deceleration onsets stored in the files, after removing artifact samples, counted per recording over the locomotion selection of all five groups with at least 3 events, as the code counts them. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance; the standard deviations are reported.

claims.statement: The probability that a dF/F increase follows an acceleration is 57.5% for Anxa1, and that one follows a deceleration is 62.4% for Vglut2 and 62.3% for Calb1.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 7f; Methods, Analysis of signaling during locomotion, paragraph 6
claims.quote: The probability that ΔF/F transients follow accelerations is 57.5% for Anxa1, and the probability that transients follow decelerations is 62.4% for Vglut2+ and 62.3% for Calb1+, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 7f.
claims.criterion: Per event, the integral of dF/F over 0.75 s from the trigger minus its value at the trigger; per recording the percent of events with a positive integral; the mean over recordings. Reproduced when all three are within tolerance, partially reproduced when all three are above 50% but one or more is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: In averages triggered on decelerations, the dF/F peak comes later for Vglut2 (0.35 s) than for Calb1 (0.23 s), P = 0.01.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 6f legend
claims.quote: Timing of the calcium transient peak in triggered averages on decelerations (Fig. 2g, right) for each recording from Calb1 and Vglut2. Means Vglut2 = 0.35, Calb1 = 0.23; p-value for comparison between subtypes = 0.01 (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
claims.criterion: Time of the maximum of each recording's smoothed deceleration-triggered average between 0 and 1 s (Methods); the code's report, 0.01 s later, is a variant. A two-sided rank-sum test without correction, as the legend states. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance and p < 0.05; partially reproduced when Vglut2 peaks significantly later but a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Transient amplitude grows with the size of the deceleration (Vglut2 214%, Calb1 243%) or acceleration (Anxa1 206%) from the smallest to the largest quintile (P = 0.01, 0.002, 0.002).
claims.source: Figure 5a,b; Results, Subtypes show different responses to rewards and aversive stimuli, paragraphs 1 and 2
