claims.statement: Differences across sustained states have significant anterior-posterior gradients, for ACh comparing high and low facial movement, with larger increases in anterior areas, and for calcium comparing locomotion and high facial movement.
claims.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 3; Discussion; Figure S7
claims.quote: there was a significant anterior-posterior gradient in the differences across states measured with Spearman’s rank correlation for the cholinergic signal comparing sustained high and low facial movement and for calcium activity comparing sustained locomotion and high facial movement
claims.criterion: Spearman correlation of the mean difference over mice with the anterior-posterior rank. Reproduced when ACh (high minus low face) has rho < 0 with p < 0.05 and calcium (locomotion minus high face) has p < 0.05; partially reproduced when one holds.

claims.statement: During high facial motion ACh3.0 amplitude is higher in frontal-motor areas than in visual areas (paired t-test, p < 0.05).
claims.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 4; Figure 3d
claims.quote: increased motor activity (e.g., facial movement) is associated with significantly higher ACh release in motor versus visual areas
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the high-face ACh amplitude averaged over MOp and MOs against that averaged over the eight visual areas, as in the Methods. Reproduced when frontal-motor exceeds visual with paired t-test p < 0.05; partially reproduced when it exceeds it in every mouse with p >= 0.05; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The muscarinic blocker scopolamine decreases cortical activity in motor but not visual areas, and the nicotinic blocker mecamylamine has no significant effect.
claims.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 4; Figure 3e
claims.quote: treatment with the muscarinic blocker scopolamine selectively decreased cortical activity in motor but not visual areas ... In contrast, treatment with the nicotinic blocker mecamylamine had no significant impact on cortical activity

claims.statement: Increased facial movement is associated with significant increases in between-area correlations of ACh in anterior somatosensory and motor areas.
claims.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 1; Figure 4a
claims.quote: We found that increased facial movement was associated with significant increases in between-area pairwise correlations in anterior somatosensory and motor areas for ACh signal
claims.criterion: Peak cross-correlation within ±5 frames for the 253 pairs of the 23 left parcels, per matched epoch, Fisher z averaged per mouse; the high minus low face difference averaged over mice; stratified permutation of epoch labels within mice (10,000 permutations), two-sided, and Benjamini-Yekutieli FDR at q = 0.01, as in the code. Motor-somatosensory pairs are those with both areas in MOs, MOp, SSp-* or SSs. Reproduced when at least one pair increases significantly, significant increases outnumber significant decreases, and the fraction of motor-somatosensory pairs with a significant increase exceeds that of the other pairs. Partially reproduced when the first two hold but not the third. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Locomotion is associated with a reduction in between-area correlations of ACh that is significant across the cortex.
claims.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 1; Figure 4a
claims.quote: locomotion was associated with a reduction in the between-area correlations of cholinergic activity that was significant across the cortex
claims.criterion: As fig4a-ach-correlations-up-with-face, for locomotion minus high face. Area groups are the code's visual, retrosplenial, auditory, posterior parietal, somatosensory and frontal-motor. Reproduced when significant decreases outnumber increases, at least 25% of pairs decrease significantly, and every area group has at least one area in a significantly decreased pair. Partially reproduced when decreases outnumber increases and at least one is significant, but not broadly. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Increased facial movement is associated with broad, significant increases in between-area calcium correlations.
claims.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 1; Figure 4b
claims.quote: We found that increased facial movement was associated with ... broad, significant increases for calcium signal
claims.criterion: As fig4a-ach-correlations-down-with-locomotion, for calcium, high minus low face, with increases in place of decreases.

claims.statement: Locomotion occurs with modest decreases in calcium correlations that are significant primarily across posterior cortical areas.
claims.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 1; Figure 4b
claims.quote: Locomotion also occurred with modest decreases in correlation for calcium signals that were significant primarily across posterior cortical areas
claims.criterion: As fig4a-ach-correlations-up-with-face, for calcium, locomotion minus high face. Posterior pairs are those with both areas from VISam on in the Methods' order (ranks 12 to 23). Reproduced when significant decreases outnumber increases, at least one is significant, and the fraction of posterior pairs with a significant decrease exceeds that of the other pairs. Partially reproduced when the first two hold but not the third. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Sustained facial movement is associated with a significant increase in the correlation between ACh and calcium signals broadly across the cortex.
claims.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 2; Figure 5
claims.quote: Sustained facial movement was associated with a significant increase in correlation between the two signals broadly across the cortex
claims.criterion: Within-parcel peak cross-correlation (±5 frames) of ACh with calcium for the 23 left parcels, with the permutation test and FDR of fig4a-ach-correlations-up-with-face over the 23 parcels. Reproduced when at least half of the parcels increase significantly and none decreases significantly. Partially reproduced when increases outnumber decreases with at least one significant. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Sustained locomotion is associated with a significant reduction in the correlation between ACh and calcium that is restricted to the frontal cortex.
claims.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 2; Figure 5
claims.quote: sustained locomotion was associated with a significant reduction in the correlation between the two channels that was restricted to the frontal cortex
claims.criterion: As fig5-coupling-up-with-face, for locomotion minus high face. Frontal parcels are MOs and MOp (the code's frontal-motor group). Reproduced when at least one frontal parcel decreases significantly and no more parcels outside the frontal group than inside it decrease significantly. Partially reproduced when significant decreases exist but more of them lie outside the frontal group. Not reproduced when no parcel decreases significantly.

claims.statement: The spatial regression on 395 nm signals removes stimulus-evoked and behaviour-related negative hemodynamic transients better than pixel-wise regression, shown in GFP and mCherry control mice and in ACh3.0 mice.
claims.source: Results, Dual-color mesoscopic ACh and calcium imaging, paragraph 1; Methods, Validation of hemodynamics correction; Figures S3, S4
claims.quote: This method outperformed conventional pixel-wise regression in its ability to remove stimulus-induced and spontaneous behavior-associated negative transients in fluorescence corresponding to hemodynamic absorption

claims.statement: ACh3.0 specifically reports cholinergic signalling, ex vivo (carbachol, blocked by scopolamine) and in vivo (basal forebrain stimulation).
claims.source: Results, Dual-color mesoscopic ACh and calcium imaging, paragraph 1; Figure S2
claims.quote: we confirmed both ex vivo and in vivo that ACh3.0 specifically reported cholinergic signaling

claims.statement: The relationship between behavioural state and cholinergic signalling is also seen with mesoscopic imaging of GCaMP6s in cholinergic axons.
claims.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 3; Figure S8
claims.quote: we observed a similar relationship between behavioral state and cholinergic axonal signaling measured via mesoscopic imaging of genetically targeted GCaMP6s-expressing fibers

claims.statement: The per-cell descriptors computed from the dandiset (event rate, IEI CV, mean amplitude, spontaneous and task) agree with the per-cell table the paper deposited on Zenodo, so that table can give the cells' first occurrences.
claims.source: Key resources table, Deposited data; Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.14727695
claims.criterion: Cells matched by session and cell name (C, D, reading i). The link holds (reproduced) when at least 90% of matched cells have event rate and amplitude within 1% of the table's values (rounding), partially reproduced for 50 to 90%, not reproduced below 50%. The number of unmatched cells on either side is reported.

claims.statement: In SMA 129, 61 and 63 cells were identified in monkeys Q, F and U, and in M1 37 and 23 cells in monkeys U and V.
claims.source: Results, General description of calcium activity, paragraph 2 (Table S2)
claims.quote: In the SMA, we identified 129, 61, and 63 cells in monkeys Q, F, and U, respectively. In M1, we identified 37 and 23 cells in monkeys U and V, respectively
claims.criterion: Accepted cells per site over the sessions listed in the opening comment. Readings (i) unique cells, each counted once (C), as Fig. 2A treats 129 Q cells over seven sessions; (ii) the sum of accepted cells over sessions. The Limitations call 23 to 129 the number imaged per session, which fits neither reading for Q (129 cells over seven sessions, Fig. 2A); the two readings are of which count is meant, so either may match. Table S2, which gives the counts, is not in the text read. Reproduced when all five counts are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: About 18% of cells were tracked across up to three recording sessions.
claims.source: Results, General description of calcium activity, paragraph 2
claims.quote: We could track a small portion of cells (18%) across up to three recording sessions.
claims.criterion: Needs the cross-session cell identity (C). The fraction of unique cells, over all five sites, that appear in two or more sessions; the maximum number of sessions per cell is reported. Blocked when no cross-session identity is available from the dataset or the Zenodo table.

claims.statement: Calcium event rates did not differ between the spontaneous and reaching task conditions in either SMA or M1.
claims.source: Results, General description of calcium activity, paragraph 3; Figure 1D
claims.quote: The calcium event rates and the coefficient of variation of the inter-event intervals (IEI CV) did not differ between the spontaneous and reaching task conditions in either cortical region
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test of spontaneous against task event rate, paired by cell, cells with both parts (C, D), with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR and significance at p < 0.05 (Methods, Statistical comparisons; Figure 1 legend). The grouping and the FDR family are not given; readings, groups (i) per region with monkeys pooled, (ii) per monkey and region (Q SMA, U SMA, U M1, and V M1 when its second part is taken as task); families (a) all spontaneous against task tests of the three measures of Fig. 1D-F, (b) the tests of this measure only; with D readings (i) and (ii). Reproduced when no reading finds a significant difference, not reproduced when every reading does, blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ. Median rates per condition and the effect size are reported.

claims.statement: The IEI CV did not differ between the spontaneous and reaching task conditions in either SMA or M1.
claims.source: Results, General description of calcium activity, paragraph 3; Figure 1E
claims.quote: The calcium event rates and the coefficient of variation of the inter-event intervals (IEI CV) did not differ between the spontaneous and reaching task conditions in either cortical region
claims.criterion: As fig1d-rate-no-change, for the IEI CV. Cells with fewer than two inter-event intervals in a part have no CV and are left out.

claims.statement: In monkey U's SMA, event amplitude was significantly higher in the spontaneous state than during the reaching task.
claims.source: Results, General description of calcium activity, paragraph 3; Figure 1F
claims.quote: In the SMA, the amplitude of the events was significantly higher in the spontaneous state, compared to the reaching task recordings in monkey U
claims.criterion: Wilcoxon signed-rank test of spontaneous against task mean amplitude, paired by cell, for U SMA cells with both parts (C, D), FDR as in fig1d-rate-no-change, families (a) and (b), D readings (i) and (ii). Reproduced when every reading gives corrected p < 0.05 with the spontaneous median higher, not reproduced when none does, blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ.

claims.statement: In monkey U the event rate was higher in M1 than in SMA, in both the spontaneous and the reaching task conditions.
claims.source: Results, General description of calcium activity, paragraph 3; Figure 1D
claims.quote: In monkey U, we found that the event rate was higher in M1 than in SMA, both during the spontaneous and reaching task conditions
claims.criterion: For each condition, a Wilcoxon rank-sum test of U M1 cells against U SMA cells (C, D, readings i and ii). The Methods apply Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, the Results do not say it for these tests; readings uncorrected, and corrected over the two region comparisons of each measure. Per reading, reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with the M1 median higher, partially reproduced when one does; the outcome is the one every reading gives, blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ.

claims.statement: In monkey U, event amplitude during the task was higher in M1 than in SMA.
claims.source: Results, General description of calcium activity, paragraph 3; Figure 1F
claims.quote: Similarly, the amplitude of the events was higher for the task in M1, compared to SMA
claims.criterion: As fig1d-rate-m1-above-sma-u, for the task mean amplitude. Reproduced when every reading gives p < 0.05 with the M1 median higher, not reproduced when none does, blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ.

claims.statement: In monkey Q's SMA, 43 of 129 cells (34%) significantly changed their activity after the rewarded target appeared.
claims.source: Results, Calcium traces in SMA and M1 show changes in activity, paragraph 2; Figure 2A
claims.quote: We found that in monkey Q's SMA, 34% (43/129) of cells significantly modulated their activity in response to the presentation of the rewarded target and the immediately ensuing movement
claims.criterion: Method Z on the seven Q SMA sessions with TTL data, each cell in its first session. Reproduced when the count of modulated cells is within tolerance under the main method; the variants of Z are reported.

claims.statement: Of the 129 Q SMA cells, 11 (9%) had task responses that were not direction-related and 32 (25%) responded more for one target position.
claims.source: Results, Calcium traces in SMA and M1 show changes in activity, paragraph 2; Figure 2B and 2C
claims.quote: In 11/129 cells (9%), the activity was not direction-related, but 32/129 cells (25%) showed larger changes in activity in trials where the target was located at a specific position
claims.criterion: Method Z, classes as defined there. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: In Q's SMA the size of the response did not differ between cells whose activity rose and cells whose activity fell, and was similar for all target positions.
claims.source: Results, Calcium traces in SMA and M1 show changes in activity, paragraph 2 (data not shown)
claims.quote: The magnitude of the responses did not differ between cells responding with an increase or decrease in firing (Mann-Whitney rank-sum test) and was similar regardless of the target position (Kruskal-Wallis test; data not shown)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's tests (Methods, Alignment to behavioral events). Magnitude is the absolute change in mean z between the 1 s before and the 1 s after target onset, per modulated cell and significant condition; increase or decrease is the sign of the change (the code's Ratio1). A Mann-Whitney test of increase against decrease magnitudes, and a Kruskal-Wallis test across right, center and left, each at p < 0.05. Which values enter is not given; readings (i) one value per significant cell and condition, (ii) one value per modulated cell (mean over its significant conditions). Reproduced when no reading finds a difference in either test; not reproduced when every reading finds one in either; blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise.

claims.statement: In monkey U's SMA, 6 of 14 cells (43%) were modulated at rewarded target onset, all six direction-related, and the proportions were the same when aligned to movement onset.
claims.source: Results, Calcium traces in SMA and M1 show changes in activity, paragraph 3; Figure S1
claims.quote: In monkey U's SMA, we found that 43% (6/14) cells had significant modulation of activity when the calcium traces were aligned to the appearance of the rewarded target, and in all cases (6/6) these changes in activity were related to the direction of the movement. These proportions were the same when the data were aligned to the movement onset
claims.criterion: Method Z on the U SMA session with TTL data (14 cells), for both alignments. Which session holds the TTL data is the author's to find; the Figure S1 legend is not in the text read. Reproduced when all four counts match; partially reproduced when the target-onset counts match and the movement-onset counts do not.

claims.statement: In monkey U's M1, aligned to rewarded target onset, 4 of 6 cells (67%) changed their activity, none direction-related.
claims.source: Results, Calcium traces in SMA and M1 show changes in activity, paragraph 4; Figure S1
claims.quote: In monkey U's M1, when the calcium traces were aligned to the appearance of the rewarded target, 4/6 cells (67%) showed changes in activity, without directional relation.
claims.criterion: Method Z on the U M1 session with TTL data (6 cells), aligned on side target onset. Reproduced when both counts match.

claims.statement: In monkey U's M1, aligned to movement onset, all 6 cells were modulated and half of them were direction-related.
claims.source: Results, Calcium traces in SMA and M1 show changes in activity, paragraph 4; Figure S1; Discussion, paragraph 7
claims.quote: When the data were aligned to the movement onset, 100% (6/6) cells were modulated, and 50% of them showed direction-related activity
claims.criterion: Method Z on the U M1 session with TTL data, aligned on the center release. Reproduced when both counts match; partially reproduced when the modulated count matches only.

claims.statement: Pairs of neurons with synchronous activity occur in both SMA and M1, in both the spontaneous and the task conditions.
claims.source: Results, Cells in SMA and M1 show coactivation, paragraph 1; Figure 3A to 3C
claims.quote: Pairs of neurons exhibited neuronal synchrony in both the SMA and M1 during the spontaneous and task conditions
claims.criterion: Method J. Reproduced when, in each of SMA and M1 and each condition, at least one session has pairs with |Z-Jaccard| > 1.96, the paper's definition of a synchronized pair. The paper compares the proportions with no chance level; the proportion per session and the 0.05 a two-sided 1.96 threshold gives under the null are reported, not used to decide.

claims.statement: Synchrony between cell pairs was not related to the distance between their centroids, in SMA or M1.
claims.source: Results, Cells in SMA and M1 show coactivation, paragraph 1; Figure 3A and 3B; Discussion, paragraph 9
claims.quote: The cell pairs exhibiting synchrony were not related to the centroid distances in either SMA or M1
claims.criterion: The paper shows a loess smoother (span 1) of Z-Jaccard on centroid distance per pair for example sessions of monkey U (SMA and M1, both conditions) and reports no test; the legend calls the panels correlation plots. Method J; distance in um (pixels times 3.2, code). Open details, with readings. The test, (i) Pearson and (ii) Spearman correlation of Z-Jaccard with distance, two-sided p < 0.05; the example sessions, which are not named, each U SMA and U M1 session (which session is meant, so any may match). Per test reading, reproduced when there is a U SMA session and a U M1 session where neither condition shows a significant correlation, not reproduced when every U session shows one in some condition; the outcome is the one both test readings give, blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ. The loess curves and the correlations of all sessions of all monkeys are reported.

claims.statement: The proportion of synchronized cell pairs did not differ between spontaneous and task conditions in SMA (p = 0.07) or M1 (p = 0.22).
claims.source: Results, Cells in SMA and M1 show coactivation, paragraph 1; Figure 3C
claims.quote: The proportion of cells that were synchronized did not significantly differ between spontaneous and reaching tasks in either SMA or M1
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test (Methods; 1_JaccardIndexAnalysisAllSessions.R). Per session and condition, the proportion of pairs with |Z-Jaccard| > 1.96 (method J); per region, a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of spontaneous against task, paired by session, over the sessions with both conditions, at p < 0.05. Reproduced when neither region shows a significant difference; not reproduced when either does. The p-values, the median change and the code's 10-shift null for SMA are reported.

claims.statement: In an example session of monkey Q's SMA with 40 cells, 13 sequences were detected in the spontaneous condition and 17 during the task, and the specific sequences differed between the two even where they involved the same cells.
claims.source: Results, Cells in SMA and M1 show sequential activation patterns, paragraph 2; Figure 4A
claims.quote: In an example imaging session in monkey Q's SMA, we detected 13 such sequences in spontaneous and 17 sequences during the task ... While some of the sequences detected involved the same cells ... the specific sequences differed
claims.criterion: Method S on the Q SMA session with 40 cells (Figure 4A legend); the session is not named, so every Q SMA session with 40 accepted cells is a reading of which session is meant. Per reading of S, reproduced when for some such session both counts are within tolerance and the two sets of sequences (ordered cell lists) are not the same; the outcome is the one every reading of S gives, blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ; the number of sequences found in both is reported.

claims.statement: In another Q SMA session with 18 cells and 20 min of spontaneous recording, 8, 13 and 9 sequences were found in the two spontaneous halves and the task, and the sequences differed between all three segments.
claims.source: Results, Cells in SMA and M1 show sequential activation patterns, paragraph 2; Figure 4B; Discussion, paragraph 10
claims.quote: We detected 8, 13, and 9 unique sequences during ... The detected sequences differed between all three states
claims.criterion: Method S, spontaneous split into its first and second 10 min, on the Q SMA session with 18 cells and a spontaneous part of about 20 min; each such session is a reading of which session is meant. Per reading of S, reproduced when for some such session the three counts are within tolerance and no two segments have the same set of sequences; the outcome is the one every reading of S gives, blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ. The number of sequences shared by each pair of segments, and by all three (the preprint says none), is reported.

claims.statement: The number of sequences per cell, their repetition and the proportion of cells in sequences varied across conditions and imaging sites.
claims.source: Results, Cells in SMA and M1 show sequential activation patterns, paragraph 3; Figure 4D
claims.quote: We found that these factors varied across conditions and across imaging sites, similar to observations made in monkey Q's SMA.
claims.criterion: Method S on every session and segment (spontaneous 1, spontaneous 2 where there are 20 min, task). Per segment, the number of sequences over the number of cells, the median number of repetitions of its sequences, and the fraction of cells in at least one sequence (Figure 4D legend). The paper reports no test. Reproduced when the per-site medians of each measure are not all equal across segments, and not all equal across sites; the per-session values are compared with the Zenodo Fig. 4D table (doi:10.5281/zenodo.14976005) where they match by session.

claims.statement: Cells involved in sequences were spread across the field of view, with no preferred spatial relation between them.
claims.source: Results, Cells in SMA and M1 show sequential activation patterns, paragraph 4; Figure 4C and Figure S2
claims.quote: Plotting the distribution of distances between pairs of cells that were involved in sequences, as well as the overall distribution of distances between all detected cells showed that there is no preferred spatial relation between cells involved in sequences
claims.criterion: The paper compares distributions by eye and reports no test; Figure S2 is not in the text read. What is compared is read two ways, (i) the centroid positions of cells in sequences against those of all cells, spontaneous condition, Q SMA and U M1 (Figure 4C legend), (ii) the distances between cells of the same sequence against the distances between all cell pairs (Results). The test is open; readings a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and a Mann-Whitney test, p < 0.05, on distances (ii) or on each centroid coordinate (i). Reproduced when no reading finds a difference; not reproduced when every reading does; blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise.

claims.statement: Lenses and prisms were placed in the arm regions of SMA and M1, in deep cortical layers, with monkey Q's SMA lens at the anterior edge of SMA.
claims.source: Results, Expression of GCaMP6f and lens localization, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure S3A
claims.quote: Postmortem histological examination confirmed that the lens and prism were placed in the arm regions of SMA and M1
claims.criterion: Histology, not imaging data. Judged from the MAP2 sections on Zenodo against the atlas of Paxinos et al. (2000); reproduced when each of the five lens tracks ends in deep layers of the arm region of SMA or M1 and Q's SMA lens lies at the anterior edge of SMA (Results).

claims.statement: GCaMP6f expression was robust around most imaging sites, sparse in monkey U's SMA, and GCaMP6f-positive cells were not GABAergic.
claims.source: Results, Expression of GCaMP6f and lens localization, paragraph 2; Figure S3B to S3D
claims.quote: We observed robust GFP expression around the lens/prism for most sites, except in monkey U's SMA, where the GFP expression was sparse ... We confirmed that GCaMP6f expression was specific for non-GABAergic neurons by performing a double immunofluorescence assay for GABA and GFP
claims.criterion: Histology, not imaging data. From the GFP and GABA double-label images on Zenodo, reproduced when no GFP-positive cell body is also GABA-positive; GFP density per site is described.

claims.statement: After excluding two sessions, 46 sessions are analysed, in which 883 single units pass the 0.1 Hz rate filter, 351 in the hippocampus and 532 in the amygdala, of 950 isolated.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 3; STAR Methods, Spike sorting
claims.quote: In total, we isolated 950 neurons across both areas of the MTL. Neurons with a firing rate lower than 0.1 Hz in either the WM or the LTM tasks were excluded from analysis (67 neurons (7.1%)). Analyses are based on 351 isolated neurons in the hippocampus and 532 in the amygdala
claims.criterion: Counts of sessions and of units by area, before and after the rate filter of U, in the sessions of S. Tolerance zero, as these are counts of the deposited units. Reproduced when all four match; partially reproduced when the counts after the filter match but the isolated count does not (Table S1 sums to 973 recorded units, so the paper itself gives two totals). The Table S1 total is reported beside them.

claims.statement: Per session, the numbers of recorded units in the hippocampus and the amygdala are those of Table S1.
claims.source: Table S1
claims.criterion: Per session, matched by the session labels of Table S1 to the dataset's subject and session through the patient metadata, the count of units per area in the dataset (before and after the rate filter of U) against the table's recorded count. Reproduced when every one of the 46 sessions matches under one of the two counts; partially reproduced when some do and others do not, the sessions that differ being listed. The category-selective and memory-selective counts per session of the table are compared with those of claims category-neuron-counts and ms-neuron-counts, as a report, not a test.

claims.statement: Patients answered 93.3% of WM trials and 70.3% of LTM trials correctly (d' 1.19), both above the 50% chance level.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Patients performed well in both parts of the task, with an average accuracy of 93.3 ± 7.6 % (mean ± SD) in the WM task and 70.3 ± 9.8 % (d’ = 1.19 ± 0.62) in the LTM task, respectively (both p < 0.0001 as compared to 50 % chance; permutation-based t-test
claims.criterion: Per session of S, the proportion of correct WM trials and of correct LTM trials (all 400), and d' as z(hit rate) - z(false-alarm rate) of old and new pictures; means across sessions. The tolerances are the standard errors of the mean (the stated SD over the square root of 46), since the paper's stated spread is the SD across sessions and these are means of the same sessions; the 10% default would be looser. The correction for hit or false-alarm rates of 0 or 1 is not given; none is applied unless a rate is 0 or 1, in which case the 1/(2N) rule, a standard choice, is used and said. Reproduced when the three means are within tolerance and each accuracy exceeds 50% by a one-sample permutation test (P) at p < 0.0001.

claims.statement: WM accuracy is higher in load 1 than in load 3 trials.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1c
claims.quote: In the WM task, patients performed with higher accuracy (Fig. 1c; load 1 – load 3: t(45) = 4.89, p < 0.0001
claims.criterion: Per session of S, the proportion correct in load 1 and in load 3 trials (plot_behavior.m), compared by the paired permutation t-test of P. Reproduced when load 1 is higher at p < 0.0001; partially reproduced when it is higher at p < 0.05 only.

claims.statement: WM responses are faster in load 1 than in load 3 trials.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1d
claims.quote: and faster (Fig. 1d; t(45) = −4.29, p < 0.0001) in load 1 than load 3 trials
claims.criterion: Per session of S, the mean response time of load 1 and of load 3 trials, response times above 5 s set to missing as in plot_behavior.m (the Methods name no exclusion; the variant without it is shown), compared by the paired permutation t-test of P. Reproduced when load 1 is faster at p < 0.0001; partially reproduced when it is faster at p < 0.05 only. All trials are used, as in the code; the paper does not restrict to correct trials.

claims.statement: LTM recognition is more accurate in high-confidence than in low-confidence trials.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1e
claims.quote: In the LTM task, retrieval was more accurate (Fig. 1e; t(44) = 8.66, p < 0.0001; one patient did not use confidence ratings and was therefore excluded from all confidence-related analyses)
claims.criterion: Per session of S with confidence ratings, LTM accuracy over all trials (old and new) of high and of low confidence (L), compared by the paired permutation t-test of P. Open, the text says "Low confidence was defined as an average of “unsure” and “guessing” responses"; readings (a) accuracy of the unsure and guessing trials pooled, as plot_behavior.m computes it, and (b) the mean of the unsure accuracy and the guessing accuracy. Reproduced when high is more accurate at p < 0.0001; partially reproduced when at p < 0.05 only.

claims.statement: LTM responses are faster with high confidence (mean 1.83 s) than with low confidence (2.62 s).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2
claims.quote: and faster (mean RT high: 1.83 ± 0.57 s; mean RT low: 2.62 ± 0.66 s; t(44) = −11.13, p < 0.0001) when patients indicated high confidence in their responses
claims.criterion: Per session with confidence ratings, the mean response time of high- and low-confidence LTM trials (L), all trials; means across sessions; the paired permutation t-test of P. Tolerances are the standard errors of the mean (stated SD over the square root of 45), for the reason given in behaviour-overall-accuracy. Open, (a) all response times, as the text names no exclusion, or (b) response times above 5 s set to missing, as plot_behavior.m does for every response time it reads; and low confidence pooled or averaged as in fig1e-ltm-confidence-accuracy. Reproduced when, under one reading, both means are within tolerance and high is faster at p < 0.0001; partially reproduced when high is faster at p < 0.05 but a mean is outside tolerance under every reading.

claims.statement: Pictures held in load 1 WM trials are later recognized better than pictures held in load 3 trials.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1f
claims.quote: Items that were encoded in load 1 trials in the previous WM task were remembered better than items encoded during load 3 trials (Fig. 1f; t(45) = 2.42; p = 0.018)
claims.criterion: Per session of S, the hit rate (old pictures answered old over all old pictures) for pictures from load 1 and from load 3 trials, from the LTM trials' load field, as plot_behavior.m computes it; the paired permutation t-test of P. Reproduced when load 1 is higher at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Pictures that were also used as WM probes, and so shown twice, are later recognized better than pictures shown once.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1g
claims.quote: items that were also used as the probe and therefore presented twice were remembered better than items not used as the probe (Fig. 1g; t(45) = 7.25, p < 0.0001)
claims.criterion: Per session of S, the hit rate for old pictures shown twice and shown once in the WM task (the LTM trials' num_times_shown field, plot_behavior.m); the paired permutation t-test of P. Reproduced when shown twice is higher at p < 0.0001; partially reproduced when at p < 0.05 only.

claims.statement: 104 hippocampal units (29.65%) and 220 amygdala units (41.35%) are category neurons.
claims.source: Results, Category neurons remain persistently active when their preferred category is held in WM, paragraph 1
claims.quote: In the hippocampus, 104 (29.65 %) neurons qualified as category neurons, and in the amygdala 220 (41.35 %) neurons qualified as category neurons
claims.criterion: Selection C on the units of U in the sessions of S. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance (10% of each, which also covers the run-to-run variation of the permutation tests that the code warns of).

claims.statement: Hippocampal category neurons are persistently active above baseline during maintenance and fire more when an image of their preferred category is held in WM.
claims.source: Results, Category neurons remain persistently active, paragraph 2; Figure 2b
claims.quote: In the hippocampus, category neurons remained persistently active throughout the maintenance period (intercept: beta = 17.86, p = 1.38 × 10−3; mixed-effects GLM) and had significantly higher FRs during trials in which images from the preferred category were maintained in WM (Fig. 2b; preferred category: beta = 12.47, p = 8.82 × 10−7)
claims.criterion: Hippocampal category neurons of C; all correct WM trials, both loads; the rate 0 to 2.5 s after maintenance onset, normalized as B; outliers removed as O; the GLM of G with the fixed effect preferred category (true when an encoding picture of the trial is of the neuron's preferred category). Open, (a) one row per trial, as the text describes, or (b) the rows of the code's table (one per encoding picture later tested in the LTM test, the preferred flag per picture); and the baseline B1 or B2. Reproduced when, under the readings, the intercept and the preferred-category effect are positive at p < 0.05 and both betas within tolerance; partially reproduced when both are positive at p < 0.05 but a beta is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: When the preferred category is held, hippocampal category neurons fire more in correct than incorrect trials and more in load 1 than load 3 trials.
claims.source: Results, Category neurons remain persistently active, paragraph 2; Figure 2c
claims.quote: Using only preferred trials and modelling WM accuracy (2 levels, WM correct/incorrect, categorical) as well as load (2 levels, load 1/load 3, categorical) as fixed effects, we further observed that category neurons in the hippocampus had higher FRs in (1) correct than incorrect trials (beta = 16.22, p = 0.046) and (2) in load 1 than in load 3 trials (Fig. 2c; beta = 13.769, p = 0.0023)
claims.criterion: Hippocampal category neurons of C; WM trials holding a picture of the neuron's preferred category, correct and incorrect, both loads; maintenance rate (0 to 2.5 s) normalized as B; O; the GLM of G with fixed effects WM accuracy (incorrect as reference) and load (load 3 as reference). Open, (a) main effects only, as the text names two effects, or (b) with their interaction; and B1 or B2. Reproduced when, under the readings, both effects are positive at p < 0.05 and both betas within tolerance; partially reproduced when the load effect holds and the accuracy effect is positive but p >= 0.05 (its reported p is 0.046), or when both hold with a beta outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Amygdala category neurons are also persistently active during maintenance and fire more for the preferred category.
claims.source: Results, Category neurons remain persistently active, paragraph 3; Figure 2e
claims.quote: In the amygdala, category neurons also remained persistently active throughout the maintenance period across all correct trials (intercept: beta = 9.78, p = 6.76 × 10−4) with FRs higher for preferred than unpreferred categories (Fig. 2e; preferred category: beta = 6.91, p = 9.38 × 10−7)
claims.criterion: As fig2b-hippocampus-persistent, with the amygdala category neurons.

claims.statement: When the preferred category is held, amygdala category neurons fire more in load 1 than load 3 trials, but not more in correct than incorrect trials.
claims.source: Results, Category neurons remain persistently active, paragraph 3; Figure 2f
claims.quote: using only preferred trials category neurons in the amygdala showed a significant main effect only for load (Fig. 2f; load 1 – load 3; beta = 12.309; p = 2.46 × 10−7), but the effect for WM accuracy (correct – incorrect: beta = −6.13; p = 0.24) was not significant
claims.criterion: The model of fig2c-hippocampus-correct-load, with the amygdala category neurons and the same readings. The accuracy part is a claim of absence, judged on the same GLM at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the load effect is positive at p < 0.05 with its beta within tolerance and the accuracy effect has p >= 0.05 under every reading; partially reproduced when only one part holds. The accuracy beta is reported either way.

claims.statement: In a GLM over category neurons of both areas, no main effect of LTM accuracy, confidence or area is significant, nor the LTM accuracy by confidence interaction, but every interaction with area is, so the relation of maintenance activity to later memory differs between hippocampus and amygdala.
claims.source: Results, Persistent activity of category neurons in the hippocampus - not the amygdala - predicts LTM formation, paragraph 1; Figure 3a
claims.quote: We did not observe any significant main effects nor was the interaction between LTM accuracy and confidence significant (Fig. 3a; all p > 0.26). However, all interaction terms including area showed significant modulations (confidence × area: beta = 16.88, p = 0.025; LTM accuracy × area: beta = 59.78, p = 0.0030; confidence × LTM accuracy × area: beta = −28.64, p = 0.0029)
claims.criterion: As NWB_computeGLM.m, which is the paper's code for this panel. Category neurons of C in both areas; one row per WM picture later shown in the LTM test; maintenance rate 0 to 2.5 s after maintenance onset, normalized as B (mean baseline over all the neuron's rows); then rows kept when the WM trial was correct and the picture is of the preferred category, with a confidence rating; confidence recoded as the Methods say (forgotten sure 1, unsure 2, guessing 3; remembered guessing 1, unsure 2, sure 3; the code maps 4, 5, 6 to 1, 2, 3 and keeps 1, 2, 3, which is the same under L); FR ~ LTMacc * conf * area with the random effects of G, area with amygdala as reference so that the interactions are hippocampus minus amygdala. Outliers O-M for the main result, O-C (the code) shown as a variant. Reproduced when the three interactions with area have p < 0.05 with the reported signs and betas within tolerance, and the main effects and the LTMacc by conf interaction have p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when the three interactions hold in sign and significance with a beta out of tolerance or a main effect significant.

claims.statement: In the hippocampus, maintenance activity of category neurons for the preferred category predicts later LTM accuracy and confidence, with an interaction between the two, so activity is higher for pictures later remembered than forgotten.
claims.source: Results, Persistent activity of category neurons in the hippocampus, paragraph 1; Figure 3b
claims.quote: This revealed a significant main effect of confidence (Fig. 3b; beta = 20.30, p = 4.17 × 10−3) and LTM accuracy (beta = 67.90, p = 4.43 × 10−4), as well as a significant interaction between the two terms (beta = −30.80, p = 7.74 × 10−4) in the hippocampus
claims.criterion: The table of fig3a-area-interactions restricted to hippocampal category neurons, FR ~ LTMacc * conf with the random effects of G (the Fig. 3a code with the area term dropped, as the text says the analysis was "repeated ... in each area separately"). Outliers O-M, with O-C as a variant; O applied over both areas together as in Fig. 3a (a) or within the hippocampus (b), the text not saying which. Reproduced when, under the readings, the three effects have p < 0.05 with the reported signs and betas within tolerance; partially reproduced when the three hold in sign and significance with a beta out of tolerance.

claims.statement: In the amygdala, maintenance activity of category neurons does not predict later LTM accuracy or confidence.
claims.source: Results, Persistent activity of category neurons in the hippocampus, paragraph 1; Figure 3b
claims.quote: in the hippocampus but not in the amygdala (confidence: beta = 1.54, p = 0.69; LTM accuracy: beta = −2.27, p = 0.82; confidence × LTM accuracy: beta = 1.02, p = 0.83)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the model of fig3b-hippocampus-predicts-ltm on amygdala category neurons, with the same readings. Reproduced when none of the three effects has p < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. The betas are reported either way.

claims.statement: Across hippocampal category neurons, maintenance firing for the preferred category is higher for pictures later remembered than forgotten with high confidence, but not with low confidence.
claims.source: Results, Persistent activity of category neurons in the hippocampus, paragraph 2; Figure 3c
claims.quote: In the hippocampus, FRs were higher for remembered than forgotten trials for high confidence (Fig. 3c; t(82) = 2.16, p = 0.028; some neurons were removed due to insufficient data in at least one of the conditions or since they differed ±3 SD from the mean across all neurons and conditions; see Methods), but not low confidence trials (t(68) = −1.38, p = 0.17)
claims.criterion: Hippocampal category neurons of C; the rows of fig3a-area-interactions (correct WM trials, preferred pictures later tested). Per neuron, the mean maintenance rate (0 to 2.5 s) of pictures remembered with high confidence (L, rating 6) and of pictures forgotten with high confidence (rating 1); for low confidence, remembered 4 or 5 against forgotten 2 or 3. Neurons without trials in a condition, or outliers by O-M, are removed; the paired permutation t-test of P. Open, the rate is (a) normalized as B, as the betas of Fig. 3 are, or (b) in spikes per second, the legend not naming the unit of panel c. The low-confidence part is a claim of absence on the same test at p < 0.05. Reproduced when, under both readings, the high-confidence difference is positive at p < 0.05 and the low-confidence one has p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when only the high-confidence part holds. The numbers of neurons tested (83 and 69 in the paper) are reported.

claims.statement: Across amygdala category neurons, maintenance firing does not differ between later remembered and forgotten pictures, with high or low confidence.
claims.source: Results, Persistent activity of category neurons in the hippocampus, paragraph 2; Figure 3d
claims.quote: In the amygdala, we neither observed a significant effect for high (Fig. 3d; t(158) = 0.84, p = 0.41) nor low confidence trials (t(152) = 1.15, p = 0.26)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the test of fig3c-hippocampus-high-confidence applied to amygdala category neurons, with the same readings. Reproduced when neither comparison has p < 0.05; not reproduced when either does. Mean differences are reported.

claims.statement: In hippocampal category neurons, firing differs between pictures later remembered and forgotten with high confidence early in the maintenance period, from 0 to 650 ms.
claims.source: Results, Persistent activity of category neurons in the hippocampus, paragraph 3; Figure 3e
claims.quote: In the hippocampus, FRs during the beginning of the maintenance period (0 – 650 ms) differed significantly between the two conditions (Fig. 3e; cluster-p = 0.0042; cluster-based permutation test
claims.criterion: The high-confidence remembered and forgotten conditions and neurons of fig3c-hippocampus-high-confidence; per neuron, time-resolved rates over the maintenance period 0 to 2.5 s; a cluster-based permutation test as FieldTrip's ft_freqstatistics (Methods, Statistics), paired across neurons (dependent-samples t), 10,000 permutations, alpha 0.025 for each one-sided cluster. Open, (T1) the binning, (a) 200 ms windows stepped by 25 ms, the only PSTH binning the paper gives (Fig. 2a legend), or (b) 50 ms bins, the code's PSTH bin (spikePlotParams in NWB_calcCatSelective_SB.m), each time point at the window centre; (T2) the cluster-forming threshold, not given, taken as FieldTrip's default clusteralpha 0.05, a standard choice that could change the cluster's extent; (T3) the rate normalized as B or in spikes per second, as in fig3c. Reproduced when, under the readings, a cluster with remembered above forgotten has cluster p < 0.025, begins within 65 ms of maintenance onset and ends within tolerance of 650 ms; partially reproduced when such a significant cluster exists but its bounds are outside these.

claims.statement: In amygdala category neurons, no period of the maintenance period shows a significant difference between later remembered and forgotten pictures.
claims.source: Results, Persistent activity of category neurons in the hippocampus, paragraph 3; Figure 3f
claims.quote: In the amygdala, we did not observe any significant cluster throughout the entire maintenance period of the WM task (Fig. 3f; cluster-p = 0.16)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the test of fig3e-early-delay-cluster applied to amygdala category neurons (the high-confidence conditions of fig3d), with the same readings. Reproduced when no cluster has cluster p < 0.025 on either side; not reproduced when one does. The smallest cluster p is reported.

claims.statement: Maintenance activity of category neurons while non-preferred pictures are held does not predict later LTM accuracy or confidence.
claims.source: Results, Persistent activity of category neurons in the hippocampus, paragraph 4; Figure 3g
claims.quote: None of the main effects nor interactions in either of the mixed-effects GLMs showed any significant relationship between FR and the factors tested (all p > 0.06)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the model of fig3a-area-interactions (LTMacc * conf * area, both areas) on the rows of non-preferred pictures in place of preferred ones (Fig. 3g legend). Open, which rows, (a) every non-preferred picture of the code's table (pref false), or (b) only pictures of trials that held no preferred picture. Reproduced when no fixed effect other than the intercept has p < 0.05 under every reading; not reproduced when any does under every reading. The coefficients are reported.

claims.statement: Activity of category neurons during the presentation of the first encoding picture, for preferred pictures, does not predict later LTM accuracy or confidence.
claims.source: Results, Persistent activity of category neurons in the hippocampus, paragraph 4; Figure 3h; STAR Methods, Relating WM maintenance activity to LTM formation, paragraph 2
claims.quote: or for the visually evoked response of category neurons when images were shown on the screen during encoding (Fig. 3h; encoding 1; 0 – 2s after picture onset; preferred trials only). None of the main effects nor interactions in either of the mixed-effects GLMs showed any significant relationship between FR and the factors tested (all p > 0.06)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the model of fig3a-area-interactions with the rate 0 to 2 s after the onset of encoding picture 1 in place of the maintenance rate, normalized as B, correct WM trials only (Fig. 3h legend). Open, which trials, (a) those whose first encoding picture is of the preferred category, with the LTM outcome of that picture, or (b) those holding a preferred picture in any encoding slot, with the LTM outcome of the preferred picture and the rate of the picture 1 window. Reproduced when no fixed effect other than the intercept has p < 0.05 under every reading; not reproduced when any does under every reading.

claims.statement: 53 of the 351 hippocampal units (15.10%) are memory-selective, 25 of them (47%) firing more to familiar than novel pictures.
claims.source: Results, Activity during WM maintenance is linked to subsequent memory signal, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Out of the 351 recorded cells, n = 53 (15.10 %) were MS cells. Of these, 25 (47%) responded more to familiar than novel items, with the remaining responding more to novel than to familiar items.
claims.criterion: Selection M on the hippocampal units of U in the sessions of S. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance. The amygdala count (68 in Table S1) is reported, not tested.

claims.statement: Hippocampal memory-selective neurons separate old from new pictures better for high-confidence than for low-confidence decisions (higher ROC AUC), so they carry a memory-strength signal.
claims.source: Results, Activity during WM maintenance is linked to subsequent memory signal, paragraph 2; Figure 4b; STAR Methods, Single-neuron AUC analysis
claims.quote: The response of MS neurons differed significantly more for high- as compared to low-confidence trials (Fig. 4b; t(40) = 2.89, p = 0.0039; 12 neurons excluded due to insufficient data in either one of the conditions, see Methods)
claims.criterion: Hippocampal MS neurons of M. Spike counts 0.2 to 1.2 s after LTM picture onset; per neuron an ROC with 25 thresholds linearly spaced from the minimal to the maximal count observed, AUC by the trapezoid rule; for FS neurons all true negatives against high-confidence true positives (rating 6) and, separately, against low-confidence true positives (4, 5); for NS neurons all true positives against high-confidence (1) and low-confidence (2, 3) true negatives (Methods, Single-neuron AUC analysis). The AUC is oriented so that the neuron's preferred response (old for FS, new for NS) above 0.5 means selectivity, the reading under which the paper's "AUC was significantly higher for high than low confidence" holds across both types. Open, which neurons are kept, (a) at least ten correct novel and ten correct familiar trials, as the Methods say, or (b) at least ten trials in each of the groups compared; O-M then applies. High against low AUC by the paired permutation t-test of P. Reproduced when, under both readings, high exceeds low at p < 0.05; the number of neurons kept (41 in the paper) is reported.

claims.statement: 20 hippocampal neurons are both memory-selective and category neurons, an overlap no greater than chance.
claims.source: Results, Activity during WM maintenance is linked to subsequent memory signal, paragraph 3; Figure 4c
claims.quote: Of the 53 MS neurons and the 104 category neurons, 20 neurons (37.8% of MS cells; 19.2 % of category neurons) were part of both groups ... This revealed that the overlap between category neurons and MS cells was not significantly higher than chance (Fig. 4c; p = 0.11)
claims.criterion: With the hippocampal category and MS sets of C and M, the overlap count; the null as the paper describes, drawing as many hippocampal neurons as there are category neurons, without replacement, 1000 times, and counting how many are MS; p as the fraction of draws with an overlap at least the observed (a standard choice; the seed likewise). The absence part is judged on this test at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the overlap is within tolerance and p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when p >= 0.05 but the overlap is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: During LTM retrieval, hippocampal category neurons code neither familiarity nor confidence for pictures of their preferred category.
claims.source: Results, Activity during WM maintenance is linked to subsequent memory signal, paragraph 4; Figure 4d
claims.quote: None of the effects revealed significant modulations of FRs (Fig. 4d top; confidence: beta = 6.05, p = 0.28; familiarity: beta = 4.49, p = 0.71; confidence × familiarity: beta = −4.32, p = 0.57). To further confirm this result, we directly compared FRs of category neurons between preferred old and new items and did not observe a significant difference (Fig. 4d bottom; t(94) = −0.28, p = 0.78).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's two tests. Hippocampal category neurons of C; correct LTM trials showing a picture of the neuron's preferred category; rate 0.2 to 1.2 s after picture onset; the GLM of G with fixed effects confidence (continuous, 3 levels), familiarity (old or new) and their interaction; and, per neuron, mean rate of preferred old against preferred new pictures by the paired permutation t-test of P, after O-M. Open, (D1) the confidence coding, (a) the coding of the Fig. 3a code (sure new 1 to guessing new 3, guessing old 1 to sure old 3) or (b) certainty, sure 3, unsure 2, guessing 1 for both responses; (D2) the rate, (a) spikes per second in the window, the measure the text names, or (b) normalized as B to the WM baseline, the only baseline the paper defines; (D3) the trials of the t-test, (a) correct LTM trials only, as for the GLM in the sentence before, or (b) all trials of preferred old and new pictures, the sentence on the t-test not restricting them. Reproduced when no GLM effect and not the t-test reach p < 0.05 under every reading; not reproduced when any does under every reading.

claims.statement: Familiarity-selective hippocampal neurons respond more during LTM retrieval to familiar pictures that were held with strong, compared with weak, maintenance activity of a simultaneously recorded category neuron.
claims.source: Results, Activity during WM maintenance is linked to subsequent memory signal, paragraphs 5 and 6; Figure 4e; STAR Methods, Interaction between simultaneously recorded category- and memory-selective neurons
claims.quote: This analysis revealed that FRs of familiarity-selective MS cells during LTM retrieval of items that were previously accompanied by high persistent activity in the WM task were higher than those previously accompanied by low persistent activity (Fig. 4e left; Maintenance FR: beta = 14.63, p = 1.39 × 10−3)
claims.criterion: Pairs of a hippocampal MS neuron (M) and a hippocampal category neuron (C) of the same session. Per category neuron, its maintenance rates (0 to 2.5 s) in correct WM trials holding a preferred picture later shown in the LTM test, median-split into strong and weak separately within load 1 and load 3 trials (Methods); a rate equal to the median goes to weak (a standard choice). The MS neuron's rate 0.2 to 1.2 s after onset of those pictures in the LTM test. The GLM of G with the fixed effect maintenance (strong or weak), FS pairs only; and, per pair, the mean MS rate after strong against after weak by the paired permutation t-test of P (O-M applied). Open (the Methods sentence on this GLM lost its variable names), (E1) the random intercept within patient is (a) the MS neuron or (b) the pair; (E2) the LTM trials are (a) all trials of those old pictures or (b) only those answered old; (E3) a neuron that is both MS and category is (a) paired with itself or (b) not; (E4) the rate is (a) spikes per second or (b) normalized as B to the WM baseline. Reproduced when, under the readings, both tests give strong above weak at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when one of them does under every reading. The pair counts and beta are compared with expected values as a report, since E3 changes the counts.

claims.statement: The response of novelty-selective hippocampal neurons to familiar pictures does not depend on whether the paired category neuron's maintenance activity was strong or weak.
claims.source: Results, Activity during WM maintenance is linked to subsequent memory signal, paragraphs 5 and 6; Figure 4f
claims.quote: No significant relationship was observed for the activity of novelty-selective MS neurons (Fig. 4f left; Maintenance FR: beta = 0.09, p = 0.98)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's two tests of fig4e-fs-strong-maintenance applied to NS pairs, with the same readings. Reproduced when neither test has p < 0.05 under every reading; not reproduced when either does under every reading. The number of NS pairs (122 in the paper) and the beta are reported.

claims.statement: Ten participants (four male, six female, 19 to 50 years) were recorded with two 128-electrode grids each; all ten did the CORR, SYN-P, SYN-C and SEM conditions, five of them the combined violation (COM) and the other five the non-linguistic task (NL).
claims.source: Methods, Participants, paragraph 1, and The Chinese language and stimuli design, paragraph 3; Supplementary Table 1
claims.quote: This study included ten participants (age range, 19–50 years; four males, six females) ... All the ten participants performed under CORR, SYN-P, SYN-C and SEM conditions. Five participants performed under COM and the other five performed under NL conditions.
claims.criterion: Counts of distinct subjects in the dataset, their sex, and the tasks each has. Tolerance zero, as these are counts the paper gives exactly. Reproduced when all match; partially reproduced when the dataset holds a subset of the participants with matching metadata. Ages are compared with Supplementary Table 1 (30, 39, 19, 30, 50, 34, 42, 36, 40, 31 for participants 1 to 10) where the dataset gives them.

claims.statement: Each of the CORR, SYN-P, SYN-C, SEM and COM conditions has 32 sentences, with six words per sentence in CORR, SYN-C and SEM and seven in SYN-P and COM, each word shown for 400 ms with a 100 ms interval after an 800 ms fixation and a 500 ms blank.
claims.source: Methods, The Chinese language and stimuli design, paragraph 4; Supplementary Information, stimulus sentence lists
claims.quote: Each trial started with an 800 ms fixation followed by a 500 ms blank screen, and then each word of the sentence (or geometric shape) was displayed for 400 ms, with a 100 ms interstimulus interval. There were six words per sentence in the CORR, SYN-C and SEM conditions and seven words in the SYN-P and COM conditions.
claims.criterion: The 32 sentences per condition are read from the numbered lists in the supplement (no sentence of the text gives the count). Per participant, the number of trials of each condition (before bad-interval exclusion, where the dataset says which were excluded) and the word timing from the event times. The timing tolerance of 10 ms is one sample of the 100 Hz HGA. Reproduced when every count matches and the timings are within tolerance in every participant; partially reproduced when they do in some.

claims.statement: Most participants responded fast and accurately in the linguistic task, most response times lying around 0.5 to 1.0 s.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure 2b legend
claims.quote: Most of the responding time is around 0.5-1.0 second.
claims.criterion: Response times of the linguistic trials of all ten participants pooled, measured from the onset of the question as the dataset times it. The paper gives no measure of "most"; the reading taken is that more than half of the response times lie in the range widened by 10% of each bound (0.45 to 1.1 s), and no other is named in the text. Accuracy is reported (proportion of correct judgements per participant) but has no number to match. Reproduced when more than half lie in the range.

claims.statement: High-gamma components above 70 Hz classify the linguistic conditions with the highest accuracy (above 80%), and the evoked responses are more prominent in the 70 to 150 Hz band than in other bands.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 1b; Supplementary Figure 3a to 3e
claims.quote: Results showed that high-gamma (HG) components (>70 Hz) discriminated conditions with the highest accuracy (>80%, Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 3a) and ERPs were more prominent in the HG band (70–150 Hz) compared with other frequency bands
claims.criterion: Needs the broadband signal, from which the analytic amplitude of bands from 0 to 150 Hz in 10 Hz steps is taken as the first principal component across band-passes, and classified with the SVM, logistic regression and k-nearest-neighbour settings of the Methods (Frequency component extraction) into correct, syntactic violation, semantic violation and resting state. If the dataset holds only high-gamma activity, as its description says, the claim cannot be tested. Otherwise, open, the cross-validation and the features (time samples of the band amplitude in the keyword window). The paper reports the band accuracies for the SVM (Fig. 1b legend) and for logistic regression (Supplementary Fig. 3a legend) only; reproduced when, under both, a band with lower bound at or above 70 Hz gives the highest accuracy and, for the SVM, it exceeds 0.72 (80% less the tolerance). The kNN result is shown as a variant. The ERP part is judged from the measure of Supplementary Fig. 3d (the peak power during violation against the peak power during CORR, per responding electrode), and holds when the mean difference is largest in the 70 to 150 Hz band.

claims.statement: Most electrodes showing enhanced activity to linguistic stimuli lie in the IFG.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 1c; Supplementary Figure 3f
claims.quote: Most of the electrodes showing enhanced activities to linguistic stimuli were located in the IFG
claims.criterion: The rest against stimulus test of E (with readings E1a and E1b) applied to every electrode of every participant, regardless of location, with HGA higher during stimuli. Reproduced when more than half of the responsive electrodes carry an IFG label. Open, which labels form the IFG, (a) pars opercularis and pars triangularis, the labels of E, or (b) these and pars orbitalis.

claims.statement: The enhanced activity for violation conditions relative to CORR appears only after the keyword.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 1d
claims.quote: In the linguistic task, the enhanced activity of violation conditions relative to CORR was only observed after the keywords, indicating that the responses were highly linked to the violation manipulations (Fig. 1d).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence before the keyword, judged on the paper's test, the test of V (the discriminating period of Fig. 1e and the ERP amplitude Methods), applied to the electrodes of E over the sentence before the keyword, aligned to the first word (words 1 to 3, 0 to 1,500 ms). Reproduced when no electrode and condition pair passes V before the keyword; not reproduced when any does. The count of passing pairs, before and after the keyword, is reported either way. The SEM verb (word 2) differs from the CORR verb; the test without SEM samples 500 to 1,000 ms is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: 58 IFG electrodes respond to at least one violation type more strongly than to correct sentences.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 2b
claims.quote: we defined a significant effect in each electrode if its response to a certain type of violation was reliably enhanced compared with the CORR condition for more than 50 ms (P < 0.05, ANOVA, two tailed, Bonferroni correction for the number of electrodes, n = 256 for each participant); there were 58 electrodes satisfying this criterion
claims.criterion: Electrodes of E (readings E1a, E1b) passing V (readings V1a, V1b, V2a, V2b) for at least one of SYN-P, SYN-C and SEM, over the ten participants. Reproduced when the count is within tolerance under at least one combination of readings (a count that a reading can move is a reported number read in more than one way, so any reading may match); not reproduced when none is. The count under every combination is reported.

claims.statement: Most responding electrodes (49 of 58) respond strongly to only one violation type; few (9 of 58) are co-activated by two types, mainly SYN-P and SYN-C.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 2b
claims.quote: We found that most of the electrodes (49 of 58) strongly responded to only one type of violation (Fig. 2b, one-way ANOVA F statistic > 4). Only a few electrodes were co-activated by two violation types (9 of 58) and were mainly co-activated by SYN-P and SYN-C
claims.criterion: Among the electrodes of fig2b-violation-electrodes, an electrode strongly responds to a violation when its F (readings F1, F2, F3) exceeds 4. Counts of electrodes strongly responding to exactly one, and to two, of the three types. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, both counts are within tolerance and the SYN-P and SYN-C pair is the most frequent pair among the co-activated electrodes; partially reproduced when the single-type electrodes are a majority and SYN-P with SYN-C is the most frequent pair, but the counts are outside tolerance under every reading. The 10% tolerance on 9 is below one electrode, so the second count must match exactly.

claims.statement: When half of the sentences select the responding electrodes and the other half are analysed, most electrodes (46 of 62) still respond to one violation type only and 16 of 62 to two, mainly SYN-P and SYN-C.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Supplementary Figure 6a legend
claims.quote: We used first half sentences to identify the linguistic responding electrodes and used the remaining sentences for further analysis, to resolve non-independence issue. We found that most of the electrodes (46/62) strongly responded to only one type of violation (below figure). Only a few electrodes were ... by two violation types (16/62) and were mainly ... by SYN-P and SYN-C
claims.criterion: As fig2b-violation-electrodes and fig2b-single-type, with E and V computed on the trials of the first half of the sentences and F on the remaining trials. Open, (a) "first half" as sentences 1 to 16 of each condition's list, or (b) the first half of each condition's trials in presentation order. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all three counts are within tolerance and SYN-P with SYN-C is the most frequent pair; partially reproduced when the single-type electrodes are a majority and the pair is the most frequent, with counts outside tolerance.

claims.statement: When the length of the period differing from CORR is used in place of amplitude, most electrodes (61 of 79) respond to one violation type only and 18 of 79 to two, mainly SYN-P and SYN-C.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 5; Supplementary Figure 6b legend
claims.quote: We found that most of the electrodes (61/ 79) strongly responded to only one type of violation (below figure). Only a few electrodes were ... by two violation types (18/79) and were mainly ... by SYN-P and SYN-C
claims.criterion: The paper does not say how 79 electrodes are selected or what length counts as a response. Readings, (a) electrodes of E with a significant period (V, without the amplitude rule V2) of more than 50 ms for a violation count as responding to it; (b) as (a) with the amplitude rule kept. The length of an electrode's significant period is the number of significant samples times 10 ms. Reproduced when, under one reading (crossed with V1a and V1b), all three counts are within tolerance and SYN-P with SYN-C is the most frequent pair; partially reproduced when the single-type electrodes are a majority and the pair is the most frequent, with counts outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The response time courses of SYN-P and SYN-C are more similar (Euclidean distance 48.43) than those of the syntactic and semantic conditions (62.17).
claims.source: Results, paragraphs 5 and 6; Figure 2c
claims.quote: the similarity between SYN-P and SYN-C (Euclidean distance, 48.43) was greater than that between syntactic and semantic conditions (Fig. 2c, Euclidean distance, 62.17)
claims.criterion: Distances computed with scipy's hierarchical clustering on Euclidean distance (Methods, Electrode selection, paragraph 3), between condition vectors built from the responding electrodes of fig2b-violation-electrodes. Open, (a) each condition's vector is the trial-mean HGA from 0 to 1,000 ms of every responding electrode, concatenated over electrodes; (b) the trial-mean HGA time course from 0 to 1,000 ms averaged over the responding electrodes (the Methods call it a "time-course similarity", so a reading without time is not allowed); and the "syntactic to semantic" distance read as (i) SEM to SYN-P, (ii) SEM to SYN-C, (iii) the mean of the two, or (iv) the linkage height at which SEM joins the SYN-P and SYN-C cluster. Fig. 2c's y axis is a "relative distance", so absolute values depend on the vector. Reproduced when, under every reading, the syntactic to semantic distance is larger than SYN-P to SYN-C, and under at least one reading both values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the order holds under every reading but no reading matches the values; not reproduced when the order fails under every reading; blocked otherwise. The values under each reading are reported.

claims.statement: Of the electrodes responding to the combined violation (COM), 78.3% also respond to SYN-P but only 26.1% to SEM.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 6; Supplementary Figure 7a
claims.quote: for the electrodes responding to the combined violation condition (COM), 78.3% of them also showed enhanced activity to the syntactic violation (SYN-P), but only 26.1% of them responded to the semantic violation (SEM)
claims.criterion: In the five participants with COM, electrodes of E passing V for COM against CORR (COM keyword at word 5, as in SYN-P). Fractions of those that also pass V for SYN-P, and for SEM. Open, whether "responded" to SYN-P and SEM means passing V or having F > 4 (F1 to F3), as Supplementary Fig. 7a plots F values. The smallest count the two percentages fit is 18 and 6 of 23 electrodes (an inference; the paper gives no count), so the 10% tolerance on 26.1% is below one electrode there. Reproduced when both fractions are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when, under every reading, the SYN-P fraction exceeds the SEM fraction but the values are outside tolerance.

claims.statement: The electrodes responding to linguistic violations do not respond to the non-linguistic violation in the high-gamma band.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 6; Supplementary Figure 7b and 7c legend
claims.quote: at 70 -150 Hz, the linguistic responding electrodes were almost completely not responding to the non-linguistic task
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. In the five NL participants, the electrodes of fig2b-violation-electrodes tested for NL-VIO against NL-CORR with the test of V, NL trials aligned to the onset of the shape in the keyword's position. The paper's NL test is a one-way ANOVA at P < 0.01, corrected (Supplementary Fig. 4b); the threshold read is 0.01/256 per sample, with 0.05/256 (the linguistic test) as a variant. "Almost completely not" is read as at most 5% of those electrodes passing, the rate a test at the paper's alpha allows. Reproduced when no more than 5% pass; not reproduced otherwise. The count and the electrodes' NL-VIO minus NL-CORR differences are reported either way.

claims.statement: Across participants, the activation centres and epicentres of the SYN-P, SYN-C and SEM electrodes are not spatially separated in the IFG.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 7; Figure 2d and 2e; Supplementary Figure 8a
claims.quote: Unlike the result at the electrode level, we failed to observe a tendency of spatial separation for the activation centre of syntactic and semantic conditions. Likewise, the epicentre of these responses failed to show separations using a permutation test of the clusters of electrodes (Fig. 2e).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a non-parametric permutation test of the spatial segregation among SYN-P, SYN-C and SEM electrodes on the MNI152 template (Methods, Spatial organization). The Methods do not give the statistic or the permutation scheme. Readings, (a) for each pair of conditions, the distance between the mean MNI coordinates of their electrodes; (b) the distance between the peaks of their kernel density estimates (bandwidth 20, as the Methods give, in mm); in both, condition labels permuted among the electrodes of the pair 1,000 times (the permutation count the Methods give for ALE), two-sided, p < 0.05. Co-activated electrodes count in each of their conditions. Reproduced when no pair is significant under every reading; not reproduced when a pair is under every reading; blocked otherwise. The distances are reported. The ALE analysis (GingerALE) is not repeated.

claims.statement: Even within individual participants the SYN-P, SYN-C and SEM electrodes show no clear spatial separation.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 7; Supplementary Figure 8b
claims.quote: However, even at the individual level, we were unable to obtain a clear separation pattern (Supplementary Fig. 8b).
claims.criterion: The paper shows one representative participant and reports no test. The test of fig2de-no-spatial-separation, reading (a), run per participant on native or MNI coordinates, for pairs of conditions with at least three electrodes each (a standard minimum, not the paper's). A claim of absence, reproduced when no participant has a pair significant at p < 0.05 uncorrected; not reproduced otherwise. The number of participants with a significant pair is reported.

claims.statement: From the fraction of co-activated electrodes, the diameter of the functional circuits is estimated as no greater than about 3.25 mm.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 8; Figure 2f; Methods, Functional circuit size estimation
claims.quote: The results showed that the diameter of functional circuits was no greater than ~3.25 mm (Fig. 2f)
claims.criterion: The Methods give p(co-activation) = 1 - (r - 0.5 mm)/r for an electrode of radius 0.5 mm and a circuit of diameter r, so r = 0.5 mm / p. p is the fraction of co-activated electrodes from fig2b-single-type (9 of 58 gives 3.22 mm, matching the paper's 15.6% and 3.25 mm on Fig. 2f). Reproduced when r from the dataset's fraction is within tolerance under a reading that also reproduces fig2b-single-type, or under any reading if none does.

claims.statement: Electrode types (SYN-P, SYN-C, SEM, non-responding) can be predicted from responses to correct sentences above the 25% chance level, with accuracies of 45.6%, 73.0%, 69.3% and 38.4%.
claims.source: Results, paragraph 9; Supplementary Figure 9 legend; Methods, Predicting different types of electrodes
claims.quote: our data showed the predicted electrode types with accuracies significantly higher than chance level (SYN-P 45.6%, SYP-C 73.0%, SEM 69.3%, and not-responding electrodes 38.4%; all P < 0.0001 relative to chance level 25%, Supplementary Fig. 9)
claims.criterion: k-nearest neighbours (Supplementary Fig. 9 legend) with the settings the Methods give for the frequency decoding (5 neighbours, Minkowski p = 2, uniform weights; the Methods state them for that analysis, and no other kNN settings are given), features from the CORR response of each electrode only, onset, offset, peak (L), area and amplitude at T0 (Methods, Predicting different types of electrodes). Open, (a) the electrodes and labels, single-type electrodes of fig2b-single-type labelled by their type, and non-responding electrodes either (a1) the electrodes of E that pass V for no condition or (a2) the IFG electrodes outside E; co-activated electrodes left out; (b) the cross-validation, (i) stratified 5-fold repeated 100 times with the t-test over repeats, or (ii) leave-one-out with the t-test over electrodes of each class (correct as 1, wrong as 0); (c) features standardized or raw; (d) L readings. Accuracy per class is the fraction of that class's electrodes predicted correctly. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all four accuracies are within tolerance and each exceeds 25% with two-sided t-test p < 0.0001; partially reproduced when, under every combination, all four exceed chance at p < 0.0001 but the values miss tolerance; not reproduced when any class fails to exceed chance under every combination.

claims.statement: SYN-P responses start and peak earliest (onset 113 ms, peak 480 ms), then SEM (122 ms, 524 ms) and SYN-C (283 ms, 579 ms).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 10; Figure 3c, 3d and 3f
