claims.source: Results 3.2, Adcyap1 expression in maternal placenta; Figure 11
claims.quote: we find no difference in hyperlocomotion in PACAPko mice bred from heterozygous dams versus those from homozygous PACAPko dams ( Figure 11 )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test (Figure 11 legend). Per behaviour, a Mann-Whitney U test of the two groups, Holm-Šídák across the four. Reproduced when all four have adjusted p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any has p < 0.05. U values are shown.

claims.statement: Fasting lowers light-phase body temperature in both WT and PACAPko mice, and it returns on refeeding to the fed level.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 12B
claims.quote: Removal of food causes significantly decreased Tb in both wild-type and PACAPko mice, indicating that this aspect of thermoregulation is intact
claims.criterion: From Methods 2.1 (Body temperature telemetry) and the Figure 12B legend. Mean Tb over each 12-h light period (fed, fasting, refed) per mouse; a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA of feeding status by genotype (Geisser-Greenhouse corrected, as the fractional degrees of freedom show), Tukey comparisons of feeding status within genotype. Which baseline light period is "fed" is open (5 baseline days were recorded, three light periods are plotted); readings are (a) the last light period before food removal, (b) the mean of the baseline light periods. Reproduced when, under one reading, fasting Tb is below fed and refed in both genotypes at p < 0.05, and fed against refed has p >= 0.05 in both.

claims.statement: PACAPko mice have a higher body temperature than WT, averaging 36.21 against 35.63 degrees C across light cycles.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 12B
claims.quote: We also see a significant main effect of genotype (F (1, 36) = 11.12, p < 0.0001), with PACAPko mice averaging 36.21°C across light cycles and WT mice averaging 35.63°C.
claims.criterion: Same ANOVA and readings as fig12b-pacapko-fasting-hypothermia; the averages are over the three light periods. Tolerances - 10% of the difference; for each mean, half the difference (0.29), since 10% of a body temperature would admit any physiological value. The printed p (< 0.0001) does not match F(1, 36) = 11.12 (p near 0.002); the genotype effect is judged at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the genotype effect has p < 0.05 with PACAPko higher and the difference is within tolerance; partially reproduced when the effect holds and the difference is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: PACAPko mice are more active than WT mice in most 12-h periods.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 1; Figure 12D
claims.quote: PACAPko mice are significantly more active than WT mice in most of the time periods.
claims.criterion: From the Figure 12D legend. Mean telemetry activity per 12-h period (three light and three dark, fed, fasting and refed) per mouse; unpaired t-tests per period with Holm-Šídák across the six. "Most" is read as more than half, so at least 4 of 6 periods. The fed baseline periods take the readings of fig12b-pacapko-fasting-hypothermia. Reproduced when PACAPko is higher at adjusted p < 0.05 in at least 4 of the 6 periods.

claims.statement: In Sim1-Cre::PACAP fl/fl mice, body temperature does not differ from WT, and the fasting-induced Tb decrease and its recovery on refeeding are intact.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 13A
claims.quote: Restriction of the PACAP knockout to hypothalamus abrogates the effect of PACAP loss on locomotion and on body temperature, while normal Tb decrease after fasting remains intact ( Figure 13a , b ).
claims.criterion: As fig12b-pacapko-fasting-hypothermia, with its readings, for Sim1-Cre::PACAP fl/fl against Cre-negative littermates, sexes pooled as the legend's single ANOVA implies. Unlike Figure 12B, the time effect has integer degrees of freedom (F(2,30), and F(2,24) in Figure 13C), so no Geisser-Greenhouse correction was applied in Figure 13. The genotype effect and interaction are a claim of absence, on the paper's test. Reproduced when the genotype effect and interaction have p >= 0.05, fasting Tb is below fed and refed in both genotypes at p < 0.05, and fed against refed has p >= 0.05 in both.

claims.statement: Activity of Sim1-Cre::PACAP fl/fl mice does not differ from WT in any period.
claims.source: Figure 13B
claims.quote: Activity of Sim1-Cre::PACAP fl/fl mice does not differ from activity of WT mice in any period (multiple unpaired t-tests with Holm-Šídák correction).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test. Mean activity per 12-h period per mouse, unpaired t-tests per period, Holm-Šídák across the six; fed baseline periods with the readings of fig12b-pacapko-fasting-hypothermia. Reproduced when no period has adjusted p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In PAC1ko mice, body temperature does not differ from WT, and the fasting-induced Tb decrease and its recovery on refeeding are intact.
claims.source: Results 3.3, paragraph 2; Figure 13C
claims.quote: Similarly, body temperature, activity, and fasting-induced thermoregulation did not differ between PAC1ko and wild-type mice ( Figure 13c , d ).
claims.criterion: As fig13a-sim1-tb-unchanged, for PAC1ko against WT littermates. Reproduced when the genotype effect and interaction have p >= 0.05, fasting Tb is below fed and refed in both genotypes at p < 0.05, and fed against refed has p >= 0.05 in both.

claims.statement: Activity of PAC1ko mice does not differ from WT in any period except the initial fed light cycle, when it is slightly lower.
claims.source: Figure 13D
claims.quote: activity of PAC1ko mice does not differ from activity of WT mice in any period except during the initial fed light cycle (p = 0.026), when PAC1ko animals show slightly lower levels of activity than WT mice.
claims.criterion: Mean activity per 12-h period per mouse, unpaired t-tests per period, Holm-Šídák across the six; fed baseline periods with the readings of fig12b-pacapko-fasting-hypothermia. Reproduced when the initial fed light period is lower in PAC1ko at adjusted p < 0.05 and no other period has adjusted p < 0.05 (absence, on the paper's test); partially reproduced when only the absences hold.

claims.statement: Seven mice were recorded over 66 sessions, yielding 3892 hippocampal CA1 units and 2557 medial prefrontal units after curation and cell type classification.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 1; Supplementary Table 1
claims.quote: we recorded single unit and local field potential activity in dorsal hippocampal CA1 and medial prefrontal cortex during behavior ( n = 3892 units in hippocampus, n = 2557 units in medial prefrontal cortex
claims.criterion: Counts from the dandiset. Animals and sessions are design counts and must match exactly (tolerance 0, reason: they are the experiment, not a measurement). Units are counted per region over all sessions, all three cell types (Supplementary Table 1 note: final counts after curation and cell type classification); the per-animal counts of Supplementary Table 1 are reported beside them.

claims.statement: In the final task 65% of trials are delay only, 25% switch and 10% stay trials.
claims.source: Methods, Behavioral task and training, paragraph 2; Results, first section, paragraph 1
claims.quote: These trial types consisted of delay only trials (65% of trials)
claims.criterion: Fractions of final-task trials (warm-up trials excluded, Methods; code maze_id 4) of each type, pooled over the 66 sessions. Readings for the denominator, all reported: (a) all final-task trials; (b) the per-session fractions averaged over sessions. Reproduced when all three fractions are within tolerance under one reading. Note: the paper's own counts do not give these fractions. Supplementary Table 1 lists 8104 delay, 1840 switch and 717 stay completed trials (0.76, 0.17, 0.07), and the Results counts (7172 delay only, 1840 switch) with the 717 stay trials give 0.74, 0.19, 0.07; both fall outside the tolerances, so the percentages read as the task's programmed trial probabilities (Methods). The realized fractions are reported beside the result.

claims.statement: The delay on delay only trials lasted 10.56 s on average, the shortened delay before the update cue on switch trials 1.40 s, and the delay after the update cue 6.02 s; trials lasted about 21 s from start to choice.
claims.source: Results, first section, paragraph 1; Supplementary Fig. 1a
claims.quote: The mice had to maintain the memory of the correct goal arm during the delay period (10.56 ± 0.07 seconds, n = 7172 trials, Supplementary Fig. 1 ). On a subset of trials, a second visual cue appeared when mice reached a specific location after a shortened delay period (1.40 ± 0.03 seconds, n = 1840 trials)
claims.criterion: From the trial table of final-task trials. The delay on delay only trials runs from original cue offset to choice made (Supplementary Fig. 1a legend); trial duration from trial start to choice made (Supplementary Fig. 1a legend; code behavior_analyzer, t_choice_made minus start_time). The first delay on switch trials runs from original cue offset to update cue onset. The second delay is open; readings (a) second delay onset (t_delay2) to choice made, (b) update cue onset to choice made. The Results do not say which trials the 6.02 s second delay covers (Methods give a second delay on stay and update trials); readings for it (e) switch trials, (f) switch and stay trials pooled. The trial set is open (n = 7172 delay only and 1840 switch trials in the text, 7313 and 1886 in the legend, 8104 and 1840 completed in Supplementary Table 1); readings (c) all final-task trials, (d) correct trials. Reproduced when each value is within tolerance under one reading; the trial counts under each reading are reported.

claims.statement: Animals performed above 50% correct on delay only trials (65 +/- 2%) and on switch trials (74 +/- 2%).
claims.source: Results, first section, paragraph 1; Figure 1b; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 1b
claims.quote: animals learned to remember and follow the cues across all trial types and performed above 50% accuracy (delay only mean ± SEM: 65 ± 2%, switch mean ± SEM: 74 ± 2%, p = 6.197e−10 delay only vs. 50% correct, p = 3.410e−11 switch vs. 50% correct
claims.criterion: Final-task trials (code maze_id 4). The test is a two-sided one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test against 0.5 (Methods, Supplementary Table 2). Its sample is open; readings (a) one proportion correct per session and trial type (the code runs this test on session proportions minus 0.5, and the printed W values fit a sample of tens, not thousands); (b) the 40-trial windows that Supplementary Table 2 names. The mean is open; readings (c) over sessions, (d) over the 7 animals. Reproduced when the test gives p < 0.05 with the mean above 0.5 for both trial types and the means are within tolerance under one reading of the mean.

claims.statement: Over rolling windows of trials, proportion correct averaged 0.68 on delay only and 0.78 on switch trials.
claims.source: Figure 1b legend; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 1b
claims.quote: Box plots indicate median and quartiles of 40-trial bins. (delay only: 0.68 ± 0.00, n = 6252 windows of 40 trials; switch: 0.78 ± 0.01, n = 1002 windows)
claims.criterion: Proportion correct in rolling windows of consecutive trials of one type within a session (Methods "a rolling window of proportion correct"; code behavior_analyzer, pandas rolling with min_periods equal to the window), final-task trials. The window length is 40 trials in the Methods and legend, while the code default used for Figure 1 is 15 trials (trial_window); 15-trial windows give a window count close to the reported 6252 (7172 minus 66 times 14), 40-trial windows cannot. Readings (a) 40 trials, (b) 15 trials; the number of windows of each reading is reported. Reproduced when means and medians are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: On switch trials the animals’ heading (view angle) shifts from the initial toward the new side after the update cue, while on delay only trials it stays toward the initial side.
claims.source: Results, first section, paragraph 2; Figure 1d
claims.quote: We found that on switch trials around the update cue onset, the animals’ heading direction shifted from one direction to the opposite in response to the cue indicating the reward location had changed (Fig. 1d
claims.criterion: Average view angle trajectories by position (Methods, Behavioral analysis: the mean per position bin over trials, left and right trials separately; code behavior_analyzer, 50 position bins), across all delay only and switch trials (Figure 1d legend), separately for initial-left and initial-right trials. Reproduced when, for both sides, the mean view angle of switch trials points toward the initial side at the update cue onset position and toward the new side in the last central-arm bin before the choice point, while delay only trials point toward the initial side in that last bin. The paper reports no test.

claims.statement: Animals performed very well on stay trials (proportion correct 0.92 over windows).
claims.source: Figure 5a legend; Results, Goal codes for updating behaviors are not due simply to new visual information, paragraph 1
claims.quote: accuracy on stay trials showing median and quartiles ( n = 7 animals; stay: 0.92 ± 0.01, n = 117 40-trial windows)
claims.criterion: As fig1b-window-performance, for stay trials, with the same two window-length readings. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Spatial tuning curves of hippocampal and prefrontal neurons tile the virtual track.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figs. 2c and 5a
claims.quote: we found that neurons in both hippocampus and prefrontal cortex had spatial tuning curves that tiled the virtual environment (Supplementary Fig. 2c , Supplementary Fig. 5a )
claims.criterion: Position tuning curves of the encoder model (shared method S2, S3; 80% of delay only trials, Supplementary Fig. 2c legend), all units of included sessions, per region. The paper gives no measure. Readings (a) every one of the 50 position bins is the peak of at least one unit; (b) the distribution of peak positions over units covers the central arm and both goal arms with no run of more than 3 empty bins outside the gaps between track segments. Reproduced for a region when both readings hold.

claims.statement: Hippocampal and prefrontal population activity decodes the animal’s current position across the track.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figs. 2d and 5b
claims.quote: We first confirmed that hippocampal and prefrontal activity could reliably decode the animals’ current location in the environment; decoded positions from neural activity represented the animals’ true position across locations in the environment (Supplementary Figs. 2d and 5b )
claims.criterion: Held-out delay only trials decoded with the shared method (S1 to S4); error is the absolute difference between true and peak decoded position (Supplementary Fig. 2d legend). The paper gives no threshold. Readings (a) in most included sessions the median error is below the median error between true positions and positions drawn uniformly over the decoded bins; (b) the session-averaged confusion matrix has its column maximum within 2 bins of the true bin for more than half of the occupied position bins. Reproduced for a region when both readings hold; if they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: After the update cue, hippocampal decoding of both the initial and the new goal arm is higher on switch trials than on delay only trials.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 2; Figure 2c to e; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 2e
claims.quote: the overall probability of goal locations being decoded, the posterior probability integrated over each goal arm, was elevated on switch trials compared to delay only trials (p = 2.630e-8, initial, switch vs. initial, delay only, p = 4.157e−7, new, switch vs. new, delay only
claims.criterion: CA1 position decoding by the shared method (S1 to S9), correct switch and delay only trials, trial value the mean integrated goal arm probability over 0 to 1.5 s. LME on trial values with goal arm by trial type as predictor, ANOVA, Tukey contrasts. Which trial types enter the model is open; readings (a) switch and delay only only (code plot_goal_coding_stats for Figure 2; the reported denominator df 4400.90 fits about 2 x 2221 rows); (b) switch, delay only and stay together (Supplementary Table 2 note "linear mixed effects models included delay, update, and stay trials"). Reproduced when, under every reading, the ANOVA and both switch against delay only contrasts give p < 0.05 with switch higher; trial counts are reported against 1295 and 926.

claims.statement: Within trials, hippocampal decoding of the initial and the new arm after the update cue does not differ: the initial minus new difference is not different from zero and does not differ between switch and delay only trials.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 3; Figure 2e right; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 2e
claims.quote: when we compared differences between the amount of initial goal location and new goal location representations on a trial-by-trial basis, the differences were not significantly different from zero and were not significantly different between switch and delay only trials ( p = 0.7806 switch vs. delay only
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests: an LME (S9) on the per-trial initial minus new difference (0 to 1.5 s) with trial type as predictor, ANOVA at p < 0.05; and two-sided one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of per-session means of the difference against zero, per trial type (Supplementary Table 2, n = 56 sessions). Reproduced when none of the three tests gives p < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. Effect sizes are reported either way.

claims.statement: Within single 200 ms bins hippocampal goal decoding is strongly biased to one arm (43% of bins highly biased), yet within a trial both arms are represented (70% of trials have a mean goal bias index between -0.5 and 0.5).
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 3; Supplementary Fig. 2e
claims.quote: each bin strongly represented one arm or the other with 43% of bins highly biased for one arm or the other (having a goal bias index close to 1 or −1)
claims.criterion: Goal bias index per bin = (new minus initial) / (new plus initial) integrated arm probability (Methods); highly biased when above 0.93 or below -0.93 (Methods); per-trial index the mean of its bin indices (code plot_goal_coding_indtrials, ave_bins); correct switch trials, CA1, n = 1295 (Supplementary Fig. 2e legend). The window is open; readings (a) 0 to 1.5 s after the update cue (Methods quantification window), (b) 0 to 2.5 s, all aligned bins at or after the cue (code). Bins on the 0.2 s alignment grid. Reproduced when both fractions are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: On switch trials after the update cue, both goal arms are decoded more than retrospective non-local positions at the start of the track.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 4; Supplementary Fig. 3c
claims.quote: We found that both initial and new goal arms were represented significantly more than retrospective non-local locations after the update cue on switch trials (retrospective vs. initial: p = 0.04, retrospective vs. new: p = 0.0011, Supplementary Fig. 3c )
claims.criterion: As fig2e-hpc-goal-increase with a third zone, the retrospective zone, the first 0.15 of the track (Results); the code integrates linearized positions 5 to 50 (quantify_aligned_data with prospective_reps). LME with zone as predictor on correct switch trials, Tukey contrasts. Reproduced when both goal arms exceed the retrospective zone with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Retrospective non-local decoding after the update cue does not differ between switch and delay only trials.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 4; Supplementary Fig. 3c ii
claims.quote: Comparing switch and delay only trials, we found that non-local retrospective codes did not differ significantly (retrospective switch vs delay only: p = 0.0513, Supplementary Fig. 3c )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test: the LME of fig2e-hpc-goal-increase with zone (retrospective, initial, new) by trial type, Tukey contrast of the retrospective zone between switch and delay only. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the effect is reported either way.

claims.statement: Goal arm decoding also rises during the original cue, but then favours the back half of the goal arms, while after the update cue it favours the front half.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 6; Supplementary Fig. 3a, b
claims.quote: during the original cue we found higher decoding of the back half of the goal arm (initial: p = 4.842e−9, new: p = 3.919e−14), while during the update cue decoding of the front half of the goal arms was higher (initial: p = 0.0100, new: p = 1.020e−7
claims.criterion: Correct switch trials, CA1. Decoding aligned to the original cue (trial start, code time_label start_time with no time before it) and to the update cue, each over 0 to 1.5 s. Each goal arm split into front (toward the choice point) and back halves by its bins (code quantify_aligned_data, half front and rearhalf; the Figure code passes front for both panels, so it does not settle the back half, and the split by bins is used). LME with cue by arm half, Tukey contrasts between cues. Reproduced when the four contrasts give p < 0.05 in the stated directions.

claims.statement: With all trial types in the encoding model, the increase of hippocampal goal arm decoding after the update cue on switch trials remains similar.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 5; Supplementary Fig. 2f
claims.quote: we also ran the analysis using all trials in the encoding model and found that while there was more accurate representation of the animals’ current location during the update cue, the non-local coding results remained similar (Supplementary Fig. 2f )
claims.criterion: The test of fig2e-hpc-goal-increase repeated with encoders built from 80% of all trial types (delay only, switch, stay; Methods "we used all trial types ... to build our encoding model as a control"). Which trials are decoded is open. Supplementary Fig. 2f lists 1322 switch and 4538 delay only trials; 4538 is close to the 926 held-out correct delay only trials of Figure 2e divided by 0.2 (about 4630), so the decoded trials do not look restricted to a 20% test set. Readings (a) encoder built from all trials of all types and every trial decoded with it; (b) encoder from 80% of all trial types, the held-out 20% decoded. Readings for outcome (c) correct trials as in Figure 2e (1322 is near the 1295 correct switch trials), (d) correct and incorrect. Trial counts under each reading are reported against 1322 and 4538. Reproduced when both arms remain higher on switch than on delay only trials with Tukey p < 0.05 under every reading.

claims.statement: Decoded position distributions are spatially wider in prefrontal cortex than in CA1.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 7; Supplementary Fig. 5f
claims.quote: Indeed, we found the spatial spread of decoded positions was significantly wider in PFC than in CA1 (CA1 vs PFC: p = 0.0001, Supplementary Fig. 5f )
claims.criterion: Sessions with at least 20 cells in each region and 50 trials; the region with more cells randomly subsampled to the same number; delay only trials, correct and incorrect (Methods; Supplementary Fig. 5f legend). Spread per decoding bin is the distance in front of and behind the posterior peak at which the posterior drops below the peak minus one standard deviation of that posterior (Methods); the code takes it in feature bins, using bins where the animal is past 120.35 (after the original cue), and averages per trial (plot_region_error_distribution). The unit is open; readings (a) feature bins (code), (b) linearized track units. Expected values are compared under reading (a). Region compared by LME with animal and session random effects (Methods; the Methods also list region and trial as random effects, which cannot be read as written, so the S9 model is used). Reproduced when PFC spread exceeds CA1 with p < 0.05 and the values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Before the update cue, goal arms are decoded more strongly from CA1 than from prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 7; Supplementary Fig. 5g
claims.quote: Goal locations were more strongly represented in CA1 than in the prefrontal cortex before any changes due to the update cue (CA1 vs PFC initial: p = 4.641e−14; new: p < 4.462e−61, Supplementary Fig. 5g )
claims.criterion: Correct delay only trials, sessions with both regions meeting S1, cells subsampled to equal numbers (Methods; legend), at positions before the update cue location; the code uses -2 to 0 s around the pseudo update time (time_window (-2, 0)). The CA1 initial arm value is printed 0.010, beside 0.11 for the new arm, and is not used as an expected value. LME with region by arm, Tukey contrasts. Reproduced when CA1 exceeds PFC for both arms with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Prefrontal position decoding of the goal arms after the update cue does not differ between switch and delay only trials, and the two arms are represented equally.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 7; Figure 2f, g; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 2g
claims.quote: Non-local representations in medial prefrontal cortex were not significantly different across trial types and both goal locations were equally represented until the animals approached the goal arm ( p = 0.3496, initial, switch vs. initial, delay only, p = 0.3148, new, switch vs. new, delay only, p = 0.9111, switch vs. delay only, Fig. 2g
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests, applied to PFC position decoding as in fig2e-hpc-goal-increase and fig2e-hpc-arms-equal (shared method, correct trials, 0 to 1.5 s). Reproduced when the ANOVA on arm by trial type, the two Tukey contrasts, the ANOVA on the within-trial difference and the two per-session Wilcoxon tests all give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any does not. Effects are reported either way.

claims.statement: Prefrontal goal arm decoding on switch and delay only trials does not differ in shorter windows after the update cue either.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced non-local codes of both goal locations in hippocampus, paragraph 7; Supplementary Fig. 5e
claims.quote: There was a small increase in prefrontal decoding of goal locations on switch trials versus delay only trials, however these trial types did not differ significantly over several time windows examined (0–0.5 s, 0–1 s, 0–1.5 s after the update cue onset, Supplementary Fig. 5e )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test (as fig2g-pfc-no-goal-increase) in each window the paper names; the text lists 0 to 0.5, 0 to 1 and 0 to 1.5 s and the legend 0 to 0.5, 0 to 1 and 0.5 to 1 s, so all four windows are run. Reproduced when no switch against delay only contrast gives p < 0.05 in any window; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: After the update cue on switch trials, hippocampal non-local goal codes are strongest in the first half of the theta cycle and local codes in the second half.
claims.source: Results, Theta phase segregation of non-local and local position codes, paragraph 2; Figure 3b, c; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 3c
claims.quote: we found that codes for prospective goal locations (non-local) were represented significantly more on the opposite theta phase as current location representations (local) (p = 0.0275, −π to 0, initial vs. central arm, p = 0.0106, −π to 0 new vs. central arm, p = 9.284e−9, 0 to π, initial vs. central arm, p = 6.672e−14, 0 to π, new vs. central arm, Fig. 3a–c )
claims.criterion: CA1 decoding in 25 ms bins (Methods; code decoder_bin_size 0.025), correct switch trials. Theta from the CA1 pyramidal-layer channel, 4 to 12 Hz FIR equiripple band-pass, phase from peaks and troughs, 0 set at the phase of maximal CA1 pyramidal cell firing in 30 degree bins per session (Methods; code theta_phase/get_phase_reference.py). The phase at each decoding bin centre; integrated probability per zone averaged per trial in each half cycle (-pi to 0, 0 to pi) over 0 to 1.5 s after the cue (Methods; Figure 3b legend; code calc_theta_phase_data). The central zone is open; readings (a) the whole central arm, (b) a central window the size of a goal arm centred on the update cue location (code home_boundaries). LME with location by half, Tukey contrasts. Reproduced when, under every reading, both goal arms exceed central in the first half and central exceeds both in the second half, all four with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: At the theta timescale, goal arm decoding increases and central decoding decreases from before to after the update cue on switch trials.
claims.source: Results, Theta phase segregation of non-local and local position codes, paragraph 2; Figure 3b; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 3b
claims.quote: When comparing before and after the update cue onset, we found that there was a significant increase in the amount of goal location (non-local) decoding, but the local vs. non-local phase preferences were maintained ( p = 6.439e−14, pre- vs. post-update initial arm, p = 5.329e-14 pre- vs. post-update new goal, Fig. 3b–d )
claims.criterion: As fig3c-theta-phase-segregation with pre (-1.5 to 0 s) and post (0 to 1.5 s) windows (Figure 3b legend). Which phases enter the values is open; readings (a) the first half cycle (Supplementary Table 2 labels the Figure 3b data "first half of theta cycle"), (b) the whole cycle. LME with time by location, Tukey contrasts. Reproduced when, under every reading, both goal arms increase and central decreases with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: At the theta timescale, goal arm decoding after the update cue is larger on switch than on delay only trials.
claims.source: Results, Theta phase segregation of non-local and local position codes, paragraph 2; Supplementary Fig. 6; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 3c, d
claims.quote: non-local codes at the timescale of individual theta cycles were also significantly larger on switch trials compared delay-only trials ( p = 1.450e−27, initial arm, switch vs. delay only, p = 1.367e−13 new arm, switch vs. delay only Supplementary Fig. 6 )
claims.criterion: As fig3c-theta-phase-segregation, one LME per goal arm with trial type (switch, stay, delay only, as Supplementary Table 2 lists) by phase half, correct trials, 0 to 1.5 s. Reproduced when, for both arms, the ANOVA and the switch against delay only contrasts in both halves give p < 0.05 with switch higher.

claims.statement: After the update cue, decoding of the new goal arm differs between theta half cycles while decoding of the initial arm does not.
claims.source: Results, Theta phase segregation of non-local and local position codes, paragraph 2; Figure 3d; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 3d
claims.quote: The new goal location was more strongly theta modulated compared to the old goal location ( p = 0.0008, new arm − π to 0 vs 0 to π , p = 0.6496, initial arm − π to 0 vs 0 to π
claims.criterion: As fig3c-theta-phase-segregation, one LME per arm with phase half as predictor (Supplementary Table 2), correct switch trials, 0 to 1.5 s. Reproduced when the new arm gives p < 0.05 and the initial arm, a claim of absence judged on the same test, gives p >= 0.05. The text and the table print different initial arm p values (0.6496, 0.4203); both are above 0.05.

claims.statement: An LSTM predicting the final choice from behaviour is near chance at the start of the trial and highly accurate by the end, with session-averaged log likelihoods of -0.98, -0.63, -0.43 and -0.17 in the original cue, delay, update and second delay phases.
claims.source: Results, Rapid switch from old to new choice estimates in prefrontal cortex, paragraph 1; Figure 4a
claims.quote: The choice estimate varied throughout the course of a trial, starting at chance-level accuracy at the start of the trial on average, and ending with a highly accurate, or −0.17 ± 0.02 log likelihood on average, prediction of the animals’ final choice
claims.criterion: LSTM as shared method S10, one model set per session, 66 sessions. Log likelihood at each time point is y log2(p) + (1 - y) log2(1 - p) of the final choice y (Methods; code _log2_likelihood). Phases by forward position as fractions of the track, with boundaries at the original, delay, update and second delay cue start locations 5, 120.325, 145.125 and 215.125 of a track from 5 to 285 (code choice_visualizer plot_choice_commitment), on held-out delay only trials; mean over time points per phase and session, then over sessions. Reproduced when the four session means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the order original < delay < update < second delay holds but some value falls outside. The LSTM is stochastic; one run with the code's seeds is reported.

claims.statement: After the update cue, prefrontal decoding of the initial choice is lower and of the new choice higher on switch than on delay only trials.
claims.source: Results, Rapid switch from old to new choice estimates in prefrontal cortex, paragraph 2; Figure 4b to f; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 4f
claims.quote: We observed that the choice estimates of the initial and new choice began to diverge preceding the update and then rapidly flipped after the reward location changed ( p = 5.192e−49 initial switch vs. initial, delay only, p = 2.934e−7 new, switch vs. new, delay only Fig. 4b–f
claims.criterion: PFC choice decoding by shared method S1, S3 to S9 and S11, correct trials, 0 to 1.5 s. LME with choice by trial type (readings for the trial types in the model as in fig2e-hpc-goal-increase), Tukey contrasts. Reproduced when, under every reading, initial choice is lower and new choice higher on switch trials, each with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The within-trial initial minus new choice difference in prefrontal cortex is negative on switch trials and positive on delay only trials, and differs between them.
claims.source: Results, Rapid switch from old to new choice estimates in prefrontal cortex, paragraph 2; Figure 4f right
claims.quote: Furthermore, the difference between initial and new choice decoding was significantly different between switch and delay trial types (p = 8.610e-33 initial – new for switch vs. delay only Fig. 4f )
claims.criterion: As fig4f-pfc-choice-flips, on the per-trial difference, LME with trial type, ANOVA. Reproduced when p < 0.05, the switch mean is below zero, the delay only mean above zero, and both are within tolerance.

claims.statement: On average, the switch of prefrontal choice decoding from the initial to the new choice precedes the change in rotational velocity.
claims.source: Results, Rapid switch from old to new choice estimates in prefrontal cortex, paragraph 2; Figure 4d
claims.quote: On average, the change in neural activity choice decoding preceded the movement change (Fig. 4d )
claims.criterion: Correct switch trials, PFC choice decoding aligned to the update cue on the 0.2 s grid (S5), rotational velocity mirrored like the decoding. Two times defined in the Figure 4d legend; the neural time, the first time after the cue at which the trial-averaged new choice decoding exceeds the initial; the motor time, the first time after the cue at which the slope of the trial-averaged rotational velocity changes to negative. Reproduced when the neural time is earlier than the motor time; not reproduced when it is later; equal times are reported as not decided at this grid. The paper reports no test.

claims.statement: Aligned to each trial's motor response, prefrontal initial choice decoding has already decreased and new choice decoding increased before the response, and new overtakes initial at about the time of the response.
claims.source: Results, Rapid switch from old to new choice estimates in prefrontal cortex, paragraph 2; Supplementary Fig. 7d
claims.quote: Examining when animals began changing head direction (rotational velocity began decelerating away from the initial choice) on a single trial basis, we found initial choice codes decreased and new choice codes increased before the motor response (Supplementary Fig. 7d )
claims.criterion: Correct switch trials. The motor response is the first time after the update cue at which the derivative of rotational velocity switches from positive to negative (Supplementary Fig. 7d legend). Variant (code plot_motor_timing), the first bin after the cue at which the mirrored rotational velocity is negative. Decoding re-aligned to each trial's motor response and averaged. Reproduced when the mean initial decoding in the bin before the motor response is below its value at update cue onset and the mean new decoding above it, and the mean new decoding first exceeds the initial within one 0.2 s bin of the motor response. The paper reports no test.

claims.statement: On correct trials, prefrontal initial choice decoding 1.5 to 0.5 s before the update cue is lower on switch than on delay only trials, a difference attributed to selecting correct trials.
claims.source: Results, Rapid switch from old to new choice estimates in prefrontal cortex, paragraph 2; Supplementary Fig. 7e
claims.quote: We also found differences in pre-update cue decoding of the initial choices in prefrontal cortex between switch and delay only trials (p = 0.0031 switch vs. delay-only 1.5–0.5 s preceding update cue, Supplementary Fig. 7e )
claims.criterion: As fig4f-pfc-choice-flips over -1.5 to -0.5 s (Results; code time_window (-1.5, -0.5)), correct trials, and again with all outcomes. Reproduced when the correct-trial initial contrast gives p < 0.05 with switch lower, and the all-trial initial contrast gives p < 0.05 with switch higher.

claims.statement: In hippocampus, initial choice decoding is lower and new choice decoding higher after the update cue on switch than on delay only trials.
claims.source: Results, Rapid switch from old to new choice estimates in prefrontal cortex, paragraph 4; Figure 4g, h; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 4h
claims.quote: We found that initial choice representations in hippocampus were higher than the alternative choice preceding the update, and then decreased after the update cue was presented and the new choice representation increased (Fig. 4g, h
claims.criterion: CA1 choice decoding as fig4f-pfc-choice-flips, over 0 to 1.5 s after the cue (Methods quantification window). Variant (code, plot_goal_coding_stats with time_window (0, 2) for this panel), 0 to 2 s, shown but not deciding, since the Methods come first where they disagree with the code. Reproduced when initial is lower and new higher on switch trials with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: After the update cue on switch trials, hippocampus represents the initial and new choices equally; the within-trial difference is not different from zero.
claims.source: Results, Rapid switch from old to new choice estimates in prefrontal cortex, paragraph 4; Figure 4h right
claims.quote: both choices were represented equally and the difference on a trial-by-trial basis was not significantly different from zero ( p = 0.5625, initial – new vs. zero, Fig. 4h )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-sided one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the initial minus new difference against zero (Methods). The sample is not fixed by the paper; readings (a) per-trial differences (the legend gives n = 1205 trials), (b) per-session means (as Supplementary Table 2 does for Figures 2e and 2g); window 0 to 1.5 s as fig4h-hpc-choice-switches. Reproduced when no reading gives p < 0.05; not reproduced when all do; otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified with every result shown.

claims.statement: The switch from initial to new choice decoding evolves more slowly in hippocampus than in prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: Results, Rapid switch from old to new choice estimates in prefrontal cortex, paragraph 4; Figure 4d, g
claims.quote: However, while the decoded activity followed a similar pattern of switching from the initial to the new choice as in prefrontal cortex, this change evolved over a longer period of time in hippocampus.
claims.criterion: Correct switch trials, trial-averaged choice decoding per region on the 0.2 s grid. The crossing time is the first time after the update cue at which mean new choice decoding exceeds mean initial (Figure 4d legend arrow). Reproduced when the CA1 crossing is later than the PFC crossing, or CA1 does not cross within 2.5 s while PFC does. The paper reports no test.

claims.statement: Hippocampal goal arm decoding after the second cue on stay trials does not differ from delay only trials.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes for updating behaviors are not due simply to new visual information, paragraph 2; Figure 5c, d; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 5d
claims.quote: we found that the amount of non-local representations on stay trials was not significantly different from delay-only trials (p = 0.9927, initial, stay vs. delay only; p = 0.6267, new, stay vs. delay only)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the LME of fig2e-hpc-goal-increase with three trial types (switch, stay, delay only), correct trials, 0 to 1.5 s, Tukey contrasts. Reproduced when both stay against delay only contrasts give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when either gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Hippocampal goal arm decoding after the second cue is lower on stay trials than on switch trials.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes for updating behaviors are not due simply to new visual information, paragraph 2; Figure 5c, d
claims.quote: Non-local codes were in fact significantly lower on stay trials compared to switch trials ( p = 2.358e-8 initial, stay vs. switch, p = 0.0274 new, stay vs. switch, Fig. 5c, d )
claims.criterion: As fig5d-stay-hpc-like-delay. Reproduced when both stay against switch contrasts give p < 0.05 with stay lower.

claims.statement: In the first 0.5 s after the stay cue, hippocampal decoding of the new arm is transiently higher on stay than on delay only trials, with no difference for the initial arm.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes for updating behaviors are not due simply to new visual information, paragraph 2; Supplementary Fig. 10
claims.quote: Examining that period (0–0.5 s after the update cue), we found significantly more decoding of the new arm on stay trials than on delay only trials (initial, stay vs delay only: p = 0.9806; new, stay vs delay only: p = 0.0375, Supplementary Fig. 10a, b )
claims.criterion: As fig5d-stay-hpc-like-delay over 0 to 0.5 s after the cue. Reproduced when the new arm contrast gives p < 0.05 with stay higher; the initial arm part is a claim of absence judged on the same test (p >= 0.05). The text and the table print different p values; both are below 0.05 for the new arm.

claims.statement: Prefrontal new choice decoding after the second cue on stay trials is similar to delay only trials and lower than on switch trials.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes for updating behaviors are not due simply to new visual information, paragraph 3; Figure 5e, f; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 5f
claims.quote: We found that new choice coding on stay trials was also at similar levels to delay only trials, and significantly lower than switch trials ( p = 0.7914, stay vs. delay only, p = 0.0072, stay vs. switch, Fig. 5e, f )
claims.criterion: PFC choice decoding as fig4f-pfc-choice-flips with three trial types, correct trials, 0 to 1.5 s. The stay against delay only part is a claim of absence judged on its Tukey contrast (p >= 0.05); the stay against switch part holds when its contrast gives p < 0.05 with stay lower. Reproduced when both hold.

claims.statement: Prefrontal initial choice decoding after the second cue on stay trials stays higher than on switch trials but is lower than on delay only trials.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes for updating behaviors are not due simply to new visual information, paragraph 3; Figure 5f
claims.quote: The decoded initial choice estimate remained relatively constant on stay trials, in contrast to switch trials, though also significantly lower than on delay trials ( p = 0.0032, stay vs. delay only, p = 1.908e-10 stay vs. switch)
claims.criterion: As fig5f-stay-pfc-new-choice. Reproduced when stay is lower than delay only and higher than switch, both with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The prefrontal within-trial initial minus new choice difference on stay trials differs from both switch and delay only trials.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes for updating behaviors are not due simply to new visual information, paragraph 3; Figure 5f right
claims.quote: Furthermore, the difference between initial and new choice decoding was significantly different between trial types ( p < 4.462e−61 initial-new for switch vs. stay, p = 0.0033 initial-new for stay vs. delay only)
claims.criterion: As fig5f-stay-pfc-new-choice on the per-trial difference. Reproduced when both contrasts give p < 0.05, with stay between delay only (0.08) and switch (-0.02).

claims.statement: On incorrect switch trials, hippocampal new goal arm decoding after the update cue is less elevated than on correct trials, after accounting for speed and rotation.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes predict ability to accurately update decisions in response to new information, paragraph 1; Figure 6a, b; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 6b
claims.quote: We found that indeed on incorrect trials in hippocampus, the new goal choice coding was not as elevated as correct trials (p = 0.0025, new correct vs. incorrect, Fig. 6a, b )
claims.criterion: CA1 position decoding, switch trials of both outcomes, 0 to 1.5 s. Residual goal codes (Methods, GLM analysis): a GLM with rotational and translational velocity as predictors and the integrated goal probability as response, one model per goal representation, 200 ms bins over 2.5 s before and after the cue, Pearson residuals; the code uses a Poisson family and statsmodels GLM (aggregator get_residuals). The GLM is fit on the bins of all trial types and animals together (Methods "across all trial types and animals"); the code fits it per session on the switch trials of the comparison (by_session=True), which is shown as a variant and does not decide, since the Methods come first where they disagree with the code. Trial value the mean residual in the window; LME with outcome by arm, Tukey contrasts. Reproduced when the new arm contrast gives p < 0.05 with correct higher.

claims.statement: Hippocampal initial goal arm decoding after the update cue does not differ between correct and incorrect switch trials.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes predict ability to accurately update decisions in response to new information, paragraph 1; Figure 6b
claims.quote: There was also no significant difference in initial goal choice coding on correct versus incorrect trials after the update cue (p = 0.2967 initial correct vs. incorrect, Fig. 6b )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the Tukey contrast of fig6b-hpc-new-lower-incorrect for the initial arm, with its Methods GLM (the per-session code GLM shown as a variant). Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Before the update cue, hippocampal initial goal arm decoding is higher on incorrect than on correct switch trials, beyond motor differences.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes predict ability to accurately update decisions in response to new information, paragraph 1; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 6b pre update
claims.quote: Interestingly, preceding the update cue there was a noticeable increase in the initial goal arm representation on incorrect trials that could not be explained by motor differences alone ( p = 0.002, initial correct vs. incorrect)
claims.criterion: As fig6b-hpc-new-lower-incorrect over -1.5 to 0 s (Methods baseline window). Reproduced when the initial arm contrast gives p < 0.05 with incorrect higher (Methods GLM; code GLM as a variant).

claims.statement: On incorrect switch trials prefrontal new choice decoding is smaller after the update cue and does not overtake the initial choice.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes predict ability to accurately update decisions in response to new information, paragraph 2; Figure 6c, d; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 6d
claims.quote: This lack of switching choice representations was driven by significantly smaller decoding of the new choice in prefrontal cortex on incorrect trials ( p = 0.002, new correct vs. incorrect)
claims.criterion: PFC choice decoding with the residuals of fig6b-hpc-new-lower-incorrect (Methods GLM; code GLM as a variant), switch trials of both outcomes, 0 to 1.5 s. Reproduced when the new choice contrast gives p < 0.05 with correct higher.

claims.statement: Prefrontal initial choice decoding does not differ between correct and incorrect switch trials after the update cue, nor, after accounting for motor differences, before it.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes predict ability to accurately update decisions in response to new information, paragraph 2; Figure 6d
claims.quote: In contrast, there was no significant difference in initial choice coding on correct and incorrect trials when accounting for motor differences ( p = 0.5874, initial correct vs. incorrect, Fig. 6d )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests, the Tukey contrasts of fig6d-pfc-new-lower-incorrect for the initial choice over 0 to 1.5 s and over -1.5 to 0 s, Methods GLM (code GLM as a variant). Reproduced when both give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when either gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Within trials, prefrontal new choice decoding exceeds initial on correct switch trials but not on incorrect ones.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes predict ability to accurately update decisions in response to new information, paragraph 2; Figure 6d right
claims.quote: on incorrect trials the old and new choices were decoded at similar amounts even after new information was presented, in contrast to the significantly stronger new choice coding on correct trials (p = 0.0001, initial-new for correct vs. incorrect, p = 0.3531 initial-new vs. zero, incorrect trials, p = 0.0113 initial-new vs. zero, correct trials)
claims.criterion: As fig6d-pfc-new-lower-incorrect on the per-trial difference. One-sample two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests against zero; their sample is open, readings per-trial values and per-session means. Reproduced when the correct against incorrect test gives p < 0.05 and the correct-trial difference is below zero with p < 0.05 while the incorrect-trial difference gives p >= 0.05, under every reading.

claims.statement: On delay only trials, hippocampal goal arm decoding in the update period does not differ between correct and incorrect trials.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes predict ability to accurately update decisions in response to new information, paragraph 3; Supplementary Fig. 12a
claims.quote: On delay only trials we found no differences in hippocampal decoding of position for either initial or new goal arms ( p -values ≥ 0.942)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests, the residual analysis of fig6b-hpc-new-lower-incorrect applied to delay only trials at the pseudo update time (S5; Results "the same period as we examined for switch trials"), Methods GLM (code GLM as a variant). Reproduced when all three p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any p < 0.05.

claims.statement: On correct delay only trials prefrontal cortex decodes the initial (rewarded) choice more strongly, and on incorrect trials the new (unrewarded) choice.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes predict ability to accurately update decisions in response to new information, paragraph 3; Supplementary Fig. 12b
claims.quote: On correct trials the initial goal arm (the one that will be rewarded on delay only trials) was decoded more strongly than the other goal arm throughout the delay period ( p = 5.934e−11, initial correct vs. incorrect, Supplementary Fig. 12b )
claims.criterion: As sfig12-delay-hpc-no-outcome-difference for PFC choice decoding. Reproduced when the initial contrast gives p < 0.05 with correct higher and the new contrast p < 0.05 with incorrect higher (Methods GLM; code GLM as a variant).

claims.statement: The post-update difference between initial and new goal codes predicts whether a switch trial is correct, above shuffled labels, with 61.43% accuracy from prefrontal choice decoding and 55.83% from hippocampal position decoding.
claims.source: Results, Goal codes predict ability to accurately update decisions in response to new information, paragraph 3; Figure 6e
claims.quote: We found that in both hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, the population representation of the initial and new goals after the update cue was presented predicted whether the animals would choose the correct or incorrect side (hippocampus: p < 4.462e−61, prefrontal cortex: p < 4.462e−61, permutation test, Fig. 6e )
claims.criterion: Per region, switch trials of both outcomes; one feature, the initial minus new integrated probability averaged over 0 to 1.5 s after the cue (Methods; code calc_prediction_data on raw values, not residuals). Classes balanced by resampling the smaller class with replacement to the size of the larger (code random_state 123). RBF SVM; C and gamma by randomized search, 10 iterations, leave-one-out (Methods); the code draws C from loguniform(1, 1000) and gamma from loguniform(1e-4, 1). Accuracy by leave-one-out. Shuffled control, the same procedure on shuffled labels 1000 times (Methods; code iterations=1000). Reproduced when, for both regions, accuracy exceeds the 95th percentile of shuffled accuracies and lies within tolerance; partially reproduced when only the permutation test holds.

claims.statement: The more committed the animal was to the initial arm at the update cue (view angle toward it), the larger the post-cue increase in hippocampal decoding of the new arm.
claims.source: Results, Increased goal representations are correlated with choice commitment, paragraph 1; Figure 7b, c; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 7c
claims.quote: the view angle preceding new information was positively correlated with the increase in non-local goal representation of the new arm (new goal codes vs. view angle: p = 1.330e-5, r s = 0.12370, Fig. 7b, c
claims.criterion: Correct switch trials, CA1 (code plot_group_comparisons_full). View angle at update cue onset (Methods), taken at the last aligned sample before time 0 (code calc_choice_commitment_data), signed so that positive points toward the initial arm (Results; the code negates it on trials with a right original cue). Change in decoding per trial is the mean over 0 to 1.5 s minus the mean over -1.5 to 0 s (Methods; code normalize=True). Two-sided Spearman correlation across trials. Quartile means of Figure 7c are reported beside it. Reproduced when rho > 0 with p < 0.05 and rho is within tolerance; partially reproduced when only the sign and p hold.

claims.statement: The change in hippocampal initial arm decoding after the update cue is not correlated with view angle at the cue.
claims.source: Results, Increased goal representations are correlated with choice commitment, paragraph 1; Figure 7c
claims.quote: It is important to note that the correlation between view angle and prospective codes was only observed for the new arm and not the initial arm
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the Spearman correlation of fig7c-hpc-commitment-new-arm for the initial arm. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The more committed the animal was to the initial side at the update cue, the larger the decrease in prefrontal initial choice decoding.
claims.source: Results, Increased goal representations are correlated with choice commitment, paragraph 1; Figure 7d, e; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 7e
claims.quote: In prefrontal cortex, when the animals were more committed to the initial side, the update cue induced a larger decrease in the initial choice representation compared to trials where animals were less committed (initial goal codes vs. view angle: p = 0.0002, r s = −0.1108
claims.criterion: As fig7c-hpc-commitment-new-arm for PFC choice decoding. Reproduced when rho < 0 with p < 0.05 and rho within tolerance; partially reproduced when only the sign and p hold.

claims.statement: The post-cue increase in prefrontal new choice decoding is weakly correlated with view angle at the cue, smallest when the animal was already heading to the new arm.
claims.source: Results, Increased goal representations are correlated with choice commitment, paragraph 1; Figure 7e; Supplementary Table 2, Figure 7e
claims.quote: After the update cue, prefrontal decoding of the new arm increased on all trial types, but the increase was the smallest when animals were already more committed to the new arm.
claims.criterion: As fig7e-pfc-commitment-initial for the new choice. The sign of rho differs between the text (positive, which fits the quartile means of the Figure 7e legend and the sentence quoted) and Supplementary Table 2 (negative). Reproduced when rho > 0 with p < 0.05; a result with rho < 0 and p < 0.05 matches only the table and is partially reproduced; not reproduced when p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: The dataset comes from 25 mice of both sexes, 11 males and 14 females, aged 17 to 31 weeks at the end of the experiments.
claims.source: Methods, Animals, paragraph 1
claims.quote: The mice of both sexes (11 males and 14 females) were used for the experiments. The age ranged from 17–31 weeks at the end of experiments.
claims.criterion: Counts of subjects are exact, so the tolerance is 0. Reproduced when the subjects with any session number 25 with 11 males and 14 females, and every subject's age at its last session lies within 17 to 31 weeks widened by 10% of each bound (15.3 to 34.1 weeks), age taken from the subject metadata (age or date of birth) and the session dates.

claims.statement: Of the 375 task training sessions (25 mice by 15 sessions), data were collected from 364 (97%); the 11 others lacked complete imaging. All 15 sessions were collected for 16 of the 25 mice.
claims.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 3; Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3d legend
claims.quote: Of the 375 task training sessions conducted, we successfully collected data from 364 sessions ( Fig. 3d ; Table 1 ) and completed data collection for all 15 sessions in 16 out of 25 animals.
claims.criterion: Counts of deposited sessions are exact, so the tolerance is 0. A task session is one whose session description or file name marks it as a task (lever-pull) session; recordings deposited more than once count once. Reproduced when 364 distinct task sessions are found and 16 mice have all 15. The Data Records sentence (15 task and 4 resting-state sessions per mouse) also bears on the count of resting-state sessions, which is reported without a criterion, as Table 1's contents are not in the text.

claims.statement: Each task session was imaged for 30 min (108000 frames at 60 Hz, so 54000 frames per excitation channel at 30 Hz), each resting-state session for 10 min and the sensory-mapping session for 15 min.
claims.source: Methods, Acquisition of wide-field one-photon image, paragraph 1; Data Records, Imaging Raw Data
claims.quote: We imaged 108000 frames (30 min) in each task session, 36000 frames in each resting-state session (10 min on recording days 1, 7, 15), and 54000 frames in the sensory mapping session (recording day 16).
claims.criterion: The paper's 60 Hz counts are read as the sum over the two channels, from the Methods sentence that the effective rate is 30 Hz and the Data Records sentence on TIFF frame counts. Reproduced when the 30 Hz ROI series (and, where they are read, the TIFF stacks) of most sessions of each type have these lengths; sessions that differ are listed with their lengths.

claims.statement: Training had 3.1 +/- 0.6 breaks per mouse of 2.3 +/- 0.7 days each (mean +/- s.d., 25 mice), and recording days 1 to 16 spanned 24.28 +/- 3.2 calendar days.
claims.source: Methods, Behavioral task, paragraph 1
claims.quote: There were occasional training breaks of typically 2–3 days without any handling ( e.g. over weekends; 3.1 ± 0.6 breaks throughout training; 2.3 ± 0.7 days per break; mean ± s.d., n = 25 mice). ... The entire recording period (recording day 1 to 16) spanned 24.28 ± 3.2 calendar days (mean ± s.d.).
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the paper's stated s.d. Dates are the session start dates. A break is a run of calendar days without a task session between consecutive task sessions (days 1 to 15), and its length is the number of days in the run. The span is from the day 1 task session to the sensory-mapping session (day 16), counted inclusively or as a difference (both shown). Open details, each run. (1) Which gaps are breaks, read as (a) every run of one or more days, (b) runs of two or more days only (the text's "typically 2–3 days" and the Methods' "two or more days" for breaks over weekends). (2) Whether "days per break" is the mean over all breaks pooled or the mean over mice of each mouse's mean. (3) For the 8 mice with two sensory-mapping sessions, day 16 read as (a) the first (the session Figure 4 uses), (b) the last. A task session that was run but not deposited cannot be told from a break in the deposited dates; such gaps are listed. If no sensory-mapping session is deposited, the span is blocked and the other two values are still tested.

claims.statement: Across the population the response rate to the tone rose over training, from about 0.55 in task session 1 to about 0.85 in task session 15 (median over mice).
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3c, top panel
claims.quote: The response rate to the sound cue tended to increase overall (∼0.55 in task training session 1 to ∼0.85 in task training session 15; median)
claims.criterion: From the Figure 3 legend, the response rate is the number of valid pulls over the number of tones, a valid pull being a pull (lever beyond 1 mm) initiated within 1 s of the tone onset; per session, then the median over the mice with that session (thick black line of Figure 3c). How a valid pull is identified is open, with two readings, both run. (a) From the trial table's outcome labels, counting successes and failures (aborted pulls) as valid and misses as not, following the Methods' trial outcomes. (b) From the lever trace, a trial being valid when the lever crosses 1 mm within 1 s of tone onset. Reproduced when, under one reading, both medians are within tolerance and session 15's exceeds session 1's.

claims.statement: The population success rate stayed roughly constant across the 15 task sessions.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3c, middle panel
claims.quote: while the success rate seemed to be constant as a whole ( Fig. 3c )
claims.criterion: The success rate is the number of successful (rewarded) pulls over the number of tones (Figure 3 legend), per session, and the population value is the median over mice. The paper gives no test and no bound for "constant", so the readings are (a) the session-15 median within 10% (relative) of the session-1 median, the protocol's default tolerance; (b) no monotonic trend of the 15 session medians, Spearman correlation with session index at p >= 0.05. Successes are counted from reward deliveries and, where the trial table has them, from its outcome labels (both shown). The claim holds when both readings hold, fails when both fail, and is blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ. The change in the response rate over the same sessions is shown alongside for contrast.

claims.statement: Hierarchical clustering (Ward's method) of the session-by-session T_pull_final divides the mice into two clusters, A with 7 mice and B with 18.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3d and 3e legends
claims.quote: The hierarchical clustering revealed that mice could be divided into two clusters in terms of T pull_final ( Fig. 3d ).
claims.criterion: Cluster sizes are counts, with tolerance 0 (10% of 7 is under one mouse). T_pull_final is the required pull duration at the end of each session (Methods, Tone-triggered lever-pull task), read from the trial table's required-duration field at the last trial; where no such field exists, the author asks. Each mouse is a vector of its T_pull_final over task sessions 1 to 15, clustered by Ward's method (Figure 3d legend) on Euclidean distance and cut at two clusters; cluster A is the one with the higher mean T_pull_final. Open details, each run. (1) The feature, "the chronological change in T_pull_final", read as (a) the 15 values themselves, (b) the 14 differences between consecutive sessions. (2) Missing sessions (9 mice), read as (i) linear interpolation from the neighbouring sessions (carrying the nearest value at the ends), (ii) the previous session's value carried forward, (iii) the next session's initial T_pull plus 100 ms where that session exists, following the Methods' rule. Reproduced when a reading gives clusters of 7 and 18.

claims.statement: Mice of cluster A had high success rates in the early sessions (about session 5), which led to a high T_pull_final that was often maintained into the late sessions.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3e
claims.quote: Mice belonging to one cluster (cluster A) showed high success rates in the early sessions (∼5) leading to high T pull_final which were often maintained even in the late sessions.
claims.criterion: Uses the clusters of fig3d-tpull-clusters (under each reading that gives 7 and 18). The paper gives no test; "high" is read against cluster B, the contrast of Figure 3e. Reproduced when (1) cluster A's median success rate exceeds cluster B's in the early sessions, read as (a) sessions 1 to 5, (b) session 5 alone, and (2) cluster A's median T_pull_final exceeds cluster B's in the late sessions, read as (a) sessions 11 to 15, (b) session 15 alone. Per-mouse values are shown.

claims.statement: Mice of cluster B rarely reached a high T_pull_final, but in the late sessions their response and success rates were similar to those of cluster A.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3e; Figure S1c
claims.quote: Mice belonging to the other cluster (cluster B) rarely achieved a high T pull_final , while they accomplished a response rate and success rate similar to the cluster A mice in the late sessions ( Fig. 3e , Fig. S1).
claims.criterion: Uses the clusters of fig3d-tpull-clusters. The paper gives no test or bound. "High T_pull_final" is read as (a) the 400 ms maximum, (b) above the median of all mice's T_pull_final values; "rarely" holds when the fraction of cluster B's mouse-sessions above that level is below cluster A's and below one half. "Late sessions" are read as (a) sessions 11 to 15, each mouse's mean, (b) session 15. "Similar" is read as (a) a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test of A against B with p >= 0.05, (b) group medians within 10% of cluster A's median. Response and success rates as in fig3c-response-rate-increase and fig3c-success-rate-constant. The claim holds when the T_pull_final part holds and, for both rates, the similarity holds under both readings of "similar"; when these readings differ it is blocked as methods_underspecified, with every result shown.

claims.statement: Fluorescence signal degradation across imaging sessions was not observed.
claims.source: Methods, Acquisition of wide-field one-photon image, paragraph 1
claims.quote: The total power of excitation lights (blue and violet) was set at ∼10 mW and the fluorescent signal degradation across imaging sessions was not observed.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence for which the paper names no measure and no test. The readings the text allows are (a) the raw 470 nm fluorescence (the ROI baseline F_B0, the median over time, where the dataset holds raw ROI signals; otherwise the session-mean intensity of the blue TIFF stack within the cortical ROI masks) against task-session index, (b) the s.d. of the corrected dF/F per ROI against task-session index. For each, a per-mouse Spearman correlation with session index, and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the 25 correlations against 0 at p < 0.05. The claim holds when neither reading finds a significant decline, fails when both do, and is blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ; the size of the change (session 15 over session 1, median over mice) is reported either way.

claims.statement: MesoNet-inferred skull landmarks used to register the Allen CCF agreed with manual annotations of three representative sessions from each of the 25 mice (75 sessions).
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3; Figure 4a,b legend
claims.quote: We validated the accuracy of this method by comparing the MesoNet-based skull-landmark annotations with the manual annotations, based on three representative sessions from each of the 25 animals ( Fig. 4a,b ).
claims.criterion: The paper gives no number or bound for the agreement. The test needs the manual landmark annotations, which the paper does not describe as deposited; the dataset's atlas_to_data_transform alone cannot be compared with them. Reproduced only if the manual annotations are found, when the warped manual landmarks fall near the CCF reference landmarks as in Figure 4b; the distances (median and 95th percentile, in atlas pixels) are reported.

claims.statement: In the sensory-mapping sessions, visual stimulation of the left eye evoked the strongest activity in the right occipital cortex, at VISp in the registered atlas.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3; Figure 4d
claims.quote: Visual stimuli to the left eye of mice elicited prominent activity in the right occipital cortex ( Dräger 1975 ; Grinvald et al. 1986 ; Schuett, Bonhoeffer, and Hübener 2002 ) corresponding to VISp (primary visual area) in the atlas.
claims.criterion: From the Figure 4d legend, the first sensory-mapping session of each mouse; the response is the trial-averaged activity over 2 s from stimulus onset, normalized to 0 to 1 per mouse and stimulus; the area is the region above the 80th percentile of the normalized map. Open details, each run. (1) The map, read as (a) the 44 ROI dF/F series in the NWB file, (b) pixel maps from the blue TIFF stack as dF/F against the session median (the Methods' dF/F), without hemodynamic correction, as the Methods describe it for ROIs only. (2) The baseline, read as (a) none (dF/F is already relative to the session median), (b) the mean over the 2 s before stimulus onset subtracted. Stimulus onsets are the visual stimulus TTL onsets. Reproduced when, under one reading, right VISp is the ROI with the largest response (or, for pixel maps, the peak falls inside right VISp) in the mean over mice (the animal-averaged map of Figure 4d); the number of mice in which it holds is reported. If no sensory-mapping session is deposited the claim is blocked.

claims.statement: Vibration of the right whisker pad evoked a robust response in the left barrel cortex (SSp-bfd), with marked laterality.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3; Figure 4d
claims.quote: Tactile stimuli to the right whisker pad elicited a robust response in the left SSp-bfd, a primary sensory cortex for processing whisker-related sensory information with marked hemispheric laterality
claims.criterion: As fig4d-visual-map, with the tactile stimulus TTL onsets (vibration or air puff, both included). Reproduced when, under one reading, left SSp-bfd is the ROI with the largest response (or holds the pixel peak) in the mean over mice, and its response exceeds that of right SSp-bfd; the number of mice in which each holds is reported.

claims.statement: White-noise stimulation evoked spreading activity that included a multimodal sensory area in the parietal cortex.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3; Figure 4d
claims.quote: Auditory stimuli evoked spreading activity, including a multimodal sensory area in the parietal cortex
claims.criterion: As fig4d-visual-map, with the auditory stimulus TTL onsets. The parietal multimodal area is not named; it is read as any of the posterior parietal ROIs of the Allen CCF dorsal map (VISa, VISrl, or a ROI named PTLp), in either hemisphere. "Spreading" is read as an 80th-percentile region covering more than one ROI. Reproduced when, under one reading, the 80th-percentile region of the mean over mice includes a parietal ROI and more than one ROI.

claims.statement: The mice showed no sign of the aberrant short-duration, large-amplitude calcium transients reported in some transgenic lines; no cluster of transients had high prominence (> 0.1 dF/F) and narrow width (< 0.5 s).
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3; Figure S2b legend
claims.quote: High prominence (> 0.1 in Δ F / F ) and narrow width (< 0.5 s) of the transients were not detected in each animal (right).
claims.criterion: From the Figure S2b legend. Each mouse's first resting-state recording (day 0); the left frontal, left barrel, left retrosplenial and right visual ROIs; transients detected in the corrected dF/F with their prominences and widths; per mouse and region, K-means (k = 2) on (prominence, width), and the two cluster centres. Reproduced when no centre in any mouse and region has prominence > 0.1 and width < 0.5 s, and not reproduced when any does. Open details, each run. (1) Peak detection, which the paper does not name, read as scipy.signal.find_peaks (SciPy is the library the Methods name) (a) with no threshold, (b) with a minimum prominence of 0.01 dF/F; width at half prominence in seconds at 30 Hz. (2) The ROIs, "frontal" read as MOs or MOp, "visual" as VISp, "barrel" as SSp-bfd, "retrosplenial" as RSPd or RSPagl. (3) K-means features raw or z-scored. (4) The signal, which the legend calls ΔF/F, read as (a) the hemodynamics-corrected dF/F, (b) the uncorrected ΔF_B/F_B (the Methods' ratio before band-pass filtering), where the dataset holds the raw blue ROI signal. The number of transients per mouse is reported.

claims.statement: DeepLabCut keypoints differed from manual annotations only by minor errors on validation frames (192 frames from 25 mice for the body and face cameras, 190 for the eye).
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 4; Figure 5a-c legend
claims.quote: Comparison of DeepLabCut model-based keypoint annotations with manual annotations showed minor errors, validating the quality of our models ( Fig. 5a-c ).
claims.criterion: The paper gives no number in the text (the 95th percentiles are in the figure, which could not be read). The test needs the manual annotations of the validation frames (from task sessions 3, 6, 9 and 12, Figure S3 legend), which the paper does not describe as deposited. Blocked unless they are found; if found, the 95th-percentile error per keypoint is reported, and the claim holds when it is small against the keypoint spacing.

claims.statement: The lever-tip position tracked from the body video correlated highly with the encoder lever position, R = 0.98 +/- 0.02 (mean +/- s.d.).
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 4; Figure 5e,f
claims.quote: Moreover, the lever tip position estimated from the videography showed a markedly high correlation (0.98 ± 0.02; mean ± s.d.) with the encoder-based lever position ( Fig. 5e,f ).
claims.criterion: Tolerance is the paper's stated s.d. From the Figure 5 legend, Pearson's R between the keypoint's y position and the encoder-based lever position, over the frames of all successful trials of a session, per task session with body video and at least one successful trial (354 sessions, 25 mice). Open details, each run. (1) Sampling, read as (a) keypoints at the 100 Hz video rate with the lever position averaged over each video frame (each dot is a video frame in Figure 5e), (b) the down-sampled 30 Hz series. (2) Keypoints with likelihood below 0.2 dropped (the Methods' cut-off, confirmed in bdbc_nwb_packager/tracking/dlc.py) or kept. (3) The frames of a trial, read as (a) the trial interval of the trial table, (b) tone onset to tone onset plus 1 s plus the trial's T_pull. (4) The summary, read as (a) mean and s.d. over sessions (the text), (b) over the per-mouse means (the Figure 5f legend). (5) The sign, as computed and as an absolute value, since the image y axis points down. Reproduced when, under one reading, the mean R is within tolerance.

claims.statement: The right forepaw, which pulls the lever, correlated with the lever position (R = 0.49 +/- 0.23), and the left forepaw did not (R = 0.05 +/- 0.19), over 354 task sessions from 25 mice.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 4; Figure 5d-f
claims.quote: We found this is exactly the case, based on the 354 task-recording sessions of our dataset that successfully included upper-body videos ( Fig. 5d-f ; right forepaw, 0.49 ± 0.23; left forepaw, 0.05 ± 0.19; mean±s.d., n = 354 sessions from 25 animals
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the paper's stated s.d.; the session count is exact. As fig5f-lever-tip-correlation, with the right and left forepaw keypoints, under the same readings. The sessions are the 355 task sessions with an upper-body video less the one with no successful trial. Reproduced when, under one reading, both means are within tolerance and the right forepaw's exceeds the left's.

claims.statement: In the example session, the forepaws and the nose began moving before lever-pull onset, and the jaw and pupil diameter changed after it.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 5; Figure 6b
claims.quote: While some body parts, such as forepaws and nose, began moving before the lever-pull onset, others, including jaw and pupil diameter, moved afterward at least in this session.
claims.criterion: The example session is not identified, so the readings are (a) the mean over all task sessions with videos of each session's trial average, (b) the fraction of sessions in which the order holds, the claim holding under (b) when it holds in more than half. The paper states the finding for its example session only ("at least in this session"), so when no reading holds the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified (the session cannot be identified), not judged not reproduced; the per-session results are shown. Lever- pull onset is the lever crossing 1 mm (Methods), for pulls in (a) successful trials, (b) all valid pulls.
