Traces are taken from -1 s to 3 s around onset (the range of Figure 6c), as the keypoint's displacement from its mean position over -1 to -0.5 s. A trace's onset is the first time its trial average leaves the mean +/- 2 s.d. of that baseline window; this rule is not in the paper and is a standard choice, shown also with 3 s.d. Reproduced when, under one reading, both forepaws and the nose have onsets before 0 and the jaw and pupil diameter after 0.

claims.statement: In the example session, MOs activity returned quickly to baseline after the pull, while MOp and the upper-limb and nose somatosensory areas (SSp-ul, SSp-n) stayed slightly above baseline after reward delivery.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 5; Figure 6b
claims.quote: The secondary motor cortex (MOs) quickly recovered to the baseline level. In contrast, the primary motor (MOp) and somatosensory cortex (SSpul and SSpn) showed slightly higher activity than the baseline level after the reward delivery.
claims.criterion: The example session is not identified; readings (a) and (b) for sessions and pulls as in fig6b-movement-order. Trial-averaged corrected dF/F aligned to lever-pull onset, baseline the mean over -1 to 0 s. After reward is read as (a) 1 to 3 s after onset (to the end of the Figure 6c range), (b) 0.5 to 2 s after reward delivery in successful trials. The hemisphere is not given, read as left (contralateral to the pulling forelimb), right, and their mean. Reproduced when, under one reading, MOs's post-reward mean minus baseline is smaller than each of MOp's, SSp-ul's and SSp-n's, and those three are above baseline. As the paper states it for its example session only, when no reading holds the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, as in fig6b-movement-order.

claims.statement: In the example session, OB, RSPagl, AUDs and VISp had activity time courses that closely matched pupil dilation.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 5; Figure 6b
claims.quote: Other sensory-related areas (OB, olfactory bulb; RSPagl, retrosplenial area, lateral agranular part; AUDs, secondary auditory areas; VISp, primary visual area) showed activity traces that shared time courses closely matching the pupil dilation.
claims.criterion: Readings for sessions, pulls and hemisphere as in fig6b-motor-somatosensory-after-reward, over -1 to 3 s around lever-pull onset. The paper gives no measure of the match; the reading here is the contrast the paragraph draws, motor and somatosensory areas tracking the lever and these areas tracking the pupil. Reproduced when, under one reading, each of the four areas' trial-averaged traces has a higher Pearson correlation with the trial-averaged pupil diameter than with the trial-averaged lever position, and MOp's does not. As the paper states it for its example session only, when no reading holds the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, as in fig6b-movement-order.

claims.statement: Cortical activity varied less across trials after lever-pull onset than before it.
claims.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 5; Figure 6b
claims.quote: The data also revealed a decrease in activity variability after the lever-pull onset, exemplifying how stereotypic movements like lever-pull constrain cortical activity.
claims.criterion: Readings for sessions and pulls as in fig6b-movement-order. Variability is the across-trial s.d. of the corrected dF/F at each time point, averaged over a window, per ROI; before is -1 to 0 s, after is read as (a) 0 to 1 s, (b) 0 to 3 s. The paper names no test; reproduced when, under one reading, the after value is lower than the before value in more than half of the 44 ROIs, with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over ROIs at p < 0.05 reported. As the paper states it for its example session (Figure 6b), when no reading holds the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified, as in fig6b-movement-order.

claims.statement: The TEM model trained on mouse images segments the mouse test images with a mean three-class pixel-wise accuracy of 95% (0.9451 in Table 3, mean over 24 test images).
claims.source: Results, Segmentation, paragraph 1; Table 3, row TEM, Mice
claims.quote: The TEM model trained on mice microscopy achieved a pixel-wise accuracy of 95% on mice samples
claims.criterion: Segment each mouse TEM image of the dandiset with default_TEM_model_v1 at commit 7f60132, by segment.py with its defaults (0.01 um working pixel size, overlap 25, the input contrast inverted once as segment.py does for this model, see the opening comment), using the pixel size the dandiset gives for each image (Table 1 gives 0.002 um). The result without the inversion is shown as a variant. Pixel-wise accuracy is, per image, the fraction of pixels whose class (background, myelin, axon) in the prediction equals the class in the dandiset's segmentation, at the native pixel size (Methods, Pipeline overview and Pixel-wise accuracy); the value is the mean over images (Table 3 legend). The test set is open, as the paper names neither the mice nor their group. The readings are (a) every mouse image in the dandiset, which also holds the model's training images; (b) the images of the control mice only, following the Discussion's statement that the models were trained and tested on healthy tissues. Neither reading is the paper's test set (3 of the 20 mice, disjoint from the 17 training mice, Table 1), so both may hold training images and a match is weaker evidence than a test on held-out mice. When a mouse has more than 8 images, all its images are used (the paper does not say which 8 it took). Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance under both readings; when the readings differ in outcome the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified. The per-mouse means, and the cuprizone mice apart, are reported.

claims.statement: On the mouse test images the TEM model reaches a mean axon Dice of 0.9493, a mean myelin Dice of 0.8552, a mean axon detection sensitivity of 0.9597 and a mean precision of 0.9647.
claims.source: Table 3, row TEM, Mice
claims.criterion: Segmentations and test-set readings as in table3-tem-mice-accuracy. Dice per image is 2|A and B| / (|A| + |B|) between the predicted and the ground-truth masks, for axon and for myelin apart (Methods, Equation 1; pw_dice in segmentation_scoring.py). Sensitivity and precision per image are TP / (TP + FN) and TP / (TP + FP) over axon objects matched by centroids (Methods, Detection metrics), computed with score_analysis as the opening comment states. Each value is the mean over images. Reproduced when all four means are within tolerance under both readings; partially reproduced when two or three are under both.

claims.statement: In both models and every test sample the myelin Dice is lower than the axon Dice, which the authors attribute to myelin having two boundaries (with the axon and with the background).
claims.source: Discussion, Performance metrics, paragraph 1; Table 3
claims.quote: In both models and all test samples, computed myelin Dice was lower than axon Dice.
claims.criterion: Tested on the mouse TEM images only, with the values of table3-tem-mice-dice-detection. Which units "all test samples" covers is open. The readings are (i) the rows of Table 3, so that for the mice the means over images are compared, and (ii) every single test image, as the Table 3 legend calls each of the 24 mouse images a sample. Reproduced when the myelin Dice is below the axon Dice under either of (i) and (ii), for both test-set readings; the result under each, and the fraction of single images with myelin Dice below axon Dice, are reported. The SEM rows and the macaque row cannot be tested on this dandiset; the paper's values (Table 3) hold the order in all five rows.

claims.statement: Axon detection sensitivity is above 93% in every test set (Table 3 gives 0.9300 for the human sample, so there the bound is met only with rounding).
claims.source: Discussion, Performance metrics, paragraph 1; Table 3
claims.quote: In all test sets, sensitivity was high (>93%, see Table 3 ), indicating good capability to detect true positive axons.
claims.criterion: Tested on the mouse TEM images only, with the mean sensitivity of table3-tem-mice-dice-detection. Reproduced when the mean is above 0.93 under both test-set readings. The other test sets (rat 1, rat 2, human, macaque) are not in the dandiset.

claims.statement: The SEM model trained on rat spinal cord reaches a pixel-wise accuracy between 85% and 88% on the two rat test images (0.8510 and 0.8822 in Table 3).
claims.source: Results, Segmentation, paragraph 1; Table 3, rows SEM, Rat 1 and Rat 2
claims.quote: The SEM model trained on rat microscopy was able to achieve a pixel-wise accuracy between 85% and 88% on the rat test samples
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset, which holds no SEM images. If the two rat test images and their ground truth were found, segment with default_SEM_model_v1 at commit 7f60132 by segment.py with its defaults (0.1 um working pixel size, overlap 25) and compute the accuracy as in table3-tem-mice-accuracy.

claims.statement: On the human spinal cord SEM test image the rat-trained SEM model reaches a pixel-wise accuracy of 81% (0.8114), the lowest of all test samples, which the authors attribute to the human sample's different contrast, quality and noise.
claims.source: Results, Segmentation, paragraph 1; Table 3, row SEM, Human; Discussion, Performance metrics, paragraph 1
claims.quote: while the pixel-wise accuracy on human test sample was 81%
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset, which holds no SEM images. Method as in table3-sem-rat-accuracy.

claims.statement: On the macaque corpus callosum TEM test image the mouse-trained TEM model reaches a pixel-wise accuracy of 84% (0.8438).
claims.source: Results, Segmentation, paragraph 1; Table 3, row TEM, Macaque
claims.quote: and a pixel-wise accuracy of 84% on macaque samples
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset, which holds mouse images only. Method as in table3-tem-mice-accuracy, on the single macaque image of ref. 7.

claims.statement: For the SEM test images and the macaque TEM image the axon Dice, myelin Dice, sensitivity and precision are rat 1 0.9089, 0.8193, 0.9699, 0.8468; rat 2 0.9244, 0.8389, 0.9876, 0.7987; human 0.8089, 0.7629, 0.9300, 0.7306; macaque 0.9069, 0.7519, 0.9429, 0.8129.
claims.source: Table 3, rows Rat 1, Rat 2, Human and Macaque
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset. Methods as in table3-tem-mice-dice-detection, with the SEM model for the rat and human images.

claims.statement: The TEM model slightly underestimates the myelin sheaths of the macaque sample compared with its ground truth.
claims.source: Discussion, Performance metrics, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Note that myelin sheaths of the macaque TEM sample are slightly underestimated when compared to the ground truth segmentation.
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset, which holds no macaque image. The paper gives no measure; the reading would be a predicted myelin area below the ground-truth myelin area on the macaque image.

claims.statement: Segmenting a full rat cervical spinal cord SEM slice took 5 hours on a Mac laptop (2.9 GHz).
claims.source: Results, Segmentation, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Processing time was 5 hours in a Mac laptop (2.9 GHz).
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset, which holds no SEM slice; the time also depends on the machine.

claims.statement: In the corticospinal tract of the rat cervical spinal cord the segmentation gives small axon diameters (around 1 um), very high axon density (around 200,000 axons per mm2) and g-ratios around 0.6.
claims.source: Results, Morphometrics extraction, paragraph 1; Figure 7
claims.quote: In the corticospinal tract (tract
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset, which holds no rat spinal cord. Per the Methods (Morphometrics extraction), with AxonSeg (ref. 16) as the paper used, the segmentation of the full slice is aggregated into 50 x 50 um2 cells, within a white matter mask; axon diameter is the equivalent diameter sqrt(4 Area / pi) of each axon object, density is axons per mm2, and g-ratio is sqrt(1 / (1 + MVF / AVF)). The paper gives the tract only as a schematic diagram (Figure 7, refs. 34 to 36), so the cells that form the tract are open.

claims.statement: Larger axons are found close to the periphery of the rat spinal cord.
claims.source: Results, Morphometrics extraction, paragraph 1; Figure 7
claims.quote: Larger axons are found close to the spinal cord periphery.
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset. Method as in fig7-corticospinal-tract; the paper gives no measure of distance to the periphery.

claims.statement: The diameter map agrees with the literature in that the ventral spinothalamic tract has the largest axons and the spinocerebellar tracts are mostly large-diameter fibres (both stated with citations, as known anatomy the map is consistent with), and axons of the cuneate fasciculus are observed to be larger than those of the gracile fasciculus.
claims.source: Discussion, Morphometrics extraction, paragraph 1; Figure 7
claims.quote: The ventral spinothalamic tract (#3 in tract reference of Fig. 7 ) contains the largest axons ... We also observe that axons in the cuneate fasciculus (#7 in tract reference) are larger than those found in the gracile fasciculus
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset. Method as in fig7-corticospinal-tract, comparing the mean axon diameter between tracts; the tract boundaries are open.

claims.statement: Across the rat spinal cord white matter the g-ratio ranges between 0.5 and 0.75, in agreement with other rat studies.
claims.source: Discussion, Morphometrics extraction, paragraph 1; Figure 7
claims.quote: G-ratio ranges between 0.5 and 0.75, which is in agreement with other rat microstructure studies
claims.criterion: Not testable on this dandiset. Method as in fig7-corticospinal-tract, over all 50 x 50 um2 white matter cells; the claim holds when the g-ratios lie within 0.45 to 0.825 (the range widened by 10% of each bound). Whether isolated cells at the edge of the mask count is open.

claims.statement: The simulated M1 network is composed of 10,073 neurons of seven excitatory pyramidal cell types (IT, PT5B, CT) and two interneuron cell types (PV, SOM).
claims.source: Figure 1 legend; Methods, Microcircuit composition, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Simulated primary motor cortex (M1) is composed of 10,073 neurons.
claims.criterion: In each of the four files of set sM1_12-12-2023, count the units whose population is one of the 15 M1 populations of sim/cfg.py (allpops), leaving out the input spike generators. Reproduced when the count is 10,073 in each file. The tolerance is zero because the number is a count of a fixed model, not a measurement.

claims.statement: In the parkinsonian condition the PT5B neuron model was changed (BK and NaT conductances) so that its spike count across current injections fell by 64%, as in 6-OHDA mouse slices.
claims.source: Methods, paragraph 2 and Morphology and physiology of neuron classes, paragraph 3; Supplementary Fig. 1 (not read)
claims.quote: In the simulated parkinsonian mouse M1 PT5B currents (BK and NaT) were modified so that they showed a 64% decrease in excitability as reported by Chen et al.
claims.criterion: Needs single-neuron current-injection simulations of the control and parkinsonian PT5B model (README parameter settings; cfg.gpeak and cfg.gnafbar). The current amplitudes, step duration and averaging behind the 64% are those of Fig. 1D of Chen et al. 2021 (J. Neurosci. 41, 5553) and Supplementary Fig. 1, which was not available to this reader. The claim can be tested only if the dataset holds these current-injection simulations and the supplement or the question process supplies the protocol; otherwise the detail is open and the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: The results hold across four sets of four simulations with different random seeds; set sM1_12-12-2023 is a typical example and the other three sets are analysed in Supplementary Table 2.
claims.source: Methods, paragraph 2; Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Figs. 2 to 5 (not read)
claims.quote: To demonstrate robustness, we ran 4 sets of 4 simulations (Supplementary Table 2 ), each set including the control and parkinsonian conditions in rest state and in the activated (movement) state.
claims.criterion: Supplementary Table 2, which gives the measures and values for the other three sets, was not in the text supplied, so this reader cannot fix the measures, the expected values or what counts as holding. The claim is blocked as methods_underspecified until a reader with the supplement completes it. The author may report, for each set the dataset holds, the measures of the claims below, without an outcome.

claims.statement: In the control condition at rest, M1 activity is dominated by beta-band activity of about 20 Hz, particularly clear in the PT5B spike count histogram.
claims.source: Figure 2A legend; Results, Control simulations, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Resting state (250 ms at midpoint of 4.3 s simulation) displayed dominant beta-band activity (~20 Hz; particularly clear in the PT5B spike count histogram).
claims.criterion: File -01. The frequency of the largest peak of the time-averaged power spectrum in W of (a) the PT5B SCH (the legend's measure) and (b) the LFP under E1 and E2. The paper reports separate 2 Hz activity in the rest LFP (Fig. 3A), so the peak is searched (i) above 0 Hz and (ii) above 5 Hz, a range the paper does not fix. Reproduced when the peak is within 18 to 22 Hz under every reading of the SCH; the LFP readings are reported as variants, since the legend names the SCH.

claims.statement: In the control condition, the activated state shifts M1 activity to gamma-band activity of about 44 Hz.
claims.source: Figure 2B legend; Results, Control simulations, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Activated state showed change to high-frequency gamma-band activity (~44 Hz).
claims.criterion: File -03, the measure and readings of fig2-control-rest-beta. Reproduced when the largest spectral peak of the PT5B SCH in W is within 39.6 to 48.4 Hz under every reading; the LFP readings (E1, E2) are reported as variants.

claims.statement: In the control condition PT5B neurons fire more in the activated state than at rest (11.7 +/- 9.4 against 26.8 +/- 18.2 spikes/s, p < 0.001).
claims.source: Figure 2C legend; Results, Control simulations, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Pyramidal tract neurons had the highest spike rate of any neuron population during the rest state, and increased further in the activated state (rest: 11.7 ± 9.4 spikes/s; activated: 26.8 ± 18.2 spikes/s; p < 0.001; Fig. 2C ).
claims.criterion: Files -01 and -03, rates in W, readings R1 and R2. Reproduced when, under one rate reading, all four values are within tolerance and the activated rates are higher with p < 0.001 under every test reading T1 to T4.

claims.statement: In the control condition IT2/3 neurons fire more in the activated state than at rest (1.2 +/- 1.6 against 6.7 +/- 8.9 spikes/s, p < 0.001).
claims.source: Figure 2C legend; Results, Control simulations, paragraph 5
claims.quote: IT2/3 neurons significantly increased their firing rate (rest: 1.2 spikes/s; activated: 6.6 spikes/s; p < 0.001).
claims.criterion: Files -01 and -03, population IT2, rates in W, readings R1 and R2. The legend gives 6.7 and the text 6.6 spikes/s for the activated mean; the tolerance of 6.7 covers both. Reproduced when, under one rate reading, all four values are within tolerance and the activated rates are higher with p < 0.001 under every test reading T1 to T4.

claims.statement: In the control condition IT6 neurons fire less in the activated state than at rest (5.8 +/- 5.8 against 3.5 +/- 5.2 spikes/s, p < 0.001).
claims.source: Figure 2C legend; Results, Control simulations, paragraph 5
claims.quote: IT6 firing rates decreased from 5.8 spikes/s at rest to 3.5 spikes/s in the activated state ( p < 0.001).
claims.criterion: Files -01 and -03, rates in W, readings R1 and R2. Reproduced when, under one rate reading, all four values are within tolerance and the activated rates are lower with p < 0.001 under every test reading T1 to T4.

claims.statement: In the control condition IT5A and IT5B neurons fire at about 3 spikes/s at rest (3.3 and 3.1 spikes/s) and stop firing (0 spikes/s) in the activated state.
claims.source: Results, Control simulations, paragraph 5; Figure 2B
claims.quote: In contrast, IT5A and IT5B firing rates decreased from 3 Hz (IT5A... 3.3 spikes/s; IT5B... 3.1 spikes/s) at rest, to 0 spikes/s in the activated state
claims.criterion: Files -01 and -03, rates in W, reading R1 (under R2 an activated mean is undefined when no neuron fires; if some fire, R2 is reported as a variant). The tolerance of the zero rates is 0.05 spikes/s, the rounding of the paper's one decimal place, since 10% of zero is zero. Reproduced when all four values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: In the control condition the IT4 population rate rises from 2.6 spikes/s at rest to 4.7 spikes/s in the activated state.
claims.source: Results, Control simulations, paragraph 5
claims.quote: The IT4 neuron population firing rate increased from 2.6 Hz during rest to 4.7 Hz during the activated state.
claims.criterion: Files -01 and -03, rates in W, readings R1 and R2. Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance. The paper reports no test.

claims.statement: PT5B neurons have the highest mean spike rate of any population in the control rest state and in both the parkinsonian rest and activated states.
claims.source: Results, Control simulations, paragraph 5; Results, Parkinsonian condition, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Pyramidal tract neurons had the highest spike rate of any neuronal population during the rest and activated states in the parkinsonian condition
claims.criterion: Files -01, -02 and -04, mean rates in W of every M1 population. "Any neuron population" can be read as (a) all 15 M1 populations, interneurons included, or (b) the seven excitatory pyramidal cell types (Methods, Morphology and physiology of neuron classes, paragraph 1), the excitatory cell types of Figs. 2C and 5C. Reproduced when the PT5B mean is the highest in all three simulations under one rate reading (R1 or R2) and both population readings; when the population readings disagree, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified with both shown.

claims.statement: In the control condition PT5B interspike-interval CV is highly variable at rest (0.59 +/- 0.37; 47.8% regular with CV <= 0.5, 52.2% irregular) and mainly irregular in the activated state (0.61 +/- 0.30; 25.7% regular, 74.3% irregular).
claims.source: Results, Control simulations, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The CV was found to be highly variable across the PT5B population during rest (0.59 + /−0.37), indicating the presence of both regular (CV < = 0.5; 47.8%) and irregular activity (CV > 0.5; 52.2%).
claims.criterion: Files -01 and -03. CV of each PT5B neuron's ISIs (standard deviation over mean), mean and standard deviation over neurons, and the share with CV <= 0.5 (regular) and > 0.5 (irregular), as in the Results. Open, with readings - the window, (a) W (the window of the rates in the same figure) or (b) the whole 4.3 s; which neurons, (i) neurons with at least two ISIs or (ii) at least one ISI (a single ISI gives CV 0). Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, all six values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: In the control condition subthreshold membrane-potential oscillations appear in 57.4% of PT5B neurons in the activated state and not at rest.
claims.source: Results, Control simulations, paragraph 3; Figure 2A,B
claims.quote: Oscillations in subthreshold membrane potentials appeared frequently during the activated state (57.4% of PT5B neurons) but not during rest
claims.criterion: Files -01 and -03, somatic membrane potentials of the PT5B neurons recorded. Neither the paper nor its code says how a subthreshold oscillation is detected or over which neurons the 57.4% is taken, and no reading follows from the text. The claim is blocked as methods_underspecified unless a question to a reader settles it; the number of PT5B neurons with recorded voltage is reported.

claims.statement: In the control condition the PT5B duty cycle, the share of each oscillation period with activity above half-height, is 31% at rest and 48% in the activated state.
claims.source: Results, Control simulations, paragraph 4; Figure 2A,B; Methods, Duty cycle
claims.quote: The duty cycle was 31% during rest (Fig. 2A ) and 48% during activated state (Fig. 2B ; dashed vertical lines not shown).
claims.criterion: Files -01 and -03, the PT5B SCH (2 ms bins, unsmoothed, as the legends describe it). A period runs from one rising crossing of half-height to the next, and the duty cycle is the time above half-height divided by the period (Results, paragraph 4; the Methods sentence that a period runs from the rising to the falling crossing would make every duty cycle 100% and is read as defining the time on). Open, with readings - half-height, (a) halfway between the minimum and maximum of the window shown (one line per panel, Fig. 2 legend) or (b) halfway between the trough and peak of each period (Methods); the window, (i) the 250 ms of Fig. 2A,B, 2.0 to 2.25 s (the notebooks) or (ii) W; the summary over periods, which the paper does not give, (x) the mean of the per-period duty cycles or (y) the total time above half-height over the total time of complete periods. Reproduced when, under one combination, both values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: In the control rest state the LFP spectrogram shows virtually continuous power around 2 Hz and 15 to 25 Hz beta bursts recurring every 600 ms (1.7 Hz).
claims.source: Figure 3A legend; Results, Control simulations, paragraph 6
claims.quote: The rest state simulation revealed virtually continuous power around 2 Hz, as well as 15–25 Hz beta-band bursts (Fig. 3A ), occurring every 600 ms (or with a burst-rate of 1.7 Hz).
claims.criterion: File -01, LFP spectrogram in W, readings S1, S2 and E1, E2. Power around 2 Hz is present when the time-averaged spectrum has a local maximum within 1 to 3 Hz, the reading of "power around 2 Hz" as a spectral peak. The paper does not define a burst. The one reading the paper's text offers is its own half-height convention (Methods, Duty cycle) applied to the 15 to 25 Hz band power over time - a burst is an epoch above halfway between the minimum and maximum of that band power in W. Reproduced when the 2 Hz peak is present and the burst rate is within tolerance under every reading; the author may ask a reader for a burst definition.

claims.statement: Social isolation changes alcohol licking in opposite directions in the two sexes, raising it in males and lowering it in females, a significant sex by housing interaction.
claims.source: Figure 1c legend; Results, Social isolation increases alcohol drinking in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Social isolation produced opposite effects on alcohol licking in males and females ( N = 14 male and 11 female mice, two-way ANOVA, interaction: F (1, 23) = 21.04, *** P = 0.0001; Sidak’s multiple comparisons test), increasing alcohol licking in males while decreasing it in females.
claims.criterion: Per mouse, alcohol licks averaged over the last 3 baseline days and over the 11 isolation days (Methods, 2BC drinking). A two-way ANOVA of sex (between) by housing (within, repeated measures), as the error df of 23 with 25 mice implies; Sidak post hoc tests of housing within each sex. Reproduced when the interaction has p < 0.05, males rise and females fall, and the Sidak test is significant in males. Partially reproduced when the interaction holds but one sex's change is in the wrong direction.

claims.statement: A three-way ANOVA over sex, liquid (alcohol, water) and housing finds a significant three-way interaction.
claims.source: Results, Social isolation increases alcohol drinking in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2
claims.quote: A three-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) across sex, liquid and housing condition revealed a significant interaction ( F (1, 46) = 14.68; P < 0.001), indicating that social isolation altered alcohol and water drinking differently across sexes.
claims.criterion: The licks of fig1c-isolation-alcohol-sex-opposite, alcohol and water. The error df of 46 fits 50 mouse-by-liquid series less four groups, so the reading is housing as the repeated factor and sex and liquid as between factors; the fully repeated reading (liquid and housing within mouse) is shown as a variant. Reproduced when the three-way interaction has p < 0.05 under the first reading (paper p < 0.001).

claims.statement: In males alcohol drinking rises progressively over the days of isolation, peaking after about one week and staying high, with a significant effect of time.
claims.source: Figure 1d legend; Results, Social isolation increases alcohol drinking in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Time course of escalated alcohol drinking during social isolation ( N = 14 male mice, one-way ANOVA, F (4, 65) = 2.83, * P = 0.03; post hoc Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test).
claims.criterion: The df give five time levels and an ordinary (not repeated) one-way ANOVA over 70 values. The levels are not stated; the readings are baseline (last 3 baseline days) and the 11 isolation days in four blocks of (a) days 1 to 3, 4 to 6, 7 to 9, 10 to 11, or (b) days 1 to 2, 3 to 5, 6 to 8, 9 to 11. Dunnett tests against baseline. Reproduced when under every reading the ANOVA has p < 0.05 and the largest block mean is at or after day 6; when the readings disagree the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Isolation does not change water licking, while females lick more water than males (main effect of sex).
claims.source: Figure 1e legend; Results, Social isolation increases alcohol drinking in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Social isolation did not impact water licking, but females drink more water than males ( N = 14 male and 11 female mice, two-way ANOVA, main effect of sex: F (1, 23) = 13.87, ** P = 0.001).
claims.criterion: Water licks as in fig1c-isolation-alcohol-sex-opposite, same ANOVA. The sex effect is reproduced when p < 0.05 with females higher. The absence of an isolation effect is judged on the same ANOVA at p < 0.05, for the housing main effect and the interaction; the size of the housing change is given either way. Both parts must hold for reproduced.

claims.statement: In group-housed males social rank correlates with alcohol licks, lower-ranked mice drinking more, and rank 4 mice drink more than the others.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1c legend; Results, Social isolation increases alcohol drinking in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Rank correlates with alcohol licks ( N = 26 male mice, Pearson correlation, r 2 = 0.25, Bonferroni adjusted * p = 0.01). Inset, Rank 4 mice drink more alcohol ( N = 26 male mice, one-way ANOVA, F(3, 22) = 4.68, * p = 0.01; Sidak’s post hoc, * p < 0.05).
claims.criterion: Rank under both M8 readings; licks are baseline alcohol licks (last 3 baseline days). The Bonferroni family is not stated; readings (a) two tests (alcohol and water, panels c and d), (b) no correction (the printed p = 0.01 matches the uncorrected p for r2 = 0.25 and 26 mice). Reproduced when r2 is within tolerance, licks rise toward subordinate ranks, the corrected p < 0.05 under every reading, and the one-way ANOVA over integer ranks has p < 0.05 with rank 4 highest.

claims.statement: In group-housed males social rank does not correlate with water licks.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1d legend
claims.quote: No correlation between social rank and water licks ( N = 26 male mice, Pearson correlation, r 2 = 0.06, p = 0.43).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence on the paper's test, a Pearson correlation of rank (M8, both readings) with baseline water licks at p < 0.05. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; r2 is given either way.

claims.statement: During isolation rank still correlates with alcohol licks in males, but not with water licks.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1e,f legend
claims.quote: Rank correlates with alcohol licks during isolation ( e ; N = 14 male mice, Pearson correlation, r 2 = 0.41, Bonferroni adjusted * p < 0.05), but not water ( f ; N = 14 male mice, Pearson correlation, r 2 = 0.002, Bonferroni adjusted p = 1).
claims.criterion: Licks averaged over the 11 isolation days; rank under both M8 readings. The Bonferroni family is not stated; read as two tests (e and f). A four-test family (c to f) is not allowed: with r2 = 0.41 and 14 mice it gives p of about 0.054, against the printed p < 0.05. Reproduced when r2 for alcohol is within tolerance with corrected p < 0.05, and the water correlation has corrected p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Subordinate males increase their alcohol licks per bout during isolation (rank by isolation interaction), with no change in water licks per bout.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1g,h legend
claims.quote: Subordinate males increase alcohol licks per bout during isolation ( g ; N = 4 male mice/group, two-way ANOVA, interaction: F (1, 6) = 20.84, *** p < 0.003, main effect of isolation: F(1, 6) = 28.84, ** p < 0.01; Sidak’s post hoc, *** p = 0.001 compared to group-housed), with no effect on water licks per bout ( h ).
claims.criterion: Licks per bout (M1). Two groups of four, dominant and subordinate; which mice form them is not stated. Readings (a) rank 1 against the lowest rank of each cage, (b) rank 1 against rank 4 only. Two-way ANOVA, rank group by housing, housing repeated (df 6 = 8 mice less 2). Reproduced when the interaction has p < 0.05 with the subordinate rise significant (Sidak) and the water ANOVA shows no effect at p < 0.05, under every reading that yields four mice per group.

claims.statement: Isolation increases the number of alcohol bouts in dominant males, with no change in water bouts.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1i,j legend
claims.quote: Isolation increases alcohol bout number in dominant males ( i ; N = 4 male mice/group, two-way ANOVA, main effect of isolation: F (1, 6) = 10.23, * p = 0.01), with no effect on water bouts ( j ).
claims.criterion: Bouts per session (M1), groups and ANOVA as in ed1g-subordinate-licks-per-bout. Reproduced when the main effect of isolation on alcohol bouts has p < 0.05 with dominants rising and no effect on water bouts at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In females rank correlates with alcohol licks (one-tailed test, direction from males) but not with water licks.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1l,m legend
claims.quote: Rank correlates with alcohol licks ( N = 9 female mice, one-tailed Pearson correlation, based on male mice, r 2 = 0.46, Bonferroni adjusted * p = 0.04), but not water licks ( m , Pearson correlation, r 2 = 0.08, Bonferroni adjusted p = 0.45).
claims.criterion: Baseline licks; rank under both M8 readings; one-tailed in the male direction for alcohol. The Bonferroni family is not stated; read as the two tests (l, m), which matches the printed p = 0.04 for r2 = 0.46 and 9 mice. Reproduced when r2 is within tolerance, corrected one-tailed p < 0.05, and the water correlation has corrected p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: At baseline males lick more alcohol and less water than females (main effects of sex and of liquid).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1n legend
claims.quote: Males show higher alcohol and lower water licking than females ( N = 26 male and 14 female mice/group, two-way ANOVA, main effect of sex: F(1, 38) = 10.77, ** p = 0.002; main effect of liquid: F(1, 38) = 17.29, *** p = 0.0002).
claims.criterion: Baseline alcohol and water licks; two-way ANOVA sex (between) by liquid (within), df 38 = 40 mice less 2. Reproduced when both main effects have p < 0.05 and male alcohol exceeds female alcohol while male water is below female water. The paper is not consistent here: the Results say females show a "trend in higher baseline alcohol intake" (Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability, paragraph 2), so the direction of the alcohol difference is reported either way.

claims.statement: Alcohol licks correlate strongly with blood alcohol concentration.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1r legend; Results, Social isolation increases alcohol drinking in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Alcohol licks (15% alcohol + 10% sucrose) correlates with blood alcohol concentrations, ( N = 19 male mice, Pearson’s correlation, r 2 = 0.67, **** p < 0.0001).
claims.criterion: Licks of the session after which trunk blood was taken (Methods, Blood alcohol concentration). Reproduced when r2 is within tolerance with p < 0.0001.

claims.statement: After isolation BLA-mPFC neurons of males fire more action potentials across current injections than those of group-housed males.
claims.source: Figure 2c legend; Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Social isolation increases excitability of BLA–mPFC neurons in males (group-housed: n = 21 neurons/ N = 7 male mice; social isolation: n = 30 neurons/ N = 9 male mice, two-way ANOVA, interaction effect: F (25, 1225) = 4.3, **** P < 0.0001; Sidak’s multiple comparisons post hoc, * P < 0.05).
claims.criterion: M6, labeled neurons of males. Reproduced when the current by housing interaction has p < 0.05 (paper p < 0.0001), isolated neurons fire more at most steps, and at least one Sidak test across steps is significant, under both spike readings.

claims.statement: After isolation BLA-mPFC neurons of females fire fewer action potentials across current injections than those of group-housed females.
claims.source: Figure 2d legend; Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Social isolation decreases excitability of BLA–mPFC neurons in females (group-housed: n = 18 neurons/ N = 9 female mice; social isolation: n = 15 neurons/ N = 7 female mice, two-way ANOVA, interaction effect: F (25, 775) = 2.16, *** P = 0.0009; Sidak’s multiple comparisons post hoc, * P < 0.05).
claims.criterion: M6, labeled neurons of females. Reproduced when the interaction has p < 0.05, isolated neurons fire less at most steps, and at least one Sidak test is significant, under both spike readings.

claims.statement: Group-housed females have more excitable BLA-mPFC neurons than group-housed males.
claims.source: Figure 2e legend; Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Group-housed females exhibited higher baseline excitability of BLA–mPFC neurons compared with group-housed males (group-housed females: n = 18 neurons/ N = 9 female mice; group-housed males: n = 21 neurons/ N = 7 male mice, two-way ANOVA, interaction effect: F (25, 925) = 13.2, **** P < 0.0001; Sidak’s post hoc test, * P < 0.05).
claims.criterion: M6, group-housed labeled neurons. Reproduced when the current by sex interaction has p < 0.05, female neurons fire more at most steps, and at least one Sidak test is significant, under both spike readings.

claims.statement: A three-way ANOVA over sex, current and housing finds a significant interaction for BLA-mPFC firing.
claims.source: Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2
claims.quote: A three-way ANOVA across sex, current injection and housing condition revealed a significant interaction ( F (25, 2,000) = 5.6; P < 0.0001), indicating that social isolation altered BLA–mPFC excitability differently across sexes.
claims.criterion: M6, the four groups of Fig. 2c,d; df 2000 = 25 times (84 neurons less 4 groups), current repeated. Reproduced when the three-way interaction has p < 0.05 under both spike readings.

claims.statement: Isolation raises the input resistance of male BLA-mPFC neurons.
claims.source: Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2; Supplementary Table 1
claims.quote: Post hoc two-way analyses showed that social isolation increased the intrinsic excitability of BLA–mPFC neurons in males, reflected by greater action potential firing across current injections (Fig. 2c ) and elevated input resistance (Supplementary Table 1 )
claims.criterion: Input resistance from the steady-state response to the -120 pA step (Methods). The steady-state window is not given; readings the last 100 ms and the last 50 ms of the step. Unpaired t-test between housing groups, p < 0.05 (Supplementary Table 1 legend). Reproduced when isolated male neurons have higher input resistance with p < 0.05 under both readings. The table's values are not in the text read, so no number is checked.

claims.statement: Isolation lowers the input resistance and raises the firing threshold of female BLA-mPFC neurons.
claims.source: Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 3; Supplementary Table 1
claims.quote: In contrast to males, isolation decreased BLA–mPFC excitability in females (Fig. 2d ), accompanied by reduced input resistance and a higher firing threshold (Supplementary Table 1 )
claims.criterion: Input resistance as in supt1-male-input-resistance-up; threshold is the smallest current step eliciting an action potential (Methods), under both M6 spike readings. Unpaired t-tests, p < 0.05. Reproduced when both differ in the stated directions; partially when one does. No number is checked (table values not in the text read).

claims.statement: Isolation also increases the excitability of nonspecific BLA neurons in males, a small but significant interaction, which the Results call minimal.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2e legend; Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Social isolation increases excitability of non-specific BLA neurons in males (Group-housed: n = 50 neurons from N = 11 male mice; Social isolation: n = 54 neurons from N = 12 male mice; two-way ANOVA, interaction effect: F (25, 2550) = 1.58, * p = 0.03).
claims.criterion: M6, unlabeled neighbouring neurons of males. Reproduced when the interaction has p < 0.05 with isolated neurons firing more, under both spike readings. The paper gives no measure of "minimal"; the F and the size of the difference are reported beside those of fig2c-male-blampfc-excitability-up, not tested.

claims.statement: Nonspecific BLA neurons of males show no rank differences in excitability, group-housed or isolated, and isolation does not change their firing at 300 pA within any rank.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2b–d legend; Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 3
claims.quote: No detectable social rank-dependent differences were observed in non-specific BLA neurons from group-housed ( b ; Rank 1: n = 10 cells from N = 3 male mice; ... d . Social isolation did not alter the number of action potentials elicited by a 300 pA current injection across each social rank in males.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The legend names no test; the Statistics section gives two-way ANOVA with repeated measures for three or more groups, so b and c are tested by M6 with rank (1 to 3) in place of housing, and d by a two-way ANOVA of rank by housing on spikes at 300 pA, each at p < 0.05. Reproduced when no rank main effect or interaction reaches p < 0.05 in b and c, and no housing effect or interaction in d. The Results text cites these panels as Extended Data Fig. 3; the legends place them in Extended Data Fig. 2.

claims.statement: Among group-housed males, dominant (rank 1) mice have less excitable BLA-mPFC neurons than intermediate (rank 2) and subordinate (rank 3) mice.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3c legend; Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Dominant male mice showed reduced basal BLA-mPFC excitability compared to Intermediate and Subordinate male mice (Rank 1: n = 13 neurons from N = 4 male mice; Rank 2: n = 9neurons from N = 4 male mice; Rank 3: n = 14 neurons from N = 5 male mice, two-way ANOVA, interaction effect: F (50, 825) = 4.25, **** p < 0.0001; Tukey’s post hoc, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, compared to Rank 1).
claims.criterion: M6 with rank (1 to 3) as the group factor, group-housed labeled male neurons. Reproduced when the interaction has p < 0.05, rank 1 fires least, and Tukey tests show rank 1 below both rank 2 and rank 3 at some step; partially when only one of the two differs.

claims.statement: Group-housed females show no rank differences in BLA-mPFC excitability.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 3d legend
claims.quote: No detectable social rank-dependent differences were observed in BLA-mPFC neurons from group-housed female mice
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. No test is named; M6 with rank as the group factor (the test of ed3c-male-rank-blampfc-excitability) at p < 0.05. Reproduced when neither the rank main effect nor the interaction reaches p < 0.05.

claims.statement: ChrimsonR stimulation of BLA-mPFC terminals decreases social interaction against tdTomato controls, both group-housed and after isolation.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4e,f legend
claims.quote: BLA-mPFC stimulation decreased social interaction in ChrimsonR vs. tdTomato males under group-housed ( e ; two-way ANOVA, interaction: F(9,140) = 4.94, **** p < 0.0001; Sidak’s post hoc, *** p < 0.001) and social isolation ( f ; interaction: F(9,140) = 4.99, **** p < 0.0001; Sidak’s post hoc, *** p < 0.001) conditions ( N = 8 male mice/group).
claims.criterion: Frames of the 3-min stimulation epoch (Methods, Optogenetic stimulation during resident-juvenile intruder task). The df imply 10 levels crossed with group, with 16 mice and no repeated-measures error (140 = 160 less 20). The levels are not named; readings (a) 10 UMAP behavioural clusters (legend c: unsupervised UMAP clustering of ChrimsonR and tdTomato frames), with the measure the fraction of frames per cluster; (b) 10 time bins of 18 s, with the measure the fraction of frames scored as interaction by the head-to-body distance of 60 pixels or less and angle of 135 degrees or less (Methods, SLEAP). UMAP parameters and the clustering of its embedding are not given; reading (a) uses the umap-learn defaults on the pairwise features the Methods list and the cluster count fixed at 10. Reproduced when, under every reading, the interaction has p < 0.05 in both housing conditions and ChrimsonR mice spend less time in interaction (Sidak significant for the interaction cluster or for some bins); methods_underspecified when readings disagree.

claims.statement: Neither ChrimsonR stimulation nor NpHR inhibition changes total distance travelled against controls.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4g,m legend
claims.quote: Total distance traveled did not differ between ChrimsonR and tdTomato mice (ChrimsonR: N = 15; tdTomato: N = 16 male mice).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. No test is named; the Statistics section gives t-tests for two groups, read as two-sided unpaired, p < 0.05. How distance was tracked is not given: behaviour was recorded with EthoVision (body-centre tracking) and pose was tracked with SLEAP; readings the EthoVision body centre where the dataset holds it, and the SLEAP skull base and haunch points. The epoch is not given; readings the 3-min stimulation epoch and the whole 6-min interaction. Reproduced when neither comparison (ChrimsonR 15 against tdTomato 16; NpHR 16 against eYFP 16) has p < 0.05 under any reading.

claims.statement: NpHR inhibition of BLA-mPFC terminals decreases social avoidance when group-housed and increases social interaction after isolation.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4k,l legend; Results, Social isolation increases BLA–mPFC neuronal excitability in males and decreases it in females, paragraph 4
claims.quote: BLA-mPFC inhibition decreased social avoidance in NpHR vs. eYFP males under group-housed ( k ; two-way ANOVA, interaction: F(6,98) = 4.02, ** p = 0.001; Sidak’s post hoc, *** p < 0.001) and increased social interaction under social isolation ( l ; two-way ANOVA, interaction: F(6,97) = 3.57, ** p = 0.003; Sidak’s post hoc, ** p < 0.01) conditions ( N = 8 male mice/group).
claims.criterion: As in ed4ef-chrimson-decreases-social with 7 levels (UMAP clusters of NpHR and eYFP frames, or 7 time bins). Reproduced when, under every reading, both interactions have p < 0.05, NpHR mice show less avoidance when group-housed and more interaction after isolation. The Results describe only the isolation effect ("increased social interaction selectively during isolation"); both parts are reported.

claims.statement: GRIN lens implants do not change baseline alcohol licks.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 5c legend
claims.quote: GRIN lens implants do not alter baseline alcohol licks (No GRIN: N = 12 male mice; BLA GRIN: N = 22 male mice; mPFC GRIN: N = 6 male mice, one-way ANOVA, F (2, 37) = 0.47, p = 0.62).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence on the paper's test, a one-way ANOVA over the three groups at p < 0.05. Reproduced when p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Both BLA populations respond to the cue with a modest, transient increase below 0.5 z-score.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 5d legend
claims.quote: Both populations exhibited modest, transient increases in activity (<0.5 z-score) following cue onset
claims.criterion: Cue-onset z-scores per M3 with cue onset in place of bout onset. The Methods give baselines only for bouts ("3- or 5-s"); readings 3 s and 5 s before cue onset (the intertrial interval of 53 to 73 s allows both). Reproduced, under both readings, when the population mean trace of each population peaks above 0 and below 0.5 within 3 s of cue onset and falls back toward 0 by the end of the 3-s cue.

claims.statement: Hierarchical clustering of alcohol responses gives several functional clusters, and BLA-mPFC neurons distribute across them differently from nonspecific BLA neurons.
claims.source: Figure 3d–f legends; Results, BLA–mPFC activity robustly encodes and predicts alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The distribution of BLA–mPFC neurons across functional clusters suggests that projection-defined BLA–mPFC neurons may represent a distinct functional subpopulation with specific response properties to alcohol, distinct from nonspecific BLA neurons (Fig. 3f ).
claims.criterion: One clustering of the 736 neurons of both populations pooled ("Hierarchical clustering of responses to alcohol for all recorded BLA neurons", Results, paragraph 3). Ward linkage, Euclidean distance on each neuron's mean alcohol z trace (M3), the cut set to the highest linkage giving at least one nonresponsive cluster (Methods, Agglomerative hierarchical clustering); "nonresponsive" read as a cluster whose mean trace stays within +-1.98 after onset (M4). The trace span is not given; readings -3 to +5 s and 0 to +3 s around onset. Percentage enrichment per cluster as in Methods, Enrichment analysis. The paper gives no test; the Statistics section names chi-square for distributions, so a chi-square test of population by cluster at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the test has p < 0.05 under both trace readings.

claims.statement: Neurons excited by alcohol and those excited by water are largely separate ensembles.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 5e,f legend; Results, BLA–mPFC activity robustly encodes and predicts alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Nonspecific BLA and BLA–mPFC neurons excited to alcohol and water consisted of largely nonoverlapping neurons (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f ).
claims.criterion: Excited neurons per M4 for alcohol and for water bouts, in each population; the Wilcoxon reading of M4 is shown too. "Largely" is not quantified; read as fewer than half of the smaller excited set also excited by the other liquid. Reproduced when this holds in both populations under the threshold reading.

claims.statement: Nonspecific BLA population activity distinguishes alcohol from water drinking with about 85% accuracy.
claims.source: Figure 3h; Results, BLA–mPFC activity robustly encodes and predicts alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 4
claims.quote: We found that population activity in nonspecific BLA neurons could distinguish alcohol from water consumption with ~85% accuracy (Fig. 3h ).
claims.criterion: M5 on the 540 nonspecific BLA neurons of 10 mice. Reproduced when the mean accuracy over folds is within tolerance under every M5 reading; methods_underspecified when readings disagree.

claims.statement: BLA-mPFC population activity decodes alcohol against water drinking more accurately than nonspecific BLA activity.
claims.source: Figure 3h legend; Results, BLA–mPFC activity robustly encodes and predicts alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 4
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC activity predicts alcohol drinking with greater accuracy than nonspecific BLA neurons (nonspecific BLA: n = 540 neurons/ N = 10; BLA–mPFC: n = 196 neurons/ N = 11 male mice, Kruskal–Wallis test, H (2) = 8.06, ** P = 0.009; Dunn’s multiple comparisons test, * P = 0.02).
claims.criterion: M5 for nonspecific BLA, BLA-mPFC and all BLA neurons (the three groups of the H(2) df, Extended Data Fig. 6b). Fold accuracies are the units. Reproduced when, under every M5 reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test has p < 0.05 and Dunn's test shows BLA-mPFC above nonspecific BLA at p < 0.05. The comparison of populations of different size (196 against 540 neurons) is as the paper did it; a size-matched subsample of nonspecific neurons is a variant only.

claims.statement: Nonspecific BLA, BLA-mPFC and all BLA populations each decode alcohol against water above chance (shuffled data).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 6b legend
claims.quote: Population-level activity of non-specific BLA, BLA-mPFC, and all BLA neurons decodes alcohol vs. water drinking above chance (shuffled data), using a support vector machine ... two-way ANOVA, main effect: F(1,24) = 174.2, **** p < 0.0001; Sidak’s post hoc, **** p < 0.0001).
claims.criterion: M5 with the shuffled control under both chance readings; two-way ANOVA population by data (real, shuffled) over fold accuracies (df 24 = 30 less 6). Reproduced when the main effect has p < 0.05 and every Sidak test of real against shuffled within a population has p < 0.05, under every M5 reading.

claims.statement: Across mice, the mean BLA-mPFC response to alcohol correlates positively with the number of alcohol bouts.
claims.source: Figure 3k legend; Results, BLA–mPFC activity robustly encodes and predicts alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 5
claims.quote: We correlated the number of alcohol bouts with the mean BLA–mPFC response to alcohol and found a significant positive relationship, such that greater BLA–mPFC activity predicted higher alcohol consumption (Fig. 3k ).
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the mean over its BLA-mPFC neurons of the M3 alcohol response, against its number of alcohol bouts (M1) in the imaging session (mean over sessions if a mouse has more than one). Bonferroni family readings (a) four tests (Fig. 3i to l), (b) two tests (k and l). Reproduced when r2 is within tolerance, r is positive and the corrected two-sided p < 0.05 under both readings.

claims.statement: Nonspecific BLA responses do not correlate with alcohol or water bouts, and BLA-mPFC water responses do not correlate with water bouts.
claims.source: Figure 3i,j,l legends; Extended Data Fig. 6e,f legend; Results, BLA–mPFC activity robustly encodes and predicts alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 5
claims.quote: No such relationship was observed for nonspecific BLA neurons, water consumption or cue responses (Fig. 3i,j,l and Extended Data Fig. 6e–j ).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, as fig3k-blampfc-response-predicts-bouts, on the paper's test (Pearson, Bonferroni over Fig. 3i to l) at p < 0.05. Reproduced when none of the nonspecific alcohol, nonspecific water and BLA-mPFC water correlations reaches corrected p < 0.05; r2 given for each.

claims.statement: Cue-evoked responses of neither population correlate with alcohol bouts.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 6i,j legend
claims.quote: Scatter plots showing non-specific BLA neurons ( i , r 2 = 0.04, p = 0.53) and BLA-mPFC neurons ( j , r 2 = 0.005, p = 0.84) cue-evoked responses did not correlate with alcohol bouts.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence on the paper's test (Pearson, p < 0.05). Per mouse mean cue response as in ed5d-cue-response-modest (mean z 0 to 3 s after cue onset) against alcohol bouts. Reproduced when neither correlation has p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Average bout duration does not correlate with the number of bouts.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 6k legend; Results, BLA–mPFC activity robustly encodes and predicts alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 5
claims.quote: No correlation was observed between the average bout duration and the number of bouts ( N = 11 male mice, Pearson correlation, r 2 = 0.0, p = 0.84).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence on the paper's test (Pearson, p < 0.05), alcohol bouts (M1) of the 11 BLA-mPFC mice. Reproduced when p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: The BLA-mPFC alcohol response correlates with alcohol bouts in lower-ranked (ranks 3 and 4) males but not in higher-ranked (ranks 1 and 2) males.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 6c,d legend; Results, BLA–mPFC activity robustly encodes and predicts alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 5
claims.quote: BLA-mPFC alcohol responses correlate with alcohol bout number in lower-ranked (Ranks 3-4) males ( d ; Pearson correlation, r 2 = 0.94, Bonferroni adjusted * p = 0.01) but not higher-ranked (Ranks 1-2) males ( c ; r 2 = 0.42, Bonferroni adjusted p = 1).
claims.criterion: The measures of fig3k-blampfc-response-predicts-bouts split by rank. Bonferroni readings (a) four tests (Extended Data Fig. 6c, d, g, h), (b) two tests (c and d). Reproduced when the lower-rank correlation is positive with corrected p < 0.05 and the higher-rank one has corrected p >= 0.05 under both readings, and both r2 are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Lick-triggered BLA-mPFC terminal stimulation increases alcohol licks in ChR2 mice against eYFP controls, returning to baseline in the recovery session.
claims.source: Figure 4e legend; Results, BLA–mPFC terminal stimulation increases alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 1
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC terminal stimulation increased alcohol drinking in ChR2-expressing males compared with eYFP controls ( N = 6 male mice per group, two-way ANOVA, F (2, 20) = 4.7, * P = 0.02; Tukey’s multiple comparisons test).
claims.criterion: Alcohol licks per session for baseline, stimulation and recovery sessions (Methods, Optogenetic stimulation during 2BC drinking). Two-way ANOVA group by session, session repeated (df 20 = 2 times 10). The legend does not say which effect F(2, 20) is; both the session main effect and the group by session interaction have these df, so both are readings. Baseline is not defined; readings the last baseline session and the mean of the last 3 baseline days (Methods, 2BC drinking). Reproduced when, under every reading, the effect has p < 0.05, Tukey shows ChR2 stimulation above ChR2 baseline, and ChR2 recovery is not above baseline at p < 0.05; methods_underspecified when readings disagree.

claims.statement: BLA-mPFC terminal stimulation does not change sucrose or water drinking.
claims.source: Figure 4c,d legends; Results, BLA–mPFC terminal stimulation increases alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 1
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC terminal stimulation did not alter sucrose ( c , N = 6 male mice per group) or water ( d , N = 6 male mice per group) drinking.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The test is not named; the same two-way ANOVA as fig4e-chr2-increases-alcohol (group by session) on sucrose licks (1% sucrose baseline against stimulation session) and on water licks, at p < 0.05. Reproduced when neither has a significant interaction or group effect.

claims.statement: BLA-mPFC stimulation lengthens alcohol bouts and increases licks per bout in ChR2 mice.
claims.source: Figure 4h,i legends; Results, BLA–mPFC terminal stimulation increases alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC stimulation increased alcohol bout duration ( h ; N = 6 male mice, two-sided unpaired t -test, **** P < 0.0001) and the number of alcohol licks per bout ( i ; N = 6 male mice, two-sided unpaired t -test, **** P < 0.0001).
claims.criterion: Bouts (M1) of ChR2 mice, OFF against ON (stimulation session); an unpaired test with P < 0.0001 from 6 mice implies bouts as units. Every lick onset triggers stimulation in the test session, so OFF is another session, not named; readings the preceding baseline session and the recovery session. Reproduced when, under both readings, both measures are larger ON with two-sided unpaired p < 0.0001; partially when p < 0.05. The same test in eYFP mice (Fig. 4f) is reported; the paper says the effects were absent there.

claims.statement: Stimulation does not change the total number of alcohol bouts.
claims.source: Figure 4g inset; Results, BLA–mPFC terminal stimulation increases alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Analysis of lick microstructure revealed that BLA–mPFC activation prolonged individual alcohol drinking bouts (Fig. 4h ) and increased the number of licks per bout (Fig. 4i ), without changing the total number of bouts (Fig. 4g ).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence; no test named. Read as a two-sided paired t-test over the 6 ChR2 mice, bouts OFF against ON (two groups per Statistics section), p < 0.05. Reproduced when p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Isolation increases mPFC neuron responses to alcohol.
claims.source: Figure 5b legend; Extended Data Fig. 8l legend; Results, Social isolation increases mPFC responses to alcohol while decreasing responses to sucrose in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Social isolation increased mPFC responses to alcohol (group-housed: n = 240 neurons/ N = 6 male mice; social isolation: n = 281 neurons/ N = 5 male mice, one-sided unpaired t -test, ** P = 0.006).
claims.criterion: M3 alcohol responses of mPFC neurons in the alcohol stimulation session before and after isolation (imaging was obtained during the stimulation sessions, Methods, Optogenetic stimulation and calcium imaging during cued-2BC drinking; the neuron counts equal those of Fig. 6c,f). Which trials enter is not said; readings (a) nonstimulated trials only, (b) all trials. Neurons are units. Reproduced when, under both readings, the isolated mean exceeds the group-housed mean with one-sided p < 0.05; the two-sided p of Extended Data Fig. 8l is reported (its p = 0.03 is not twice 0.006, so the two panels may use different trials).

claims.statement: Isolation does not change mPFC responses to water.
claims.source: Figure 5c legend; Results, Social isolation increases mPFC responses to alcohol while decreasing responses to sucrose in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: No detectable effect of social isolation was observed for mPFC responses to water (group-housed: n = 240 neurons/ N = 6 male mice; social isolation: n = 281 neurons/ N = 5 male mice).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence on the test of fig5b-isolation-increases-mpfc-alcohol applied to water bouts, both trial readings; neither direction is stated, so two-sided unpaired t-test at p < 0.05. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 under both.

claims.statement: Isolation decreases mPFC neuron responses to sucrose.
claims.source: Figure 5d legend; Results, Social isolation increases mPFC responses to alcohol while decreasing responses to sucrose in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: In contrast to alcohol, social isolation decreased mPFC responses to sucrose (group-housed: n = 284 neurons/ N = 7 male mice; social isolation: n = 343 neurons/ N = 7 male mice, one-sided unpaired t -test, * P = 0.01).
claims.criterion: As fig5b-isolation-increases-mpfc-alcohol for sucrose bouts of the sucrose stimulation sessions, both trial readings. Reproduced when, under both, the isolated mean is below the group-housed mean with one-sided p < 0.05. Extended Data Fig. 8g says the sucrose responses before and during isolation were not significantly different; that conflict is reported, and the two-sided p is given.

claims.statement: In group-housed mice, mPFC responses to alcohol, sucrose and social interaction do not change between two imaging time points 2 to 3 weeks apart.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 7b–d legend; Results, Social isolation increases mPFC responses to alcohol while decreasing responses to sucrose in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: No effect of time on mean mPFC responses to alcohol drinking in the cued 2-bottle choice drinking task (T1: n = 275 neurons and T2: n = 275 neurons from N = 4 male mice).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. No test is named; read as the two-sided unpaired t-test over neurons of fig5b-isolation-increases-mpfc-alcohol (the paired test is a variant for b, where T1 and T2 counts are equal), at p < 0.05, M3 responses, social bouts with the M3 social baselines. Reproduced when none of alcohol, sucrose and social interaction differs at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In group-housed mice, BLA-mPFC stimulation increases mPFC responses to alcohol, mimicking isolation.
claims.source: Figure 6c legend; Results, BLA–mPFC stimulation mimics social-isolation-induced mPFC responses to alcohol and sucrose in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC stimulation increased mPFC alcohol responses in group-housed mice, mimicking social isolation ( n = 240 neurons/ N = 6 male mice, one-sided paired t -test, * P = 0.03).
claims.criterion: M3 alcohol responses of each neuron on stimulated and nonstimulated choice trials of the group-housed alcohol stimulation session; paired over neurons. Reproduced when stimulated exceeds nonstimulated with one-sided p < 0.05. Extended Data Fig. 8h says stimulation did not alter alcohol responses before isolation; that conflict is reported with the two-sided p.

claims.statement: BLA-mPFC stimulation lowers the proportion of mPFC neurons inhibited by alcohol, without changing the proportion excited.
claims.source: Figure 6d,e legend; Results, BLA–mPFC stimulation mimics social-isolation-induced mPFC responses to alcohol and sucrose in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC stimulation decreased inhibited mPFC alcohol responses ( e ; N = 6 male mice, one-sided paired t -test, t (5) = 4.6, ** P = 0.005) without affecting excited responses ( d ); threshold of ±1.98.
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the percentage of its neurons inhibited (and excited) per M4 threshold on stimulated and on nonstimulated trials, group-housed; paired over mice. Reproduced when the inhibited proportion falls with p < 0.05 and the excited proportion does not change at p < 0.05. The printed P = 0.005 matches a two-sided p for t(5) = 4.6 (one-sided would be about 0.003), so both sidedness readings are shown; the outcome must agree under both.

claims.statement: After isolation, BLA-mPFC stimulation decreases mPFC responses to alcohol.
claims.source: Figure 6f legend; Results, BLA–mPFC stimulation mimics social-isolation-induced mPFC responses to alcohol and sucrose in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC stimulation decreased mPFC alcohol responses during social isolation ( n = 281 neurons/ N = 5 male mice, one-sided paired t -test, * P = 0.02).
claims.criterion: As fig6c-stim-increases-mpfc-alcohol-gh in the isolation session. Reproduced when stimulated is below nonstimulated with one-sided p < 0.05. Extended Data Fig. 8j says stimulation did not alter alcohol responses during isolation; the conflict is reported with the two-sided p.

claims.statement: BLA-mPFC stimulation does not change mPFC responses to water, nor the proportions of excited or inhibited water neurons, before or after isolation.
claims.source: Figure 6g–j legends; Extended Data Fig. 8q,r legend; Results, BLA–mPFC stimulation mimics social-isolation-induced mPFC responses to alcohol and sucrose in males, paragraph 2
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC stimulation had no effect on mPFC water responses in group-housed ( g – i , N = 6) or social isolation ( j , N = 5) male mice.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence on the tests of fig6c-stim-increases-mpfc-alcohol-gh (paired over neurons) and fig6de-stim-fewer-alcohol-inhibited (paired over mice) on water bouts, both housing conditions, at p < 0.05; sidedness not given for absence, so two-sided. Reproduced when none reaches p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In group-housed mice, BLA-mPFC stimulation decreases mPFC responses to sucrose, mimicking isolation.
claims.source: Figure 6k legend; Extended Data Fig. 8c legend; Results, BLA–mPFC stimulation mimics social-isolation-induced mPFC responses to alcohol and sucrose in males, paragraph 3
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC stimulation decreased mPFC sucrose responses in group-housed mice, mimicking social isolation ( n = 284 neurons/ N = 7 male mice, one-sided paired t -test, ** P = 0.008).
claims.criterion: As fig6c-stim-increases-mpfc-alcohol-gh on sucrose bouts of the group-housed sucrose stimulation session. Reproduced when stimulated is below nonstimulated with one-sided p < 0.05.

claims.statement: BLA-mPFC stimulation lowers the proportion of mPFC neurons excited by sucrose, without changing the proportion inhibited.
claims.source: Figure 6l,m legend; Results, BLA–mPFC stimulation mimics social-isolation-induced mPFC responses to alcohol and sucrose in males, paragraph 3
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC stimulation decreased excited mPFC sucrose responses ( l ; N = 7 male mice, one-sided paired t -test, t (6) = 2.76, * P = 0.03) without affecting inhibited responses ( m ); threshold of ±1.98.
claims.criterion: As fig6de-stim-fewer-alcohol-inhibited on sucrose, group-housed. Reproduced when the excited proportion falls with p < 0.05 and the inhibited proportion does not change at p < 0.05. The printed P = 0.03 matches a two-sided p for t(6) = 2.76; both sidedness readings are shown.

claims.statement: After isolation, BLA-mPFC stimulation no longer changes mPFC responses to sucrose.
claims.source: Figure 6n legend; Extended Data Fig. 8e legend; Results, BLA–mPFC stimulation mimics social-isolation-induced mPFC responses to alcohol and sucrose in males, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Social isolation occluded BLA–mPFC stimulation effects on mPFC sucrose responses ( n = 343 neurons/ N = 7 male mice).
claims.criterion: A claim of absence on the paper's paired t-test over neurons (as fig6k), stimulated against nonstimulated in the isolation sucrose session; read two-sided at p < 0.05. Reproduced when p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: During isolation, BLA-mPFC stimulation lowers the proportion of mPFC neurons inhibited by sucrose, with no change in those excited.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 8m,n legend
claims.quote: BLA-mPFC stimulation significantly decreased the proportion of mPFC neurons inhibited to sucrose ( n ; paired t-test, ** p = 0.005) with no effect on mPFC neurons excited to sucrose ( m ), based on a mean Z-score response ±1.98, during social isolation.
claims.criterion: As fig6lm-stim-fewer-sucrose-excited in the isolation sucrose session, paired over mice, two-sided. Reproduced when the inhibited proportion falls with p < 0.05 and the excited proportion does not change at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: During isolation, BLA-mPFC stimulation does not change the proportions of mPFC neurons excited or inhibited by alcohol.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 8o,p legend
claims.quote: BLA-mPFC stimulation did not alter the proportion of mPFC neurons responsive to alcohol during social isolation.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. No test is named; the test of the neighbouring panels (Extended Data Fig. 8m,n), a two-sided paired t-test over the 5 mice of the isolation alcohol stimulation session, on the percentages of neurons excited and inhibited per M4 threshold, stimulated against nonstimulated trials, at p < 0.05. Reproduced when neither reaches p < 0.05.

claims.statement: During isolation, NpHR inhibition of BLA-mPFC terminals decreases the number of alcohol bouts, without changing water drinking.
claims.source: Figure 6q legend; Results, BLA–mPFC inhibition during social isolation reduces alcohol drinking in males, paragraph 1
claims.quote: BLA–mPFC inhibition decreased alcohol bouts ( N = 8 male mice per group, two-way ANOVA, main effect of stimulation: F (1,13) = 9.707, ** P = 0.008; Sidak’s post hoc test, * P = 0.05).
claims.criterion: Alcohol bouts (M1) on inhibited and noninhibited choice trials of the isolation inhibition session; two-way ANOVA group by stimulation, stimulation repeated (df 13 implies 15 mice). Bouts read as counts per condition; per-trial rates are a variant (equal halves of choice trials make them proportional). Reproduced when the stimulation effect has p < 0.05 with fewer bouts on inhibited trials in NpHR mice (Sidak p <= 0.05), and the same ANOVA on water bouts finds no stimulation effect or interaction at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: About 30% of mPFC neurons are co-registered across all four social sessions.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9c legend
claims.quote: ~ 30% of mPFC neurons co-registered across all four sessions
claims.criterion: CellReg on CNMF-E footprints (Methods). The denominator is not given; readings (a) neurons of the reference session, (b) the mean neuron count over the four sessions, (c) all distinct registered cells. Reproduced when one reading is within tolerance, as the protocol allows for denominators. If the dataset holds only the co-registered 199 neurons the claim cannot be tested.

claims.statement: Isolation decreases mPFC responses to social interaction.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9e legend
claims.quote: Isolation decreases mPFC responses to interaction ( n = 199 neurons/ N = 6 male mice, two-way RM-ANOVA, interaction: F (49, 19404) = 1.538, ** p = 0.009).
claims.criterion: M3 z traces of the 199 co-registered neurons around interaction-bout onsets (UMAP social clusters, Methods, SLEAP) on no-stimulation sessions, before and after isolation. 50 time points (df 49) at 10 Hz; readings 0 to 5 s after onset, and -2.5 to 2.5 s. Baselines 3 s and 5 s (M3). Reproduced when the time by housing interaction has p < 0.05 and the isolation trace is below the group-housed trace after onset, under every reading.

claims.statement: BLA-mPFC stimulation does not change mPFC responses to social interaction before isolation but increases them during isolation.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9f,g legend
claims.quote: BLA-mPFC stimulation did not affect mPFC responses before isolation ( n = 199 co-registered neurons from N = 6 male mice). g . BLA-mPFC stimulation increases mPFC responses during isolation ( n = 199 neurons/ N = 6 male mice, two-way ANOVA, interaction: F (49, 7350) = 1.631, ** p = 0.003).
claims.criterion: As ed9e-isolation-decreases-social-response, stimulation against no-stimulation session in each housing condition. Reproduced when the isolation interaction has p < 0.05 with stimulated above and the group-housed interaction has p >= 0.05. The error df 7350 (150 times 49) does not match 199 neurons; this is reported, not resolved.

claims.statement: In group-housed mice, mPFC social responses with and without stimulation are negatively correlated across neurons (stimulation inverts their sign); during isolation they are uncorrelated.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9h,i legend; Results, BLA–mPFC stimulation mimics social-isolation-induced mPFC responses to alcohol and sucrose in males, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Stimulation and no-stimulation mPFC responses are negatively correlated in group-housed mice ( h ; n = 199 neurons/ N = 6 male mice, Pearson correlation, r 2 = 0.02, Bonferroni adjusted * p = 0.04) but uncorrelated during isolation ( i ; r 2 = 0.0, p = 1).
claims.criterion: Per neuron, scalar M3 social response (0 to 3 s) with and without stimulation. The Bonferroni family is not stated. A two-test family cannot give the printed p = 0.04: with r2 = 0.02 and 199 neurons the uncorrected p is about 0.046, and r2 below 0.025 keeps the doubled p above 0.05. Readings (a) uncorrected, (b) two tests, reported both; the outcome is judged on (a), the only reading consistent with the printed numbers. Reproduced when the group-housed r is negative with p < 0.05 and the isolation correlation has p >= 0.05, under both baseline readings.

claims.statement: In group-housed mice mPFC activity decodes social interaction above chance with and without stimulation; isolation abolishes decoding without stimulation and lowers accuracy, and BLA-mPFC stimulation raises accuracy in both housing conditions, rescuing it after isolation.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9k–o legends
claims.quote: mPFC decodes interaction above chance under both conditions (two-way ANOVA, main effect of group: F(1,36) = 54.29, **** p < 0.0001; ... m . Isolation decreases mPFC decoding accuracy (unpaired t-test, * p = 0.02). n,o . BLA-mPFC stimulation increases decoding accuracy in group-housed ( n , unpaired t-test, * p = 0.01) and isolation ( o , unpaired t-test, * p = 0.005) conditions.
claims.criterion: M5 with interaction against noninteraction bouts (noninteraction bouts over 20 s split, bouts 2 s apart; Methods) for each of the four sessions. The df 36 imply 10 accuracy values per cell, so k = 10 folds here (readings: 10 folds; 5 folds repeated twice). Panels k and l are read as one two-way ANOVA per housing condition, data (real, shuffled) by stimulation, over fold accuracies (2 by 2 by 10 values, error df 36). Reproduced when, under every reading, the group-housed ANOVA has a real against shuffled main effect at p < 0.05 with real above shuffled in both stimulation conditions (Sidak); the isolation ANOVA has a data by stimulation interaction at p < 0.05, with isolation no-stimulation accuracy not above shuffled and stimulation accuracy above shuffled (Sidak); isolation no-stimulation accuracy is below group-housed no-stimulation (unpaired p < 0.05); and stimulation exceeds no-stimulation in both housing conditions (unpaired p < 0.05). Partially reproduced when some but not all of these hold.

claims.statement: BLA-mPFC stimulation recruits an mPFC ensemble resembling the isolation pattern, with greater overlap of excited neurons than in the group-housed comparison.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 9p–r legends; Results, BLA–mPFC stimulation mimics social-isolation-induced mPFC responses to alcohol and sucrose in males, paragraph 4
claims.quote: BLA-mPFC stimulation recruits a mPFC ensemble resembling isolation-induced patterns, with greater overlap of excited neurons vs. group-housed ( n = 199 neurons/ N = 6 male mice , Chi 2 = 6.94, * p = 0.03).
claims.criterion: Excited neurons by M4 in each session. The contingency table is not given; readings (a) among neurons excited by stimulation in the group-housed session, those also excited in the isolation no-stimulation session, against those also excited in the group-housed no-stimulation session; (b) clusters from the concatenated clustering (Extended Data Fig. 9p) cross-tabulated by session.
