OLS of each session's mean OL latent distance on session order, per participant. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 in both participants; not reproduced when p < 0.05 in either. Slopes are reported either way.

claims.statement: CL latent distances between actions increase across days in both participants (slope 1.655 in B1, 2.371 in B3).
claims.source: Results, Changes in representational statistics with closed-loop control, paragraph 2; Figure 2K-L
claims.quote: CL was characterized by a striking increase in separability (via a random intercept LMM over CL1 and CL2, B1: β = 1.655 ± 0.563 , t ( 18 ) = 2.937, p = 0.0087 , Fig. 2 K ; B3: β = 2.371 ± 0.495 , t ( 20 ) = 4.786 , p = 1 × 10 – 3 , Fig. 2L )
claims.criterion: Methods (trend paragraph). Per participant, a mixed model of session mean latent distance on session order over CL1 and CL2 together, with CL1 and CL2 as random intercepts; p is the fraction of 1000 permutations (day order shuffled within CL1 and within CL2) whose |t| is at least the observed. The slope is in the latent space's own units, which depend on each autoencoder; the values are read as approximate. Reproduced when both slopes are positive with p < 0.05 and within tolerance; partially reproduced when both are positive and significant but outside tolerance.

claims.statement: In the full feature space, too, CL distances increase across days while OL distances stay stable, in both participants.
claims.source: Figure S6G-H legend; Results, Changes in representational statistics with closed-loop control, paragraph 2
claims.quote: A linear mixed effect (LME) model combining CL1 and CL2 showed a significant increase in the separation between movements across-days (magenta line with slope indicated, t ( 18 ) = 2.1213 , p = 0.048 )
claims.criterion: As fig2kl-ol-distance-stable and fig2kl-cl-distance-increase, on the mean pairwise Mahalanobis distance of each session's features instead of latent values. Open detail. "Full high dimensional neural data" is not defined for B1; readings (a) the 96 decoder features (2x2 pooled, L2-normalized), (b) the 384 unpooled channel features. B3 uses its 759 features. The outcome is the one both readings give; if they differ, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified. Reproduced when the CL slope is positive with p < 0.05 and the OL slope has p >= 0.05, in both participants.

claims.statement: Across sessions, the mean latent distance between actions predicts the session's decoding accuracy (leave-one-out logistic regression, better than permuted data), in both participants.
claims.source: Results, Changes in representational statistics with closed-loop control, paragraph 2; Figure 2M-N
claims.quote: These across-days increases in average distances were significantly predictive of improved decoding accuracies in B1 and B3 ( Fig. 2M and 2N , leave-one-out cross validated logistic regression with permutation B1: CV log loss of 0.51, p = 0.002 , B3: CV log loss of 0.392, p = 0.002 )
claims.criterion: Methods (paragraph on logistic regression). Per participant, the points are the sessions' OL, CL1 and CL2 values (the Methods say accuracy "from each individual session", and the figure plots each session's distance against its accuracy); logistic regression of accuracy (a proportion) on mean latent distance; leave-one-out log loss averaged over points; p is the fraction of 1000 permutations of the accuracies whose log loss is smaller. Open details. (1) Whether points are 30 and 33 (all three contexts) or 10 and 11 (one per session); readings (a) all contexts, (b) CL2 only, (c) mean of the contexts. (2) The fit with a fractional outcome; reading a binomial GLM with the proportion as response, unweighted. Reproduced when under one reading of (1) both p < 0.05 and both losses are within tolerance; partially reproduced when both p < 0.05 only.

claims.statement: Daily autoencoder manifolds are similar across days (CKA); in B1, 80% of day pairs have all five layers significantly similar and the rest at least four; in B3, 83.64% have all five, 12.72% four and 3.64% three.
claims.source: Results, Stability of action representations, paragraph 1; Figure 3C
claims.quote: In B1, 80% of all pairwise comparisons had all 5 layers significantly similar; the remaining 20% had at least 4 of 5 similar layers. In B3, 83.64% of all pairwise comparisons had all layers similar; 12.72% had at least 4 of 5 similar layers and the remaining 3.64% had at least 3 of the 5 similar layers
claims.criterion: Methods (Representational stability analyses). For each pair of days, linear CKA between the two autoencoders' activations at each of the five hidden layers (48, 16, 2, 16, 48 units), activations mean-centered; the null is 1000 CKA values after randomly shuffling the weights and biases of the two layers compared; p is the fraction of null values at least the observed; FDR at 0.05 over all layers and pairs. Open details. (1) Which samples are fed to both networks, which CKA needs to match; readings (a) the pooled samples of both days, (b) day X's samples through both networks and day Y's through both, averaging the two CKAs. (2) What "shuffled" permutes; readings (a) entries of the layer's weight matrix and bias vector are permuted, (b) the layer's units (rows) are permuted. There are 45 day pairs in B1 and 55 in B3, five layers each. Reproduced when both "all 5" fractions are within tolerance and no B1 pair has fewer than 4 similar layers; partially reproduced when at least 75% of pairs in each participant have at least 4 similar layers. (1) and (2) are method details, so the outcome is the one all four combinations give; if they differ, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In B1, daily initialized ReFit-KF velocity commands are less discernible between targets in latent space than the discrete actions; feedforward commands are more discernible than all commands within 45 degrees.
claims.source: Figure S7B legend; Results, Stability of action representations, paragraph 2
claims.quote: daily initialized discrete representations had greater median Mahalanobis distances between targets across sessions as compared to daily initialized early feedforward velocity commands (first ~ 2.5 s , Mann Whitney U test p = 1.2 × 10 - 5 ) or all intended velocity commands to the target within a 45 degree tolerance
claims.criterion: Methods (Representational analyses of denovo BCI velocity commands). Five days of ReFit-KF data in B1, six target classes, daily autoencoders on OL, CL1 and CL2 bins, either the first 2.5 s of each trial or all bins whose decoded velocity is within 45 degrees of the target; the session value is the mean pairwise latent distance; CL1 and CL2 values are pooled and compared with the discrete sessions' CL values by Mann Whitney U. Reproduced when all three tests give p < 0.05 in the stated directions.

claims.statement: In B1, the daily manifolds of ReFit-KF velocity commands are much less stable across days than those of discrete actions; most day pairs (65%) share no similar layer, feedforward commands never do, and commands within 45 degrees share 1.5 layers on average.
claims.source: Figure S7C-D legend; Results, Stability of action representations, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Specifically, the majority of the pairwise comparisons (65%, averaged for both types of commands) between individual days’ autoencoders had no significantly similar layers between them
claims.criterion: As fig3c-manifold-stable, with its readings, on the ReFit-KF daily autoencoders; the layer-wise CKA values of all day pairs are compared between command types by Mann Whitney U. Reproduced when the 65% and 1.5 values are within tolerance, no feedforward day pair has a similar layer, and the three tests give p < 0.05 with discrete highest. As in fig3c-manifold-stable, the outcome is the one all combinations of its readings give; if they differ, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Trajectories to cardinal targets deviate less from the straight line under IBID than under the ReFit-KF.
claims.source: Figure S7I legend; Results, PnP control of a virtual robotic arm, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Results revealed greater median error in trajectories when using ReFit-KF after closed-loop decoder adaptation as compared to IBID after closed-loop decoder adaptation (Mann Whitney U test, z = 6.967 , p = 3.2442 × 10 - 12 )
claims.criterion: Methods (Robot kinematics analyses). Per trial, the square root of the summed squared differences between decoded and ideal straight-line positions over all time points, divided by the number of points; Mann Whitney U between IBID and ReFit-KF CL2 trials. Open detail. The Results name 48 IBID and 18 ReFit-KF trials on one testing day, but with 48 and 18 values a Mann Whitney z cannot exceed about 6.2, below the reported 6.967; the reported test therefore used more values (more trials or sessions, or per-time-point errors), which the paper does not say. The test is run on per-trial errors as the Methods define them, and the z and p are not expected to match. Reproduced when p < 0.05 with the ReFit-KF median higher.

claims.statement: For right thumb OL trials in B1, the mean high-gamma map is preserved across three days (average pairwise r = 0.88), but channel-level high-gamma means over M1/S1 differ between days.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 1; Figure 4A-B
claims.quote: Even with a preserved neural map and somatotopy (average pairwise r = 0.88 ), there was little distributional overlap between days ( Fig. 4B , permutation t – tests show significant differences in γ H mean over trials, Day 1 vs. Day 4, t ( 11 ) = 17.87 , p = 1 × 10 – 4
claims.criterion: Open details, as the paper names neither which three days (called "three random days"; the tests name days 1, 4 and 8), nor which channels form the M1/S1 rectangle, nor what the 12 observations behind t(11) are. Readings (a) days 1, 4 and 8 of the daily sessions, channels the dataset marks as M1/S1 hand area, a paired permutation t-test over 12 channels of trial-mean high gamma; (b) the same days, a two-sample permutation t-test over trials of the mean over those channels. Reproduced when under one reading the mean pairwise map correlation is within tolerance and day 1 differs from days 4 and 8 with p < 0.05; partially reproduced when only the differences hold. The day 4 against day 8 result is reported.

claims.statement: The recording day can be decoded from held-out OL samples on a common multi-day manifold (90.96% in B1, chance 10%; 98.4% in B3, chance 9.09%).
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 1; Figure 4C-D
claims.quote: In general, the recording day could be classified from held-out samples on the common manifold ( Fig. 4C – D B1: cross-validated decoding accuracy of 90.96% [90.68% - 91.24%], chance = 10%, B3: cross-validated decoding accuracy of 98.4% [98.24% - 98.54%], chance = 9.09%)
claims.criterion: Methods (Across-day drifts in centroids). OL samples of all days (about 22k), 40 random splits of 68% training, 12% validation and 20% test; an autoencoder as in fig2i-distance-cl-vs-ol trained with day labels as additional class memberships; accuracy of the classification layer for the day of recording on test samples, averaged over splits. Open details. (1) How day labels enter; readings (a) the classifier layer has one unit per day, (b) one unit per day and action combination, scored on day. (2) Whether samples are split by sample or by trial; the Methods say samples, so (a) by sample, with (b) by trial shown as a variant. The interval tolerances are the paper's own and very narrow; the claim is reproduced when both accuracies are within their tolerance, and partially reproduced when both are within 10% of the reported values and far above chance. (1) is a method detail, so the outcome is the one both readings give; if they differ, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: After mean-centering each day's data, the recording day can no longer be decoded (B1 10.03%, B3 8.77%, not different from chance).
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 1; Figure 4C-D
claims.quote: In contrast, centering and demeaning each day’ data before building a common manifold eliminated discernibility ( Fig. 4C , B1 decoding accuracy: 10.03% [9.71% - 10.37%], chance = 10%, WSR: p = 0.282 , Fig. 4D : decoding accuracy of 8.77% [8.617% - 9.138%], chance = 9.09%, WSR: p = 0.3 )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. As fig4cd-day-decodable after subtracting each day's mean from its samples; a Wilcoxon signed rank test of the 40 split accuracies against chance (10% in B1, 9.09% in B3). Reproduced when p >= 0.05 in both participants; not reproduced when p < 0.05 in either. The accuracies are reported.

claims.statement: A two-layer MLP on the full feature space also decodes the recording day from held-out trials, significantly above chance in both participants.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 1; Figure S8A-B
claims.quote: A MLP in high-dimensional channel-feature space revealed similar significant trial-level decoding accuracies ( Fig. S8A – B )
claims.criterion: Methods (Across-day drifts, paragraph on the MLP). Trials of all days split 70/15/15 by trial, 10 random splits; MLP with two layers of 64 units, leaky ReLU, dropout 0.4, trained on samples; trial-level day accuracy averaged over splits; p from the binomial (as in fig2e-above-chance) with the number of held-out trials and chance 1/10 (B1) or 1/11 (B3). Open detail. How a trial's samples give its label is not stated for this decoder; readings (a) max vote over the trial's samples, as for the other trial-level decoders (Methods, Action decoding), (b) the fraction of the trial's samples decoded correctly, averaged over trials. The outcome is the one both readings give; if they differ, blocked as methods_underspecified. Reproduced when p < 0.05 in both participants.

claims.statement: Distances between actions on held-out days increase linearly with the number of prior days used to build the common manifold, in both participants.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 2; Figure 4F-G
claims.quote: we found that the pairwise distances between actions on a given day linearly increased as a function of the number of prior days used to build the common manifold (robust linear regression on median Mahalanobis distances, B1: slope b = 0.258 , z = 6.474 , p = 1.847 × 10 – 10 , Fig. 4F
claims.criterion: Methods (Across-day drifts, paragraph on cumulative days). For k = 1 to n - 1 days, an OL autoencoder is built on days 1 to k (as in fig2i-distance-cl-vs-ol); each held-out day k+1 to n is projected and its mean pairwise latent distance taken; the median over held-out days is regressed robustly on k. Open details. (1) The robust weighting is not named; readings (a) bisquare (MATLAB robustfit default), (b) Huber. (2) The statistic is called z, which suggests a normal approximation on 9 or 10 points; the p is taken from the fit as reported by the software. (3) The printed slope is identical for B1 and B3, so it belongs to one of them and the paper does not say which; readings (a) it is B1's, (b) it is B3's. Reproduced when both slopes are positive with p < 0.05 and the slope of the participant named by reading (a) or (b) is within tolerance (either reading may match); partially reproduced when both are positive and significant only. (1) is a method detail, so the outcome is the one both weightings give; if they differ, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In B1, a boundary between two hand actions trained on more prior days generalizes better to a new day, with decoding accuracy rising by 5.5 points per added day.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 2; Figure 4I
claims.quote: in B1 trends in decoding performance assessed via linear regression, slope, b = 5.541 ± 0.966 , t ( 8 ) = 5.735 , p = 4.365 × 10 – 4
claims.criterion: Methods (Across-day drifts, last paragraph). A two-layer MLP in the common latent space classifies left thumb against both middle fingers, trained on days 1 to k (k = 1 to 10) and tested on a day distinct from the 10 daily sessions; OLS of accuracy on k. Open details. The held-out day is not identified ("a new day distinct from the 10 daily experimental days"); the MLP width is not given; 64 units per layer, as for the day-decoding MLP, is a standard choice, not the paper's, and widths 32 and 128 are shown as variants. Reproduced when the slope is positive with p < 0.05 and within tolerance; if the widths give different outcomes, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In B1's first PnP experiment (fixed MLP, 28 days) the average accuracy was 87.43%, time to target 1.195 s and bit rate 1.72 bps.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 3; Figure 5A-C
claims.quote: The average accuracy across the entire PnP period was 87.43% [84.0%–90.8%] and the average time to target was 1.195 s [1.087s – 1.33s] ( Fig. 5A – B ). This resulted in a mean bitrate of 1.72 bps [1.51 – 1.94]
claims.criterion: Methods (Discrete PnP experiments; PnP experiments, performance metrics). A trial's output is the first non-zero output of the 5-bin mode filter (the action decoded in more than 50% of the accumulated above-threshold bins, ties giving none, OSF code runningMode.m); a trial is accurate when that output is the cued action, and its time is from trial start to that output; trials time out at 5 s. Bit rate per block is log2(C - 1) max(0, N_acc - N_fail) / T with C = 7, T the block's total time. Open details. (1) Whether the averages are over blocks or pooled over trials; readings (a) mean of block values, (b) pooled trials, (c) mean of daily values. (2) Timed-out trials count as failures with 5 s, the reading the bit-rate formula implies. Reproduced when under one reading of (1) all three values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: In B1's second PnP experiment (38 days, decoder updated with the first experiment's data) the average accuracy was 80.71%, time to target 0.875 s and bit rate 1.848 bps.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 3; Figure 5D-F
claims.quote: The average accuracy was 80.71% [77.6% – 83.5%] and the average time to target was 0.875 s [0.842 s – 0.917 s ] resulting in an effective mean bit rate of 1.848 bps [1.68 – 2.02]
claims.criterion: As fig5abc-pnp1-b1, with its readings.

claims.statement: Bit rates do not differ between B1's two PnP experiments.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 3
claims.quote: There were no significant differences in performance between the two PnP experiments (Mann-Whitney U test on bitrates z = – 0.9574 , p = 0.338 )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Mann-Whitney U on the block bit rates of the two experiments; reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05. The difference in medians is reported.

claims.statement: Daily median PnP accuracy shows no linear trend across days in either B1 experiment or in B3.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 3; Figure S8C-E
claims.quote: a linear fit to the daily median revealed stable performance across-days for both ( Fig. S8C – D , p = 0.897 for PnP Exp 1 and p = 0.11 for PnP Exp 2)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. OLS of each PnP day's median accuracy (median over blocks) on day, per experiment. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 in all three experiments; not reproduced when p < 0.05 in any. Slopes are reported.

claims.statement: Over both B1 PnP experiments the mean effective bit rate was 1.8 bps, with a maximum of 3.351 bps.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Across both experiments, the mean effective bit rate was 1.8 bps [1.66 – 1.93] and the highest was 3.351 bps
claims.criterion: As fig5abc-pnp1-b1, pooling the blocks of both experiments; the maximum is over blocks. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: In B3's PnP experiment (39 days) the average accuracy was 84.9%, time to target 0.818 s and bit rate 2.22 bps (maximum 3.508 bps), and accuracy stayed stable across days.
claims.source: Results, Plug-and-play control in presence of distributional drift, paragraph 4; Figure 5G-I
claims.quote: The average accuracy was 84.9% [82.14% – 87.43%], and the average time to target was 0.818 s [0.789 s – 0.848 s ] with a mean bit rate of 2.22 bps [2.046 bps – 2.394 bps ] (maximum of 3.508 bps )
claims.criterion: As fig5abc-pnp1-b1, with its readings. Stability is claim figs8cde-pnp-stable.

claims.statement: Under IBID, the angular error between integrated and ideal diagonal velocities is centred on zero (mean 1.885 degrees, not different from zero), showing integrated off-axis control.
claims.source: Results, PnP control of a virtual robotic arm, paragraph 3; Figure 6G
claims.quote: The mean of this circular distribution was 1.885 degrees [95% C.I. −1.44 degrees to 5.206 degrees] and not significantly different from zero (circular median, p = 0.348 )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test (Methods, Robot kinematics analyses), the CircStat circular median test (circ_medtest) of the instantaneous angular errors between IBID velocities and the ideal diagonal velocity, over all time points and trials to diagonal XY targets; reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05. The circular mean and its interval are reported (expected value with the paper's interval). The Methods take the errors "across time and trials", so the test is run on all time points; excluding time points with zero velocity is shown as a variant only, since a claim of absence is judged on the paper's test as written.

claims.statement: PCA of velocities during diagonal reaches shows covariation between X and Y velocity, unlike the non-integrated null model whose components recapitulate the cardinal axes.
claims.source: Results, PnP control of a virtual robotic arm, paragraph 3; Figure 6F-G
claims.quote: In contrast, data revealed significant velocity covariation due to the integration in IBID ( Fig. 6G , left, middle)
claims.criterion: Methods (Robot kinematics analyses). PCA of 2D (X, Y) velocities over the diagonal trials. The paper calls the covariation "significant" but gives no test, threshold or number for it, in the Methods or the legend. The attempt reports the PC loadings and angles. As a variant only, it reports whether the first component lies more than 20 degrees from both cardinal axes with both loadings above 0.3 in absolute value; this threshold is not the paper's and cannot decide the outcome. The claim is recorded as methods_underspecified, with the loadings shown.

claims.statement: B1 used the PnP decoder proficiently under changed visual perspectives, with 86% (allocentric) and 94% (left-handed) accuracy over 42 trials each.
claims.source: Results, PnP control of a virtual robotic arm, paragraph 4; Figure S8H-I
claims.quote: We found that B1 could immediately and proficiently use the decoder even with significant visual perturbations, with 86% and 94% decoding accuracies when operating the PnP decoder from either an allocentric or left-handed reference frame respectively (42 trials each
claims.criterion: Trial accuracy as for the PnP experiments (fig5abc-pnp1-b1), over the 42 trials of each perturbation. Reproduced when both are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Imagined coactivations of two actions are discernible from the single actions.
claims.source: Results, PnP control of a virtual robotic arm, paragraph 3; Figure S8G
claims.quote: B1 was also able to access off-axis directions by coactivating multiple representations simultaneously
claims.criterion: Methods (Coactivations of representations). A decoder (3-layer MLP of 64 units, as for the PnP decoder) classifies right thumb or right hand, left leg, head and the coactivations; trial accuracy by max vote. The legend reports "significant discernability" without naming the test; the paper's test of decoder significance elsewhere (Methods, Action decoding) is the binomial test of fig2e-above-chance, used here with m the number of classes (five, right hand, left leg, head and the two coactivations, per the Methods). Reproduced when it gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: B1 reached 100% accuracy with the mode switch in the virtual reach-to-grasp and transport task after about one week of practice, with a median completion time of 45 s.
claims.source: Results, Flexible control of reaching and grasping, paragraph 2; Figure 7D-E
claims.quote: B1 gained rapid proficiency in using the mode-switch with 100% accuracy after ~1 week of practice ( Fig. 7D – E , median task completion time of 45s)
claims.criterion: Over the 10 sessions of the task. Open detail. Which sessions count as "after ~1 week" and which trials the median time is over; readings (a) sessions from day 7 on, (b) the last session, (c) all sessions for the median time. Reproduced when under one reading the success rate is within tolerance and the median time is within tolerance.

claims.statement: With the fixed RNN, B1 completed the real-world reach and rotate task with a median success rate of 90% and completion times of 60.8 s.
claims.source: Results, Long-term control of grasping and object manipulation using the Kinova Jaco robot, paragraph 1; Figure 7I-J
claims.quote: The median success rate was 90% with task completion times of 60.8 s [54.76 s – 76.95 s ]
claims.criterion: Methods (Robot reach-to-grasp metrics). A trial succeeds only when all phases are completed and the reoriented object is placed at the target; completion time runs from the start of robot control to gripper release. Open details. (1) The median success rate is over days or blocks; readings (a) per day, (b) per block. (2) Whether 60.8 s is a median or a mean of successful trials; readings (a) median, (b) mean. Reproduced when under one reading both values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: In the wall task, B1 reached and grasped the object off the wall proficiently across the whole PnP window (median success 100%, mean 94.6%, median time 38.053 s).
claims.source: Results, Long-term control of grasping and object manipulation using the Kinova Jaco robot, paragraph 1; Figure 7K top
claims.quote: B1 was able to perform the first part (reach and grasp the target off the wall center) proficiently across the entire PnP testing window and for all levels of approach difficulty ( Fig. 7K top, median success rate of 100%, mean of 94.6%, median time to reach and grasp object 38.053 s [26.825 s – 45.458 s ])
claims.criterion: As fig7ij-reach-rotate, for the first part of the wall task (object grasped off the wall), over all PnP days before recalibration, with the same readings of the median.

claims.statement: Full wall-task success declined after PnP day 35 (median 88.19% over the first 35 days against 69.05% over days 35 to 210), with longer completion times.
claims.source: Results, Long-term control of grasping and object manipulation using the Kinova Jaco robot, paragraph 1; Figure 7K bottom, 7L
claims.quote: Here, we observed a drop in performance after PnP day 35 (first 35 days median accuracy of 88.19%, total task completion time 75.52 s [70.22 s – 85.326 s ]; days 35–210 median accuracy of 69.05%, total task completion time 104.854 s [94.648 s – 126.639 s ])
claims.criterion: As fig7ij-reach-rotate, for the full wall task. Open detail. Day 35 falls in both ranges as printed; readings (a) day 35 in the first period, (b) in the second. Reproduced when under one reading the four values are within tolerance and the later median success is lower; partially reproduced when the later success is lower but values fall outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Recalibrating the RNN with about 8 min of data immediately restored full wall-task success to 100%, with a median completion time of 80.73 s.
claims.source: Results, Long-term control of grasping and object manipulation using the Kinova Jaco robot, paragraph 2; Figure 7K-L
claims.quote: Notably, recalibration of the RNN (data required for decoder update was ~8 min, Methods ), immediately improved the success rate to 100% with a median completion time of 80.73 s [51.277 s – 108.247 s ]
claims.criterion: As fig7ij-reach-rotate, over the wall-task trials after recalibration (day 0 in Figure 7K). Reproduced when both values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The biLSTM decoder was trained on about 14 hours and 48 minutes of open-loop and closed-loop data from B1's virtual and real-world hDoF experiments, before augmentation and segmentation.
claims.source: Methods, RNN decoders based on spatiotemporal activity patterns, paragraph 2
claims.quote: By the point we got to training a LSTM, we had already collected roughly 14 hours and 48 minutes of experimental open-loop and closed-loop data (prior to data augmentation and segmentation) in the virtual 3D environment and with practice with the Kinova Jaco in the real-world using the MLP
claims.criterion: The total duration of the trials used to train the RNN, before segmentation. Open detail. Which part of a trial counts; the RNN segments come from "the active portions of the task" (Methods), and the OSF code (get_lstm_features.m) takes task states 2 and 3 and pads from state 4; readings (a) the whole stored trial, (b) the active (cue and control) portion only. The dataset may also hold the later real-world fine-tuning trials, which the 14 h 48 min precede; when it labels contexts, the duration is shown with and without real-robot fine-tuning trials. Reproduced when under one reading the duration is within tolerance.

claims.statement: In B1, 2x2 spatial pooling of the grid makes single-trial high-gamma activity more consistent and improves online decoding in pilot blocks.
claims.source: Figure S3C and S3F legend
claims.quote: A Mann Whitney U test revealed significant differences in median variance between pooled and unpooled channels ( z = 8.721 , p = 2.748 × 10 - 18 )
claims.criterion: Methods (Spatial feature extraction). Variance over time and trials of binned (200 ms) high gamma during right thumb trials, per channel, for the 128 raw channels against the 32 channels after a 1 s running average and 2x2 pooling with stride 2; Mann Whitney U. The block accuracy comparison uses online pilot blocks, which only the online decodes can give. Reproduced when the variance test gives p < 0.05 with pooled lower; the accuracy part is reported when testable.

claims.statement: The dandiset's somatic current-step recordings are those behind the paper's somatic excitability figures, and the spike counts computed from them agree with the paper's per-cell tables.
claims.source: Figures 1E, 3C, 6C, 7C and 9D; the paper's tables at Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.17307059
claims.criterion: Groups are matched by name. Each dandiset cell is compared with every row of the paper's table for its group over the steps from 20 to 300 pA present in both, and its best match is the row with the smallest summed absolute difference in spike counts. The link holds (reproduced) when, over all groups the dandiset holds, the cell counts per group equal the paper's n, and at least 80% of cells have an exact match and at least 95% a best match within 3 spikes in total. Partially reproduced when at least 50% match exactly; not reproduced otherwise. Rheobase agreement with the best match is reported.

claims.statement: The dandiset's dendritic line scans are those behind the paper's dendritic excitability index figures, and the index computed from them agrees with the paper's per-cell values.
claims.source: Figures 1I, 3F, 6D and 7F; the paper's tables at Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.17307059
claims.criterion: Where the paper's table names cells by date and letter (Figure 6D), cells are matched by that identifier (letter a, b, c for the first, second and third cell of the day). Elsewhere the paper's rows are taken to follow the dandiset's order by date and cell number, an assumption checked by the somatic link, where rows follow that order. Reproduced when the counts of cells with an index equal the paper's n in at least 7 of the 10 groups and the matched values differ from the paper's by a median of at most 10% of the paper's value. Partially reproduced when only one of these holds.

claims.statement: The dandiset's Sr2+-oEPSC recordings are cells of the paper's Figures 2 and 4, and their events agree with the paper's per-cell values.
claims.source: Figures 2G to 2I and 4F to 4H; the paper's tables at Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.17307059
claims.criterion: Cells are matched by date and session letter (the paper's identifiers are the date followed by a letter). Reports the fraction of the paper's cells that are in the dandiset and, for those, the events found by lid.detect_events against the paper's event counts and mean amplitudes. Reproduced when every dandiset cell matches a paper identifier and the per-cell mean amplitude and event count are within 25% of the paper's for at least 75% of cells; partially reproduced when every cell matches but the values do not; not reproduced when cells do not match.

claims.statement: The dandiset's GRAB-ACh recordings are regions of the paper's Figure 5F, and the normalised areas computed from them agree with the paper's per-region values.
claims.source: Figure 5F; the paper's tables at Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.17307059
claims.criterion: The paper's regions carry no identifier that links them to the dandiset's mice, so each mouse's vector of single-pulse areas (no drug, quinpirole, sulpiride, and dopamine where present) is matched to the paper's region in the same group with the smallest summed absolute difference. Reproduced when the counts per group are those of the paper and every mouse has a match within 0.05 per treatment; partially reproduced when the dandiset holds part of the regions and at least half of its mice match within 0.05 per treatment; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The dandiset's AIM score tables are mice of the paper's Figures 8 and 10, with genotypes and scores that agree with the paper's tables.
claims.source: Figures 8B, 8C and 10B; the paper's tables at Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.17307059
claims.criterion: Mice are matched by their numeric identifier. The paper's total AIM score per session is taken to be the sum over the session's time points of the three scores. Reproduced when every dandiset mouse matches a paper mouse and every matched session total is equal; partially reproduced when the matched mice agree but some dandiset mice are not in the paper or the dandiset's genotype labels disagree with the paper's; not reproduced when matched values differ.

claims.statement: During recordings the rats performed the odor-place task at a high level, 77.0% correct (mean and s.e.m. over the 8 rats, 1.3%).
claims.source: Results, Odor-place associative memory and decision-making task, paragraph 2; Figure 1b
claims.quote: animals maintained a high level of performance on the task, indicating accurate decision making based on cued recall of odor-place associations ( Figure 1b , n=8 rats, 77.0% ± 1.3%, mean ± s.e.m.)
claims.criterion: Performance is the proportion of correct trials (Methods, Odor-place association task training), per session (run epochs of a recording day), odor-cued sessions only. The code computes it per epoch and averages (F16/Behavior/cs_performanceScatter.m); the Methods do not say whether trials with sampling under 0.5 s count, and the code keeps them in the performance vector (cs_getNosepokeWindow.m lines 186 to 223). Readings (a) mean over rats of each rat's mean session performance, (b) mean over all sessions, each with and without the short-sampling trials. Reproduced when one reading falls within 77.0 +/- 1.3%.

claims.statement: Odor sampling lasted 0.82 s on average (s.e.m. across sessions 0.02 s; s.d. across trials 0.25 s) and did not differ between correct and incorrect trials.
claims.source: Results, Odor-place associative memory and decision-making task, paragraph 3; Figure 1c; Figure 1-figure supplement 1a
claims.quote: The average odor-sampling duration before odor port disengagement and odor offset was 0.82±0.02 s (mean ± s.e.m. across sessions), and this duration was similar between correct and incorrect trials ( Figure 1c ; within-session signed-rank test, p=0.71
claims.criterion: Duration is odor port beam-break offset minus onset (Methods). Per session the mean duration on correct and on incorrect trials; a Wilcoxon signed-rank test across the 38 sessions, as the Results and legend name it. Absence claim, reproduced when that test gives p >= 0.05. The code tests the same per-session means with a rank-sum test (F16/Behavior/cs_nosepokeDuration_2.m line 65), shown as a variant. The effect size (median paired difference) is reported.

claims.statement: On most trials the rat turned away from the odor port toward the side of the reward arm it then chose, on correct and incorrect trials alike, so the choice is made during odor sampling.
claims.source: Results, Odor-place associative memory and decision-making task, paragraph 3; Figure 1d
claims.quote: Notably, we observed that on a majority of trials (95.4% ± 0.12%), the animals' turn direction away from the odor port matched the direction of the T-maze reward arm that they would ultimately choose on that trial
claims.criterion: Sessions on the truncated mazes are excluded (legend). Turn direction as in F16/Behavior/cs_turnFromNPDirection.m, which the Methods do not describe - the 41 position samples from odor port exit, the sample furthest in x from the odor port position, its sign giving left or right, trials within 40 samples of the epoch end dropped. A binomial test of same against opposite with null probability 0.5 (the code's binopdf(...,0.5)), per outcome. The 95.4% (with a spread of 0.12% as printed) is read as (a) the mean over sessions or (b) the pooled fraction of all trials; the counts give 97.6% pooled. Reproduced when both binomial tests give p < 0.05 with more same than opposite turns and the counts fall within tolerance; the fraction is reported under both readings.

claims.statement: Sniff rate measured by the nasal thermocouple rose slightly during odor sampling (7.1 Hz) compared with time-matched pre-odor periods (6.2 Hz).
claims.source: Results, Odor-place associative memory and decision-making task, paragraph 3; Figure 1-figure supplement 1e
claims.quote: There was a small but significant increase in sniff rate during the odor sampling period (within-session increase 7.1±0.39 Hz, mean ± s.e.m.) compared to time matched pre-odor periods (6.2±0.29 Hz, mean ± s.e.m.)
claims.criterion: Thermocouple signal of the two implanted animals. The Methods do not describe sniff detection; the code (F16/Behavior/cs_sniffRate.m) takes a pre-odor window of the same length as each trial's sampling ending at odor onset, smooths and downsamples by 25, counts peaks (Chronux findpeaks, whose threshold is not in the repository) and divides by window length, averaged per day, with a signed-rank test across days. Peaks are counted here as local maxima of the smoothed signal; a peak rule with a prominence threshold is shown as a variant. Reproduced when the signed-rank test gives p < 0.05 with odor above pre-odor and both rates within tolerance.

claims.statement: Performance on the odor-cued task was higher than on the air-cued sessions, where no odor cue was given.
claims.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 1f
claims.quote: Performance of three animals on the odor-cued task (n = 24 sessions) versus the air-cued task (n = 4 sessions) in which animals were presented with only air as a neutral stimulus
claims.criterion: Per session the fraction correct (correct meaning the well the paper's task scores as rewarded), in the animals that ran an air session; a rank-sum test of odor-cued against air-cued sessions (legend; code F16/Behavior/cs_odorVsAirPerf.m line 98). Reproduced when p < 0.05 with odor-cued performance higher. The paper gives three animals in this legend and four in the Methods; both sets are shown.

claims.statement: Beta power rose from the time-matched pre-odor period to the odor sampling period in CA1, PFC and OB.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 1; Figure 2d top
claims.quote: We observed a strong increase in power in the beta band (20–30 Hz) during this decision-making period compared to a time-matched pre-odor period across all three regions
claims.criterion: Beta power (20 to 30 Hz) per region, per session the mean over trials of odor minus pre-odor power; Wilcoxon signed-rank across sessions. Run under LFP readings A and B of the opening comment. Reproduced when all three regions show an increase with p < 0.05; partially reproduced for one or two regions. The outcome is the one both readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified with both shown.

claims.statement: RR power did not rise after odor onset; it fell slightly in CA1 and did not change in PFC or OB.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 2; Figure 2d top
claims.quote: power increases were seen during the odor sampling period only in the beta band ( Figure 2d signed-rank tests, n=38 sessions, CA1 p=2.84e-3, PFC p=1.80e-4, OB p=8.3e-6) and not in the RR band
claims.criterion: As fig2d-beta-power-increase, for 7 to 8 Hz. The paper's test is the signed-rank test at 0.05. Reproduced when no region shows a significant increase, CA1 shows a significant decrease and PFC and OB show no significant change; the effect sizes are reported. Run under readings A and B; if they disagree, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified with both shown.

claims.statement: Beta coherence between all three region pairs rose from the pre-odor period to odor sampling.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 3; Figure 2e top
claims.quote: This coherence was specific to the odor-sampling period... it significantly increased compared to time-matched pre-odor periods ( Figure 2e top , signed-rank test, n=38 sessions, CA1-PFC p=2.8e-3, CA1-OB p=5.1e-5, PFC-OB p=3.7e-5)
claims.criterion: Beta (20 to 30 Hz) coherence per region pair, per session the mean over trials of odor minus pre-odor coherence; Wilcoxon signed-rank across sessions, under LFP readings A and B of the opening comment. Reproduced when all three pairs increase with p < 0.05; partially reproduced for one or two pairs. The outcome is the one both readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified with both shown.

claims.statement: RR coherence also rose from the pre-odor period to odor sampling for all three region pairs.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 3; Figure 2e top
claims.quote: Network wide coherence in the RR band also increased from the pre-odor to the odor-sampling period ( Figure 2e top , signed-rank test, CA1-OB p=6.4e-4, CA1-PFC p=3.9e-3, PFC-OB p=2.4e-4)
claims.criterion: As fig2e-beta-coherence-increase, for 7 to 8 Hz.

claims.statement: Beta coherence in the last 500 ms of odor sampling was higher than in the last 500 ms before reward well exit, for all three region pairs, so it is not a sign of movement preparation.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 4; Figure 2e middle
claims.quote: We confirmed that beta coherence observed during the decision-making period was significantly higher than coherence at the reward well between all three pairs ( Figure 2e middle , signed-rank test, CA1-PFC p=0.010, CA1-OB p=0.0012, PFC-OB p=0.0024)
claims.criterion: Windows from the Results - the last 500 ms of odor sampling and the last 500 ms before reward well exit, correct trials (rewarded) with sampling over 0.5 s, as F7/ClaireCrossCoherence.m lines 1040 to 1064 do. Reward well exit is the end of the reward-well beam break; the code takes the next DIO event after the pump turns off (F16/Behavior/cs_getRewardTimes.m line 101), shown as a variant. Coherence under LFP reading B (its pipeline) and reading A's settings on the same windows; per session odor minus reward, signed-rank across sessions. Path A's windows centred on exit (F16/LFPAnalysis/cs_cohOdorVsReward.m, 0.5 s either side) are a variant. Reproduced when all three pairs are higher during odor with p < 0.05; partially for one or two. The outcome is the one both settings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified with both shown.

claims.statement: For RR, coherence was higher during odor sampling than at the reward well for CA1-OB and PFC-OB but not for CA1-PFC.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 4; Figure 2e middle
claims.quote: Interestingly, this effect in RR was observed for CA1-OB and PFC-OB, but not between CA1-PFC ( Figure 2e middle , signed-rank test CA1-PFC p=0.569, CA1-OB p=0.0044, PFC-OB p=0.00064)
claims.criterion: As fig2e-beta-coherence-odor-vs-reward, for 7 to 8 Hz. Reproduced when CA1-OB and PFC-OB are higher during odor with p < 0.05 and CA1-PFC gives p >= 0.05 (the paper's test for the absence); partially when two of the three parts hold.

claims.statement: Beta power in all three regions differed between the odor sampling and reward periods, while RR power differed only in OB.
claims.source: Figure 2d middle (legend)
claims.quote: Change in LFP Power from odor-to-reward period (signed-rank tests ... CA1 p=0.0012, PFC p=5.3e-4, OB p=4.4e-4 ... CA1 p=0.11, PFC p=0.062, OB p=4.4e-4)
claims.criterion: Power in the windows of fig2e-beta-coherence-odor-vs-reward, per session odor minus reward, signed-rank across sessions. The legend gives no direction; the figure was not seen, so the direction found is reported. Reproduced when the three beta tests and the OB RR test give p < 0.05 and the CA1 and PFC RR tests give p >= 0.05; partially when four or five of the six hold.

claims.statement: Neither power nor coherence, in beta or RR, differed between correct and incorrect trials.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 7; Figure 2d and 2e bottom
claims.quote: There was no significant change in the level of coherence or power in the CA1-PFC-OB network in either frequency band between correct and incorrect trials ( Figure 2e bottom , signed-rank tests; all p's>0.05)
claims.criterion: Twelve comparisons (power in three regions and coherence in three pairs, each band). Correct trials subsampled at random to the number of incorrect trials in each session (legend, "trial-count matched"; F7/ClaireCrossCoherence.m lines 249 to 257). Per session correct minus incorrect. The paper names two tests - signed-rank across sessions (Results; code line 470) and rank-sum on sessions (legend). Absence claim. Reproduced when neither test finds a difference at p < 0.05 in any of the twelve comparisons, not reproduced when both find one in any, blocked as methods_underspecified when they differ; under LFP readings A and B. Effect sizes are reported.

claims.statement: Beta coherence for all three region pairs was lower on air-only trials than on odor-cued correct trials, while RR coherence did not differ.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 5; Figure 2g
claims.quote: RR coherence was unchanged between odor- and air-cued sessions, but beta coherence was significantly lower in the absence of odor cues during air-only sessions ( Figure 2g )
claims.criterion: One value per trial, the z-scored coherence averaged over the sampling period (legend and code, F16/LFPAnalysis/cs_LFPcoherence_noOdor.m), pooled over sessions; odor trials are correct trials of odor-cued sessions (legend). Bootstrap as the Methods give it - odor trials resampled with replacement to the number of air trials, 1000 times, the mean each time, compared with the observed air mean. The Methods count bootstrap means >= the air mean, which would give a p near 1 for a lower air mean; the code takes the smaller of the two tails. The lower tail is used (the fraction of bootstrap means <= the air mean), and the code's two-tail minimum is reported too. Coherence under LFP reading A (the code's pipeline here) and reading B. Reproduced when all three beta pairs give p < 0.05 with air lower and all three RR pairs give p >= 0.05; partially when four or five of the six hold. The outcome is the one both readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified with both shown.

claims.statement: Sharp-wave ripples were rare during odor sampling and frequent at the reward wells.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 6; Figure 2f
claims.quote: However, a distinct lack of SWR events at the odor port ( Figure 2f ; signed-rank test, p=1.1e-7) suggests that SWR replay is unlikely to play a direct role in decision making
claims.criterion: Detection from the Methods (Sharp-wave ripple detection) - locally referenced CA1 LFP, 150 to 250 Hz, Hilbert envelope above 3 s.d. of its mean for at least 15 ms on at least one CA1 tetrode; tetrodes are the CA1 tetrodes with cells (F16/Ripples/cs_riptettag_anycells.m). The code keeps events at speed under 4 cm/s (cs_rippletimes.m), followed here. Number of SWRs per trial on correct trials (legend). Windows, which the Methods do not fix - (a) the odor sampling period and the reward-well period (reward-well beam break onset to exit); (b) the code's speed-defined stops around the odor port and around reward onset, the latter extended to at least 1 s (cs_rippleRate_NPvsReward.m). Per session the mean count per trial in each window; signed-rank across sessions (legend; the code's rank-sum over trials is a variant). Reproduced when p < 0.05 with fewer SWRs at the odor port under a reading, and the readings agree.

claims.statement: Beta amplitude was coupled to RR phase in CA1, PFC and OB during odor sampling.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 2; Figure 2-figure supplement 1f
claims.quote: During the decision-making period, we also found phase-amplitude coupling between beta and RR rhythms in all three regions
claims.criterion: Tort modulation index as in the Methods (Cross-frequency coupling) - RR phase in 18 bins of 20 degrees, mean beta amplitude per bin normalized to sum 1, MI from the KL distance to the uniform; null from 500 shuffles of the trial assignment of RR phase series (Methods and legend). Per region, the local tetrode with most cells (as for phase locking; the Methods do not name the tetrode for this analysis), odor sampling periods. The Methods do not say which trials; readings all completed trials and correct trials only. The code restricts samples to high OB beta periods and shuffles amplitudes across samples (F16/LFPAnalysis/cs_cfc.m), a variant. The legend shows one real MI per region against a trial-shuffled null, so MI is pooled over the trials of all sessions; per-session MIs are reported as a variant. Reproduced when the pooled MI exceeds all 500 shuffles in each region; partially when that holds in one or two regions. The outcome is the one both trial readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: During odor sampling CA1 beta led PFC beta, and CA1 RR led PFC and OB RR, though offsets varied widely across sessions.
claims.source: Figure 2-figure supplement 2d; Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 7
claims.quote: During the full odor sampling window, CA1 beta lead PFC (p = 2e-4) and there was no consistent phase difference between OB and PFC or CA1 beta (all p>0.05). Similarly, CA1 RR lead PFC RR (p < 1e-5), as well as OB (p < 1e-5)
claims.criterion: The paper names no test. From F7/ClairePhaseOffset.m - per trial the circular mean of the instantaneous phase difference over the last 500 ms of sampling (trials of 0.5 to 2 s), the circular mean over trials per session, one tetrode per region (most units), and a test of the session offsets against zero by a sign-flip null of 100,000 draws taking the smaller tail; the code's circ_mtest is a variant. The legend's "full odor sampling window" against the code's last 500 ms gives readings (a) whole sampling period, (b) last 500 ms. The legend also says no consistent offset between OB and CA1 RR, which contradicts CA1 RR leading OB; only the stated leads are tested for RR. Reproduced when the CA1 beta lead over PFC and the two RR leads are significant (p < 0.05) in the stated direction and the beta OB pairs are not. The outcome is the one both window readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: After odor port exit, as the rat ran, the dominant LFP frequency in CA1 and PFC shifted slightly from RR up into the theta band.
claims.source: Results, Beta and RR coherence is elevated during odor sampling and decision making, paragraph 1; Figure 2-figure supplement 1e
claims.quote: Following odor port disengagement and the initiation of running down the track, we observed a small shift in the dominant LFP frequency from RR to the theta band in CA1 and PFC
claims.criterion: Full-maze animals only (legend). The paper gives no test; the code (F16/LFPAnalysis/cs_peakFreqOdorVRun.m with cs_PSD.m) takes power spectra (fpass 0 to 20 Hz, 1 s windows) from 0 to 3 s after odor onset, splits them at 0.8 s into odor and run parts, finds the peak frequency per day and compares odor and run by a signed-rank test. The search range in the code is set by array indices; it is read as the theta band the paper defines, 6 to 12 Hz. Readings for the windows (a) the code's 0 to 0.8 s and 0.8 to 3 s after odor onset, (b) the odor sampling period and run after exit at speed over 3 cm/s. Reproduced when the run peak is higher than the odor peak with signed-rank p < 0.05 in CA1 and in PFC; partially for one region. The outcome is the one both window readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: The recordings gave 1,309 CA1 and 717 PFC units, of which 934 and 508 were active, 813 CA1 and 464 PFC active units were putative pyramidal cells (121 and 44 interneurons), 170 and 234 pyramidal cells were active in the odor period, and 138 and 185 of these were task responsive.
claims.source: Results, Single neurons in CA1 and PFC exhibit choice selectivity during decision-making period, paragraph 1; Figure 3g-h
claims.quote: we first selected units that fired at least 100 spikes during the run epochs ( Figure 3g–h , 'Active Cells', 934 in CA1, 508 in PFC) and categorized them into pyramidal cells and interneurons based on firing rate and spike width
claims.criterion: Selections as defined in the opening comment (active units, cell types, odor period active, task responsive), each under the readings named there; a reading is one choice for each open detail. Reproduced when one reading gives every count within tolerance; partially when the totals and active counts match but some later counts do not. The dandiset's units may already be curated, in which case the totals compare what was deposited.

claims.statement: About a third of task-responsive pyramidal cells were choice selective, 47 of 138 in CA1 and 59 of 185 in PFC.
claims.source: Results, Single neurons in CA1 and PFC exhibit choice selectivity during decision-making period, paragraph 2; Figure 3
claims.quote: To determine significance, the SI value for each task responsive pyramidal cell was compared to a distribution of SIs generated by shuffling the odor identities across trials (n=47/138, 34% CA1 selective cells, n=59/185, 31% PFC selective cells)
claims.criterion: Choice selectivity as defined in the opening comment, in task-responsive pyramidal cells, under each reading of unit-counts. Reproduced when the fractions fall within tolerance under a reading (the counts too when that reading reproduces 138 and 185).

claims.statement: In choice-selective pyramidal cells the selectivity index on incorrect trials was anti-correlated with that on correct trials, so the cells code the upcoming choice and not the odor.
claims.source: Results, Single neurons in CA1 and PFC exhibit choice selectivity during decision-making period, paragraph 3; Figure 3i-j
claims.quote: the SIs on correct trials were anti-correlated with the SIs on incorrect trials ... Spearman Rank Correlation, CA1 pyr correct-incorrect SI r =–0.58, p(47) = 1.82e-5, PFC pyr correct-incorrect SI r =–0.68, p(59) = 3.47e-9
claims.criterion: SI on incorrect trials with the same formula and odor labels as on correct trials. The Methods define SI on sampling-period rates; the code (F16/OdorSelectivitySingleCell/ cs_odorSelectivity_v2.m) uses 50 ms PSTH bins with empty bins set to 0 and averages the per-bin SI from 0.2 to 1 s after odor onset. Readings (a) whole sampling period rates, (b) the code's binned SI. Cells without incorrect trials of both odors are dropped and counted. Spearman correlation (paper); the code's Pearson is a variant. Reproduced when both correlations are negative with p < 0.05 and r within tolerance; partially when negative and significant but r out of tolerance. The outcome is the one both SI readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: The Results say the correct-incorrect anti-correlation was not significant among task-responsive cells that were not choice selective, while the legend reports a significant anti-correlation (r = -0.34 in both regions).
claims.source: Results, Single neurons in CA1 and PFC exhibit choice selectivity during decision-making period, paragraph 3; Figure 3-figure supplement 1e
claims.quote: This pattern was not significant within the population of neurons that were task-responsive but did not meet the selectivity threshold ( Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–e )
claims.criterion: As fig3ij-si-anticorrelated, in task-responsive pyramidal cells that are not choice selective. The paper disagrees with itself, so two readings - (a) the Results, no significant anti-correlation (Spearman p >= 0.05); (b) the legend, r near -0.34 (tolerance 0.034) with p < 0.05. Reproduced under whichever reading the result matches, and the inconsistency is recorded; r and p are reported for each region.

claims.statement: Firing rates of task-responsive pyramidal cells differed between odor sampling and reward consumption, in CA1 and in PFC.
claims.source: Figure 3-figure supplement 1c
claims.quote: Firing rates of task-responsive pyramidal neurons during odor sampling and reward consumption (Signed-rank tests ... n = 138 cells, p = 5.1e-13 ... n = 185 cells, p = 0.009)
claims.criterion: No code for this panel was found. Per cell the mean rate over odor sampling periods and over reward periods (reward-well beam break onset to exit) of the same trials; the Methods do not fix the reward window or the trials, so readings are correct trials (rewarded) and all completed trials. Signed-rank test across cells. The direction is shown only in the figure, which was not seen, and is reported. Reproduced when both regions give p < 0.05 under a reading.

claims.statement: CA1 choice-selective interneurons also had selectivity on incorrect trials anti-correlated with that on correct trials; PFC interneurons, few in number, did not.
claims.source: Results, Single neurons in CA1 and PFC exhibit choice selectivity during decision-making period, paragraph 4; Figure 4c
claims.quote: For CA1 interneurons, the selectivity response showed anti-correlation during correct versus incorrect trials similar to that of pyramidal cells ( Figure 4c top , r(32) = –0.80, p=3.4e-8)
claims.criterion: Task responsiveness and choice selectivity as for pyramidal cells (Results, "using the same criteria"), in interneurons; correlation and readings as fig3ij-si-anticorrelated. Reproduced when CA1 interneurons give a negative correlation with p < 0.05 and r within tolerance, and PFC interneurons give p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Among CA1-PFC pairs with significant cross-correlation peaks during odor sampling, PFC interneurons tended to lead CA1 interneurons and CA1 pyramidal cells, CA1 interneuron-PFC pyramidal pairs were skewed too, and pyramidal-pyramidal pairs showed no skew.
claims.source: Results, Single neurons in CA1 and PFC exhibit choice selectivity during decision-making period, paragraph 5; Figure 4d
claims.quote: We found a significant skew in CA1-PFC interneuron pairs towards the PFC interneurons leading (sign rank test, x=–0.028, p=3.5e-8) ( Figure 4d ), as well as for CA1 pyramidal cell - PFC interneuron pairs in the same direction (sign rank test, x=–0.013, p=0.0034)
claims.criterion: Method from the Methods (Corrected spike cross-correlogram) - for simultaneously recorded task-responsive CA1-PFC pairs, cross-correlogram from -0.15 to 0.15 s in 2.5 ms bins, one cell's spikes jittered by up to +/-50 ms 1000 times, pointwise z-score against the jitter, the highest peak within +/-100 ms that is significant at p < 0.05 taken as the pair's lag; positive lag is CA1 leading (legend). Open details and readings - spikes from (a) whole sampling periods (Methods) or (b) the last 0.5 s of sampling (code, F7/ClaireCellCellInteractions.m line 1298), correct and incorrect trials as the code uses; pointwise p < 0.05 as one-sided z > 1.645 or two-sided |z| > 1.96. The code's 200 jitters and z > 3 are a variant. Signed-rank test of lags against 0 per pair type. The Results' x is not named; the median and the mean lag are both compared with the expected values, a match under either counting. Reproduced when the two interneuron-involving tests quoted are significant with negative lags, the CA1 interneuron-PFC pyramidal test is significant and the pyramidal-pyramidal test gives p >= 0.05; partially when two or three of these four hold. The outcome is the one all window and threshold readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified. Pair counts are reported against 87, 283, 111 and 224.

claims.statement: Most CA1 task-responsive cells and a minority of PFC cells were locked to local RR; a modest share of CA1 pyramidal cells and a large share of CA1 interneurons were locked to local beta, while PFC cells were locked to beta no more than chance.
claims.source: Results, CA1 and PFC cells phase lock to beta and respiratory rhythms during decision making, paragraph 1; Figure 5c
claims.quote: Surprisingly though, while a modest but significant proportion of CA1 pyramidal cells were also coherent to local beta (28/138, 20% binomial test p=4.6e-11) a large fraction of CA1 interneurons were coherent to local beta (36/83, 43%)
claims.criterion: Phase locking as in the opening comment, to the local tetrode, task-responsive cells. The interneuron denominators differ between the Results (83 CA1, 28 PFC) and the Figure 5c legend (96 and 36); both are counted and reported. Chance is 0.05, the dotted line of Figure 5-figure supplement 1c and the code's chance line (F7/ClaireBetaAnalysis.m line 622); binomial test, one-sided, of the number locked against n and 0.05. The 1-count tolerance on the smallest counts is a floor, not 10%. Reproduced when the CA1 pyramidal beta proportion exceeds chance with p < 0.05, the PFC beta proportions do not, and the fractions fall within tolerance (counts scaled to the n found when the denominators differ); partially when the significance pattern holds but some fractions do not.

claims.statement: More CA1 interneurons were locked to PFC beta than chance, while CA1 pyramidal cells and PFC cells showed no cross-regional beta locking beyond chance.
claims.source: Results, CA1 and PFC cells phase lock to beta and respiratory rhythms during decision making, paragraph 1; Figure 5c-d
claims.quote: When we assessed cross-regional spike-beta coherence, we found that there were significantly more CA1 interneurons locked to PFC beta than chance
claims.criterion: Each task-responsive cell tested against beta on the CA1, PFC and OB tetrodes; locked to a region when the Rayleigh p is below 0.05/3 (Results; F7/ClaireBetaAnalysis.m pcrit = .05/3) and assigned to the region with the smallest p (legend 5d; line 320). Binomial test of each count against chance; the chance probability is not stated, readings 0.0167 and 0.05. The paper gives some OB denominators as 138 where the population is PFC (185); counts are compared, not denominators. Reproduced when the CA1 interneuron count to PFC beta exceeds chance at p < 0.0167 and the CA1 pyramidal and PFC counts do not. The outcome is the one both chance readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified with both shown.

claims.statement: Preferred beta and RR phases were consistent across task-responsive CA1 cells, while in PFC only interneurons had a consistent preferred RR phase.
claims.source: Results, CA1 and PFC cells phase lock to beta and respiratory rhythms during decision making, paragraph 2; Figure 5g-h
claims.quote: phase preference across cells was consistent in CA1 for both rhythms ( Figure 5g–h , Rayleigh Z-test, CA1... pyr n=138, beta p=5.4e-5, RR P =5.9e-4, int n=83 beta p=2.62e-4 RR p=5.61e-6)
claims.criterion: Each task-responsive cell's preferred phase is the mean phase of its spikes on correct trials (Methods, the circular mean under a von Mises model), whether or not it is locked (Results, "regardless of the significance"); local tetrode. Rayleigh test across cells per region, cell type and rhythm. Reproduced when the five significant tests give p < 0.05 and the three PFC tests give p >= 0.05; partially when six or seven of the eight hold.

claims.statement: More cells were phase locked to RR than to beta, and the depth of RR modulation was stronger, in CA1 and in PFC.
claims.source: Results, CA1 and PFC cells phase lock to beta and respiratory rhythms during decision making, paragraph 2; Figure 5c; Figure 5-figure supplement 1a
claims.quote: even though a higher percentage of cells in both regions were phase locked to RR ( Figure 5c and z-test for proportions ... and depth of this modulation was much stronger for RR compared to beta
claims.criterion: Proportions of task-responsive cells locked to RR and to beta compared by a pooled z-test for two proportions (code F16/PhaseLocking/cs_plCellProportions.m, which counts a cell locked to CA1 or PFC LFP; readings local LFP only, and CA1 or PFC LFP as the code does), two-sided and one-sided (the code's ztestprop.m is one-sided). Rayleigh Z of each task-responsive pyramidal cell's spikes for RR against beta by rank-sum (legend). Reproduced when, in each region, RR has the larger proportion with p < 0.05 and larger Rayleigh Z with p < 0.05. The outcome is the one all readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: The share of cells locked to both beta and RR did not differ from that expected by chance from the share locked to each, in CA1 and PFC, for pyramidal cells and interneurons.
claims.source: Results, CA1 and PFC cells phase lock to beta and respiratory rhythms during decision making, paragraph 3; Figure 5-figure supplement 1d-e
claims.quote: in both CA1 and PFC, the proportion of cells that were phase locked to both beta and RR was no different than chance, given the percentages of cells that were modulated by either rhythm
claims.criterion: Chance probability the product of the fractions locked to beta and to RR (legend; code F16/Spiking/jhb_plotAllProportions.m line 389); binomial test of the number locked to both against n and that probability, two-sided (the legend shows a 95% binomial interval). Absence claim on the paper's test - reproduced when all four give p >= 0.05, not reproduced when any gives p < 0.05; the observed and chance fractions are reported.

claims.statement: Choice-selective cells were no more or less likely than chance to be phase locked to beta or to RR, in CA1 and PFC.
claims.source: Results, CA1 and PFC cells phase lock to beta and respiratory rhythms during decision making, paragraph 4; Figure 5-figure supplement 1f-h
claims.quote: Interestingly, we found that the number of cells that met both criteria was no different than chance for either CA1 or PFC ( Figure 5—figure supplement 1f , binomial tests; all p>0.05)
claims.criterion: As fig5s1de-beta-rr-overlap, with chance the product of the fractions choice selective and phase locked among task-responsive cells. "Phase locked" is to any region's rhythm (Results, "within and across regions"); the local-only count is a reading too. Absence claim - reproduced when all six tests give p >= 0.05, not reproduced when any gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Beta-locked CA1 pyramidal cells and interneurons and PFC pyramidal cells were more strongly locked to local beta on correct than on incorrect trials.
claims.source: Results, CA1 and PFC cells phase lock to beta and respiratory rhythms during decision making, paragraph 5; Figure 5e
claims.quote: We found that both pyramidal cells and interneurons in CA1 and pyramidal cells in PFC that were phase-locked to the local beta rhythm exhibited a lower MVL on incorrect trials
claims.criterion: Cells - task-responsive cells locked to local beta. Method from the Methods (Phase locking) - correct-trial spikes subsampled to the number of incorrect-trial spikes, the MVL of the subsample bootstrapped 1000 times, the mean bootstrapped MVL compared with the incorrect-trial MVL; signed-rank test across cells. The code resamples trials, not spikes, 500 times (Path A, cs_phaselockBootstrap_v2.m) or subsamples both conditions 200 times and prints a t-test (Path B, F7/ClaireBetaAnalysis.m lines 155 to 172 and 890); variants. Reproduced when the three groups give lower incorrect MVL with p < 0.05; partially for one or two.

claims.statement: Locking to local RR did not differ between correct and incorrect trials.
claims.source: Results, CA1 and PFC cells phase lock to beta and respiratory rhythms during decision making, paragraph 5; Figure 5f
claims.quote: There was no significant effect for local RR phase locking ( Figure 5f , signed-rank test, no significance found)
claims.criterion: As fig5e-beta-mvl-correct-incorrect, for RR-locked cells. Absence claim - reproduced when none of the four groups gives p < 0.05; the median differences are reported.

claims.statement: CA1 interneurons locked to PFC beta were more strongly locked on correct than on incorrect trials.
claims.source: Results, CA1 and PFC cells phase lock to beta and respiratory rhythms during decision making, paragraph 5; Figure 5-figure supplement 2a
claims.quote: Interestingly, cross-region spike-phase coherence showed a similar relationship to decision accuracy for CA1 phase-coherent interneurons ( Figure 5—figure supplement 2 n=20, p=0.0023)
claims.criterion: As fig5e-beta-mvl-correct-incorrect, for CA1 interneurons significantly locked to PFC beta; the other cross-regional combinations (legend, all p > 0.05) are reported. Which interneurons form the 20 is not stated - readings locked to PFC beta at p < 0.05, or at p < 0.0167 (as in fig5d-cross-region-beta). Reproduced when correct exceeds incorrect with signed-rank p < 0.05 under a reading.

claims.statement: CA1 and PFC ensemble trajectories for the two choices separated within the odor sampling period, at similar times (CA1 200 to 800 ms, PFC 400 to 700 ms after odor onset).
claims.source: Results, Neural ensemble responses in CA1 and PFC during decision making predict the upcoming choice, paragraph 2; Figure 6c-d
claims.quote: Neural discrimination times for CA1 and PFC (n=24 sessions across 8 animals; threshold of 4 task-responsive cells, CA1... 200–800ms; PFC... 400–700ms) were similar ( Figure 6d ; p=0.68, sign-rank test)
claims.criterion: Method from the Methods (PCA) - sessions with at least 4 task-responsive cells per region; spikes in 100 ms bins from 0 to 1 s after odor onset, correct trials (the code, F16/pca/sj_columnVectors_day_npCells.m line 71); first 3 PCs; Euclidean distance between the mean left-bound and right-bound trajectories; null from 1000 shuffles of trial labels (code sj_PCA_AvgDis_Sess_npcells_update2.m line 232); discrimination time is the first bin whose distance exceeds the null's upper bound. Cells are task-responsive pyramidal cells (Results, "We first considered only pyramidal cells that were task-responsive for the ensemble analyses"); the code's pyramidal cells and interneurons (npCells_PyrInt) are a variant. Open details and readings - PCA fitted (c) on the session's trial-averaged bins by neurons matrix (Methods) or (d) per bin on single trials (code lines 175 to 176); the bound the 95th (code) or 97.5th percentile (the upper edge of a 95% interval). The code's window from -0.2 s is a variant. Each reading gives per-session times; reported are the range per region and a signed-rank test of CA1 against PFC over sessions with both. Reproduced when the ranges fall within the expected bounds widened by tolerance and the signed-rank test gives p >= 0.05 (the absence part judged on that test). The outcome is the one all readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: A control distance between even and odd trials of the same odor never crossed significance in any session.
claims.source: Results, Neural ensemble responses in CA1 and PFC during decision making predict the upcoming choice, paragraph 2; Figure 6c
claims.quote: A second even-odd shuffle ( Figure 6c black lines) failed to cross significance in any session, suggesting the emergence of a robust discriminatory neural code during decision-making
claims.criterion: For each session and region of fig6d-discrimination-time, the distance between the mean trajectories of even and odd trials of each odor, averaged over the two odors (legend; code F16/pca/Run_PCA_SJ_copy.m lines 107 to 112), compared with the same null bound bin by bin. The trace the figure code labels even-odd (sj_PCA_AvgDis_Sess_npcells_update2.m line 332) is the first shuffle's distance, a variant. Reproduced when no session crosses the bound in any bin; partially when at most 10% of sessions do.

claims.statement: A GLM on task-responsive pyramidal ensembles predicted the upcoming choice before odor port exit, from 0.1 s before exit in CA1 and 0.3 s before in PFC.
claims.source: Results, Neural ensemble responses in CA1 and PFC during decision making predict the upcoming choice, paragraph 3; Figure 6e left
claims.quote: When we performed this analysis using task-responsive putative pyramidal cells we found that reward choice could be accurately predicted 0.1 s prior to odor port disengagement by CA1 ensembles, and 0.3 s prior by PFC ensembles ( Figure 6e left )
claims.criterion: Method from the Methods (GLM) - task-responsive cells active on at least 10 trials, spike counts per cell as predictors, choice (the well chosen, all completed trials, as the code labels them, cs_predictChoice_GLM.m line 122) as response; binomial GLM, with the Methods' log link or the code's logit (line 142); five-fold cross-validation, accuracy the fraction of test trials correct; null from shuffled choice labels; rank-sum test of real against shuffled accuracy over sessions per window. Tolerance is one 0.1 s window step. The alignment is open, as the Methods use cumulative windows from odor onset (0-0.1 to 0-1.0 s; the plotted code, cs_trialPredictionGLM.m) and the Results speak of time before exit. Readings (a) windows from odor port exit minus 0.6 s to exit plus w, w from -0.5 to 0.2 s in 0.1 s steps (code cs_predictChoice_GLM_v3.m), the time of a window its end; (b) the onset-aligned windows, a window's time before exit read as the mean sampling duration (0.82 s, fig1c) minus its length. The earliest window from which all later windows are significant is reported. Shuffles - 100 per session as the code does (cs_predictChoice_GLM.m line 155), each with its own fold split. The code's t-test is a variant. Reproduced when both regions predict above chance before exit and both earliest times fall within tolerance; partially when only one does. The outcome is the one both alignment readings give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Adding interneurons made CA1 prediction accurate earlier, 0.2 s before exit, PFC prediction did not change, and resampling pyramidal cells to the same ensemble size gave 0.1 s again.
claims.source: Results, Neural ensemble responses in CA1 and PFC during decision making predict the upcoming choice, paragraph 3; Figure 6e right
claims.quote: In this case, we found an improvement in prediction for CA1 ensembles... reward prediction was now accurate starting earlier, at 0.2 s prior to decision execution. Prediction by PFC ensembles remained the same
claims.criterion: As fig6e-glm-choice-prediction with task-responsive pyramidal cells and interneurons. The control resamples pyramidal cells with replacement to the number of pyramidal cells plus interneurons (Results); no code was found for it, and the number of resamples is not stated - read as 100 resamples per session with accuracy averaged, a standard choice. Reproduced when CA1 with interneurons is significant earlier than CA1 pyramidal alone, PFC unchanged and the control as for pyramidal cells, with the times within tolerance. The outcome is the one both alignment readings of fig6e-glm-choice-prediction give; when they differ the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Many CA1 and PFC cells had spatial fields on the track, 344 of 585 in CA1 and 159 of 288 in PFC.
claims.source: Results, Representations of choice and space are maintained independently during stem running, paragraph 1; Figure 7b
claims.quote: A large fraction of cells in CA1 and PFC exhibited spatial activity on the maze (see Methods for details on spatial parameters, n=344 out of 585 CA1 cells; n=159 out of 288 PFC cells had fields on the track)
claims.criterion: Full-maze sessions (Results, 26 sessions from 6 rats; Methods, the five full-maze animals; both sets shown). Cells are pyramidal cells that fire during run (code F7/SummaryObjPlaceInteractions.m lines 349 to 351). Place fields from the Methods (Place field determination) - run epochs at speed over 3 cm/s, each outbound trajectory linearized into 100 bins, rate map smoothed with a Gaussian of 2 bins, peak at least 1 Hz, peak at least 2 s.d. above the mean of a null from circularly shifting spikes within each run, field under 75% of the trajectory. Shuffle count from the code, 500 (F7/CalcLinPlaceField.m); the code's one-tailed p < 0.05 in place of 2 s.d. is a variant. Reproduced when the counts fall within tolerance.
