claims.statement: HMM state spaces are higher-dimensional in human and murine organoids than in primary cultures.
claims.source: Results, Comparing sequences across neurodevelopmental models, paragraph 4; Figure 7F; Supplementary Fig. 25
claims.quote: With θ = 0.75, human organoids were separable from slice data ( P = 0.04, linear mixed-effects model with Poisson observations), while primary cultures had significantly lower dimensionality than both human ( P < 0.0001) and murine organoids ( P = 0.003) ( Fig. 7F )
claims.criterion: HMMs as in supp18-hmm-likelihood-real-above-shuffled for all 31 recordings, K from 10 to 30. Per model, PCA of the K by units matrix of Poisson rates (exp of the fitted log lambdas, Supplements.py); dimensionality, the smallest number of components whose cumulative explained variance exceeds theta = 0.75 (counted up to 10). Test as in lmem.R, a Poisson GLMM (glmer, log link) of dimensionality on model type with a random intercept per recording, emmeans pairwise contrasts (Tukey adjustment, the emmeans default). Reproduced when primary cultures are lower than human and murine organoids with p < 0.05. The human organoid against slice contrast is reported; the legend's "but not compared with slices" next to P = 0.036 is not judged.

claims.statement: Non-rigid units fire more irregularly (higher CV2) than backbone units in every model type.
claims.source: Results, Comparing sequences across neurodevelopmental models, paragraph 4; Supplementary Fig. 24C
claims.quote: The CV2 scores are significantly larger for non-rigid units compared to backbone units, reflecting a more Poisson-like firing of non-rigid units (Human organoids P ≤ 10-20, Murine organoids P ≤ 10-20, Murine slices P = 7x10-13, Murine primary cultures P ≤ 10-20
claims.criterion: CV2 per unit as in Holt et al. (mean over consecutive interval pairs of 2|I2 - I1|/(I2 + I1)), units with at least 30 spikes. The panel does not say whether raw or shuffle z-scored CV2 (Methods) is tested; readings (a) raw, (b) z-scored to the 100 shuffles. Model, CV2 on unit type, model type and their interaction with a random intercept per recording. Reproduced when non-rigid exceeds backbone with p < 0.05 in all four model types under both readings. (The paper prints "P ≤ 10-20"; p_relation "<" stands for it.)

claims.statement: Given the HMM hidden state, non-rigid units fire mostly like Poisson units, while backbone units fire less variably than Poisson in a sizable fraction of states.
claims.source: Results, Comparing sequences across neurodevelopmental models, paragraph 4; Supplementary Fig. 24D; Supplementary Methods, Non-Poisson Units
claims.quote: Across models, non-rigid units were predominantly Poisson, while backbone units were non-Poisson ( Supplementary Fig. 24 )
claims.criterion: As the Supplementary Methods, Non-Poisson Units, and Supplements.py (poisson_test, unit_consistency, mean_consistency). HMMs as in fig7f-hmm-dimensionality (all 31 recordings, K from 10 to 30). For each unit, model and state, the spike counts of the unit in the realizations of the state (bins where it is the most likely state; the code keeps only bins inside burst windows); a one-sided chi-square test of variance below the Poisson variance (the mean count) at the 1% level, statistic (n - 1) s² / mean against the lower tail of chi-square with n - 1 degrees of freedom (code). A unit that never fires in a state counts as Poisson there (code). Per unit, the fraction of states passing, weighted by their numbers of realizations, over all its fitted HMMs. No test of the group difference is reported. "Sizable" and "almost all states" are not fixed; reproduced when, in every model type, the median fraction of backbone units exceeds that of non-rigid units and the median fraction of non-rigid units is at most 0.1 (read as at least 90% of states Poisson). The medians and a linear mixed-effects model of the fraction on unit type with a random intercept per recording are reported.

claims.statement: The consistency of backbone sequence order across bursts differs between model types, and is higher in human organoids than in primary cultures.
claims.source: Supplementary Fig. 10B
claims.quote: Main effect of sample type P = 0.004 ... Human organoids vs Murine primary cultures P = 0.0004
claims.criterion: Normalized Spearman rank-order correlations of backbone sequences for all burst pairs as in ed4d-gabazine-rank-order, both normalization readings. Model, value on model type with a random intercept per recording. Reproduced when the main effect and the human organoid against primary culture contrast (higher in organoids) have p < 0.05 under both readings. The other five contrasts (P = 0.066, 0.061, 0.99, 0.38, 0.65) are reported.

claims.statement: HMM state traversal rates during the backbone period are higher in primary cultures than in human organoids and slices, while human and murine organoids do not differ.
claims.source: Results, Comparing sequences across neurodevelopmental models, paragraph 4; Supplementary Fig. 26
claims.quote: In particular, human and murine organoid cannot be distinguished (P = 0.93), whereas the higher state traversal rate of murine primary cultures is significantly different from that of human organoids (P = .021) and murine acute slices (P < 0.0001) but not significant relative to murine organoids (P = 0.064)
claims.criterion: As state_traversal_df in hmmsupport.py. Per model and burst, the number of distinct most likely states in the bins of the backbone window after the peak offset, averaged over bursts and divided by the window length. Model as in lmem.R, rate on model type plus K (as a factor) with a random intercept per recording, emmeans pairwise contrasts. Reproduced when primary cultures exceed human organoids and slices with p < 0.05 and the human against murine organoid contrast is non-significant (absence at alpha 0.05); the primary against murine organoid contrast is reported.

claims.statement: A subset of every preparation type shows near-critical temporal dynamics (d2 between 0 and 0.1), and shuffling spike times raises d2 well above that.
claims.source: Results, Firing pattern stability, paragraph 1; Supplementary Fig. 27A; Supplementary Methods, d2 calculation
claims.quote: Spike-time shuffling consistently abolished temporal criticality across preparations, producing significantly larger d 2 values ( P < 10 −10 compared to intact data, two-sided Welch t-test)
claims.criterion: As the Supplementary Methods, d2 calculation. Spike counts over all units in 30 ms bins, z-scored; an order-20 AR model by Yule-Walker; d2 from the AR coefficients with the code of Sooter et al. (figshare article 25927081, version 1, as r_download.sh fetches). Shuffled control, each neuron's spike times shuffled independently keeping its rate (not the Okun swap). Preparations are kept when the AR model's simulated avalanche size and duration distributions and power spectrum lie within one order of magnitude of the data's; the comparison is not specified further, so counts that differ by one are reported as near matches. The counts are exact numbers of recordings and are given no tolerance; reproduced when shuffled d2 exceeds intact d2 by a two-sided Welch t-test with p < 0.05 and the kept intact preparations have d2 at most 0.1; partially reproduced when the test holds but the counts differ. The code's table lists 7 primary cultures (Pr5 absent) of the 8.

claims.statement: Backbone units have higher mean rates than non-rigid units in the Sharf organoid slices (HO1 to HO4) but not in the whole Alam El Din organoids (HO5 to HO8).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2D
claims.quote: (Sharf et al. P < 10 −20 , Alam El Din et al . P = 0.40, two-sided linear mixed-effect model, n = 4 organoids each)
claims.criterion: Log mean rate per unit (units with at least 30 spikes) on unit type with a random intercept per organoid, fitted separately to HO1 to HO4 and to HO5 to HO8. Reproduced when the Sharf fit has backbone higher with p < 0.05 and the Alam El Din fit has p >= 0.05 (absence judged on the same test); the effect sizes are given.

claims.statement: Rate-normalized burst-to-burst correlations are higher for backbone than non-rigid units in both sets of human organoid recordings.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2E
claims.quote: Note the significant difference between backbone and non-rigid units present for both sets of recordings (Sharf et al . P = 1×10 −10 , Alam El Din et al . P = 0.0092, two-sided linear mixed-effect model, n = 4 organoids each)
claims.criterion: Normalized burst-to-burst correlation as in fig7b-normalized-b2b ("after average rate normalization"), on unit type with a random intercept per organoid, fitted separately to HO1 to HO4 and HO5 to HO8. Reproduced when backbone is higher with p < 0.05 in both.

claims.statement: In both sets of human organoid recordings, only backbone pairs have rate-normalized pairwise correlations significantly above zero.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 2F
claims.quote: Note that only the normalized correlation for backbone pairs are significantly larger than 0 for both sets of recordings (Sharf et al . P = 0.0001, 0.145 and 1 respectively, Alam El Din et al . P = 7×10 −11 , 1 and 1 respectively, one-sided linear mixed-effect model, n = 4 organoids each)
claims.criterion: Normalized pairwise correlations as in fig7c-normalized-pairwise, per pair, for each pair type; one-sided test of the intercept above 0 in a linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept per organoid, separately for HO1 to HO4 and HO5 to HO8. Reproduced when backbone pairs are above 0 with p < 0.05 in both sets and the other two pair types are not (absence at alpha 0.05); partially reproduced when the backbone result holds but another type is also significant.

claims.statement: Single-cell RNA sequencing shows that the murine ESC organoids are of predominantly forebrain identity and express AMPA, NMDA and GABA receptor subunit genes.
claims.source: Supplementary Fig. 5B and 5C
claims.quote: Expression patterns of brain-region specific marker genes reveal predominant forebrain identity of the murine brain organoids used in this study
claims.criterion: The PIPseq data of 30-day organoids from three lines (4031 cells after filtering), as in the Supplementary Methods (Seurat 5.1.0, SCTransform, 40 PCs, Leiden clustering at resolution 0.5, canonical markers). Not testable on the dandiset, which holds electrophysiology only. The markers are those of Supplementary Fig. 5B, which the text does not list, so the set of markers and what counts as predominant are open; the claim is recorded and not tested here.

claims.statement: Imaging data come from 94 sessions of 8 mice (2, 10, 5, 14, 15, 15, 12 and 21 sessions for mice 1 to 8); PPC layers 2, 3 and 5 were imaged in 17, 15 and 14 sessions and PM layers 2, 3 and 5 in 16, 15 and 17.
claims.source: Online Methods, Behavioral analysis; Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 1
claims.quote: In total, we analyzed data from 94 sessions in 8 mice (mouse 1, 2 sessions; mouse 2, 10 sessions; mouse 3, 5 sessions; mouse 4, 14 sessions; mouse 5, 15 sessions; mouse 6, 15 sessions; mouse 7, 12 sessions; mouse 8, 21 sessions)
claims.criterion: Counts of named sessions and animals, so the tolerance is 0 for each, and the sessions per mouse must match the list as a multiset (the dataset's subject labels need not follow the paper's numbering). Reproduced when all counts match; partially reproduced when the totals match and at most two per-group counts differ by one.

claims.statement: 41,031 neurons were imaged, 8,371, 7,108 and 4,859 in PPC layers 2, 3 and 5 and 7,788, 7,005 and 5,900 in PM; these are active cells, 99.6% of the manually selected ROIs.
claims.source: Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 1; Supplementary Table 1
claims.quote: In total, we imaged the activity of 41,031 neurons in 94 sessions (PPC ... 8,371, 7,108 and 4,859 neurons from 17, 15 and 14 sessions in layers 2, 3 and 5, respectively; PM ... 7,788, 7,005 and 5,900 neurons from 16, 15 and 17 sessions, respectively)
claims.criterion: The per-session averages of Supplementary Table 1 (active cells 492, 474, 347, 487, 467, 347) times the session counts give these totals, so they count active cells. Readings of what the dataset's ROIs are, (a) all ROIs, (b) ROIs with a dR/R excursion beyond 3 s.d. of the session trace (the paper's "signal beyond 3σ"). Reproduced when, under one reading, all seven counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Mice got the reward 7.4 ± 0.1 s after the trial start and spent 860 ± 10 ms in each no-sound zone of the intermittent conditions (mean ± s.e.m. over 94 sessions).
claims.source: Online Methods, Behavioral training, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Mice got the reward in 7.4 ± 0.1 s (mean ± s.e.m., n = 94). In intermittent conditions, mice spent 860 ± 10 ms (n = 94) in each no-sound zone.
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the stated s.e.m. Per session, the mean over the analysed trials (first 150, without trials over 20 s or error trials), then the mean over sessions. Which no-sound zones count is not given; readings (a) every complete no-sound zone after the first 33 cm and before the goal, (b) every no-sound zone the mouse enters, including the one around the goal in intermittent 1 up to the reward. Reproduced when the reward time and, under one reading, the zone time are within tolerance.

claims.statement: In every session the start-to-first-lick distance correlated with the start-to-goal distance, with r from 0.258 to 0.822 over the 94 sessions (r = 0.798 in the example session).
claims.source: Results, Licking indicates action-dependent distance estimation, paragraph 2; Figure 1b; Online Methods, Behavioral analysis
claims.quote: Mice increased licking frequency as they approached the goal (r = 0.798, P = 2.11 × 10−34; Fig. 1b; 94 sessions of 8 mice ... r = 0.258 to 0.822, P = 0.00229 to 9.05 × 10−38)
claims.criterion: The Results do not name the two variables of r. They are read as those of the Methods' session selection, since every reported P is below its 0.01 threshold. The Methods define that correlation as start-to-lick distance against start-to-goal distance, first lick meaning the first lick more than 33 cm from the start, over the analysed trials of all conditions. The coefficient is not named; readings (a) Pearson, (b) Spearman. Reproduced when, under one reading, every session has r > 0 with P < 0.01 and all r lie within 0.232 to 0.904 (the range widened by 10% of each bound).

claims.statement: Licking increased as mice approached the goal in all conditions, and in both intermittent conditions it increased even within the no-sound zones (41.9-25.1 and 8.4-0 cm in intermittent 1, 25.1-8.4 cm in intermittent 2).
claims.source: Figure 1c; Results, Licking indicates action-dependent distance estimation, paragraph 2
claims.quote: In intermittent conditions, anticipatory licking increased even when the sound was omitted (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P = 4.87 × 10−8 to 1.22 × 10−15; Fig. 1c)
claims.criterion: Licks per trial in goal-distance bins, mean per session, for each condition (Fig. 1c). The text does not state the bins or the pairs compared; they are read from the figure. The boxes are 4.2 cm wide (32 from 134 to 0 cm), and each of the four brackets compares a bin with the bin 8.4 cm (two boxes) farther from the goal. The tested bins are 29.3-25.1, 20.9-16.7, 12.6-8.4 and 4.2-0 cm. The text confirms this. Its no-sound range, P = 4.87e-8 to 1.22e-15, is exactly the set of the first and fourth intermittent 1 values and the second and third intermittent 2 values, the comparisons whose tested bin is silent. Bin edges at multiples of 4.2 cm from the goal are a standard choice read from the figure. One-sided signed-rank test over the 94 sessions (tested bin higher), at the Bonferroni threshold P < 0.01 (Statistics; the legend marks P < 1e-7). Reproduced when licking rises with P < 0.01 in the four no-sound comparisons (intermittent 1, first and fourth; intermittent 2, second and third) and in all four continuous comparisons. The other comparisons are shown.

claims.statement: During no-sound zones licking rose more steeply in fast-locomotion trials than in slow ones, in both intermittent conditions.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 1; Results, Licking indicates action-dependent distance estimation, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Slope of licking ... was significantly steeper in fast trials than slow trials, suggesting that mice use action-dependent distance estimation
claims.criterion: Per trial, lick frequency in a no-sound zone regressed on time (Lick(t) = b0 + b1 t, Supplementary Fig. 1); trials split into equal slow and fast halves per session (O9); per session, mean slope of slow and of fast trials; signed-rank test over sessions per condition. Reproduced when, under every reading of O9, fast slopes exceed slow with P < 0.01 in both intermittent conditions.

claims.statement: Silencing PPC with muscimol lowered the correlation between start-to-lick and start-to-goal distance, making lick initiation more variable.
claims.source: Figure 1d; Results, Licking indicates action-dependent distance estimation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Correlation coefficients decreased after muscimol injection, indicating that silencing of PPC made lick initiation more variable (Mann-Whitney U test, P = 3.08 × 10−4, z = 3.61)
claims.criterion: Session correlations as in lick-goal-correlation, muscimol sessions against PBS sessions (no-injection sessions are shown in Fig. 1d but not tested), two-sided Mann-Whitney U. Reproduced when muscimol correlations are lower with P < 0.05.

claims.statement: After muscimol the distance between the first lick and the goal was more variable than after PBS, in all three conditions.
claims.source: Figure 1e; Results, Licking indicates action-dependent distance estimation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Variance of the distance was compared between PBS and muscimol-injected trials
claims.criterion: First-lick-to-goal distance per trial, PBS against muscimol trials, Ansari-Bradley test per condition. Reproduced when muscimol trials have the larger spread with P < 1e-14 (the legend's threshold) in all three conditions.

claims.statement: After muscimol, licking no longer increased significantly in the no-sound zones of the intermittent conditions, while after PBS it did. The increase of licks between adjacent bins in those no-sound zones was smaller after muscimol than after PBS.
claims.source: Figure 1f,g; Results, Licking indicates action-dependent distance estimation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The effect of PPC silencing was most prominent in intermittent conditions, with no increase in licking in no-sound zones (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P = 0.485 to 0.0212; Fig. 1f; Mann-Whitney U-test, P = 0.00761 and 4.84 × 10−6; Fig. 1g)
claims.criterion: Fig. 1f, licks per trial in 4.2-cm bins and the same four comparisons as fig1c-licking-without-sound (each tested bin against the bin 8.4 cm farther from the goal; the figure draws the same brackets), separately for the 12 muscimol and the 12 PBS sessions, one-sided signed-rank test over sessions, P < 0.01 (legend). The text's muscimol range for no-sound zones, P = 0.485 to 0.0212, is again the first and fourth intermittent 1 values and the second and third intermittent 2 values. Fig. 1g, per trial, the change of lick count from the 8.4-cm bin 25.1-16.7 cm to 16.7-8.4 cm and from 16.7-8.4 cm to 8.4-0 cm (the legend's 25-17, 17-8.4 and 8.4-0 cm), PBS against muscimol trials, Mann-Whitney U, P < 0.01. Reproduced when none of the four no-sound comparisons has P < 0.01 after muscimol, all four have P < 0.01 after PBS (the paper's largest is 0.00464), and the Fig. 1g increase is larger after PBS with P < 0.01 for intermittent 1 at 17-8.4 to 8.4-0 cm and intermittent 2 at 25-17 to 17-8.4 cm.

claims.statement: Silencing PPC increased overrun, the start of licking more than 8.3 cm past the goal, most in the intermittent 1 condition.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 2d; Results, Licking indicates action-dependent distance estimation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Silencing of PPC increased overrun (start licking over 8.3 cm past the goal)
claims.criterion: Per trial, the distance of the licking for reward acquisition relative to the goal (the first lick at or past the goal), PBS against muscimol trials per condition, Mann-Whitney U. Reproduced when muscimol trials lick farther past the goal with P < 0.01 in continuous and intermittent 1 (the legend's threshold); intermittent 2 (reported P = 0.0221) is shown.

claims.statement: PPC inactivation lowered locomotion speed and raised anticipatory licking in the continuous condition, but changed neither in the intermittent conditions.
claims.source: Online Methods, Muscimol injection, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Inactivation of PPC decreased the locomotion speed of mice in the continuous condition (MannWhitney U-test, P = 9.63 × 10−12, z = 6.81), which was most probably caused by increased anticipatory licking (Mann-Whitney U-test, P = 6.92 × 10−11, z = 6.52). In intermittent conditions, inactivation of PPC did not change the locomotion speed (P = 0.106, z = 1.62) and the licking (P = 0.0828, z = 1.73).
claims.criterion: Per trial, muscimol against PBS trials, Mann-Whitney U (two-sided, Statistics); intermittent 1 and 2 pooled, as the text reports one test. The paper does not define the measures. Readings for speed, (a) mean speed from start to goal, (b) mean speed from start to reward. Readings for licking, (a) lick count from start to goal, (b) lick count from start to reward. The no-change parts are claims of absence, judged at P < 0.05. Reproduced when, under every reading, continuous speed is lower and licking higher after muscimol with P < 0.05, and neither differs with P < 0.05 in intermittent trials.

claims.statement: PPC and PM neurons responded to sounds; in layer 3, PM had more sound-responsive neurons than PPC (4.78% against 1.48%).
claims.source: Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 2; Supplementary Figure 4b
claims.quote: On average, PM had more sound-responsive neurons than PPC in layer 3 (PPC, 1.48%, PM, 4.78%; Mann-Whitney U test, P = 0.0402)
claims.criterion: Sound-mapping trials (Online Methods, Imaging sound responses of neurons). Activity after sound from two adjacent speakers pooled into six azimuths; 500 ms moving average; a neuron is sound responsive when, at some azimuth, activity in the first 1.5 s after sound onset exceeds activity in the 1 s before (one-sided t-test, P < 1e-5). Percentages per field of view, readings of O5. Reproduced when, under one reading, both percentages are within tolerance and the per-session Mann-Whitney U test gives PM higher with P < 0.05.

claims.statement: Goal-distance neurons numbered 1,116, 1,054 and 483 in PPC layers 2, 3 and 5 and 601, 479 and 129 in PM; of these, 744, 854 and 367 in PPC and 193, 204 and 54 in PM were after-reaching neurons; per session, on average 65.6, 70.3 and 34.5 in PPC and 37.6, 31.9 and 7.59 in PM were goal-distance neurons.
claims.source: Figure 2d; Figure 3c legend; Supplementary Figure 6 legend; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Number of after-reaching neurons in layers 2, 3, 5 was 744, 854, 367 in PPC and 193, 204, 54 in PM ... (average number of goal-distance neurons in layers 2, 3 and 5; PPC, 65.6, 70.3 and 34.5; PM, 37.6, 31.9 and 7.59)
claims.criterion: The classification of the opening comment (Online Methods, Task-relevant neurons), under readings O1, O2 and O3. Before-reaching counts follow by subtraction and match Supplementary Fig. 9a (372, 200, 116; 408, 275, 75); the per-session averages are the totals over session counts. Fig. 2d also gives goal-distance or reward neurons (1,745, 1,456 and 651 in PPC; 816, 625 and 183 in PM), so reward neurons are 629, 402, 168; 215, 146, 54. These are shown, not judged. This claim selects the neurons other claims use. Reproduced when, under every reading, at least 10 of the 12 counts are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at least 6 are. The counts under each reading are shown.

claims.statement: Task-relevant neurons made up 41.3, 33.8 and 20.0% of active neurons in PPC layers 2, 3 and 5 and 19.6, 16.7 and 5.70% in PM, more in PPC than in PM in every layer.
claims.source: Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 4; Figure 2d
claims.quote: Among active neurons (99.6% of all neurons; Supplementary Table 1), the proportions of task-relevant neurons in layers 2, 3 and 5 were 41.3, 33.8 and 20.0% in PPC, and 19.6, 16.7 and 5.70% in PM, indicating that more neurons were recruited to the task in PPC than PM
claims.criterion: Task relevance as in neuron-classes (O1, O2). Percentages under the two readings of O5 (Fig. 2d shows pooled counts 3,497, 2,376, 1,045 and 1,533, 1,180, 317 task-relevant neurons, which over the active counts give 41.8, 33.4, 21.5, 19.7, 16.8 and 5.37%. These differ from the reported values by up to 1.5 percentage points, so the reported values are probably per-session means, reading (a); the pooled values still lie within tolerance). Mann-Whitney U over per-session proportions, PPC against PM per layer. Reproduced when, under one O5 reading, all six values are within tolerance and, under every method reading, PPC exceeds PM with P < 0.05 in all three layers.

claims.statement: PPC had more goal-distance neurons than PM in all three layers.
claims.source: Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 4; Figure 2d
claims.quote: PPC had more goal-distance neurons than PM in all layers (Mann-Whitney U test, P = 0.00415, 0.0152 and 4.98 × 10−4, z = 2.87, 2.43 and 3.48, respectively; Fig. 2d)
claims.criterion: Per session, goal-distance neurons, PPC against PM per layer, Mann-Whitney U over sessions. Whether counts or proportions of active neurons are compared is not said; readings (a) proportion of active neurons, (b) count. Reproduced when, under every reading of O1 to O3 and of the measure, PPC is higher with P < 0.05 in all three layers.

claims.statement: PPC had more after-reaching than before-reaching neurons in every layer, whereas PM tended the other way, significantly in layer 2.
claims.source: Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 4; Figure 2d
claims.quote: PPC had more after-reaching neurons than before-reaching neurons (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P = 0.0319, 0.00568 and 0.0176, z = 2.15, w = 13.5 and 9.5), whereas PM had the opposite tendency (P = 0.00771, 0.287 and 0.427, z = 2.66, w = 70 and 57.5)
claims.criterion: Per session, counts (or proportions, O5) of after-reaching and before-reaching neurons, paired over sessions, two-sided signed-rank test per area and layer. Reproduced when, under every reading of O1 to O3, after-reaching exceeds before-reaching in all PPC layers with P < 0.05, and in PM before-reaching exceeds after-reaching in layer 2 with P < 0.05 and PM layers 3 and 5 do not show PPC's direction significantly.

claims.statement: In both PPC and PM, goal-distance neurons in layers 3 and 5 preferred distances closer to the goal than those in layer 2.
claims.source: Figure 2d insets and legend; Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 4
claims.quote: in both areas, goal-distance neurons in layers 3 and 5 were more tuned to the distance near the goal than those in layer 2 (Mann-Whitney U test, P = 0.00319 to 2.25 × 10−16)
claims.criterion: Distance preference per goal-distance neuron (O4), Mann-Whitney U over neurons between layers within each area, Bonferroni threshold P < 0.01 (Statistics, Fig. 2d). Reproduced when, under every reading of O1 to O3, layers 3 and 5 each have smaller preferred distances than layer 2 with P < 0.01 in both areas. The layer 3 against 5 comparisons are shown.

claims.statement: In PPC and PM, more goal-distance neurons were best fit by goal distance than by the time to reach the goal.
claims.source: Figure 3b; Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 6
claims.quote: More neurons represented the goal distance than the time to goal in PPC and PM (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P = 0.00348 to 4.33 × 10−4)
claims.criterion: Single-neuron regression with BIC selection over the 11 variable sets (opening comment; O6). A neuron represents distance when its best set contains distance, and time when it contains time. Per session, counts of distance and of time neurons among goal-distance neurons, paired two-sided signed-rank test over sessions per area and layer. Reproduced when, under every reading, distance neurons outnumber time neurons with P < 0.01 in all six area-layer groups.

claims.statement: Goal-distance and after-reaching neurons were fit better by goal distance than by a distance held constant during no-sound zones or by the sound intensity.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 6; Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 6
claims.quote: RMSE of Distance was significantly smaller than of other variables both in goal-distance neurons and after-reaching neurons, indicating goal distance representation
claims.criterion: Per neuron, y(t) = b0 + b1 phi(variable(t)) with the Gaussian basis of equation (3), variable Distance, Step (goal distance held at its value on entering each no-sound zone) or Sound (intensity, 100 dB SPL at 25 cm and 6 dB lower per doubling of distance; Online Methods). Intensity during no-sound zones and below 25 cm is not given; readings (a) zero during no-sound zones and the formula below 25 cm with distance floored at 0.42 cm; (b) the same with intensity capped at 100 dB below 25 cm. Frames as O6. RMSE of each fit, paired signed-rank test over neurons, Distance against Step and against Sound, for goal-distance and for after-reaching neurons in each area and layer. Reproduced when, under every reading, Distance has the lower RMSE with P < 0.05 in all 24 comparisons; partially when in at least 20.

claims.statement: The distance tuning curves of goal-distance neurons, as fitted coefficients, did not differ between PPC and PM.
claims.source: Results, Goal-distance representation in PPC and PM, paragraph 6
claims.quote: Fitted coefficients for goal-distance representation revealed that the distance tuning curves of neurons were similar between PPC and PM (Online Methods; Mann-Whitney U test, P = 0.268 to 0.106, z = 1.11 to 1.62)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The coefficient compared is not named; the fit is the distance model of equation (2) for goal-distance neurons. Readings (a) the width s of the distance basis; (b) the distance coefficient b1. Mann-Whitney U over neurons, PPC against PM per layer, two-sided. Reproduced when no layer differs with P < 0.05; not reproduced when any does; effect sizes are shown. If the readings disagree the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In the continuous condition, after-reaching neurons increased their activity as mice approached the goal, in both PPC and PM.
claims.source: Figure 3c; Results, PPC represents goal distance estimated from action, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Activity in the continuous condition gradually increased in both PPC and PM as mice approached the goal (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P = 0.00507 to 0, z = 2.80 to 25.0; Fig. 3c, and Supplementary Figs. 7 and 8a)
claims.criterion: Per after-reaching neuron, its trial-averaged dR/R in the condition, binned every 0.42 cm (equation 5); whether the 8.37 cm moving average of the classification is applied first is not said, readings (a) not applied, (b) applied. Slope of activity against approach in the zones 25.1-8.4 and 8.4-0 cm (Supplementary Fig. 8a), signed-rank test of slopes against zero over neurons per area and layer. Reproduced when, under every reading, the median slope is positive (activity rising toward the goal) with P < 0.01 in all 12 area, layer and zone tests.

claims.statement: In the intermittent conditions, PPC after-reaching neurons in all layers increased activity toward the goal both with and without sound.
claims.source: Figure 3c; Supplementary Figure 8a; Results, PPC represents goal distance estimated from action, paragraph 1
claims.quote: In intermittent conditions, increased activity was observed with and without sound inputs in all PPC layers (sound zones ... P = 1.37 × 10−4 to 0, z = 3.81 to 23.2; no-sound zones ... P = 1.19 × 10−6 to 0, z = 4.86 to 17.9)
claims.criterion: Slopes as in fig3c-continuous-ramp (both readings), in intermittent 1 and 2 trials, zones 25.1-8.4 and 8.4-0 cm (one with and one without sound in each condition). Reproduced when, under every reading, the median slope is positive with P < 0.01 in all 12 PPC tests (3 layers, 2 conditions, 2 zones).

claims.statement: In PM, after-reaching neurons showed positive slopes in some no-sound zones, but in the intermittent 1 condition their slopes without sound were not significantly positive.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 8a; Results, PPC represents goal distance estimated from action, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Slopes were significantly positive with and without sound in PPC in all conditions, but in PM in intermittent 1 condition they were not significantly positive without sound.
claims.criterion: Slopes as in fig3c-continuous-ramp, PM after-reaching neurons, no-sound zones (intermittent 1, 8.4-0 cm; intermittent 2, 25.1-8.4 cm), signed-rank against zero per layer, P < 0.01 (the legend's threshold). Supplementary Fig. 8a marks all three PM layers significant in intermittent 2 at 25.1-8.4 cm and none in intermittent 1 at 8.4-0 cm. Reproduced when, under every reading, all three PM intermittent 2 no-sound tests are positive with P < 0.01 and no PM intermittent 1 no-sound test is (the latter a claim of absence, judged by the paper's test). Per layer results are shown.

claims.statement: Slopes of after-reaching activity were lower without sound than with sound.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 8b
claims.quote: Although slopes were significantly positive even without sound in a, they were less steep than those with sound
claims.criterion: For each after-reaching neuron and zone (25.1-8.4 and 8.4-0 cm), the slope with sound (from the condition with sound in that zone) against without (the other intermittent condition), paired signed-rank over neurons. Reproduced when, under every reading of fig3c-continuous-ramp, the slope without sound is lower with P < 0.01 in all six PPC comparisons and in at least four of six PM comparisons (the paper reports five).

claims.statement: Without sound, PPC after-reaching neurons in layers 2 and 3 had steeper slopes than PM, while slopes in PM were equal to or lower than in PPC.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 8c; Results, PPC represents goal distance estimated from action, paragraph 1
claims.quote: In layers 2 and 3, PPC had steeper slopes than PM without sound
claims.criterion: No-sound slopes per neuron as in supp8b-slopes-lower-without-sound, PPC against PM neurons per layer and zone, Mann-Whitney U. The legend gives two P values per zone and layer; they are read in the order intermittent 1, intermittent 2, as the other legends list conditions, which puts the without-sound value second in 25.1-8.4 cm and first in 8.4-0 cm (the only order under which the legend supports the text's layers 2 and 3). The figure confirms it, since in each zone the red intermittent 1 pair is drawn first, and the stars fall on the no-sound pairs as read. Reproduced when, under every reading, PPC no-sound slopes exceed PM with P < 0.05 in layer 3 in both zones and in layer 2 in at least one zone, and PM is significantly steeper in no comparison.

claims.statement: PPC neurons kept the distance preference they had in the continuous condition in the intermittent conditions, especially near the goal, more than PM neurons did.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 9b; Results, PPC represents goal distance estimated from action, paragraph 2
claims.quote: PPC neurons preserved the distance representation, especially near the goal, significantly more than neurons in PM (Mann-Whitney U test, P = 0.0429 to 6.82 × 10−14, z = 2.02 to 7.49)
claims.criterion: Per goal-distance neuron, the difference between its distance preference (O4) in continuous trials and in intermittent 1 (and 2) trials. The legend says only "difference"; it is read as the absolute difference, the only reading under which a smaller value means a better preserved preference (signed differences are shown); PPC against PM per layer and neuron group, Mann-Whitney U. Groups as Supplementary Fig. 9a, before-reaching neurons in four groups by continuous preference and after-reaching neurons; the four groups' borders are not given, readings (a) equal 16.75 cm quarters of 67 to 0 cm, (b) the zone borders 58.6, 25.1 and 8.4 cm. Reproduced when, under every reading, in intermittent 1 PPC after-reaching neurons have the smaller difference with P < 0.05 in at least one layer, and PM has a significantly smaller difference in no comparison. "Especially near the goal" is read as the after-reaching group, the one nearest the goal.

claims.statement: Decoders built from goal-distance neurons estimated goal distance above chance in both PPC and PM.
claims.source: Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 2; Figure 4b
claims.quote: Both areas estimated the goal distances reliably above chance level (Wilcoxon signed rank test, P = 0, z = 181 to 439)
claims.criterion: Decoder of the opening comment (O7, O8). Chance level is not defined. The z values imply a paired test over frames. Readings of chance (a) the RMSE of the flat prior over 0 to 67 cm at each frame; (b) the RMSE of a decoder whose training trials have their distances permuted across trials. Paired signed-rank test of decoder RMSE against chance over frames, per area, layer and condition. Reproduced when, under every reading, decoder RMSE is lower with P < 0.01 in all 18 settings.

claims.statement: The decoding error (RMSE) from layer 2 neurons was lower in PPC than in PM.
claims.source: Figure 4c; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 2
claims.quote: the estimation in PPC had significantly less deviation from the actual distance than in PM (Mann-Whitney ... U-test in layer 2, P = 0.00765 to 0, z = 2.67 to 17.1)
claims.criterion: Per trial, mean RMSE within each goal-distance bin (O8), PPC trials against PM trials per bin and condition, Mann-Whitney U, P < 0.01 (legend threshold). The legend's ranges (continuous P = 0.893 to 0) show that not every bin differs. Reproduced when, under every reading, in each condition PPC has the lower median RMSE in more than half of the bins and significantly lower RMSE in at least one, and PM is significantly lower in no bin. Layers 3 and 5 (Supplementary Fig. 10) are shown.

claims.statement: PPC and PM gave similar MAP estimates, but near the goal PPC estimates were better than PM.
claims.source: Figure 4d; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 2
claims.quote: PPC and PM had similar MAP estimates, but the estimations near the goal were better in PPC than in PM (P = 0.00549 to 2.47× 10−11, z = 2.78 to 6.68; Fig. 4d)
claims.criterion: Per trial, mean MAP within each bin (O8), PPC against PM, Mann-Whitney U per bin, layer 2, P < 0.01. "Near the goal" is read as the bins between 8.4 and 0 cm. Reproduced when, under every reading, in the continuous condition at least one bin in 8.4-0 cm has PPC MAP closer to the actual distance with P < 0.01 and no bin in that range has PM closer with P < 0.01.

claims.statement: The uncertainty (posterior s.d.) of distance estimates was lower in PPC than in PM at every goal distance and in every condition.
claims.source: Figure 4e; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 2
claims.quote: uncertainty of distance estimation was significantly less in PPC than PM (P = 1.09 × 10−12 to 0, z = 7.12 to 22.9; Fig. 4e)
claims.criterion: Per trial, mean posterior s.d. within each bin (O8), PPC against PM per bin and condition, layer 2, Mann-Whitney U. Reproduced when, under every reading, PPC is lower with P < 0.01 in every bin of every condition; partially when in at least 90% of bins. Layers 3 and 5 (Supplementary Fig. 10) are shown.

claims.statement: Decoding errors decreased with sound and increased without it. Within zones, the change per cm of the RMSE difference (intermittent minus continuous) was lower in sound zones than in no-sound zones, in all PPC layers and in PM layers 2 and 3.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 11b,c; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Decoding errors decreased with sound and increased without sound (Mann-Whitney U test, P = 0.00295 to 1.56 × 10−6, z = 2.97 to 4.80; Supplementary Fig. 11)
claims.criterion: Supplementary Fig. 11b,c. Per session, dRMSE, the difference of median RMSE (over trials) between each intermittent condition and the continuous condition in 0.42-cm bins. Linear regression of dRMSE on distance within each zone, y = b0 - b1 distance, so b1 is the rise per cm of approach (Fig. 11c axis, "dRMSE per cm"). Then b1 of sound zones against b1 of no-sound zones, Mann-Whitney U. Fig. 11b shows four zones per intermittent condition (58.6-41.9, 41.9-25.1, 25.1-8.4 and 8.4-0 cm). The legend's "n = 68 (that is, 17 sessions times 4)" allows two readings. (a) Four sound and four no-sound zones per session, n = 68 per group. (b) 68 zones in all, the zones 25.1-8.4 and 8.4-0 cm of both conditions, two sound and two no-sound per session. Decoder sessions exclude the 3 with no goal-distance neurons, which fits PM layer 5's 14 sessions. Reproduced when, under every reading, b1 is lower with sound with P < 0.01 in all PPC layers. PM is shown.

claims.statement: In the continuous condition, decoded MAP distances followed the actual distance in all layers of PPC and PM.
claims.source: Figure 5a; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In the continuous condition, MAPs followed the actual distances in all layers of PPC and PM (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P = 9.56 × 10−14 to 0, z = 7.45 to 34.1; Fig. 5a)
claims.criterion: Per trial and zone (O8, four zones), MAP decrease per cm (equation 10); signed-rank test of slopes against zero over trials. Reproduced when, under every reading, the median slope is positive with P < 0.01 in all 24 area, layer and zone tests.

claims.statement: In the intermittent conditions, MAPs decreased with and without sound in most zones, and in every zone in PPC layers 3 and 5.
claims.source: Figure 5a; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 3; Discussion, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In intermittent conditions, MAPs decreased with and without sound inputs in most distance zones, and especially in all zones in PPC layers 3 and 5 (sound zones ... P = 0.00293 to 0, z = 2.98 to 14.7; no-sound zones ... P = 6.59 × 10−4 to 0, z = 3.41 to 8.56)
claims.criterion: As fig5a-map-follows-continuous, in intermittent 1 and 2 trials. Reproduced when, under every reading, in PPC layers 3 and 5 every zone of both conditions (16 tests) has a positive median slope with P < 0.01, and over all 48 tests more than half do.

claims.statement: MAP slopes were shallower without sound than with sound.
claims.source: Figure 5b; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Slopes of MAPs without sound were lower than those with sound (Mann-Whitney U test, P = 5.14 × 10−12 to 0; Fig. 5b)
claims.criterion: Per trial MAP slopes in the zones 25.1-8.4 and 8.4-0 cm; for each zone, trials of the condition with sound there against trials of the one without, Mann-Whitney U (Fig. 5b legend). Reproduced when, under every reading, the no-sound slope is lower with P < 0.01 in all six PPC comparisons and in at least four of six PM comparisons.

claims.statement: In intermittent 1, without sound between 8.4 and 0 cm, MAPs decreased more steeply in PPC layer 3 than layer 2, while the s.d. of the estimates did not differ between these layers.
claims.source: Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In the intermittent 1 condition, the decrease of MAPs in PPC layer 3 was significantly steeper than that in layer 2 without sound between 8.4 and 0 cm (Mann-Whitney U test, P = 0.00685, z = 2.70), whereas the s.d. of distance estimation showed no significant difference (P = 0.247, z = 1.16)
claims.criterion: Per trial MAP slope and s.d. slope (equation 10) in intermittent 1 trials, zone 8.4-0 cm, PPC layer 3 trials against layer 2 trials, Mann-Whitney U. The s.d. part is a claim of absence judged at P < 0.05. Reproduced when, under every reading, the layer 3 MAP slope is steeper with P < 0.05 and the s.d. slopes do not differ with P < 0.05.

claims.statement: During no-sound zones, decoded MAPs fell faster in fast-locomotion trials than in slow ones.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 13; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Slopes of MAPs were steeper in fast trials than slow trials, suggesting action-dependent distance prediction of mice
claims.criterion: Per trial, MAP regressed on time within no-sound zones (y(t) = b0 + b1 t); trials split into slow and fast halves (O9); fast against slow trials per area, layer and condition, Mann-Whitney U. Reproduced when, under every reading, fast trials have the steeper median slope with P < 0.05 in PPC layers 2 and 3 in both conditions; the other eight tests are shown (the paper reports PM significant in intermittent 1 only).

claims.statement: In all PPC layers, between 25.1 and 0 cm, uncertainty of the estimated distance fell more steeply with sound than without, the updating step of dynamic Bayesian inference.
claims.source: Figure 5c,d; Results, Distance prediction with dynamic Bayesian inference, paragraph 3; Discussion, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Uncertainty of estimated distance decreased with sound inputs compared with no sound in all layers of PPC between 25.8 and 0 cm (P = 0.0153 to 6.92 × 10−11; Fig. 5c,d)
claims.criterion: Per trial s.d.-of-posterior slopes (decrease per cm, equation 10) in the zones 25.1-8.4 and 8.4-0 cm, sound trials against no-sound trials per zone as in fig5b-map-slope-lower-without-sound, Mann-Whitney U. Reproduced when, under every reading, the decrease is larger with sound with P < 0.05 in all six PPC comparisons. PM results are shown (the paper reports them mixed).

claims.statement: In all PPC layers, the uncertainty of the decoded distance (s.d. of the posterior) decreased during sound presentation between 8.4 and 0 cm.
claims.source: Figure 5c and legend
claims.quote: Uncertainty decreased during sound presentations in PPC between 8.4 cm and 0 cm.
claims.criterion: Per trial s.d.-of-posterior slope (decrease per cm, equation 10) in the zone 8.4-0 cm, signed-rank test against zero over trials per area, layer and condition, P < 0.01 (Fig. 5c, "Data presentation as in a"). The legend gives only the range over all Fig. 5c tests (P = 0.892 to 0), so no statistic is recorded. Fig. 5c marks, in the 8.4-0 cm zone of each PPC layer, the continuous and intermittent 2 tests, the two conditions with sound there. Reproduced when, under every reading of O7 and O8, the decrease is positive with P < 0.01 in all six (three PPC layers, continuous and intermittent 2). PM and intermittent 1 are shown.

claims.statement: The decoder with a log-normal likelihood estimated goal distance better than one with a Gaussian likelihood in 17 of 18 settings, all but PM layer 5 in the continuous condition.
claims.source: Online Methods, Probabilistic decoding of goal distance, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The decoder with log-normal distribution gave better estimates for goal distance than that with a Gaussian distribution in the 18 settings ... except for layer 5 in PM in continuous condition (P = 0.834, z = 0.209)
claims.criterion: The same decoder with a Gaussian likelihood of raw activity (mean and s.d. per bin as for the log-normal). "Better" is not defined; readings (a) lower RMSE, (b) lower absolute MAP error, paired over frames (the z values imply frames), signed-rank test per setting (3 layers x 2 areas x 3 conditions). Reproduced when, under every reading, the log-normal decoder is better with P < 0.01 in at least 16 of the 18 settings.

claims.statement: An SVM decoder trained on recorded data did not estimate distance better than one trained on trial-shuffled data, except in one setting, so ignoring correlations between neurons cost the decoder little.
claims.source: Online Methods, Probabilistic decoding of goal distance, paragraph 8
claims.quote: Recorded-SVM did not estimate distance better than shuffled-SVM (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P = 0.957 to 1, z = 1.71 to 12.5), except in 1 setting (layer 3 in PM in intermittent1 condition, P = 0.00572, z = 2.53)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. SVM (Matlab) on goal-distance neurons' activity, trained and validated as the probabilistic decoder. The paper says only "shuffled data" (refs. 49, 50); the shuffle is read as the standard one of those references, each neuron's activity permuted independently across training trials at the same goal distance (4.2-cm bin). Kernel, classes and error measure are not given; readings (a) linear multiclass SVM over 4.2-cm distance bins, error the absolute difference of the predicted bin centre from the actual distance; (b) linear SVM regression, absolute error. One-sided signed-rank test (recorded better) over frames per setting. Reproduced when, under every reading, no more than one of the 18 settings shows the recorded SVM better with P < 0.01; not reproduced when more do.

claims.statement: The data are 2286 single and multi-units from 29 patients (17 female), 30 to 137 units per patient, in the amygdala (580), hippocampus (794), entorhinal cortex (440), parahippocampal cortex (373) and piriform cortex (99).
claims.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1d; Results, Patient-wise decoding performance, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We recorded from 29 patients (17 female ... a total of 2286 single- and multi-neurons across the amygdala (A; 580 neurons, 25.37%), hippocampus (H; 794, 34.73%), entorhinal cortex (EC; 440, 19.25%), parahippocampal cortex (PHC; 373, 16.32%), and piriform cortex (PIC; 99, 4.33%) ... units per patient range from 30 to 137
claims.criterion: Counts of patients, units and female patients are exact, as the dandiset should hold the recordings the paper analysed. Regions as fixed in the opening comment. Reproduced when every value is within tolerance and units per patient range from 30 to 137; partially reproduced when the patient, unit and sex counts match but a region count does not; not reproduced when the patient or unit count differs.

claims.statement: Over half of the parahippocampal neurons responded to camera cuts (193 of 373, 51.74%).
claims.source: Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 2b; Table S1
claims.quote: Over half of the parahippocampal neurons responded to Camera Cuts during the movie (193/373, 51.74%
claims.criterion: Responsive neurons by the Methods' test as fixed in the opening comment. The fraction is compared, as the dandiset's PHC count differs from the paper's; the count is reported against 193. Readings are alpha 0.001 and alpha 0.01; reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance under either; partially reproduced when it is outside tolerance but above 25% under either; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Camera cuts evoked responses in a large share of neurons in every region (amygdala 46.90%, entorhinal cortex 45.68%, hippocampus 38.92%).
claims.source: Table S1; Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We found individual neurons with significant stimulus-evoked responses in all regions for visual transitions
claims.criterion: Same test and readings as fig2b-phc-camera-cuts. Reproduced when all three fractions are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when not, but every region has more than 25% responsive units under one reading; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Few parahippocampal neurons responded to scene cuts (25 of 373, 6.70%), but the modulation was consistent across the responsive neurons (cluster permutation test, p = 0.018).
claims.source: Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 2b; Table S1
claims.quote: Comparatively few parahippocampal neurons responded to Scene Cuts (25/373, 6.70%), although there was nonetheless a consistent pattern of modulation across responsive neurons (p = 0.018, cluster permutation test)
claims.criterion: The tolerance is the 95% binomial interval of a proportion of 6.70% among the paper's 373 units (1.96 times the standard error); 10% of the value (0.67 points) is smaller than the sampling error of a count of 25. Readings alpha 0.001 and 0.01. The cluster permutation test as in the Methods (z-scored trial-averaged rate per unit in 100 ms bins from -1000 to 1000 ms, two-sided independent t-test per bin between responsive and non-responsive units, clusters of adjacent bins with p < 0.005, summed absolute t, 1000 permutations of the unit labels, p of a cluster the fraction of permutations whose largest cluster sum exceeds it). Reproduced when, under one reading, the fraction is within tolerance and the largest cluster has p < 0.05; partially reproduced when one of the two holds; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Only a few neurons responded to the onset of semantic features (Summer 46, Tom 216, Persons 6 and Outdoor 4 of 2286 neurons), in contrast to camera cuts (1025).
claims.source: Abstract; Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons; Table S1
claims.criterion: The tolerance for Summer is the 95% binomial interval of 46 among 2286 units (10% of 46 is smaller than its sampling error); for Tom 10%. Readings alpha 0.001 and 0.01. Reproduced when, under one reading, both counts are within tolerance and every semantic label tested (Summer, Tom, McKenzie, Persons, Indoor, Outdoor, Summer Presence) has fewer than 10% of all units responsive while camera cuts have more than 25%; partially reproduced when that contrast holds but a count is outside tolerance; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: No neuron responded to the onset of indoor scenes.
claims.source: Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons, paragraph 1; Table S1
claims.quote: No responses were detected for the onset of indoor scenes.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test at alpha 0.001, the threshold stated in the same Results paragraph. Reproduced when no unit is responsive to Indoor onsets; not reproduced when any is. The count at alpha 0.01 and the counts for McKenzie and Summer Presence (also 0 in Table S1) are reported as variants.

claims.statement: By the cluster permutation test, parahippocampal neurons responded to the largest set of features (Summer, Persons, Camera Cuts, Scene Cuts, Outdoor), compared with the hippocampus (Tom, Camera Cuts, Outdoor), the amygdala (Camera Cuts) and the entorhinal cortex (none).
claims.source: Results, Stimulus-aligned responsive neurons, paragraph 1
claims.quote: neurons in the parahippocampal cortex responded to the largest set of stimulus features (Summer, Persons, Camera Cuts, Scene Cuts, Outdoor ... as compared to the hippocampus (Tom, Camera Cuts, Outdoor), amygdala (Camera Cuts), and entorhinal cortex (None).
claims.criterion: The cluster test of fig2b-phc-scene-cuts is run for 8 labels (Summer, Tom, McKenzie, Persons, Camera Cuts, Scene Cuts, Indoor, Outdoor) in 4 regions (A, H, EC, PHC); a cell is significant when its largest cluster has p < 0.05; with fewer than 2 responsive units a cell is not significant. Readings alpha 0.001 and 0.01 for the responsive split. Reproduced when, under one reading, at least 28 of the 32 cells agree with the paper's list and PHC has the most significant labels; partially reproduced when one of the two holds or at least 24 cells agree; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Thresholding the activity of single neurons does not reliably predict whether Summer is on screen; most neurons perform near chance, below the population decoder.
claims.source: Results, Decoding from neuronal activity, paragraph 1; Figure 3b; Methods, Single-neuron decoding performance
claims.quote: Decoding performances obtained by simply applying a threshold to single-neuron activity did not reliably predict the content, as the majority of neurons in the population performed near chance level (Fig. 3b). ... surpassing the performances achieved by individual neurons alone.
claims.criterion: For each unit, the summed spike count from 800 ms before to 800 ms after each sample; on each fold's validation set the threshold and its direction (above or below) that maximise kappa among up to 50 quantiles of the counts; kappa of that rule on the test set, averaged over the five folds. Reproduced when the median unit's kappa is below 0.05 and no unit reaches the paper's population kappa for Summer (0.31); partially reproduced when one of the two holds; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: A logistic regression on spike counts decodes characters and location about as well as the LSTM; pooled over patients it reaches kappa 0.28 for Summer and 0.31 for Indoor/Outdoor.
claims.source: Results, Choice of architecture, paragraph 2, and Patient-wise decoding performance, paragraph 2; Figure 3c; Figure 4a
claims.quote: The logistic regression model showed lower performances for the Scene and Camera Cut features (by 0.1 and 0.07, respectively), whereas no drop for character-related or location-related features was observed. ... the overall pooled performance of 0.28. ... an overall pooled performance of 0.31
claims.criterion: The tolerances are the SEMs over folds the paper gives for these labels (Table S2, LSTM), the nearest stated spread, as the paper gives none for the logistic regression. The logistic regression as fixed in the opening comment. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance and Tom, McKenzie and Persons each reach at least the LSTM value less its SEM (0.17, 0.235, 0.312); partially reproduced when 3 or 4 of these 5 conditions hold; not reproduced otherwise. Permutation p-values per fold are reported.

claims.statement: For scene and camera cuts the logistic regression performs below the LSTM, by 0.1 and 0.07, that is about kappa 0.10 and 0.11.
claims.source: Results, Choice of architecture, paragraph 2; Figure 3c; Table S2
claims.quote: The logistic regression model showed lower performances for the Scene and Camera Cut features (by 0.1 and 0.07, respectively)
claims.criterion: The values are the LSTM's (Table S2, 0.20 and 0.18) less the stated drops, and the tolerances the LSTM's SEMs, the nearest stated spread. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when both are below the LSTM values and above chance (permutation p < 0.001 in every fold) but one or both are outside tolerance; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Without temporal gaps between training, validation and test samples, decoding of Summer is almost perfect (kappa 0.99), and it falls to 0.31 as the gap grows to 32 s.
claims.source: Results, Avoiding spurious decoding performance, paragraph 1; Figure 3e; Figure S9
claims.quote: For instance, a random split without any temporal gaps achieves an almost perfect score of 0.99 ± 0.0005. However, as temporal gap sizes increase to 32 s, the performance drops precipitously to 0.31 ± 0.06
claims.criterion: Tested with the logistic regression in place of the LSTM. A random split assigns each sample at random to training, validation and test in the proportions of the 32 s split, five times; gaps of 4, 8, 16 and 32 s use the dataset's code layout. Reproduced when the random-split kappa is at least 0.9 and above the 32 s value; partially reproduced when it exceeds the 32 s value by at least 0.2 but is below 0.9; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Decoding from a single patient's neurons is lower than from the pooled population; no patient matches the pooled performance, for Summer, Scene Cuts or Indoor/Outdoor.
claims.source: Results, Patient-wise decoding performance, paragraph 2; Figure 4
claims.quote: Generally, decoding performance was lower at the individual patient level compared to the pooled neuronal population, with no single patient matching the performance of the aggregated data.
claims.criterion: The logistic regression per patient, same folds and procedure as the pooled model. Reproduced when, for all three labels, every patient's mean kappa is below the pooled mean kappa; partially reproduced when this holds for two labels; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: For Summer, patients 7, 10, 15 and 22 exceed kappa 0.2; for Indoor/Outdoor, patients 2, 13, 20 and 25 exceed 0.2.
claims.source: Results, Patient-wise decoding performance, paragraph 2; Figure 4b and 4d
claims.quote: certain patients (specifically 7,10,15, and 22) achieved decoding performances exceeding 0.2 ... Notably, patients 2,13,20 and 25 achieved performances exceeding 0.2
claims.criterion: Assumes the dandiset's subject ids are the paper's patient numbers; the dandiset and paper give no mapping. Of the 8 named patient and label pairs, reproduced when at least 7 have mean kappa above 0.2; partially reproduced for 4 to 6; not reproduced below 4. The patients above 0.2 here are listed either way.

claims.statement: Decoding from single regions depends on the feature; the amygdala is best and the hippocampus worst for Summer, and the parahippocampal cortex is best and the amygdala worst for Indoor/Outdoor.
claims.source: Results, Parahippocampal cortex drives decoding of visual transitions and location, paragraph 2; Results, Distribution of information across MTL regions, paragraph 1; Figure 5
claims.quote: the parahippocampal cortex yielded the highest performance for predicting indoor versus outdoor content ... For entorhinal cortex and amygdala, we observed lower performances ... The amygdala and parahippocampal cortex showed the highest decoding performances for Summer and Tom, respectively ... The hippocampus had the lowest performance for Summer
claims.criterion: Tested with the logistic regression in place of the LSTM, restricted to the units of one region (A, H, EC, PHC as fixed in the opening comment). The four orderings are A highest and H lowest for Summer, PHC highest and A lowest for Indoor/Outdoor, by mean kappa. Reproduced when all four hold; partially reproduced when 2 or 3 hold; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Responsive neurons drive decoding of camera cuts but not of Summer; without them, Summer is decoded about as well as from all neurons while camera cuts drop the most, and responsive neurons alone decode camera cuts about as well as all neurons but Summer less well.
claims.source: Results, Decoding with non-responsive versus responsive neurons, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 6
claims.quote: these subpopulations yielded performances comparable to those of the complete population (Fig. 6a, Complete) for the character Summer. ... restricting to only responsive neurons produced a decrease in overall performance ... the Camera Cuts feature, which exhibited the greatest performance drop when responsive neurons were excluded ... remained comparable to that of the complete population for the entire MTL
claims.criterion: Tested with the logistic regression in place of the LSTM, over all regions together. Responsive units at alpha 0.001. Conditions (a) Summer without responsive units is at least the complete kappa less 0.05; (b) Summer with responsive units only is below the complete kappa less 0.05; (c) the drop without responsive units is larger for camera cuts than for Summer; (d) camera cuts with responsive units only is at least the complete kappa less 0.05. Reproduced when all four hold; partially reproduced when 2 or 3 hold; not reproduced otherwise. Size-matched non-responsive sets (three draws) are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Across the five rankings of neurons by logistic regression weights for Summer, the top 500 neurons share 78 neurons, against about 1 expected by chance.
claims.source: Results, Top-ranked neurons and their distribution across patients and MTL regions, paragraph 1; Figure 7b; Methods, Intersection of top-performing neurons
claims.quote: Analyzing the top-performing 500 neurons from each of the five rankings revealed a common set of 78 neurons. ... the expected number of overlapping neurons is equivalent to one.
claims.criterion: Twenty sub-splits, four per test fold, each taking one of the other four folds as validation and the remaining three as training; each fit as the pooled logistic regression. Ranking per test fold as in the Methods (units grouped by the number of the four models with a non-zero coefficient, then by mean absolute coefficient); units tied at zero are ordered by a seeded random draw. Chance is computed for 2286 units and five sets of 500. Reproduced when the overlap is within tolerance; partially reproduced when it is outside tolerance but at least ten times chance; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: An LSTM decodes every label above chance from the pooled population, with kappa 0.36 for Persons, 0.31 for Indoor/Outdoor, 0.31 for Summer, 0.32 for McKenzie, 0.23 for Tom, 0.20 for Scene Cuts and 0.18 for Camera Cuts.
claims.source: Results, Decoding from neuronal activity, paragraph 1; Figure 3c; Table S2
claims.quote: Decoding performances for all tested labels significantly exceeded chance level (zero for Cohen's Kappa), as shown in Fig. 3c. The Persons label achieved the highest performance (mean ± standard error of the mean, SEM: 0.36 ± 0.05), followed by the location-related label Indoor/Outdoor (0.31 ± 0.06).

claims.statement: Shuffling the order of time bins in the test data lowers the LSTM's performance, most for visual transitions.
claims.source: Results, Choice of architecture, paragraph 2; Figure 3d
claims.quote: we assessed trained models using temporally-modified test data ... A pattern consistent with the LSTM decoding results emerged, with a noticeable decline in performance, especially for the visual transition labels.

claims.statement: Face labels decode slightly better than character labels (Summer 0.33, Tom 0.27), and Summer Presence (0.27) is decoded best from the amygdala (0.26).
claims.source: Results, Differences in character's visual appearances, paragraph 2; Figure 5b and 5c
claims.quote: Face labels for both characters elicited a slight improvement in performance ... with Summer increasing from 0.31 ± 0.06 to 0.33 ± 0.06 and Tom increasing from 0.23 ± 0.06 to 0.27 ± 0.07. ... The Summer Presence label had an overall performance of 0.27 ± 0.04 ... with the amygdala clearly dominating the regional distribution (0.26 ± 0.07).
claims.criterion: Tested with the logistic regression in place of the LSTM, as fixed in the opening comment, on the dandiset's summer-faces, tom-faces and summer-presence labels. The face labels hold only 0 and 1, so the frames the Methods exclude (a face neither shown nor clearly absent) stay in as negatives. Three conditions, by mean kappa over the five folds; (a) Summer Faces pooled is above Summer pooled; (b) Tom Faces pooled is above Tom pooled; (c) for Summer Presence the amygdala is highest among A, H, EC and PHC. Reproduced when all three hold; partially reproduced when one or two hold; not reproduced when none holds. Kappas by region for all three labels and permutation p-values per fold are reported.

claims.statement: Decoding Summer from the 500 top-ranked neurons gives the peak performance (kappa 0.38), above that of the full population.
claims.source: Results, Training on pre-selections of top-ranked neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 7a
claims.quote: observed an increase in performance when restricting the input activity to smaller populations (peak at 0.38 (Cohen's Kappa) for 500 neurons, 21.9% of the total population)
claims.criterion: Tested with the logistic regression in place of the LSTM. For each test fold, the ranking of fig7b-top500-overlap from its four sub-splits; on each of these sub-splits a logistic regression on the top k units of that ranking, scored on the shared test fold; kappa averaged over the four sub-splits and then over the five test folds (Methods, nested cross-validation). Sizes k of 23, 114, 150, 229, 500, 750, 1000, 1500 and 2286 units (1% to 100%, with the 500 and 150 the Results name). Reproduced when the kappa for 500 units is above that of all 2286 units and is the highest of the sizes; partially reproduced when it is above that of all units but another size is higher; not reproduced when it is not above that of all units.

claims.statement: The dandiset is the data the paper's analysis code reads, so that the code's choices fixed in this file apply to it.
claims.source: Code availability; the dandiset description; README of NuoLiLabBCM/KakuEtAl2025 at commit fbc0abe
claims.criterion: Reproduced when process_mat.py's inputs can be built from the NWB files (spike times per trial, unit quality metrics, CCF coordinates, airflow at 25 kHz with its timestamps, side and bottom DeepLabCut jaw and tongue traces and likelihoods, 3D jaw and tongue tracks) and the count of units passing get_good_units over all files is within 10% of 20,300 (with or without the drift metric, V1). Partially reproduced when the inputs exist but the count is outside 10%.

claims.statement: Mice licked at 6.23 +- 2 Hz (95% range 3.59 to 8.91 Hz) and breathed at lower frequencies, 4.02 +- 1.24 Hz (95% range 2.12 to 7.17 Hz).
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 2; Figure 1d
claims.quote: Licking occurred at 6.23 ± 2 Hz (mean ± std, 95% range: 3.59 - 8.91 Hz) while breathing occurred at lower frequencies (4.02 ± 1.24 Hz, 95% range: 2.12 - 7.17 Hz; Figure 1d)
claims.criterion: Neither the Methods nor the code say how the frequencies are taken. Readings (a) the inverse of every interval between consecutive tongue onsets, and between consecutive inspiration onsets, within trials, pooled over all sessions; (b) the same within lick bouts only (code bouts). Onsets as in the header. The 95% range is the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile. Reproduced when, under one reading, all six values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the two means are and a bound is not.

claims.statement: Inspiration always occurred between licks and never coincided with licking; licking preceded inspiration at a fixed latency.
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 2; Figure 1f
claims.quote: Inspiration always occurred between licks and thus never coincided with licking. Licking preceded inspiration at a fixed latency
claims.criterion: The paper shows this in raster plots and gives no measure. Measure, from the paper's definitions, the fraction of inspiration onsets inside lick bouts that fall within a tongue protrusion (tongue onset to tongue offset, code get_movement_timing), per session. "Never" is read (a) literally, no such inspiration in any session, and (b) as a rounded statement, under 5% of inspirations in pooled data (a standard choice, named here). Reproduced when (b) holds; the result under (a) is reported. The latency from the last lick to the next inspiration is reported per number of licks in the cycle.

claims.statement: For breath cycles with two licks, the second lick was delayed preceding a slower breath compared to a fast breath, in all mice (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, p < 0.001), so breathing influences the licking rhythm.
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 2; Figure 1g
claims.quote: In all mice, the lick timing was significantly delayed preceding a slower breath compared to a fast breath (Figure 1g, p<0.001, one sample t-test, two-tailed)
claims.criterion: The per-session peak difference of the header (Lick-to-breath timing, code get_peak_diff_lick_behv), slow minus fast. One-sample two-tailed t-test against 0 under O4 (a) sessions and (b) mice. Reproduced when the mean is positive with p < 0.001 under a reading and every mouse's mean difference is positive; partially reproduced when p < 0.001 with a positive mean but one or more mice are not positive.

claims.statement: During slow breathing, licking frequency increased abruptly to add licks within the breathing cycle (1, 2, 3 or 4 licks between breaths), keeping the fixed lick latency before the next inspiration, so licking shifted between modes of oscillation with breathing frequency.
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 3; Figure 1f
claims.quote: During slow breathing, when the next lick could not be delayed further to accommodate the next breath, licking frequency abruptly increased to add additional licks within the breathing cycle to maintain the fixed lick latency preceding the next inspiration
claims.criterion: The paper shows this in a raster grouped by the number of licks in the cycle (code volcano_plot_licking). With the breath cycles of the header, pooled per session, reproduced when the median inter-breath interval rises strictly from 1 to 2 to 3 licks per cycle (and to 4 where a session has at least 20 such cycles) in most sessions (more than half), and the median latency from the last lick to the next inspiration differs by less than 20% between the groups (a standard choice, named here).

claims.statement: Inspirations following licking were significantly delayed for slower licking frequencies, anticipating the next lick (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, p < 0.001), so licking influences breathing.
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 4; Figure 1i
claims.quote: inspirations following licking were significantly delayed for slower licking frequencies to anticipate the next lick (Figure 1i, p<0.001, one sample t-test, two-tailed)
claims.criterion: The per-session peak difference of the header (Breath-to-lick timing, code get_peak_diff_breath_behv), slow minus fast; one-sample two-tailed t-test against 0 under O4 (a) and (b). Reproduced when the mean is positive with p < 0.001 under a reading.

claims.statement: Neither a free-running breathing oscillator that sets lick timing nor a free-running licking oscillator that sets breath timing reproduces the observed lick-breath relationship, suggesting that the two oscillators are bidirectionally coupled.
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 4; Extended Data Figure 1d-i; Methods, Simulation of licking-breathing coupling
claims.quote: This pattern of lick-breath temporal relationship also cannot be produced by a free-running licking oscillator unidirectionally setting the timing of breathing rhythm
claims.criterion: Simulate as the Methods say, drawing intervals from the empirical frequency distributions of fig1d-lick-breath-frequencies, Gaussian timing noise SD 10 ms. The paper gives no value for the fixed latency or the number of simulated cycles; standard choices, named here, are the median latency from the last lick to the next inspiration (breathing model) and from the last inspiration to the next lick (licking model) in the data, and as many simulated cycles as the pooled data. Apply the two peak-difference measures of the header to each simulation. Reproduced when the breathing-driven model gives a Fig 1i difference whose mean is not positive or not significant (two-tailed t-test over simulated sessions of the data's sizes, p >= 0.05, a standard choice named here since the paper reports no test) and the licking-driven model fails likewise on the Fig 1g measure, while the data give both differences positive.

claims.statement: Licking and breathing in freely moving rats showed a similar lick-breath temporal relationship.
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 4; Extended Data Figure 2
claims.quote: Independent analysis of breathing and licking in freely moving rats yielded similar temporal relationship (Extended Data Figure 2)
claims.criterion: Rat data (7 rats, lickometer contacts, thermocouple inspiration onsets at 10% of onset amplitude after 1-20 Hz filtering, Methods). Licks from bouts shorter than 1.75 s left out as the Methods say. The two peak-difference measures of the header computed per rat with tongue contacts as licks. Reproduced when both differences are positive in a majority of rats and positive on average (one-sample t-test over rats, two-tailed, p < 0.05, a standard choice named here since the paper reports no test).

claims.statement: Licking was paused during detected swallows but not during ordinary expirations, so the detected events are genuine swallows.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 1b-c; Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Licking was paused during swallowing. Bottom, lick timing aligned to all expirations as a control. Lick was not paused during expiration.
claims.criterion: Swallows detected as in the header. Per session, the probability of a tongue onset in 3.4 ms bins from -0.3 to 0.3 s around swallow onsets and around all expiration onsets inside lick bouts. The paper does not define expiration onset; it is taken as the Hilbert phase crossing pi (a standard choice, named here), and the bins and window are plotting choices. Reproduced when the mean lick probability from 0 to 100 ms after onset is lower around swallows than around expirations in most sessions with at least 20 swallows, by a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05 (a standard choice, named here).

claims.statement: Inspirations and licks followed swallowing at relatively fixed latencies despite different breath and lick timing before the swallow, suggesting that swallowing interrupted the ongoing rhythms.
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1k and 1m
claims.quote: Inspirations and licks followed swallowing at relatively fixed latencies despite different breath and lick timing before the swallow (Figure 1k and m)
claims.criterion: Swallow events and ranking as in O5 (a) and (b). For licks and for breaths separately, reproduced when the difference in median latency from swallow onset to the first following lick (inspiration) between the top and bottom thirds is smaller than the difference in their median cycle -1 (as Figure 1k right compares the two thirds) under a reading.

claims.statement: The inter-lick interval before and after swallowing was preserved (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, P = 0.649).
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1l
claims.quote: The inter-lick-interval before and after swallowing was preserved (Figure 1l, P=0.649, one-sampled t-test, two-tailed)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Delta(1,-1) per swallow event as in the header, bottom third by O5 (a), the code's selection, pooled across sessions. Reproduced when the one-sample two-tailed t-test against 0 gives p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The mean Delta(1,-1) is reported, and O5 (b), (c) and (d) are shown as variants.
