claims.statement: The lick cycle in which swallowing occurred was significantly prolonged, by 33.3 ms (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, P < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1l
claims.quote: whereas the lick cycle in which swallowing occurred was significantly prolonged by 33.3 ms (Figure 1l, P<0.001, one-sampled t-test, two-tailed)
claims.criterion: Delta(0,-1) per swallow event, readings O5 (a) to (d). Reproduced when, under one reading, the mean is within tolerance and the one-sample two-tailed t-test gives p < 0.001; partially reproduced when the test holds and the mean is outside tolerance under every reading. Under O5 (a) the selection of the longest cycles 0 favours a positive Delta(0,-1); the result under (b) and (c) is reported beside it.

claims.statement: The inter-breath interval before and after swallowing was preserved (P = 0.225).
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1n
claims.quote: P=0.225 for inter-breath-interval before vs. after swallowing
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, as fig1l-lick-interval-preserved with inspiration onsets and the breath limits of the header (cycle 0 between 1/15 and 1/2 s). Reproduced when p >= 0.05 under O5 (a); not reproduced when p < 0.05. The other readings are variants.

claims.statement: The breath cycle in which swallowing occurred was significantly prolonged, by 48.0 ms (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, P < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1n
claims.quote: P<0.001 for inter-breath-interval in which swallowing occurred, one-sample t-test, two-tailed, prolonged by 48.0 ms
claims.criterion: As fig1l-lick-cycle-prolonged, with breaths.

claims.statement: Across 339 insertions in 31 mice, 20,300 single units passed quality control (60 +- 22 per probe), 5,700 in the cerebellum, 3,700 in the pons and 10,900 in the medulla.
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 2; Methods, Preprocessing, spike sorting, and quality metrics, paragraph 2
claims.quote: we obtained 20,300 clear single units, including 5,700 units in the cerebellum, 3,700 units in the pons, and 10,900 units in the medulla
claims.criterion: Units by the quality filter of the header, V1 both ways; region from the unit's CCF label (cerebellum CB, pons P, medulla MY, with their subregions). Insertions and mice are counted exactly. Extended Data Figure 4c gives 19,000 units with amplitude > 150 uV, a second reading of the total; a count within tolerance of either is reported as such.

claims.statement: Neurons in the cerebellum (22 +- 29 spikes/s) and vestibular nucleus (38 +- 32) fired faster than neurons in the medulla (11 +- 14).
claims.source: Methods, Preprocessing, spike sorting, and quality metrics, paragraph 2; Figure 2e
claims.quote: Neurons in the cerebellum and the vestibular nucleus exhibited higher spike rates than neurons in the medulla (22 ± 29 spikes/s, mean ± std, for cerebellum, 38 ± 32 spikes/s for vestibular nucleus, and 11 ± 14 spikes/s for medulla
claims.criterion: The rate is not defined; readings (a) the quality metric avg_firing_rate; (b) spikes over the session's trial time. Vestibular nucleus is the CCF VNC; medulla is MY with (i) and (ii) without VNC. Reproduced when the three means are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Units showed significant phase tuning to licking (3551 of 20,300) or breathing (1015 of 20,300), but rarely to both (182 of 20,300).
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Individual units exhibited significant phase tuning to either licking (3551/20300), or breathing (1015/20300), but rarely to both (182/20300)
claims.criterion: Phase tuning and MI as in the header, tuned at P < 0.001 and MI > 0.6, readings V2 (a) and (b) and V3 (a) and (b). The text does not say whether the licking and breathing counts include the 182 units tuned to both; readings (i) they include them; (ii) they exclude them. Reproduced when the three counts are within tolerance under (i) or (ii), for every reading of V2 and V3; partially reproduced when the counts are not but both-tuned units are under 10% of licking-tuned units and under 25% of breathing-tuned units, for every reading of V2 and V3 (a standard choice, named here; the paper's ratios are 5% and 18%, and the Methods say only that the relative proportions were robust to the MI criterion). The code's choices (order 5, 100 resamples) are shown as variants.

claims.statement: Of 18,485 units, 427 were modulated by swallowing only, 175 by both licking and swallowing and 55 by both breathing and swallowing.
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 3; Extended Data Figure 5e-f
claims.quote: Most units were modulated by swallowing only (427/18485), with a smaller group modulated by both licking and swallowing (175/18485) (Extended Data Figure 5f). Another small subset of units with swallowing-related activity were also modulated by breathing (55/18485)
claims.criterion: Swallow modulation as in the header, readings V4 (a) and (b). The denominator 18,485 is not defined; readings (a) units of sessions with at least one detected swallow; (b) units with at least 20 swallows (code). "Swallowing only" is read (i) not licking- or breathing-tuned; (ii) not licking-tuned. Reproduced when the four numbers are within tolerance under one combination of (a) or (b) with (i) or (ii), for both readings of V4.

claims.statement: Units encoding breathing clustered near the preBotzinger complex and in the posterior ventral IRN.
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 4; Figure 2f
claims.quote: Units encoding breathing were near the preBötzinger complex 22, as well as posterior ventral IRN
claims.criterion: The paper shows a map and gives no test. Regions by O3 (a) and (b). Reproduced when the fraction of breathing-tuned units among the units of each of the two regions exceeds the fraction among all pons and medulla units, each by a one-sided Fisher exact test at p < 0.05 (a standard choice, named here), under both readings of O3.

claims.statement: Licking-related units were broadly distributed, including the hypoglossal (12N) and trigeminal (5N) motor nuclei, extensive portions of the IRN and parts of the pons.
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 4; Figure 2g
claims.quote: The regions containing licking-related activity were remarkably broad, including the tongue- and jaw-related motor nuclei (hypoglossal nucleus, 12N; trigeminal nucleus, 5N) as well as extensive portions of the IRN and parts of pons
claims.criterion: As fig2f-breathing-units-location, with licking-tuned units and the CCF regions XII, V and IRN, and the pons taken whole (P). Reproduced when the fraction exceeds that of all pons and medulla units in each of XII, V and IRN (Fisher exact, one-sided, p < 0.05) and licking units are present in the pons at more than 1% of its units.

claims.statement: Swallowing-related units clustered in the trigeminal nucleus (5N), lateral to the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) and above the nucleus ambiguus (10N), with further clusters in the inferior colliculus and the nucleus of the lateral lemniscus.
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 4; Figure 2h; Extended Data Figure 6a-d
claims.quote: Units with swallowing-related activity were clustered in the trigeminal nucleus (5N), lateral to the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS), and above the nucleus ambiguus (10N)
claims.criterion: As fig2f-breathing-units-location, with swallow-modulated units. Regions are CCF V, IC and NLL; "lateral to NTS" is units within (a) 300 um or (b) 500 um lateral of NTS at its AP extent; "above 10N" is units within the same distances dorsal of AMB. Reproduced when the fraction exceeds that of all units of the same sessions in all five regions under both distance readings; partially reproduced in three or four under both.

claims.statement: Swallow-related activity in 5N and IRN leads swallowing, while activity in the inferior colliculus and nucleus of the lateral lemniscus follows it.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 6e; Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Activities in 5N and IRN lead swallowing while activities in the IC and NLL follow swallowing.
claims.criterion: Swallow PSTHs as in the code (1 ms bins, 50 ms boxcar, -1 to 1 s). Per swallow-modulated unit, the time of the PSTH peak within -0.15 to 0.15 s (the paper gives no window or latency measure; a standard choice, named here). Reproduced when the median peak time is negative for units in V and IRN and positive for units in IC and NLL, and the two groups differ by a two-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05 (a standard choice, named here).

claims.statement: A GLM on the tracked features found separate clusters of units predicted by licking or by breathing movements.
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 5; Extended Data Figure 7c-d
claims.quote: The GLM found separate clusters of units predicted by either licking or breathing movement (Extended Data Figure 7c-d)
claims.criterion: The GLM of the Methods (17 ms bins, jaw and tongue x, y, z and airflow, z-scored, tongue set to 0 when its likelihood is below 0.05 in both views, every 5th trial held out, lags of +-5 bins), readings O8. The paper shows maps of the weights (Extended Data Fig 7c, airflow weights around and below 10N; 7d, jaw and tongue weights in the premotor regions) and gives no measure. Among units with validation VAF > 0.05, each unit is assigned to airflow or to jaw and tongue by its largest absolute weight (threshold and assignment are standard choices, named here). Reproduced when airflow units lie ventral of jaw and tongue units (CCF DV, one-sided Mann-Whitney test, p < 0.05) and the fraction of airflow units near the preBotzinger complex exceeds that of jaw and tongue units (one-sided Fisher exact test, p < 0.05), under every reading of O3 and O8; both tests are standard choices, named here.

claims.statement: The autoencoder embedding predicted a larger fraction of activity variance than the tracked features for most units across the brainstem (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 6; Extended Data Figure 7g
claims.quote: The CAE predicted a larger fraction of activity variance than the tracked features for most units across the brainstem (Extended Data Figure 7g; CAE vs. features, P<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test)
claims.criterion: CAE as in reference 40 and the Methods (two residual blocks of three convolutions, linear readouts of 128 and 32, frames downsampled to 120 x 112, one network per mouse trained on 80% of trials for 20,000 iterations with L2 regularization), which needs the raw videos; GLM readings O8. Reproduced when, over all units, CAE VAF exceeds feature VAF in more than half of the units and the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives P < 0.001.

claims.statement: Units in the preBotzinger complex were the exception, where the autoencoder gave worse predictions than the tracked features (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 6; Extended Data Figure 7g-h
claims.quote: the only exceptions were units in the preBötzinger complex where activity prediction using CAE led to worse predictions (CAE vs. features, P<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test
claims.criterion: As ed7g-cae-better-than-features, for units near the preBotzinger complex (O3 (a) and (b)), and for breathing-tuned units there (Extended Data Fig 7g marks breathing units). Reproduced when feature VAF exceeds CAE VAF with P < 0.001 under every reading of O3 and O8.

claims.statement: Breathing-related units in the preBotzinger complex preferentially fired at the inspiration phase of breathing.
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 5; Extended Data Figure 8a-c
claims.quote: units in the preBötzinger complex preferentially fired at inspiration phase of breathing
claims.criterion: Preferred phases of the fitted tuning curves (header), breathing units by O1 (b) as Extended Data Fig 8b states, located by O3 (a) and (b). Inspiration phase is the half cycle starting at inspiration onset (phase 0 to pi in the convention where inspiration onset is 0). Reproduced when more than half of those units prefer that half cycle and their phases are non-uniform by a Rayleigh test at p < 0.05 (a standard choice, named here), under both readings of O3.

claims.statement: Licking-related units were mostly active when the tongue was fully protruded.
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 5; Extended Data Figure 8d-f
claims.quote: Units with licking-related activity were mostly active when the tongue was in the fully protruded state
claims.criterion: Licking units by O1 (b). For each session, the jaw phase at the frame of maximal tongue protrusion in each lick (the frame of largest 3D tongue distance from its onset position; the paper does not define full protrusion, a standard choice named here) gives the protrusion phase; a unit's preferred phase is compared with its session's circular median protrusion phase. Reproduced when more than half of licking units prefer a phase within pi/2 of it (a standard choice, named here).

claims.statement: Licking-related neurons showed selectivity for ipsilateral licking, while individual units within each hemisphere had diverse direction preferences, including the center direction.
claims.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 7; Extended Data Figure 8g-i
claims.quote: Overall, licking-related neurons showed selectivity for ipsilateral licking (Extended Data Figure 8i)
claims.criterion: Lick angle by O9 (a) and (b); spikes from -50 to 100 ms around each lick onset (Extended Data Fig 8g); left and right licks are those with angle below and above the midline. Per licking unit (O1 (a)), left-lick rate minus right-lick rate. Reproduced when this difference is larger for left-hemisphere than right-hemisphere units (CCF medial- lateral position against the midline) by a one-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05 (a standard choice, named here) and each hemisphere's median favours the ipsilateral side, under both readings of O9.

claims.statement: The licking activity map was insensitive to spike-sorting quality; raising the amplitude threshold from 150 to 500 uV left 2223 of 19,000 units and the same map.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 4c; Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Licking activity map was insensitive to the quality of spike sorting. To obtain units with the highest amplitude, the waveform amplitude quality metric was increased from 150 μV to 500 μV. This filtered the 19,000 units with amplitude > 150 μV to 2223 unit with amplitude > 500 μV.
claims.criterion: Units passing the filter of the header with amplitude > 500 uV. Reproduced when the count is within tolerance and, over CCF regions with at least 20 such units, the mean licking MI per region in this subset correlates with that in all units (Spearman, p < 0.05, positive; a standard choice, named here). The paper's 19,000 against 20,300 units is not resolved here; both are reported.

claims.statement: Premotor neurons of the masseter and genioglossus occupied largely distinct regions of the pons and medulla, overlapping in the dorsal IRN.
claims.source: Results, A licking premotor network with autonomous rhythm-generation properties, paragraph 3; Figure 3a; Extended Data Figure 9a-b
claims.quote: Premotor neurons for the masseter and genioglossus muscles occupied largely distinct regions of the pons and medulla, with some overlap in the dorsal IRN (Figure 3a)
claims.criterion: Not testable on the dandiset. From the premotor neuron positions in CCF, the density contours of Extended Data Fig 9a (genioglossus 0.0063 and masseter 0.0019 neurons per mm3); reproduced when the overlap of the two contours is under half of the smaller and lies in IRN dorsal to its DV midpoint (both standard choices, named here).

claims.statement: Units inside the tongue-jaw premotor regions showed significantly higher licking modulation than position-shuffled populations (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, A licking premotor network with autonomous rhythm-generation properties, paragraph 3; Figure 3b
claims.quote: Units inside these regions showed significantly higher licking modulation compared to position-shuffled populations (P < 0.001 Wilcoxon rank sum test)
claims.criterion: Premotor regions are the union of the two density contours of Extended Data Fig 9a built from reference 43's premotor neurons. Position shuffling is not described; readings (a) licking MI of units inside against the MIs of the same number of units drawn at random from all units (positions shuffled across units); (b) inside against outside. Reproduced when the inside MIs are higher with rank-sum P < 0.001 under both readings.

claims.statement: Photostimulation of ALM (n = 11 mice) or latSC (n = 3 mice) elicited sustained rhythmic licking at the naturalistic 7 Hz frequency.
claims.source: Results, A licking premotor network with autonomous rhythm-generation properties, paragraph 4; Figure 3c and 3e
claims.quote: Photostimulation of ALM or latSC (20 or 40 Hz pulse trains for 2 or 1.3 s) elicited sustained rhythmic licking at the naturalistic 7 Hz frequency (Figure 3c and e)
claims.criterion: Photostimulation trials of the ALM mice (cued licking task) and latSC mice. Lick rate as tongue onsets per second from the first lick to the end of the light, mean per mouse then across mice (the paper does not say how the rate is taken; a standard choice, named here). Reproduced when the mean across mice is within tolerance for each group and licking lasts to the end of the light in most trials (a lick in the last 300 ms, a standard choice, named here).

claims.statement: ALM and latSC axons targeted the contralateral brainstem and engulfed the tongue-jaw premotor regions; constant photostimulation of Phox2b+ neurons in the posterior-dorsal IRN/PARN elicited rhythmic licking, while anterior sites locked the jaw.
claims.source: Results, A licking premotor network with autonomous rhythm-generation properties, paragraphs 4 and 5; Figure 3d, 3f, 3g and 3h
claims.quote: In contrast, photostimulating a posterior-dorsal region of IRN and the adjacent region in PARN (anterior-lateral to 12N) elicited rhythmic jaw movement and tongue protrusions
claims.criterion: Anatomy and fibre-site data, with no stated deposit. For the fibre sites (46 sites, 27 mice, Figure 3h), reproduced when the sites classed rhythmic lie posterior and dorsal of those not rhythmic (median CCF AP and DV positions) and within or next to IRN or PARN.

claims.statement: Of the brainstem photostimulation sites, 18 evoked rhythmic jaw movement with a peak at 7 Hz and rhythmic tongue protrusions, 11 evoked no rhythmic jaw movement and 4 evoked only a transient tongue protrusion.
claims.source: Extended Data Figure 10b, 10e and 10h
claims.criterion: Jaw position Fourier spectrum during the 2 s of light (Extended Data Fig 10b). Sites are classed rhythmic when the spectrum has a peak between 3 and 15 Hz (the jaw band of the Methods) higher than in the 2 s before the light; classing rules beyond that are not given. The three classes sum to 33 of the 46 sites of Figure 3h; the paper does not say how the other 13 were classed, or whether the 4 transient sites are among the 11. Reproduced when the counts are within tolerance and the peak of the mean spectrum of rhythmic sites is within tolerance.

claims.statement: During ALM-induced licking the lick-breath relationship of voluntary licking was recapitulated; lick timing anticipated the next breath at a fixed latency across breathing frequencies.
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 2; Figure 4b
claims.quote: Notably, the same lick-breath temporal relationship was recapitulated during artificially induced licking. Lick timing anticipated the next breath and proceeded inspiration at a fixed latency across different breathing frequencies (Figure 4b)
claims.criterion: Cued licking task of the ALM mice. The Fig 1g measure (header) on photostimulation trials (licks during the 2 s light) and on Go-cue trials separately, pooled per mouse (Figure 4b, "across all mice"); session pooling as needed for the minimum of 40 cycles per half. Reproduced when the photostimulation difference is positive on average across mice by a one-sample two-tailed t-test at p < 0.05 (the paper's test of Fig 1g; the threshold is a standard choice, named here).

claims.statement: During ALM-induced licking, inspiration timing was still influenced by future lick timing.
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 2; Figure 4c
claims.quote: Conversely, inspiration timing was influenced by future lick timing (Figure 4c)
claims.criterion: As fig4b-artificial-licking-keeps-lick-timing, with the Fig 1i measure of the header.

claims.statement: In a subset of mice, ALM photostimulation also increased breathing rate.
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 2; Extended Data Figure 11b
claims.quote: In a subset of mice, ALM photostimulation also induced an increase in breathing rate (Extended Data Figure 11b)
claims.criterion: Breathing rate (inspiration onsets per second) in the 2 s of light against the 1 s before, per photostimulation trial. Reproduced when at least one and fewer than all 11 mice show an increase by a paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over trials at p < 0.05 (a standard choice, named here).

claims.statement: Preceding a slower breath, the activity of licking neurons was slowed in anticipation of the next inspiration.
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 3; Figure 4e
claims.quote: Preceding a slower breath, the activity of licking neurons was slowed in anticipation of the next inspiration (Figure 4e)
claims.criterion: The unit peak difference of the header (code get_peak_diff_lick_unit), slow minus fast, per licking unit, units by O1 and recordings by O2. The legend says "Same as b", the test of Fig 1g; one-sample two-tailed t-test over units at p < 0.05 (threshold a standard choice, named here). Reproduced when the mean is positive and significant under all readings; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: Preceding a slower lick, the activity of breathing neurons was slowed in anticipation of the upcoming lick.
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 3; Figure 4f
claims.quote: Preceding a slower lick, the activity of breathing neurons was slowed in anticipation of the upcoming lick (Figure 4f)
claims.criterion: As fig4e-licking-units-anticipate-breath, with breathing units and the code's get_peak_diff_breath_unit.

claims.statement: Licking and breathing oscillators were recorded simultaneously in 43 recordings from 21 mice, with 1 to 28 licking-related and 1 to 12 breathing-related units per recording.
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 3; Figure 4d
claims.quote: 43 recordings in 21 mice; 1-28 licking-related units and 1-12 breathing-related units per recording
claims.criterion: Recordings with two probes, one with licking units (O1) in the posterior-dorsal IRN/PARN and one with breathing units near the preBotzinger complex (O3). Reproduced when the counts are within tolerance and the unit ranges per recording are within 1 to 28 and 1 to 12 widened by 10%, under every reading of O1 and O3.

claims.statement: Activity of simultaneously recorded breathing and licking units was significantly correlated for most pairs compared to trial-shuffled controls (103 of 119 pairs; 43 positively correlated, 60 anticorrelated).
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 4; Figure 4g
claims.quote: Activity was significantly correlated for most pairs compared to trial-shuffled controls (Figure 4g; 103/119 pairs with significant cross-correlation relative to shuffled control, 43 positively correlated, 60 anticorrelated
claims.criterion: Pairs from fig4d-simultaneous-recordings; correlograms by O6. Reproduced when, under every reading of O6, the four counts are within tolerance; partially reproduced when, under every reading, more than three quarters of pairs are significant with anticorrelated pairs outnumbering positive ones.

claims.statement: The cross-correlation was temporally symmetric; breathing units lagged licking units for 57 pairs, licking units lagged breathing units for 34 pairs, and 12 pairs peaked at zero.
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 4
claims.quote: breathing units lagged licking units for 57 pairs, while other licking units lagged breathing units for 34 pairs, (the remaining 12 pairs had cross-correlation peak at 0)
claims.criterion: Significant pairs and lags by O6. Reproduced when the three counts are within tolerance under every reading of O6; partially reproduced when, under every reading, both lag directions each hold at least a quarter of significant pairs.

claims.statement: Significant cross-correlation between licking and breathing unit pairs was observed even when mice were not licking.
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 4; Extended Data Figure 12c
claims.quote: Notably, significant cross-correlation between the unit pairs was observed even when mice were not licking, i.e. when the licking oscillator was inactive (Extended Data Figure 12c)
claims.criterion: As fig4g-licking-breathing-pairs-correlated, on the baseline of the cued licking task (trial start to Go cue, no tongue detected; Extended Data Fig 12c). Reproduced when more than half of the pairs are significant under every reading of O6.

claims.statement: Units outside the licking oscillator were less often cross-correlated with breathing units (54 of 110 pairs), a significantly lower proportion than licking-breathing oscillator pairs (Chi-square test, p < 0.0001).
claims.source: Results, Coupled brainstem oscillators autonomously coordinate licking and breathing, paragraph 4; Figure 4h
claims.quote: units outside of the licking oscillator exhibited less cross correlation with the breathing units (Figure 4h; 54/110 pairs with significant cross correlation; a significantly lower proportion compared to licking-breathing oscillator unit pairs, p<0.0001, Chi-square test)
claims.criterion: Non-licking units are not defined; readings (a) units of the licking-oscillator probe not licking-tuned (O1); (b) units of that probe outside the posterior-dorsal IRN/PARN (O3). Correlograms by O6. Chi-square test on the 2 x 2 table of significant and not significant pairs, without continuity correction (i) and with it (ii). Reproduced when the proportion is lower with p < 0.0001 under (a) or (b), for every reading of O6 and of the continuity correction; the counts are reported against the expected values.

claims.statement: Mice initiated licking 127.6 +- 29.6 ms after the Go cue (mean +- std across mice, n = 11).
claims.source: Results, Descending control patterns oscillators at movement initiation, paragraph 2; Figure 5a-b
claims.quote: Mice initiated licking 127.6 ± 29.6 ms after the Go cue onset (defined as the onset of tongue appearance in the video, mean ± std across mice, n=11 mice
claims.criterion: Cued licking task, Go-cue trials, first tongue onset after the cue within the 0.5 s response window; mean per mouse, then mean across the 11 mice.

claims.statement: Before voluntary licking, breathing phase deviated from random 115 +- 19 ms before lick onset and became entrained to a phase that put expiration at the first lick (two-sample Kuiper test with Bonferroni correction, p < 0.0001).
claims.source: Results, Descending control patterns oscillators at movement initiation, paragraph 2; Figure 5c
claims.quote: 115 ± 19 ms before licking onset (mean ± s.e.m., bootstrap), breathing phase began to deviate significantly from random distribution and became entrained to a specific phase (Figure 5c; p<0.0001, two sample Kuiper test with Bonferroni correction)
claims.criterion: Go-cue trials of the cued licking task; breathing phase (Hilbert, header) aligned to the first lick; test and latency by O7 (a) and (b). Reproduced when, under both readings of O7, the latency is within tolerance and the phase at lick onset lies in expiration (phase pi to 2 pi).

claims.statement: ALM photostimulation evoked licking with a latency of 230.7 +- 31.5 ms, significantly longer than voluntary licking (paired t-test, two-tailed, p < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Descending control patterns oscillators at movement initiation, paragraph 3; Figure 5e
claims.quote: Photostimulation evoked licking with a latency of 230.7 ± 31.5 ms (Figure 5e), which was significantly longer than voluntarily initiated licking (p<0.001, paired t-test, two-tailed)
claims.criterion: First tongue onset after light onset on photostimulation trials, mean per mouse. The paper does not give the unit of the paired test; readings (a) the 11 mice, against the Go-cue latencies of fig5b-voluntary-lick-latency; (b) sessions, Go-cue and photostimulation means of the same session. Reproduced when the mean across mice is within tolerance and the paired two-tailed t-test gives p < 0.001 under one reading.

claims.statement: Artificially induced licking did not recapitulate the pre-emptive breath adjustment; breathing phase changed only 47.6 +- 10 ms before lick onset, a significantly shorter latency than before voluntary licking (bootstrap, P < 0.0001).
claims.source: Results, Descending control patterns oscillators at movement initiation, paragraph 3; Figure 5f (the Results also cite a Figure 5g that the legend does not describe)
claims.quote: Breathing phase was altered only shortly before licking onset (Figure 5f; 47.6 ± 10 ms), a significantly shorter latency than the pre-emptive adjustment before voluntary licking (Figure 5g; P<0.0001, bootstrap)
claims.criterion: As fig5c-preemptive-breath-adjustment on photostimulation trials, aligned to the first tongue protrusion after light onset. The bootstrap comparison is not described; the reading used is 10,000 resamples of trials with replacement, drawn within each condition, p the fraction where the induced latency is at least the voluntary one (a standard choice, named here; P < 0.0001 needs at least 10,000 resamples). Reproduced when, under both readings of O7, the latency is within tolerance and the comparison gives P < 0.0001.

claims.statement: In monkey V, 112 neurons were studied before MPTP and 159 after, of which 49 and 54 were PTNs and 31 and 48 CSNs; three neurons in all were activated from both the peduncle and the putamen.
claims.source: Supplementary table (monkey V); Results, Database, paragraph 1; Table 1
claims.quote: Of these, 66 were activated antidromically from peduncle stimulation (PTNs: 49 in monkey V and 17 in monkey L; Table 1) and 56 were activated from the putamen (CSNs: 31 in monkey V and 25 in monkey L)... Only 3 cells were activated antidromically from both the putamen and the peduncle
claims.criterion: Counts of monkey V units with at least 5 perturbations per direction, by MPTP state and projection type; dual-projecting units counted over all files. Reproduced when every count is within tolerance.

claims.statement: In monkey L, 57 of 115 neurons before MPTP and 35 of 73 after responded to torque perturbations of the wrist, and the monkey L responses enter all pooled results.
claims.source: Supplementary table (monkey L); Table 1
claims.criterion: Needs the torque perturbation trials of monkey L (direction and onset). Blocked if no monkey L file marks them.

claims.statement: Before torque onset, the firing rate of M1 neurons was lower after MPTP, because PTN rates fell (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001) while CSN rates did not change (p = 0.5). In monkey V the rates were 12.6 and 8.9 spikes/s for all cells, 20.3 and 14.8 for PTNs, and 3.5 and 3.4 for CSNs, before and after MPTP.
claims.source: Supplementary table; Table 1; Results, Database, paragraph 3
claims.quote: The pre-torque firing rate of PTNs was reduced by 27% following MPTP treatment (Mann–Whitney U-test, p < 0.001; Table 1) whereas the mean activity of CSNs remained unchanged (Mann–Whitney U-test, p = 0.5).
claims.criterion: Mean baseline rate per group of cells studied. Reproduced when all six means are within tolerance, the PTN rate is lower after MPTP (Mann-Whitney p < 0.05) and the CSN rate does not differ (p >= 0.05). Partially reproduced when the two tests hold and some means are outside tolerance, or the means hold and a test does not. The M1 test (p < 0.05/2 in the paper) is reported.

claims.statement: Before MPTP, PTNs fired much faster than CSNs at rest (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Database, paragraph 2; Table 1
claims.quote: resting neuronal firing rates measured immediately prior to torque onset were markedly higher for PTNs (mean rate: 16.3-spikes/s, range: 0.2–45; Table 1) than for CSNs (mean rate: 3.6-spikes/s, range: 0–22; Mann–Whitney U-test, p < 0.001).
claims.criterion: Pre-MPTP baseline rates of monkey V PTNs and CSNs. Reproduced when PTNs are higher with Mann-Whitney p < 0.001; partially when p < 0.05; not reproduced otherwise. The text gives means of 16.3 and 3.6 spikes/s and Table 1 gives 18.3 and 3.2; these pooled values are reported, not judged.

claims.statement: PTN antidromic latencies did not change after MPTP (1.9 ms, p = 0.9), while CSN latencies were longer (5.1 against 6.1 ms, p < 0.05/3).
claims.source: Results, Database, paragraph 3; Table 1
claims.quote: The antidromic latencies of PTNs remained unchanged between pre- and post-MPTP periods (mean = 1.9-ms; Mann–Whitney U-test, p = 0.9; Table 1) whereas those of CSNs were significantly longer following MPTP administration
claims.criterion: Antidromic latency of monkey V PTNs and CSNs studied (the expected values pool both monkeys). Reproduced when the CSN latency is longer after MPTP (Mann-Whitney p < 0.05/3), the PTN latency does not differ (p >= 0.05), and the four means are within tolerance. Partially reproduced when the two tests hold and a mean does not, or the reverse. A variant adds every monkey L PTN and CSN unit, as their selection by perturbations cannot be made.

claims.statement: The detection threshold, p < 0.01 divided by 5 independent comparisons, holds the chance of a false response over the 200 ms epoch near 0.01.
claims.source: Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 6
claims.quote: The threshold for significance was adjusted to account for multiple comparisons [p < 0.01/(200-ms epoch/40-ms gamma filter half-width = 5 independent comparisons) = 0.002].
claims.criterion: The same detection at a pseudo onset 600 ms before the torque, on the monkey V cells studied, both directions. Reproduced when the fraction of cell-directions with any threshold crossing over 0 to 200 ms is between 0.0033 and 0.03 (the factor-of-3 rule above; the tolerance field gives the upper bound). The rate for a response with onset in 20 to 60 ms is also reported.

claims.statement: In monkey V, 84 of 112 M1 neurons (75%) were torque-related before MPTP and 108 of 159 (68%) after; for PTNs 27 of 49 (55%) and 37 of 54 (68%); for CSNs 14 of 31 (45%) and 10 of 48 (21%).
claims.source: Supplementary table; Table 1; Figure 3A
claims.criterion: A cell is torque-related when it has a response in at least one direction. Reproduced when all six percentages are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at least four are; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: MPTP did not change the fraction of torque-related neurons, in M1, in PTNs or in CSNs (chi-square, p > 0.05/3).
claims.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP, paragraph 1; Figure 3A
claims.quote: induction of parkinsonism did not increase the prevalence of torque responses in the general population of M1 cells (62% for both states), in CSNs (26%), or in PTNs (68%; χ2 < 6.4 p > 0.05/3; Figure 3A, Table 1).
claims.criterion: Absence claim, judged on the paper's test. A Yates-corrected chi-square test of torque-related against not, pre against post, for monkey V M1, PTNs and CSNs. Reproduced when none of the three has p < 0.05/3; not reproduced when any does. The size of each change is given.

claims.statement: PTNs responded to torque more often than CSNs (68% against 31% over both monkeys, chi-square 32.3, p < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, prevalence, paragraph 1; Figure 3A
claims.quote: Torque responses were observed in 68% (89/131) of PTNs but only 31% (35/114) of CSNs (χ2 = 32.3, p < 0.001; Table 1 and Figure 3A).
claims.criterion: Pre and post pooled. The expected values are the monkey V counts of the supplementary table (64 of 103 PTNs, 24 of 79 CSNs). Reproduced when both are within tolerance and the Yates-corrected chi-square test gives p < 0.001 with PTNs higher; partially reproduced when the test holds and a fraction does not, or the fractions hold and p is between 0.001 and 0.05.

claims.statement: About half of the torque-related cells (124 of 284, 44%) responded to only one direction of rotation.
claims.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, prevalence, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Half of these torque-related cells (124/284, 44%) responded for only one direction of rotation (flexion or extension).
claims.criterion: Monkey V, pre and post pooled (the paper's value pools both monkeys). Reproduced when the percentage is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Most torque responses were increases in firing (86% of M1 responses before and 88% after MPTP; 70% and 75% for PTNs), and MPTP did not change the PTN balance (chi-square 0.1, p = 0.7).
claims.source: Table 1; Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP, paragraph 2
claims.quote: For PTNs, most torque-evoked changes in activity consisted of an increase in firing (72% of responses... That high prevalence of torque-evoked increases in firing did not differ between pre- and post-MPTP periods (χ2 = 0.1, p = 0.7; Table 1).
claims.criterion: Responses counted per direction, monkey V (the paper's values pool both monkeys). The PTN part is an absence claim judged on a Yates-corrected chi-square test at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the four percentages are within tolerance and the PTN test does not find a change; partially reproduced when only one of these holds; not reproduced when neither.

claims.statement: The magnitude of torque responses did not differ before and after MPTP, for M1 cells or for PTNs, by any of three measures (mean change, maximum change, area; Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Mann-Whitney, all p > 0.15).
claims.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP, paragraph 2; Figure 4A
claims.quote: None of these comparisons yielded a significant difference between pre- and post-MPTP periods (Kolmogorov two-sample test and Mann–Whitney U-test, all p's > 0.15; Figure 4A).
claims.criterion: Absence claim, judged on the paper's tests. Responses counted per direction, both directions pooled; for M1 and for PTNs, each of the three measures compared pre against post with a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and a Mann-Whitney test (12 tests). Reproduced when none has p < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. Per-direction tests are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: In monkey V, the mean response magnitudes were 42.4 and 37.9 spikes/s for M1 flexion responses, 50.9 and 42.6 for M1 extension responses, 33.4 and 26.1 for PTN flexion and 38.8 and 29.3 for PTN extension responses, before and after MPTP.
claims.source: Supplementary table
claims.criterion: The table does not say which measure "magnitude" is. Readings, in order, (a) the maximum change from baseline, (b) the mean firing rate during the response, (c) the mean change from baseline. Reproduced when all eight values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when at least five are under one reading; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Response latencies were shorter after MPTP for M1 cells and for PTNs, for flexion and extension (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, all p < 0.05). In monkey V the means were 39.2 and 34.6 ms (M1 flexion), 40.4 and 33.4 ms (M1 extension), 43.9 and 35.5 ms (PTN flexion) and 44.4 and 36.7 ms (PTN extension), before and after MPTP.
claims.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP, paragraph 3; Figure 4B; supplementary table
claims.quote: The latencies of torque-evoked responses, however, were significantly shorter following MPTP administration. This observation held true for the general population of M1 neurons and specifically for PTNs, and for responses to flexions and extensions, all considered separately
claims.criterion: Response onset per direction. Reproduced when the post-MPTP latencies are shorter with Kolmogorov-Smirnov p < 0.05 in all four comparisons (M1 and PTN, each direction) and at least six of the eight means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when two or three comparisons are significant and shorter, or all four are and fewer than six means hold; not reproduced otherwise. The pooled means (M1 41 and 35 ms, PTN 46 and 38 ms) are reported under two readings, responses per direction and each cell's earliest response.

claims.statement: The latency shortening was not a history effect; latencies did not correlate with the days of training (monkey V Spearman |rho| = 0.02, p = 0.85).
claims.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP, paragraph 3
claims.quote: we found no correlation between the latencies of torque-evoked responses and the days of training an animal experienced (monkey V: Spearman |rho|= 0.02 p = 0.85
claims.criterion: Absence claim. Spearman correlation, over monkey V torque-related cells, of each cell's latency (its earliest response) with the days since the first monkey V session in the dandiset, pre and post pooled as the text reads. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. Within each state is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Torque-evoked increases in PTN firing were briefer after MPTP; the FWHM fell from 73 to 50 ms over both monkeys (Mann-Whitney, p < 0.05 for each direction). In monkey V the PTN FWHM was 97 and 52 ms for flexion and 57 and 41 ms for extension, before and after MPTP.
claims.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP, paragraph 4; supplementary table
claims.quote: For these responses, the response FWHM was reduced by 31% from a mean of 73-ms (80-ms for flexion, and 66-ms for extension) pre-MPTP to 50-ms (54-ms for flexion, and 46-ms for extension) post-MPTP (Mann–Whitney U-test, p's < 0.05).
claims.criterion: FWHM of monkey V PTN responses that are increases, per direction. Reproduced when the FWHM is shorter after MPTP with Mann-Whitney p < 0.05 in both directions and at least three of the four means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when one direction is significant, or both are and fewer than three means hold; not reproduced otherwise. The supplementary table may include decreases; the means over all PTN responses are reported.

claims.statement: Directional selectivity fell after MPTP; reciprocal and unidirectional responses became less common and bidirectional and non-directional ones more common (by about 10% of torque-related M1 cells; chi-square 22.2, p < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Response directionality, pre- vs. post-MPTP, paragraph 1; Figure 6
claims.quote: highly directional (reciprocal and unidirectional) response types became less common following MPTP administration (10% reduction in incidence), and bi-directional or non-directional response types became more common (10% increase in incidence; χ2 = 22.2, p < 0.001
claims.criterion: Monkey V torque-related cells. Chi-square test of the four categories (2 x 4), pre against post. Reproduced when the fraction of reciprocal plus unidirectional cells is lower after MPTP and p < 0.001; partially reproduced when it is lower and p < 0.05, or lower by at least 5 percentage points without significance; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: In monkey V the mean DSI of torque-related cells was 0.72 and 0.66 for M1, 0.73 and 0.75 for PTNs and 0.81 and 0.83 for CSNs, before and after MPTP.
claims.source: Supplementary table
claims.criterion: Mean DSI over torque-related cells; tolerances are 2 SD / sqrt(n) with n the torque-related cells of the table. Reproduced when all six are within tolerance; partially when at least four are; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The loss of selectivity was not due to resting rates, as pre-torque rates did not differ between directional categories (one-way ANOVA, F = 0.77, p = 0.46).
claims.source: Results, Response directionality, pre- vs. post-MPTP, paragraph 1
claims.quote: pre-torque mean firing rates did not differ between the different directional categories (One-Way ANOVA, F = 0.77 and p = 0.46).
claims.criterion: Absence claim. One-way ANOVA of baseline rate across the four categories, monkey V torque-related cells, pre and post pooled. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. Three groups (reciprocal and unidirectional merged) are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: After MPTP, torque-induced displacements were slower and smaller; mean peak velocity fell by 16.2% and amplitude by 6.6% (ANOVA, F > 515 and F > 49).
claims.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP, paragraph 2; Figure 1
claims.quote: Induction of parkinsonism also led to a slowing of torque-induced displacements of the arm (ANOVA; F > 515, p < 0.001; Figure 1) and a reduction in movement amplitude (F > 49, p < 0.01).
claims.criterion: Session means per direction, monkey V only (the paper's ANOVA has animal as a third factor). Two-way ANOVA (type II) of MPTP state and direction with their interaction. The change is the post mean over the pre mean, minus 1. Readings, in order, (a) both directions pooled, (b) flexion only (Figure 1). Reproduced when both changes are within tolerance under one reading and MPTP reduces both measures with ANOVA p < 0.01; partially reproduced when both are reduced with p < 0.05 and a change is outside tolerance; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The latency of torque-induced displacements did not change after MPTP (F < 0.2, p > 0.05).
claims.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP, paragraph 2; Figure 1
claims.quote: The latencies of torque-induced displacements remained unmodified post-MPTP (F < 0.2 and p > 0.05; Figure 1)
claims.criterion: Absence claim. The MPTP effect in the two-way ANOVA of session mean movement onset latency (monkey V). Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The paper's MPTP by direction interaction (F > 94) is reported.

claims.statement: The long-latency (m2, 41 to 80 ms) EMG response of the stretched triceps was larger after MPTP (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, p < 0.05).
claims.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP, paragraph 3; Figure 2
claims.quote: Following the administration of MPTP, the m2 component was markedly larger (Kolmogorov two-sample test, p < 0.05; Figure 2).
claims.criterion: Session m2 values for flexion torques, pre against post, two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov. The paper names one triceps longus; the dandiset has two channels, and either may be the paper's. Reproduced when m2 is larger after MPTP (higher median) with p < 0.05 for the triceps lateralis and for at least one triceps longus channel; partially reproduced when this holds for one muscle only; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The total duration of EMG responses to torque increased after MPTP, from 57 +/- 6 to 79 +/- 3 ms (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, p < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP, paragraph 3; Figure 2
claims.quote: The total duration of EMG responses to torque perturbations also increased (from 57 ± 6 to 79 ± 3-ms; Kolmogorov two-sample test, p < 0.001)
claims.criterion: Durations of the session-average responses of the three triceps channels to flexion torques, pooled over channels. Reproduced when both means are within tolerance and the durations are longer after MPTP with Kolmogorov-Smirnov p < 0.001; partially reproduced when they are longer with p < 0.05 and a mean is outside tolerance; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The latency of the earliest EMG responses did not change after MPTP (p > 0.05).
claims.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP, paragraph 3
claims.quote: latencies of the earliest EMG responses showed no significant change (p > 0.05).
claims.criterion: Absence claim. Onsets of the same responses as emg-duration-longer, pre against post, two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (the test the paper uses for the EMG). Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The short-latency m1 component (15 to 40 ms) was poorly formed and generally much smaller than the m2 component.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral effects of MPTP, paragraph 3; Figure 2
claims.quote: The short-latency response defined as the m1 component (muscle activity occurring between 15 ± 3 and 40 ± 4-ms post-torque) was poorly formed and generally much smaller than the long-latency response
claims.criterion: Session m1 and m2 of the three triceps channels for flexion torques, pre and post separately. Reproduced when m2 exceeds m1 in at least 75% of channel-sessions and the median of m1 / m2 is below 0.5 in both states; partially reproduced when this holds in one state; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: In sessions with equivalent torque-induced velocities (130 to 200 deg/s), MPTP did not change the magnitude of responses (Mann-Whitney, p = 0.19 for flexion and 0.46 for extension, with 24 and 33 flexion and 22 and 31 extension responses).
claims.source: Results, Torque-evoked neuronal responses, pre- vs. post-MPTP, paragraph 2; Supplementary Figure 1
claims.quote: We confirmed our main result in this subset by observing that MPTP did not change the magnitude of torque-evoked responses in M1 (Mann–Whitney U-test, all p's > 0.19).
claims.criterion: Absence claim. Responses (monkey V) from sessions whose mean peak velocity for that direction is 130 to 200 deg/s; maximum change from baseline compared pre against post with a Mann-Whitney test per direction. Reproduced when neither direction has p < 0.05; not reproduced when either does. The counts are reported against the expected values but do not decide the outcome; the other magnitude measures are a variant.

claims.statement: Across sessions, the mean PTN response latency did not correlate with the peak velocity of the torque-induced movement (|rho| < 0.18) or with the m2 EMG response (|rho| < 0.26; Spearman, p > 0.05 with threshold 0.05/4).
claims.source: Results, Analysis of neural-behavioral correlations, paragraph 1
claims.quote: No significant correlation was found for either analysis (Velmax, Spearman |rho| < 0.18 p > 0.05; or m2max, |rho| < 0.26 p > 0.05).
claims.criterion: Absence claim. Monkey V sessions with at least one torque-related PTN; the session's mean PTN latency (earliest response per cell) against the session's mean peak velocity (both directions) and its triceps longus channel 1 m2 for flexion torques. Spearman, threshold p < 0.0125. Reproduced when neither correlation reaches it; not reproduced when either does.

claims.statement: Trial by trial, PTN response latencies did not correlate with the peak velocity or the m2 EMG response (Spearman |rho| < 0.34, p > 0.05).
claims.source: Results, Analysis of neural-behavioral correlations, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Measures of PTN response latencies did not correlate with any of the measures of LLSR (Spearman |rho| < 0.34; p > 0.05).
claims.criterion: Needs a single-trial response latency, which the Methods do not define. Blocked unless one is defined by the paper.

claims.statement: The analysis covers 60,221 trials in 70 recording sessions from six rats, of which 39,175 are choice trials, 12,707 no-choice trials and 8329 error trials.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral data, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Here, we report the results of all 60,221 trials in 70 recording sessions performed by six rats, consisting of 39,175 choice trials (65.1%), 12,707 no-choice trials (21.1%), and 8329 error trials (13.8%)
claims.criterion: The rat count must match exactly. Choice trials are successful tone-A trials, no-choice trials successful tone-B trials, and error trials those ended by the error tone (Behavioral task). Readings of the total are (a) all trials started; (b) trials in which a cue tone was presented. Reproduced when, under one reading, every count is within tolerance.

claims.statement: A block took 105.6 trials on average, and a session held 8.1 blocks on average, from 5 to 12.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral data, paragraph 1
claims.quote: On average, 105.6 trials were required in one block, and 8.1 blocks (from 5 to 12 blocks) were performed in one session
claims.criterion: The paper does not say which trials a block counts or whether a session's last, possibly unfinished, block counts. Readings are (a) all trials, including no-choice and error trials, every block; (b) as (a), completed blocks only; (c) choice trials only, every block; (d) as (c), completed blocks only. Reproduced when, under one reading, all four values are within tolerance (the range bounds are whole numbers, so the fewest blocks must be 5 and the most 11 to 13).

claims.statement: In choice trials the time from center-hole exit to L or R hole entry was under 1 s in 72% of trials, with a median of 0.75 s.
claims.source: Results, Reaction time and tone discrimination, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The reaction time in the choice trials, the time period from the exit of the center hole to the entry of the left or right hole, was <1 s in 72% of the trials and had a median of 0.75 s
claims.criterion: Over all choice trials of the 70 sessions, pooled. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Rats rarely failed to poke after tone A (0.39% of choice trials) or poked wrongly after tone B (0.73% of no-choice trials), so they discriminated the tones well.
claims.source: Results, Reaction time and tone discrimination, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The errors in the choice trials, in which rats did not perform any nose pokes within 1 min for tone A presentation, were only 0.39% of the choice trials. The errors in no-choice trials, in which rats performed a nose poke at the left or right hole within 1 s for tone B presentation, were 0.73% of the no-choice trials
claims.criterion: The denominators are not fixed. Readings are (a) the error count over the successful trials of that tone (39,175 and 12,707); (b) the error count over the successful trials of that tone plus those errors. Errors from leaving the center hole during the cue are not counted in either. Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Both L1 and R0 in the previous trial raise the left-choice probability (0.68 and 0.62), more after L1; both R1 and L0 lower it (0.30 and 0.39), more after R1. So rewarded experience modulates choice more than unrewarded experience.
claims.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 1; Figure 2B
claims.quote: Both the experience L1 and R0 in the previous trial increased the probability of a left choice in the current trial [Fig. 2B, green arrow, P(L|L1) = 0.68; green arrowhead, P(L|R0) = 0.62]. The left choice probability after L1 was significantly higher than after R0 (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.0001) ... The left probability after R1 was significantly lower than after L0 [Fig. 2B, brown arrow, P(L|R1) = 0.30; brown arrowhead, P(L|L0) = 0.39] (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.0001)
claims.criterion: Conditional probabilities as the Methods define them (opening comment), pooled over all sessions; histories as O7; tests as O8. Reproduced when, under every reading, the four values are within tolerance, P(L|L1) > P(L|R0) > 0.5 > P(L|L0) > P(L|R1), and both tests give p < 0.0001.

claims.statement: The experience two trials back still affects choice; P(L|R0 L1) = 0.66 differs from P(L|L1 L1) = 0.72.
claims.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 2; Figure 2B and 2C
claims.quote: the conditional probability P(L|R0 L1) = 0.66 (Fig. 2B,C, blue arrowhead), which is the probability of a left choice (at trial t) after R0 (at trial t − 2) and L1 (at trial t − 1), significantly differs from P(L|L1 L1) = 0.72 (Fig. 2B,C, blue arrow) ... (Mann– Whitney U test, p < 0.0001)
claims.criterion: As fig2b-reward-stronger-than-noreward (O7, O8). Reproduced when, under every reading, both values are within tolerance, P(L|L1 L1) > P(L|R0 L1), and the test gives p < 0.0001.

claims.statement: Of the 128 mirror-paired four-trial sequences, L1 L1 L1 L1 (with R1 R1 R1 R1) is the most frequent (6.87%), R0 L1 L1 L1 (with L0 R1 R1 R1) the second (2.87%), R0 L0 R0 L0 (with L0 R0 L0 R0) the third (2.55%), and L0 L0 L0 L0 with R0 R0 R0 R0 make 1.28%.
claims.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraphs 2 and 3
claims.quote: the sequence L1 L1 L1 L1 and R1 R1 R1 R1 was observed most frequently (6.87% of all observed sequences of four trials). The sequence R0 L1 L1 L1 and L0 R1 R1 R1 was observed second most frequently (2.87%) ... The sequences R0 L0 R0 L0 and L0 R0 L0 R0 were observed third most frequently (2.55%) ... L0 L0 L0 L0 and R0 R0 R0 R0, which consisted of 1.28% of all observed sequences across the four trials
claims.criterion: All windows of four consecutive choice trials, histories as O7. Whether a pair's percentage is the sum of the two mirror sequences or each one's share is not fixed; readings are (a) the sum; (b) the mean of the two. Reproduced when, under one reading, all four values are within tolerance and the first three are the three most frequent pairs in that order.

claims.statement: After repeated L1 the left-choice probability rises and converges near 0.75, and the effect of an earlier R0 fades under following L1s, so P(L|L1 L1 L1 L1) and P(L|R0 L1 L1 L1) do not differ (both 0.74).
claims.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
claims.quote: increased with the number of L1 experiences and converged around 0.75 ... There was no significant difference between P(L|L1 L1 L1 L1) = 0.74 and P(L|R0 L1 L1 L1) = 0.74 (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.94)
claims.criterion: Prefix probabilities as the opening comment, histories as O7. The absence is judged on the paper's test, a Mann-Whitney U test at p < 0.05 (two-sided), under reading O8 (a), the 0/1 choices that follow each history; reading O8 (b) is shown as a variant. Reproduced when the test does not find a difference, both values are within tolerance, and P(L|L1) < P(L|L1 L1) < P(L|L1 L1 L1 L1), as the paper's own values are (0.68, 0.72, 0.74), with P(L|L1 L1 L1 L1) within 0.075 (10%) of 0.75; P(L|L1 L1 L1) is reported. The difference is reported either way.

claims.statement: After an unrewarded choice rats tended to choose the other action (switching), as seen in the alternating unrewarded sequences R0 L0 R0 L0 and L0 R0 L0 R0.
claims.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 3; Figure 2D
claims.quote: These results illustrate that there was a “switching” behavior in which rats tended to choose the other action after one action was not rewarded
claims.criterion: Prefix probabilities for R0 L0 R0 L0 and L0 R0 L0 R0 (O7), with 99% intervals. Reproduced when, under every reading, after each prefix ending in L0 the left-choice probability is below 0.5 and after each prefix ending in R0 it is above 0.5. The paper gives no test; the 99% intervals are reported.

claims.statement: After two or more unrewarded left choices the left-choice probability gradually rises, and P(L|L0 L0 L0) and P(L|L0 L0 L0 L0) are both above 0.5, so rats sometimes persevere after repeated non-reward.
claims.source: Results, History dependence of action choice, paragraph 3; Figure 2E
claims.quote: The probability of a left choice gradually increased after two or more left choices with no reward. In particular, P(L|L0 L0 L0) and P(L|L0 L0 L0 L0) were both >0.5
claims.criterion: Prefix probabilities for L0 L0 L0 L0 (and mirrored for R0 R0 R0 R0, as 1 - P(L)), O7. The paper gives no test. Reproduced when, under every reading, P(L|L0 L0) < P(L|L0 L0 L0) < P(L|L0 L0 L0 L0) ("gradually increased after two or more") and both P(L|L0 L0 L0) and P(L|L0 L0 L0 L0) exceed 0.5 for the left sequence; partially reproduced when this holds for the probabilities above 0.5 but not for the rise.

claims.statement: Fitted by least squares to the six four-trial sequences of Fig. 2C and 2D, the local matching law and standard Q-learning cannot represent switching, while F-Q and DF-Q can; the averaged residual errors are 0.0102, 0.0073, 0.0010 and 0.0002.
claims.source: Results, Modeling rats' strategies with a reinforcement learning model, paragraph 3; Figure 3; Table 1
claims.quote: The results showed that the local matching law (Fig. 3A) and the standard Q-learning model (Fig. 3B) were not able to represent switching behavior, whereas the F-Q- and DF-Q-learning models were (Fig. 3C,D). The averaged residual errors of the local matching law, the standard Q, F-Q, and DF-Q models were 0.0102, 0.0073, 0.0010, and 0.0002, respectively
claims.criterion: Data are the prefix probabilities of L1 L1 L1 L1, R1 R1 R1 R1, R0 L1 L1 L1, L0 R1 R1 R1, R0 L0 R0 L0 and L0 R0 L0 R0 (24 points). Each model starts from QL = QR = Q0 (a free parameter), applies the sequence and predicts P(L) after each prefix; parameters minimize the squared error (Results, paragraph 3; Table 1). Model equations as O1. The "averaged residual error" is not defined; readings are (a) the mean squared error over the 24 points; (b) the mean squared error over the 12 points of the three left-ending sequences with each mirror pair averaged. "Represents switching" is read from Fig. 3 as the model's P(L) after each L0 of R0 L0 R0 L0 below 0.5 and after each R0 above 0.5. Reproduced when, under every reading, the residuals are in the order local matching > standard Q > F-Q > DF-Q, each within tolerance, and switching is represented by F-Q and DF-Q but not by the local matching law and standard Q. Partially reproduced when the order and the switching hold but a value is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: The least-squares fits give the parameters of Table 1 (alpha1, alpha2, kappa1, kappa2, Q0) for each model.
claims.source: Table 1
claims.criterion: As fig3-lsq-switching. A reported 0.00 cannot take 10% of itself, so it is given 0.01, one step of the table's printed precision (two decimals). Readings as O1 (the parameter values depend on the form of the update). Reproduced when, under one reading of O1, all values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at least 10 of the 14 are. The O1 reading that gives the match is reported.

claims.statement: The first- to fourth-order Markov models reach normalized likelihoods of 0.528, 0.532, 0.534 and 0.532 on test data; the third order is best and the fourth is lower, presumably by overfitting its 256 parameters.
claims.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "Figure 5 shows"; Figure 5
claims.quote: The normalized likelihood of the first-order Markov model was 0.528 ... The normalized likelihood for the second- and third-order Markov models increased to 0.532 and 0.534, respectively ... The performance of the fourth-order model was 0.532, lower than that of the third-order model
claims.criterion: Markov prediction as the Methods give it, counts from the 35 training sessions, scored on the 35 test sessions with the normalized likelihood (O2); split O3; first trials O6; histories over choice trials within a session. Reproduced when, under every reading, all four values are within tolerance and order 3 is the highest. Partially reproduced when order 3 is highest but a value is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: With constant parameters, standard Q, F-Q and DF-Q (0.527, 0.531, 0.531) predict much better than the local matching law (0.508), but worse than the first- or second-order Markov models.
claims.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "Predictions by the standard Q-"; Figure 5; Table 2
claims.quote: Predictions by the standard Q-, F-Q-, and DF-Q-learning models with constant parameters (α and κ) were much better (0.527, 0.531, and 0.531, respectively) than the predictions of the local matching law (0.508), but poorer than that of the first- or second-order Markov models
claims.criterion: Parameters constant across sessions, fitted by maximum likelihood on the training sessions (O4), Qi(1) = 0 in each session, scored on the test sessions (O2, O3); equations O1; local matching law with P(L) = QL / (QL + QR). Reproduced when, under every reading, all four values are within tolerance and the three Q models exceed the local matching law. The comparison with the Markov models is reported; the paper's own numbers place F-Q and DF-Q (constant) above the first-order Markov model (opening comment), so it is not part of the outcome.

claims.statement: With time-varying parameters standard Q, F-Q and DF-Q improve to 0.5304, 0.5375 and 0.5368, and F-Q with time-varying parameters predicts best of all models.
claims.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "With time-varying parameters"; Figure 5
claims.quote: With time-varying parameters, the performance of the standard Q, F-Q, and DF-Q models improved (0.5304, 0.5375, and 0.5368, respectively). The F-Q-learning model with time-varying parameters produced the best prediction performance
claims.criterion: Particle filter as the supplemental Methods and the opening comment give it, 5000 particles, sigma_alpha and sigma_kappa fitted on the training sessions (O4), drift O5, equations O1, scored on the test sessions (O2, O3). Each variable model is reported against its constant version. Reproduced when, under every reading, the three values are within tolerance, each exceeds its constant version, and F-Q (variable) has the highest normalized likelihood of all models of Fig. 5; partially reproduced when F-Q or DF-Q (variable) is highest and the values are in tolerance but F-Q is not first.

claims.statement: Per test session, the F-Q and DF-Q models with time-varying parameters predict significantly better than every other model, including the third-order Markov model.
claims.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "A statistical test"; Figure 5 legend
claims.quote: the prediction accuracies of both the F-Q- and DF-Q-learning models with time-varying parameters were significantly higher than those of all other models (paired-sample Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p < 0.05 for third Markov model, p < 0.01 for other models)
claims.criterion: Per-session normalized likelihoods of the 35 test sessions (O2), two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of F-Q (variable) and of DF-Q (variable) against each of the other nine models of Fig. 5 (standard Q variable, three constant Q models, local matching law, Markov orders 1 to 4). The paper does not say whether the tests are one- or two-sided; both are readings. Readings O1, O3 to O6. Reproduced when, under every reading, both models exceed every other model with p < 0.05 against the third-order Markov model and p < 0.01 against the rest; partially reproduced when all comparisons give p < 0.05 with the F-Q and DF-Q medians higher.

claims.statement: The F-Q and DF-Q models with time-varying parameters do not differ in prediction accuracy (p = 0.067), so F-Q, with fewer parameters, is regarded as the better model.
claims.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "A statistical test"
claims.quote: There was no significant difference between these two models (paired-sample Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p = 0.067)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test of per-session normalized likelihoods of F-Q (variable) against DF-Q (variable) over the 35 test sessions at p < 0.05, under every reading of O1, O3 to O5. The paper does not give the side; the test is run two-sided, as a test of no difference with no direction named, and the one-sided p is shown as a variant. Reproduced when the test does not find a difference; the median difference is reported either way.

claims.statement: Taking left when the predicted P(L) exceeds 0.5 and right otherwise, the best model predicts 68% of choices correctly, averaged over the 35 test sessions.
claims.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "With time-varying parameters"
claims.quote: If we take binary predictions from the choice probability [left for PL(t) > 0.5, right for PL(t) < 0.5], the average percentage of correct predictions over 35 test sessions is 68%
claims.criterion: The sentence follows the statement that F-Q (variable) is best and does not name the model; read as F-Q (variable). Percentage correct per test session, averaged over the 35 sessions; trials with P(L) = 0.5 exactly count as half correct. Readings O1, O3 to O5. Reproduced when, under every reading, the value is within tolerance.

claims.statement: The maximum-likelihood parameters on the training data are those of Table 2 (for example F-Q constant alpha 0.55, kappa1 1.25, kappa2 0.55; F-Q variable sigma_alpha 0.005, sigma_kappa 0.07).
claims.source: Table 2
claims.criterion: As fig5-constant-models and fig5-variable-models-best. The parameter values depend on O1 and O3 to O5, and a grid step (O4 a) is coarser than 10% for the smallest values. O1 is a reading of what the reported values are (the parameterization), O3 to O5 readings of method. Reproduced when, under one reading of O1 and every reading of O3 to O5, all 16 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at least 8 are. The O1 reading that matches is reported.

claims.statement: Across all data the time-varying estimates average, for F-Q, alpha1 0.47 ± 0.25, kappa1 1.61 ± 0.77, kappa2 1.10 ± 0.87, and for DF-Q, alpha1 0.45 ± 0.19, alpha2 0.46 ± 0.19, kappa1 1.69 ± 0.77, kappa2 1.24 ± 0.92; standard Q alpha1 0.45 ± 0.23, kappa1 1.86 ± 0.68.
claims.source: Table 3
claims.criterion: Per-trial estimates (O13) from the time-varying models with the Table 2 sigmas, over all 70 sessions. The paper does not say over what the average and SD are taken; readings are (a) over all choice trials pooled; (b) over sessions, of per-session means. The tolerance of each mean is its SD (protocol); each SD is also reported against the table. Readings O1, O5, O13. Reproduced when, under every reading, all nine means are within tolerance.

claims.statement: With time-varying parameters, F-Q and DF-Q capture win-stay-lose-switch behaviour by raising kappa2 close to kappa1, and persevering behaviour by a negative kappa2, which the standard Q model cannot.
claims.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraphs beginning "Figure 4A–F" and "Figure 4, B, D, and F"; Figure 4
claims.quote: This behavior was captured by the F-Q- and DF-Q-learning models, with both models showing an increase in the nonreward aversion parameter κ2 close to the reward reinforcement parameter κ1 ... The F-Q and DF-Q models captured this behavior by exhibiting a negative value for the aversion parameter κ2 (Fig. 4H)
claims.criterion: The paper shows representative sessions and does not identify them, so the claim is tested as existence of such episodes. Win-stay-lose-switch episode, a run of at least 10 choice trials in which the rat repeated every rewarded choice and switched after every unrewarded one, as Results describe it. Persevering episode, a run of consecutive choices of the less advantageous side, rewarded or not, in a (10, 50) or (50, 10) block, as the Results describe Fig. 4B, D, F ("continued to choose the less advantageous left action"). The paper gives no run length; 5, 10 and 15 trials are readings for both kinds of episode, and the outcome is the one they all give. Reproduced when, under every reading of O1, O5 and O13, some win-stay-lose-switch episode has F-Q (variable) kappa2 within 25% of kappa1 at its end, some persevering episode has F-Q (variable) kappa2 below 0, and over all such episodes the F-Q (variable) mean per-trial likelihood exceeds that of standard Q (variable). The 25% reads "close to"; the paper gives no bound.

claims.statement: The actual left-choice probability, plotted against QL - QR from the standard Q, F-Q and DF-Q models, confirms that the models' predictions are meaningful.
claims.source: Results, Prediction of choices by models, paragraph beginning "With time-varying parameters"; supplemental Data 1 (not available)
claims.quote: the meaningful performances of the standard Q, F-Q, and DF-Q models were also conformed by plotting the actual left-choice probability for the difference between QL and QR (supplemental Data 1
claims.criterion: Supplemental Data 1 is not in the text read, so its bins and models (constant or variable) are not known. Readings are the variable and the constant versions of each model, with QL - QR (O13 a) in ten equal-count bins over all choice trials. Reproduced when, under every reading, the left-choice fraction rises with QL - QR (Spearman correlation of bin centres and fractions above 0.9) for all three models.

claims.statement: Analysis used 148 NAc neurons and 66 VP neurons from six rats in 70 sessions.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal recording data, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Subsequent analysis was performed for a total of 148 NAc neurons and 66 VP neurons from six rats during 70 sessions
claims.criterion: Units whose estimated position lies in the NAc or VP (Histology). Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: VP neurons fire faster than NAc neurons during the task (10.2 ± 9.1 against 2.6 ± 2.6 Hz, mean ± SD).
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 1
claims.quote: VP neurons showed a higher firing rate than NAc neurons overall. The average and SD of the firing rate of VP neurons and NAc neurons during the task were 10.2±9.1 and 2.6±2.6 Hz, respectively
claims.criterion: Per neuron, spikes over the task period divided by its duration (O15); mean and SD over neurons per region. The paper gives no test. Reproduced when, under every reading, the VP mean exceeds the NAc mean and the two means are within tolerance; the SDs are reported and partially reproduced is given when a mean holds but an SD is outside 10%.

claims.statement: After cue onset (phase 2), 54% of NAc neurons (80 of 148) and 50% of VP neurons (33 of 66) fire differently for the choice and the no-choice tone (state-coding neurons).
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B
claims.quote: After the onset of the cue tone (phase 2), 54% (80 of 148) of NAc neurons and 50% (33 of 66) of VP neurons showed different firing patterns in response to the choice tone and the no-choice tone
claims.criterion: Mann-Whitney U test at p < 0.01 of phase-2 spike counts, choice against no-choice trials (opening comment), trials O14. Reproduced when, under every reading, both counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: By block comparison of firing, few neurons code an action value; QL-coding neurons are 6, 8 and 7% of NAc neurons and 11, 18 and 21% of VP neurons in phases 1 to 3, and QR-coding neurons 7, 8 and 5% (NAc) and 11, 9 and 11% (VP).
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B; Figure 7E and 7F
claims.quote: Before the onset of the nose poke action at the center hole (phase 1), the percentage of QL-coding neurons in the NAc was 6% (9 of 148), and 11% (7 of 66) in the VP ... The percentage of QR-coding neurons in the NAc was 7% (11 of 148), and 11% (7 of 66) in the VP ... The percentage of QL-coding neurons in the NAc was 8% (12 of 148) and 18% (12 of 66) in the VP. The percentage of QR-coding neurons in the NAc was 8% (12 of 148) and 9% (6 of 66) in the VP. Before the initiation of action (phase 3), QL-coding neurons represented 7% (11 of 148) of the neurons in the NAc and 21% (14 of 66) of those in the VP. QR-coding neurons represented 5% (8 of 148) of the neurons in the NAc and 11% (7 of 66) of those in the VP
claims.criterion: Block comparisons by Mann-Whitney U test at p < 0.01 on the last 20 choice trials of each block (opening comment). Several blocks of one type in a session are pooled. The 10% tolerance is under one neuron for most counts, so each count is also judged within ±2 neurons. Reproduced when, under that rule, all 12 counts match; partially reproduced when at least 9 do and every count is below 25% of its region.

claims.statement: Before action initiation (phase 3), 11% of NAc neurons (17 of 148) and 18% of VP neurons (12 of 66) code the action to be chosen (action command-coding neurons).
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B
claims.quote: Neurons encoding the action to be chosen before execution represented 11% (17 of 148) of the neurons in the NAc and 18% (12 of 66) of those in the VP (action command-coding neurons)
claims.criterion: Mann-Whitney U test at p < 0.01 of phase-3 spike counts, left against right choice trials. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: After action onset (phase 4), 41% of NAc neurons (61 of 148) and 39% of VP neurons (26 of 66) code the selected action.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B
claims.quote: After the action onset (phase 4), the proportion of action-coding neurons increased to 41% (61 of 148) in the NAc and 39% (26 of 66) in the VP
claims.criterion: Mann-Whitney U test at p < 0.01 of phase-4 spike counts, left against right choice trials. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: After the reward or no-reward tone (phase 5), 63% of NAc neurons (93 of 148) and 68% of VP neurons (45 of 66) code reward availability.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 4; Figure 8B
claims.quote: After the onset of the reward tone or no-reward tone (phase 5), 63% (93 of 148) of NAc neurons and 68% (45 of 66) of VP neurons coded reward availability
claims.criterion: Mann-Whitney U test at p < 0.01 of phase-5 spike counts, rewarded against unrewarded choice trials. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The NAc and VP do not differ in the percentages of neurons coding trial type, action command, chosen action and reward outcome.
