claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 5; Figure 8B
claims.quote: Comparison of the percentages of coding neurons in the NAc and VP revealed no differences with trial type, action command, chosen action, and reward outcome (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.59, p = 0.19, p = 0.80, and p = 0.45, respectively)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a Mann-Whitney U test as O9 at p < 0.05, for each of the four types. Reproduced when none of the four finds a difference; not reproduced when any does. The four differences of percentages are reported either way.

claims.statement: QL-coding neurons are a larger share of VP than of NAc neurons after cue onset (phase 2) and before action initiation (phase 3).
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 5; Figure 8B
claims.quote: Surprisingly, the percentages of QL-coding neurons both after cue onset (phase 2) and before action initiation (phase 3) were significantly higher in the VP than in the NAc (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.03 < 0.05, p = 0.004 < 0.01, respectively)
claims.criterion: Mann-Whitney U test as O9 on QL-coding indicators, NAc against VP, per phase. Reproduced when, in both phases, the VP percentage is higher with p < 0.05; partially reproduced when this holds in one phase.

claims.statement: QR-coding neurons do not differ in share between the VP and NAc in phases 2 and 3.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 5; Figure 8B
claims.quote: whereas those of QR-coding neurons were not significantly different between areas at the two different times (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.81, and 0.17)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a Mann-Whitney U test as O9 at p < 0.05 on QR-coding indicators, NAc against VP, in phases 2 and 3. Reproduced when neither finds a difference; the differences are reported either way.

claims.statement: Among state-coding neurons (48% NAc, 36% VP preferring tone A), action command-coding neurons (53%, 50% preferring left) and action-coding neurons (57%, 50% preferring left), the share with each preference does not differ from 50%.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 6
claims.quote: Of the state-coding neurons, 48% (38 of 80) in the NAc and 36% (12 of 33) in the VP showed a greater response to tone A than to tone B. Of the action command-coding neurons, 53% (9 of 17) in the NAc and 50% (6 of 12) in the VP showed greater activity in left-selected trials than in right-selected trials. In the action-coding neurons, 57% (35 of 61) in the NAc and 50% (13 of 26) in the VP showed greater activity in left-selected than in right-selected trials. All of these populations were not significantly different from 50% (Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p > 0.05)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at p < 0.05 within each of the six populations. The test as written is reading O11 (a); the sign test, O11 (b), is shown as a variant. Preference is the sign of the difference of mean spike counts in the coding bin. Reproduced when none of the six tests finds a departure from 50%; the six percentages are reported against the expected values either way.

claims.statement: 73% of NAc reward-coding neurons (68 of 93) respond more to the no-reward than to the reward tone, more than the 50% of chance, while the VP share (56%, 25 of 45) does not differ from 50%.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 6
claims.quote: However, 73% (68 of 93) of the reward-coding neurons in the NAc showed a larger response to the no-reward than to the reward tone. This percentage of cells was significantly larger than the 50% predicted by chance (Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p < 0.0001). The percentage of reward-coding neurons in the VP (56%; 25 of 45), however, was not significantly different from 50% (Wilcoxon's signed rank test, p > 0.05)
claims.criterion: Preference by the sign of the phase-5 difference of mean spike counts. For the NAc, under both readings of O11, the NAc percentage is above 50% and the test gives p < 0.0001. The VP part is a claim of absence judged on O11 (a) at p < 0.05, with O11 (b) as a variant. Reproduced when the NAc part holds under every reading and the VP test finds no departure; partially reproduced when one part holds.

claims.statement: Splitting NAc neurons into tentative core and shell groups by electrode position, the same analyses find no difference between core and shell neurons.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 7; supplemental Data 3 (not available)
claims.quote: The same analysis described above found no significant differences between core and shell neurons (supplemental Data 3
claims.criterion: Supplemental Data 3, which holds the tests, is not in the text read. A claim of absence, read as the analysis of fig8b-nac-vp-same-event-coding and fig8b-ql-vp-higher (Mann-Whitney U test as O9 at p < 0.05 on per-neuron coding indicators) with core and shell in place of NAc and VP, for state, action command, action, reward, and QL and QR coding in phases 1 to 3. Core and shell as assigned in the dataset from Fig. 6; if the dataset does not assign them, the claim cannot be tested. Reproduced when no test finds a difference.

claims.statement: By regression on the block reward probabilities, QL-coding neurons are 9, 10 and 7% of NAc neurons and 15, 24 and 26% of VP neurons in phases 1 to 3, and QR-coding neurons 11, 9 and 6% (NAc) and 9, 17 and 14% (VP).
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8C
claims.quote: QL-coding neurons, which were found to have a significant regression coefficient to QL (t test, p < 0.01) but not to QR, were present in percentages of 9, 10, and 7% in the NAc, and 15, 24, and 26% in the VP for different time bins (Fig. 8A, phases 1–3) ... QR-coding neurons, which were found to have a significant regression coefficient to QR (t test, p < 0.01) but not to QL, were present in percentages of 11, 9, and 6% in the NAc, and 9, 17, and 14% in the VP
claims.criterion: Regression as the opening comment, y = b0 + b1 QL + b2 QR with QL and QR the block's reward probabilities as fractions; the equation is missing, and the text names no other regressor, so none is added. The 10% tolerance is under one neuron for most values, so each is also judged within ±2 neurons of the reported percentage. Reproduced when, under that rule, all 12 values match; partially reproduced when at least 9 do.

claims.statement: In the regression analysis, QL-coding neurons are a larger share of VP than of NAc neurons in phases 2 and 3.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8C
claims.quote: In phases 2 and 3, there were significant differences in the size of the population of QL-coding neurons in the NAc, and in the VP (p = 0.007 and 0.0001 < 0.01, Mann–Whitney U test)
claims.criterion: Mann-Whitney U test as O9, NAc against VP, on regression QL-coding indicators. Reproduced when, in both phases, the VP share is higher with p < 0.01; partially reproduced when both give p < 0.05 or one gives p < 0.01.

claims.statement: Regression detects slightly more action value-coding neurons (Fig. 8C) than the block comparison (Fig. 8B), and the two are consistent.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8
claims.quote: These regression analysis results were consistent with those obtained by comparing the perievent time histograms (Fig. 8B). However, the number of the detected action value-coding neurons was slightly larger in Figure 8C than in Figure 8B
claims.criterion: Total QL- plus QR-coding neurons over phases 1 to 3 and both regions, regression against block comparison. Reproduced when the regression total is larger, and the region with the larger QL share in phases 2 and 3 is the VP in both analyses.

claims.statement: State value-coding neurons are 12, 8 and 8% of NAc neurons and 18, 20 and 20% of VP neurons in phases 1 to 3, with the VP share larger in phases 2 and 3.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8D
claims.quote: State value-coding neurons, which were found to have a significant regression coefficient to [QL(t) + QR(t)] but not to [QL(t) − QR(t)], were present in percentages of 12, 8, and 8% in the NAc, and 18, 20, and 20% in the VP (Fig. 8D). In phases 2 and 3, these differences between the sizes of the populations in the NAc and VP were significant (p = 0.02 and 0.02 < 0.05, respectively; Mann–Whitney U test)
claims.criterion: Regression y = b0 + b1 (QL + QR) + b2 (QL - QR) on the last 20 choice trials of each block (Methods, Regression analysis); t test at p < 0.01; Mann-Whitney U test as O9. Percentages judged within ±2 neurons where 10% is under one neuron. Reproduced when the six values match and the VP share is higher in phases 2 and 3 with p < 0.05; partially reproduced when the test result holds and at least four values match.

claims.statement: Policy-coding neurons are 10, 9 and 7% of NAc neurons and 11, 15 and 14% of VP neurons in phases 1 to 3.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8D
claims.quote: Policy-coding neurons, which were found to have a significant regression coefficient to [QL(t) − QR(t)] but not to [QL(t) + QR(t)], were present in percentages of 10, 9, and 7% in the NAc, and 11, 15, and 14% in the VP (Fig. 8D)
claims.criterion: As fig8d-state-value-vp-higher, for the QL - QR coefficient. Reproduced when the six values match (±2 neurons where 10% is under one neuron); partially reproduced when at least four do.

claims.statement: Every coding population of Figure 8 is larger than expected by chance.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 8; Figure 8 legend
claims.quote: All percentages shown in Figure 8 were significantly larger than those predicted by chance (p < 0.01, binomial test)
claims.criterion: One-sided binomial test of each count of Fig. 8B to 8D against the chance level O10. Reproduced when, under every reading, every population gives p < 0.01; partially reproduced when at least 90% of them do.

claims.statement: Information about the trial type (state) in the NAc and VP rises right after cue onset and again after center-hole exit.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 9; Figure 9A and 9B
claims.quote: The information coding state in the NAc and VP (green lines) increased immediately after the onset of the cue tone, and again after exiting from the center hole
claims.criterion: MI as the opening comment, tone A against tone B, choice and no-choice trials, averaged per region, windows O12. "Immediately after" is read as within 0.5 s of cue onset. Reproduced when, under every reading and in both regions, the state MI exceeds the threshold within 0.5 s after cue onset and is higher there than in the 0.5 s before it, and the curve aligned to center-hole exit has a local maximum above threshold after the exit that exceeds its value at the exit.

claims.statement: Information about the chosen action is very weak before center-hole exit, rises rapidly after it, and peaks around entry to the L or R hole.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 9; Figure 9B
claims.quote: Information related to action choice was very weak in both the NAc and VP before the onset of the choice (before the exit of the center hole), but increased rapidly after the choice onset, and showed a peak around the time of entry to the left or right hole
claims.criterion: MI between firing and left or right choice, choice trials, aligned to center-hole exit, windows O12. Reproduced when, under every reading and in both regions, the mean MI over windows before the exit is below a fifth of the peak, and the peak lies after the exit within 0.5 s of the median reaction time (L or R entry).

claims.statement: Information about reward rises when the reward or no-reward tone is presented at L or R entry, then decreases gradually but lasts until the next trial.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 9; Figure 9B; Discussion, Information coding in NAc and VP, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Information related to the reward started to increase at the presentation of reward/no-reward tone, which was presented at the time of entry to the left or right hole. The reward information gradually decreased, but was sustained until the subsequent trial
claims.criterion: MI between firing and reward outcome, choice trials, aligned to center-hole exit (Fig. 9B) and, for the next trial, to the next cue onset (Fig. 9A, "previous reward"), with the previous trial's outcome as the event; windows O12. Reproduced when, under every reading and in both regions, reward MI is below threshold before the L or R entry, rises above it after, and the previous-trial reward MI is above threshold around the next cue onset.

claims.statement: Information about the action values QL and QR is above the significance threshold in the NAc and VP but low and without clear peaks, while state, action and reward information are robust.
claims.source: Results, Neuronal activity in the NAc and VP, paragraph 10; Figure 9; Discussion, Information coding in NAc and VP, last paragraph but one
claims.quote: Information regarding action values QL and QR in the NAc and VP were found to be larger than the threshold values, indicating a significant level of information (p < 0.01) (see Materials and Methods). However, this level of information was still relatively low and without clear peaks, whereas information about state, action, and reward was robustly represented in the NAc and VP
claims.criterion: QL and QR from F-Q with time-varying parameters (Table 2 sigmas), binarized at the median (O13), MI as the opening comment, windows O12. Reproduced when, under every reading and in both regions, QL and QR MI exceed the threshold in most windows (over half), their peak is below the peaks of state, action and reward MI, and their maximum is less than twice their median over windows (no clear peak); partially reproduced when the comparison with the other events holds but the above-threshold or flatness part does not.

claims.statement: Information about the chosen action in the NAc and VP lasts beyond the peak of reward information.
claims.source: Discussion, Information coding in NAc and VP, paragraph 3; Figure 9
claims.quote: In particular, we showed that a representation of information regarding action in the NAc and VP lasted beyond the peak of information regarding reward (Fig. 9)
claims.criterion: On the curves of Fig. 9B (O12). Reproduced when, under every reading and in both regions, action MI is above threshold at the time of the reward MI peak and in the window 0.5 s after it.

claims.statement: The analysis covers 78,107 trials in 86 recording sessions from seven rats, of which 12,185 are single fixed-choice, 22,234 double fixed-choice, 36,292 free-choice and 3505 extinction-test trials.
claims.source: Results, opening section, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Here, we report the results of all 78,107 trials in 86 recording sessions, performed by seven rats, consisting of 12,185 single fixed-choice trials (16.4%), 22,234 double fixed-choice trials (30.0%), 36,292 free-choice trials (48.9%), and 3505 extinction test trials (4.7%)
claims.criterion: The rat count must match exactly. The paper does not say which trials it counts (the four categories sum to 74,216, not 78,107). Readings are (a) all trials started, including wait-error and error trials; (b) trials with an L/R choice only. Reproduced when, under one reading, every count is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Completing a block took 22.56 ± 8.70 trials for single fixed-choice blocks, 47.11 ± 20.29 for double fixed-choice blocks and 41.10 ± 27.58 for free-choice blocks (mean ± SD).
claims.source: Results, opening section, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Numbers of trials required to complete one block were 22.56 ± 8.70 for single fixed-choice blocks, 47.11 ± 20.29 for double fixed-choice blocks, and 41.10 ± 27.58 for free-choice blocks, (mean ± SD)
claims.criterion: The tolerance of each mean is the stated SD (protocol); each SD is checked to 10%. The paper leaves open which trials are counted and which blocks enter. Readings are (a) choice trials only (the block rule counts "choice trials"), completed blocks only; (b) all trials including wait-error and error trials, completed blocks only; (c) as (a) with the last, possibly unfinished, block of a session included; (d) as (b) with it included. Extinction trials are not counted in any reading. Reproduced when, under one reading, all six values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: During extinction tests, choice probabilities for the left and right tones differ significantly from those for the choice tone.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral performance, paragraph 1; Figure 2B and 2C
claims.quote: Choice probabilities during extinction tests were significantly different between the left and right tones and the choice tone (Fig. 2C; p < 0.0001, χ2 test)
claims.criterion: Choices over the five trials of each extinction test (Fig. 2C legend). The contingency table of the χ2 test is not given. Readings are (a) left-tone trials against choice-tone trials after a left-optimal free-choice block, and right-tone trials against choice-tone trials after a right-optimal block, each a 2 x 2 table of left and right choices; (b) one 2 x 2 table of choices of the previously optimal action, fixed tones pooled against the choice tone pooled. Reproduced when, under every reading, every test gives p < 0.0001 with the fixed tones further from 50% than the choice tone.

claims.statement: In extinction tests the choice-tone choice probability shifts toward 50% after the first unrewarded trial, while the left- and right-tone choice probabilities stay biased after five unrewarded trials.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral performance, paragraph 1; Figure 2B
claims.quote: whereas the choice probabilities for the free-choice tone shifted toward 50% following the first nonrewarded trial (orange lines, Fig. 2B), choice probabilities for the left and right tones remained biased even after five no-reward trials
claims.criterion: Left-choice probability at each of the five extinction trials, per tone, with the choice tone split by the optimal action of the previous free-choice block (Fig. 2B legend), with 95% confidence intervals of a binomial proportion (the interval method is not given; the readings are Wilson and Clopper-Pearson intervals). Reproduced when, under both readings, (1) for both choice-tone groups the probability at trial 2 is closer to 0.5 than at trial 1, and (2) at trial 5 the 95% interval for the left tone lies above 0.5 and that for the right tone below 0.5.

claims.statement: Choice-tone choices depend on the previous one or two trials' actions and rewards (a decision tree that expands symmetrically), while left- and right-tone choices stay biased toward left and right whatever the previous experience.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral performance, paragraph 2; Figure 2D to 2F
claims.quote: The decision tree for choice tones expands symmetrically (Fig. 2D), indicating that action selection was sensitive to past experiences ... action probabilities for the left or right tones (in both single and double fixed-choice blocks) are biased toward 1 (Fig. 2E) or 0 (Fig. 2F), respectively, indicating insensitivity to past experiences
claims.criterion: Conditional left-choice probabilities for d = 1 and d = 2 from counts NL and NR after each experience sequence, within choice-tone trials and within left- and right-tone trials (single and double fixed-choice blocks), as the Methods define (Decision trees); 95% binomial intervals as in fig2b-extinction-time-course. Experience sequences are taken over consecutive trials of the same tone within a session (the Methods say "sequences of choice behavior in choice-tone trials"); whether they run across block borders is open, and both are readings. The paper gives no test or threshold. Reproduced when, under every reading, (1) for choice tones P(L) after L1 exceeds P(L) after R1 with non-overlapping 95% intervals, and (2) every d = 1 and d = 2 conditional probability is above 0.5 for the left tone and below 0.5 for the right tone. For (2), the readings are all sequences, and sequences with at least 10 trials (a sparse branch is not a reliable estimate; the paper gives no floor).

claims.statement: Of six DFQ-learning variants and the Markov models, the FQ-learning model with time-varying parameters predicts held-out rat choices in free-choice blocks best.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral performance, paragraph 5; Figure 2G
claims.quote: found that the FQ-learning model with time-varying parameters predicted rat behaviors best (Fig. 2G). Prediction accuracy was higher than that of Markov models
claims.criterion: Choice-tone trials of free-choice blocks; models Q (alpha2 = kappa2 = 0), FQ (alpha1 = alpha2) and DFQ, each with constant or time-varying parameters, and Markov models of order d (Methods, Evaluation of decision-making models). Sessions split into training and test halves (the paper used 101 and 101 sessions; how the split was made is not given, so the readings are alternate sessions and a seeded random half, both shown); parameters fitted by maximum likelihood on training data, the time-varying models with a particle filter of 5000 particles. Model equations as O8 (opening comment). The normalized likelihood formula is missing; it is read as the geometric mean of per-trial choice likelihoods, which is 0.5 at chance, computed per test session for the paired Wilcoxon test across sessions. Reproduced when, under every reading, FQ (variable) has the highest normalized likelihood of test data and exceeds every Markov model.

claims.statement: A regular actor-critic model with constant parameters predicts test choices close to chance, with normalized likelihood 0.5080.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral performance, last paragraph
claims.quote: We also tested a regular actor-critic model with constant variables (Sutton and Barto, 1998), but the normalized likelihood of test data was close to the chance level (0.5080; data not shown)
claims.criterion: The paper names the model only as a regular actor-critic model with constant parameters (Sutton and Barto, 1998) and gives neither its equations nor its parameters. "Constant" is read as in Fig. 2G, parameters constant across sessions, fitted by maximum likelihood on the training sessions and scored on the test sessions as in fig2g-fq-variable-best. The readings of the model are the tabular actor-critic for one state and two actions (critic V and actor preferences both updated by the reward prediction error, softmax choice with a free inverse temperature) with (a) one learning rate shared by critic and actor, (b) separate learning rates. Reproduced when every reading is within tolerance; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: Stable recordings were made from 260 DLS, 178 DMS and 179 VS neurons, of which 190, 105 and 119 were phasically active neurons.
claims.source: Results, Activity patterns of phasically active neurons, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Stable recordings were made from 260 neurons in DLS, 178 neurons in DMS, and 179 neurons in VS from seven rats ... Among these, 190, 105, and 119 neurons from DLS, DMS, and VS, respectively, were classified as PANs
claims.criterion: Counts of units per region; PANs by the rule of the Methods (proportion of time in ISIs longer than 1 s greater than 0.4), over the whole session. The Results also name waveforms as a basis of the PAN class, but the Methods give no waveform rule, so none is applied. If the dataset holds only curated units, the stable counts are compared as deposited and the PAN rule is applied to them. Reproduced when all six counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: More than 60% of VS PANs increase their activity as the rat approaches the center hole (Phase 1), significantly more than in DLS and DMS.
claims.source: Results, Activity patterns of phasically active neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 4B
claims.quote: The proportion of neurons that increased their activity as a rat approached the center hole (trial Phase 1) was >60% in VS, significantly larger than in DLS and DMS (p = 0.0015 and p < 0.0001, respectively, χ2 test)
claims.criterion: Per PAN, the EASH over all trials (O3), normalized to a maximum of 1 (Fig. 4A legend), smoothing as O2. A neuron is activated in a phase when its normalized EASH reaches 0.5 during that phase (Fig. 4B legend); readings are (a) any bin at or above 0.5 in the phase, (b) the first crossing of 0.5 falls in the phase (the sort of Fig. 4A). 2 x 2 χ2 tests between regions, O4. Reproduced when, under every reading, the VS proportion exceeds 0.54 and VS exceeds DLS and DMS with p < 0.05 in both tests.

claims.statement: More than 60% of DMS PANs are activated between center-hole exit and L/R-hole entry (Phase 5), significantly more than in DLS and VS.
claims.source: Results, Activity patterns of phasically active neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 4B
claims.quote: After a rat's exit from the center hole until its entrance into the L/R hole (trial Phase 5), >60% of DMS neurons were activated, which was significantly larger than the proportions of DLS and VS (p = 0.00021 for DLS, p = 0.040 for VS, χ2 test)
claims.criterion: As fig4b-vs-phase1, for Phase 5. Reproduced when, under every reading, the DMS proportion exceeds 0.54 and DMS exceeds DLS and VS with p < 0.05 in both tests.

claims.statement: During pellet retrieval (Phase 7) the proportion of activated neurons is significantly larger in VS than in DLS.
claims.source: Results, Activity patterns of phasically active neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 4B
claims.quote: During the trial phase of receiving a sugar pellet (trial Phase 7), the proportion of activated neurons was significantly larger in VS than in DLS (p = 0.0040, χ2 test)
claims.criterion: As fig4b-vs-phase1, for Phase 7. Reproduced when, under every reading, the VS proportion exceeds the DLS proportion with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: VS PANs stay active longer than DLS and DMS PANs, and DLS PANs have the shortest activation, shorter than VS and DMS.
claims.source: Results, Activity patterns of phasically active neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 4C
claims.quote: VS neurons maintained activation longer (more than half of peak activity) than DLS (p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test) and DMS neurons (p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test), and DLS neurons had shorter durations of activation than VS neurons and DMS neurons (p < 0.0001 for VS, p = 0.040 for DMS, Mann–Whitney U test)
claims.criterion: Per PAN, the activity ratio of each phase (time the normalized EASH is above 0.5, divided by the phase duration), averaged over the seven phases (Fig. 4C legend); EASH as in fig4b-vs-phase1 (O2, O3). Two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests between regions. Reproduced when, under every reading of O2 and O3, the region means (Fig. 4C plots the average) order VS > DMS > DLS and all three tests give p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Information about the block type (fixed- or free-choice) is strongest in VS, especially during the approach to the center hole (Phase 1).
claims.source: Results, Information coding of state, action, and reward, paragraph 2; Figure 5A and 5B
claims.quote: State information (fixed- or free-choice block) was strongest in VS, especially, during the approach to the center hole (trial Phase 1) (p < 0.0001 for DLS, p = 0.022 for DMS, Mann–Whitney U tests)
claims.criterion: Per PAN, MI between firing and block type (fixed-choice blocks, single and double, against free-choice blocks) in each 100 ms EASH bin over all trials (Methods, Mutual information; O1, O3). The test's unit of comparison is not stated; readings are per-neuron MI (a) averaged over the bins of Phase 1, (b) in each Phase 1 bin, the result read from the bins that pass. Two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests. Reproduced when, under every reading, VS exceeds DLS and DMS with p < 0.05 and the VS region average exceeds the shuffle threshold in Phase 1.

claims.statement: Action information (left or right choice) starts rising during cue presentation (Phase 3) only in DLS.
claims.source: Results, Information coding of state, action, and reward, paragraph 2; Figure 5C to 5E; Discussion, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Action information (left or right hole choice) started increasing during the tone presentation (trial Phase 3) specifically in DLS (Fig. 5C–E)
claims.criterion: Region averages of per-PAN action MI in 100 ms EASH bins (O1, O3), against the shuffle threshold of the Methods (100 random-event repeats, second largest, p < 0.01). Reproduced when, under every reading, the DLS average exceeds its threshold in at least one Phase 3 bin and the DMS and VS averages exceed theirs in no Phase 3 bin.

claims.statement: In the 100 ms before cue offset, action information is significantly higher in DLS than in DMS and VS.
claims.source: Results, Information coding of state, action, and reward, paragraph 3; Figure 5E
claims.quote: Action information during the 100 ms before the offset of the cue tone was significantly higher in DLS than in DMS and VS (p = 0.0175 for DMS, p = 0.00091 for VS, Mann–Whitney U tests)
claims.criterion: Per-PAN action MI in the 100 ms EASH bin ending at E3 (O1, O3); two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests. Reproduced when, under every reading, DLS exceeds DMS and VS with p < 0.05 in both tests.

claims.statement: In the 100 ms before center-hole exit, action information in DMS is higher than in DLS (not significant) and VS, and is weakest in VS.
claims.source: Results, Information coding of state, action, and reward, paragraph 3; Figure 5D and 5E
claims.quote: Immediately after the offset of the cue tone (trial Phase 4) action information in DMS rapidly increased and became higher than that in DLS and VS during the 100 ms before the offset from the center hole, while information in VS was weakest (p = 0.16 for DLS, p = 0.0027 for VS, p < 0.0001 for DLS vs VS, Mann–Whitney U tests)
claims.criterion: Per-PAN action MI in the 100 ms EASH bin ending at E4 (O1, O3); two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests. Reproduced when, under every reading, the region means order DMS > DLS > VS, and DMS against VS and DLS against VS give p < 0.05. DMS against DLS is reported; its significance is not part of the claim.

claims.statement: During action execution (Phase 5), action information is highest in DMS.
claims.source: Results, Information coding of state, action, and reward, paragraph 3; Figure 5D
claims.quote: During action execution (trial Phase 5), the action information was the highest in DMS (p < 0.0001 for DLS, p < 0.0001 for VS, p < 0.0001 for DLS vs VS, Mann–Whitney U tests)
claims.criterion: Per-PAN action MI in the 100 ms EASH bins of Phase 5 (O1, O3); the bins compared are not stated, so the readings are (a) the mean over Phase 5 bins, (b) the bin of the DMS region peak. Two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests. Reproduced when, under every reading, DMS exceeds DLS and VS with p < 0.05 in both tests. The DLS against VS test is reported.

claims.statement: Reward information rises in all regions after L/R-hole entry and is strongest in VS, then DMS, with DLS significantly below both.
claims.source: Results, Information coding of state, action, and reward, paragraph 4; Figure 5F and 5G
claims.quote: Reward information was strongest in VS, followed by DMS, and reward information in DLS was significantly less than that in VS and DMS (p = 0.012 for DLS vs DMS, p < 0.0001 for DLS vs VS, p = 0.13 for DMS vs VS, Mann–Whitney U tests)
claims.criterion: Per-PAN reward MI (rewarded against unrewarded choices) in 100 ms EASH bins (O1, O3). The window of the test is not stated; readings are the mean over the bins of (a) Phase 6, (b) Phases 6 and 7, (c) the bin of the VS region peak. Two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests. Reproduced when, under every reading, (1) the region average of each region first exceeds its shuffle threshold (Methods, Mutual information) after E5, in Phase 6, and (2) the means order VS > DMS > DLS and DLS is below DMS and VS with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Proportions of event-coding neurons follow the MI results. State-coding neurons during cue presentation are most common in VS, action-coding neurons in DLS before action execution and in DMS during it, and reward-coding neurons in VS during L/R poking.
claims.source: Results, Information coding of state, action, and reward, paragraph 4; Figure 6D
claims.quote: the proportion of state-coding neurons during cue presentation (trial Phase 3) was the largest in VS, and the proportion of action-coding neurons was the largest in DLS before action execution and in DMS during action execution. The proportion of reward-coding neurons was the largest in VS during the L/R poking (Fig. 6D)
claims.criterion: Over all trials (Fig. 6D; O3), a PAN codes an event when firing differs between the two conditions by a Mann-Whitney U test with p < 0.01 (Fig. 6 legend). Windows from the legend; action command (AC) the 500 ms before E4, action the 500 ms after E4, Reward1 the 500 ms before E6, Reward2 the 500 ms after E6. The state window is drawn only in Fig. 6A, which could not be read; readings are (a) all of Phase 3 on the EASH axis, (b) the 500 ms before E3. Reward "during the L/R poking" is read as Reward1. Reproduced when, under every reading, VS has the largest state and Reward1 proportions, DLS the largest AC proportion and DMS the largest action proportion. The paper's χ2 tests between regions (O4) are reported; which pairs it marked significant could not be read from the figure.

claims.statement: Every proportion of event-coding neurons, in every region, in fixed-choice blocks, free-choice blocks and all trials, is significantly larger than chance.
claims.source: Figure 6B to 6D legend
claims.quote: All populations are significantly larger than the chance level (binomial test, p < 0.01)
claims.criterion: As fig6-event-coding-proportions, for fixed-choice trials (Fig. 6B), free-choice trials (Fig. 6C) and all trials (Fig. 6D); state coding exists only for all trials. The chance level is not given; it is read as 0.01, the selection threshold. One-sided binomial test per region and event. Reproduced when every test gives p < 0.01.

claims.statement: The proportions of action- and reward-coding neurons are similar in fixed- and free-choice blocks.
claims.source: Results, Information coding of state, action, and reward, paragraph 4; Figure 6B and 6C
claims.quote: These proportions in the population were similar in fixed-choice and free-choice blocks (Fig. 6B,C)
claims.criterion: The paper names no test. Proportions of AC, action, Reward1 and Reward2 neurons per region, computed separately in fixed-choice and free-choice trials, as in fig6-event-coding-proportions. Reproduced when the region with the largest proportion is the same in both block types for each event. The difference per event and region, with a 2 x 2 χ2 test (O4), is reported.

claims.statement: Substantial proportions of neurons in all three regions code the current action before and after action execution and the reward after L/R poking, and rewards of the previous trial are coded in all phases in all regions; a significant proportion of DMS neurons codes the previous action during action execution.
claims.source: Results, Model-based analysis of action value and state value coding, paragraph 3; Figure 8A to 8D
claims.quote: Substantial proportions of neurons in DLS, DMS, and VS coded actions before and after action execution (Fig. 8A) ... a significant proportion of DMS neurons coded previous actions during action execution (trial Phase 5; Fig. 8B). Substantial proportions of neurons in all subareas coded rewards after the start of L/R hole poking (Fig. 8C), and rewards in the previous trial were also strongly coded in all trial phases in all striatal regions (Fig. 8D)
claims.criterion: Regression with BIC selection as the Methods give it (opening comment; O6, O7, O8), coding at p < 0.01 per coefficient. Proportions per region and window against chance by a one-sided binomial test at p < 0.01 (Fig. 8 legend); the chance level is not given and is read as 0.01. Reproduced when, under every reading, (1) a(t) is coded above chance in every region in at least one window before and one after E4, (2) r(t) above chance in every region in at least one window after E5, (3) r(t-1) above chance in every region in at least one window of every phase, and (4) a(t-1) above chance in DMS in a Phase 5 window.

claims.statement: The proportion of action-value-coding neurons is highest in DMS during action execution, significantly above DLS.
claims.source: Results, Model-based analysis of action value and state value coding, paragraph 4; Figure 8E
claims.quote: the proportion of action-value coding neurons was highest in DMS during action execution (Fig. 8E; p = 0.00058 for DLS, p = 0.081 for VS, Mann–Whitney U test)
claims.criterion: Action-value coding is QL or QR coded (Fig. 8E legend), regression as in fig8a-d-action-reward-coding. Per-neuron 0/1 indicators in the Phase 5 windows compared by Mann-Whitney U tests (O5). Reproduced when, under every reading, DMS has the highest proportion of the three regions in a Phase 5 window and exceeds DLS there with p < 0.05. DMS against VS is reported; its significance is not part of the claim.

claims.statement: Most action-value-coding DMS neurons represent QR, and the proportion coding QR during action execution is significantly larger in DMS than in DLS.
claims.source: Results, Model-based analysis of action value and state value coding, paragraph 4
claims.quote: The majority of these action value-coding neurons in DMS represented QR, the action value for right hole choice, and the proportion of neurons coding QR during action execution was significant larger in DMS than in DLS (p = 0.00017, Mann–Whitney U test)
claims.criterion: As fig8e-action-value-dms, with QR coding alone. Reproduced when, under every reading, more than half of the DMS action-value-coding neurons in the Phase 5 window code QR and the DMS proportion coding QR exceeds the DLS proportion with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: State-value-coding neurons (QL and QR coded with the same sign) are most common in VS in all phases, significantly more than in DLS and DMS in Phase 1 and in the first half of Phase 4.
claims.source: Results, Model-based analysis of action value and state value coding, paragraph 5; Figure 8F (cited as Fig. 7F in the text)
claims.quote: The proportion of state-value coding neurons was the highest in VS in all trial phases, especially in starting phase (trial Phase 1) and action initiation phase (trial Phase 4), the proportion was significantly larger in VS than in DLS and DMS (p = 0.039 for DMS and p = 0.0027 for DLS, in trial Phase 1; p = 0.024 for DMS and p = 0.0045 for DLS, first half of Phase 4; Mann–Whitney U test)
claims.criterion: State-value coding as the Fig. 8F legend defines it, regression as in fig8a-d-action-reward-coding, Mann-Whitney U tests on 0/1 indicators (O5). Reproduced when, under every reading, VS has the largest proportion in every phase (at least one window per phase) and exceeds DLS and DMS with p < 0.05 in a Phase 1 window and in the window covering the first half of Phase 4.

claims.statement: No region has a significant number of policy-coding neurons (QL and QR coded with opposite signs) in any time bin.
claims.source: Results, Model-based analysis of action value and state value coding, paragraph 5
claims.quote: We did not find significant numbers of policy-coding neurons (those with significant correlations with both action values with opposite signs), in any subarea or in any time bin (data not shown)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test for Fig. 8, a one-sided binomial test of the proportion against chance at p < 0.01, with chance read as 0.01 (as in fig8a-d-action-reward-coding; the paper names one chance level for all panels of Fig. 8 and does not give it). Reproduced when, under every reading of O6 to O8, no region and window gives p < 0.01; not reproduced when, under every reading, one does; blocked when they disagree. The largest proportion is reported either way.

claims.statement: In every block type, action information rises first in DLS during cue presentation, then in DMS after cue offset (Phase 4), and last in VS after the onset of action execution (Phase 5); the pattern holds in free-choice blocks too.
claims.source: Results, Action-command information in fixed- and free-choice blocks, paragraph 1; Figure 9A to 9D
claims.quote: Action information in the single and double fixed-choice blocks started to rise first in DLS during cue presentation and then in DMS after cue offset (trial Phase 4), and finally in VS after onset of action execution (trial Phase 5) (Fig. 9A,B). Contrary to expectation, this temporal pattern of action information was seen also in free-choice blocks (Fig. 9C,D)
claims.criterion: Per PAN and block type (single fixed, double fixed, free with higher probabilities (90, 50) and (50, 90), free with lower probabilities (50, 10) and (10, 50)), action MI from the last 20 trials of each block, in a sliding window of the preceding 500 ms with 50 ms steps (Fig. 9 legend), averaged per region; first time the average exceeds the p < 0.01 shuffle threshold (the triangle of Fig. 9). How the last 20 trials of several blocks of one type in a session are combined is not stated; readings are (a) pooled into one MI estimate per neuron, (b) MI per block, averaged. O1 applies. The rise of a region is the start of its sustained rise into action execution, the first crossing after which the average stays above threshold through Phase 5, since Fig. 10C reports a transient VS peak during cue presentation in single fixed-choice blocks, which the paper does not count as the VS rise. The first crossing is reported too. Reproduced when, under every reading, (1) in single and double fixed-choice blocks the rise falls in Phase 3 for DLS, in Phase 4 for DMS and in Phase 5 for VS, and (2) in both free-choice block types the rises come in the same order, DLS, then DMS, then VS (the text says only that "this temporal pattern" was seen; Fig. 10A says the DLS rise is later in free-choice blocks); their phases are reported.

claims.statement: In no block type is the action command in DMS stronger than in DLS.
claims.source: Results, Action-command information in fixed- and free-choice blocks, paragraph 1; Figure 9
claims.quote: There were no conditions in which the action command in DMS was stronger than in DLS
claims.criterion: A claim of absence for which the paper gives no test. Action command is action MI before action execution (Fig. 9 legend, upcoming action for Phases 2 to 4), as in fig9-temporal-order-all-blocks, in the two windows the paper tests in Fig. 10 (the 500 ms before E3 and the 500 ms before E4). Judged with the test the paper uses to compare MI between regions (Results, Information coding of state, action, and reward), a Mann-Whitney U test across neurons, two-sided at p < 0.05. Reproduced when, under every reading, DMS is not significantly above DLS in any block type and window; not reproduced when, under every reading, it is somewhere; blocked when the readings disagree. The differences are reported either way. Note that fig5e-action-info-center-exit has DMS above DLS, not significantly, in the 100 ms before E4 over all trials.

claims.statement: In DLS, action information is significantly stronger in fixed-choice than in free-choice blocks in Phase 3 and Phase 4; it rises right after cue onset in fixed-choice blocks, more slowly in free-choice blocks with higher rewards, and later and weaker with lower rewards.
claims.source: Results, Action-command information in fixed- and free-choice blocks, paragraph 2; Figure 10A
claims.quote: Action information in free-choice blocks with higher rewards increased more slowly than that in fixed-choice blocks, and action information in free-choice blocks with lower rewards appeared later and was weaker. There were significant differences in action information between fixed-choice blocks and free-choice blocks in trial Phase 3 (during the 500 ms before cue presentation) and trial Phase 4 (during the 500 ms before center hole exit) (p = 0.00047 and p = 0.00037, respectively, paired-Mann–Whitney U test)
claims.criterion: Per-PAN action MI as in fig9-temporal-order-all-blocks. Windows from the text, the 500 ms windows ending at the end of Phase 3 and of Phase 4 ("500 ms before cue presentation" is read as the 500 ms before cue offset, the end of Phase 3, since the window must lie in Phase 3; the 500 ms before cue onset is shown as a variant). Fixed is SF and DF, free is FH and FL; readings of how they are combined are (a) the per-neuron mean of the two block types, (b) trials pooled. "Paired-Mann-Whitney U test" is read as (a) the Wilcoxon signed-rank test over neurons, (b) the Mann-Whitney U test unpaired. Reproduced when, under every reading, fixed exceeds free with p < 0.05 in both windows and the DLS region average crosses threshold first in SF or DF, then FH, then FL, with FL's peak in Phases 3 and 4 the lowest of the four.

claims.statement: In DMS too, action information is significantly stronger in fixed-choice than in free-choice blocks in Phases 3 and 4, against the paper's prediction.
claims.source: Results, Action-command information in fixed- and free-choice blocks, paragraph 2; Figure 10B
claims.quote: In DMS, action information was stronger in single and double fixed-choice blocks than in free-choice blocks (Fig. 10B), similar to that in DLS, with significant differences in trial Phases 3 and 4 (p = 0.040 for Phase 3, p = 0.0029 for Phase 4, paired-Mann–Whitney U test)
claims.criterion: As fig10a-dls-fixed-above-free, for DMS, without the order of crossings. Reproduced when, under every reading, fixed exceeds free with p < 0.05 in both windows.

claims.statement: In VS, action information shows a transient peak during cue presentation only in single fixed-choice blocks and stays low until action execution, with no significant difference between fixed- and free-choice blocks in Phases 3 and 4.
claims.source: Results, Action-command information in fixed- and free-choice blocks, paragraph 2; Figure 10C
claims.quote: Action information in VS had a transient peak during cue presentation only in single, fixed-choice blocks and remained low until the onset of action execution (Fig. 10C) with no significant differences between fixed- and free-choice blocks in trial Phases 3 and 4 (p = 0.23 and p = 0.28, respectively, paired-Mann–Whitney U test)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test as in fig10a-dls-fixed-above-free (each of its readings of the test, as the test itself is ambiguous), at p < 0.05. Reproduced when, under every reading, neither window gives p < 0.05; not reproduced when, under every reading, either does; blocked when the readings disagree. The effect sizes are reported. The SF peak is reported, as whether the SF region average crosses threshold in Phase 3 while DF, FH and FL do not.

claims.statement: In free-choice blocks, DLS action information is stronger in stay trials than in switch trials in Phase 3, while DMS shows no difference between stay and switch trials.
claims.source: Results, Action-command information in fixed- and free-choice blocks, paragraph 3; Figure 10D and 10E
claims.quote: In DLS, action information was stronger in stay trials than in switch trials in trial Phase 3 (during the 500 ms before cue presentation) (p = 0.019, Mann–Whitney U test). In DMS, however, we could not find any difference in the action-command signal between switch and stay trials
claims.criterion: Free-choice trials split by whether the action repeats the previous trial's (stay) or not (switch). The trials used are not stated; the Fig. 9 legend and the Results for Fig. 9 say the last 20 trials of each block (the Fig. 10 legend does not), so readings are (a) the last 20 trials of each free-choice block, (b) all free-choice trials. Per-PAN action MI in the Phase 3 window of fig10a-dls-fixed-above-free (O1); two-sided Mann-Whitney U test. Reproduced when, under every reading, DLS stay exceeds switch with p < 0.05 and, for DMS (a claim of absence on the same test), neither the Phase 3 nor the Phase 4 window gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Across 388 imaging sessions, the number of ROIs per session ranged from 21 to 286 (95 plus or minus 56, mean and s.d.), and was stable over time.
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 1d
claims.quote: Across a total of 388 sessions, the number of ROIs per session ranged from 21 to 286 (95 ± 56 (mean ± s.d.)) and was stable over time
claims.criterion: ROIs are the CNMF_E segments of each imaging session (Methods, Miniscope recordings), counted per session over all imaging sessions of mice 1 to 10. The session count holds when 388 sessions are found; the paper does not say whether sessions of mice 6 to 10 are included, so the readings are (a) all imaging sessions and (b) mice 1 to 5 only. "Stable over time" has no test in the paper; it is judged per mouse within the Fig. 1 protocol as no monotonic trend, read as a Spearman correlation of ROI count with session number that is not significant at p < 0.05 in a majority of mice, and the correlations are shown.

claims.statement: In the four-week circular protocol, the median proportion of ROIs detected as HD cells per animal was 0.2, 0.7, 0.4, 0.7 and 0.2, with 72, 42, 197, 48 and 102 ROIs per session on average, over 19, 20, 19, 19 and 20 recordings.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 1e legend
claims.quote: Median proportion ± s.d. per animal = 0.2 ± 0.03, 0.7 ± 0.04, 0.4 ± 0.05, 0.7 ± 0.05, 0.2 ± 0.04. n = 19, 20, 19, 19, 20 recordings per animal, with a respective mean ± s.d. of ROIs detected 72 ± 16, 42 ± 5, 197 ± 18, 48 ± 12, 102 ± 25
claims.criterion: The ROI means use the s.d. given per animal as tolerance; the recording counts must match exactly. The HD cell is as in the opening comment, per session (split-half correlation at least 0.4 and session HDI at least 0.11 among ROIs whose across-session HDI exceeds 0.1). The paper does not say whether the CellReg and six-session conditions apply to this proportion; readings (a) with them and (b) without. Reproduced when, under one reading and one smoothing reading, at least four of the five proportions are within tolerance.

claims.statement: An Isomap projection of the HD cell population activity forms a ring, reflecting the circular representation of head direction.
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 1h
claims.quote: Low-dimensional projection of HD cell population activity using Isomap (Methods), a technique for... high-dimensional data by preserving its geometric structure, revealed a ring topology
claims.criterion: Method from the Methods (Dimensionality reduction). HD cells with split-half correlation above 0.8 and HDI above 0.1 in the session; dF/F smoothed with a Gaussian of sigma 133 ms, normalized (OPEN, readings z-score and division by the maximum), averaged in 0.25 s bins; bins where the mean normalized activity is below 0.1 dropped; Isomap with 50 neighbours to two dimensions. The paper judges the ring by eye with head direction as colour. The criterion is read from Extended Data Fig. 7d, which plots the Isomap angle against head direction, as a circular-circular correlation between the angle of each point around the embedding's centroid and the head direction, significant at p < 0.05 in an example session of each of the five mice. Reproduced when this holds for all five; partially reproduced for three or four. This test and its counts are the reader's, not the paper's, and are recorded as a deviation.

claims.statement: In an example mouse, the population change in preferred direction relative to the last session was concentrated around 0 degrees (V-test, v = 17.06, P < 0.001, 18 sessions, median absolute deviation 5.0 degrees).
claims.source: Fig. 1f legend; Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 3
claims.quote: Population average of across-session angular difference in preferred direction, relative to the last session for one example mouse (V-test, not different from 0°, v = 17.06, two-tailed P < 0.001, n = 18 sessions, median absolute deviation from 0° = 5.0°)
claims.criterion: Per session, the change in preferred direction relative to the last session of the circular protocol (opening comment). The example mouse is not named in Fig. 1. Readings are (a) animal 4, which Extended Data Fig. 1g names as the animal of Fig. 1, and (b) any mouse with 18 compared sessions. Reproduced when, under one reading, V and the median absolute deviation are within tolerance and the V-test p is below 0.001.

claims.statement: Across all five mice, the population change in preferred direction relative to the last session was concentrated around 0 degrees (V-test, v = 75.21, P < 0.001, 84 sessions), with per-mouse means of 15.4, 2.1, -5.5, -7.8 and -6.9 degrees.
claims.source: Fig. 1g legend
claims.quote: Distribution of population-wise angular difference relative to the last session for all five mice (V-test, not different from 0°, v = 75.21, two-tailed P < 0.001, n = 84 sessions). Per mouse... 15.4 ± 24.7°, 2.1 ± 18.7°, −5.5 ± 15.2°, −7.8 ± 23.6°, −6.9 ± 41.5° (mean ± s.d.)
claims.criterion: As fig1f-example-stable, pooled over the five mice. The per-mouse means use the per-mouse s.d. as tolerance. Reproduced when the pooled V is within tolerance with p below 0.001 and at least four per-mouse means are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The V statistic of the change in preferred direction relative to the last session was 14.1, 17.1, 17.3, 14.6 and 12.2 per animal, against shuffle medians of 3.0, 3.2, 5.7, 4.8 and 2.0, and 75.2 pooled against a shuffle median of 18.6; each animal's distribution was concentrated around 0 degrees (P < 0.001).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4a,b legends
claims.quote: V statistic per animal = 14.1, 17.1, 17.3, 14.6, 12.2. Median of V statistic shuffles per animal = 3.0, 3.2, 5.7, 4.8, 2.0. Left... V-test statistic for pooled animals (75.2) versus the distribution of V statistic for within-day shuffled cell identity (median = 18.6)
claims.criterion: Shuffle of HD cell identity within a day, 1,000 times (Methods, Orientation remapping). The per-animal V of Extended Data Fig. 4b and the Fig. 1f value (17.06) do not agree for animal 4 (14.6); this is recorded, not resolved. Reproduced when at least four of the five per-animal V are within tolerance and each exceeds its shuffle median.

claims.statement: The change in preferred direction relative to the previous session was also concentrated around 0 degrees across the five animals (V-test, P < 0.001, 75 sessions; pooled V 69.9 against a shuffle median of 21.9).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4c,d legends
claims.quote: Distribution of population- wise angular difference relative to the previous session for all five animals (V-test, not different from 0°, two-tailed p < 0.001, n = 75 sessions)
claims.criterion: As edf4ab-vtest-per-animal, with each session compared to the previous session. Reproduced when the pooled V is within tolerance with p below 0.001 and at least four of the five per-animal V are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The Jaccard index of HD cell detection between sessions of the circular protocol remained high regardless of the delay between sessions.
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 2a,b
claims.quote: The Jaccard index remained high regardless of... the delay between sessions, suggesting that most ROIs were... registered and continued to exhibit activity across time
claims.criterion: Method from the Methods (Jaccard score). Per mouse and pair of sessions, the Jaccard index of the binary vectors of presence (1) or absence (0) of HD tuning in each ROI, over the ROIs registered across the session pairs; the median over all session pairs with the same interval. OPEN, which ROIs count as registered across "all relevant session pairs", readings (a) ROIs registered in both sessions of the pair and (b) ROIs registered in every session of the protocol. The paper gives no test or level for "high". Reproduced when, in at least four of five mice, the median index at the longest interval is at least 80% of that at an interval of one day; this threshold is the reader's and is recorded as a deviation. The Spearman correlation of the median index with interval is shown.

claims.statement: The shift in preferred direction between the first and last recording was not significantly related to the displacement of the ROI centroid in the field of view (p = 0.290) or to the CellReg score (p = 0.344), while centroid displacement was related to CellReg score (p = 0.004).
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 2c-e
claims.quote: the change in preferred direction was not significantly correlated with the quality of cell registration nor the drift of the ROI in the Miniscope field of view
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the two-sided Wald test of the slope of a linear regression (as scipy.stats.linregress gives it) at 0.05 Bonferroni-corrected over the tests of the figure. Per HD cell registered in the first and last recording of the circular protocol, the shift in preferred direction (cross-correlation, opening comment), the centroid displacement and the CellReg score. OPEN, readings for which cells give n = 72, (a) pooled over the five mice and (b) the Fig. 1 example mouse; and for the shift, (i) signed and (ii) absolute. Reproduced when the two absence tests are not significant and the displacement against score test is significant; the slopes are shown.

claims.statement: The absolute change in preferred direction grew slowly with the days between recordings, at a drift rate of 7.1 plus or minus 4.4 degrees per week across mice.
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 3; Fig. 1h
claims.quote: we computed the absolute change in preferred direction as a function of days passed between recordings and observed... a slow drift rate (7.1 ± 4.4° per week)
claims.criterion: Per pair of sessions of the circular protocol, the absolute change in preferred direction; OPEN, readings for the value (a) the absolute value of the session-level circular mean over cells and (b) the median over cells of each cell's absolute change. Drift rate per mouse by the readings of the opening comment, averaged over the five mice. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance and positive under one combination of readings.

claims.statement: The drift in preferred direction was not diffusive (not a random walk) but fluctuated around a fixed direction, as shown by the cumulative variance of orientation across days.
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 4e,f
claims.quote: Analysis of the cumulative variance of orientation across days suggested that this drift, although modest, was not diffusive (that is, not a random walk) but instead... around a fixed direction
claims.criterion: Extended Data Fig. 4e plots the mean variance of the absolute change in preferred direction against the number of recordings included, from the first to the last day. The paper gives no test. A random walk predicts a variance growing in proportion to the number of recordings. OPEN, the variance is read (a) as that of the session-level changes relative to the last day over the first k recordings and (b) relative to the first day. Reproduced when, under the reading run, the variance at the full number of recordings is less than half the value a line through the origin fitted to the first five points predicts, in at least four of five mice. This threshold is the reader's and is recorded as a deviation.

claims.statement: The absolute change in overall preferred direction with respect to the last day was smaller than for shuffled cell identities in every animal (median 15.9, 5.1, 7.9, 26.3 and 24.0 degrees; one-tailed Wilcoxon, p from 3.8e-6 to 1.5e-4).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 4f legend
claims.quote: Absolute change in overall preferred direction, per session, with respect to the last day of the experiment in Fig. 1. Median absolute change per animal in degrees... 15.9, 5.1, 7.9, 26.3, 24.0
claims.criterion: Per session the absolute change against the same session's shuffled-identity value. OPEN, the shuffle value per session is read as (a) the median and (b) the mean over 1,000 shuffles. Reproduced when every animal's one-tailed Wilcoxon is below 0.05 and at least three medians are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The change in pairwise angular offset across all registered HD cell pairs was strongly biased towards 0, with per-animal medians of 12, 9, 12, 24 and 12 degrees against shuffle medians of 51 to 54 degrees (p < 0.001 per animal, 25,901 pairs).
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 4g
claims.quote: The change in pairwise angular offset across all registered cell pairs (... of interleaving days) was strongly biased towards 0 (Extended Data Fig. 4g), suggesting highly coherent population dynamics
claims.criterion: Method from the Methods (Change in the angular offset) over all session pairs of the circular protocol. The per-animal tolerances are the s.d. that Extended Data Fig. 4g gives with each median. Reproduced when every animal's median is below all 1,000 shuffled medians and at least four medians are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The change in pairwise angular offset drifted more slowly (4.1 plus or minus 4.8 degrees per week) than single cell tuning, though not significantly so.
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 4; Fig. 1i
claims.quote: the change in pairwise angular offset drifted more slowly (4.1 ± 4.8° per week), yet this was not significantly different from single cell tuning drift rate
claims.criterion: Per pair of sessions, the median over cell pairs of the absolute change in offset (Fig. 1i axis, "Median delta angular offset"); drift rate per mouse by the readings of the opening comment. The test against the fig1h-drift-rate values is not named. A claim of absence; OPEN, readings (a) two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank and (b) paired t-test across the five mice, at 0.05 (with five mice, reading (a) cannot reach p below 0.0625). Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance and neither test is significant; not reproduced when either is. Effect size shown.

claims.statement: Decoders of head direction trained on one session and tested on another decoded significantly better than chance for nearly the whole four weeks of the experiment.
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 5; Fig. 1j,k
claims.quote: we trained and tested non-linear decoders (extreme gradient-boosted trees (Methods)) on every recording session pair and observed statistically significant decoding for nearly the entire duration of the experiment
claims.criterion: Decoder as in the opening comment, on every ordered pair of sessions of the circular protocol, error per pair as the median over time bins, chance from time-reversed head direction in the test session (both median and mean error are run, as the Methods and legend differ). The paper does not name its test. OPEN, readings (a) per day difference, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank of data against chance over all session pairs of all mice, and (b) per day difference, one-sided Wilcoxon across the five mice of per-mouse means. Reproduced when, under one reading, the error is below chance at p < 0.05 for every day difference up to 20 days except at most one, read as "nearly the entire duration"; partially reproduced when that holds up to 10 days.

claims.statement: The population vector coherence decayed slowly over the course of the recording.
claims.source: Results, The tuning of HD cells is stable over time, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 4h-j
claims.quote: This is in line with a slow decay in the population vector coherence over the course of the recording
claims.criterion: Population vector correlation between two sessions with activity in 12 head-direction bins (Extended Data Fig. 4h). OPEN, readings (a) the mean over bins of the correlation across cells of the two sessions' population vectors at the same head-direction bin and (b) the correlation of the two flattened cell by bin matrices. Reproduced when the correlation decreases with the days between sessions (negative Spearman correlation, p < 0.05, in at least four of five mice) and its mean at the longest day difference stays above 0.

claims.statement: Across the four environments, HD cells preserved their pairwise angular offsets, with per-animal median changes of 24, 12, 18, 29 and 12 degrees against shuffle medians of 54 to 57 degrees, and a drift rate of 1.9 plus or minus 1.02 degrees per week.
claims.source: Results, Internal organization across time and environments, paragraph 1; Fig. 2e; Extended Data Fig. 6b
claims.quote: We observed the same tendency of preserved pairwise angular difference in preferred directions across... all sessions and mice (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 6)
claims.criterion: Over all session pairs of the 40-session multi-environment protocol. The per-animal tolerances are the s.d. that Extended Data Fig. 6b gives with each median. The Methods exclude mouse 2 from this analysis while Extended Data Fig. 6b lists five values; readings (a) mouse 2 excluded, (b) mouse 2 included, (c) mouse 2 with only pairs within one Miniscope epoch. Reproduced when, under one reading, every included animal's median is below all 1,000 shuffled medians and the mean drift rate (opening comment readings) is within tolerance.

claims.statement: The tuning of HD cells was stable within each environment, with changes in preferred direction relative to the last day concentrated around 0 degrees in all four, and no difference between environments (repeated-measures ANOVA, F = 0.44, P = 0.73).
claims.source: Results, Internal organization across time and environments, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 5c
claims.quote: The tuning of HD cells was stable within each environment for all mice
claims.criterion: Per environment, the change in preferred direction of each session relative to the last session of that environment (for mouse 2 in the square, the next-to-last day, as the legend says). The ANOVA is a claim of absence judged on a repeated-measures ANOVA over environments with mice as subjects (n = 5, giving 3 and 12 degrees of freedom) at 0.05; the per mouse and environment value is OPEN, readings (a) mean absolute change and (b) median absolute change. Reproduced when all four V-tests are significant, at least three V are within tolerance and the ANOVA is not significant.

claims.statement: Electrophysiological recordings confirmed that pairwise angular offsets of HD cells are preserved across environments, with per-animal median changes of 18, 12, 27 and 15 degrees against shuffle medians of 54 degrees (p < 0.001).
claims.source: Results, Internal organization across time and environments, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 7e
claims.quote: To confirm that this long-tailed distribution is not specific to the imaging... we confirmed these results with electrophysiological recordings
claims.criterion: HD cells with firing rate above 1 Hz and HDI above 0.3; spike-count tuning curves (bins and smoothing OPEN, the imaging values as the reading); offsets compared across the three environment pairs of the day. Tolerances are the s.d. given with each median. Reproduced when every animal's median is below all 1,000 shuffled medians.

claims.statement: Electrophysiologically recorded HD cells have broader waveforms than non-HD cells (median trough-to-peak 0.54 against 0.295 ms, half-peak width 0.21 against 0.165 ms).
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 7g legend
claims.quote: Note HD cells tend to have broader waveforms, consistent with pyramidal cells. Median HD trough-to-peak = 0.54 ms, median HD half-peak width = 0.21 ms, versus 0.295 and 0.165 respectively for non-HD cells; n = 254 cells
claims.criterion: Mean waveform per unit on its largest channel; trough-to-peak from trough to the following maximum, half-peak width the width at half the trough amplitude. These definitions are not in the paper and are OPEN; they are the standard ones. Reproduced when at least three of the four medians are within tolerance and HD medians exceed non-HD medians for both.

claims.statement: For recordings 7 days apart, decoders trained and tested in the same environment tended to be better than across environments, and the change in pairwise offset tended to be smaller, neither significantly (p = 0.063 for both).
claims.source: Results, Environmental modulation of the HD cell population, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 8b,c
claims.quote: Decoders of head direction of mice trained and tested in the same environment one week apart showed a tendency for better (yet non-significant) accuracy than decoders trained across environments with the same delay between sessions
claims.criterion: Pairs of sessions 7 days apart in the multi-environment protocol, "single" when both are in one environment and "mixed" otherwise; per mouse the mean over pairs. The decoder measure is the variance of the error between predicted and actual direction (OPEN, readings the circular variance and the linear variance of the signed circular error in radians). The tendency claim is reproduced when every mouse is lower for single than mixed (W = 0) under one reading and the means are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Classifiers of environment identity trained on pairwise correlations of HD cell tuning curves were more accurate than shuffles (proportion correct 0.7 against 0.3; one-sided Wilcoxon, P = 0.031, W = 15).
claims.source: Results, Environmental modulation of the HD cell population, paragraph 1; Fig. 2f,g
claims.quote: These classifiers showed higher accuracy than controls (Fig. 2f,g)... the idea that the HD signal in the PoSub is environment specific
claims.criterion: Method as in the opening comment. The random half split is OPEN; the criterion runs 100 random splits per mouse and uses the mean proportion correct, and also a single split with a fixed seed, as readings. Reproduced when, under one reading, the one-sided Wilcoxon of data against shuffle across the five mice has p below 0.05 and the means are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The remapping of the HD system between the three environments of one room seemed random across mice (Rayleigh test, P = 0.36 circular to square, 0.61 square to radial maze, 0.032 radial maze to circular).
claims.source: Results, Environmental modulation of the HD cell population, paragraph 2; Fig. 2h,i
claims.quote: Notably, this remapping seemed random across mice, although more data would be required to support a true random remapping
claims.criterion: Average remapping per mouse and environment pair as in the opening comment, over all session pairs of the two environments, in room coordinates; mouse 2 included (Methods, Inclusion and exclusion criteria). Rayleigh's test over the five mice. Reproduced when the first two tests are not significant at 0.05 and the third is, matching the paper, with z within tolerance; partially reproduced when the first two are not significant but the third pattern differs.

claims.statement: While the internal structure of the HD system was largely kept across environments, its absolute orientation was specific to each environment, the HD cells of a mouse shifting together (coherent remapping) compared with shuffled cell identities.
claims.source: Results, Environmental modulation of the HD cell population, paragraph 2; Fig. 2c,d,h,i
claims.quote: Whereas the internal structure of the HD system was largely preserved across environments, with only minor... its absolute orientation was specific to each environment
claims.criterion: Per mouse and pair of environments, the mean vector length over HD cells of the shift in preferred direction, for each pair of recordings of the two environments (Methods, Orientation remapping), compared with 1,000 shuffles of cell identity within a day. The paper gives no threshold; the 95th percentile of the shuffle distribution, the bound Fig. 3e draws for its controls, is used. Per mouse and environment pair, coherent when the median over recording pairs of the mean vector length exceeds the median over recording pairs of the shuffle 95th percentile. The environment pairs are the three of Fig. 2i (circular to square, square to radial maze, radial maze to circular), the environments of one room whose alignment the paper measures in room coordinates; the open field, in another room, is shown as a variant. Reproduced when this holds for at least 80% of the mouse and environment pairs (mouse 2 included, as for remapping in the Methods), and the average remapping of at least one environment pair differs from 0 by more than 30 degrees in at least three mice, read as an orientation specific to each environment. The 80% and 30 degree thresholds are the reader's, not the paper's, and are recorded as a deviation.

claims.statement: After a delay without visits, the orientation of the HD system in each environment was retained, drifting slowly with the delay; it was concentrated around 0 degrees for delays under 1, 2 and 4 weeks (V-test, P = 0.002, 0.02, 0.03) but not at 6 weeks (P = 0.191), with mean absolute changes of 3.6, 23.9, 39.6 and 70.0 degrees.
claims.source: Results, HD system forms long-term memories of orientation, paragraph 1; Fig. 3d
claims.quote: the average alignment of the HD system to external environments across mice drifted gradually, albeit slowly, as the interval between sessions increased, becoming significantly... from 0° only at the 6-week delay
claims.criterion: Per mouse (mice 1 to 4; mouse 5 excluded, Methods) and environment, the remapping between the last visit of the two-week protocol and the probe trial (Methods, Orientation remapping), HD cells with CellReg score above 0.6 detected in at least two sessions. The delays are those of the environment order, open field under 1 week, radial maze 2 weeks, square 4 weeks, circular 6 weeks (OPEN, the probe order is not given; the delays are taken from the session dates). Reproduced when the V-tests are significant at 0.05 for the first three delays and not at 6 weeks, and the mean absolute change increases with delay; partially reproduced when the 6-week test is not significant but one earlier delay also fails.

claims.statement: The mean vector length of the remapping angles across mice decreased with delay (0.998, 0.79, 0.79 and 0.536 for under 1, 2, 4 and 6 weeks), compared with shuffled HD cell identities.
claims.source: Fig. 3d (the mvl values printed in the panel) and Fig. 3e
claims.quote: Mean vector length of animal remapping angles (that is, probe versus last visit of each environment, for n = 4 mice) as a function of delay between visits compared to controls (shuffled HD cell identity)
claims.criterion: Mean vector length of the four mice's remapping angles at each delay, from fig3de-probe-memory. Reproduced when at least three of the four values are within tolerance and the 6-week value is the lowest.

claims.statement: The absolute change in individual preferred directions drifted with delay at 10.8 plus or minus 0.1 degrees per week, while the pairwise angular offsets stayed coherent, drifting at 2.5 plus or minus 0.1 degrees per week.
claims.source: Results, HD system forms long-term memories of orientation, paragraph 1; Fig. 3f,g
claims.quote: We further tested this drift by assessing the absolute changes in individual neuronal preferred directions and observed a similar drift from the original direction (Fig. 3f). Of note, the population structure maintained its coherence across these recordings
claims.criterion: The legend calls its spread (0.1, for both rates) the s.d. over mice; a spread this small for four mice is doubtful, so 10% of the value is used as tolerance, and whether the rates fall within 0.1 of the values is also shown. Values against delay in weeks, drift rate per mouse by the readings of the opening comment, mean over mice 1 to 4. The Methods exclude mouse 2 from the 6-week delay "of pairwise angular offset (Fig. 3f)"; readings (a) mouse 2 excluded at 6 weeks from the pairwise offset (Fig. 3g) and (b) from the preferred direction (Fig. 3f). Reproduced when both rates are within tolerance under one combination of readings; partially reproduced when the preferred-direction rate exceeds the pairwise-offset rate but a value is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: After four further weeks of visits to the four environments in random order, the system showed reduced retention of the original preferred direction, though changes relative to week 1 stayed centred on 0 degrees (V = 11.3, 10.1, 10.8), and pairwise offsets drifted at a mean of 1.6 degrees per week.
claims.source: Results, HD system forms long-term memories of orientation, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 9b,d
claims.quote: this orientation memory may be affected by cognitive load as after four additional weeks of extensive experience with the different... the systems showed reduced retention of the original preferred direction
claims.criterion: V-tests against 0 degrees over 20, 20 and 18 sessions (weeks 2, 3 and 4). The legend gives no p and says only that the V-tests are significant; p below 0.05 is the reading. "Reduced retention" has no test in the paper. OPEN, it is read as the mean over mice of the absolute change in preferred direction relative to week 1 at week 4 (Extended Data Fig. 9e) being larger than the mean absolute change at the 4-week probe delay of fig3de-probe-memory. Reproduced when the V statistics and drift rate are within tolerance and that comparison holds.

claims.statement: After a single visit, the orientation of the HD cell population was retained four weeks later as well as with weekly visits; the change in preferred direction from first to last session was smaller than shuffles in both groups (one-sided Wilcoxon, P = 0.031) and did not differ between groups (P = 0.438; weekly 12.4, single 6.6 degrees).
claims.source: Results, Memory from a single visit is stable over weeks, paragraph 1; Fig. 4d
claims.quote: We observed a highly maintained absolute orientation of the HD cell... for both environments
claims.criterion: Mice 6 to 10; per mouse and environment, the absolute change in preferred direction between the first and the last session in that environment, HD cells detected in at least two sessions with CellReg score above 0.8 (Methods; the 0.6 score is allowed for Fig. 3 only); shuffle of cell identity within a day, 1,000 times (Methods, Orientation remapping). OPEN, the shuffle value per mouse, readings (a) the median and (b) the mean over the 1,000 shuffles.
