claims.statement: The frequency of spontaneous EPSCs is lower in VENs than in neighbouring PCs.
claims.source: Results, Altered connectivity profile of deep-layer AIC neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 5b
claims.quote: The frequencies of both excitatory and inhibitory events were significantly lower in VENs than in PCs (Fig. 5b )
claims.criterion: Per cell, sEPSCs are detected in the recording held at -70 mV (inward events), and the cell's frequency is the number of events over the duration analysed, in Hz (Methods, "Recordings of synaptic events were assessed for frequency (Hz)"; the code's tables give one frequency per cell as events over duration). The Methods fix the event threshold at "the maximus root mean squared noise level (5 pA)" and give no other detection parameter (miniAnalysis settings such as baseline window or area threshold are not given, and the code holds no detection step); a standard peak detector on the baseline-subtracted trace is used, and the threshold has two readings, (a) a fixed 5 pA amplitude and (b) the recording's own RMS noise level. The peak detector itself is a standard choice, not the paper's (miniAnalysis is not reproduced). The Methods say each trace was recorded for at least 5 min after the signal had stabilized (no shift beyond 4 s.d. of the baseline) and that at least 200 events were included for analysis, but not how long a stretch was analysed; the analysis uses the whole stable recording, and the code's 30 s per cell (its mIPSC table) is shown as a variant. Cell types are the dataset's labels; the paper's n is 8 VENs and 11 PCs (Fig. 5b legend), of which the code's 11 PCs are 10 distinct cells (one cell's two traces counted twice), so the PC group is read (a) as the paper's 11 entries and (b) as 10 distinct cells. Test, as in the legend and in Fig5ab_ana_sPSC.m, a two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test of VEN against PC per-cell frequencies, uncorrected, at p < 0.05 (conventional; the panel's p-value was not readable). Reproduced when, under every combination of the readings, the VEN median is below the PC median with p < 0.05; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree, with every result shown. Group medians and ranges are reported.

claims.statement: The frequency of spontaneous IPSCs is lower in VENs than in neighbouring PCs.

claims.criterion: As fig5b-sepsc-frequency, for sIPSCs, with n = 7 VENs and 8 PCs (Fig. 5b legend) and no duplicate reading. The Methods hold IPSCs at -60 mV with a CsCl internal (inward events); the code's metadata names the sIPSC recordings "+20mV", which would make the events outward. Events are detected in the direction implied by the holding potential the file records, and the notebook says which it is. Threshold readings (a) 5 pA and (b) the recording's RMS noise; whole stable recording, with the code's 30 s as a variant. Two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum, uncorrected, p < 0.05 (conventional). Reproduced when both readings give the VEN median below the PC median with p < 0.05; blocked as methods_underspecified when they disagree.

claims.statement: The frequency of miniature EPSCs (in tetrodotoxin) is lower in VENs than in neighbouring PCs.

claims.statement: In flight, after an initial period, hippocampal place cells on the Escher staircase showed normal, spatially specific firing, with spatial information per spike not different from the same rats' preflight cells.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "During the Neurolab Space Shuttle mission", last sentence; supported by the paragraphs beginning "Spatial firing patterns of 16 active place cells" and "The mean spatial-information content for all 7" and Figures 2a, 2c and 3a; also the standfirst
claims.quote: Nonetheless, place cells eventually demonstrated normal, spatially specific firing properties.
claims.criterion: The paper supports this finding by its three comparisons of spatial information per spike in flight with the same rat's preflight cells (main text, paragraphs beginning "Spatial firing patterns of 16 active place cells" and "The mean spatial-information content for all 7"), which are the claims this one depends on. Reproduced when all three are reproduced; partially reproduced when the two FD9 comparisons (rats 1 and 2, the sessions the word "eventually" points to) are reproduced and the FD4 comparison is not, or when no FD9 comparison is not reproduced and one or more of the three is partially reproduced; not reproduced when either FD9 comparison is not reproduced. When a dependency is blocked as methods_underspecified, so is this claim, unless the others already decide it.

claims.statement: For rat 2, the spatial information per spike of the 16 active cells recorded on the Escher staircase on flight day 9 (1.13 +/- 0.09 bits) did not differ significantly from that of its 19 active preflight cells (1.12 +/- 0.08 bits), by Mann-Whitney test.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "Spatial firing patterns of 16 active place cells", sentences 1 and 3; Figure 2a,b
claims.quote: An index of spatial tuning specificity ... did not significantly differ between cells recorded preflight and those recorded on FD9 (for active cells, defined as having a mean firing rate > 0.05 Hz on the track; mean information per spike ± s.e. preflight, 1.12 ± 0.08 bits, n = 19; FD9, 1.13 ± 0.09 bits, n = 16; not significant by Mann-Whitney)
claims.criterion: From the paper's text. Cells are the active cells of each session, mean firing rate above 0.05 Hz over the session on the track (main text), the FD9 cells from the Escher staircase session and the preflight cells from the rectangular track (Fig. 2b). The measure is Skaggs' information per spike (ref. 13), computed with off-track positions kept (Fig. 1 legend). The test is the paper's, a Mann-Whitney test of FD9 against preflight values; the level is not printed and is read as two-sided p < 0.05. Tolerances are the paper's standard errors, and 10% for the counts. Bin size, smoothing, minimum occupancy and which sessions are open; the readings M-a and M-b and S-a and S-b of the opening comment are each run. Answers of 2026-10-20, the paper gives none of these details. The paper compares one index computed the same way for both groups, so each comparison with preflight uses the same map reading on both sides; a reading that cannot be computed for one side is not run for that comparison, the outcome rests on the readings that can be run, and a test of M-b flight values against M-a preflight values is a variant, not judged. The paper names no preflight epoch (it does not mention ES or MC epochs), so under S-a each preflight epoch is a candidate session; under S-b each epoch of the recording day closest before launch is run on its own, the paper describing rat 2's preflight cells as recorded on one track, and neither epoch is preferred. A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Reproduced when, under every reading, the test does not find a difference and, under at least one reading, both means fall within tolerance; partially reproduced when the test finds no difference under every reading but no reading puts both means within tolerance; not reproduced when the test finds a difference under every reading; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree on the test. The difference of the means and the test's p-value are given under every reading.

claims.statement: For rat 1, the mean spatial information of its 21 active cells on flight day 9 (1.19 +/- 0.09 bits) did not differ significantly from its preflight cells (1.37 +/- 0.10 bits, n = 28).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "Spatial firing patterns of 16 active place cells", sentences 4 and 5; Figure 2c
claims.quote: We also determined the spatial tuning of 21 active cells from rat 1 on FD9 (Fig. 2c). ... did not significantly differ from that rat's preflight data (1.37 ± 0.10; n = 28).
claims.criterion: As for si-comparable-to-preflight, for rat 1. The sentence names no test; it is read as the Mann-Whitney test named for rat 2 in the sentence before, the only test the paper names. Units are not printed for these means; they are read as bits per spike, as for rat 2. The paper says "that rat's preflight data" and does not say these are active cells; the 0.05 Hz definition given for rat 2 is applied. The paper does not say on which track the preflight cells were recorded, so any preflight session is a candidate (S-a), and S-b takes the one closest before launch. The same readings are run and the same rule decides the outcome.

claims.statement: For rat 3, the mean spatial information of all 7 active place cells on flight day 4 (1.12 +/- 0.27 bits, session 2) was not different from its preflight cells (1.48 +/- 0.11 bits, n = 24).
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "The mean spatial-information content for all 7", sentence 1; Figure 3a
claims.quote: The mean spatial-information content for all 7 active place cells from rat 3 on the fourth day of flight (FD4) was 1.12 ± 0.27 bits (Fig. 3a), which was not different from the information content measured for this rat's place cells before the flight (1.48 ± 0.11 bits; n = 24).
claims.criterion: As for si-comparable-to-preflight, for rat 3. The FD4 cells are from the session of Fig. 3a, the second exposure to the staircase that day (the first was lost, Fig. 3 legend). The sentence names no test; it is read as the Mann-Whitney test named for rat 2, the only test the paper names. The paper says "this rat's place cells" for the preflight value; the 0.05 Hz definition of active cells given for rat 2 is applied. The paper does not say on which track the preflight cells were recorded, so any preflight session is a candidate (S-a), and S-b takes the one closest before launch. The same readings are run and the same rule decides the outcome.

claims.statement: For rat 3 on flight day 4, most of the 7 cells kept the same firing fields in a third session that followed the second immediately; the fourth cell lost its field, and a few other cells gained a field in session 3.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "The mean spatial-information content for all 7", sentence 2; Figure 3a,b and legend
claims.quote: Another recording session followed immediately, and most cells maintained the same firing fields in both sessions (Fig. 3b), demonstrating that the spatial tuning was stable across different exposures to the track.
claims.criterion: The cells are the 7 active cells of session 2 (si-rat3-fd4-vs-preflight), followed into session 3 on the same track. The paper judges "the same firing fields" from the maps of Fig. 3 and gives no measure, so the measure is open; "most" is read as at least 4 of the 7. Readings of keeping a field, each run on the maps of reading M-a and of M-b (opening comment) (a) the Pearson correlation of a cell's session 2 and session 3 rate maps, over bins visited in both, exceeds the 95th percentile of the correlations between different cells across the two sessions; (b) the bin of peak rate in session 3 lies in the session 2 field, taken as the bins with at least 20% of the session 2 peak rate (a common field definition, not the paper's). "Most" means more than half of the cells shown, the active cells of session 2 (answer of 2026-10-20); with the paper's 7 cells this is at least 4, and with another count of active cells it is more than half of that count, not a count of 4. Cells are paired across sessions as the same unit ("the same seven cells", Fig. 3 legend); the paper says nothing on how the deposited maps are tied to units, so a pairing through the unit whose spike-count map a deposited map best matches is allowed for M-a when each map is tied to one unit and no unit to two maps, and is reported with the match; otherwise M-a is not run for this claim. Reproduced when more than half of the cells keep their field under every reading; not reproduced when half or fewer do under every reading; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. Which cell lost its field, and the cells silent in session 2 that gained a field in session 3, are reported but not judged, as the figure's cell order is not given in the text.

claims.statement: Some cells had place fields only when the rat moved counterclockwise through a location, showing the direction selectivity seen on such tracks on Earth.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "The rats occasionally turned around on the track", sentences 1 and 2
claims.quote: Some cells demonstrated place fields when the rat was moving only counterclockwise through a single location, thus demonstrating the direction selectivity that is seen on such tracks under normal terrestrial conditions
claims.criterion: The paper names no session, cells or measure. Sessions are the in-flight Escher staircase sessions with position (FD4 and FD9), active cells as in si-comparable-to-preflight. Direction of travel is open; it is read as the sign of the rat's movement along the track's circuit, from successive positions, clockwise being the trained direction (main text). For each cell and position bin of the maps of reading M-b, rates are computed separately for clockwise and counterclockwise samples. A cell has a counterclockwise-only field when, at some bin with counterclockwise occupancy, its counterclockwise rate is at least 1 Hz and its clockwise spike count there is lower than expected from the counterclockwise rate by a one-sided Poisson test at p < 0.05 (the thresholds are standard choices, not the paper's). "Some cells" is read as at least two cells over all sessions. Reproduced when at least two cells have such a field; partially reproduced when one does; not reproduced when none does. The paper gives no method, no time base by direction and no track layout (answer of 2026-10-20); it allows no reading without time spent per bin in each direction and the direction of travel, so when the data lack these the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Hippocampal EEG showed normal theta rhythm during active locomotion, in all rats on flight days 4 and 9.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "The rats occasionally turned around on the track", sentences 3 and 4
claims.quote: Hippocampal EEG activity was also ... recorded during baseline and behavioral sessions in all rats on FD4 and FD9. Although the small number of subjects precluded a statistical analysis, they showed normal theta rhythm during active locomotion
claims.criterion: Needs the hippocampal EEG of the FD4 and FD9 behavioral sessions. The paper reports no statistical analysis and no measure of "normal". Read as a peak in the EEG power spectrum within the theta band during locomotion that is absent or smaller during immobility. Locomotion is read as speed above the session median and the band as 6 to 10 Hz; both are standard choices, not given in the paper. Reproduced when every rat and flight day with EEG shows this; partially reproduced when some do; not reproduced when none does.

claims.statement: Hippocampal EEG showed normal sharp waves and ripples during quiet inactivity in the sleeping pouch, on both flight days.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "The rats occasionally turned around on the track", sentence 4
claims.quote: they showed normal theta rhythm during active locomotion and normal sharp waves and ripples15 during quiet inactivity in the sleeping pouch on both flight days.
claims.criterion: Needs the hippocampal EEG of the sleeping pouch baseline sessions on FD4 and FD9. The paper reports no statistical analysis and no detection method; it cites Buzsaki 1986 (ref. 15) for the events. Read as ripple events in the 100 to 250 Hz band, detected where the band envelope exceeds its mean by 3 standard deviations during immobility, coinciding with a large negative sharp wave in the filtered 0.5 to 30 Hz signal. The band, the threshold and the sharp wave filter are standard choices, not given in the paper or by ref. 15 as cited. Reproduced when every rat and flight day with pouch EEG shows such events; partially reproduced when some do; not reproduced when none does.

claims.statement: On the first experience of the Escher staircase on flight day 4, place cells of rats 1 and 2 showed abnormal patterns of spatial selectivity, which differed between the two rats.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "It is interesting to note", sentence 1 (given as unpublished observations)
claims.quote: on the first experience on the Escher staircase on FD4, firing of place cells showed abnormal patterns of spatial selectivity that differed between rats 1 and 2
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure or test for "abnormal"; its only measure of normal spatial selectivity is spatial information per spike compared with the same rat's preflight cells by Mann-Whitney. Read so (one reading for the comparison, with the map and session readings of the opening comment) abnormal is a spatial information of active cells on FD4 significantly lower than preflight for that rat (two-sided p < 0.05), in each of rats 1 and 2. As in si-comparable-to-preflight (answers of 2026-10-20), both sides of a comparison use the same map reading, and each preflight epoch is a candidate session. Reproduced when this holds for both rats under every reading; partially reproduced when it holds for one rat; not reproduced when it holds for neither; blocked as methods_underspecified when readings disagree. That the patterns differed between the rats has no measure in the paper and is reported, not judged.

claims.statement: Hippocampal cells formed distinct, reliable representations of position on the three orthogonal surfaces of the Escher staircase in microgravity.
claims.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "It is interesting to note", sentence 2; also the standfirst
claims.quote: Thus hippocampal cells can form unique, reliable representations of position on three orthogonal surfaces in microgravity
claims.criterion: The paper reports no analysis per surface; the finding rests on the spatial information and stability results. Read as (i) flight-spatial-code and fig3-stability-across-sessions reproduced, and (ii) in each FD9 session (rats 1 and 2), the peak-rate bins of the active cells, on maps of readings M-a and M-b, fall on each of the track's three surfaces (at least one cell per surface), the surfaces drawn from the track outline in the position frame. Reproduced when both hold under every reading; not reproduced when (i) fails, that is when either dependency is not reproduced; partially reproduced otherwise (a dependency partially reproduced, or (ii) failing for a rat or a reading). Whether the code is one three-dimensional map or separate two-dimensional maps is left open by the paper and is not judged.

claims.statement: After a block transition, mice transiently increase their probability of switching ports, which brings them to the new high-reward-probability port.
claims.source: Results, Adaptive switching in decision-making, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 1b,c
claims.quote: After successive unrewarded trials resulting from reversals of the reward probability at block transitions, the mice transiently increase their probability of switching ports between trials
claims.criterion: From the behaviour code (block_transition_stats.ipynb), P(switch) and P(high port) by trial position from the block transition, per mouse, over the n = 8 mice of Extended Data Fig. 1. Reproduced when, in the mean over mice (the panels show mean ± s.e.m.), P(switch) over the first 10 trials after the transition exceeds the mean over the 10 trials before it, P(switch) returns towards the pre-transition level later in the block, and P(high port) rises after the transition (the exponential time constant tau_highport, fitted over block positions 0 to 30 as in the code, is positive). The per-mouse values are reported. The 10-trial span is a standard choice for a plotting range; the paper does not fix it.

claims.statement: The three-parameter RFLR model (alpha, beta, tau) predicts the switching dynamics at block transitions and the conditional switch probabilities given the past two trials.
claims.source: Results, Adaptive switching in decision-making, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 1f-j
claims.quote: the RFLR model accurately predicts the switching dynamics at block transitions as well as the probability of switching on the current trial, which depends on the choice and reward history of previous trials
claims.criterion: RFLR fitted by maximum likelihood with stochastic gradient descent (Supplementary Methods, Behavior performance analysis; bandit_models.py). The paper does not say how train and test sessions are split; the readings are (a) fit and evaluate on held-out sessions per mouse, (b) on all sessions pooled. Reproduced when, under both, the model's conditional switch probabilities for the two-trial histories of Extended Data Fig. 1j fall within the binomial standard error bars of the mice's for most histories, and the predicted P(switch) and P(high port) around block transitions follow the observed curves (correlation above 0.9 across block positions; a standard threshold for "accurately", named as such).

claims.statement: After side-port entry, unrewarded trials show a lower mean DA and a larger delta-Ach than rewarded trials, in DA (13 mice) and Ach (14 mice) recordings.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA are dynamically regulated, paragraph 2; Fig. 1d,e
claims.quote: Reward outcome greatly alters DA and Ach transients, with unrewarded trials resulting in a robust decrease in mean DA and a consistent increase in ∆Ach (Fig. 1e )
claims.criterion: Shared method in the header (signal, windows W1 and W2, per-trial measures, T1 per mouse, T2 across mice), rewarded against unrewarded trials, post window, as in aa_processStats_final_Fig1_AllDA.m and _Fig1_Ach_Words.m. Reproduced when, under each window reading, mean DA is lower and delta-Ach higher in unrewarded trials in more than half of the mice with T1 p < 0.05. "Robust" and "consistent" are read as this count, a reading named here; the paper does not give one. T2 across mice is reported, as the header says, and does not decide.

claims.statement: Before side-port entry, mean DA and delta-Ach do not differ significantly between rewarded and unrewarded trials.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA are dynamically regulated, paragraph 2; Fig. 1e
claims.quote: Notably, the changes are significant after ('post'), but not before ('pre') side entry
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, T1 per mouse (two-sided t-test, p < 0.05) on the pre window, readings W1 and W2 (header). Reproduced when fewer than half of the DA mice and fewer than half of the Ach mice show a significant pre difference (the count mirrors that of fig1e-reward-outcome-post; the paper gives none); not reproduced otherwise. The per-mouse differences and T2 across mice are reported either way.

claims.statement: An LDA classifier separates rewarded from unrewarded trials with accuracy above 80% when trained on post-side-entry signals and around 50% (chance) when trained on pre-side-entry signals.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA are dynamically regulated, paragraph 3; Fig. 1e
claims.quote: the LDA classification accuracy is very high when trained on the signals post-side entry (higher than 80%), but not when trained on those pre-side entry (around 50%) (Fig. 1e )
claims.criterion: LDA as in the header, windows W1 and W2, DA and Ach separately. The post value is a bound, met when accuracy exceeds 80%. The paper prints a percentage per mouse and does not say whether "higher than 80%" means every mouse or the mean; the readings are (a) the mean over mice, (b) every mouse. Reproduced when post accuracy exceeds 80% and pre accuracy is within the expected value under one reading, for both DA and Ach.

claims.statement: DA and Ach transients do not differ between trials to the port ipsilateral and contralateral to the fibre; DA shows no significant difference and Ach differences are inconsistent in direction with poor LDA accuracy.
claims.source: Supplementary Results, Analysis of lateralization of DA and Ach signals; Extended Data Fig. 3d-f
claims.quote: Differences between these trials were not statistically different for DA (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Any significant differences for Ach were inconsistent in directionality, and the LDA classification accuracy was poor
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, T1 per mouse at p < 0.05, ipsilateral against contralateral trials, rewarded and unrewarded separately, post window (W1, W2), as in processStats_Fig1_DA_RL_RewNR.m (right against left port). Which side is ipsilateral needs the hemisphere of each fibre. Reproduced for DA when no DA mouse shows a significant difference; for Ach when the significant differences do not share one direction across mice and the LDA accuracy is below 65% on average ("poor", a threshold named here). The effect sizes are reported either way.

claims.statement: In rewarded trials with the LED cues omitted, DA after side entry is larger and DA before side entry smaller than with cues, while Ach changes in the opposite direction.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA are dynamically regulated, paragraph 4; Fig. 1f; Extended Data Fig. 4a
claims.quote: the DA transient in cue-omission rewarded trials is significantly increased after side-port entry and decreased before side entry, whereas Ach transients are modulated in the opposite direction
claims.criterion: Header method, cue-omission session against a cued session of the same mouse, as paired in aa_processStats_Fig1_DA_Ach_LED.m (which cued session is compared is fixed there by date). The Extended Data Fig. 4a legend measures Ach as the mean minimum z-scored signal, not delta-Ach; both are shown and the legend's minimum decides. Reproduced when, under each of W1 and W2, in more than half of the 4 mice (at least 3, the count of fig1e-reward-outcome-post; the paper gives none) mean DA post is higher and pre lower without cues with T1 p < 0.05, and the Ach minimum moves the other way.

claims.statement: In trials that repeat the previous port, lose-win trials have a larger mean DA and delta-Ach after side entry than win-win trials, and win-lose trials have a deeper DA dip and a larger delta-Ach than lose-lose trials.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA are dynamically regulated, paragraph 5; Fig. 1g; Extended Data Fig. 4d,e
claims.quote: Indeed, mean DA and ∆Ach signals increase post-side entry in the 'lose–win' scenario ... Conversely, for an unrewarded trial, mean DA dips more and ∆Ach rises more if this trial was preceded by a rewarded trial ('win–lose')
claims.criterion: Header method, stay trials, aA against AA and Aa against aa (the code's w_aA/w_AA and w_aa/w_Aa in aa_processStats_final_Fig1_DA_Words.m and _Fig1_Ach_Words.m), post window W1 and W2. Reproduced when, under each window reading, each of the four comparisons (two signals, two contrasts) goes in the stated direction in more than half of the mice with T1 p < 0.05 (the count of fig1e-reward-outcome-post). T2 across mice is reported and does not decide.

claims.statement: When the mouse switches ports, the previous outcome does not change DA or Ach after side-port entry.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA are dynamically regulated, paragraph 5; Fig. 1h; Extended Data Fig. 4d,e
claims.quote: Notably, these effects of expectation on DA and Ach are absent if the mouse switches ports between trials ... the signals after side-port entry are similar
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, T1 per mouse at p < 0.05, switch trials, aB against AB and Ab against ab (w_aB/w_AB, w_ab/w_Ab in the Fig. 1 scripts), post window W1 and W2. Reproduced when, for each comparison and signal, fewer than half of the mice show a significant difference; not reproduced otherwise. Effect sizes and T2 are reported.

claims.statement: In switch trials, DA during the move from centre to side port is larger when the previous trial was unrewarded.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA are dynamically regulated, paragraph 5; Fig. 1h
claims.quote: Instead, the DA signals during the transition from centre to side port are greater when the previous trial was unrewarded (Fig. 1h )
claims.criterion: Header method, mean DA in the pre window (W1, W2), switch trials with a previous loss (aB and ab) against a previous win (AB and Ab), as in the code's (pre Sw)aX/AX condition (FNoRewSw against FRewSw). Reproduced when, under each window reading, the previous-loss mean is higher in more than half of the 13 DA mice with T1 p < 0.05 (the count of fig1e-reward-outcome-post). T2 across mice is reported and does not decide.

claims.statement: DA and Ach are modulated more around port entries in unrewarded trials than around the same port entries during the ITI; after side entry DA dips more and Ach rises more in unrewarded trials, with the opposite before side entry.
claims.source: Supplementary Results, ITI analysis of signals; Extended Data Fig. 4b,c
claims.quote: DA and Ach signals are modulated to a greater extent during unrewarded trials than during the ITI ... DA signals dip more while Ach signals rise more after side port entry, and the opposite changes occur prior to side port entry
claims.criterion: ITI events as the Supplementary Methods define them, centre and side entries between one trial's side exit and the next centre entry, separated by at least 15 samples (0.81 s) from other port entries and exits; windows of 14 samples (0.756 s) before and after side entry, readings as W1 and W2 shortened to 14 samples; Extended Data Fig. 4a,c use mean DA and the mean minimum of Ach. Unrewarded trial side entries against ITI side entries. Reproduced when, under each window reading, post DA is lower and post Ach higher in unrewarded trials, and pre the reverse, each in more than half of the mice with T1 p < 0.05.

claims.statement: A base GLM of behavioural events explains about a fifth of the variance of trial-associated DA and Ach signals (test R2 0.206 for each).
claims.source: Results, Action-outcome history shapes DA and Ach, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 5c,d
claims.quote: We find that it captures substantial variance across the trial-associated data (DA GLM R 2 = 0.206; Ach GLM R 2 = 0.206)
claims.criterion: GLM as in Methods, GLM. Binary event predictors at 54-ms bins; design matrix of 20 shifts forward and backward (41 coefficients per predictor); ITI data excluded, data from shortly before centre entry to after side exit kept, with overlapping boundary samples duplicated; trials split 50/50 into training and test; OLS (the Supplementary GLM section says OLS suffices); R2 on the test set averaged over runs. DA n = 8 mice, Ach n = 9 mice. Open, as the GLM code is not published. (1) The predictor set; the leave-out text names centre entry, centre exit, side entry, side exit, lick and reward; reading P1 uses these six, P2 adds the other recorded events (lick offset, LED onset and offset). (2) Pooling; G1 one model over all sessions of all mice; G2 one model per mouse, R2 averaged; G3 one per session, averaged. (3) Runs; Y = 10 or Y = 3. "Shortly before" and "after" are open; a standard choice of the 20-shift span (1.08 s) is used. Reproduced when both R2 fall within tolerance under every reading; blocked as methods_underspecified when readings disagree.

claims.statement: Leaving out side entry or reward raises the GLM's MSE for both DA and Ach, leaving out side exit or lick raises it for Ach, and leaving out centre entry or centre exit alone does not change it.
claims.source: Results, Action-outcome history shapes DA and Ach, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 5f
claims.quote: For both DA and Ach models, the closely timed centre entry and centre exit are redundant because loss of either alone does not affect the model fit ... DA and Ach signals are more accurately reconstructed with the addition of side entry and reward predictors, and, additionally, side exit and lick enable better reconstructions of the Ach signal
claims.criterion: GLM as in ed5-base-glm-r2, with its open readings; Y = 10 runs, each with a 50/50 trial split held for all models, and within training a 10-fold group shuffle split by trial (80/20) for validation MSE (Methods, GLM). The paper reports no test; reproduced when, under each reading, the median validation MSE over runs rises when side entry or reward is left out (DA and Ach) and when side exit or lick is left out (Ach), with the 10 runs' ranges not overlapping the full model's, while leaving out centre entry or centre exit alone leaves the median within the full model's range. The range rules are a reading of "greatly increased" and "does not affect" named here; the paper gives no rule.

claims.statement: Adding side entries split by the eight action-outcome histories improves the GLM, to a test R2 of 0.213 for DA and 0.214 for Ach, with a lower MSE and no overfitting.
claims.source: Results, Action-outcome history shapes DA and Ach, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 5f-i
claims.quote: This reflects an improvement in the ability of the history GLMs to capture the variance of the trial-associated data (DA GLM R 2 = 0.213; Ach GLM R 2 = 0.214) without overfitting
claims.criterion: As ed5-base-glm-r2, with side entry replaced by eight side-entry predictors, one per two-trial action-outcome combination (the paper does not list them; the reading is the eight combinations of stay or switch, previous outcome and current outcome). Reproduced when both R2 are within tolerance and the history model's test MSE is below the base model's in every run ("reduced the MSE", read as every run, a reading named here), under each reading.

claims.statement: DA signals recorded with rDAh and dLight1.1 in opposite hemispheres of the same mice are comparable in shape, with consistently smaller amplitudes for rDAh.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA release are anticorrelated, paragraph 1; Fig. 2a; Extended Data Fig. 6d
claims.quote: Both sensors yield comparable signals, but with consistently reduced amplitudes for rDAh
claims.criterion: Extended Data Fig. 6d compares the maximum or minimum z-scored signal in the indicated periods; the periods are not given in the text. The readings are the pre and post windows W1 and W2 (header), rewarded and unrewarded trials. Reproduced when, under each reading, the absolute peak (maximum post in rewarded, minimum post in unrewarded) is smaller for rDAh than for dLight1.1 in all 3 mice, and the trial-averaged traces of the two sensors correlate above 0.8 ("comparable", a threshold named here).

claims.statement: DA release is highly correlated across the two hemispheres of the same mouse.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA release are anticorrelated, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 6c
claims.quote: we exploited the fact that the release of DA is highly correlated across hemispheres within the same mouse
claims.criterion: Cross-correlation of trial-segregated dLight1.1 signals from the two hemispheres, as in the header (n = 4 mice). Reproduced when the peak normalized cross-correlation is positive and above 0.7 ("highly", a threshold named here) in every mouse. The lag of the peak is reported; the paper says nothing of it.

claims.statement: Simultaneously recorded DA and Ach in the same hemisphere are highly anticorrelated over whole sessions, with the minimum at a positive lag (Ach changes follow DA changes after a short delay).
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA release are anticorrelated, paragraph 2; Fig. 2d
claims.quote: reveal that DA and Ach responses are highly anticorrelated with a positive time lag, which indicates that increases in DA might suppress Ach with a short delay (Fig. 2d )
claims.criterion: Supplementary Methods, Cross-variance analyses, and Signal demodulation (72-sample windows, 18-ms samples for Fig. 2d). Whole-session normalized cross-correlation of rDAh and Ach3.0 (n = 6 mice); controls are Ach against DA from another session of the same mouse, and DA circularly shifted by a random 1 to 10000 samples. The Fig. 2d legend says "DA lags Ach"; the sign is taken from the Methods (a positive lag means DA changes precede Ach changes). Reproduced when the mean over mice has its minimum at a positive lag below 0.3 s ("short delay", a bound named here), with a value below the minima of both controls (the comparison the controls are drawn for; the paper states no result for them). The controls' values at that lag are reported.

claims.statement: Trial-segregated DA and Ach signals are anticorrelated with an offset of about 100 ms in rewarded and unrewarded trials, and their noise components show a similar structure.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA release are anticorrelated, paragraph 2; Fig. 2e; Extended Data Fig. 6f
claims.quote: We observed that the trial-segregated DA and Ach signals are anticorrelated with a time offset of around 100 ms across rewarded and unrewarded trials ... This revealed a similar correlation structure (Fig. 2e )
claims.criterion: Header cross-correlation, 40 samples before and 100 after centre-port entry, rewarded and unrewarded trials separately, signal and noise, n = 6 mice. The tolerance is one 54-ms sample, the resolution of the signal; "around 100 ms" is two samples. The code's alignment to side entry and s.d.-scaled residuals are variants. Reproduced when, for both trial types, the signal and the noise cross-correlations have a negative minimum at a lag within tolerance in the mean over mice.

claims.statement: The two-dimensional covariance of DA and Ach fluctuations has a negative off-diagonal at which DA changes precede Ach changes by about 100 ms at most times, and it nearly disappears when the mouse enters the side port.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA release are anticorrelated, paragraph 3; Fig. 2f,g
claims.quote: This revealed a strong time-lagged negative covariance (Fig. 2f ), which we call the off-diagonal (Fig. 2g ), showing that, at most time points, changes in DA precede changes in Ach by approximately 100 ms ... Notably, the negative, off-diagonal covariance nearly disappears when the mouse enters the side port
claims.criterion: K(t1, t2) as the Supplementary Methods equation gives it, the trial mean of the product of residuals (each trial minus the trial-averaged signal) of DA at t1 and Ach at t2, per mouse and trial type, 40 samples before and 100 after centre entry; the code's division of residuals by the across-trial s.d. (anaCrossCor.m) is a variant. The off-diagonal is K(t, t + lag) at the lag of the minimum found in fig2e. Reproduced when, in the mean over the 6 mice, the off-diagonal is negative at more than half of the time points and its magnitude in the samples within one sample of side entry is below a quarter of its median magnitude ("nearly disappears", a threshold named here). The side-entry time in centre-aligned trials varies by trial; the readings are (a) side-aligned windows, (b) centre-aligned windows with the median side-entry time.

claims.statement: Kernels of a GLM that predicts one neuromodulator from the other show a negative interaction at about 100 ms; photometry alone predicts weakly (R2 0.116 for DA, 0.171 for Ach), and adding the photometry kernels to the history GLMs raises R2 to 0.336 for DA and 0.388 for Ach.
claims.source: Supplementary Results, GLM with photometry variable; Fig. 2h; Extended Data Fig. 6h
claims.quote: Although the DA or Ach photometry signal alone is insufficient to robustly predict the other (Extended Data Fig. 6h) (DA GLM R2 = 0.116; Ach GLM R2 = 0.171), incorporation of these photometry kernels into history GLMs for DA and Ach improves model performance without overfitting (DA GLM R2 = 0.336; Ach GLM R2 = 0.388)
claims.criterion: GLM as in ed5-base-glm-r2 and ed5-history-glm-r2, with all their open readings, on the 6 simultaneous rDAh and Ach3.0 mice, with the other channel's z-scored signal as a continuous predictor with the same 41 shifts. Reproduced when the four R2 are within tolerance and the mean kernel has its most negative coefficient at a shift of 54 to 162 ms with the predicted signal following the predictor, under every reading.

claims.statement: DA and Ach recorded in separate hemispheres are also anticorrelated at a positive lag, with a smaller positive correlation at a negative lag.
claims.source: Supplementary Results, Cross correlation analysis of DA and Ach transients recorded from independent hemispheres; Extended Data Fig. 6a,b
claims.quote: Cross correlation analysis of these trial-segregated signals in which DA lags Ach reveals an anticorrelation with a positive time lag ... In addition, there is a smaller positive correlation at a negative time lag
claims.criterion: Header cross-correlation of trial-segregated dLight1.1 and Ach3.0 signals from opposite hemispheres (n = 3 mice in the legend). Reproduced when the mean has a negative minimum at a positive lag and a positive maximum of smaller magnitude at a negative lag.

claims.statement: TelC expressed in VLS CINs suppresses Ach release measured in vivo during rewarded trials.
claims.source: Results, Striatal DA dynamics do not require CINs, paragraph 1; Fig. 3d
claims.quote: potently inhibits the release of Ach from CINs in vitro (Fig. 3c ) and in vivo (Fig. 3d
claims.criterion: The legend gives ∆F/F0 averages (n = 3 mice); the paper reports no test and does not give the baseline F0. The readings for F0 are (a) the session median of the demodulated signal, (b) a rolling 1-min baseline. Reproduced when, under both, the peak-to-trough range of the trial-averaged Ach ∆F/F0 within 2 s of side entry in TelC mice is below half that of mCherry mice for every TelC mouse ("potently", a threshold named here).

claims.statement: In acute striatal slices, optogenetic activation of Chrimson-expressing CINs evokes DA release (carbon-fibre amperometry) when the CINs coexpress mCherry, and this is blocked when they coexpress TelC, showing that TelC inhibits Ach release from CINs in vitro.
claims.source: Results, Striatal DA dynamics do not require CINs, paragraph 1; Fig. 3c
claims.quote: potently inhibits the release of Ach from CINs in vitro (Fig. 3c )
claims.criterion: Methods, Amperometry recordings and Preparation of acute brain slices; 593-nm light, 5.86 mW, 2 ms, at 180-s intervals; +600 mV constant potential, current converted to DA concentration by calibration. The paper gives no n, test or window for this panel. Per sweep, the peak DA after the light pulse minus the mean over the 1 s before it (a standard choice named here), averaged per slice. Reproduced when the mCherry slices show a DA rise and the TelC slices' mean peak is below a quarter of the mCherry mean ("potently", a threshold named here). A two-sample two-sided t-test across slices is reported.

claims.statement: Striatum-wide TelC in CINs causes severe behavioural defects (changed mean ITI, decision time and RFLR alpha), yet DA still has opposite polarity after side entry for rewarded and unrewarded trials.
claims.source: Results, Striatal DA dynamics do not require CINs, paragraph 1; Fig. 3e; Extended Data Figs. 7k and 9f-i
claims.quote: This widespread loss of Ach induced severe behavioural defects and greatly altered behaviourally evoked DA signals ... Nevertheless, DA retained its capacity to encode for reward, such that DA signals (Fig. 3e ) and their associated GLM kernels (Extended Data Fig. 7k ) maintain opposing polarity with reward outcome
claims.criterion: Behaviour metrics per mouse (behaviour code, block_transition_stats.ipynb) compared with the tests named. Reproduced when mean ITI and decision time differ with p < 0.05 (two-sided t-test), RFLR alpha differs with p < 0.05 (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum), and, in TelC mice, mean z-scored DA in the post window (W1, W2) is above zero in rewarded and below zero in unrewarded trials in the mean over mice. The direction of the ITI, decision-time and alpha changes is not stated in the text and is reported.

claims.statement: Blocking Ach release from VLS CINs in one hemisphere does not change DA dynamics there compared with the control hemisphere, in any trial type or history up to three trials back.
claims.source: Results, Striatal DA dynamics do not require CINs, paragraphs 2-3; Fig. 3f; Extended Data Fig. 8d-k
claims.quote: VLS-specific loss of Ach release did not affect DA dynamics in trials recorded with dLight1.1 (Fig. 3f ) or with rDAh ... but we did not observe any significant changes in DA dynamics or in the underlying GLM kernels of DA for each input feature after loss of Ach
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, T1 per mouse at p < 0.05, TelC hemisphere against mCherry hemisphere, mean DA in the pre and post windows (W1, W2) for rewarded, unrewarded and history-parsed trials one, two and three back, as in aa_processStats_Fig3_DA_Ach_mCh_tet_FINAL.m. The paper does not say how per-mouse results are combined into "no significant changes"; the reading used here is that no comparison is significant in a consistent direction across mice (significant differences, if any, do not share a sign in more than half of the mice). Reproduced when that holds; not reproduced otherwise. All per-mouse effects are reported, and the count of mice with any significant comparison is reported as the strict reading.

claims.statement: In the simultaneous rDAh and Ach3.0 recordings, the TelC hemisphere has suppressed Ach release, validating the perturbation.
claims.source: Results, Striatal DA dynamics do not require CINs, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 8g
claims.quote: or with rDAh, in which we simultaneously validated the suppression of Ach release
claims.criterion: The paper does not say how the suppression was validated; Extended Data Fig. 8g shows z-scored traces, and z-scoring can hide a loss of amplitude. The readings are (a) the header's delta-Ach in the post window (W1, W2) of the z-scored Ach, TelC against mCherry hemisphere, T1 per mouse; (b) the peak-to-trough range of the trial-averaged Ach ∆F/F0 within 2 s of side entry, as in fig3d-telc-abolishes-ach. Reproduced when, under each reading, Ach is lower in the TelC hemisphere in every one of the 4 mice (with T1 p < 0.05 under (a)); the "every mouse" rule is a reading of "validated" named here.

claims.statement: Mice with VLS-selective TelC in CINs show no behavioural deficits.
claims.source: Results, Striatal DA dynamics do not require CINs, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 9j-m
claims.quote: Mice did not exhibit behavioural deficits (Extended Data Fig. 9j–m )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests (Supplementary Methods, Behavior performance analysis), two-sided t-test for mean ITI, decision time, lose-switch, win-switch and mean left rates; Wilcoxon rank-sum for tau_highport, maximum P(switch) and RFLR coefficients; bootstrapped 95% CI of the difference (1000 resamples) for conditional switch probabilities, against controls, at p < 0.05. The legend's groups are TelC and mCherry mice; since each mouse has one hemisphere of each, the paper does not say what the control group is; the readings are (a) the cohort against the striatum-wide mCherry mice of Fig. 3e, (b) the cohort before and after expression, (c) the same mice's sessions split by the hemisphere recorded (TelC or mCherry). Each reading the data allow is run. Reproduced when no test is significant under any of them; when they disagree the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Loss of local Ach release does not consistently change the amplitude of DA sensor transients (∆F/F0).
claims.source: Results, Striatal DA dynamics do not require CINs, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 8f
claims.quote: we analysed the amplitudes of DA sensor fluorescence transients (∆ F / F 0 ), but this analysis did not reveal consistent effects
claims.criterion: The paper names no test. Per mouse, the peak ∆F/F0 of the trial-averaged DA after side entry in the TelC and mCherry hemispheres (F0 readings as in fig3d-telc-abolishes-ach). Reproduced when the sign of the TelC minus mCherry difference is not the same in all 4 mice (a reading of "did not reveal consistent effects" named here).

claims.statement: Optogenetic inhibition of DANs with stGtACR2 during rewarded trials significantly reduces DA in the VLS.
claims.source: Results, Striatal DA dynamics do not require CINs, paragraph 3; Fig. 3g
claims.quote: inhibition of DAN activity robustly alters DA release, as evidenced by a significant reduction in the levels of DA after optogenetic inhibition of DANs with stGtACR2
claims.criterion: Laser (463 nm, 0.7 mW, 5 s) triggered at side entry (Methods, Optogenetic manipulations); rDAh ∆F/F0 in stimulated rewarded trials of opsin mice against opsin-free mice (n = 3 each). The paper names no test for this panel; the readings are (a) T1 per mouse, stimulated against unstimulated rewarded trials, mean over 0 to 5 s after side entry; (b) a two-sample t-test across mice of the stimulated minus unstimulated difference, opsin against no opsin. Reproduced when DA is lower under stimulation in all 3 opsin mice with p < 0.05 under (a), or p < 0.05 under (b).

claims.statement: Optogenetic activation of Chrimson-expressing VLS CINs during the task evokes a small, significant DA release, without changing decision or side-port occupancy times.
claims.source: Supplementary Results, Optogenetic activation of the CINs; Extended Data Fig. 7e,f
claims.quote: We demonstrated that CIN stimulation consistently and significantly evokes DA release (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Therefore, exogenous activation of CINs is sufficient to drive DA release
claims.criterion: 590-nm laser, 15 mW, 1.5 s in 25% of trials at side entry (Methods, Optogenetic manipulations); stimulation artefact removed. Peak dLight1.1 change from a baseline over 1.5 s before the laser (the head-fixed baseline of the Methods; the task baseline is not given, and the reading is that same span), per mouse, paired two-sided t-test across the 7 mice (the legend's connected pairs). The legend does not say what the two dots of a pair are; the readings are (a) Chrimson against mCherry hemisphere, stimulated trials, (b) stimulated against unstimulated trials in the Chrimson hemisphere. Reproduced when, under each reading, p < 0.05 with the Chrimson or stimulated value higher, and decision and occupancy times show p > 0.05.

claims.statement: In head-fixed mice, optogenetic activation of DANs lowers Ach and inhibition of DANs raises it, opposite to the change in DA, and both effects are abolished by the D2R antagonist eticlopride.
claims.source: Results, DA inhibits Ach release through D2Rs, paragraph 1; Fig. 4b,c
claims.quote: These manipulations altered the levels of Ach in the direction opposite to optogenetically evoked changes in DA levels, consistent with DA inhibiting Ach release (Fig. 4b,c ). Notably, these effects are D2R-dependent as they are abolished by the administration of eticlopride
claims.criterion: Methods, Optogenetic manipulations, 45-s ITI, 20 sweeps per session, baseline = mean over 1.5 s before the laser; n = 3 mice per opsin. The Methods give two durations for these panels, 5 s ("For optogenetic manipulation of DANs (Figs. 3g and 4b,c)") and 1.5 s (head-fixed mice on a wheel); the readings are a 1.5-s and a 5-s window from laser onset, and the laser timestamps, where the data hold them, say which was used. The paper names no test. Per mouse, the mean ∆F/F0 change over the stimulation relative to baseline. Reproduced when, with saline, DA rises and Ach falls under Chrimson and DA falls and Ach rises under stGtACR2 in all 3 mice, and with eticlopride the Ach change is less than a quarter of its saline size or of the opposite sign in all 3 mice ("abolished", a threshold named here). The DA change under eticlopride is reported; the paper says nothing of it.

claims.statement: In striatal slices, DA released by stimulating ChR2-expressing DAN terminals reduces CIN firing in wild-type mice, and this is absent in CINs of Drd2-cKO mice.
claims.source: Results, DA inhibits Ach release through D2Rs, paragraph 2; Fig. 4d-f
claims.quote: In wild-type mice, release of DA after laser stimulation of channelrhodopsin-expressing DAN terminals robustly reduced CIN firing, as measured by cell-attached recordings, but this effect was absent in CINs from Drd2-cKO mice
claims.criterion: Cell-attached recordings, one 2-ms 473-nm pulse every 120 s (Methods); 9 WT and 9 Drd2-cKO cells. The paper names no test or windows. Per cell, firing rate in the 1 s after the pulse against the 1 s before (a standard choice of window, named as such; readings 0.5 s and 2 s are also shown). Reproduced when the rate falls in most WT cells (paired t-test across cells, p < 0.05) and not in Drd2-cKO cells (same test, p > 0.05), under each window.

claims.statement: In Drd2-cKO mice the two dips in Ach that coincide with DA rises (moving from centre to side port, and after side entry in rewarded trials) are lost, so Ach signals are significantly larger than in Drd2 f/f and wild-type mice.
claims.source: Results, DA inhibits Ach release through D2Rs, paragraph 3; Fig. 4g; Extended Data Fig. 11d
claims.quote: We found that the loss of D2Rs in CINs abolished both instances of Ach suppression that coincide with an increase in DA levels (Fig. 4g ). Together, these changes lead to significantly increased Ach signals (Extended Data Fig. 11d )
claims.criterion: Header measures on z-scored Ach, in the windows of aa_processStats_final_Fig4_cKO_Ach_Words.m (post +1 to +18 and +9 to +16, all trials pre -18 to -1 and -18 to -9 samples about side entry), the Extended Data Fig. 11d schematic not being legible in the text. The legend prints "Open circles denote a significant difference ... (two-sided ANOVA, open circle, P > 0.05)"; as open circles mark significance, "P > 0.05" is read as a misprint for P < 0.05. The unit of the ANOVA is open (its code is not published); the readings are (a) one value per mouse, the mean over its trials; (b) every trial pooled within genotype. Reproduced when, under each reading, the ANOVA gives p < 0.05 for delta-Ach in the pre window and in the rewarded post window, and two-sided t-tests show Drd2-cKO higher than both Drd2 f/f and WT at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: DA dynamics during the task do not differ significantly across WT, Drd2 f/f and Drd2-cKO mice.
claims.source: Results, DA inhibits Ach release through D2Rs, paragraph 3; Fig. 4g; Extended Data Fig. 11d
claims.quote: these changes occurred despite no significant changes in DA dynamics during the task across the three genotypes (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 11d )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-sided one-way ANOVA across the three genotypes at p < 0.05, on mean z-scored rDAh in the windows of fig4g-cko-ach-suppression-lost, with its unit readings (a) and (b) shown. Reproduced when no window and trial type gives p < 0.05 under reading (a), the unit the legend's mean ± s.d. by genotype implies; reading (b) is a variant. Effect sizes are reported.

claims.statement: In Drd2-cKO mice the anticorrelation between DA and Ach is significantly smaller in magnitude, and the off-diagonal negative covariance is reduced.
claims.source: Supplementary Results, GLM for DA and Ach signals upon D2R deletion in CINs; Fig. 4h,i; Extended Data Fig. 11e
claims.quote: As a result, the relationship between Ach and DA signals in Drd2-cKO mice is severely disrupted (Extended Data Fig. 11a), with a significant reduction in the magnitude of their anticorrelation (Fig. 4h; Extended Data Fig. 11e) and the off-diagonal negative covariance
claims.criterion: Header cross-correlation and the off-diagonal of fig2fg-off-diagonal, per mouse; the amplitude of the minimum covariance per mouse compared between Drd2-cKO and each control group with a two-sample two-sided t-test across mice. Reproduced when the Drd2-cKO minimum is smaller in magnitude than both controls with p < 0.05, for signal or noise correlations, and the mean off-diagonal magnitude is smaller in Drd2-cKO.

claims.statement: History GLMs fit DA and Ach signals of the three genotypes with test R2 of 0.129, 0.122 and 0.155 for DA and 0.202, 0.262 and 0.214 for Ach (WT, Drd2 f/f, Drd2-cKO); side-entry Ach kernels are greatly altered in Drd2-cKO mice while DA kernels are comparable.
claims.source: Supplementary Results, GLM for DA and Ach signals upon D2R deletion in CINs; Extended Data Fig. 11b,c
claims.quote: DA kernels are comparable across the three cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 11c). In contrast, all side-entry Ach kernels are greatly altered in Drd2-cKO mice
claims.criterion: History GLM as in ed5-history-glm-r2 with its open readings, per genotype. Reproduced when the six R2 are within tolerance under every reading, and the Drd2-cKO side-entry Ach kernels have larger coefficients than both controls at negative shifts for all histories, with the s.d. bands of runs not overlapping ("greatly altered", a threshold named here), and the DA kernels' s.d. bands overlap across genotypes ("comparable", likewise).

claims.statement: General performance metrics and block-transition dynamics of Drd2-cKO mice do not differ from Drd2 f/f and WT mice.
claims.source: Results, DA inhibits Ach release through D2Rs, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 11f-h
claims.quote: Although general performance metrics, block transition dynamics and RFLR coefficients (Extended Data Fig. 11f–i ) are comparable between Drd2-cKO mice and both control groups
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests (Supplementary Methods, Behavior performance analysis, and block_transition_stats.ipynb), two-sided t-tests on mean ITI, decision time, lose-switch, win-switch and mean left rates, and Wilcoxon rank-sum on tau_highport and maximum P(switch), Drd2-cKO against each control, at p < 0.05. Reproduced when none is significant; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The Extended Data Fig. 11i legend reports significant differences in the RFLR beta and tau of Drd2-cKO mice, although the main text calls the RFLR coefficients comparable.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 11i legend
claims.quote: RFLR coefficients for mice in Fig. 4g . Bars denote mean with 95% C.I. Significance is determined using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (* P ... β = 0.014; τ = 0.018)
claims.criterion: RFLR per mouse (bandit_models.py), Wilcoxon rank-sum, Drd2-cKO against each control group. The legend does not name the control group; the readings are Drd2 f/f, WT, and both pooled. Reproduced when beta and tau differ with p < 0.05 under one reading; the main text's "comparable" (no difference) is reported against it, and the conflict between the two statements is recorded as a deviation.

claims.statement: Drd2-cKO mice are impaired in switching ports after some action-outcome histories compared with both Drd2 f/f and WT mice.
claims.source: Results, DA inhibits Ach release through D2Rs, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 11j
claims.quote: Drd2-cKO mice are impaired in their ability to switch selection ports across some histories when compared to both Drd2 f/f and wild-type cohorts
claims.criterion: Conditional switch probabilities for each two-trial (or three-trial, seq_nback = 3 in bandit_plots.py; the legend does not say) action-outcome history; per Supplementary Methods, 1000 resamples of each dataset, the difference of the parameter between groups, significant when its 95% CI excludes zero. The resampling unit (trials or sessions) is open; both are run. Reproduced when, under each reading, at least one history shows a lower switch probability in Drd2-cKO than both Drd2 f/f and WT, significant against both.

claims.statement: Retrograde tracing from the VLS labels cells across many cortical regions and, in the thalamus, mainly in the parafascicular nucleus.
claims.source: Results, The cortex and thalamus drive Ach release, paragraph 2; Fig. 5a
claims.quote: We find that a broad distribution of cells from multiple cortical regions send afferents into the VLS (Fig. 5a ). Meanwhile, thalamic inputs into this striatal region originate predominantly from the parafascicular nucleus
claims.criterion: Histology (Ctb in the VLS, n = 3 mice). The paper gives no counts. Reproduced when labelled cells are found in at least three cortical areas ("multiple", a threshold named here) and the parafascicular nucleus holds more labelled thalamic cells than any other thalamic nucleus ("predominantly"), in every mouse.

claims.statement: Striatal glutamate varies during the task and does not differ between ipsiversive and contraversive trials.
claims.source: Results, The cortex and thalamus drive Ach release, paragraph 3; Fig. 5b
claims.quote: we find that striatal glutamate levels vary during the task but are not lateralized (Fig. 5b
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper names no test for this panel; the test of its other lateralization claim (ed3-not-lateralized), T1 per mouse at p < 0.05 on the mean z-scored iGluSnFR signal in the pre and post windows (W1, W2), ipsiversive against contraversive trials, is used. Reproduced when fewer than half of the 4 mice show a significant difference.

claims.statement: Glutamate is suppressed before the choice and rises at side-port entry like Ach, and in rewarded trials shows a sustained rise during consumption that is absent in unrewarded trials.
claims.source: Results, The cortex and thalamus drive Ach release, paragraph 3; Fig. 5c
claims.quote: Glutamate signals are suppressed before the choice and increase during side-port entry in an analogous manner to Ach (Fig. 5c ). In rewarded trials, glutamate exhibits an extra phase of sustained increase during consumption, which is absent in unrewarded trials
claims.criterion: Trial-averaged z-scored iGluSnFR (n = 4 mice) and Ach3.0 (n = 9 mice), aligned to side entry. The paper gives no test. Reproduced when, in the mean over mice, glutamate in the pre window is below its value at centre entry, glutamate rises within 0.5 s of side entry, the correlation of the mean glutamate and Ach traces from -1 to +1 s about side entry is positive, and mean glutamate from 1 to 3 s after side entry is higher in rewarded than unrewarded trials with T1 p < 0.05 in at least 3 of 4 mice. The time spans are standard choices named here; the paper does not fix them.

claims.statement: Calcium activity in cortical and thalamic terminals in the VLS coincides with glutamate release in rewarded and unrewarded trials.
claims.source: Results, The cortex and thalamus drive Ach release, paragraph 3; Fig. 5d
claims.quote: The activities of cortical and thalamic terminals in the VLS, measured with genetically encoded calcium sensors, coincide with glutamate release across both trial types
claims.criterion: Trial-averaged z-scored jRCaMP1b (thalamic terminals, 6 mice) and GCaMP8 (cortical terminals, 5 mice) against iGluSnFR (4 mice), separate mice. The paper gives no test. Reproduced when, for each trial type, the mean calcium trace of each input correlates positively with the mean glutamate trace over -2 to +3 s about side entry (r above 0.5, a threshold named here).

claims.statement: Silencing cortical or thalamic glutamatergic inputs with TelC robustly lowers Ach sensor ∆F/F0 across all trials, consistently across mice.
claims.source: Results, The cortex and thalamus drive Ach release, paragraph 4; Fig. 5e,f; Extended Data Fig. 13e
claims.quote: Loss of neurotransmission from each region robustly dampened Ach transients across all trials, as seen in the lowered ∆ F / F 0 of the Ach sensor signal ... The degree of suppression of ∆ F / F 0 was strong and consistent across mice
claims.criterion: Ach3.0 ∆F/F0 (F0 readings as in fig3d-telc-abolishes-ach), cortex TelC 5 mice against mCherry 4, thalamus TelC 5 against mCherry 3. The paper names no test. Reproduced when, under each F0 reading, the peak-to-trough range of every TelC mouse's trial-averaged ∆F/F0 within 2 s of side entry is below the smallest range among its mCherry group, for both inputs ("strong and consistent across mice", a threshold named here).

claims.statement: In unrewarded trials, loss of cortical but not thalamic input perturbs Ach after side-port entry, and loss of thalamic input shifts the timing of Ach transients more than loss of cortical input.
claims.source: Results, The cortex and thalamus drive Ach release, paragraph 5; Fig. 5e,f
claims.quote: In unrewarded trials, loss of cortical but not thalamic inputs perturbs Ach transients after side-port entry, suggesting that the cortex has a specific role in driving this signal. In addition, loss of the thalamic input shifts the timing of Ach transients more than does loss of the cortical input
claims.criterion: Z-scored Ach (Fig. 5e,f, bottom), TelC against mCherry per input, unrewarded trials. The paper names no test or measure. Delta-Ach in the post window (W1, W2), the paper's Ach measure elsewhere, compared between the TelC and mCherry groups with a two-sample two-sided t-test across mice (a standard choice named here); timing as the latency of the trial-averaged Ach peak after side entry (likewise a choice named here). Reproduced when the cortex comparison gives p < 0.05 and the thalamus comparison does not, and the absolute peak-latency shift from mCherry is larger for thalamic than cortical TelC, under each window reading.

claims.statement: Cortical or thalamic TelC impairs performance, with lower reward rate and win-switch differences, and the RFLR shows a smaller beta and a larger tau.
claims.source: Results, The cortex and thalamus drive Ach release, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 13f-m
claims.quote: Consistent with this impairment, the RFLR model description revealed a reduction in β and an increase in τ
claims.criterion: Behaviour code (block_transition_stats.ipynb, bandit_models.py) with the tests the legends name, TelC against mCherry per input. Reproduced when, for each input, beta is lower and tau higher in TelC mice with p < 0.05 (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum), and reward rate is lower with p < 0.05 (two-sided t-test). The win-switch direction is not stated and is reported. The legend prints p = 0.05 for cortical beta; a value at or just above 0.05 is recorded as a match to the paper.

claims.statement: The DA and Ach transients depend on neuromodulator binding, being absent with the ligand-binding-site mutant sensors.
claims.source: Results, Ach and DA are dynamically regulated, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 2k-p
claims.quote: and that depended on neuromodulator binding, because they were absent in ligand-binding-site mutants of the sensors
claims.criterion: Rewarded-trial ∆F/F0 of dLight1.1 against its D103A mutant and Ach3.0 against its mutant (n = 4 mice each; F0 readings as in fig3d-telc-abolishes-ach). The paper gives no test. Reproduced when the peak-to-trough range of the trial-averaged mutant trace within 2 s of side entry is below a quarter of the wild-type sensor's in every mouse ("absent", a threshold named here).

claims.statement: After 6 weeks of SCC-DBS, monkeys N and T spent more time moving and more time foraging in the home cage than before, in the same direction in both animals.
claims.source: Results, SCC-DBS induces selective macroscale remodeling in the CB, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 1
claims.quote: Time spent moving and foraging both increased after SCC-DBS, with concordant effects observed across subjects
claims.criterion: From Methods (Behavior analysis) and the Extended Data Fig. 1 legend. For N and T, the 60 binary 10-s bins of each pre and post session, for movement and for foraging separately (240 values each). ANOVA of the binary values on condition (pre, post) with monkey as a fixed effect, under readings (a) condition, monkey and their interaction (the reported df) and (b) condition and monkey. Reproduced when, under both readings, the condition effect has P < 0.05 with the post probability higher, for both behaviors, and the post probability is higher than the pre in each monkey for both behaviors; the F values and partial eta squared are compared with the expected values under reading (a).

claims.statement: In the unstimulated lead-implanted monkey D, the amount of movement and foraging did not change between before and 6 weeks after implantation.
claims.source: Results, The impact of SCC-DBS lead insertion on functional and structural brain networks, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 1 (monkey D)
claims.quote: First, there was no change in the amount of movement or foraging in naturalistic behavior
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper shows monkey D's probabilities (Extended Data Fig. 1) but reports no test for monkey D; the legend says only N and T were analysed. The test the Methods describe for this measure, applied to one monkey, is a one-way ANOVA of the 120 binary bins on condition (pre, post), at the Methods' P < 0.05. Reproduced when neither movement nor foraging differs at P < 0.05; not reproduced when either does. The pre and post probabilities and their difference are given either way.

claims.statement: After 6 weeks of SCC-DBS, fractional anisotropy (FA) increased in the cingulum bundle of the stimulated hemisphere, with a significant PrePost x side interaction and a significant pre against post difference in the stimulated CB.
claims.source: Results, SCC-DBS induces selective macroscale remodeling in the CB, paragraph 3; Fig. 2a and legend
claims.quote: We found there was a selective increase in FA in the CB in the stimulated hemisphere, particularly the mid-cingulate portion, after 6 weeks of SCC-DBS
claims.criterion: From Methods (FA analysis) and the Fig. 2a legend. Voxel FA (1.5 mm) within the CB, UF and FM masks of each hemisphere of N and T, both sessions in the pre-DBS T1w space, voxels on the lead track excluded; the voxel counts should match the legend's n. ANOVA as fixed in the opening comment (DBS x side x tract full factorial plus monkey; Tukey-Kramer over the 12 cells). Reproduced when the PrePost x side interaction has P < 0.05 and the stimulated CB's pre against post comparison has P < 0.05 with post FA higher. F and partial eta squared are compared with the expected values.

claims.statement: FA did not change in the stimulated UF or FM, nor in any of the three tracts of the control hemisphere.
claims.source: Results, SCC-DBS induces selective macroscale remodeling in the CB, paragraph 3; Fig. 2a bottom graphs
claims.quote: No consistent changes were apparent in either the stimulated UF or the FM ... or in the same tracts within the control hemisphere
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the Tukey-Kramer post hoc of the model of fig2a-cb-fa-increase at P < 0.05. Reproduced when none of the five pre against post comparisons (stimulated UF, stimulated FM, control CB, control UF, control FM) has P < 0.05; not reproduced when any does. The mean change and P of each are given either way.

claims.statement: The FA increase in the stimulated CB was in the same direction in both monkeys.
claims.source: Results, SCC-DBS induces selective macroscale remodeling in the CB, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 2
claims.quote: Importantly, both monkeys exhibited changes in the same direction
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test per monkey. With the voxels of fig2a-cb-fa-increase, reproduced when the mean post minus pre FA in the stimulated CB is positive in monkey N and in monkey T.

claims.statement: Of the four CB subregions, only the mid-cingulate portion (MCC-CB) of the stimulated hemisphere showed an FA increase, and it did so in both animals.
claims.source: Results, SCC-DBS induces selective macroscale remodeling in the CB, paragraph 3; Fig. 2b and legend; Extended Data Fig. 4a
claims.quote: Comparing the FA values before and after 6 weeks of DBS in four CB subregions revealed that only the mid-cingulate region on the stimulated side showed an increase in FA in both animals
claims.criterion: From Methods (FA analysis) and the Fig. 2b legend. The CB voxels split into four subregions by the D99 atlas (SCC part, CB adjacent to areas 25 and 32; dACC, to area 24; MCC, to area 24'; PCC, to area 23). The Methods do not define "adjacent"; if the dataset labels voxels by subregion those labels are used, and the voxel counts should match the legend. ANOVA DBS x side x subregion full factorial plus monkey, Tukey-Kramer over the 16 cells. Reproduced when the interaction has P < 0.05, the stimulated MCC-CB pre against post comparison has P < 0.05 with post higher, no other subregion and side has a significant increase, and the stimulated MCC-CB mean post minus pre is positive in each monkey.

claims.statement: The proportion of CC1-positive (myelinating oligodendrocyte) cells among DAPI-positive cells in the MCC-CB was higher in the stimulated than in the control hemisphere, in both animals.
claims.source: Results, SCC-DBS induces increased myelinating oligodendrocytes and the degree of myelination, paragraph 1; Fig. 3b,c and legend
claims.quote: The proportion of CC1 positive cells in the whole DAPI stained population was higher in the mid-cingulate portion of the CB on the stimulated side compared to the control side in both animals
claims.criterion: From Methods (Immunofluorescence of myelinating oligodendrocytes) and the Fig. 3c legend. The CC1/DAPI ratio (%) of each of the 112 MCC-CB fields of N and T. ANOVA on side with monkey as a fixed effect, readings (a) and (b) of the opening comment. Reproduced when, under both readings, side has P < 0.05 with the stimulated side higher, and each monkey's mean ratio is higher on the stimulated side.

claims.statement: In the MCC-CB the number of CC1-positive cells was higher on the stimulated side, while the number of DAPI-positive cells did not differ between hemispheres.
claims.source: Extended Data Fig. 5 legend
claims.quote: The main effect of side for the number of CC1 positive cells was significant ... while no significant difference was observed for the number of DAPI positive cells
claims.criterion: As fig3c-cc1-dapi-ratio, on the CC1-positive and DAPI-positive counts per field. Reproduced when, under both model readings, the CC1 count has a side effect at P < 0.05 with the stimulated side higher and the DAPI count has none (P >= 0.05, the paper's test for the absence).

claims.statement: Neither the CC1/DAPI ratio nor the numbers of CC1-positive and DAPI-positive cells differed between hemispheres in the anterior (dACC) portion of the CB, nor in the region where the FM and UF overlap.
claims.source: Results, SCC-DBS induces increased myelinating oligodendrocytes and the degree of myelination, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 6a,b
claims.quote: No changes were observed in the anterior portion of CB, consistent with the lack of FA alterations there ... Similarly, the region where the FM and UF overlap showed no oligodendrocyte changes
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the ANOVA of fig3c-cc1-dapi-ratio on the dACC-CB fields (112) and the UF/FM overlap fields (80), at P < 0.05 (Extended Data Fig. 6 legend, which tests the ratio and both counts). Reproduced when the side effect on the CC1/DAPI ratio, the CC1 count and the DAPI count has P >= 0.05 in both regions under reading (a) of the model (the reported df); not reproduced when any has P < 0.05. Reading (b) and the effect sizes are given either way.

claims.statement: The g-ratio of myelinated axons in the MCC-CB was lower in the stimulated than in the control hemisphere, in both animals, meaning thicker myelin.
claims.source: Results, SCC-DBS induces increased myelinating oligodendrocytes and the degree of myelination, paragraph 2; Fig. 3d-f and legend
claims.quote: In the stimulated hemisphere, the MCC-CB g -ratio was decreased compared to the control hemisphere in both animals
claims.criterion: From Methods (Electron microscopy analysis of myelin thickness) and the Fig. 3f legend. One g-ratio per axon, as defined in the opening comment, axons with aspect ratio above 2 excluded (700 axons; the Fig. 3f legend calls the 350 per hemisphere "individual fields", but the df, 696 = 700 - 4, and the Methods' 175 axons per hemisphere per animal on average make them axons). ANOVA on side with monkey as a fixed effect, readings (a) and (b). Reproduced when, under both readings, side has P < 0.05 with the stimulated side lower, and each monkey's mean g-ratio is lower on the stimulated side.

claims.statement: After SCC-DBS, whole-brain functional connectivity between cortical areas decreased and connectivity between subcortical areas increased.
claims.source: Results, Whole-brain functional connectivity changes following SCC-DBS, paragraph 1; Fig. 4a top right, Fig. 4b top
claims.quote: Broadly, we observed a reduction in cortico–cortical functional connectivity and a concurrent increase in subcortico–subcortical functional connectivity
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test of the blocks; the pattern is read from the difference connectome (Fig. 4a) and the per-ROI changes (Fig. 4b). Connectome as in the opening comment, DBS group (N and T). Readings (a) the mean of the off-diagonal entries of the group difference connectome within the cortical (CHARM) block and within the subcortical (SARM) block; (b) each ROI's mean change to all other ROIs (the Fig. 4b measure), with the median over cortical ROIs and over subcortical ROIs. Reproduced when, under both readings, the cortical value is negative and the subcortical value positive.

claims.statement: Per ROI, functional connectivity changed significantly between pre and post scans in 69 of the 122 CHARM and SARM ROIs in the DBS group and in 44 of 122 in the nonsurgical control group.
claims.source: Fig. 4b and legend; Supplementary Tables 1 and 2
claims.criterion: From Methods (EPI data analysis) and the Fig. 4b legend. For each of the 122 ROIs, its 122 connectivity values (Fisher Z, group mean) pre against post with a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Open, and run under each reading. The test's pairing of values (a) rank-sum of the 122 pre values against the 122 post values, as the Methods name; (b) the 122 change values against zero (signed-rank), as the legend's "changes ... from zero". The threshold (a') P < 0.01/122, Bonferroni over ROIs; (b') the Bonferroni-adjusted P (P x 122) < 0.01, which is the same, so the open part is whether the listed P values are adjusted (see the opening comment); a third reading takes the listed P values as raw and the threshold P < 0.01, uncorrected. Whether the 122 values include the ROI's own diagonal is not stated (121 or 122 values are both run). Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Sorted by cortical network membership, functional connectivity within and across networks was reduced after SCC-DBS.
claims.source: Results, Whole-brain functional connectivity changes following SCC-DBS, paragraph 1; Fig. 4c left
claims.quote: When the functional connectivity was sorted based on cortical networks membership, it was clear that connectivity within and across networks was reduced
claims.criterion: The paper does not give which network each of the 122 ROIs belongs to for Fig. 4c, nor a test (the circular plot draws changes with |Z| > 0.1). If the paper's code deposited in the dandiset assigns the ROIs to networks, use it; reproduced when, in the DBS group's difference connectome, the mean change over all within-network ROI pairs and the mean change over all between-network ROI pairs are both negative (the sentence's "within and across networks").
