claims.statement: Optogenetic activation of Anxa1+ DANs evokes DA release in the dCP at varying intensities, and the evoked release in the cCP has a lower amplitude.
claims.source: Results, Specialized organization of Anxa1+ DANs, paragraph 2; Figure S2
claims.quote: Optogenetic activation of Anxa1+ DANs at varying intensities elicited DA release in the dCP ... optogenetically evoked DA release in the cCP exhibited a lower amplitude compared to the dCP signal
claims.criterion: dLight1.3b z-scored signal aligned to ChRmine stimulation (1 s at 40 Hz, Methods). The intensities, window, test and n are in Figure S2, which was not read; all are open. Reproduced when the peak of the mean evoked response after stimulation onset exceeds the pre-stimulus baseline in dCP and is lower in cCP than in dCP, per recording, by a two-sided unpaired t-test (the Methods' two-group test) at p < 0.05. Peak within 0 to 1 s and within 0 to 2 s of onset are both run. These windows are set here (the train lasts 1 s, Methods); whether dCP and cCP were recorded in the same or in different mice is not given, and a paired t-test is run as well where the same mice hold both. The main text says only "at varying intensities"; which powers enter the comparison, the unit (session or mouse) and the pre-stimulus baseline window are not given (Figure S2 not read). The readings are (a) each session's mean over all trains, all powers pooled, the session as unit; (b) each power alone, the session as unit. A per-mouse summary is reported, not judged (two mice per site). The baseline is the mean z-score over (i) 1 s and (ii) 2 s before train onset; both are run.

claims.statement: Anxa1+ DAN axons in dorsolateral CP are enriched in MOR+ striosomes and the subcallosal streak, suggesting a nigro-striato-nigral loop.
claims.source: Results, Specialized organization of Anxa1+ DANs, paragraph 3; Figure 2I
claims.quote: eYFP axonal labeling in the dorsolateral CP was enriched in the mu-opioid receptor (MOR) immunoreactive striosomes and subcallosal streak
claims.criterion: Images only; no measure or test is given. Reproduced when eYFP density inside MOR+ patches is higher than in the surrounding matrix of dorsolateral CP. This rule is set here.

claims.statement: After low-dose 6-OHDA, degeneration of eYFP+ Anxa1+ SNc neurons is accompanied by near-complete loss of their eYFP+ axons in the dCP across the anteroposterior axis.
claims.source: Results, Specialized organization of Anxa1+ DANs, paragraph 4; Figure 2J to 2N
claims.quote: Degeneration of the eYFP+ SNc neurons was accompanied by near-complete ablation of the corresponding eYFP+ axons in the dCP across the anteroposterior axis
claims.criterion: eYFP optical density in dCP, lesioned against intact side, per section (Figure 2N, n = 5 mice). No test is given. "Near-complete" is not quantified; reproduced when the lesioned dCP density is below 10% of the intact side (background subtracted) at every anteroposterior level in the mean over mice, partially reproduced when it is reduced at every level but not below 10%. The 10% bound is set here, as the paper gives none; the measured ratio is reported.

claims.statement: Anxa1+ and DAT+ axons in dCP ramp up before a water drop, peak at contact with it, and return quickly to baseline during water consumption.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DANs do not encode motivational value, paragraph 1; Figure 3D
claims.quote: Recordings showed that the Anxa1+ as well as the DAT+ axons in dCP exhibited a ramping activity that peaked upon contact with the water droplet, followed by a rapid return to baseline during water consumption
claims.criterion: Z-scored signals aligned to the water drop touch; per recording, the mean over touches of the AUC in three windows; RM one-way ANOVA (Geisser-Greenhouse corrected, as the fractional degrees of freedom show) with Sidak's post hoc, the recording as unit (legend). The first window is the baseline (legend of 3F-G). The window edges are drawn only in Figure 3D, which was not seen; they are open. Readings are (a) 1 s windows, -2 to -1, -1 to 0 and 0 to 1 s from touch, the width the paper uses for motif AUC in Figure 4, and (b) 2 s windows, -4 to -2, -2 to 0 and 0 to 2 s. Reproduced when, under a reading, the Anxa1 ANOVA has p < 0.05 and AUC is larger in the second window than the third at Sidak p < 0.05, and the DAT ANOVA has p < 0.05 with the second window larger than the first. A reader may be asked for the edges from the figure. The event is "the water drop touch" (legend) and "contact with the water droplet" (Results); the paper names no event types. Readings are (i) correct (drop retrieved) touches only and (ii) every contact with a drop (correct, drop and semidrop); empty-spout events are not touches of a drop and are excluded in both. Each window reading is run with both. The paper gives no rule for which recordings enter (legend n of 10, 4, 13 and 11) and does not say whether "Artifacts and instances of signal intensity loss were excluded" (Methods) drops whole recordings or stretches of signal. Every recording of the group and site with at least one event is used; the n used is reported against the legend's, and a per-mouse summary is reported, not judged.

claims.statement: DA release in dCP follows the same ramp-and-drop dynamics as Anxa1+ axons, while in cCP it shows a classical reward-related profile, ramping before contact and peaking during consumption before returning to baseline.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DANs do not encode motivational value, paragraph 1; Figure 3E
claims.quote: Similarly, the recorded DA signals in the dCP showed the same dynamics ... In contrast, recordings from the cCP revealed a typical reward-related phasic DA release profile, showing a ramping signal before droplet contact with a peak during reward consumption that then returned to baseline
claims.criterion: As in fig3d-anxa1-ramp-to-touch, with the same window, event and recording readings. Reproduced when, under a reading, dLight-dCP has ANOVA p < 0.05 and the second window larger than the third at Sidak p < 0.05, and dLight-cCP has ANOVA p < 0.05 with both the second and third windows larger than the first at Sidak p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Against the baseline window, the legend lists three AUC changes, the second window of DAT GCaMP-dCP (p = 0.0308) and of dLight-cCP (p = 0.0028) and the third window of dLight-cCP (p = 0.0148), with only the dLight-cCP second window marked significant; the other groups and windows are not listed.
claims.source: Figure 3F and 3G
claims.criterion: Per recording, the AUC of the second and of the third window minus that of the first; one-sample two-tailed t-test against 0, Bonferroni corrected over the eight tests (four groups, two windows), window, event and recording readings as in fig3d-anxa1-ramp-to-touch. Only dLight-cCP second carries an asterisk in the legend; whether the printed p are corrected, and over how many tests, is open. The single asterisk fits printed raw p with Bonferroni over eight tests (all groups and windows) or over four (the groups, per window); both families are run. Reproduced when, under a window reading, the dLight-cCP second-window change is positive and significant after Bonferroni under a family, and the other two listed changes are positive; their raw and corrected p and the other five tests are reported.

claims.statement: Optogenetic activation of DAT+ neurons strongly reinforces self-stimulation in the first two days, while activation of Anxa1+ DANs does not.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DANs do not encode motivational value, paragraph 2; Figure 3I and 3J
claims.quote: We found that optogenetic activation of DAT+ neurons strongly reinforced self-stimulation during the first two days of the task ... In contrast, optogenetic activation of the Anxa1+ DANs did not support self-stimulation behavior
claims.criterion: Days 1 and 2 (right port active). Active pokes per mouse over the two days (sum or mean give the same ranks, so the choice cannot change the outcome). Preference is not defined in the text; readings are (a) active over total pokes and (b) active minus inactive pokes. Kruskal- Wallis over the three groups with Dunn's post hoc. Reproduced when, under a reading of preference, both Kruskal-Wallis tests have p < 0.05, DAT-ChRmine exceeds both other groups at Dunn p < 0.05 for active pokes and for preference against Anxa1-ChRmine, and Anxa1-ChRmine does not differ from Ctrl-Tdtomato.

claims.statement: When the active port is reversed, DAT-ChRmine mice quickly switch to the newly active left port, while Anxa1-ChRmine mice develop no significant preference for the active port in the last reversal days.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DANs do not encode motivational value, paragraph 2; Figure 3K and 3L
claims.quote: When active and inactive port assignment was reversed, DAT-Cre mice quickly reversed their responding from the inactive (right) to the active (left) port ... mice did not develop any significant preference for the active port during the last days of the reversal
claims.criterion: The legend does not say which group the RM two-way ANOVA and Friedman test belong to; F(4, 32) fits 9 mice over five days, so the reading is DAT-ChRmine, days -1 and 1 to 4 (the other reading, all six days, is run as well). Per group, RM two-way ANOVA side by day on left and right pokes with Sidak's post hoc, and Friedman test on preference over days with Dunn's post hoc, preference read as in fig3i. Reproduced when for DAT-ChRmine the interaction has p < 0.05 and the Friedman test has p < 0.05 with preference changed from day -1 to day 1, and, as a claim of absence, Anxa1-ChRmine shows no left against right difference at Sidak p < 0.05 on reversal days 3 and 4.

claims.statement: Mice with silenced Anxa1+ DANs show no significant change in total nosepokes in the FR5 or PR stages.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DANs do not encode motivational value, paragraph 2; Figure 3M to 3O
claims.quote: Mice with genetic silencing of Anxa1+ DANs exhibited no significant changes in the total number of nosepokes during FR5 or PR tasks
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The legend names no test and no n; the Methods' test for two groups is the two-sided unpaired t-test, used here. Total pokes per mouse over the two FR5 days and over the two PR days, Anxa1-TeTx against control. Reproduced when neither comparison reaches p < 0.05; the difference and its size are reported.

claims.statement: Anxa1+ axonal activity in the dCP correlates positively with linear speed during open field exploration, above a shuffled control, and DA release in dCP shows a similar correlation.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN projections are activated during vigorous actions, paragraph 1; Figure 4B
claims.quote: We found a significant positive correlation between Anxa1+ axonal activity in the dCP and linear speed, and this correlation was similar when we recorded DA release in the dCP
claims.criterion: Per recording, the correlation over the 20 min session of the z-scored FP signal with linear speed, against the same with the signal shuffled; two-sided paired t-test over recordings (legend). Pearson's r, the paper's R. Open, (1) the shuffle, read as (a) a random permutation of samples and (b) a circular shift by a random lag; (2) the time base, the FP signal at 60 fps averaged onto the 30 fps video frames, a standard choice; (3) speed as in the header. Reproduced when, under a reading, both groups have a mean correlation above 0 and above the shuffle at p < 0.05. The printed p equal the exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank p when all 9 (or 8) recordings lie on one side (2/512 and 2/256); the Wilcoxon test is run as a variant. DAT GCaMP-dCP (5 mice, 7 recordings) has no p in the legend and is reported.

claims.statement: DA release in the cCP correlates negatively with locomotion speed.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN projections are activated during vigorous actions, paragraph 1; Figure 4B
claims.quote: The recorded DA release in cCP instead showed a negative correlation with locomotion speed
claims.criterion: As in fig4b-speed-correlation-dcp. Reproduced when the mean dLight-cCP correlation is below 0 and below the shuffle at p < 0.05 under a reading (p = 0.016 equals the exact Wilcoxon p 2/128 for 7 recordings on one side; Wilcoxon as a variant).

claims.statement: Unsupervised VAME analysis of open field pose identifies 37 kinematic motifs, grouped into action categories.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN projections are activated during vigorous actions, paragraph 2; Figure 4C; Methods, Behavioral analysis
claims.quote: This unsupervised analysis of postural dynamics identified 37 kinematic motifs, which we categorized into seven communities of actions
claims.criterion: A count of the distinct motif labels in the paper's motif labelling (header). The tolerance is 0, as a label set is counted exactly. The text names seven communities while the legend of Figure 4C names six categories (Stationary/Sniffing, Turn, Rear, Groom, Walk, Sniff/Walk) and Figure 5G five; the category of each motif is drawn only in Figure 4C and is taken from the dataset if it holds it, otherwise it is open.

claims.statement: Anxa1+ axon activity is associated with the onset of high-speed motifs regardless of action type, as is DA in dCP, while DA in cCP rises strongly after the onset of low-speed motifs.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN projections are activated during vigorous actions, paragraph 2; Figure 4D and 4E; Figure S3
claims.quote: This analysis demonstrated that the activity of Anxa1+ projections was associated with high-speed motifs independently of the action type, and this profile was also observed in DA signals recorded in the dCP ... However, DA signals recorded in the cCP demonstrated a different pattern with strong activation after the onset of low-speed motifs
claims.criterion: Mean z-scored signal aligned to each motif onset (first frame of a run of that label), motifs ranked by mean linear speed. Judged by fig4f-auc-correlations and fig4h-auc-motif-speed; in addition, reproduced for "independently of the action type" when, within at least two action categories, the Spearman correlation of Anxa1 AUC (0 to 1 s) with motif speed is positive, and for cCP when its AUC correlates negatively with motif speed. Spearman within categories is set here, as the paper gives no test for this sentence.

claims.statement: Across motifs, the onset AUC of Anxa1+ terminal activity correlates positively with that of dLight in dCP (R = 0.70) and negatively with that of dLight in cCP (R = -0.52).
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN projections are activated during vigorous actions, paragraph 2; Figure 4F and 4G
claims.quote: the area under the curve (AUC, 0 to 1 sec) calculated for each motif from Anxa1-terminal activity showed a positive correlation with the AUC of dLight signals recorded in the dCP (Figure 4F) and a negative correlation with the AUC of dLight signals recorded in the cCP
claims.criterion: Per motif, the AUC from 0 to 1 s after onset of the z-scored signal (legend), then Pearson's R over motifs between groups. Open, how traces are averaged; readings are (a) all onsets of all recordings of a group pooled, then the mean trace, and (b) the mean per recording, then the mean over recordings. Whether a pre-onset baseline is subtracted is open; readings are (i) the AUC of the z-scored trace as is and (ii) minus its mean over -1 to 0 s. Reproduced when, under a reading, both R are within tolerance and p < 0.01.

claims.statement: The onset AUC of Anxa1+ terminal activity is highly correlated with mean motif linear speed across motifs (R = 0.83).
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN projections are activated during vigorous actions, paragraph 2; Figure 4H
claims.quote: Furthermore, the AUC from Anxa1-terminal activity was highly positively correlated with motif speed
claims.criterion: AUC readings as in fig4f-auc-correlations; motif speed is the mean linear speed over the frames of the motif (legend of 4H), over the Anxa1 recordings or over all mice of the motif set, both run. Reproduced when R is within tolerance and p < 0.01 under a reading.

claims.statement: Anxa1-TeTx mice show moderate reductions in linear and angular speed in the open field, with a slight increase in immobility time.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN silencing produces a prodromal PD bradykinetic profile, paragraph 1; Figure 5B to 5E
claims.quote: we found that Anxa1-tetanus mice showed moderate reductions in linear and angular speed, accompanied by a slight increase in immobility time
claims.criterion: Per mouse, mean linear speed, mean angular speed and immobility time over the open field session; two-sided unpaired t-test against Ctrl-Tdtomato (legend). Speed and immobility as in the header. Reproduced when linear and angular speed are lower at p < 0.05 and immobility is higher; partially reproduced when one speed is lower at p < 0.05. Which panels carry asterisks is in the figure, not seen (the legend gives only the key *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, with n = 18 Ctrl-Tdtomato and 14 Anxa1-TeTx); the p of immobility is reported.

claims.statement: The mild locomotor phenotype and acceleration distribution of Anxa1-silenced mice resemble the early-stage PD models (mild 6-OHDA, MP-early), consistent with a bradykinetic and not an akinetic/rigid profile.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN silencing produces a prodromal PD bradykinetic profile, paragraph 1; Figure 5C to 5F; Figure S4
claims.quote: The mild locomotor phenotype and acceleration distribution pattern in Axna1-silenced mice was similar to the early-stage PD models suggesting that loss of Anxa1+ DANs is linked primarily to a bradykinetic
claims.criterion: No test of similarity is given. For each experimental group, the change of mean linear speed, mean angular speed and immobility against its own control (in percent of the control mean), and the acceleration density (legend of 5F). Reproduced when the changes of Anxa1-TeTx lie within the range spanned by 6OHDA-low and MP-early, or closer to theirs than to MP-middle's, for at least two of the three measures. The rule is set here; the values, including those of MP-middle, are reported.

claims.statement: In a PCA of motif usage, PC1 separates the groups by PD stage, with Anxa1-TeTx mice between the early and middle PD models, and PC2 separates middle-stage MitoPark mice from the others.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN silencing produces a prodromal PD bradykinetic profile, paragraph 2; Figure 5G
claims.quote: We found that the first principal component (PC1) effectively separated the groups according to PD stage (Figure 5G). The motif usage profile of Anxa1-tetanus mice positioned them between early and middle PD models along the PC1 axis ... PC2 separated middle-stage MitoPark mice from the other groups
claims.criterion: PCA of per-mouse motif usage time (37 motifs) over all mice of the eight groups. Open, the scaling; readings are (a) standardized usage (Prism's default) and (b) centred only; usage as fraction of session time (equal sessions make seconds equivalent). The sign of a PC is arbitrary and is set so that MP-middle has the largest group mean. Reproduced when, under a reading, the group mean PC1 of Anxa1-TeTx lies between the means of the early models (6OHDA- low, MP-early) and MP-middle, controls lie on the low side, and the MP-middle mean on PC2 lies farther from the mean of all other groups than any other group's mean.

claims.statement: Walk and stationary motifs lie at opposite extremes of PC1 in the loading plot.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN silencing produces a prodromal PD bradykinetic profile, paragraph 2; Figure 5H
claims.quote: “Walk” and “stationary” motifs were prominently represented at the opposite extremes of the PC1 axis
claims.criterion: Loadings of PC1 per motif, readings of fig5g. Reproduced when, under a reading, the five highest-loading motifs on one end are mostly walk motifs and the five on the other end are mostly stationary motifs. Motif categories from the dataset, else open (fig4c-vame-motifs).

claims.statement: Motif PC1 values correlate negatively with mean motif speed (R = -0.762), while PC2 shows no significant correlation (R = -0.1494, p = 0.3772), nor do PC3 and PC4.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN silencing produces a prodromal PD bradykinetic profile, paragraph 2; Figure 5I; Figure S5
claims.quote: linear regression analysis between motif speed and PC1 eigenvalues revealed a significant negative correlation (Figure 5I). In contrast, we did not observe any significant correlation between the eigenvalues of PC2 (Figure 5I), PC3, PC4 and motif speed
claims.criterion: Per motif, the PC1 (and PC2 to PC4) loading, called eigenvalue in the paper, against mean motif linear speed over all mice; Pearson R. The printed p = 0.3772 for R = -0.1494 fits 37 motifs. A PC's sign is arbitrary, so the magnitude is judged and the sign reported, with PC1 oriented as in fig5g. Reproduced when, under a reading of fig5g, |R| for PC1 is within tolerance with p < 0.0001, and PC2, PC3 and PC4 each have p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Anxa1-silenced mice show significant downregulation of five high-speed motifs (42, 34, 16, 0 and 25), not of all vigorous high-speed motifs.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN silencing produces a prodromal PD bradykinetic profile, paragraph 3; Figure 5J
claims.quote: Specifically, we found that Anxa1-silenced mice displayed significant downregulation of five high-speed motifs (42, 34, 16, 0 and 25)
claims.criterion: Per mouse, usage time of each of the 37 motifs; Anxa1-TeTx against Ctrl-Tdtomato, two-sided unpaired t-test per motif, Holm-Sidak adjusted over the 37 motifs at alpha 0.05 (legend). Motif numbers are the paper's labels. Reproduced when exactly these five motifs are reduced at adjusted p < 0.05; partially reproduced when at least three of them are and no more than one other motif is changed.

claims.statement: Motifs 42 and 34 are reduced in all PD models; motifs 0 and 25 are reduced among the models only in middle-stage MitoPark mice; stationary motifs 3, 39, 27 and 28 are increased only in middle-stage MitoPark mice.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN silencing produces a prodromal PD bradykinetic profile, paragraph 3; Figure 5J
claims.quote: we found a subset of motifs that were significantly reduced across all the PD models (motifs 42 and 34), while another subset was reduced only in the middle-staged MitoPark group (motif 0 and 25 ... the stationary-related motifs (3, 39, 27, and 28) were significantly increased only in the middle-stage MitoPark group
claims.criterion: As in fig5j-tetx-five-motifs, each model against its own control (6OHDA-low against Ctrl-Asc Acid, MP-early against Ctrl-early, MP-middle against Ctrl-middle). "All the PD models" is read as (a) the three disease models and (b) these with Anxa1-TeTx. Reproduced when, under a reading, 42 and 34 are reduced in each, 0 and 25 are reduced in MP-middle and in no other disease model, and 3, 39, 27 and 28 are increased in MP-middle and in no other group. Partially reproduced when two of the three parts hold.

claims.statement: Anxa1+ DAN silencing has no major effect on the overall structure of motif sequences, but the reduced high-speed walk motifs form a small network of high-probability transitions (motif 0 to 16 to 34).
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DAN silencing produces a prodromal PD bradykinetic profile, paragraph 4; Figure 5K to 5M; Figure S5
claims.quote: We did not observe any major effects in the overall structure of motif sequences after Anxa1+ DANs silencing (Figure S5); however, we identified that the significantly reduced high-speed “walk” motifs formed a small network with high-probability transition connections (motif 0 -> motif 16 -> motif 34
claims.criterion: Transition probability from one motif to the next different motif, from the motif label sequence (self-transitions excluded, as in VAME's transition matrix; including them is a variant), pooled over control mice (Ctrl-Tdtomato). Reproduced when the probability from 0 to 16 is the highest from motif 0 among walk motifs, and that from 16 to 34 the highest from motif 16 among walk motifs. The legend's n = 3 mice for Figure 5M does not match n = 14 in Figure 5C, and the "overall structure" test is in Figure S5, not read; the Fisher's exact tests per transition on pooled transition counts, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted, are run on all mice and reported.

claims.statement: In the arrow maze, Anxa1-silenced mice show only a small decrease in linear speed on the fourth day and no change in immobility time.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DANs are necessary for procedural motor learning, paragraph 1; Figure 6C; Figure S6
claims.quote: we found that Anxa1-silenced mice displayed only minor changes in locomotion, showing a small decrease in linear speed on the fourth day of the test without any changes in immobility time
claims.criterion: Per mouse and day (days 1 and 4), mean linear speed and immobility time over the 10 min session; RM two-way ANOVA group by day with Sidak's post hoc. Reproduced when the speed group effect has p < 0.05 with Anxa1-TeTx slower, the Sidak test is p < 0.05 on day 4 only, and, as a claim of absence on the same test, immobility shows no group effect and no Sidak difference at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Control mice learn to prefer the rewarded arm over four days, while Anxa1-silenced mice show no increase in preference for the rewarded arm.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DANs are necessary for procedural motor learning, paragraph 1; Figure 6B and 6D left
claims.quote: Control mice successfully learned the basic task strategy over the four days, as evidenced by a significant increase in the preference for the rewarded arm ... However, mice with silenced Anxa1+ DANs failed to show any increase in the preference for the rewarded arm
claims.criterion: Per mouse and day, the number of rewarded transitions (centre to the left, rewarded, end zone) minus error transitions (centre to the right end zone), from the Bonsai end-zone entries, days 1 and 4; RM two-way ANOVA group by day with Sidak's post hoc. The legend's "Day 1 vs. Day 2" is read as the first against the fourth day, the days plotted. Reproduced when the interaction has p < 0.05, controls increase from day 1 to day 4 at Sidak p < 0.05, Ctrl exceeds Anxa1-TeTx on day 4 at Sidak p < 0.05, and Anxa1-TeTx do not increase at p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Control mice improve task efficiency (reward relative to distance traveled) over the four days, while Anxa1-silenced mice do not.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DANs are necessary for procedural motor learning, paragraph 1; Figure 6D right; Figure S6
claims.quote: a significant increase in task efficiency quantified as the received reward relative to the traveled distance ... and did not improve their motor efficiency in the task
claims.criterion: Per mouse and day, rewards received divided by distance traveled (Results), days 1 and 4; whether the central initiation drops count as rewards is open, readings (a) lateral rewards only and (b) all drops. RM two-way ANOVA group by day with Sidak's post hoc. Reproduced when, under a reading, the interaction has p < 0.05, controls rise from day 1 to day 4 at Sidak p < 0.05, Anxa1-TeTx do not, and Ctrl exceeds Anxa1-TeTx on day 4 at Sidak p < 0.05. The legend's two group differences (p = 0.0027 and p < 0.0001) imply a difference on day 1 as well; it is reported.

claims.statement: Control mice improve reaching accuracy over four sessions; Anxa1-TeTx mice have normal accuracy in the first session but fail to improve, and Anxa1-Arch mice show reduced accuracy during the last three sessions with optogenetic inhibition.
claims.source: Results, Anxa1+ DANs are necessary for procedural motor learning, paragraph 2; Figure 6H to 6J; Figure S6
claims.quote: As expected, control mice improved their reaching accuracy over the four training sessions ... In contrast, Anxa1-tetanus mice exhibited normal accuracy during the first session but failed to refine their grasping movements in subsequent sessions ... as Anxa1-Arch mice showed a significant reduction in reaching accuracy during the last three sessions
claims.criterion: Per mouse and session, the fraction of grasp attempts with the preferred forelimb whose measured distance from the target is within a threshold (Results; distances measured by hand in Kinovea). The threshold is given as < 0.2 cm in the Results and < 0.1 cm in the legend of 6J; both are run. RM two-way ANOVA group by day on days 1 and 4 with Sidak's post hoc. Reproduced when, under a reading, the interaction has p < 0.05, controls improve from day 1 to day 4 at Sidak p < 0.05, controls exceed both Anxa1-TeTx and Anxa1-Arch on day 4 at Sidak p < 0.05, and Anxa1-TeTx does not differ from controls on day 1. The residual df of 14 fits 17 mice with both days, one fewer than 8 + 4 + 6; which mouse was left out is not given, so all 18 are used and each single exclusion is shown as a variant. The paper does not define a grasp attempt by event type. It describes a reaching attempt as start, "grasping upon contact with the water droplet" and retraction (Results), and Figure 6F shows on- and off-target efforts. The readings are (a) every labelled reach with a distance, and (b) all but empty-spout and unknown events. The preferred forelimb is not defined; readings are (i) per mouse over all its sessions, (ii) per session. Day 1 and day 4 are the first and fourth of four consecutive training sessions after habituation (Methods); the paper does not map these to session labels, so the first and fourth training sessions of each mouse are used. For Arch, the laser is off on day 1 and on during days 2 to 4 (Methods, Results); a session labelled otherwise is reported as departing from the paper. The legend has one control group (Ctrl, n = 8) in a single ANOVA with both silenced groups, so the controls are one pooled group; the paper does not say from which cohort they come, and controls of both cohorts are pooled. Mice recorded after the preprint (22 December 2024) cannot be in the figure; the main run uses mice recorded before it, all mice with both days are a variant.

claims.statement: WT pairs reach significantly higher match (coordination) rates than Fmr1 pairs under both the 100% and the 50% reward contingency.
claims.source: Figure 1E and legend; Results, A spatial cooperation task for social coordination in rat pairs
claims.quote: WT pairs demonstrated significantly higher coordination rates than both Fmr1 pairs ( Fig. 1 E , I )
claims.criterion: Per pair and session, the match rate, a match being a simultaneous nose-poke of the two rats at corresponding wells (Methods, Cooperative learning task), counted under rate readings r1 and r2 of the opening comment; WT and Fmr1 pairs, first 21 sessions at 100% and first 35 at 50% (Methods, Behavioral quantification). The genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under readings A and B of the opening comment. Reproduced when, in both contingencies, the genotype effect has p < 0.05 with the WT mean higher.

claims.statement: Fmr1 rats make fewer task-related arm transitions than WT rats (they are slower in the task), under both contingencies.
claims.source: Figure 1F and legend; Results, A spatial cooperation task for social coordination in rat pairs
claims.quote: Fmr1 and mixed pairs were generally slower in the task, as reflected by a reduced number of task-related transitions ( Fig. 1 F , G ; Fig. S1 D )
claims.criterion: Per rat and session, the number of transitions (visits to a well other than the rat's previous one), under rate readings r1 and r2; rats of the WT and Fmr1 pairs; first 21 and first 35 sessions. The genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under readings A and B, with rats as units (the df show 20 rats). Reproduced when, in both contingencies, p < 0.05 with the WT mean higher.

claims.statement: In the 50% condition, match rate rises linearly with transition rate in both genotypes, with a steeper slope and a better fit in WT (beta 0.79, R2 0.74) than in Fmr1 (beta 0.64, R2 0.44).
claims.source: Figure 1G legend
claims.quote: Linear regression between cooperative match event rates and transition rates for 50% reward condition
claims.criterion: An ordinary least-squares regression of match rate on transition rate per genotype, first 35 sessions at 50%. The legend gives n = 35 sessions, but its p-values imply far more points than 35, and the units of the rates are not given. Readings of the points are (a) one per pair and session, with the pair's summed transitions; (b) one per rat and session, the rat's transitions against its pair's matches; (c) one per session, pairs averaged; each under rate readings r1 and r2. Reproduced when, under one reading, both slopes and both R2 values are within tolerance and both regressions have p < 0.05; partially reproduced when both are significant with WT having the higher slope and R2 but the values are out of tolerance.

claims.statement: Both WT and Fmr1 pairs coordinate no better than chance early in training, and above chance late in training, by a permutation test that circularly shifts one rat's sequence of well visits.
claims.source: Figure 1H and legend; Results, A spatial cooperation task for social coordination in rat pairs
claims.quote: Both WT and Fmr1 rat pairs exhibited performance indistinguishable from chance during early training on both reward contingency tasks; however, by late training, their performance improved significantly, exceeding chance levels ( Fig. 1 H , I )
claims.criterion: Per pair and session, performance (Eq. 1) against a null from 1,000 circular time shifts of one rat's whole sequence of reward well visits within the session, p being the fraction of shifts whose performance equals or exceeds the observed one (Methods, Permutation testing of coordination performance). Open, not fixed by the paper are which rat is shifted (the readings, the first rat as the dataset orders them, and the second; the result is reported for both) and the range of shifts (a uniform random shift over the session length is the standard choice). The paper shows one pair per genotype. "Early" and "late" can be read as (a) the first session at 100% and the last analysed session at 50%, as the legend's examples; (b) the first and last analysed session of each contingency, as the Results say. The Results state it for "Both WT and Fmr1 rat pairs", that is every pair. The early and late readings name which sessions the paper means, and one of them suffices; the shifted-rat readings are a method detail, and the outcome must hold under both of them, else the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified. Reproduced when every pair of both genotypes has p >= 0.05 in the early session(s) and p < 0.05 in the late session(s); partially reproduced when that holds in at least 3 of 5 pairs per genotype, or when the late sessions are above chance in every pair but the early ones are too.

claims.statement: Cooperative performance (matches relative to transitions, Eq. 1) is significantly lower in Fmr1 pairs than in WT pairs under both contingencies, so their impairment is not only due to slower transitions.
claims.source: Figure 1I and legend; Results, A spatial cooperation task for social coordination in rat pairs
claims.quote: Performance metrics for WT and Fmr1 −/y pairs in 100% (left) and 50% (right) reward contingencies shows significant impairment in Fmr1 −/y pairs compared with WT pairs
claims.criterion: Performance per pair and session as Eq. 1 (opening comment), first 21 and first 35 sessions; the genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under readings A and B. Reproduced when, in both contingencies, p < 0.05 with the WT mean higher.

claims.statement: A multinomial logistic regression predicts a rat's next choice from its partner's current location above chance in both genotypes, and more accurately in WT than in Fmr1 rats, under both contingencies.
claims.source: Figure 1J and legend; Results, A spatial cooperation task for social coordination in rat pairs
claims.quote: This predictive relationship exceeded chance levels across all rat pairs. However, prediction accuracy was significantly higher in WT pairs compared with both Fmr1 and mixed-genotype pairs
claims.criterion: As in the Methods (Multinomial logistic regression and cross-validation), per rat and contingency, a scikit-learn multinomial logistic regression (default settings, the standard choice) of the rat's next well on the partner's current well, one-hot encoded, scored by accuracy averaged over fivefold stratified cross-validation; the null is 1,000 independent shuffles of the two vectors with the cross-validation repeated, each rat's null value being its mean shuffled accuracy; groups compared with a two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test; 10 WT and 10 Fmr1 rats (U = 100 implies 10 per group). Open, not fixed by the paper is the moment at which the partner's location is read. Readings are the partner's well (a) when the focal rat leaves its current well; (b) at the focal rat's last poke before the choice; (c) at the moment the focal rat arrives at its next well. Also open is whether a rat's sessions of a contingency are pooled (reading p1, as "for each rat individually" suggests) or scored per session and averaged (p2). Reproduced when, under every reading, in both contingencies real accuracy exceeds shuffled in each genotype (p < 0.05) and WT real accuracy exceeds Fmr1 real accuracy (p < 0.05); blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree.

claims.statement: Mixed WT-Fmr1 pairs also reach lower coordination rates and performance, make fewer transitions and have lower partner-based prediction accuracy than WT pairs.
claims.source: Results, A spatial cooperation task for social coordination in rat pairs; Figure S1A to S1D (not read)
claims.quote: WT pairs demonstrated significantly higher coordination rates than both Fmr1 pairs ( Fig. 1 E , I ) and mixed pairs ( Fig. S1 A ) under both 100% and 50% reward contingencies ... prediction accuracy was significantly higher in WT pairs compared with both Fmr1 and mixed-genotype pairs
claims.criterion: The tests of Figure S1 are in the supplement, which was not read. The readings are the tests of the matching Figure 1 panels, with mixed pairs in place of Fmr1 pairs, as in fig1e-match-rate-wt-higher, fig1f-transition-rate-wt-higher, fig1i-performance-wt-higher and fig1j-partner-location-predicts-choice, each under the readings named there. Reproduced when, in both contingencies, WT exceeds mixed pairs with p < 0.05 for match rate and for prediction accuracy; partially reproduced when that holds in one contingency. Transitions and performance are reported.

claims.statement: Replacing the transparent divider with an opaque one (with white noise) lowers the performance of WT and Fmr1 pairs compared with standard 50% sessions, with no genotype difference in this effect.
claims.source: Figure 2B and legend; Results, Cooperation deficits in Fmr1 rats are not due to sensory or learning deficits
claims.quote: Compared with the 50% reward condition, rats showed a significant reduction in performance in the SD sessions ( Fig. 2 B , C )
claims.criterion: Performance per session as Eq. 1. Per pair, the mean over its SD sessions and the mean over its transparent 50% sessions, these being the last 9 transparent sessions (legend, right panel); a mixed-design ANOVA (genotype between, condition within, pair as subject; the df F(1,4) fit 6 pairs) and a paired t test per genotype. Open for the left panel is which transparent sessions are compared; readings are (a) the last 9 transparent sessions, (b) the transparent sessions interspersed with the SD sessions. Reproduced when, under one reading, the condition effect has p < 0.05 with SD lower, both paired t tests have p < 0.05 with SD lower, and the genotype x condition interaction of the same ANOVA has p >= 0.05 (the absence part, judged on that test); partially reproduced when the condition effect holds but a paired test does not, or the interaction is significant.

claims.statement: In mixed pairs the opaque barrier also lowers performance (condition effect with WT pairs), though the paired test within mixed pairs is not significant.
claims.source: Figure 2C and legend
claims.quote: Comparison of mean performance of rat pairs between standard and sensory-deprived conditions
claims.criterion: As fig2b-opaque-barrier-lowers-performance, with the 3 WT pairs and 5 mixed pairs. Reproduced when the condition effect has p < 0.05 with SD lower; the mixed-pair paired t test is reported with its p (the paper's is not significant).

claims.statement: Both WT and Fmr1 rats learn the visual cue-reward association task; performance rises over sessions at 100% reward, and there is no significant genotype effect or genotype x session interaction at 100% or 50%. The Results also say Fmr1 rats learned more slowly, which the reported interaction tests do not show.
claims.source: Figure 2E and legend; Results, Cooperation deficits in Fmr1 rats are not due to sensory or learning deficits
claims.quote: Both WT and Fmr1 rats learnt to approach the reward-associated arm based on the visual cue ( Fig. 2 E ), demonstrating intact visual cue-reward associative learning
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Percent correct per rat and session; per contingency a linear mixed-effects model with genotype, session (continuous, as the df of 1 show) and their interaction as fixed effects and a random intercept per rat (legend, Figure 2), F tests with Satterthwaite df (the fractional df). Reproduced when the genotype effect has p >= 0.05 in both contingencies and the session effect at 100% has p < 0.05 with performance rising; not reproduced when the genotype effect is significant. The genotype x session terms are reported. The Methods give p = 0.981 for genotype in a model with contingency as a factor; that model (rat random intercept, session, genotype and contingency fixed) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: In the visual-cue task WT rats respond to the cue with shorter latency than Fmr1 rats over pooled responses (100%, 22.0 against 42.2 s; 50%, 14.0 against 28.4 s); in the session-wise mixed-effects models with rat as random intercept the genotype effect is not significant (p = 0.058 at 100%, 0.064 at 50%).
claims.source: Figure 2F and legend
claims.quote: WT rats respond to the visual LED cue with lower latency relative to Fmr1 −/y rats under both 100% (left) and 50% (right) reward contingencies
claims.criterion: Latency from cue onset to the correct poke, pooled over responses of all rats of a genotype (the n are responses), two-sided Mann-Whitney U test per contingency. Open is whether latency is counted to the correct poke only (the Methods say "latency to correct choice") or to any poke; the reading is the correct poke, with any poke shown as a variant. Reproduced when both tests have p < 0.05 with WT shorter and the means are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the tests hold but a mean is out of tolerance. The session-wise latency models of the legend (genotype, session and their interaction fixed, random intercept per rat, per contingency) are run and reported; they are not the basis of the outcome.

claims.statement: Under 100% reward rats mostly alternate between two arms, while under 50% they explore all three arms through the optimal 1-2-3 or 1-3-2 triplets, especially WT rats.
claims.source: Figure 3B and 3C; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: Parsing each session's transitions into nonoverlapping triplets revealed that rats in the 100% condition predominantly alternated between two adjacent arms, while those in the 50% condition engaged in comprehensive exploration of all three arms through either the 1-2-3 or 1-3-2 sequences, especially for WT pairs
claims.criterion: The paper shows example rats and gives no test. Per rat and session, the choice sequence (opening comment) cut into consecutive nonoverlapping triplets from its first visit (Methods, Choice triplet counts); the fraction of optimal triplets. The Methods list eight possible triplets, though twelve without a repeated well exist (2-1-3, 2-3-1, 3-1-2 and 3-2-1 are missing), and name 1-2-3 and 1-3-2 as optimal because they visit all three wells. Readings are (o1) every triplet that visits all three wells is optimal, as the rationale says; (o2) only the literal 1-2-3 and 1-3-2. Per rat, over all its triplets of the first 21 (100%) or first 35 (50%) sessions, the fraction of alternation triplets (x-y-x, the same under both readings) and the fraction of optimal triplets. The paper gives no number for "predominantly"; it is read as more than half. Reproduced when, under every reading, the median WT and median Fmr1 alternation fractions at 100% exceed 0.5, the median WT optimal fraction at 50% exceeds the WT median at 100%, and the WT median optimal fraction at 50% exceeds the Fmr1 median at 50%; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. The fractions per rat are reported.

claims.statement: The entropy of WT rats' choice sequences is lower than that of Fmr1 rats, a genotype effect under both contingencies. The legend describes a larger decrease with learning in WT rats, but the genotype x session interaction is not significant at either contingency.
claims.source: Figure 3D and legend; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: Session-wise comparison of entropy of choice sequences of WT and Fmr1 −/y rats during 100% (left) and 50% (right) reward contingencies, showing significantly higher decrease in entropy with learning for WT rats
claims.criterion: Per rat and session, the sample entropy of the full choice sequence (Methods). The embedding dimension m and tolerance r are not given; with wells coded 1, 2, 3 any r below 1 means exact matching, the usual r = 0.2 SD falls there, and readings are m = 2 (the standard) and m = 3 (the triplet unit of the Methods), with r = 0.2 times the sequence SD. The genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under readings A and B, first 21 and first 35 sessions. Reproduced when, under every reading, in both contingencies the genotype effect has p < 0.05 with WT entropy lower; partially reproduced when, under every reading, that holds in the 50% contingency only; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. The slope of entropy over sessions per genotype and the genotype x session terms are reported.

claims.statement: WT rats have higher exploration efficiency (fraction of optimal choice triplets) than Fmr1 rats, strongly in the 50% condition and modestly in the 100% condition.
claims.source: Figure 3E and legend; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: Exploration efficiencies of WT and Fmr1 −/y rats during 100% (left) and 50% (right) contingency sessions, showing significantly higher exploration efficiency for WT rats in the 50% condition
claims.criterion: Exploration efficiency per rat and session (Methods, Eq. 2), the number of optimal triplets over all nonoverlapping triplets, under the readings o1 and o2 of optimal named in fig3c-triplets-by-contingency; the genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under readings A and B; first 21 sessions at 100%, and at 50% the first 33 and first 35 sessions. Reproduced when at 50% the genotype effect has p < 0.05 with WT higher under every reading; the 100% result is reported and, if also p < 0.05 with WT higher, the claim is reproduced in full, otherwise partially.

claims.statement: When foraging with a virtual agent under a 50% contingency, WT and Fmr1 rats perform alike.
claims.source: Figure 3G and legend; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: In this task, both WT and Fmr1 rats achieved similar levels of task performance with comparable learning rates ( Fig. 3 G )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Percent of correct rewarded responses per rat and session (Methods), 8 sessions; the genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under reading A, the test the reported df show (as an absence claim it is judged on that test alone; reading B is shown as a variant), and a Mann-Whitney U test on per-rat means. Reproduced when the genotype effect has p >= 0.05; not reproduced when it is significant. The Mann-Whitney result and the group means are reported.

claims.statement: With a virtual agent, WT and Fmr1 rats have similar exploration efficiency; both adopt structured transition strategies.
claims.source: Figure 3H and legend; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: Notably, both genotypes independently demonstrated the capacity to adopt such structured transition strategies when interacting with the virtual agent ( Fig. 3 H )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Exploration efficiency per rat and session as in fig3e-exploration-efficiency-wt-higher (optimal as reading o1, the Methods' rationale, with o2 shown as a variant); the genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under reading A, the test the reported df show (reading B shown as a variant). Reproduced when the genotype effect has p >= 0.05; not reproduced when it is significant. The group means are reported.

claims.statement: Within pairs, choice sequences are similar for both genotypes under 100% reward, but under 50% reward WT pairs have more similar choice sequences than Fmr1 pairs; in the sensory-deprived condition similarity falls in both genotypes alike.
claims.source: Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior; Figure S2 (not read)
claims.quote: Under the 100% reward condition, Jaccard similarity ( Fig. S2 A ; see Materials and Methods) between the choice sequences of paired rats was high for both genotypes ( Fig. S2 B,C ). In contrast, under the 50% probabilistic condition, WT pairs exhibited significantly higher similarity in their choice sequences compared with Fmr1 pairs ... similarity decreased comparably across genotypes
claims.criterion: The Jaccard similarity of Eq. 3, every session of one rat against every session of its partner (Methods, Cross-rat choice sequence similarity analysis). The test and the summary per pair are in the unread supplement. Open are the sets compared; readings are the sets of (a) distinct ordered transitions (from-well, to-well), (b) distinct nonoverlapping triplets, (c) distinct overlapping triplets. Open is the summary per pair; readings are the mean over (i) all entries of the matrix, (ii) the lower triangle, (iii) the diagonal (same-session pairs). The genotype test is not in the text read; the stand-in is a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test on per-pair values (5 against 5), the test the paper uses for per-rat means in Figures 3G and 5D. It is the reader's choice, and the claim should be revised once Figure S2 is read. Reproduced when, under every reading, the 50% WT similarity exceeds Fmr1 with p < 0.05; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. The 100% and SD values are reported.

claims.statement: During match events WT pairs arrive at the wells with shorter lags between the two rats than Fmr1 pairs, under both contingencies; in WT pairs the lag falls over 100% training.
claims.source: Figure 4B and legend; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: We observed that, under the 100% reward contingency, the mean arrival lag during match events progressively decreased in WT pairs, whereas it remained consistently elevated in Fmr1 pairs ( Fig. 4 B ). This difference persisted under the 50% reward contingency, with WT pairs exhibiting significantly shorter arrival lags than Fmr1 pairs
claims.criterion: The Methods do not define arrival lag (the legend refers to them). Per match, the absolute difference between the two rats' arrival times at the matched wells; readings of arrival are (a) the start of the rat's first poke at that well, (b) the first frame its head is within 40 pixels of the well centre (the radius of the Methods' cross-correlation section). Mean per pair and session; genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under readings A and B; first 21 and first 35 sessions. Reproduced when, under every reading, the genotype effect has p < 0.05 with WT lower in both contingencies; blocked as methods_underspecified when readings disagree. The slope of the WT lag over the 100% sessions is reported.

claims.statement: After match events WT rats depart from the wells with shorter lags between partners than Fmr1 rats, under both contingencies.
claims.source: Figure 4C and legend; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: A similar pattern emerged for mean departure lag following match events, with WT rats departing more promptly than Fmr1 rats ( Fig. 4 C )
claims.criterion: Departure lag is not defined in the Methods. Per match, the absolute difference between the two rats' departure times from the matched wells; readings of departure are (a) the end of the rat's last poke at that well before it visits another, (b) the last frame its head is within 40 pixels of the well centre. Mean per pair and session; genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under readings A and B; first 21 sessions at 100%, first 33 and first 35 at 50%. Reproduced when, under every reading, p < 0.05 with WT lower in both contingencies; blocked as methods_underspecified when readings disagree.

claims.statement: Fmr1 rats spend longer at reward wells per visit than WT rats (Results), though the legend's genotype effects are not significant (p = 0.25 at 100%, p = 0.063 at 50%).
claims.source: Figure 4D and legend; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: Additionally, Fmr1 rats exhibited longer dwell times at reward wells compared with WT rats ( Fig. 4 D )
claims.criterion: Dwell time per visit, for all visits, match or not (Results); readings are (a) from the first poke to the end of the last poke at the well before the rat visits another, (b) the time the head is within 40 pixels of the well centre. Mean per rat and session; genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under reading A, the test the reported df show (B as a variant). The Results state a difference that the legend's tests do not support. Reproduced when the Fmr1 mean exceeds the WT mean in both contingencies and the genotype effect has p >= 0.05 in both, as the legend reports; partially reproduced when the Fmr1 mean is higher in both but the genotype effect is significant in one or both (the Results sentence holds, the legend's tests do not); not reproduced when WT dwell times are longer.

claims.statement: Cross-correlation of the two rats' well-arrival times has peaks above shuffled controls in both genotypes, but correlation is higher in WT pairs and only WT pairs show prominent peaks near zero lag (near-synchronous transitions).
claims.source: Figure 4E to 4G and legends; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: Cross-correlation of arrival times at reward wells revealed significant peaks at multiple lags for both groups, exceeding shuffled controls ... Importantly, only WT rats showed prominent peaks near zero lag ... Fmr1 rats lacked this short-lag synchrony
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Cross-correlation analysis of well arrivals) give it. Head position assigned to the nearest well when within 40 pixels of its centre, else null; downsampled to 1 Hz; an arrival where the well identity differs from the preceding time point; binary arrival series per rat; scipy.signal.correlate in full mode divided by the product of the two series' Euclidean norms; positive lag when rat 2 follows rat 1. The df (40 for lag) fix 41 lags, -20 to +20 s. Open are the well centres (the reading, the median head position during pokes at each well), the downsampling (readings, every 30th frame; the modal well in each 1 s bin), whether a change from a well to null and back to the same well is an arrival (readings, yes as the text says; no), and the shuffle (the reading, a circular shift of one rat's series, as in Figure 1H). Per pair, session and lag, the coefficient; a linear mixed-effects model coefficient ~ genotype x lag (lag categorical) with a random intercept per pair (the df fit one row per pair, session and lag). Reproduced when, in both contingencies, genotype and genotype x lag have p < 0.05 with WT higher, and the mean WT coefficient at lags -1 to +1 s exceeds the Fmr1 value; the near-zero peaks are shown per genotype. The paper gives no test for the peaks exceeding shuffled controls; observed and shuffled coefficients per genotype and lag are reported, not judged.

claims.statement: The distribution of lags at peak cross-correlation differs between WT and Fmr1 pairs in the 50% condition but not in the 100% condition.
claims.source: Figure 4H and legend; Results, Development of structured spatial and temporal coordination strategies supports cooperative behavior
claims.quote: Correspondingly, the distribution of lags at peak correlation coefficients differed between WT and Fmr1 rats, particularly under the 50% condition ( Fig. 4 H )
claims.criterion: The absolute lag at the maximum of each session's cross-correlation, as in fig4eg-cross-correlation-wt-higher, pooled over sessions and pairs per genotype; a two-sample KS test (scipy.stats.ks_2samp). Open is the range searched for the maximum; readings are (a) -20 to +20 s, the lags of Figure 4G; (b) all lags of the full correlation. Reproduced when, under every reading, the 50% test has p < 0.01 and the 100% test has p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when the 50% test is significant and the 100% test is too.

claims.statement: Session-wise peak cross-correlation coefficients are higher in WT than in Fmr1 pairs under both contingencies.
claims.source: Figure 4I and legend
claims.quote: Session wise peak correlation coefficients for WT and Fmr1 −/y rat pairs, showing greater temporal coordination for WT rat pairs
claims.criterion: The maximum coefficient of each pair-session cross-correlation (fig4eg), under the two peak ranges of fig4h-peak-lag-distribution; genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under readings A and B. Reproduced when, under every reading, both contingencies give p < 0.05 with WT higher; blocked as methods_underspecified when readings disagree.

claims.statement: Leadership is not fixed; on average rats of both genotypes lead about half of the match events, with no genotype difference in the mean probability of leading estimated by a state-space model.
claims.source: Figure 5C and 5D and legends; Results, Dynamic turn-taking in the initiation of coordinated responses
claims.quote: On average, both genotypes led approximately half of the match events under both 100% and 50% reward contingencies ( Fig. 5 D , E )
claims.criterion: Per match the leader is the rat whose poke at its matched well began first (Methods, Assignment of leader and follower). Per rat, the binary leadership series over all its match events of a contingency, sessions in order, fitted with the state-space model of Smith et al. (2004) as the Methods give it (Gaussian random walk, logistic observation, EM with Newton-Raphson). b0 is not given; the reading is that of Smith et al. (2004), b0 = log(p0 / (1 - p0)) with p0 = 0.5, chance for two rats, so b0 = 0. The rat's mean of p_k over events; a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test of WT against Fmr1 rats (10 and 10) per contingency. A claim of absence for the genotype test. Reproduced when both Mann-Whitney tests have p >= 0.05 and every genotype mean is within 0.45 to 0.55; partially reproduced when the tests are not significant but a mean is outside that range; not reproduced when a test is significant. Since every pair is of one genotype and each event has one leader, the raw proportions of the two rats of a pair sum to 1, so a genotype mean near 0.5 follows by construction; the per-rat means are reported to show the spread.

claims.statement: The within-pair difference in the proportion of leading events does not differ by genotype at 100%, but shows a small significant genotype effect at 50%, present at the start of training and gone later in training (Results).
claims.source: Figure 5E and legend; Results, Dynamic turn-taking in the initiation of coordinated responses
claims.quote: However, under the 50% reward condition, a small but significant genotype-specific difference emerged, with WT and Fmr1 rats differing significantly in their likelihood of assuming the leader role at the start of training ( Fig. 5 E )
claims.criterion: Per pair and session, the difference between the two rats' proportions of match events led; the sign is not given and rat order is arbitrary, so the reading is the absolute difference, with the signed difference (first rat minus second, as the dataset orders them) as a variant. Genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under readings A and B; first 21 sessions at 100%, first 33 and first 35 at 50%. The 100% part is a claim of absence, judged on reading A (the test the reported df show) with the absolute difference. Reproduced when the 50% genotype effect has p < 0.05 under every reading and the 100% effect has p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when the 50% effect holds under some readings only. The genotype means of the first five and the last five analysed 50% sessions are reported (the paper does not say which sessions are the start; five is a display choice and decides nothing).

claims.statement: A rat's chance of leading on a given match event depends on whether it led on the preceding events.
claims.source: Results, Dynamic turn-taking in the initiation of coordinated responses; Figure S3C and S3D (not read)
claims.quote: Furthermore, the likelihood of a rat assuming the leader role on a given trial was modulated by its leadership status over the preceding trials
claims.criterion: The analysis and its test are in the unread supplement (Figure S3C, S3D); the Methods do not describe it, so no test can be taken from the text read. Until the supplement is read into this file, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified. Leader per match event as in fig5d-leading-near-half. Shown, not judged, are per rat (a) P(lead | led the previous event) against P(lead | followed it), compared across rats by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test; (b) a logistic regression of leading on lead status in each of the previous 1 to 3 events. These are the reader's choices, not the paper's.

claims.statement: In a multiagent reinforcement learning model of the task, partner-aware agents learn to coordinate far better than partner-unaware and random agents, reaching about 70% coordination efficiency after the switch to 50% reward.
claims.source: Figure 6C and legend; Results, Differential reliance on two hierarchical strategies for successful coordination
claims.quote: Partner-aware agent pairs achieved markedly higher performance than both partner-unaware and random agent pairs ( Fig. 6 C )
claims.criterion: A simulation, not a test on recorded data; no code is published. As the Methods give it, tabular Q-learning, two agents on three-location grids, one agent chosen at random to act first each timestep, reward +1 when both choose the same location and it differs from the last rewarded location, epsilon decaying exponentially from 1.0 to 0.01 over 90% of episodes, 100 episodes at 100% then 100 at 50% reward. Not given are the learning rate, discount factor, timesteps per episode, number of runs and the state encoding; these must be named as readings by whoever runs it. Reproduced when partner-aware agents exceed both other types (Wilcoxon p < 0.05 over episodes) and reach 63 to 77% after the switch.

claims.statement: Under 50% reward, a larger proportion of Fmr1 pairs' matches occur in asynchronous trials (rats starting at different wells) than WT pairs' matches; at 100% there is no genotype difference.
claims.source: Figure 7A and 7B and legend; Results, Differential reliance on two hierarchical strategies for successful coordination
claims.quote: whereas Fmr1 pairs showed a higher proportion of matches occurring during asynchronous trials, particularly under the 50% reward condition ( Fig. 7 A , B )
claims.criterion: A match is synchronous when, before it, the two rats were at corresponding wells and moved together to the matched wells, and asynchronous when they started from different (noncorresponding) wells (Results). Per pair and session, the proportion of matches that are asynchronous. At 100%, a claim of absence, the genotype effect of the two-way ANOVA under reading A, the test the reported df show (B as a variant); at 50%, a linear mixed-effects model with genotype, session and their interaction and a random intercept per pair (the df F(1,280) also fit reading A, which is shown). Reproduced when the 50% genotype effect has p < 0.05 with Fmr1 higher and the 100% effect has p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Session mean trial duration is negatively correlated with cooperative performance in both genotypes (WT R = -0.51, Fmr1 R = -0.40).
claims.source: Figure 7C and legend; Results, Differential reliance on two hierarchical strategies for successful coordination
claims.quote: Next, we found that session-level mean trial duration was negatively correlated with cooperative performance, indicating that shorter, more efficient trials were associated with higher performance ( Fig. 7 C )
claims.criterion: Pearson correlation of session mean trial duration with performance (Eq. 1), 100% and 50% sessions combined. The trial is not defined for this panel; readings are (a) the asynchronous trial of the gaze analysis, from the rats being at their initial wells to the follower's departure (Methods); (b) the interval between consecutive matches; (c) the interval between consecutive transitions of the pair. The p-values imply a different number of points per genotype; readings of the points are one per pair and session, and one per rat and session. Reproduced when, under one reading, both R are within tolerance and p < 0.05; partially reproduced when both are negative with p < 0.05 but out of tolerance.

claims.statement: Follower-only gaze toward the leader increases from the first to the later quartiles of a trial and is greatest just before departure; mutual gaze shows no quartile effect, and there is no genotype effect.
claims.source: Figure 7D and 7E and legend; Results, Differential reliance on two hierarchical strategies for successful coordination
claims.quote: A mixed-effects ANOVA revealed significant effects of quartile for follower-only gaze
claims.criterion: Asynchronous trials as the Methods define them (rats at distinct, nonopposing wells; the follower moves while the leader waits; the trial ends when the follower departs). The bearing angle of Eq. 11, from the neck-to-head vector and the head-to-partner-body vector, peer-directed below 40 degrees. Per trial quartile, the fraction of frames with follower-only gaze (follower toward leader, leader not toward follower) and with mutual gaze; mean per rat and quartile; a mixed ANOVA with genotype between and quartile within, rat as subject (the df fit 20 rats), Holm-corrected post hoc tests. Which sessions enter is not given; the reading is all analysed sessions of both contingencies. Reproduced when the follower-only quartile effect has p < 0.001 with quartile 4 highest, the Holm-corrected post hoc tests show quartile 1 below each of quartiles 2, 3 and 4 (p < 0.05), the mutual-gaze effect has p >= 0.05, and genotype and its interactions have p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: Under 100% reward, follower-only gaze becomes a stronger predictor of matching over training, driven by Fmr1 pairs; in the late block the Fmr1-minus-WT contrast is positive for follower-only gaze (0.34) and mutual gaze (0.60), while early and mid contrasts are not significant.
claims.source: Figure 7F and 7G and legends; Results, Differential reliance on two hierarchical strategies for successful coordination; Table S1 (not read)
claims.quote: Under the 100% reward condition, the models revealed that follower-only gaze became an increasingly strong predictor of successful cooperation across training ( Fig. 7 G , left; Table S1 ). Post hoc comparisons indicated that this effect was driven primarily by Fmr1 pairs
claims.criterion: Per asynchronous trial at 100% (fig7e), outcome match or not, predictors follower-only and mutual gaze durations normalised by trial duration (Results), genotype and session block; the model of Eq. 12, logit(P(match)) ~ (gF + gM) * Genotype * Block + (1 | animal / session), binomial, logit link (glmmTMB), and between-genotype contrasts of emtrends per block, Tukey adjusted (Methods, Post hoc analyses). Tolerances are the paper's stated spread (the ± values). Open are the blocks (readings, thirds of the 21 sessions as 7, 7 and 7; thirds by the pair's own session count) and the scaling of gF and gM ("normalized"; readings, fraction of trial duration as the Results say; that fraction z-scored). Reproduced when, under one reading, both late contrasts are positive with p < 0.05 and within tolerance and the early and mid follower-only contrasts have p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when the late contrasts are positive and significant but out of tolerance.

claims.statement: Under 50% reward, Fmr1 pairs depend more than WT pairs on follower-only gaze in every training block (contrasts 0.38, 0.39 and 0.44), while mutual-gaze contrasts are not significant.
claims.source: Figure 7H and legend; Results, Differential reliance on two hierarchical strategies for successful coordination; Table S2 (not read)
claims.quote: Fmr1 pairs remained significantly more dependent on follower-only gaze, i.e., the follower monitoring the leader throughout, compared with WT pairs ( Fig. 7 H , left)
claims.criterion: As fig7g-gaze-100-late, for the 50% sessions; block readings are thirds of the 35 sessions (12, 12 and 11, or 11, 12 and 12) and thirds by each pair's own session count. Reproduced when, under one reading, all three follower-only contrasts are positive with p < 0.05 and within tolerance and the three mutual-gaze contrasts have p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when the follower-only contrasts are positive and significant but out of tolerance.

claims.statement: After a partner's cooperative choice, WT rats are more likely to cooperate under both contingencies, Fmr1 rats only under 100% reward.
claims.source: Figure 8B and legend; Results, Partner cooperation history shapes cooperative behavior
claims.quote: For the 100% reward contingency, both WT and Fmr1 rats were more likely to cooperate after their partner had just done so in the previous trial ( Fig. 8 B ). In contrast, for the 50% reward contingency, only WT rats adjusted their behavior based on recent partner choices
claims.criterion: Follower trials as the Methods define them (the leader enters an arm first; the follower cooperates when it chooses the matching arm). For each follower trial, the partner's choice on its own most recent follower trial (Methods, Partner behavior history analysis). Per rat, P(cooperate | partner cooperated) and P(cooperate | partner did not); a Wilcoxon signed-rank test across rats per genotype and contingency (10 per genotype). Open is whether a partner's most recent trial is sought within the session only or across sessions; the reading is within the session, as Δt is a within-session interval, with across sessions as a variant. Reproduced when WT is significant (p < 0.05, higher after cooperation) at 100% and 50%, Fmr1 at 100%, and Fmr1 at 50% is not significant.

claims.statement: The time between the partner's most recent follower choice and the subject's current follower choice is longer in Fmr1 than in WT rats under both contingencies.
claims.source: Figure 8D and legend
claims.quote: Across both contingencies, Fmr1 −/y rats showed significantly longer partner-referenced Δ t intervals than WT rats
claims.criterion: Δt per follower trial as in fig8b-partner-history-cooperation, pooled over trials of all rats per genotype, a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test per contingency. Reproduced when both tests have p < 0.0001 with the Fmr1 median longer; the U values are reported.

claims.statement: In a GLMM of cooperation on each follower trial, the partner's previous cooperation has a larger effect in WT rats at 50% (beta 0.77) than in Fmr1 rats (beta 0.13), a significant genotype interaction (beta 0.64); at 100% both genotypes show an effect (WT 0.36, Fmr1 0.26).
claims.source: Figure 8E and legend; Results, Partner cooperation history shapes cooperative behavior
claims.quote: However, under the 50% contingency only WT rats adjusted their choices based on recent partner behavior, while Fmr1 rats did not ( Fig. 8 E )
claims.criterion: Per contingency, a binomial GLMM (logit) of cooperation on each follower trial with fixed effects partner's previous choice (binary), Δt (continuous) and their interaction, each interacting with genotype, plus covariates for the subject's own recent choice history, random intercepts for rat and session (Methods, Generalized linear mixed-effects modeling; pymer4 0.8 / lme4). Open are the own-history covariates (readings, the subject's own previous follower choice; its previous two), the scaling of Δt (readings, seconds; z-scored), and how the per-genotype betas are read (readings, simple effects with WT as the reference level and with Fmr1 as reference). The legend gives Fmr1 at 50% beta 0.13 with p < 0.01 while the Results say Fmr1 rats did not adjust; the finding tested is the 50% genotype interaction and the WT effects. Reproduced when, under one reading, the 50% interaction is positive with p < 0.001 (WT larger), the WT effects are positive with p < 0.001, and the betas are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the signs and significance hold but a beta is out of tolerance.

claims.statement: The expert sessions of the behavioural data come from 41 mice and number 201, with an average of 23 context blocks per session.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 2; Figure 1C legend; Figure 1 figure supplement 1A and 1B
claims.quote: Mice were trained in this task until they reached expert performance, completing an average of 23 blocks per session
claims.criterion: The Methods (Behavioral task and training curriculum) define a block contrast, for each block but the first and last, as the mean of the absolute differences in whisker hit rate between the block and its two neighbours, and call a session expert when its contrasts are significantly above 0.375. The test is that of the code, the lower bound of a 95% bootstrap interval (scipy.stats.bootstrap, 10,000 resamples, defaults otherwise) of the mean contrast above 0.375 (process main_analysis/figure1_supp_analysis.py:53-187), with early-lick trials dropped. Blocks are the context epochs of the session (the Methods); the code cuts blocks of 20 non-early-lick trials (figure1_supp_analysis.py:72-85), shown as a variant. Blocks per session are counted from the context epochs. Applied to every behavioural session of the dataset, reproduced when the three counts are within tolerance; the overlap with the code's list sessions_Context_sessions_expert.yaml is reported.

claims.statement: In expert sessions mice lick to the auditory tone in both contexts, with hit rates of 96 ± 4% in W+ and 94 ± 5% in W- (mean ± SD over 41 mice).
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 2; Figure 1C
claims.quote: In expert sessions, mice showed consistent licking responses to the auditory stimulus in both contexts (Auditory hit rate: W+ = 96 ± 4 %, W- = 94 ± 5 %; n = 41 mice)
claims.criterion: Lick probability in auditory trials, per mouse as in the opening comment (behaviour), over the expert sessions under either reading of the selection. The tolerances are the paper's stated SDs over mice.

claims.statement: Licking to the whisker stimulus depends strongly on context, 84 ± 6% in W+ against 32 ± 7% in W- (mean ± SD over mice).
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 2; Figure 1C
claims.quote: and strong context-modulated licking in response to whisker stimuli (W+ = 84 ± 6 %, W- = 32 ± 7 %) (Figure 1C)
claims.criterion: As fig1c-auditory-hit-both-contexts, for whisker trials. The tolerances are the paper's stated SDs over mice.

claims.statement: The context modulation of whisker licking holds whichever background noise (pink or brown) is associated with each context.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 2; Figure 1D
claims.quote: irrespective of which background noise was associated to each context (Figure 1D)
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test for this panel, and the code computes none (plot utils/figure1D.py), which splits the mouse-level lick probabilities by the noise identity (context_background). The mice are split by the noise assigned to W+ (Methods, each mouse randomly assigned a whisker-rewarded context). Reproduced when, in both groups of mice, the mean whisker lick probability is higher in W+ than in W- and the paired t-test across the mice of the group (the paper's test for Figure 1C) gives p < 0.05; partially reproduced when W+ is higher in both groups but the test passes in one only. The number of mice per group is reported.

claims.statement: Catch-trial (spontaneous) lick rates are low but slightly higher in W+ blocks, 13 ± 7% against 4 ± 2% in W-.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 2; Figure 1C
claims.quote: Lick rates in catch trials were overall low, although slightly higher in W+ blocks (Catch false alarm rate: W+ = 13 ± 7 %, W-: 4 ± 2%; t-value = −9, p-value = 1.6 x 10-10)
claims.criterion: Per mouse catch-trial lick probability per context, as in the opening comment (behaviour); a two-sided paired t-test of W- against W+ across mice, uncorrected, as plot utils/figure1C.py:78-82. Reproduced when both means are within the stated SDs, W+ is higher and p < 0.05.

claims.statement: When the two context noises are replaced by constant white noise, keeping the block reward structure, mice no longer discriminate between the context blocks in their whisker responses.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 2; Figure 1E; Figure 1 figure supplement 1E
claims.quote: After removing the explicit contextual information mice were unable to discriminate between context blocks (Figure 1E and Figure 1 – figure supplement 1E)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The sessions are the Context Off days of the 7 mice (process configs sessions_Context_sound_off_only.yaml, the middle of three days in sessions_Context_sound_off.yaml).
