The paper reports no test for the panel and the code computes none for Figure 1E (plot utils/figure1E.py); for supplement 1E the code runs the Figure 1G test, a paired t-test across mice of the last whisker trial before against the first after the transition, on the Off days (plot utils/figure1_supp.py:85-125), and prints it. That is the only test the paper's material holds, so the absence is judged on it alone (protocol, claims of absence), for each transition direction, two-sided, p < 0.05. Reproduced when both directions give p >= 0.05, not reproduced when either gives p < 0.05 in the direction of the new context. A two-sided paired t-test across the 7 mice of whisker lick probability in W+ against W- blocks on the Off day is shown as a variant. The W+ minus W- difference on the Off day and on the On days is reported.

claims.statement: Mice change their whisker response at the first whisker trial after a context change, from 26 ± 8% to 73 ± 13% from W- to W+, and from 87 ± 7% to 57 ± 13% from W+ to W-.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 3; Figure 1G
claims.quote: The probability of licking in response to whisker deflection was significantly different comparing the first trial after context change with the last trial of the previous block (transition from W- to W+: pre = 26 ± 8 %, post = 73 ± 13 %, t-value = 21, p-value = 2.8 x 10-23; transition from W+ to W-: pre = 87 ± 7 %, post = 57 ± 13 %, t-value = −14, p-value = 7.3 x 10-17)
claims.criterion: Whisker trial -1 is the last non-early-lick whisker trial of a block and +1 the first of the next (cicada cicada_tools/behavior/behavior_analysis_utils.py:214-274); per mouse the mean over transitions within a session, then over sessions (Methods, Figure 1G; cicada behavior_analysis_plots.py:787-792); a two-sided paired t-test, post against pre, across mice, per direction (plot utils/figure1FG.py:62-63). The code also saves a Bonferroni value (x2); whether the printed p is corrected is not stated, so both are reported. Reproduced when the four values are within the stated SDs and both tests give p < 0.05 in the stated direction.

claims.statement: After the first whisker trial of a new block, whisker responses adapt slightly further over the following whisker trials, the second whisker trial already closer to the new context than the first.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 3; Figure 1F; Results, paragraph 5 (Figure 1L)
claims.quote: Mice changed their licking behavior as early as the first whisker trial following the context transition with a slight gradual further adaptation over subsequent whisker trials (Figure 1F)
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test. Mean lick probability over mice at whisker trials +1 to +4 after each transition, built as in fig1g-first-trial-switch (the code's window, 3 trials before to 4 after). Reproduced when, for both directions, trial +2 is closer than trial +1 to the new context (higher after W- to W+, lower after W+ to W-) and trial +4 is at least as close as +2; partially reproduced when this holds in one direction. The paired t-test across mice of +2 against +1 (the paper's test for Figure 1G) is reported per direction.

claims.statement: The lick probability to the first whisker trial of a block rises with the time elapsed since a transition to W+ and falls with it after a transition to W-, while the last whisker trial before a transition shows no sign of anticipating the switch.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 3; Figure 1H
claims.quote: We observed a progressive increase in lick probability in W+ and a corresponding decrease in W−, suggesting temporal integration of contextual information after context switch. However, there was no apparent sign of anticipation of the context switch in the behavior of the mice.
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Figure 1H) and the code give it, for each session the last whisker trial of each block and the first of the next (the first of the first block and the last of the last block left out), timed from the transition (negative before it), assigned to 10 s bins, bin -1 being [-10, 0) s and bin +1 [0, 10) s (cicada behavior_analysis_plots.py:1076-1145; plot utils/figure1H.py:107-116); trials pooled over all sessions and mice, the lick probability of a bin being its licked trials over its trials. The code keeps early-lick trials here; the variant without them is shown. The paper reports no test. The rise and fall are judged by the code's fit (plot utils/misc/stats.py:139-212), an exponential A exp(-t/tau) + C over bin -1 (as t = 0) and bins +1 to +5, tau bounded in 0.1 to 50 bins; reproduced for the first part when, for W+, the fitted values increase from bin +1 to bin +5 and, for W-, decrease. The absence of anticipation has no test in the paper; readings (a) the Pearson correlation of bin lick probability with bin time over bins -5 to -1, per direction, p >= 0.05, (b) the lick probability of bin -1 against bins -5 to -2 pooled, Fisher's exact test, p >= 0.05. The second part holds when both readings find no effect, fails when both find one toward the coming context, and is otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified. Reproduced when both parts hold, partially reproduced when one does.

claims.statement: Before the whisker stimulus, pupil area is larger in W+ than in W- (0.52 ± 0.13 against 0.50 ± 0.12 mm2), while whisker angle and jaw opening show no general effect of context.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 4; Figure 1I; Figure 1 figure supplement 1G
claims.quote: Pupil area was significantly modulated by context with larger values in W+ compared to W- (W+: 0.52 ± 0.13 mm2, W-: 0.50 ± 0.12 mm2, t-value = 3.7, p-value = 0.023)
claims.criterion: Sessions are the four widefield expert groups with face video (24 mice, 97 sessions in the code, process main_analysis/process_deeplabcut_data.py:266-268). Body parts filtered by likelihood (Methods, Figures 1I-J, 80% whisker, 60% jaw, 50% pupil), a body part dropped for a session when under 70% of its points pass; pupil area as the polygon of its four points, all four above 50% likelihood (Methods, Behavioral kinematics). Whisker trials only; the mean over the 2 s pre-stimulus quiet window per trial, then per session, then per mouse, by context (plot utils/figure1IJ.py:26-147); a two-sided paired t-test across mice, W+ against W-, Bonferroni corrected by 20 as in the code. Reproduced when the pupil means are within the stated SDs, W+ is larger with corrected p < 0.05, and whisker angle and jaw opening give corrected p >= 0.05 (the absence judged on the same test).

claims.statement: Independently of context, before trials in which the mouse then licks to the whisker stimulus the jaw rests more open (0.27 ± 0.05 against 0.23 ± 0.04 mm) and the whisker is more posterior (97.3 ± 13 against 98.6 ± 12 degrees).
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 4; Figure 1 figure supplement 1G
claims.quote: Whisker angle and jaw opening were modulated by trial outcome with larger values in the baseline preceding lick for jaw opening (Lick: 0.27 ± 0.05 mm, No-Lick-: 0.23 ± 0.04 mm, t-value = 4.6, p-value = 0.0035), and smaller values in the baseline preceding lick for whisker angle (Lick: 97.3 ± 13 °, No-Lick-: 98.6 ± 12 °, t-value = −4, p-value = 0.0103)
claims.criterion: As fig1i-pupil-larger-wplus, with trials split by lick outcome over both contexts (plot utils/figure1IJ.py:171-189). Jaw opening is the vertical distance from the session's 5th percentile of the jaw trace, whisker angle as the Methods (Behavioral kinematics) define it, 180 degrees for a whisker parallel to the body. Reproduced when the four means are within the stated SDs and both tests give corrected p < 0.05 in the stated directions.

claims.statement: Pre-stimulus jaw speed is higher in the rewarded context (3.0 ± 1.0 against 2.5 ± 0.8 mm/s), and also before lick than before no-lick trials, while whisking speed shows no effect of context or lick.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 4; Figure 1J; Figure 1 figure supplement 1H
claims.quote: Jaw speed was significantly higher in W+ compared to W- (W+: 3.0 ± 1.0 mm/s, W-: 2.5 ± 0.8 mm/s, t-value = 5.1, p-value = 0.0011) and before Lick compared to No-Lick (Lick: 2.8 ± 0.1 mm/s, No-Lick: 2.6 ± 0.7 mm/s, t-value = −3.7, p-value = 0.0254)
claims.criterion: As fig1i-pupil-larger-wplus. Speed is the absolute first derivative of the trace times the frame rate (Methods, Figures 1I-J; the code multiplies by 200, plot utils/figure1IJ.py, which holds only for 200 Hz video; the frame rate of each session is used, the fixed 200 is a variant). The lick SD of 0.1 mm/s is far below the others and the t-value's sign is opposite to the stated direction (paper_inconsistency); the tolerance for the lick mean is 10%. The claim stands on the stated directions. Reproduced when the four means are within tolerance, jaw speed is higher in W+ and before lick with corrected p < 0.05, and whisker speed gives corrected p >= 0.05 for both context and lick (the absence judged on the same test).

claims.statement: A gradient-boosted tree model of the whisker-trial lick choice, from task, history and orofacial features, reaches a cross-validated accuracy of 0.78 on held-out test trials.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 5; Figure 1K
claims.quote: Our model reached a cross-validated accuracy of 0.78 on held-out test trials (Figure 1K)
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Gradient boosted decision tree model) and the code give it. The Methods say "all expert sessions"; the orofacial features exist only for sessions with face video, and the code settles the set. Sessions are the code's 60 sessions of 21 mice (session_context_expert_behaviour_model.yaml), sessions failing the code's 30% missing-value rule on the DLC features skipped, early licks dropped, whisker trials only (process main_analysis/model_context_behaviour.py:34-175); features as in configs/analysis_params/whisker_classification.yaml and explain_behaviour preprocessing/trial_features.py; one session held out (rng seed 20); a stratified 67/33 trial split of the rest (random_state 123); XGBoost tuned by Optuna (TPE, seed 123, 1000 trials, 80/20 inner split, binary log loss, early stopping 100 rounds); balanced accuracy on the 33% test split (explain_behaviour models/behavioural_analysis_GBM.py:80-186). The code's early stopping uses the test split as its evaluation set; this is followed, and the variant with early stopping on the inner validation split is shown. Reproduced when the balanced accuracy is within tolerance; the accuracy on the held-out session is reported.

claims.statement: Among the model's features, context gives the largest drop in accuracy when permuted, followed by whether the previous whisker trial was rewarded, the cumulative number of rewards and the index of the whisker trial in the block.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 5; Figure 1K
claims.quote: Among all model features, context information was the one leading to the strongest accuracy drop in the permutation test, followed by whether or not the previous whisker trial was rewarded, the cumulative number of rewards, and the index of the whisker trial of the block (Figure 1K)
claims.criterion: Permutation importance as the Methods (Figure 1K) and plot utils/figure1KL.py:512-523 give it, each feature shuffled 10,000 times on the test split, the drop in balanced accuracy recorded. Reproduced when context has the largest mean drop and the next three are, in order, previous whisker rewarded, cumulative water, whisker trial in block; partially reproduced when context is first and the other three are in the top five in any order.

claims.statement: The SHAP values of the whisker-trial-in-block feature follow the behaviour, with a single-trial change after a context transition and a slower further component.
claims.source: Results, Rapid behavioral adaptation to sensory stimuli in a changing context, paragraph 5; Figure 1L
claims.quote: we examined the SHAP value of the parameter “whisker trial in block”, finding a pattern consistent with the mouse behavior capturing both single trial adaptation after context transition and a slower component
claims.criterion: SHAP values by the interventional TreeExplainer with 100 background trials from the training set (Methods, Figure 1L; explain_behaviour models/behavioural_analysis_GBM.py:516-534), over train and test trials; whisker trials 5 to 8 of a block relabelled -4 to -1 (plot utils/figure1KL.py:568). The paper gives no measure. Reproduced when, for both transition directions, the mean SHAP value of whisker trial 1 of the new block differs in sign from that of trial -1 of the previous block, in the direction of the new context, and trial 2 lies further in that direction than trial 1; partially reproduced when only the sign change holds.

claims.statement: Whisker-rewarded context blocks last longer than whisker-non-rewarded blocks (196 ± 13 against 185 ± 4 s).
claims.source: Figure 1 figure supplement 1C
claims.quote: Whisker rewarded context blocks were significantly longer than whisker non-rewarded blocks (W+: 196 ± 13 s, W-: 185 ± 4 s, t-value = 4.3, p-value = 2.0 x 10-4)
claims.criterion: Block duration from the context epochs of the expert sessions, averaged within a session then over sessions per mouse (the legend; process main_analysis/figure1_supp_analysis.py lines 324-351, plot utils/figure1_supp.py:39-67); a two-sided paired t-test across mice, uncorrected. Reproduced when both means are within the stated SDs, W+ longer, p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Spout contact after the stimulus is slightly faster in W+ than in W-, for auditory (370 ± 9 against 400 ± 9 ms) and whisker trials (392 ± 9 against 418 ± 9 ms).
claims.source: Figure 1 figure supplement 1D
claims.quote: Average spout contact time in response to auditory and whisker trials in W- and W+ showing slightly faster response in W+ compared to W- for both auditory and whisker trials (Auditory: W+: 370 ± 9 ms, W-: 400 ± 9 ms, t-value = −8.7, p-value = 1.8 x 10-10, Whisker: W+: 392 ± 9 ms, W-: 418 ± 9 ms, t-value = −4, p-value = 6.0 x 10-4)
claims.criterion: Lick time minus stimulus onset on lick trials without early lick (cicada behavior_analysis_plots.py:978-1033), averaged per session then per mouse; a two-sided paired t-test across mice per trial type, Bonferroni x2 (plot utils/figure1_supp.py:128-174; the code labels this panel 1E). The paper's ± of 9 ms for every group may be an SEM; the stated value is the tolerance, and the SD and SEM over mice are both reported. Reproduced when the four means are within tolerance and both tests give corrected p < 0.05 with W+ faster; partially reproduced when the directions and tests hold but a mean is outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Optogenetic inactivation of cortical sites has little effect on licking in catch trials in either context.
claims.source: Results, Distributed cortical areas are involved in task execution, paragraph 1; Figure 2C
claims.quote: In catch trials, optogenetic inactivation had little effect on licking behavior in either context (Figure 2C)
claims.criterion: The opto-map rule of the opening comment, catch trials, 7 VGAT-ChR2 mice. A claim of small effect, with no test or threshold in the paper. Reproduced when, under each threshold and null reading, at most 3 of the 39 sites (under 10%) have an effect in either context, and the largest mean |ΔP| over sites is reported; not reproduced when, under every reading, more do; otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In auditory trials, inactivating auditory cortex and frontal premotor regions reduces lick probability, similarly in both contexts.
claims.source: Results, Distributed cortical areas are involved in task execution, paragraph 1; Figure 2D
claims.quote: However, in auditory trials, there was a reduction in lick probability when inactivating auditory cortex and frontal premotor regions, which was similar across contexts (Figure 2D)
claims.criterion: The opto-map rule, auditory trials. Frontal premotor regions are read as the sites wM1, wM2 and ALM (the Results name these "anterior premotor regions" and the paper's section summary lists wM1/2 and ALM). Reproduced when A1 and at least one of wM1, wM2, ALM have a negative effect in both contexts; partially reproduced when this holds in one context only. Each threshold and null reading is run; the outcome is the one they all give, otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified. Similarity across contexts is reported as the W+ and W- mean ΔP at those sites.

claims.statement: In whisker trials, inactivating wS1, wS2 and anterior premotor regions (wM1/2, ALM) reduces lick probability in both contexts.
claims.source: Results, Distributed cortical areas are involved in task execution, paragraph 1; Figure 2E; Results, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Finally, in whisker trials, we observed that inactivating primary and secondary whisker somatosensory cortices (wS1 and wS2), as well as anterior premotor regions led to a reduction of lick probability across both contexts (Figure 2E)
claims.criterion: The opto-map rule, whisker trials. Reproduced when wS1, wS2 and at least one of wM1, wM2, ALM have a negative effect in both W+ and W-; partially reproduced when they do in W+ only (where the whisker lick rate is high). Each threshold and null reading is run; the outcome is the one they all give, otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Inactivating tongue-jaw somatosensory cortex (tjS1) or retrosplenial cortex (RSC) increases lick probability in whisker trials specifically in the W- context.
claims.source: Results, Distributed cortical areas are involved in task execution, paragraph 1; Figure 2E right
claims.quote: Interestingly, during whisker trials, inactivation of the tongue–jaw primary somatosensory cortex (tjS1) and the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) increased lick probability with respect to the control condition specifically in W− trials, indicating a context-dependent effect of these two regions (Figure 2E, right panel)
claims.criterion: The opto-map rule, whisker trials. RSC is the site (-1.5, 0.5); the Methods give the RSC coordinates as 1.5 mm posterior to bregma and 0.5 mm lateral (Pharmacological inactivation), and the tracing used "the coordinates defined in our optogenetic and imaging experiments" (Results, paragraph 2 of the Figure 3 section). The code's second "RSC" site (-0.5, 0.5) is a variant. Reproduced when tjS1 and RSC have a positive effect in W- and neither has a positive effect in W+; partially reproduced when one of the two does. Each threshold and null reading is run; the outcome is the one they all give, otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified. The mean ΔP of each in both contexts is reported.

claims.statement: In control mice without ChR2, light at the grid sites causes no significant change in lick probability at any site.
claims.source: Results, Distributed cortical areas are involved in task execution, paragraph 1; Figure 2 figure supplement 1C and 1D
claims.quote: In control mice without ChR2 expression, we did not observe any significant changes in lick probability following optogenetic inactivation at any site (Figure 2 – figure supplement 1C&D)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the d' of the opto-map rule for the 4 control mice (process sessions_Context_sessions_opto_control.yaml), with the null by shuffling all trials as the supplement 1D legend says (reading ii). The paper fixes no threshold; under each threshold reading, reproduced when no site in any trial type and context passes it, and not reproduced when one does. When the thresholds disagree, blocked as methods_underspecified. The largest d' and |ΔP| over sites are reported.

claims.statement: Muscimol in wS1 significantly reduces whisker-trial lick probability in W- and W+, while muscimol in RSC gives a non-significant positive trend in whisker-trial licking in W-; pharmacological inactivation is consistent with the optogenetic results.
claims.source: Figure 2 figure supplement 1E to 1G; Results, Distributed cortical areas are involved in task execution, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Muscimol injection in wS1 significantly reduced lick probability in response to whisker trials in W- and W+ (hierarchical bootstrapping, p-value < 1.0 x 10-5) ... Same as E, but for RSC inactivation, which leads to a non-significant positive trend in lick probability for whisker trials in W- (hierarchical bootstrapping, p-value = 0.059)
claims.criterion: As process main_analysis/figure2_supp_stats.py gives it. Per area, trial type and context, the change in lick probability from the baseline day to the injection day, early licks dropped; the statistic is the muscimol change minus the Ringer change; two-level bootstrap (mice with replacement, then trials within mouse), each drug and day resampled independently, seed 42, a two-sided p of twice the smaller tail; the code's default is 10,000 iterations and its docstring names 100,000 for the paper's run, which is used (a p below 1e-5 needs it). Reproduced when wS1 gives a negative change with p < 0.05 in both contexts (p < 1e-5 is reported against the resolution) and RSC in W- gives a positive change with 0.05 <= p < 0.1; partially reproduced when only the wS1 part holds. fpS1 is reported.

claims.statement: Lick latency increases during inactivation of frontal areas but does not change during inactivation of RSC or tjS1.
claims.source: Results, Distributed cortical areas are involved in task execution, paragraph 1; Figure 2F
claims.quote: While lick latency increased during inactivation of frontal areas, presumably correlated with decreased motor function, there was no change in lick latency associated with inactivation of RSC or tjS1 (Figure 2F and Figure 2 – figure supplement 1H)
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Figure 2F) and plot utils/figure2F.py give it. Spout contact time minus stimulus onset on lick trials without early lick, auditory trials of both contexts pooled and whisker trials of W+; per mouse and site the mean minus that of control trials, averaged over mice; d' between the site and control distributions over mice, |mean difference| over the root of the mean of the two variances (ddof 0). Thresholds as the opto-map rule readings. Frontal areas are wM1, wM2 and ALM; RSC is (-1.5, 0.5), as fig2e-rsc-tjs1-increase-wminus. Reproduced when at least one frontal site shows an increase passing the threshold in a trial type, and RSC and tjS1 show no change passing it in either trial type; partially reproduced when one of the two parts holds. Each threshold reading is run; the outcome is the one they all give, otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Inhibiting RSC does not change performance in catch or auditory trials, so the effect of RSC inactivation needs the context-sensitive whisker stimulus.
claims.source: Results, Optogenetic inhibition drives cortical activity modes predictive of behavior, paragraph 1; Figures 2C and 2D
claims.quote: Importantly, inhibition of RSC in catch or auditory trials did not lead to any changes in performance, indicating that the presence of the context-sensitive stimulus is necessary for the effect of RSC inactivation to become apparent.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's measure for Figures 2C and 2D, the d' of the opto-map rule of the opening comment, 7 VGAT-ChR2 mice, at the RSC site (-1.5, 0.5) as in fig2e-rsc-tjs1-increase-wminus, catch and auditory trials, W+ and W-. The paper fixes no threshold; under each threshold and null reading, reproduced when RSC has no effect of either sign in any of the four trial type and context groups, and not reproduced when it has one. When the readings disagree, blocked as methods_underspecified. The ΔP and d' of RSC in each group are reported, and the site (-0.5, 0.5) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Jaw opening, the first movement, begins 108 ± 24 ms after the sensory stimulus, so the first 120 ms after the stimulus largely precede movement.
claims.source: Results, Context-dependent flow of activity during sensorimotor transformation, paragraph 1; Figures 3B and 3C
claims.quote: We focused our analyses on the first 120 ms after sensory stimuli, largely preceding the onset of jaw opening (108 ± 24 ms) (Figures 3B&C)
claims.criterion: The jRGECO1a widefield mice, correct trials, jaw opening traces filtered at 60% likelihood and centered on the 250 ms before the stimulus (Methods, Figure 3B). The onset rule of the Methods and the code differ, and the Methods decide (protocol, step 2), on each mouse-average trace the first time after the stimulus at which the d' between jaw opening values and the pre-stimulus 250 ms is >= 1 (Methods, Figure 3C). The code's rule, per trial the first time after the stimulus at which |jaw| over its pre-stimulus SD exceeds 3, averaged per session, then mouse (plot utils/figure3_supp.py:602-674, criterion 3 in figure_files/figure3.py:34), is a variant. Which trial types are pooled is open in the text; the code uses auditory and whisker hits. Reproduced when the mean onset is within tolerance (the ± is the paper's, SEM or CI width in the code).

claims.statement: Auditory-evoked cortical activity is similar in W+ and W-, beginning in A1, then RSC, then medial secondary motor regions (wM1/2), then orofacial motor cortices (tjS1, ALM).
claims.source: Results, Context-dependent flow of activity during sensorimotor transformation, paragraph 1; Figure 3E; Figure 3G right
claims.quote: We observed comparable patterns of cortical activity in auditory trials across W+ and W-contexts, which was dominated by an early increase in fluorescence in the primary auditory cortex (A1), followed by RSC (and nearby regions), and, subsequently, activity propagated anteriorly towards a medial part of secondary motor region (including wM1/2), before transitioning to the orofacial motor cortices (including tjS1 and ALM) (Figures 3D&E)
claims.criterion: The widefield conventions of the opening comment, auditory hits, jRGECO1a mice. The paper gives no measure of similarity or order. Similarity, no ROI reaches |d'| > 2 between W+ and W- from 20 to 120 ms (the paper's Figure 3H threshold and window). Order, readings (a) the time of the peak of the mouse-average trace within 0 to 120 ms, (b) the first time the trace exceeds half that peak. Reproduced when similarity holds and A1 comes before RSC, RSC before wM1 or wM2, and these before tjS1 and ALM, in both contexts; partially reproduced when similarity holds and A1 is first. Each order and baseline reading is run; the outcome is the one they all give, otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: In whisker trials, wS1 and wS2 activate similarly in both contexts early after the stimulus, and from about 50 ms activity diverges, with more activity in RSC and wM1/2 in W+ than in W-.
claims.source: Results, Context-dependent flow of activity during sensorimotor transformation, paragraph 1; Figure 3F
claims.quote: Early after stimulus onset, whisker deflection evoked similar activation of primary and secondary whisker somatosensory cortices (wS1 and wS2) in both W+ and W− contexts. However, after ∼50 ms post-stimulus, cortical dynamics began to diverge, with increased activity in RSC and wM1/2 in the W+ context compared to the W-context.
claims.criterion: The widefield conventions, W+ hits against W- misses, jRGECO1a mice. Reproduced when wS1 and wS2 have |d'| <= 2 from 20 to 50 ms, and RSC and wM1 (or wM2) have d' > 2, W+ higher, at some time between 50 and 120 ms; partially reproduced when only one of RSC and wM1/2 does. The d' threshold and window are those of the Methods (Figure 3H). Each baseline reading is run; the outcome is the one they all give, otherwise methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: RSC is the first cortical area to discriminate the contexts in whisker trials, both in the pixel-wise maps and in the ROI averages, the time of the first d' above 2 between W+ and W-.
claims.source: Results, Context-dependent flow of activity during sensorimotor transformation, paragraph 1; Figure 3H
claims.quote: This analysis, performed both on pixel-wise activity maps and on the average fluorescence of target regions, revealed RSC as the first area to show significant context discriminability (Figure 3H)
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Figure 3H) and plot utils/figure3H.py give it. Per ROI (wS1, wS2, wM1, RSC, ALM, tjS1, as the code ranks) and per pixel, the first time at which the signed W+ minus W- d' across the 6 jRGECO1a mice exceeds 2, the first 20 ms after the stimulus excluded (the code keeps the 20 ms frame; frames from 30 ms is the Methods' reading, 20 ms the code's, both run). For pixels, the earliest crossing among the pixels within each ROI's 1 mm circle, after the code's Gaussian smoothing of sigma 1 pixel (plot utils/misc/plot_average_widefield_timecourse.py:60-63), and without it as a variant. Reproduced when RSC has the earliest time in both the ROI ranking and the pixel version, under every baseline and every exclusion reading (the outcome is the one they all give, otherwise methods_underspecified); a tie with another ROI at the first time counts as partially reproduced, and so does RSC first in one version only.

claims.statement: GCaMP6f mice show whisker-evoked dynamics consistent with jRGECO1a mice, and calcium-insensitive tdTomato and GFP control mice show none of these dynamics.
claims.source: Results, Context-dependent flow of activity during sensorimotor transformation, paragraph 1; Figure 3 figure supplement 1A and 1B
claims.quote: Importantly, these dynamics were not observed in control mice expressing tdTomato or GFP (Figure 3 – figure supplement 1A&B)
claims.criterion: The widefield conventions per mouse line (GCaMP6f 8 mice, tdTomato 4, GFP 6, from the code's lists). The paper gives no measure. An evoked response at an ROI is read as the Methods' rule for Figure 3C applied to ΔF/F0, a d' >= 1 across mice between the post-stimulus value and the pre-stimulus baseline at some time from 20 to 120 ms. Reproduced when GCaMP6f mice show a whisker-evoked response in wS1 and W+ greater than W- in RSC or wM1/2 (d' > 2, as fig3f-whisker-divergence-after-50ms), and tdTomato and GFP mice show no evoked response in wS1 and no ROI with |d'| > 2 between contexts; partially reproduced when only the controls part or only the GCaMP6f part holds.

claims.statement: Axons of RSC neurons project strongly and directly to frontal motor regions (wM1/2).
claims.source: Results, Context-dependent flow of activity during sensorimotor transformation, paragraph 2; Figure 3 figure supplement 1C
claims.quote: finding strong direct connectivity between RSC and frontal motor regions such as secondary motor cortex (wM1/2), consistent with previous anatomical studies
claims.criterion: Light-sheet images of cleared brains after AAV-Chronos-GFP injection into RSC, registered to the Allen atlas. Reproduced when GFP-labelled axons are present in M2 at the wM1/2 coordinates in the injected mice the dataset holds. The paper reports no number of mice or quantification, so the claim is judged by presence.

claims.statement: Before correct trials, pre-stimulus correlations are higher in W- than W+ among orofacial regions, between whisker motor and orofacial regions, between wS1 and wS2, and between wS2 and wM1/2.
claims.source: Results, Inter-area functional connectivity is modulated by context and upcoming choice, paragraph 1; Figure 4B; Figure 4 figure supplement 1C
claims.quote: We observed higher correlation values among orofacial regions, and between whisker motor and orofacial regions in W- compared to W+ in the baseline preceding correct trials. Similarly, there was also an increase in correlation between wS1 and wS2 and between wS2 and wM1/2 in W-.
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Seed correlations; Figures 4A&B) and the code give it (process main_analysis/pixel_correlation_analysis.py, pixel_correlation_processing.py; plot utils/figure4A_B.py). jRGECO1a widefield mice; the 2 s before each trial start; seeds wS1, wS2, wM1, RSC, ALM, tjM1, tjS1 (1 mm circles); per trial the zero-lag Pearson correlation of seed and pixel; the null by 1,000 shuffles of block identity; averages over trials per session, context and correct or incorrect, then over sessions per mouse; grid-space values of the masked maps (>= 1.8 SD of the null). The pairs are the code's fixed list (figure4A_B.py:494-495); orofacial pairs ALM-tjM1, ALM-tjS1, tjM1-tjS1; whisker motor to orofacial wM1-ALM, wM1-tjM1; and wS1-wS2, wS2-wM1. The paper's comparison has two forms; readings (a) the Figure 4B line rule, W- minus W+ with paired d' >= 0.8 (Methods, Figures 4A&B), (b) the related t-test across mice with Bonferroni correction (the code corrects over the 7 targets, figure4A_B.py:656-685), p < 0.05. Reproduced when W- is higher for all seven pairs; partially reproduced when it is for at least four, including one of each group the quote names. Both readings are run; the outcome is the one they both give, otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Before incorrect trials the contextual modulation of correlations is absent, because correlations increase in incorrect W+ trials.
claims.source: Results, Inter-area functional connectivity is modulated by context and upcoming choice, paragraph 1; Figure 4B
claims.quote: Such contextual modulation of correlation was absent in baseline periods preceding an incorrect trial. This was due to an increase in correlation in incorrect trials in the W+ context
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the same pairs and methods as fig4b-wminus-higher-correlation-correct, before incorrect trials. The Figure 4B rule is the paper's test (lines with d' >= 0.8 drawn in colour, the others grey; Methods, Figures 4A&B); the related t-test with Bonferroni correction is the variant. Reproduced when no pair has a W- minus W+ d' >= 0.8 before incorrect trials, and the W+ incorrect minus W+ correct difference is positive for most of the seven pairs; not reproduced when a pair passes the d' rule.

claims.statement: The pre-stimulus network of significantly correlated seeds connects whisker sensory regions, tongue-jaw orofacial regions and RSC, with wM1/2 as intermediary node, and pairs such as wS1 and wS2 or ALM and tjM1 are connected in both contexts for correct and incorrect trials.
claims.source: Results, Inter-area functional connectivity is modulated by context and upcoming choice, paragraph 1; Figure 4B; Figure 4 figure supplement 1B
claims.quote: We found a pattern of significant connectivity between whisker sensory regions, tongue-jaw orofacial regions and RSC with wM1/2 acting as intermediary node in the spontaneous pre-stimulus activity.
claims.criterion: As fig4b-wminus-higher-correlation-correct; a pair is connected when its grand-mean correlation is >= 1.8 SD of the null (Methods, Figures 4A&B; figure4A_B.py:100-101, 469). Reproduced when wS1-wS2 and ALM-tjM1 are connected in all four context and outcome groups and, in each group, wM1 is connected to RSC and to at least one whisker sensory and one tongue-jaw region; partially reproduced when only the first part holds.

claims.statement: Inhibiting wS1 decreases activity widely across cortex, inhibiting wM1/2 decreases activity among motor areas while leaving whisker sensory responses intact, and inhibiting RSC does not increase activity in wM1/2 or tongue-jaw motor regions.
claims.source: Results, Optogenetic inhibition drives cortical activity modes predictive of behavior, paragraph 1; Figure 4C
claims.quote: For instance, inhibition of wS1 (which leads to a strong decrease in lick probability) resulted in widespread decrease in cortical activity, whereas inhibiting wM1/2, which also generated strong decreases in lick probability, concentrated the downstream inhibitory effect among motor areas while leaving the whisker sensory responses intact.
claims.criterion: The 4 widefield-with-optogenetics mice, whisker trials in W+ (Figure 4C legend), grid ROI ΔF/F0 averaged per session, context and site, then per mouse, then over mice (Methods, Figure 4C), compared with control trials (laser off the brain). The paper gives no measure. Peak ΔF/F0 from 50 to 120 ms (the Figure 3G window) per ROI; a decrease is the site value below control by more than the SD of control over mice. Reproduced when wS1 inhibition decreases a majority of ROIs, wM1 (or wM2) inhibition decreases wM1/2, ALM or tjM1 but not wS1 or wS2, and RSC inhibition does not raise wM1, wM2, ALM, tjM1 or tjS1 above control by more than that SD; partially reproduced when two of the three parts hold.

claims.statement: Projected onto PC3, inactivation of wS1, wS2, wM1/2 and ALM drives the trajectory away from the control-lick trajectory toward no-lick, while inhibition of RSC and tjS1 gives trajectories that follow the control-lick trajectory in both contexts.
claims.source: Results, Optogenetic inhibition drives cortical activity modes predictive of behavior, paragraph 1; Figure 4D
claims.quote: For regions of interest that decreased task performance (wS1, wS2, wM1/2 and ALM), inactivation strongly deviated the trajectories away from the control-lick trajectory, towards no-lick. Only inhibition of RSC and tjS1, regions which led to increased licking, had trajectories that followed that of the control-lick in both contexts.
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Principal component analysis; Figure 4D) and plot utils/figure4C_G.py:434-535 give it. Grid ROI traces of control trials, whisker and catch trials, averaged per mouse then over mice by context, trial type, lick and time, from -150 to 150 ms (the Methods' 300 ms window); StandardScaler then PCA with 15 components, signs set as the code sets them; trials at each stimulated site projected per mouse with all trials pooled. Closeness is measured on PC3 from 0 to 150 ms as the mean squared distance to the control-lick and to the control-no-lick trajectories. Reproduced when, in both contexts, wS1, wS2, wM1/2 and ALM are closer to no-lick and RSC and tjS1 closer to lick; partially reproduced when RSC and tjS1 are closer to lick in both contexts and at least two of the others closer to no-lick.

claims.statement: The PC3 trajectories under RSC and tjS1 inhibition make smaller angles with the control-lick trajectory than those under inhibition of the other regions, which decreased lick probability.
claims.source: Results, Optogenetic inhibition drives cortical activity modes predictive of behavior, paragraph 1; Figure 4E
claims.quote: RSC and tjS1 – areas that increased licking in W- – had smaller angles with respect to the lick trajectories compared to the other regions, which decreased lick probability in all contexts (Figure 4E)
claims.criterion: The angle as the Methods (Figures 4E-G) give it, the arccos of the normalised dot product of the per-mouse stimulated-site PC3 trace and the grand-average control-lick PC3 trace, in degrees, over the post-stimulus samples of the window (plot utils/figure4C_G.py:214-237). The code first adds the minimum of the stimulated trace to both traces, which the Methods do not describe; the Methods' angle decides and the code's is a variant. Reproduced when, in each context, the mean angles over mice of RSC and tjS1 are both smaller than those of wS1, wS2, wM1 (or wM2) and ALM; partially reproduced when this holds in one context.

claims.statement: Across all inactivated sites, in W+ and in W-, the angle between the inhibition and control-lick trajectories relates to the change in lick probability the inhibition evokes.
claims.source: Results, Optogenetic inhibition drives cortical activity modes predictive of behavior, paragraph 1; Figures 4F and 4G
claims.quote: This relationship held generally true across all inactivated regions in W+ and W-contexts (Figures 4F&G)
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Figures 4E-G) and plot utils/figure4C_G.py:318-341 give it. Per context, a linear regression (scipy linregress, Pearson) over sites of the mean angle over mice against the mean whisker-trial ΔP(Lick) of the same 4 mice from the opto-map rule. Sites are paired by coordinate; the code pairs two tables by sorted position, which may mis-pair them, and is shown as a variant. Reproduced when the correlation is negative (smaller angles with larger ΔP) with p < 0.05 in both contexts; partially reproduced when in one context, or when negative in both without p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In mice expressing jRGECO1a without ChR2, the laser gives only a local photoactivation effect and none of the widespread inhibition seen in ChR2 mice.
claims.source: Figure 4 figure supplement 1D; Results, Optogenetic inhibition drives cortical activity modes predictive of behavior, paragraph 1
claims.quote: This control experiment shows a locally restricted jRGECO1a photo-activation effect (jRGECO1a is based on mApple, which shows photoconversion upon blue light stimulation), but no widespread inhibition as observed in mice expressing the ChR2 opsin in inhibitory neurons
claims.criterion: The photoactivation-control mice (2 mice, 6 sessions in the code's list), laser at wS1 and wM1/2, whisker trials, analysed as fig4c-inhibition-propagates-forward. Reproduced when the stimulated ROI rises above control and fewer than half of the other ROIs fall below control by more than the control SD, for both sites.

claims.statement: Mice are less accurate in the olfactory search task in the DOI session than in the saline session, going more often to the incorrect side.
claims.source: Results, DOI alters olfactory search behavior, paragraph 2; Figure 1B
claims.quote: Indeed, mice more often navigated to the incorrect side of the arena in the DOI condition ( Figure 1B ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.024, n = 22)
claims.criterion: As the Methods (Figure 1) and fig1_cleaned.Rmd define it, accuracy is the percent of a session's odor trials (odor_setting 0) that were correct, sessions with fewer than 40 trials dropped. A two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test of DOI against saline accuracy over the mice. Reproduced when the median DOI minus saline difference is negative and p < 0.05; partially reproduced when it is negative with 0.05 <= p < 0.1. Omission-trial accuracy, which the code also tests, is reported as a variant.

claims.statement: Over the session, odor-trial accuracy in 5 min bins is higher in the saline condition than the DOI condition after the first 10 min, except in the 30 to 35 min bin, so the effect is spread across the session.
claims.source: Results, DOI alters olfactory search behavior, paragraph 2; Figure 1C
claims.quote: In odor trials, accuracy was higher in the saline condition after the first 10 min, except for the 30 – 35 min bin ( Figure 1C ; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p < 0.01 for time points within 10 – 25 min, p = 0.039 for 35 – 40 min)
claims.criterion: As in the Methods (Figure 1) and fig1_cleaned.Rmd. Odor trials only; for each trial the rolling accuracy, the percent correct of the session's odor trials up to and including that one; trials binned by start time into 5 min bins from 0 to 40 min; per mouse and bin, the mean rolling accuracy; per bin, a two-sided unpaired Wilcoxon rank-sum test of DOI against saline mouse values, uncorrected (the Methods give the rank-sum test because some mice have no trials in some bins). Reproduced when saline is higher at p < 0.05 in the bins 10 to 15, 15 to 20, 20 to 25 and 35 to 40 min, with p < 0.01 in the first three, and the 30 to 35 min bin is not significant; partially reproduced when saline is higher at p < 0.05 in at least two of those four bins. The 0 to 10 min and 25 to 30 min bins, which the text does not state separately, are reported. The per-bin fraction correct (not rolling) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Mice complete fewer trials in the 40 min DOI session than in the saline session.
claims.source: Results, DOI alters olfactory search behavior, paragraph 3; Figure 1D
claims.quote: Mice completed fewer trials in the DOI condition ( Figure 1D ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.011, n = 22)
claims.criterion: Trials completed is the number of trials in the session (the Methods, Figure 1, "the sum of all trials in a session"). fig1_cleaned.Rmd counts only the odor trials (odor_setting 0) for this test, while the Methods' wording counts all trials; both are run, readings (a) odor trials, the code, and (b) all trials, the Methods. A two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the 22 mice. Reproduced when, under a reading, DOI is lower with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The drop in trials completed under DOI is driven by females; female mice perform fewer trials on DOI than saline, while male mice show no significant difference.
claims.source: Results, DOI alters olfactory search behavior, paragraph 3; Figure 1D
claims.quote: This effect was driven by female mice; female mice performed fewer trials on DOI compared to saline ( Figure 1D ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.011, n = 12), whereas male mice did not show a significant difference ( Figure 1D ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.39, n = 10)
claims.criterion: The trial counts of fig1d-fewer-trials under both of its readings, split by sex (females as listed in the opening comment, from the code). Two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests within each sex, as in fig1_cleaned.Rmd. Reproduced when, under a reading, females are lower on DOI at p < 0.05 and males do not differ at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when only one of the two holds.

claims.statement: Mice poke into the initiation port during the ITI at the same rate in the DOI and saline conditions, showing an equivalent motivation to do the task.
claims.source: Results, DOI alters olfactory search behavior, paragraph 3; Figure 1E
claims.quote: We found that mice poked into the initiation port, but there was not a significant difference between conditions ( Figure 1E ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.27, n = 17)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. As in the Figure 1E legend and fig1_cleaned.Rmd, the repoke rate is the session's number of initiation-port pokes during ITIs divided by the number of ITIs (trials minus one), for the 17 mice after the first cohort. Two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, DOI against saline. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the median difference is reported either way.

claims.statement: Mice rarely enter a reward port during the ITI after a trial-initiation attempt, and DOI does not make them do so more than saline.
claims.source: Results, DOI alters olfactory search behavior, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Mice rarely entered the reward port during the ITI after trial initiation attempt (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p = 1)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The Methods (Figure 1) define a false odor report as an initiation-port beam break followed by crossing the decision line during the ITI, for the 17 mice after the first cohort; the code in the repository does not compute it (the trial table of the later cohort has a false_alarm column, which is used if the dataset holds it). The per-mouse measure is not fixed; readings (a) the count of false reports per session and (b) that count divided by the number of ITIs. The paper's test, a two-sided unpaired Wilcoxon rank-sum test of DOI against saline sessions. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 under the readings, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the counts per session are reported to show whether they are rare. The Results describe the event as entering the reward port during the ITI after an initiation attempt; that count is shown as a variant, the Methods' definition deciding. "Rarely" has no threshold in the paper and is not judged.

claims.statement: After correct trials, mice stay longer in the reward port on DOI odor trials than on saline odor trials and saline omission trials.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
claims.quote: Reward port duration was increased in the DOI odor trial condition compared to both saline odor and saline odor omission trials ( Figure 2A ; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p < 0.001, n = 17)
claims.criterion: Reward-port duration after a correct trial is the time from entering the reward port to exiting it, re-entries not added (Methods, Figure 2), for the 17 mice after the first cohort. Every event is a sample, pooled over mice, in four groups (DOI odor, DOI omission, saline odor, saline omission). As the Methods and fig2_cleaned.Rmd do, a Kruskal-Wallis test over the four groups, then pairwise two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Bonferroni adjustment over the six pairs (R pairwise.wilcox.test). Reproduced when DOI odor durations are higher than both saline groups at adjusted p < 0.001; partially reproduced when both hold at adjusted p < 0.05, or only one at p < 0.001. Which port entry counts is not fixed by the paper (the files the code reads are pre-computed); readings (a) the first reward-port entry after the trial's response, (b) the first entry within the 5 s window the Methods give for collecting a reward. The per-mouse medians of fig2b are reported alongside.

claims.statement: Reward-port duration after correct trials does not depend on sex in either condition.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 1; Figure 2A supplemental
claims.quote: We did not find a sex effect of condition ( Figure 2A supplemental , p = 1)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The events of fig2a, grouped by condition and sex (DOI female, DOI male, saline female, saline male). The paper does not name the test. Readings (a) a Kruskal-Wallis test over the four groups, as fig2_cleaned.Rmd runs it; (b) pairwise two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Bonferroni adjustment over the six pairs, as the Methods give for the duration groups and as the Results name for the matching test of Figure 2C, judged on female against male within each condition. Reproduced when no reading finds a sex difference at p < 0.05, not reproduced when every reading does; when they disagree, blocked as methods_underspecified with both results shown. The p-values are reported.

claims.statement: Per mouse, the median reward-port duration after correct trials is longer in the DOI session than in the saline session.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 1; Figure 2B
claims.quote: When comparing the median duration between conditions, mice in the DOI condition spent longer in the reward port compared to saline ( Figure 2B ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.002)
claims.criterion: The correct-trial events of fig2a, odor and omission trials together; per mouse and condition the median duration; a two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, DOI against saline, as in fig2_cleaned.Rmd. Reproduced when DOI is higher with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The longer median reward-port duration under DOI is driven by odor trials.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 1; Figure 2B supplemental
claims.quote: This effect was driven by the odor trial ( Figure 2B supplemental ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.001)
claims.criterion: As fig2b, with odor trials only, as in fig2_cleaned.Rmd. Reproduced when DOI is higher with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: After correct omission trials, the median reward-port duration does not differ between DOI and saline.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 1
claims.quote: as we did not see a difference between median duration after an omission trial (Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.60)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. As fig2b, with omission trials only, mice without events in both conditions dropped, as in fig2_cleaned.Rmd; two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the median difference is reported.

claims.statement: After incorrect (unrewarded) trials, mice stay longest in the reward port on DOI odor trials, longer than on DOI omission, saline odor and saline omission trials, and longer on saline odor than saline omission trials.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
claims.quote: We found an increased duration in DOI odor trials compared to DOI odor omission trials ( Figure 2C ; Wilcoxon rank sum test for all comparisons, p < 0.001), saline odor trials (p = 0.030), and saline odor omission trials (p < 0.001). Additionally, there was an increased reward port duration for the saline odor trial compared to the saline odor omission trial (p < 0.001)
claims.criterion: As fig2a (same duration definition, same port-entry readings, same Kruskal-Wallis and Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise rank-sum tests over the four groups, as in the Methods and fig2_cleaned.Rmd), with the events after incorrect trials. Reproduced when all four stated comparisons go in the stated direction at adjusted p < 0.05; partially reproduced when three of the four do.

claims.statement: After incorrect trials, reward-port duration does not differ between the sexes within either condition.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 2; Figure 2C supplemental
claims.quote: Sex differences within each condition were not significant ( Figure 2C supplemental , Wilcoxon rank sum, p = 1)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's named test. The incorrect-trial events grouped by condition and sex; pairwise two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Bonferroni adjustment over the six pairs of the four groups (the Methods' post hoc test); female against male within DOI and within saline. Reproduced when neither is significant at adjusted p < 0.05, not reproduced when either is. The Kruskal-Wallis test over the four groups, which fig2_cleaned.Rmd runs, is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Per mouse, the median reward-port duration after incorrect trials does not differ between DOI and saline.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 2; Figure 2D
claims.quote: When comparing the median duration between conditions, there was no difference between DOI and saline ( Figure 2D ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.21)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Per mouse and condition the median duration over incorrect-trial events, odor and omission together; two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, mice without both values dropped, as in fig2_cleaned.Rmd. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the median difference is reported.

claims.statement: After incorrect omission trials, mice stay longer in the reward port in the DOI condition than in the saline condition.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 2; Figure 2D supplemental
claims.quote: However, after an odor omission trial, mice spent longer in the reward port in the DOI condition ( Figure 2D supplemental , Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.049)
claims.criterion: As fig2d, with incorrect omission trials only, mice without both values dropped, as in fig2_cleaned.Rmd. Reproduced when DOI is higher with p < 0.05; partially reproduced when it is higher with 0.05 <= p < 0.1.

claims.statement: Mice take longer to complete odor trials in the DOI condition than in the saline condition.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 3; Figure 3A
claims.quote: In odor trials, mice took longer to complete a trial in the DOI condition compared to the saline condition ( Figure 3A ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p < 0.001, n = 22)
claims.criterion: Trial duration is trial end minus trial start; per mouse and condition the mean over odor trials (Methods, Figure 3; fig3_cleaned.Rmd); two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Reproduced when DOI is longer with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The duration of omission trials does not differ between DOI and saline.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In contrast, there was no difference in trial duration in omission trials between DOI and saline (Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.26, n = 22)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. As fig3a with omission trials. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the median difference is reported.

claims.statement: ITI duration does not differ between DOI and saline.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 3; Figure 3B
claims.quote: However, there was no difference in ITI duration between conditions ( Figure 3B ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p = 0.19, n = 22)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. ITI duration is the next trial's start minus this trial's end (Methods, Figure 3); per mouse and condition the mean over all trials of the session, as in fig3_cleaned.Rmd; two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the median difference is reported.

claims.statement: DOI lowers movement speed within trials, odor and omission trials pooled, compared with saline.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 4; Figure 3C
claims.quote: We found that DOI decreased movement speed both within trial ( Figure 3C ; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p = 0.011, pooled trial type)
claims.criterion: Nose-keypoint speed as in the Methods (Figure 3) and fig3_cleaned.Rmd (see the opening comment), per mouse and condition the mean over the frames within any trial. The Results name the rank-sum test; the Methods ("For trial durations, ITI duration, and overall task speed, Wilcoxon signed rank tests were used") and the code use the two-sided paired signed-rank test, which decides here, the Methods coming first; the unpaired rank-sum test is shown as a variant. Reproduced when DOI is lower with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: DOI lowers movement speed during the ITI compared with saline.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 4; Figure 3D
claims.quote: and during the ITI ( Figure 3D ; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p = 0.036) compared to saline
claims.criterion: As fig3c, with the frames outside every trial. Reproduced when DOI is lower with p < 0.05 under the paired signed-rank test; the rank-sum test is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Within odor trials alone, speed does not differ between DOI and saline sessions.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 4; Figure 3 supplemental
claims.quote: In odor trials specifically, the speed between DOI and saline sessions were not different ( Figure 3 supplemental ; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p = 0.059)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. As fig3c with the frames of odor trials only. The Results name the rank-sum test; the Methods and fig3_cleaned.Rmd (which runs every pair of the six condition and period means as paired signed-rank tests, uncorrected) use the two-sided paired signed-rank test, which decides, the Methods coming first. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05. The rank-sum result and the median difference are reported.

claims.statement: Within the DOI condition, mice move more slowly in the ITI than in odor trials.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 4; Figure 3 supplemental
claims.quote: Within the DOI condition, speed was decreased in the ITI compared to an odor trial ( Figure 3 supplemental ; Wilcoxon signed rank test, p < 0.001)
claims.criterion: Per mouse, DOI session mean speeds over ITI frames and over odor-trial frames (as fig3c); two-sided paired signed-rank test, as in fig3_cleaned.Rmd. Reproduced when ITI is slower with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Within the DOI condition, speed does not differ between odor and omission trials, nor between the ITI and omission trials.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 4
claims.quote: However, there was no difference in speed between the odor and odor omission trials in the DOI condition (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p = 0.21), nor the ITI and odor omission trials (Wilcoxon rank sum, p = 0.068)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, for two comparisons. Per-mouse DOI session mean speeds over odor-trial, omission-trial and ITI frames (as fig3c); two-sided paired signed-rank tests, the Methods' test and the code's, uncorrected; the rank-sum tests the Results name are shown as variants. Reproduced when neither comparison has p < 0.05; partially reproduced when one does; not reproduced when both do. Effect sizes are reported.

claims.statement: In saline sessions, mice move more slowly in the ITI than in odor trials and in omission trials.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 4
claims.quote: In comparison, in saline sessions the ITI speed was slower compared to odor (p = 0.002) and odor omission trials (p = 0.017)
claims.criterion: Per-mouse saline session mean speeds over ITI, odor-trial and omission-trial frames (as fig3c); two-sided paired signed-rank tests, uncorrected, as in fig3_cleaned.Rmd and the Methods; the rank-sum test is shown as a variant. Reproduced when the ITI is slower than both at p < 0.05; partially reproduced when it is slower than one.

claims.statement: In saline sessions, speed does not differ between odor and omission trials.
claims.source: Results, DOI impacts speed and timing, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Speed within the odor and odor omission trials were not different in the saline condition (Wilcoxon rank sum, p = 0.54)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Per-mouse saline session mean speeds over odor-trial and omission-trial frames (as fig3c); two-sided paired signed-rank test, the Methods' and code's; the rank-sum test is shown as a variant. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the median difference is reported.

claims.statement: Pooling all sessions with a usable sniff signal, sniff frequency is higher in DOI sessions than in saline sessions.
claims.source: Results, DOI increases sniff frequency, paragraph 1; Figure 4A to 4C
claims.quote: When all sessions with sniff measurement were combined, sniff frequency was higher in DOI sessions ( Figure 4A – C ; Fisher-Pitman Permutation test, Z = 24.9, p < 0.001)
claims.criterion: Sniff frequency is 1000 over the interval in ms between consecutive inhalation times (Methods, Figure 4; fig4_cleaned.Rmd), sniffs with a missing exhalation dropped. Further exclusions from the Methods, applied when the dataset gives raw inhalation times; sniff durations below the 5th or above the 95th percentile, computed where the Methods do not say (the MATLAB code that applied it is not in the repository), so run under readings (a) per session and (b) over all sessions of a condition, and durations outside 10 to 1000, read as ms (the Methods print "s", which cannot hold for a sniff). Where the dataset holds only the thermistor signal, the Methods give a 25 ms moving-window smoothing and peak and trough detection, and the detection settings are open; the inhalation times are then a deviation. Sessions are those with a usable signal; the code drops DOI sessions 2195 17 and 2198 17 and saline sessions 2198 19 and 2213 18 as faulty, and the counts are compared with 14 and 13. Every sniff is a sample; a two-sample Fisher-Pitman permutation test (coin oneway_test, 10000 resamples) of DOI against saline. Reproduced when the DOI mean frequency is higher with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Every mouse with matched DOI and saline sniff sessions has a sniff-frequency distribution shifted higher in the DOI condition.
claims.source: Results, DOI increases sniff frequency, paragraph 1; Figure 4 supplemental
claims.quote: All mice with a matched DOI and saline session had a higher-shifted distribution sniff rates in the DOI condition ( Figure 4 supplemental ; Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p < 0.001 for 13 of 13 mice)
claims.criterion: The sniff frequencies of fig4abc; for each mouse with usable DOI and saline sessions, a one-sided two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test that DOI frequencies are stochastically larger (R ks.test(doi, saline, alternative = "less"), as in fig4_cleaned.Rmd). Reproduced when every matched mouse has p < 0.001 and their number is within the tolerance; partially reproduced when at least two thirds of them do.

claims.statement: Mice sniff faster in the DOI condition in odor trials, in omission trials and during the ITI.
claims.source: Results, DOI increases sniff frequency, paragraph 1; Figure 4D
claims.quote: mice sniffed faster in the DOI condition for each trial type and during the ITI ( Figure 4D ; Fisher-Pitman Permutation test for all trial types; Odor trials: Z = 3.38, p < 0.001; Omission trials: Z = 2.71, p= 0.007; ITI: Z = 18.4, p < 0.001)
claims.criterion: The sniffs of fig4abc, each placed by its inhalation time in an odor trial, an omission trial (between a trial's start and end) or the ITI (otherwise), as in fig4_cleaned.Rmd; a Fisher-Pitman permutation test (10000 resamples) of DOI against saline in each period. Reproduced when DOI is higher with p < 0.05 in all three; partially reproduced in two.

claims.statement: Per-mouse median sniff frequency does not differ between DOI and saline.
claims.source: Results, DOI increases sniff frequency, paragraph 1; Figure 4E
claims.quote: We did not observe a difference in median sniff frequencies between conditions ( Figure 4E ; Wilcoxon signed rank test; p = 0.11)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Per mouse and condition the median of the sniff frequencies of fig4abc; two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over mice with both, as in fig4_cleaned.Rmd. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the median difference is reported.

claims.statement: Mice occupy the arena similarly in the DOI and saline conditions; DOI does not make them spend more time in task-irrelevant areas such as the corners or spread more evenly.
claims.source: Results, Mice occupy allocentric space similarly but head twitch preferentially in proximity to odor ports, paragraph 1; Figure 5A and 5B
claims.quote: Contrary to this prediction, mice showed similar occupancy across DOI and saline conditions ( Figure 5A, B )
claims.criterion: The paper reports no test. Occupancy is the fraction of a session's tracked frames in each 1 cm bin (48 pixels in fig5_cleaned.Rmd), from the nose keypoint, frames above 160 cm/s dropped, x flipped for the first cohort; the maps are the mean over the 22 mice (Figure 5A legend, Methods Figure 5, code). The measures come from the prediction the paper tested ("more time in areas irrelevant to the task such as corners of the arena, with a more even distribution"); per mouse and condition (a) the Shannon entropy of the occupancy map and (b) the fraction of frames in the four arena corners, with the corner size open, read as squares of 5 cm and of 10 cm side (choices, as the paper fixes none). Each is compared DOI against saline with a two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, the Methods' paired test. Reproduced when no measure differs at p < 0.05; not reproduced when every one does, in either direction, as the claim is one of similar occupancy; otherwise blocked as methods_underspecified with all results shown. The Pearson correlation between the two grand-mean maps is reported as a description.

claims.statement: During trials, HTR rate (normalized to occupancy) varies with the X coordinate of the arena but not with the Y coordinate.
claims.source: Results, Mice occupy allocentric space similarly but head twitch preferentially in proximity to odor ports, paragraph 2; Figure 5 supplemental A
claims.quote: During a trial, HTR rate occurred throughout the arena without spatial predictability on the Y-coordinate ( Figure 5 supplemental ; Permutation test, p = 0.92), but with preference for the X-coordinate ( Figure 5 supplemental ; Permutation test, p = 0.002)
claims.criterion: DOI sessions with HTR times. As in the Methods (Figure 5) and fig5_cleaned.Rmd; nose position at each frame (x flipped for the first cohort, frames above 160 cm/s dropped); each HTR assigned to the frame nearest its time; the arena in bins of 100 pixels (about 2.5 cm), the last bin column and row (x bin 1200, y bin 700) dropped; per mouse and bin, HTRs within trials over within-trial occupancy, in HTR per min, bins the mouse visited in the session filled with zero where it had no within-trial time. Statistic the Pearson correlation of the per-mouse, per-bin rates with bin x and with bin y; null from 10000 permutations of the bin coordinates; two-sided p as the fraction of permuted absolute correlations at or above the observed one (seed 123 in the code, a choice that cannot change the outcome). Reproduced when p < 0.05 for x and p >= 0.05 for y; partially reproduced when only one holds. The sign of the x correlation is reported, positive meaning toward the odor and reward ports.

claims.statement: With trial and ITI periods combined, mice head-twitch more often closer to the odor end of the arena, as the X coordinate increases.
claims.source: Results, Mice occupy allocentric space similarly but head twitch preferentially in proximity to odor ports, paragraph 2; Figure 5E
claims.quote: and when conditions were combined ( Figure 5E ; Permutation test, p < 0.001 for X-coordinates)
claims.criterion: As fig5supp-htr-within-trial-x-not-y with all frames of the DOI session (trial and ITI combined), rows for the bins each mouse occupied, as fig5_cleaned.Rmd does. Reproduced when the x correlation is positive (rate rising toward the odor and reward ports) with p < 0.001; partially reproduced when it is positive with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: During the ITI, mice head-twitch more often toward the end of the arena past the decision line (as X increases), but not specifically next to the reward ports on the Y coordinate.
claims.source: Results, Mice occupy allocentric space similarly but head twitch preferentially in proximity to odor ports, paragraph 2; Figure 5 supplemental B
claims.quote: Similarly, during the ITI, we found that mice HTR more frequently closer to the end of the arena after crossing the decision line (as X-coordinate increases), but not immediately next to the reward ports (on the Y-coordinate)
claims.criterion: The paper gives no test for the ITI alone and the code runs none; the test of fig5supp-htr-within-trial-x-not-y is applied to ITI frames and ITI HTRs (per-mouse rates over ITI occupancy, the code's htr_normalized_permouse_iti, edge bins dropped), the reading the paper's "Similarly" implies. Reproduced when the x correlation is positive with p < 0.05 and the y test has p >= 0.05; partially reproduced when only the x part holds.

claims.statement: HTR rate does not differ between time within trials and time in the ITI.
claims.source: Results, Mice occupy allocentric space similarly but head twitch preferentially in proximity to odor ports, paragraph 2; Figure 5F
claims.quote: We normalized HTR rate based on within trial and ITI duration and found no difference in HTR rate based on whether the mouse was in a trial or ITI ( Figure 5F ; Wilcoxon signed rank, p = 1)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. As in fig5_cleaned.Rmd; per DOI session, HTRs whose time lies within a trial divided by the summed trial durations, and the other HTRs divided by 2400 s minus the summed trial durations, in HTR per min; two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the median difference is reported.

claims.statement: HTR rate over the 40 min DOI session does not differ between male and female mice.
claims.source: Results, Mice occupy allocentric space similarly but head twitch preferentially in proximity to odor ports, paragraph 2; Figure 5 supplemental C
claims.quote: Additionally, we did not see a sex difference in HTR rate over the 40 m session ( Figure 5 supplemental ; Wilcoxon rank sum, p = 0.31)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Per DOI session the number of HTRs divided by 40 min; a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (normal approximation, exact = FALSE in fig5_cleaned.Rmd), female against male. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the group medians are reported.

claims.statement: Each frame holds seven MARS keypoints (nose, left ear, right ear, neck, left hip, right hip, tail base) for each of two mice, the resident (mouse 0) and the intruder (mouse 1), in pixel coordinates of a 1024 x 570 image, at 30 Hz, with a confidence score from 0 to 1 for each keypoint.
claims.source: Section 3 and Figure 3; Appendix C (data format), paragraph 4; Appendix D.1
claims.quote: mouse 0 is the resident and mouse 1 is the intruder), image (x,y) coordinates in pixels, and keypoint ID. For keypoint ID, there are seven tracked body parts, ordered (nose, left ear, right ear, neck, left hip, right hip, tail base).
claims.criterion: Judged on the dandiset's CalMS21 file. Reproduced when it holds 14 keypoint series named for these seven parts on the resident and the intruder, in pixels, sampled at 30 Hz, with every coordinate within 0 to 1024 (x) and 0 to 570 (y), and a confidence value for each keypoint and frame within 0 to 1. Partially reproduced when the positions meet all of this but the confidence values are missing or out of range. Not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Mouse 0, the resident, is the black C57Bl/6J mouse, and mouse 1, the intruder, is the white BALB/c mouse.
claims.source: Appendix C; Appendix B (Collection Process); Appendix D.1
claims.quote: In this assay, a black (C57Bl/6J) male "resident" mouse is filmed in its home cage, and a white (BALB/c) male or female "intruder" mouse is manually introduced to the cage ... mouse 0 is the resident and mouse 1 is the intruder
claims.criterion: On the dandiset's video and pose. Every 30th frame, the mean grey level of the video in a patch of 12 x 12 pixels centred on each mouse's body centre (the mean of its neck and two hip keypoints), using frames where the two body centres are at least 60 pixels apart. Reproduced when the resident's patch is darker than the intruder's in at least 90% of these frames; partially reproduced for 50% to 90%; not reproduced below 50%.

claims.statement: Task 1 frames are annotated by one annotator (annotator id 0) with exactly one label per frame from the vocabulary attack 0, investigation 1, mount 2 and other 3.
claims.source: Section 3; Appendix C (metadata and vocab)
claims.quote: In Tasks 1 and 2, each frame is assigned one label ... In Task 1, GROUPNAME is annotator_id-0 ... and there is only one GROUP in the file. ... For example, in Task 1 vocab is attack: 0, investigation: 1, mount: 2, other: 3.
claims.criterion: On the dandiset's CalMS21 file. Reproduced when its catalogue of behaviors holds these four names with these integer codes, the annotator is given as 0, and the bouts give exactly one label to every frame of the session (no frame uncovered, none covered twice). Partially reproduced when the names and codes hold but the annotator or the one-label rule does not. Not reproduced when the names or codes differ.

claims.statement: The source videos of Task 1 are released, recorded at 30 Hz and 1024 x 570 pixels.
claims.source: Section 3.1, paragraph 3; Appendix D.1
claims.quote: In addition to pose data, we also release all source videos for Task 1 ... Videos are acquired at 30 fps and 1024x570 pixel resolution
claims.criterion: On the dandiset's video of mouse071. Reproduced when it is 1024 x 570 pixels at 30 frames per second and has as many frames as the pose. Partially reproduced when it is present but one of the three differs; not reproduced when it is absent or unreadable.

claims.statement: Close investigation, attack and mount are behaviors in which the resident is in close contact with the intruder; other frames include the animals apart.
claims.source: Appendix D.2 (behavior definitions)
claims.quote: Close investigation: resident (black) mouse is in close contact with the intruder (white) and is actively sniffing the intruder anywhere on its body or tail. ... animals may be apart from each other exploring other parts of the arena
claims.criterion: On the dandiset's pose and bouts. Per frame, the distance from the resident's nose to the nearest intruder keypoint. Reproduced when, for each social label present in the session, the median distance in its frames is below the median in "other" frames, with a 95% moving-block bootstrap interval (blocks of 300 frames, 2000 resamples) of the difference that excludes 0. Partially reproduced when this holds for some labels only. A label with no frames in the session is reported as untested.

claims.statement: Errors in pose estimation are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly.
claims.source: Appendix B (Composition, errors and noise)
claims.quote: some errors in pose estimation and noise in keypoint placement still occur. These are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly.
claims.criterion: On the dandiset's pose alone, as it holds no usable confidence values. A frame is counted as a pose error when any of four body lengths of either mouse (nose to neck, neck to tail base, left to right ear, left to right hip) lies outside the session's quartiles widened by 3 times the interquartile range. Close frames are the lowest 10% of the distance between the two mice's centroids; fast frames are the highest 10% of the faster mouse's centroid speed after a 15-frame running median. Reproduced when the error fraction is higher in close frames than in the others and higher in fast frames than in the others, each with a 95% moving-block bootstrap interval (blocks of 300 frames, 2000 resamples) of the difference that excludes 0. Partially reproduced when this holds for one of the two. Thresholds of 5% and 20%, and a factor of 1.5, are shown as variants.

claims.statement: The dandiset's CalMS21 sequence is the CalMS21 Task 1 test sequence mouse071, with the same keypoints, confidence scores and frame annotations.
claims.source: Appendix C; CaltechDATA record 10.22002/D1.1991, file task1_classic_classification.zip
claims.criterion: Records are matched by name (session mouse071_task1 against the key task1/test/mouse071_task1_annotator1). Reproduced when the frame counts are equal, every keypoint coordinate agrees within 0.001 pixel with mice, parts and axes in the stated order, and the frame labels from the bouts agree with the CaltechDATA annotations (through the catalogue's codes) on every frame. Partially reproduced when at least 99% of coordinates and of frames agree. Not reproduced otherwise. The confidence scores are compared and reported; the dandiset's are known to be empty (data check), which is recorded under format-keypoints and as a finding, and does not decide the link.

claims.statement: Errors in pose estimation are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly, as shown by the MARS confidence scores.
claims.source: Appendix B (Composition, errors and noise)
claims.quote: some errors in pose estimation and noise in keypoint placement still occur. These are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly.
claims.criterion: The confidence scores come from CaltechDATA's copy of mouse071, matched frame by frame; positions, distances and speeds come from the dandiset.
