Per frame, the mean confidence over the 14 keypoints. Close and fast frames as in pose-errors-close-fast. Reproduced when the median confidence is lower in close frames than in the others and lower in fast frames than in the others, each with a 95% moving-block bootstrap interval (blocks of 300 frames, 2000 resamples) that excludes 0; partially reproduced when this holds for one of the two.

claims.statement: Task 1 has 70 training sequences with 507,738 frames and 19 test sequences with 262,107 frames.
claims.source: Table 5; Section 3.1; Figure 4A
claims.quote: There are 70 videos in the public training set ... Training and test set instances counts for each task and category.
claims.criterion: Counts of a fixed deposited file, so the tolerance is 0. Frames are counted as the length of each sequence's annotations, checked against its scores. Reproduced when all four match; partially reproduced when all are within 10% of the reported value; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Task 2 has, for annotators 1 to 5, 6 training sequences each with 139,112, 135,623, 107,420, 108,325 and 92,383 frames, and 13, 6, 4, 4 and 20 test sequences with 286,810, 150,919, 77,079, 76,174 and 364,007 frames.
claims.source: Table 5; Section 3.2
claims.quote: we provide six 10-minute training videos for each of five annotators unseen in Task 1 ... Training and test set instances counts for each task and category.
claims.criterion: As table5-task1-counts, over the 20 counts.

claims.statement: Task 3 has, for approach, disengaged, grooming, intromission, mount attempt, sniff face and white rearing, 3, 2, 2, 1, 4, 3 and 2 training sequences with 20,624, 35,751, 45,174, 19,200, 46,847, 19,244 and 36,181 frames, and 25, 1, 13, 10, 12, 47 and 1 test sequences with 126,468, 19,088, 156,664, 55,218, 85,836, 251,793 and 17,939 frames.
claims.source: Table 5; Section 3.3; Figure 4A
claims.quote: This task contains annotations on seven behaviors not labeled in Tasks 1 & 2, where some behaviors are very rare ... Training and test set instances counts for each task and category.
claims.criterion: As table5-task1-counts, over the 28 counts.

claims.statement: In the Task 1 training set, 2.76% of frames are labelled attack, 28.9% investigation, 5.64% mount and 62.7% other.
claims.source: Table 6; Figure 4B
claims.quote: The percentage of frames labeled as attack, investigation, mount, and other in the Task 1 training set.
claims.criterion: Percentages of a fixed deposited file, so the tolerance is half a unit of the last digit reported. Readings of the frames counted are (a) the training split, as the table says, and (b) training and test together. Reproduced when all four are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when all four are within 10% of the reported value under one reading; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The five Task 2 annotators label different fractions of frames as other, investigation, mount and attack (annotator 1 60.0, 20.6, 16.2 and 3.2%; annotator 2 65.5, 25.8, 3.4 and 5.3%; annotator 3 68.9, 13.5, 9.5 and 8.1%; annotator 4 75.2, 11.6, 4.5 and 8.7%; annotator 5 69.5, 26.4, 1.0 and 3.0%).

claims.quote: Annot 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are different domain experts, whose annotations for attack, mount, and investigation are used in Task 2.
claims.criterion: The pie charts carry no class names for Task 2; the order is read from the Task 1 pie (other, investigation, mount, attack). Tolerance is half a unit of the last digit, as in table6-task1-label-fractions. Readings are (a) the training split and (b) training and test together, and for the classes (i) the Task 1 order and (ii) the four values of each annotator matched to the four classes in whatever order fits best. Reproduced when all 20 values are within tolerance under one combination of readings; partially reproduced when at least 16 are; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: In Task 3 the behaviors occupy 3.25% (approach), 1.47% (disengaged), 14.0% (groom), 19.3% (intromission), 0.90% (mount attempt), 4.74% (sniff face) and 9.29% (white rearing) of frames.
claims.source: Table 7; Figure 4B
claims.quote: This task contains annotations on seven behaviors not labeled in Tasks 1 & 2, where some behaviors are very rare
claims.criterion: Tolerance is half a unit of the last digit, as in table6-task1-label-fractions. Readings are (a) the training split of each behavior and (b) training and test together. Reproduced when all seven are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced when all are within 10% of the reported value; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: The unlabeled set has 282 videos and about 6 million frames; the dataset holds over 1 million annotated frames, over 70 hours of tracked poses and over 10 hours of frame-by-frame annotation.
claims.source: Abstract; Section 3; Figure 4A; Section 5 (Discussion), paragraphs 1 and 3
claims.quote: The dataset consists of 6 million frames of unlabeled tracked poses of interacting mice, as well as over 1 million frames with tracked poses ... The released data include over 70 hours of tracked poses from pairs of mice, and over 10 hours of manual, frame-by-frame annotation ... unlabeled trajectory data from 282 videos
claims.criterion: Unlabeled frames are counted from the scores of each sequence. The statements "over" a value are read (a) over Task 1 only (training and test), (b) over all labelled sets of the three tasks, and (c) as (b) with sequences deposited more than once counted once; tracked poses add the unlabeled set to each reading. Hours are frames / 30 / 3600. Reproduced when the two expected values hold and each of the three "over" statements holds under at least one reading; partially reproduced when only some of these hold; not reproduced when none does.

claims.statement: On Task 3, classifier performance depends on the percentage of frames in which a behavior is observed and on its average bout duration, with shorter bouts giving lower performance.
claims.source: Section 4.4, paragraph 2; Tables 7 and 10
claims.quote: We found classifier performance to depend both on the percentage of frames during which a behavior was observed, and on the average duration of a behavior bout, with shorter bouts having lower classifier performance.
claims.criterion: Across the seven behaviors, Spearman correlations of the baseline model's F1 score in Table 10 with (i) the percentage of frames labelled with the behavior and (ii) its mean bout length (runs of consecutive labelled frames), computed from the data on (a) the training split or (b) the test split. Reproduced when, under one reading, both correlations are positive with a one-sided exact permutation p below 0.05; partially reproduced when both are positive under one reading but not both significant; not reproduced otherwise. The F1 of the baseline with task programming features is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Among baseline architectures trained on Task 1, the 1D convolutional network performs best (F1 0.793, MAP 0.856), ahead of fully connected (0.659), LSTM (0.675) and self-attention (0.610) models.
claims.source: Table 1; Section 4.1, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Among the explored architectures, we obtained the highest performance using the 1D convolutional neural network (Table 1).

claims.source: Table 2 and Table 8; Section 4.2, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We found that including task programming features improved model performance.

claims.statement: On Task 2 the fine-tuned baseline reaches an annotator-averaged F1 of 0.754, 0.774 with task programming features and 0.809 for the top entry, and all models do better on annotators 1 and 2 than on 3, 4 and 5.
claims.source: Table 3 and Table 9; Section 4.3 and Appendix G.2, paragraph 1
claims.quote: We observe that all classifiers generally performs better on annotators 1 and 2, while performing worse on annotators 3, 4, and 5.

claims.statement: On Task 3 the baseline reaches a behavior-averaged F1 of 0.338 (0.328 with task programming features, 0.319 for the top entry), far below Tasks 1 and 2.
claims.source: Table 4 and Table 10; Section 4.4; Appendix G.3, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Based on performance metrics, Task 3 is more difficult than the other two Tasks

claims.source: Figure 7; Section 4.2, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Many prediction errors of the baseline models were localized around behavior transition boundaries (Figure 7).

claims.statement: The annotator embedding learned by the top Task 2 entry places annotators 3 and 4 close to each other and apart from annotators 1, 2 and 5.
claims.source: Figure 11; Section 4.3, paragraph 2, and Appendix G.2
claims.quote: Annotators 3 and 4 were found to be similar to each other, and different from annotators 1, 2, and 5.

claims.statement: Of 480 IRD patients in the cohort, 7 (1.45%) carried IMPG1 or IMPG2 mutations; 2 (0.41%) were diagnosed with RP and 5 (1.04%) with VMD.
claims.source: Results, opening paragraph (before 3.1)
claims.quote: In our study, 7 out of 480 patients with IRDs (1.45%) were found to have mutations in IMPG genes. Of these, two patients (0.41%) were diagnosed with RP, while five patients (1.04%) exhibited characteristics of VMD.
claims.criterion: Counts are of patients and must match exactly (tolerance 0, as a count of people has no measurement error); percentages take the default 10%. The carriers and their diagnoses are counted from the dataset; the denominator of 480 is the cohort of Methods 2.1 (IRDs Clinic, March 2015 to June 2024). If the dataset holds only the seven carriers, the numerators are tested and the denominator is recorded as taken from the paper. The paper prints 1.45% and 0.41% where 7/480 and 2/480 give 1.458% and 0.417%; both truncation and rounding fall within tolerance, so this does not change the outcome. The Discussion's "1 in 68" is 480/7 and is tested with the same counts.

claims.statement: All seven patients with IMPG mutations were Caucasian.
claims.source: Results, opening paragraph (before 3.1)
claims.quote: All seven patients with IMPG mutations were Caucasian.
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the dataset records race or ancestry as Caucasian (white, European) for all seven patients; not reproduced when any is recorded otherwise; blocked when the dataset does not record it.

claims.statement: The seven patients carry the variants of Table 1 (F32 IMPG1 c.2218C>T p.Leu740Phe heterozygous; M83 IMPG2 c.3056G>A p.Cys1019Tyr and c.391C>T p.Arg131Cys, compound heterozygous; M75 IMPG1 c.1269C>A p.Asp423Glu heterozygous; M82 IMPG2 c.745C>T p.Leu249Phe heterozygous; M73 and F57 IMPG2 c.2890C>T p.Arg964* heterozygous; M34 IMPG2 c.3262C>T p.Arg1088* heterozygous).
claims.source: Table 1; Results, opening paragraph (before 3.1)
claims.quote: All the patients are represented in Table 1.
claims.criterion: For each of the seven patients, the gene, cDNA change, protein change and zygosity in the dataset are compared with Table 1. Table 1 writes the gene of F32 as "IMGP1"; the text (3.1, Figure 1) makes it IMPG1, and IMPG1 is the reading used. Reproduced when all seven patients match in every field; partially reproduced when some but not all do; not reproduced when none does. Reference transcripts are not named in the paper, so a cDNA position that differs only by a transcript offset, with the same protein change, is reported and counted as a match.

claims.statement: F32 (female, 32 years) has sectoral RP and M83 (male, 83) RP; M75 (male, 75), M82 (male, 82), M73 (male, 73), F57 (female, 57) and M34 (male, 34) have VMD.
claims.source: Table 1
claims.criterion: Diagnosis and sex must match exactly for each patient. Age is the number in the identifier and the "N-year-old" of section 3; the paper does not say at which date it was taken. Readings allowed by the text are (a) age at the most recent visit, the visit whose BCVA is reported for M83 and M75, and (b) age at data collection for the study (2024). Age takes the default tolerance of 10%. Reproduced when diagnoses and sexes all match and ages match under one reading; partially reproduced when diagnoses match but sex or age does not for some patient.

claims.statement: The RP mutations are all missense, dominant in IMPG1 and recessive (compound heterozygous) in IMPG2; all VMD mutations are dominant (heterozygous), either missense or nonsense.
claims.source: Results, opening paragraph (before 3.1); Figure 1; Table 1
claims.quote: Our findings show all missense mutations for the RP phenotype with dominant inheritance in IMPG1 and recessive in IMPG2 ... all patients expressing VMD harvest dominant mutations, which can be either mis- or non-sense
claims.criterion: Read from the genotypes and diagnoses of the two claims it depends on. Dominant and recessive are the paper's reading of zygosity (one heterozygous variant is dominant, two variants on different alleles recessive); family segregation is not reported. Reproduced when the dataset's genotypes and diagnoses give the pattern stated.

claims.source: Table 1; Results, 3.1 and 3.2, the paragraph on each patient
claims.criterion: Snellen fractions must match exactly, eye by eye (no tolerance, as Snellen acuity is read in discrete lines). The paper says for M83 and M75 that the value is from the most recent visit and does not say so for the others. Readings are (a) the most recent visit recorded and (b) any visit recorded. Reproduced when all 14 eyes match under one reading; partially reproduced when some do; not reproduced when none does.

claims.statement: Patient F32 has sector RP of the inferior retina; FF shows inferior sectoral bone spicule pigmentation, FAF reduced autofluorescence, SD-OCT a normal foveal architecture without significant thinning, and GVF a superior depression in both eyes.
claims.source: Results, 3.1 RP Patients, paragraph on Patient F32; Figure 2A,B
claims.quote: Clinically, Patient F32 presented with sector RP primarily affecting the inferior retina ( Figure 2 A,B). ... The FF examination revealed dystrophy of the inferior retina, characterized by sectorial bone spicule pigmentation (yellow arrows). The FAF imaging showed reduced autofluorescence corresponding to a superior visual field defect in both eyes
claims.criterion: The paper grades its images by clinical inspection and gives no quantitative measure; the arrows in Figure 2A,B mark the features. Each feature (inferior bone spicule pigmentation on FF, reduced FAF, foveal architecture without significant thinning on SD-OCT, superior depression on GVF) is judged by viewing the patient's image of that modality and eye against the place the Figure 2 legend marks. Reproduced when the dataset holds the four modalities for both eyes and each feature is visible; partially reproduced when some are; blocked for a modality the dataset lacks. This visual reading is the only method the paper allows and is recorded as a deviation.

claims.statement: Patient M83 has bilateral outer retinal atrophy sparing the central fovea with a bull's eye pattern, 360 degree bone spicules, pale discs and attenuated vessels on FF; reduced FAF; an inferior residual crescent and small central field on GVF; and diffuse ellipsoid zone and outer nuclear layer loss on SD-OCT, sparing part of the central fovea in the left eye.
claims.source: Results, 3.1 RP Patients, paragraph on Patient M83; Figure 2C,D
claims.quote: The FF revealed bilateral outer retinal atrophy sparing the central fovea, with a bull's eye pattern surrounding the fovea ( Figure 2 C,D). ... The GVF demonstrated an inferior residual crescent in both eyes and a small central visual field. The SD-OCT shows diffuse loss of the ellipsoid zone and outer nuclear layer, sparing part of the central fovea in the left eye.
claims.criterion: As for f32-sector-rp-phenotype, by visual inspection of each modality and eye against the features the text and the Figure 2C,D legend name (atrophy, bull's eye pattern, bone spicules, reduced FAF, GVF crescent and central field, ellipsoid loss). Reproduced when every named feature is visible; partially reproduced when some are; blocked for a modality the dataset lacks.

claims.statement: Patient M75 has bilateral subretinal vitelliform material in the macula on SD-OCT, macular hypopigmentation on FF, FAF hypo-autofluorescence in the right macula and hyper-autofluorescence in the left, early blockage and late window defects on FA, and a superior macular nevus.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 VMD Patients, paragraph on Patient M75; Figure 3A,B
claims.quote: Subretinal vitelliform material was detected bilaterally in the macula by SD-OCT ( Figure 3 A,B). The FF shows hypopigmentation in the macula of both eyes. Hypo-autofluorescence, suggesting retinal atrophy, was observed in the right macula, while hyper-autofluorescence, indicative of vitelliform deposits, was noted in the left macula using FAF.
claims.criterion: By visual inspection of each modality and eye, as for f32-sector-rp-phenotype. The text and the legend disagree on the left eye's FAF; the legend says "FAF shows hypo-autofluorescence in the right and left macula". Both readings are named; the FAF feature holds when the left macula is hyper-autofluorescent (text) or hypo-autofluorescent (legend), and the notebook says which. The nevus is looked for on FF and, where the dataset holds it, the infrared image, where the text says it was seen. Reproduced when the SD-OCT, FF, FAF and FA features and the nevus are visible; partially reproduced when some are.

claims.statement: Patient M82 has late-stage VMD with foveal atrophy; SD-OCT shows an attenuated ellipsoid and retinal thinning in the right eye and a vitelliform lesion with small ellipsoid disruption in the left; FF shows foveal hypopigmentation and FA window defects in both eyes.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 VMD Patients, paragraph on Patient M82; Figure 3C,D
claims.quote: SD-OCT of the right eye showed attenuated ellipsoid and retinal thinning, while the left eye displayed a vitelliform lesion with a small ellipsoid zone disruption. The FF shows hypopigmentation of the fovea in both eyes. The FFA demonstrates a bilateral window defect.
claims.criterion: By visual inspection of each modality and eye, as for f32-sector-rp-phenotype, against the features of the text and the Figure 3C,D legend. Reproduced when every named feature is visible; partially reproduced when some are.

claims.statement: Patient M73 has bilateral macular subretinal hyporeflective spaces and ellipsoid disruption on SD-OCT, foveal hypopigmentation, dot-blot hemorrhages and peripheral cobblestone degeneration on FF, and bilateral hyper-autofluorescence on FAF.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 VMD Patients, paragraph on Patient M73; Figure 3E,F
claims.quote: Patient M73, a 73-year-old male, presented with bilaterally macular subretinal hyporeflective spaces on SD-OCT, suggesting the reabsorption of vitelliform material ( Figure 3 E,F). Additional findings included ellipsoid disruption.
claims.criterion: By visual inspection of each modality and eye, as for f32-sector-rp-phenotype. The text does not say which eye has the ellipsoid disruption; the Figure 3E,F legend says the right eye, and either eye satisfies the feature. Reproduced when every named feature is visible; partially reproduced when some are.

claims.statement: Patient F57 has subretinal vitelliform lesions in the macula of both eyes on SD-OCT, foveal hypopigmentation on FF, and bilateral hypo-autofluorescence on FAF, more pronounced in the left eye.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 VMD Patients, paragraph on Patient F57; Figure 3G,H
claims.quote: exhibiting subretinal vitelliform lesions in the macula of both eyes on SD-OCT ( Figure 3 G,H). ... FAF showed hypo-autofluorescence bilaterally, which was more pronounced in the left eye.
claims.criterion: By visual inspection of each modality and eye, as for f32-sector-rp-phenotype. "More pronounced" is judged by comparing the extent of the hypo-autofluorescent area in the two eyes' FAF images; the paper gives no measure. Reproduced when every named feature is visible; partially reproduced when some are.

claims.statement: Patient M34 has bilateral subretinal vitelliform lesions on SD-OCT, glaucomatous optic nerves and mild macular hypopigmentation on FF, and faint hyper-autofluorescence on FAF.
claims.source: Results, 3.2 VMD Patients, paragraph on Patient M34; Figure 3I,J
claims.quote: The SD-OCT shows subretinal vitelliform lesions on both eyes. The FF is primarily indicative of glaucomatous optic nerves and mild macular hypopigmentation. FAF showed faint hyper-autofluorescence.
claims.criterion: By visual inspection of each modality and eye, as for f32-sector-rp-phenotype. The text and the legend disagree on FAF; the Figure 3I,J legend says "The FF and FAF reveal bilateral hypopigmentation and hypo-autofluorescence". Both readings are named; the FAF feature holds under either, and the notebook says which. Reproduced when every named feature is visible; partially reproduced when some are.

claims.statement: Both RP patients have superior visual field limitation (inferior retina affected first), and neither has cystoid maculopathy.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 3 (on Patient M83 and the RP patients)
claims.quote: Both RP patients experienced visual field limitations in the superior visual field. ... Cystoid maculopathy did not occur in either young or old patients.
claims.criterion: The superior limitation is read from the GVF of F32 and M83 by visual inspection; the absence of cystoid maculopathy from their SD-OCT, where cystoid spaces are looked for in the macula of each eye (Methods 2.1 names cystoid macular edema as an OCT indicator for RP). The paper gives no test. Reproduced when both GVFs show the superior limitation and no macular SD-OCT shows cystoid spaces; not reproduced when either fails.

claims.statement: In most VMD patients visual acuity was not significantly reduced; the only exception is M73 (20/100 OD, 20/50 OS).
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 5
claims.quote: Interestingly, in most VMD patients, visual acuity was not significantly reduced. The only exception is patient M73, who has a BCVA of 20/100 OD and 20/50 OS.
claims.criterion: The paper gives no threshold for a significant reduction and does not say whether it is judged on the worse or the better eye. Its text counts M75 (20/40 in both eyes) as not reduced and M73 (20/100 OD, 20/50 OS) as reduced, so the readings it allows are a threshold of worse than 20/40 applied to the worse eye, or to the better eye, and, on the worse eye, any threshold up to 20/100 (worse than 20/40, 20/50 or 20/70). Each reading is run on the five VMD patients. Reproduced when under every reading M73 is the only one reduced; not reproduced when under every reading he is not; blocked as methods_underspecified when the readings differ.

claims.statement: The two unrelated carriers of IMPG2 p.Arg964* (M73 and F57) have similar vitelliform macular lesions, but the older (M73) has peripheral cobblestone lesions and macular lesions with increased autofluorescence.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 6
claims.quote: Both patients have similar vitelliform macular lesions. However, the oldest patient (M73) presents with peripheral cobblestone lesions, and the macular lesions have increased autofluorescence.
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure of similarity. Judged by visual inspection of the two patients' SD-OCT and FAF images; reproduced when both show macular vitelliform lesions on SD-OCT, M73's FAF is hyper-autofluorescent where F57's is hypo-autofluorescent, and M73's FF shows peripheral cobblestone degeneration that F57's does not.

claims.statement: Patient M73, who also carries a BEST1 variant, had a normal EOG, which the authors read as against Best disease.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 5 (on Patient M73)
claims.quote: However, the patient's EOG results were normal, a finding inconsistent with Best disease but more indicative of IMPG2-associated retinal dystrophy.
claims.criterion: The paper reports no EOG values, no Arden ratio and no normal range, and its Methods do not describe the EOG. Reproduced when the dataset holds M73's EOG and it is reported as normal there, or when its light-peak to dark-trough (Arden) ratio is in the normal range the recording gives; blocked when the dataset holds no EOG. The normal range is not fixed by the paper and is recorded as open.

claims.statement: Besides their IMPG variants, F32 carries a JAG1 variant, M73 a BEST1 variant, and M83 heterozygous variants of uncertain significance in ALMS1, CEP164, COL11A1, CPLANE1, EYS, KIF7, NPHP4 and PHYH.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraphs 2, 3 and 5
claims.quote: It is also important to note that this patient had two diseased gene variants ... IMPG1 and JAG1 .
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the dataset's genetic reports list each of the named genes for the named patient; partially reproduced when some are listed; blocked when the dataset holds no genetic report beyond the IMPG variants. The quote states the JAG1 variant of F32; the BEST1 variant of M73 and the M83 gene list are stated in Discussion paragraphs 5 and 3.

claims.statement: The variants lie in or near named protein domains. In IMPG1, p.Leu740Phe is near (3.1) or in (3.5, Discussion) the EGF-like domain next to SEA2, and p.Asp423Glu is between SEA1 and SEA2. In IMPG2, p.Arg131Cys is near SEA-1, p.Leu249Phe in SEA1, p.Arg964* in SEA2, p.Cys1019Tyr in the EGF-1-like domain and p.Arg1088* in the EGF-like 2 domain.
claims.source: Figure 1; Results, 3.1 and 3.2, the paragraph on each patient; Results, 3.5
claims.quote: He is heterozygous for the p.Cys1019Tyr mutation in one allele, which affects the EGF-1-like domain, and the p.Arg131Cys mutation in the other allele, which is located near the non-proteolytic SEA-1 domain.
claims.criterion: Uses outside domain annotations, not the dataset. The paper names no source for the domain boundaries of Figure 1. Readings are the UniProt feature annotations of the canonical entries (IMPG1 Q17R60, IMPG2 Q9BZV3) and the InterPro (Pfam, SMART) domain annotations of the same sequences. "Near" is not defined by the paper and is recorded as open; the distance in residues to the named domain is reported, and a "near" placement matches when the residue lies in no other named domain and the named domain is the closest. For p.Leu740Phe the paper says both "near" and "in"; either matches. Reproduced when every variant is placed as stated under one reading; partially reproduced when some are.

claims.statement: In silico tools predict all IMPG2 variants and the novel IMPG1 p.Asp423Glu to be pathogenic, and IMPG1 p.Leu740Phe to be likely benign, with the scores of Table 2.
claims.source: Results, 3.3 Pathogenicity Prediction; Table 2
claims.quote: In IMPG1, the novel variant p.Asp423Glu is predicted to be pathogenic, while the known variant p.Leu740Phe is considered likely benign.
claims.criterion: Uses outside tools, not the dataset. Scores are recomputed with the tools of Methods 2.2 (SIFT, PolyPhen-2, MutationTaster, CADD, FATHMM) for the variants of Table 1. The paper names no tool version, genome build or reference transcript; PolyPhen-2, CADD, MutationTaster and FATHMM were accessed on 10 November 2024, SIFT with no date. Readings for the build are GRCh37 and GRCh38, and for the transcript the canonical (MANE Select) one of each gene; CADD version is the one current in November 2024 (v1.7) or the one before (v1.6); for PolyPhen-2 the HumDiv and HumVar models. Scores take the default 10%; SIFT scores of 0 must be 0 (below 0.05, the damaging range). The flattened Table 2 rows each hold seven entries, with "-" for a missing score, so the FATHMM and MutationTaster columns are read by column order. The paper does not say which MutationTaster output its "score" is, nor which FATHMM model gives the coding scores; the attempt reports the outputs each tool gives and says which, if any, matches. The paper gives no rule for turning scores into the Prediction column; 3.3 says the IMPG2 nonsense calls rest on the premature stop codon and the IMPG2 missense calls on SIFT, PolyPhen and MutationTaster, and the attempt reports each tool's own classification for every variant. Reproduced when, under one reading, the scores are within tolerance and the Prediction column (pathogenic for all but p.Leu740Phe) is matched; partially reproduced when the predictions match but some scores do not.

claims.statement: IMPG1 p.Asp423Glu, found in M75, is a novel variant with no ClinVar entry, and its association with VMD is reported here for the first time.
claims.source: Table 2 (Existing Variant ID column); Discussion, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Notably, patient M75 harbored a novel missense mutation, p.Asp423Glu, in IMPG1, marking its first reported association with VMD.
claims.criterion: Uses outside data (ClinVar, dbSNP), not the dataset. The paper does not say which release it searched; readings are the releases current at submission (November 2024) and the release current when the attempt is run. Reproduced when no entry for IMPG1 c.1269C>A (p.Asp423Glu) existed in the November 2024 release; a later entry is reported but does not change the outcome.

claims.statement: All five missense variants are predicted to destabilize the protein by every tool (all ΔΔG negative), and p.Leu249Phe shows the largest destabilizing effect.
claims.source: Results, 3.4 Prediction of Protein Stability for Point Mutations; Table 3
claims.quote: Our analysis revealed that all the variants, including p.Leu740Phe, p.Asp423Glu, p.Cys1019Tyr, p.Leu249Phe, and p.Arg131Cys, lead to destabilizing effects on the proteins ... Specifically, the p.Leu249Phe variant exhibited the largest destabilizing effect
claims.criterion: Uses outside tools, not the dataset. ΔΔG is recomputed with mCSM, SDM, DUET, iMutant and MuPRO (Methods 2.4) for the five missense variants; the 25 values of Table 3 are listed under expected with the default 10% each. mCSM, SDM and DUET need a structure; Methods 2.3 says it is the I-TASSER model with the highest confidence score and over 80% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions, and the model is not deposited, so a rerun of I-TASSER is the only reading and its stochastic output is a source of difference (recorded as a deviation). iMutant and MuPRO run from sequence; the paper names no UniProt entry, and the canonical isoforms (IMPG1 Q17R60, IMPG2 Q9BZV3) are the reading used. The paper names no unit; the tools report kcal/mol. All negative is tested on every value. "Largest" is not defined; readings are (a) the mean ΔΔG over the five tools, (b) the largest magnitude in a majority of tools, (c) the largest in every tool. Table 3 itself satisfies (a) and (b) but not (c) (SDM gives p.Cys1019Tyr and iMutant p.Arg131Cys a larger magnitude). Reproduced when all signs are negative and p.Leu249Phe is largest under (a) or (b).

claims.statement: In IMPG1, neither p.Asp423Glu nor p.Leu740Phe changes hydrogen bonds, van der Waals interactions or polar contacts significantly.
claims.source: Results, 3.5, paragraph 1; Figure 4A,B
claims.quote: In IMPG1, no significant differences were observed in hydrogen bonds, van der Waals interactions or polar contacts between the reference and mutant proteins.
claims.criterion: A claim of absence; the paper names no test or threshold. Uses outside tools (DynaMut, Methods 2.5, on the I-TASSER models of Methods 2.3, not deposited). Reproduced when DynaMut lists the same hydrogen bonds, van der Waals and polar contacts of residue 423 and residue 740 in the reference and mutant models, as Figure 4A,B shows; the contacts gained or lost are reported either way. The model is re-predicted, which is recorded as a deviation.

claims.statement: In IMPG2, p.Cys1019Tyr replaces the polar bond of Cys1019 with Ser1023 and its hydrogen bond with Cys1036 by new bonds with Ser1023, Gln1017 and Cys1025; p.Leu249Phe loses the hydrogen bonds of Leu249 with Val305, Lys252, Leu373 and Val307; p.Arg131Cys loses the hydrogen bond with Tyr134 and a van der Waals interaction.
claims.source: Results, 3.5, paragraphs 3 to 5; Figure 4C to 4E
claims.quote: In the reference protein, Cysteine 1019 interacts with Serine 1023 through polar bonds and with Cysteine 1036 via hydrogen bonds ( Figure 4 C). In the mutant protein, Tyrosine 1019 replaces Cysteine 1019, disrupting these original interactions. Instead, Tyrosine 1019 forms new bonds with Serine 1023, Glutamine 1017, and Cysteine 1025.
claims.criterion: Uses outside tools (DynaMut on re-predicted I-TASSER models, as for impg1-interactions-unchanged). The contacts of residues 1019, 249 and 131 in reference and mutant are compared with the residues the text names. The text names the van der Waals partner of Arg131 as Gln1236 and then as His135; both readings are named and either matches. Reproduced when the named contacts are lost and, for p.Cys1019Tyr, the named new contacts appear, for all three variants; partially reproduced for one or two.

claims.statement: ProtParam gives reference IMPG1 a molecular weight of 89,387 Da, pI 4.79, instability index 53.57 and aliphatic index 75.63; p.Asp423Glu raises the weight (89,419), pI (4.81) and instability index (53.76), and p.Leu740Phe raises the weight (89,421) and lowers the aliphatic index (75.14).
claims.source: Results, 3.5, paragraph 2; Table 4
claims.quote: The molecular weight increased from 89.387 KDa in the reference protein to 89.419 KDa in the p.Asp423Glu mutant and 89.421 KDa in the p.Leu740Phe mutant
claims.criterion: Uses an outside tool (ExPASy ProtParam, Methods 2.6), not the dataset. Tolerances are half the last printed digit, not 10%, because ProtParam is deterministic for a given sequence and the finding is a difference between forms far smaller than 10% of any value. The paper names no sequence; readings are (a) the canonical UniProt IMPG1 sequence (Q17R60) and (b) the same without its signal peptide. Reproduced when every value matches under one reading; partially reproduced when the directions of change stated in the text (weight up for both, pI and instability index up for p.Asp423Glu, aliphatic index down for p.Leu740Phe) hold but some values do not. A single Asp to Glu change adds one CH2 (14 Da, 3 atoms), not the 32 Da and 7 atoms of Table 4, so the p.Asp423Glu weight and atom count may not reproduce under either reading; this is reported. The Discussion (paragraph 2) attributes the higher pI and instability index to p.Leu740Phe, which Table 4 does not show; the claim follows Results 3.5 and Table 4.

claims.statement: In gnomAD, IMPG2 p.Cys1019Tyr occurs in about 1 in 93,300 European (non-Finnish) individuals; p.Arg131Cys in about 1 in 4100 European (non-Finnish) and 1 in 3000 Middle Eastern; p.Arg964* in about 1 in 18,700 African/African American and 1 in 59,000 European (non-Finnish); and IMPG1 p.Leu740Phe in about 1 in 332 European (non-Finnish).
claims.source: Results, 3.1 RP Patients, paragraph on Patient M83; Results, 3.2 VMD Patients, paragraph on M73 and F57; Discussion, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The Cys1019Tyr variant is a rare mutation found exclusively in the European (non-Finnish) population, with an estimated frequency of approximately 1 in 93,300 individuals.
claims.criterion: Uses outside data (gnomAD), not the dataset. The paper names no gnomAD version and does not say whether "1 in N" is the inverse of allele frequency or of carrier frequency. A Middle Eastern population is in gnomAD v3.1 and later, so the version readings are v3.1.2 genomes and v4.1 (exomes and genomes joint, and each alone); the frequency readings are 1/allele frequency and 1/(2 x allele frequency). Default 10% tolerance. Reproduced when every value matches under one combination of readings; partially reproduced when some do.

claims.statement: The paper analysed 1394 PL neurons from 9 shocked mice and 847 neurons from 7 non-shocked mice on day 1, and 1031 (shocked) and 967 (non-shocked) cells on day 2.
claims.source: STAR Methods, Miniscope data processing; Figure 1K and 1L legends
claims.quote: We identified 1394 neurons across 9 mice in Shock animals and 847 neurons across 7 mice in Non-shock animals.
claims.criterion: Counts of accepted cells per session and of mice with imaging, by group and day. Tolerance zero, as these are counts of the recorded cells. The day 2 counts are from the Figure 1K and 1L legends ("Cells analyzed... Day 2 1031" and "Day 2 967").

claims.statement: Cell registration across days tracked about 40% of neurons, 463 cells from 6 shocked mice and 322 cells from 7 non-shocked mice.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 2; Figure 1N legend
claims.quote: we used cell registration to track ~40% of neurons across sessions (shocked mice ... 463 cells from 6 mice, NS controls ... 322 cells from 7 mice
claims.criterion: Counts of cells matched between day 1 and day 2 (CellReg on the Minian footprints, Methods), by group. Tolerance zero for counts. If the dataset holds no registration, the claim cannot be tested without redoing it, which the author reports.

claims.statement: During learning, shocked mice spent a progressively larger fraction of the tone on the safety platform, and this differed from non-shocked controls.
claims.source: Results, Tracking changes in PL activity during PMA; Figure 1E
claims.quote: During learning, shocked mice exhibited progressive increases in time spent on the platform ... These behaviors were significantly different than NS controls
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the fraction of tone time on the platform in blocks of three tones on each day (opening comment). Two-way repeated measures ANOVA (group by block) with Geisser-Greenhouse correction and Sidak's post hoc tests, per day (Methods; Figure 1 legend, day 1 Shk N=11, NS N=9; day 2 Shk N=8, NS N=8). Reproduced when in shocked mice the day 1 block means rise from block 1 to block 4 with at least one Sidak-corrected block difference at p < 0.05, and at least one Sidak comparison of shocked against NS mice at a block is p < 0.05 on day 1 or day 2. The Sidak family is not stated; readings are all pairwise block comparisons within the shocked group, and each block against block 1; both are run.

claims.statement: Shocked mice showed a progressive increase in the proportion of successful trials, in which the footshock was completely avoided, which differed from non-shocked controls.
claims.source: Results, Tracking changes in PL activity during PMA; Figure 1F
claims.quote: in the proportion of successful trials (where mice completely avoided a footshock)
claims.criterion: As fig1e-platform-time, with the per-mouse proportion of successful trials per block (success rule in the opening comment).

claims.statement: Shocked mice showed a progressive increase in freezing during the tone, which differed from non-shocked controls.
claims.source: Results, Tracking changes in PL activity during PMA; Figure 1G
claims.quote: and in freezing levels
claims.criterion: As fig1e-platform-time, with the per-mouse fraction of tone time freezing per block (BehaviorDEPOT freezing labels).

claims.statement: Shocked mice showed a progressive decrease in the latency to enter the platform after tone onset, which differed from non-shocked controls.
claims.source: Results, Tracking changes in PL activity during PMA; Figure 1H
claims.quote: and a progressive decrease in latency to enter the platform during the tone
claims.criterion: As fig1e-platform-time, with the per-mouse latency per block (opening comment), and with the day 1 block means falling from block 1 to block 4 in shocked mice.

claims.statement: In each period (BL, D1, D2), the overall proportion of PL neurons encoding PMA features was similar between shocked and non-shocked mice, and it increased modestly across learning.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 1; Figure 1K and 1L (black and gray pie charts)
claims.quote: In each period (BL, D1, D2), the overall proportion of PL neurons encoding PMA features was similar between groups and modestly increased across learning
claims.criterion: Per period and group, the fraction of all recorded cells (Figure 1K and 1L denominators) responsive to at least one of tone, platform or freezing (opening comment). The paper compares pie charts with chi-square (Methods; two-sided with Yates' correction, Figure 1 legend) and reports no test for this. Similar is judged by that test, a 2x2 chi-square with Yates' correction of responsive against non-responsive cells, shocked against NS, in each period; it holds when p >= 0.05 in all three periods. The increase holds when in each group the D2 fraction exceeds the BL fraction. Run under each period and frame reading (opening comment).

claims.statement: On day 1, shocked and non-shocked mice had similar proportions of PL neurons encoding the tone, the safety platform, freezing, or their combinations.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 1; Figure 1K and 1L (colored wheel plots); Figure S1F, G
claims.quote: On day 1, shocked and NS control mice had similar proportions of PL neurons that encoded the tone, safety platform, freezing behavior, or their combinations
claims.criterion: For BL and D1, among the responsive cells, the counts of tone-only, platform-only, freezing-only and mixed cells, shocked against NS. The paper's test for these pie charts is the two-sided chi-square with Yates' correction (Methods; Figure 1 legend), applied as for the day 2 mixed cells, a 2x2 table of the category against the other responsive cells. Reproduced when no category gives p < 0.05 in either period; the differences in percentage points are given either way. Run under each period and frame reading. Figure S1F and S1G were not read.

claims.statement: In both shocked and non-shocked mice, the proportion of tone-encoding PL neurons was greatest in the baseline period, and the activity of tone-encoding neurons at tone onset was similar between groups.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 3; Figure 1K, 1L, 1P1 and 1Q1
claims.quote: We also revealed that in both shocked and NS control mice, the proportion of tone-encoding neurons was greatest during the baseline period, when tones are novel, and their activity during tone onset was similar across groups.
claims.criterion: Proportion, per group and period (BL, D1, D2), the fraction of all cells (Figure 1K and 1L denominators) that encode the tone. Which cells count as tone-encoding is open, reading G1, any cell responsive to the tone category (opening comment), and G2, tone-only cells (the colored wheel plots). The paper gives no test; greatest holds when in each group the BL fraction exceeds the D1 and the D2 fractions. Activity, as fig1p-platform-exit-excited-day2 for the cells excited and the cells suppressed at tone onset (the code's toneonVector and 5 s window; 61 and 52 shocked, 24 and 25 NS on day 1, 34 and 37 shocked, 34 and 22 NS on day 2, STAR Methods, Cells Analyzed for Figure 1), Welch's t-test of shocked against NS on each day; similar holds when none gives p < 0.05, with the differences reported. Reproduced when both parts hold. Run under each period and frame reading and under G1 and G2; where they give different outcomes the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: By day 2, shocked mice had a significantly larger proportion of mixed-selective PL neurons (encoding more than one PMA feature) than non-shocked mice, 51% against 25%.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 1; Figure 1K-M
claims.quote: By day 2, shocked mice had a significantly greater proportion of PL neurons exhibiting mixed selectivity (i.e., encoding multiple features of PMA; shocked ... 51%, non-shocked ... 25%
claims.criterion: Mixed cells on day 2 (period D2, opening comment), shocked against NS, 2x2 chi-square with Yates' correction (Figure 1K legend). The denominator is open. Reading R1, the responsive cells (the multi-colored pie charts show "profiles of" encoding cells, Figure 1K legend); reading R2, all day 2 cells (1031 and 967). A chi-square near 43 with 51% against 25% needs about 300 cells per group, which fits R1 and not R2, but both are shown. Reproduced when under a reading the percentages fall within tolerance and the test gives p < 0.05 with shocked higher. Run under each period and frame reading.

claims.statement: Among registered cells, neurons that selectively encoded the tone at the end of day 1 were more likely to be mixed-selective on day 2 in shocked mice than in non-shocked mice.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 2; Figure 1O
claims.quote: In shocked mice, neurons that selectively encoded the tone at the end of day 1 were more likely to exhibit mixed selectivity on day 2 compared to NS controls
claims.criterion: Registered cells only (Methods, Tracking cell encoding across days). Among the cells that were tone-only at D1, the fraction that are mixed at D2, shocked against NS, 2x2 chi-square with Yates' correction (Figure 1O legend). Reproduced when the shocked fraction is higher and p < 0.05. Run under each period and frame reading.

claims.statement: Among registered cells, neurons not modulated at the end of day 1 were more likely to become mixed-selective on day 2 in shocked mice than in non-shocked mice.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 2; Figure 1O
claims.quote: Non-modulated neurons were also more likely to develop mixed selectivity on day 2 in shocked mice
claims.criterion: As fig1o-tone-to-mixed, for the cells non-modulated (no tone, platform or freezing response) at D1.

claims.statement: On day 2, platform-excited neurons of shocked mice showed a large increase in activity after platform exits compared with non-shocked mice.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 3; Figure 1P3
claims.quote: Shocked mice had a large increase in the activity of platform-excited neurons following platform exits on day 2
claims.criterion: Method from compile_pooled_avg_heatmaps.m and trialAvg.m, where the Methods are silent. Cells are those called excited for platform exits on day 2, by an ROC over the whole session (the code uses the session-wide vectors; cell counts in the STAR Methods, Cells Analyzed for Figure 1). For each cell, DeltaF/F averaged over all exits of the session in a window from 4 s before to 4 s after the exit (exits whose window leaves the recording are dropped), z-scored by the mean and SD of its pre-exit half, and the area (trapezoid sum over frames at 15 frames/s) of the post-exit half. Welch's t-test of these per-cell areas, cells pooled across mice, shocked against NS (Figure 1P legend). Reproduced when the shocked mean is higher and p < 0.05.

claims.statement: On day 2, the activity of platform-inhibited neurons after platform exits did not differ between shocked and non-shocked mice.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 3; Figure 1Q3
claims.quote: but no differences in the activity of platform-inhibited neurons
claims.criterion: As fig1p-platform-exit-excited-day2, for cells called suppressed for platform exits on day 2 (74 shocked, 82 NS in the STAR Methods). The paper's test is Welch's t-test at p < 0.05; reproduced when it gives p >= 0.05, with the difference of means reported.

claims.statement: On day 2 there were subtle differences between shocked and non-shocked mice in the activity of freezing-modulated neurons after freezing onset and offset.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 3; Figure 1P2 and 1Q2
claims.quote: On day 2, there were subtle changes in activity following freezing onset and offset
claims.criterion: As fig1p-platform-exit-excited-day2, for freezing-excited and freezing-suppressed cells on day 2 (171 and 283 shocked, 150 and 198 NS), aligned to freezing onset and to freezing offset with a 3 s window on each side (code). The paper does not say which comparison differed or in which direction. Reproduced when at least one of the four Welch's t-tests (excited or suppressed, onset or offset) gives p < 0.05; the four results are reported.

claims.statement: Excited mixed-selective neurons showed a significant increase in activity during platform exits in shocked mice on day 1 only, not on day 2.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 3; Figure 1R3
claims.quote: Excited mixed selective neurons exhibited a significant increase in activity during platform exits only on day 1
claims.criterion: As fig1p-platform-exit-excited-day2, for mixed cells (opening comment) that are excited, aligned to platform exits, on day 1 and on day 2. Which mixed cells enter is open, readings M1, mixed cells with an excited platform-exit call, and M2, mixed cells whose calls include any excited call (the code's split into excited and suppressed mixed cells counts a cell as excited when any call is excited). Reproduced when Welch's t-test gives shocked higher with p < 0.05 on day 1 and p >= 0.05 on day 2.

claims.statement: The larger platform-exit response of platform-excited neurons in shocked mice on day 2 was not due to premature exits followed by footshocks.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 3; Figure S1H
claims.quote: This was not due to premature platform exits resulting in footshocks
claims.criterion: The Methods (ROC analysis) split exit bouts by whether the 2 s after the exit hold a shock. As fig1p-platform-exit-excited-day2 with exits followed by a shock within 2 s removed. Reproduced when shocked mice remain higher with Welch's p < 0.05. Figure S1H was not read.

claims.statement: Escape, jumping and rearing were rare; shocked mice jumped more on day 1; few PL neurons encoded these behaviors and their activity was similar between groups, except escape-excited neurons, which were more active in shocked mice on both days.
claims.source: Results, Learning-induced increase in PL neurons with mixed-selective encoding, paragraph 4; Figure S2
claims.quote: While these behaviors were relatively rare ( Figure S2C - E ), shocked mice jumped more on day 1 ... Shocked mice had significantly higher levels of activity in escape-excited neurons on both days
claims.criterion: Figure S2 was not read, and its tests are not in the main text; the Methods give Welch's t-test for comparisons not otherwise named. Jumping, per mouse, the number of jumping bouts on day 1, shocked against NS, Welch's t-test p < 0.05 with shocked higher. Activity, as fig1p-platform-exit-excited-day2, for escape-excited cells aligned to escape onset, on each day, Welch's t-test p < 0.05 with shocked higher on both days. Similar activity, as fig1p-platform-exit-excited-day2 for the other cells excited or suppressed for escape, jumping or rearing, on each day, Welch's t-test; it holds when none gives p < 0.05 (the paper's test, with the differences reported). That these behaviors were rare and that few neurons encoded them is reported as counts and not judged, as Figure S2 was not read. The averaging window for escape, jumping and rearing is not given; the code uses 5 s for the tone, 4 s for the platform and 3 s for freezing on each side of the event, so the readings are 3, 4 and 5 s; where they give different outcomes the claim is methods_underspecified. Reproduced when the jumping, escape-excited and similar-activity parts all hold.

claims.statement: On day 1, neurons encoding platform entries or exits were more strongly modulated when the entry or exit occurred during the tone than during the inter-tone interval, in both shocked and non-shocked mice.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced encoding of avoidance actions during threatening cues, paragraph 1; Figure 2C1 and 2D1
claims.quote: On day 1, neurons encoding platform entries or exits were more strongly modulated during the tone for both shocked and NS control mice
claims.criterion: Per cell called excited or suppressed for platform entries (or exits) during the tone, and separately during the ITI (code vector names such as itiPlatentVector), the auROC, with suppressed values folded as 1 - auROC (Methods, Frequency distributions of auROC values). Ordinary two-way ANOVA (group by tone/ITI) with Fisher's LSD (Methods). What enters the ANOVA is open, reading H1, the folded auROC of each cell pooled across mice, and H2, the per-mouse modulation scores of fig2e-modulation-entries. Reproduced when, for entries and for exits, the tone values exceed the ITI values with Fisher's LSD p < 0.05 in each group.

claims.statement: On day 2, shocked mice showed a further increase in the strength of platform entry and exit encoding during the tone.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced encoding of avoidance actions during threatening cues, paragraph 1; Figure 2C2 and 2D2
claims.quote: On day 2, shocked mice had a further increase in encoding strength during the tone
claims.criterion: As fig2-day1-tone-stronger, on day 2. Reproduced when, for entries and for exits, the shocked tone values exceed the NS tone values with Fisher's LSD p < 0.05, and exceed the shocked day 1 tone values.

claims.statement: Per animal, shocked mice had significantly higher modulation scores than non-shocked mice for platform entries occurring during the tones on day 2.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced encoding of avoidance actions during threatening cues, paragraph 1; Figure 2E
claims.quote: Again, shocked mice had significantly higher modulation scores for both platform entries and exits occurring during the tones on day 2
claims.criterion: Per mouse, the folded auROC values of its cells called for platform entries during the tone (or during the ITI); mice with fewer than 3 such cells are left out (Methods). The modulation score is 1 minus the area under the mouse's cumulative frequency histogram (Methods). For an exact cumulative distribution over the auROC axis from 0.5 to 1, this is the mean folded auROC; over an axis rescaled to 0 to 1 it is 2 times that mean minus 1; the two give the same ANOVA. The histogram bins are not given (Prism); the exact cumulative distribution is used, a standard choice that changes the score only by binning. Two-way ANOVA (group by tone/ITI) with Fisher's LSD (Methods; Figure 2E legend, day 2 Shk N=7, NS N=7). Reproduced when on day 2 the shocked tone score exceeds the NS tone score with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Per animal, shocked mice had significantly higher modulation scores than non-shocked mice for platform exits occurring during the tones on day 2.
claims.source: Results, Enhanced encoding of avoidance actions during threatening cues, paragraph 1; Figure 2F
claims.quote: shocked mice had significantly higher modulation scores for both platform entries and exits occurring during the tones on day 2 ( Figure 2E , F )
claims.criterion: As fig2e-modulation-entries, for platform exits (Figure 2F legend, day 2 Shk N=6, NS N=7).

claims.statement: Decoding of trial outcome from all recorded PL neurons on day 1 was significantly better in shocked than in non-shocked mice in the pre-shock and shock epochs.
claims.source: Results, Population dynamics prospectively represent trial outcomes early in learning; Figure 3A
claims.quote: Decoder performance using all recorded neurons was significantly greater for shocked mice than NS controls in the pre-shock and shock epochs
claims.criterion: Decoding as in the opening comment, all cells, day 1, per mouse (Figure 3 legend, Shk N=7, NS N=7). Two-way repeated measures ANOVA (group by epoch) with Geisser-Greenhouse correction and Sidak's test of shocked against NS at each epoch (Methods). Reproduced when shocked mice are higher with Sidak p < 0.05 in the pre-shock and in the shock epoch. Run under C1 and C2, N1 and N2; the code's pre-shock epoch (22 to 27 s) is shown as a variant.

claims.statement: Decoding performance in shocked mice was already better than in non-shocked mice before tone onset.
claims.source: Results, Population dynamics prospectively represent trial outcomes early in learning, paragraph 1; Figure 3A
claims.quote: Notably, decoding performance was already better even before the onset of the tone.
claims.criterion: As fig3a-decoding-shock-gt-ns. The Methods define no epoch before the tone; the code's pre-cue epoch, -5 to 0 s, is the one used. The paper reports no test for it. Reproduced when the shocked mean over that epoch exceeds the NS mean; the Sidak comparison is reported beside it and decides nothing.

claims.statement: In shocked mice on day 1, decoding of trial outcome peaked immediately before the shock.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 5; Figure 3A
claims.quote: we found that decoder performance peaked immediately before the shock, and further showed that decoding trial outcomes was possible before animals established a stable avoidance strategy
claims.criterion: Decoding as in fig3a-decoding-shock-gt-ns, all cells, shocked mice, day 1. The paper gives no test. What "peaked" is measured on is open, reading P1, of the four Methods epochs the pre-shock epoch (23 to 28 s) has the highest mean normalized F1 across mice; P2, the highest bin of the across-mouse mean trace from 0 to 38 s after tone onset lies in the pre-shock epoch. Run under C1 and C2, N1 and N2; where the readings give different outcomes the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Decoding from only ROC-defined feature-encoding neurons enhanced decoder performance in shocked mice.
claims.source: Results, Population dynamics prospectively represent trial outcomes early in learning, paragraph 2; Figure 3B
claims.quote: Using only feature-encoding neurons enhanced decoder performance in shocked mice
claims.criterion: Decoding as in fig3a-decoding-shock-gt-ns with modulated cells only (opening comment). What "enhanced" is compared with is open. Reading E1, against the all-cell decoder of the same shocked mice, the mean normalized F1 in the pre-shock and shock epochs is higher with modulated cells. Reading E2, against NS mice decoded the same way, the two-way repeated measures ANOVA with Sidak's test gives shocked higher with p < 0.05 in at least as many epochs as with all cells. Both are run, each under the cell readings K1 and K2; when they disagree the claim is methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Decoding from only non-modulated PL neurons worsened decoder performance.
claims.source: Results, Population dynamics prospectively represent trial outcomes early in learning, paragraph 2; Figure 3C
claims.quote: whereas using only the non-modulated PL neurons worsened performance
claims.criterion: As fig3b-feature-cells-enhance with non-modulated cells only, and with lower in place of higher (E1) and fewer significant epochs in place of at least as many (E2).

claims.statement: The fraction of tone time on the platform was best fitted by the hybrid Rescorla-Wagner model, which learns from both shock and avoid trials.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 1; Figure 4A-C
claims.quote: The fraction of time on the platform was best modeled by the hybrid approach
claims.criterion: The three models of the opening comment fitted per shocked mouse (N=9, Figure 4B legend). Per mouse and model, the mean over blocks of three trials of the squared residual between the predicted and observed fraction (Figure 4A and 4B legends). Repeated measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction (Methods). Reproduced when the hybrid model has the lowest mean squared residual and the ANOVA gives p < 0.05. Run under T1 and T2, S1 and S2.

claims.statement: On day 1, the mean Euclidean distance between latent trajectories of successful and unsuccessful trials in the tone-onset epoch was positively correlated with the avoid learning rate.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 2; Figure 4E
claims.quote: On days 1 and 2, the mean Euclidean distance during the tone-onset epoch, but not during the pre-shock epoch, was significantly correlated with learning rate
claims.criterion: Mean Euclidean distance (opening comment) in the tone-onset epoch on day 1, per shocked mouse, against the hybrid model's avoid learning rate; Pearson's correlation, N=8 (Figure 4E legend). Reproduced when r > 0 (positive per the Discussion, "positively correlated with learning rates ( Figure 4E , G , J )") and p < 0.05. The paper's r and p are in Table S1, not read. Run under W1, W2 and W3, L1 and L2, T1 and T2, S1 and S2.

claims.statement: On day 1, the mean Euclidean distance in the pre-shock epoch was not significantly correlated with the learning rate.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 2; Figure 4F
claims.quote: but not during the pre-shock epoch
claims.criterion: As fig4e-day1-onset-distance in the pre-shock epoch (23 to 28 s). The paper's test is Pearson's correlation at p < 0.05; reproduced when p >= 0.05, with r reported.

claims.statement: On day 2, the mean Euclidean distance between successful and unsuccessful trajectories in the tone-onset epoch was positively correlated with the avoid learning rate.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 2; Figure 4G
claims.quote: On days 1 and 2, the mean Euclidean distance during the tone-onset epoch ... was significantly correlated with learning rate
claims.criterion: As fig4e-day1-onset-distance on day 2, under D-a and D-b as well.

claims.statement: On day 2, the mean Euclidean distance in the pre-shock epoch was not significantly correlated with the learning rate.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 2; Figure 4H
claims.quote: but not during the pre-shock epoch, was significantly correlated with learning rate
claims.criterion: As fig4f-day1-preshock-distance-none on day 2, under D-a and D-b as well.

claims.statement: On day 1, trajectory distance in the tone-onset epoch on the trials of interest was not significantly correlated with learning rate.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 3; Figure 4I
claims.quote: On day 1, there were no significant correlations between trajectory distance and learning rate during the tone onset epoch
claims.criterion: Trajectory distance (opening comment, Methods measure) in the tone-onset epoch on the first shock trial and on the first avoidance trial of day 1, per shocked mouse, against the avoid learning rate; Pearson's correlation, N=8 (Figure 4I legend). The paper's test is Pearson's at p < 0.05; reproduced when every trial of interest gives p >= 0.05, with r reported. The code's distance and its extra trials (last shock, last avoid) are shown as variants. Run under W1, W2 and W3, L1 and L2.

claims.statement: On day 1, trajectory distance in the pre-shock epoch on the first avoidance trial was positively correlated with learning rate.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 3; Figure 4J
claims.quote: but there was a positive correlation during the pre-shock epoch on the first avoidance trial
claims.criterion: As fig4i-day1-onset-trajectory-none in the pre-shock epoch, first avoidance trial. Reproduced when r > 0 with p < 0.05. The Discussion calls this correlation trend-level ("some trend-level correlations (e.g. Figure 4I , J )"); the Results are followed, and the r and p are reported whatever the outcome.

claims.statement: On day 2, trajectory distance in the tone-onset epoch on the first shock trial was negatively correlated with learning rate.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 3; Figure 4K
claims.quote: On day 2, during the tone onset period, we observed a significant negative correlation between the trajectory distance and learning rate on the first shock trial
claims.criterion: As fig4i-day1-onset-trajectory-none on day 2, first shock trial. Reproduced when r < 0 with p < 0.05. Run under D-a and D-b as well.

claims.statement: On day 2, trajectory distance in the pre-shock epoch on the trials of interest was not significantly correlated with learning rate.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 3; Figure 4L
claims.quote: and no significant correlations during the pre-shock period
claims.criterion: As fig4i-day1-onset-trajectory-none on day 2 in the pre-shock epoch. Reproduced when every trial of interest gives p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: On day 1, the mean Euclidean distance 5 to 10 s after tone onset was positively correlated with learning rate, while the distance just before tone onset was not.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 2; Figure S3A, B
claims.quote: On day 1, we also observed a significant positive correlation between Euclidean distance and learning rate during the 5–10s period after (but not in the moments before) the tone onset
claims.criterion: As fig4e-day1-onset-distance in the post-onset window (5 to 10 s) and the pretone window (-6 to -1 s) (Methods). Reproduced when the post-onset correlation has r > 0 and p < 0.05 and the pretone correlation has p >= 0.05. Figure S3 was not read.

claims.statement: On day 1, the Euclidean distances between successful and unsuccessful population trajectories were comparable in shocked and non-shocked mice.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 4; Figure S3C, D
claims.quote: On day 1, Euclidean distances between population vectors for successful and unsuccessful trials were comparable for shocked and NS mice
claims.criterion: Mean Euclidean distance (opening comment) on day 1 in the tone-onset and pre-shock epochs, per mouse, shocked against NS. Figure S3 was not read; the test is Welch's t-test (Methods, "All other comparisons"). Reproduced when both epochs give p >= 0.05, with the differences reported. Run under W1, W2 and W3.

claims.statement: Following the first successful trial, trajectory distance was significantly higher in shocked than in non-shocked mice in the tone-onset epoch and significantly lower in the pre-shock epoch.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 4; Figure S3E, F
claims.quote: Following the first successful trial, trajectory distance was significantly higher in shocked mice during tone onset, but significantly lower than NS controls during the pre-shock epoch
claims.criterion: Trajectory distance (opening comment) on day 1, per mouse, shocked against NS, Welch's t-test (Methods). Which trial "following the first successful trial" means is open, reading A1, the trial after the first avoidance trial, and A2, the first avoidance trial itself (the code's event-aligned distances run from it to the trial after). Reproduced when shocked mice are higher at tone onset and lower at pre-shock, each with p < 0.05. Figure S3 was not read.

claims.statement: Behaviour of shocked and non-shocked mice was similar during the tone-onset and pre-shock epochs.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 4; Figure S3G, H
claims.quote: Behaviors of shocked and NS mice were similar during both epochs
claims.criterion: Figure S3G and S3H were not read. The same paragraph names avoidance and freezing as the behaviours compared, so the measures are the fraction of time on the platform and the fraction of time freezing in the tone-onset and pre-shock epochs, per mouse. Which trials enter is open, reading B1, day 1 trials 4 to 12, and B2, the trial of interest of figs3ef-first-success-trajectory (the sentence follows that result). Welch's t-test (Methods), shocked against NS. Reproduced when no comparison gives p < 0.05, each reading shown.

claims.statement: In the ITI and mid-tone epochs, trajectory distance was not significantly related to learning rate.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 4; Figure S4A, B
claims.quote: We also examined epochs during the ITI and in the middle of the tone, finding no significant relationships between trajectory distance and learning rate in either
claims.criterion: As fig4i-day1-onset-trajectory-none in the mid-ITI (-25 to -20 s) and mid-tone (14 to 19 s) windows (Methods), on days 1 and 2. Reproduced when no correlation gives p < 0.05. Figure S4 was not read.

claims.statement: The only differences in trajectory distance between shocked and non-shocked mice in the control epochs occurred during the ITI before the first avoidance trial.
claims.source: Results, PL population activity states relate to individual learning rates, paragraph 4; Figure S4C, D
claims.quote: The only differences in trajectory distance between shocked and NS mice occurred during the ITI before the first avoidance trial
claims.criterion: As figs3ef-first-success-trajectory in the mid-ITI and mid-tone windows, on each trial of interest. Reproduced when the mid-ITI window on the first avoidance trial gives p < 0.05 and no other comparison does. Figure S4 was not read.

claims.statement: Grin2b+/- rats have more SWDs than WT across the 24-h day; hour of day has no effect and does not interact with genotype (linear mixed model, genotype F = 55.36, p < .00001; hour p = .16; interaction p = .49).
claims.source: Figure 2B
claims.quote: Hour of the day had no effect on the number of seizures between the two genotypes, and Grin2b+/− rats had significantly more seizures overall when compared to wild‐type littermates
claims.criterion: SWD counts per ZT hour per animal (mean of the two days); split-plot ANOVA with genotype between and hour within animals. Reproduced when the genotype effect has p < 0.05 with Het higher and neither hour nor the interaction has p < 0.05. Partially reproduced when Het are higher on average but the genotype p >= 0.05, or hour or the interaction is significant. Not reproduced when Het are not higher.

claims.statement: Grin2b+/- rats have more SWDs over 24 h than WT (Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 4.5, p = .0002).
claims.source: Figure 2C, left
claims.quote: The above reflected a statistically significant increase in the total number of SWDs over the full 24 h in Grin2b+/− rats when compared to wild‐type
claims.criterion: Number of SWD events per day, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, judged by the rule for genotype differences in the opening comment (Het higher).

claims.statement: SWDs are longer on average in Grin2b+/- rats than in WT (two-sample t test, df = 22, T = -5.26, p = .00003).
claims.source: Figure 2C, middle
claims.quote: Furthermore, Grin2b+/− rats had a longer average SWD duration and total SWD duration than
claims.criterion: Mean SWD duration per day, two-sample t test, judged by the rule for genotype differences (Het higher). An animal with no SWDs has no mean duration and is left out of this test; the count left out is reported.

claims.statement: The total time in SWDs over 24 h is higher in Grin2b+/- rats than in WT (Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 5.5, p = .0002).
claims.source: Figure 2C, right
claims.quote: Furthermore, Grin2b+/− rats had a longer average SWD duration and total SWD duration than
claims.criterion: Total SWD duration per day, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, judged by the rule for genotype differences (Het higher).

claims.statement: Over 24 h, Grin2b+/- rats spend on average 59.97 min in SWDs, while WT littermates average less than a minute.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Over 24 h, Grin2b+/− mutants had on average of 59.97 min of SWDs, almost an entire hour of the day in an absence seizure. In contrast, wild‐type littermates had average totals of less than a minute.
claims.criterion: Mean over animals of the total SWD duration per day. Reproduced when the Het mean is within tolerance and the WT mean is below 1 min; partially reproduced when one of the two holds; not reproduced when neither does.

claims.statement: The number of SWDs does not differ between the light and dark phases, and Grin2b+/- rats have more SWDs than WT in both (linear mixed model, genotype p < .00001, phase p = .28, interaction p = .53).
claims.source: Figure S5A; Results, Absence seizures in Grin2b+/- rats, paragraph 2
claims.quote: Number of SWD events during the light and dark phases did not differ significantly but were increased significantly in Grin2b+/− rats
claims.criterion: SWD counts in ZT 0-12 and ZT 12-24 per animal (mean of the two days); split-plot ANOVA with genotype between and phase within. Reproduced when phase has p >= 0.05 and the genotype effect has p < 0.05 with Het higher. Partially reproduced when phase has p >= 0.05 and Het are higher on average without p < 0.05. Not reproduced when phase has p < 0.05 or Het are not higher.

claims.statement: Sex does not affect the number, mean duration or total duration of SWDs (two-way ANOVA sex x genotype, sex p = .74, .99 and .99).
claims.source: Figure S8B
claims.quote: Grin2b+/− rats had a statistically greater number of SWDs, with longer average and total durations than Grin2b+/+ rats, and these differences were not influenced by the animals’ sex
claims.criterion: The paper's two-way ANOVA with interaction cannot be fitted, as both WT are female. The sex term of a two-way ANOVA (type II) with genotype and sex, without interaction, is used for each of the three measures. Reproduced when none of the three sex terms has p < 0.05; not reproduced when any has.

claims.statement: The EEG spectrum during SWDs has a clear peak in the theta range with a harmonic, in both genotypes.
claims.source: Figure 2D; Results, Absence seizures in Grin2b+/- rats, paragraph 3
claims.quote: In SWD epoch averages we found a clear peak in the theta frequency range with a secondary harmonic in both genotypes
claims.criterion: Mean Welch spectrum (absolute, uV^2/Hz) of the SWD epochs in the raw windows, per animal with at least 5 usable SWD epochs. A peak is a local maximum of log10 power between 3 and 30 Hz with a prominence of at least 0.1. Reproduced when every such animal has a peak at 5-10 Hz (f0) and another within 1 Hz of 2 x f0, and both genotypes have such an animal.
