Blocked when the data set holds no such pair of intensities.

claims.statement: Both ON and ON-OFF direction-selective RGCs are found in mutant retinas.
claims.source: Results, Functional visual circuits form in the absence of Pcdh- γ s, paragraph 3; Figure 9B
claims.quote: Both ON and ON-OFF direction-selective cells were encountered in mutant retinas ( Figure 9B and data not shown)
claims.criterion: The stimulus is from the Figure 9B legend, a grating moving in 8 directions (wavelength 664 um, speed 664 um/s), with the average firing rate per direction. The paper defines no direction selectivity index and no threshold. Readings are (a) the vector-sum index |sum r e^(i theta)| / sum r above 0.3; (b) (preferred minus opposite) / (preferred plus opposite) above 0.5; in each also requiring the index to exceed the 95th percentile of 1000 shuffles of the direction labels over trials. ON and ON-OFF are taken from the flash readings of fig9a-response-variety. The Results also name moving bars ("moving bars and gratings", with "data not shown"), whose parameters are not given; mutant moving-bar recordings are analysed the same way, per direction. Reproduced when, under every reading, at least one mutant ON cell and one mutant ON-OFF cell are direction selective. Blocked when the data set holds no moving-grating or moving-bar recordings from mutant retinas.

claims.statement: Some control and mutant RGCs have receptive field surrounds of opposite sign to the centre, so lateral inhibition functions in mutant circuits.
claims.source: Results, Functional visual circuits form in the absence of Pcdh- γ s, paragraph 3; Supplementary Figure 3 (not read)
claims.quote: Some control and mutant RGCs had receptive field surrounds, where light has the opposite effect of the center
claims.criterion: The supplementary figure was not available and the text gives no measure. Read from the spatial profile b(x) of fig9d-rf-size-similar, a surround is a lobe of b(x) of sign opposite to the centre peak on both flanks, with readings for its size of (a) any minimum beyond 10% of the centre peak; (b) beyond 20%. Reproduced when, under every combination of these, the separation and the recording readings of fig9d-rf-size-similar, at least one mutant and one control cell have a surround.

claims.statement: Receptive field centre size varies greatly among RGCs, but its distribution is similar in control and mutant retinas.
claims.source: Results, Functional visual circuits form in the absence of Pcdh- γ s, paragraph 4; Figure 9D
claims.quote: The size of the receptive field center varied greatly among RGCs, but the distribution was similar in control and mutant retinas ( Figure 9D )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Methods, Electrophysiology, Eqns 1 and 2, and Figure 9D legend. The spike-triggered average of the flickering-bar stimulus, intensity with its time average subtracted, over all spikes of the cell. The paper does not say which recording of a retina is used; it names bars of 8.3 or 16.6 um width but not their orientation, and says nothing of retinas with more than one such recording. Readings are (A) the first vertical-bar recording at 8.3 or 16.6 um; (B) all vertical-bar recordings at 8.3 or 16.6 um pooled, spikes and frames together; (C) the horizontal-bar recording where the retina has one, otherwise as A. The same readings hold for every claim on the flicker stimulus. Its length in time is not given, and a window of 0.5 s (30 frames) before each spike is used as a standard choice that holds the response. The separation h(x, t) = b(x) a(t) is not specified; readings are (i) the leading singular vectors of h, (ii) b(x) as h at the time of its largest absolute value and a(t) as h at the bar of its largest absolute value. Centre size is the full width at half maximum of |b(x)| around its peak, in um from the bar width (8.3 or 16.6 um) of each recording, with linear interpolation between bars as a standard choice. Reproduced when the 95% bands of the two cumulative histograms overlap under every combination of the CI readings (header), the recording readings and the separation readings; not reproduced when they separate under all; blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise. The medians and a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: The time course of the light response is significantly slower in mutant retina, measured as the time to peak of the temporal integration function a(t).
claims.source: Results, Functional visual circuits form in the absence of Pcdh- γ s, paragraph 4; Figure 9E
claims.quote: On the other hand, the time course of the light response was significantly slower in mutant retina ( Figure 9E )
claims.criterion: The paper names no test; the Figure 9E legend gives the measure, the time to peak of a(t) from Eqn 2, and 95% confidence bands. a(t) as in fig9d-rf-size-similar (both separation readings and the three recording readings); the peak is the extremum of largest absolute value, so that OFF cells are timed at their trough. Its time is read (a) at the 16.6 ms frame resolution, (b) with parabolic interpolation over the three frames around the extremum. Reproduced when, under every combination of the CI, recording, separation and peak readings, the mutant curve lies at longer times and the bands separate; not reproduced when the bands overlap under all; blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise. Group medians and a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test are reported.

claims.statement: Mutant RGCs fire at much lower rates than control RGCs in response to flickering gratings.
claims.source: Results, Functional visual circuits form in the absence of Pcdh- γ s, paragraph 4; Figure 9F
claims.quote: Moreover, mutant RGCs fired at much lower rates in reponse to flicker stimuli ( Figure 9F )
claims.criterion: Figure 9F legend, the average firing rate observed during stimulation with flickering gratings, per cell as its spike count over the duration of the flicker stimulus, in the recording chosen by the recording readings (A, B, C) of fig9d-rf-size-similar; under B, the spike count and duration of the pooled recordings. Reproduced when the mutant curve lies at lower rates and the 95% bands separate under every combination of the CI readings (header) and the recording readings; not reproduced when they overlap under all; blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise. Group medians and their ratio are reported.

claims.statement: In a Linear-Nonlinear model fitted to the flicker responses, the response threshold of mutant RGCs is unaltered.
claims.source: Results, Functional visual circuits form in the absence of Pcdh- γ s, paragraph 4; Figure 9G
claims.quote: Based on fitting with a Linear-Nonlinear model ... we found that the threshold is unaltered, but the gain is reduced in mutants ( Figures 9G-H )
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. Methods, Eqn 3, the generator y(t) is the stimulus filtered by the cell's spike-triggered average h(x, t) (Eqn 1), summed over bars and scaled by Z to unit variance; the rate is N(y) = B for y below theta and B + G y above. The fitting procedure is not given; readings are (a) least squares of the model against the firing rate in bins of one stimulus frame (16.6 ms); (b) least squares against the mean rate in bins of y (the empirical nonlinearity of Chichilnisky 2001), with 20 bins of equal count as a standard choice. The printed form B + G y is discontinuous at theta unless B is adjusted; the continuous form B + G (y - theta) is a second reading of the nonlinearity. The filter and the fit use the same data, the recording chosen by the recording readings of fig9d-rf-size-similar, as the Methods describe no split. Judged on the paper's comparison, the overlap of the 95% bands of the cumulative histograms of theta. Reproduced when they overlap under every combination of the CI, recording, fit and form readings; not reproduced when they separate under all; blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise. Medians and a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test are shown as a variant.

claims.statement: In the same Linear-Nonlinear model, the gain of mutant RGCs is reduced.
claims.source: Results, Functional visual circuits form in the absence of Pcdh- γ s, paragraph 4; Figure 9H
claims.quote: we found that the threshold is unaltered, but the gain is reduced in mutants ( Figures 9G-H )
claims.criterion: G from the fits of fig9g-threshold-unaltered, under the same readings. Reproduced when, under every combination of the CI, recording, fit and form readings, the mutant curve lies at lower gains and the 95% bands separate; not reproduced when they overlap under all; blocked as methods_underspecified otherwise. Group medians are reported.

claims.statement: Warmer spring air advanced bud swelling in both species, by 1.1 days per degree in beech and 2.3 days per degree in oak, across 2020 and 2021 and the four treatments.
claims.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1A and 1B
claims.quote: Higher daily air temperatures in spring were linked to an earlier bud swelling in both species, where beech was advanced by −1.1 d °C−1 and oak by −2.3 d °C−1 across the 2 yr and treatments
claims.criterion: Phenology regression (opening comment) of bud swelling day of year on Tspring. Reproduced when, under one of the readings P1 or P2 with H1 or H2, both slopes are within tolerance and each regression has P <= 0.05.

claims.statement: Warmer spring air shortened leaf development duration by 0.7 days per degree in both species.
claims.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1C and 1D
claims.quote: A shorter leaf development duration was also found, with a reduction of −0.7 d °C−1 in both species
claims.criterion: Phenology regression (opening comment) of development duration (stage 1 to stage 4) on Tspring. Reproduced when, under one of the readings P1 or P2 with H1 or H2, both slopes are within tolerance and each regression has P <= 0.05.

claims.statement: Warmer fall air extended leaf senescence duration by 3.4 days per degree in beech and 3.1 days per degree in oak.
claims.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1G and 1H
claims.quote: Similarly, senescence duration was extended by +3.4 d °C−1 in beech and +3.1 d °C−1 in oak
claims.criterion: Phenology regression (opening comment) of senescence duration (10% to 90% of leaves coloured or fallen, linearly interpolated between observation dates as the Methods say) on Tfall. Reproduced when, under one of the readings P1 or P2 with H1 or H2, both slopes are within tolerance and each regression has P <= 0.05.

claims.statement: Warmer annual air lengthened the growing season by 4.5 days per degree in beech and 5.7 days per degree in oak.
claims.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1I and 1J
claims.quote: The growing seasons were extended by +4.5 d °C−1 and +5.7 d °C−1 for beech and oak, respectively, with an increase in daily mean annual air temperature
claims.criterion: Phenology regression (opening comment) of growing season length (bud swelling to onset of senescence) on Tannual. Reproduced when, under one of the readings P1 or P2 with H1 or H2, both slopes are within tolerance and each regression has P <= 0.05.

claims.statement: The temperature-driven advance was larger in oak than in beech (P = 0.004, least squares analysis).
claims.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1
claims.quote: However chronic warming was more advantageous to oak than to beech as the advancement of bud swelling extension was higher in oak (P = 0.004 using Least-squares analysis)
claims.criterion: The paper names the analysis only as least squares, and "advancement of bud swelling extension" is ambiguous. Readings (a) the species by Tspring interaction in a linear model of bud swelling date on Tspring, species and their interaction; (b) the same for growing season length on Tannual. Each fit on the units of the phenology regression (P1 and P2, H1 and H2). Reproduced when, under one reading, the interaction has p < 0.05 with the oak slope the larger in magnitude; p is reported against 0.004.

claims.statement: The onset of senescence was not related to fall air temperature in either species.
claims.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1E and 1F
claims.quote: No relationship between the onset of senescence and fall daily air temperatures was found, suggesting that the onset of senescence is not driven by temperature changes in the fall for both species
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test, the phenology regression (opening comment) of onset of senescence on Tfall at P <= 0.05. Reproduced when neither species' regression has P <= 0.05. The unit and sensor are open (P1, P2, H1, H2); the outcome is the one they all give, and the slopes are reported.

claims.statement: No phenological trait was related to soil moisture in either species.
claims.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Supplemental Figure S1
claims.quote: We observed no significant relationship between phenology and soil moisture for both species (Supplemental Fig. S1)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test, linear regressions as in the phenology regression (opening comment), with soil moisture at 25 cm in place of air temperature, bud swelling and development duration on Mspring, onset and duration of senescence on Mfall, growing season length on Mannual (Supplemental Figure S1 legend, Methods, Statistical analysis). Reproduced when none of the ten regressions has P <= 0.05. The unit (P1 or P2) is open; the outcome is the one both give.

claims.statement: The more chilling days trees received, the fewer growing degree days they needed to reach bud swelling, in both species, following a negative exponential.
claims.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 2; Figure 2A and 2B
claims.quote: With an increase in the number of chilling days, both species had lower GDD requirements to budburst (Fig. 2)
claims.criterion: Per species, monoculture trees in 2020 and 2021, one value per tree and year (Figure 2 legend). GDD is accumulated from January 1 to the bud swelling date over daily mean air temperatures above 5 C, and chilling days are days with daily mean below 5 C from November 1 (Methods, Phenology, paragraph 2), from the chamber's record. Open, (a) GDD as the sum of the excess over 5 C or (b) as the sum of the daily means above 5 C; the end of the chilling count at (c) bud swelling (Methods) or (d) leaf flushing, stage 4 (Figure 2 legend); the sensor (H1 or H2); and the negative exponential as (e) GDD = a exp(b CD) or (f) GDD = a + b exp(c CD), the paper giving only nls. Reproduced when, under every reading, the fitted curve decreases with chilling days and its rate parameter has p <= 0.05 in both species; blocked as methods_underspecified when readings differ.

claims.statement: Even without warming, trees received at most 97 chilling days.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 1; Figure 2
claims.quote: In our experiment, trees were exposed to a maximum of 97 d even in the absence of warming (Fig. 2)
claims.criterion: Chilling days as in fig2-gdd-chilling, readings (c) and (d) and H1 and H2. Reproduced when the maximum over C and MR trees is within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Warming made predawn leaf water potential more negative in 2020 in both species, and midday leaf water potential more negative in 2020 in beech only.
claims.source: Results, Leaf water potential, paragraph 1; Figure 3
claims.quote: Warming resulted in more negative ΨPD in 2020 in both species and more negative ΨMD in 2020 but only in beech (Fig. 3)
claims.criterion: Treatment test (opening comment), untransformed, readings T1 and T2. Reproduced when, in 2020, W is significantly more negative than C for predawn potential in both species and for midday potential in beech, and not in oak; partially reproduced when two or three of these four hold. The outcome is the one T1 and T2 both give.

claims.statement: Lower soil moisture alone made predawn leaf water potential more negative in 2020 in oak only.
claims.source: Results, Leaf water potential, paragraph 1; Figure 3
claims.quote: lower soil moisture reduced ΨPD in 2020 but only in oak (Fig. 3)
claims.criterion: Treatment test (opening comment), untransformed, readings T1 and T2. Reproduced when, in 2020, MR predawn potential is significantly below C in oak and not in beech; the outcome is the one T1 and T2 both give.

claims.statement: Combined warming and drier soil made predawn leaf water potential more negative in 2021 in both species.
claims.source: Results, Leaf water potential, paragraph 1; Figure 3; Supplemental Table S1
claims.quote: However, combined warming and drier soils resulted in more negative ΨPD in 2021 in both species (Fig. 3, Supplemental Table S1)
claims.criterion: Treatment test (opening comment), untransformed, readings T1 and T2. Reproduced when, in 2021, WMR predawn potential is significantly below C in both species; partially reproduced in one. The outcome is the one T1 and T2 both give.

claims.statement: Under the low moisture treatment trees reached predawn water potentials of about -1.9 MPa in beech and -1.2 MPa in oak.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 3; Figure 3
claims.quote: As the predawn (ΨPD) and midday leaf water potential (ΨMD) of our trees were slightly affected by our low moisture treatment (Fig. 3), we considered the water availability level as moderate. Indeed, trees reached ΨPD of about −1.9 and −1.2 MPa in beech and downy oak, respectively
claims.criterion: The paper does not say which value "reached" is. Readings (a) the lowest yearly treatment mean of MR in 2020 or 2021 (Figure 3); (b) the lowest yearly treatment mean of MR or WMR; (c) the lowest campaign treatment mean of MR or WMR; (d) the most negative single measurement of a monoculture tree under MR or WMR, as "trees reached" allows. Yearly means are of the tree-year means of monoculture trees, in 2020 and 2021. Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: In beech, warming alone had no effect on starch, sugar, Asat, or height, diameter and AGWB increments.
claims.source: Results, Leaf-level carbon relations and tree growth, paragraph 1; Figure 4; Supplemental Table S1
claims.quote: In beech, warming had no impact on leaf-level carbon relations and growth (Fig. 4, Supplemental Table S1)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test, the treatment test (opening comment). Reproduced when no W against C contrast is significant (alpha 0.05) for any of the six traits in 2020 or 2021 in beech; not reproduced when any is. The contrasts' sizes and the Table S1 warming terms are reported. Table S1 also gives a significant warming by year term for beech Asat (F = 5.22, p = 0.006), which the statistics above leave out; the claim rests on the W against C contrasts. Readings T1, T2, S1, S2 and S3, the square-root readings applying to negative starch, sugar and Asat values as to negative increments (the paper does not say how they were handled); the outcome is the one they all give.

claims.statement: In oak, warming alone reduced height, diameter and AGWB increments, in 2021 only.
claims.source: Results, Leaf-level carbon relations and tree growth, paragraph 1; Figure 4G to 4L; Supplemental Table S1
claims.quote: In oak, warming reduced height increment, diameter increment, and AGWB increment but only in 2021 (Fig. 4, Supplemental Table S1)
claims.criterion: Treatment test (opening comment), readings T1, T2, S1, S2 and S3. Reproduced when, in oak, W is significantly below C in 2021 for all three increments and for none in 2020; partially reproduced when one or two of the 2021 contrasts are significant and none in 2020. The outcome is the one all readings give.

claims.statement: In oak, warming had no effect on Asat or on starch and sugar concentrations.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 4; Figure 4A to 4F
claims.quote: downy oak, which occurs in environments of 19 °C MAT (Pasta et al. 2016), showed no effect of warming on Asat and NSC but a substantial decrease in growth (Fig. 4)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test, the treatment test (opening comment). Reproduced when no W against C contrast is significant for starch, sugar or Asat in oak in 2020 or 2021. Readings T1, T2, S1, S2 and S3; the outcome is the one all give.

claims.statement: In beech, lower soil moisture alone reduced Asat in 2021, height increment in 2021, diameter increment in 2020 and 2021, and AGWB increment in 2021.
claims.source: Results, Leaf-level carbon relations and tree growth, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: In beech, lower soil moisture led to a significant reduction of Asat in 2021, height increment in 2021, diameter increment in 2020 and 2021, and AGWB increment in 2021
claims.criterion: Treatment test (opening comment), readings T1, T2, S1, S2 and S3. Reproduced when MR is significantly below C in all five named trait-years; partially reproduced in three or four; not reproduced otherwise. The other MR against C contrasts are reported. The outcome is the one all readings give.

claims.statement: In oak, lower soil moisture alone reduced Asat and height, diameter and AGWB increments in both 2020 and 2021.
claims.source: Results, Leaf-level carbon relations and tree growth, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: Similarly, we observed a substantial reduction in Asat, height increment, diameter increment, and AGWB increments in oak in 2020 and 2021 (Fig. 4, Supplemental Table S1)
claims.criterion: Treatment test (opening comment), readings T1, T2, S1, S2 and S3. Reproduced when MR is significantly below C in all eight trait-years; partially reproduced in four to seven; not reproduced otherwise. The outcome is the one all readings give.

claims.statement: In beech, combined warming and low moisture reduced Asat and diameter increment in 2020 and 2021.
claims.source: Results, Leaf-level carbon relations and tree growth, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: Under combined warming and low moisture, we observed a reduction of Asat, and diameter increment in 2020 and 2021 in beech
claims.criterion: Treatment test (opening comment), readings T1, T2, S1, S2 and S3. Reproduced when WMR is significantly below C in all four trait-years; partially reproduced in two or three. The outcome is the one all readings give.

claims.statement: In oak, combined warming and low moisture reduced Asat and height, diameter and AGWB increments in 2020 and 2021.
claims.source: Results, Leaf-level carbon relations and tree growth, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: In oak, a reduction of Asat, height increment, diameter increment, and AGWB increment in 2020 and 2021 was observed
claims.criterion: Treatment test (opening comment), readings T1, T2, S1, S2 and S3. Reproduced when WMR is significantly below C in all eight trait-years; partially reproduced in four to seven. The outcome is the one all readings give.

claims.statement: Responses to combined warming and low moisture did not differ from responses to low moisture alone.
claims.source: Results, Leaf-level carbon relations and tree growth, paragraph 1; Figure 4
claims.quote: No significant differences were found between responses to lower moisture alone and combined warming and soil moisture reduction (Fig. 4, Supplemental Table S1)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test, the treatment test (opening comment). Reproduced when no MR against WMR contrast is significant for the six traits of Figure 4 in either species in 2020 or 2021; not reproduced when any is, with the number and sizes of such contrasts reported. Readings T1, T2, S1, S2 and S3; the outcome is the one all give.

claims.statement: Drier soils did not change starch and sugar concentrations in either species.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 5; Figure 4A to 4D
claims.quote: Chronically drier soils strongly reduced the leaf-level carbon relations and growth of both species, except for NSC where we found no changes (Fig. 4)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test, the treatment test (opening comment). Reproduced when no MR against C contrast is significant for starch or sugar in either species in 2020 or 2021. WMR against C is shown as a variant. Readings T1, T2, S1, S2 and S3; the outcome is the one all give.

claims.statement: Low soil moisture impaired Asat more strongly in beech than in oak.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 5; Figure 4E and 4F
claims.quote: However, while both species were negatively impacted by low soil moisture, beech Asat was more strongly impaired (Fig. 4)
claims.criterion: No test is reported. The measure, from Figure 4, is the reduction of mean Asat over monoculture tree-year means, which the paper does not define. Open, the measure, (r1) the relative reduction (C - X) / C or (r2) the absolute reduction C - X; which treatment X (MR alone, or MR and WMR); and which year (2020, 2021, or both pooled). Reproduced when the reduction is larger in beech than in oak under every reading; blocked as methods_underspecified when readings differ.

claims.statement: Asat, starch and sugar did not vary among the three campaigns of the growing season.
claims.source: Methods, Statistical analysis, paragraph 2; Supplemental Table S6
claims.quote: As leaf-level responses (assimilation and starch and sugar concentrations) did not vary during the growing season, we averaged them per year before the analyses (Supplemental Table S6)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test (Table S6 footnote), lme(trait ~ (warming + moisture reduction + season)^3, random = ~1|Chamber) on square-root values, season the campaign (early, middle, late). Reproduced when the season term has p > 0.05 for all three traits. Table S6 has no species or year column, so open, (a) both species pooled, (b) per species; the years, (y1) 2019 to 2021, the years of the treatment test whose averaging Table S6 justifies (Methods, Statistical analysis, paragraph 2), or (y2) 2020 and 2021, the years reported; and the trees (monocultures, as that paragraph concerns, or monocultures and mixtures). The paper does not say whether its F tests are sequential (the default of nlme's anova) or marginal, and links no code; both are readings, (F1) sequential and (F2) marginal. Negative values as S1, S2 or S3 (opening comment). The outcome is the one all readings give.

claims.statement: Species mixture did not change phenology in either species, except a development duration about 2 days shorter in oak mixtures than monocultures under lower moisture, whose net biodiversity effect was not significant.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 1; Supplemental Table S2
claims.quote: In both species, no impact of species interactions on phenology was found in any treatment, except in oak where we observed a slightly shorter development duration of 2 d in mixtures compared to the monocultures under lower moisture (Supplemental Table S2), but the net biodiversity effect was not significant
claims.criterion: Interaction test (opening comment) on the five phenological traits, readings I1 and I2, with the years of reading Y1 (bud swelling and development duration on 2020 and 2021, the three fall and season traits on 2019 to 2021, as the F and p pairs of Table S2 imply); Y2 (2020 and 2021 for all five) is reported as a variant. Reproduced when the only significant mixture against monoculture contrast is oak development duration under MR, shorter in mixtures by a difference within tolerance (in one year under I1, or pooled under I2); partially reproduced when that contrast holds and one other is also significant. The NBE of oak development duration under MR, in the year or years of the contrast, must not differ from zero by the t-test of the biodiversity effects procedure (readings B1 and B2, which must agree, or blocked as methods_underspecified); when it does, the claim is at most partially reproduced.

claims.statement: Under warming, species mixture did not change beech leaf-level carbon relations or growth in 2020 and 2021, and beech showed no net biodiversity effect on these traits in 2021.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 2; Supplemental Table S3; Figure 5
claims.quote: In beech, no impact of species interactions on leaf-level carbon relations or growth was found under the warming treatment in 2020 and 2021 (Supplemental Table S3). Consequently, beech did not show any impact of net biodiversity in response to warming in terms of leaf-level carbon relations or growth in 2021 (Fig. 5)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's tests. Reproduced when, in beech under W, no mixture against monoculture contrast of the interaction test (opening comment) is significant for the six traits of Figure 5 in 2020 or 2021, and no 2021 NBE differs from zero by the t-test of the biodiversity effects procedure. The 2020 NBEs are reported, not judged, as the paper states the absence for 2021 only. Readings I1, I2, B1, B2, L1 and L2; the outcome is the one all give.

claims.statement: Under warming, beech Asat showed a positive selection effect, too weak to change the net biodiversity effect.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 2; Supplemental Figure S2E
claims.quote: However, we observed a positive selection effect on beech Asat under warming (Supplemental Fig. S2), suggesting positive interactions in the mixtures; although, this effect was not strong enough to influence the overall net biodiversity effect
claims.criterion: Biodiversity effects procedure (opening comment). The year is not stated; it may be 2020 or 2021. Reproduced when, in one of these years, the beech Asat selection effect under W is positive and differs from zero by the t-test, and the NBE does not. The method readings (B1, B2, L1, L2, and the reading of Eq. 4) must all agree; when they do not, blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Under warming, oak in mixtures had a diameter increment about 0.3 cm per year lower than in monocultures, and no other difference between mixtures and monocultures.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 2; Supplemental Table S3
claims.quote: For oak, no differences between mixtures and monocultures were found under warming, except for lower diameter increment of approximately 0.3 cm per year in mixtures compared to monocultures (Supplemental Table S3)
claims.criterion: Interaction test (opening comment), readings I1 and I2. The unit is open, as the paper prints cm here but Table S4 gives diameters in mm; readings (u1) 0.3 cm and (u2) 0.3 mm. Reproduced when, under W, the oak diameter increment contrast is significant and lower in mixtures with a difference within tolerance under one unit reading, and no other oak trait contrast under W is significant.

claims.statement: Under warming in 2020, oak showed a negative net biodiversity effect on AGWB increment, explained by a negative complementarity effect.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 2; Figure 5L; Supplemental Figure S3L
claims.quote: Moreover, oak trees showed a negative net biodiversity effect for the AGWB increment in response to warming in 2020 (Fig. 5), explained by a negative complementarity effect (Supplemental Fig. S3)
claims.criterion: Biodiversity effects procedure (opening comment). Reproduced when, for oak AGWB increment under W in 2020, the NBE and the complementarity effect are both negative and differ from zero by the t-test. The Discussion (paragraph 8) calls this complementarity effect positive; the sign found is reported. Readings B1 and B2 must agree; when they do not, blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Under lower soil moisture, beech in mixtures had a smaller diameter increment than in monocultures.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 3; Supplemental Table S3
claims.quote: Under lower soil moisture, we found a reduced diameter increment in mixtures compared to the monocultures in beech (Supplemental Table S3)
claims.criterion: Interaction test (opening comment). The year is not stated. Reproduced when, under MR, the beech diameter increment is significantly lower in mixtures than in monocultures in 2020 or 2021 (I1) or over both years (I2).

claims.statement: Under low soil moisture, beech showed a negative net biodiversity effect on sugar concentration, driven by a negative complementarity effect.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 3; Figure 5C; Supplemental Figure S3C
claims.quote: Similarly, a negative net biodiversity effect on sugar concentration in response to low soil moisture was found in beech (Fig. 5), driven by a negative complementarity effect (Supplemental Fig. S3)
claims.criterion: Biodiversity effects procedure (opening comment). The Results give no year; the Discussion (paragraph 8) places it in 2020 and calls the complementarity effect positive. Reproduced when, for beech sugar under MR in 2020 or 2021, the NBE is negative and differs from zero by the t-test, and the complementarity effect is negative and differs from zero; the year and sign found are reported. The method readings (B1, B2, L1, L2) must agree; when they do not, blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Under low soil moisture alone, oak showed no effect of species interactions and no net biodiversity effect.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 3; Supplemental Table S3; Figure 5
claims.quote: In contrast, we observed no impact of species interactions and net biodiversity effect in oak (Supplemental Table S3, Fig. 5)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's tests. Reproduced when, in oak under MR, no mixture against monoculture contrast of the interaction test is significant for the six traits of Figure 5 in 2020 or 2021, and no NBE differs from zero by the t-test (opening comment). Readings I1, I2, B1, B2, L1 and L2; the outcome is the one all give.

claims.statement: Under combined warming and lower moisture, beech height increment was about 2 cm per year larger in monocultures than in mixtures.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 4; Supplemental Table S3
claims.quote: Under combined warming and lower moisture, a larger height increment by approximately 2 cm per year was found in monocultures compared to the mixtures in beech (Supplemental Table S3)
claims.criterion: Interaction test (opening comment). Reproduced when, under WMR, beech height increment is significantly larger in monocultures, with a difference within tolerance, in 2020 or 2021 (I1) or over both years (I2).

claims.statement: Under combined warming and lower moisture, oak diameter increment was 1.4 cm larger in mixtures than in monocultures.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 4; Supplemental Table S3
claims.quote: In oak, diameter increment was larger by 1.4 cm in mixtures compared to the monocultures (Supplemental Table S3)
claims.criterion: Interaction test (opening comment), readings I1 and I2. The unit is open, as in tables3-oak-warming-diameter, (u1) cm or (u2) mm. Reproduced when, under WMR, oak diameter increment is significantly larger in mixtures with a difference within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Under combined warming and drier soils in 2021, oak showed a positive net biodiversity effect on Asat, explained by complementarity.
claims.source: Results, Impact of species interactions, paragraph 4; Figure 5F; Supplemental Figure S3F
claims.quote: We also observed a positive net biodiversity effect for Asat in 2021 in oak (Fig. 5). This effect was explained by complementarity effects, indicating a resource complementarity under warmer air and drier soils (Supplemental Fig. S3)
claims.criterion: Biodiversity effects procedure (opening comment). Reproduced when, for oak Asat under WMR in 2021, the NBE and the complementarity effect are positive and differ from zero by the t-test; partially reproduced when the NBE holds and the complementarity effect is positive but not significant. Readings B1, B2, L1 and L2 must agree; when they do not, blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: The treatments raised air temperature by 5.19 C (W) and 5.02 C (WMR) and reduced soil moisture by 52.77% (MR) and 51.96% (WMR) relative to the control.
claims.source: Materials and methods, Experimental set-up, paragraph 2; Figure 6
claims.quote: an air warming treatment with an increase of around 5 °C (i.e. +5.19 ± 0.2 °C) relative to the (ambient) air temperature in the control (W) ... a soil moisture reduction treatment with a reduction of soil moisture of around 50% (i.e. −52.77 ± 9.7%) relative to the control ... (WMR, i.e. +5.02 ± 0.2 °C and −51.96 ± 10.3%, Fig. 6, Supplemental Table S5)
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the paper's stated spreads. From the chamber records, treatment means of daily means (n = 4 chambers per treatment, Figure 6). Open, the period (from June 2019 to the end of 2021, or 2020 and 2021) and the air sensor (H1, H2). Reproduced when all four values are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Soil moisture at 25 cm did not differ between the single and the combined treatments.
claims.source: Discussion, paragraph 6; Figure 6E and 6F
claims.quote: We found no differences in soil moisture conditions at 25 cm depth between single and combined treatments (Fig. 6)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the paper's test, Tukey's HSD at alpha 0.05 on the averages over the entire time per treatment (Figure 6 legend). Reproduced when MR and WMR do not differ; W against C is shown as a variant. Open, the unit of the test, (a) chamber means over the period (n = 4 per treatment) or (b) daily treatment means; the outcome is the one both give.

claims.statement: Annual mean air temperature was about 12 C without warming and 16 to 17 C with warming, and annual soil moisture about 10% without and 5% with moisture reduction, in 2020 and 2021.
claims.source: Supplemental Table S5
claims.criterion: Treatment means of the chamber records, January to December (Table S5). Air temperature tolerances are the table's stated spread (0.4); the soil moisture spread is printed as 0.0, below the table's precision, so 10% is used. The air sensor is open (H1, H2). Reproduced when all 16 values are within tolerance under one reading; partially reproduced for 10 to 15.

claims.statement: Before the treatments began, tree height and diameter did not differ among the four climatic treatments in either species.
claims.source: Materials and methods, Experimental set-up, paragraph 2; Supplemental Table S4
claims.quote: Tree sizes were statistically similar when delivered and planted (Supplemental Table S4)
claims.criterion: Tolerances are the standard deviations Table S4 gives. Table S4 gives spring 2019 values. A claim of absence; the paper names no test. Readings (a) a one-way ANOVA of treatment per species and trait, (b) the treatment test's model without year (opening comment), on (c) the measured trees of monocultures and mixtures or (d) monocultures only, at p <= 0.05. Reproduced when no reading finds a treatment difference in any species and trait, and the 16 means are within tolerance; blocked as methods_underspecified when readings differ.

claims.statement: The deposited data are the specimens the paper modelled, 27 366 in total, giving 177 species-years and 11 798 birds for HY allometry, 174 and 12 318 for spring AHY, and 171 and 3250 for autumn AHY, and 11 731, 11 481 and 3122 birds in the three preliminary models.
claims.source: Methods, Morphological data, paragraph 1; Methods, Identifying key climatic variables, paragraph 2; Methods, Testing whether climate drives changes in wing length allometry, paragraph 6
claims.quote: HY allometry was estimated for 177 unique species-year combinations using 11 798 individuals, AHY spring allometry was estimated for 174 unique species-year combinations using 12 318 individuals, and AHY autumn allometry was estimated for 171 unique species-year combinations using 3250 individuals
claims.criterion: Counts after the class split and the dropping of species-years with missing predictors, as the header describes for the main models and as Script02 does for the preliminary models (which drop more species-years, having more predictors). Reproduced when every count is within tolerance (10% of the reported value, the default) under one of the filtering readings; the exact counts are reported, as they show which reading matches.

claims.statement: In HY birds, warmer temperature in the wintering season before the autumn of collection is associated with a more positive allometric slope (beta 0.02, pd 94.8%) but not with the allometric intercept (beta 0.01, pd 76.1%).
claims.source: Results, Spring migration, pre-breeding and wintering season temperatures do not have long-term impacts on wing length allometry, paragraph 1; Table 1
claims.quote: we find that the wintering season temperature prior to the autumn when HY birds were collected is significantly and positively associated with the allometric slope (β = 0.02, probability of direction (pd) = 94.8%) but is not significantly associated with the allometric intercept (β = 0.01, pd = 76.1%)
claims.criterion: HY main model as in the header (PrevTempWinMo). Reproduced when the slope effect is positive with pd at least 90% and the intercept effect has pd below 90%, with both means within tolerance, under each filtering reading; partially reproduced when the signs and means hold but an effect falls on the other side of 90%.

claims.statement: In HY birds, warmer pre-breeding temperature is associated with a more positive allometric intercept (beta 0.05, pd 98.7%) and not with the slope (beta -0.01, pd 89.5%).
claims.source: Results, Spring migration, pre-breeding and wintering season temperatures do not have long-term impacts on wing length allometry, paragraph 1; Table 1
claims.quote: We also find that the pre-breeding temperature prior to when HY birds are collected has a significant and positive association with the allometric intercept (β = 0.05, pd = 98.7%), but no significant association with the allometric slope (β = −0.01, pd = 89.5%)
claims.criterion: HY main model as in the header (AvgTempPreBreedBase). Reproduced when the intercept effect is positive with pd at least 90%, the slope effect has pd below 90%, and both means are within tolerance, under each filtering reading; partially reproduced when the signs and means hold but an effect falls on the other side of 90% (the slope pd of 89.5% is near the line).

claims.statement: Spring migration temperature has no significant effect on wing length, or interaction with body size, in any of the three preliminary phylogenetic mixed models, and so is left out of the main models.
claims.source: Results, Spring migration, pre-breeding and wintering season temperatures do not have long-term impacts on wing length allometry, paragraph 1; Tables S4 to S6
claims.quote: We do not include temperature during spring migration as a parameter in any of our main models of allometry because it does not have a significant effect in any of the phylogenetic mixed models
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the preliminary MCMCglmm models of Script02 (scaled wing on scaled tarsus, sex, every climate variable and year, each with its tarsus interaction; species random with the phylogenetic inverse matrix; inverse Wishart priors V 1, nu 0.02; 4 chains of 15 000 iterations, 5000 burn-in). The terms are every spring migration temperature (MinTempSpringMig, MinTempNextSpringMig, PrevMinTempSpringMig) and their tarsus interactions. Reproduced when every such 95% interval includes 0, under interval readings (i) and (ii) of the header; not reproduced when any excludes 0. The estimates and intervals are reported either way.

claims.statement: Pre-breeding and wintering season temperatures have no significant association with AHY wing length in the preliminary models of spring and autumn AHY birds.
claims.source: Results, Spring migration, pre-breeding and wintering season temperatures do not have long-term impacts on wing length allometry, paragraph 1; Tables S5 and S6
claims.quote: However, temperatures during these periods do not have any significant associations with AHY allometry (electronic supplementary material, tables S5–S6)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the preliminary models as in s4-s6-spring-migration- temperature-none. Terms are the main effects and tarsus interactions of every wintering temperature (TempWinMo, PrevTempWinMo, PrevPrevTempWinMo) and pre-breeding temperature (AvgTempPreBreedBase, PrevAvgTempPreBreedBase) in the spring AHY and autumn AHY models. Reproduced when every such 95% interval includes 0, under interval readings (i) and (ii); not reproduced when any excludes 0.

claims.statement: In HY birds, warmer breeding season temperature is associated with a more negative allometric intercept (beta -0.06, pd 99.1%), that is shorter wings for a given body size, and not with the slope (beta 0.01, pd 78.1%).
claims.source: Results, Colder breeding season temperatures during development are associated with increases in relative wing length, paragraph 1; Table 1
claims.quote: we find that breeding season temperature has a significant negative association with the allometric intercept of the relationship between body size and wing length (β = −0.06, pd = 99.1%) and no relationship with the allometric slope (β = 0.01, pd = 78.1%)
claims.criterion: HY main model as in the header (TempBreedMoBase). Reproduced when the intercept effect is negative with pd at least 90%, the slope effect has pd below 90%, and both means are within tolerance, under each filtering reading; partially reproduced when the signs and means hold but an effect falls on the other side of 90%.

claims.statement: In spring AHY birds, the temperature of the breeding season in which they developed has no significant association with the allometric intercept (beta -0.01, pd 72.7%) or slope (beta -0.01, pd 83.5%).
claims.source: Results, Colder breeding season temperatures during development are associated with increases in relative wing length, paragraph 1; Table 2
claims.quote: The association with the allometric intercept is not significant among AHY birds collected during the following spring (allometric intercept β = −0.01, pd = 72.7%; allometric slope β = −0.01, pd = 83.5%; table 2)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the spring AHY main model as in the header (TempBreedMoBase). Reproduced when both effects have pd below 90%, not reproduced when either reaches 90%; the means and pd are reported either way, under each filtering reading.

claims.statement: In autumn AHY birds, warmer temperature in the breeding season of their development (the year before the most recent) is again associated with a more negative allometric intercept (beta -0.09, pd 99.5%) and not with the slope (beta -0.01, pd 75.1%).
claims.source: Results, Colder breeding season temperatures during development are associated with increases in relative wing length, paragraph 1; Table 3
claims.quote: but it is significant again among AHY birds collected in the following autumn (allometric intercept β = −0.09, pd = 99.5%; allometric slope β = −0.01, pd = 75.1%; table 3)
claims.criterion: Autumn AHY main model as in the header (PrevTempBreedBase). Reproduced when the intercept effect is negative with pd at least 90%, the slope effect has pd below 90%, and both means are within tolerance, under each filtering reading; partially reproduced when the signs and means hold but an effect falls on the other side of 90%.

claims.statement: In the autumn AHY preliminary model, temperature of the most recent breeding season is not significantly associated with wing length.
claims.source: Results, Colder breeding season temperatures during development are associated with increases in relative wing length, paragraph 1; Table S6
claims.quote: However, temperature during the breeding season most recent to when autumn AHY birds were collected is not significantly associated with wing length among autumn AHY birds
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the autumn AHY preliminary model as in s4-s6-spring-migration- temperature-none (TempBreedMoBase and its tarsus interaction). Reproduced when both 95% intervals include 0, under interval readings (i) and (ii); not reproduced when either excludes 0.

claims.statement: In the HY preliminary model, autumn migration temperature has no significant association with wing length.
claims.source: Results, Autumn migration temperatures have mixed effects on wing length allometry of after hatch-year birds, paragraph 1; Table S4
claims.quote: Temperature during autumn migration does not have a significant association with HY wing length
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, on the HY preliminary model as in s4-s6-spring-migration- temperature-none (MinTempFallMig and its tarsus interaction). Reproduced when both 95% intervals include 0, under interval readings (i) and (ii); not reproduced when either excludes 0.

claims.statement: In spring AHY birds, warmer temperature during the preceding autumn migration is associated with a more negative allometric intercept (beta -0.04, pd 94.8%) and not with the slope (beta 0.00, pd 55.6%).
claims.source: Results, Autumn migration temperatures have mixed effects on wing length allometry of after hatch-year birds, paragraph 1; Table 2
claims.quote: temperature during the autumn migration prior to when spring AHY birds were collected is significantly and negatively associated with the allometric intercept (β = −0.04, pd = 94.8%) and has no significant relationship with the allometric slope (β = 0.00, pd = 55.6%)
claims.criterion: Spring AHY main model as in the header (MinTempFallMig). claims.statement: The increase in phage resistance after phage exposure did not differ between the two temperatures (no phage by temperature interaction).
claims.source: Results, SCVs have relatively higher phage resistance, paragraph 1; Figure 2A; Supplementary Table S3a
claims.quote: phage × temperature: F1,15 = 2.099, p = .168
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, the phage by temperature term of the ANOVA of fig2a-phage-exposed-more-resistant at p < .05 (Methods). Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the effect size is reported either way. The clone unit and the sums of squares readings are shown as variants.

claims.statement: SCVs were much more phage-resistant than mucoid clones, whether or not they had been exposed to phage during selection, with a significant colony type by phage interaction.
claims.source: Results, SCVs have relatively higher phage resistance, paragraph 1; Figure 2A; Supplementary Table S3a
claims.quote: Interestingly, SCVs were much more resistant to phages compared to mucoid colonies (colony morphology: F1,15 = 445.207, p < .001 Supplementary, Table S3a, Figure 2A) regardless of if they had been exposed to phages during the selection experiment (colony type × phage: F1,15 = 86.063, p < .001
claims.criterion: The ANOVA and readings of fig2a-phage-exposed-more-resistant. Reproduced when the colony type effect and the colony type by phage interaction both have p < 0.05 under all readings and the mean R of SCVs exceeds that of mucoid clones both among -P clones and among +P clones.

claims.statement: Mucoid clones from one 25 degrees C phage replicate were the exception, showing increased phage resistance.
claims.source: Results, SCVs have relatively higher phage resistance, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
claims.quote: The only exception was mucoid colonies isolated from one treatment replicate at 25 °C in the presence of phage that also showed an increase in phage resistance (phage: F1,18 = 174.5, p < .001)
claims.criterion: One-way ANOVA of clone R (Methods). The paper does not say what the mucoid clones of this replicate are compared with; df (1, 18) imply 20 clones. Readings are (a) against the mucoid clones of the 25 degrees C -P treatment, (b) against the mucoid clones of both -P treatments. Reproduced when R of these clones is higher and p < 0.05 under each reading.

claims.statement: SCVs had a higher maximum growth rate than mucoid clones, regardless of prior phage or temperature exposure.
claims.source: Results, SCVs show increased growth rate but reduced carrying capacity, paragraph 1; Figure 2B; Supplementary Table S3b
claims.quote: We found that SCVs had higher growth rate compared to mucoid colonies (colony type: F1,15 = 29.393, p < .001, Supplementary Table S3b, Figure 2B) regardless of the prior phage exposure (phage × colony type: F1,15 = 2.898, p = .109, Supplementary Table S3b, Figure 2B) or temperature exposure (temperature × colony type: F1,15 = 0.002, p = .967
claims.criterion: Maximum growth rate is the mu of a logistic model fitted with grofit gcFitModel to OD600 over time (Methods). The code's default fit, the best of four models by AIC with failed fits set to 0, is shown as a variant. The Methods speak of 13 time points but list nine; all time points the data hold are used. The code fits one curve per combination of the growth file's replicate and strain columns, on the mean OD600 at each time point within it; when the replicate column is the technical replicate, a clone's mu and A are the mean of its three fits. The ANOVA terms, unit, clone variant and sums of squares readings are those of fig2a-phage-exposed-more-resistant. Reproduced when the colony type effect has p < 0.05 with SCVs higher and both interactions have p >= 0.05 under all readings.

claims.statement: SCVs had a lower carrying capacity than mucoid clones, not affected by prior temperature or phage exposure.
claims.source: Results, SCVs show increased growth rate but reduced carrying capacity, paragraph 1; Figure 2C; Supplementary Table S3c
claims.quote: non-mucoid SCVs showed a clear reduction in their carrying capacity (colony type: F1,15 = 87.965, p < .001, Supplementary Table S3c, Figure 2C), which was not affected by prior temperature (temperature × colony type: F1,15 = 3.222, p = .093, Supplementary Table S3c, Figure 2C) and phage exposure treatments (phage × colony type: F1,15 = 2.900, p = .109
claims.criterion: Carrying capacity is the A of the growth fits of fig2b-scv-higher-growth-rate, with the same readings and variant. Reproduced when the colony type effect has p < 0.05 with SCVs lower and both interactions have p >= 0.05 under all readings.

claims.statement: Prior temperature or phage exposure had no effect on the twitching motility of SCVs.
claims.source: Results, Phage resistance and loss of mucoidy leads to reduced R. solanacearum virulence, paragraph 1; Figure 2D; Supplementary Table S3d
claims.quote: While prior temperature or phage exposure had no effect on the twitching motility of SCVs (all p > .05, Supplementary Table S3d)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, Table S3d, an ANOVA of twitching diameter over the 28 evolved clones (residual df 21, so one value per clone, the mean of three technical replicates) with temperature, phage, colony type and the three two-way interactions. The test includes mucoid clones although the claim is about SCVs. Reproduced when the temperature, phage and temperature by phage terms all have p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any has p < 0.05. Sums of squares read sequential in table order and type II. The same ANOVA on SCV clones alone is shown as a variant. The diameter is taken as given in the data, at 72 h.

claims.statement: Phage-resistant mucoid clones from the 25 degrees C phage treatment showed clearly reduced twitching motility.
claims.source: Results, Phage resistance and loss of mucoidy leads to reduced R. solanacearum virulence, paragraph 1; Figure 2D
claims.quote: phage-resistant mucoid colony types from the treatment at 25 °C in the presence of phage showed a clear reduction in twitching motility (F1,6 = 27.22, p < .01, Figure 2D)
claims.criterion: One-way ANOVA of clone twitching diameter (Methods); df (1, 6) imply four clones against four. The comparison group is not named. Readings are (a) the four mucoid clones of 25 degrees C -P, (b) the four mucoid clones of 35 degrees C -P. Reproduced when the 25 degrees C +P mucoid clones have the smaller mean diameter and p < 0.05 under both readings. The ancestor's diameter (9.38 cm, the dashed line in the code for Figure 2D) is reported alongside.

claims.statement: Mucoid clones formed more biofilm than the ancestor, while SCVs kept ancestral-level biofilm formation.
claims.source: Results, Phage resistance and loss of mucoidy leads to reduced R. solanacearum virulence, paragraph 1; Figure 2E; Supplementary Table S3e
claims.quote: overall, mucoid colonies showed increased biofilm formation relative to ancestral strain, while SCVs retained ancestral-level biofilm formation (colony type: F1,21 = 42.370, p < .001
claims.criterion: Biofilm OD570, each clone the mean of three technical replicates; the ANOVA of Table S3e as in fig2d-scv-twitching-no-exposure-effect. The paper gives no test against the ancestor; the comparison is read from Figure 2E, which draws the ancestor as a dashed line beside boxplots of the clones. Readings are (a) the ancestor's value lies below the interquartile range of the mucoid clones and within that of the SCVs, (b) it lies below the median of the mucoid clones and within the range of the SCVs. Reproduced when the colony type effect has p < 0.05 with mucoid higher and the comparison holds under both readings; when the readings differ, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Prior temperature or phage exposure had no significant effect on biofilm formation.
claims.source: Results, Phage resistance and loss of mucoidy leads to reduced R. solanacearum virulence, paragraph 1; Supplementary Table S3e
claims.quote: Prior temperature or phage exposure had no significant effects on biofilm formation (all p > .05, Supplementary Table S3e)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the ANOVA of Table S3e. Reproduced when the temperature, phage and temperature by phage terms all have p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any has p < 0.05. Effect sizes are reported.

claims.statement: Prior exposure to phage reduced virulence in tomato, irrespective of the temperature at which the bacteria evolved; the main effect of temperature was not significant.
claims.source: Results, Phage resistance and loss of mucoidy leads to reduced R. solanacearum virulence, paragraph 1; Figure 2F; Supplementary Table S3f
claims.quote: We found that prior exposure to the phage resulted in reduced virulence, irrespective of the temperature environment in which the bacteria had evolved (phage: F1,21 = 20.310, p < .001, Supplementary Table S3f, Figure 2F; the main effect of temperature was nonsignificant)
claims.criterion: Disease incidence is the share of wilted plants per block at the end of the experiment, each clone the mean of its three blocks (Methods; Table S3f is on the proportion scale). The ANOVA terms are those of fig2d-scv-twitching-no-exposure-effect, sums of squares read both ways. Reproduced when the phage effect has p < 0.05 with lower incidence in +P clones and the temperature effect has p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: All SCVs showed complete loss of virulence regardless of prior phage exposure.
claims.source: Results, Phage resistance and loss of mucoidy leads to reduced R. solanacearum virulence, paragraph 1; Figure 2F; Supplementary Table S3f
claims.quote: Moreover, all SCVs showed complete loss of virulence regardless of if they had previously been exposed to phage (colony type: F1,21 = 33.413, p < .001
claims.criterion: Reproduced when every SCV clone has a disease incidence of 0 in every block and the colony type effect of the ANOVA of fig2f-phage-exposure-reduces-virulence has p < 0.05 with SCVs lower. Partially reproduced when the effect holds but some SCV clones wilt plants.

claims.statement: The phage-resistant mucoid clones from the 25 degrees C phage treatment lost their virulence.
claims.source: Results, Phage resistance and loss of mucoidy leads to reduced R. solanacearum virulence, paragraph 1; Figure 2F; Supplementary Table S3f
claims.quote: Interestingly, the phage-resistant mucoid colonies isolated from 25 °C-phage treatment lost their virulence (colony type × phage: F1,21 = 9.992, p < .01
claims.criterion: The ANOVA of fig2f-phage-exposure-reduces-virulence. Reproduced when the colony type by phage interaction has p < 0.05 and the mean disease incidence of the four 25 degrees C +P mucoid clones is below that of every -P mucoid group and of the ancestor. The Discussion says all mutants showed complete loss of virulence; whether each of the four clones has a disease incidence of 0 is reported alongside.

claims.statement: Sequenced clones carried on average 8.5 nonsynonymous mutations, and the number did not depend on colony morphology.
claims.source: Results, Genetic changes associated with SCVs and phage resistance, paragraph 1; Supplementary Table S4
claims.quote: Sequenced clones had an average of 8.5 nonsynonymous mutations each... The average number of detected mutations was not affected by the colony morphology.
claims.criterion: Variants called with Snippy 4.6.0 against the RS-N reference (GenBank CP099579 to CP099581) after FastQC and cutadapt, annotated with PROKKA 1.14.5 (Methods). Counted per clone are variants that change a protein, which the Results say include small deletions, small insertions and SNPs. The paper names no test for the morphology comparison; the Methods' one-way ANOVA is used, mucoid against SCV counts at p < .05. Reproduced when the mean is within tolerance and the ANOVA gives p >= 0.05.

claims.statement: SCVs carried mutations in the quorum-sensing histidine kinase gene phcS (13 of 16 SCV clones), while no mucoid clone did.
claims.source: Results, Genetic changes associated with SCVs and phage resistance, paragraph 2; Table 1
claims.quote: Interestingly, SCVs were also associated with mutations in phcS quorum sensor histidine kinase gene (Table 1 and Figure 3)
claims.criterion: Variant calls as in sequencing-mutation-count. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Two of the four mucoid phage-resistant clones from 25 degrees C with phage had mutations in pilD, which no other clone carried.
claims.source: Results, Genetic changes associated with SCVs and phage resistance, paragraph 2; Table 1
claims.quote: Interestingly, two of four mucoid phage-resistant clones that had evolved at 25 °C temperature treatment in the presence of phage had mutations in pilD gene (Table 1 and Figure 3)
claims.criterion: Variant calls as in sequencing-mutation-count. Counts of four clones allow no tolerance. Reproduced when two of the four carry a pilD mutation and no other clone does.

claims.statement: Three of four SCVs from 35 degrees C with phage had mutations in the type II secretion genes gspE or gspF.
claims.source: Results, Genetic changes associated with SCVs and phage resistance, paragraph 3; Table 1
claims.quote: Finally, three of four sequenced small colony types that had evolved at 35 °C in the presence of phage had mutations in T2SS genes gspF and gspE (Table 1 and Figure 3)
claims.criterion: Variant calls as in sequencing-mutation-count. Reproduced when three of the four carry a gspE or gspF mutation (Table 1, gspE 2 of 4, gspF 1 of 4) and no clone of another treatment does.

claims.statement: The pilM and pilB mutants were fully resistant to phage NNP42, unlike their wild types.
claims.source: Results, Genetic changes associated with SCVs and phage resistance, paragraph 2; Supplementary Table S6
claims.quote: we used previously constructed pilM and pilB mutant strains for phage infections and found that both mutants were fully resistant to phage NNP42 relative to the wildtype strains (Supplementary Table S6)
claims.criterion: The resistance assay of the Methods (24 h, MOI 0.1, three technical replicates), means as in Table S6. Reproduced when all eight values are within tolerance. If the data hold only resistance ratios, the ratios from Table S6 (pilB 0.92, pilM 1.01, OE1-1 0.25, QL-Rs1115 0.32) are compared at 10%.

claims.statement: pilD mutants showed reduced phage adsorption, while the phcS and the T2SS (gspE, gspF) mutants showed no reduction.
claims.source: Results, Genetic changes associated with SCVs and phage resistance, paragraphs 2 and 3; Supplementary Figure S3
claims.quote: However, either of the T2SS mutants or any of the tested phcS mutants showed no reduction in phage adsorption (Supplementary Figure S3), which suggests that these mutations were not associated with phage binding.
claims.criterion: Percentage adsorption is the loss of free phage after 30 min relative to the initial density (Figure S3 legend). Figure S3 marks differences at P < 0.05 with letters; the Methods name one-way ANOVA with Tukey for pairwise comparisons. Reproduced when, in a one-way ANOVA across strains with Tukey comparisons, every pilD mutant adsorbs less than the ancestor at p < 0.05 and no phcS, gspE or gspF mutant adsorbs significantly less than the ancestor. The paper's sentence for pilD is "We also confirmed that pilD mutants observed in our experiment showed reduced phage adsorption".

claims.statement: After 6 h of phage exposure, 1477 R. solanacearum genes were differentially expressed, 707 up and 770 down.
claims.source: Results, Activation of restriction modification and abortive infection phage defense systems..., paragraph 1; Figure 4A
claims.quote: We found that a total 1477 of R. solanacearum genes were differentially expressed after phage exposure (|log2foldchange| > 1, FDR < 0.05, Figure 4A). Of these, around half (707) were upregulated, and another half (770) downregulated in the presence of phage.
claims.criterion: From the Methods, reads trimmed with cutadapt (error rate 0.1, overlap 5, minimum length 15), mapped to the RS-N reference with Hisat, counted with HTSeq, and tested with DESeq2 between five phage and five control samples; differentially expressed means |log2 fold change| > 1 and FDR < 0.05. Tool versions and DESeq2 options are not given; DESeq2 defaults (Wald test, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p as the FDR, no fold-change shrinkage) are the standard choice. Reproduced when all three counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: Five KEGG pathways were enriched in the phage compared to the control treatment, namely propanoate metabolism, RNA degradation, synthesis and degradation of ketone bodies, bacterial secretion system and valine, leucine and isoleucine degradation.
claims.source: Results, Activation of restriction modification and abortive infection phage defense systems..., paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure S5
claims.quote: Based on KEGG pathway enrichment analysis, a total of five metabolic pathways were significantly enriched in phage compared to control treatment (p < .05, Supplementary Figure S5).
claims.criterion: KOBAS KEGG enrichment of the differentially expressed genes of rnaseq-differential-expression-count at p < .05 (Methods; Figure S5). The KOBAS version, the background set and whether p is corrected are not given; readings are uncorrected and corrected p. Reproduced when the five named pathways are enriched at p < 0.05 under both readings; when the readings differ, the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified.

claims.statement: Under phage exposure phcR and phcS were upregulated and pilD and other pilus and fimbrial genes downregulated; seven of the 13 genes mutated under phage selection were differentially expressed.
claims.source: Results, Activation of restriction modification and abortive infection phage defense systems..., paragraph 1; Figure 4B and 4C
claims.quote: For example, phcR and phcS virulence-associated genes that were significantly upregulated, while pilD and other pilus biogenesis and adherence (fimbriae) associated genes were significantly downregulated in the presence of phage (Figure 4B and C). Of 13 mutated genes that were selected for in the presence of phage, seven showed differential gene expression
claims.criterion: The analysis of rnaseq-differential-expression-count, with the thresholds of the Figure 4B legend (FDR < 0.05, |log2FC| > 1). The 13 genes are those of Figure 4B; Table 1 lists 14 named genes mutated in +P clones (RSc1174 among them), so the set is read from the figure and not from the table. Reproduced when phcR and phcS are up, pilD is down, and seven of the 13 meet the thresholds.

claims.statement: Phage exposure upregulated type I restriction-modification genes (MTases, REases) and CBASS genes (SMODS cyclase, Gros effector) and downregulated the Wadjet gene JetC.
claims.source: Results, Activation of restriction modification and abortive infection phage defense systems..., paragraph 1; Figure 4C
claims.quote: Specifically, JetC gene belonging to Wadjet system, was downregulated, while genes linked to MTases and Reases belonging to Restriction-Modification type I system, and SMODS (cyclase) and Gros (effector) genes belonging to CBASS abortive infection system, were upregulated (Figure 4C).
claims.criterion: The analysis of rnaseq-differential-expression-count, with the Figure 4C thresholds (padj < .05, |log2FC| > 2). The paper names the genes by system and not by locus tag, so which loci are the five defense genes is open; the readings are the loci annotated as these system genes in the RS-N annotation. Reproduced when each named gene meets the thresholds in the stated direction.

claims.statement: Phage exposure downregulated motility genes and type II (e.g. gspG, rcpA, tadC) and type III secretion system genes (several hrp and hrc genes).
claims.source: Results, Activation of restriction modification and abortive infection phage defense systems..., paragraph 1; Figure 4C
claims.quote: We also found that phage exposure led to downregulation of several virulence genes associated with motility and type II and III secretions systems (Figure 4C).
claims.criterion: The analysis of rnaseq-differential-expression-count, with the Figure 4C thresholds (padj < .05, |log2FC| > 2). Reproduced when gspG, rcpA and tadC and at least two hrp or hrc genes meet the thresholds downward and none of these is upregulated. "Several" is read as at least two.

claims.statement: The object sessions yielded 1,189 unique CA1 principal cells from 9 rats, the control sessions 219 CA1 principal cells from 3 rats, and up to 620 CA1 cells were recorded simultaneously.
claims.source: Figure 2D legend; Introduction, paragraph 3; Results, Decoding the presence of an object, paragraph 1
claims.quote: n = 1,189 principal cells recorded from 9 rats) and the corresponding pair of control trials (as in Figure 2B; brown lines; n = 219 principal cells recorded from 3 rats)
claims.criterion: Cells are counted after the paper's inclusion rules (Methods, Spike sorting and cell-inclusion criteria, and Histology), CA1 only. Unique cells under both readings of the opening comment. Reproduced when the three counts are within tolerance.

claims.statement: 19.9% of CA1 cells (237 of 1,189) were object-tuned by the template matching procedure, significantly more than the 5.03% (11 of 219) found by the same procedure in control trials without objects.
claims.source: Results, Object cells and object-vector cells in the hippocampus, paragraph 3; Figure 1C
claims.quote: Using the template matching procedure, 19.9% of CA1 cells were classified as object-tuned (237/1,189 cells) ... This fraction was significantly higher than a chance level determined by running the same template matching procedure on control trials without objects (11/219 cells, 5.03%
claims.criterion: Template matching as in the opening comment, under each template-width reading, on the O and OM trials of every CA1 cell. Chance level as in the Methods (Template matching, Chance level), on the 219 control cells with the object placed at (75, 75) cm in the trial standing for O and at (35, 120) cm in the trial standing for OM. The paper does not say which control trials stand for O and OM; readings (a) CON2 and CON3, the trials in the same place in the session; (b) CON1 and CON2. Rate maps are smoothed as the opening comment's "Smoothing and unvisited bins" says (rate per bin, unvisited bins 0, then smoothed; calculateRateMap.m and the Methods, Firing rate maps). Reproduced when, under one reading, both fractions are within tolerance and a binomial test of the object-tuned count against the chance fraction gives p < 0.05 (two-sided, as all the paper's tests are; Methods, Statistical tests).

claims.statement: Firing fields of object-tuned cells lay at a wide range of distances from the object (4.8 to 80.7 cm, mean 37.7 cm, SD 16.0 cm) and covered all directions around it.
claims.source: Results, Object cells and object-vector cells in the hippocampus, paragraph 3; Figure 1D
claims.quote: The firing fields of the object-tuned cells covered a wide range of distances from the object (range: 4.8–80.7 cm; mean ± SD: 37.7 ± 16.0 cm) and the entire azimuthal range
claims.criterion: The tolerance on the mean is 10% of it, as the SD of 16.0 cm is the spread over cells, not an uncertainty of the mean. Fields detected as in the opening comment. The paper does not say which point of a field gives its distance, in which trial, or which field of a cell with several. Readings (a) the centroid of the field (the point Supplementary Figure 5G plots) in the O trial, nearest field; (b) as (a) averaged over the O and OM trials; (c) the field's peak bin in the O trial. The 1 Hz rule of field detection is not given further (Methods, Firing rate maps); each point reading is run with the field readings (a) peak at least 1 Hz and (b) every bin at least max(3 x MAD, 1 Hz). Reproduced when, under one reading, the mean is within tolerance, the range lies within 4.8 to 80.7 cm widened by 10% of each bound, and every 45 degree sector around the object holds at least one field.

claims.statement: About 4.1% of all recorded CA1 cells (49 of 1,189) were object cells, object-tuned with fields under 15 cm from the object, and 13.3% (158) were object-vector cells, with fields 15 cm or more away; 30 object-tuned cells had no detectable field.
claims.source: Results, Object cells and object-vector cells in the hippocampus, paragraph 4; Figure 1E; Methods, Template matching procedure
claims.quote: we estimated that 4.1% of all recorded cells were object cells (49/1,189 cells, object-tuned cells with firing fields <15 cm from the object ... and 13.3% were object-vector cells (158/1,189 cells
claims.criterion: Field distance under the readings of fig1d-field-distances. Reproduced when, under one reading, the three values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The nearer an object-tuned cell's firing field is to the object, the larger the range of orientations around the object that its fields cover.
claims.source: Figure 1F legend
claims.quote: The nearer the cell’s firing field is to the object, the larger is the orientation coverage.
claims.criterion: Orientation coverage is the fraction of 0 to 360 degrees around the object covered by the cell's firing fields (Supplementary Figure 3C legend), taken as the angular span, seen from the object centre, of the field bins; distance as in fig1d-field-distances. The paper reports no test; its stated test for correlations is Pearson's (Methods, Statistical tests). Reproduced when, under one distance reading, the Pearson correlation of coverage with distance over object-tuned cells is negative with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The object-tuning score did not change with the number of days the animal had been exposed to the object (r = -0.080, p = 0.574, 62 cells).
claims.source: Results, Object cells and object-vector cells in the hippocampus, paragraph 4; Figure 1G
claims.quote: We observed no significant effect of day of exposure to the object on the object-tuning score (Figure 1G)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a Pearson correlation at alpha 0.05 of the object-tuning score (opening comment) against the number of days the rat had been exposed to the object, over the cells recorded on more than one day and object-tuned on at least one. The legend says each dot is a cell (n = 62) and does not say which day's score stands for a cell; readings (a) the score on the first day the cell passed as object-tuned; (b) the cell's highest score; (c) every cell-day, in case the dots are cell-days. Reproduced when p >= 0.05; not reproduced when p < 0.05. The r and the number of cells are given either way. Needs cell identities across days.

claims.statement: Of 35 object-tuned cells recorded on more than one day, few passed the object-tuning criteria on more than one day, yet object-tuned cells passed again on later days more often than other cells (13/35 against 36/370, p = 3.35e-4).
claims.source: Results, Object cells and object-vector cells in the hippocampus, paragraph 5; Figure 1H
claims.quote: Only 13 of these cells (31.4%) had significant object-tuning scores on more than 1 day (Figure 1H). However, object-tuned cells were more stable than expected by chance, with higher probability of passing the classification on later days compared to other cells (13/35 object-tuned cells vs. 36/370 other cells
claims.criterion: The paper gives 13 in the text and 11 in the Figure 1H legend, with 31.4% for both; the readings are 13 (text) and 11 (legend, which matches 31.4%). Day 0 is the first day a cell was recorded (Figure 1H legend). Reproduced when the counts are within tolerance, the number of object-tuned cells passing on more than one day is within 10% of 13 or of 11, and a two-sided binomial test (Methods, Statistical tests) of that count among the 35 against the fraction of other cells passing on a later day gives p < 0.05. The y axis of Figure 1H runs to 62 cells while its legend says 35; the count found is reported. Needs cell identities across days.

claims.statement: Within a single trial, object-tuned cells with larger object-tuning scores were more stable (r = 0.45 between within-trial stability and score).
claims.source: Results, Object cells and object-vector cells in the hippocampus, paragraph 5; Supplementary Figure 2E
claims.quote: cells with larger object-tuning scores tended to be more stable than cells with lower scores (Figure S2E) (Pearson correlation between within-trial stability and object-tuning score, r = 0.45
claims.criterion: Within-trial stability is the Pearson correlation of rate maps from the first and second halves of the O trial (Supplementary Figure 2E legend), rate maps as in the opening comment. Reproduced when r is within tolerance and p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The percentage of object-tuned cells did not depend on the proximodistal location of the recording site (r = 0.42, p = 0.22).
claims.source: Results, Object cells and object-vector cells in the hippocampus, paragraph 3; Supplementary Figure 2C
claims.quote: There was no significant linear correlation between the proximodistal site and the percentage of object related cells (r = 0.42, p = 0.2216
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Per implant (rat, with the two probes of rat 27207 apart), the percentage of object-tuned cells against the proximodistal order of the implant site; Pearson correlation. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; r is given either way. Needs the implant sites, which the paper shows in Supplementary Figure 1.
