claims.statement: Object-related activity was present also in CA3, where 23% of cells (72 of 313) were object-tuned.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 3A
claims.quote: In CA3, 23% of the cells were object tuned (72/313 cells; 7 object cells and 58 object vector cells)
claims.criterion: Template matching as for CA1 (opening comment), on the CA3 cells. Reproduced when, under one template-width reading, the fraction is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Introducing the object changed spatial firing more than the passage of time did, with lower NO-O rate-map correlations than CON1-CON2 correlations in control sessions.
claims.source: Results, The majority of hippocampal cells change spatial firing patterns, paragraph 1; Figure 2D, top left
claims.quote: introducing the object led to larger changes in spatial firing patterns (i.e., smaller Pearson correlations of rate maps) than in pairs of control trials with no object
claims.criterion: Spatial correlation as in the opening comment. Reproduced when the NO-O correlations are lower than the CON1-CON2 correlations (lower median) with a two-sided rank-sum p < 0.05.

claims.statement: The overall rate change between NO and O, measured by rate overlap, did not differ from that between control trials.
claims.source: Results, The majority of hippocampal cells change spatial firing patterns, paragraph 1; Figure 2D, top right
claims.quote: the overall rate change, estimated as the mean firing rate in the less active trial divided by mean firing rate in the more active trial (rate overlap), was not different between trial pairs with objects (NO-O) and control trials (CON1-CON2)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test of NO-O against CON1-CON2 rate overlaps at alpha 0.05. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the difference in medians is given either way, under both rate-overlap readings of the opening comment.

claims.statement: About two thirds of CA1 cells (67.5%, 803 of 1,189) changed their spatial firing, their rate, or both between NO and O.
claims.source: Results, The majority of hippocampal cells change spatial firing patterns, paragraph 1
claims.quote: we estimated that 67.5% of the cells (n = 803/1,189 cells) expressed either spatial change, rate change, or both between NO and O
claims.criterion: The Methods' classification (Spatial correlation and rate overlap). Within-trial distributions from the NO trial, split 500 times at random into two groups of 1 s bins; between- trial distributions from a random half of each trial's 1 s bins, 500 times. A cell changes on a measure when the mean between-trial value is below the 1st percentile of the within-trial distribution and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the two distributions gives p < 0.05 (alpha from Methods, Statistical tests; the 500 values are paired by repetition, as the signed-rank test needs pairs and the paper does not say how they are paired). A cell counts when it changes on spatial correlation, rate overlap or both. Reproduced when the fraction is within tolerance.

claims.statement: Moving the object also changed spatial firing and rate more than in control trials, and 69.7% of cells (829 of 1,189) changed between O and OM.
claims.source: Results, The majority of hippocampal cells change spatial firing patterns, paragraph 1; Figure 2D, second row
claims.quote: Considerable change was also observed between the O and OM trials ... In these trials, 69.7% of the cells changed their spatial firing pattern, firing rate, or both when the object was moved (n = 829/1,189 cells)
claims.criterion: As fig2d-spatial-change-no-o and fig2-fraction-changed-no-o, for O-OM against CON2-CON3. Reproduced when both rank-sum tests give p < 0.05 with lower O-OM medians, and the fraction is within tolerance; partially reproduced when one of the three holds.

claims.statement: Removing the object changed spatial firing more than in control trials (OM-NO' against CON3-CON4), without a significant difference in rate overlap, and many cells kept fields from the preceding trial.
claims.source: Results, The majority of hippocampal cells change spatial firing patterns, paragraph 1; Figure 2D, third row
claims.quote: Major changes were evoked also when we removed the object ... Upon removal of the object, many cells retained firing fields from the preceding trial
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the spatial correlations are lower for OM-NO' with rank-sum p < 0.05, and the rate-overlap rank-sum test gives p >= 0.05 (the absence part, judged on the paper's test). Sessions without a NO' trial are left out.

claims.statement: Spatial firing in NO' differed from that in NO more than CON4 differed from CON1.
claims.source: Results, The majority of hippocampal cells change spatial firing patterns, paragraph 1; Figure 2D, fourth row
claims.quote: major changes in spatial firing were also observed between NO and NO0 (Figure 2D, fourth row
claims.criterion: Reproduced when NO-NO' spatial correlations are lower than CON1-CON4 correlations with rank-sum p < 0.05. The paper prints the same z and p as for OM-NO'; that is noted, not tested.

claims.statement: In CA3 too, spatial correlations between trials differed between object and control sessions for every trial pair, while rate overlaps did not.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 3F
claims.quote: As for CA1, we found that spatial correlation values between pairs of trials was always significantly different between Object sessions and control sessions, whereas rate overlap was not significantly different between the two types of sessions.
claims.criterion: 313 CA3 cells against the 59 CA3 control cells, measures as for CA1. Reproduced when all four spatial-correlation tests give p < 0.05 and all four rate-overlap tests give p >= 0.05 (the absence part judged on the paper's test); partially reproduced when the spatial part holds and one or more rate-overlap tests is significant.

claims.statement: 18.3% of CA1 cells (218 of 1,189) had object-trace fields, firing in NO' where they had fired in OM, well above the 1% chance level.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 4B to 4D legend; Methods, Region-of-interest analysis for object traces
claims.quote: We found that 18.3% of CA1 cells had trace responses ... (n = 218/1189 cells in total, significantly above chance level of 1%
claims.criterion: The Methods' procedure. Cells changing between NO and NO' as in fig2-fraction-changed-no-o; fields in NO' (opening comment); a circular ROI per field moved to the same place in OM; rate overlap between the NO' ROI and the OM ROI against 1,000 shuffles placing the ROI at random in OM with wrap-around; a trace field above the 99th percentile. The ROI's size is open, as the Methods refer to a section that is not in the paper. Readings (a) a circle of the field's area centred on its centroid; (b) the smallest circle centred on the centroid containing the field. A cell counts when any of its fields passes (the Supplementary Figure 4A legend tests each field). Reproduced when, under one reading, both values are within tolerance and a two-sided binomial test (Methods, Statistical tests) against 1% gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Removing object traces from the OM trial did not significantly change the number of object-tuned cells (256 of 1,189 after removal, against the expected 19.9%).
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 2D
claims.quote: The number object tuned cells was not significantly different after removing traces (using expected percentage 19.9% from Fig. 1c and observed count of 256/1189
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a two-sided binomial test of the count of object-tuned cells after removal against 19.9% at alpha 0.05. The paper does not say how traces were removed; readings (a) leave the OM rate-map bins inside the trace ROIs of figs4-object-traces out of the template correlations; (b) set the rate in those bins to zero. Reproduced when p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05; the count is given either way.

claims.statement: The object-vector score method of earlier studies classified 40 cells (3.4%) that the template matching did not, mostly false positives on inspection.
claims.source: Methods, Object-vector score and object-vector cell criteria, last paragraph
claims.quote: 40 out of 1189 cells (3.4%) were classified by this method but not by the template matching procedure.
claims.criterion: The Methods' four criteria, after excluding cells whose fields would fall outside the arena in OM. The vector map's distance and direction bins and its smoothing are not given; the paper directs to the method of its references 11 and 12 (Hoydal et al. 2019; Andersson et al. 2021), and those papers' bins and smoothing are used. Reference 12 (Andersson et al. 2021, Methods, OV score) gives them, read for the answer of 2026-10-21; "distance bins of 2 cm and orientation bins of 10°", rate as spikes over time per bin, "circularly smoothed with a 2D Gaussian kernel with s.d. of 1.5 bins (3 cm, 15°)", 0° East. Neither paper gives the range of distances; readings (r-a) 0 to the largest distance sampled in either trial, the correlation over bins with a value in both maps; (r-b) 0 to the largest distance sampled in both trials. Reproduced when, under one range reading, the count is within tolerance. The manual inspection is not repeated.

claims.statement: A Bayesian decoder using 1 s population spike counts told the NO trial from the O trial above chance (50%) in every session.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 1; Figure 3B
claims.quote: The decoding accuracy was above chance (50%) in all experimental sessions (Figure 3B)
claims.criterion: The whole-arena decoder (opening comment), on each decoding session. The paper reports no test per session; it gives chance as 50%, and its chance level comes from the label-shuffling procedure (Methods, Shuffling trial labels; 50 shuffles per session, Supplementary Figure 5E). Reproduced when, under both speed readings, every session's accuracy exceeds 0.5 and the mean accuracy of that session's 50 label shuffles.

claims.statement: Decoding accuracy grew roughly logarithmically with the testing bin size, rising quickly up to 1 s and saturating beyond.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 1; Figure 3C; Methods, Performance of decoder
claims.quote: The decoder’s performance increased approximately logarithmically with the bin size of the testing data vector (Figure 3C)
claims.criterion: The whole-arena decoder with testing bins of 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 5000 and 10000 ms (Methods). The paper gives no test. Reproduced when the median accuracy over sessions rises from 10 to 1000 ms at each step, and its gain from 1000 to 10000 ms is smaller than its gain from 100 to 1000 ms.

claims.statement: Decoding accuracy increased with the number of cells used.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 1; Figure 3D; Methods, Effect of number of cells
claims.quote: the success of decoding increased with the number of cells included (Figure 3D)
claims.criterion: Random subsets of k cells, 100 per k, whole-arena decoder (Methods). The data are open; readings (a) the Methods', the 620-cell Neuropixels session, k = 1, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500; (b) the legend's, the four datasets pooled (two tetrode, two Neuropixels), k up to each dataset's size. The paper gives no test; its stated test for correlations is Pearson's (Methods, Statistical tests). Reproduced when, under one reading, mean accuracy is higher at the largest k than at k = 1 and the Pearson correlation of accuracy with k over all subsets is positive with p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Decoding accuracy fell gradually with the animal's distance from the object, over 5 equal-sample distance bins, with significant steps between bins 1 and 2, 2 and 3, and 4 and 5.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 2; Figure 4B
claims.quote: we found that decoding performance decreased gradually with increasing distance from the object (Figure 4B)
claims.criterion: The distance decoder (opening comment), on the decoding sessions. Reproduced when, under every reading of speed and sessions, the Kruskal-Wallis test across the 5 bins gives p < 0.05 with median accuracy falling from bin 1 to bin 5, and signed-rank tests of bins 1 vs 2, 2 vs 3 and 4 vs 5 each give p < 0.05 with the nearer bin higher. Partially reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis part holds and one or two of the pairs do not. The population mean of bin 1 minus bin 5 (0.19 in the paper, Results, Distance-specific reorganization, paragraph 2) is reported.

claims.statement: Every session showed decoding accuracy decreasing with distance from the object.
claims.source: Figure 4C legend
claims.quote: Note that all experimental sessions have decreasing curves.
claims.criterion: The paper's two measures of the decrease (Methods, Measuring strength of distance-specific reorganization) give the readings (a) the least-squares slope of accuracy on distance-bin index is negative; (b) accuracy in bin 1 minus bin 5 is positive. Reproduced when, under one reading, every session meets it; partially reproduced when more than half do; not reproduced otherwise.

claims.statement: Decoding accuracy did not differ between 5 angular sectors around the object, so the distance effect is not specific to compass directions.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 3; Figure 4E and 4F
claims.quote: The decoding accuracy was the same in different angular bins (Figures 4E and 4F)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a Kruskal-Wallis test across the 5 angular bins at alpha 0.05. Distance decoder with 72 degree sectors of allocentric angle from the object in place of distance rings (Figure 4D legend, Methods). The sectors' starting angle is not given; readings (a) sectors starting at 0 degrees (the positive x axis, the code's angle origin in templateMatchingScore.m); (b) sectors starting at 36 degrees. Reproduced when p >= 0.05 under the readings, not reproduced when p < 0.05; H is given either way.

claims.statement: Correlations between NO and O population vectors were lowest near the object and rose stepwise with distance before saturating, with significant steps between bins 1 and 2, 2 and 3, and 3 and 4.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 5; Figure 4G and 4H
claims.quote: This showed a stepwise linear increase in correlation values as a function of distance from object, with saturation at larger distances (Figure 4H)
claims.criterion: Methods, Population vector correlation. Per session, rate maps of the whole NO and O trials (3 cm bins, 50 x 50, as the Methods give m = n = 50), the Pearson correlation across cells at each spatial bin, and the mean correlation in each of 5 distance bins. The bins are open; readings (a) the Methods' fixed 20 cm rings (0 to 100 cm); (b) 5 bins with equal numbers of spatial bins, which the reported 489 values per bin implies. The Methods do not say whether these maps are speed-filtered or blanked (answered 2026-10-21); readings (pv-a) speed-filtered, as the Methods' general rule for rate maps; (pv-b) not filtered, as the decoder code; each with (bl-a) unvisited bins blanked and left out of that bin's correlation or (bl-b) not blanked, as the decoder's 3 cm maps. Reproduced when, under one reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p < 0.05 with correlation rising from bin 1 to bin 5 and the three signed-rank tests give p < 0.05 with the farther bin higher.

claims.statement: The NO trial could also be decoded from the NO' trial, above chance, consistent with trace fields.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure 5A
claims.quote: we were also able to decode the NO trial from the NO0 trial using population activity (Figure S5A)
claims.criterion: As fig3b-decode-presence, with NO' in place of O, on sessions with a NO' trial. Reproduced when the accuracy exceeds 0.5 and the mean of the session's label shuffles in every session; partially reproduced when in more than half.

claims.statement: With fixed distance bins (0-20 to 80-100 cm) decoding accuracy still fell with distance.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 5B; Methods, Fixed distance bins
claims.quote: Decoding accuracy as a function of distance from object when using fixed distance bins ... Decoding accuracy decreases as a function of distance from object
claims.criterion: The distance decoder with bin edges 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 cm (Methods). Samples beyond 100 cm are left out, as the Methods' bins stop there. Reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p < 0.05 with median accuracy highest in bin 1 and lowest in bin 4 or 5.

claims.statement: Decoding the first from the second half of the NO trial showed no decrease of accuracy with distance.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 4; Supplementary Figure 5C
claims.quote: we observed no decrease in decoding accuracy across the same distance bins when attempting to decode the first half of the NO trial from the second half of the NO trial (Figure S5C)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. The NO trial is split at its midpoint and each half split again into training and testing quarters (Methods, Decoding 1st half vs. 2nd half); distances from the O trial's object position (the Methods give no other). Reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis test across the 5 bins gives p >= 0.05, not reproduced when p < 0.05.

claims.statement: In control sessions without an object (CON1 against CON2), decoding accuracy did not fall with distance.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 4; Supplementary Figure 5D
claims.quote: attempting to perform the decoding in control experiments without the object (Control trial 1 vs. Control trial 2). We observed no decrease in accuracy as a function of distance
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test. Distance decoder on CON1 against CON2. The object position used for distances in control sessions is not given for this analysis; readings (a) the arena centre (75, 75) cm, the pseudo-object position the Methods use for the control chance level; (b) (35, 120) cm, the other one. The control sessions used are not stated; those with at least 25 simultaneously recorded cells are used (the rule for population analyses). Reproduced when p >= 0.05 under the readings, not reproduced when p < 0.05.

claims.statement: With shuffled trial labels the decoder performed at 50% in every distance bin.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 4; Supplementary Figure 5E
claims.quote: On the shuffled data, the decoder performed with a mean accuracy of 50% in all distance bins (Figure S5E)
claims.criterion: Labels of the testing samples shuffled 50 times per session (Methods, Shuffling trial labels); session values are the means over shuffles. Tolerances are the SDs the legend gives. Reproduced when every bin's mean is within 0.49 to 0.51 and no one-sample t test against 0.5 gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Partitioning training and testing samples at random gave the same decline of accuracy with distance.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 4; Supplementary Figure 5F
claims.quote: The results from this decoder showed the same decline in decoding accuracy as a function of distance from the object (Figure S5F)
claims.criterion: The distance decoder with training and testing timepoints drawn by a random permutation (Methods, Random partitioning). The timepoints are the 1 s spike-count vectors (answered 2026-10-21); the random partitioning is "analogous to the shuffling procedure above", where the permuted timepoints are "N×1 spike count vectors" (Methods, Shuffling trial labels). Training rate maps are built from the position and spike samples within the training windows. Reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p < 0.05 with accuracy highest in bin 1 and lowest in bin 5.

claims.statement: Firing fields were spread across the arena, not concentrated at the object, and firing rates were similar between NO and O and highest at middle distances (bin 3).
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 4; Supplementary Figure 5G to 5I
claims.quote: across all cells, firing fields were widely distributed across the environment and not concentrated at the object location (Figures S5G and S5H), whereas firing rates were similar between trials, being largest at middle distances from the object (peaking in distance bin 3; Figure S5I)
claims.criterion: The paper gives no test. Field centroids in NO and O relative to the object (Supplementary Figure 5G); per session, the mean firing rate of each cell in each of the 5 equal-sample distance bins of the whole trial, averaged over cells, then over sessions. Reproduced when (i) the proportion of fields per unit area within 20 cm of the object is not higher in O than in NO by a two-sided rank-sum test over sessions at p < 0.05 (the paper's test for unpaired data); (ii) the mean rate peaks in bin 2, 3 or 4 in both trials, and in bin 3 in at least one; (iii) no bin shows a NO against O difference by signed-rank test at p < 0.05. Partially reproduced when two of the three hold.

claims.statement: Decoders of trial type based on speed, head direction or occupancy performed only slightly above 50% and their accuracy did not depend on distance from the object.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral analyses, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure 6A, 6C and 6E
claims.quote: Decoders for speed, head direction, and occupancy performed only slightly above 50% correct, with accuracies independent of object distance (Figures S6A, S6C, and S6E)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests. Behavioural decoders as in the Methods (Behavioral analyses I), with gamma likelihoods for speed (Lowess-smoothed, 25 Hz, all speeds), two-Gaussian mixtures for head direction, and occupancy ratios, 50 x 50 spatial bins, same training and testing split and distance bins. The Lowess span is not given; it cannot change the absence much, and a span of 0.5 s is used as a standard choice. Reproduced when all three Kruskal-Wallis tests give p >= 0.05; not reproduced when any test gives p < 0.05. The paper gives no number for "slightly above 50%", so the median accuracy of each decoder is reported, not judged.

claims.statement: After matching the distributions of speed, head direction or occupancy between NO and O within each distance bin, decoding accuracy on neural data still fell with distance.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral analyses, paragraph 2; Supplementary Figure 6H to 6J
claims.quote: We still observed a graded decrease in decoding accuracy for the neural activity decoder after matching distributions for speed (Figure S6H), head direction (Figure S6I) and occupancy (Figure S6J)
claims.criterion: Matching as in the Methods (Behavioral analyses II), speed bins of 5 cm/s to 100 cm/s, head direction bins of pi/10, occupancy bins of 30 cm, random removal of the excess samples from the trial with more. The samples matched are the 1 s testing samples (the decoder's samples), with the behaviour averaged over the second; the Methods do not say, so a second reading matches 25 Hz position samples and keeps the 1 s bins whose samples all survive. Reproduced when, under one reading, each of the three Kruskal-Wallis tests gives p < 0.05 with bin 1 highest.

claims.statement: Replacing the occupancy prior by a uniform prior did not change the decline of decoding accuracy with distance.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral analyses, paragraph 2; Supplementary Figure 6K
claims.quote: removal of this prior had no effect on our results (Figure S6K)
claims.criterion: Distance decoder with a uniform prior over the spatial bins of each distance bin (Methods, Removing effects of prior). Reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p < 0.05 with bin 1 highest.

claims.statement: Using only spatial bins visited for at least 100, 500, 1000 or 2000 ms in both trials, the decline of accuracy with distance remained.
claims.source: Results, Behavioral analyses, paragraph 3; Supplementary Figure 6L
claims.quote: Regardless of the threshold value, the result was the same as before, with accuracy declining along with object distance (Figure S6L
claims.criterion: Distance decoder with rate-map bins of 10 cm (the Methods' "10 cm2" read as 10 cm sides, as 3 cm2 is used for the 3 cm bins), spatial bins below the threshold in either trial left out of both. The Methods do not say whether the sampling time is that of the whole trial or of the training half, nor whether testing samples in a left-out bin are kept (answered 2026-10-21; the code holds no sampling analysis); the four combinations are readings. Reproduced when, under one reading, all four Kruskal-Wallis tests give p < 0.05 with bin 1 highest.

claims.statement: The effect of distance on decoding accuracy held when the bin nearest the object was left out.
claims.source: Supplementary Figure 6L legend, last sentence; Supplementary Table 1, first row
claims.quote: all the main statistics hold even after excluding distance bin 1
claims.criterion: The distance decoder results of fig4b-distance-decline, bins 2 to 5 only. The table's p-value has lost its exponent in the text; it was read from PDF page 49. Reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p < 0.05 with bin 2 highest; H is compared with the expected value.

claims.statement: Population words (patterns of spiking and silence in 10 ms bins) carried much more information about the trial than population spike counts.
claims.source: Results, Objects are encoded by distinct patterns of joint activity, paragraph 1; Figure 5B
claims.quote: Words were much more informative than counts (Figure 5B)
claims.criterion: Methods, Definition of words and counts, and Mutual information. Spike counts in 10 ms bins; tetrode sessions with all cells, Neuropixels sessions subsampled to 30 cells; the all-zero word and zero count left out; mutual information with trial, from frequency distributions, minus the mean over 50 label shuffles. Distance bins as in Figure 4B (Figure 5B legend), each 10 ms bin taking the distance of the nearest position sample, 5 equal-sample bins per trial. Open readings (a) one random subset of 30 Neuropixels cells; (b) the mean over 20 subsets (the number the Methods use for subsampling the decoder). Which samples are compared is open; readings (c) per distance bin, 16 against 16 sessions; (d) all bins pooled. Reproduced when, under one combination, every rank-sum test gives p < 0.05 with words higher.

claims.statement: The information from words decreased with distance from the object, as decoding did.
claims.source: Results, Objects are encoded by distinct patterns of joint activity, paragraph 1; Figures 5B and 5C
claims.quote: Importantly, the amount of information gained from words decreased as a function of distance from the object (Figures 5B and 5C)
claims.criterion: Mutual information of words as in fig5b-words-more-informative, under its subset readings. Reproduced when, under one reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test across the 5 bins gives p < 0.05 with bin 1 highest.

claims.statement: The information from counts did not depend on distance and was not significantly above zero.
claims.source: Results, Objects are encoded by distinct patterns of joint activity, paragraph 1; Figure 5B
claims.quote: In contrast, the amount of information from counts did not depend on object distance ... and was not significantly above zero
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests. Bias-subtracted mutual information of counts as in fig5b-words-more-informative. Reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p >= 0.05 and no per-bin two-sided one-sample t test against zero gives p < 0.05; not reproduced otherwise. Values given either way.

claims.statement: The KL divergence between the word distributions of NO and O fell with distance from the object, from bin 1 to bin 5, while shuffled data showed no decrease.
claims.source: Results, Objects are encoded by distinct patterns of joint activity, paragraph 3; Figure 5E
claims.quote: divergence between the NO and O distributions became smaller with increasing object distance (Figure 5E, blue curve) ... No decrease in the KL divergence was present in shuffled data
claims.criterion: Methods, Kullback-Leibler divergence, words and distance bins as in fig5b-words-more-informative, D(NO||O) over all words, probabilities as counts over all timepoints. Words seen in NO and never in O make the sum infinite, and the paper does not say how that was handled; the one finite reading its text allows is to sum over words seen in both trials, recorded as a deviation. Shuffled data assign trial labels to words at random (Figure 5E legend). Reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis test and the bin 1 against bin 5 signed-rank test give p < 0.05 with bin 1 higher, and the shuffled divergences show no Kruskal-Wallis effect at 0.05.

claims.statement: The entropy of words was higher than that of counts (1.65 against 0.84 bits).
claims.source: Results, Objects are encoded by distinct patterns of joint activity, paragraph 4
claims.quote: the entropy was higher for words than counts (entropy of words: 1.65 bits ± 0.06; entropy of counts: 0.84 bits ± 0.02; mean ± SEM)
claims.criterion: Entropy as in the Methods, words and counts as in fig5b-words-more-informative. The SEM is over an unstated unit, so the tolerance is 10%. The unit and whether the all-zero word is in are open; readings (a) per session and trial over the whole trial, all-zero word left out (as in the mutual information); (b) as (a) with it included; (c) per session, trial and distance bin. Reproduced when, under one reading, both means are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The number of distinct words did not differ between trial types or across distance bins.
claims.source: Results, Objects are encoded by distinct patterns of joint activity, paragraph 3; Supplementary Figure 7C and 7D
claims.quote: In contrast to the identity of words, the number of words was independent of trial type and distance from the object (Figures S7C and S7D)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests (from the Supplementary Figure 7 legend, an image on PDF page 46, not in the text). Distinct words per session, trial and distance bin as in fig5b-words-more-informative. The values of the rank-sum test are not given (answered 2026-10-21); the legend says "n = 16 experiments" and Supplementary Figure 7C and 7D plot only values per session and distance bin. Readings (w-a) each session's distinct words over the whole trial, 16 against 16; (w-b) the 80 session and distance bin values of each trial. Reproduced when, under one reading, all three tests give p >= 0.05, not reproduced when any gives p < 0.05.

claims.statement: After downsampling words to as many states as counts, words still carried more information than counts.
claims.source: Results, Objects are encoded by distinct patterns of joint activity, paragraph 4; Supplementary Figure 7E
claims.quote: after downsampling the number of states to be equal for words and counts, words were still much more informative (Figure S7E)
claims.criterion: Methods, Downsampling words. Per session and distance bin, keep the c most frequent words, c the number of distinct counts, and renormalise. Whether the bias subtraction is applied is not said; readings (a) with, (b) without. Reproduced when, under one reading, a signed-rank test over the 80 pairs gives p < 0.05 with words higher.

claims.statement: Single cells decoded with almost flat accuracy across distance; their distance tuning (bin 1 minus bin 5 accuracy) averaged 0.02, 98.7% lay between -0.2 and 0.2, 12.2% (145) had significant positive and 3.8% (45) significant negative tuning.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 2; Figure 6A and 6B
claims.quote: CA1 cells had a slight positive bias in distance tuning (mean: 0.02; for reference, the same mean calculated from populations is 0.19; Figure 4C) and nearly all cells were contained between the bounds ... and 0.2 (98.7% of cells) ... some cells had significant positive distance tuning (12.2%, n = 145/1,189 cells) ... and some cells had significant negative distance tuning (3.8%, n = 45/1,189 cells)
claims.criterion: The distance decoder run with one cell at a time; distance tuning is accuracy in bin 1 minus bin 5 (Equation 1). Significance from 100 circular shifts of the spike train by 20 s to the trial length less 20 s, above the 99th or below the 1st percentile (Methods). The tolerance on the within-bounds fraction is 10% and stops at 1. The mean of 0.02 is printed to one significant figure, so the tolerance on it is 0.005 (half the last digit) in place of 10%. Which cells are open; readings (a) all 1,189 unique cells, each in its session; (b) the cells of the decoding sessions (Figure 6A legend). Reproduced when, under one reading, all four values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the mean and within-bounds fraction are and a significant fraction is not.

claims.statement: After removing the cells with significant positive distance tuning, decoding accuracy still fell gradually with distance.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 2; Supplementary Figure 5L
claims.quote: after removing cells with significant positive distance tuning (12.2%), we still observed a gradual drop in decoding accuracy ... obtained with population data as a function of object distance (Figure S5L)
claims.criterion: Distance decoder on the decoding sessions without the cells found in fig6ab-single-cell-distance-tuning. Reproduced when the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p < 0.05 with bin 1 highest.

claims.statement: After removing all object-tuned cells, decoding accuracy still fell gradually with distance.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 5; Supplementary Figure 5M
claims.quote: After removing all object-tuned cells (19.9%) from the data and re-running the decoder, we observed the same gradual fall in decoding accuracy as a function of distance (Figure S5M)
claims.criterion: Distance decoder on the decoding sessions without the object-tuned cells of fig1c-object-tuned-fraction (each template-width reading). Reproduced when, under one reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p < 0.05 with bin 1 highest.

claims.statement: In the 620-cell session, random subsets of every size except a single cell showed decoding accuracy falling with distance.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 3; Figure 6C
claims.quote: All curves showed reduced decoding accuracy as a function of distance, except the curve constructed using only a single cell (Figure 6C)
claims.criterion: Distance decoder on 20 random subsets per size of the 620 cells (Methods, Subsampling for decoder). The sizes are open, as three lists are given; readings (a) Results, 1, 5, 10, 30, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500; (b) legend, 1, 5, 20, 30, 50 to 500; (c) Methods, 1, 5, 10, 30, 100 to 500. The test is open, as the printed W values are not integers; readings (d) signed-rank of bin 1 against bin 5 over the 20 subsets; (e) Kruskal-Wallis across the 5 bins over the 20 subsets. Reproduced when, under one reading of the test, the single-cell curve gives p >= 0.05 and every other size gives p < 0.05 with bin 1 higher.

claims.statement: The difference between bins 1 and 5 grew, and the slope of accuracy over distance became more negative, as more cells were used, both reaching their extremes at 500 cells.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 3; Figure 6D
claims.quote: The difference between bins #1 and #5 grew systematically with the number of cells (Figure 6D; left y axis, blue)
claims.criterion: The 20 subsets per size of fig6c-subsets-decline; per subset, accuracy in bin 1 minus bin 5 and the least-squares slope over bin indices 1 to 5 (Methods, Measuring strength). Reproduced when, under one size reading, both Kruskal-Wallis tests across sizes give p < 0.05 and the largest mean difference and most negative mean slope are at 500 cells, as the Results say.

claims.statement: The growth of distance reorganization with the number of cells held in the tetrode sessions and in the 135-cell Neuropixels session.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 3; Supplementary Figure 8A to 8D
claims.quote: The finding was upheld in data from animals with smaller numbers of cells (135 cells in a Neuropixels recording; 25–39 cells in tetrode recordings)
claims.criterion: As fig6d-reorganization-grows-with-cells, on the tetrode decoding sessions pooled (sizes up to each session's count) and on the 135-cell session. Subset sizes for the tetrode sessions are not given beyond n = max (29 to 35 cells); sizes from reading (a) of fig6c-subsets-decline up to each session's count, then the session's full count, are used. Reproduced when all four Kruskal-Wallis tests give p < 0.05 with the difference rising and the slope falling with size.

claims.statement: Even the 20% of cells with the lowest distance tuning showed distance reorganization, with a bin 1 minus bin 5 difference of 0.121 and a slope of -0.0267.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 4; Figure 6E and 6F
claims.quote: even the 20% of cells with lowest tuning was sufficient to demonstrate the distance modulation, in the form of positive distance tuning as well as a negative slope (Figures 6E and 6F; rightmost point on blue curve: 0.121; on orange curve
claims.criterion: Cells of the 620-cell session sorted by single-cell distance tuning (fig6ab-single-cell-distance-tuning), the lowest 100, 80, 60, 40 and 20% kept, distance decoder run on each. Reproduced when both 20% values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when the difference is positive and the slope negative but outside tolerance.

claims.statement: Single-cell properties barely predicted distance tuning; correlations with object-tuning score (r = 0.12), spatial information (r = -0.13), spatial correlation (r = -0.08) and rate overlap (r = -0.18) were significant but weak.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 5; Figure 7A to 7D
claims.quote: The object-tuning score had a significant positive correlation with distance tuning, but very weakly so (r = 0.12 ... Spatial information had a significant negative correlation, but also this was very weak ... spatial correlation and rate overlap were also negatively but weakly correlated with distance tuning
claims.criterion: Pearson correlations over cells of distance tuning with the object-tuning score (opening comment), spatial information in bits per spike in the O trial (Methods), and NO-O spatial correlation and rate overlap. The mean rate lambda is not defined beyond "the mean firing rate in the trial" (answered 2026-10-21); readings (si-a) the trial's speed-filtered spikes over speed-filtered time; (si-b) the occupancy-weighted mean of the smoothed map, sum of Pi li with Pi the occupancy over the trial's duration. The r values are printed to two digits, so a tolerance of 0.05 is used in place of 10%, being half a unit in the first digit at the scale the claim calls weak. Reproduced when, under one cell reading of fig6ab-single-cell-distance-tuning and one lambda reading, all four r are within 0.05 of the printed values with the same sign and p < 0.05, and each |r| is below 0.3.

claims.statement: Using the slope of accuracy against distance in place of distance tuning gave similar weak correlations with the same four properties.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 5
claims.quote: We obtained similar results when, instead of distance tuning, we used the slope of the regression line fitted to decoding accuracy vs. distance as a measure of reorganization
claims.criterion: As fig7-single-cell-properties with the single-cell least-squares slope. Reproduced when all four r are within 0.05 of the printed values with the same sign. The printed sign for spatial correlation (negative for both measures, while the others flip) is noted.

claims.statement: The arena walls did not act as a pivot as the object did; position decoding error and population vector correlations were comparable near (under 15 cm) and far from the walls.
claims.source: Results, Decoding the presence of an object from neural-population activity, paragraph 5; Supplementary Figure 5J and 5K
claims.quote: The internal walls of the recording environment did not play a similar role as the free-standing object, since position decoding accuracy and population vector correlations were comparable near and far away from the walls (Figures S5J and S5K)
claims.criterion: A claim of absence. The paper reports no test; its test for paired data is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Methods, Statistical tests), applied here over the decoding sessions, near against far, at alpha 0.05. Near is under 15 cm from a wall, far more than 15 cm (Supplementary Figure 5J legend). (J) Position decoding error in the NO trial, the Euclidean distance between the animal's position and the decoded position. The position decoder is not described in the Methods; the reading allowed is the paper's Bayesian decoder (Methods, Bayesian decoding algorithm) with the posterior over the 50 x 50 spatial bins of the NO trial, 1 s samples, the same training and testing halves, and the decoded position the bin of maximum posterior. Open, could change the outcome; reading (b) takes the posterior mean. (K) The population vector correlation (Methods, Population vector correlation) between rate maps of the first and second halves of the NO trial, mean over the near and over the far spatial bins. Reproduced when neither signed-rank test gives p < 0.05 under any reading; not reproduced when one does. Differences are given either way.

claims.statement: In the tetrode sessions and the 135-cell Neuropixels session too, keeping only the cells with the lowest distance tuning weakened but did not at first remove the distance reorganization; the slope reached zero when 60% (tetrode) or 50% (135-cell session) of the least-tuned cells were kept.
claims.source: Results, Distance-specific reorganization of the hippocampal map is widely distributed, paragraph 4; Supplementary Figure 8E to 8H
claims.quote: As before, the finding also held in smaller-sized tetrode and Neuropixels data (Figures S8E–S8H)
claims.criterion: As fig6ef-least-tuned-cells (100, 80, 60, 40 and 20% of cells with the lowest single-cell distance tuning kept), on the tetrode decoding sessions pooled (Supplementary Figure 8E, 14 sessions) and on the 135-cell session. The tolerance is one step of the kept fraction (the paper's grid is in steps of 20%), not 10%. Reproduced when, for both datasets, the 100% curve has a positive bin 1 minus bin 5 difference and a negative slope, both shrink as fewer cells are kept, and the largest kept fraction with a mean slope of zero or above is within tolerance. The Results say the 20% finding "held", while the legends say the slope reached zero at 0.6 and 0.5; the 20% values are reported.

claims.statement: The deposit holds the measurements of the 22 Apollo 64455 glass subsamples that failed the paleointensity selection criteria, named as in Table 2, and replicate measurements for the twelve single crystals of Table 1.
claims.source: Background & Summary, Glass, paragraph 2; Methods, paragraph 2; Table 2; Data Records
claims.quote: Plots for all the data not meeting paleointensity criteria1 (n=22) are provided26 with photomicrographs of specimens that were measured
claims.criterion: Specimens are matched by the names in Table 2 and Table 1 (s11 in Table 2 may be ss11; both are accepted). Holds when each named specimen has measurements with steps, moments, declinations and inclinations as the Data Records describe. Reported either way, which glass specimens have AF steps, compared with the reading of the Table 2 marks given in the opening comment (12 without, 10 with).

claims.statement: Of the Apollo 64455 glass subsamples given thermal paleointensity experiments, 12% passed the selection criteria (3 of 25, 13 run without and 12 with AF pre-treatment).
claims.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 3; Methods, paragraph 2
claims.quote: In the thermal studies1 of Apollo 64455 (Methods), the success rate was 12%
claims.criterion: The three successful specimens are in ref. 1 and its dataset, not in this deposit, so the rate is 3 over (3 plus the failed specimens found here). The split by AF pre-treatment is counted from AF steps in the deposit's failed specimens plus the Methods' count of successful ones (one without, two with AF). Holds when 22 failed specimens are found and 10 of them have AF steps.

claims.statement: For the nine failed glass specimens with a line fit (ss19, ss43, ss22, ss41, ss6, ss9, ss10, ss30, ss34), the number of points, temperature range, MAD, R2 and pTRM check differences are as in Table 2, which lists the criteria each failed.
claims.source: Methods, Paleointensity Selection criteria, paragraph 2; Table 2
claims.quote: Reasons for de-selection are provided in Table 2
claims.criterion: Per specimen, the field-off and field-on steps within the Table 2 temperature range (the range and n fix the points), NRM lost against TRM gained as in the opening comment, R2 of the least-squares line, MAD of a principal component fit to the field-off directions, and the pTRM check percentage at each listed temperature. MAD and pTRM check percentages are computed under each reading named in the opening comment; a value matches when one reading puts it within tolerance. Reproduced when n matches for all nine and at least 80% of the MAD, R2 and pTRM values match; partially reproduced for 50 to 80%. Whether each listed failure follows is reported against the stated thresholds (n of 4 or more, pTRM within 15%, R2 about 0.9), not judged, as ss6 is listed as failing R2 at 0.91 while ss43 at 0.90 is not, and no MAD threshold is given.

claims.statement: The other thirteen failed glass specimens (g2, ss8, s11, ss18, ss24, ss27, ss29, ss36, ss38, ss39, ss45, ss46, ss48) gave no fit, most because they did not acquire TRM in a regular fashion and some because their directions trend out of the origin.
claims.source: Methods, Paleointensity Selection criteria, paragraph 2; Table 2
claims.quote: We note that some specimens did not acquire TRM in a regular fashion, or showed directions that trended out of ... the origin of their respective orthogonal vector plots
claims.criterion: The paper gives no measure of regular TRM acquisition. Over each specimen's Table 2 range, TRM gained per step is computed as in the opening comment and the pTRM check percentages listed for these specimens are compared with Table 2 as in table2-fit-statistics. Regularity is read as (a) TRM gained increasing with each temperature step, or (b) a TRM gained against temperature curve with no step falling by more than 15% (the pTRM tolerance of the selection criteria). Reproduced when, under one reading, at least 9 of the 11 specimens marked "no regular TRM acquisition" show irregular acquisition, and ss36 and ss39 have field-off vectors whose distance from the origin grows over the last steps of the range. The counts under each reading are reported. The pTRM check comparison is reported and does not decide the outcome.

claims.statement: Glass subsamples ss43 and ss19, which failed the reliability criteria, show hints of linear directional components on orthogonal vector plots, from which nominal paleointensities can be calculated with the 18 uT laboratory field.
claims.source: Background & Summary, Glass, paragraph 2; Figure 1
claims.quote: some of these data reveal linear directional components, and nominal paleointensities can be calculated (Fig. 1)
claims.criterion: Over the Table 2 ranges (ss43 250 to 400 C, ss19 175 to 450 C), MAD and R2 as in table2-fit-statistics, and the nominal paleointensity as the absolute slope times 18 uT (Figure 1 legend). The figure's values were not seen (no PDF), so none is expected. Holds when both MADs and R2 values match Table 2 under one reading; the nominal paleointensities are reported under each reading.

claims.statement: Glass subsamples ss41 and ss22 show field-off directions that change over a temperature interval, consistent with a changing ambient field during magnetization, and curved NRM lost against TRM gained plots.
claims.source: Background & Summary, Glass, paragraph 2; Figure 2; Table 2
claims.quote: Other specimens show a changing vector, consistent with a changing ambient field (Fig. 2)
claims.criterion: The arrows marking the interval in Figure 2 were not seen, so the Table 2 ranges are used (ss41 500 to 580 C, ss22 250 to 500 C), with the earlier steps shown. The paper names no measure of a changing direction. Readings (a) the angle between the first and the last field-off direction of the range exceeds the MAD of a line fit over the range, (b) a great-circle fit over the range has a smaller MAD than a line fit. Reproduced when both specimens show a changing direction under one reading and R2 is within tolerance of Table 2 (0.38 each); the angles and MADs are reported.

claims.statement: The field-off directions of the failed glass specimens, as seen on orthogonal vector plots, are not random, implying the presence of an ambient field.
claims.source: Background & Summary, Glass, paragraph 2
claims.quote: The directions, as viewed on orthogonal vector plots, are not random and imply the presence of an ambient field
claims.criterion: The paper names no test. Per specimen, the field-off directions of its thermal steps are tested for randomness with Watson's test (n directions, resultant length R, p < 0.05), a standard choice. Reproduced when more than half of the 22 specimens reject randomness, partially reproduced for a quarter to a half. Because successive demagnetization steps of one remanence are not independent, the count is also given for the steps within each specimen's Table 2 range where one is printed.

claims.statement: For nearly all glass samples given AF pre-treatment, AF cleaning did not significantly change the NRM direction or magnitude.
claims.source: Methods, paragraph 2
claims.quote: For nearly all samples, AF cleaning did not significantly change the NRM direction or magnitude
claims.criterion: Per specimen with AF steps, the angle between the NRM direction and the direction after the last AF step, and the ratio of the moments. The paper gives no threshold for "significantly". Readings (a) angle under 15 degrees and moment change under 15% (the pTRM check tolerance of the selection criteria), (b) angle under the specimen's Table 2 MAD where one is printed and moment change under 15%. Reproduced when, under one reading, all but at most two of the AF-treated specimens show no significant change.

claims.statement: For each of the twelve single crystals, the maximum field that cannot be excluded, given the magnetometer threshold of 8e-11 emu and the moment acquired at 590 C in a 20 uT field, is as in Table 1, between 0.20 and 0.51 uT.
claims.source: Background & Summary, Single crystal measurements, paragraph 4; Table 1; Technical Validation, Example of threshhold detection limit
claims.quote: Considering a magnetometer threshold value (see Methods) the maximum field that cannot be excluded by the data can be calculated from the data for each crystal. These values are presented in Table 1
claims.criterion: Max intensity = 8e-11 emu / M590 x 20 uT (Technical Validation). M590 is computed under the readings named in the opening comment, (a) or (b) crossed with (i) or (ii). Reproduced when, under one reading, all 24 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced when at least 18 are. The reading that matches is reported, and whether Table 1 max intensities equal the formula applied to its own M590 column to two places.

claims.statement: The maximum fields that the single crystal data cannot exclude define a baseline of about 0.2 to 0.5 uT below which fields cannot be evaluated with these data.
claims.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 7
claims.quote: they nevertheless define a baseline of ~0.2 to ~0.5 μT below which fields cannot be evaluated with the present data
claims.criterion: Holds when the lowest and highest of the twelve values computed in table1-max-intensity, under the reading that matches there, lie in 0.18 to 0.22 and 0.45 to 0.55 uT.

claims.statement: For crystal 14053g1, the threshold field detection limit computed from the magnetometer sensitivity (8e-14 A m2) and a TRM at 590 C of 8e-12 A m2 in a 20 uT field is 0.2 uT.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Example of threshhold detection limit
claims.quote: Threshold field detection = Magnetometer sensitivity (8 × 10−14 A m2) / TRM590o (8 × 10−12 A m2) × Lab Field (20 μT) = 0.2 μT
claims.criterion: The example conflicts with Table 1, which gives 14053g1 3.203E-09 emu and 0.51 uT. Readings (a) the example as written, for 14053g1; (b) a misprint of the crystal name, the numbers belonging to 12040g1 (8.002E-09 emu, 0.20 uT in Table 1). TRM computed as in table1-max-intensity. Reproduced as written when reading (a) matches; when only (b) matches, the claim is reported as matching the misprint reading, with the 14053g1 values shown.

claims.statement: For most crystals the replicate NRM measurements have a consistent direction, as shown on stereonets for 12040g1 and 14053g2.
claims.source: Background & Summary, Single crystal measurements, paragraph 2; Figure 3a and 3d
claims.quote: These show that for most of the crystals there is consistency of the NRM direction (Fig. 3a,d)
claims.criterion: Per crystal, the replicate NRM (step 0.0) directions, with Fisher mean, k and alpha95. Readings for "consistent", named in the opening comment, (a) k of the NRM replicates higher than k of the 590.0 replicates, (b) Watson's test rejects randomness of the NRM replicates at p < 0.05. Reproduced when, under one reading, more than half of the twelve crystals are consistent, including 12040g1 and 14053g2.

claims.statement: After demagnetization at 590 C in zero field, the replicate directions of the crystals are inconsistent, consistent with a null magnetization state.
claims.source: Background & Summary, Single crystal measurements, paragraph 2; Figure 3b and 3e; Methods, Thermal measurements, paragraph 5
claims.quote: but this consistency is not seen after demagnetization at 590 °C (Fig. 3b,e)
claims.criterion: Per crystal, the replicate 590.0 directions, with Fisher mean, k and alpha95. Readings (a) k of the 590.0 replicates lower than k of the NRM replicates, (b) Watson's test does not reject randomness of the 590.0 replicates at p < 0.05. Reproduced when, under one reading, more than half of the twelve crystals are inconsistent, including 12040g1 and 14053g2. The 590.0 moments are reported against the 8e-11 emu threshold.

claims.statement: The replicate directions after the zero-field alteration check at 590 C are also inconsistent.
claims.source: Background & Summary, Single crystal measurements, paragraph 2; Figure 3c and 3f
claims.quote: The directions are also inconsistent after the alteration check at 590 °C (Fig. 3c,f)
claims.criterion: As fig3-590-inconsistent, for the replicate 590.3 directions.

claims.statement: Crystal 14053g1, measured after heating to 400 C during initial tests, held a stable remanence, which was removed by treatment at 590 C.
claims.source: Background & Summary, Single crystal measurements, paragraph 3
claims.quote: One crystal (14053g1) was measured after heating to an intermediate temperature (400 °C) during initial tests, and found to be stable
claims.criterion: Applies only if the deposit holds 400 C measurements for 14053g1. The paper names no measure of stability; stable is read, as for the NRM, as replicate 400 C directions consistent under fig3-nrm-consistent's readings, with the 590.0 replicates of the same crystal inconsistent; or (b), where 400 C was measured once, the 400 C direction lies within the alpha95 of the Fisher mean of the NRM replicates. Reproduced when the 590.0 replicates are inconsistent and (a) or (b) holds.

claims.statement: Alteration during the laser heating of the single crystals was not significant; apparent recording efficiencies far above 100% were not observed and the alteration checks did not fail.
claims.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 5
claims.quote: If alteration had resulted in the formation of new magnetic minerals, apparent recording efficiencies ≫ 100% should have be observed (but these were not), and alteration checks should fail
claims.criterion: The paper does not define recording efficiency or the failure of the alteration check for the crystals. Readings (a) the 590.3 moment does not exceed the 590.0 moment by more than the 8e-11 emu threshold, and the 590.3 directions are inconsistent as in fig3-alteration-check-inconsistent; (b) the 590.4 TRM (40 uT, vector difference from 590.3) is no more than about twice the 590.1 TRM (20 uT), as linear recording predicts; the paper gives no bound for "far above 100%", so the ratios are reported and a ratio of the 590.4 TRM to twice the 590.1 TRM above 2 is taken as failing, a choice not from the paper. Reproduced when every crystal passes under one reading; the ratios are reported. Recording efficiency against a theoretical TRM needs grain properties the paper does not give, so it is not computed.

claims.statement: Together with ref. 1, the data are consistent with impact plasma magnetization of the 64455 glass and with the absence of a long-lived lunar core dynamo recorded in the 3.9 to 3.2 Ga crystals.
claims.source: Abstract; Background & Summary, paragraphs 2 and 7
claims.quote: These 64455 field strengths1 match those predicted by the charge separation mechanism
claims.criterion: An interpretation that rests on ref. 1 and on models of impact plasmas, not on a measurement this deposit can repeat. Not tested; it is judged as following from the outcomes of fig2-changing-field, glass-directions-not-random, fig3-590-inconsistent and table1-max-intensity, which are reported together.

claims.statement: The User Responses Dataset holds 134,699 voter responses, each with answers to the 39 statements, along with demographics, the three most salient statements and the parties the respondent would and would never vote for, for most responses.
claims.source: Data Records, User Responses Dataset; Table 1
claims.quote: This raw dataset provides n = 134,699 individual Likert-scale responses to a series of 39 policy issues and value statements along with additional user demographics and preferences for most of the responses
claims.criterion: Count the rows of the raw user responses file (data_without_email.csv) and check that it has the columns of Table 1 (TIME.STAMP, S1 to S39, the would-not-vote columns such as UN26, GENDER, AGE, EDUCATION, EMAIL_ID). Reproduced when the row count is within tolerance and the columns are present. The count is of the raw file, before cleaning, as the Data Records say ("This raw dataset"); the count after removing incomplete rows is reported as well.

claims.statement: The responses were gathered during the 26 days leading up to and including election day, from the launch on 5 September 2023 to the election on 30 September 2023.
claims.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 3; Methods, Volebný Kompas implementation and usage, paragraph 5
claims.quote: gathered during the 26 days leading up to and including the day of the 2023 snap Slovak Parliamentary Elections
claims.criterion: From TIME.STAMP of the raw rows. The time zone of TIME.STAMP is not stated, so it is open, readings (a) dates as given and (b) the timestamp read as UTC and converted to Slovak time (CEST, UTC+2). Reproduced when, under one reading, every timestamp falls between 2023-09-05 and 2023-09-30 inclusive. Table 1's sample entry (2023-10-09 08:57:38) falls outside this window, so the number of rows outside it and their dates are reported under each reading. The paper sets no share of rows that may fall outside.

claims.statement: The Party Positions Dataset lists the 39 statements in Slovak, Hungarian and English and holds 429 party positions, both party self-placements and expert-coded positions, with sources, snippets and links.
claims.source: Data Records, Party Positions Dataset
claims.quote: This dataset lists the n = 39 statements used in the survey across three languages — Slovak, Hungarian, and English and offers detailed information on various parties’ positions concerning specific statements with n = 429 observations
claims.criterion: Tolerance 0, as these are counts of a fixed design (11 parties by 39 statements). Reproduced when the file holds 39 statements, each with a Slovak, Hungarian and English wording, and 429 party-by-statement positions with expert-coded positions, self-placement columns, and source, snippet and link columns.

claims.statement: Eleven parties are positioned on the 39 statements.
claims.source: Methods, Party selection and coding, paragraph 1
claims.quote: Out of 25 political parties, 11 met the inclusion criteria and were incorporated into our VAA
claims.criterion: Tolerance 0, a count. Reproduced when the Party Positions Dataset names 11 distinct parties, each with positions on the 39 statements.

claims.statement: Four of the eleven parties returned the self-placement questionnaire.
claims.source: Methods, Party selection and coding, paragraph 4
claims.quote: Responses were garnered from four political entities out of eleven
claims.criterion: Tolerance 0, a count. Reproduced when exactly 4 of the 11 parties have self-placement values in the Party Positions Dataset. A party counts when it has a self-placement for at least one statement; the number of statements each answered is reported.

claims.statement: Agreement between the two expert coders of party positions was high, with a weighted Cohen's kappa of 0.84.
claims.source: Methods, Party selection and coding, paragraph 3
claims.quote: we employed Weighted Cohen’s Kappa37, which provided a value of κ = 0.84, indicating a high level of consistency among coders
claims.criterion: Weighted Cohen's kappa (Methods, citing ref. 37) between the two coders' positions over the 429 party-by-statement positions, ordered Completely Disagree, Tend to Disagree, Neutral, Tend to Agree, Completely Agree. Two details are open in the text. The weights, readings (a) linear and (b) quadratic. The "No Opinion" category, readings (i) pairs with No Opinion from either coder left out, (ii) No Opinion scored as Neutral (50), as the cleaning does for users. Reproduced when kappa is within tolerance under one reading; every reading is reported. The claim needs each coder's separate positions; whether the dataset holds them is the author's to find.

claims.statement: The platform placed each party on five uni-dimensions, using 18 of the 39 statements, and on a two-dimensional socio-economic and socio-cultural landscape from 0 to 100, using 16 statements; the placements (Figs. 2 and 3) conform to the anticipated placements of Slovak parties.
claims.source: Methods, Volebný Kompas implementation and usage, paragraphs 3 and 4; Figs. 2 and 3; Technical Validation, Content validation, last paragraph
claims.quote: Out of the 39 statements, 18 were assigned to the five uni-dimensions ... Of the 39 statements, 16 influenced this two-dimensional political landscape
claims.criterion: The dimensions and polarities of each statement come from Supplementary Table 1, which was not in the text read; the author takes them from it or from the data dictionary. Party positions on 0 to 100 as in the Methods (Completely disagree 0 to Completely agree 100). The scoring is said to follow the euandi method (ref. 30) and is not given in full. Readings for a dimension score (a) the mean over its statements of the position for polarity +1 and 100 minus the position for polarity -1; (b) for the landscape, a start at 50 moved by each statement's polarity-adjusted deviation from 50, averaged over the axis's statements. How "No Opinion" party positions enter is not stated, readings (i) left out and (ii) scored as 50, as the cleaning does for users. Reproduced when the counts of assigned statements are 18 and 16 and, under one reading, the order of the parties on each uni-dimension and each landscape axis matches Figs. 2 and 3 of the published paper. The figures were not readable here, so the expected placements are read from the published figures by the author.

claims.statement: Hierarchical clustering of the parties' recoded positions, by Manhattan distance and average linkage, groups the parties largely as anticipated (Fig. 7).
claims.source: Technical Validation, Content validation, paragraph 7; Fig. 7
claims.quote: We used the ‘recoded_party_positions’ dataset and computed pairwise Manhattan distances to emphasize the absolute differences in policy positions, applying average linkage clustering
claims.criterion: Method from the Technical Validation; party positions coded 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 as in the Methods; pairwise Manhattan distances between the 11 parties over the 39 statements; average linkage. The recoding behind 'recoded_party_positions' is made by the deposited R code and is not described; for "No Opinion" the readings are (a) recoded to 50, as the cleaning does for users, and (b) left out of each pairwise distance. Which positions are clustered is not stated either; the final positions adopted by the team (Methods, Party selection and coding, paragraph 4) are the natural reading, and the expert-coded positions are a variant if the dataset holds them separately. Reproduced when, under one reading, the dendrogram's merge order (its topology) matches Fig. 7 of the published paper. The text names no expected grouping and the figure was not readable here, so the author reads it from the published figure.

claims.statement: Of the responses counted in Table 2, 41.61% are female (44,919), 57.08% male (61,626) and 1.32% other or prefer not to say (1,420).
claims.source: Table 2, Gender rows
claims.criterion: The paper does not say which rows Table 2 counts. Each of its three blocks sums to 107,965 (computed here from the table), fewer than the 134,699 raw rows, and each percentage is over that sum. That the gender, age and education blocks share one total suggests the table counts rows with all three given. Readings (a) rows left after the cleaning (no -1 in S1 to S39), with gender not NA; (b) all raw rows with gender not empty; (c) cleaned rows with gender, age and education all given; (d) raw rows with all three given. Reproduced when, under one reading, every count and percentage is within tolerance. The total under each reading is reported.

claims.statement: Respondents are skewed toward younger ages; 32.32% are 25 to 34 (34,894) and 25.79% are 35 to 44 (27,847), with 2,716 aged 65 to 74 and 683 aged 75 or older (Table 2).
claims.source: Technical Validation, Content validation, paragraph 2; Table 2, Age rows
claims.quote: the substantial numbers within the younger age brackets, particularly those aged 25–34 (n = 34,894, 32.32%) and 35–44 (n = 27,847, 25.79%), highlight this trend (Table 2)
claims.criterion: The rows counted are open, with the readings of table2-gender (a) cleaned rows with age not NA, (b) raw rows with age not empty, (c) cleaned rows with gender, age and education all given, (d) raw rows with all three given. Reproduced when, under one reading, every count and the two percentages are within tolerance. The other percentages of Table 2 (1.17, 6.50, 11.38, 14.06, 5.63, 2.52, 0.63) are reported against the result.

claims.statement: Respondents are skewed toward the well educated; 64.41% have a university degree or academic higher education (69,542), with 990 reporting no education and 1,665 only primary education (Table 2).
claims.source: Technical Validation, Content validation, paragraph 2; Table 2, Education rows
claims.quote: The pronounced presence of individuals with university degrees or academic higher education (n = 69,542, 64.41%)
claims.criterion: The rows counted are open, with the readings of table2-gender (a) cleaned rows with education not NA, (b) raw rows with education not empty, (c) cleaned rows with gender, age and education all given, (d) raw rows with all three given. Reproduced when, under one reading, every count and the percentage are within tolerance.

claims.statement: The multivariate check found 40 respondents under 18 and 400 aged 18 to 20 reporting university-level education, which is not congruent with their age.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Structural validation, paragraph 3
claims.quote: specifically n = 40 cases under the age of 18 and n = 400 cases aged ‘18–20’, which were not congruent with university-level education attainment
claims.criterion: Count rows with EDUCATION "University degree/Academic higher education" and AGE "Under 18", and with AGE "18–20". The rows checked are open; the structural validation is run "After cleaning" (Structural validation, paragraph 1), so reading (a) is the cleaned rows and reading (b) all raw rows. Whether "university-level" also takes in "Applied higher education" is open, readings (i) the university category only, as the paragraph names it, and (ii) both higher education categories. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance under one reading.

claims.statement: Opinions on S2 (higher earners should face a higher income tax rate) and S3 (the retirement age should rise with life expectancy) span a wide range, with means of 43 and 42, standard deviations of 33 and medians of 25.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Content validation, paragraph 4; Fig. 5
claims.quote: S2 — ‘People who earn higher wages should have a higher income tax rate’ (mean = 43, s.d. = 33, median = 25) and S3— ‘The retirement age should rise as life expectancy increases’ (mean = 42, s.d. = 33, median = 25) highlight the diversity of opinions
claims.criterion: Statistics are taken "prior to the re-coding of ‘no opinion’ with a value of 50" (same paragraph), so "no opinion" answers are left out. The rows are open, readings (a) rows left after removing those with -1 in S1 to S39; (b) all raw rows, leaving out -1 and empty answers to the statement. Standard deviation with the n - 1 denominator (R's sd), a standard choice that cannot change the outcome at this sample size. Reproduced when, under one reading, all six values are within tolerance.

claims.statement: S4 (more personal responsibility in health care) and S5 (heavier taxes on banks and big corporations) show stronger consensus, with medians of 75 (means 70 and 69, standard deviations 26 and 29), though more than 17,435 respondents for S4 and 23,344 for S5 disagree with scores of 0 or 25.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Content validation, paragraph 4; Fig. 5
claims.quote: S4 — ‘In the health care system, more emphasis should be placed on the personal responsibility of the individual’ (mean = 70, s.d. = 26, median = 75,) and S5 —‘Banks and big corporations should be taxed more heavily’ (mean = 69, s.d. = 29, median = 75) suggest a stronger consensus ... more than n = 17,435 for S4 and n = 23,344 for S5 — diverging on these views, with scores of 0 and 25
claims.criterion: Rows as in s2-s3-wide-range, readings (a) cleaned rows and (b) raw rows, "no opinion" left out. "More than n = 17,435" can be read as (i) the count of answers 0 or 25 is about 17,435 (within tolerance) or (ii) the count exceeds 17,435; likewise for S5. Reproduced when, under one combination of readings, the six statistics are within tolerance and both counts hold.

claims.statement: Parallel analyses on both the polychoric and the Pearson correlation matrices of S1 to S39 indicated that 11 factors should be extracted.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Content validation, paragraphs 5 and 6; Fig. 6
claims.quote: Both parallel analyses indicated that 11 factors should be extracted.
claims.criterion: Tolerance 0, a count of factors. Method from the Technical Validation, R package psych (ref. 45) on S1 to S39, with negatively worded statements reversed (which ones is in Supplementary Table 1 or the R code; reversing an item does not change the eigenvalues, so this cannot change the count). Open details, all of which could change the count. Rows, readings (a) the cleaned rows with "no opinion" as 50 and (b) the cleaned rows with "no opinion" as missing, pairwise complete. The parallel analysis settings are not given; reading psych's fa.parallel defaults (minres factoring, 20 iterations, the factor count it reports, not the component count), once with cor "poly" and once with "cor". The random seed is a standard choice that may move the count by one; it is reported. Reproduced when both counts are 11 under one reading of the rows.

claims.statement: With 11 factors and promax rotation, maximum likelihood and principal axis factoring gave consistent results, and S1 (real estate tax raised to lower labour taxes) and S3 (retirement age) loaded strongly.
claims.source: Technical Validation, Content validation, paragraph 6
claims.quote: various estimation strategies were employed, including Maximum Likelihood (ML) and principal axis factoring, with promax rotation. This approach yielded consistent results. Notably statements such as S1 — ‘Real estate tax should be increased to lower labor taxes rises’ and S3 — ‘The retirement age should rise as life expectancy rises’ had strong loadings
claims.criterion: psych fa with nfactors 11, rotate "promax", fm "ml" and fm "pa", on the matrices and rows of efa-eleven-factors. "Strong" and "consistent" are not defined in the paper; the thresholds here are this file's choices and an outcome resting on them rests on an assumption. S1 and S3 have strong loadings when their largest absolute loading is at least 0.4 under reading (i) and 0.5 under reading (ii). The two solutions are consistent when each statement's factor of largest absolute loading, matched between solutions by Tucker congruence, agrees for at least 35 of 39 statements. Reproduced when, under one reading, S1 and S3 load strongly in both solutions and the solutions are consistent; all loadings are reported.

claims.statement: The 11 selected parties were the top 11 vote recipients in the 2023 election; each received at least 2% of the vote and no excluded party reached 1%.
claims.source: Methods, Party selection and coding, paragraph 1
claims.quote: The inclusion closely corresponded to election results, correctly anticipating the top 11 vote recipients. All of the 11 selected parties received at least 2% of the vote while no excluded party reached the 1%.
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the 11 parties of the Party Positions Dataset are the 11 lists with the most votes, each at 2% or more, and every other list is below 1%.

claims.statement: The platform registered 270,836 website views in the 26 days leading up to the election.
claims.source: Methods, Volebný Kompas implementation and usage, paragraph 6; Fig. 4
claims.quote: registering 270,836 website views within the 26-day span leading up to the elections
claims.criterion: Reproduced when the platform's view count for 5 to 30 September 2023 is within tolerance. The user responses alone cannot test it, since views are not responses.

claims.statement: The deposited dataframe is the JECFA index of May 2024, with 6552 rows and the fields of Table 1.
claims.source: Data Records, paragraphs 1 and 2
claims.quote: As of May 2024, the final dataframe consists of 6552 rows. The RDS file contains a structured data frame to reflect the fields described in Table 1 of the manuscript
claims.criterion: The tolerance of 3 rows is chosen here in place of 10% (655 rows), which would not test an exact count. The paper says both that the final dataframe has 6552 rows (Data Records) and that the dataframe is cleaned of duplicates to 6549 unique pages (Methods), so the deposit may hold either; 3 rows covers both. Reproduced when jecfa.rds has 6552 rows within tolerance and holds a column for each of the 17 fields of Table 1 (by the code's names in process_df.R, or an evident equivalent); partially reproduced when the row count holds and at most three fields are missing (a threshold chosen here). JECFA.csv is compared with jecfa.rds and any difference in rows or columns is reported.

claims.statement: The 6552 scraped entries, cleaned of the duplicates of page 6316 and of test pages, give 6549 unique pages.
claims.source: Methods, Web-scraping, paragraph 2
claims.quote: We validated the effectiveness of this method by identifying 6552 entries, which were then cleaned to remove duplicates of (E)-N-[2-(1,3-BENZODIOXOL-5-YL)ETHYL]-3- (3,4-DIMETHOXYPHENYL)PROP-2-ENAMIDE ... and test pages, resulting in 6549
claims.criterion: The tolerance of 2 rows is chosen here in place of 10% (655 rows), which would not test an exact count; the Technical Validation gives the same number as "6,551 minus a duplicate and a test page". The paper names page 5883 as the test page and the chemical of page 6316 as the duplicate, without saying how a duplicate is detected. Readings, (D1) rows with distinct URL; (D2) rows with distinct JECFA name, then removing the row of URL 5883; (D3) the 6552 rows less the rows of URL 5883 and less all but one row whose JECFA name is that of page 6316. Reproduced when one reading gives 6549 within tolerance and page 6316's chemical appears more than once in the 6552 rows.

claims.statement: The share of pages carrying each Table 1 field is 100% for URL and JECFA name, 82% chemical names, 79% synonyms, 35% CAS number, 71% JECFA number, 65% FEMA number, 46% COE number, 98% functional class, 98% evaluation year, 97% report and its link, 93% Tox monograph and its link, 92% specification and its link, and 93% FAS.
claims.source: Methods, Web-scraping, paragraph 3; Table 1, column Availability (%)
claims.criterion: For each field the percentage of rows where it is present (E, opening comment), under U1 or U2. FAS is the FAS column the code derives (process_df.R, add_metadata.R), empty when the Tox monograph is not a FAS. Reproduced when, under one reading, at least 15 of the 17 values are within tolerance; partially reproduced for 10 to 14 (thresholds chosen here, as the paper gives none). The paper does not say whether the denominator is 6552 rows or the 6549 cleaned pages, which differ by under 0.1%.
