attempts.label: DANDI:000036
attempts.paper_title: Measuring Stimulus-Evoked Neurophysiological Differentiation in Distinct Populations of Neurons in Mouse Visual Cortex
attempts.entry_title: Neurophysiological differentiation in mouse visual cortex (Mayner, Marshall, Billeh et al. 2022)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Mayner, Marshall, Billeh et al. (2022) on dandiset 000036, which holds two-photon dF/F, running and the movie stimuli of the OpenScope differentiation experiment. It links the dandiset's 57 sessions to the 44 the paper analysed, then tests the spectral differentiation contrasts by layer and area, their sensitivity to the measure's parameters, the per-session permutation tests, decoding, the differences among natural clips, the relation to stimulus differentiation, multivariate differentiation in UMAP space, and the correlation of effect size with running. Claims that need L0 calcium events or the Methods' pupil diameter are blocked.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Mayner et al. (2022) from dandiset 000036
Multivariate differentiation (Figure 5) from dandiset 000036
Arousal and effect size (Figure 4) from dandiset 000036 and the paper's Zenodo deposit

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's sessions can be matched to the 44 sessions the paper analysed (the results/main.parquet of the paper's code), and matched sessions agree on mouse, Cre line, area, depth and number of cells, and give the paper's per-trial ND.
outcomes.source: Code accessibility; results/main.parquet of github.com/wmayner/openscope-differentiation at commit 2d959bd
outcomes.notes: All 44 sessions of main.parquet match one dandiset session each on mouse id and start time (NWB session_start_time minus 7 hours, to the millisecond; no other whole-hour offset matches any session). All 44 agree on Cre line, layer, area and depth, and on the number of cells once the 14 ROIs whose dF/F is NaN at every frame are left out (37 of 44 agree with them counted). With the trial start moved by 0 to -6 frames, the dandiset's dF/F gives the paper's unnormalised per-trial ND to a relative 1e-6 in all 5280 trials (5279 at one shift, 1 at two). With the trial windows the NWB times give, per-trial log10 ND correlates with the paper's at r = 0.9974 (difference SD 0.0465). Thirteen dandiset sessions are unmatched; the one in L5 AL (mouse 402796, 741889312) has 63586 frames at 15.08 Hz and fits the session the paper excluded, which the deposit's metadata.csv also marks invalid (seen while preparing, not in the notebook).
deviations: The 7 hour offset was found while preparing the attempt; the criterion was written after it.

outcomes.statement: Data come from 45 two-photon sessions in nine mice (three per Cre line for L2/3, L4 and L5), 15 sessions per line and 9 per area over V1, LM, AL, PM and AM, with one L5 AL session excluded for recording problems.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1 and 2; Materials and Methods, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Data were collected from L2/3, L4, and L5 in each of five areas (V1, LM, AL, PM, and AM; Fig. 1 E ) across 45 experimental sessions (15 sessions per transgenic line; 9 sessions per area; 5 ± 1 sessions per mouse ... One imaging session in L5 of AL was excluded from our analyses because of technical problems with the two-photon recording
outcomes.notes: The 44 linked sessions plus the half-rate L5 AL session give the paper's design exactly (45 sessions from 9 mice, 3 mice and 15 sessions per line, 9 per area, 3 per layer and area pair, 4 to 6 per mouse). The dandiset holds 12 more, 57 sessions in all (25 Cux2, 15 Rorb and 17 Rbp4; 11 to 13 per area); the 12 (10 second recordings in Cux2 mice 389014 and 389020, and one more PM session in each of Rbp4 mice 402796 and 405808) are not described in the paper and are recorded as a finding. The files hold no sex; the code's table gives 2, 3 and 1 males for Cux2, Rorb and Rbp4, as the paper states. The excluded session is identified by its absence from main.parquet and its half frame rate.
deviations: The criterion does not anticipate a dataset that holds more sessions than the paper. The outcome is judged on the paper's 45 sessions, which are all present, found through the link claim; the round-1 version of this record gave partially_reproduced on the deposited counts.

outcomes.statement: 4018 cells were recorded over the 44 analysed sessions, 1683 in L2/3, 1781 in L4 and 554 in L5, with per layer and area totals from 62 (L4 AM) to 649 (L4 V1).
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 1-2
outcomes.inferred: Extended Data Figure 1-2 shows the counts as an image not in the text; the numbers are the code's own output of that figure (results/table-s1.csv at the commit named in the opening comment), the sums of the session metadata's ncells per layer and area.
outcomes.notes: Over the 44 linked sessions there are 4032 ROIs, 14 of them NaN at every frame; the 4018 others are 1683, 1781 and 554 per layer, and all 15 layer and area totals equal table-s1.csv (15 of 15 within 10%). With the NaN ROIs counted, the totals (4032; 1687, 1790, 555) are also within tolerance. The files carry no validity flag.

outcomes.statement: Calcium indicator kinetics, measured as the half-life of an exponential fit to each cell's mean isolated-event-locked dF/F, do not differ across layers, areas or their interaction.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 1-3 legend
outcomes.quote: we found no layer × area interaction (likelihood ratio test; χ 2 (8) = 1.293, p = 0.996). We tested for main effects of layer and area in two further models and likewise found none
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds no L0 events. The criterion's detector, l0_analysis.py of github.com/AllenInstitute/visual_coding_2p_analysis (commit 3ceca10), is Python 2 code (cPickle) that imports allensdk and FastLZeroSpikeInference. That package is not on PyPI; its repository (github.com/jewellsean/FastLZeroSpikeInference, commit cdfaade) fails to build with pip from git because its setup.py expects the C++ sources copied into the python directory, and its current Python API has no arfpop, which l0_analysis.py calls. The latest commit that defines arfpop (7b80ccd) has a Python 2 fast.py (a SyntaxError under Python 3) and a FitSegmentModel.cpp that uses std::numeric_limits without including <limits>; the notebook's section on the L0 detector prints each of these from the published sources. Running the detector would mean patching the package and porting l0_analysis.py to Python 3. While preparing the round-1 revision, outside the notebook and not run there, the 7b80ccd sources were patched that way (<limits> added, without which g++ stopped at std::numeric_limits, and the print statements of fast.py rewritten for Python 3); the package then built and arfpop ran on a synthetic trace. l0_analysis.py was not ported and no events were computed from this dataset, so the build decides nothing; the published software still cannot be installed as released, which is the reason given. The NWB files hold no path naming events (listing of all 57 files in the notebook). The paper's own events are in its Zenodo deposit (events/, 4125 members, 4.1 GB), which the criterion does not name.

outcomes.statement: Unscrambled stimuli evoke higher ND than their phase-scrambled versions in L2/3 but not in L4 or L5, with a significant layer by stimulus category interaction.
outcomes.source: Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to excitatory cells in L2/3; Figure 3A
outcomes.quote: We fitted an LME model with stimulus category (unscrambled or scrambled), layer, and their interaction as fixed effects and found a significant interaction (likelihood ratio test, χ 2 (2) = 13.379, p = 0.00124). Post hoc tests showed that the unscrambled versus scrambled difference was specific to L2/3

statistics.statistic: z = 3.866, Cohen's d = 0.164, 95% CI of the contrast [0.051, inf)

outcomes.notes: 2200 contrast trials of 44 sessions. Interaction chi2(2) = 14.09, p = 0.00087. Post hoc L2/3 z = 3.83, adjusted p = 0.0002, lower bound 0.050 (paper 0.051); L4 z = 0.10, p = 0.84; L5 z = -1.35, p = 0.999. Cohen's d L2/3 0.163, L4 0.006, L5 -0.079 (paper 0.164, 0.011, -0.067). The L2/3 effect is positive in all three Cux2 mice (d 0.15, 0.43, 0.29). Variant on all 56 complete dandiset sessions, chi2(2) = 8.74, p = 0.013, L2/3 the only significant layer.
deviations: Trials are cut where the NWB stimulus times put them, 0 to 6 frames later than the paper's stimulus table (the shift grows through the session).
ROIs with all-NaN dF/F are left out (none in the paper's counts).
LME, likelihood ratio and glht tests are run with statsmodels and scipy, not R; on the paper's own per-trial values they give its printed chi2, z, p and interval bounds.

outcomes.statement: The higher ND for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM, with a significant area by stimulus category interaction.
outcomes.source: Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM; Figure 3B
outcomes.quote: We fitted an LME model with stimulus category, area, and their interaction as fixed effects and found a significant interaction (likelihood ratio test, χ 2 (4) = 15.203, p = 0.00430). Post hoc tests showed that the unscrambled versus scrambled difference was specific to AL and AM

statistics.statistic: z = 2.873, Cohen's d = 0.200, 95% CI of the contrast [0.022, inf)
z = 2.446, Cohen's d = 0.268, 95% CI of the contrast [0.128, inf)

outcomes.notes: Interaction chi2(4) = 15.58, p = 0.0036. AL z = 2.65, adjusted p = 0.020; AM z = 2.54, p = 0.028; V1, LM and PM p 0.81 to 1.0. Cohen's d AL 0.181 (within tolerance of 0.200) and AM 0.132, outside the tolerance of 0.268. The paper's own per-trial values give AM d = 0.127, and 0.128 with the pooled SD as the code computes it; the paper's text prints d = 0.268 with interval [0.128, inf), where the post hoc test on the paper's per-trial values gives the interval bound 0.0048, so 0.268 looks like a transcription slip in the paper and the dataset agrees with the paper's computation. The criterion's rule rests on the significance pattern, which holds. Variant on all 56 complete dandiset sessions, chi2(4) = 14.39, p = 0.006, AM significant but AL not (p = 0.072). With the pooled SD as the code computes it (variant), the paper's per-trial values give AL 0.200 and AM 0.128, and this dataset 0.184 and 0.133. A question asks a reader whether 0.268 is a misprint (questions/000036.yaml).
deviations: As fig3a-layer-specific (trial windows from the NWB times, NaN ROIs left out, statistics in Python).

outcomes.statement: Over all 12 stimuli, naturalistic stimuli evoke higher ND than artificial ones in L2/3 and L5 (not L4) and in AL and AM (not V1, LM or PM), with significant interactions with layer and with area.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 3-1 legend
outcomes.quote: In this analysis, post hoc tests showed a significant effect also in L5; however, this contrast does not control for low-level stimulus characteristics and is thus harder to interpret

statistics.about: area x category interaction, as printed (the layer values repeated; the code's output is chi2(4) = 22.213, p = 0.0001817)

outcomes.notes: 5280 trials. Layer chi2(2) = 16.09, p = 0.0003; area chi2(4) = 21.84, p = 0.0002 (the code prints 22.213). L2/3 (adjusted p < 0.0001) and L5 (p = 0.0004) significant, L4 not (p = 0.98); AL and AM significant (p <= 0.0001), V1, LM and PM not (p 0.28 to 1.0). All four Cohen's d within tolerance.
deviations: As fig3a-layer-specific.

outcomes.statement: The L2/3, AL and AM specificity of the unscrambled against scrambled ND difference holds for nearly all choices of distance metric, state length, frequency spacing and spectral window.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figures 3-2, 3-3 and 3-4 legends; Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: For nearly all other combinations of parameters, we likewise find that unscrambled stimuli elicit increased ND specifically in L2/3 of AL and AM
outcomes.notes: 36 of 108 parameter sets meet the agreement rule (33.3%), below 90% and 80%; the looser rule also gives 36. L2/3 is the only significant layer in all 108 sets and the layer and area interactions are significant in 108 and 102. The areas vary; AL and AM both significant in 36 sets, AL alone in 41, AM alone in 24, neither in 7. Agreement by window is rectangular 39%, Kaiser 33%, Tukey 28%; by state length 0% at 10 s and 72% at 2 s. The same rule on the paper's own results/stats.parquet gives 28 of 108 (25.9%); there L2/3 is also the only significant layer in all 108 sets, and AL and AM are both significant in 28, AL alone in 50, AM alone in 24, neither in 6. So the paper's outputs do not meet this reading of "nearly all" either; the difference is between the claims file's rule and the paper's sentence, not between the dataset and the paper's computation. The spectra are the paper's. For six sets, one per window and frequency spacing, this dF/F at the start shift found for the main set gives the paper's per-trial ND (results/sensitivity_analysis.parquet) to a relative 1.1e-14 in all 2199 contrast trials with a single matching shift, and over all 108 sets per-trial log10 ND with the NWB windows correlates with the paper's at r = 0.993 to 0.9999. A question asks a reader whether the paper supports a different agreement rule (questions/000036.yaml).
deviations: As fig3a-layer-specific.

outcomes.statement: With locomotion and pupil diameter as covariates in the LME models, L2/3 of AL and AM remain the populations where ND is greater for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli, for nearly all parameter combinations.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figures 3-5, 3-6 and 3-7 legends; Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Consistent with the simpler models, for nearly all parameter combinations, L2/3 of AL and AM emerged as the cell populations in which ND is greater for unscrambled versus scrambled stimuli
outcomes.notes: The criterion crosses the readings of pupil diameter, and the Methods reading (twice the semi-major axis of the fitted ellipse) is in no public file. The dandiset has no eye tracking at all; the Zenodo deposit holds pupil area per session (eye/*_area.npy), from which only the code's reading can be computed. For fig4-pupil-effect-size the two computable artifact readings already disagree in sign. Locomotion per trial is available under both readings.

outcomes.statement: Spectral ND of L0 calcium events gives results similar to dF/F, with greater ND for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in L2/3 and in AL, while AM is at the threshold (p = 0.050).
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 3-8 legend
outcomes.quote: Results are similar to the main analysis on ΔF/F 0 traces shown in Figure 3
outcomes.notes: Needs L0 events; see ext1-3-kinetics-no-difference.

outcomes.statement: With the 200 ms after each L0 event removed from dF/F, ND remains greater for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in L2/3 and in AL, with significant interactions; AM is not significant (p = 0.0958).
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 3-9 legend
outcomes.quote: Results are similar to the main analysis shown in Figure 3 , indicating that our ND results are not driven solely by initial transients in the calcium response
outcomes.notes: Needs L0 events to mark the 200 ms to remove; see ext1-3-kinetics-no-difference.

outcomes.statement: Part of the effect of stimulus category on ND is mediated by mean calcium event magnitude and part is direct (mediated 0.1351, direct 0.0951, proportion mediated 0.59).
outcomes.source: Results, Increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: We also analyzed whether the mean magnitude of calcium events (a proxy for firing rate) mediated the effect of stimulus category and found evidence for both mediated and direct effects
outcomes.notes: The mediator is the mean L0 event magnitude, which cannot be computed (see ext1-3-kinetics-no-difference). The pupil covariate also needs the Methods' diameter, which is in no public file (data_missing).

outcomes.statement: Per-session permutation tests find ND greater for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in all 6 sessions of L2/3 AL and AM, in 8 of 15 L2/3 sessions, 1 of 15 L4 and 0 of 14 L5 sessions.
outcomes.source: Table 1; Results, Permutation tests for individual experimental sessions
outcomes.quote: In all sessions recorded from L2/3 of AL and AM, responses to unscrambled stimuli were significantly more differentiated than to scrambled stimuli ( p < 0.05)
outcomes.notes: Methods rule, log10 ND, 20,000 permutations per session (own seed). L2/3 AL 3 of 3, AM 3 of 3, L2/3 8 of 15, L4 1 of 15, L5 0 of 14; the 15-cell table equals the code's printed table cell by cell, and the code's rule gives the same. The six L2/3 AL and AM sessions have p 0.00005 to 0.029. Untransformed ND (variant) gives 5 of 15 in L2/3 (2 of 3 in AL and in AM).
deviations: As fig3a-layer-specific; random permutations are not the paper's.

outcomes.statement: In L2/3 of AL and AM, the per-session effect size of unscrambled against scrambled ND is positively correlated with the fraction of time spent running (r = 0.896).
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal is correlated with effect size; Figure 4, top left
outcomes.quote: We found that in L2/3 of AL and AM, effect sizes were positively correlated with locomotion activity (Pearson’s r = 0.896; two-sided t test; t (4) = 4.030, p = 0.0157, 95% CI [0.308, 1.00]
outcomes.notes: Over the six L2/3 AL and AM sessions, reading (a) r = 0.842, t(4) = 3.13, p = 0.035; reading (b) r = 0.844, p = 0.035; both within tolerance (0.792 to 1) and significant. Reading (b) gives the code's printed locomotion fractions to within 0.0001 and reading (a) to within 0.0008, so the lower r comes from the effect sizes (one session d = 1.111 against the code's stored 1.258). With d computed with the pooled SD as the paper's code computes it (variant), r = 0.892 (p = 0.017) under reading (a) and 0.894 (p = 0.016) under reading (b). Over all 44 sessions r = -0.03. The deposit is now streamed over parallel range requests and reached all required members after 176 s in the final run (217 s in the run reviewed in round 2), so the executed copy shows both readings.
deviations: Reading (b) uses the deposit's parameters and vsync alignment on the dandiset's running velocity, whose first sample is dropped (the rest equal the deposit's run_speed).
Effect sizes use trial windows from the NWB times, as fig3a-layer-specific.

outcomes.statement: In L2/3 of AL and AM, the per-session effect size is positively but not significantly correlated with mean normalized pupil diameter (r = 0.716, p = 0.109).
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal is correlated with effect size; Figure 4, top right
outcomes.notes: The dandiset has no pupil data. With the deposit's pupil area and the code's diameter (2*sqrt(area/pi)), reading (b) of artifact removal reproduces the code's printed per-session pupil values exactly and gives r = 0.651, p = 0.16 (positive, within tolerance of 0.716); reading (a), without artifact removal, gives r = -0.647, p = 0.17, because unremoved artifacts set the maximum the diameter is normalised by. The criterion requires every reading of pupil diameter, and the Methods' semi-major axis reading cannot be computed from any public file. The deposit's data/eye/ holds 45 pupil area files and a parameter file, and no ellipse fit (listed in the arousal notebook). That is the main reason (data_missing); the two computable readings also disagree, which the criterion would block as methods_underspecified.

outcomes.statement: Within single L2/3 AL and AM sessions effect sizes are medium to very large (Cohen's d 0.57 to 1.25), while the effect over these sessions pooled is 0.34.
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 6
outcomes.quote: while we observed medium to very large effect sizes within individual experimental sessions in L2/3 of AL and AM (Cohen’s d = 0.57–1.25), the overall effect was relatively subtle (Cohen’s d = 0.34)
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' pooled SD, per-session d 0.572 to 1.111, all six within 0.513 to 1.375; smallest and pooled (0.340) within tolerance; the largest is below the tolerance of 1.25 (1.125 to 1.375), printed as a failed check in the notebook. For that session (719080059, paper 719334668) the paper's main.parquet gives 1.155 and its effect_size.parquet 1.258. The effect_size.parquet values equal, to 4e-15 in all 44 sessions, Cohen's d from main.parquet with the pooled SD as the code's analysis.pooled_std_dev computes it, each group's SD weighted by the other group's n - 1; the paper's 0.57 to 1.25 and 0.34 come from that. With that SD (variant) this dataset gives 0.584 to 1.194 and a pooled 0.343, all within tolerance. The claims file and the Methods give the standard formula, so the outcome rests on it; a question asks a reader which the criterion means (questions/000036.yaml).
deviations: As fig3a-layer-specific.
The criterion gives no partial rule; partial is used because two of three values and the range hold and one extreme is 0.014 outside its tolerance.

outcomes.statement: Multivariate ND (mean distance to the centroid in an 8-dimensional UMAP embedding) is higher for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli specifically in L2/3.
outcomes.source: Results, Multivariate analysis also shows increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli; Figure 5A
outcomes.quote: The mean centroid distance was higher in response to unscrambled compared to scrambled stimuli ( Fig. 5 ), and this effect was specific to L2/3
outcomes.notes: Interaction chi2(2) = 18.535, p = 9.4e-5. L2/3 z = 5.12, adjusted p < 0.0001; L4 p = 0.112; L5 p = 0.997. Cohen's d L2/3 0.192 (paper 0.194). Per-trial values correlate with the paper's at r = 0.995. umap-learn 0.5.12 with numba 0.68.0. The first version of this record gave 18.99 and 0.194 from the author run; the author-answers run and both runs of this revision give 18.535 and 0.192.
deviations: UMAP version differs from the paper's run; trial windows from the NWB times.

outcomes.statement: Multivariate ND is higher for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli specifically in AL and AM.

outcomes.quote: and areas AL and AM [area × stimulus category interaction ... likelihood ratio test, χ 2 (4) = 16.232, p = 0.00272
outcomes.notes: Interaction chi2(4) = 16.142, p = 0.0028. AL adjusted p = 0.0094, AM p < 0.0001; V1, LM, PM p 0.94 to 0.95. Cohen's d AL 0.181, AM 0.274 (paper 0.184, 0.277).

outcomes.statement: Multivariate ND of L0 events is also higher for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in L2/3 and in AL and AM, and in V1 as well.
outcomes.source: Results, Multivariate analysis also shows increased differentiation for unscrambled stimuli, paragraph 3; Extended Data Figure 5-1
outcomes.quote: The results of multivariate differentiation analysis of these data were consistent with our results using ΔF/F 0 traces (Extended Data Fig. 5-1 ), with the additional finding of significantly greater differentiation for unscrambled versus scrambled stimuli in L2/3 of V1 as well as AL and AM
outcomes.notes: Needs L0 events; see ext1-3-kinetics-no-difference.

outcomes.statement: Stimulus category (unscrambled or scrambled) can be decoded accurately from most layers and areas, well above chance, without the layer and area specificity of ND.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding analysis does not reveal layer or area specificity; Figure 6
outcomes.quote: Decoding performance was high for most areas and layers ( Fig. 6 ), in contrast to the unscrambled-scrambled difference in ND
outcomes.notes: Mean balanced accuracy is at least 0.75 in 14 of 15 populations and at least 0.9 in 12; per layer 0.86 to 0.95, per area 0.83 to 0.96, all above 0.5; per session 0.575 to 1.0. Lowest populations L4 AM 0.66 and L4 PM 0.75. Per-session scores correlate with the paper's at r = 0.990 (mean difference -0.005). The populations with the ND effect are not the best decoded (L2/3 AL and AM 0.93, L2/3 LM 0.98).

outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 6-1 legend; Results, Decoding analysis does not reveal layer or area specificity
outcomes.quote: Stimulus identity can be accurately decoded from most layers and areas using responses to all 12 stimuli
outcomes.notes: At least 0.75 in 14 of 15 populations and at least 0.9 in 10; per layer 0.83 to 0.97, per area 0.79 to 0.95, chance 0.083; L4 AM lowest at 0.51. Per-session scores correlate with the paper's at r = 0.998.

outcomes.statement: ND differs among the five continuous naturalistic clips, over all layers and areas.
outcomes.source: Results, Differences in ND among individual stimuli
outcomes.quote: We fitted an LME model with stimulus as a fixed effect and found it was significant (likelihood ratio test, χ 2 (4) = 32.115, p = 1.812e–6)
outcomes.notes: 2200 trials of the five continuous natural clips over 44 sessions; chi2(4) = 31.55, p = 2.4e-6 (paper 32.115).

outcomes.statement: The snake (predator) clip evokes higher ND than the conspecifics, crickets and man writing clips, and the mousecam clip higher ND than man writing.
outcomes.source: Results, Differences in ND among individual stimuli; Figure 7
outcomes.quote: revealed that the predator stimulus (a snake) evoked significantly higher differentiation than clips of conspecifics ... prey (crickets ... and a man writing ... The “mousecam” clip of movement through a wooded environment also evoked significantly higher differentiation than the clip of a man writing
outcomes.notes: Tukey-adjusted p for snake against conspecifics 0.012, crickets 0.0008, man writing 2.8e-6, and mousecam against man writing 0.006; none of the other six pairs below 0.05 (smallest 0.18). Estimated differences 0.096, 0.118, 0.154 and 0.103 lie inside the paper's intervals. emmeans' Tukey adjustment is computed from the studentized range with infinite degrees of freedom. On the paper's own per-trial values the same code gives the paper's chi2(4) = 32.115, p = 1.812e-6, and its printed z, adjusted p and intervals for the four named pairs (z 3.229, 3.928, 5.249 and 3.396; p 0.0109, 0.00082, 2e-6 and 0.0061), with the other six pairs not significant.

outcomes.statement: Arousal alone does not account for the differences among continuous clips, with a mixture of direct and arousal-mediated effects; for the largest contrast, snake against man writing, there is evidence only for a direct effect of stimulus on ND, with locomotion or pupil diameter as mediator.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 7-1 legend
outcomes.quote: Notably, for the largest contrast (predator vs man writing), for both locomotion and pupil diameter we found evidence only for a direct effect

outcomes.notes: r = 0.746, t(10) = 3.55, one-sided p = 0.0027 over 12 stimuli and the six L2/3 AL and AM sessions (720 trials); noise has the largest Cook's distance, 2.113 (next 0.219). Stimulus differentiation from the files' movies equals the code's printed values (max difference 0.0 in log10), so the movies are the paper's.

outcomes.quote: If we exclude this stimulus, we find a weaker correlation ( r = 0.258; one-sided t test; t (9) = 0.801, p = 0.222, 95% CI [–0.307, 1.00] ii ). Furthermore, there was no evidence of a relationship with ND when considering only the scrambled stimuli and their unscrambled counterparts

statistics.about: 5 contrast stimuli, as printed in Results (the legend prints p = 0.523)

outcomes.notes: Without noise r = 0.271, one-sided p = 0.21 (paper 0.258); five contrast stimuli r = -0.423, two-sided p = 0.48 (paper -0.378). Neither test finds a relation.

outcomes.statement: ND in L2/3 of AL and AM is not explained by stimulus luminance, contrast or spectral energy.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 8-1 legend; Results, SD does not explain ND
outcomes.quote: We also did not find a relationship with stimulus luminance, contrast, or spectral energy
outcomes.notes: Two-sided, no property has p < 0.05 (luminance r = -0.26, p = 0.42; contrast r = 0.26, p = 0.42; spectral energy r = 0.51, p = 0.087 with per-pixel DC removal and r = 0.55, p = 0.066 with the code's global mean). One-sided, spectral energy has p = 0.044 and 0.033 under the two DC readings. The readings differ, which the criterion blocks. The code's spectral energy values are reproduced to 2e-15.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds 57 sessions where the paper analysed 44 and excluded one. The 12 extra sessions (second recordings of each area in Cux2 mice 389014 and 389020, and a second PM session in Rbp4 mice 402796 and 405808) are not described in the paper, and nothing in the files or the dandiset metadata says which sessions the paper used or that the L5 AL session 741889312 was excluded. They can be identified only through the paper's code outputs. Run on all complete sessions, the area result changes (AL no longer significant).

The NWB identifier is not the session id the paper and its code use (for example 717235570 against 717911143); it is the id that names the deposit's pupil files. The paper's ids appear nowhere in the dandiset, so the sessions can be linked to the paper only by start time.

session_start_time is 7 hours later than the start times of the paper's metadata in all 57 files while labelled -07:00; recordings appear to start between 15:00 and 00:46 local time, against 08:00 to 17:44 in the paper. The times look like UTC labelled as Pacific time (consistent with the data, not shown).

Against the 2p frame times, the NWB stimulus and running timestamps run late by an amount that grows through each session, compared with the vsync-to-frame alignment of the paper's sync files, from about 0 frames in the first minute to 1.3 to 4.4 frames (40 to 146 ms) in the last; the paper's trials start 0 to 6 frames earlier than the NWB stimulus times give. The frame timestamps themselves equal the paper's 2p vsync times.

Every running_velocity series has one sample more than its timestamps; the extra sample is the first (the rest equal the deposit's run_speed, shifted by one), and in one session it is an artifact of -742.7 cm/s. In 39 of 57 files the dF/F timestamps have one entry more than the data has frames.

15 ROIs (14 in the paper's sessions) have dF/F that is NaN at every frame, with no flag or description; without them the cell counts equal the paper's. The PlaneSegmentation table holds only image masks, with no validity or cell id columns.
The imaging plane states an imaging rate of 30.0 Hz; the frame timestamps step by 33.17 ms (30.15 Hz), and by 66.33 ms (15.08 Hz) in the excluded session 741889312, which was imaged at half the rate.

The dandiset holds no L0 calcium events, no eye tracking or pupil data, and no sex, age or date of birth of the mice, all of which the paper uses or reports. The events and pupil area are in the paper's Zenodo deposit (doi:10.5281/zenodo.5781567); the fitted pupil ellipse whose semi-major axis the Methods define as the diameter is in neither. Eight claims are blocked for these data.

The L0 event detector the paper names (l0_analysis.py of AllenInstitute/visual_coding_2p_analysis) is Python 2 code that needs allensdk and the compiled FastLZeroSpikeInference, which is not on PyPI, does not build with pip from its repository, and no longer has the arfpop function the detector calls.

For area AM in Figure 3 the paper prints Cohen's d = 0.268, 95% CI [0.128, inf). Its own per-trial values (results/main.parquet) give d = 0.128 with the pooled SD as its code computes it, and the post hoc test on them a lower bound of 0.0048. The paper's value looks like a transcription slip.

The code's pooled SD (analysis.pooled_std_dev) weights each group's SD by the other group's n - 1, where the Methods give the standard formula; its groupby sorts the labels, so s1 is the SD of "artificial" while n1 counts "natural". The per-session effect sizes of results/effect_size.parquet (0.570 to 1.258 in L2/3 AL and AM, the paper's 0.57 to 1.25, and the figure 4 correlation r = 0.896) come from this. They equal Cohen's d from results/main.parquet with the swapped weights to 4e-15, while the Methods' formula gives 0.592 to 1.155.

The paper says that for nearly all parameter combinations unscrambled stimuli elicit increased ND specifically in L2/3 of AL and AM; in its own sensitivity statistics (results/stats.parquet) AL and AM are both significant in 28 of 108 sets, AL alone in 50, AM alone in 24 and neither in 6, while L2/3 is the only significant layer in all of them.

attempts.label: DANDI:000037
attempts.paper_title: Responses of pyramidal cell somata and apical dendrites in mouse visual cortex over multiple days
attempts.entry_title: Somata and apical dendrites of mouse V1 pyramidal cells over days (Gillon, Lecoq et al. 2023)
attempts.description: Tests the data descriptor of Gillon, Lecoq et al. (2023) on dandiset 000037, which holds two-photon imaging of L2/3 and L5 pyramidal cell somata and distal apical dendrites in 13 mice over 50 sessions, with Gabor sequence and visual flow stimuli. It checks the subjects, sessions and stimuli against the paper's tables and Methods, the ROI counts and tracking across days, the ROI signal to noise ratios, pairwise correlations and stimulus-locked responses of the Technical Validation, and the file sizes.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Gillon, Lecoq et al. (2023) from dandiset 000037

outcomes.statement: The dataset holds 13 mice whose subject ids, sex, date of birth, imaged cell type (L2/3 or L5 pyramidal) and imaging plane (somata or distal apical dendrites) are as listed in Table 1.
outcomes.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, Table 1
outcomes.inferred: The values are those of Table 1; no sentence states them.
outcomes.notes: All 13 subjects of Table 1 are in the dataset, and sex and genotype (cell type) agree for all 13. The files record no date of birth and no plane. As variants, the plane implied by the recorded depth matches for 13 of 13, and the date of birth implied by the recorded age for 12 of 13; for 418779 it is one day late, and matches when the start clock is read as UTC.
deviations: Table 1 values are read from Supplementary Table 1, which holds the same values.

outcomes.statement: Thirteen mice were imaged, three L2/3 dendritic, three L2/3 somatic, four L5 dendritic and three L5 somatic, each with at least three imaging sessions.
outcomes.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: 13 mice in total underwent imaging (L2/3-D: n = 3, L2/3-S: n = 3, L5-D: n = 4, L5-S: n = 3) with at least three optical imaging sessions recorded in each
outcomes.notes: 3 L2/3 dendritic, 3 L2/3 somatic, 4 L5 dendritic and 3 L5 somatic mice, with 3 to 6 sessions each. Line is read from the genotype and plane from the recorded depth; both agree with Supplementary Table 1 for every session.

outcomes.statement: Seven of the mice are male and six female, and only one L2/3 dendritic mouse is female.
outcomes.source: Data Records, Animal and recording session attributes, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: while the dataset is well-split between male (7) and female (6) subjects, splitting the data further by sex may result in some groups with N = 1 (e.g., there is only 1 female L2/3-D mouse)
outcomes.notes: 7 male and 6 female mice; one L2/3 dendritic mouse (433414) is female.

outcomes.statement: The dataset holds 50 imaging sessions from 13 animals, each session in its own files grouped by subject.
outcomes.source: Data Records, Data organization, paragraph 1; Animal and recording session attributes, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: data for 50 recording sessions total were gathered from 13 animals
outcomes.notes: 50 distinct sessions in 13 subject folders, three files per session (150 NWB files), each file in its subject's folder.

outcomes.statement: The 50 sessions have the subject ids, session ids, imaging dates, imaging depths, ROI counts, tracked ROI counts, QC results and stimulus seeds listed in Table 2.
outcomes.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, Table 2
outcomes.inferred: The values are those of Table 2; no sentence states them.
outcomes.notes: All 50 sessions are present; subject, ROI count and tracked ROI count agree for all 50, the date for 46 and the depth for 47. 43 of 50 sessions agree in every recorded field, below the 45 the criterion asks for partial reproduction. The three sessions of 433414 are recorded at 60 um against 75 in Table 2. Four sessions (412933 local session 3, and 418779 sessions 1 to 3) start a day later in the files than Table 2's date. Their start times are early-morning clock values (00:18 to 03:01) stated with a Pacific offset; read as UTC they fall on the evening before in Pacific time. Supplementary Table 1 gives the same clock values as UTC for all 50 sessions. Read as UTC and converted to Pacific time, all 50 dates agree and 47 sessions agree in every field; that reading is not in the criterion and does not decide the outcome. The files hold no other wall-clock time to settle it, since timestamps_reference_time equals session_start_time and file_create_date gives the conversion dates (2022 and 2023). The depth difference holds under either reading. QC and stimulus seed are not recorded in the files.
deviations: The date of a session is taken from its start time as the file states it; the reading of the clock as UTC is shown as a variant. The claims file does not say how a date is read from a time.
Table 2 values are read from Supplementary Table 1, which holds the same values.

outcomes.statement: Two animals had at least one session that failed the Allen Institute's QC thresholds, and some animals had more than three sessions, for example when an early session failed QC.
outcomes.source: Data Records, Animal and recording session attributes, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Of these, two animals had at least one session that did not meet the Allen Institute's previously-described 15 quality control thresholds
outcomes.notes: The files hold no QC status (no QC field in the subject, session or trial table metadata), and the dandiset metadata gives none; the criterion blocks the claim in that case. For reference, Supplementary Table 1 marks failed sessions in three mice (411400 and 412933 sessions 1 to 3, 440889 sessions 5 and 6), so (a) gives 3 and (b) gives 2. Mice with more than three sessions in the files are 411400, 412933, 433448, 433458 and 440889, so that part of the claim holds. None of the 23 small datasets and attributes under general and at the top level of each of the 50 files mentions QC, quality, pass, fail, exclusion or rejection; all are printed for 759666166, a failed session of 411400.

outcomes.statement: Each mouse had three 70-minute imaging sessions within three to six days, with at most one session per day.
outcomes.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Following habituation, they underwent three 70-minute optical imaging sessions within a span of three to six days, with no more than one session occurring per day
outcomes.notes: Under combination (i)(b), local sessions 1 to 3 with calendar days counted inclusively, all 13 mice span 3 to 6 days and no mouse has two sessions on one date; this holds with the dates as stated and with the clock read as UTC. With the dates as stated, (i)(a) fails for 6 mice (2-day spans), (ii)(a) for 5, and (ii)(b) for 411400 (7 days). Sessions last 70.06 to 70.37 min by the stimulus table and 70.22 to 70.53 min by the imaging.
deviations: Local session numbers are the order of the start times in each subject, which equals Supplementary Table 1's numbering; the selection of reading (ii) uses its QC results.

outcomes.statement: Somata were imaged at 175 um (L2/3) and 375 um (L5) depth, and distal apical dendrites at 50 to 75 um (L2/3) and 20 um (L5).
outcomes.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: two-photon calcium imaging was performed in either the cell body layer for somatic recordings (175 μ m depth for layer 2/3 and 375 μ m depth for layer 5) or in cortical layer 1 for distal apical dendritic recordings (50–75 μ m depth for layer 2/3 and 20 μ m depth for layer 5)
outcomes.notes: All 50 sessions are at the depth the criterion gives for their line and plane (175 and 375 um for somata, 20 um for L5 dendrites, 50 to 75 um inclusive for L2/3 dendrites). The three sessions of L2/3 dendritic mouse 433414 are recorded at 60 um, inside the range. What the answer changed is that the criterion first admitted only 50 or 75 um for L2/3 dendrites, under which 47 of 50 sessions passed and the claim was not reproduced. The answer of 2026-10-22 (questions/000037.yaml) replaced the two values with the Methods' range, so the outcome is now reproduced. Table 2 gives 75 um for these sessions; that difference is recorded under table2-sessions and as a finding.

outcomes.statement: Calcium movies were recorded at 30 Hz over a 400 um field of view at 512 x 512 pixels, and running was recorded at 60 Hz in cm/s.
outcomes.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 2; Running and pupil tracking, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Calcium fluorescence movies were recorded at 30 Hz with resonant scanners over a 400 μ m field of view with a resolution of 512 × 512 pixels
outcomes.notes: Imaging at 30.08 to 30.15 Hz by the timestamps (stated 30 Hz), running at 59.95 Hz in cm/s in every session, and 512 x 512 pixel masks and projection images. The statement's 400 um field of view is not recorded in the files and was not tested.

outcomes.statement: ROIs that were too noisy, with a mean dF/F below 0 or a median dF/F above the midpoint between the trace's minimum and maximum, were rejected, so no retained ROI has either property.
outcomes.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: any remaining ROIs identified as being duplicates or unions, overlapping the motion border or being too noisy (defined as having a mean ΔF/F below 0 or a median ΔF/F above the mid-range ΔF/F, i.e., the midpoint between the minimum and maximum) were rejected
outcomes.notes: 0 of 19115 ROIs over the 50 sessions have a mean dF/F below 0 or a median above the mid-range; the lowest ROI mean is 0.0006. The duplicate, union and motion-border rules were not tested, as the criterion says.

outcomes.statement: Somatic planes yielded 15 to 224 ROIs per mouse per session and dendritic planes 159 to 1636.
outcomes.source: Methods, Experimental animals and calcium imaging, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: In the somatic layers, 15–224 ROIs per mouse per session were identified and retained for analysis, compared to 159–1636 ROIs in the dendritic layers.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), the 33 analysed sessions, somatic planes hold 15 to 224 ROIs and dendritic planes 159 to 1636. Reading (b), sessions passing QC, gives the same, and reading (c), all 50 sessions, gives 15 to 227 and 159 to 1636; all three are within tolerance.

outcomes.statement: Matching produced 254 tracked ROIs in L2/3 dendritic planes, 261 in L2/3 somatic, 516 in L5 dendritic and 129 in L5 somatic, about 100 to 500 per plane and about 32 to 75% of the theoretical maximum number of trackable ROIs.
outcomes.source: Methods, ROI tracking across sessions, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: In total, the modified matching algorithm produced ~100–500 highly plausible matched ROIs per plane, i.e., ~32–75% of the theoretical maximum number of trackable ROIs (L2/3-D: n = 254, L2/3-S: n = 261, L5-D: n = 516, L5-S: n = 129)
outcomes.notes: Summed over the 11 mice of the paper's analyses, 254, 261, 516 and 129 tracked ROIs, equal to the stated totals. With the theoretical maximum read as (a), the smallest ROI count of each mouse's three tracked sessions, the plane percentages run from 32.9 to 75.0%; reading (b), the mean count, gives 25.4 to 65.7%, outside. Over all 13 tracked mice the dendritic totals are 352 and 678.

outcomes.statement: The same imaging planes were recorded over three days and many ROIs could be identified in each day's recording, so that individual dendritic segments and somata can be followed over the three sessions.
outcomes.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: By segmenting the data in each plane into regions of interest (ROIs), and registering these ROIs across recording days, we were able to identify single ROIs that were present in each day's recording.
outcomes.notes: All 13 tracked mice have three tracked sessions with equal counts (12 to 353), each index once per session, and the same indices in the three sessions. In an added check on the mask centroids (masks not registered), the same index lies a median of 1.9 to 14.5 pixels apart across sessions against 11.5 to 62.4 pixels to the nearest other tracked ROI, and is the closest for 55% (411400) to 100% of ROIs.
deviations: The mask centroid check is added; it is not in the criterion and decides nothing.

outcomes.statement: In the example L2/3 dendritic mouse of Fig. 8a, removing four conflicting pairwise matches from the union over session orderings left 136 final matches.
outcomes.source: Figure 8a legend
outcomes.quote: In this example, four pairwise matches were identified as conflicts and removed, yielding 136 final matches.
outcomes.notes: Mouse 413663 has 136 tracked ROIs in each of its three sessions.

outcomes.statement: For the same mouse, the union of matches over all session orderings held four conflicting matches, which were removed.
outcomes.source: Figure 8a legend
outcomes.quote: In this example, four pairwise matches were identified as conflicts and removed
outcomes.notes: The repository's matching files give a union of 140 matches for 413663; 140 - 136 tracked ROIs in the dataset = 4. The files of its three sessions agree.

outcomes.statement: In the example L5 somatic mouse of Fig. 8b, removing two conflicting pairwise matches left 47 final matches.
outcomes.source: Figure 8b legend
outcomes.quote: Combining matched ROIs across all permutations did nonetheless, in this example mouse, enable two of the pairwise matches to be identified as conflicts and removed, yielding 47 final matches.
outcomes.notes: Mouse 411771 has 47 tracked ROIs in each of its three sessions.

outcomes.statement: For the same L5 somatic mouse, two conflicting matches were removed from the union over session orderings.
outcomes.source: Figure 8b legend
outcomes.quote: enable two of the pairwise matches to be identified as conflicts and removed
outcomes.notes: The repository's matching files give a union of 49 matches for 411771; 49 - 47 = 2.

outcomes.statement: The number of matched ROIs varied less across session orderings for somata than for dendrites.
outcomes.source: Figure 8b legend
outcomes.quote: The variation in number of matched ROIs across session orderings for somata was generally far less than that for dendrites due to their larger sizes and more regular shapes.
outcomes.notes: Of the 39 matching files in the repository (13 mice), only those of 413663 and 411771 hold counts per session ordering; the dataset holds only the final matches, and the paper's modified matching code is not linked. In the two examples the range over orderings is 3 matches for the dendritic mouse (129 to 132, 2.2% of 136) and 1 for the somatic mouse (47 to 48, 2.1% of 47), smaller for somata in absolute terms and about equal as a fraction.

outcomes.statement: Gabor sequences are repeating 1.5-s sequences of five 300-ms images (A-B-C-D-G), each non-grey image holding 30 Gabor patches, with inconsistent sequences replacing D by U, whose mean orientation is shifted by 90 degrees (drawn from 90, 135, 180 and 225 degrees, against 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees for the other images).
outcomes.source: Methods, Visual stimulation, paragraphs 2 and 3
outcomes.quote: it consisted of repeating 1.5-second sequences, each comprising five consecutive images ( A-B-C-D-G ) presented for 300 ms each ... “Inconsistent” sequences were created by replacing D images with U images in the sequence ( A-B-C-U-G ) ... namely from {90°, 135°, 180°, 225°}
outcomes.notes: In all 50 sessions the 1360 sequences follow A-B-C-D-G or A-B-C-U-G, every non-grey image holds 30 patches (kappa 16), A to D take mean orientations 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees, and U takes 90, 135, 180 and 225, always the sequence's mean plus 90. The median image lasts 300 ms. Every image is within 300 ms +/- 10% in 46 of 50 sessions; four sessions hold 1 to 5 images outside it (13 of 340000 in all, up to 604 ms), three of them the failed-QC sessions of 411400, for which Supplementary Table 1's experimental notes record dropped stimulus frames (printed in the notebook). The criterion asks for every image in every session, so that part holds in 46 of 50. The criterion names no partial outcome; the claim holds in part, the protocol's partially reproduced, and a strict reading that admits only reproduced or not would give not reproduced.

outcomes.statement: Visual flow is 105 white squares of 8 by 8 degrees moving at 50 degrees per second, in two consecutive periods (rightward and leftward) in random order, with 25% of squares reversed for 2 to 4 s during inconsistent flow.
outcomes.source: Methods, Visual stimulation, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: The visual flow stimulus consisted of 105 white squares moving uniformly across the screen at a velocity of 50 visual degrees per second, with each square being 8 by 8 visual degrees in size.
outcomes.notes: In all 50 sessions the table records 105 squares and a reversed proportion of 0.25, and the directions run as two consecutive periods (rightward first in 26). Reversals last 1.99 to 4.01 s. At the first frame of each session's first reversal a median of 24.8% of squares move against the flow (15.2 to 32.4%). Size and speed in degrees are not testable, as the table gives the unwarped stimulus in pixels (128 pixels, 780 pixels/s); their ratio, 6.09 per second, is within 3% of the paper's 50/8 = 6.25.

outcomes.statement: Each imaging session lasted 70 min, with 34 min of Gabor sequences and 17 min of visual flow in each direction, each stimulus period flanked by 30 s of grey screen.

findings.statement: The session start times are stated with a Pacific offset (-07:00 or -08:00), but their clock values are those Supplementary Table 1 gives as UTC, for all 50 sessions. For four sessions (412933 session 765427689, and 418779's three sessions) the stated date is a day after the imaging date of Table 2, and the date of birth implied by 418779's age is a day after Table 1's.
The three sessions of mouse 433414 are recorded at a depth of 60 um; Table 2 and Supplementary Table 1 give 75 um. Which is right is not known from the files.

The files hold no QC result, local session number or stimulus seed. The paper's analyses use only sessions 1 to 3 that passed QC, and the dandiset's description points to an outside table (the metadata repository) for which sessions were excluded.
The imaging plane (somata or distal apical dendrites) is not recorded; it follows from the depth. The field of view in um is not recorded.
Visual flow square size and position are given in pixels of the unwarped stimulus, with no screen geometry to convert them to the degrees the paper states (8 degrees, 50 degrees/s).

The dF/F of the 28 dendritic sessions is stored gzip-compressed in small chunks (991 to 1994 frames by 5 to 26 ROIs), and the chunk index is spread through the file, so streaming it through remfile and h5py is slow; the 22 somatic files store it contiguous. The notebook therefore streams each basic file whole into memory before reading it.

In two sessions the dF/F response to grey screen transitions does not exceed the 99th percentile of the responses at shifted times (777496949, 15 ROIs, above 94.6% of them; 838633305, which failed QC and whose experimental notes in Supplementary Table 1 say the laser was set to 800 nm, while the file states 910 nm), so their alignment to the trial table could not be shown. It is shown in the other 48.

The per-ordering ROI matching counts behind Fig. 8 are published for two mice only, and the paper's modified matching code is not linked, so the comparison of order dependence between somata and dendrites cannot be repeated.

attempts.label: DANDI:000041
attempts.paper_title: Network Homeostasis and State Dynamics of Neocortical Sleep
attempts.entry_title: Firing rates across sleep states in rat frontal cortex (Watson et al. 2016)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Watson, Levenstein, Greene, Gelinas and Buzsaki (2016) on dandiset 000041, which holds silicon probe recordings of units, LFP and sleep states from the frontal cortex of 10 rats in their home cage. It compares firing rates and bursting across WAKE, nonREM and REM, how rates of fast and slow firing cells change over sleep and within nonREM packets, how they relate to LFP band power, and the rate changes across state triplets. UP and DOWN state and spindle analyses are blocked, as their methods are in the unavailable supplement.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Watson et al. (2016) from dandiset 000041

outcomes.statement: The recordings come from 11 rats and 27 sessions of 294 plus or minus 137 min, yielding 995 putative pyramidal cells and 126 putative interneurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of brain states, paragraph 1; Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 1; Experimental Procedures
outcomes.quote: We recorded across different brain states from 11 rats ... Recordings from 27 sessions (294±137 min) ... This resulted in 995 putative pyramidal (pE) cells ... and 126 putative interneurons (pI)
outcomes.notes: Two of five values are within tolerance, 10 rats and a mean session duration of 286.8 min (SD 150.2). The files hold 22 sessions, 826 excitatory and 96 inhibitory units (and 23 of unknown type); the 21 usable sessions hold 812 pE and 89 pI cells. Per session the pE count is close to the paper's (mean 38.7, range 10 to 105, against 36.9 and 10 to 104).
deviations: Counted on the files as deposited, with session duration from the state table.

outcomes.statement: Median firing rates of pE cells are 0.76 Hz in WAKE, 0.69 Hz in nonREM and 0.88 Hz in REM; of pI cells 5.59, 4.69 and 4.25 Hz.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 2; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: Median rates (±SD) of putative pyramidal cells in each state were: WAKE: 0.76±1.53 Hz, nonREM: 0.69±0.86 Hz, REM: 0.88±1.33 Hz; and for putative interneurons were: WAKE: 5.59±7.25 Hz, nonREM: 4.69±5.62 Hz, REM 4.25±9.43 Hz.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a) the three pE medians are within tolerance (0.755, 0.662 and 0.825 Hz) and the three pI medians are below it (3.92, 2.73 and 3.06 Hz, against 5.59, 4.69 and 4.25). Reading (b) gives the same counts (pE WAKE 0.748). The pI sample is 89 cells in 9 subjects, with per-subject medians from 0.07 to 13.4 Hz across subjects and states.
deviations: 812 pE and 89 pI cells from 21 sessions, against 995 and 126 from 27.
WAKE excludes microarousals derived from the Awake label, not the paper's scored MAs.

outcomes.statement: The distribution of pE firing rates is strongly positively skewed and spans three orders of magnitude, from 0.05 to 5 Hz.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 2; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: the distribution of per-cell mean firing rates for putative pyramidal neurons was strongly positively skewed ... spanning three orders of magnitude range from 0.05 Hz to 5 Hz (Figure 2A)
outcomes.notes: WAKE rates have skewness 4.57 and a 97.5th percentile of 7.17 Hz (within a factor of 2 of 5 Hz), but the 2.5th percentile is 0.0124 Hz, about four times below 0.05 Hz. 13 of 812 cells have a WAKE rate of zero. The log10 rates are skewed to the left (-0.74).
deviations: The paper's range is read from a log axis; the factor-of-2 tolerance was fixed in the criterion.

outcomes.statement: The fraction of pE cells firing above 2 Hz is 19.2% in WAKE, 19.2% in REM and 8.8% in nonREM (chi-square, p < 1e-10).
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 2; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: The right tail extended toward higher rates during WAKE and REM compared to nonREM (Figure 2A; fraction of >2 Hz neurons: WAKE= 19.2%; REM= 19.2%; nonREM= 8.8%; Chi-Square Test
outcomes.notes: REM (18.7%) and nonREM (9.1%) are within tolerance, WAKE (17.0%) is not. nonREM is lower than WAKE (chi-square 21.5, p = 3.5e-06) and REM (30.5, p = 3.4e-08), but neither test reaches p < 1e-10, which the criterion requires. The direction of the effect is as in the paper, with fewer cells than the paper had. Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked against the spikes, WAKE is 20.2% (within tolerance) and both tests still miss p < 1e-10.

outcomes.statement: Per-cell nonREM and WAKE rates are highly correlated (R = 0.82), and the slope of their relation is below 1 (95% confidence interval 0.66 to 0.71), so state transitions act differently across the rate spectrum.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 2; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: Whereas nonREM and WAKE firing rates remained highly correlated on a per-cell basis (R = 0.82 ... the slope of this relationship significantly deviated from 1 (Figure 2B) ... (95% confidence interval of slope: 0.66 – 0.71)

statistics.about: correlation of nonREM and WAKE rates
slope of the nonREM against WAKE rate relation

outcomes.notes: On log10 rates (799 cells, 13 with a zero rate left out), R = 0.862 and the slope of nonREM on WAKE is 0.757 (95% CI 0.727 to 0.788). In Hz the slope is 0.583 (0.560 to 0.607), outside the widened interval. The reverse regression on log10 rates gives 0.982 (0.942 to 1.022), so the slope below 1 may in part be regression to the mean. Per subject the slope ranges from 0.41 to 0.91. A split-half control (alternate WAKE epochs of each cell) gives a slope of 0.936 between halves and a reliability of 0.961 for the log10 WAKE rate; corrected for this noise the slope is 0.788 (0.756 to 0.821), still below 1. The rest of the gap to 1 comes from the WAKE-nonREM correlation being below 1, which is also regression to the mean. The ratio of the SDs of log10 rates, nonREM over WAKE, is 0.878 (Pitman-Morgan p = 9.8e-13, 95% interval resampling sessions 0.777 to 0.971), so the spread of rates is narrower in nonREM.
deviations: The paper does not say whether the slope is on log or linear rates; both readings are shown and the log reading matches.

outcomes.statement: The burst index (fraction of spikes with inter-spike intervals under 15 ms) is highest in nonREM (median 11.8%), lowest in WAKE (4.0%), with REM (5.5%) slightly above WAKE (Kruskal-Wallis, p < 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Burst index was highest during nonREM (median in nonREM = 11.8%) and lowest during WAKE (4.0 %), with REM (5.5 %) slightly higher than WAKE (p < 0.05; Kruskal-Wallis test).
outcomes.notes: The order nonREM > REM > WAKE holds under both readings, with Kruskal-Wallis p = 5.7e-36 (a) and 7.3e-38 (b), and REM above WAKE (paired Wilcoxon p = 1e-32). Reading (a), the fraction of intervals under 15 ms, gives medians of 6.35, 2.64 and 3.65%, none within tolerance; reading (b), the fraction of spikes in such an interval, gives 11.67% in nonREM (within tolerance), 4.95% in WAKE and 6.71% in REM (above). The measured values are those of reading (a), the first listed. The paired Friedman test over the 753 cells with all three values gives p = 3.9e-151.
deviations: The definition "fraction of spikes with ISIs under 15 ms" can be read two ways; both are shown and neither matches all three medians.

outcomes.statement: The average spike autocorrelogram of pE cells peaks near 8 ms in nonREM, with a smaller peak near 125 ms (theta) in REM and WAKE.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: a large peak occurred at approximately 8ms inter-spike interval during nonREM, whereas smaller peaks were present at ~125 ms (i.e., theta frequency) during REM and WAKE (Figure 2C)
outcomes.notes: The nonREM autocorrelogram peaks at 8.5 ms. The smoothed REM and WAKE autocorrelograms are highest at the 60 ms edge of the 60 to 250 ms window, so the criterion finds no theta peak. In a variant that divides the 21 ms smoothing by a 101 ms one, WAKE has a maximum at 118.5 ms (ratio 1.016) and REM at 142.5 ms (1.017). Per subject the REM maximum falls within 112.5 to 137.5 ms in two subjects (Bogey 135.5, Dino 125.5). Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked, the nonREM peak is at 6.5 ms, outside 7 to 9 ms, so the nonREM part rests on the sample as well as on the method. A fix to the binning (lags rounded to 1 ns, so that float error does not move a lag on a bin edge) moved the nonREM peak from 7.5 to 8.5 ms.
deviations: The peak location criteria (windows, 21 ms smoothing) were fixed here; the paper shows the peaks in a figure only.

outcomes.statement: The autocorrelogram of pE cells decays faster in nonREM than in WAKE and REM (decay fit exponent medians -1.35, -0.83 and -0.80; Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: Time decay of the autocorrelograms of pyramidal neurons was significantly faster during nonREM compared to WAKE and REM (Figure 2C; decay fit exponent median nonREM = – 1.35, WAKE = – 0.83, REM = – 0.80; p < 0.05; Kruskal-Wallis test).
outcomes.notes: The main text gives decay fit exponents but not what is fitted (function, lag range); the Supplemental Experimental Procedures, which would say, could not be retrieved (PubMed Central and the publisher answer with a browser check). The autocorrelograms themselves are computed for fig2c-acg-peaks.

outcomes.statement: In nonREM, pairs of fast-firing pE cells are positively correlated, while pairs of one slow and one fast cell are negatively correlated.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, paragraph 5; Figure 2F
outcomes.quote: the fastest and slowest firing neurons tended to be positively correlated within groups, but were actually negatively correlated across groups (Figure 2F).
outcomes.notes: Over 20764 same-session pE pairs (169 without a defined correlation), the (6,6) mean correlation of 100 ms counts in nonREM is 0.0424, the largest of the 21 group combinations, and correlations rise with the rates of both cells. The (1,6) mean is 0.0089, above zero (t = 10.85, p = 8.7e-26); 22.8% of all pairs are negative, but no group combination has a negative mean. Reading (b) gives the same pattern ((6,6) 0.0401, (1,6) 0.0087).
deviations: The correlation measure is Pearson correlation of raw counts in 100 ms bins; the paper's measure and test are in the unavailable supplement and may differ (for example a correction for the shared UP/DOWN modulation).

outcomes.statement: Microarousals have a median duration of 15.9 plus or minus 3.3 s, occur 0.32 plus or minus 0.12 times per minute and occupy 9.1 plus or minus 3.5% of SLEEP (790 in total).
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of brain states, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: There were a total of 790 MAs in our dataset (median duration = 15.9±3.3sec; frequency = 0.32±0.12 per minute; 9.1±3.5% of time in SLEEP).
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), median MA duration 19.0 s (within the spread), 0.096 MAs per minute of SLEEP and 3.22% of SLEEP time; reading (b) gives 19.0 s, 0.127 per min and 4.23%. The paper reports 0.32 and 9.1%. 391 MAs in 21 sessions (262 inside SLEEP periods), against 790 in 27. Looser rules raise the counts but none reaches both values: Non-REM on at least one side and under 60 s gives 0.177 per min and 7.63% of SLEEP; every Awake epoch inside SLEEP gives 0.245 per min and 13.66%. outcomes.statement: The dataset holds 54 WAKE-SLEEP episodes (at least 7 min of WAKE followed by at least 20 min of SLEEP), an average of 2.0 per session, and sessions without one were discarded.

outcomes.statement: The mean firing rate of pE cells declines over the course of SLEEP, restricted to nonREM (R = -0.11, p < 1e-3).

30 cycles from 21 sessions, against 54 from 27.

outcomes.statement: The mean pE rate is lower in the last than in the first nonREM packet of SLEEP (1.04 plus or minus 1.20 against 0.88 plus or minus 0.91 Hz; Wilcoxon p < 0.02).
outcomes.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 1

outcomes.notes: Over 1070 cell and cycle pairs, 1.0915 plus or minus 1.483 Hz in the first packet and 0.9679 plus or minus 1.241 Hz in the last (the upper bound of tolerance is 0.968), Wilcoxon p = 3.9e-06. Without the seven sessions whose LFP could not be checked, the last mean is 1.006 Hz, outside tolerance.
deviations: 30 cycles from 21 sessions, against 54 from 27.

outcomes.statement: Comparing the same neurons in the first and last nonREM packets of SLEEP, the regression slope departs from 1 (95% confidence interval 0.827 to 0.880), as fast cells slow down and slow cells speed up.
outcomes.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, paragraph 2; Figure 3D
outcomes.quote: we assessed spike rates of the same neurons in the first versus the last nonREM packets of SLEEP and found the slope of this correlation significantly departed from unity (slope 95% confidence interval 0.827–0.880)
outcomes.notes: On log10 rates (1021 pairs, 49 with a zero rate left out) the slope of last on first is 0.801 (95% CI 0.768 to 0.834); in Hz 0.723. The reverse regression gives 0.864 (0.829 to 0.900), and the second half of the first packet regressed on its first half gives 0.855 (0.829 to 0.881), above the first-to-last slope. Corrected for the noise of the first-packet rate (reliability 0.946 from its halves), the slope is 0.846 (0.812 to 0.881), still below 1. The ratio of the SDs of log10 rates, last over first packet, is 0.963, a narrowing of about 4% that is significant over pairs (Pitman-Morgan p = 0.028) but not when cycles are resampled (95% interval 0.892 to 1.029). Most of the slope below 1 comes from the first-to-last correlation being below 1 (R = 0.832), so the claim's reading that fast cells slow down and slow cells speed up is weakly supported. The criterion, fixed before the analysis, judges the slope alone.
deviations: The paper does not say whether the regression is on log or linear rates; both are shown.

Reading (b), 727 cells, gives the same pattern (population p = 1.4e-09, sextile 1 p = 0.36). In 23 of 30 cycles the WAKE after SLEEP is shorter than 300 s. With the pre-sleep window cut to the length of the post-sleep one, the result is the same (population p = 1.7e-09, sextile 1 p = 0.18, sextile 6 p = 1.8e-05). findings.statement: The dandiset holds 22 sessions from 10 rats, where the paper and the dandiset's own description report 27 sessions from 11 rats; the files hold 945 units (826 excitatory, 96 inhibitory, 23 unknown) against the 995 putative pyramidal cells and 126 interneurons analysed. Which sessions and units were left out, and why, is not stated.

In sub-Dino_ses-Dino-072114 the spike times are whole seconds divided by 20000 (8451 distinct values from 0 to 0.4252 s, in a recording of 7959 s). The conversion read this session's spikes from a CellExplorer file with a hard-coded 20 kHz rate. The session's spikes cannot be used.

In sub-Dino_ses-Dino-061914 the LFP has 125 columns for 128 electrodes, lasts 331.7 min against 291.9 min of states and spikes, and its samples are scrambled (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.28 on the reference channel, against 0.99 or more in every other session), consistent with a 128-channel file read as 125 channels.

The state table holds only Awake, Non-REM and REM. The paper scores microarousals as a state of their own and builds WAKE-SLEEP episodes, nonREM packets and episodes, UP/DOWN states and spindles, none of which is in the dandiset. MAs derived from short Awake epochs are fewer than the paper reports (391 in 21 sessions, against 790 in 27).

The dandiset does not say how the state table was scored. The conversion code takes it from each session's SleepState.states.mat; it yields 30 WAKE-SLEEP cycles in 21 sessions (3 sessions with none, though the paper kept only sessions with a full cycle), and only 49 of 534 REM epochs are followed directly by Non-REM, so it may not be the scoring the paper used.

The dandiset description gives 11 animals, 27 sessions and 1360 units, the paper's numbers, while the files hold 10 animals, 22 sessions and 945 units (the archive's summary counts 10 subjects). The description gives an age of 4-7 months, the files 3-7 months.
The LFP is stored as int16 with unit volts and conversion NaN, so it cannot be converted to volts.

Every electrode's location is "unknown" and every unit's region is "CTX" or "unknown", although the paper records from medial prefrontal, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate and secondary motor cortex; only the electrode groups carry a region.
23 units of sub-BWRat21_ses-BWRat21-121613 have cell type and region "unknown", with no description of what the label means.
No movement, accelerometer or EMG data are in the dandiset, though the paper uses EMG to score states and movement to define WAKE and to relate WAKE to rate changes.

The state labels are consistent with the spikes in 20 of 21 sessions (not established for BWRat21-121813), but in 14 sessions the best agreement is with the table shifted 5 to 60 s earlier, so state boundaries may lag the activity. The LFP agrees with the spikes to within 50 ms in 14 of 21 sessions. Of the other seven, three (BWRat21-121113, Bogey-012615, Dino-072414) have a clear cross-correlation extreme 56 to 64 ms from zero lag; in three (BWRat17-121912, BWRat21-121613, BWRat21-121813) the extreme is less than three times the value at plus or minus 1 s, so agreement is not established; and the LFP of Dino-061914 is scrambled.
