attempts.label: DANDI:000044
attempts.paper_title: Diversity in neural firing dynamics supports both rigid and learned hippocampal sequences
attempts.entry_title: Rigid and plastic hippocampal sequences (Grosmark and Buzsaki 2016)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) on dandiset 000044, which holds eight sessions of CA1 units, LFP, sleep states and track positions from four rats, each with sleep before and after exploring a novel track. It decodes candidate ripple events with a Bayesian decoder, compares sequence scores across PRE, MAZE and POST, estimates each place cell's contribution to sequences, and relates firing rate and ripple gain to coactivation and replay.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) from dandiset 000044

outcomes.statement: Recordings were made in four rats, in eight novel exploration sessions, each a PRE sleep, a MAZE epoch on one of two linear tracks or a circular track, and a POST sleep.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure S1 (as cited in the text)
outcomes.quote: Simultaneous recordings of well-isolated CA1 pyramidal single units were performed in four rats ... exploration of one of two linear or a circular track (MAZE) ... preexperience sleep (PRE) and postexperience sleep (POST) ... (eight novel exploration sessions)
outcomes.notes: 4 subjects and 8 sessions, each with PRE, MAZE and POST epochs in that order (8 of 8), on a 1.6 m linear track (4 sessions), a 2 m linear track (1) and a circular track (3). PRE lasts 2.98 to 5.37 h, MAZE 34.5 to 92.7 min and POST 2.22 to 4.51 h. The rooms the paper names are not in the files.

outcomes.statement: The Bayesian decoder was built from 491 place cells over the eight sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: a spatial Bayesian decoder (2), constructed from the firing-rate vectors of place cells (n = 491 cells) during track running (eight novel exploration sessions)
outcomes.notes: 417 of the 562 pyramidal units have a smoothed rate-map peak of 1 Hz or more on running, below 491 by more than the tolerance of 49. At 0.5 Hz the count is 480 (within tolerance), at 2 Hz 352, so the count depends strongly on the threshold; the criterion fixes 1 Hz and the other thresholds are variants that do not decide the outcome. By subject, Achilles 181, Buddy 30, Cicero 127, Gatsby 79.
deviations: The place-cell definition is a common choice (peak of 1 Hz or more on running above 5 cm/s, 2 cm bins, 4 cm smoothing); the paper's definition is in the supplementary Methods, which were not available.

outcomes.statement: Sequence scores (rZ) of candidate events are higher in POST sleep than in PRE sleep (replay).
outcomes.source: Figure 1C
outcomes.quote: Cumulative distribution of rZ for PRE, MAZE, and POSTevents, and 95% confidence intervals. ... Inset, mean ± SE of sequence scores in each condition. *P < 0.05; **P < 0.005; ***P < 0.0005 (Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by post hoc Tukey-Kramer tests).
outcomes.notes: Pooled over sessions, as the criterion fixes the test, POST does not exceed PRE (mean rZ 0.763 against 0.770, Tukey on ranks after Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.412). Within sessions it does; POST is higher in 8 of 8 sessions (sign test p = 0.0039; one-sided rank-sum p < 0.05 in 6), and with each session's PRE mean subtracted POST is higher by 0.106 (p = 2.3e-14). The pooled test is dominated by the three circular-track sessions, which score lower in every epoch (PRE 0.161 and POST 0.260 against 1.112 and 1.207 on the linear tracks, where the event takes the better of two templates) and supply 11161 of 23801 POST events but 5912 of 16448 PRE events. The same test run on each kind of track finds POST above PRE on the five linear-track sessions (Tukey on ranks p = 5.1e-07) and on the three circular-track sessions (p = 1.1e-05). By subject, POST minus PRE is +0.089 (Achilles), +0.185 (Buddy), +0.021 (Cicero) and -0.173 (Gatsby) when pooled within subject.
deviations: Candidate events are population bursts of all units holding a ripple (150 to 250 Hz envelope above 3 SD on one LFP channel per session), outside REM in PRE and POST and below 5 cm/s in MAZE; the paper's detection is in the unavailable Methods.
The rZ null is 200 column-cycle shuffles of the posterior; the paper's shuffle is not stated in the main text.
On the linear tracks each event takes the better of the two direction templates, which raises their scores over those of the single-template circular track.
The Tukey comparison is scipy's Tukey HSD on the pooled ranks, not MATLAB's Tukey-Kramer after kruskalwallis.
Immobility for MAZE candidate events is taken from the 2D head speed, while running for the rate maps is taken from the speed of the linearized position, both at 5 cm/s.

outcomes.statement: Sequence content is higher in MAZE immobility events than in PRE sleep events.
outcomes.source: Figure 1C; Figure 2C legend
outcomes.quote: the marked increase in sequence content observed in the MAZE and POSTepochs is driven by the recruitment of plastic cells
outcomes.notes: MAZE events score higher than PRE events (mean rZ 1.270 against 0.770, n = 2460 and 16448; Tukey on ranks p printed as 0), and MAZE is higher in all 8 sessions (one-sided rank-sum p from below 0.0001 to 0.0405). It holds on the linear-track sessions (p printed as 0) and on the circular-track sessions (p = 0.0007) separately. MAZE has 76 to 953 scored events per session.
deviations: Events and scores as for fig1c-post-gt-pre.

outcomes.statement: 216 neurons showed significant PCC scores in PRE or POST and were considered to contribute strongly to sequences.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: Neurons that showed significant PCC scores in either PRE or POST were considered to be strongly contributing to sequence formation (n = 216 neurons (Fig. 2B)
outcomes.notes: The test fixed in the criterion (one-sided signed-rank test of a cell's contributions over its events, p < 0.05) finds 303 strongly contributing cells (72.7% of 417 place cells), against 216. With every rate map shifted it calls 56.1% of cells significant (0.843 on the 1.6 m tracks, 0.905 on the 2 m track, 0.140 on the circular track), so about 234 would be expected by chance. The paper calls these PCC scores significant, which implies a 5% false-positive rate; this test is far from it, so it is not the paper's procedure. The excess is on the linear tracks, where the contribution is taken on the template the event was selected for. A best-template variant of the contribution has a false-positive rate of 0.206 (0.132 in PRE, 0.118 in POST) and finds 188 cells, outside the tolerance; at alpha 0.001 its false-positive rate is 0.031 and it finds 95. The false-positive rates are measured on every fourth PRE and POST event, so on all events they would likely be higher. The best-template numbers are not identical across machines (the verifier's executed copy printed 190 cells and 0.129 in PRE); no conclusion rests on the difference. The PCC definition and its test are in the unavailable Methods.
deviations: The PCC and its significance test are choices made here, as the Methods were not available.
The 20 shifts of a cell's map are drawn afresh for every event.

outcomes.statement: Most neurons strongly contributing to PRE sequences (73%) also contributed to POST sequences.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2C as cited
outcomes.quote: Importantly, the majority of neurons strongly contributing to PRE (73%) also contributed to POST sequences (Fig. 2C and fig. S19)
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Of 248 PRE strongly contributing cells, 235 (94.8%) also contribute in POST, against a chance level of 69.5%. With the best-template variant 72 of 102 (70.6%), within 73 +/- 7.3, against a chance level of 37.9%.

outcomes.statement: The PRE to POST increase in sequence score is eliminated when the place fields of the 10 to 20% of cells with the highest dPCC are shuffled, and remains after shuffling the bottom 75%.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: Replay (POST > PRE) was eliminated after shuffling or removal of the top 10 to 20% of cells with the highest ΔPCC scores, whereas it remained after shuffling or removal of the bottom 75%
outcomes.notes: On the pooled test of the criterion replay is absent after shuffling the top 10% (POST minus PRE -0.100, p = 1.0) and the top 20% (-0.127, p = 1.0), but also after shuffling the bottom 75% (+0.022, p = 0.21), so one of the two conditions holds. The pooled test finds no replay before shuffling either (-0.008, p = 0.916), so on all sessions it cannot show a removal. On the five linear-track sessions replay is present before shuffling (+0.101, p < 0.0001), absent after shuffling the top 10% (+0.015, p = 0.23) or 20% (-0.039, p = 0.995) and present after the bottom 75% (+0.098, p < 0.0001); shuffling a random 10% or 20% leaves it (+0.099, +0.088). dPCC is measured on the events that are decoded again. Ranking cells on the even-numbered events and measuring replay on the odd-numbered ones, on the linear tracks replay falls from +0.116 to +0.046 (p = 0.024) after the top 10% and +0.042 (p = 0.038) after the top 20%, so out of sample it is reduced but not removed.
deviations: Variant decodes use 50 column-cycle shuffles per event in place of 200.
dPCC is the difference of the criterion's PCC, whose significance test is not the paper's (fig2b-strong-contributors); the ranking does not use that test.

outcomes.statement: The PRE to POST increase in sequence content is attributable to a small number of plastic cells; removing them, unlike removing rigid cells, removes the increase.
outcomes.source: Figure 2E
outcomes.quote: The PRE to POST increase in sequence content is attributable to only a small number of plastic cells.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. On the pooled test, removing plastic cells gives POST minus PRE -0.168 (p = 1.0) and removing rigid cells +0.038 (p = 0.019); removing as many random strongly contributing cells gives -0.023 (p = 0.99). On the linear-track sessions -0.060, +0.136 and +0.094. With classes from the even-numbered events and replay on the odd-numbered ones, the linear tracks give -0.009 (p = 0.54) and +0.090 (p = 0.0027). With the best-template classes, pooled, -0.125 and +0.020 (p = 0.24).

outcomes.statement: Rigid and plastic neurons were similarly distributed along the track.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; fig. S2 as cited
outcomes.quote: Rigid and plastic neurons were similarly distributed along the track (fig. S2).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Rate-map peaks of rigid and plastic cells do not differ by the KS test (medians 0.419 and 0.486 of the track, D = 0.145, p = 0.072); with the split over all place cells p = 0.079, with the best-template classes p = 0.12.

outcomes.statement: Plastic neurons had higher place-specific indices and fewer place fields than rigid cells.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 3A
outcomes.quote: Plastic neurons had higher place-specific indices and fewer place fields compared with rigid cells (Fig. 3A)
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Plastic cells carry more spatial information (median 0.904 against 0.594 bits per spike, p = 1.9e-05; best-template classes p = 0.0035), but the number of fields does not differ (means 1.484 and 1.685, p = 0.073).

outcomes.statement: Plastic but not rigid neurons increased their spatial specificity (in-field versus out-of-field firing ratio) steadily during the MAZE session.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 3B
outcomes.quote: plastic but not rigid neurons increased their spatial specificity steadily during learning (Fig. 3B and fig. S13)
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Both groups raise their in-field ratio over the session (change of log10 ratio, plastic median 0.155, p = 0.0079; rigid 0.129, p = 0.030; between groups p = 0.41). With the best-template classes plastic p = 0.020 and rigid p = 0.28.

outcomes.statement: Session-wide firing rates of rigid neurons were higher than those of plastic neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: Session-wide firing rates of rigid neurons were significantly higher compared with plastic neurons (Fig. 4, A and B, and figs. S14 and S15).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Rigid cells fire somewhat faster (median 0.700 against 0.591 Hz) without significance (p = 0.062; split over all place cells p = 0.053; best-template classes p = 0.74).

outcomes.statement: Ripple-related spiking, bursting and pairwise coactivation were higher in plastic than in rigid neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: Ripple-related spiking, bursting, and pair-wise coactivation were higher in plastic versus rigid neurons (Fig. 4A and figs. S14 to S16).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Ripple gain (4.489 against 3.939, p = 0.015) and bursting (0.180 against 0.147, p = 0.028) are higher in plastic cells; coactivation is not (0.028 against 0.027, p = 0.90). With the best-template classes none reaches p < 0.05 (gain p = 0.15, bursting p = 0.11).

outcomes.statement: In PRE sleep, coactivation was dominated by fast-firing neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: In PRE sleep, coactivity was dominated by fast-firing neurons, and these correlations remained unchanged into POST sleep.
outcomes.notes: PRE coactivation rises with firing rate, from 0.0208 in the slowest window to 0.0486 in the fastest; Spearman correlation 0.861 on the averaged curve, positive in 6 of 8 sessions. The POST minus PRE change of the fastest window does not differ from 0 over sessions (sign-rank p = 0.383), which fits the statement that these correlations remain into POST.
deviations: Coactivation over whole epochs, all states; the paper's restriction, if any, is not stated in the main text.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing neurons showed the strongest increases in coactivation from PRE to POST sleep.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: In contrast, slow-firing neurons showed the strongest increases in coactivation from PRE to POST sleep (Fig. 4B).
outcomes.notes: The POST minus PRE change does not fall with firing rate; Spearman correlation -0.068 on the averaged curve (p = 0.55), negative in 5 of 8 sessions. The averaged change is 0.0019 in the slowest window and -0.0007 in the fastest, with a maximum of 0.0090.
deviations: Coactivation over whole epochs, all states.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing cells showed the greatest replay, the partial correlation between RUN and POST coactivation accounting for PRE.
outcomes.source: Figure 4C legend
outcomes.quote: Moreover, it was the slow-firing cells that showed the greatest replay (partial correlation across coactivation values between RUN and POST, accounting for PRE).
outcomes.notes: The partial correlation of MAZE running and POST coactivation given PRE is 0.186 in the slowest window and 0.115 in the fastest, but the Spearman correlation over windows is 0.095 and negative in only 4 of 8 sessions. By subject it is -0.588 (Achilles), -0.646 (Buddy), -0.070 (Cicero) and 0.671 (Gatsby).
deviations: MAZE coactivation is taken over running bins (above 5 cm/s on the track).

outcomes.statement: Place cells divided into equal groups by sleep firing rate have medians of 0.39 Hz (low-rate) and 1.12 Hz (high-rate).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6
outcomes.quote: we divided place cells into equal subgroups by either “off-line” sleep-firing rate or ripple-rate gain ... Low-rate neurons (median, 0.39 Hz) ... than high-rate cells (median, 1.12 Hz)
outcomes.notes: Split by non-REM sleep rate, the low-rate median is 0.435 Hz under both readings, just outside 0.39 +/- 0.039, and the high-rate median 1.091 Hz (a, within sessions) or 1.092 (b, pooled), within 1.12 +/- 0.112. With the rate over all of PRE and POST (a variant) both are within tolerance (0.395 and 1.041 under reading a). The split is of 417 place cells, not 491.
deviations: The paper does not say whether the split is within sessions or pooled; both readings are shown and give the same medians.
Off-line sleep rate is taken as the non-REM rate in PRE and POST; the rate over all of PRE and POST is a variant.

outcomes.statement: Low-rate neurons carried more spatial information per spike on the maze, and increased their within-ripple firing-rate gain from PRE to POST more than high-rate cells.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6; fig. S16 as cited
outcomes.quote: Low-rate neurons (median, 0.39 Hz) contributed more spatial information per spike on the maze and displayed increased within-ripple firing-rate gains from PRE to POST sleep than high-rate cells
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), which the criterion selects as neither reading of rate-split-medians matched, low-rate cells carry more spatial information (median 0.975 against 0.622 bits per spike, p = 4.1e-08), but their ripple-gain change from PRE to POST is not larger (0.251 against 0.155, p = 0.948). Reading (b) gives the same.
deviations: Ripple gain is the rate within candidate events over the epoch rate; the paper's definition is in fig. S16, which was not available.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing, but not fast-firing, neurons increased their contribution to sequences from PRE to POST sleep, in a decoding restricted to each group.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figure 4D
outcomes.quote: Slow-firing, but not fast-firing, neurons increased their contribution to neuronal sequences from PRE to POST sleep (Fig. 4D).
outcomes.notes: On the pooled test neither half shows replay (low-rate POST minus PRE -0.024, p = 0.964; high-rate -0.049, p = 0.9999), as for all cells (-0.008, p = 0.916). In the within-session variant both halves show replay, larger for low-rate cells (+0.116 against +0.058, p of at most 0.0001 for each), which would be the criterion's partial pattern. On the linear-track sessions alone the pooled test also finds both, larger for low-rate cells (+0.077, p = 0.0046, against +0.044, p = 0.018).
deviations: Variant decodes use 50 column-cycle shuffles per event in place of 200.

outcomes.statement: PRE to POST increases in sequence content were limited to cells with high ripple-specific recruitment (gain).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figure 4E
outcomes.quote: Conversely, PRE to POST increases in sequence content were limited to cells that showed a high degree of ripple-specific recruitment (gain) (Fig. 4E and figs. S20 to S22)
outcomes.notes: On the pooled test neither half shows replay (high-gain -0.001, p = 0.71; low-gain -0.111, p = 1.0). In the within-session variant high-gain cells show replay (+0.111, p < 0.0001) and low-gain cells do not (+0.016, p = 0.14), the paper's pattern. On the linear-track sessions alone the pooled test finds replay in neither half (+0.023, p = 0.25; +0.010, p = 0.21) and the within-session variant finds it in both (+0.045, p = 0.029; +0.050, p = 0.0028).
deviations: Gain is the rate within PRE and POST candidate events over the PRE and POST rate, split at the session median.
Variant decodes use 50 column-cycle shuffles per event in place of 200.

findings.statement: In versions 0.210812.1516 and 0.250624.0426 every position series stores its sampling period (0.0256 s) as its rate, so the positions span about 880 to 2360 hours in place of the MAZE epoch. Version 0.261005.2101 stores 39.06 Hz, which matches the epoch lengths.
In Gatsby_08022013 the POST epoch ends at 30413.6 s, while the LFP, the spikes and the sleep states run to about 32000 s.
The dandiset description lists neck EMG and head-mounted accelerometer signals, and the files hold neither; they also hold no wide-band data (acquisition is empty), only the LFP at 1250 Hz.

The paper's derived data are not deposited. There are no candidate or ripple events, no place-cell list, no sequence scores and no PCC values or rigid and plastic labels, so the paper's selections cannot be checked against the dandiset and every one must be rebuilt.

Neither the paper nor the dandiset links analysis code, and the supplementary Materials and Methods, which define the candidate events, place cells, the PCC and its test, are not openly available (PMC and Science serve them only behind a browser check).

Every electrode's location is "unknown" and no depth or layer is given, so the channel for ripple detection has to be chosen from the signals. Units carry only the hemisphere (lCA1 or rCA1). Subject age is "/".

On the circular track the animals ran toward decreasing linearized position (47 to 63% of samples against 7 to 16% the other way). The series description says the position increases clockwise but not which way the animals ran.

disagreements.reason: This claim ranks all place cells by dPCC and does not use the strong-contributor selection, so the block reason does not apply (problem 4). By the criterion replay is absent after shuffling the top 10% or 20% but also after shuffling the bottom 75% (p = 0.35); the unmanipulated baseline has no pooled replay either (p = 0.92), so "eliminated" cannot be judged (uninformative). The within-session variant shows the paper's pattern. dPCC is computed from the same PRE and POST events that are decoded again, so the result is circular and there is no control that shuffles a random X% of cells (problem 3).

Replay is absent without plastic cells (p = 1.0) and present without rigid cells (p = 0.020). The result is circular (problem 3), and with the shift-test classes removing rigid cells leaves no replay (p = 0.11).
KS p = 0.034 (cell 37). This is fragile, p = 0.051 under reading (b) and 0.12 under the shift-test variant.
Spatial information is higher in plastic cells (p = 3e-4). The number of fields does not differ (p = 0.52) (cell 39).
Both groups increase: plastic p = 0.015, rigid p = 0.032 (cell 41).
Rigid cells have the higher median, but p = 0.059 (cell 43).
Gain is higher in plastic cells (p = 0.037). Bursting (p = 0.20) and coactivation (p = 0.79) are not (cell 45).

attempts.label: DANDI:000045
attempts.entry_title: Standardized and reproducible decision-making in mice (The International Brain Laboratory 2021)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of The International Brain Laboratory (2021) on dandiset 000045, which holds the trial tables of 178 mice trained in seven laboratories from June 2019 to March 2020. It recomputes basic and full task proficiency from the trials and compares training times, psychometric parameters, block effects, the choice model and session ends with the paper, across laboratories. The dandiset holds no sessions before June 2019 and no training status.

notebooks.title: Reproducing The International Brain Laboratory (2021) from dandiset 000045

outcomes.statement: Of 206 mice that started training, 140 reached proficiency in the basic task and 98 in the full task.
outcomes.source: Results, opening section, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Out of 206 mice that started training, 140 achieved proficiency in the basic task, and 98 in the full task
outcomes.notes: The dataset holds 177 mice of the paper's project; 136 have their whole training in it (first session a first-stage session), against 206 that started training. Under the main reading 83 reach basic task proficiency (61 first with status 1a, 22 with 1b), against 140; the pipeline's contrast check gives 85, and 1b replacing 1a from 2019-09-12 gives 70 and 71. 60 reach full task proficiency, against 98. No count is within tolerance under any reading. The answers of 2026-10-22 changed P1 (each session and the two before it, any protocol; all trials counted; percent correct over 50% and 100% contrasts; 1a or 1b at any date), which moved the count from 75 to 84 under the earlier readings to 83 under the main one; the outcome is the same as before (not_reproduced). The dataset holds sessions from 2019-06-11 to 2020-03-23; the Methods say training of these mice began in January 2019. No window fails the 1b or P2 criteria only because missing stimulus onsets leave its reaction time undefined (0 windows under every reading), so the missing onsets do not lower the counts. P2 slides over full-task days; 10 days with more than one full-task session fall at or before a mouse's P2 day, or on any day of a mouse without P2, in 7 mice, so a count over sessions could differ for at most 7 mice.
deviations: Proficiency is recomputed from the trials, as the files carry no training status.
P2 is computed over three consecutive full-task days, not sessions (see notes).
Mice whose first session in the dataset is not a first-stage session (41) are left out, as their training began before the dataset does.

outcomes.statement: Basic task training took 18.4 +- 13.0 days (s.d., n = 140 mice), from 3 days for the fastest mouse to 59 days for the slowest.
outcomes.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 2g
outcomes.quote: The average training took 18.4 ± 13.0 days (s.d., n = 140, Figure 2g )
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading (83 mice) the mean days to P1 is 19.87 counting the P1 day and 18.87 without, both within 18.4 +- 1.84, and the slowest mouse takes 58 and 57 days, within 59 +- 5.9. The s.d. is 11.39 (against 13.0 +- 1.3) and the fastest mouse takes 5 or 4 days (against 3 +- 0.3); two of four values are within tolerance. The variants give means of 17.73 to 23.17 days and at most two values within tolerance. Six of the 136 whole-training mice have their first session in the dataset's first 7 days, where an earlier start would go unseen; without the 2 of them that reach P1 the mean is 19.40 days (s.d. 10.98, fastest 5, slowest 58), again two of four within tolerance. The five fastest mice start between 2019-08-06 and 2019-11-21. The answers changed P1 (see cohort-counts); the outcome is the same as before (partially_reproduced). Measured is the main reading, counting the P1 day.
deviations: 83 mice, against 140.

outcomes.statement: The number of days to basic task proficiency differed across laboratories; within-lab interquartile ranges ranged from 8 days (Lab 2) to 22 days (Lab 6).
outcomes.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 2g
outcomes.quote: The number of days needed to achieve basic task proficiency was different across laboratories ( Figure 2g , p<0.001, Kruskal-Wallis nonparametric test followed by a post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparisons test)

statistics.test: Kruskal-Wallis nonparametric test, then post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparisons test

outcomes.notes: Kruskal-Wallis across labs p = 0.029 under the main reading (0.023 to 0.088 under the variants), never below 0.001; the code's switch gives the same tests. Lab 2 interquartile range 7.75 days (within 8 +- 0.8), Lab 6 5.75 days (against 22 +- 2.2). The labs differ at p < 0.05 but not at the p < 0.001 the criterion requires, and one of the two ranges matches, so the effect is present but weaker. Changed from not_reproduced after the verifier's round 1, which gave partially_reproduced for this reason.
deviations: 6 to 26 mice per lab.

outcomes.statement: Measured in trials, basic task training took 10.8 +- 8.6 thousand trials (s.d., n = 140), from one thousand for the fastest mouse to 43 thousand for the slowest; reaching 80% correct on easy trials took on average about 7.4 thousand trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 2, figure supplement 1
outcomes.quote: For mice that learned the task, the average training took 10.8 ± 8.6 thousands of trials (s.d., n = 140) ... The fastest learner met training criteria in one thousand trials, the slowest 43 thousand trials. To reach 80% on easy trials took on average ~7.4 thousand trials.
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading the mean trials to P1 is 11,839 counting the P1 day and 11,104 without, within 10,800 +- 1,080; the s.d. (7,515 and 7,472), fastest (2,357 and 1,687) and slowest (34,998 and 34,265) are outside tolerance. The mean cumulative trials when mean easy-trial performance first exceeds 80% is 7,329 (within 7,400 +- 740), and 6,659 to 7,306 under the variants. The answers changed P1; the outcome is the same as before (partially_reproduced).
deviations: The median filter over 3 sessions is pandas' centred rolling median with partial windows at the ends, a standard choice; the claims file does not fix the edges.

outcomes.statement: About 80% of mice that started training would learn the basic task within the 40 days usually allotted (Kaplan-Meier estimate over all 206 mice).
outcomes.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 4; Figure 2h
outcomes.quote: there was a 80% probability that mice would learn the task within the 40 days that were usually allotted, and when mice were trained for a longer duration, the success rate rose even further ( Figure 2h )
outcomes.notes: Over the 136 mice that started training in the dataset, mice without P1 censored, the Kaplan-Meier proportion at day 40 is 0.749 counting the P1 day and 0.749 without under the main reading, within 0.8 +- 0.08, and 1.000 at the last day. Since round 1 a mouse without P1 is censored at its last training day counted the same way as the events (before, at the count including the P1 day under both counts), which moved the count without the P1 day from 0.741 to 0.749. The pipeline's contrast check, a variant, gives 0.768; 1b replacing 1a from 2019-09-12 gives 0.600 to 0.602, outside tolerance. The code's variant, leaving out mice still in training at the cutoff, gives 0.815 under the main reading. The answer to the question on "all contrasts introduced" (each of the three sessions, the main reading; the pipeline's check of the current session a variant; pooling given by neither) settled the reading that blocked the claim, and the change of P1 to the pipeline's computation moved the proportion under that reading from 0.670 to 0.678 to 0.741 to 0.749. Earlier outcome blocked (methods_underspecified).
deviations: Without status labels, time is the training days to P1 for proficient mice and the total training days otherwise, as the criterion says; mice without P1 are censored.
The variant takes "still in training at the cutoff" as a session in the last 7 days of the dataset, a choice for a variant that decides nothing.

outcomes.statement: Contrast threshold and bias varied little during training; the threshold interquartile range slightly decreased from 12-29% in the first 10 training days to 11-23% thereafter, and the bias interquartile range went from -5.2 to 7.1% to -5.6 to 6.5%.
outcomes.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 2b,c
outcomes.quote: Estimates of contrast threshold did not vary much during training ( Figure 2b ), with an interquartile range that slightly decreased from 12–29% during the first 10 training days, and 11–23% thereafter. Likewise, bias did not vary much, with an interquartile range of −5.2% to 7.1% during the first 10 days to −5.6% to 6.5% thereafter ( Figure 2c ).
outcomes.notes: Under every reading the threshold interquartile range narrows after day 10 (main, filtered, days 10 to 39, 11.5-23.7% against 11.1-24.3%), but no reading puts all eight bounds within tolerance; the main reading puts at most four (filtered, days 10 on). The answer on 50:50 sessions (the basic-task sessions with all their trials) confirms the sessions used; the change of P1 changed the mice. Earlier outcome the same (partially_reproduced). Measured is the main reading, filtered, days 10 to 39.
deviations: Fits are per training day, all sessions of the day pooled (1,427 days).

outcomes.statement: During training mice were not systematically biased to one side; absolute bias averaged 9.8 +- 12.1 (s.d.), and contrast threshold, which stabilized after about 10 sessions, averaged 17.8 +- 11.7%.
outcomes.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 2; Figure 2b,c
outcomes.quote: Mice across laboratories were not systematically biased towards a particular side and the absolute bias was similar across laboratories (9.8 ± 12.1 [s.d.] on average). Likewise, measures of contrast threshold stabilized after the first ~10 sessions, which was on average 17.8 ± 11.7% on average across institutions.
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading both means are within tolerance under every reading pooled over sessions. Under the first reading listed (filtered, pooled) the absolute bias is 8.821 and the threshold after day 10 18.39%; without the filter 9.759 and 18.56%. The s.d.s are below the paper's under every reading (6.30 to 8.72 against 12.1; 8.55 to 9.89 against 11.7). The statement's "similar across laboratories" is not tested by the criterion; lab means of the signed bias run from -5.11 to 2.55 (main, filtered). The answers changed P1; earlier outcome the same (reproduced).

outcomes.statement: Variability in performance across mice decreased with training but did not disappear; between training days 15 and 40, mean easy-trial performance rose from 80.7% to 91.1% while its s.d. across mice fell from 19.1% to 10.1%.
outcomes.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 3; Figure 2, figure supplement 2
outcomes.quote: For example, between training days 15 and 40, when the average performance on easy trials of the mice increased from 80.7% to 91.1%, the variation across mice (s.d.) of performance on easy trials decreased from 19.1% to 10.1%.
outcomes.notes: The mean rises and the s.d. falls between days 15 and 40 under every reading, and the means are within tolerance under every reading, but no reading has both s.d.s within tolerance (15.03 to 17.12% at day 15 against 19.1%; 6.86 to 12.19% at day 40 against 10.1%). The answers changed P1 and confirm the 50:50 sessions of reading (2); earlier outcome the same (partially_reproduced).
deviations: Reading (3) averages each mouse's days within the bin before taking the mean and s.d. over mice; the claims file does not say how the bin is pooled.

outcomes.statement: A Random Forests decoder applied to the change in easy-trial performance over the first five sessions predicted whether a mouse would be in the bottom quartile of learning speed with 53% accuracy (chance 25%), and misclassified a top-quartile mouse as bottom-quartile only 7% of the time.
outcomes.source: Results, Training succeeded but with different rates across mice and laboratories, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: A Random Forests decoder applied to change in performance (% correct with easy, high-contrast stimuli) in the first five sessions was able to predict whether a mouse would end up in the bottom quartile of learning speed (the slowest learners) with accuracy of 53% (where chance is 25%). Conversely, the chance of misclassifying a fast-learning, top quartile mouse as a slow-learning, bottom quartile mouse, was only 7%.
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading of P1 the criterion's readings disagree on whether the accuracy is near 53%; 3 of 20 accuracy values are within 0.53 +- 0.053 (features (b), four quartiles from days, recall 0.571, four-class accuracy 0.518, precision 0.571), the others run from 0.143 to 0.667. Top-quartile mice classed as bottom quartile, 0.000 to 0.143. The answers changed P1 but not the readings that block the claim; earlier outcome the same. Measured is features (a), four quartiles from days, recall.
deviations: The Random Forest's seed is a standard choice (0).
The criterion's readings are run under the main reading of P1 only, to keep the notebook within its time limit.

outcomes.statement: At basic task proficiency, errors on easy (50% and 100%) contrasts were low, 9.5 +- 3.6%, with no significant difference across laboratories.
outcomes.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 3c
outcomes.quote: The lapse rates (i.e., the errors made in response to easy contrasts of 50% and 100%) were low (9.5 ± 3.6%, Figure 3c ) with no significant difference across laboratories.
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading easy-trial errors at proficiency are 8.41 +- 3.79% (81 mice); the s.d. is within tolerance, the mean just outside 9.5 +- 0.95. The pipeline's contrast check, a variant, gives 9.66 +- 3.69% (85 mice), both within tolerance; 1b replacing 1a gives 5.26 and 5.84%. Two of the 83 mice with P1 have no basic-task session in S1. The answers changed P1, and the main reading now decides; earlier outcome reproduced (8.56 +- 3.77% under 1a/each). The statement's "no significant difference across laboratories" is fig3cde-no-lab-difference-medians.

outcomes.statement: At basic task proficiency the contrast threshold was similar across laboratories at 14.3 +- 3.8 (s.d., n = 7 laboratories) and the response bias was small at 0.3 +- 8.4.
outcomes.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 3d,e
outcomes.quote: The slope of the curves, which measures contrast sensitivity, was also similar across laboratories, at 14.3 ± 3.8 (s.d., n = 7 laboratories, Figure 3d ). Finally, the horizontal displacement of the curve, which measures response bias, was small at 0.3 ± 8.4 (s.d., n = 7, Figure 3e ).
outcomes.notes: Over mice, under the main reading, threshold 14.09 +- 3.80 and bias -0.46 +- 8.09, all four within tolerance; also under the pipeline's contrast check (13.89 +- 3.92 and 0.16 +- 9.05). Over the seven lab means the s.d.s are 1.14 to 2.24. The answers changed P1; earlier outcome the same (reproduced).

outcomes.statement: At basic task proficiency, easy-trial performance, contrast threshold and bias did not differ in median across laboratories.
outcomes.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 3c-e
outcomes.quote: None of these measures showed a significant difference across laboratories, either in median (performance: p=0.63, threshold: p=0.81, bias: p=0.81, FDR corrected Kruskal-Wallis test)
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading the corrected Kruskal-Wallis p are 0.287 (performance), 0.439 (threshold) and 0.730 (bias), all >= 0.05; the code's switch to ANOVA gives the same. Lab medians, performance 89.0 to 93.1%, threshold 12.3 to 17.1, bias -6.1 to 1.8. The pipeline's contrast check gives the same outcome (smallest 0.395); with 1b replacing 1a from 2019-09-12, a variant, performance differs across labs (corrected p = 0.038 and 0.026). The answers removed the pooled reading of "all contrasts introduced" and made "1a or 1b at any date" the main reading, so the readings that disagreed no longer decide. Earlier outcome blocked (methods_underspecified).
deviations: 6 to 25 mice per lab.

outcomes.statement: At basic task proficiency, easy-trial performance, contrast threshold and bias did not differ in variance across laboratories.
outcomes.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 1; Figure 3c-e
outcomes.quote: or in variance (performance: p=0.09, threshold: p=0.57, bias: p=0.57, FDR corrected Levene's test)
outcomes.notes: Corrected Levene p for performance, threshold and bias are 0.268, 0.268 and 0.299 under the main reading and all >= 0.05 under every variant (smallest 0.212). Lab s.d.s (main), performance 1.48 to 4.35, threshold 2.35 to 4.75, bias 4.66 to 10.57. The answers changed P1; earlier outcome the same (reproduced).

outcomes.statement: At basic task proficiency the median trial duration (stimulus onset to feedback) was 468 +- 221 ms, with some differences across laboratories.
outcomes.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 4; Figure 3, figure supplement 2a
outcomes.quote: The median time from stimulus onset to feedback (trial duration, a coarse measure of reaction time) was 468 ± 221 ms, showing some differences across laboratories ( Figure 3—figure supplement 2a , p=0.004, Kruskal-Wallis nonparametric test)
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading the median trial duration is 420.45 ms, just below 468 +- 46.8, with s.d. 219 ms (within 221 +- 22.1). The Kruskal-Wallis test across labs gives p = 0.061 uncorrected (0.12 corrected), and 0.068 to 0.40 under the variants, so the difference across labs that the criterion requires (p < 0.05) is not found. Lab 4's median is 702 ms against 370 to 455 ms for the others. One of the two values is within tolerance and the other just outside, and the lab difference is not significant, so the claim holds in part. Changed from not_reproduced after the verifier's round 1, which gave partially_reproduced.
deviations: Trials without a stimulus onset time (6% of all trials) have no duration and are left out.

outcomes.statement: At basic task proficiency mice performed 719 +- 223 trials per session; the difference across laboratories was significant but only in one laboratory relative to the rest.
outcomes.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 4; Figure 3, figure supplement 2b
outcomes.quote: Mice on average performed 719 ± 223 trials per session ( Figure 3—figure supplement 2b ). This difference was significant (p<10 −6 , one-way ANOVA) but only in one laboratory relative to the rest.
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading 706.8 trials per session (within 719 +- 71.9), s.d. 196.9 (outside 223 +- 22.3). One-way ANOVA p = 1.2e-04, below 0.05 and not below 1e-6; the five significant Tukey pairs all involve Lab 7 (412 trials per session against 635 to 836). The variants give p = 9.2e-05 to 0.0026, every pair with Lab 7. The answers changed P1; earlier outcome the same (partially_reproduced).

outcomes.statement: A Naive Bayes classifier could not identify a mouse's laboratory from its basic-task performance, threshold and bias; its accuracy was 0.12 +- 0.051 against a chance level of 0.11, and the 95% range of its distribution included chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 5; Figure 3f
outcomes.quote: Its mean accuracy was 0.12 ± 0.051, and a 95th percentile of its distribution included the chance level of 0.11 (mean of the null distribution).
outcomes.notes: The answer on the subsample size (the Methods' rule, the lowest lab count over the datasets classified, one size for every classifier claim) let the classifier run with 5 mice per lab (Lab 4 and Lab 7 in S2, Lab 7 in the first full-task sessions). Naive Bayes on S1 (81 mice) has accuracy 0.140 +- 0.063 (within 0.12 +- 0.051) against a shuffled mean of 0.106 (within 0.11 +- 0.011); its 2.5th percentile, 0.029, is below the shuffled mean, so it is not above chance. Under the pipeline's contrast check, 0.138, 2.5th percentile 0.029, null 0.110. The code's 8 mice per lab cannot run (Lab 4 and Lab 7 hold 7 and 6 mice in S1). Earlier outcome blocked (other, fewer than 8 mice in some labs).
deviations: 5 mice per lab, 35 per subsample, against 8 and 56 in the paper.
The leave-one-out Naive Bayes is computed directly; it agrees with scikit-learn's GaussianNB on every subsample checked (synthetic data and 20 subsamples of S1).

outcomes.statement: With the laboratory's time zone added as a feature, the classifier performed above chance and confused labs in the same time zone.
outcomes.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 5; Figure 3f; Figure 3, figure supplement 3b
outcomes.quote: If the classifier was given this variable during training and testing it performed above chance ( Figure 3f , Positive control ) and the confusion matrix showed clusters of labs located in the same time zone
outcomes.notes: With the time zone as a fourth feature and 5 mice per lab, accuracy 0.405 +- 0.084; the 2.5th percentile (0.257) and the code's 0.001th percentile (0.171) are above the shuffled mean of 0.118. In the mean confusion matrix all off-diagonal mass lies on labs in the same time zone (4.166 over 12 cells, against 0.000 over 30 cells of other zones); Lab 7, alone in its zone, is always classified correctly. The time zones come from the code (lab-link); the start times in the files cannot confirm them. The subsample answer let the claim run; earlier outcome blocked (other).
deviations: 5 mice per lab, as for fig3f-classifier-chance-basic.

outcomes.statement: Random Forest and Logistic Regression classifiers also failed to predict laboratory membership from basic-task behavior.
outcomes.source: Results, Performance in the basic task was indistinguishable across laboratories, paragraph 5; Figure 3, figure supplement 3d-i
outcomes.quote: Similar results were obtained with two other classifier algorithms ( Figure 3—figure supplement 3d–i ).
outcomes.notes: With 5 mice per lab (answer of 2026-10-22), Logistic Regression is not above chance (accuracy 0.071 +- 0.054, 2.5th percentile 0.000, shuffled mean 0.070, 2000 subsamples). The Random Forest (100 trees, leave-one-out) now runs in 4 processes at 3.7 s per subsample, about 2 h for the 2000 subsamples of the criterion, so the first 50 of the same sequence are run; its accuracy is 0.130 +- 0.055, 2.5th percentile 0.035 (bootstrap 95% interval 0.029 to 0.057) against a shuffled mean of 0.100, so it is not above chance; the first 25 give the same (0.046 against 0.098). Earlier outcome blocked (not_runnable), with 6 subsamples; the verifier's round 1 noted the run time is not a data limit and asked for a larger run. Measured is the Random Forest's 2.5th percentile and shuffled mean.
deviations: The Random Forest is run on the first 50 of the 2000 subsamples, to keep the notebook within its time limit.

Logistic Regression with solver liblinear is fitted one-vs-rest, as scikit-learn did for several classes with this solver when the paper's code ran (the installed version refuses more than two classes); the direct Newton fit of liblinear's objective agrees with scikit-learn's OneVsRestClassifier on every subsample checked.

outcomes.statement: The institutions named in the dandiset's files are the paper's seven laboratories, so that the code's lab numbers (Lab 1 to 7) and time zones can be given to the dataset's mice.
outcomes.source: Claims file header, code lab numbers and time zones (paper-behavior at commit edc4531)

The start times do not bear out the time zones, as they are local clock times stated as UTC (median start hours 11.0 to 14.4 h in every lab, Lab 7 at 11.0 h). Not affected by the answers.

outcomes.statement: In the basic task, mouse choices were no more consistent within laboratories than across laboratories.
outcomes.source: Figure 3, figure supplement 1a legend
outcomes.quote: This averaged consistency was not significantly higher (p=0.73) than a null distribution generated by randomly shuffling lab assignments between mice and computing the average within-lab choice variability 10,000 times ( violin plot ). Therefore, choices were no more consistent within labs than across labs.

statistics.test: permutation test against 10,000 shuffles of lab labels

permutation test against 10,000 shuffles of lab labels

outcomes.statement: With a looser proficiency criterion (80% correct on easy trials over three sessions, n = 150 mice), behavior was again consistent across laboratories; only the number of trials per session differed slightly, and a classifier failed to identify a mouse's laboratory.

outcomes.statement: In the first three sessions of the full task, bias in each block, contrast threshold in each block and performance on 100% contrast trials did not vary significantly across laboratories, and a classifier could not predict lab membership.

outcomes.statement: Mice incorporated the block priors into their choices from the first sessions of the full task.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds 178 mice and 6,615 sessions from 2019-06-11 to 2020-03-23. The paper's mice began training in January 2019 (206 mice, 10,903 sessions), so 41 mice of the project begin mid-training in the dandiset and the mice trained before June 2019 are missing.

The training status of each session (in_training, trained_1a, trained_1b, ready4ephysrig and so on), on which every analysis of the paper selects sessions, is not in the files. It has to be recomputed from the trials, which leaves open details of the criteria.
One recording is deposited twice, under two mice (CSHL_013 and CSHL_015, 2019-07-15, identical trials and start time).

probabilityLeft is described as the probability of a left stimulus for the current block, but in every basic-task session it varies from trial to trial between 0 and 1 (24% of basic-task trials are not 0.5), with the stimulus side following it.
session_start_time is stated in UTC (+00:00) but holds local clock times; all seven labs, from London to Berkeley, have median start hours between 11.0 and 14.4 h.

In 807 files the wheel position data and its timestamps differ in length (for example 181,623 samples against 340,799 timestamps); 16 files have no wheel series. In one session checked (ibl_witten_07), the wheel moves the opposite way to the choice on every trial.

257,021 trials (6%) have no stimulus onset time, and 185 sessions have none; 1,541 trials in 220 sessions have a response time before the stimulus onset (down to -5,638 s). No proficiency window of this attempt fails for the missing onsets alone.
One session (ZM_1367, 2019-06-11) uses contrasts of 4% and 8%, which the paper does not describe.

The Methods give the 1a/1b performance criterion on easy trials and the Results give the lapse criterion as a maximum of 0.2 for the sum of the lapses, while Appendix 1, table 1d gives performance on 100% contrast and a bound on each lapse rate. After the answers of 2026-10-22 the claims file follows the pipeline's code for performance (easy trials) and the table for the lapses; with performance on 100% contrast only, 84 mice reach P1 against 83.
The dandiset's metadata do not say which of its 178 mice are the paper's; one mouse (SWC_029) belongs to another project by its subject record.

attempts.label: DANDI:000056
attempts.paper_title: Internally organized mechanisms of the head direction sense
attempts.entry_title: Head-direction cells across waking and sleep (Peyrache et al. 2015)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Peyrache, Lacroix, Petersen and Buzsaki (2015) on dandiset 000056, which holds spike times, LED positions and sleep states from 40 sessions of 7 mice recorded in the anterior thalamus and post-subiculum. It classifies head-direction cells, compares their rates and pairwise correlations across waking, REM and slow-wave sleep, estimates the speed of the internal head-direction signal from cross-correlograms, and tests noise correlations and decoding. The units carry no brain region, so the comparisons between the two structures cannot be made.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Peyrache et al. (2015) from dandiset 000056

outcomes.statement: Of the recorded cells, 242 of 720 in the anterior thalamus and 111 of 357 in the PoS were classified as HD cells, 353 of 1077 in all.
outcomes.source: Methods, Head direction cells, paragraph 2; Results, first paragraph
outcomes.quote: 242 out of 720 recorded cells (41% on average) in the anterior thalamus, and 111 out of 357 (31%) cells in the PoS were classified as HD cells.
outcomes.notes: By the Methods' criteria 378 units are HD cells in the 38 sessions with position, within 353 plus or minus 35.3. They are 0.218 of the 1731 units with spikes in the open-field epoch (reading a) and 0.205 of all 1848 unit rows of those sessions (reading b), both outside 0.328 plus or minus 0.033. The files hold 1959 unit rows in 40 sessions against the paper's 1077 recorded cells in 42 sessions. By mouse the fraction is 0.108 to 0.386; in the mice that appear to be thalamus only it is 0.133 (133 of 1000) against the paper's thalamic 0.336, and in the mice that appear dual-site 0.335 (245 of 731). With a concentration threshold of 0.8 or 1.2 the count is 424 or 357. None of the 34 units with unsorted spike times in these sessions is an HD cell. The count passes only with Mouse12-120808 as deposited, where position and spikes do not share a clock and no unit passes the criteria. With position realigned by the best shift of each quarter of the epoch, that session has 13 HD cells (12 with one constant shift of -2.6 s), and the count is 391 (390), above the upper bound of 388.3, so the match of the count is fragile. The unit rows cannot be brought down to the paper's 1077 cells from the files (1826 rows fire at 0.05 Hz or more and 1526 at 0.5 Hz or more; unit ids are 0 to N-1 and carry no shank or cluster number). The agreement of the count may therefore also be coincidental. The split into 242 thalamic and 111 PoS HD cells cannot be tested.
deviations: Regions pooled, as the units carry no region.

The von Mises fit (maximum likelihood fit to the tuning curve as a distribution of angles) and the Rayleigh test (resultant length of the tuning curve with the number of waking spikes) are choices made here; the Methods do not specify them.
The open-field epoch is found from position, as the files do not mark it.
Mouse17-130201 and Mouse32-140820 have no processed position and are left out.
Mouse12-120808 is counted as deposited, with position and spikes on different clocks; the realigned session is a variant.

outcomes.statement: The firing rates of HD neurons are strongly correlated between waking and SWS and between waking and REM sleep.
outcomes.source: Figure 2a (ADn n = 215, PoS n = 62 cells)
outcomes.quote: First, the firing rates of HD neurons remained strongly correlated across brain states (Fig. 2a).
outcomes.notes: Over 378 HD cells in 37 sessions with sleep states, Pearson r of waking against SWS rates is 0.838 (p = 3.7e-101) and against REM rates 0.891 (p = 4.5e-131); with log rates 0.806 and 0.883. By mouse r is 0.718 to 0.889 for SWS and 0.866 to 0.942 for REM. The cell count (378 against the paper's 277) does not decide the outcome; the paper does not say which HD cells were in its figure.
deviations: ADn and PoS cells pooled; the paper plots them separately.

outcomes.statement: The pairwise correlations between HD neurons, within and across structures, are similar across brain states.
outcomes.source: Results, second paragraph; Figure 2b (ADn pairs n = 970, PoS pairs n = 92)
outcomes.quote: Second, the pairwise correlations between HD neuron pairs both within and across structures were robustly similar across states (Fig. 2b)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), 1573 pairs in 33 sessions, waking against SWS pair correlations r = 0.938 and against REM r = 0.963. Reading (b), 2246 pairs, r = 0.925 and 0.952. Every mouse gives r of at least 0.913. 888 of 2461 pairs fail reading (a) for low rates.
deviations: Pairs within and across structures are pooled, and pairs on the same shank cannot be removed.
Bin sizes are those of Figure 3a; Figure 2b does not state them.

outcomes.statement: The zero-lag correlation between HD cell pairs falls with the offset of their preferred directions, positive below 60 degrees, negative above it and near zero at about 60 degrees, and this holds in waking, REM and SWS.
outcomes.source: Results, third paragraph; Figure 3a
outcomes.quote: Pairs of neurons with <60° offset showed positive correlations, pairs with >60° offset showed negative correlations, and pairs with approximately 60° offset were uncorrelated (Fig. 3a). The relationship between the 0-lag correlation and the preferred angular direction was preserved across brain states
outcomes.notes: The mean zero-lag correlation, in 10 degree bins of the offset of preferred directions, crosses zero at 54.2 degrees in waking, 56.9 in REM and 55.9 in SWS (measured gives the waking value, the lowest), all within 54 to 66. The Pearson correlation of pair correlation with offset is -0.751, -0.741 and -0.671 (p below 1e-200). With 15 degree bins the crossings are 55.4, 57.9 and 57.7 degrees; under reading (b) 54.1, 57.1 and 56.5, the waking value just outside the tolerance. The waking crossing of reading (a) is 0.2 degrees inside the tolerance, so the pass is close to the boundary.
deviations: ADn-ADn, ADn-PoS and PoS-PoS pairs are pooled.

outcomes.statement: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal, estimated from the temporal profile of pairwise cross-correlograms, is about tenfold faster during SWS than during waking.
outcomes.source: Results, second paragraph; Figure 2e,f; Abstract ("accelerated tenfold")
outcomes.quote: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal, either estimated by a Bayesian decoder or from the temporal profile of pairwise cross-correlograms ... was approximately tenfold faster during SWS than during waking (Fig. 2e,f)
outcomes.notes: Over 1509 pairs (64 of 1573 dropped for a fit at the edge of the speed range), the median ratio of SWS to waking angular velocity is 8.33 (quartiles 5.91 to 11.31), below 9 to 11; SWS is faster in 1420 pairs (sign test p = 4.1e-309). Median speeds are 36.9 deg/s in waking, 33.5 in REM and 324.4 in SWS. By mouse the ratio is 7.89 to 13.52. The Bayesian decoder variant gives a median of 11.53 over 28 sessions. Under reading (b) the median is 8.02 over 2129 pairs; with pairs whose fits reach R2 of 0.25 or 0.5 in every state, 8.46 (1063 pairs) and 8.56 (748 pairs). Median R2 is 0.84 in waking, 0.55 in REM and 0.78 in SWS. The waking estimates are 0.60 times the measured mean angular speed of the head (median over sessions) and correlate with it at r = 0.20 across 33 sessions. On Poisson surrogates driven by the measured head direction and the waking tuning curves, the estimator returns 0.37 of the true mean speed (median 37.0 deg/s, as on the data, against a true 99.9), and for the same trajectory played ten times faster it gives a median ratio of 4.99 (quartiles 2.76 to 7.02), not 10. Scaled by that compression the data's 8.33 becomes 16.69, so the data are consistent with a speed-up below, at or above tenfold. The estimator shows that SWS is faster but does not determine the fold; how far its bias in SWS matches that of the surrogates is not known.
deviations: The paper does not say how the expected and observed cross-correlograms are put on one scale; a free scale and offset are fitted here.
The lag range (4 s) and speed grid are chosen here.
The expectation over the chi-squared speed distribution is computed exactly from its characteristic function.
Pairs within and across structures are pooled; the paper shows ADn-ADn and PoS-PoS pairs.

outcomes.statement: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal is similar during REM sleep and waking.
outcomes.source: Results, second paragraph; Figure 2e,f
outcomes.quote: Angular velocity of the internal HD signal was similar during waking and REM (Fig. 2e,f).
outcomes.notes: The median REM to waking ratio is 0.87 over 1509 pairs (quartiles 0.60 to 1.26), inside 0.67 to 1.5, and 0.85 over 2129 pairs under reading (b); by mouse 0.69 to 1.07; the decoder variant gives 1.05. By a Wilcoxon test of the log ratio the median REM speed is below the waking one (p = 6.3e-18, median log10 ratio -0.060, about 13%), a test the paper does not make, but REM is faster in 581 of 1509 pairs.
deviations: The paper names no test for "similar"; the range 0.67 to 1.5 is chosen here.

outcomes.statement: During waking, the observed correlations of HD cell pairs exceed those expected from independent rate-coded neurons for pairs with overlapping fields (0 plus or minus 15 degrees), and fall below them for pairs at about 60 degrees.
outcomes.source: Results, fourth paragraph; Figure 4a,b
outcomes.quote: However, correlations expected from independent rate-coded neurons could not fully account for the observed pairwise correlations of HD cells (Fig. 4a). ... were observed for neuron pairs with overlapping fields (0±15°), with a marked negative signal correlation at 60±15° offset (Fig. 4b,c)
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' formula (mean cross-products over bins where the head direction is known at both times), the noise correlation of pairs at 0 plus or minus 15 degrees is positive in 110 of 118 pairs (median 7.84 Hz2, 0.81 of the chance product, Wilcoxon p = 5.3e-19) and of pairs at 60 plus or minus 15 degrees positive in only 35 of 256 (median -4.08 Hz2, p = 4.2e-32). Under reading (b) the medians are 4.22 and -1.63 Hz2 (p = 2e-24 and 6.8e-42). On independent Poisson surrogates with tuning curves estimated from their own spikes, the measure is biased in the same direction, median +0.64 Hz2 at 0 degrees and -0.37 Hz2 at 60, about a tenth of the observed values; the data exceed their surrogates in 110 of 118 pairs at 0 degrees (p = 5e-19) and fall below them in 223 of 256 at 60 degrees (p = 1.6e-31). It holds in the mice that appear thalamus only. Under the first criterion, with both cross-correlations on a Pearson scale, the 0 degree pairs are negative (median -0.78), which reflects the scale and not the data.
deviations: The criterion was revised after a first run, before this outcome was recorded, from a Pearson scaling that contradicted the Methods' stated formula to that formula; the first version is shown as a variant.
Regions pooled.

outcomes.statement: The HD signal decoded with a Bayesian decoder from the HD cells faithfully tracks the head direction of the waking mouse.
outcomes.source: Methods, Bayesian reconstruction of head-direction; Figure 1c
outcomes.quote: These estimates faithfully tracked the head position in the waking mouse.
outcomes.notes: In 28 sessions with at least 6 HD cells, two-fold cross-validated decoding has a pooled median absolute error of 11.7 degrees (chance 90); session medians 8.1 to 27.2, all at or below 30. With HD cells selected on the training half alone, the same 28 sessions give a pooled median of 11.7 degrees (session medians 8.1 to 24.7).
deviations: HD cells of both structures are decoded together; the paper decodes one structure at a time.
The threshold of 30 degrees for "faithfully" and the 6 degree angle bins are chosen here.

outcomes.statement: ADn HD cells have peak rates almost three times those of PoS HD cells (p < 1e-10, Mann-Whitney, 242 ADn and 111 PoS HD cells).
outcomes.source: Results, first paragraph; Supplementary Figure 2b
outcomes.quote: ADn neurons exhibited peak rates almost three times higher than PoS cells (Supplementary Fig. 2b
outcomes.notes: The units table holds only spike times, with no electrode, shank or region, and every electrode's location is "unknown", so units cannot be assigned to the ADn or the PoS.

outcomes.statement: ADn HD cells convey 30% more head-direction information than PoS HD cells (1.44 against 1.11 bits per spike, p < 1e-6).
outcomes.source: Results, first paragraph; Supplementary Figure 2c
outcomes.quote: conveyed 30% more head-direction information than PoS cells (1.44 bit per spike vs. 1.11 bit per spike
outcomes.notes: No region per unit (see adn-pos-peak-rate).

outcomes.statement: Ensembles of 8.4 plus or minus 5.1 (s.d.) HD units per session were recorded in the ADn and 5 plus or minus 2.8 in the PoS.
outcomes.source: Results, first paragraph
outcomes.quote: Ensembles of HD neurons from ADn (8.4 ± 5.1 s.d. units per session) and PoS (5 ± 2.8 s.d.) were recorded by multi-site silicon probes
outcomes.notes: No region per unit. Pooled, the sessions hold 0 to 26 HD cells (median 10). In the mice that appear thalamus only there are 7.4 plus or minus 6.2 (s.d.) HD cells per session over 18 sessions (7.8 plus or minus 6.1 without Mouse12-120808), against the ADn's 8.4 plus or minus 5.1; in the mice that appear dual-site 12.2 plus or minus 5.9 over 20 sessions, both structures together. The assignment of mice is consistent with the files but not shown by them, so these numbers do not decide the claim.

outcomes.statement: Pairwise correlations of HD cells closer than 60 degrees are stronger in the ADn than in the PoS in every brain state (p < 1e-5, 345 ADn-ADn and 55 PoS-PoS pairs).
outcomes.source: Results, third paragraph; Supplementary Figure 5
outcomes.quote: HD signal was more strongly preserved in the ADn than in the PoS as shown by the stronger pairwise correlations in any brain state

statistics.n: 345 ADn-ADn and 55 PoS-PoS pairs closer than 60 degrees

outcomes.notes: No region per unit.

outcomes.statement: The activity packets in the ADn and the PoS are coherent with the packet expected from the Bayesian decoded HD in waking, REM and SWS.
outcomes.source: Results, third paragraph; Figure 3b
outcomes.quote: The actual activity packets, both in the ADn and the PoS, and across brain states, were highly similar to the predictions given by the signal decoded from a Bayesian estimator (Fig. 3b) in waking, REM and SWS
outcomes.notes: The coherence is shown per structure, and units have no region. The measure is also described only by reference to earlier work (the bootstrap of population vectors is not fully specified), which would block it as methods_underspecified as well. A version pooled over regions could be run, but the Methods do not say how the actual and expected packets are compared or how the probability is formed from the 5,000 random waking population vectors, so it is not run here.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlations of HD cell pairs are stronger in the ADn than in the PoS (p < 1e-9, Kruskal-Wallis).
outcomes.source: Results, fourth paragraph; Figure 4c
outcomes.quote: These signal correlations were stronger for ADn than PoS neurons

statistics.n: ADn-ADn pairs 96 and 200, ADn-PoS pairs 77 and 157, PoS-PoS pairs 29 and 57, at 0 and 60 degrees

outcomes.notes: No region per unit.

outcomes.statement: In the ADn the covariance-based optimal linear estimator of HD is about 50% better than the signal-based one, and this gain is larger than in the PoS (p < 0.05, 20 ADn and 8 PoS ensembles).
outcomes.source: Results, fourth paragraph; Figure 4d,e
outcomes.quote: In the ADn, where noise correlations were highest for overlapping HD cells, the covariance-based OLE was approximately 50% better than the signal-based OLE (Fig. 4d,e), and significantly stronger than in the PoS
outcomes.notes: The claim compares ADn and PoS ensembles, and units have no region.

outcomes.statement: The HD signal decoded from ADn assemblies during sleep gives tuning curves of PoS cells more similar to their waking tuning than the signal decoded from PoS assemblies does for ADn cells, in all brain states.
outcomes.source: Results, fifth paragraph; Figure 5a,b
outcomes.quote: However, the HD signal extracted from ADn assemblies resulted in tuning curves more similar to actual HD fields than the HD signal decoded from PoS assemblies, in all brain states
outcomes.notes: Decoding from one structure to compute tuning in the other needs the region of each unit.

outcomes.statement: ADn assemblies predict PoS spike trains in all brain states better than PoS assemblies predict ADn spike trains, with optimal readout windows of 123 ms (waking), 133 ms (REM) and 79 ms (SWS).
outcomes.source: Results, fifth paragraph; Figure 5c to e
outcomes.quote: Optimal readout windows were similar between waking and REM (median: 123 ms and 133 ms respectively) and shorter during SWS (median: 79 ms). In the reverse direction, PoS cell assemblies predicted spike trains of ADn neurons more weakly, especially during SWS
outcomes.notes: Predicting one structure from the other needs the region of each unit.

outcomes.statement: Fast synchrony between ADn HD cell pairs decreases with the difference of their preferred directions in all brain states (p < 1e-10, Kruskal-Wallis, 970 pairs).
outcomes.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 6
outcomes.quote: The degree of synchrony decreased with the magnitude of difference between the preferred head directions of the neurons (Fig. 6b ... in all brain states (Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 7a).
outcomes.notes: The claim is about ADn pairs on different shanks; units have neither region nor shank. The mice that appear thalamus only could stand in for the ADn, but that assignment is not shown by the files, and without shanks the pairs on the same shank, whose fast synchrony at 1 to 5 ms is distorted by spike sorting, cannot be removed.

outcomes.statement: Putative monosynaptic connections were found in 4.45% of 6960 ADn to PoS pairs and 0.35% of PoS to ADn pairs; among pyramidal PoS cells, 0.41% against 0.18% (p = 0.014).
outcomes.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 7a,b
outcomes.quote: revealed putative synaptic connections in a fraction of the pairs (4.45% of 6960 pairs from ADn to PoS, 0.35% from PoS to ADn ... (0.41% ADn-PoS pairs versus 0.18% PoS-ADn pairs

statistics.n: 3394 ADn and PoS pyramidal cell pairs

outcomes.notes: Needs the region of each unit, and for the pyramidal subset waveforms, which the dandiset does not hold for units (raw broadband data are in only 3 of the 40 files).

outcomes.statement: PoS HD cells postsynaptic to ADn HD cells share the preferred direction of their presynaptic cell (12 pairs), and such PoS pyramidal cells convey more HD information than those without an identified presynaptic cell (p = 0.011).
outcomes.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 7d,e
outcomes.quote: PoS HD cells that were post-synaptic to ADn HD cells shared the same preferred direction as their presynaptic neuron (Fig. 7d ... Pyramidal neurons in PoS that were synaptically driven by ADn HD cells conveyed more HD information than PoS neurons for which a presynaptic cell could not be identified

statistics.about: preferred direction of postsynaptic PoS against presynaptic ADn HD cells
statistics.test: Rayleigh test followed by Wilcoxon's signed rank test

statistics.about: HD information of driven against other PoS pyramidal neurons

outcomes.notes: Depends on the ADn to PoS connections, which need the region of each unit.

outcomes.statement: ADn HD cell spikes are associated with high-frequency oscillations of the PoS LFP.
outcomes.source: Results, sixth paragraph; Figure 7c
outcomes.quote: ADn cell spiking was associated with high frequency LFP oscillations in the PoS (Fig. 7c)
outcomes.notes: Needs the region of the units and of the LFP channels; electrode locations are "unknown".

findings.statement: The units tables hold only spike times. No unit has an electrode, shank, brain region, waveform or quality measure, and every electrode's location is "unknown". Units cannot be assigned to the antero-dorsal thalamus or the post-subiculum, which blocks 13 of the paper's 21 claims. The electrode groups and ripple annotations are consistent with Mouse24, Mouse25 and Mouse28 being the three dual-site mice, but the files do not say so.

The files hold 1959 unit rows (103 with no spikes) in 40 sessions, against the paper's 1077 recorded cells in 42 sessions. Mouse12-120809 alone has 292 units, 167 of them firing below 0.5 Hz. Unit ids run from 0 to N-1 and carry no shank or cluster number, the units table has no quality measure, and 1526 rows fire at 0.5 Hz or more, so the paper's 1077 cells cannot be recovered. Nothing marks which units or sessions the paper analysed (its Methods discard some sessions).

The open-field exploration (the paper's waking epoch) is not marked. The "Awake" state also covers waking in the home cage, and some sessions hold a second exploration or a larger second environment. The epoch had to be found from position.

In 36 of 40 files one unit's spike times are not sorted. Each such unit holds exactly two sorted runs, and in all 36 the first run ends at an index of the form k x 65536 - 1. The second run starts within 36 s of the start of the recording and the first between 24 and 13704 s, and the two end within 15 s of each other. In 26 units no time of the second run appears in the first; in 10, 821 to 22281 times do. This suggests an error in the conversion.

In Mouse12-120808 the position and the spikes do not share a clock. Head-direction tuning is best with position shifted by -1.5 s at the start of the exploration and -3.4 s at its end, and no unit passes the HD criteria as deposited; with position realigned by the best shift of each quarter, 13 units do. In all other sessions the best shift is -0.2 to 0 s.
The raw LED positions in `acquisition` are stated in meters with a conversion of NaN but hold camera pixels (values in the hundreds).

Mouse32-140820 has no sleep-state table and no processed position, and Mouse17-130201 has no processed position; both have raw LED series only. In three Mouse20 sessions the position series ends 11 to 109 minutes before the recording.
The annotation series `dow`, `hdD` and `rip` (labels such as "DOWN ON 5", "HD UP ON", "Ripple peak 1") have no description.

The dandiset's related resource for the paper gives its name and identifier as "nternally organized mechanisms of the head direction sense" (first letter missing, and the title in place of a DOI); the URL is correct.

Neither the paper nor the dandiset links analysis code, so the von Mises fit, the Rayleigh test, the scaling in the cross-correlogram estimate of angular velocity and the coherence measure had to be chosen or could not be repeated.
