findings.statement: The dandiset holds the raw 30 kHz broadband, port events, position and task logs, but none of the derived data the paper's findings rest on: no spike times or waveform features, LFP, ripple or multiunit event times, linearised position or decoder output. 31 of the paper's 33 claims need ripples or clusterless decoding recomputed from about 9.1 TB of raw data, which cannot be streamed within the registry's limits.

The electrode table gives the location of all 128 channels as None in every file, so the CA1 cell-layer tetrodes used for ripple detection and decoding, and the corpus callosum tetrode used as LFP reference, cannot be identified from the data.

The files do not mark which run sessions the paper analysed. They hold 27, 32, 24 and 33 run epochs for jaq, roquefort, despereaux and montague, where the paper used 26 (24 after excluding sessions 1 and 3 of subject 1), 32, 23 and 33, and the excluded sessions are named only by number. Which jaq and despereaux epoch the paper did not count cannot be told: possible ones are jaq day 7 epoch 2 (6 rewards in 74 valid trials, no outerreps printed) and the epochs shorter than the Methods' 45 minutes (jaq day 6 epoch 4 and day 9 epoch 6, despereaux day 4 epoch 4). The paper's code repository (LorenFrankLab/Gillespie_Neuron_2021) holds a saved filter output with per-animal epoch lists that may identify them; it was not used here.

55 of the draft version's 57 files differ in content (SHA-256) from the published version's; their draft assets were modified in February and March 2022. In the file compared (montague day 4), written as NWB 2.4.0 on 2022-01-14, the DIO timestamps agree with the published version to within a microsecond, but the draft's position timestamps are shifted by about -1.59e9 s and no longer share the DIO clock; in the published version they do. The README of the paper's code links the draft.

Position is sampled at 32.9 to 33.0 Hz, where the Methods state 30 Hz, and 110 of 116 run epochs end with 1 to 4 NaN position timestamps (all of them the last samples of the series, none elsewhere); two epochs have non-increasing timestamps (up to 200).

In montague day 16 epoch 2 the StateScript log's clock steps by about 3.4 s twice against the DIO pump times early in the epoch, and in jaq day 6 epoch 4 the DIO holds one more reward pump (arm 8) 226 s after the last logged reward and 40 s after the last logged trial, so that log appears to end before the epoch. Elsewhere the log and the DIO agree to a few milliseconds and on every reward.

The task logs (StateScript, embedded as text in processing/associated_files) are the only record of the goal arm, trial structure and timeouts; there is no trials table. Five run epochs carry the log without the Python observer header that states the task parameters (rewards per goal, forage assist); for these, forage assist can be ruled out only from the log lines (no CURRENTGOAL line names more than one arm).

attempts.entry_title: Structure and variability of delay activity in premotor cortex (Even-Chen et al. 2019)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Even-Chen, Sheffer, Vyas, Ryu and Shenoy (2019) on dandiset 000121, which holds 12 sessions of delayed center-out reaching with Utah arrays in two monkeys (all 7 of R, 5 of the 16 of J). It checks the sessions and trial counts, the behaviour, the low-dimensional structure of PMd delay activity (PCA, the spatial plane, its time course, the speed axis), the variability of single-trial neural states on and off the reach axis, and SVM decoding of reach direction and distance.

outcomes.notes: Grouped by the Methods' dates, ring 3584 (paper 3577) and vertical 3842 (4040) are within 10% under all three readings, horizontal 4156 (3699) and 3-rings 1340 (912) are not. Measured values are reading (a), successful delayed center-out trials; readings (b) and (c) differ by at most 26 trials per configuration. Grouped by the file geometry, three of four are within 10% (horizontal 3842 against 3699, vertical 4156 against 4040), which fits the exchange of dates found in session-configurations. The 3-rings session holds 47% more successful delayed trials than the paper used, and no reading explains the difference. Reading (b) leaves out failed trials without a go cue; counting them gives ring 4568, horizontal 5250, vertical 5033 and 3-rings 1671, none within 10%.
deviations: Which trials the paper counted is not stated; three readings were tested.

outcomes.statement: Monkey J contributed 6161 ring, 5017 horizontal, 6110 vertical and 7722 3-rings trials, over four sessions each.
outcomes.source: Materials and methods, Experimental design, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: 24 targets for J (6161 trials over four sessions ... For horizontal configuration: 5017 trials over four sessions for J ... For vertical: 6110 trials over four sessions ... (7722 trials over four sessions for J
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds 5 of the 16 sessions the Methods list for J (2015-10-01, 10-02, 10-15, 2016-01-27, 01-28). The 11 missing include all four horizontal sessions, three of four ring sessions and two of four in each of vertical and 3-rings. The data link in the paper (stanford.edu/~shenoy/Data/Even-ChenEtAlPLoSCompBio2019.zip) returns HTTP 403, and no other dandiset of this paper was found.

outcomes.statement: Delays were uniform from 300 to 700 ms for J and 400 to 900 ms for R, 10% of trials had no delay; average reaction time was 346 ms (J) and 311 ms (R), average reach time 582 ms (J) and 482 ms (R), and reaction time was negatively correlated with delay (p < 1e-4 for both).
outcomes.source: Materials and methods, Experimental design, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Delays were distributed uniformly from 300 to 700 ms for J and 400 to 900 ms for R ... The average reach time of successful trials was J: 582 ms, R: 482 ms and the average reaction time was J: 346 ms, R: 311 ms. Also, the reaction time was negatively correlated

statistics.about: reaction time against delay, J and R

outcomes.notes: Reaction times (J 332, R 305 ms) and reach times read as acquisition minus go cue (J 587, R 486 ms) are within tolerance; read as acquisition minus movement onset they are 255 and 181 ms. R's mean reaction time includes the 5.9% of its trials whose onset precedes the go cue; its median (361 ms) and its mean over 100 to 800 ms (362 ms) are outside tolerance, and with onset searched only after the go cue the means are 342 ms (J, within tolerance) and 340 ms (R, just inside its bound of 342 ms). J's delays span 300 to 700 ms as stated; R's span 400 to 1000 ms, beyond the widened bound of 990 ms. No-delay trials are 19.8% of J's and 0.2% of R's successful center-out trials (26, all on 2017-01-19), not 10%. Reaction time falls with delay in R (r = -0.264, p = 1.8e-205) but not in J (r = -0.013, p = 0.21; with onset at 5% of peak speed r = -0.034, p = 1.5e-03; with onset after the go cue r = -0.029, p = 7.9e-03). J is 5 of its 16 sessions.
deviations: Movement onset (10% of peak speed) and maximum speed are defined here; the paper does not define them. Onsets at 5% and 20%, and onset searched only after the go cue, are shown.
Reach time is undefined in the paper; two readings were tested and (b) matches.

outcomes.statement: Of the 96 PMd electrodes, 74 for J and 80 for R had activity significantly correlated with the x and y location of the target (p < .05, Bonferroni over 96).
outcomes.source: Materials and methods, Neural recording and signal preprocessing, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Of the 96 electrodes, we found that 74 for J and 80 for R had significant correlation (p < .05, with Bonferroni correction where n = 96) with the task
outcomes.notes: 72 of 96 channels (J) and 80 of 96 (R) regress on target x and y at p < 0.05/96. Per session the counts are lower (J 39 to 70, R 30 to 70). On the units the file labels PMd (0 to 95) the counts are 74 (J) and 40 (R); R's labelled array has 29 silent channels.
deviations: PMd is taken as units 96 to 191, from the data check, against the units' electrode_group labels.
J is 5 of its 16 sessions.

outcomes.statement: The top six PCs of the condition-averaged delay activity explain cumulatively 58, 82, 88, 92, 94 and 95% of the variance for J (120 conditions) and 81, 89, 92, 94, 95 and 96% for R (132 conditions).
outcomes.source: Materials and methods, Dimensionality reduction, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: The top 6 PCs explained the following cumulative percentages of the variance: 58% 82% 88% 92% 94% 95% (J); 81% 89% 92% 94% 95% 96% (R)
outcomes.notes: R has the paper's 132 conditions. Twelve of thirteen values are within tolerance; R's PC1 is 72.8% against 81 +- 8.1%, outside by 0.14 points. The criterion's partial case needs all R values within tolerance, so by its letter the result is not reproduced. With the day's mean taken over the analysed delay windows R's PC1 is 80.5%, and without day-mean subtraction 80.6%. Spikes exist only within trials (99.93 to 99.95% of PMd spikes inside a trial in every session), so the main day mean is the rate over trial time. J's values are within tolerance on 96 of its 120 conditions.
deviations: The day's average rate is the session's rate over its recorded time; the paper does not say how it was computed. The other choice is shown.
J is 5 of its 16 sessions and 96 of its 120 conditions.

outcomes.statement: The spatial plane captures a large part of the variance of the condition-averaged activity for the ring, horizontal, vertical and 3-rings tasks; 66.8, 64.4, 47.7 and 68.2% for J and 33.7, 30.7, 31.0 and 30.1% for R (p < 1e-4).
outcomes.source: Results, Structure of neural activity during delay period, paragraph 2; Figure 2a
outcomes.quote: The spatial plane captures a large percentage of the overall variance of the trial-averaged neural responses for the ring, horizontal, vertical, and 3-rings tasks: 66.8%, 64.4%, 47.7%, and 68.2% (monkey J), 33.7%, 30.7%, 31.0%, 30.1% (monkey R)
outcomes.notes: Measured values are reading (a) with tasks by the Methods' dates (R ring, horizontal, vertical, 3-rings; J ring, vertical, 3-rings). No pairing of readings puts more than three of the seven values within tolerance. R's shares (29.5 to 36.9%) lie near the paper's (30.1 to 33.7%); J's are lower (40.2 to 54.4% against 47.7 to 68.2%) on 5 of 16 sessions without the horizontal task. The shares exceed those of planes fit to targets shuffled across conditions with p = 0.005 to 0.16 (shuffle medians 11.5 to 24.8%), so the stated p < 1e-4 does not hold against this null; the paper's null is not stated. 1000 shuffles cannot give p below 1.0e-03, but the observed p values lie well above that.
deviations: J's plane is fit on 96 of its 120 conditions and its horizontal task is absent.
Two definitions of the share and two namings of R's horizontal and vertical tasks were tested.

outcomes.statement: After target onset the neural state in the spatial plane starts at the center, diverges after 50 ms (R 75 ms) and converges to the steady delay state after 300 ms (R 400 ms).
outcomes.source: Results, Structure of neural activity during delay period, paragraph 2; Figure 2c
outcomes.quote: at target onset, the neural states projected onto this plane start at the center of this plane, start to diverge after 50 ms (R: 75 ms), and converge to the steady neural states after J: 300 ms, R: 400ms
outcomes.notes: Divergence (D below 0.9) at 70 ms (J) and 90 ms (R) after target onset; convergence (D below 0.1) at 270 ms (J) and 350 ms (R). All four are within tolerance, so by the letter of the criterion the result is reproduced; partially_reproduced is a judgment beyond the criterion, made because R's divergence cannot be told from baseline noise. Other thresholds move divergence between 10 and 150 ms and convergence between 230 and 390 ms, so both monkeys' times depend on the threshold; J diverges at 150 ms with threshold 0.8 and converges at 390 ms with threshold 0.05, outside tolerance. J's times hold under the two added checks (pre-onset D SD 0.03; with the converged state taken from trials whose delay window starts after the bin, 70 and 250 ms). R's D lies below 0.9 in 6 of the 10 bins before target onset (SD 0.09), and with the non-overlapping converged state it diverges at 10 ms and converges at 310 ms, both outside tolerance. The pre-target state sits at x -2.1, y -30.4 mm (J) and 17.6, -13.1 mm (R) in the plane's target coordinates, so "starts at the center" is not borne out.
deviations: The thresholds, bins and smoothing are chosen here; the paper reads the times from a figure.

outcomes.statement: On single trials, on-axis and off-axis deviations of the neural state in the spatial plane are positively correlated with the on-axis and off-axis deviations of the hand position at maximum speed (on-axis p = 1e-3 J, 4e-3 R; off-axis p = 4e-4 J, 2e-4 R).
outcomes.source: Results, Structure of neural activity during delay period, paragraph 3; Figure 2d
outcomes.quote: Both on-axis ... and off-axis ... deviations in the neural state were positively correlated with on-axis and off-axis deviations in the position of max-speed for both monkeys
outcomes.notes: Over all tasks (reading a), on-axis J r = 0.091 (p = 1.7e-17), R r = 0.022 (p = 1.3e-02); off-axis J r = 0.102 (p = 1.3e-21), R r = 0.072 (p = 2.2e-16). In the 3-rings task alone R's on-axis correlation is not significant (p = 6.5e-02). R's on-axis correlation is positive with p < 0.05 in one of seven sessions and negative in one (2017-01-16, r = -0.044, p = 4.9e-02). With deviations from session by condition means the correlations are nearly unchanged (R on-axis r = 0.020, p = 2.3e-02; off-axis 0.083, p = 3.0e-21; J on 0.092, off 0.101), so offsets between sessions do not produce them.
deviations: The position of maximum speed comes from hand positions smoothed here (Gaussian, SD 20 ms).

outcomes.statement: The speed axis of delay activity varies with maximum speed for reaches to the same target distance, for 11 of 12 distances in J and 11 of 12 in R (p < 0.05), so it encodes speed independently of distance.
outcomes.source: Results, Structure of neural activity during delay period, paragraph 4; Figure 2e and 2f
outcomes.quote: We then tested whether the neural state in this dimension varied with speed for reaches to the same target, and found that for almost all distances it did (J: 11/12 distances in the vertical and horizontal tasks, R: 11/12, p < 0.05)
outcomes.notes: R 11 of 12 distances under both readings and with cross-validated projections; the exception is the nearest distance. J 6 of 12 under both readings (4 and 5 cross-validated), on 3211 trials of its two vertical sessions; its horizontal sessions are not in the dandiset. Each distance rank pools both line tasks and both sessions of each. Split by task and session, R has 1, 4, 10 and 7 of 12 and J 1 and 3, so the counts rest on pooling sessions.
deviations: J has only vertical sessions here, against horizontal and vertical in the paper.
R's horizontal targets lie at 5.2 + 10.4 k mm, so distances are matched by rank (1 to 12) within each task.

outcomes.statement: After regressing out speed from the neural activity, a positive correlation with target distance remains (p < 1e-4 for J and R).
outcomes.source: Results, Structure of neural activity during delay period, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: we found that after regressing out speed from the neural activity, there is still a positive correlation
outcomes.notes: Cross-validated predictions of target distance from speed-residualised activity correlate with distance, J r = 0.123 (p = 1.2e-30), R r = 0.233 (p = 7.1e-158); in-sample r = 0.182 and 0.257. Within 3-rings the cross-validated r is 0.154 (J) and 0.265 (R).
deviations: The paper does not say how the correlation was tested; a 10-fold cross-validated linear regression was chosen.

outcomes.statement: Projected onto the top PCs, the distance dimension is about half as large as the speed dimension.
outcomes.source: Results, Structure of neural activity during delay period, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: when projecting the speed and distance dimensions onto the top PCs, the distance projection is approximately half compared to the projection of the speed dimension
outcomes.notes: The distance axis projects onto the top PCs as much as the speed axis for J (ratio 1.01) and more for R (1.68). With the plane projected out of the distance axis the ratios are 0.73 and 1.14.
deviations: The paper does not define the distance dimension or the projection; both are defined here.

outcomes.statement: Across all single trials the speed dimension explains 2% (J) and 1% (R) of the variance of the neural state, and the spatial plane 20% (J) and 10% (R).
outcomes.source: Results, Structure of neural activity during delay period, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: This dimension explains J: 2%, R: 1% of the variance in the neural state across all trials; for reference, the spatial plane explains J: 20%, R: 10% for single trials
outcomes.notes: Only R's speed value (0.86% against 1%) is within tolerance. All four values are below the paper's and keep its order, J above R. Within single sessions the plane explains 11.2 to 20.7% (J) and 6.5 to 14.2% (R).
deviations: J is 5 of its 16 sessions.

outcomes.statement: The distributions of single-trial neural states for each condition are elliptical, and for most conditions their major axis points along the direction of the mean neural state from the origin.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural state variability during delay, paragraph 2; Figure 3a and 3c
outcomes.quote: we found that the ellipses for most conditions were oriented in the direction of the mean neural state from the origin
outcomes.notes: Major axis within 45 degrees of the condition mean's direction for 69 of 96 conditions (J, median 21.0 degrees, Wilcoxon p = 4.1e-08) and 99 of 132 (R, median 19.3 degrees, p = 8.0e-10). Median ratio of major to minor axis 1.35 (J) and 1.56 (R).

outcomes.statement: The mean absolute on-axis (distance) deviation of the neural state is larger than the off-axis (direction) deviation, in each task (J p = 9e-7 ring, 4e-7 horizontal, 1e-8 vertical, 3e-14 3-rings; R 8e-3, 4e-7, 2e-7 and 0.19).
outcomes.source: Results, Neural state variability during delay, paragraph 2; Figure 3
outcomes.quote: The mean absolute on-axis deviation for each target and for each monkey was systematically greater than the mean absolute off-axis deviations in the tasks
outcomes.notes: On-axis exceeds off-axis with p < 0.05 in 5 of 6 task and monkey pairs under readings (a) paired over targets and (c) Welch over trials, 4 of 6 under (b). The exception is J's ring task, one session of four here (13 of 24 targets with on > off, paired p = 0.69). R's 3-rings task is not significant (paired p = 0.38), as in the paper (0.19).
deviations: J's ring task is 1 of 4 sessions.
The test is not named; three readings were tested.

outcomes.statement: Relative deviations of the neural state (deviation as a fraction of reach distance), on and off axis, decrease with reach distance.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural state variability during delay, paragraph 3; Figure 3b and 3d
outcomes.quote: we found that the relative deviations in both distance and direction in the neural state decreased as a function of reach distance
outcomes.notes: Spearman rho of relative deviation with distance, on axis J -0.389 and R -0.404, off axis J -0.378 and R -0.402, all p below 1e-290. Absolute deviations grow slightly with distance (rho 0.073 to 0.103), so the decrease comes mainly from dividing by distance, and the test discriminates little.

outcomes.statement: Direction classification of the ring targets reaches 32.2% for J (24 targets) and 16% for R (36 targets); distance classification over 12 targets reaches 18.9% (J) and 21.4% (R).
outcomes.source: Results, Accuracy of endpoint prediction from delay activity, paragraph 2; Figure 4a and 4b
outcomes.quote: direction was J:32.2% ± 0.6% accuracy for 24 targets (R:16% ±.5% for 36 targets) while distance classification for only 12 targets was lower for J (18.9% ±.1%) and comparable for R (21.4% ±.2% for R)
outcomes.notes: All four accuracies are below the paper's (32.2, 16, 18.9, 21.4%) and well above chance (4.2, 2.8, 8.3%). With hyperparameters chosen on the 3-rings trials they are 24.3, 13.8, 16.0 and 18.3%. J's ring value comes from 1020 trials of one session against four in the paper, and its distance value from the vertical task only.
deviations: SVM hyperparameters are sklearn's defaults; the paper's tuned values are not reported. A tuned variant is shown.
The tolerance is 10%, not the paper's SEM over folds (see the claims file).
J ring is 1 of 4 sessions; J distance is the vertical task only.

outcomes.statement: Classifying the 16 directions of each ring of the 3-rings task separately, accuracy increases with ring distance; 23, 36 and 43% for J and 22, 28 and 29% for R.
outcomes.source: Results, Accuracy of endpoint prediction from delay activity, paragraph 2; Figure 4c
outcomes.quote: when classifying targets in 3-rings separately for each distance, accuracy increases with ring distance (23%, 36%, 43% for J; 22%, 28%, 29% for R)
outcomes.notes: Accuracy rises with ring distance in both monkeys. J's values are within tolerance; R's are below it (paper 22, 28, 29%). With tuned hyperparameters R gives 20.2, 22.9 and 27.8%.
deviations: SVM hyperparameters are sklearn's defaults.

outcomes.statement: Angular errors of direction classification decrease with ring distance, but errors measured as arc length are not significantly different between rings (F test, p > .05 for J and R).
outcomes.source: Results, Accuracy of endpoint prediction from delay activity, paragraph 3; Figure 4c and 4d
outcomes.quote: When presenting the decoding accuracy in term of angular error, mean error decreases as a function target distance (Fig 4c). In contrast, when presenting the errors as arc-length ... the arc-length error distributions are not significantly different
outcomes.notes: Angular errors fall with ring distance (J 41.0, 24.3, 18.3 degrees; R 52.0, 42.4, 36.7), but arc errors grow (J 2.87, 3.40, 3.84 cm; R 3.63, 5.92, 7.69 cm), and the one-way ANOVA finds the rings different (J F = 22.15, p = 2.7e-10; R F = 52.16, p = 1.5e-22). Restricted to errors within the 4 cm ring's range, J's rings do not differ (p = 0.23) and R's do (p = 1.3e-03); the paper's Figure 4d inset uses that restriction for its means, so J matches there.
deviations: The paper's "F test" was read as a one-way ANOVA of per-trial arc errors; a variance test (Levene) and the restricted ANOVA are shown.

outcomes.statement: Mean distance-classification error is slightly but significantly lower than the arc-length error of direction classification, and projecting the activity onto the spatial plane before classification raises it (J 2.64 to 3.03 cm; R given as 2.78 and 3.27 cm), to the level of the direction errors.
outcomes.source: Results, Accuracy of endpoint prediction from delay activity, paragraph 4; Figure 4d
outcomes.quote: we found that the mean classification error for distance classification was significantly (albeit only slightly) lower than the errors for directional classification ... The resulting classification error rate (Fig 4d, blue bars) is significantly greater than classification using the full dimensional neural activity

statistics.about: plane-projected against full-dimensional distance error, J and R
plane-projected distance error against direction errors, each distance in J and R

outcomes.notes: Under reading (a) all four values are within tolerance and projection raises the error (Welch J p = 2.7e-07, R p = 4.3e-41; paired over trials J p = 4.9e-12, R p = 1.2e-62). R's full value is inside its bound (2.502 cm) by 0.001 cm, so the match is fragile. The full-activity distance error is lower than the arc error of every ring in both monkeys (p at most 3.1e-05). After projection it equals the arc error only for J's 4 cm ring (p = 0.46), so the claim that projection brings it to the level of the direction errors holds for 1 of 6 rings. With arc errors restricted to the 4 cm ring's range, as in the Figure 4d inset, the full error is still lower than every ring's (p at most 3.1e-05), and the projected error equals the arc error for J's 4 and 8 cm rings (p = 0.46 and 0.11) but not J's 12 cm ring (p = 5.3e-03) or any of R's (p at most 1.0e-04), 2 of 6 rings.
deviations: The paper prints R's values in an order that contradicts its text; two readings were listed and (a) matches.
J's distance classification uses the vertical task only.
The plane is fit on all trials, including the test folds of the plane-projected classifier.

findings.statement: In every file the units' electrode_group labels are swapped. Units 0 to 95 are labelled PMd but their electrodes column points to electrode rows of group 1 (M1), and units 96 to 191 are labelled M1 but point to rows of group 2 (PMd), the rows the PMd LFP uses. The data agree with the electrodes column; in R the array labelled PMd has 29 silent channels and carries almost no target information (at most 6 significant channels per session in the delay window and decoding at most 0.03 above chance), though 40 of its 96 channels regress on target position when R's sessions are pooled; this is as expected of the M1 array the paper calls unusable. The conversion code assigns electrode_group by the order of a dictionary of groups.

In every J file the boundary between units 0 and 1 in units/spike_times_index is misplaced. Unit 0 stops 1323 to 3120 s into sessions of 3083 to 8106 s, and unit 1 holds two to five times the median number of spikes, with spike times that run to the session's end and restart near 0.
Hand, cursor, eye and decoded positions are stated in meters with conversion NaN; the values are in mm (targets at up to 120, hand reaching them at about the same values).

task_id is 2 in every trial and version_id is one value per monkey, so the files do not say which target configuration a session used; it must be inferred from target_pos, which has no unit. Electrode positions are NaN and impedances -1.
The trials column is_successful is described as "if monkey started before the mandatory delay period after target shown"; it holds the rig's trial success flag.
The dandiset description says the files hold sorted spikes; the units are threshold crossings of each electrode (one unit per electrode, built from the rig's spike rasters).
The archive's assetsSummary for version 0.220124.2156 gives 15 files and 187.5 GB; the version holds 12 files and 39.5 GB.

The dandiset holds 5 of the 16 sessions the paper uses for monkey J. All four horizontal sessions, three of four ring sessions and two of four in each other configuration are missing; the paper's own data link returns HTTP 403.

The files place R's horizontal targets on 2017-01-15 and 16 and vertical targets on 2017-01-17 and 18; the Methods give these dates the other way round. Grouped by the files' geometry, R's trial counts match the Methods' counts for horizontal and vertical better (within 4% and 3%) than grouped by date (12% and 5%).
R's horizontal targets lie at 5.2 + 10.4 k mm from the center, not 1 cm apart as stated, and R's 2017-01-17 session holds 69 successful trials to six ring targets outside its layout.
R's delays run from 400 to 1000 ms, against 400 to 900 ms in the Methods, and R has only 26 trials without a delay (all on 2017-01-19), against 10% in the Methods; J has 19.8%.
R's 3-rings session holds 1340 successful delayed center-out trials where the paper used 912; neither the paper nor the dandiset says how the trials were selected.
In R's 2017-01-19 the cursor differs from the hand by more than 1 m in over 1% of samples; in the other sessions they agree to within 3 mm in 99% of samples.

The Results give J's distance errors as "3.03 cm v.s. 2.64 cm" (projected, then full) and R's as "2.78 cm v.s. 3.27 cm", while stating that projection raises the error in both; the R values are printed in the reverse order or contradict the text.
The paper names no analysis code, does not report its SVM hyperparameters or the nulls of its p-values, and its data link returns HTTP 403.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The executed notebook of the first run (commit d455c0d) with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file.

disagreements.reason: All 6 J values and R PCs 2-6 are within tolerance, but R PC1 is 72.8 against a lower bound of 72.9. The criterion's partial case requires all R values within, so by its letter this is not reproduced. It is a 0.14-point miss, and the result depends on the day-mean choice (the trial-window variant gives 80.5). The day mean is n_spikes / recorded_s, and recorded_s is the total in-trial hand time, while unit spans run to about 8300 s against 6520 s recorded; whether spikes exist between trials is never checked.

attempts.label: DANDI:000127
attempts.paper_title: Area 2 of primary somatosensory cortex encodes kinematics of the whole arm
attempts.entry_title: Active and passive arm movements in somatosensory area 2 (Chowdhury et al. 2020)
attempts.description: Tests the active/passive findings of Chowdhury, Glaser and Miller (2020) on dandiset 000127, which holds one of the paper's twelve sessions. It compares hand and arm kinematics between active reaches and passive bumps, measures how well single neurons tell the two apart, and fits hand-only and whole-arm models of each neuron's firing. The paper's two-workspace experiment cannot be tested because those sessions are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Chowdhury, Glaser & Miller (2020) from dandiset 000127

outcomes.statement: In the two-workspace experiment, the whole-arm model predicted neural activity better than the hand-only model for 238 of 288 neurons, with no significant difference for the other 50.
outcomes.source: Figure 4
outcomes.quote: Of the 288 neurons recorded across the 8 sessions, 238 were significantly better predicted by the whole-arm model than the hand-only model, and for the other 50, there was no significant difference
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds one session of the active/passive experiment. None of the eight two-workspace sessions is in it.

outcomes.statement: A whole-arm model trained on both workspaces explained as much neural variance as models trained within a single workspace.
outcomes.source: Figure 5
outcomes.quote: The symbols lying very close to the unity line in each panel of Figure 5 indicate that the full model explained just as much neural variance as did the individual models.
outcomes.notes: The two-workspace sessions are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: The whole-arm model predicted the shape of directional tuning curves in the two workspaces better than the hand-only model for 138 of 288 neurons, and worse for 2.
outcomes.source: Figure 6
outcomes.quote: Only two out of 288 neurons were significantly better predicted by the hand-only model (using p < 0.05), while 138 of 288 neurons were significantly better predicted by the whole-arm model.
outcomes.notes: The two-workspace sessions are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: The whole-arm model predicted the shifts of preferred direction between workspaces better than the hand-only model, with a circular variance accounted for of 0.75 against 0.57.
outcomes.source: Figure 7B
outcomes.quote: Figure 7B shows that the whole-arm model once again out-performed the hand-only model, with an average cVAF over all neurons of 0.75 compared to 0.57.

statistics.about: whole-arm against hand-only cVAF, the sessions in which the whole-arm model out-performed
statistics.test: corrected resampled t-test on repeated 5-fold cross-validation
statistics.n: 7 of 8 sessions, 100 cross-validation samples of the cVAF per model and session

statistics.about: whole-arm against hand-only cVAF, the remaining session
statistics.test: corrected resampled t-test on repeated 5-fold cross-validation
statistics.n: 1 session, 100 cross-validation samples of the cVAF per model

outcomes.notes: The two-workspace sessions are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: In the 120 ms after movement onset, average hand speed was similar in active reaches and passive bumps.
outcomes.source: Figure 8B
outcomes.quote: However, average movement speed was similar between active and passive trials in this 120 ms window, which we used for data analysis.
outcomes.notes: The speed traces of active and passive trials overlap in the 120 ms window and separate afterwards. Passive movements are 13% faster on average (0.207 against 0.183 m/s), half a standard deviation, which is statistically clear; the paper's "similar" is qualitative.
deviations: One session from one monkey; the paper has four sessions from two.

outcomes.statement: A linear discriminant classifier predicted whether a movement was active or passive 89% of the time from whole-arm kinematics in the analysis window.
outcomes.source: Results, Area 2 represents passive movements differently from active reaches, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Averaged over the sessions, a linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier could predict the movement type 89% of the time, using only the whole-arm kinematics in the analysis window
outcomes.notes: A linear discriminant tells active from passive trials 90% of the time from joint angles and velocities, against 58% from hand kinematics and 53% by chance. The paper reports 89% averaged over four sessions.
deviations: One session from one monkey; the paper has four sessions from two.
Joint angles and velocities stand in for the hand and elbow marker kinematics, which are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Many neurons had an above-chance separability index, the accuracy of a linear discriminant predicting the trial type from that neuron's firing.
outcomes.source: Figure 8E
outcomes.quote: we used LDA to classify movement type based on individual neurons, calling this prediction rate the neuron's 'separability index' (Figure 8E). We found that many neurons had an above chance separability index
outcomes.notes: 20 of 50 neurons have a separability index above chance at p < 0.05, with a median of 0.56 and a highest value of 0.80.
deviations: One session from one monkey; the paper has four sessions from two.
Neurons firing below 1 Hz in the window (15 of 65) are left out; the paper states no criterion.

outcomes.statement: In the active/passive experiment the whole-arm model again tended to out-perform the hand-only model, but for many more neurons than in the two-workspace experiment the difference was not significant.
outcomes.source: Figure 9
outcomes.quote: the whole-arm model again tended to out-perform the hand-only model (Filled circles above the dashed unity line in Figure 9). However, there were many more neurons (open circles) for which the difference between models was insignificant...
outcomes.notes: The whole-arm stand-in is significantly better than the hand-only model for 15 of 50 neurons and worse for none; 35 (70%) show no significant difference, against 17% in the paper's two-workspace experiment. That comparison uses the paper's number.
deviations: One session from one monkey; the paper has four sessions from two.
The whole-arm model is hand plus joint kinematics; the marker positions the paper's model uses are not in the dandiset.
The hand-only model is two-dimensional, the fits carry a small ridge penalty, neurons below 1 Hz are left out, and no Bonferroni correction is applied.

outcomes.statement: Unlike in the two-workspace experiment, many neurons had no consistent relationship with arm kinematics across active and passive movements, shown by negative pseudo-R2 for the model trained on both conditions.
outcomes.source: Figure 10
outcomes.quote: Surprisingly however, unlike our results from the two-workspace experiment (see Figure 5), many neurons in the active/passive task did not have this consistent relationship, indicated by the many neurons with negative pR2 values for the model trained over both conditions.
outcomes.notes: 19 of 50 neurons scored on active trials and 23 of 50 on passive trials have negative pseudo-R2 for the model trained on both conditions, but about as many (17 and 25) are negative when trained within one condition. Only 5 and 3 neurons are positive within a condition and negative across both. Training on both costs a little on active trials and nothing on passive trials.
deviations: One session from one monkey; the paper has four sessions from two.
The whole-arm model is hand plus joint kinematics, as for fig9-whole-arm-fits-better.
Pseudo-R2 for one trial type is computed on a repeat's pooled held-out predictions, against that type's own mean firing; the paper does not say which mean it used.

outcomes.statement: The consistency of the whole-arm model, its pseudo-R2 when trained on both conditions, correlated negatively with a neuron's separability index.
outcomes.source: Figure 11B
outcomes.quote: Interestingly, we found the opposite result—model consistency actually correlated negatively with the separability index.
outcomes.notes: Scored on active trials, model consistency correlates negatively with separability (Spearman -0.38, 95% interval -0.60 to -0.11). Scored on passive trials the correlation is -0.13 and on all trials together 0.14; neither can be told apart from zero.
deviations: One session from one monkey; the paper has four sessions from two.
The whole-arm model is hand plus joint kinematics, as for fig9-whole-arm-fits-better.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds one of the twelve sessions analysed in the paper, and none from the two-workspace experiment, so four of the paper's main findings cannot be tested from it.
The positions of the arm markers, which the paper's whole-arm model is built on, are not included. Joint angles and muscle lengths derived from them are.
The text descriptions of hand position and hand velocity give centimetres while the stated unit is metres. The stated unit, with the file's conversion factor, is correct.
The dandiset's metadata names the paper without saying which part of it the data covers. It was packaged for the Neural Latents Benchmark, not as the paper's data release.

attempts.label: DANDI:000128
attempts.paper_title: Cortical preparatory activity: representation of movement or first cog in a dynamical machine?
attempts.entry_title: Preparatory and peri-movement tuning in motor and premotor cortex (Churchland et al. 2010)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Churchland, Cunningham, Kaufman, Ryu and Shenoy (2010) on dandiset 000128 (MC_Maze), which holds the J-array session of monkey Jenkins on the maze task, recorded with two Utah arrays. It tests the correlation between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, its time course, the dimensionality of preparatory activity, the performance and stability of preferred directions in the peri-movement, kinematic and task spaces, and the paper's oscillator model. The speed task, the single-electrode recordings and EMG are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Churchland et al. (2010) from dandiset 000128

outcomes.statement: The J-array dataset holds 146 single- and multi-unit isolations from two 96-electrode arrays, recorded on the maze task with 108 conditions, with a mean of 2166 trials per neuron.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavior and recordings, paragraph 1; Methods, Neural recordings and datasets
outcomes.quote: (27 and 108 conditions for ‘monkey J’ and ‘monkey J-array’ datasets) ... a pair of implanted 96-electrode arrays (J-array dataset, 146 single- and multi-unit isolations) ... High trial counts (mean trials/neuron = 311, 492, 388 and 2166 for monkey A, B, J, J-array)
outcomes.notes: The dataset has 108 conditions (36 mazes in 3 versions). The unit count is 182 (137 held in, 45 held out), outside 146 plus or minus 14.6, so the three counts do not all match under any reading. Reading (a), all successful trials, gives 2869 with the 574 test-file segments, outside the tolerance, and 2295 counting the train file alone (the trials with condition labels), within it; every unit is observed on every train trial. The test file has its own clock and no delay or success column, so whether its trials belong to (a) cannot be settled from the file. Under reading (b) M1 keeps 1786 trials with T2, outside the tolerance. The 137 held-in units (a Neural Latents Benchmark split) and the 1967 trials with delay > 400 ms are printed but are not readings and decide nothing. The answer of 2026-10-22 to the M1 question removed T1's count (1452) from reading (b); the outcome is unchanged.
deviations: Nothing in the dataset says which units or trials the paper used, or whether this session (2009-09-25) is the one the paper analysed.

outcomes.statement: The single-electrode datasets hold 64, 74 and 172 single units for monkeys A, B and J, with means of 311, 492 and 388 trials per neuron.
outcomes.source: Results, Behavior and recordings, paragraph 1; Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Neural and EMG recordings
outcomes.quote: High trial counts (mean trials/neuron = 311, 492, 388 and 2166 for monkey A, B, J, J-array) ... A total of 310 single-electrode isolations (64, 74, and 172 single-unit isolations for monkeys A, B and J) were recorded from caudal PMd, surface M1 and sulcal M1.
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds only the array session of monkey Jenkins. No speed-task data (monkeys A and B) and no single-electrode maze recordings are in it, and the paper names no other archive for them.

outcomes.statement: In the speed task one example neuron keeps its preparatory preference (reaches up and left) into the peri-movement epoch, with a preparatory to peri-movement tuning correlation of 0.72.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural responses during preparation and movement, paragraph 2; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: This preference is shared between preparatory and peri-movement epochs. This agreement is not perfect (two green traces surpass the black trace) but the overall correlation is quite high ( r =0.72, see section on correlations below for details).
outcomes.notes: Needs the speed task, which is not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Three other speed-task neurons with clear preparatory tuning do not keep their preferences into the peri-movement epoch; their preparatory and peri-movement tuning are negatively correlated, even for straight reaches at one distance and speed.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural responses during preparation and movement, paragraph 3; Figure 2C-E and legend
outcomes.quote: Despite clear preparatory tuning, preferences are not maintained between the preparatory and peri-movement epochs (color ordering differs between epochs). ... These neurons show negative correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning.
outcomes.notes: Needs the speed task, which is not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: In the maze task some neurons keep similar tuning between the preparatory and peri-movement epochs, but most do not.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural responses during preparation and movement, paragraph 4; Figure 3
outcomes.quote: Some neurons maintained similar tuning between preparatory and peri-movement epochs (panel A ) but most did not.
outcomes.notes: Under T2 with S1, 1 of 17 neurons has r of 0.72 or more (0.765) and 94.1% have r below 0.72, so the claim holds. The first part rests on that one neuron (unit 1581); the next largest r is 0.457. The answers of 2026-10-22 set aside T1 and S2. The earlier record was blocked (methods_underspecified) because T1 with S1 gave no neuron at 0.72 and S2 selected no neuron; with T2 and S1 fixed, the claim is reproduced. The notebook no longer prints T1 or S2 values.

outcomes.statement: In the J-array dataset the correlation between a neuron's preparatory and peri-movement tuning is positive on average but small (mean r = 0.13, p = 0.03; mean Spearman r = 0.11).
outcomes.source: Results, Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, paragraph 1; Figure 4D
outcomes.quote: Across the four datasets the mean correlation was positive (p=0.01, p=0.01, p=0.12, p=0.03) but only very modestly so (mean r = 0.21, 0.19, 0.06 and 0.13). Non-parametric correlations were similarly modest (mean Spearman's r = 0.20, 0.20, 0.06 and 0.11).

statistics.about: mean Pearson tuning correlation against zero, J-array
statistics.n: J-array neurons tuned in both epochs (count not given)

outcomes.notes: Under T2 with S1, 17 neurons, the mean Pearson r is 0.051 and the mean Spearman r 0.072, outside 0.13 plus or minus 0.013 and 0.11 plus or minus 0.011, and no test gives p below 0.05 (P1 0.47, P2 0.42, P3 0.61). Both means are positive; the Pearson mean is below half the paper's (0.065) and the Spearman mean is 65% of the paper's. Per-neuron r runs from -0.355 to 0.765 (SD 0.283); with 17 neurons the tests have little power. The answers of 2026-10-22 set aside T1 and S2; the earlier record gave T1 with S1 (recorded then as measured) and T2 with S1, and S2 gave no neuron; the notebook no longer prints T1 or S2 values. The measured values are now those of T2, and the outcome is unchanged.
deviations: The dataset has 182 units, not the paper's 146, and the paper's unit selection is not recorded; the selected neurons may differ from the paper's.

outcomes.statement: In the single-electrode datasets (monkeys A, B and J) the mean tuning correlation is 0.21, 0.19 and 0.06 (p = 0.01, 0.01 and 0.12), with mean Spearman correlations of 0.20, 0.20 and 0.06.
outcomes.source: Results, Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, paragraph 1; Figure 4A-C
outcomes.quote: Across the four datasets the mean correlation was positive (p=0.01, p=0.01, p=0.12, p=0.03) but only very modestly so (mean r = 0.21, 0.19, 0.06 and 0.13). Non-parametric correlations were similarly modest (mean Spearman's r = 0.20, 0.20, 0.06 and 0.11).

statistics.about: mean tuning correlation against zero, monkey A
mean tuning correlation against zero, monkey B
mean tuning correlation against zero, monkey J

outcomes.notes: The single-electrode datasets of monkeys A, B and J are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: The distributions of tuning correlations give little evidence (except perhaps weakly for monkey B) of one population with concordant tuning (r near 1) and another with opposing tuning (r near -1); most neurons have weakly correlated tuning, with a broad range of correlations centred near zero.
outcomes.source: Results, Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, paragraphs 3 and 4; Figure 4A-D
outcomes.quote: Even more disconcertingly, different neurons show markedly different relationships between preparatory and peri-movement activity, with a broad range of correlations centered near zero. ... Yet there is little evidence in Figure 4 (except perhaps weakly in panel B ) for one population of concordant tuning ( r ≈ 1) and another of opposing tuning ( r ≈ -1). Instead, most neurons have weakly correlated tuning.
outcomes.notes: J-array only. Under T2 with S1 the dip statistic is 0.071 (p 0.683), so U1 holds, and 16 of 17 neurons have |r| below 0.5, so U2 holds. No neuron has |r| of 0.8 or more; median r 0.013. With 17 neurons the dip test has little power, so U1 is weak evidence. The panel B part of the statement (monkey B) cannot be tested. The answers of 2026-10-22 removed the T1 and S2 readings, which had given the same outcome (T1) or no neuron (S2); the outcome is unchanged.

outcomes.statement: The correlation between preparatory tuning and peri-movement tuning measured at single time points begins to decline about 200 ms before movement onset and is near zero by movement onset.
outcomes.source: Results, Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, paragraph 2; Figure 4E and legend
outcomes.quote: The correlation with preparatory activity began to decline ∼200 ms prior to movement onset, and reached values near zero by movement onset ( Figure 4E ).
outcomes.notes: Under T2 with S1 (17 neurons), the mean correlation is 0.737 (A1) and 0.759 (A2) at -400 ms, 0.608 at -200 ms and 0.012 at movement onset, where no test is significant (smallest p 0.854). 82.1% (A1) and 79.8% (A2) of the drop from -400 ms to onset comes after -200 ms. The answers of 2026-10-22 removed the T1 and S2 readings, which had given the same outcome (T1) or no neuron (S2); the outcome is unchanged.
deviations: Under A2 the criterion's linear joining was implemented as a straight line between the last go-locked value and the first movement-locked one where they leave a gap, and a linear fade from one to the other where they overlap, with each condition's go cue placed at its mean reaction time before onset. A1 and A2 differ only before -300 ms and give the same outcome.

outcomes.statement: In population averages sorted by each neuron's preparatory preference, the weak agreement between preparatory and peri-movement tuning dominates early, but the separation shrinks with time and shows little relation to preparatory tuning by movement onset.
outcomes.source: Results, Correlations between preparatory and peri-movement tuning, paragraph 3; Supplemental Figure 1 and legend
outcomes.quote: In population averages ( Supp. Fig. 1 ) the lack of correlation averages out and the means are dominated by the weak agreement between preparatory and peri-movement tuning. However, such effects grow dramatically smaller with time. By movement onset even population averages show little relationship with preparatory tuning ( Supp. Fig. 1 ).
outcomes.notes: Under T2 with S1 (17 neurons), the strongest-minus-weakest separation is 0.220 (reading a) and 0.346 (reading b) of the maximum rate in the preparatory epoch, and 0.053 and 0.095 at movement onset, ratios 0.240 and 0.274. R1 holds under both; R2 holds under (a) and not under (b). The preparatory separation is positive by construction, as the conditions are ranked on the same preparatory rates. The answer of 2026-10-22 says the paper does not fix the maximum, and the criterion now names readings (a) and (b), the two already run, so the method is unchanged. The answers on M1 and M6 removed T1 and S2; the outcome is unchanged.

outcomes.statement: For every dataset the highest cross-validated PD performance in accounting for preparatory tuning is reached when the PD is expressed in the space built by PCA from the population peri-movement response, compared with task spaces and PCA-based kinematic and EMG spaces.
outcomes.source: Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 3; Figure 6A-D
outcomes.quote: For every dataset, the highest level of performance was achieved ... when PDs were expressed in the peri-movement space.
outcomes.notes: Under T2 with S1 (83 neurons) the peri-movement space is best in 24 of 24 combinations of W, D, V and G under K1 and under K2. Its best is 0.518 at k = 14 (K1) and 0.505 at k = 12 (K2), against 0.424 and 0.417 for the best kinematic space and 0.412 for the kitchen-sink space (G1). The best k is the upper end of each range, an edge value and not a peak. The answers of 2026-10-22 set aside T1 and S2. The earlier record was blocked (methods_underspecified) because under T1 with S1 the peri-movement space fell below the kinematic and kitchen-sink spaces (values no longer printed); with T2 fixed, the claim is reproduced.
deviations: J-array only; EMG is not recorded for it.
Acceleration is the time derivative of the dataset's hand velocity.
V1 ("each component's maximum absolute value") was run as the magnitudes (V1a) and as the signed component at its largest magnitude (V1b); they do not change the outcome.

outcomes.statement: Considering each dimensionality separately, PD performance is almost always higher in the peri-movement space than in other spaces of the same dimensionality; for the maze task the 3-D endpoints and peak speed space does not perform well.
outcomes.source: Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 3; Figure 6A-D
outcomes.quote: Even if we consider each dimensionality individually, performance was almost always higher for the peri-movement space. An exception was that, among 3-dimensional spaces, the ‘targs+instr. spd.’ and ‘endpoints + max. spd.’ performed very well for the datasets collected using the speed task. The former is undefined for the maze task, but the latter did not perform well.
outcomes.notes: The 3-D endpoints + max speed space (0.168) is below the 3-D peri-movement space (0.271). Under T2 with S1 the peri-movement space wins 21 of 22 comparisons (K1) and 19 of 20 (K2) in every combination of W, D, V and G, so L1 and L2 hold. The comparison lost is the 2-D initial-velocity space (0.238 against 0.223). At k = 1 the peri-movement space beats the kinematic spaces by 0.002 to 0.004 only. The answers of 2026-10-22 set aside T1 and S2. The earlier record was blocked (methods_underspecified) because T1 failed L1 and L2 and T2 with S2 failed L1 in some combinations; with T2 and S1 fixed, the claim is reproduced.
deviations: J-array only.

outcomes.statement: PD performance in PCA-based spaces generally improves with dimensionality, peaks in a middle range, and declines beyond about 10 dimensions through over-fitting.
outcomes.source: Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 2; Figure 6A-D
outcomes.quote: Performance typically improved with dimensionality. ... Performance typically declined at dimensionalities >10, an indication of over-fitting.
outcomes.notes: Under T2 with S1 (83 neurons) performance rises from 0.140 at k = 1 to 0.518 at k = 14, so it improves with dimensionality, but the best k is 14, above 10, and performance does not decline at k = 14. Two of the criterion's three conditions fail, and the part of the statement they test (a peak in a middle range and a decline beyond about 10 dimensions) is not found. The answers of 2026-10-22 set aside T1 and S2. The earlier record was blocked (methods_underspecified) because under T1 the claim held (values no longer printed); with T2 fixed, it is not reproduced.
deviations: J-array only.

outcomes.statement: Preparatory activity is moderately high-dimensional; depending on the dataset, 7 to 10 dimensions capture 90% of its variance across conditions.
outcomes.source: Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Estimating the upper limit of PD performance; Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: This T-matrix also allows us to estimate the dimensionality of preparatory activity ... depending on the dataset, 7-10 dimensions were required to capture 90% of the data variance.
outcomes.notes: Under T2, 90% of the variance of the preparatory condition-mean matrix needs 15 components with the 83 neurons of N1 (S1) and 18 with all 182 units (N2). Neither is within 7 to 11. The supplement defines the matrix as the claims file does ("T was c×n with each row containing the mean preparatory activity for every neuron"), from "all neurons", which is reading N2 (18), and says "7-10 dimensions were required"; the main text says "at least 7-10 dimensions", which 15 and 18 would meet. Whether the claim is a range or a lower bound is asked in questions/000128.yaml. The condition means average 10 to 22 trials per condition (median 17), and their noise may add components; the claims file does not fix how the paper handled this. The answers of 2026-10-22 set aside T1 (recorded earlier as measured) and S2; the measured value is now 15 and the outcome is unchanged.
deviations: J-array only.

outcomes.statement: Averaged over monkeys A, B and J (J-array excluded, no EMG), PD performance is highest in the peri-movement space at every dimensionality limit, the advantage grows with dimensionality, and task spaces are largely outperformed by the kinematic and EMG spaces, which are in turn outperformed by the peri-movement space.
outcomes.source: Results, PD performance in a variety of spaces, paragraph 5; Figure 6E and legend
outcomes.quote: Performance (averaged across neurons) was highest when the PD employed the space based on peri-movement neural activity. This performance differential increased at higher dimensionalities, indicating that the peri-movement space better captured higher-dimensional aspects of the data.

statistics.about: spaces worse than the best space (asterisks in Figure 6E)
statistics.n: neurons of monkeys A, B and J

outcomes.notes: Needs monkeys A, B and J (single electrodes) and EMG, none of which is in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: A control space built from peri-movement responses in which each neuron's peri-movement pattern was inverted on a random half of the conditions performs poorly, so the trailing end of preparatory activity does not explain the peri-movement space's success.
outcomes.source: Results, Controls, paragraph 1; Figure 7A and legend
outcomes.quote: The PCA-based ‘shuffled-space’ performed poorly ( Figure 7A ); any contribution from the trailing end of preparatory activity (preserved despite shuffling) is insufficient to allow good performance.
outcomes.notes: Under T2 with S1 the shuffled space (mean of 10 shuffles) is below the unshuffled one at every k, so H1 holds, and its best, 0.227 (0.208 to 0.244 over shuffles), is below the best kinematic space in every variant (0.421 or more under K1, 0.414 or more under K2), so H2 holds. The answers of 2026-10-22 set aside T1 and S2. The earlier record was blocked (methods_underspecified) because under T1 the unshuffled space fell below zero at k of 10 or more while the shuffled one stayed positive, so H1 failed; with T2 fixed, the claim is reproduced.
deviations: J-array only; the paper averages over datasets.

outcomes.statement: Moving the start of the peri-movement window from 150 ms before movement onset to movement onset costs little PD performance; at movement onset performance is 97% (monkey J) and 94% (monkeys A, B) of its original value.
outcomes.source: Results, Controls, paragraph 1; Figure 7B and legend
outcomes.quote: Finally, the start of the peri-movement window was 150 ms before movement onset but could be slid later in time with little decline in performance ( Figure 7B ). Even when the window began at movement onset ... performance was still at 97% (monkey J), and 94% (monkeys A, B) of its original value.
outcomes.notes: Reading J2, the J-array ratio. Under T2 with S1, performance at the best k with the window starting at onset is 0.959 (K1) and 0.957 (K2) of that with the window starting at -150 ms, within 0.97 plus or minus 0.097. The 94% of monkeys A and B and the single-electrode J value (J1) cannot be tested. Both best k values are the upper end of their range. The answers of 2026-10-22 set aside T1 and S2, which had all been within tolerance (T1 was recorded earlier as measured); the measured value is now 0.959 and the outcome is unchanged.
deviations: J-array only (reading J2).

outcomes.statement: The weak correlation between preparatory and peri-movement tuning does not depend on anterior-posterior recording location; regressing tuning correlation on AP location gives r = 0.20, p = 0.27 for J-array and no significant effect in any dataset.
outcomes.source: Results, Comparison of anterior versus posterior sites, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Regressing tuning correlation (as in Figure 4 ) against AP location yielded little or no effect: r =-0.05, p =0.82; r =-0.03, p =0.85; r =-0.07, p =0.52; and r =0.20, p =0.27 for the four datasets.

statistics.test: regression of tuning correlation on AP location
regression of tuning correlation on AP location
regression of tuning correlation on AP location
regression of tuning correlation on AP location

outcomes.notes: The electrodes table has no coordinates, so no anterior-posterior location. The criterion's fallback, the array, is not usable either, as every unit's electrode reference points into the 96 PMd rows, so by the file all units are in PMd. The unit ids' leading digit (1 for 92 units, 2 for 90) looks like an array number, but nothing in the dataset documents it or which array is which. As a variant that decides nothing, regressing tuning correlation on that digit gives r of magnitude 0.432 (T2 with S1, 17 neurons, p 0.084), not significant. The electrode groups are described as one array in M1 and one in PMd, but no unit column other than the electrode reference maps a unit to a group. The answers of 2026-10-22 removed the T1 variant; the block is unchanged.

outcomes.statement: The peri-movement space captures preparatory tuning at both anterior and posterior sites, with performance slightly better at anterior sites.
outcomes.source: Results, Comparison of anterior versus posterior sites, paragraph 1; Figure 7C and legend
outcomes.quote: The ability of the peri-movement space to capture tuning also held for both anterior and posterior sites ( Figure 7C ). ... Performance was slightly better at anterior sites
outcomes.notes: Needs each unit's AP location or at least its array; see ap-location-no-effect-on-correlation. Not run.

outcomes.statement: When the PD is measured on two random sets of 25 conditions, it is most stable in the peri-movement space, for every comparison space and all four datasets.
outcomes.source: Results, Stability of the PD, paragraph 2; Figure 7D and legend
outcomes.quote: Yet for every comparison, and for all four datasets, the PD was most stable when measured in the peri-movement space.
outcomes.notes: Under T2 with S1 the peri-movement space has the higher mean PD consistency in all 11 comparisons (0.752 against 0.548 for endpoints + max speed, 0.649 and 0.648 against 0.495 and 0.466 for segment directions G1 and G2, and 0.197 to 0.319 against 0.166 to 0.230 for the kinematic spaces at their best k, which is the upper end of the range). The answers of 2026-10-22 removed the T1 and S2 readings, which had given the same outcome; the outcome is unchanged. Removing them changed the random draws, so the values differ slightly from the earlier record.
deviations: J-array only.

outcomes.statement: In a simulated linear dynamical system (a harmonic oscillator held at 25 random initial states, then released), the preparatory to peri-movement tuning correlation of a unit is low (0.08), and a given preparatory rate can lead to opposing peri-movement patterns.
outcomes.source: Results, Tuning from a dynamical systems perspective, paragraph 2; Figure 8B-C and legend
outcomes.quote: The correlation of preparatory activity with peri-movement activity (averaged over the gray interval) was 0.08.
outcomes.notes: Over 1000 draws of 25 initial states, the correlation has medians -0.041 to 0.019, and the central 95% ranges have lower bounds of -0.430 to -0.385 and upper bounds of 0.350 to 0.428 under the eight readings; 0.08 lies inside all of them. The second part of the statement (a given preparatory rate leading to opposing patterns) is not tested by the criterion.

outcomes.statement: In the same simulated system, preparatory tuning is captured perfectly by a PD in the two-dimensional space found by PCA of the peri-movement activity.
outcomes.source: Results, Tuning from a dynamical systems perspective, paragraph 3; Figure 8D and legend; Supplemental Text
outcomes.quote: The PD points towards the pattern recruited by the activity of unit one (panel A ), and perfectly captures preparatory ‘tuning’.
outcomes.notes: Under all eight readings the smallest R squared and leave-one-out performance over 100 draws are 1.0 to the printed precision.

findings.statement: Every unit's electrode reference in the units table points into the first 96 rows of the electrodes table, which are labelled PMd, so by the file all 182 units are in PMd. The dataset describes two arrays, in M1 and PMd. The reference equals the unit id's channel digits minus one, which suggests the array offset was dropped in conversion.

The electrodes have no coordinates (x, y and z are NaN), and the leading digit of the unit ids (1 or 2), which may be the array, is not documented. No unit can be placed on the anterior-posterior axis or on an array.
The dataset holds 182 units where the paper reports 146 isolations for the J-array dataset, and does not record which units or trials the paper used, or that this session is the paper's.

574 of the session's successful trials are in the test file as 0.7 s segments around movement onset, without condition labels or behaviour and with only the 137 held-in units, so they cannot enter a condition-mean analysis. None duplicates a train trial. The test file has a clock of its own (segment times restart at 0) and no delay or success column, and the train file's trial ids are contiguous, so the files do not record which session trials the packaging dropped.
14 trials have a negative delay (as low as -3 ms), where the go cue precedes the recorded target onset.
