attempts.label: DANDI:000130
attempts.paper_title: Bayesian computation through cortical latent dynamics
attempts.entry_title: Bayesian computation through cortical latent dynamics (Sohn et al. 2019)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Sohn, Narain, Meirhaeghe and Jazayeri (2019) on dandiset 000130, the Neural Latents Benchmark's DMFC_RSG set, which holds one session of monkey H performing the Ready-Set-Go task with 54 units from dorsomedial frontal cortex. It tests the behaviour and the Bayesian observer model, single-unit sensitivity to the prior and elapsed time, the geometry and speed of population trajectories, the alternative mechanisms, and single-trial GPFA trajectories. Monkey G and the recurrent network models are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Sohn et al. (2019) from dandiset 000130

outcomes.statement: Regression slopes of tp on ts are positive and less than one in every condition, so the animals estimated ts and their responses were biased toward the mean of the prior.
outcomes.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 3; Figure 1E and S1; Table S1
outcomes.quote: The regression slopes were positive, indicating that animals were able to estimate ts, and were less than unity, indicating that responses were biased toward to the mean of the prior (Figure 1E and S1, Table S1).
outcomes.notes: Six of 8 weighted slopes of tp on ts lie between 0 and 1 (0.50 to 0.90) and 5 of 8 have 95% intervals excluding 0 and 1. The Short prior slopes with the eye are 1.11 (Eye Right, interval 1.01 to 1.21) and 1.01 (Eye Left). All 8 are positive, so the animal estimated ts; the part of the statement about bias toward the mean fails in the two eye Short conditions.
deviations: One session of monkey H; the paper's slopes come from 17 sessions of H and 12 of G.
Outliers removed with the file's `is_outlier` flag, which a refit of the Methods' mixture model does not reproduce (see findings).

outcomes.statement: At the overlapping ts of 800 ms, biases were in opposite directions for the two priors (rank-sum test, p < 1e-43 in animal H over 17 sessions).
outcomes.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 3; Figure 1E; Table S2
outcomes.quote: The effect of the prior was most conspicuous at the overlapping ts for which biases were in opposite directions for the two prior conditions
outcomes.notes: At ts = 800 ms the median bias is +28.3 ms for Short (93 trials) and +47.6 ms for Long (107 trials), both positive; rank-sum p = 0.073. The Long tp is the longer in 2 of 4 datasets (Hand Right p = 0.00099, Hand Left p = 0.069, where the Short bias is -61.6 ms); in the eye datasets the Short tp is the longer (Eye Left +79.1 against +18.6 ms, p = 0.051).
deviations: One session; the paper's p < 1e-43 pools 17 sessions of monkey H.

outcomes.statement: Increments of tp between neighbouring ts are smaller at the extremes of the prior than near its mean, as the sigmoidal Bayesian estimator predicts (signed-rank test, p < 1e-11 in animal H).
outcomes.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 4; Figure 2E and 2F
outcomes.quote: Consistent with this prediction, tp increments at the extrema of the prior were smaller than increments near the mean
outcomes.notes: The middle increment of mean tp exceeds the extreme one in 7 of 8 conditions (median difference 31.3 ms), two-sided signed-rank p = 0.0156. Hand Left, Short is the exception (-10.7 ms).
deviations: The test is over the 8 conditions of one session; the paper's is over sessions and conditions of both animals.

outcomes.statement: Biases are larger for the Long prior than for the Short prior, as scalar variability predicts; regression slopes are smaller for Long.
outcomes.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 4; Figure 2G and 2H
outcomes.quote: Third, due to scalar variability, biases for the Long prior should be larger than the Short prior condition (Figure 2G), which we confirmed empirically (Figure 2H, Table S1).
outcomes.notes: The Long slope is below the Short slope in all 4 datasets (mean 0.716 against 0.898), weighted or unweighted.
deviations: One session.

outcomes.statement: A Bayesian observer model with scalar measurement and production noise fit to the behaviour captures the bias and the variance of tp in all conditions.
outcomes.source: Results, Task and behavior, paragraph 4; Figure 2C and 2D; Table S3
outcomes.quote: Accordingly, fits of the model to behavior captured the bias and variance (Figure 2C,D) for both animals and across all experimental conditions (Figure S1, Table S3).
outcomes.notes: The predicted SD of tp correlates positively with the observed one in all 4 datasets (r = 0.28 to 0.91), but the bias R2 reaches 0.8 in 2 of 4 (0.12, 0.67, 0.87, 0.98). The poorly fit datasets are the eye ones, whose Short slopes exceed 1, with wm = 0.013 and 0.025. All fits converged. Table S3 was not available, so the fitted wm (0.013 to 0.117) and wp (0.090 to 0.106) are not compared.
deviations: Fit to one session per effector and direction; the paper pools sessions.
The prior is taken as continuous uniform over each range, as the Results describe; the task used 5 discrete values.
The bias R2 threshold of 0.8 is a choice made here; the paper shows the fit graphically.

outcomes.statement: About 30% of neurons were modulated by elapsed time (27% in monkey H) and more than 60% were sensitive to the prior (65% in monkey H), by a Poisson GLM of spike counts before Set compared by BIC.
outcomes.source: Results, Single-neuron response profiles, paragraph 3; Figure 3E; Methods, Generalized linear model
outcomes.quote: Results indicated that approximately 30% of neurons were modulated by elapsed time (27% Monkey H, 31% Monkey G), and more than 60% were sensitive to the prior condition (65% Monkey H, 62% Monkey G).
outcomes.notes: 36 of 48 units are prior-dependent (75.0%, 95% interval 61.2 to 85.1%) and 22 of 48 are ts-dependent (45.8%, interval 32.6 to 59.7%), against 65% and 27% for monkey H. Both are outside tolerance and higher; the interval of the prior fraction includes 65%, that of the ts fraction excludes 27%. A likelihood-ratio test gives higher fractions still (prior 77.1 to 87.5%, ts 66.7 to 77.1% at p < 0.01 and 0.05). Chance levels by the same BIC rule are far lower; prior labels shuffled within effector and direction give 0 to 8.3% and labels shifted along the session by 50 to 200 trials, which keeps the prior blocks, 2.1 to 14.6%; time points shuffled within trials give 0 to 2.1% ts-dependent. The ts test in the Short prior alone gives 31.2% and in the Long prior alone 33.3%, both above 27 +/- 2.7%.
deviations: 48 units from one session, where the paper's fractions use 536 units of monkey H over 17 sessions.
The GLM design with attrition (rows for every trial whose Set comes after each time point) is read from the Methods; the paper's code was not available.

The Long prior's ts test uses the Long ts as time points (800 to 1200 ms after Ready); Eq. 3 of the paper does not say which time points were used, and a unit counts as ts-dependent when either prior's test finds it.

outcomes.statement: At the overlapping ts of 800 ms, firing rates differ between priors, with the largest difference during the support of the prior, between 480 and 800 ms after Ready.
outcomes.source: Results, Single-neuron response profiles, paragraph 3; Figure 3C and 3D
outcomes.quote: The influence of prior was most evident at the overlap ts of 800 ms (Figure 3C) ... many neurons had highly distinct firing rate patterns depending on the prior condition, with a maximum difference in firing rate during the support of the prior between 480 and 800 ms (Figure 3D).
outcomes.notes: The mean RMS rate difference at ts = 800 ms is largest at 480 to 640 ms after Ready (6.86 spikes/s), above the 95th percentile of the shuffled maximum (3.11). Before Ready it is at the shuffle level. Per dataset the largest bin is 480-640 (2 datasets), 640-800 and 800-960 ms, and the mean is also high just after Set (6.07 at 800 to 960 ms). Over 200 bootstrap samples of trials the peak is in 480 to 640 ms in 192 and in 800 to 960 ms in 8 (96% within 480 to 800 ms).
deviations: The time range (320 ms before Ready to 640 ms after Set) and the shuffle reference are chosen here.

outcomes.statement: Population activity is low dimensional; 3 to 4 principal components in the estimation epoch and 5 to 10 in the production epoch explain about 75% of the variance.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry and dynamics of population activity, paragraph 2; Figure S3
outcomes.quote: For all datasets, the population activity in each epoch was relatively low dimensional: 3–4 principal components (PC) in the estimation epoch and 5–10 PCs in the production epoch explained nearly 75% of total variance (Figure S3).
outcomes.notes: Two components reach 75% of the variance in the estimation epoch in all 4 datasets (3 explain 86 to 90%), and 2, 2, 5 and 4 in the production epoch; 1 of 8 values is in range. The count depends on normalisation, which the Methods do not mention; with rates z-scored per unit (a variant) the counts are 3 or 4 and 6 to 10, all 8 in range, and with soft normalisation (range plus 5 spikes/s) 6 of 8 are in range. The outcome is judged on unnormalised rates, as the claims file fixed.
deviations: 48 simultaneously recorded units, where the paper's trial-averaged PCA pools units over 17 sessions; more units can add dimensions.
Rates not normalised before PCA; the Methods do not say.

outcomes.statement: Projections of estimation-epoch neural states onto the encoding axis match the Bayesian estimates from the model fitted to the behaviour (R2 = 0.993 for the Short prior, 0.996 for the Long prior, monkey H, Hand Left).
outcomes.source: Results, Encoding Bayesian estimate along curved trajectory, paragraph 1; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: Neural projections onto u exhibited biases that matched the Bayesian model fitted to the behavior (R2 = 0.993 for the Short prior, 0.996 for the Long prior; Figure 4C)
outcomes.notes: Both readings match. (a) Hand Left R2 = 0.998 (Short) and 0.996 (Long), given as measured; (b) the mean of 4 datasets 0.959 and 0.989. With only 2 PCs in the estimation epoch, random unit axes also fit te well (median R2 0.73 to 0.98); the R2 on u exceeds 95% of random axes in 3 of 8 dataset-priors (Hand Right Long and both Hand Left), so the paper's statement that the match is specific to u (Figure S5) holds only for those. With normalised rates (3 or 4 PCs) R2 stays above 0.94 in every dataset-prior, and u beats 95% of random axes in 2 of 8 (soft normalisation) and 0 of 8 (z-scored).
deviations: te comes from the observer model fitted to this session.
The encoding axis averages difference vectors up to the middle of the support, a choice made here.

outcomes.statement: Neural projections are better explained by the Bayesian model than by a linear function of ts with the same number of parameters, for both priors (signed-rank test on RMSE, p = 0.008 for each prior).
outcomes.source: Results, Encoding Bayesian estimate along curved trajectory, paragraph 1; Figure 4D top
outcomes.quote: Indeed, the neural projections were better explained by the Bayesian model than a linear model for both priors (signed-rank test for RMSE, p=0.008 for the Short prior, p=0.008 for the Long prior; Figure 4D).
outcomes.notes: The Bayesian RMSE is lower in 4 of 4 datasets for Long and 3 of 4 for Short (Hand Right Short 0.99 against 0.80). Where the Bayesian model wins it is better by 0.045 to 0.573 spikes/s; in Hand Right Short it is worse by 0.186. With the RMSE weighted by trial counts, as in the fit, the counts are the same. In the matched control period of the Long prior (short-in-long-control) the Bayesian model is also better in 3 of 4 datasets, so in this session the advantage is not specific to the support of the prior.
deviations: 4 datasets, where the paper had 8; a signed-rank test over 4 cannot reach p < 0.05, so the criterion counts datasets.

outcomes.statement: In the Long prior during the period matched to the support of the Short prior ("Short In Long"), there is no sigmoidal representation; the Bayesian model is not better than the linear one (signed-rank test, p = 0.74).
outcomes.source: Results, Encoding Bayesian estimate along curved trajectory, paragraph 1; Figure 4D top
outcomes.quote: As a negative control, we also analyzed neural data in the Long prior condition during a period temporally matched to support of the Short prior (“Short In Long” in Figure 4D) and found no evidence of sigmoidal representations

statistics.about: interaction of prior condition and model on RMSE
Bayesian against linear model for Short In Long

outcomes.notes: Judged on the paper's test as the claims file fixes; signed-rank p = 0.25 over 4 datasets, where the smallest attainable p is 0.125, so the test could not have found an effect. The effect sizes do not show the control's contrast; the Bayesian model is better in 3 of 4 datasets with a median relative RMSE difference of -0.089, at least as large as in the Short prior (-0.060). This outcome carries no evidence for the absence the paper reports.
deviations: 4 datasets, where the paper had 8.

outcomes.statement: Neural projections show more bias for the Long prior than for the Short prior, as a smaller regression slope of Xu on ts (signed-rank test, p = 0.008).
outcomes.source: Results, Encoding Bayesian estimate along curved trajectory, paragraph 2; Figure 4D bottom
outcomes.quote: the Long prior exhibited more bias than the Short prior as measured by slope of a regression line relating projections to ts (signed-rank test, p=0.008; Figure 4D).
outcomes.notes: The Long slope of Xu on ts is below the Short slope in 4 of 4 datasets (ratios 0.55, 0.63, 0.34, 0.97).
deviations: 4 datasets, where the paper had 8.

outcomes.statement: Larger projections on the encoding axis at Set are followed by slower neural trajectories in the production epoch (Pearson correlation, rho Short = -0.74, rho Long = -0.51).
outcomes.source: Results, Controlling speed based on Bayesian estimate, paragraph 1; Figure 4E
outcomes.quote: For both conditions, larger projections along the encoding axis were associated with slower speeds across all conditions (Figure 4E; Pearson correlation, ρShort=−0.74 ... ρLong=−0.51
outcomes.notes: Both correlations are negative and significant (Short p = 6.2e-10, Long p = 3.7e-07) and stronger than reported, outside tolerance. Within datasets -0.75 to -1.00; with Xu z-scored per dataset -0.759 and -0.779, and the speed divided by mean tp gives -0.917 and -0.923. Both quantities change with ts; with the residuals of each on ts within dataset and prior the correlation is -0.195 (Short) and +0.069 (Long), so the pooled relation is carried by the common dependence on ts. The paper's control (z-scoring within ts) is on single-trial GPFA states of the production epoch, not computed here.
deviations: 20 points per prior (4 datasets), where the paper had 40.
Speed is the mean step between 20 ms states up to the shortest tp; the Methods' division by the Set to Go duration is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: The initial speed of production trajectories (Set to Set + 400 ms) is biased toward the middle of the prior; its dependence on ts is shallower than the unbiased profile proportional to 1/ts (signed-rank test, p < 1e-3 over conditions and animals).
outcomes.source: Results, Controlling speed based on Bayesian estimate, paragraph 1; Figure 4F
outcomes.quote: The speed profile for each prior condition, however, demonstrated systematic biases with a central tendency: trajectories associated with shorter ts were slower than expected from an unbiased speed profile, and vice versa (Figure 4F

statistics.test: Wilcoxon sign-rank test on measured versus unbiased regression slopes relating speed to ts

outcomes.notes: The initial speed falls with ts in 8 of 8 dataset-priors and is shallower than the 1/ts profile in 7 of 8 (Eye Right Long is the exception), two-sided signed-rank p = 0.039. No trial had tp below 400 ms.
deviations: 8 dataset-priors of one animal, where the paper's test combines 16 over two animals.

outcomes.statement: The speed of neural trajectories in the production epoch predicts the mean tp (Pearson correlation, rho Short = -0.58, rho Long = -0.52).
outcomes.source: Results, Controlling speed based on Bayesian estimate, paragraph 1; Figure 4G
outcomes.quote: we verified that the overall speed of dynamics throughout the production epoch was predictive of the resulting tp across both priors and across all experimental conditions (Figure 4G; Pearson correlation, ρShort=−0.58 ... ρLong=−0.52
outcomes.notes: Faster trajectories go with shorter mean tp in both priors (Short p = 0.00024, Long p = 0.00017), more strongly than reported and outside tolerance. Within datasets -0.80 to -0.99. The Neural Latents Benchmark's trial-by-trial variant gives r = -0.195 to -0.740 (mean -0.519), 7 of 8 conditions with p < 0.05. With speed and tp z-scored within each ts trial by trial, as in the paper's control, r = -0.317 (Short, 481 trials, p = 1.1e-12) and -0.201 (Long, 502 trials, p = 5.5e-06), negative in 8 of 8 dataset-priors and p < 0.05 in 6. A Poisson null at constant rates with each trial's own duration gives mean null r of -0.071 (Short) and -0.033 (Long) over 20 simulations, and the observed values are below every null value, so the shorter averaging of short trials accounts for a small part. Residuals on ts of the 20 condition means give +0.084 and -0.283.
deviations: 20 points per prior, where the paper had 40.

outcomes.statement: Instantaneous speed of neural trajectories in the full neural space is not modulated during the support of each prior (signed-rank test for zero regression slopes, p = 0.64 for Short, p = 0.08 for Long).
outcomes.source: Results, Alternative mechanisms (speed hypothesis); Figure 5B
outcomes.quote: for both prior conditions, speed remained unmodulated throughout the support of each prior (Figure 5b; signed-rank test for zero regression slopes during the support, p=0.64 for Short, p=0.08 for Long).

statistics.test: signed-rank test for zero regression slopes
signed-rank test for zero regression slopes

outcomes.notes: Judged on the paper's test as the claims file fixes; signed-rank p = 0.125 for each prior, the smallest a test over 4 datasets can give, so the outcome carries no evidence for the absence of modulation. All 8 slopes are positive, but noise produces slopes of this size, as later bins average fewer trials. For Poisson units at constant rates with the same trials and Set times, the mean null slope is above the observed one in 8 of 8 and no observed slope exceeds the null's 95th percentile. With only the trials of the longest ts, which last the whole support, slopes are -0.106 to +0.529 per 100 ms and outside the null's 95% range in 1 of 8 (below it). The bootstrap intervals over trials are biased upward (the point estimate is below the interval in 2 of 8) and are not used. The observed slopes are below the null mean in 8 of 8 with all trials and in 8 of 8 with fixed trials, while the null's mean speed over the support is below the observed one in 7 of 8 (null / observed 0.65 to 1.18), so the null is not noisier than the data. This points to a speed that falls during the support, if the units' noise is no larger than Poisson; it was not tested further. The session shows no speed increase beyond what noise produces.
deviations: 4 datasets, where the paper had 8.
Speed from smoothed trial-averaged rates with attrition in 20 ms bins of 48 units; the paper's smoothing for this measure is not stated.

outcomes.statement: In the first 200 ms after Set, trajectories for different ts run parallel; their distance to the middle ts trajectory does not change (signed-rank test for zero slopes, p = 0.92 for the shortest ts, p = 0.13 for the longest).
outcomes.source: Results, Alternative mechanisms (transient hypothesis); Figure 5D
outcomes.quote: Results indicated that neural trajectories for different ts in each prior evolved parallel to one another (signed-rank test for zero regression slopes relating the distance to time after Set, p=0.92 for the shortest ts, p=0.13 for the longest ts

statistics.test: signed-rank test for zero regression slopes
signed-rank test for zero regression slopes

outcomes.notes: For the longest ts the distance to the middle trajectory falls in the first 200 ms after Set in 6 of 8 dataset-priors (median -15.3% of the mean distance per 100 ms), signed-rank p = 0.039; for the shortest ts p = 0.078 (6 of 8 rising, median +26.7%). The PCA kept 1 to 4 components, one in Eye Left. For the longest ts p = 0.016 with 60% of the variance, 0.039 with 90%, 0.023 in the full space and 0.039 with z-scored rates; with soft-normalised rates 0.055.
deviations: 8 dataset-priors of one animal, where the paper's test used 16.
Rates smoothed over 100 ms before to 300 ms after Set and cut to the first 200 ms, a choice made here.

outcomes.statement: Aligned to the response, distances between trajectories for different ts decrease steadily up to movement initiation, without the converging then diverging pattern a ts-dependent threshold would produce.
outcomes.source: Results, Alternative mechanisms (threshold hypothesis); Figure 5F
outcomes.quote: However, the distance profile of neural trajectories did not show this converging-diverging pattern; instead, the distance between trajectories appeared to drop steadily throughout the production epoch, even near the time of motor initiation (Figure 5F

statistics.test: one-tailed sign-rank test for time of minimum distance occurring strictly before movement initiation

outcomes.notes: With the components reaching 60% of the variance (1 to 3), the median time of the minimum distance is 210 ms before Go; 6 of 32 curves have their minimum in the last 40 ms and 14 in the last 200 ms. Distances do fall overall (the distance at Go is below that 800 ms earlier in 26 of 32). With 75% of the variance the median minimum is 80 ms before Go and in the full space 40 ms, which would meet the criterion, so the outcome depends on the number of components. With one component (eye datasets, 16 curves) the signed difference changes sign at the minimum in 12, so those minima are crossings; 4 have the minimum at Go (3 of them not crossings), and the distance at Go is more than 10 times the minimum in 5. With at least 2 components the median minimum is 230 ms before Go, with at least 3 it is 70 ms before Go.
deviations: The paper's test (one-tailed signed-rank, p = 1.5e-4) cannot be read unambiguously; the criterion on the median time of the minimum was fixed before the analysis.
The 60% of variance follows the figure legend; the 75% of the Methods is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: The variance across single trials of the GPFA neural state at Set projected on the encoding axis has an inverted-U profile over ts, lower at the extremes of each prior (one-tailed signed-rank test on quadratic coefficients, p = 0.0273, monkey H).
outcomes.source: Results, The curved manifold hypothesis captures the variance, paragraph 3; Figure 6C
outcomes.quote: The resulting variance profile of single-trial projections resembled an inverted U-shape on average, with a tendency for lower variances at the extrema of each prior (one-tailed signed-rank test on coefficients for quadratic term in polynomial fitting, p=0.0273

statistics.test: one-tailed signed-rank test on coefficients for quadratic term in polynomial fitting

outcomes.notes: The quadratic coefficient is negative in 5 of 8 dataset-priors; one-tailed signed-rank p = 0.125 (paper 0.0273). Cross-validation chose 8 latent dimensions in all 4 datasets, the larger candidate. 12 latents, scored on the same folds as a variant, beat 8 in all 4 datasets; with them the coefficient is negative in 5 of 8, p = 0.125. After 100 EM iterations the training log-likelihood still rose by 0.064 to 0.085% over the last 25 iterations.
deviations: Latent dimensionality chosen only from 4 and 8, with 100 EM iterations, to keep the run short; the paper's cross-validation range is not stated.
One GPFA per effector and direction with both priors; the paper does not say how trials were grouped.

outcomes.statement: The mean of the single-trial GPFA projections is sigmoidal (signed-rank test on increments, p = 0.0078) and has a higher slope for the Short prior (one-tailed signed-rank, p = 0.0625).
outcomes.source: Results, The curved manifold hypothesis captures the variance, paragraph 3; Figure 6D
outcomes.quote: the mean of the single-trial projections inferred from GPFA had a sigmoidal shape ... and higher slope for the Short prior

statistics.test: signed-rank test between increments of mean Xu around extreme ts versus those near middle ts

statistics.test: one-tailed signed-rank test for regression slope between Short and Long

outcomes.notes: Middle increments of the mean projection exceed the extreme ones in 8 of 8 (two-sided signed-rank p = 0.0078) and the Short slope is the higher in 4 of 4 datasets (one-tailed p = 0.0625), the paper's values; the mean rises with ts in 8 of 8. With 12 latents, 8 of 8 (p = 0.0078) and 4 of 4.

outcomes.statement: Recurrent neural networks trained on the two-prior task with scalar measurement noise behave like a Bayesian observer and show curved trajectories during the support of the prior, like DMFC.
outcomes.source: Results, Recurrent network models, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 7A to 7C and S7
outcomes.quote: we were able to build RNNs whose behavior was captured by a Bayesian observer model (Figure 7B) ... For instance, the network trajectories also exhibited curvature during the support of the prior (Figure 7C and S7).
outcomes.notes: The claim is about recurrent networks trained in silico. The dandiset holds only the two NWB files of spikes and trials, and the trained networks and the training code are not public (the code is available from the corresponding author on request). Training new networks from the Methods would be a new study, not a test against this data.

outcomes.statement: In trained networks, compressing states along the encoding axis increases the regression to the mean of tp, and translating them shifts tp.
outcomes.source: Results, Recurrent network models, paragraph 4; Figure 7D and 7E
outcomes.quote: tp values exhibited progressively larger regression to the mean for larger compressive perturbations (Figure 7D), and underwent an overall upward or downward shift as a result of translation (Figure 7E).
outcomes.notes: As for rnn-curved-manifold; the perturbation experiments are on the trained networks.

outcomes.statement: The behavioural and neural results hold in monkey G as in monkey H.
outcomes.source: Results throughout; Figures 1 to 6 and S1 to S6
outcomes.inferred: Summarises results reported for monkey G throughout the Results and Figures 1 to 6 and S1 to S6; no single sentence states it.
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds one session of monkey H. A search of the DANDI archive for Jazayeri, Sohn, DMFC and Ready-Set-Go finds no other dandiset with these recordings (only 000620, 000897 and 001275 of the same lab, on other tasks). The paper says the data are in the article and the code is available on request.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds one recording session (2016-12-11) of monkey H, with 54 units, where the paper analyses 17 sessions of H and 12 of monkey G (617 and 741 units recorded, 536 and 636 kept for analysis). The dandiset's description does not say that it holds one session of the paper's 29 or which one. The 48 units that pass the paper's rate rule match its count for the single session of H used for GPFA.

Following the Neural Latents Benchmark design, 283 trials of the session are in the test file without ts, tp, prior, effector or direction and without 14 of the 54 units, on a separate clock. These trials cannot be used for any analysis of the paper.
The description of the `iti` column says 500 ms after Short prior trials and 1220 ms after Long ones; the values are the reverse (Short 1220, Long 500), as the paper states.

`tp` is described as the time between Set and Go, but is a median 17.9 ms longer than go_time minus set_time (5th to 95th percentile 1.1 to 29.8 ms, up to 200.6 ms in used trials). `ts` is the nominal interval, within 23.5 ms of ready_time minus set_time. Neither difference is documented.

The `is_outlier` flag is described only as a probabilistic mixture model. It flags 46 completed trials (4.47%); a refit of the Methods' Gaussian and uniform mixture per prior, ts, effector and direction flags 10 of these and no others, and the other 36 have tp from 0.53 to 1.60 times ts.

Units carry no single-unit or multi-unit label and no electrode or probe; the electrode table has no positions or impedances and gives the filtering as unknown. The paper distinguishes 456 single units from 902 multi-units.
The paper's analysis code is available only on request. The code the dandiset links (nlb_tools) loads the data and scores benchmark models, and holds none of the paper's analyses.
For the single high-yield session of each monkey used for GPFA, the Results give the number of neurons as N = 48 for monkey H and N = 107 for monkey G, the Methods as N = 48 in H and 96 in G.

attempts.label: DANDI:000147
attempts.paper_title: Stability of motor representations after paralysis
attempts.entry_title: Finger representations in human posterior parietal cortex after paralysis (Guan et al. 2022)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Guan, Aflalo et al. (2022) that dandiset 000147 can support. It checks online and offline finger decoding, single-unit tuning and whether the cue location can be decoded, builds the cross-validated finger RDMs of the ten sessions, compares them with the able-bodied fMRI models from the authors' repository, and tests whether the representation changed across sessions and runs. The calibration and control tasks, the component model RDMs and sorting quality metrics are not in the dandiset, so the claims that need them are blocked.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Guan, Aflalo et al. (2022) from dandiset 000147

outcomes.statement: Over 10 sessions the recordings yielded 95.8 (SD 6.7) sorted neurons and 408 (SD 40.8) trials of the main finger task per session.
outcomes.source: Results, "Intracortical recordings during finger flexion", paragraphs 1 and 3
outcomes.quote: We recorded single and multineuron activity (95.8 ± standard deviation [SD] 6.7 neurons per session over 10 sessions) ... We repeated this online-control finger flexion task over multiple sessions (408 ± SD 40.8 trials/session over 10 sessions)
outcomes.notes: The ten files hold 95.8 units per session (SD 6.7) and 408.0 trials per session (SD 40.8), 4080 trials in all, as reported.

outcomes.statement: Online BCI classification of the cued finger was 86% accurate (SD 4% across sessions, weighted by trials) over 4016 trials in 10 sessions, against a chance level of 17%. No-Go trials of the first session are excluded because the classifier could not output No-Go that day.
outcomes.source: Figure 1b, Figure 1-figure supplement 3, Results, "Accurately decoding fingers from PPC single-neuron activity", paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: High classification accuracy during online control (86% ± SD 4% over 10 sessions; chance = 17%) (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
outcomes.notes: The recorded decoder outputs match the cued finger on 85.96% of the 4016 scored trials, with a trial-weighted SD across sessions of 3.6%. Shuffling the outputs gives 16.9%, the paper's chance level of 17%.

outcomes.statement: Most (70%) of the online classification errors were middle-ring or ring-pinky confusions.
outcomes.source: Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 2; Figure 1b
outcomes.quote: The majority (70%) of the online classification errors were middle-ring or ring-pinky confusions (Figure 1b).
outcomes.notes: Of the 379 online errors between two fingers, 69.7% confuse middle with ring or ring with pinky. Counting errors that involve No-Go, the fraction is 46.8% of 564 errors, or 59.2% of the 446 errors on finger trials.
deviations: The paper does not say which errors form the denominator. Only errors between two fingers, leaving out No-Go, give the paper's 70%.

outcomes.statement: Offline classification of the cued finger from sorted firing rates in the window 0.5 to 1.5 s after the cue, with diagonal LDA and leave-one-out cross-validation within each session, was 92% accurate (SD 2% across sessions) over 4080 trials.
outcomes.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 4a, Results, "Accurately decoding fingers from PPC single-neuron activity", paragraph 1, Methods "Finger classification"
outcomes.quote: offline cross-validated classification (92% ± SD 2%; Figure 1—figure supplement 4a) demonstrated that the finger representations were reliable and linearly separable.
outcomes.notes: Diagonal LDA with leave-one-out cross-validation within sessions gives 93.4% (weighted SD 1.6%) over 4080 trials. The classifier and eight stratified folds of the authors' code give 92.4% (SD 1.7%).
deviations: The paper's methods say leave-one-out; the authors' code uses eight folds, a mean-count cutoff of 0.5, z-scoring and LDA with identity covariance. Both are reported, and the measured value is the leave-one-out one.

outcomes.statement: In the calibration task, offline cross-validated finger classification was 96% accurate (SD 3%) over 530 trials in nine sessions.
outcomes.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 4b, Results, "Accurately decoding fingers from PPC single-neuron activity", paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: During the calibration task, cross-validated classification was similarly robust (accuracy = 96% ± SD 3%; Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds only the main finger task. The calibration task, recorded at the start of each day, is not in any of the ten files.

outcomes.statement: Most (89%) neurons were significantly tuned to at least one finger movement, by a two-tailed t-test of each finger's firing rate in the 0.5 to 1.5 s window against No-Go trials, p < 0.05 after FDR correction, with neurons below 0.1 Hz excluded and neurons pooled across sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, "Accurately decoding fingers from PPC single-neuron activity", paragraph 2, Figure 1-figure supplement 5, Methods "Single-unit tuning to finger flexion"
outcomes.quote: At the single-neuron level, most (89%) neurons were significantly tuned to individual finger-press movements (significance threshold: p < 0.05, FDR-corrected) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
outcomes.notes: With FDR correction over all units and fingers pooled, 87.9% of 958 units are tuned to at least one finger. FDR within each session gives 87.5%, within each unit 83.9%, and no correction 91.7%. No unit fell below the 0.1 Hz cutoff, whether the rate is taken in the window over all trials (lowest 0.113 Hz) or over the whole recording (lowest 0.147 Hz).
deviations: The FDR family is not stated in the paper; the measured value pools all units and fingers.
Student's t-test with equal variances; the paper does not say which form of the t-test.

outcomes.statement: Linear regression could not decode the cue's screen coordinates from neural activity in the attempted-movement window; cross-validated r2 was close to 0 in every session.
outcomes.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 6a
outcomes.quote: Linear regression could not decode target location [x, y] coordinates from the neural activity during the attempted-movement period. Violin plot shows that cross-validated regression r2 values are close to 0 across sessions
outcomes.notes: The trials table gives the cue location as an index from 1 to 12 on the grid of three rows and four columns, described only as a screen location index, with no map to the grid or to screen coordinates. As a check, the coordinates were regressed on spike counts under the two plain orders of the index. Ordinary least squares gives a cross-validated r2 below 0 for both coordinates in all ten sessions under both orders. Ridge regression gives r2 up to 0.097 for x and 0.104 for y, with both coordinates at or below 0.05 in 5 (row order) or 6 (column order) of the ten sessions. The result depends on the regression as well as on the unknown layout.
deviations: The check assumes the index runs along the rows or down the columns; neither is documented.
The paper does not say whether its regression was regularised, so both ordinary least squares and ridge regression are shown, each with eight unshuffled folds per session.

outcomes.statement: A diagonal LDA classifier could not classify the cue location from neural activity in the attempted-movement window.
outcomes.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 6b
outcomes.quote: A linear classifier (diagonal linear discriminant analysis [LDA]) could not classify the gaze location from neural activity during the attempted-movement period.
outcomes.notes: Diagonal LDA classifies the 12 cue locations at 11.5% against a chance level of 8.3% (binomial p = 1e-12), above all 500 label shuffles across trials (highest 10.0%) and all 500 shuffles within finger (highest 10.2%). The authors' classifier gives 11.2%, and removing each finger's mean activity first gives 11.7%. Five of the ten sessions are above chance at p < 0.05. With folds that never split a screen the accuracy is 11.1%, above all 200 shuffles of location within screens (highest 9.8%), and with folds that never split a run it is 11.3%. Every screen cues each location once; location and position within the screen are weakly associated over all trials (chi-square p = 0.037). The cued finger is classified at 93.4% from the same features. With folds that never split a run, 11.3% is above all 200 shuffles of location within runs (highest 9.8%). Position within the screen is itself decoded at 10.5%, above all 200 shuffles within screens (highest 9.5%), but after removing each position's mean activity location is still classified at 11.1%.
deviations: Eight stratified folds within each session; the paper does not say how this classifier was cross-validated, and the authors' code uses eight folds for its classifiers.
The paper shows a confusion matrix without an accuracy or a test, so the comparison is with its statement that the location could not be classified.

outcomes.statement: Fingers could not be classified from neural activity during the control task, in which the participant viewed the cues without attempting movements.
outcomes.source: Figure 1-figure supplement 6c
outcomes.quote: a linear classifier (diagonal LDA) could not classify finger movements from neural activity during passive observation (orange) of the finger press task.
outcomes.notes: The no-movement control task is not in the dandiset; every file is described as the main task and contains only its trials.

outcomes.statement: In the session-averaged representational dissimilarity matrix (cross-validated Mahalanobis distance, window 0.5 to 1.5 s, No-Go excluded), the thumb is distinct, while the middle, ring and pinky fingers are close.
outcomes.source: Figure 2d and 2e, Results, "Finger representational structure matches the structure of able-bodied individuals", paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: For visual intuition, we also projected the representational structure to two dimensions in Figure 2e, which shows that the thumb is distinct, while the middle, ring, and pinky fingers are close in neural space.
outcomes.notes: In the session-averaged RDM, max-scaled, the distances among middle, ring and pinky are 0.21 to 0.48 and every distance involving the thumb is 0.64 or more. This holds in 9 of the 10 sessions on their own.
deviations: The noise covariance uses OAS shrinkage, as in the authors' code; the paper names Ledoit-Wolf.

outcomes.statement: The measured RDMs match the able-bodied PC-IP fMRI model better than the unstructured (pairwise-equidistant) model, by whitened unbiased cosine similarity (WUC), p = 5.7e-5.
outcomes.source: Figure 2f, Results, "Finger representational structure matches the structure of able-bodied individuals", paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: The measured representational structure matched the able-bodied representational structure significantly over the unstructured model (p = 5.7 × 10–5, two-tailed t-test) (Figure 2f)
outcomes.notes: Mean WUC is 0.881 with the able-bodied PC-IP model and 0.781 with the unstructured model. The PC-IP model is higher in all 10 sessions; the bootstrap 95% interval of the difference is 0.074 to 0.127, and the bootstrap t-test gives p = 4.4e-5 (paper 5.7e-5).
deviations: The model RDMs are read from the authors' code repository at the commit archived with the paper, not from the dandiset.
The p-value comes from 1000 resamples of the sessions (mean difference over its bootstrap SD, nine degrees of freedom); the paper used rsatoolbox's bootstrap t-test.

outcomes.statement: The measured RDMs match the able-bodied motor cortex (MC) fMRI model better than the able-bodied PC-IP fMRI model (p = 1.9e-6), and the WUC with the MC model is close to the noise ceiling.
outcomes.source: Figure 2-figure supplement 5a, Results, "Finger representational structure matches the structure of able-bodied individuals", paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: PC-IP BCI finger representations matched the able-bodied fMRI finger representational structure in the MC ... even better than that of able-bodied PC-IP (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). The WUC similarity with the MC RDM was close to the noise ceiling
outcomes.notes: Mean WUC with the MC model is 0.969, higher than with the PC-IP model in all 10 sessions (difference 0.088, bootstrap 95% interval 0.060 to 0.112, p = 7.9e-5; paper 1.9e-6). It is 0.015 below the lower noise ceiling of 0.984, and at or above its own session's ceiling in 1 of 10 sessions.
deviations: The model RDMs are read from the authors' code repository, as for fig2f-able-bodied-over-unstructured.
The criterion's margin of 0.05 below the noise ceiling is a choice; the paper says only "close to".

outcomes.statement: Compared with the RDMs of individual able-bodied fMRI participants, participant NS's average PC-IP RDM was statistically typical (permutation test, p = 0.55).
outcomes.source: Results, "Finger representational structure matches the structure of able-bodied individuals", paragraph 4, Figure 2-figure supplement 4
outcomes.quote: When compared among the RDM distribution of individual able-bodied participants, participant NS's average PC-IP RDM was statistically typical (permutation shuffle test, p = 0.55)

statistics.n: participant NS's average RDM against 29 able-bodied participants

outcomes.notes: The test needs the RDMs of the 36 individual able-bodied fMRI participants. Neither the dandiset nor the authors' code repository holds them; the repository has only the group means.

outcomes.statement: The finger RDMs were consistent across sessions, with an average pairwise correlation between session RDMs of r = 0.90 (SD 0.04, min 0.83, max 0.99).
outcomes.source: Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Indeed, participant NS's finger RDMs were largely consistent across different recording sessions (average pairwise correlation, excluding the diagonal: r = 0.90 ± SD 0.04, min 0.83, max 0.99).
outcomes.notes: The 45 pairs of session RDMs correlate at a mean Pearson r of 0.928 (SD 0.041, min 0.817, max 0.990), against 0.90 (SD 0.04, min 0.83, max 0.99). The mean is 0.028 above the paper's, inside the tolerance of 0.03.

outcomes.statement: Over sessions the model fit did not trend from the able-bodied model toward the unstructured model (session by model interaction t(6) = 0.50, one-tailed p = 0.32).
outcomes.source: Figure 3a, Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: However, we did not find conclusive evidence for a trend from the able-bodied model toward the unstructured model (linear-model session × model interaction: t(6) = 0.50, one-tailed t-test p = 0.32 ... (Figure 3a).

statistics.test: one-tailed t-test of the linear-model session × model interaction

outcomes.notes: The session by model interaction is t(16) = 1.47, one-tailed p = 0.080 toward the unstructured model (paper t(6) = 0.50, p = 0.32). The WUC with the PC-IP model alone declines across sessions (slope -0.009 per session, p = 0.038); the slopes for the unstructured and MC models are not significant (p = 0.20 and 0.23). In other specifications the trend is also not significant. The same t read with 6 degrees of freedom gives p = 0.096; the difference between the unstructured and PC-IP fits regressed on session gives t(8) = 1.30, p = 0.116; with the MC model in place of PC-IP the slope is negative (p = 0.84).
deviations: Ordinary least squares on the twenty session-by-model WUC values, with sixteen residual degrees of freedom. The paper's t(6) implies a different model or degrees of freedom, which it does not describe, and its code for this test is not in the repository.
Three specifications are shown, since the paper's t(6) is not explained.
No Bayes factor is computed.

outcomes.statement: The distances between the most confused finger pairs (middle-ring and ring-pinky) did not increase across sessions (one-tailed p > 0.99) or across runs within sessions (one-tailed p = 0.67).
outcomes.source: Figure 3b, Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 2, Methods "Measuring changes in the representational structure"
outcomes.quote: the middle-ring and ring-pinky distances did not increase over the course of the experiment (across sessions: t(8) = −4.5, one-tailed t-test p > 0.99 ... across runs within sessions: t(82) = −0.45, one-tailed t-test p = 0.67
outcomes.notes: For the middle-ring and ring-pinky distances of 85 per-run RDMs, the session term is t(8) = -3.56 (paper -4.5) and the run term t(83) = -1.05 (paper -0.45). In all six estimates the coefficients are negative and the one-tailed p for an increase is 0.73 or more.
deviations: The paper's code for this regression is not in its repository. The regression follows the methods' formula on per-run RDMs, with degrees of freedom of sessions minus two for the session term and runs minus two for the run term, as the paper's t(8) and t(82) suggest.
The dandiset has 85 runs; the paper's t(82) implies 84.

Per-run RDMs use five folds of eight trials each, so a fold's noise covariance rests on one or two trials per finger and inflates the distances (mean 5.06 against 0.68 for session RDMs). A variant with the session's noise covariance (mean 0.76) is reported.
No Bayes factors are computed.

outcomes.statement: Across all finger pairs the inter-finger distances did not increase; they decreased slightly across sessions (t(8) = -4.0, two-tailed p = 0.004) and across runs within sessions (t(82) = -2.4, p = 0.019), with very small effect sizes (Cohen's f2 of 0.008 and 0.005).
outcomes.source: Figure 3-figure supplement 1, Results, "Representational structure did not trend toward task optimum", paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Inter-finger distances instead decreased slightly (across sessions: t(8) = −4.0, two tailed t-test p = 0.004; across runs within sessions: t(82) = −2.4, two-tailed t-test p = 0.019), although the effect size was very small (across sessions: Cohen's f2 = 0.008 ...
outcomes.notes: Over all ten pairs the session and run coefficients are negative in all six estimates, and Cohen's f2 is 0.006 for session and 0.012 for run in the main regression, and 0.017 and 0.013 with the session's noise covariance (paper 0.008 and 0.005). In the main regression the session decrease is t(8) = -2.28, p = 0.052, and the run decrease t(83) = -3.12, p = 0.0025. With the session's noise covariance they are t(8) = -3.76, p = 0.0055, and t(83) = -3.29, p = 0.0015, against the paper's t(8) = -4.0, p = 0.004, and t(82) = -2.4, p = 0.019.
deviations: The same regression and choices as fig3b-confused-pairs-no-increase.

The session decrease is significant at 0.05 only in the variant with the session's noise covariance; the pre-registered criterion asks for negative coefficients and small effect sizes, not significance. The per-run fold covariance inflates the distances of the main regression, so the variant with the session's covariance is the better estimate of the session term.

outcomes.statement: In a time-resolved decomposition of the RDM into muscle and somatotopy component models, the muscle model emerged 170 ms before the somatotopy model (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test across sessions, p = 0.002).
outcomes.source: Figure 4e, Figure 4-figure supplement 2
outcomes.quote: RDA of the measured RDM over time shows an early fit to the muscle model and a late fit to the somatotopy model ... Difference in model start time (170 ms, Methods) was significant (p = 0.002, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
outcomes.notes: The decomposition needs the muscle and somatotopy model RDMs of Ejaz et al. (2015). They are not in the dandiset, and the authors' code repository loads them from a models folder that holds only the two fMRI models and the unstructured model at the archived commit.

outcomes.statement: Among combinations of the hand-usage, muscle and somatotopy models, the hand usage plus somatotopy and muscle plus somatotopy combinations matched the data best.
outcomes.source: Figure 4-figure supplement 1, Results, "Finger representational structure is motor-like and then somatotopic", paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Through a model selection procedure (Methods), we found that the hand usage + somatotopy and muscle + somatotopy model combinations matched the data best (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
outcomes.notes: The hand-usage, muscle and somatotopy model RDMs are not in the dandiset or the authors' code repository.

outcomes.statement: The able-bodied match and the representational dynamics hold when only well-isolated units (lowest third of L-ratio) are used.
outcomes.source: Figure 4-figure supplement 4c and 4d
outcomes.quote: showing that the measured RDMs match the able-bodied fMRI RDM significantly better than they match the unstructured model ... Representational dynamics analysis, repeated using only well-isolated units, shows an early fit to the muscle model and a late fit to the somatotopy model.

statistics.test: two-tailed t-test, able-bodied fMRI RDM against unstructured model, well-isolated units

outcomes.notes: The units table has spike times, observation intervals, electrodes and electrode groups only, the same in every file. There are no waveforms, features or L-ratio values from which to select well-isolated units, and the representational dynamics part also needs the missing component models.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds only the main finger task. The calibration task (nine sessions) and the no-movement control task (six sessions) analysed in the paper are not included.

The model RDMs that the paper's main comparisons rest on are not in the dandiset. The two able-bodied fMRI group RDMs and the unstructured model are in the authors' code repository; the muscle, hand-usage and somatotopy models and the individual fMRI participants' RDMs are in neither.
The units have no waveforms or sorting quality metrics, so the paper's selection of well-isolated units by L-ratio cannot be repeated.

Spike times are not in ascending order within units. In nearly every unit the spikes of the first seconds of each run are stored before the rest of the previous run (590 to 1016 backward jumps per file). No trial's analysed range meets an affected span, so sorted spike times give the same counts, but tools that assume ascending spike times could be misled near run boundaries.

The cue location is an index from 1 to 12, described as the screen location index of the cue, with no map to the grid of three rows and four columns or to screen coordinates. The trials table's Run and TrialNumber columns read "no description", and the start time has only the NWB default description. Decoding the finger over time is consistent with a start time at the cue onset, but does not pin it to the cue within a few hundred milliseconds.
Electrode coordinates and impedances are missing (NaN), and the participant is identified as P1 in the files and as NS in the paper.
The paper says the first session had 84 No-Go trials. The file has 64, and the paper's own total of 4016 scored trials (4080 minus the first session's No-Go trials) implies 64.

The two published versions hold the same ten files. The earlier version, which the authors' download script pins, names the bioRxiv preprint; the later one names the eLife paper. Neither says which of the paper's tasks the data cover.

attempts.label: DANDI:000207
attempts.paper_title: Neurons detect cognitive boundaries to structure episodic memories in humans
attempts.entry_title: Cognitive boundaries and human medial temporal lobe neurons (Zheng et al. 2022)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Zheng et al. (2022) that can be tested on dandiset 000207, which holds spike times of medial temporal lobe neurons and the behaviour of 19 patients in a task with video clips that contain no boundary, a soft boundary or a hard boundary. It compares memory for temporal order and for scenes across the three kinds of clip, looks for boundary cells and event cells with the paper's definitions, counts neurons that respond to clip onsets, and measures how far the population state moves after a boundary. Eleven of the paper's twenty findings cannot be tested, because the dandiset has no local field potentials, no neurons outside the medial temporal lobe, no labels for the paper's cell classes, and no way to link test trials with soft or hard boundaries to the clips they came from.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Zheng et al. (2022) from dandiset 000207

outcomes.statement: In the time discrimination task, subjects chose the frame that was shown first in 73% of trials when the two frames were separated by no boundary or by a soft boundary, and in 53% of trials, significantly fewer, when they were separated by a hard boundary.
outcomes.source: Figure 2a; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: subjects correctly identified which frame was shown first in 73 ± 7% and 73 ± 8% of trials when the two frames were separated by no boundary (NB) or a soft boundary (SB) ... subjects performed significantly worse when discriminating the order of frames separated by a hard boundary (HB) (Fig. 2a, red, HB: 53 ± 5%
outcomes.notes: Time discrimination accuracy is 0.528 across a hard boundary, 0.728 with no boundary and 0.720 with a soft boundary (paper 0.53, 0.73, 0.73). It is lower across a hard boundary in 18 of 19 subjects (paired p < 1e-6 against both).
deviations: 19 of the paper's 20 subjects; the twentieth is not in the dandiset.
Trials without a response are kept as coded in the file; leaving them out moves no mean by more than 0.01.
Paired tests over subjects are added to the paper's one-way ANOVA.

outcomes.statement: Reaction times in the time discrimination task were longer when the two frames were separated by a hard boundary (2.10 s) than by no boundary (1.62 s) or a soft boundary (1.59 s).
outcomes.source: Figure 2b; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Subjects also showed longer reaction times (Fig. 2b; HB: 2.10 ± 0.37 seconds; NB: 1.62 ± 0.28 seconds; SB: 1.59 ± 0.34 seconds; F (2, 57) = 14.25
outcomes.notes: Mean reaction time is 2.05 s across a hard boundary, 1.62 s with no boundary and 1.54 s with a soft boundary (paper 2.10, 1.62, 1.59 s), longer across a hard boundary in 18 of 19 subjects. The file's RT column is used, which runs from the disappearance of the frames.
deviations: 19 of the paper's 20 subjects.
Trials without a response have an RT of 0 in the file and are kept; leaving them out gives 2.08, 1.64 and 1.56 s.

outcomes.statement: Confidence ratings in the time discrimination task were lower when the two frames were separated by a hard boundary (1.95 on a scale of 1 to 3) than by no boundary (2.52) or a soft boundary (2.59).
outcomes.source: Figure 2c; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: lower confidence ratings when discriminating the order of frames separated by a hard boundary (Fig. 2c; HB: 1.95 ± 0.45; NB: 2.52 ± 0.29; SB: 2.59 ± 0.23; F (2, 57) = 20.41
outcomes.notes: Mean confidence is 1.98 across a hard boundary, 2.45 with no boundary and 2.51 with a soft boundary (paper 1.95, 2.52, 2.59), lower across a hard boundary in 18 of 19 subjects.
deviations: 19 of the paper's 20 subjects.
Trials without a response have a confidence of 0 in the file and are kept; leaving them out gives 2.00, 2.48 and 2.55.

outcomes.statement: Scene recognition accuracy did not differ between frames from clips with no boundary (76%), a soft boundary (75%) and a hard boundary (75%).
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 2a; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: the ability to recognize a frame as ‘old’ did not differ significantly between the types of boundaries preceding the frame (Extended Data Fig. 2a; NB: 76% ± 10%; SB: 75% ± 9%; HB: 75% ± 8%, F (2, 57) = 0.07, p = 0.94).
outcomes.notes: Scene recognition accuracy over targets and foils is 0.738, 0.739 and 0.718 for clips with no, a soft and a hard boundary (paper 0.76, 0.75, 0.75), with no difference in a one-way ANOVA (F(2, 54) = 0.38, p = 0.69). Accuracy for hard-boundary clips is the lowest in every variant, by 0.01 to 0.05, without reaching significance.
deviations: 19 of the paper's 20 subjects.
The paper does not say whether foils are counted. Targets and foils are; targets alone give 0.737, 0.718 and 0.688 (p = 0.59).

outcomes.statement: Recognition accuracy for a target frame fell with the time between the frame and the boundary before it, for soft boundaries (r = -0.61) and hard boundaries (r = -0.44), but not for clips with no boundary (r = 0.085).
outcomes.source: Figure 2d-f; Results, Boundaries boost recognition but disrupt serial order memory, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: Target frames presented shortly after a SB and HB were remembered better than those farther away from the boundary (Fig. 2e and 2f; SB: r = −0.61 ... recognition accuracy did not differ significantly as a function of time relative to NBs (Fig. 2d, Pearson correlation; NB: r = 0.085, p = 0.65).
outcomes.notes: The dandiset does not give the position of a tested frame within its clip. Its name says frameA or frameB, which by the paper's Methods (one frame from each half) is probably the first or the second half; no column states it. For clips with soft or hard boundaries the frame names also do not identify the clip.

outcomes.statement: 42 of 580 medial temporal lobe neurons (7.24%) were boundary cells, which changed their firing in the second after soft and hard boundaries but not in the middle of clips with no boundary; 2.11% were expected by chance.
outcomes.source: Figure 3a-c; Results, Medial temporal lobe neurons demarcate episodic transitions, paragraph 1; Methods, Boundary cell
outcomes.quote: 42/580 MTL neurons (7.24%; expected proportion by chance for all MTL neurons= 2.11%) were classified as boundary cells (Fig. 3c).
outcomes.notes: The analysis was run, but the procedure behind the paper's count could not be determined. 1 of 549 units (0.18%) meets the Methods' definition of a boundary cell, against 42 of 580 (7.24%) in the paper. The paper's chance level is 2.11%; the literal definition gives 0.03% here, alpha = 0.10 gives 0.10% and a looser pooled reading 0.55%, and the verifier found in simulation that the five-test definition stays at or below about 1% for every response profile it tried. No reading tried here produces the paper's chance level, so the paper's count came from a different procedure. Under the pooled reading there are 15 boundary cells (2.73%), more than in any of 300 shuffles. The authors' published code contains no cell selection. Recorded as not_reproduced before verification.
deviations: 549 units from 18 sessions against the paper's 580 from 19. Subject 19 is left out because its spike times are not on the clock of the trial tables, and the dandiset's units differ from the paper's in number and in their split by region.
The paper's "permutation t-test" is implemented as a sign-flip test for before against after and a one-sided label-permutation test between conditions, with 1000 permutations.

Soft-boundary trials are every soft boundary of a session, in SB clips and in HB clips (75 per session). The Methods do not say; this follows the authors' published plotting code (B01_raster_psth_encoding_BAligned_BSep_NWB.m, lines 29 to 37). The first soft boundary of each SB clip, used before that code was read, is kept in the notebook as an alternative.

findings.statement: In the most recent published version (0.230530.1822) the spike times of subjects 13, 17 and 18 are shifted by 191.5, -16.8 and 9.3 s against the encoding trials, which did not move, so spikes and clips no longer line up. The version the paper cites (0.220216.0323) does not have this shift.
The spike times of subject 19 are near -7.02e12 s while its events run from 0 to 2892 s, in both versions read. Its 16 units cannot be aligned to the task.

Scene recognition and time discrimination trials with soft or hard boundaries cannot be linked to the clips they test. Their frame names are numbered differently from the clips (10 distinct numbers in recognition, 1 to 60 in time discrimination, against clips 1 to 30). The position of a tested frame within its clip is not given.
The dandiset does not say which units the paper classified as boundary cells or event cells, so the paper's selection cannot be compared with a new one cell by cell.

The dandiset has no local field potentials, no units outside the medial temporal lobe (the paper has 405), no similarity ratings and no stimuli, and it lacks the behaviour of one of the paper's 20 subjects.

The dandiset has 565 medial temporal lobe units where the paper analyses 580, with a different split by region (hippocampus 279 against 343, amygdala 233 against 169, parahippocampal gyrus 53 against 68). Nothing says how the two sets relate.

Several column descriptions do not match the values. stimCategory holds 0, 1, 2 and is described as 1, 2, 3. A missing second or third boundary is stored as the clip's start time and described as 0. The accuracy code 0 for "no response" is never used; trials without a response are coded incorrect, or, in 20 time discrimination trials, correct. resp_value is 1 for those trials and described as -1. RT is measured from the disappearance of the frames, which its description does not say, and is negative in 151 time discrimination trials.
The events series holds 43 entries with a code 0 that its description does not list, with timestamps as low as -7.0e12 s. The spike times have no stated unit.

The paper's Methods do not specify the permutation test, which soft boundaries are used, or how trials are matched across subjects for the pseudopopulation. The definitions of boundary and event cells, read literally, give a chance level about seventy times lower than the paper reports.

The code the dandiset links to (github.com/rutishauserlab/cogboundary-zheng, commit 60f7ece) is four scripts that plot rasters from the NWB files. It contains none of the paper's analyses, no cell selection, chance level, statistics, state-space or reinstatement analysis, and nothing that links a tested frame to its clip.

The authors' plotting code drops missing boundaries by testing for a stored time above 0. In version 0.220216.0323 a missing boundary is stored as the clip's start time, so the code would keep 150 soft-boundary rows where 75 exist and its fixed row ranges for the three conditions would be wrong. In version 0.230530.1822 missing boundaries are NaN and the code works, but that version has the shifted spike times.

Methods and published code disagree on the firing-rate traces. The Methods give a 200 ms window moved in 2 ms steps; the code uses 10 ms bins smoothed with a Gaussian window of 20 bins. The code shows 0.5 s before and 1 s after a boundary. It also treats every soft boundary, including those inside hard-boundary clips, as a soft-boundary trial (75 per session), which the Methods do not state.

Four hard-boundary clips (HB_7, HB_11, HB_14, HB_15) drive strong population activity in the half second before the hard boundary; all contain a soft boundary between 2.75 and 3.40 s. This raises the baseline of a before-against-after test of the hard boundary.

attempts.paper_title: Transformation of a Spatial Map across the Hippocampal-Lateral Septal Circuit
attempts.entry_title: Spatial phase coding in the lateral septum (Tingley and Buzsaki 2018)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Tingley and Buzsaki (2018) on dandiset 000213, which holds 67 sessions of simultaneous hippocampal and lateral septum recordings from five rats running on alternation mazes and a linear track. It decodes position from the spike rate and the spike theta phase of each LS and hippocampal unit, finds place fields, measures spatial information, relates phase coding to recording depth, and measures hippocampal-LS theta coherence and theta-gamma coupling, and detects hippocampal-LS cell assemblies on a random sample of pairs.

The hippocampal fraction is 8.0% to 13.6% per rat. With a Gaussian of SD 5 bins the fractions are 4.9% and 11.6%; with the 5-bin box map 5.8% and 6.3% (p = 0.40); with the 1% threshold of the code's default 0.4% and 4.6%.
