attempts.label: DANDI:001170
attempts.paper_title: Conserved neural dynamics and computations across species in olfaction
attempts.entry_title: ON and OFF odor responses in the mouse olfactory bulb and locust antennal lobe (Ling et al. 2023)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Ling, Moss, Smith, Deng, Kroeger, Reimer, Raman and Arenkiel (bioRxiv 2023, v2 2024) on dandiset 001170, which holds two-photon imaging of olfactory bulb glomeruli in awake mice, seven sessions from four mice under the paper's block protocol and five random-order sessions. It compares glomerular ON and OFF responses, contrast enhancement between sequential odors, and odor classification after offset, and tests the locust findings on the recordings the paper deposited on Figshare.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Ling et al. (2023) from dandiset 001170

outcomes.statement: The mouse block-protocol data (four odors, 5 s pulses, 55 s between trials, blocks of ten, 15 min between blocks) come from seven imaging sessions in four mice, with a median of 215 glomeruli per imaging session.
outcomes.source: Results, OFF responses form anticorrelated odor afterimages across species, paragraph 5; Figure 2H and 4B legends; Methods, Odor delivery to mice
outcomes.quote: With this approach, we monitored calcium signals from hundreds of glomeruli (median: 215 glomeruli per imaging session) ... Summary of the median angular distances for 4 odors (n = 7 imaging sessions from 4 mice)
outcomes.notes: The trials tables give seven block-protocol sessions from mice 134, 141, 148 and 149. The median ROI count over these is 210 (reading a); over all twelve sessions it is 296 (reading b). The ROI counts of sub-141 ses-8 (198), sub-149 ses-1 (219) and sub-148 ses-3 (318) equal the glomerulus counts the Methods give for Figures 2F and 4C, 6D and 7. The published version's Table 1 gives the same seven counts in four mice, but puts the 318 session with the 219 session (mouse 4), where the dandiset puts it with the 286 session (sub-148).
deviations: Sessions are matched to the paper's figures by ROI count; no identifier links them.

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's raw fluorescence of the 198-glomerulus session is the data the paper deposited for its Figure 2D to 2F and 4C (Figshare data1_mouse_glom198.mat), up to the normalisation, with glomeruli in the same order.
outcomes.source: Methods, Time-bin-by-time-bin correlation analysis (n = 198 glomeruli for Fig. 2F); the paper's Figshare record
outcomes.quote: For mouse data, dF/F values were taken to be a n-dimensional population glomerular activity vectors (where n=198 glomeruli for Fig. 2F
outcomes.notes: Matched by ROI count (sub-141 ses-8, the only 198-ROI session) and ROI order. With the code's frame-counted windows the median within-trial r between the dandiset's raw F and the deposited array is 0.968 (5th percentile 0.834, 0.947 to 0.994 by block), and every deposited glomerulus correlates best with the dandiset ROI of the same index. With windows placed in seconds the median r is 0.307, as the code counts 16 frames per second in a session imaged at 15.5 Hz. The deposited values are close to F z-scored within each trial window (r = 0.927). No other claim depends on this one.

outcomes.statement: In the mouse OB the angle between glomerular ON and OFF response vectors is greater than 90 degrees for each odor (mean 121.8 +/- 2.98 SEM, 4 odors, 7 sessions), so ON and OFF responses are inverted relative to each other.
outcomes.source: Results, OFF responses form anticorrelated odor afterimages across species, paragraph 6; Figure 2G and 2H
outcomes.quote: the angle between ON and OFF trajectories was greater than 90° for each odor presented (mean = 121.8° +/- 2.98 SEM, n = 4 odors, 7 sessions) (Fig. 2G, H), revealing that, as in the locust, odor ON and OFF responses in mouse OB glomeruli are inverted relative to each other
outcomes.notes: With the code's procedure (median subtraction, vectors centred over the 160 frames) the median ON-OFF angle exceeds 90 degrees in all 28 session-odor pairs (101.7 to 153.9) and in each odor's mean (111.0 to 140.0), but the mean is 127.9 (SEM 3.2), outside 121.8 +/- 2.98. After centring the mean ON vector is exactly opposite the mean OFF vector (cosine -1 in every case), and without centring the mean angle is 71.8 with 2 of 28 above 90. The same centred procedure gives 101.1 between the two halves of the ON window (28 of 28 above 90), 101.6 between the halves of OFF and 129.7 between the 2 s before onset and ON, and on synthetic frames around patterns 2.4 to 13.0 degrees apart it gives 91.6 to 115.6; so the angles above 90 follow the criterion but do not show that ON and OFF are inverted. Without the median subtraction the mean is 124.2 and with per-trial z-scored traces 119.5, both within tolerance; with F z-scored on the 2 s before onset 125.8 and with frame-counted windows 126.1. By mouse the means are 136.3 (134), 136.3 (141), 116.0 (148) and 117.9 (149).
deviations: dF/F with F0 from the 2 s before onset; the paper's deposited arrays are close to per-trial z-scores. The z-scored result is shown as a variant.
Windows placed in seconds on a 16 Hz grid; the code counts frames at a nominal 16 per second.

outcomes.statement: Time-averaged glomerular ON and OFF responses to the same odor are anticorrelated; glomeruli active during the odor tend to be suppressed after it and the reverse.
outcomes.source: Results, OFF responses form anticorrelated odor afterimages across species, paragraph 6; Results, ON and OFF responses occupy distinct regions of feature space, paragraph 3; Figure 2D, 2F and 4C
outcomes.quote: glomeruli responding to odors during odor presentation tended to be suppressed following odor offset, and that glomeruli responding most strongly to odor offset were suppressed during the odor presentation ... odor ON and OFF responses were not just distinct, but were anticorrelated.
outcomes.notes: The time-averaged ON and OFF vectors are positively correlated in all 28 session-odor pairs (median r 0.481, Wilcoxon p = 7.5e-09), for every odor (0.391 to 0.535) and every mouse (0.245 to 0.596). The median subtraction does not change r, by construction. With F z-scored on the 2 s before onset the median r is 0.526 and with frame-counted windows 0.446 (0 of 28 below 0 in both). With per-trial z-scored traces the median r is 0.068 (12 of 28 below 0, p = 0.33); on synthetic glomeruli with excitation only, that normalisation gives r = -0.90 between ON and 10 to 15 s after offset, against 0.30 with the pre-onset z-score. The angles of fig2h exceed 90 degrees only after centring, which makes the mean ON and OFF vectors opposite by construction.
deviations: dF/F with F0 from the 2 s before onset, not the paper's (undocumented) normalisation.

outcomes.statement: In the mouse OB the ON response to a reference odor is closer in angle to the ON responses of the other odors than to any OFF response, including its own, and this holds for every odor of the panel.
outcomes.source: Results, ON and OFF responses occupy distinct regions of feature space, paragraph 3; Figure 4B and S4B
outcomes.quote: As in locusts, angular separations between a reference odor and all other odor ON responses were smaller than angular separations between the reference ON response and all odor OFF responses (Fig. 4B). This result was true for all odors in the panel (Fig. S4B).
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) holds for acetophenone only (ON-ON 105.7, ON-OFF 127.5 degrees, paired p = 0.018). Methyl salicylate and eugenol show no difference (p = 0.76 and 0.83), and allyl sulfide goes the other way (ON-ON 112.1, ON-OFF 59.6, p = 0.00035). Reading (b) holds in none of the seven sessions for any reference odor. Full-dimensional vectors give the same pattern. The session-mean ON-ON angles are 85.6 to 123.1 degrees, against a median of 44.7 for the acetophenone reference in the published version (Figure 2G), so the paper's procedure probably differs from the one used here.
deviations: The mouse code for this figure is not in the Figshare record (it loads precomputed angles); the locust code's procedure (top three PCs, mean vectors) was used.

outcomes.statement: Hierarchical clustering of glomerular responses cleanly separates ON responses from OFF responses.
outcomes.source: Results, ON and OFF responses occupy distinct regions of feature space, paragraph 3; Figure 4D
outcomes.quote: Supporting this, hierarchical clustering of mouse odor responses cleanly separated ON and OFF responses (Fig. 4D)
outcomes.notes: In 0 of 7 sessions, the 198-glomerulus session included, does the two-cluster cut put the four ON vectors apart from the four OFF vectors, with dF/F or with z-scored traces.
deviations: The paper shows one representative session without naming it; the 198-glomerulus session is taken as it, and all seven are reported.

outcomes.statement: Methyl salicylate presented 1 s after another odor evokes a response less correlated with that odor's solitary response than the solitary methyl salicylate response is (history dependent contrast enhancement; one-tailed t-test p < 0.01, 3 sessions from 2 mice).
outcomes.source: Results, History-dependent suppression enhanced between sequentially presented odors, paragraph 3; Figure 6D and 6E (left)
outcomes.quote: Correlation values between solitary presentations of msc and other odors (left boxes in D) compared to correlation values between sequential msc and odors across imaging sessions (right boxes in D, n = 3 imaging sessions from 2 mice; one-tailed t test, p < 0.01)
outcomes.notes: Over 21 session-odor pairs the solitary r (0.229) and the sequential r (0.219) do not differ (difference 0.009, positive in 10 of 21, one-tailed paired p = 0.39); per session p = 0.40, per first odor p = 0.33 to 0.51. On the three sessions the published version's Table 1 names (sub-148 ses-2, sub-148 ses-3, sub-149 ses-1) the solitary r is 0.133 and the sequential r 0.064 (p = 0.082). With F z-scored on the 2 s before the pair's onset there is no difference (0.251 against 0.258, p = 0.58). With per-trial z-scored traces the solitary r is 0.289 and the sequential r 0.118 (p = 5.6e-07; 0.0025 on the three sessions), as the claim states, but that normalisation can produce negative correlations with later activity by itself (fig2f).
deviations: All seven block sessions are used, as the preprint does not identify its three sessions from two mice; the three the published version names are shown as a variant.
dF/F with F0 from the 2 s before the pair's first onset.

outcomes.statement: Acetophenone presented 1 s after another odor evokes a response less correlated with that odor's solitary response than solitary acetophenone (one-tailed t-test p < 0.05, 4 sessions from 2 mice).
outcomes.source: Figure 6E (right) and Figure S6
outcomes.quote: Correlation values between solitary presentations of ace and the three other odors (see also Figure S5) compared to correlation values between sequential ace and odors across imaging sessions (n = 4 imaging sessions from 2 mice; one-tailed t test, p < 0.05).
outcomes.notes: No sequential pair in the dandiset ends in acetophenone; in all seven block sessions the second odor is always methyl salicylate (ace, als or eug first). The Figshare code builds only (X)msc sequences too, so the (X)ace data of Figure 6E (right) and S6 were not found in public form. The published version's Table 1 assigns this panel to the 73-, 210-, 153- and 198-glomerulus sessions, which in the dandiset hold only (X)msc pairs; in those sessions the first odor's response in the pairs correlates 0.94 to 0.99 with solitary acetophenone when the first odor is labelled acetophenone, and the second odor's response 0.76 to 0.95 with solitary methyl salicylate, consistent with the dandiset's labels.

outcomes.statement: After odor offset the glomerular population activity stays negatively correlated with the odor-evoked ON response for several tens of seconds, although overall activity returns to baseline quickly.
outcomes.source: Results, Odor OFF responses persist long after odor offset, paragraph 1; Figure 7B, 7D and S7C
outcomes.quote: neuronal activity in the AL and OB maintained negative correlations with the odor-evoked ON responses for several tens of seconds following stimulus termination ... although the overall neural activity after stimulus termination returns rapidly to pre-stimulus levels, network activity remains negatively correlated
outcomes.notes: The median r with the ON vector over the 28 pairs is 0.481 at 0 to 5 s after offset, 0.312 to 0.328 from 5 to 20 s and 0.094 at 45 to 50 s, above 0 in every bin (p <= 0.014), while the mean dF/F falls from 0.071 to 0.005. With F0 from before each block r is positive in every bin (0.304 to 0.600); for the first block of sub-134 and sub-141 that baseline is only 14 to 24 s. With F z-scored on the 2 s before onset r is positive in every bin (0.152 to 0.527), and with frame-counted windows too (0.152 to 0.446). With per-trial z-scored traces r is negative from 5 s on (-0.344 to -0.480, 26 to 28 of 28), as the claim states, but on synthetic glomeruli with excitation only that normalisation gives negative values of the same sign and larger size (-0.90 and -0.93). Mice 148 and 149 keep r near 0.2 to 0.4 for the whole 50 s.
deviations: Correlation of the ON vector with 5-s bins, a summary of the paper's frame-by-frame matrix.
dF/F with F0 from the 2 s before onset.

outcomes.statement: Glomerular activity averaged over the 50 s after each odor offset classifies the preceding odor with high accuracy (k-NN, k = 20).
outcomes.source: Results, Odor OFF responses persist long after odor offset, paragraph 2; Figure 7G and 7H; Methods, Classification analysis of average ITI periods
outcomes.quote: We observed a similar clustering of 55-second ITI activity from the mouse OB (Fig. 7G), which contributed to highly accurate classification of odors from ITI glomerular responses (Fig. 7H).
outcomes.notes: In sub-148 ses-3 (318 glomeruli) accuracy is 45%, above the null's 99th percentile (37.5%, null mean 16.7%) but below 50%; by odor 0.9, 0.0, 0.3 and 0.6. The code's choice (cosine on the top three PCs) gives 12.5%. Across the seven sessions accuracy is 22.5% to 47.5%, above the null's 99th percentile in three. The null mean of this leave-one-out vote (16.7% to 17.4%) is below the nominal 25%, as with k = 20 only 9 of the 39 other trials share the own odor; the paper gives no chance value for this panel. With k at or below the class size accuracy is 90.0% (k = 5) and 82.5% (k = 9) in sub-148 ses-3 and 80.0% to 100% in every session (null 99th percentiles 42.5% to 45.0%). All trials of one odor lie in one block, so neither k separates the odor from slow differences between blocks (fig7j).
deviations: k = 20 from the legend; the Methods' k = 50 exceeds the 39 other vectors.
dF/F with F0 the session median of each ROI.

outcomes.statement: A time-bin k-NN classifier identifies the preceding odor from glomerular activity throughout the 55 s inter-trial interval; accuracy stays high for its whole duration and falls to chance with shuffled labels.
outcomes.source: Results, Odor OFF responses persist long after odor offset, paragraph 3; Figure 7J and S8C
outcomes.quote: We found that classifier accuracy remained high for the duration of the 55-second ITI (Fig.7J) ... Shuffling odor labels results in chance-level classifier performance throughout the ITI (Fig. S8C).
outcomes.notes: In sub-148 ses-3 accuracy is 88.5% in the first 10 s after offset and 71.9% to 75.6% from 10 to 50 s, above 50% and the null's 99th percentile (32.5% to 35.9%); the other sessions give 72.2% to 99.4% in every segment. The statement's reading as odor memory is not supported by the outputs. The trial-label null does not keep the block structure, and as each odor has one block no label permutation that keeps whole blocks can serve as a null. On pseudo-trials within the 15 min after each block, where no odor is given, the same classifier names the preceding block at 69.6% to 96.9% (sub-148 ses-3 69.6% to 71.2%), nearly as high as in the ITIs (the pseudo-trial maximum is below the ITI minimum in 4 of 7 sessions), so slow differences between blocks are enough for most of this accuracy.
deviations: dF/F with F0 the session median of each ROI.
The shuffled-label control is a permutation of whole-trial labels with the neighbours kept.

outcomes.statement: During the 15 min between blocks odor-specific information is no longer present; classification of 1-min bins of the inter-block interval by the preceding odor is near chance (34.8%).
outcomes.source: Results, Odor OFF responses persist long after odor offset, paragraph 2; Figure S7D and S7E, Figure 7K
outcomes.quote: during the IBI, network activity ceased to contain odor-specific information ... The overall classification rate of the glomerular IBI activity was 34.8%.
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' k = 50 on 60 one-minute bins the rate is 0.0% to 13.3% (mean 3.8%) in the four sessions with complete IBIs, and this procedure's permutation null averages 10.8%, not the 25% chance of four odors, so the paper's 34.8% cannot come from it. With k = 20 the IBI bins are classified by the preceding block at 73.3% to 95.0% in those four sessions and 35.0% to 66.7% in the other three (permutation p <= 0.02), and with k at or below the 14 other bins of the own IBI at 69.4% to 98.3% (k = 10) and 90.0% to 98.3% (k = 5) in all seven (null means 21.8% to 25.5%, p < 0.001). These rates contradict the claim, but each odor has one IBI per session, so no validation can hold out a block, and slow drift between neighbouring minutes could give them.
deviations: The 318-glomerulus session has only three complete IBIs (54 bins), so k = 50 was run on the four sessions that have four.

outcomes.statement: When eleven odors are presented in random order (1 s pulses, 19 s apart), odor information after offset is variable across odors and on average declines to chance after several seconds.
outcomes.source: Results, Odor OFF responses persist long after odor offset, paragraph 4; Figure S8D and S8E
outcomes.quote: Classifier accuracy across the ITI was variable across odors (Fig. S8D), but, on average, declined to chance after several seconds (Fig. S8E).
outcomes.notes: In all five random-order sessions accuracy in the first 2 s after offset is above the null (24.4% to 56.8% against 99th percentiles of 10.6% to 12.3%, chance 9.1%), with large differences between odors. In the last 5 s it is 9.6% to 15.3%, still above the null's 95th percentile in four of five sessions (not in sub-134 ses-6). The published version's Table 1 lists random-order sessions with 175, 340, 323, 306, 286, 204, 250 and 280 glomeruli; only sub-126 ses-1 (323) and sub-134 ses-6 (306) have one of these counts. In those two early accuracy is 24.4% and 29.0%, and late accuracy is above the null's 95th percentile in sub-126 ses-1 (9.6% against 9.0%) and not in sub-134 ses-6 (9.9% against 10.0%).
deviations: The paper's random-order session (286 glomeruli, mouse 129 in the Figshare code) is not in the dandiset; five sessions with the same paradigm, four of them from mice not in the block sessions, were used.
In three of these sessions odors have different concentration values; the first 10 presentations of each odor were used regardless.

outcomes.statement: Photoionization detector recordings at the nostril show odor concentration rising and decaying quickly at onset and offset, for every odor.
outcomes.source: Figure S2; Results, Odor OFF responses persist long after odor offset, paragraph 3; Methods, Odor delivery to mice
outcomes.quote: PID recordings confirmed that, for all odors, concentrations near the nares decayed rapidly after odor offset (Fig. S2).
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds no photoionization detector recordings (acquisition holds the movies, treadmill and in one file respiration). No PID file is in the Figshare record's file list.

outcomes.statement: In the locust antennal lobe the median angle between PN population ON and OFF response vectors exceeds 90 degrees for every one of 11 odors (mean 106.7 +/- 0.84 SEM).
outcomes.source: Results, OFF responses form anticorrelated odor afterimages across species, paragraph 4; Figure 1F and 1G, S1
outcomes.quote: For every odor the median angle between the ON and OFF responses was more than 90 degrees (mean = 106.7° +/- 0.84 SEM, n = 11 odors)
outcomes.notes: All 11 odors give a median ON-OFF angle above 90 degrees (99.2 to 108.7); the mean is 104.9 (SEM 0.87), 1.8 degrees below 106.7 +/- 0.84. Without centring the mean is 58.5; with each PN's pre-odor mean subtracted and no centring it is 91.9, with 9 of 11 above 90. The centring alone gives angles above 90 degrees; the two halves of the ON window are 96.0 apart on average (11 of 11 above 90).
deviations: Data from the Figshare record of the published version; the preprint's data may differ.

outcomes.statement: In the locust the ON response to a reference odor is closer to other odors' ON responses than to OFF responses for most reference odors, significantly for 5 of 11.
outcomes.source: Results, ON and OFF responses occupy distinct regions of feature space, paragraph 1; Figure 3B and S4A
outcomes.quote: While this finding was consistent for most reference odors, the difference in angular separation was significant for 5 out of 11 odors in the panel (Fig. S4A).
outcomes.notes: Four reference odors have ON angles significantly smaller than OFF angles (hex, hxa, phn, vny), and 9 of 11 have smaller ON angles on average. Ammonia differs significantly the other way (ON 107.3, OFF 52.5 degrees, p = 0.0033). The 11 ON angles include the reference's own 0 degrees, as the criterion states; without it the count is still 4, and ON is smaller on average for 8 of 11. Benzaldehyde (p = 0.052) and octanoic acid (p = 0.059) are near the threshold.

outcomes.statement: In the locust, PN responses to geraniol presented 0.5 s after another odor are less correlated with that odor's solitary response than solitary geraniol is (one-tailed t-test p < 0.05, 5 odor pairs).
outcomes.source: Results, History-dependent suppression enhanced between sequentially presented odors, paragraph 2; Figure 5D and 5E
outcomes.quote: we found that the correlation between high-dimensional odor response vectors was lower when the odors were sequentially presented, compared to when the odors were presented in isolation (Fig. 5D, E).
outcomes.notes: Solitary first odors correlate with solitary geraniol at 0.486 on average and with geraniol after them at 0.227, lower for all five (one-tailed paired p = 0.0055). With hexanol as the second odor the difference is smaller (0.407 against 0.321, p = 0.13).

outcomes.statement: In the locust, PN activity averaged over the 20 s after odor offset classifies the preceding odor (k-NN on angular distance), so ITI activity is odor specific.
outcomes.source: Results, Odor OFF responses persist long after odor offset, paragraph 2; Figure 7E and 7F; Methods, Classification analysis of average ITI periods
outcomes.quote: A k-nearest neighbor classifier, using angular distances of the full-dimensional ITI data, robustly discriminated odors (Fig. 7F). This confirmed the interpretation from the PCA analysis and showed that ITI activity was odor-specific.
outcomes.notes: The 20-s ITI averages classify all 70 trials correctly (null 99th percentile 25.7%, chance 14.3%); the code's choice (k = 4, cosine on three PCs) gives 97.1%. The published version's Table 1 gives this dataset a solitary block structure; the Figshare file holds only the 40 s around each trial, so no control for slow differences between blocks can be built, and the accuracy cannot be attributed to the odor alone.

outcomes.statement: In the locust a time-bin k-NN classifier's accuracy decays across the 20 s after offset to about 40% averaged over odors, but for most odors does not fall to chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Odor OFF responses persist long after odor offset, paragraph 3; Figure 7I
outcomes.quote: Classifier accuracy decreased to ∼40% across odors throughout the 20-second post stimulus ITI, but notably, for most odors, accuracy did not fall to chance levels during the entire ITI period (Fig.7I).
outcomes.notes: Accuracy decays from 78.7% in the first 2 s after offset to 29.0% averaged over odors in the last 5 s, below 40 +/- 4; every one of the 7 odors stays above its null's 99th percentile in the last 5 s (16.0% to 54.0% against 14.0% to 27.6%). Averaged over the whole 0 to 21 s the accuracy is 39.6%, a reading of "about 40%" the criterion did not list. As for fig7f, the files allow no control for the block structure.
deviations: The paper's ~40% is read from its text; the last 5 s of the ITI was taken as the end.

findings.statement: The fluorescence traces are raw F (unit "n.a.") with no description of how they were extracted or of the normalisation the paper applied. The paper's deposited arrays are close to F z-scored within each 57-s trial window. With that normalisation the contrast enhancement and negative correlations between the ON response and activity from 5 s after offset appear in these data, and they do not with dF/F relative to the 2 s before each odor or with F z-scored on those 2 s. The time-averaged ON and OFF vectors are not anticorrelated with any of these (median r 0.068 with the whole-window z-score, 12 of 28 below 0). On synthetic glomeruli with excitation only, the whole-window z-score gives such anticorrelations by itself.

The trials table has one row per second of valve opening, without a description; odor presentations, blocks and sequential pairs have to be rebuilt from timing. Five block sessions fill the gaps with "Empty" rows and two do not. The concentration column has no unit, gives 0.0 to two odorants (2-ethylphenol, anisaldehyde) in three random-order sessions, and 0.1 to the Empty rows of sub-141 ses-5.

In sub-134 ses-22, sub-141 ses-5 and sub-141 ses-8 the raw TwoPhotonSeries holds half the frames of the fluorescence traces (91000 against 182000 in sub-134 ses-22) at twice the frame interval; the conversion notes give 182000 frames for sub-134 ses-22.

No sequential pair ends in acetophenone (Figure 6E right, S6) and no PID recordings are included (Figure S2). The published version's Table 1 assigns the acetophenone panel to the 73-, 210-, 153- and 198-glomerulus sessions, which in the dandiset hold only pairs ending in methyl salicylate. The random-order session of Figure S8D and S8E (286 glomeruli) is not in the dandiset, and of the eight random-order sessions that Table 1 lists (175, 340, 323, 306, 286, 204, 250 and 280 glomeruli) only two (323 and 306) match a dandiset session by ROI count.

The dandiset holds the paper's seven block-protocol sessions from four mice and five random-order sessions from five mice (four not in the block sessions) with odor-specific concentrations, apparently from a second study (the conference paper it also names, whose authors are the dandiset's contributors). Neither the metadata nor the description says which sessions belong to which paper, and the description is that of the second study.

No identifier links the paper's datasets to the dandiset's sessions. They match by ROI count (198, 219, 318), but the session names in the paper's Figshare code (for example m149_3_1, m129_1_2) do not all exist in the dandiset (it has no mouse 129 and only session 1 of mouse 149).

The dandiset and the published version's Table 1 disagree on which mouse one session belongs to. The dandiset puts the 318-ROI session under sub-148 with the 286-ROI session; Table 1 puts the 318-glomerulus session under mouse 4 with the 219-glomerulus session (sub-149 here). Which is right cannot be told from the data.

The random-order odorant names differ from the paper's; the files have 2-ethylphenol and anisaldehyde where the Methods list 2-ethylpyrizine (2ep) and isoamyl acetate (asa). Names are spelled differently across sessions ("Anisole" and "anisole"), and "2-methypyrazine" is misspelled.
The genotype (Thy1-GCaMP6f) and the ages are not stated, and every session starts at 00:00, so the time of day is missing. In sub-124 ses-3 the last trial ends 8.9 s after the last imaging frame.

The paper's code counts windows in frames at a nominal 16 per second, while the sessions are imaged at 13.7 to 17.8 Hz, so a nominal 57-s window of 912 frames lasts 51.2 to 66.4 s; in sub-141 ses-8 (15.5 Hz) the deposited trial windows match the dandiset only when counted in frames (r 0.968) and not in seconds (r 0.307).

The Methods give k = 50 for the ITI-average classifier of Figure 7H, which has 40 vectors, while the legend gives k = 20 and the code uses k = 20 on three PCs. For the IBI classifier (60 vectors, k = 50) the procedure's own null is 10.8%, not the 25% chance of four odors.
The Figure 5E legend states a one-tailed t-test; Script_Fig4.m uses MATLAB's ttest, which is two-tailed (p = 0.011 against 0.0055 one-tailed here).

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier had no attempt record and took its counts from the claims file. bioRxiv refused the preprint download, so it read the v2 abstract and the published version (iScience, PMC13066794); the preprint's Fig 4B ON-ON value and Table S1 were not checked. It gave its own outcome for each claim; 18 of 19 agree with the record.

disagreements.reason: The k = 50 rate is 3.8%, far below 34.8 +/- 3.48 and below chance, because the k = 50 classifier is degenerate; on random data with 4 x 15 vectors it gives 10.7%, so the <= 38.3% criterion is met by construction (problem 1). The only usable classifier (k = 20) gives 73 to 95% with permutation p = 0 in the four complete sessions, which contradicts "no longer present", though adjacent 1-minute bins of the same IBI serve as each other's neighbours, so slow drift alone could explain it.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook with conclusions and summary, the README, the attempt record, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier read the v2 preprint text (bioRxiv API JATS, saved in paper/), which confirms 121.8, 106.7, 34.8, n = 286 and the 11-odor list; its Fig 4B text gives no ON-ON value, and Table S1 is an image and was not checked. It agrees with 19 of 19 outcomes.

attempts.label: DANDI:001172
attempts.paper_title: Dual color mesoscopic imaging reveals spatiotemporally heterogeneous coordination of cholinergic and neocortical activity
attempts.entry_title: Cholinergic and calcium dynamics across behavioural states (Lohani, Moberly et al. 2022)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Lohani, Moberly et al. (2022) on dandiset 001172, which holds dual-colour mesoscopic imaging of ACh3.0 and jRCaMP1b with face video, pupil and wheel data from 4 of the paper's 6 mice. It tests the regression of both signals on behaviour, transients at face movement and locomotion onsets, amplitudes in sustained states, and the state dependence of correlations between areas and between the two signals, using the Allen parcel masks of the paper's code. ECoG, pharmacology, control mice and cholinergic axon imaging are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Lohani, Moberly et al. (2022) from dandiset 001172

outcomes.statement: The paper's Allen parcel masks, from its code, can be laid on the dandiset's ΔF/F pixels, so that the areas the paper names can be found in the data.
outcomes.source: Methods, Preprocessing of imaging data and Post-processing analysis; parcells_updated121519.mat and brainMask.mat in the paper's code at commit c337686
outcomes.notes: Per session (pixels non-zero in either ΔF/F movie) the non-zero pixels equal the code's brainMask.mat rotated by 180 degrees in all 9 sessions (agreement 1.0; best other orientation 0.98). Per movie, 25 of the 26 movies of the 13 sessions (the 9 state sessions and the 4 visual stimulus sessions) agree at 1.0; the calcium movie of grabAM08 11232019 spont agrees at 0.996, as 263 pixels inside the mask, all in the right AUD parcel, are zero in every frame and none outside is non-zero. With 100% contrast gratings in one visual stimulus session per mouse (47 to 49 trials), the largest calcium response of the 46 parcels is in a left visual parcel in all 4 mice and left VISp exceeds right VISp in all 4 (0.108 to 0.216 against -0.024 to 0.065 percent ΔF/F), but left VISp ranks 1, 1, 3 and 2, so first in 2 of 4 mice where the criterion asks 3 for reproduced. The dependent claims are tested; the partial result bears on parcel borders, not on which areas are where.
deviations: The criterion's "pixels with non-zero ΔF/F in the blue and green movies" can be read per movie or per session; the per-session reading was chosen after seeing that one movie fails the 99.9% bar under the per-movie reading. Under the per-movie reading the mask part fails on that movie and the claim would be not reproduced by the letter of the criterion. The failing pixels are all in the right AUD parcel, which the left-hemisphere analyses do not use.

outcomes.statement: The variance of ACh3.0 and jRCaMP1b signals explained by a ridge regression on FaceMap PCs 1 to 25, locomotion speed and pupil area differs across cortical areas (Friedman's ANOVA p < 0.001 for both, n = 6 mice).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 1; Figure 2a,b
outcomes.quote: For ACh3.0 and jRCaMp1b, the variance explained ... using this full model differed significantly across cortical areas
outcomes.notes: Friedman across the 23 left parcels with 4 mice, ACh chi2 = 67.98, p = 1.4e-06, calcium chi2 = 63.51, p = 6.7e-06. Full-model R2 ranges 0.030 to 0.397 (ACh) and 0.084 to 0.387 (calcium). Spontaneous sessions alone give p = 6e-07 and 0.005. With |speed| as the wheel predictor p = 1.3e-06 and 7.7e-06. For the three mice that match rows of the paper's own R2 file (grabAM05, grabAM07, grabAM08), mean full-model R2 is 0.182, 0.126 and 0.140 (ACh) and 0.207, 0.216 and 0.227 (calcium) against the file's 0.166, 0.126 and 0.142 and 0.193, 0.229 and 0.254.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice; spontaneous and air-puff sessions (9) averaged per mouse, as the Methods do not say which sessions were used.
The ridge regression code is not public; the penalty is chosen per parcel by marginal likelihood over a grid of 91 values, as ridgeMML does by optimisation.

The wheel predictor is the files' WheelSpeed, which is signed, as the Methods ("a differential of distance") and the code's wheel_changepoints.m (db1SpeedMpS) define speed. The first revision had switched to |speed|; the second revision returned to the signed series, and |speed| is a variant.
Predictors are scaled with the training folds' statistics; the first run z-scored them over the whole session.

outcomes.statement: The coupling of behaviour to fluorescence has anterior-posterior gradients that are inverted between the signals, with ACh most strongly linked to behaviour in frontal areas and calcium in posterior areas.
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 1; Figure 2b
outcomes.quote: We also observed significant anterior-posterior gradients in the coupling between behavioral state and fluorescence activity that were inverted for cholinergic versus calcium signals ... with ACh release and calcium signaling most strongly linked to behavioral state variables in frontal and posterior areas, respectively
outcomes.notes: Spearman of mean R2 with anterior-posterior rank (1 = MOs) gives ACh rho = -0.761 (p = 2.5e-05) and calcium rho = 0.555 (p = 0.0059). Per mouse ACh rho -0.44 to -0.87; calcium 0.57 to 0.70 in three mice and -0.01 in grabAM05. Spontaneous sessions alone give -0.897 and 0.655. With |speed| -0.758 and 0.558.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: For ACh3.0, facial movement (FaceMap PC1) predicts activity better than locomotion or pupil, in single-variable models (Friedman p = 0.006, face against locomotion and against pupil p = 0.031) and as unique contribution (Friedman p = 0.003).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 1; Figure 2c
outcomes.quote: Facial movements yielded the strongest prediction accuracy compared to locomotion and pupil variation for Ach 3.0
outcomes.notes: Single-variable R2 averaged over left parcels, face PC1 0.081, wheel 0.026, pupil 0.009; face highest in all 4 mice, Friedman p = 0.018 (exact p = 0.0046). Unique contributions face 0.081, pupil 0.016, wheel 0.004, face largest in all 4 mice, Friedman p = 0.039 (exact p = 0.042). The same holds with |speed|. Signed-rank tests give p = 0.125, the smallest possible with 4 mice, so the paper's p = 0.031 cannot be reached.
deviations: The paper's post hoc signed-rank tests are replaced by the direction in every mouse.
Unique contribution of face is from shuffling PC1 only; the Methods do not say which face PCs were shuffled.

outcomes.statement: For jRCaMP1b, facial movement (FaceMap PC1) is the most robust predictor of activity (single-variable Friedman p = 0.006; face against locomotion and pupil p = 0.031).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 1; Figure 2c
outcomes.quote: Again, facial movement (PC1) was the most robust predictor
outcomes.notes: Changed to reproduced in the third verification round, from the partially_reproduced of the first revision, which rested on |speed| as the wheel predictor. With the signed speed of the Methods and the code, now the main analysis, single-variable R2 is face PC1 0.112, wheel 0.084, pupil 0.010, face best in all 4 mice by 0.016 to 0.053 over wheel speed, Friedman p = 0.018 (exact p = 0.0046). Unique contributions face 0.058, pupil 0.025, wheel 0.014, face largest in all 4 mice (in grabAM05 by 0.002 over pupil), Friedman p = 0.039. With |speed| wheel speed is higher in grabAM06 (0.147 against 0.142), face is best in 3 of 4 mice and the claim would be partial. In the paper's own per-mouse values (Fig2RawData.mat) face PC1 is the best single variable in all 6 mice, and in grabAM05 (row 1, matched by full-model R2 across parcels, Spearman 0.94 to 0.98) the wheel R2 is 0.0246 for calcium against 0.0253 here with signed speed and 0.0483 with |speed|. The paper found face against pupil not significant for the unique contribution here (p = 0.063).
deviations: As for fig2c-face-best-predictor-ach.
The regression code is not public; signed speed follows the Methods and wheel_changepoints.m.

outcomes.statement: Facial movement onset without locomotion is associated with significant whole-cortex transients in ACh (0.64 ± 0.09 ΔF/F, p = 0.001) and calcium (0.69 ± 0.15 ΔF/F, p = 0.006).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 2; Figure S7
outcomes.quote: Facial movement onset (quantified using FaceMap PC1) in the absence of locomotion was associated with desynchronization of local neuronal firing as estimated by ECoG and significant whole cortex-averaged transients in both ACh ... and calcium ... signals
outcomes.notes: ACh 0.728 ± 0.119 percent ΔF/F (paper 0.55 to 0.73), calcium 0.920 ± 0.131 (paper 0.54 to 0.84), positive in all 4 mice, one-sample t-test p = 0.0089 and 0.0060. 12 to 31 onsets per mouse. The ACh mean is inside tolerance by 0.002. The same peak at random times in sustained quiescence (200 draws) has per mouse means 0.049 to 0.088 (ACh) and 0.113 to 0.177 (calcium); every mouse's transient is above the null's 95th percentile. Keeping the quiescent period after the last locomotion epoch (which the code's onset function drops) gives 0.728 and 0.871.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice; face onsets from the code's procedure, which the Methods describe only in part.

outcomes.statement: Locomotion onset is associated with transient increases in ACh (0.68 ± 0.17 ΔF/F, p = 0.010) and calcium (1.50 ± 0.11 ΔF/F, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 2; Figure S7
outcomes.quote: Locomotion onset co-occurred with an increase in facial movement and local desynchronization and was also associated with transient increases in ACh ... and calcium ... signals
outcomes.notes: ACh 0.761 ± 0.272 percent ΔF/F (paper 0.51 to 0.85, p = 0.068 here), calcium 1.985 ± 0.489 (paper 1.39 to 1.61, p = 0.027), positive in all 4 mice; grabAM08 has the largest values (ACh 1.555, calcium 3.436). 17 to 39 onsets per mouse. Null peaks at random quiescent times have per mouse means 0.044 to 0.082 (ACh) and 0.111 to 0.212 (calcium); every mouse's transient is above the null's 95th percentile.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: ACh transients vary across cortical areas (p < 0.001) but do not differ between locomotion and facial motion onsets (p = 0.734, two-way repeated measures ANOVA).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 2; Figure S7
outcomes.quote: ACh transients varied significantly across cortical areas ... but were not significantly different between locomotion and facial motion onsets
outcomes.notes: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA (4 mice), onset type F = 0.03, p = 0.88; area F = 9.39, p < 0.0001. Whole-cortex locomotion minus face per mouse -0.285 to 0.625 (three negative, one positive), mean 0.034 percent ΔF/F. An absence result with 3 denominator degrees of freedom, which carries little weight.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Calcium transients vary across cortical areas (p < 0.001) and states (p = 0.005), with locomotion onset associated with the largest signal.
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 2; Figure S7
outcomes.quote: Calcium transients varied significantly across cortical areas ... and states ... with locomotion onset associated with the largest signal
outcomes.notes: Locomotion transient above face transient in all 4 mice (by 0.447 to 2.245, mean 1.065 percent ΔF/F), onset type F = 6.94, p = 0.078; area F = 31.6, p < 0.0001.
deviations: 4 of 6 mice; the ANOVA has 3 denominator degrees of freedom for onset type.

outcomes.statement: Transient magnitudes show a significant anterior-posterior gradient for ACh but not for calcium.
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 2; Figure S7
outcomes.quote: We also found a significant anterior-posterior gradient in the transient magnitudes for cholinergic but not calcium signals
outcomes.notes: ACh rho = -0.605 (p = 0.0022) at face onset and -0.752 (p = 3.5e-05) at locomotion onset, larger anteriorly; calcium rho = 0.014 (p = 0.95) and 0.106 (p = 0.63).
deviations: The paper does not say which onsets the gradient refers to; both are tested.

outcomes.statement: Sustained facial movement and locomotion are associated with progressively increasing 30 to 100 Hz ECoG power.
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 3; Figure 3b
outcomes.quote: Sustained increases in facial movement and locomotion were associated with progressively increasing local circuit desynchronization, as evidenced by an increase in high frequency power

statistics.about: main effect of state on 30-100 Hz power

outcomes.notes: The files hold no ECoG; the conversion code reads the Spike2 LFP channel but does not write it. The paper offers its data on request only.

outcomes.statement: Sustained facial motion elevates whole-cortex ACh (low face -0.13 ± 0.04, high face 0.18 ± 0.08 ΔF/F; low against high p = 0.046, post hoc LSD), with a main effect of state (p = 0.015).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 3; Figure 3c
outcomes.quote: ACh activity varied significantly across cortical areas ... and differed by state ... Sustained facial motion significantly elevated whole-cortex Ach activity
outcomes.notes: With 3 mice (grabAM07 has no sustained high face epoch), low face -0.129 ± 0.031 and high face 0.158 ± 0.047 percent ΔF/F, both inside the paper's ranges; high above low in all 3 mice (0.138 to 0.384), LSD p = 0.027; state effect F = 11.1, p = 0.023. Matched epochs per mouse 10, 2 and 13 (71.7, 14.6 and 93.7 s per state). Without grabAM06, high exceeds low in both other mice but LSD p = 0.207.
deviations: 3 of the paper's 6 mice; grabAM06 contributes 2 epochs per state.

outcomes.statement: Locomotion does not further increase whole-cortex ACh beyond high facial motion (locomotion 0.16 ± 0.06 ΔF/F; locomotion against high face p = 0.717).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 3; Figure 3c
outcomes.quote: but locomotion did not further increase the Ach signal
outcomes.notes: Locomotion minus high face LSD t = 1.09, p = 0.34. The locomotion mean, 0.250 percent ΔF/F, is above the paper's 0.10 to 0.22, and exceeds high face in all 3 mice (by 0.027 to 0.179), so the data point against the claim; the outcome rests on an absence test with 3 mice, which carries little weight.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Sustained facial movement and locomotion both increase whole-cortex calcium (low face -0.02 ± 0.02, high face 0.17 ± 0.04, locomotion 0.63 ± 0.19 ΔF/F; low against high p = 0.020, locomotion against high p = 0.044), with a main effect of state (p = 0.005).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 3; Figure 3c
outcomes.quote: Similarly, sustained calcium activity varied significantly for cortical area ... and state ... Sustained facial movement and locomotion both increased whole cortex calcium activity
outcomes.notes: Low face -0.002, high face 0.164 (inside the paper's ranges), locomotion 1.106 percent ΔF/F (paper 0.44 to 0.82). High above low in all 3 mice (0.124 to 0.222) but LSD p = 0.24; locomotion above high in all 3 (0.656 to 1.2), LSD p = 0.001; state effect F = 48.3, p = 0.0016. Without grabAM06 high minus low has p = 0.266 and locomotion minus high p = 0.019.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Differences across sustained states have significant anterior-posterior gradients, for ACh comparing high and low facial movement, with larger increases in anterior areas, and for calcium comparing locomotion and high facial movement.
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 3; Discussion; Figure S7
outcomes.quote: there was a significant anterior-posterior gradient in the differences across states measured with Spearman’s rank correlation for the cholinergic signal comparing sustained high and low facial movement and for calcium activity comparing sustained locomotion and high facial movement
outcomes.notes: ACh high minus low face rho = -0.801, p = 4.3e-06 (larger anteriorly); calcium locomotion minus high face rho = 0.329, p = 0.125. Without grabAM06 (2 epochs per state) ACh rho = -0.874 (p = 5.3e-08) and calcium rho = 0.437 (p = 0.037), so the calcium half would be met with 2 mice; the criterion fixes the 3 mice.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: During high facial motion ACh3.0 amplitude is higher in frontal-motor areas than in visual areas (paired t-test, p < 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 4; Figure 3d
outcomes.quote: increased motor activity (e.g., facial movement) is associated with significantly higher ACh release in motor versus visual areas
outcomes.notes: High face ACh, frontal-motor 0.166 to 0.427 against visual 0.032 to 0.108 percent ΔF/F, higher in all 3 mice, paired t = 4.34, p = 0.049. Without grabAM06 (2 epochs per state) the difference holds in both other mice but p = 0.247.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice; p is just below 0.05.

outcomes.statement: The muscarinic blocker scopolamine decreases cortical activity in motor but not visual areas, and the nicotinic blocker mecamylamine has no significant effect.
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 4; Figure 3e
outcomes.quote: treatment with the muscarinic blocker scopolamine selectively decreased cortical activity in motor but not visual areas ... In contrast, treatment with the nicotinic blocker mecamylamine had no significant impact on cortical activity
outcomes.notes: No drug or vehicle sessions are in the dandiset (its sessions are spontaneous, air-puff and visual stimulus); the paper offers its data on request only.

outcomes.statement: Increased facial movement is associated with significant increases in between-area correlations of ACh in anterior somatosensory and motor areas.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 1; Figure 4a
outcomes.quote: We found that increased facial movement was associated with significant increases in between-area pairwise correlations in anterior somatosensory and motor areas for ACh signal
outcomes.notes: High minus low face, 64 of 253 pairs increase significantly (BY q = 0.01) and none decreases; 39 of 45 motor-somatosensory pairs (0.867) against 25 of 208 other pairs (0.120). Mean change in z per mouse 0.095, 0.314 and 0.362. At q = 0.05, 98 increases.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice; the permutation test permutes epochs within mice, so its power comes from epochs (25 per state in all) more than mice.

outcomes.statement: Locomotion is associated with a reduction in between-area correlations of ACh that is significant across the cortex.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 1; Figure 4a
outcomes.quote: locomotion was associated with a reduction in the between-area correlations of cholinergic activity that was significant across the cortex
outcomes.notes: Locomotion minus high face, 243 of 253 pairs (0.960) decrease significantly, none increases, all six area groups involved; mean r 0.539 against 0.791; per mouse mean change in z -0.337 to -0.648.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Increased facial movement is associated with broad, significant increases in between-area calcium correlations.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 1; Figure 4b
outcomes.quote: We found that increased facial movement was associated with ... broad, significant increases for calcium signal
outcomes.notes: High minus low face, 161 of 253 pairs (0.636) increase significantly, none decreases, all six area groups involved; per mouse mean change in z 0.227 to 0.567.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Locomotion occurs with modest decreases in calcium correlations that are significant primarily across posterior cortical areas.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 1; Figure 4b
outcomes.quote: Locomotion also occurred with modest decreases in correlation for calcium signals that were significant primarily across posterior cortical areas
outcomes.notes: Locomotion minus high face, 100 pairs decrease significantly and none increases; 55 of 66 posterior pairs (0.833) against 45 of 187 other pairs (0.241). Per mouse mean change in z -0.183 to -0.513.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice; posterior is defined here as ranks 12 to 23 of the Methods' order.

outcomes.statement: Sustained facial movement is associated with a significant increase in the correlation between ACh and calcium signals broadly across the cortex.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 2; Figure 5
outcomes.quote: Sustained facial movement was associated with a significant increase in correlation between the two signals broadly across the cortex
outcomes.notes: ACh-calcium coupling increases in all 23 left parcels (z 0.173 to 0.737) and significantly in 10 (none decreases), short of the 12 the criterion asks; 22 have uncorrected p < 0.05 and 20 pass BY at q = 0.05. Mean r 0.573 against 0.185; per mouse mean change 0.182 to 0.694.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice.

outcomes.statement: Sustained locomotion is associated with a significant reduction in the correlation between ACh and calcium that is restricted to the frontal cortex.
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent modulation of cortical network architecture, paragraph 2; Figure 5
outcomes.quote: sustained locomotion was associated with a significant reduction in the correlation between the two channels that was restricted to the frontal cortex
outcomes.notes: No parcel decreases significantly at q = 0.01 (2 at q = 0.05). Coupling is lower with locomotion in all 23 parcels (z -0.370 to -0.037) and in each mouse (-0.138 to -0.269); the largest decreases are in PTLp and SSp-tr (p = 0.0007 and 0.0006), and MOs and MOp have p = 0.072 and 0.076. The decrease is broad here, not restricted to frontal cortex.
deviations: 3 of 6 mice, with 25 matched epochs per state in all.

outcomes.statement: The spatial regression on 395 nm signals removes stimulus-evoked and behaviour-related negative hemodynamic transients better than pixel-wise regression, shown in GFP and mCherry control mice and in ACh3.0 mice.
outcomes.source: Results, Dual-color mesoscopic ACh and calcium imaging, paragraph 1; Methods, Validation of hemodynamics correction; Figures S3, S4
outcomes.quote: This method outperformed conventional pixel-wise regression in its ability to remove stimulus-induced and spontaneous behavior-associated negative transients in fluorescence corresponding to hemodynamic absorption
outcomes.notes: The comparisons rest on GFP, mCherry and backscatter data from control mice, which are not in the dandiset. The ACh3.0 part (visual stimulus negativity in V1 before and after correction) would need the uncorrected blue ΔF/F, which is not in the files. It could in principle be recomputed from the raw blue and violet movies of the visual stimulus sessions (about 50 GB each), but that needs a reimplementation of the spatial regression and the atlas areas in native space, because the code's registration transforms are not in the files; this attempt did not do it. A check on one session (data check) shows the archived blue ΔF/F shares almost no fluctuation with the violet ΔF/F (r = 0.070) where the raw movies share much (r = 0.576), consistent with a correction having been applied.

outcomes.statement: ACh3.0 specifically reports cholinergic signalling, ex vivo (carbachol, blocked by scopolamine) and in vivo (basal forebrain stimulation).
outcomes.source: Results, Dual-color mesoscopic ACh and calcium imaging, paragraph 1; Figure S2
outcomes.quote: we confirmed both ex vivo and in vivo that ACh3.0 specifically reported cholinergic signaling
outcomes.notes: The slice imaging with carbachol and scopolamine and the basal forebrain stimulation sessions are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: The relationship between behavioural state and cholinergic signalling is also seen with mesoscopic imaging of GCaMP6s in cholinergic axons.
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium and cholinergic signals encode behavioral state, paragraph 3; Figure S8
outcomes.quote: we observed a similar relationship between behavioral state and cholinergic axonal signaling measured via mesoscopic imaging of genetically targeted GCaMP6s-expressing fibers
outcomes.notes: No ChAT-Cre Ai162 (GCaMP6s) mice are in the dandiset.

findings.statement: The ΔF/F series (DFFOnePhotonSeriesBlue, Green and Violet) are given the starting time of the first LED pulse, the time of raw frame 0, but their frame 0 is raw frame 499, as the detrending drops the first frames. Their times are 49.9 s early in every session; both the raw movies and the alignment of calcium with wheel speed show it.

The FaceMap, pupil, eye and video timestamps are spaced 111 ms (9 Hz) where the camera pulses are 100 ms apart, span about 10% longer than the session, and end with two values equal to the first camera pulse. With these timestamps face movement and wheel speed are misaligned by 23 to 60 s; with frame i at camera pulse i, as the paper's code does, they align.

RoiResponseSeriesParcellated holds the calcium (green excitation) ΔF/F averaged over its ROIs, but its segmentation is linked to the ACh imaging plane. Its image masks are transposed relative to the ΔF/F images, and its starting time is that of the first green pulse, 64.9 s before its first frame (150 frames after the ΔF/F's first frame).

The ΔF/F descriptions mention detrending only; the blue and green ΔF/F are also hemodynamically corrected and registered to the Allen atlas, rotated by 180 degrees, as the paper's code shows (the data are consistent with the correction, in one session checked). The Allen parcels the paper analyses are not in the files; they come from the paper's code. The parcellation in the files is a different, functional one with 89 to 107 ROIs per session and no area names.
In the VisualStimulus tables the columns from stimulus_size on are shifted by one; stimulus_size holds the duration (2) and the first screen coordinate holds the size (20 degrees).
The air-puff session grabAM07 11262019 has no Airpuff table, so its puff times are unknown.

No air puff in the Airpuff tables is followed by a locomotion onset within 5 s (29 puffs), which fits the paper's code keeping only puffs without running. The tables then hold a selection of the puffs given, which the files do not say.

WheelSpeed and pupil_area have the unit "unknown"; the paper's code treats wheel speed as m/s, and its range fits that. WheelSpeed is signed (minimum -0.07 to -0.14 per session), which its description does not say.

In the calcium ΔF/F of grabAM08 11232019 spont, 263 pixels inside the brain mask, all in the right AUD parcel, are zero in every frame; in the other 25 ΔF/F movies every pixel of the mask is non-zero.
The VisualStimulus tables give screen coordinates but not where the monitor stood relative to the mouse, so the hemisphere expected to respond cannot be read from the files.

The dandiset holds 4 of the 6 ACh3.0 and jRCaMP1b mice of the paper's code (grabAM05 to grabAM08, not grabAM09 and grabAM10), and no ECoG, drug sessions, control mice or ChAT-GCaMP6s mice. Five of the paper's findings cannot be tested.

disagreements.reason: The arithmetic is not disputed; with |speed| wheel beats face in grabAM06 (0.147 vs 0.142), so the result is partial. The reason for switching to |speed| is disputed. The Methods define speed as "a differential of distance" after unwrapping, which keeps its sign; the paper's code computes it signed (wheel_changepoints.m line 50, db1SpeedMpS) and takes abs only for the threshold on mean epoch speed (line 135); the file's WheelSpeed is very likely that same series. The code repository contains Figure2Regression/Fig2RawData.mat, the paper's own per-mouse R2 (6 x 52); for calcium its single-variable face R2 is above wheel in all 6 mice; if its rows 1 to 4 are grabAM05 to grabAM08 (not established), its wheel R2 for mouse 1 is 0.0246 (calcium) and 0.0014 (ACh), against 0.0253 and 0.0017 here with signed speed and 0.0483 and 0.0031 with |speed|; the other mice are mixed. On this evidence signed speed is the better-supported reading, and under it the claim is reproduced. The outcome should either go back to reproduced with |speed| as the variant, or stay partial with a reason that matches the sources. Compare the per-mouse values with Fig2RawData.mat after confirming its row-to-mouse mapping; this would also give the first external check of the ridgeMML port.

attempts.label: DANDI:001453
attempts.paper_title: Neural circuits underlying divergent visuomotor strategies of zebrafish and Danionella cerebrum
attempts.entry_title: Optomotor swimming of zebrafish and Danionella cerebrum (Fouke et al. 2025)
attempts.description: Tests the freely swimming findings of Fouke, He, Loring and Naumann (2025) on dandiset 001453, which holds the tracking data of 25 zebrafish and 12 Danionella cerebrum larvae during the optomotor protocol. It compares swimming speed, turning and angular acceleration between species and stimuli, the response to monocular stimuli, and how steady the swimming is. The imaging and head-fixed tail tracking of the paper's Figures 2 to 4 are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Fouke et al. (2025) from dandiset 001453

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's stimulus codes can be linked to the stimuli the paper names, using the paper's analysis code and the protocol file of its stimulus software, and the values computed through that link agree with those the paper's code printed.
outcomes.source: Data and Code Availability; the paper's Fig1-S1.ipynb at GitLab commit 33a5c29
outcomes.notes: Codes are matched by their integer value. All 21 codes are in the dandiset, including every code the analysis uses. Through the link, 17 of 18 species and stimulus speed medians are within 10% of the values printed by Fig1-S1.ipynb (DC static is 10.52 against 11.9 mm/s), and the angular velocities differ from the printed ones by a median of 0.02 deg/s. The fish counts (25 ZF, 12 DC) match the code's lists; fish cannot be matched one by one, as no identifier links the dandiset's subjects to the code's folders. The static window is the code's (first 35 s of the code-20 block, measured from 3 s), and no fish median is exactly 0, so the code's exclusion of zero medians changes nothing. On codes 9 and 11 the ZF medians are 0.02 and 1.59 deg/s. Over 3 to 35 s DC turn more to the right for code 11 than for code 9 (median difference 5.82 deg/s, 10 of 12 fish, Wilcoxon p = 0.0093), and ZF go the same way without significance (1.66 deg/s, 16 of 25 fish, p = 0.141). If fish turn with lateral motion as they do with medial motion, code 11 is lateral right, as the protocol file has it; the data do not show that they do, so the assignment is not settled.
deviations: The code's filter on a `vel` column is not applied to DC trials, as the DC files have no such series; this is the remaining difference that may explain the one DC static value outside 10%.
The timing of the DC stimulus labels could not be confirmed from the turning response (the contrast is 4.6 deg/s with true labels and 0.1 with shifted ones); the DC labels are taken as they are.

outcomes.statement: Danionella cerebrum (DC) swim at a higher median velocity than zebrafish (ZF) across the visual stimuli.
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: DC show a significantly higher median velocity across all stimuli than ZF
outcomes.notes: Over all 21 codes, the median over fish and code values is 94.0 pixels/s for DC and 55.2 for ZF; species effect F = 78.4, p = 6.3e-18. The ANOVA treats each fish and code value as independent; with one value per fish, DC 87.4 against ZF 52.9 pixels/s, Mann-Whitney p = 0.02. With positions resampled to 30 Hz, 95.2 against 53.8 (p = 1.3e-08). DC are faster within each frame-rate group.
deviations: Tested over all stimulus codes without their names; the paper's figure uses nine whole-field stimuli.
The comparison assumes one spatial scale for all rigs, which the files do not state.

outcomes.statement: Across the whole-field stimuli DC have a higher median velocity than ZF (9.8 against 6.4 mm/s), with a significant main effect of species in a two-way ANOVA.
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: In contrast, DC show a significantly higher median velocity across all stimuli than ZF (DC = 9.8 mm/s, ZF = 6.4 mm/s
outcomes.notes: All four readings put both values within tolerance; (a) median of stimulus medians DC 10.02 and ZF 6.39 mm/s, (b) median of fish and stimulus values 9.87 and 6.41 (given as measured), (c) median of fish medians 9.36 and 6.33, (d) median of trials 9.88 and 6.28. Species effect F = 20.8, p = 7.5e-06. With 30 Hz positions DC 9.43 to 10.15 and ZF 6.07 to 6.30 (p = 0.0011). Without the trial rejection (4487 trials in place of 4458) readings (a) to (c) are unchanged and (d) gives DC 9.85 and ZF 6.30 (p = 6.7e-06).
deviations: The paper does not say how the overall median is taken; four readings are shown, and all match.
25 ZF, where the paper states 26.
Speeds rely on the code's scale of 10 pixels per mm, which the dandiset does not state.

outcomes.statement: ZF modulate their velocity with the direction of motion; forward motion increases their median velocity (static 5.0 mm/s, forward 8.8 mm/s).
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: ZF strongly modulate their velocity depending on the motion direction, e.g., with forward motion increasing velocity (static = 5.0 mm/s, forward = 8.8 mm/s)
outcomes.notes: ZF static 4.84 mm/s over 18 fish and forward 8.78 mm/s over 25 fish. Of 18 fish with both, 14 are faster to forward motion (median difference 3.67 mm/s, Wilcoxon p = 0.0077). The static value is 8.31 mm/s in the 5 fish from 167 to 171 Hz files and 4.50 in the 13 from 32 to 35 Hz files. Static is the start of the blank block after all motion trials (4 hours in the protocol, 0.2 to 787.3 min in the files), one period per fish, and 7 ZF have none.
deviations: 25 ZF, where the paper states 26.

outcomes.statement: DC lack the direction-dependent velocity modulation seen in ZF.
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1; Figure 1D legend
outcomes.quote: In contrast, DC show a significantly higher median velocity across all stimuli than ZF ... and lacks direction-dependent velocity modulation
outcomes.notes: By the paper's test (Tukey's HSD over the 18 species and stimulus groups) 3 of 36 DC pairs differ, all static against a motion direction (backward left, backward right, forward left; adjusted p 0.030 to 0.049). The DC static values come from 9 fish and include one at 106.5 mm/s and two near 0. Among the eight directions no DC pair differs (smallest adjusted p 0.999), DC per-stimulus medians span 8.81 to 10.52 mm/s (ratio 1.19, ZF 2.03), and a one-way ANOVA across the nine DC stimuli gives p = 0.479 (ZF p = 0.00082). With values above 100 mm/s left out, no DC pair differs. The same Tukey test finds no ZF pair over the 18 groups (smallest p 0.835). The printed output of Fig1-S1.ipynb finds the same three DC pairs significant (adjusted p 0.0236, 0.0373 and 0.0397), so the paper's own test disagrees with the claim and this result matches the paper's computation. The DC-sub-2 static value of 106.5 mm/s is one trial measured over a 14.6 s motion phase in a 100 mm dish, likely a tracking artefact. It passes the code's speed check because the check covers 0 to 35 s (21.9 mm/s from the stored `dist`, 92.5 from positions); computing the check from positions, or leaving out zero medians as the code does, gives the same 3 pairs. The outcome is a property of the paper's test on this data, not evidence that DC modulate their speed with stimulus direction.
deviations: The DC static block is the code's window, but the code's filter on DC `vel` cannot be applied (DC static 10.52 against the code's printed 11.9 mm/s).

outcomes.statement: DC swim at a significantly higher velocity than ZF for oblique stimuli.
outcomes.source: Figure 1D legend
outcomes.quote: DC swims at a statistically higher velocity than ZF for oblique stimuli
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b), motion at 90 degrees or more, DC are significantly faster than ZF for right (p = 0.0002) and backward right (p = 0.0047), 2 of 4; under reading (a), the intercardinal directions, for 1 of 4 (backward right). Backward motion also differs (p = 0.0002).
deviations: The legend's "oblique" can be read two ways; the claim is reproduced under one of them (b) and not under the other (a).

outcomes.statement: Both species follow the direction of optic flow, turning right (positive angular velocity) to rightward motion and left to leftward motion.
outcomes.source: Figure 1G; Results, Optic flow induces angular matching and turns in DC, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Median angular velocity shows that both species follow the direction of optic flow, with positive and negative angular velocity indicating rightward and leftward turning, respectively
outcomes.notes: ZF turn with the motion; the rightward minus leftward difference is positive in 23 of 25 fish (median 29.51 deg/s, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 9.8e-07). DC do not by this test; 7 of 12 positive, median 0.88 deg/s, p = 0.151, and the DC median for left motion is +0.25 deg/s, the same sign as the paper's code printed (+0.3). DC turn right to right motion (8.67 deg/s).
deviations: The paper gives no test for following the direction; the per-fish rightward minus leftward difference and its test were chosen here before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: Across directional stimuli ZF have higher angular acceleration than DC, and the distributions of the two species differ for every stimulus.
outcomes.source: Results, Optic flow induces angular matching and turns in DC, paragraph 2; Figure 1H (Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni correction)
outcomes.quote: Across directional stimuli, ZF maintained higher angular acceleration than DC
outcomes.notes: With angular acceleration as the Methods define it, DC are higher than ZF for all nine stimuli (medians 143 to 191 against 55.4 to 66.4 deg/s2, Kruskal-Wallis p below 0.05/9 for each), the reverse of the claim. Per-fish medians, and the files at 128 to 171 Hz alone (ZF 84.9, DC 178.6 deg/s2, p = 6.3e-05), give the same. The quantity Fig1-S1.ipynb computes gives ZF higher with p below 0.05/9 for 7 of 9 stimuli; it divides the heading change per frame by the file's mean frame interval, which in DC files is a median 8.73 times the frame interval (ZF 1.37), as DC files hold only trial frames. Part of the DC values may be tracking noise. In the 3 s stationary phase the DC median is 205 deg/s2, higher than the 171 during motion (per fish median ratio 1.24, p = 0.016), but ZF are also higher at rest (66.9 and 60.8, ratio 1.07, p = 0.00012), so this does not separate the species. In frames where the fish is still (below 1 mm/s) DC are higher than ZF (per-fish medians 72.4 and 34.9 deg/s2, Mann-Whitney p = 0.00014), and DC are higher in every speed band (at 5 mm/s or more, 207 and 85.8). The outputs cannot say whether the higher values in moving DC are noise or turning during continuous swimming. With the heading from the unwrapped `f0_theta` DC are higher still (218 to 278 against ZF 61.8 to 77.3 deg/s2, 0 of 9). The reversal should not be read as evidence against the paper.
deviations: Follows the Methods' definition (degrees per second squared) on heading resampled to 30 Hz; the code's quantity, which disagrees with the Methods, is shown as a variant.
Heading is taken from the cumulative sum of `f0_vtheta`, as the code does; in DC files it does not match `f0_theta`.

outcomes.statement: DC generally respond less than ZF to monocular stimuli, suggesting that they need more visual motion input to drive the optomotor response.
outcomes.source: Results, Optic flow induces angular matching and turns in DC, paragraph 2; Figure S1E
outcomes.quote: DC generally responded less to monocular stimuli, suggesting that DC require more visual motion input to drive OMR behaviors
outcomes.notes: Species effect F = 23.3, p = 2.5e-06. DC turn less toward the stimulus than ZF for medial stimuli (3.26 against 13.48 deg/s, p = 0.0003) and binocular ones (2.87 against 21.87, p = 0.0002). For lateral stimuli DC are below ZF only nominally (-1.07 against -0.13 deg/s, p = 0.96); neither species turns toward lateral motion. With the protocol file's assignment of codes 9 and 11, the lateral medians change sign and DC are no longer below ZF there, which would make the claim partially reproduced. The DC turning to codes 9 and 11 leans toward the protocol file's assignment (see stimulus-code-link), so the lateral part is fragile.
deviations: Codes 9 and 11 are assigned as the figure code has them; the stimulus software's conversion has them the other way, and the data do not settle it.

outcomes.quote: These visually evoked bouts in ZF consist of sharp velocity increases ... followed by interbout glides, resulting in characteristic periodic patterns. While DC also match the optic flow direction, they swim continuously, maintaining a relatively constant velocity
outcomes.notes: The median-to-mean ratio of instantaneous speed is 0.306 in ZF (25 fish, 0.244 to 0.580) and 0.908 in DC (12 fish, 11 above 0.74, one at 0.140), Mann-Whitney p = 5.4e-05. It holds in files at 128 to 171 Hz alone (0.298 against 0.898, p = 0.0028) and in forward trials alone.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds only the freely swimming tracking of Figure 1 and Figure S1. The two-photon imaging and the head-fixed tail tracking behind Figures 2 to 4 are not in it, and the GitLab repository the paper names for all behavioural and imaging data holds analysis notebooks only. Nine of the paper's main findings cannot be tested.

The stimulus codes 0 to 20 have no names or description in the files or the dandiset metadata. They can be named only from the paper's analysis notebook and the protocol file of its stimulus software.

The paper's analysis notebook labels code 9 as lateral right and 11 as lateral left, while its conversion of the stimulus software's names gives the reverse (it carries a remap that swaps them). The data do not settle which is right; zebrafish barely turn to either, and Danionella turn more to the right for code 11, which fits the stimulus software's assignment only if the fish turn with lateral motion.

Subject ids 0 to 11 are each used for one zebrafish and one Danionella cerebrum, so subject_id does not identify an animal. The archive's summary counts 25 subjects and lists only Danio rerio; the files hold 37 fish of two species.

f0_vtheta is stated in radians/s but holds the heading change per frame in radians, and f0_vx and f0_vy are stated in pixels/s but are per frame. In most Danionella files the sum of f0_vtheta over a trial does not match the change of f0_theta (median ratios 0.09 to 0.89).

18 of 25 zebrafish files and 1 of 12 Danionella files are sampled at 32 to 35 Hz, where the Methods state tracking at more than 150 Hz. Their timestamp intervals are regular (28.8 to 30.8 ms) and their trials last the protocol's 35 s, so these are the acquisition rates. Some measures differ with frame rate, such as the zebrafish static speed (8.31 against 4.50 mm/s).

No spatial scale is given; positions are in pixels. They are consistent with the 10 pixels per mm in the paper's code, except one Danionella file (sub-5) whose positions reach 1490 pixels against about 1120 in the others.

Zebrafish and Danionella files were exported differently. Zebrafish files keep untracked frames and frames between trials; Danionella files hold only tracked trial frames and add a `dist` series. The paper's code filters Danionella frames on a `vel` column that is not in the files.

The paper's code computes the angular acceleration of Figure 1H as the heading change per frame divided by the file's mean frame interval, an angular velocity. In Danionella files the mean interval includes the gaps between trials (a median 8.73 times the frame interval), which scales their values down. With the Methods' definition Danionella have the higher angular acceleration.

Figure 1H and its legend state a Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni correction; the code runs two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, and its loop selects the stimulus with a variable left from an earlier loop, so the nine tests compare the same stimulus.

The Results state that Danionella lack the direction-dependent speed modulation of zebrafish, but the Tukey test printed by Fig1-S1.ipynb for Figure 1D finds three Danionella pairs significant (static against backward left, backward right and forward left, adjusted p 0.024 to 0.040), as this attempt does.

The `dist` series of the Danionella files does not agree with the positions; over the first 35 s of a trial its sum is a median 1.11 times the path length of the smoothed positions, with a 5th to 95th percentile of 0.31 to 3.79. The paper's speed check uses it, though computing the check from positions passes the same trials.
The Figure 1D legend gives 26 zebrafish; the paper's code lists 25, its ANOVA degrees of freedom fit 25, and the dandiset holds 25.
The dandiset holds the 25 zebrafish and 12 Danionella the code keeps after exclusion (its comments give 28 and 40 recorded). The dandiset does not say that the excluded fish were left out or why.
