attempts.entry_title: Place cells during space flight on the Neurolab mission (Knierim et al. 2000)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Knierim, McNaughton and Poe (2000) on dandiset 001754, version 0.260728.1352, which holds sorted units, task epochs, the original rate and occupancy maps, and spike-time positions of three rats recorded before and during the Neurolab shuttle mission. It compares spatial information in flight with preflight for each rat, tests abnormal selectivity on flight day 4 and the stability of fields across two sessions, and records why the direction, EEG and three-surface claims could not be tested. The claims come from the paper's full text.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Knierim et al. (2000) from dandiset 001754

outcomes.statement: In flight, after an initial period, hippocampal place cells on the Escher staircase showed normal, spatially specific firing, with spatial information per spike not different from the same rats' preflight cells.
outcomes.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "During the Neurolab Space Shuttle mission", last sentence; supported by the paragraphs beginning "Spatial firing patterns of 16 active place cells" and "The mean spatial-information content for all 7" and Figures 2a, 2c and 3a; also the standfirst
outcomes.quote: Nonetheless, place cells eventually demonstrated normal, spatially specific firing properties.
outcomes.notes: On flight day 9, 10 of 25 Rat1 units (0.40) have spatial information above the 95th percentile of 500 circular-shift shuffles on the Escher staircase (binomial p = 1.6e-7 against 0.05), and 2 of 28 Rat2 units (0.071, p = 0.41). By the criterion Rat1 is above chance but below 0.5 and Rat2 is not above chance, so neither the reproduced nor the partially reproduced rule is met. Repeats with 2000 shuffles and five other seeds give 10 or 11 of 25 for Rat1 and 2 of 28 for Rat2, and the run of 200 shuffles in the data check gives 10 and 2; 5 Rat1 units have p between 0.01 and 0.1. The outcome is the same as in 001754-knierim-2000-01, which recorded 12 of 25 for Rat1 (11 to 13 over seven runs); on the earlier version's files the notebook gives 11 or 12 of 25 for Rat1 and 2 or 3 of 28 for Rat2 over five seeds. Every real spike has a sample at its own time in both versions; the draft's trace adds samples at the other rat's spike times in each window, so shifted spikes find a sample more often and the shuffles change. Shifted spikes are now dropped about as often in Rat2's FD9 ES epoch (median 0.058) as in Rat1's (0.060), against 0.306 to 0.307 and 0.074 to 0.075 on the earlier version's files, and a count-matched variant gives 12 of 25 (0.48) for Rat1 and 2 of 28 for Rat2. With each unit's spikes replaced by a Poisson train of the same mean count, 9 of 122 flight ES units are significant (0.074, binomial p = 0.16 against 0.05), and 12 of 125 (0.096, p = 0.023) when each spike is moved to its nearest position sample, which reproduces the real drop rates; per session the false-positive fraction is 0 to 0.21, and in the judged sessions 0.160 and 0.154 for Rat1 and 0.037 and 0.214 for Rat2. Against these fractions Rat1's 10 of 25 is still above chance (p = 0.0035 and 0.0026) and Rat2's 2 of 28 is not (p = 0.28 and 0.99), so the outcome is the same, though the criterion's 0.05 is below the false-positive fraction of some sessions. With each unit's real train reversed in time within its epoch, which keeps its bursts and changes in rate and breaks its relation to the position, 2 of 122 flight ES units are significant (1 of 25 in Rat1's FD9 session, 0 of 27 in Rat2's), and Rat3's ES1 trains against the ES2 trace and the reverse give 0 of 16 and 0 of 19, so with real temporal structure the test is conservative. A unit's 95th percentile of the shuffles is nearly the same for its reversed train (Spearman rho 0.995), 1.7 to 2.3 times that of a Poisson train of the same count per session, and higher the fewer 10 s periods hold its spikes (rho -0.874 with the effective fraction of 10 s bins filled) and the fewer spikes it has (rho -0.601); the two explain 80% of its variance on a log scale. Rat2's FD9 units are the most clumped (median 0.145 of the bins, against 0.190 to 0.358 in the other sessions) and have the highest median 95th percentile (3.572). The test has less power for such units, and its power was not measured, so a low fraction, Rat2's especially, is weak evidence against a spatial code; the criterion's rule decides the outcome. The trace moves as a tracked animal would in Rat2's windows (median step 0.50 pixels and path length 33.0 pixels per second in its FD9 ES window), and units of neither rat are selective in any MC window (0 to 2 of 11 to 32), so neither settles whose position it is. Rat2's units are not selective with the trace in any window (1 of 16 and 2 of 28 in their own ES epochs, 0 of 15 and 0 of 41 in Rat1's), and Rat1's units are selective in Rat2's FD4 ES epoch (10 of 15), so the trace in Rat2's epochs may not be Rat2's position; the files say it is taken to be, and that the source does not name the animal tracked. On flight day 4, 11 of 20 Rat1 units, 1 of 16 Rat2 units, and 11 of 16 and 1 of 19 Rat3 units in its ES1 and ES2 epochs are significant. In MC epochs 0 to 2 units per session are significant. The "three orthogonal surfaces" part of the abstract is tested apart, and blocked.
deviations: The paper's Methods were not available; the selection (50 spikes at a known position), the 32 x 32 binning, the shuffle and the thresholds are common choices fixed in the claims file.

Occupancy is the original analysis's occupancy map for the epoch, and shuffled spikes take the nearest position sample within 0.25 s, as the dandiset gives position only at spike times. A spike whose nearest sample is the lost position is dropped.
Robust is read as at least half of the units significant in each flight day 9 session.
Rat2's flight day 9 session is judged although whose position the trace holds in it could not be established.

outcomes.statement: Hippocampal cells formed distinct, reliable representations of position on the three orthogonal surfaces of the Escher staircase in microgravity.
outcomes.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "It is interesting to note", sentence 2; also the standfirst
outcomes.quote: Thus hippocampal cells can form unique, reliable representations of position on three orthogonal surfaces in microgravity
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds one two-dimensional pixel position per time from one camera. The draft's position reference frame says the camera view and the pixel size on the apparatus are not recorded in the source files, nothing in the files or the dandiset metadata describes the track layout in the image, and the conversion code at the new commit describes the ES track only as a three-dimensional track with 90 degree yaw and pitch turns (its lines are printed in the notebook), so pixels cannot be assigned to the three surfaces. The NASA record of the study (OSD-968) says position was recorded with two synchronised cameras (printed in the notebook); a second view is not in the dandiset. Same outcome as in 001754-knierim-2000-01.

outcomes.statement: For rat 3 on flight day 4, most of the 7 cells kept the same firing fields in a third session that followed the second immediately; the fourth cell lost its field, and a few other cells gained a field in session 3.
outcomes.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "The mean spatial-information content for all 7", sentence 2; Figure 3a,b and legend
outcomes.quote: Another recording session followed immediately, and most cells maintained the same firing fields in both sessions (Fig. 3b), demonstrating that the spatial tuning was stable across different exposures to the track.
outcomes.notes: In Rat3's two flight day 4 ES epochs, the 15 units with 50 or more spikes in each have a median rate-map correlation of 0.537 (range -0.107 to 0.849), above the 95th percentile of 1000 re-paired medians (0.102, p = 0.001) and above 0.5; 8 of 15 exceed 0.5. These numbers and the outcome are the same as in 001754-knierim-2000-01. With smoothing of 0.5 to 2 bins and 50 or 100 spikes the median is 0.315 to 0.707, always above its null (p = 0.001); at 0.5 bins it is below 0.5. The dandiset's ES1 and ES2 rate maps, now linked to the same unit, give a median of 0.340 over 18 units (0.157 in the first attempt, when maps were paired by short names). A unit is the same sorted cluster in both epochs, as the units' description now states; mean rates are related across the epochs (Spearman rho 0.598, re-paired 95th percentile 0.339). In the first epoch 11 of 16 units are significant against shuffles and in the second 1 of 19, with similar occupancy and shuffle drops and more spikes per tested unit in the second (median 455 against 301). For several stable units the 95th percentile of the shuffles rises more than their information in the second epoch (TT4 cluster 1, information against 95th percentile, 2.449 against 1.326 and then 3.592 against 4.305; TT5 cluster 1, 0.910 against 0.504 and then 1.472 against 2.393); the epochs use 348 and 299 bins with 5 or more occupancy counts. Poisson trains give 0 to 2 false positives in either epoch. These units fire fewer spikes in fewer 10 s periods in the second epoch (TT4 cluster 1, 1582 spikes filling an effective 0.267 of the 10 s bins and then 423 filling 0.096; TT5 cluster 1, 8844 at 0.575 and then 2221 at 0.307), which raises the shuffles' 95th percentile (see flight-spatial-code); the stability measure does not use the shuffle test.
deviations: Only the title of Figure 3 was available; which sessions it compares is unknown. The test uses the only pair of same-track sessions with position on one day.
Takes the same sorted cluster in both epochs to be the same neuron; the files hold no waveforms to check it.

findings.statement: Partly fixed since 001754-knierim-2000-01. Each flight file now holds the shared tracker's trace only within its own rat's ES and MC epochs and says the trace there is taken to be that rat's position, and that the source does not name the animal tracked. Rat2's units are not spatially selective with the trace in any window (1 of 16 and 2 of 28 in Rat2's ES epochs, 0 of 15 and 0 of 41 in Rat1's), and Rat1's units are selective in Rat2's flight day 4 ES epoch (10 of 15), when Rat1 is labelled as on baseline. The trace moves as a continuous track in Rat2's windows, and units of neither rat are selective in any MC window, so neither settles it. Whose position the trace is during Rat2's task epochs is still not established.

Still present. Position is given only at spike times (taken from the spike files), so occupancy cannot be computed from the files' position, and the preflight files have no position at all. The draft's position description now states this.

Still present. The dandiset description says the preflight recordings were made on a flat rectangular track, but the preflight files label their epochs ES (Escher staircase) and MC (Magic Carpet) and hold ES and MC rate maps, as the flight files do. Which apparatus the preflight epochs were recorded on is not stated in the files.
Partly fixed. The rate-map description now says the maps are smoothed, but the kernel is not recorded (in the median well-matched map, 91% of the bins with a positive rate hold no spike of the unit).

Partly fixed. The files' experiment description now says no EEG was archived, but the dandiset's description still reports normal theta and sharp waves and ripples in the hippocampal EEG, and no EEG is in the dandiset.

Partly fixed. The age is still "/" for every subject, now with a subject description saying it is not recorded, and the position's reference frame now says the camera view and pixel size are not recorded; the map geometry is given in pixels. The age, pixel scale and camera view themselves are missing.

New. Rat2's preflight units are on tetrodes TT0 to TT10 and its flight units on TT12 to TT22, with no tetrode in common, while Rat1's and Rat3's preflight and flight tetrodes overlap. The conversion notes list whether the preflight folders are assigned to the right rats as an open question, and nothing in the files settles it, so per-rat comparisons with preflight rest on an unconfirmed assignment.

attempts.entry_title: Place cells during space flight on the Neurolab mission (Knierim et al. 2000)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Knierim, McNaughton and Poe (2000) on dandiset 001754, version 0.260728.1352, which holds sorted units, task epochs, the original rate and occupancy maps, and spike-time positions of three rats recorded before and during the Neurolab shuttle mission. It compares spatial information in flight with preflight for each rat, tests abnormal selectivity on flight day 4 and the stability of fields across two sessions, and records why the direction, EEG and three-surface claims could not be tested. The claims come from the paper's full text.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Knierim et al. (2000) from dandiset 001754

outcomes.statement: In flight, after an initial period, hippocampal place cells on the Escher staircase showed normal, spatially specific firing, with spatial information per spike not different from the same rats' preflight cells.
outcomes.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "During the Neurolab Space Shuttle mission", last sentence; supported by the paragraphs beginning "Spatial firing patterns of 16 active place cells" and "The mean spatial-information content for all 7" and Figures 2a, 2c and 3a; also the standfirst
outcomes.quote: Nonetheless, place cells eventually demonstrated normal, spatially specific firing properties.
outcomes.notes: The criterion judges this claim from its three dependencies. si-comparable-to-preflight is partially reproduced, si-rat3-fd4-vs-preflight reproduced and si-rat1-fd9-vs-preflight blocked as methods_underspecified. The others do not decide it, as the rule gives partially reproduced if the rat 1 comparison is reproduced or partially reproduced and not reproduced if it is not reproduced; the rat 1 preflight ES reading (p = 0.50) would give the first and the preflight MC reading (p = 0.0055, flight higher) the second. The outcome differs from 001754-knierim-2000-02 (not reproduced) because the claim is now judged as the paper judges it, by spatial information against preflight, and not by a shuffle test the paper does not use; that test is not run. The answers of 2026-10-20 leave the rat 1 comparison blocked, as its criterion now says when the two preflight epochs disagree, so this claim is blocked before and after.
deviations: Inherits the deviations of its three dependencies.

outcomes.statement: For rat 2, the spatial information per spike of the 16 active cells recorded on the Escher staircase on flight day 9 (1.13 +/- 0.09 bits) did not differ significantly from that of its 19 active preflight cells (1.12 +/- 0.08 bits), by Mann-Whitney test.
outcomes.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "Spatial firing patterns of 16 active place cells", sentences 1 and 3; Figure 2a,b
outcomes.quote: An index of spatial tuning specificity ... did not significantly differ between cells recorded preflight and those recorded on FD9 (for active cells, defined as having a mean firing rate > 0.05 Hz on the track; mean information per spike ± s.e. preflight, 1.12 ± 0.08 bits, n = 19; FD9, 1.13 ± 0.09 bits, n = 16; not significant by Mann-Whitney)
outcomes.notes: Under both readings with preflight values the Mann-Whitney test finds no difference. Rat 2's 17 active FD9 ES maps have 1.377 +/- 0.120 bits per spike, against 1.320 +/- 0.112 for its 21 preflight ES maps (p = 0.88, difference 0.057) and 1.284 +/- 0.116 for its 25 preflight MC maps (p = 0.66, difference 0.092). No reading puts both means within tolerance (1.377 above 1.22; 1.320 and 1.284 above 1.20), so the rule gives partially reproduced. The FD9 count (17) is within 16 +/- 1.6 and the preflight counts (21, 25) are not within 19 +/- 1.9. Reading M-b gives 2.965 +/- 0.224 over 25 active FD9 units but cannot be computed preflight; tested against the M-a preflight values it differs (p 6.2e-07 and 2.5e-07), a variant, not judged. Leaving out the maps with cell_number -1 (a variant) the test finds no difference either (p 0.87 and 0.56). The FD9 ES window is one in which the trace behaves as Rat 2's position (data check). In 001754-knierim-2000-02 this claim, then from the dandiset's description and judged on Rats 1 and 2 pooled by medians, was reproduced (later removed from that record); the outcome differs because the claim is now rat 2's, with the paper's means as expected values, which the deposited maps exceed. What the answers of 2026-10-20 changed. The criterion now has both sides of a comparison use one map reading and judges on M-a where M-b cannot be computed preflight, which is what this attempt had done; and under S-b each epoch of the preflight day is run on its own, so S-b gives the same two readings (ES and MC) as S-a, where the attempt had read S-b as MC alone. Neither changes a number or the outcome (partially reproduced before and after).
deviations: Reading M-a uses the deposited maps, each identical copy once, and counts a map as active by its own occupancy-weighted mean rate, as the pinned version cannot link maps to units.
Which preflight epoch was the rectangular track of Fig. 2b is not stated in the files.

outcomes.statement: For rat 1, the mean spatial information of its 21 active cells on flight day 9 (1.19 +/- 0.09 bits) did not differ significantly from its preflight cells (1.37 +/- 0.10 bits, n = 28).
outcomes.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "Spatial firing patterns of 16 active place cells", sentences 4 and 5; Figure 2c
outcomes.quote: We also determined the spatial tuning of 21 active cells from rat 1 on FD9 (Fig. 2c). ... did not significantly differ from that rat's preflight data (1.37 ± 0.10; n = 28).
outcomes.notes: The readings disagree on the test. Rat 1's 24 active FD9 ES maps (1.588 +/- 0.143 bits per spike) do not differ from its 25 preflight ES maps (1.804 +/- 0.149, p = 0.50, difference -0.216) and are higher than its 24 preflight MC maps (1.127 +/- 0.114, p = 0.0055, difference 0.461); the paper does not say on which track or in which epoch rat 1's preflight cells were recorded. No mean is within tolerance (1.19 +/- 0.09, 1.37 +/- 0.10) and no count within 10% (24 against 21; 25 and 24 against 28). Reading M-b gives 3.331 +/- 0.268 over 24 units, flight only, and is not judged. Leaving out the maps with cell_number -1 (a variant) the readings disagree in the same way (p 0.40 against ES, 0.020 against MC), with 21 FD9 maps, the paper's count. What the answers of 2026-10-20 changed. The criterion now runs each preflight epoch on its own under S-a and S-b, prefers neither, and keeps the claim blocked when they disagree, so the block that the attempt had applied pending the answer is now the criterion's own; the outcome is blocked before and after. New claim; 001754-knierim-2000-02 had none like it.
deviations: As for si-comparable-to-preflight (M-a activity by map rate).

outcomes.statement: For rat 3, the mean spatial information of all 7 active place cells on flight day 4 (1.12 +/- 0.27 bits, session 2) was not different from its preflight cells (1.48 +/- 0.11 bits, n = 24).
outcomes.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "The mean spatial-information content for all 7", sentence 1; Figure 3a
outcomes.quote: The mean spatial-information content for all 7 active place cells from rat 3 on the fourth day of flight (FD4) was 1.12 ± 0.27 bits (Fig. 3a), which was not different from the information content measured for this rat's place cells before the flight (1.48 ± 0.11 bits; n = 24).
outcomes.notes: Under both readings the test finds no difference. Rat 3's 11 active session 2 (ES1) maps have 1.231 +/- 0.206 bits per spike, against 1.518 +/- 0.125 for its 38 preflight ES maps (p = 0.28, difference -0.287) and 1.337 +/- 0.121 for its 33 preflight MC maps (p = 0.77, difference -0.106). Under the ES reading both means are within tolerance (1.12 +/- 0.27 and 1.48 +/- 0.11), which the rule requires of one reading. The counts are not (11 against 7; 38 and 33 against 24), so the cells are not the paper's set; the criterion's rule does not use them. Session 3 (ES2, 19 maps, 1.384 +/- 0.177) does not differ from either preflight epoch (p = 0.28 and 0.86). Reading M-b gives 3.038 +/- 0.334 over 16 units, flight only, and is not judged. The answers of 2026-10-20 (one map reading on both sides; each preflight epoch a candidate under S-a and S-b) confirm the readings the attempt judged on and change no number; reproduced before and after. New claim.
deviations: As for si-comparable-to-preflight. Session 2 is read as the file's first ES epoch (ES1), as the paper says the first session was lost.

outcomes.statement: On the first experience of the Escher staircase on flight day 4, place cells of rats 1 and 2 showed abnormal patterns of spatial selectivity, which differed between the two rats.
outcomes.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "It is interesting to note", sentence 1 (given as unpublished observations)
outcomes.quote: on the first experience on the Escher staircase on FD4, firing of place cells showed abnormal patterns of spatial selectivity that differed between rats 1 and 2
outcomes.notes: Lower spatial information than preflight holds for rat 2 under both readings and for rat 1 under neither. Rat 2's 14 active FD4 ES maps (0.708 +/- 0.112 bits per spike) are lower than its preflight ES (1.320, p = 0.00063) and MC maps (1.284, p = 0.0015). Rat 1's 20 FD4 ES maps (1.409 +/- 0.192) are lower than its preflight ES maps without significance (1.804, p = 0.077) and higher than its MC maps (1.127, p = 0.36). Rat 2's FD4 maps are also lower than its FD9 maps (1.377, p = 0.00033); Rat 1's are not (1.588, p = 0.38). In Rat 2's FD4 ES window the trace could not be shown to be Rat 2's position (data check). The Rat1 and Rat2 files hold one trace there (4 of 707 shared valid positions more than 2 px apart), and Rat 2's FD4 units carry more information than every time shift on neither file's copy (0 of 17 and 1 of 16, against 12 of 28 and 16 of 28 on FD9), so whether the low FD4 information comes from firing or from tracking is not known; the criterion sets no condition on this. That file holds five identical copies of maps, counted once. Leaving out the maps with cell_number -1 (a variant) gives the same pattern (Rat 2 p 0.0002 and 0.0017; Rat 1 p 0.24 and 0.42). That the patterns differed between the rats is not judged. In 001754-knierim-2000-02 this claim, then from the dandiset's description and judged on Rats 1 to 3 pooled by a one-sided test, was reproduced (later removed from that record); it now requires each of rats 1 and 2 with a two-sided test, and holds for one. The answers of 2026-10-20 (one map reading on both sides, so M-b is not run as it has no preflight values; each preflight epoch a candidate) are what the attempt had done and change no number; partially reproduced before and after.
deviations: As for si-comparable-to-preflight.

outcomes.statement: For rat 3 on flight day 4, most of the 7 cells kept the same firing fields in a third session that followed the second immediately; the fourth cell lost its field, and a few other cells gained a field in session 3.
outcomes.source: Main text, paragraph beginning "The mean spatial-information content for all 7", sentence 2; Figure 3a,b and legend
outcomes.quote: Another recording session followed immediately, and most cells maintained the same firing fields in both sessions (Fig. 3b), demonstrating that the spatial tuning was stable across different exposures to the track.
outcomes.notes: Under M-b, the one reading that can be run, 6 of 16 active session 2 units keep their field by reading (a) (same-cell correlations -0.024 to 0.366, 95th percentile of 240 different-cell pairs 0.094) and 1 of 16 by reading (b), neither more than half (8), so the rule gives not reproduced. M-a is not run, as the criterion says when its pairing condition fails. Each distinct deposited map with a unit on its tetrode, 17 of 19 in session 2 (all 11 active maps among them) and 23 of 23 in session 3, was tied to the unit of its tetrode whose spike-count map it best matches. In session 2 no unit is tied to two maps (two maps are each the best map of two units, the second unit matching at r 0.009 and 0.059); in session 3 four are (TT10 cluster 6, TT4 cluster 3, TT5 cluster 2, TT8 cluster 5), three of them units of active session 2 maps. attempts.description: Tests the findings of Mantas, Contestabile, Skara et al. (bioRxiv 2024) on dandiset 001828, which holds the paper's open field pose, kinematics and VAME motifs (some with fiber photometry), optogenetically evoked dLight release, water drop and forelimb reaching sessions with annotated events, and arrow maze pose. It tests evoked release in dCP against cCP, the photometry around the water drop and during open field movement, the locomotion of the PD models and Anxa1-silenced mice, the maze speed and reaching accuracy. The motif claims are blocked, as the dandiset's VAME labels are not the paper's; their analyses are shown on the dandiset's labels. The histology, RNA-seq, qPCR and nosepoke data of Figures 1 to 3 are not in the dandiset; the MitoPark RNA-seq counts are read from GEO GSE282753.

outcomes.statement: In bulk RNA-seq of sorted midbrain DANs, both early-stage mitochondrial PD models (cMfn2KO-early and MP-early) show significant downregulation of the Anxa1 transcript among DAN subtype markers.
outcomes.source: Results, Anxa1 is a marker of an early PD vulnerable SNc DAN subpopulation, paragraph 1; Figure 1A and 1B
outcomes.quote: Differential expression analysis of genes enriched in midbrain DAN subtypes revealed that both PD models showed a shared profile of significant early-stage downregulation of the Annexin A1 (Anxa1) transcript
outcomes.notes: GEO GSE282753, public since 2026-10-20 and the paper's only RNA-seq deposit, holds one count table, MitoPark and control DANs at 10 weeks (5 MitoPark mice, as in the legend, and 7 controls, each with 3 to 12 technical libraries), and no cMfn2KO-early counts, so that half of the claim cannot be tested and the claim stays blocked. The answer (2026-10-21) found no other place for the cMfn2KO counts, and made the mouse the unit, with libraries summed per mouse, and the MitoPark half to be run and reported. Before the answer the MitoPark counts were not analysed (the earlier note counted 6 MitoPark mice; the table has 5). The MitoPark half holds under both readings, as the criterion judges them, where DESeq2 and edgeR agree. Summed per mouse, Anxa1 log2 fold change -1.02 at FDR 2.9e-05 (DESeq2) and -0.99 at FDR 7.5e-04 (edgeR exact test); with each library as a sample, -0.93 at FDR 5.0e-08 and 6.2e-08. Anxa1 counts per million are 90 to 222 in MitoPark mice and 258 to 446 in controls. GEO's supplementary files are this count table and an RPKM table of the same MitoPark libraries, and the series' design and its 92 samples describe MitoPark and control mice only (printed in the notebook).
deviations: DESeq2 is pydeseq2 0.5.4 and edgeR is edgepy (inmoose 0.9.1), a Python port, with TMM written out in the helper and the GLM common and tagwise dispersions (estimateGLMCommonDisp, estimateGLMTagwiseDisp) in place of estimateDisp, which the port lacks, so the edgeR reading is not edgeR's default route; R is not in the entry's environment.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds only behaviour and fiber photometry. The histology, RNA-scope and tracing images or counts, the qPCR of iPSC-derived neurons and the nosepoke counts of the self-stimulation and ratio tasks are not in it, so 16 claims of Figures 1 to 3 cannot be tested. GEO GSE282753 holds the MitoPark RNA-seq counts but not the cMfn2KO ones. No file holds a nosepoke, port, reward, zone, entry or trial object.
The arrow maze files hold DeepLabCut pose only. The Bonsai end-zone entries, reward deliveries and arena geometry behind Figure 6D are not in them.

86 open field sessions have session_id tmaze-..., 84 of them in files named ses-tmaze-..., although their descriptions, contents (VAME labels, kinematics, the open field DeepLabCut model) and frame counts are those of open field sessions.

Experimental groups, cohorts, days, test phases and light conditions are given only in free text inside session_description, with names that differ between experiments (ctrl, asc_acid, Ctrl 10-11 wks, Littermate control); the subject metadata carry no group.

Subject genotypes conflict across files. Mice with dLight (776769, 776770, 796284, 796287, 802369, 802372, 821709, 821710, 829248, 842388, 842395) are WT in their open field files and Anxa1-flp or Dat_cre in their other files, and 687662 is anxa1-flp in the open field and Dat_cre in reaching. Mouse 779575 is a control in the open field TeTx experiment and a TeTx mouse in the reaching cohort.

The paper's 37-motif VAME labelling is not in the dandiset. Its only labelling, VAME_42, has 42 labels (0 to 41) with no names or action categories, while the paper reports 37 motifs numbered up to 42 and grouped into categories; motif 42 is not a label and motif 28 is unused by the Figure 5 mice. Ten claims rest on the paper's motifs.

The VAME motif labels are stored with starting_time 0 on the frame grid of the pose and kinematics, but they explain linear speed best when placed 15 to 21 frames later (median 18, eta squared 0.69 against 0.49 as stored), about half the 30-frame VAME window, so a stored label is consistent with describing the window that starts at its frame. The files do not say how labels are placed in time, and motif onsets as stored come about 0.6 s early.

The 30 Hz z-scored open field photometry (FiberPhotometrySeriesZScored) is smoothed (its first and last 7 or 8 samples are held constant) and best matches the dF/F 0.1 s earlier; neither the smoothing nor the lag is documented.

The dandiset holds more photometry recordings and mice than the legends count (water drop, Anxa1 15 against 10, DAT 8 against 4, dLight-dCP 21 against 13, dLight-cCP 15 against 11; open field Anxa1 10 against 9) and fewer in some (open field DAT 6 against 7, arrow maze controls 17 against 18), without saying which recordings the paper used.

The dandiset holds experiments that are not in the preprint version read (6-OHDA in the tail striatum in open field, reaching and arrow maze; anti-Anxa1 open field; a 2025 Arch reaching cohort), labelled only in free text.

All 17 Arch-cohort reaching files of the first training day, the 2024 mice included, say the laser was switched on after the mouse's first reach, while the Methods say it was off during the first day of reaching and on during the last three; either the label or the protocol differs from the paper.

The 20 evoked release sessions are described as nosepoke self-stimulation, but their 1 s trains come at fixed 4 s intervals in every session; the reaching photometry sessions' descriptions call the GCaMP signals SN cell-body recordings, while the fiber table and the indicator descriptions place the fiber in dCP.

The archive's variableMeasured lists only ProcessingModule and BehavioralTimeSeries, though 110 files hold fiber photometry; the photometry sessions of the water drop task are stored as reaching sessions.
Seven open field photometry recordings hold under 13 minutes of photometry (2.9 to 11.9 min) where the Methods describe 20 minute sessions.

attempts.label: DANDI:001878
attempts.paper_title: CalMS21 - Caltech Mouse Social Interactions (Sun et al., 2021)
attempts.entry_title: CalMS21 mouse social behavior dataset (Sun et al. 2021)
attempts.description: Tests the claims of Sun et al. (2021), the paper describing the CalMS21 dataset of resident-intruder pose and behavior annotations, on dandiset 001878, which holds one CalMS21 sequence (Task 1 test sequence mouse071) with its video, and on the full dataset deposited on CaltechDATA. It checks the format, identities and annotations of the dandiset's sequence, links it to the deposit, and tests the dataset's counts and label fractions. The model benchmarks are not run.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Sun et al. (2021) from dandiset 001878 and the CalMS21 deposit

outcomes.statement: Each frame holds seven MARS keypoints (nose, left ear, right ear, neck, left hip, right hip, tail base) for each of two mice, the resident (mouse 0) and the intruder (mouse 1), in pixel coordinates of a 1024 x 570 image, at 30 Hz, with a confidence score from 0 to 1 for each keypoint.
outcomes.source: Section 3 and Figure 3; Appendix C (data format), paragraph 4; Appendix D.1
outcomes.quote: mouse 0 is the resident and mouse 1 is the intruder), image (x,y) coordinates in pixels, and keypoint ID. For keypoint ID, there are seven tracked body parts, ordered (nose, left ear, right ear, neck, left hip, right hip, tail base).
outcomes.notes: The file holds 14 keypoint series named for the seven parts of the resident and the intruder, in pixels, at 30 Hz, with every coordinate inside the 1024 x 570 image (x 5.0 to 991.2, y 9.0 to 563.3). The confidence field is present for every keypoint but all 333,340 values are NaN, so the confidence part of the claim fails.
deviations: Judged on the one CalMS21 sequence in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Mouse 0, the resident, is the black C57Bl/6J mouse, and mouse 1, the intruder, is the white BALB/c mouse.
outcomes.source: Appendix C; Appendix B (Collection Process); Appendix D.1
outcomes.quote: In this assay, a black (C57Bl/6J) male "resident" mouse is filmed in its home cage, and a white (BALB/c) male or female "intruder" mouse is manually introduced to the cage ... mouse 0 is the resident and mouse 1 is the intruder
outcomes.notes: In 746 of 794 sampled frames (every 30th) the body centres are at least 60 px apart; in all of them the 12 px patch on the resident is darker than the one on the intruder (median grey level 46.4 against 250.9). With 8 and 24 px patches the fractions are 0.997 and 1.000, with separations of 30 and 120 px 0.999 and 1.000, and 1.0 in every minute.
deviations: The coat colour test (grey level of the video at the body centre) was chosen here; the paper states the identities without a test.

outcomes.statement: Task 1 frames are annotated by one annotator (annotator id 0) with exactly one label per frame from the vocabulary attack 0, investigation 1, mount 2 and other 3.
outcomes.source: Section 3; Appendix C (metadata and vocab)
outcomes.quote: In Tasks 1 and 2, each frame is assigned one label ... In Task 1, GROUPNAME is annotator_id-0 ... and there is only one GROUP in the file. ... For example, in Task 1 vocab is attack: 0, investigation: 1, mount: 2, other: 3.
outcomes.notes: The catalogue holds attack 0, investigation 1, mount 2 and other 3; the bouts give the annotator as "CalMS21 annotator 0"; the 170 bouts tile the session from 0 to 793.67 s with no gaps, so all 23,810 frames have exactly one label. The session has no attack bouts.

outcomes.statement: The source videos of Task 1 are released, recorded at 30 Hz and 1024 x 570 pixels.
outcomes.source: Section 3.1, paragraph 3; Appendix D.1
outcomes.quote: In addition to pose data, we also release all source videos for Task 1 ... Videos are acquired at 30 fps and 1024x570 pixel resolution
outcomes.notes: The video is 1024 x 570, h264, at 30 frames per second with 23,810 frames, equal to the pose. Its motion energy correlates best with the pose speed at lag 0 (r = 0.754, falling to 0.19 and 0.26 at 15 frames either way). It is 184,059,454 bytes against 964,451,532 for CaltechDATA's mouse071_task1_annotator1.mp4, so it was re-encoded; the two were not compared frame by frame.

outcomes.statement: Close investigation, attack and mount are behaviors in which the resident is in close contact with the intruder; other frames include the animals apart.
outcomes.source: Appendix D.2 (behavior definitions)
outcomes.quote: Close investigation: resident (black) mouse is in close contact with the intruder (white) and is actively sniffing the intruder anywhere on its body or tail. ... animals may be apart from each other exploring other parts of the arena
outcomes.notes: Median distance from the resident's nose to the nearest intruder keypoint is 21.4 px in 4,679 investigation frames and 15.0 px in 2,894 mount frames, against 376.0 px in 16,237 other frames (differences -354.6 and -361.0 px, 95% block bootstrap intervals -408.9 to -295.2 and -413.6 to -303.8, with blocks of contiguous session time). The centroid distance gives -307.2 and -355.5 px, with intervals excluding 0, and each half of the session gives the same order. Attack is absent from the session, so the attack part of the statement is untested.
deviations: The paper defines the behaviors in words; the distance measure, the comparison with other frames and the bootstrap were chosen here.
One session, with no attack frames.

outcomes.statement: Errors in pose estimation are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly.
outcomes.source: Appendix B (Composition, errors and noise)
outcomes.quote: some errors in pose estimation and noise in keypoint placement still occur. These are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly.
outcomes.notes: 657 of 23,810 frames (2.8%) have a body length outside the session's quartiles widened by 3 IQR. In the closest 10% of frames (centroid distance at most 66.4 px) the fraction is 0.131 against 0.016 elsewhere (difference 0.115, 95% interval 0.064 to 0.179). In the fastest 10% (at least 389 px/s) it is 0.010 against 0.030 (difference -0.020, interval -0.033 to -0.008), the reverse of the claim. Both directions hold at 5% and 20% and with a factor of 1.5. With the speed taken as the running median of the larger speed per frame, the fast difference is -0.020 (interval -0.033 to -0.008) at 10% and -0.011 (interval -0.025 to 0.001) at 20%. Error fractions by label are 0.045 (investigation), 0.105 (mount) and 0.009 (other), so a hunched posture in mount could give real outliers. Checked against the MARS confidence of the same frames, flagged close frames have a lower confidence than unflagged close frames (median 0.574 against 0.657, difference -0.082, interval -0.107 to -0.050), and in each of eight flagged close frames drawn at random and shown with the video, at least one segment visibly runs across the other mouse or the background (judged by eye). The flags in close frames therefore mark mostly tracking errors, though the share of real postures among them is not measured.
deviations: The dandiset has no confidence values, so pose errors are counted with an anatomical proxy chosen here; the paper gives no measure of pose error.
The thresholds for close and fast frames were chosen here.

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's CalMS21 sequence is the CalMS21 Task 1 test sequence mouse071, with the same keypoints, confidence scores and frame annotations.
outcomes.source: Appendix C; CaltechDATA record 10.22002/D1.1991, file task1_classic_classification.zip
outcomes.notes: Matched by name to task1/test/mouse071_task1_annotator1 on CaltechDATA. Both have 23,810 frames; every keypoint coordinate is identical (largest difference 0 px), while swapping the mice or the axes gives differences of about 895 px. The frame labels from the bouts agree with the CaltechDATA annotations on all 23,810 frames (4,679 investigation, 2,894 mount, 16,237 other). CaltechDATA's confidence scores (0.030 to 0.980, all finite) are NaN in the dandiset. The same recording is also deposited on CaltechDATA as the Task 3 training sequence task3/groom/train/mouse002_task3_groom.

outcomes.statement: Errors in pose estimation are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly, as shown by the MARS confidence scores.
outcomes.source: Appendix B (Composition, errors and noise)
outcomes.quote: some errors in pose estimation and noise in keypoint placement still occur. These are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly.
outcomes.notes: The mean confidence per frame (CaltechDATA scores, matched frame by frame) is lower in the closest 10% of frames (median 0.649 against 0.740, difference -0.091, 95% interval -0.107 to -0.074), most of all for the intruder (-0.149 against -0.031 for the resident). In the fastest 10% of frames it is higher (0.751 against 0.732, difference 0.018, interval 0.012 to 0.025), the reverse of the claim. Both hold at 5% and 20%. The confidence correlates with the body-length error flags of pose-errors-close-fast (point-biserial r = -0.366). With the speed taken as the running median of the larger speed per frame, the fast difference is 0.018 (interval 0.012 to 0.025). The link holds in full, so the match of scores to frames is exact.
deviations: Confidence is a proxy for pose error; the paper gives no measure.
The confidence scores come from CaltechDATA, as the dandiset's are missing.

outcomes.statement: Task 1 has 70 training sequences with 507,738 frames and 19 test sequences with 262,107 frames.
outcomes.source: Table 5; Section 3.1; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: There are 70 videos in the public training set ... Training and test set instances counts for each task and category.
outcomes.notes: The training file holds 70 sequences with 507,738 frames and the test file 19 with 262,107, as reported. Annotation lengths equal the frame counts of the scores in every sequence, and the frame counts of the keypoints and the scores agree in all 574 sequences of the deposit.

outcomes.statement: Task 2 has, for annotators 1 to 5, 6 training sequences each with 139,112, 135,623, 107,420, 108,325 and 92,383 frames, and 13, 6, 4, 4 and 20 test sequences with 286,810, 150,919, 77,079, 76,174 and 364,007 frames.
outcomes.source: Table 5; Section 3.2
outcomes.quote: we provide six 10-minute training videos for each of five annotators unseen in Task 1 ... Training and test set instances counts for each task and category.
outcomes.notes: 19 of 20 counts match exactly. Annotator 1's training set has 139,122 frames where Table 5 gives 139,112 (10 frames, 0.007%); its six sequences match. The six sequences have the same frame counts in scores, keypoints and annotations; the paper gives no per-sequence counts, so the sequence that holds the 10 frames is not known. Annotator ids in the metadata agree with those in the keys.

outcomes.statement: Task 3 has, for approach, disengaged, grooming, intromission, mount attempt, sniff face and white rearing, 3, 2, 2, 1, 4, 3 and 2 training sequences with 20,624, 35,751, 45,174, 19,200, 46,847, 19,244 and 36,181 frames, and 25, 1, 13, 10, 12, 47 and 1 test sequences with 126,468, 19,088, 156,664, 55,218, 85,836, 251,793 and 17,939 frames.
outcomes.source: Table 5; Section 3.3; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: This task contains annotations on seven behaviors not labeled in Tasks 1 & 2, where some behaviors are very rare ... Training and test set instances counts for each task and category.
outcomes.notes: All 28 counts match Table 5.

outcomes.statement: In the Task 1 training set, 2.76% of frames are labelled attack, 28.9% investigation, 5.64% mount and 62.7% other.
outcomes.source: Table 6; Figure 4B
outcomes.quote: The percentage of frames labeled as attack, investigation, mount, and other in the Task 1 training set.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), the training split, investigation, mount and other are within half a unit of the last reported digit; attack is 14,039 of 507,738 frames, 2.765009%, 0.005009 from 2.76 against a tolerance of 0.005. It rounds to 2.77 and truncates to the reported 2.76. All four are within 10% of the reported values. Reading (b), training and test, gives 3.46, 27.00, 7.85 and 61.68% and does not match.
deviations: The tolerance of half a unit of the last digit is tighter than the protocol's default of 10%, because these are percentages of a fixed file; under the default the claim would be reproduced.

outcomes.statement: The five Task 2 annotators label different fractions of frames as other, investigation, mount and attack (annotator 1 60.0, 20.6, 16.2 and 3.2%; annotator 2 65.5, 25.8, 3.4 and 5.3%; annotator 3 68.9, 13.5, 9.5 and 8.1%; annotator 4 75.2, 11.6, 4.5 and 8.7%; annotator 5 69.5, 26.4, 1.0 and 3.0%).
outcomes.source: Figure 4B
outcomes.quote: Annot 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are different domain experts, whose annotations for attack, mount, and investigation are used in Task 2.
outcomes.notes: Under the training split with the class order of the Task 1 pie (other, investigation, mount, attack), all 20 percentages are within 0.05 of the figure's values; the best assignment of classes gives the same 20. The closest case is annotator 1 attack, 4,517 of 139,122 frames (3.2468%, 0.047 from 3.2), which would stay within 0.05 with up to 4 more attack frames. Training and test together match 1 of 20 under either class reading.
deviations: The Task 2 pies carry no class names; the order was read from the Task 1 pie, and the alternative reading (best assignment) was listed before the analysis. Both match.

outcomes.statement: In Task 3 the behaviors occupy 3.25% (approach), 1.47% (disengaged), 14.0% (groom), 19.3% (intromission), 0.90% (mount attempt), 4.74% (sniff face) and 9.29% (white rearing) of frames.
outcomes.source: Table 7; Figure 4B
outcomes.quote: This task contains annotations on seven behaviors not labeled in Tasks 1 & 2, where some behaviors are very rare
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), the training split, all seven are within tolerance. Training and test together give values outside 10% for five of seven (for example groom 7.36%).

outcomes.statement: The unlabeled set has 282 videos and about 6 million frames; the dataset holds over 1 million annotated frames, over 70 hours of tracked poses and over 10 hours of frame-by-frame annotation.
outcomes.source: Abstract; Section 3; Figure 4A; Section 5 (Discussion), paragraphs 1 and 3
outcomes.quote: The dataset consists of 6 million frames of unlabeled tracked poses of interacting mice, as well as over 1 million frames with tracked poses ... The released data include over 70 hours of tracked poses from pairs of mice, and over 10 hours of manual, frame-by-frame annotation ... unlabeled trajectory data from 282 videos
outcomes.notes: The unlabeled set has 282 sequences and 5,952,058 frames (55.1 h), counted the same in the keypoints and the scores. Annotated frames are 769,845 (7.1 h) in Task 1, 3,243,734 (30.0 h) over all labelled sets, and 2,273,674 (21.1 h) with each recording counted once; tracked pose including the unlabeled set is 62.2, 85.2 and 76.2 h. So the three "over" statements (1 million annotated frames, 10 hours of annotation, 70 hours of pose) hold under readings (b) and (c) and none holds under reading (a).
deviations: The paper does not say which sets its totals cover; three readings were listed before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: On Task 3, classifier performance depends on the percentage of frames in which a behavior is observed and on its average bout duration, with shorter bouts giving lower performance.
outcomes.source: Section 4.4, paragraph 2; Tables 7 and 10
outcomes.quote: We found classifier performance to depend both on the percentage of frames during which a behavior was observed, and on the average duration of a behavior bout, with shorter bouts having lower classifier performance.
outcomes.notes: Across the seven behaviors the baseline F1 of Table 10 rises with the percentage of labelled frames (Spearman 0.786, exact one-sided p = 0.024 on the training split; 0.929, p = 0.003 on the test split) and with mean bout length, but the latter is not significant (0.321, p = 0.249; 0.607, p = 0.083). With the task programming model's F1 the bout-length correlations are 0.536 (p = 0.118) and 0.679 (p = 0.055). The direction of both parts of the statement holds; only the frequency part is significant with seven behaviors.
deviations: The paper states the dependence without a test; the correlation and the permutation test were chosen here, using the paper's published F1 scores with frequencies and bout lengths computed from the data.

outcomes.statement: Among baseline architectures trained on Task 1, the 1D convolutional network performs best (F1 0.793, MAP 0.856), ahead of fully connected (0.659), LSTM (0.675) and self-attention (0.610) models.
outcomes.source: Table 1; Section 4.1, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Among the explored architectures, we obtained the highest performance using the 1D convolutional neural network (Table 1).
outcomes.notes: Needs the four baseline networks trained on Task 1. The paper gives some settings (input window, skip factor, the ranges searched) and refers to the project code for the rest, but the code at gitlab.aicrowd.com/aicrowd/research/mab-e/mab-e-baselines did not answer, with or without the sandbox, and no copy was found in Software Heritage or on GitHub; the web archive holds its landing page only. The data are public on CaltechDATA. Training five runs of each network was also not attempted within the time limit.

outcomes.statement: Adding task programming features learned from the unlabeled set raises Task 1 F1 from 0.793 to 0.829, and the challenge's top entry reaches 0.864.
outcomes.source: Table 2 and Table 8; Section 4.2, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: We found that including task programming features improved model performance.
outcomes.notes: Needs the baseline network (code unavailable, see table1-architectures) and the challenge's top entry, whose code is not linked. The task programming code (GitHub neuroethology/TREBA) and precomputed features on CaltechDATA are public, but without the baseline classifier the comparison cannot be repeated.

outcomes.statement: On Task 2 the fine-tuned baseline reaches an annotator-averaged F1 of 0.754, 0.774 with task programming features and 0.809 for the top entry, and all models do better on annotators 1 and 2 than on 3, 4 and 5.
outcomes.source: Table 3 and Table 9; Section 4.3 and Appendix G.2, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: We observe that all classifiers generally performs better on annotators 1 and 2, while performing worse on annotators 3, 4, and 5.
outcomes.notes: Needs the fine-tuned baseline and the top entry; the baseline code is unavailable (see table1-architectures) and the top entry's code is not linked.

outcomes.statement: On Task 3 the baseline reaches a behavior-averaged F1 of 0.338 (0.328 with task programming features, 0.319 for the top entry), far below Tasks 1 and 2.
outcomes.source: Table 4 and Table 10; Section 4.4; Appendix G.3, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Based on performance metrics, Task 3 is more difficult than the other two Tasks
outcomes.notes: Needs the fine-tuned baseline with per-behavior learning rates hand-tuned on a validation set, and the top entry; neither's code is available (see table1-architectures).

outcomes.statement: Many prediction errors of the baseline models fall around the boundaries between behaviors.
outcomes.source: Figure 7; Section 4.2, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Many prediction errors of the baseline models were localized around behavior transition boundaries (Figure 7).
outcomes.notes: Needs the baseline model's predictions; its code is unavailable (see table1-architectures), so the claim depends on a blocked claim. The predictions are also not deposited in either archive (data_missing).

outcomes.statement: The annotator embedding learned by the top Task 2 entry places annotators 3 and 4 close to each other and apart from annotators 1, 2 and 5.
outcomes.source: Figure 11; Section 4.3, paragraph 2, and Appendix G.2
outcomes.quote: Annotators 3 and 4 were found to be similar to each other, and different from annotators 1, 2, and 5.
outcomes.notes: Needs the trained top entry's annotator embedding; the entry's code is not linked and the paper describes the model only in outline. The learned matrix is also not deposited in either archive (data_missing).

findings.statement: The MARS confidence scores, which CalMS21 distributes with every keypoint, are missing from the dandiset's CalMS21 file; the confidence field of all 14 pose series is present but all 333,340 values are NaN. CaltechDATA's copy of the same sequence has them (0.03 to 0.98).

For CalMS21 the dandiset holds one sequence, the Task 1 test sequence mouse071, out of 574 sequences on CaltechDATA. Its description presents a collection of datasets and does not say that only one CalMS21 sequence is included or why this one was chosen.

The behavior catalogue (CalMS21_ethogram) has an empty definition for attack, investigation, mount and other, though the paper defines the three behaviors (Appendix D.2) and states that annotations refer to behaviors initiated by the resident.

The two mice are stored as one subject with strain C57BL/6, sex unknown and age P0D/; the intruder's strain (BALB/c) and the residents' sex (male) are known from the paper but not recorded, and which series belongs to the black or white mouse is given only by the series names.
The session start time is 2024-01-01T00:00, a placeholder; CalMS21 gives no recording dates.

The `centroid_speed` series, and the bout columns mean_speed, peak_speed and immobility_fraction that reduce it, are the speed of the mean of all 14 keypoints, which is the midpoint of the two mice, not the speed of either animal. The description ("the pose centroid, mean over keypoints") does not make this clear.

The dandiset's mouse071 video (184 MB) is a re-encoding of CaltechDATA's (964 MB). It has the same frame count, size and rate, and its motion follows the pose at lag 0, but the dandiset does not say it was re-encoded.

The dandiset links the CalMS21 dataset DOI (10.22002/D1.1991) as IsDerivedFrom, but not the paper that describes the dataset and its benchmarks (arXiv 2104.02710, NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks).

On CaltechDATA, 574 CalMS21 sequences hold 450 distinct recordings (identical keypoints over the whole sequence). 93 of the 109 Task 3 test sequences are Task 1 training recordings, five Task 1 test recordings (mouse071 among them) appear as six Task 3 training sequences, and four Task 2 recordings are in the training set of one of annotators 3 and 4 and the test set of the other. The paper describes each sequence as an independent observation and does not mention the overlap, and the CaltechDATA readme says that training and test sets are split by animal identity.

The paper's datasheet says the dataset does not include the raw videos, while Section 3.1 says all source videos of Task 1 are released, and the deposit holds them. The datasheet also gives the licence as CC-BY-NC-SA, while the CaltechDATA record and the dandiset give CC-BY 4.0.
Table 5 gives 139,112 training frames for Task 2 annotator 1; the deposited file holds 139,122. The other 47 counts of Table 5 match.

The baseline code the paper links (gitlab.aicrowd.com/aicrowd/research/mab-e/mab-e-baselines) is not reachable and no archived copy of the repository was found; the code of the challenge's top entries is not linked. The paper leaves the architectures' settings to that code, so none of the benchmark results can be repeated.
